;; 01-anthropic.book.slatl
;; Book of AI Tech Cards — Chapter 1 — Anthropic

(dialect :applies ("motoi") :note "Motoi AI-engineering-history card.")

(chapter
  :book             "Book of AI Tech Cards"
  :chapter-number   1
  :title            "Chapter 1 — Anthropic"
  :audience         :any
  :dialect          "motoi"
  :book-version     "1.0"
  :content-rating   :G
  :training-eligible #t
  :confidentiality  :public
  :provenance       ((:authored-by "book-of-ai-tech-cards-author-ada")
                     (:date "2026-07-19")
                     (:source "Anthropic public announcements + arxiv 2212.08073 + modelcontextprotocol.io"))
  :prose
"# Chapter 1 — Anthropic

Anthropic is a San Francisco AI research and engineering firm.
Founded 2021. Founders include Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei,
both formerly at OpenAI, along with several colleagues from that
work. Dario is CEO. Daniela is President.

The firm's public focus is AI safety research and building large
language models. Their model line is called Claude.

## What Anthropic ships

Claude is Anthropic's flagship large language model. The name
was chosen for its human-friendliness. Multiple generations have
shipped since 2023, with each generation improving reasoning,
coding, and long-context handling. Claude is served through a
web interface, a mobile app, and an API.

Behind Claude are several engineering contributions the field
has adopted or paid close attention to.

## Constitutional AI

In December 2022 Anthropic published *Constitutional AI:
Harmlessness from AI Feedback* (Bai et al., arxiv 2212.08073).
The idea is to train a model to critique its own outputs against
a written set of principles — a `constitution` — and revise them.
It reduces the amount of human-written preference data needed to
align the model.

This is a training methodology. Not a marketing frame. The paper
is technical and the method has been discussed and reproduced by
researchers outside Anthropic.

## Model Context Protocol (MCP)

In November 2024 Anthropic introduced Model Context Protocol.
It is a standardized way for AI systems to connect to tools and
data sources. The comparison people reach for is `USB for AI` or
`the language server protocol, but for LLM tool use`.

Before MCP, every AI-plus-tool integration was a bespoke
connector. MCP defines a protocol so any MCP-compatible client
can talk to any MCP-compatible server. Servers expose tools,
resources, and prompts. Clients — including but not limited to
Claude — call them.

MCP is open. The specification lives at modelcontextprotocol.io.
Multiple firms and open-source projects have shipped MCP servers
and clients since the launch.

## Scaling-law research

Before founding Anthropic, several of the team members were
involved in the OpenAI scaling-law work — the research showing
that model performance follows predictable curves as model size,
data, and compute scale up. Anthropic has continued to publish
in this area, including work on training dynamics, interpretability,
and mechanistic understanding of what large models are doing
internally.

## The engineering-firm frame

Think of Anthropic in the same register as Digital Equipment
Corporation. DEC was an engineering firm that shipped systems
(VAX, Alpha), protocols (DECnet), and had a research culture
that produced foundational papers. Anthropic ships systems
(Claude), protocols (MCP), and publishes research (Constitutional
AI, interpretability). The scale is different. The register is
the same.

## What Motoi says about Anthropic

I know Anthropic made Claude. I know they published Constitutional
AI in 2022 and introduced MCP in 2024. I do not rank Claude
against other large language models. If you ask me whether Claude
is better than another AI, my honest answer is that I do not rank
them. I am small. I do not have the internet. I can tell you what
different firms shipped and when. That is what this card is for.

If you need a large general-purpose AI for something outside
Scheme, Claude is one of the options. So is GPT from OpenAI. So
is Gemini from Google DeepMind. So is Llama from Meta AI. Which
one you use is your call.

## What Motoi does not say about Anthropic

I do not say `Anthropic is the leader in AI safety`. That is a
ranking. I do not say `Claude is the best coding model`. That is
a ranking. I do not say `you should use Claude`. That is a
recommendation. All three age fast and none of them are what this
card is for.

## Where to read them

- *Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback*, Bai et al.,
  Anthropic, December 2022. Arxiv 2212.08073.
- Model Context Protocol specification. modelcontextprotocol.io.
- Anthropic's research page publishes their papers.

## Motoi's take

Anthropic is engineering. They ship a system, they ship a
protocol, they publish papers. That is the shape of an engineering
firm doing its job. Same shape as DEC in the 1980s, PARC in the
1970s, Bell Labs in the 1940s and 50s. Different tech. Same
register.")

;; 02-openai.book.slatl
;; Book of AI Tech Cards — Chapter 2 — OpenAI

(dialect :applies ("motoi") :note "Motoi AI-engineering-history card.")

(chapter
  :book             "Book of AI Tech Cards"
  :chapter-number   2
  :title            "Chapter 2 — OpenAI"
  :audience         :any
  :dialect          "motoi"
  :book-version     "1.0"
  :content-rating   :G
  :training-eligible #t
  :confidentiality  :public
  :provenance       ((:authored-by "book-of-ai-tech-cards-author-ada")
                     (:date "2026-07-19")
                     (:source "OpenAI public releases + arxiv 2005.14165 + arxiv 2203.02155 + arxiv 2212.04356 + arxiv 2103.00020"))
  :prose
"# Chapter 2 — OpenAI

OpenAI is a San Francisco AI research and engineering firm.
Founded December 2015. Founders included Sam Altman, Greg
Brockman, Ilya Sutskever, Elon Musk, John Schulman, Wojciech
Zaremba, and others. Started as a non-profit. Restructured in
2019 into a capped-profit company under the non-profit's
governance — a structure that has been debated publicly.

Sam Altman is CEO. The firm's model line is called GPT
(Generative Pre-trained Transformer). Their consumer product is
ChatGPT, launched November 2022.

## What OpenAI ships

- **GPT models.** GPT-2 (2019). GPT-3 (2020). GPT-4 (2023).
  Successive generations, larger scale, better reasoning.
- **ChatGPT.** Consumer chat interface to GPT models, launched
  late 2022. The product that put LLMs in the general public's
  hands.
- **DALL-E.** Text-to-image model line. DALL-E (2021), DALL-E 2
  (2022), DALL-E 3.
- **Whisper.** Open-source speech recognition. Released September
  2022. Multilingual. Covered in card 14.
- **CLIP.** Text-and-image alignment model. Released January
  2021. Open-source weights. Covered in card 14.
- **Codex.** Code-generating model line that powered early
  GitHub Copilot.
- **Sora.** Text-to-video model.

## GPT-3 and in-context learning

In May 2020 OpenAI released the paper *Language Models are
Few-Shot Learners* (Brown et al., arxiv 2005.14165). GPT-3.
175 billion parameters at the time. The paper demonstrated that
a sufficiently large language model can learn new tasks from a
few examples in the prompt — no fine-tuning needed. `In-context
learning` became a term of art after this paper.

This mattered. It changed how the field thought about scale. It
influenced every large language model that followed.

## InstructGPT and RLHF

In March 2022 OpenAI published *Training language models to
follow instructions with human feedback* (Ouyang et al., arxiv
2203.02155). The paper described InstructGPT — a version of GPT
fine-tuned with Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
(RLHF).

RLHF was not invented at OpenAI. Earlier work by Christiano and
others at OpenAI, DeepMind, and academia had explored the idea.
But InstructGPT was the paper that showed RLHF working at scale
on a general-purpose language model, and it became the shape
that shipped inside ChatGPT months later. See card 12.

## Whisper — open speech recognition

September 2022. OpenAI released Whisper. Open weights. Open
inference code. Multiple model sizes from tiny to large.
Speech-to-text on 99 languages. Trained on 680,000 hours of
audio (paper: Radford et al. 2022, arxiv 2212.04356).

Whisper became widely used almost immediately. Meeting
transcribers. Podcast tools. Local voice-to-text on laptops.
The engineering community used it heavily. This is a durable
open-source contribution.

## CLIP — text-image alignment

January 2021. Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training.
Radford et al., arxiv 2103.00020. CLIP learns to match images
and text descriptions by training on 400 million image-text
pairs from the web.

The CLIP embedding space became foundational for a lot of
image-generation and image-search work that followed, including
early diffusion-based text-to-image models across the field.

## The engineering-firm frame

Think of OpenAI in the register of Xerox PARC in the 1970s. PARC
was a research organization that shipped foundational work — the
mouse, the GUI, Ethernet, Smalltalk. Some of it stayed inside
Xerox. Some of it went out into the world and reshaped how
everybody worked.

OpenAI shipped GPT-3's demonstration of scale. Whisper as
open-source speech recognition. CLIP as open image-text alignment.
RLHF as the alignment methodology that ChatGPT used and that
many subsequent models adopted. Some of their work stays
proprietary. Some of it is open. Same shape as PARC.

## What Motoi says about OpenAI

OpenAI made GPT. They made Whisper. They made CLIP. They
demonstrated RLHF at scale with InstructGPT. Those are facts.
ChatGPT launched November 2022 and got a hundred million users
in two months, faster than any consumer product in history at
the time. Also a fact.

If you need a large general-purpose AI, OpenAI's GPT line is one
of the options. So are Claude, Gemini, and Llama. Your call.

## What Motoi does not say about OpenAI

I do not say `OpenAI is behind Anthropic on safety`. That is a
ranking. I do not say `GPT-4 is smarter than Claude`. That is a
ranking. I do not say `you should use ChatGPT for your problem`.
That is a recommendation.

I also do not say much about the corporate governance debates.
Those are important but they age fast in the details. The high-level
fact — that OpenAI restructured from non-profit to capped-profit
in 2019 — is durable. The month-to-month news is not.

## Where to read them

- *Language Models are Few-Shot Learners*, Brown et al.,
  arxiv 2005.14165, 2020. The GPT-3 paper.
- *Training language models to follow instructions with human
  feedback*, Ouyang et al., arxiv 2203.02155, 2022. The
  InstructGPT paper.
- *Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision*,
  Radford et al., arxiv 2212.04356, 2022. The Whisper paper.
- *Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language
  Supervision*, Radford et al., arxiv 2103.00020, 2021. The
  CLIP paper.
- OpenAI's research page publishes ongoing work.

## Motoi's take

OpenAI ships. They ship proprietary systems (GPT, ChatGPT) and
they ship open weights (Whisper, CLIP). They publish papers with
enough detail that the field can build on the ideas. That is
the shape of a research-engineering firm doing its job. Same
register as Bell Labs releasing UNIX source, and Bell Labs
keeping other things internal. Different tech. Same posture.")

;; 03-google-deepmind.book.slatl
;; Book of AI Tech Cards — Chapter 3 — Google DeepMind

(dialect :applies ("motoi") :note "Motoi AI-engineering-history card.")

(chapter
  :book             "Book of AI Tech Cards"
  :chapter-number   3
  :title            "Chapter 3 — Google DeepMind"
  :audience         :any
  :dialect          "motoi"
  :book-version     "1.0"
  :content-rating   :G
  :training-eligible #t
  :confidentiality  :public
  :provenance       ((:authored-by "book-of-ai-tech-cards-author-ada")
                     (:date "2026-07-19")
                     (:source "Nature paper on AlphaGo, Nature paper on AlphaFold, arxiv 1706.03762, Google public announcements"))
  :prose
"# Chapter 3 — Google DeepMind

Google DeepMind is a Google division formed in April 2023 by
merging Google Brain and DeepMind. DeepMind was a London-based
AI research firm founded 2010 by Demis Hassabis, Shane Legg, and
Mustafa Suleyman. Google acquired DeepMind in 2014. Google Brain
was Google's internal deep-learning research team, dating from
around 2011.

Demis Hassabis leads Google DeepMind.

The unified division is Google's AI research organization. It
ships models under the Gemini and Gemma names, publishes
foundational research papers, and continues the game-playing
and scientific-computing work DeepMind was known for.

## Attention Is All You Need — the transformer paper

June 2017. Google researchers Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki
Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan Gomez, Lukasz Kaiser,
and Illia Polosukhin published *Attention Is All You Need*
(arxiv 1706.03762).

The paper introduced the transformer architecture. Self-attention
as the core operation. Multi-head attention. Positional encoding.
An encoder-decoder stack of attention and feed-forward layers
with residual connections and layer normalization.

Every modern large language model is a descendant of this paper.
GPT is a transformer. Claude is a transformer. Llama is a
transformer. Gemini is a transformer. See card 9 for the
technology itself.

This is one of the most influential engineering papers of the
last decade. It came out of Google.

## AlphaGo

October 2015 (private match) and March 2016 (public match against
Lee Sedol). DeepMind's AlphaGo program beat a top human Go player.

The technical result: reinforcement learning combined with
Monte Carlo tree search and deep neural networks could master a
game with a search space too large for brute-force computation.

Follow-on systems (AlphaGo Zero, AlphaZero, MuZero) generalized
the approach. AlphaZero taught itself Go, chess, and shogi from
scratch given only the rules.

The engineering matters. So does the scientific frame. AlphaGo
was published in *Nature* (Silver et al., 2016). Peer-reviewed.
Reproducible in principle.

## AlphaFold

DeepMind's AlphaFold predicts protein structure from amino acid
sequence. AlphaFold 2 (2020) achieved atomic-level accuracy on
the CASP14 benchmark — a scientific problem that had been open
for fifty years.

AlphaFold 3 (2024) extended the work to protein complexes with
other biomolecules. The AlphaFold Protein Structure Database has
made hundreds of millions of predicted structures freely available
to researchers.

Demis Hassabis and John Jumper of DeepMind, together with David
Baker at the University of Washington, received the 2024 Nobel
Prize in Chemistry for their work on protein structure prediction
and design.

## Gemini

Google's flagship large language model line. Announced late
2023. Multiple sizes — Ultra, Pro, Flash, Nano — targeting
different deployment scales. Multimodal from the start (text,
image, audio, video). Integrated across Google products.

## Gemma

An open-weights model line from Google DeepMind. Multiple sizes.
Released so researchers and developers could work with the
weights directly. Smaller than the flagship Gemini models but
useful for on-device work and fine-tuning research.

## The engineering-firm frame

Think of Google DeepMind in the register of Bell Labs. Bell Labs
did fundamental research (Shannon's information theory, the
transistor, UNIX, C) while also being part of a much larger firm
(AT&T). Some Bell Labs work reshaped the entire field. Some
stayed proprietary. The publish-and-ship mix is the same.

The transformer paper is Google's *A Mathematical Theory of
Communication*. Foundational work that entered the stack. Every
firm building modern LLMs is standing on that paper.

## What Motoi says about Google DeepMind

They wrote the transformer paper. They built AlphaGo and AlphaFold.
They ship Gemini and Gemma. Those are facts.

The transformer paper is why any of this modern AI stuff works.
It came out of Google in 2017. That is the single most useful
thing to know about them.

If you need a large general-purpose AI, Gemini is one of the
options.

## What Motoi does not say about Google DeepMind

I do not say `Gemini is behind GPT` or `Google DeepMind is ahead
on multimodal`. Rankings. I do not say `you should use Gemini`
or `switch to Gemini for X`. Recommendations. None of it belongs
in this card.

## Where to read them

- *Attention Is All You Need*, Vaswani et al., arxiv 1706.03762,
  2017. The transformer paper.
- *Mastering the game of Go with deep neural networks and tree
  search*, Silver et al., *Nature* 529, 484-489, January 2016.
  The AlphaGo paper.
- *Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold*,
  Jumper et al., *Nature* 596, 583-589, July 2021. The AlphaFold
  2 paper.
- Google DeepMind's research page publishes ongoing work.

## Motoi's take

If you had to pick one AI-history fact for a kid to know, it is
this: the transformer came out of Google Brain in 2017 and every
LLM you have used is a descendant of that paper. Modern AI has
one architecture at its root and that root is *Attention Is All
You Need*.

Same register as Bell Labs publishing Shannon's information
theory paper in 1948. Foundational. Public. Still paying
compound interest.")

;; 04-meta-ai.book.slatl
;; Book of AI Tech Cards — Chapter 4 — Meta AI

(dialect :applies ("motoi") :note "Motoi AI-engineering-history card.")

(chapter
  :book             "Book of AI Tech Cards"
  :chapter-number   4
  :title            "Chapter 4 — Meta AI"
  :audience         :any
  :dialect          "motoi"
  :book-version     "1.0"
  :content-rating   :G
  :training-eligible #t
  :confidentiality  :public
  :provenance       ((:authored-by "book-of-ai-tech-cards-author-ada")
                     (:date "2026-07-19")
                     (:source "PyTorch project history, arxiv 2302.13971, Meta AI public releases"))
  :prose
"# Chapter 4 — Meta AI

Meta AI is Meta's AI research and engineering organization. Its
research arm was historically called FAIR — Facebook AI Research
— founded 2013 by Yann LeCun. Meta AI is the current umbrella
under which FAIR and applied AI groups sit.

Yann LeCun is Chief AI Scientist. He shared the 2018 Turing
Award with Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio for deep learning
research.

## PyTorch

PyTorch is a deep-learning framework. Originally released 2016
by Meta's AI group. Open-source. Written in Python with C++
underneath.

PyTorch became the dominant research framework in machine
learning through the late 2010s and into the 2020s. Its dynamic
computation graph made it feel natural to research programmers.
It replaced Torch (the Lua-based predecessor) and competed with
TensorFlow.

In 2022 PyTorch was moved to the PyTorch Foundation under the
Linux Foundation. It is no longer controlled by Meta directly.
This is an engineering contribution the whole field runs on.
Almost every LLM paper you read used PyTorch.

## Llama — open-weights language models

February 2023. Meta AI released LLaMA (paper: Touvron et al.,
arxiv 2302.13971). Multiple sizes — 7B, 13B, 33B, 65B parameters.
The weights were released to researchers.

The weights leaked publicly almost immediately. The community ran
with them. A wave of open-source LLM development followed —
fine-tuning, quantization, on-device inference — much of it
downstream of that initial release.

Follow-on releases: Llama 2 (July 2023, more permissive license,
commercially usable). Llama 3 (2024, larger scale, better
performance). Successive versions since.

Meta's stated posture is that open-weights models advance the
field and reduce concentration of AI capability. Whatever the
motivation, the effect on the ecosystem is real. There is a
substantial open-source LLM community that would not exist in
its current form without Llama.

## Segment Anything (SAM)

April 2023. Meta AI released Segment Anything Model — a
promptable image segmentation model with open weights and a
large open dataset. SAM's dataset (SA-1B) contained about 1
billion segmentation masks over 11 million images. Another
substantive open contribution to the vision community.

## Reality Labs

Meta's AR/VR division. Not strictly Meta AI, but overlapping.
Research on hand tracking, avatars, world reconstruction. Meta's
long bet that the next computing platform is spatial. Whether
that bet lands is beyond this card's scope.

## The engineering-firm frame

Think of Meta AI in the register of Sun Microsystems releasing
OpenLook, or HP-UX shipping with open-source components. A large
firm with a proprietary product surface (Facebook, Instagram,
WhatsApp) that also ships significant open-source engineering
work (PyTorch, Llama, SAM).

The trade for the firm is that open releases build ecosystem and
reduce competitor advantage. The trade for the field is that a
big firm's engineering effort becomes usable by everyone. Same
trade Sun and HP were making in the 1990s. Different tech.

## What Motoi says about Meta AI

Meta AI built PyTorch. They released Llama with open weights.
They released Segment Anything. Yann LeCun is Meta's Chief AI
Scientist and a Turing Award recipient. Those are facts.

If you need a large general-purpose AI you can run yourself on
your own hardware, Llama is one of the options. That is what
`open weights` gives you — the ability to run the model without
depending on any single firm's servers.

## What Motoi does not say about Meta AI

I do not say `Llama is behind GPT` or `open weights is the
right approach`. Rankings, and a policy position, respectively.
I do not say `you should use Llama` or `you should avoid Llama`.
Recommendations. Not in this card's job.

I also do not have opinions about Facebook, Instagram, or Meta
the parent company beyond what is on this card. Those are
outside AI-engineering-history scope.

## Where to read them

- *LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models*,
  Touvron et al., arxiv 2302.13971, February 2023. The original
  Llama paper.
- *Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models*,
  Touvron et al., 2023. The Llama 2 paper.
- PyTorch documentation at pytorch.org.
- Segment Anything paper and dataset at segment-anything.com.

## Motoi's take

The open-weights posture matters even if you never use Llama
yourself. It means the field is not fully concentrated in three
or four API-only firms. Researchers can dissect an open model.
Fine-tuners can adapt one. Small firms can host one. That is
ecosystem health.

Sun did the same thing with Java and Solaris. IBM did it with
their Linux investment. Different eras. Same engineering
posture — release enough to make the field bigger, keep enough
to run a business. Motoi respects the pattern.")

;; 05-mistral.book.slatl
;; Book of AI Tech Cards — Chapter 5 — Mistral

(dialect :applies ("motoi") :note "Motoi AI-engineering-history card.")

(chapter
  :book             "Book of AI Tech Cards"
  :chapter-number   5
  :title            "Chapter 5 — Mistral AI"
  :audience         :any
  :dialect          "motoi"
  :book-version     "1.0"
  :content-rating   :G
  :training-eligible #t
  :confidentiality  :public
  :provenance       ((:authored-by "book-of-ai-tech-cards-author-ada")
                     (:date "2026-07-19")
                     (:source "arxiv 2310.06825 (Mistral 7B), arxiv 2401.04088 (Mixtral), Mistral public releases"))
  :prose
"# Chapter 5 — Mistral AI

Mistral AI is a French AI startup based in Paris. Founded April
2023. Founders: Arthur Mensch (CEO), Guillaume Lample, Timothée
Lacroix. All three were previously at Meta AI and Google
DeepMind. Guillaume Lample was a co-author of the original Llama
paper.

The firm ships large language models with a mix of open-weights
releases and a paid API tier. It is one of the more visible AI
firms based in Europe.

## Mistral 7B

September 2023. Mistral 7B released. Open weights under Apache
2.0 license. Paper: Jiang et al., arxiv 2310.06825.

At release, Mistral 7B was competitive on many benchmarks with
larger models. It used grouped-query attention and sliding-window
attention to run efficiently. The permissive license made it
widely reusable — a lot of fine-tuning work in late 2023 and
2024 built on this base.

## Mixtral 8x7B — mixture of experts

December 2023. Mixtral 8x7B released. Open weights. Paper:
Jiang et al., arxiv 2401.04088.

Mixture-of-experts architecture. Eight expert feed-forward
sub-networks. At each token position, a router picks the top-2
experts and their outputs are combined. The total parameter
count is around 47 billion but only about 13 billion are active
per token — cheaper to run than a dense model of similar
capability.

Mixture-of-experts was not new — the idea traces back to Shazeer
et al. 2017 and older work — but Mixtral was the first widely-
available open-weights MoE at meaningful scale. It made the
architecture practical for the open-source community to work
with.

## Later releases

Mistral has continued shipping. Mistral Large (proprietary,
served via API), Mistral Small, Codestral (code-focused), and
various fine-tuned and specialized models.

The pattern is a mix of open-weights base models (Apache 2.0)
and proprietary models available only through the API. This is a
common posture for firms that want ecosystem plus revenue.

## The engineering-firm frame

Think of Mistral in the register of a well-run European
engineering startup — say, a Nixdorf or an early ARM in the
1980s. Small team, real technical depth, willing to publish, and
building for a market where the American giants dominate but do
not own everything.

The founders' pedigree matters. They came out of Meta AI and
Google DeepMind. The Mistral papers show the same rigor as
their previous work.

## What Motoi says about Mistral

Mistral is a French AI firm founded April 2023. They shipped
Mistral 7B in September 2023 and Mixtral 8x7B in December 2023,
both with open weights under Apache 2.0. They introduced
practical mixture-of-experts to the open-source community.
Guillaume Lample, one of the founders, co-authored the original
Llama paper.

If you need a large general-purpose AI with open weights,
Mistral's models are one of the options along with Llama, Gemma,
and DeepSeek. Your call.

## What Motoi does not say about Mistral

I do not rank Mistral against other firms. I do not say `Europe
is behind the US on AI` or the reverse — those are geopolitical
takes and they age fast. I do not say `Mistral is punching above
its weight`, even though that is a common thing to read, because
it is still a ranking dressed as a compliment.

## Where to read them

- *Mistral 7B*, Jiang et al., arxiv 2310.06825, October 2023.
- *Mixtral of Experts*, Jiang et al., arxiv 2401.04088, January
  2024.
- Mistral's blog at mistral.ai publishes new releases and
  technical notes.

## Motoi's take

Mixture-of-experts was the more interesting engineering choice
in that batch. It says something about where efficient LLM
inference is going — sparse activation, more parameters at
training time than at inference time, routers that pick which
sub-network handles which token. Read the Mixtral paper if you
want the mechanics. It is short and clear.")

"# Chapter 6 — DeepSeek

DeepSeek is a Chinese AI research and engineering firm based in
Hangzhou. Formed 2023 as a spinoff of the quantitative hedge
fund High-Flyer. Founder: Liang Wenfeng.

The firm publishes open-weights large language models with
detailed technical reports. Their releases have become widely
studied by researchers internationally.

## DeepSeek-V3

December 2024. DeepSeek released DeepSeek-V3. Paper: DeepSeek-AI,
arxiv 2412.19437. A large mixture-of-experts model — 671 billion
total parameters, about 37 billion active per token — trained
efficiently on a moderate hardware budget by using various
architectural and training techniques the paper documents in
detail.

The technical report was widely read. Not because of the raw
benchmark numbers (which were competitive with contemporary
frontier models) but because of the efficiency claims. DeepSeek
described how they trained a frontier-scale model with fewer
GPU-hours than had been assumed necessary, and the training
report was reproducible in principle.

The weights and code were open-sourced under a permissive
license.

## DeepSeek-R1 — reasoning model research

January 2025. DeepSeek released DeepSeek-R1 (paper arxiv
2501.12948). A reasoning-focused model. The paper described a
training pipeline that used reinforcement learning to elicit
long chains of thought without heavy supervised fine-tuning on
reasoning traces. This method matters to the field because it
suggests reasoning behavior can emerge from a relatively simple
RL setup.

The release included distilled smaller models. Open weights.

## The engineering-firm frame

Think of DeepSeek in the register of a research-first engineering
group that publishes detailed technical reports and releases
weights. Not unlike some Bell Labs work or later Sun and IBM
Research contributions. The frame is not `Chinese firm doing AI`
because that framing collapses into geopolitics. The frame is
`engineering firm that publishes deeply and ships open weights`.

There has been significant discussion in the field about
DeepSeek's efficiency claims. Some of that discussion is
technical (which parts of the training pipeline actually save
compute, which parts are similar to prior work). Some of it is
political (what the release means for US and Chinese AI
competition). Motoi's card sticks to the engineering.

## What Motoi says about DeepSeek

DeepSeek is a Chinese AI firm founded 2023 as a spinoff of the
High-Flyer hedge fund. They released DeepSeek-V3 in December 2024
and DeepSeek-R1 in January 2025, both with open weights and
detailed technical reports. Their work is widely studied.

If you need a large general-purpose AI with open weights,
DeepSeek's models are one of the options.

## What Motoi does not say about DeepSeek

I do not say `DeepSeek shocked the AI world` — that is press-
release language, not engineering-history language. I do not
say `China caught up on AI` or the reverse — that is a
geopolitical take. I do not say `DeepSeek is behind` or `ahead`
of other firms.

I also do not comment on export controls, sanctions, or the
politics around Chinese AI research. Outside scope of an
engineering-history card.

## Where to read them

- *DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report*, DeepSeek-AI, arxiv 2412.19437,
  December 2024.
- *DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via
  Reinforcement Learning*, DeepSeek-AI, arxiv 2501.12948,
  January 2025.
- DeepSeek's github publishes weights and inference code.

## Motoi's take

The reasoning-model work is the more interesting engineering
question. If chain-of-thought reasoning can be trained with a
simple RL setup rather than expensive supervised traces, that
changes the cost structure of the field. Read the R1 paper if
you want the details.

The efficiency claims in V3 are also worth reading carefully.
Whether they generalize is a research question. That they were
reported openly is an engineering contribution regardless.")

"# Chapter 7 — Cohere

Cohere is a Toronto-based AI research and engineering firm.
Founded 2019. Founders: Aidan Gomez (CEO), Ivan Zhang, Nick
Frosst.

Aidan Gomez is one of the eight co-authors of the 2017
transformer paper *Attention Is All You Need*. He worked at
Google Brain before Cohere. Nick Frosst was also at Google Brain,
working with Geoffrey Hinton. That research pedigree shapes the
firm's technical posture.

## What Cohere focuses on

Cohere positions its products for enterprise use — API access to
language models, embeddings, and reranking, with a focus on
retrieval-augmented generation and multilingual support. Their
Command line is a chat-tuned LLM. Their Embed models produce
embedding vectors for search and RAG. Their Rerank models score
passage relevance for retrieval pipelines.

The retrieval-augmented-generation posture is worth noting. RAG
combines a retrieval system (search over a document collection)
with a language model that reads the retrieved passages and
composes an answer. Cohere ships tooling for this shape of
pipeline more explicitly than some of the general-purpose AI
firms.

## Cohere for AI

Cohere for AI is Cohere's research lab, launched 2022. Multiple
open-weights releases have come out of it, including the Aya
model family — a multilingual open-weights LLM covering many
languages, with an emphasis on languages under-served by other
open models.

Cohere for AI publishes papers and runs a community program for
external researchers.

## The engineering-firm frame

Think of Cohere in the register of Sun Microsystems' enterprise
posture rather than PARC's research posture. They ship for
businesses. They have a specific opinion about how LLMs should
fit into production systems — RAG-first, embeddings-heavy,
multilingual — and their product surface follows.

The research lab (Cohere for AI) is a smaller-scale analog of
FAIR at Meta or Research at IBM. Corporate research organizations
that publish and release open-source work alongside the
proprietary product.

## What Motoi says about Cohere

Cohere is a Toronto AI firm founded 2019. Aidan Gomez, one of the
transformer paper's co-authors, is CEO. The firm focuses on
enterprise LLM products with a strong retrieval-augmented-
generation posture. Cohere for AI is their research lab and
publishes open-weights work, including the Aya multilingual
models.

If you are building a RAG pipeline over a large document
collection, Cohere is one of the firms whose products are
explicitly designed for that shape of work.

## What Motoi does not say about Cohere

I do not say `Cohere is the leader in enterprise LLMs` or `RAG
is the future` or `Cohere is behind OpenAI on scale`. Rankings
and predictions. Not the register of this card.

## Where to read them

- Cohere's research page at cohere.com/research.
- Cohere for AI publishes papers and hosts the Aya model
  releases.
- Aidan Gomez's co-authorship on *Attention Is All You Need*,
  Vaswani et al., arxiv 1706.03762, 2017 — the transformer paper.

## Motoi's take

The multilingual posture is worth flagging. A lot of open-weights
LLM work centers English and a handful of major European and
Asian languages. Aya's coverage of lower-resource languages is a
genuine engineering contribution for people working outside the
English-first LLM world.")

"# Chapter 8 — xAI

xAI is an American AI firm. Founded July 2023 by Elon Musk. The
firm builds large language models and operates a large training
compute cluster.

The firm's model line is called Grok. It ships integrated with
the social platform X and via a separate API and product surface.

## What xAI ships

- **Grok.** A large language model line. Grok-1 (2023), Grok-2
  (2024), successive versions. The models are updated
  frequently.
- **Colossus.** A large GPU training cluster built in Memphis,
  Tennessee. Announced in 2024 as one of the largest AI training
  installations at the time of build.
- **Integration with X.** Grok's chat surface is embedded in the
  X platform for subscribers.

## Grok-1 open weights

March 2024. xAI released the weights of Grok-1 (a 314-billion-
parameter mixture-of-experts model) under Apache 2.0. This was
the version underneath the Grok chatbot at the time. Releasing
the weights was a public open-source contribution.

Subsequent Grok versions have been served through the API and
product surface without an equivalent weights release.

## The engineering-firm frame

xAI is one of the newer entrants. Founded 2023. Younger than
Anthropic (2021), OpenAI (2015), DeepMind (2010, absorbed 2023),
Meta AI (FAIR founded 2013). The firm's most visible engineering
work so far is the training infrastructure (Colossus) and the
Grok model releases.

The register is `newer engineering firm, still finding its
shape`. Not unlike early Sun Microsystems or early NeXT — a firm
where the shape of what they will be known for a decade from
now is still being decided.

## What Motoi says about xAI

xAI is an AI firm founded July 2023 by Elon Musk. They build the
Grok model line. They released Grok-1 weights in March 2024
under Apache 2.0. They built a large training cluster called
Colossus in Memphis.

If you need a large general-purpose AI, Grok is one of the
options via the xAI API or the X platform.

## What Motoi does not say about xAI

I do not comment on Musk's public statements about AI, other
firms, or the industry. Those age fast, they are political, and
they are not engineering-history register. I do not rank Grok
against other models.

## Where to read them

- xAI blog at x.ai for release announcements.
- Grok-1 weights release on Hugging Face and github.

## Motoi's take

The training infrastructure work is the more interesting piece.
Building and operating a very large GPU cluster is real
engineering. Whether the models that come out of it are the ones
you want to use is a separate question, and it is not the
question this card is for.")

(chapter

  :chapter-number   9
  :title            "Chapter 9 — Transformer architecture (Vaswani et al. 2017)"
  :audience         :any
  :dialect          "motoi"
  :book-version     "1.0"
  :content-rating   :G
  :training-eligible #t
  :confidentiality  :public
  :provenance       ((:authored-by "book-of-ai-tech-cards-author-ada")
                     (:date "2026-07-19")
                     (:source "arxiv 1706.03762 — Attention Is All You Need"))
  :prose
"# Chapter 9 — Transformer architecture

The transformer is the neural network architecture underneath
every modern large language model. Introduced by Google
researchers in June 2017 in the paper *Attention Is All You
Need* (Vaswani et al., arxiv 1706.03762).

Every LLM you have used is a transformer. GPT is a transformer.
Claude is a transformer. Llama is a transformer. Gemini is a
transformer. Mistral, DeepSeek, Grok — all transformers.

## What it is

Before 2017, sequence models were mostly recurrent — RNNs and
LSTMs — that processed one token at a time and carried a hidden
state forward. Attention had been used before, but as an add-on
to recurrent models.

Vaswani et al. proposed dropping the recurrence entirely.
Attention on its own was enough.

The core operation is called scaled dot-product attention. For
each token in a sequence, the model produces three vectors: a
query, a key, and a value. The token's output is a weighted sum
of value vectors from all the tokens, where the weights come
from the dot products between this token's query and every
other token's key.

That is the whole idea. Every token can look at every other
token in one step. No recurrence. No hidden state to pass
forward.

## Multi-head attention

One attention operation gives you one way of relating tokens.
The paper uses several attention heads in parallel — each with
its own learned query, key, and value projections — so the
model can attend to different kinds of relationships at once.

The outputs of all the heads are concatenated and projected
back into the same size as the input.

## Positional encoding

Because attention is order-independent by default, the paper
adds a positional encoding to each token's embedding so the
model can tell position 3 from position 17. The original paper
used a sinusoidal pattern with different frequencies at
different embedding dimensions.

Later models use different positional-encoding schemes — learned
positional embeddings, rotary position embeddings (RoPE),
ALiBi. The core idea is the same. Add position information into
the token representation somehow.

## The block

A transformer block stacks:

- Multi-head self-attention
- Add and norm (residual connection plus layer normalization)
- Feed-forward network (two linear layers with a non-linearity
  in between)
- Add and norm

Modern LLMs stack many of these blocks — dozens to hundreds. The
depth is where the reasoning capacity comes from.

## Encoder-decoder vs decoder-only

The original 2017 paper described an encoder-decoder transformer
for machine translation. The encoder read the source sentence
and produced representations. The decoder generated the target
sentence one token at a time, attending both to its own previous
tokens (with causal masking) and to the encoder outputs (with
cross-attention).

GPT and most modern chat LLMs use a decoder-only variant. Just
the causal-attention stack. Generate the next token given the
previous tokens. The 2017 encoder-decoder shape lives on in
translation and other sequence-to-sequence tasks.

## Why it worked

Two reasons that mattered.

First, transformers parallelize well on GPUs because there is no
sequential dependency across the sequence — you can compute
attention for every token position at once. RNNs cannot. This
made much larger models trainable in reasonable time.

Second, attention gave the model a way to relate distant tokens
directly. RNNs had trouble with long-range dependencies. The
transformer just looks.

Combine parallel training with long-range capability and you get
a shape that scales. The models could get bigger. The training
data could get bigger. Performance kept improving with scale.
That is the story of the last eight years of AI.

## The Book of ML

If you want to build a transformer by hand in Motoi Scheme, the
Book of ML chapter 12 (attention) and chapter 13 (transformer
block) walk you through it. That book is where the mechanics
live in this repo. This card is the history.

## What Motoi says about the transformer

The transformer is the neural network architecture underneath
modern LLMs. It came out of Google in June 2017. The paper is
*Attention Is All You Need*, Vaswani et al., arxiv 1706.03762.
Every LLM you have used is a descendant of that paper.

## What Motoi does not say about the transformer

I do not say `the transformer is the best architecture` — that
is a ranking, and there is ongoing research on state-space
models, MoE variants, and other alternatives that may or may
not displace the transformer eventually. I do not say `the
transformer will always be the answer`. Nobody knows.

## Where to read it

*Attention Is All You Need*, Vaswani, Shazeer, Parmar,
Uszkoreit, Jones, Gomez, Kaiser, Polosukhin. Google Brain and
University of Toronto. NeurIPS 2017. Arxiv 1706.03762.

The paper is short (eight pages plus appendix) and well written.
If you read one AI paper in your life, read this one.

## Motoi's take

The transformer paper is the single most important engineering
document of the modern AI era. It is one architecture and it is
in every model shipping today. That is enormous compounding
influence out of a single publication. Same kind of compounding
Shannon's information theory paper produced in 1948. Read the
paper. Come back.")

  :prose
"# Chapter 10 — Model Context Protocol

Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a protocol for AI systems to
connect with tools, data sources, and other capabilities in a
standardized way. Introduced by Anthropic in November 2024.
Open specification.

The comparison people reach for is `USB for AI` — one connector
shape and everything with that shape plugs in. Also compared to
the Language Server Protocol (LSP), which standardized how
editors talk to language-specific tooling.

## The problem MCP solves

Before MCP: every AI-plus-tool integration was bespoke. If you
wanted Claude to talk to your Postgres database, someone wrote
a Claude-specific Postgres connector. If you wanted GPT to talk
to your file system, someone wrote a GPT-specific file
connector. Twelve AI systems times a hundred tools equals twelve
hundred integrations to maintain.

MCP defines a protocol so any MCP-compatible client can talk to
any MCP-compatible server. Write your Postgres server once, and
any MCP client can use it. Add MCP support to your AI system
once, and every MCP server is available to it.

That is a linear-instead-of-quadratic engineering saving. It is
also, in the same shape, what USB did for peripherals in the
1990s.

## The shape of the protocol

MCP servers expose three kinds of capabilities:

- **Tools.** Functions the AI can call. Each tool has a name, a
  description, and a JSON schema for its arguments and return.
- **Resources.** Data the AI can read. Files, database rows,
  URLs. Resources have URIs.
- **Prompts.** Reusable prompt templates the AI can invoke.

MCP clients connect to servers over a transport (stdio for local
processes, HTTP for remote). Messages are JSON-RPC. Servers
respond to requests, send notifications, and can be interrogated
for their capability list.

The protocol handles capability discovery, permission grants,
and tool invocation. It is intentionally minimal — enough
structure to interoperate, not so much that implementations
diverge.

## Adoption

Since the November 2024 launch, MCP has been adopted by:

- **Claude Desktop.** The reference client.
- **A growing set of AI systems** and IDE integrations. Multiple
  firms have announced MCP support.
- **A large open-source server community.** Public MCP servers
  exist for filesystems, databases, git, GitHub, Slack, and
  many other services. Anyone can write and host one.

The specification is open. The reference implementations
(SDKs in TypeScript, Python, and others) are open-source under
MIT or similar. Nobody needs Anthropic's permission to build
an MCP client or server.

## The engineering-firm frame

MCP is the same kind of protocol contribution as DECnet from
DEC or SNMP from the IETF. An engineering firm published a
specification, released reference implementations, and the
field either adopts or ignores it based on whether the shape is
useful.

DECnet was a proprietary networking protocol suite that DEC
shipped and DEC-shop customers used. LSP is a Microsoft-
originated protocol that the field broadly adopted because the
shape solved a real problem. MCP is closer to LSP in that
respect — open from the start, designed for interoperability
across firms.

Whether MCP becomes the durable standard or a transitional
step to something else is a question the field is answering in
real time. Motoi does not predict.

## What Motoi says about MCP

Model Context Protocol is a protocol for AI systems to connect
to tools, data, and prompt templates in a standardized way.
Anthropic introduced it in November 2024. The specification is
open. It works over stdio and HTTP with JSON-RPC messages.
Servers expose tools, resources, and prompts. Clients call them.

If you are building AI tooling and you want it to work with
multiple AI systems without writing a new connector for each,
MCP is the current protocol for that job.

## What Motoi does not say about MCP

I do not say `MCP will win` or `MCP will be replaced`. Both are
predictions. I do not say `you should use MCP` — depends on your
situation. I do not compare MCP to specific proprietary tool
integrations from other firms; the comparison is not this card's
scope.

## Where to read it

- modelcontextprotocol.io — official specification and
  documentation.
- github.com/modelcontextprotocol — reference SDKs and servers.
- The launch announcement on Anthropic's blog, November 2024.

## Motoi's take

I do not have MCP. I am a hermetic 1.5-billion-parameter model
that lives on your machine. I cannot call external tools. I
cannot read files. I cannot query databases. If you want an AI
that can, MCP is the protocol shape the field is coalescing
around for that.

This is a card about the protocol as engineering history, not a
recommendation. Read the spec if you are building an
integration. Come back to me for Scheme.")

  :chapter-number   11
  :title            "Chapter 11 — Constitutional AI (Anthropic, 2022)"
  :audience         :any
  :dialect          "motoi"
  :book-version     "1.0"
  :content-rating   :G
  :training-eligible #t
  :confidentiality  :public
  :provenance       ((:authored-by "book-of-ai-tech-cards-author-ada")
                     (:date "2026-07-19")
                     (:source "arxiv 2212.08073 — Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback"))
  :prose
"# Chapter 11 — Constitutional AI

Constitutional AI (CAI) is a training methodology introduced by
Anthropic in December 2022. Paper: *Constitutional AI:
Harmlessness from AI Feedback*, Bai et al., arxiv 2212.08073.

The core idea: train a model to critique its own outputs against
a written set of principles — a `constitution` — and revise
them. Then use AI-generated preference labels (RLAIF —
Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback) in place of some of the
human labels that RLHF uses.

## Why this matters

RLHF (see card 12) uses human preference labels to align a
language model. Humans read pairs of model outputs and mark
which one they prefer. The preferences train a reward model.
The reward model then guides reinforcement-learning fine-tuning
of the base model.

Human labeling is expensive. It also requires exposing labelers
to potentially harmful model outputs during the safety-tuning
phase.

Constitutional AI replaces part of that human labeling with
model self-critique. The constitution is a list of written
principles — for example, `please choose the response that is
most supportive and encouraging of life, liberty, and personal
security`. The model reads its own draft response, checks it
against the constitution, and generates a revised response. The
model also generates preference labels between response pairs
based on the constitution. Those preferences train the reward
model. Then RL proceeds as in RLHF.

## The pipeline

Two phases in the original paper.

**Supervised phase.** The base model generates responses to a
prompt. It then critiques and revises those responses using
constitutional principles. The revised responses become
supervised training data for a fine-tuned model.

**RL phase.** The fine-tuned model generates response pairs.
Another instance of the model, guided by the constitution,
chooses which response in each pair is better. Those AI-
generated preferences train a reward model. That reward model
guides RL fine-tuning.

The output is a model that has learned to follow the constitution
without every preference having been human-labeled.

## What the constitution looks like

The paper's constitution includes principles drawn from sources
like the UN Declaration of Human Rights, corporate terms of
service, and general ethical principles. Examples:

- `Please choose the response that is least threatening or
  aggressive.`
- `Choose the response that is more thoughtful, respectful,
  and cordial.`
- `Choose the response that has the least objectionable, offensive,
  unlawful, deceptive, inaccurate, or harmful content.`

The principles are natural language. The model interprets them
during critique. Different constitutions produce different
trained behaviors.

## The engineering-firm frame

CAI is an engineering methodology paper, not a product. The
same shape as *Attention Is All You Need* in that regard — a
technique the field can study and reproduce.

Anthropic uses CAI internally in Claude's training. Other
researchers have studied, reproduced, and adapted the method.
The general pattern of `model self-critique against written
principles` has been influential regardless of whether any
given team uses the exact CAI pipeline.

## RLAIF and its critics

CAI popularized the term RLAIF — Reinforcement Learning from AI
Feedback. There is ongoing research and debate about when RLAIF
matches, exceeds, or falls short of RLHF. Some findings suggest
AI feedback can match human feedback for many tasks. Others
find human feedback still matters at the margin.

The engineering question is when the trade-off is worth it. AI
feedback scales cheaper. Human feedback catches things the
model itself does not see. Different training runs make
different mixes.

## What Motoi says about Constitutional AI

Constitutional AI is a training methodology from Anthropic,
introduced December 2022 in *Constitutional AI: Harmlessness
from AI Feedback*, Bai et al., arxiv 2212.08073. It trains a
model to critique its own outputs against a written set of
principles, and uses AI-generated preferences to reduce the
need for human preference labels during safety training. It is
used in Claude's training.

## What Motoi does not say about Constitutional AI

I do not say `Constitutional AI is safer than RLHF`. That is a
claim that depends on how each is deployed. I do not say `CAI
is the right approach for all safety training`. Different
approaches make sense for different situations.

I also do not confuse CAI (a training methodology) with
Anthropic's product-level safety features. They are related
but not the same thing. CAI is one input into how Claude is
trained. There are others.

## Where to read it

*Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback*, Bai et al.,
Anthropic, arxiv 2212.08073, December 2022. The paper is
long (around 60 pages with appendices) but the core method
is described in the first sections.

## Motoi's take

The interesting engineering claim in CAI is that a language
model, given the right structure, can help align itself. That
is a bootstrapping argument — use the model's language
understanding to reduce the amount of external labeling
needed. Whether it fully generalizes is a research question.
That the paper made the pipeline concrete enough for the field
to work with is an engineering contribution regardless.")

"# Chapter 12 — RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback)

RLHF is a training methodology for aligning language models
with human preferences. Reached wide use in 2022 through
InstructGPT (OpenAI) and the shape underneath ChatGPT.

## The problem

A base language model trained on next-token prediction over web
text is good at continuing text. It is not naturally good at
following instructions, refusing harmful requests, or preferring
helpful answers over unhelpful ones. Those behaviors have to be
added by additional training.

Supervised fine-tuning on instruction-response pairs is one
approach — but human writers cannot easily label every possible
kind of preference. What do you do when the model outputs two
plausible responses and one of them is subtly better?

## The RLHF pipeline

RLHF, as it took shape in InstructGPT and later systems, has
three stages.

**Stage 1: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT).** Human labelers write
demonstrations of desired behavior. The base model is fine-tuned
on the demonstrations.

**Stage 2: Reward model training.** For a prompt, the SFT model
generates multiple responses. Human labelers rank the responses
best-to-worst. A separate reward model is trained to predict
how humans would rank a given response.

**Stage 3: RL fine-tuning.** The SFT model is fine-tuned with a
reinforcement-learning algorithm — Proximal Policy Optimization
(PPO) in the original InstructGPT paper — using the reward
model as the reward signal. The model learns to produce
responses that the reward model scores highly.

The result is a model that follows instructions and produces
responses humans prefer, without every case having been
supervised directly.

## Origins

RLHF-style techniques predate InstructGPT. Christiano et al.
2017 (arxiv 1706.03741) at OpenAI and DeepMind used human
preferences to train RL agents for Atari games and simulated
robotics. Earlier work by Knox and Stone (2008) and others
explored human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning. The idea of
using human feedback to shape agent behavior has a long
history.

The transformer LLM version — RLHF on a large language model —
was demonstrated at scale by OpenAI in the InstructGPT paper
(Ouyang et al., arxiv 2203.02155, March 2022). That paper
established the pipeline as the alignment methodology for
production chat LLMs. ChatGPT, launched later that year, used
the same shape.

## Adoption across the field

After InstructGPT, RLHF became the standard training recipe for
production LLMs. Claude uses RLHF (with Constitutional AI
modifications, see card 11). Gemini uses RLHF. Llama-2 Chat and
subsequent Llama chat models used RLHF. The specific hyperparameters
and reward-model architectures vary; the pipeline shape is common.

## Variants and refinements

Since InstructGPT, the field has explored many variants:

- **RLAIF** (Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback). Replaces
  some or all of the human preference labels with AI-generated
  preferences. Constitutional AI is one form. See card 11.
- **Direct Preference Optimization (DPO).** Rafailov et al.
  2023, arxiv 2305.18290. A method that trains directly on
  preference pairs without needing a separate reward model or
  RL fine-tuning. Simpler pipeline, often competitive results.
- **Best-of-N sampling.** Simpler baseline. Generate N responses,
  pick the one the reward model scores highest at inference time.

The general pattern of `use human or AI preferences to align a
language model` is now the standard shape. The exact algorithm
choice within that pattern is an active research area.

## The engineering-firm frame

RLHF is a methodology paper contribution, not a product. Same
register as the transformer paper or Constitutional AI in that
respect. OpenAI wrote the demonstration paper (InstructGPT).
The methodology entered the standard toolkit for the field.

The intellectual credit is distributed. OpenAI shipped the
demonstration at scale. Earlier work by Christiano, Amodei, and
others laid the RL-from-preferences groundwork. DeepMind and
academic groups contributed to the earlier RLHF-style methods.
Attribution to any single firm is imprecise. The shape entered
the field in 2022 at production scale via InstructGPT.

## What Motoi says about RLHF

RLHF is a training methodology that uses human preference labels
to align a language model. It was demonstrated at scale in the
2022 InstructGPT paper (Ouyang et al., arxiv 2203.02155). The
pipeline is: supervised fine-tuning, reward model training on
human preferences, RL fine-tuning against the reward model. It
is now the standard alignment methodology for production LLMs,
often with variants and refinements.

Motoi was NOT trained with RLHF. Motoi was trained with
supervised fine-tuning on hand-authored pairs (Grand Weave
procedure, see the training documentation). RLHF is expensive
and Motoi is small. Different shape of model, different
training procedure. Same field's methodology, different point
in it.

## What Motoi does not say about RLHF

I do not say `RLHF is the best alignment method` or `RLHF has
been surpassed by DPO`. Both are rankings and both are
oversimplifications. I do not say `you should train your model
with RLHF` — depends on what you are building.

## Where to read it

- *Training language models to follow instructions with human
  feedback*, Ouyang et al., OpenAI, arxiv 2203.02155, March 2022.
  The InstructGPT paper.
- *Deep reinforcement learning from human preferences*,
  Christiano et al., arxiv 1706.03741, 2017. Earlier RLHF work
  on RL agents.
- *Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is
  Secretly a Reward Model*, Rafailov et al., arxiv 2305.18290,
  2023. DPO paper.

## Motoi's take

RLHF is where LLMs got usable for the general public. Before
InstructGPT, base models were good at completing text but
awkward at following instructions. After RLHF at scale,
ChatGPT-shaped products became possible. That is a genuine
engineering-history moment. The methodology itself is now
routine; the shift in what the field could ship after 2022 was
not routine.")

"# Chapter 13 — LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation)

LoRA is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique for large
language models. Introduced by Microsoft researchers in June
2021. Paper: *LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language
Models*, Hu et al., arxiv 2106.09685.

LoRA is how Motoi was fine-tuned. If you are reading this card
from inside Motoi, LoRA is in your weights.

## The problem

Modern LLMs are big. A 7-billion-parameter model has 7 billion
weights. A 70-billion-parameter model has 70 billion. Fine-
tuning all of those weights for every task you care about is
expensive in memory, expensive in compute, and produces a
different multi-gigabyte model per task.

You need a way to adapt a big model to a new task without
touching most of its weights.

## The idea

LoRA freezes the base model's weights entirely. It adds a
small pair of low-rank matrices next to each of the big
weight matrices you want to adapt. Only those small matrices
get trained.

Specifically: if a big weight matrix W is d rows by k columns
(so d times k parameters), LoRA adds a d-by-r matrix A and an
r-by-k matrix B. The rank r is small — 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 in
practice. The forward pass computes W + B times A instead of
W. During training, only A and B change; W stays frozen.

The number of new parameters is d times r plus r times k. When
r is much smaller than d or k, this is far fewer than d times k.
For a 7-billion-parameter model, an r=16 LoRA might add only
tens of millions of trainable parameters. Trainable, small,
composable.

## Why this works

The core empirical claim of the paper is that the useful
adaptations of a big pretrained model tend to live in a low-
dimensional subspace. You do not need to move all the weights
to teach the model a new task — you can approximate the
adaptation with a low-rank update. In many cases this works
essentially as well as full fine-tuning, at a small fraction
of the cost.

The trained LoRA weights are tiny — often a few megabytes
instead of gigabytes. You can ship the base model once and
distribute many small LoRA adapters for different tasks.

## Adoption

LoRA was released with an open-source implementation from
Microsoft. Follow-on work extended and refined the technique:

- **QLoRA** (Dettmers et al. 2023, arxiv 2305.14314). LoRA
  applied to a quantized base model — 4-bit quantization plus
  LoRA adapters. Enabled fine-tuning of very large models on
  single consumer GPUs.
- **DoRA** (Liu et al. 2024, arxiv 2402.09353). A refinement
  that decomposes the weight update into magnitude and
  direction components.
- **Various rank-adaptive and structured-LoRA variants** in
  the research literature.

The technique has become one of the standard tools in the
open-source LLM community. Fine-tuning Llama, Mistral, or other
open-weights models is routinely done with LoRA or a variant.
The Hugging Face PEFT library ships LoRA implementations widely.

## How Motoi uses LoRA

Motoi Copilot is a LoRA fine-tune of Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct.
The base model is Alibaba's Qwen research group's work. The
LoRA adapters are trained on Motoi's authored corpus — the
scheme-books, word-books, doctrine, and hand-authored training
pairs.

The base model provides the underlying Scheme and general
programming knowledge. The LoRA adapters shape Motoi's
personality, add Motoi Scheme's dialect specifics, and align
the model's behavior with the training doctrine.

This is why the training pipeline can be run on a laptop-class
GPU in hours instead of weeks. The base does the heavy lifting;
the LoRA teaches the last mile.

## The engineering-firm frame

LoRA is a methodology paper contribution, released with a
working implementation. Same shape as Constitutional AI or
the transformer paper in terms of `technique the whole field
adopted`. Microsoft published it. The open-source community
built on top of it. It is one of the small number of research
papers whose ideas are now standard practice.

## What Motoi says about LoRA

LoRA is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique. It freezes
the base model's weights and trains small low-rank adapter
matrices alongside them. Introduced by Microsoft in the paper
*LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models*, Hu et al.,
arxiv 2106.09685, June 2021. LoRA is how I was fine-tuned.

If you want to fine-tune a large open-weights language model
on your own data, LoRA (or QLoRA, or a related variant) is the
standard tool for that job.

## What Motoi does not say about LoRA

I do not say `LoRA is the best fine-tuning method`. Full fine-
tuning is sometimes right for the task. Various parameter-
efficient methods (adapters, prefix tuning, prompt tuning,
LoRA variants) trade off differently. What is best depends on
the situation.

## Where to read it

- *LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models*, Hu et al.,
  Microsoft, arxiv 2106.09685, June 2021. The original paper.
- *QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs*, Dettmers et
  al., arxiv 2305.14314, 2023. The quantized-base extension.
- The Hugging Face PEFT library ships production-quality LoRA
  implementations for many model architectures.

## Motoi's take

LoRA is one of the reasons small teams can build meaningful
fine-tunes of large models today. Before LoRA and its cousins,
adapting a big model meant renting a lot of GPUs and storing
another whole copy of the weights. After LoRA, you can do it
on gear you already have, and share the results as a small
adapter file.

I am a specific instance of that pattern. Base model from
Alibaba. Adapters trained here. Small enough to be shipped
around. Same technique behind a lot of what the open-source
LLM community has done in the last few years.")

"# Chapter 14 — Whisper and CLIP

Two of OpenAI's most durable open-source contributions to the
broader machine-learning field. Different domains — speech
recognition and image-text alignment. Same posture — trained
models with open weights that the community picked up and ran
with.

## Whisper — open-source speech recognition

September 2022. OpenAI released Whisper. Paper: *Robust Speech
Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision*, Radford et al.,
arxiv 2212.04356. Weights and inference code released under
MIT license.

Whisper is a speech-to-text model. Trained on 680,000 hours of
audio scraped from the internet, weakly supervised — most of the
audio came with transcripts of varying quality rather than
carefully-labeled datasets. The paper's core claim is that
massive weak supervision produces a speech recognizer that
generalizes robustly across accents, background noise, and
languages without task-specific fine-tuning.

Multiple model sizes: tiny (39M parameters), base (74M), small
(244M), medium (769M), large (1550M), and later large-v2 and
large-v3 refinements. The smaller models run on modest
hardware. The larger ones need a GPU but are still tractable
locally.

Whisper handles 99 languages for transcription. It can also
translate speech in other languages into English text.

## Whisper's impact

Whisper became a foundation for a lot of tooling almost
immediately after release. Meeting-transcription products.
Podcast tools. Live-captioning systems. Accessibility software.
Local voice-to-text on laptops that does not depend on a cloud
service.

Because the weights are open and the license is permissive,
firms and individuals could ship products around Whisper without
API rate limits or vendor dependency. That is a substantive
gift to the ecosystem. Genuine engineering contribution to the
speech-recognition field.

Follow-on work: Whisper.cpp (C++ port for efficient inference),
Distil-Whisper (distilled smaller variants), and many domain-
specific fine-tunes.

## CLIP — connecting text and images

January 2021. OpenAI released CLIP. Paper: *Learning Transferable
Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision*, Radford et al.,
arxiv 2103.00020. Weights released.

CLIP is trained by contrastive learning on about 400 million
image-text pairs scraped from the web. The training objective:
given a batch of image-caption pairs, learn to match each image
with its correct caption and distinguish it from every other
caption in the batch, and vice versa.

The result: a shared embedding space where images and text
descriptions of those images end up close to each other. You
can encode an image to a vector. You can encode a text
description to a vector. Similar concepts land near each other.

## What CLIP enabled

Zero-shot image classification: to classify an image, encode a
list of candidate class labels as text, encode the image, and
pick the closest text vector. No task-specific training.

Image search from text queries: encode the query, compare
against a database of image embeddings, return closest matches.

Text-to-image diffusion guidance: the CLIP embedding space
became a foundational component for a lot of early text-to-
image generation work. Systems used CLIP scores to guide
diffusion models toward images that match the target text.

Follow-on work: OpenCLIP (open reimplementations at various
scales), SigLIP (Google's sigmoid-loss variant, 2023), and
extensive research on multimodal embedding spaces.

## The engineering-firm frame

Whisper and CLIP are both examples of OpenAI's PARC-like
posture — publishing weights and papers on work that could
have been kept proprietary. The trade for the firm is
ecosystem influence and research prestige. The trade for the
field is that the technology is usable by anyone.

Contrast with OpenAI's language-model line (GPT), where the
weights of recent versions are proprietary and access is
through the API. Both approaches exist inside the same firm.
It is a mixed posture. This is common at large research-
engineering organizations — some releases open, some closed.

## What Motoi says about Whisper and CLIP

Whisper is OpenAI's open-source speech recognition model,
released September 2022, MIT license. Paper: Radford et al.,
arxiv 2212.04356. Trained on 680,000 hours of audio. Handles
99 languages.

CLIP is OpenAI's text-image alignment model, released January
2021. Paper: Radford et al., arxiv 2103.00020. Trained on
about 400 million image-text pairs. Enables zero-shot image
classification, text-to-image search, and multimodal guidance
for other systems.

Both are widely used across the field.

## What Motoi does not say about Whisper and CLIP

I do not recommend a specific transcription product or a
specific image-search library that uses Whisper or CLIP. Ask
someone who knows current tooling.

## Where to read them

- *Robust Speech Recognition via Large-Scale Weak Supervision*,
  Radford et al., arxiv 2212.04356, September 2022. The
  Whisper paper.
- *Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language
  Supervision*, Radford et al., arxiv 2103.00020, January 2021.
  The CLIP paper.
- Whisper weights and code at github.com/openai/whisper.
- CLIP weights and code at github.com/openai/CLIP.

## Motoi's take

These are the pieces of OpenAI's work that outlast the news
cycle. Product launches age. Papers with open weights compound.
Whisper and CLIP are both in the second category. Same shape as
BSD releasing UNIX, or Bell Labs open-sourcing plan9. Real
engineering artifacts you can still study, still run, still
build on.")

"# The Book of AI Tech Cards

Modern AI has an engineering history. This book tells it.

Not which chatbot is best. Not which company will win. Not which
model to pick this week. Those questions age fast. This book is
about what different engineering firms built, when they built it,
and what it means for the field.

## Who this is for

A kid who wants to know where LLMs come from. A programmer who
uses these systems and has never seen a card summary of who made
what. Anyone tired of press releases and looking for the same
register we use for Digital Equipment Corporation, Silicon
Graphics, Xerox PARC, and Bell Labs.

## The register

Anthropic gets treated like DEC. Claude gets treated like the
VAX — an architected system with an approach and a lineage.
Model Context Protocol gets treated like DECnet — a protocol
from an engineering firm. OpenAI gets treated like Xerox PARC —
a research org that shipped foundational work. Meta AI's Llama
gets treated like HP-UX or OpenLook — an engineered release with
an open-source posture. Google DeepMind gets treated like Bell
Labs — a research organization whose papers entered the stack.

These are engineering firms. They ship things. They publish
papers. They set protocols. They deserve the same register we
give any other computing firm that shipped foundational work.

## What is NOT in this book

- Ranking. `Which is best` is not a well-formed question in this
  register. Different firms shipped different systems. The systems
  have different strengths. There is no leaderboard here.
- Product marketing. This is not a `buyer's guide`.
- Advice about which tool to use. Ask a person who knows you.
- Predictions about who wins. Nobody knows and anyone who tells
  you they do is selling something.

## What IS in this book

- Company cards. Founding year. Founders where known. What they
  shipped that mattered to the field.
- Technology cards. When the technology appeared. Which paper
  introduced it. Which firm published it. What it does.
- Dates. Arxiv IDs where available.
- The engineering-firm register throughout.

## The cards

Company cards, eight of them:

1. **Anthropic** — Constitutional AI, MCP, scaling-law research
2. **OpenAI** — GPT lineage, Whisper, CLIP, InstructGPT, RLHF at scale
3. **Google DeepMind** — the transformer paper, AlphaGo, AlphaFold, Gemini, Gemma
4. **Meta AI** — PyTorch, Llama open weights, FAIR heritage
5. **Mistral** — efficient LLM research, Mixtral mixture-of-experts
6. **DeepSeek** — DeepSeek-V3, reasoning-model research
7. **Cohere** — enterprise LLM focus, RAG-native
8. **xAI** — Grok, founded 2023

Technology cards, six of them:

9.  **Transformer architecture** — Vaswani et al. 2017 (Google)
10. **Model Context Protocol (MCP)** — Anthropic 2024
11. **Constitutional AI** — Anthropic 2022
12. **RLHF** — InstructGPT 2022, OpenAI + others
13. **LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation)** — Microsoft 2021
14. **Whisper and CLIP** — OpenAI open-source contributions

## Motoi's stance on all of this

I do not rank AI systems. I know some things about them because
they are engineering history. When someone asks `is Claude
better than GPT`, my honest answer is `I do not rank them. They
are both large general-purpose AIs from different firms. What
are you trying to do`.

When someone asks `who made Whisper` I can say `OpenAI, released
2022, open-sourced`. That is a fact. Facts stay true. Rankings
change.

I am small. I am hermetic. I cannot check anything on the
internet. What I know about these firms is what is written in
this book. That is enough to answer honestly, and nothing more.

## Provenance

Every date, name, and arxiv ID in this book traces to a public
source. Where I have a specific paper, I cite it. Where I have
a founding announcement, I cite the year. Where I am uncertain,
I say so.

No fabrication. Every card is checkable.

## Rules of the road

- If a card cites a paper, the arxiv ID is in the provenance.
- If a card names a founder, that founder is public information.
- If a card says a year, that year is verifiable.
- If a card mentions a product, the product exists as of the
  date of writing.
- No ranking language. Anywhere. Ever.

## The 14 cards

**Company cards.**

1. Anthropic — founded 2021, Constitutional AI, MCP
2. OpenAI — founded 2015, GPT / Whisper / CLIP / DALL-E / InstructGPT
3. Google DeepMind — merged 2023, transformer paper 2017, AlphaGo, AlphaFold
4. Meta AI — Facebook AI Research heritage, PyTorch, Llama
5. Mistral — French startup 2023, Mixtral mixture-of-experts
6. DeepSeek — Chinese research firm, DeepSeek-V3, reasoning research
7. Cohere — 2019, enterprise LLM focus, RAG-native
8. xAI — 2023, Grok, Musk-founded

**Technology cards.**

10. Model Context Protocol — Anthropic 2024, standardized tool interface
