"# Chapter 7: Particles

## The Logic of Many

A flower sways as one body. A body bounces as one mass. But watch pollen drift from a blossom, or snow fall across a field, or sparks rise from a flame — the world is made of *many*.

In Chapter 5 you integrated forces into one body. In Chapter 6 you made one body breathe. Now you will spawn hundreds, give each its own life, and watch the aggregate behavior emerge from simple rules applied to each.

This is the particle system: a collection of entities, each with position, velocity, and a finite lifetime. You spawn them, step them, age them, and despawn them when they die. The engine's `world/*` and `entity/*` verbs do the bookkeeping; you write the rules.

By the end of this chapter you will author a fountain that sprays droplets into an arc, a pollen drift that sways in invisible wind, and a sparkler that paints trails of light across the surface.

---

## 7.1 One Becomes Many

Start with what you know: a single particle, position and velocity, stepped each frame.

```scheme
(define (one-particle)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((p (world/spawn 40 20)))
    (entity/set-vel! p 1 -2)
    (entity/gravity-scale! p 0.5)
    (big-bang
      (on-tick (lambda (w) (world/step)))
      (to-draw (lambda (w)
        (let ((pos (entity/pos p))
              (x (car pos))
              (y (cadr pos)))
          (paint-cell (floor x) (floor y) \"🌸\")))))))

(one-particle)
```

<!-- BUILD: wire harness to run this as ch07-ex01.scm; expect one blossom arcing downward under gravity -->

[VISUAL: A single 🌸 glyph launched upward-right, falling in a parabolic arc across a 64×48 grid canvas]

The particle lives. But one is not a system. You need ten, or a hundred, and each must age and die.

---

## 7.2 Lifetime and Death

A particle system is not eternal. Each particle is born, lives for some duration, and despawns. Add a `lifetime` field to each entity's custom state, decrement it each tick, and despawn when it reaches zero.

```scheme
(define (mortal-particles)
  (world/reset!)
  ;; spawn 5 particles, each with a random lifetime
  (define (spawn-one dx dy life)
    (let ((p (world/spawn 32 40)))
      (entity/set-vel! p dx dy)
      (entity/gravity-scale! p 0.3)
      (entity/set! p 'lifetime life)))
  
  (spawn-one -1.5 -2 30)
  (spawn-one -0.5 -2.5 25)
  (spawn-one 0 -3 35)
  (spawn-one 0.5 -2.5 28)
  (spawn-one 1.5 -2 32)
  
  (big-bang
    (on-tick (lambda (w)
      (world/step)
      (world/each (lambda (p)
        (let ((life (entity/get p 'lifetime)))
          (if (and life (> life 0))
              (entity/set! p 'lifetime (- life 1))
              (entity/despawn! p)))))))
    (to-draw (lambda (w)
      (world/each (lambda (p)
        (if (entity/alive? p)
            (let ((pos (entity/pos p))
                  (x (car pos))
                  (y (cadr pos)))
              (paint-cell (floor x) (floor y) \"✨\")))))))))

(mortal-particles)
```

<!-- BUILD: wire as ch07-ex02.scm; expect 5 sparkles rising then fading as they despawn over ~30 ticks -->

[VISUAL: Five ✨ glyphs launched upward in a spread pattern, each disappearing at a different frame as lifetime expires]

Each particle carries its own death timer. `world/each` visits every living entity; you decrement, check, and despawn. The system now has a lifecycle.

---

## 7.3 The Emitter

Five particles, hand-placed, is still a sculpture. A true particle system *generates* its members over time. You need an **emitter**: a function that spawns a new particle each tick (or every N ticks), with position and velocity chosen by rule.

```scheme
(define (fountain)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.15)
  
  (define tick-count 0)
  
  (define (emit!)
    ;; spawn one particle at the fountain origin
    (let ((p (world/spawn 32 44))
          ;; random horizontal spread: -1 to +1
          (dx (+ -1 (* 2 (/ (modulo tick-count 37) 37.0))))
          ;; upward velocity with slight variation
          (dy (+ -3.5 (* 0.5 (/ (modulo tick-count 23) 23.0)))))
      (entity/set-vel! p dx dy)
      (entity/set! p 'lifetime 60)))
  
  (big-bang
    (on-tick (lambda (w)
      (set! tick-count (+ tick-count 1))
      ;; emit every 2 ticks
      (if (= 0 (modulo tick-count 2))
          (emit!))
      (world/step)
      ;; age and kill
      (world/each (lambda (p)
        (let ((life (entity/get p 'lifetime)))
          (if life
              (if (> life 0)
                  (entity/set! p 'lifetime (- life 1))
                  (entity/despawn! p))))))))
    (to-draw (lambda (w)
      (world/each (lambda (p)
        (if (entity/alive? p)
            (let ((pos (entity/pos p))
                  (x (car pos))
                  (y (cadr pos)))
              (paint-cell (floor x) (floor y) \"💧\")))))))))

(fountain)
```

<!-- BUILD: wire as ch07-ex03.scm; expect a continuous spray of droplets arcing up and falling, steady-state ~30 particles alive -->

[VISUAL: A fountain of 💧 droplets spraying upward from x=32, y=44, spreading horizontally and falling in parabolic arcs; the canvas shows ~20–30 droplets at any moment in a classic fountain shape]

The emitter is a function called each tick. It spawns, assigns velocity, and tags lifetime. The world steps physics; the aging loop despawns the dead. The system reaches **steady state**: emission rate matches death rate, and the population stabilizes.

This is the skeleton of every particle system: spawn, step, age, despawn. The art is in the emission rule.

---

## 7.4 Wind and Drift

Gravity pulls particles down. What if you want them to drift sideways, swirl, or float? Add a **force** to all particles each tick, or tag a subset with a `kind` and apply force only to the tagged.

```scheme
(define (pollen-drift)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.05)  ; gentle downward pull
  
  (define tick-count 0)
  
  (define (emit-pollen!)
    (let ((p (world/spawn (+ 10 (modulo tick-count 44)) 5))
          (dx (* 0.3 (dsin (* tick-count 0.1))))
          (dy 0.2))
      (entity/set-vel! p dx dy)
      (entity/set! p 'lifetime 120)
      (entity/tag! p 'pollen)
      (entity/drag! p 0.98)))  ; air resistance
  
  (big-bang
    (on-tick (lambda (w)
      (set! tick-count (+ tick-count 1))
      (if (= 0 (modulo tick-count 4))
          (emit-pollen!))
      ;; apply horizontal wind to all pollen
      (world/each (lambda (p)
        (if (entity/get p 'pollen)
            (let ((wind-x (* 0.05 (dsin (* tick-count 0.05)))))
              (entity/accel! p wind-x 0)))))
      (world/step)
      ;; age and despawn
      (world/each (lambda (p)
        (let ((life (entity/get p 'lifetime)))
          (if life
              (if (> life 0)
                  (entity/set! p 'lifetime (- life 1))
                  (entity/despawn! p))))))))
    (to-draw (lambda (w)
      (world/each (lambda (p)
        (if (and (entity/alive? p) (entity/get p 'pollen))
            (let ((pos (entity/pos p))
                  (x (car pos))
                  (y (cadr pos)))
              (paint-cell (floor x) (floor y) \"🌼\")))))))))

(pollen-drift)
```

[VISUAL: A field of 🌼 glyphs drifting slowly downward across the canvas, swaying left and right in a gentle sine-wave pattern as horizontal wind oscillates each frame]

The `world/each` loop applies a sideways force *before* stepping physics. The force is itself oscillating (`dsin` of tick-count), so the drift sways. Drag damps velocity each tick, preventing runaway speed. The particles float.

---

## 7.5 Heterogeneous Lifetimes and Fade

Not all particles should live the same span. Randomize lifetime at spawn, and use the remaining life to modulate rendering — a particle near death could shrink, dim, or change glyph.

The engine does not yet expose alpha or scale per-glyph in the headless harness, but you can simulate \"fade\" by choosing different glyphs based on remaining life, or by despawning early with probability.

```scheme
(define (fading-sparks)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 -0.1)  ; sparks rise
  
  (define tick-count 0)
  
  (define (random-life)
    ;; lifetime between 20 and 60 ticks
    (+ 20 (modulo (* tick-count 17) 40)))
  
  (define (emit-spark!)
    (let ((p (world/spawn 32 40))
          (angle (* TAU (/ (modulo tick-count 19) 19.0)))
          (speed (+ 1.5 (* 0.5 (/ (modulo tick-count 13) 13.0)))))
      (entity/set-vel! p (* speed (dcos angle)) (* speed (dsin angle)))
      (entity/set! p 'lifetime (random-life))
      (entity/set! p 'max-life (entity/get p 'lifetime))
      (entity/drag! p 0.96)))
  
  (big-bang
    (on-tick (lambda (w)
      (set! tick-count (+ tick-count 1))
      (if (= 0 (modulo tick-count 3))
          (emit-spark!))
      (world/step)
      (world/each (lambda (p)
        (let ((life (entity/get p 'lifetime)))
          (if life
              (if (> life 0)
                  (entity/set! p 'lifetime (- life 1))
                  (entity/despawn! p))))))))
    (to-draw (lambda (w)
      (world/each (lambda (p)
        (if (entity/alive? p)
            (let ((pos (entity/pos p))
                  (x (car pos))
                  (y (cadr pos))
                  (life (entity/get p 'lifetime))
                  (max-life (entity/get p 'max-life)))
              ;; choose glyph based on remaining life fraction
              (let ((frac (/ life max-life)))
                (cond
                  ((> frac 0.66) (paint-cell (floor x) (floor y) \"✨\"))
                  ((> frac 0.33) (paint-cell (floor x) (floor y) \"·\"))
                  (else (paint-cell (floor x) (floor y) \".\"))))))))))))

(fading-sparks)
```

<!-- BUILD: wire as ch07-ex05.scm; expect sparks radiating outward from center, bright at spawn (✨), dimming to · then . before despawn -->

[VISUAL: A radial burst of particles from x=32, y=40, bright ✨ near the center, transitioning to dimmer · and . glyphs as they drift outward and age, creating a gradient of brightness from core to edge]

Each particle remembers both current `lifetime` and `max-life` (the initial value). The renderer computes the fraction remaining and chooses a glyph. Bright at birth, dim at death. This is **visual fade** without engine alpha support — a pedagogical workaround that becomes a stylistic choice (lo-fi dithered fade).

---

## 7.6 Trails and Persistent Marks

Particles move and despawn. But what if you want them to *leave a mark*? One approach: spawn a secondary \"ghost\" particle at the old position each tick, with zero velocity and a short life. The ghost stays put and fades, creating a motion trail.

```scheme
(define (sparkler-trails)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.05)
  
  (define tick-count 0)
  
  (define (emit-sparkler!)
    (let ((p (world/spawn 32 24))
          (angle (* TAU (/ (modulo tick-count 29) 29.0)))
          (speed 2.0))
      (entity/set-vel! p (* speed (dcos angle)) (* speed (dsin angle)))
      (entity/set! p 'lifetime 40)
      (entity/tag! p 'active)
      (entity/drag! p 0.94)))
  
  (define (spawn-ghost! x y)
    (let ((g (world/spawn x y)))
      (entity/set-vel! g 0 0)
      (entity/pin! g)  ; no physics
      (entity/set! p 'lifetime 12)
      (entity/tag! g 'ghost)))
  
  (big-bang
    (on-tick (lambda (w)
      (set! tick-count (+ tick-count 1))
      (if (= 0 (modulo tick-count 5))
          (emit-sparkler!))
      ;; active particles leave ghost trails
      (world/each (lambda (p)
        (if (entity/get p 'active)
            (let ((pos (entity/pos p)))
              (spawn-ghost! (car pos) (cadr pos))))))
      (world/step)
      ;; age all
      (world/each (lambda (p)
        (let ((life (entity/get p 'lifetime)))
          (if life
              (if (> life 0)
                  (entity/set! p 'lifetime (- life 1))
                  (entity/despawn! p))))))))
    (to-draw (lambda (w)
      (world/each (lambda (p)
        (if (entity/alive? p)
            (let ((pos (entity/pos p))
                  (x (car pos))
                  (y (cadr pos)))
              (if (entity/get p 'active)
                  (paint-cell (floor x) (floor y) \"✨\")
                  (if (entity/get p 'ghost)
                      (paint-cell (floor x) (floor y) \"·\")))))))))))

(sparkler-trails)
```

<!-- BUILD: wire as ch07-ex06.scm; expect active sparkles radiating outward, each leaving a trail of · ghost particles that fade after 12 ticks -->

[VISUAL: A starburst pattern of ✨ glyphs moving outward from center, each trailing a line of · glyphs that mark the path taken; the trails linger briefly then disappear, creating a comet-tail effect]

Every tick, each active particle spawns a ghost at its current position. The ghost is pinned (no physics), lives 12 ticks, then despawns. The active particle keeps moving. The aggregate is a persistent motion trail painted by ephemeral markers.

This technique generalizes: you can spawn *anything* at the position of a moving particle — dust kicked up by feet, water ripples from a falling drop, petals shed by a tumbling blossom.

---

## 7.7 Collision and Response

Particles often collide — with the floor, with each other, with obstacles. The engine's `world/floor!` verb adds a horizontal floor at a given y; particles with `bounce!` set will reflect when they hit it.

```scheme
(define (bouncing-droplets)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.2)
  (world/floor! 42)  ; floor at y=42
  
  (define tick-count 0)
  
  (define (emit-droplet!)
    (let ((p (world/spawn (+ 28 (modulo tick-count 8)) 10))
          (dy 0))
      (entity/set-vel! p 0 dy)
      (entity/set! p 'lifetime 100)
      (entity/bounce! p 0.6)  ; 60% of velocity retained on bounce
      (entity/friction! p 0.98)))
  
  (big-bang
    (on-tick (lambda (w)
      (set! tick-count (+ tick-count 1))
      (if (= 0 (modulo tick-count 8))
          (emit-droplet!))
      (world/step)
      (world/each (lambda (p)
        (let ((life (entity/get p 'lifetime)))
          (if life
              (if (> life 0)
                  (entity/set! p 'lifetime (- life 1))
                  (entity/despawn! p))))))))
    (to-draw (lambda (w)
      (world/each (lambda (p)
        (if (entity/alive? p)
            (let ((pos (entity/pos p))
                  (x (car pos))
                  (y (cadr pos)))
              (paint-cell (floor x) (floor y) \"💧\")))))
      ;; draw floor
      (let loop ((x 0))
        (if (< x 64)
            (begin
              (paint-cell x 42 \"═\")
              (loop (+ x 1)))))))))

(bouncing-droplets)
```

[VISUAL: Droplets 💧 falling from the top, hitting a horizontal line of ═ glyphs at y=42, bouncing upward with diminishing height, eventually settling on the floor]

`world/floor!` creates an infinite horizontal collider. `entity/bounce!` sets restitution (0.6 = 60% velocity retained). Friction damps horizontal motion on contact. The droplets bounce, lose energy, and come to rest.

For particle-particle collision, you use `world/collisions` or `entity/collisions` to find overlapping pairs, then apply impulse or separation. That's an advanced topic (covered in Chapter 13 with scenes); for now, know that particles can detect and respond to each other.

---

## 7.8 The Finale: A Living Fountain of Light

Compose everything: emitter, lifetime, gravity, wind, trails, and collision. You will author a fountain that sprays luminous droplets upward, each leaving a fading trail, swaying in an oscillating breeze, and settling onto a floor with diminishing bounces.

```scheme
(define (living-fountain)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.12)
  (world/floor! 44)
  
  (define tick-count 0)
  
  (define (emit-fountain-particle!)
    (let* ((p (world/spawn 32 43))
           ;; radial spread
           (angle (+ (* -0.5 PI) (* PI (/ (modulo tick-count 11) 11.0))))
           (speed (+ 2.0 (* 0.8 (dsin (* tick-count 0.1)))))
           (vx (* speed (dcos angle)))
           (vy (* speed (dsin angle))))
      (entity/set-vel! p vx vy)
      (entity/set! p 'lifetime 80)
      (entity/set! p 'max-life 80)
      (entity/tag! p 'fountain)
      (entity/bounce! p 0.5)
      (entity/drag! p 0.97)))
  
  (define (spawn-trail! x y life-frac)
    (let ((t (world/spawn x y)))
      (entity/set-vel! t 0 0)
      (entity/pin! t)
      (entity/set! t 'lifetime (floor (* 8 life-frac)))  ; brighter = longer trail
      (entity/tag! t 'trail)))
  
  (big-bang
    (on-tick (lambda (w)
      (set! tick-count (+ tick-count 1))
      ;; emit every 2 ticks
      (if (= 0 (modulo tick-count 2))
          (emit-fountain-particle!))
      ;; apply oscillating horizontal wind
      (let ((wind (* 0.04 (dsin (* tick-count 0.08)))))
        (world/each (lambda (p)
          (if (entity/get p 'fountain)
              (entity/accel! p wind 0)))))
      ;; fountain particles spawn trails
      (world/each (lambda (p)
        (if (entity/get p 'fountain)
            (let ((pos (entity/pos p))
                  (life (entity/get p 'lifetime))
                  (max-life (entity/get p 'max-life)))
              (if (> life 0)
                  (spawn-trail! (car pos) (cadr pos) (/ life max-life)))))))
      (world/step)
      ;; age and despawn
      (world/each (lambda (p)
        (let ((life (entity/get p 'lifetime)))
          (if life
              (if (> life 0)
                  (entity/set! p 'lifetime (- life 1))
                  (entity/despawn! p))))))))
    (to-draw (lambda (w)
      ;; draw trails first (background layer)
      (world/each (lambda (p)
        (if (and (entity/alive? p) (entity/get p 'trail))
            (let ((pos (entity/pos p))
                  (x (car pos))
                  (y (cadr pos)))
              (paint-cell (floor x) (floor y) \"·\")))))
      ;; draw fountain particles (foreground)
      (world/each (lambda (p)
        (if (and (entity/alive? p) (entity/get p 'fountain))
            (let ((pos (entity/pos p))
                  (x (car pos))
                  (y (cadr pos))
                  (life (entity/get p 'lifetime))
                  (max-life (entity/get p 'max-life)))
              (let ((frac (/ life max-life)))
                (cond
                  ((> frac 0.5) (paint-cell (floor x) (floor y) \"✨\"))
                  (else (paint-cell (floor x) (floor y) \"·\"))))))))
      ;; draw floor
      (let loop ((x 0))
        (if (< x 64)
            (begin
              (paint-cell x 44 \"▬\")
              (loop (+ x 1)))))))))

(living-fountain)
```

This is a particle system. Hundreds of entities, each with position, velocity, lifetime, and tag. An emitter spawns them with variance. Forces (gravity, wind) apply each tick. Trails paint persistence. Collision gives physicality. Aging and despawn keep the population finite.

The system is *alive* — not because any one particle is complex, but because the aggregate behavior emerges from simple rules iterated over many.

## What You Built

You moved from **one body** (Chapter 5) to **many bodies**, each ephemeral, each rule-following, the whole a living texture.

You learned:
- **Lifetime and despawn**: particles age and die.
- **Emitters**: functions that spawn particles over time, creating steady-state populations.
- **Forces applied to many**: gravity, wind, drag acting on all tagged entities.
- **Heterogeneous parameters**: randomized velocity, lifetime, rendering based on age.
- **Trails**: spawning ghost particles to paint motion history.
- **Collision**: floors, bounce, friction — particles interacting with the world.

The techniques generalize: pollen, snow, rain, sparks, dust, smoke, projectiles, debris, confetti — any phenomenon made of many small, short-lived things.

In Chapter 8 you will give particles *bodies* — sprites with expression, the 16 blossoms, glyphs that carry meaning. A particle will no longer be just a dot; it will be a character in the scene.

1. **Lifetime and steady state**: If an emitter spawns one particle every 3 ticks, and each particle lives 60 ticks, roughly how many particles will be alive at steady state? Why?

2. **Fade by glyph**: Modify the `fading-sparks` example to use four brightness levels instead of three (e.g., `\"✨\"` → `\"*\"` → `\"·\"` → `\".\"`). What lifetime fraction thresholds will you use?

3. **Directional emission**: Change the `fountain` example to spray particles only *upward-left* (angle between 90° and 180°). What `dcos`/`dsin` angle range will you use?

4. **Wind with turbulence**: The `pollen-drift` example uses a smooth sine-wave wind. Add a second, faster oscillation to create turbulence (two sine waves of different frequencies summed). How does the visual drift change?

5. **Trail length by speed**: In the `sparkler-trails` example, all ghosts live 12 ticks. Make the ghost lifetime proportional to the parent particle's speed (use `entity/vel` to compute magnitude, map it to a lifetime between 5 and 20 ticks). Fast particles leave longer trails.

6. **Bouncing with spawn limit**: Modify `bouncing-droplets` to stop emitting new droplets after 50 have been spawned total (not 50 alive, but 50 cumulative). The existing particles continue to bounce and age, but no new ones appear. How will you track the count?

"# Chapter 8: Bodies

In the last chapter we filled our world with particles — ephemeral dots born from emitters, each with its own lifetime and purpose. They flocked and drifted, appeared and vanished, carrying the feeling of life in numbers. But particles are faceless. They have position and velocity, color and size, but no *expression*. They cannot look at you, bow in greeting, or shrug in confusion. They are motion without character.

This chapter changes that. We will give our moving things *bodies* — articulated forms with parts that can gesture, emote, and respond. The runtime ships with 16 hand-drawn sprites (the *blossoms*), each a multi-part character with limbs, faces, and landmarks you can address. A sprite is not just a static image. It is a *rig* — a skeleton of named parts that can sway, nod, breathe, and compose complex expressions from simple motion primitives.

We will learn:

- How to spawn a sprite with `entity/sprite!` and choose from the 16 built-in blossoms.
- How to address individual body parts with the `part/*` verb family.
- How to compose *expressions* — gestural programs that combine motion verbs (sway, bow, breathe) with timing and intent.
- How to layer expressions onto physics — a sprite that bounces *and* bows, that walks *and* nods.

By the chapter's end, you will author **a blossom that expresses** — a character that moves with feeling, layering physics, oscillation, and gesture into a single living form.

---

## The 16 Blossoms

The runtime includes 16 named sprites, each drawn in a consistent style: rounded, friendly, built from parts (head, torso, limbs). You choose a sprite by name when you call `entity/sprite!`:

```scheme
(define (make-blossom)
  (let ((e (world/spawn 8 6)))
    (entity/sprite! e 'blossom-default)
    e))

(big-bang
  (on-tick (lambda (w)
             (when (= (world/frame) 0)
               (make-blossom))
             (world/step)))
  (to-draw (lambda (w)
             (world/camera))))
```

<!-- BUILD: wire as runnable example ch08-ex01-default-blossom.scm -->

[VISUAL: A single sprite standing at (8, 6) — rounded head, simple torso, arms at rest. The default blossom pose, centered on a 16×12 grid.]

The sprite appears at the given grid position and stands still. It has no velocity, no forces acting on it — just presence. But unlike a painted dot, it has *structure*. The `'blossom-default` form includes a head, torso, two arms, two legs, each a named part we can address.

---

## Addressing Parts

Every sprite is a hierarchy of *parts*: `'head`, `'torso`, `'arm-left`, `'arm-right`, `'leg-left`, `'leg-right`. Some sprites have additional parts (`'ears`, `'tail`, `'wings`), but the core six are universal. You manipulate a part by combining a `part/*` verb with the entity and the part name:

```scheme
(define (make-waving-blossom)
  (let ((e (world/spawn 8 6)))
    (entity/sprite! e 'blossom-default)
    (part/wave e 'arm-right 1.2 0)
    e))

(big-bang
  (on-tick (lambda (w)
             (when (= (world/frame) 0)
               (make-waving-blossom))
             (world/step)))
  (to-draw (lambda (w)
             (world/camera))))
```

<!-- BUILD: wire as runnable example ch08-ex02-wave.scm -->

[VISUAL: The blossom with its right arm raised and waving side-to-side — amplitude 1.2, phase 0. The wave is smooth and continuous, driven by the internal oscillator.]

The `part/wave` verb takes four arguments:

1. **entity** — which sprite to affect.
2. **part** — which part to move (`'arm-right`, `'head`, etc.).
3. **amplitude** — how far the wave travels (in radians; 1.2 is a gentle arc).
4. **phase** — offset in the wave cycle (0 starts mid-swing).

The wave runs indefinitely, driven by the entity's internal animation clock. No explicit `world/step` call is needed to *continue* the wave — the clock advances each frame automatically. But you must call `world/step` in `on-tick` to advance the simulation.

---

## Composing Gestures

A single gesture is expressive, but characters rarely move one part in isolation. A greeting combines a wave with a bow; surprise pairs raised arms with a head tilt. The `part/*` verbs *compose* — you can apply multiple motions to different parts of the same entity, and they will layer:

```scheme
(define (make-greeting-blossom)
  (let ((e (world/spawn 8 6)))
    (entity/sprite! e 'blossom-default)
    (part/wave e 'arm-right 1.0 0)
    (part/bow e 'torso 0.3 0.5)
    e))

(big-bang
  (on-tick (lambda (w)
             (when (= (world/frame) 0)
               (make-greeting-blossom))
             (world/step)))
  (to-draw (lambda (w)
             (world/camera))))
```

<!-- BUILD: wire as runnable example ch08-ex03-greeting.scm -->

[VISUAL: The blossom waving with its right arm while the torso bows forward — two independent motions layered into a single gesture. The wave is side-to-side; the bow is a gentle forward lean with period offset by phase 0.5.]

The `part/bow` verb tilts the torso forward and back, period-synced to the world clock. Amplitude 0.3 is a shallow bow; phase 0.5 starts the bow at the opposite point in the cycle from the wave. The two motions run in parallel, each on its own part, composing into a unified *greeting*.

---

## Breathing and Idleness

Living things breathe. Even at rest, a character should pulse gently — chest rising and falling, head bobbing slightly — to signal presence. The `part/breathe` verb adds a slow, low-amplitude oscillation to a part:

```scheme
(define (make-idle-blossom)
  (let ((e (world/spawn 8 6)))
    (entity/sprite! e 'blossom-friend)
    (part/breathe e 'torso 0.15 0)
    (part/sway e 'head 0.08 0.3)
    e))

(big-bang
  (on-tick (lambda (w)
             (when (= (world/frame) 0)
               (make-idle-blossom))
             (world/step)))
  (to-draw (lambda (w)
             (world/camera))))
```

<!-- BUILD: wire as runnable example ch08-ex04-idle.scm -->

[VISUAL: A `'blossom-friend` sprite standing still, torso gently expanding/contracting (breathing), head swaying side-to-side in a slow, lazy arc. Calm, restful, *present*.]

Breathing is slow (long period), so amplitude 0.15 feels subtle. The head sway (amplitude 0.08, phase offset) adds a second axis of gentle motion. Together, they create an *idle loop* — the kind of animation you see in a game when the player hasn't pressed a button in a while. The character isn't frozen; it's *waiting*.

---

## The 16 Sprite Names

The runtime includes these named sprites (all available via `entity/sprite!`):

- `'blossom-default` — neutral, round, friendly.
- `'blossom-friend` — softer features, wide eyes.
- `'blossom-brave` — squarer torso, determined expression.
- `'blossom-shy` — smaller head, folded arms in rest pose.
- `'blossom-wise` — taller, narrower, slightly older proportions.
- `'blossom-swift` — leaner limbs, athletic build.
- `'blossom-gentle` — rounder, lower center of gravity.
- `'blossom-bold` — wider stance, larger hands.
- `'blossom-curious` — larger head, expressive eyes.
- `'blossom-playful` — asymmetric rest pose, one arm raised.
- `'blossom-calm` — closed eyes in rest, serene.
- `'blossom-fierce` — sharper angles, narrowed eyes.
- `'blossom-dreamer` — head tilted up, gazing at the sky.
- `'blossom-guardian` — broad shoulders, protective stance.
- `'blossom-wanderer` — backpack, walking-stick in hand.
- `'blossom-scholar` — holding a book, glasses.

Each has the core six parts; some add accessories (`'backpack`, `'book`, `'staff`). Choose the sprite that fits the *character* you want to express.

---

## Layering Physics and Gesture

Sprites are entities, so everything you learned in chapters 4–7 applies: position, velocity, forces, emitters. You can spawn a sprite, apply gravity, and watch it fall — while it gestures:

```scheme
(define (make-falling-greeter)
  (let ((e (world/spawn 8 2)))
    (entity/sprite! e 'blossom-default)
    (entity/set-vel! e 0 0)
    (entity/gravity-scale! e 1.0)
    (entity/bounce! e 0.6)
    (part/wave e 'arm-right 1.0 0)
    (part/breathe e 'torso 0.15 0)
    (world/floor! 10)
    e))

(big-bang
  (on-tick (lambda (w)
             (when (= (world/frame) 0)
               (make-falling-greeter))
             (world/step)))
  (to-draw (lambda (w)
             (world/camera))))
```

[VISUAL: The blossom falls from (8, 2), waving its arm the whole way down. It hits the floor at y=10, bounces (0.6 restitution), settles, and continues waving and breathing in place. Physics and gesture in one.]

The sprite is a physics body (gravity, bounce) *and* an animated character (wave, breathe). The two layers are independent but simultaneous. The gesture does not \"pause\" during the fall or bounce — it runs on the animation clock, while the physics runs on the simulation clock. They compose.

---

## Expressions: Named Gesture Recipes

An *expression* is a named combination of part motions that conveys a specific emotion or intent. You define an expression as a procedure that applies multiple `part/*` calls to an entity:

```scheme
(define (express-joy! e)
  (part/wave e 'arm-left 1.2 0)
  (part/wave e 'arm-right 1.2 0.5)
  (part/breathe e 'torso 0.25 0)
  (part/nod e 'head 0.4 0.2))

(define (make-joyful-blossom)
  (let ((e (world/spawn 8 6)))
    (entity/sprite! e 'blossom-playful)
    (express-joy! e)
    e))

(big-bang
  (on-tick (lambda (w)
             (when (= (world/frame) 0)
               (make-joyful-blossom))
             (world/step)))
  (to-draw (lambda (w)
             (world/camera))))
```

<!-- BUILD: wire as runnable example ch08-ex06-expression-joy.scm -->

[VISUAL: A `'blossom-playful` sprite with both arms waving (opposite phase), torso breathing with slightly higher amplitude, head nodding — a full-body expression of *joy*.]

The `express-joy!` procedure is a *recipe*. It takes an entity and applies four gestures in a coordinated pattern. You can define a library of expressions — `express-surprise!`, `express-confusion!`, `express-greeting!` — and apply them as needed. Expressions are *composable programs*, not canned animations.

---

## Switching Expressions Over Time

A character's mood changes. You can switch expressions by calling a new recipe, which overwrites the previous part motions:

```scheme
(define (express-joy! e)
  (part/wave e 'arm-left 1.2 0)
  (part/wave e 'arm-right 1.2 0.5)
  (part/breathe e 'torso 0.25 0)
  (part/nod e 'head 0.4 0.2))

(define (express-confusion! e)
  (part/shrug e 'arm-left 0.6 0)
  (part/shrug e 'arm-right 0.6 0)
  (part/tilt e 'head 0.5 0)
  (part/breathe e 'torso 0.15 0))

(define (make-changing-blossom)
  (let ((e (world/spawn 8 6)))
    (entity/sprite! e 'blossom-curious)
    (express-joy! e)
    e))

(big-bang
  (on-tick (lambda (w)
             (when (= (world/frame) 0)
               (make-changing-blossom))
             (let ((e (world/find 'kind 'entity)))
               (when (and e (= (world/frame) 120))
                 (express-confusion! e)))
             (world/step)))
  (to-draw (lambda (w)
             (world/camera))))
```

<!-- BUILD: wire as runnable example ch08-ex07-expression-switch.scm -->

[VISUAL: The sprite starts joyful (arms waving, head nodding). At frame 120 (2 seconds at 60fps), the expression switches to confusion (arms shrugging, head tilted, gentler breathing). The transition is immediate — the new gestures replace the old.]

At frame 120, we find the entity and apply the new expression. The `part/*` verbs overwrite the previous motion on each part, so the sprite's gesture changes instantly. If you want a smoother transition, you could ramp amplitude or phase over several frames — but the verb layer itself is immediate.

---

## The Full Part Verb Vocabulary

Here are the `part/*` verbs available for sprite animation:

| Verb | Parts | Meaning |
|------|-------|---------|
| `part/sway` | any | Gentle side-to-side oscillation (idle, wind). |
| `part/bow` | torso, head | Forward/back tilt (greeting, respect). |
| `part/breathe` | torso | Slow expansion/contraction (life, rest). |
| `part/lean` | torso | Sustained tilt to one side (curiosity, off-balance). |
| `part/nod` | head | Up/down tilt (agreement, rhythm). |
| `part/wave` | arm-left, arm-right | Side-to-side arc (greeting, beckoning). |
| `part/tilt` | head | Side-to-side tilt (confusion, listening). |
| `part/turn` | head, torso | Rotation around vertical axis (looking around). |
| `part/twist` | torso | Rotation of torso relative to hips (windup, throwing). |
| `part/raise` | arm-*, leg-* | Lift part upward (reaching, stepping). |
| `part/lower` | arm-*, leg-* | Drop part downward (resting, landing). |
| `part/reach` | arm-* | Extend arm toward a target point. |
| `part/grasp` | arm-* | Close hand (holding, gripping). |
| `part/point` | arm-* | Extend arm and finger toward a direction. |
| `part/look-toward` | head | Turn head to face a given position. |
| `part/shake` | head, arm-* | Rapid side-to-side (refusal, emphasis). |
| `part/shrug` | arm-left, arm-right | Raise shoulders (uncertainty, \"I don't know\"). |
| `part/step` | leg-* | Lift and place leg (walking, climbing). |
| `part/expression` | (all) | Apply a named full-body expression preset. |

Each verb takes `(entity part amplitude phase)` or `(entity part target)` depending on whether it's oscillatory or positional. Consult `§19.6` (entity reference) and `§8` (sprite reference) for exact signatures.

---

## Looking Toward a Target

The `part/look-toward` verb turns the head to face a point, useful for gaze tracking or responding to touch:

```scheme
(define (make-gazing-blossom)
  (let ((e (world/spawn 8 6)))
    (entity/sprite! e 'blossom-wise)
    (part/breathe e 'torso 0.15 0)
    e))

(big-bang
  (on-tick (lambda (w)
             (when (= (world/frame) 0)
               (make-gazing-blossom))
             (let ((e (world/find 'kind 'entity)))
               (when e
                 (let ((target-x (+ 8 (* 3 (dsin (* 0.02 (world/frame))))))
                       (target-y 6))
                   (part/look-toward e 'head target-x target-y))))
             (world/step)))
  (to-draw (lambda (w)
             (world/camera))))
```

<!-- BUILD: wire as runnable example ch08-ex08-look-toward.scm -->

[VISUAL: The sprite's head slowly pans left and right, tracking an invisible point that oscillates side-to-side (±3 cells from center). The torso breathes; the head smoothly follows the target.]

The target position `(target-x, target-y)` moves sinusoidally. Each frame, `part/look-toward` recalculates the head rotation to face that point. The result is a *tracking gaze* — the character appears to watch something move across the scene.

*Note:* In a live app, you could replace the sinusoidal target with `input/buttons` touch coordinates to make the sprite's gaze follow the player's finger. That requires the live input seam (*[needs: live-app input]*), so we use a scripted target here.

---

## Multiple Sprites, Each with Character

You are not limited to one sprite. Spawn several, give each a different blossom and expression, and let them interact:

```scheme
(define (express-joy! e)
  (part/wave e 'arm-left 1.2 0)
  (part/wave e 'arm-right 1.2 0.5)
  (part/nod e 'head 0.4 0.2))

(define (express-calm! e)
  (part/breathe e 'torso 0.12 0)
  (part/sway e 'head 0.06 0.5))

(define (make-pair)
  (let ((e1 (world/spawn 5 6))
        (e2 (world/spawn 11 6)))
    (entity/sprite! e1 'blossom-playful)
    (entity/sprite! e2 'blossom-calm)
    (express-joy! e1)
    (express-calm! e2)
    (list e1 e2)))

(big-bang
  (on-tick (lambda (w)
             (when (= (world/frame) 0)
               (make-pair))
             (world/step)))
  (to-draw (lambda (w)
             (world/camera))))
```

<!-- BUILD: wire as runnable example ch08-ex09-pair.scm -->

[VISUAL: Two sprites side-by-side. Left: `'blossom-playful`, arms waving, head nodding — energetic, joyful. Right: `'blossom-calm`, gently breathing and swaying — serene, restful. Two characters, two moods, one scene.]

Each entity is independent. One could be falling while the other stands; one could be joyful while the other is confused. Sprites are first-class entities — everything from chapters 4–7 (forces, particles, emitters) applies to them.

---

## Finale: A Blossom That Expresses

We will compose everything: physics, oscillation, particles, and gesture. The sprite will fall, bounce, emit particles on impact, and express joy when it settles:

```scheme
(define (express-joy! e)
  (part/wave e 'arm-left 1.2 0)
  (part/wave e 'arm-right 1.2 0.5)
  (part/breathe e 'torso 0.25 0)
  (part/nod e 'head 0.4 0.2))

(define (express-landing! e)
  (part/bow e 'torso 0.4 0)
  (part/breathe e 'torso 0.15 0))

(define (emit-impact-particles! x y)
  (let loop ((i 0))
    (when (< i 8)
      (let ((p (world/spawn x y))
            (angle (* i (/ TAU 8)))
            (speed 2))
        (entity/set-vel! p (* speed (dcos angle)) (* speed (dsin angle)))
        (entity/gravity-scale! p 0.5)
        (entity/drag! p 0.95)
        (entity/set! p 'lifetime 30)
        (entity/set! p 'color '(1.0 0.8 0.3)))
      (loop (+ i 1)))))

(define (make-expressive-blossom)
  (let ((e (world/spawn 8 2)))
    (entity/sprite! e 'blossom-brave)
    (entity/set-vel! e 0 0)
    (entity/gravity-scale! e 1.0)
    (entity/bounce! e 0.4)
    (entity/set! e 'has-landed #f)
    (express-landing! e)
    (world/floor! 10)
    e))

(big-bang
  (on-tick (lambda (w)
             (when (= (world/frame) 0)
               (make-expressive-blossom))
             (let ((e (world/find 'kind 'entity)))
               (when e
                 (let ((vy (cadr (entity/vel e)))
                       (y (entity/y e))
                       (landed? (entity/get e 'has-landed)))
                   (when (and (not landed?) (>= y 9.8) (< (abs vy) 0.5))
                     (emit-impact-particles! (entity/x e) y)
                     (entity/set! e 'has-landed #t)
                     (express-joy! e)))))
             (world/each (lambda (p)
                           (when (entity/get p 'lifetime)
                             (let ((life (entity/get p 'lifetime)))
                               (if (<= life 1)
                                   (entity/despawn! p)
                                   (entity/set! p 'lifetime (- life 1)))))))
             (world/step)))
  (to-draw (lambda (w)
             (world/camera))))
```

"# Chapter 9: Locomotion

In the last chapter you learned to give sprites bodies — to dress a point mass in glyph and expression, to make a position feel like a *creature*. But the creatures stood still, or drifted on simple velocity. A real body doesn't just *move*; it *locomotes*. It carries weight. It takes steps. It has cadence and intent, a gait that tells you what it is and how it feels about where it's going.

This chapter teaches **locomotion**: the art of making motion *feel* like walking, running, hopping, prowling. You'll learn the **5-tuple motion vector** — position, velocity, acceleration, *cadence*, and *feel* — and how those last two invisible coordinates turn physics into performance. You'll compose gaits from timing patterns, learn to telegraph intent with anticipation and follow-through, and build a sprite that doesn't just *go somewhere* but *goes there like itself*.

The concepts layer cleanly: vectors (Ch4) give you position and velocity, forces (Ch5) give you acceleration and integration, oscillation (Ch6) gives you rhythmic phase, and bodies (Ch8) give you something visible to carry the weight. Now we add the *when* and the *how* — the beat on which a foot falls, the pocket that makes a stride feel lazy or urgent.

---

## 9.1 The Missing Coordinates

You've been animating with three dimensions: `x`, `y`, and `t` (time, measured in frames). A moving sprite has position and velocity; forces change velocity; `world/step` integrates it all forward.

But watch a real animal walk. There are two invisible axes:

1. **Cadence** — the *rhythm* of the motion. Steps happen on a beat, not continuously. A walk is 2-beat, a trot 4-beat, a gallop 3-beat with suspension.
2. **Feel** — the *shape* of the motion within the beat. A confident stride has snap and overshoot; a weary shuffle has drag and sag.

These are the **fourth and fifth coordinates** of motion. The engine calls them `cadence` and `feel`, and together with `pos`, `vel`, and `accel` they form the **5-tuple motion vector**. You won't set them directly on an entity the way you set position; instead, you'll compose them into *motion verbs* — high-level commands like \"walk to X with a prowling gait\" that bake timing and expression into the path.

We'll start simple: a sprite that takes discrete steps, one per beat. Then we'll add weight, anticipation, and character.

---

## 9.2 A Single Step

The simplest locomotion is a **step** — a single discrete motion event with a clear start, middle, and end.

Let's make a sprite hop once, in place, with a parabolic arc:

```scheme
(define (step-hop)
  (let* ((w (world/spawn))
         (s (world/spawn w 
              (entity/pos 8 12)
              (entity/sprite! 'blossom-plum))))
    
    ;; Hop: apply an upward impulse, let gravity bring it back down
    (world/gravity! w 0.5)
    (entity/bounce! s 0.6)
    (entity/friction! s 0.9)
    (world/floor! w 12)
    
    ;; Single impulse at frame 0
    (entity/accel! s 0 -8)
    
    ;; Step 60 frames and return the world
    (let loop ((i 0))
      (when (< i 60)
        (world/step w)
        (loop (+ i 1))))
    
    w))

(step-hop)
```

[VISUAL: 8-frame animation strip showing a plum blossom sprite at y=12, arcing up to ~y=6 and falling back to y=12, settling with a small bounce.]

The sprite rises under the impulse, falls under gravity, and settles. That's a hop. But it doesn't *feel* like a hop yet — there's no windup, no landing anticipation, no timing control. It just obeys physics.

To make it feel like locomotion, we need to control *when* things happen, not just *what* happens.

---

## 9.3 Cadence: Motion on the Beat

A step doesn't happen continuously — it happens *on a beat*. The foot lifts, the body shifts, the foot lands, all at discrete moments. Between those moments, the motion interpolates smoothly (or not — that's *feel*).

Let's make a sprite take a step *every 24 frames* (a \"step beat\"), alternating left and right:

```scheme
(define (march-in-place)
  (let* ((w (world/spawn))
         (s (world/spawn w 
              (entity/pos 8 12)
              (entity/sprite! 'blossom-plum))))
    
    (world/gravity! w 0.5)
    (world/floor! w 12)
    (entity/bounce! s 0.3)
    (entity/friction! s 0.85)
    
    ;; Every 24 frames, apply a small hop impulse
    (let loop ((frame 0))
      (when (< frame 120)
        (when (= (modulo frame 24) 0)
          (entity/accel! s 0 -6))
        (world/step w)
        (loop (+ frame 1))))
    
    w))

(march-in-place)
```

[VISUAL: Plum sprite hopping 5 times at regular intervals, landing back at y=12 each time, like marching in place.]

Now the hops have *cadence* — they happen on the 1 of every measure (if we treat 24 frames as one beat). But the sprite still doesn't go anywhere. Let's add horizontal motion, triggered on the same beat.

---

## 9.4 Walking: Horizontal Cadence

A walk is \"hop + drift\". On each beat, we apply a small upward impulse (to lift the foot) and a horizontal impulse (to shift weight forward).

```scheme
(define (walk-forward)
  (let* ((w (world/spawn))
         (s (world/spawn w 
              (entity/pos 2 12)
              (entity/sprite! 'blossom-plum))))
    
    (world/gravity! w 0.5)
    (world/floor! w 12)
    (entity/bounce! s 0.2)
    (entity/friction! s 0.7)
    
    ;; Every 20 frames: hop up and drift right
    (let loop ((frame 0))
      (when (< frame 100)
        (when (= (modulo frame 20) 0)
          (entity/accel! s 0 -5)    ;; lift
          (entity/accel! s 1.2 0))  ;; drift right
        (world/step w)
        (loop (+ frame 1))))
    
    w))

(walk-forward)
```

[VISUAL: Plum sprite stepping rightward across the canvas in 5 hops, each hop a small arc, ending at ~x=10.]

That's recognizable as a walk — discrete steps, regular timing, horizontal progress. But it still feels mechanical. The sprite doesn't *anticipate* the step or *recover* from the landing. It just pops up and drifts.

To add that, we need **feel** — the shape of motion *within* the beat.

---

## 9.5 Feel: The Shape of a Step

\"Feel\" is the easing curve applied to motion between keyframes. A step with *snap* has fast takeoff and slow landing (ease-out). A step with *drag* has slow takeoff and fast landing (ease-in). A step with *bounce* has overshoot and settle.

The engine provides `motion/with-feel`, which wraps a motion verb (like `entity/goto!`) and applies an easing curve over a duration. But that verb may not yet be wired in the headless harness — it's part of the motion-timing layer (`motionTimingVerbs.js`) that bridges frame-by-frame and high-level intent.

*[needs: motion-timing headless wiring (motionTimingVerbs.js → harness seam)]*

Here's what the code *will* look like once wired:

```scheme
    ;; This verb is not yet callable in headless; it will be.
    ;; (motion/with-feel 'snap
    ;;   (entity/goto! s 14 12 80))  ;; 80 frames to x=14, with ease-out
    
    ;; Fallback: manual stepped motion for now

    (world/floor! w 12)
    (entity/bounce! s 0.2)
    (entity/friction! s 0.7)
    
    (let loop ((frame 0))
      (when (< frame 100)
        (when (= (modulo frame 20) 0)
          (entity/accel! s 0 -5)
```

When `motion/with-feel` is wired, you'll be able to say:

```scheme

```

…and the sprite will move to `(target-x, target-y)` over `duration` frames with an ease-out curve — fast at first, slowing into arrival. The `'snap` symbol names the curve; others include `'drag`, `'bounce`, `'elastic`, `'linear`.

Until then, you compose feel manually by modulating impulse magnitude on each beat, which we'll show next.

---

## 9.6 Manual Feel: Varying Impulse by Phase

Even without the motion-timing verbs, you can fake feel by *varying the strength of each impulse* based on where you are in the gait cycle.

A confident stride front-loads the impulse (big push at the start, coast to the end). A weary shuffle back-loads it (slow start, push at the end to catch up).

```scheme
(define (walk-with-weight)
  (let* ((w (world/spawn))
         (s (world/spawn w 
              (entity/pos 2 12)
              (entity/sprite! 'blossom-plum))))
    
    (world/gravity! w 0.5)
    (world/floor! w 12)
    (entity/bounce! s 0.2)
    (entity/friction! s 0.75)
    
    ;; 5 steps, each 20 frames
    ;; Vary impulse: strong at start, weaker toward end (tired gait)
    (let loop ((step 0) (frame 0))
      (when (< step 5)
        (let ((strength (- 1.5 (* step 0.2))))  ;; 1.5, 1.3, 1.1, 0.9, 0.7
          (entity/accel! s 0 -5)
          (entity/accel! s strength 0)
          
          ;; Step forward 20 frames
          (let inner ((f 0))
            (when (< f 20)
              (world/step w)
              (inner (+ f 1))))
          
          (loop (+ step 1) (+ frame 20)))))
    
    w))

(walk-with-weight)
```

## 9.7 Gaits: Named Motion Patterns

A **gait** is a named composition of cadence + feel + rhythm. Humans recognize gaits instantly: walk vs. run vs. sneak vs. limp. Each has a signature timing.

Let's define three gaits as procedures:

```scheme
(define (gait-walk sprite frames-per-step step-count)
  ;; Walk: 2-beat, moderate impulse, slight hop
  (let loop ((step 0) (frame 0))
    (when (< step step-count)
      (entity/accel! sprite 0 -4)
      (entity/accel! sprite 1.0 0)
      (let inner ((f 0))
        (when (< f frames-per-step)
          (world/step (entity/parent sprite))
          (inner (+ f 1))))
      (loop (+ step 1) (+ frame frames-per-step)))))

(define (gait-run sprite frames-per-step step-count)
  ;; Run: faster cadence, bigger horizontal impulse, more lift
  (let loop ((step 0) (frame 0))
    (when (< step step-count)
      (entity/accel! sprite 0 -6)
      (entity/accel! sprite 2.0 0)
      (let inner ((f 0))
        (when (< f frames-per-step)
          (world/step (entity/parent sprite))
          (inner (+ f 1))))
      (loop (+ step 1) (+ frame frames-per-step)))))

(define (gait-sneak sprite frames-per-step step-count)
  ;; Sneak: slow cadence, tiny impulse, low to ground
  (let loop ((step 0) (frame 0))
    (when (< step step-count)
      (entity/accel! sprite 0 -2)
      (entity/accel! sprite 0.5 0)
      (let inner ((f 0))
        (when (< f frames-per-step)
          (world/step (entity/parent sprite))
          (inner (+ f 1))))
      (loop (+ step 1) (+ frame frames-per-step)))))

(define (demo-gaits)
  (let* ((w (world/spawn))
         (walker (world/spawn w (entity/pos 2 12) (entity/sprite! 'blossom-plum)))
         (runner (world/spawn w (entity/pos 2 8) (entity/sprite! 'blossom-cherry)))
         (sneaker (world/spawn w (entity/pos 2 4) (entity/sprite! 'blossom-pine))))
    
    (world/gravity! w 0.5)
    (world/floor! w 12)
    (entity/bounce! walker 0.2)
    (entity/bounce! runner 0.3)
    (entity/bounce! sneaker 0.1)
    (entity/friction! walker 0.7)
    (entity/friction! runner 0.6)
    (entity/friction! sneaker 0.8)
    
    (gait-walk walker 20 6)
    (gait-run runner 12 10)
    (gait-sneak sneaker 30 4)
    
    w))

(demo-gaits)
```

[VISUAL: Three sprites in horizontal lanes. Top (plum): steady walk, 6 steps. Middle (cherry): fast run, 10 quick steps. Bottom (pine): slow sneak, 4 tiny shuffles. All rightward, ending at different x positions.]

Three bodies, three rhythms, three *intentions*. The code is almost identical — only the impulse magnitudes and `frames-per-step` differ. That's the power of gaits: a small timing change reads as a large personality change.

---

## 9.8 Anticipation and Follow-Through

Real locomotion has **anticipation** (a windup before the action) and **follow-through** (a settle after). A jump doesn't start at full speed — the body crouches first. A landing doesn't stop instantly — the legs compress, then spring back.

Let's add a crouch before each hop:

```scheme
(define (walk-with-anticipation)
  (let* ((w (world/spawn))
         (s (world/spawn w 
              (entity/pos 2 12)
              (entity/sprite! 'blossom-plum))))
    
    (world/gravity! w 0.5)
    (world/floor! w 12)
    (entity/bounce! s 0.3)
    (entity/friction! s 0.7)
    
    ;; 4 steps, each with 6-frame anticipation + 14-frame motion
    (let loop ((step 0))
      (when (< step 4)
        ;; Anticipation: small downward accel (crouch)
        (entity/accel! s 0 1.5)
        (let crouch ((f 0))
          (when (< f 6)
            (world/step w)
            (crouch (+ f 1))))
        
        ;; Action: strong upward + forward impulse
        (entity/accel! s 0 -7)
        (entity/accel! s 1.2 0)
        (let action ((f 0))
          (when (< f 14)
            (world/step w)
            (action (+ f 1))))
        
        (loop (+ step 1))))
    
    w))

(walk-with-anticipation)
```

[VISUAL: Plum sprite taking 4 steps, each step showing a visible *squash* downward before the upward hop — clear anticipation + release.]

The sprite now *telegraphs* the step. You see it coming. That makes the motion readable — essential for game feel and character animation.

## 9.9 Weight: Integrating with Mass

In Chapter 5 you learned that `entity/mass!` affects how forces accumulate. A heavy sprite resists acceleration; a light sprite darts.

Let's make two sprites walk with the same gait code, but different masses:

## 9.10 Turning: Changing Direction Mid-Gait

A sprite that can only walk in one direction isn't very alive. Let's make one that walks forward, then turns around and walks back:

```scheme
(define (walk-and-turn)
  (let* ((w (world/spawn))
         (s (world/spawn w 
              (entity/pos 2 12)
              (entity/sprite! 'blossom-plum))))
    
    (world/gravity! w 0.5)
    (world/floor! w 12)
    (entity/bounce! s 0.2)
    (entity/friction! s 0.7)

    (let loop-right ((step 0))
      (when (< step 4)
        (entity/accel! s 0 -5)
        (entity/accel! s 1.0 0)
        (let inner ((f 0))
          (when (< f 20)
            (world/step w)
            (inner (+ f 1))))
        (loop-right (+ step 1))))
    
    ;; Pause 20 frames (turn moment)
    (let pause ((f 0))
      (when (< f 20)
        (world/step w)
        (pause (+ f 1))))
    
    ;; Walk left 4 steps
    (let loop-left ((step 0))
      (when (< step 4)
        (entity/accel! s 0 -5)
        (entity/accel! s -1.0 0)  ;; impulse left
        (let inner ((f 0))
          (when (< f 20)
            (world/step w)
            (inner (+ f 1))))
        (loop-left (+ step 1))))
    
    w))

(walk-and-turn)
```

## 9.12 The 5-Tuple in Full

Let's summarize the **5-tuple motion vector** you've been building:

| Coordinate | What it is | Set by | Integrated by | Feel layer |
|------------|------------|--------|---------------|------------|
| **pos** (x, y) | Position in space | `entity/set-pos!`, `entity/move!` | `world/step` (vel → pos) | — |
| **vel** (vx, vy) | Velocity (rate of position change) | `entity/set-vel!`, forces | `world/step` (accel → vel) | — |
| **accel** (ax, ay) | Acceleration (rate of velocity change) | `entity/accel!`, `world/gravity!`, etc. | `world/step` (impulse accumulation) | — |
| **cadence** | Rhythm / beat of action | `(modulo frame beat-length)`, gait proc | You (explicitly) | `motion/cadence`, `beat/on` |
| **feel** | Shape of interpolation (ease curve) | `motion/with-feel`, manual impulse scaling | `motion/*` verbs | `motion/with-feel`, `motion/arc`, etc. |

The first three (`pos`, `vel`, `accel`) are the physics layer — they exist per-entity, updated every frame by the engine.

The last two (`cadence`, `feel`) are the **performance layer** — they exist in *your code*, as timing logic and named curves. You don't set them on an entity; you *compose them into motion commands*.

When the motion-timing verbs are wired, you'll write:

```scheme
(motion/with-feel 'bounce
  (motion/cadence 24
    (entity/goto! sprite target-x target-y)))
```

…and the sprite will move to the target *on a 24-frame beat*, *with a bounce ease curve*. Until then, you hand-code the beat loop and vary impulse magnitude to fake the curve.

## 9.13 Chapter Finale: A Sprite That Walks with Weight

We'll make a heavy sprite (plum blossom) walk slowly with a tired gait, and a light sprite (cherry blossom) skip quickly with a bouncy gait, both crossing the same distance.

```scheme
         (cherry (world/spawn w 
                   (entity/pos 1 6)
                   (entity/sprite! 'blossom-cherry))))
    
    (world/gravity! w 0.5)
    (world/floor! w 12)
    
    ;; Plum: heavy, slow, low bounce
    (entity/mass! plum 3.0)
    (entity/bounce! plum 0.15)
    (entity/friction! plum 0.8)
    
    ;; Cherry: light, fast, high bounce
    (entity/mass! cherry 0.6)
    (entity/bounce! cherry 0.5)
    (entity/friction! cherry 0.6)
    
    ;; Plum gait: 8 steps, 24 frames each, with anticipation

        (entity/accel! plum 0 1.0)
        (let crouch ((f 0))
          (when (< f 6)
            (world/step w)
            (crouch (+ f 1))))
        
        ;; Step (action) — weakening over time (fatigue)
        (let ((strength (- 1.2 (* step 0.1))))
          (entity/accel! plum 0 -4)
          (entity/accel! plum strength 0)
          (let action ((f 0))
            (when (< f 18)
              (world/step w)
              (action (+ f 1)))))
        
        (loop-plum (+ step 1))))
    
    ;; Cherry gait: 12 steps, 16 frames each, no anticipation (instant spring)
    ;; Run this concurrently by resetting frame counter
    ;; (In real code you'd run both in parallel; here we sequence for simplicity)
    ;; Reset world to start of plum's journey and run cherry separately
    ;; OR: accept that they won't animate simultaneously in this sequential harness
    ;; We'll interleave: plum step, cherry step, etc. — requires re-structure.
    
    ;; Simplified: just run cherry's gait after plum finishes
    ;; (In a real game loop both would run each frame in parallel)
    (let loop-cherry ((step 0))
      (when (< step 12)
        (entity/accel! cherry 0 -6)
        (entity/accel! cherry 1.5 0)
        (let action ((f 0))
          (when (< f 16)
            (world/step w)
            (action (+ f 1))))
        (loop-cherry (+ step 1))))
    
    w))

(finale-walk-with-weight)
```

[VISUAL: Two sprites (plum and cherry) walking rightward across canvas. Plum: 8 slow, low, weary steps with visible crouch before each, ending at ~x=9. Cherry: 12 quick, bouncy skips with high arcs, ending past x=15. Both feel *embodied* — you can read personality in the timing.]

This is locomotion. Not just motion, not just physics — *performance*. The plum sprite trudges like it's carrying the weight of the world. The cherry sprite skips like it's late for a festival. Same engine, same verbs, different *timing* and *magnitude*.

When `motion/with-feel` and `motion/cadence` are wired, you'll be able to collapse the gait loops into single declarative commands. But even hand-coded, the principle is clear: **cadence + feel = character**.

---

## End-of-Chapter Questions

1. **What are the two \"invisible coordinates\" of the 5-tuple motion vector, and what do they control?**

2. **How does `entity/mass!` affect a sprite's response to the same impulse?** Show with a short example (pseudocode OK) of two sprites receiving identical `entity/accel!` calls but moving differently.

3. **What is \"anticipation\" in animation, and why does it make motion more readable?** Describe in one sentence, then sketch (in words or Scheme) how you'd add anticipation to a jump.

4. **Implement a `gait-limp` procedure** that makes a sprite favor one side — e.g., every other step has half the horizontal impulse. Signature: `(gait-limp sprite frames-per-step step-count)`.

5. **Why doesn't the engine store `cadence` and `feel` as entity properties the way it stores `pos` and `vel`?** (Hint: think about *when* they matter vs. *every frame*.)

6. **Compose a two-part motion**: a sprite walks forward 3 steps with a bouncy gait, pauses, then *runs* backward 5 steps with a faster cadence. Use the gait procedures from §9.7 as a starting point, or write your own beat loops.

---

*Next chapter: **Steering** — making a sprite *decide where to go* with seek, flee, arrive, and wander, so locomotion becomes autonomous.*
