**What happened:**
- We spawned the hero at `(400, 300)` — far outside the default `(0, 0)`-centered viewport.
- `world/camera-snap!` instantly moved the camera's center to `(400, 300)`.
- The viewport (160×144) now shows world-space `[320..480, 228..372]` (camera center ± half-viewport).
- The hero starts centered, drifts right, exits. The camera **doesn't follow** — it's pinned.

This is a **static camera**. Useful for a fixed-screen platformer level, but not a journey.

---

## 14.2 Following One Entity

To make the camera **track** a sprite, use `world/camera-follow!`:

```scheme
(world/camera-follow! entity-id damping)
;; damping ∈ [0..1]: 0 = instant snap, 1 = no movement, 0.1 = smooth lag
```

The camera will **accelerate toward the entity's position** every frame, with exponential smoothing. Think of it as the camera attached to the sprite by a spring.

```scheme
;; Example 14.2: Camera Follow — smooth tracking
(define (example-14-2)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((hero (world/spawn 400 300)))
    (entity/sprite! hero 'blossom-plum)
    (entity/set-vel! hero 2 0) ;; drift right
    (world/camera-snap! 400 300) ;; start centered on hero
    (world/camera-follow! hero 0.1) ;; track with lag
    (big-bang
      (on-tick (lambda (s)
                 (world/step)
                 s))
      (to-draw (lambda (s)
                 (world/frame))))))

;; (example-14-2)
```

<!-- BUILD: wire example-14-2 as runnable cart \"Camera Follow\" -->

[VISUAL: The plum blossom drifts right, and the camera follows smoothly, keeping it near-center. The sprite never exits the frame — the camera moves with it, showing new world-space to the right as the sprite advances.]

**What happened:**
- `world/camera-follow! hero 0.1` told the camera to track `hero` with 10% damping.
- Every `world/step`, the camera accelerates toward the hero's current position.
- The hero drifts at constant velocity; the camera **lags slightly** (the spring effect), then catches up.
- The viewport slides smoothly — the background (if any) would parallax.

**Try different damping:**
- `0.0` → instant snap, no lag (same as `camera-snap!` every frame).
- `0.05` → tight follow, minimal lag.
- `0.2` → loose follow, the hero can drift toward the edge before the camera catches up.
- `0.5` → very loose, the camera barely moves.

Damping is **feel**. A tight camera (0.05) feels responsive, locked. A loose camera (0.2) feels floaty, lazy, exploratory.

---

## 14.3 Bounded Worlds

An unbounded camera will follow the hero into the void. But most worlds have **edges** — a garden, a room, a map. We don't want the camera to show empty space beyond the world boundary.

Use `world/camera-bounds!` to **clamp** the camera:

```scheme
(world/camera-bounds! left top right bottom)
;; The camera's center will never move outside [left, right] × [top, bottom].
```

Typically you set bounds to *world-size minus half-viewport*, so the camera stops when the viewport edge reaches the world edge.

```scheme
;; Example 14.3: Camera Bounds — a walled garden
(define (example-14-3)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((hero (world/spawn 80 72))) ;; start near world-center
    (entity/sprite! hero 'blossom-cherry)
    (entity/set! hero 'controllable #t)
    ;; World: 0..320 wide, 0..240 tall
    ;; Viewport: 160×144
    ;; Bounds: camera center ∈ [80, 240] × [72, 168]
    ;;   so viewport never shows x<0, x>320, y<0, y>240
    (world/camera-bounds! 80 72 240 168)
    (world/camera-follow! hero 0.1)
    (big-bang
      (on-tick (lambda (s)
                 (when (entity/get hero 'controllable)
                   ;; simple 4-dir control
                   (let ((vx 0) (vy 0))
                     (when (input/down? 'left)  (set! vx -2))
                     (when (input/down? 'right) (set! vx 2))
                     (when (input/down? 'up)    (set! vy -2))
                     (when (input/down? 'down)  (set! vy 2))
                     (entity/set-vel! hero vx vy)))
                 (world/step)
                 s))
      (to-draw (lambda (s)
                 (world/frame))))))

;; (example-14-3)
```

- Camera bounds `[80, 240] × [72, 168]` ensure the viewport never shows `x < 0`, `x > 320`, `y < 0`, `y > 240`.
- When the sprite is near the center, the camera follows smoothly.
- When the sprite approaches the world edge, the camera **stops** at the bound, and the sprite drifts toward the viewport edge.

This is the **classic 2D adventure camera** — follow until you hit the world boundary, then let the hero explore the edge.

## 14.4 Framing an Ensemble

Following one sprite is easy. But what if you have a **pack** — a flock, a party, a team — and you want to **keep them all visible**?

The camera should center on the **bounding box** of the group, and zoom (or just frame) to fit them all. The runtime doesn't have dynamic zoom yet (the viewport is fixed-size), so we'll **center on the centroid** and trust that our viewport is large enough (or mark sprites that drift too far out-of-frame as \"offscreen\").

**Algorithm:**
1. Find all entities in the group (by tag or team).
2. Compute their **centroid** (average position).
3. Move the camera toward the centroid.

```scheme
;; Example 14.4: Camera Framing — follow the flock's center
(define (example-14-4)
  (world/reset!)
  ;; spawn 5 wandering sprites
  (let ((flock (map (lambda (i)
                      (let ((e (world/spawn (+ 80 (* i 20)) 72)))
                        (entity/sprite! e 'blossom-cherry)
                        (entity/tag! e 'flock)
                        (entity/set-vel! e (* (- i 2) 0.5) (* (- 2 i) 0.3)) ;; varied drift
                        (ai/wander e 1.0 0.3) ;; gentle wander
                        e))
                    '(0 1 2 3 4))))
    (world/camera-snap! 80 72)
    (big-bang
      (on-tick (lambda (s)
                 (world/step)
                 ;; compute flock centroid
                 (let ((sum-x 0) (sum-y 0) (count 0))
                   (group/each 'flock (lambda (e)
                                        (let ((p (entity/pos e)))
                                          (set! sum-x (+ sum-x (car p)))
                                          (set! sum-y (+ sum-y (cdr p)))
                                          (set! count (+ count 1)))))
                   (when (> count 0)
                     (let ((cx (/ sum-x count))
                           (cy (/ sum-y count)))
                       ;; smoothly move camera toward centroid
                       (let* ((cam (world/camera))
                              (cam-x (car cam))
                              (cam-y (cdr cam))
                              (dx (- cx cam-x))
                              (dy (- cy cam-y)))
                         (world/camera-snap! (+ cam-x (* dx 0.1))
                                             (+ cam-y (* dy 0.1)))))))
                 s))
      (to-draw (lambda (s)
                 (world/frame))))))

;; (example-14-4)
```

[VISUAL: Five cherry blossoms wandering in loose formation. The camera smoothly centers on their average position, so even as individuals drift apart, the group stays roughly centered in frame.]

**What happened:**
- We spawned 5 sprites, tagged them `'flock`, gave them initial velocity + `ai/wander`.
- Every tick, we compute the centroid: sum all `x` and `y`, divide by count.
- We move the camera 10% toward the centroid (exponential smoothing, same as `camera-follow!` but manual).
- The camera **frames the ensemble** — if they spread wide, the camera stays centered on their middle; if they cluster, the camera tightens.

**Limitation:** If the flock spreads wider than the viewport, some sprites will go offscreen. A real solution would compute the bounding box **and** adjust zoom (or mark offscreen sprites with arrows). The runtime doesn't have dynamic zoom yet, so we accept that wide flocks may partially exit frame. The camera still does its job: **keep the center of attention visible**.

---

## 14.5 Lead the Eye — Predictive Framing

A camera that follows the hero's **current position** is always a step behind. When the hero runs right, the camera lags, and the viewport shows more space *behind* than *ahead* — the opposite of what a player needs.

A **predictive camera** looks at the hero's **velocity** and frames **ahead** of them, giving the viewer space to see what's coming.

**Algorithm:**
1. Follow the hero's position (as before).
2. Add a **lead offset** proportional to the hero's velocity: `offset = velocity × lead-factor`.
3. Move the camera toward `hero-pos + offset`.

```scheme
;; Example 14.5: Predictive Camera — lead the runner
(define (example-14-5)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((hero (world/spawn 80 72)))
    (entity/sprite! hero 'blossom-plum)
    (entity/set! hero 'controllable #t)
    (world/camera-snap! 80 72)
    (big-bang
      (on-tick (lambda (s)
                 (when (entity/get hero 'controllable)
                   (let ((vx 0) (vy 0))
                     (when (input/down? 'left)  (set! vx -3))
                     (when (input/down? 'right) (set! vx 3))
                     (when (input/down? 'up)    (set! vy -3))
                     (when (input/down? 'down)  (set! vy 3))
                     (entity/set-vel! hero vx vy)))
                 (world/step)
                 ;; predictive framing
                 (let* ((pos (entity/pos hero))
                        (vel (entity/vel hero))
                        (lead-x (* (car vel) 10)) ;; 10 frames ahead
                        (lead-y (* (cdr vel) 10))
                        (target-x (+ (car pos) lead-x))
                        (target-y (+ (cdr pos) lead-y))
                        (cam (world/camera))
                        (dx (- target-x (car cam)))
                        (dy (- target-y (cdr cam))))
                   (world/camera-snap! (+ (car cam) (* dx 0.1))
                                       (+ (cdr cam) (* dy 0.1))))
                 s))
      (to-draw (lambda (s)
                 (world/frame))))))

;; (example-14-5)
```

When the sprite stops, the camera drifts back to center it. The framing feels **anticipatory**, like a cinematographer panning ahead of a runner.]

**What happened:**
- `lead-x` and `lead-y` are the hero's velocity × 10 (10 frames of lookahead).
- The camera targets `hero-pos + (lead-x, lead-y)` instead of just `hero-pos`.
- When the hero runs right at `vx = 3`, the camera shifts right by `3×10 = 30` cells, framing 30 cells ahead.
- When the hero stops (`vx = 0`), the lead vanishes, and the camera drifts back to center.

**Tuning:**
- **Lead factor** (here `10`): higher → more lookahead, feels faster but can be disorienting. Lower → tighter framing, less anticipation.
- **Damping** (here `0.1`): higher → slower camera, more lag. Lower → snappier.

This is the **platformer camera** — Mario, Celeste, Hollow Knight all use variants of predictive framing.

---

## 14.6 Screen Shake — Impact and Weight

When something **heavy happens** — a boss lands, a bomb explodes, a collision — the camera should **shake**. Screen shake is **haptic feedback** delivered visually. It makes impacts feel **real**.

`world/camera-shake!` applies a random offset to the camera every frame for a duration, then decays back to the follow target.

```scheme
(world/camera-shake! intensity duration)
;; intensity: max offset in cells (e.g. 3 = ±3 cell jitter)
;; duration: frames (e.g. 20 = shake for 20 ticks)
```

```scheme
;; Example 14.6: Screen Shake on Collision
(define (example-14-6)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.2) ;; mild gravity
  (world/floor! 120) ;; ground at y=120
  (let ((ball (world/spawn 80 10)))
    (entity/sprite! ball 'blossom-sakura)
    (entity/bounce! ball 0.6) ;; bouncy
    (entity/set-vel! ball 0 0)
    (world/camera-snap! 80 72)
    (world/camera-follow! ball 0.1)
    (big-bang
      (on-tick (lambda (s)
                 (let ((old-y (cdr (entity/pos ball))))
                   (world/step)
                   (let ((new-y (cdr (entity/pos ball))))
                     ;; detect bounce (velocity sign flip at floor)
                     (when (and (> old-y 115) (<= new-y 120) (> (cdr (entity/vel ball)) 0))
                       (world/camera-shake! 3 12)))) ;; shake for 12 frames
                 s))
      (to-draw (lambda (s)
                 (world/frame))))))

;; (example-14-6)
```

<!-- BUILD: wire example-14-6 as runnable cart \"Screen Shake Bounce\" -->

[VISUAL: A sakura sprite falls under gravity, bounces on the floor at y=120. On each bounce, the entire viewport **jitters violently** for ~12 frames (±3 cells random offset), then settles. The shake intensity matches the impact.]

**What happened:**
- We detect the bounce by checking if `y` crossed the floor threshold and velocity flipped positive (upward after impact).
- On detection, we call `world/camera-shake! 3 12` — shake ±3 cells for 12 frames.
- The camera applies a random `(dx, dy) ∈ [-3, 3]²` offset every frame, decaying exponentially over 12 frames.
- The shake **adds** to the follow/snap target — it doesn't cancel smooth following, just jitters on top.

**Tuning shake:**
- **Intensity**: 1–2 = subtle rumble, 3–5 = strong impact, 10+ = earthquake (disorienting, use sparingly).
- **Duration**: 6–10 frames = quick punch, 20–30 = sustained rumble, 60+ = nausea (avoid).

Shake is **emphasis**. Use it when the world **reacts** — explosions, stomps, crashes. Don't shake on every tiny event or it loses meaning.

---

## 14.7 Cinematic Cuts — Snap for Revelation

Sometimes you want the camera to **instantly jump** — a cut, not a pan. Revelations. Scene transitions. A character teleports and the camera snaps to follow.

`world/camera-snap!` is the instant cut. Combine it with `world/camera-follow!` to **cut, then resume smooth follow**.

```scheme
;; Example 14.7: Cut on Teleport
(define (example-14-7)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((hero (world/spawn 80 72))
        (teleport-timer 0))
    (entity/sprite! hero 'blossom-cherry)
    (entity/set-vel! hero 1 0) ;; drift right
    (world/camera-snap! 80 72)
    (world/camera-follow! hero 0.1)
    (big-bang
      (on-tick (lambda (s)
                 (set! teleport-timer (+ teleport-timer 1))
                 (when (= teleport-timer 120) ;; teleport after 2 seconds
                   (entity/set-pos! hero 300 200) ;; jump to far corner
                   (world/camera-snap! 300 200) ;; instant cut
                   (world/camera-shake! 2 10)) ;; small shake for \"pop\"
                 (world/step)
                 s))
      (to-draw (lambda (s)
                 (world/frame))))))

;; (example-14-7)
```

<!-- BUILD: wire example-14-7 as runnable cart \"Camera Cut Teleport\" -->

[VISUAL: A cherry blossom drifts right smoothly for 2 seconds. At frame 120, it **instantly vanishes** and reappears at (300, 200) — a far corner. The camera **cuts** (no pan, instant jump) to the new position, with a brief shake. Then smooth following resumes.]

**What happened:**
- At frame 120, we `set-pos!` the hero to a distant location.
- We **immediately** `camera-snap!` to that location — no smooth interpolation, just a cut.
- We add a small shake (2 cells, 10 frames) to **punctuate** the teleport (optional, but feels good).
- `camera-follow!` was never disabled, so after the cut, it resumes smooth tracking from the new position.

**Cuts vs. Pans:**
- **Cut** (`snap!`) = instant reveal, surprise, teleport, scene transition. No spatial continuity.
- **Pan** (`follow!` with low damping) = smooth, continuous, the viewer tracks motion through space.

Use cuts **sparingly** — they break spatial flow. But when you want **shock** or **transition**, a cut is the right tool.

## 14.8 The Cinematographer — Intelligent Framing

A **cinematographer** is a camera that **decides** what to show based on **context**. It's not just following the hero — it's composing the shot.

Examples of cinematic intent:
- **Dialogue**: frame both speakers, centered.
- **Chase**: lead the pursuer, keep pursued in frame.
- **Exploration**: wide framing, show the environment.
- **Combat**: tight framing, focus on the action.
- **Revelation**: cut to the discovered object, hold, then return.

We can build a **rule-based cinematographer** using `entity/get` state + conditional framing logic. The camera becomes an **AI** — it reads the scene and **decides** where to look.

```scheme
;; Example 14.8: Cinematographer — context-aware framing
(define (example-14-8)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((hero (world/spawn 80 72))
        (npc (world/spawn 160 72))
        (mode 'follow)) ;; 'follow | 'dialogue | 'reveal
    (entity/sprite! hero 'blossom-cherry)
    (entity/sprite! npc 'blossom-plum)
    (entity/tag! hero 'hero)
    (entity/tag! npc 'npc)
    (entity/set-vel! hero 1 0) ;; hero drifts right
    (world/camera-snap! 80 72)
    (big-bang
      (on-tick (lambda (s)
                 (world/step)
                 ;; simple event logic: after 60 frames, enter dialogue
                 (when (= (world/frame) 60)
                   (set! mode 'dialogue)
                   (entity/set-vel! hero 0 0)) ;; stop hero
                 ;; after 120 frames, reveal NPC
                 (when (= (world/frame) 120)
                   (set! mode 'reveal))
                 ;; after 180 frames, return to follow
                 (when (= (world/frame) 180)
                   (set! mode 'follow)
                   (entity/set-vel! hero 1 0)) ;; resume drift

                 ;; CINEMATOGRAPHER: decide framing based on mode
                 (cond
                   ((eq? mode 'follow)
                    ;; standard follow with lead
                    (let* ((pos (entity/pos hero))
                           (vel (entity/vel hero))
                           (lead-x (* (car vel) 8))
                           (target-x (+ (car pos) lead-x))
                           (target-y (cdr pos))
                           (cam (world/camera))
                           (dx (- target-x (car cam)))
                           (dy (- target-y (cdr cam))))
                      (world/camera-snap! (+ (car cam) (* dx 0.1))
                                          (+ (cdr cam) (* dy 0.1)))))
                   ((eq? mode 'dialogue)
                    ;; frame both hero and NPC (centroid)
                    (let* ((h-pos (entity/pos hero))
                           (n-pos (entity/pos npc))
                           (mid-x (/ (+ (car h-pos) (car n-pos)) 2))
                           (mid-y (/ (+ (cdr h-pos) (cdr n-pos)) 2))
                           (cam (world/camera))
                           (dx (- mid-x (car cam)))
                           (dy (- mid-y (cdr cam))))
                      (world/camera-snap! (+ (car cam) (* dx 0.05))
                                          (+ (cdr cam) (* dy 0.05))))) ;; slower pan
                   ((eq? mode 'reveal)
                    ;; cut to NPC, hold
                    (let* ((n-pos (entity/pos npc))
                           (cam (world/camera))
                           (dx (- (car n-pos) (car cam)))
                           (dy (- (cdr n-pos) (cdr cam))))
                      (world/camera-snap! (+ (car cam) (* dx 0.2))
                                          (+ (cdr cam) (* dy 0.2)))))) ;; quick pan to NPC
                 s))
      (to-draw (lambda (s)
                 (world/frame))))))

;; (example-14-8)
```

**Building a real cinematographer:**
- Replace the hardcoded frame-counts with **event triggers**: proximity, collision, dialogue start, quest state.
- Add more modes: 'chase' (lead the chaser), 'combat' (tight framing), 'vista' (wide framing on a landmark).
- Use `ai/decide` (Ch15, behavior trees) to **decide the mode** — the camera becomes an autonomous agent.

This is **cinematic AI** — the camera as **co-author** of the experience.

---

## 14.9 Finale: A Camera That Tells the Story

Let's build a **two-act journey** with intelligent framing:

**Act 1 (Exploration):** Hero wanders a world. Camera follows with lead, bounded to the world edges. The hero discovers a landmark (a distant blossom).

**Act 2 (Revelation):** Camera cuts to the landmark, holds for 2 seconds (shake for emphasis), then pans back to hero and resumes following. The hero walks toward the landmark, and the camera frames the approach (both in view).

This is a **narrative camera** — it knows when to follow, when to reveal, when to hold, when to return. It's telling the story **through sight**.

```scheme
;; Example 14.9: A Camera That Tells the Story (finale)
(define (example-14-9)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((hero (world/spawn 80 72))
        (landmark (world/spawn 280 72))
        (mode 'explore)
        (hold-timer 0))
    (entity/sprite! hero 'blossom-cherry)
    (entity/sprite! landmark 'blossom-wisteria)
    (entity/set! hero 'controllable #t)
    (entity/tag! landmark 'landmark)

    ;; world bounds: 0..320 × 0..240, viewport 160×144
    (world/camera-bounds! 80 72 240 168)
    (world/camera-snap! 80 72)

    (big-bang
      (on-tick (lambda (s)
                 ;; simple 4-dir control
                 (when (and (entity/get hero 'controllable) (eq? mode 'explore))
                   (let ((vx 0) (vy 0))
                     (when (input/down? 'left)  (set! vx -2))
                     (when (input/down? 'right) (set! vx 2))
                     (when (input/down? 'up)    (set! vy -2))
                     (when (input/down? 'down)  (set! vy 2))
                     (entity/set-vel! hero vx vy)))

                 (world/step)

                 ;; EVENT: if hero gets within 50 cells of landmark, trigger reveal
                 (when (and (eq? mode 'explore)
                            (< (entity/distance hero landmark) 50))
                   (set! mode 'reveal)
                   (set! hold-timer 0)
                   (entity/set-vel! hero 0 0)) ;; stop hero

                 ;; CINEMATOGRAPHER
                 (cond
                   ((eq? mode 'explore)
                    ;; predictive follow with bounds
                    (let* ((pos (entity/pos hero))
                           (vel (entity/vel hero))
                           (lead-x (* (car vel) 10))
                           (lead-y (* (cdr vel) 10))
                           (target-x (+ (car pos) lead-x))
                           (target-y (+ (cdr pos) lead-y))
                           (cam (world/camera))
                           (dx (- target-x (car cam)))
                           (dy (- target-y (cdr cam))))
                      (world/camera-snap! (+ (car cam) (* dx 0.1))
                                          (+ (cdr cam) (* dy 0.1)))))

                   ((eq? mode 'reveal)
                    ;; cut to landmark, hold for 60 frames, then approach
                    (when (= hold-timer 0)
                      (world/camera-snap! (car (entity/pos landmark))
                                          (cdr (entity/pos landmark)))
                      (world/camera-shake! 4 15)) ;; dramatic reveal shake
                    (set! hold-timer (+ hold-timer 1))
                    (when (= hold-timer 60)
                      (set! mode 'approach)
                      (entity/set! hero 'controllable #t))) ;; return control

                   ((eq? mode 'approach)
                    ;; frame both hero and landmark (centroid)
                    (let* ((h-pos (entity/pos hero))
                           (l-pos (entity/pos landmark))
                           (mid-x (/ (+ (car h-pos) (car l-pos)) 2))
                           (mid-y (/ (+ (cdr h-pos) (cdr l-pos)) 2))
                           (cam (world/camera))
                           (dx (- mid-x (car cam)))
                           (dy (- mid-y (cdr cam))))
                      (world/camera-snap! (+ (car cam) (* dx 0.08))
                                          (+ (cdr cam) (* dy 0.08))))))
                 s))

      (to-draw (lambda (s)
                 (world/frame))))))

;; (example-14-9)
```

- **Three framing strategies**:

  - *Reveal*: snap + hold (the landmark is the camera's subject).
  - *Approach*: centroid framing (both are the camera's subjects).
- **Shake for emphasis**: the reveal shake makes the landmark feel **important**.

**Extensions you could build:**
- Add more landmarks; the camera cuts to each on first discovery.
- Use `ai/decide` (Ch15) to make the camera an autonomous agent with a behavior tree: \"if hero idle for 10s, pan to nearest point-of-interest.\"
- Add a **director mode** where the camera ignores player input entirely and plays a scripted sequence (opening shot, credits roll).
- Track **dramatic tension** (distance to enemy, HP, quest state) and adjust framing: tighter in combat, wider in calm.

## What You've Learned

You can now:

1. **Move the camera** — `world/camera-snap!` for instant cuts, `world/camera-follow!` for smooth tracking.
2. **Bound the world** — `world/camera-bounds!` to prevent showing void beyond the map.
3. **Frame an ensemble** — center on the centroid of a group, keep the pack visible.
4. **Lead the eye** — predictive framing by targeting `position + velocity × lead-factor`.
5. **Shake for impact** — `world/camera-shake!` to emphasize collisions, explosions, drama.
6. **Cut for revelation** — instant snaps to reveal offscreen objects, then resume smooth follow.
7. **Build a cinematographer** — mode-based framing logic (follow, dialogue, reveal, approach) that **tells the story** through sight.

The camera is **not passive**. It's a **storyteller**, a **guide**, a **co-author** of the experience. In Chapter 15, we'll give it a **brain** — behavior trees, utility AI, policy — so it can **decide** what to show without hardcoded timers. The camera will become an **autonomous agent**, composing the shot frame-by-frame based on what's **interesting** in the scene.

But first, practice. Build cameras that follow, frame, reveal, shake. Make the viewer **see** what matters. Make the viewport **mean something**.

"# Chapter 15: The Director

You've given sprites bodies (Ch8), taught them to walk with weight (Ch9), sent them chasing across the surface (Ch10), orchestrated their flocking (Ch11), and plotted their paths around obstacles (Ch12). You've composed scenes from these parts (Ch13) and aimed a camera to watch them (Ch14).

But *who decides* what happens next?

Until now, every animation you've authored has been either deterministic choreography (a flower sways because you told it to sway, on a fixed schedule) or reactive behavior (a sprite seeks because you wired `ai/seek` to fire every tick). That's enough to build beautiful systems — but it's not enough to build a sprite that *chooses*.

This chapter teaches **the director**: the AI subsystem that decides *which* behavior a sprite should perform, *when* to switch, and *how* to weigh competing goals. You'll learn three decision architectures, each suited to different scales of complexity:

1. **Behavior trees** — compositional, hierarchical, debuggable. \"Try this, then that, but only if…\"
2. **Utility AI** — score every option, pick the best. \"I'm 80% hungry, 30% scared — eating wins.\"
3. **Policy-based selection** — map world-state to action directly. \"In this configuration, always do X.\"

Each has tradeoffs. Trees are readable and composable but can grow brittle. Utility scales to many competing drives but requires careful scoring. Policies are fast and data-driven but opaque without tooling. By the end of this chapter, you'll know when to reach for each, and you'll have built a sprite that decides — on its own — whether to graze, flee, or explore, moment by moment, as the world changes around it.

---

## 15.1 The simplest choice: `ai/decide`

The humblest director is a function that looks at the world and returns a behavior to run. `ai/decide` takes that function and an entity, calls it every tick, and applies whatever the function returns.

Here's a sprite that wanders unless you get close — then it flees:

```scheme
(let ((sprite (world/spawn 'x 0 'y 0 'sprite 'blossom-plum)))
  (big-bang
    (on-tick
      (lambda (w)
        (world/step)
        (let ((dist (entity/distance sprite
                      (list (world/camera-x) (world/camera-y)))))
          (ai/decide sprite
            (lambda (self)
              (if (< dist 5.0)
                (ai/flee self (list (world/camera-x) (world/camera-y)) 2.0)
                (ai/wander self 0.5 1.0)))))
        'ok))
    (to-draw (lambda (w)
               (paint-cell 0 0 'clear)
               (world/frame)))))
```

[VISUAL: A plum-blossom sprite wandering in lazy arcs across a pale surface; when the camera (or a touch cursor, in the live app) approaches within 5 cells, the sprite darts away.]

The lambda you pass to `ai/decide` receives the entity and must return a *steering force* — the same `(dx dy)` pair that `ai/seek`, `ai/flee`, and `ai/wander` produce. Every tick, `ai/decide` calls your lambda, takes the force, and applies it to the entity's velocity (respecting `ai/max-force!` if you've set it).

This is the atomic unit of agency: **look at the world, pick a force, apply it.**

---

## 15.2 Behavior trees: composing decisions

A single `if` is fine for two choices. But what if a sprite should:

- **First**, check if it's hurt → if yes, flee to safety.
- **Otherwise**, check if food is nearby → if yes, approach and eat.
- **Otherwise**, check if it's bored → if yes, explore.
- **Otherwise**, idle.

You *could* nest `if` forms, but they tangle fast. A **behavior tree** gives you composable nodes that succeed, fail, or keep running, and combinators that wire them into readable hierarchies.

The engine provides:

- `ai/bt-action` — wraps a lambda; succeeds if the lambda returns `'success`, fails if `'fail`, keeps running if `'running`.
- `ai/bt-condition` — wraps a predicate; succeeds if true, fails if false.
- `ai/bt-sequence` — tries children left-to-right; fails if any child fails, succeeds if all succeed.
- `ai/bt-selector` — tries children left-to-right; succeeds if any child succeeds, fails if all fail.
- `ai/bt-parallel` — runs all children; you specify how many must succeed for the parallel to succeed.
- `ai/bt-invert` — flips success ↔ fail.
- `ai/bt-force` — always succeeds or always fails (useful for fallback branches).
- `ai/bt-tick` — runs the tree and returns its status.

Here's a sprite that flees if hurt, seeks food if hungry, wanders if bored, else idles:

```scheme
(define (make-grazer)
  (let ((sprite (world/spawn 'x 0 'y 0 'sprite 'blossom-lotus 'hp 10 'hunger 0)))
    ;; plant some \"food\" entities
    (world/spawn 'x 8 'y 8 'kind 'food 'sprite 'grass)
    (world/spawn 'x -8 'y -8 'kind 'food 'sprite 'grass)
    
    ;; build the behavior tree
    (let ((tree
            (ai/bt-selector
              ;; branch 1: if hurt, flee to center
              (ai/bt-sequence
                (ai/bt-condition (lambda (self) (< (entity/hp self) 5)))
                (ai/bt-action (lambda (self)
                  (ai/flee self '(0 0) 1.5)
                  'success)))
              
              ;; branch 2: if hungry and food exists, seek nearest food
              (ai/bt-sequence
                (ai/bt-condition (lambda (self) (> (entity/get self 'hunger 0) 3)))
                (ai/bt-action (lambda (self)
                  (let ((food (world/find (lambda (e) (eq? (entity/kind e) 'food)))))
                    (if food
                      (begin
                        (ai/seek self (entity/pos food) 1.0)
                        'success)
                      'fail)))))
              
              ;; branch 3: if bored, wander
              (ai/bt-sequence
                (ai/bt-condition (lambda (self) (> (world/frame) 100)))
                (ai/bt-action (lambda (self)
                  (ai/wander self 0.3 0.8)
                  'success)))
              
              ;; fallback: idle (do nothing)
              (ai/bt-force 'success))))
      
      (big-bang
        (on-tick
          (lambda (w)
            (world/step)
            ;; tick the tree every frame
            (ai/bt-tick tree sprite)
            ;; hunger rises over time
            (entity/set! sprite 'hunger (+ (entity/get sprite 'hunger 0) 0.01))
            'ok))
        (to-draw (lambda (w)
                   (paint-cell 0 0 'clear)
                   (world/frame)))))))

(make-grazer)
```

**Key insight:** Each branch is isolated. You can re-order them, replace one, or nest a sub-tree inside any node. The tree is *data* — you can serialize it, diff it, or build it from a config file.

---

## 15.3 Blackboards: shared memory for trees

Behavior trees often need to remember things across ticks: \"I picked *this* food item last tick; keep seeking it until I arrive.\" A **blackboard** is a key-value store shared by all nodes in a tree.

The engine provides:

- `ai/bb-set! entity key val` — write.
- `ai/bb-get entity key default` — read.
- `ai/bb-has? entity key` — check.
- `ai/bb-del! entity key` — erase.

Here's a sprite that picks a food target, remembers it, and keeps seeking until close, then eats it:

```scheme
(define (make-persistent-seeker)
  (let ((sprite (world/spawn 'x 0 'y 0 'sprite 'blossom-cherry)))
    (world/spawn 'x 10 'y 10 'kind 'food 'sprite 'grass)
    (world/spawn 'x -10 'y -10 'kind 'food 'sprite 'grass)
    
    (let ((tree
            (ai/bt-selector
              ;; if we have a target and we're close, eat it
              (ai/bt-sequence
                (ai/bt-condition (lambda (self)
                  (and (ai/bb-has? self 'target)
                       (< (entity/distance self (ai/bb-get self 'target #f)) 1.0))))
                (ai/bt-action (lambda (self)
                  (let ((target (ai/bb-get self 'target #f)))
                    (entity/despawn! target)
                    (ai/bb-del! self 'target)
                    'success))))
              
              ;; if we have a target, keep seeking it
              (ai/bt-sequence
                (ai/bt-condition (lambda (self) (ai/bb-has? self 'target)))
                (ai/bt-action (lambda (self)
                  (ai/seek self (entity/pos (ai/bb-get self 'target #f)) 1.0)
                  'running)))
              
              ;; pick a new target
              (ai/bt-action (lambda (self)
                (let ((food (world/find (lambda (e) (eq? (entity/kind e) 'food)))))
                  (if food
                    (begin
                      (ai/bb-set! self 'target food)
                      'running)
                    'fail)))))))
      
      (big-bang
        (on-tick
          (lambda (w)
            (world/step)
            (ai/bt-tick tree sprite)
            'ok))
        (to-draw (lambda (w)
                   (paint-cell 0 0 'clear)
                   (world/frame)))))))

(make-persistent-seeker)
```

The blackboard decouples decision (pick a target) from execution (seek it). The tree can have separate branches for \"pick,\" \"pursue,\" and \"arrive,\" each checking and updating the blackboard. This is how you build multi-tick behaviors (patrol a route, gather resources, build a structure) without tangling state into each action node.

---

## 15.4 Utility AI: scoring the options

Behavior trees are great when you have a clear priority ladder: \"always flee if hurt.\" But what if priorities *shift*? A sprite might be 60% hungry, 40% tired, 20% curious. Which wins?

**Utility AI** scores every possible action and picks the highest. Each action has a *utility function* that maps world-state to a score (0.0–1.0). The director evaluates all functions and executes the winner.

The engine provides `ai/utility`, which takes an entity and a list of `(utility-fn action-fn)` pairs. It calls each utility-fn with the entity, picks the highest, and runs that action-fn.

Here's a sprite juggling hunger, fear, and boredom:

```scheme
(define (make-utility-sprite)
  (let ((sprite (world/spawn 'x 0 'y 0 'sprite 'blossom-willow 
                             'hunger 0 'fear 0 'boredom 0)))
    (world/spawn 'x 12 'y 0 'kind 'food 'sprite 'grass)
    (world/spawn 'x -12 'y 0 'kind 'threat 'sprite 'thorn)
    
    (big-bang
      (on-tick
        (lambda (w)
          (world/step)
          
          ;; drives drift over time
          (entity/set! sprite 'hunger (min 1.0 (+ (entity/get sprite 'hunger 0) 0.005)))
          (entity/set! sprite 'boredom (min 1.0 (+ (entity/get sprite 'boredom 0) 0.003)))
          
          ;; fear rises if threat is near
          (let ((threat (world/find (lambda (e) (eq? (entity/kind e) 'threat)))))
            (if threat
              (let ((d (entity/distance sprite threat)))
                (entity/set! sprite 'fear (if (< d 8.0) (- 1.0 (/ d 8.0)) 0.0)))
              (entity/set! sprite 'fear 0.0)))
          
          ;; utility AI: score three actions
          (ai/utility sprite
            (list
              ;; action 1: seek food (utility = hunger)
              (cons
                (lambda (self) (entity/get self 'hunger 0))
                (lambda (self)
                  (let ((food (world/find (lambda (e) (eq? (entity/kind e) 'food)))))
                    (if food (ai/seek self (entity/pos food) 1.0)))))
              
              ;; action 2: flee threat (utility = fear)
              (cons
                (lambda (self) (entity/get self 'fear 0))
                (lambda (self)
                  (let ((threat (world/find (lambda (e) (eq? (entity/kind e) 'threat)))))
                    (if threat (ai/flee self (entity/pos threat) 1.5)))))
              
              ;; action 3: wander (utility = boredom)
              (cons
                (lambda (self) (entity/get self 'boredom 0))
                (lambda (self) (ai/wander self 0.4 0.6)))))
          'ok))
      (to-draw (lambda (w)
                 (paint-cell 0 0 'clear)
                 (world/frame))))))

(make-utility-sprite)
```

## 15.5 Combining trees and utility

You can nest utility selection *inside* a behavior tree node, or use a tree to gate when utility runs. Here's a sprite that uses a tree to decide \"am I in danger?\" and utility to pick between foraging strategies when safe:

```scheme
(define (make-hybrid-sprite)
  (let ((sprite (world/spawn 'x 0 'y 0 'sprite 'blossom-maple 
                             'hunger 0 'energy 1.0)))
```

The tree enforces the hard rule (\"always flee if threatened\"), and utility handles the soft tradeoff (\"explore vs. beeline\"). This is a common pattern in game AI: use trees for crisp state transitions, utility for continuous value judgments.

---

## 15.6 Policies: world-state → action

The third architecture is **policy-based selection**: a lookup table (or learned function) that maps world-state directly to an action, no scoring, no tree traversal.

`ai/policy` takes a list of `(predicate-fn action-fn)` pairs. It evaluates predicates in order and runs the first action whose predicate returns true. If you order them carefully, you get a *decision table*:

```scheme
(define (make-policy-sprite)
  (let ((sprite (world/spawn 'x 0 'y 0 'sprite 'blossom-oak 'state 'calm)))
    (world/spawn 'x 8 'y 8 'kind 'food 'sprite 'grass)
    (world/spawn 'x -8 'y -8 'kind 'ally 'sprite 'blossom-pine)
    
    (let ((policy
            (ai/policy
              (list
                ;; rule 1: if an ally is near and I'm calm, follow it
                (cons
                  (lambda (self)
                    (and (eq? (entity/state self) 'calm)
                         (let ((ally (world/nearest self 'ally)))
                           (and ally (< (entity/distance self ally) 6.0)))))
                  (lambda (self)
                    (ai/seek self (entity/pos (world/nearest self 'ally)) 0.8)))
                
                ;; rule 2: if food is near, seek it (and set state to feeding)
                (cons
                  (lambda (self)
                    (let ((food (world/nearest self 'food)))
                      (and food (< (entity/distance self food) 10.0))))
                  (lambda (self)
                    (entity/set! self 'state 'feeding)
                    (ai/seek self (entity/pos (world/nearest self 'food)) 1.0)))
                
                ;; rule 3: otherwise, wander and set state to exploring
                (cons
                  (lambda (self) #t)
                  (lambda (self)
                    (entity/set! self 'state 'exploring)
                    (ai/wander self 0.3 0.7)))))))
      
      (big-bang
        (on-tick
          (lambda (w)
            (world/step)
            (ai/policy-act policy sprite)
            'ok))
        (to-draw (lambda (w)
                   (paint-cell 0 0 'clear)
                   (world/frame)))))))

(make-policy-sprite)
```

State labels ('calm', 'feeding', 'exploring') appear as small glyphs above the sprite.]

Policies are *fast* (just predicate checks, no tree traversal or utility evaluation) and *data-driven* (you can load rules from a file or generate them from a learned model). The tradeoff is opacity: a 50-rule policy is hard to debug by inspection. Use policies when speed matters and you have tooling to visualize/test them.

---

## 15.7 Learning policies: reinforcement bridge (preview)

The policies we've shown are *hand-authored*. But a policy is just a function from state to action — the same shape a reinforcement-learning agent produces. You can train a small net (or decision-tree learner) offline, export the weights, and load them as a runtime policy.

Here's the *shape* of a learned policy (the training harness is out of scope for this chapter, but the runtime interface is simple):

```scheme
;; (fictional) A policy learned offline and serialized as a decision tree.
;; Each node is (feature threshold left-action right-action).
(define learned-tree
  '((hunger 0.5
      (distance-to-food 5.0 seek-food wander)
      (distance-to-threat 8.0 flee idle))))

(define (eval-tree tree state)
  (if (not (pair? tree))
    tree  ;; leaf: return action symbol
    (let ((feature (car tree))
          (threshold (cadr tree))
          (left (caddr tree))
          (right (cadddr tree)))
      (if (< (cdr (assoc feature state)) threshold)
        (eval-tree left state)
        (eval-tree right state)))))

(define (make-learned-sprite)
  (let ((sprite (world/spawn 'x 0 'y 0 'sprite 'blossom-cedar)))
    (world/spawn 'x 10 'y 10 'kind 'food 'sprite 'grass)
    
    (big-bang
      (on-tick
        (lambda (w)
          (world/step)
          
          ;; build state vector
          (let* ((food (world/nearest sprite 'food))
                 (state (list
                          (cons 'hunger (entity/get sprite 'hunger 0))
                          (cons 'distance-to-food
                                (if food (entity/distance sprite food) 999.0)))))
            
            ;; eval tree, dispatch action
            (let ((action (eval-tree learned-tree state)))
              (cond
                ((eq? action 'seek-food)
                 (if food (ai/seek sprite (entity/pos food) 1.0)))
                ((eq? action 'wander)
                 (ai/wander sprite 0.4 0.6))
                ((eq? action 'flee)
                 ;; (flee logic would go here)
                 (ai/wander sprite 0.2 0.4))
                (else (void)))))
          
          (entity/set! sprite 'hunger (min 1.0 (+ (entity/get sprite 'hunger 0) 0.005)))
          'ok))
      (to-draw (lambda (w)
                 (paint-cell 0 0 'clear)
                 (world/frame))))))

(make-learned-sprite)
```

[VISUAL: A cedar sprite behaving according to the decision tree: when hunger < 0.5 and food is within 5 cells, it seeks; otherwise it wanders. The tree structure is overlaid as a small diagram in the corner, highlighting which branch is active each tick.]

The key insight: the tree is *data*. You can serialize it, diff it, A/B test it, or evolve it with a genetic algorithm. the runtime's determinism means you can run the same learned policy on device and in a training harness and get identical results — no floating-point drift, no RNG divergence.

This is the bridge to Chapter 16's finale: a garden where some sprites follow hand-authored trees, others run utility AI, and a few are governed by learned policies, all interacting in the same deterministic world.

---

## 15.8 Finale: The chooser sprite

Let's compose everything: a sprite with a behavior tree that gates high-level modes (flee, forage, socialize), utility AI that picks *how* to forage, a blackboard that remembers the current target, and a policy that decides which social behavior to perform when near an ally.

```scheme
(define (make-chooser-sprite)
  (let ((sprite (world/spawn 'x 0 'y 0 'sprite 'blossom-magnolia 
                             'hunger 0 'fear 0 'social 0 'state 'idle)))
    ;; populate world
    (world/spawn 'x 12 'y 12 'kind 'food 'sprite 'grass 'tag 'food-1)
    (world/spawn 'x -12 'y -12 'kind 'food 'sprite 'grass 'tag 'food-2)
    (world/spawn 'x 0 'y 15 'kind 'threat 'sprite 'thorn)
    (world/spawn 'x -8 'y 0 'kind 'ally 'sprite 'blossom-pine)
    
    ;; utility: how to forage
    (define (forage-utility self)
      (ai/utility self
        (list
          ;; if very hungry, beeline to nearest food
          (cons
            (lambda (s) (if (> (entity/get s 'hunger 0) 0.7) 1.0 0.0))
            (lambda (s)
              (let ((food (world/nearest s 'food)))
                (if food
                  (begin
                    (ai/bb-set! s 'target food)
                    (ai/seek s (entity/pos food) 1.5))))))
          
          ;; if moderately hungry, pick closest food and remember it
          (cons
            (lambda (s) (entity/get s 'hunger 0))
            (lambda (s)
              (if (not (ai/bb-has? s 'target))
                (let ((food (world/nearest s 'food)))
                  (if food (ai/bb-set! s 'target food))))
              (if (ai/bb-has? s 'target)
                (ai/seek s (entity/pos (ai/bb-get s 'target #f)) 1.0)
                (ai/wander s 0.3 0.5)))))))
    
    ;; policy: social behaviors
    (define social-policy
      (ai/policy
        (list
          ;; if ally is very close, align with it
          (cons
            (lambda (self)
              (let ((ally (world/nearest self 'ally)))
                (and ally (< (entity/distance self ally) 3.0))))
            (lambda (self)
              (let ((ally (world/nearest self 'ally)))
                (ai/align self (list ally) 5.0 0.8))))
          
          ;; if ally is near, seek it
          (cons
            (lambda (self)
              (let ((ally (world/nearest self 'ally)))
                (and ally (< (entity/distance self ally) 8.0))))
            (lambda (self)
              (ai/seek self (entity/pos (world/nearest self 'ally)) 0.6)))
          
          ;; otherwise idle
          (cons (lambda (self) #t) (lambda (self) (void))))))
    
    ;; top-level tree
    (define tree
      (ai/bt-selector
        ;; mode 1: flee if threatened
        (ai/bt-sequence
          (ai/bt-condition (lambda (self)
            (let ((threat (world/nearest self 'threat)))
              (and threat (< (entity/distance self threat) 10.0)))))
          (ai/bt-action (lambda (self)
            (entity/set! self 'state 'fleeing)
            (let ((threat (world/nearest self 'threat)))
              (ai/flee self (entity/pos threat) 2.0))
            'success)))
        
        ;; mode 2: socialize if social drive is high and ally is near
        (ai/bt-sequence
          (ai/bt-condition (lambda (self)
            (and (> (entity/get self 'social 0) 0.5)
                 (let ((ally (world/nearest self 'ally)))
                   (and ally (< (entity/distance self ally) 10.0))))))
          (ai/bt-action (lambda (self)
            (entity/set! self 'state 'socializing)
            (ai/policy-act social-policy self)
            'success)))
        
        ;; mode 3: forage (utility-based)
        (ai/bt-action (lambda (self)
          (entity/set! self 'state 'foraging)
          (forage-utility self)
          'success))))
    
    (big-bang
      (on-tick
        (lambda (w)
          (world/step)
          (ai/bt-tick tree sprite)
          
          ;; drives drift
          (entity/set! sprite 'hunger (min 1.0 (+ (entity/get sprite 'hunger 0) 0.004)))
          (entity/set! sprite 'social (min 1.0 (+ (entity/get sprite 'social 0) 0.002)))
          
          ;; fear rises if threat is near
          (let ((threat (world/nearest sprite 'threat)))
            (entity/set! sprite 'fear
              (if (and threat (< (entity/distance sprite threat) 10.0))
                0.8
                (* (entity/get sprite 'fear 0) 0.95))))  ;; decay
          
          ;; if we reached food, eat it
          (when (ai/bb-has? sprite 'target)
            (let ((target (ai/bb-get sprite 'target #f)))
              (when (< (entity/distance sprite target) 1.5)
                (entity/despawn! target)
                (ai/bb-del! sprite 'target)
                (entity/set! sprite 'hunger 0.0))))
          'ok))
      (to-draw (lambda (w)
                 (paint-cell 0 0 'clear)
                 (world/frame))))))

(make-chooser-sprite)
```

## End-of-chapter questions

1. **Concept:** What's the difference between `ai/decide` and `ai/utility`? When would you use one over the other?

2. **Behavior trees:** Write a behavior tree for a sprite that: (1) flees if HP < 3, (2) seeks the nearest ally if lonely (a custom drive), (3) wanders otherwise. Use `ai/bt-selector` and `ai/bt-sequence`.

3. **Blackboard:** Extend the persistent-seeker example (§15.3) so the sprite remembers *which* food item it ate last and refuses to seek that same one again (even if it respawns). Hint: store the food's `entity/tag` in the blackboard.

4. **Utility shaping:** In the utility-drives example (§15.4), hunger rises linearly. Change the utility function for \"seek food\" to `(* h h)` (quadratic). How does the sprite's behavior change? Why?

5. **Hybrid:** In the hybrid tree-utility example (§15.5), what happens if you move the \"flee if threatened\" branch *below* the foraging action in the selector? Why does order matter in a `bt-selector`?

6. **Finale remix:** Take the chooser sprite (§15.8) and add a fourth mode: \"rest\" — if energy < 0.3, move to the center of the world and idle until energy refills. Where in the tree should this branch go? How do you ensure it doesn't block fleeing?

"# Chapter 16: The Living Garden

You have built a language, painted cells, animated flowers, moved bodies through forces and steering, orchestrated flocks, routed paths through obstacles, composed scenes, framed them with a camera, and given an AI director the power to decide what happens next.

This final chapter is not a lesson. It is a recital.

We will author *The Living Garden*: a self-directed, emergent ecosystem where pollinators seek nectar, predators hunt, plants grow and sway, weather shifts, and a camera frames the drama without your input. Every technique from chapters 1–15 will compose into a single scene that lives, breathes, and surprises you.

The garden does not run on a script. It runs on *policy*—the utility AI and behavior trees you built in chapter 15—layered over the steering (chapter 10), flocking (chapter 11), pathfinding (chapter 12), particles (chapter 7), oscillation (chapter 6), forces (chapter 5), and the deterministic math (chapter 4) that makes it all repeatable.

You will not type \"make the bee go here.\" You will type \"the bee values nectar and safety,\" and the bee will *decide* where to go. The garden will feel alive because it *is* alive in the only sense that matters in a deterministic universe: its behavior emerges from rules you can understand, but outcomes you cannot predict without running the simulation.

This chapter has three parts:

1. **The Garden Skeleton**: spawn terrain, plants, creatures, and weather as a static scene.
2. **The Behavior Layer**: give each creature agency—decision trees that compose steering, sensing, and state.
3. **The Director and Camera**: automate focus, pacing, and environmental response so the garden directs itself.

Then you will run it. And then—if you've understood everything—you will *change* it, because a living garden is never finished.

---

## Part 1: The Garden Skeleton

A garden needs ground, plants, and inhabitants. We'll start with a `prefab` (chapter 13) for each piece, then spawn a population of them.

### The Ground Plane

A visual foundation. We'll use a grid of colored cells to mark zones: soil, stone, water.

```scheme
(define (draw-ground)
  (let loop ((x 0))
    (when (< x 40)
      (let row ((y 0))
        (when (< y 30)

                     ((< y 2) '(0.6 0.8 1.0))    ; sky
                     ((< y 20) '(0.4 0.6 0.3))   ; grass
                     (else '(0.5 0.4 0.3)))))    ; soil
            (paint-cell x y c))
          (row (+ y 1))))
      (loop (+ x 1)))))

(draw-ground)
```

### Prefab: A Predator

A dragonfly that patrols (chapter 12 waypoints) and, when it senses prey, pursues (chapter 10).

```scheme
(prefab/define 'dragonfly
  (lambda (x y patrol-points)
    (let ((eid (world/spawn x y 'dragonfly)))
      (entity/sprite! eid 'blossom-9)
      (entity/set! eid 'patrol patrol-points)
      (entity/set! eid 'patrol-index 0)
      (entity/set! eid 'behavior 'patrol)
      (entity/max-speed! eid 3.0)
      (entity/gravity-scale! eid 0)
      (ai/max-force! eid 0.8)
      eid)))

(define (animate-dragonfly eid frame)
  (let ((behavior (entity/get eid 'behavior)))
    (cond
      ((eq? behavior 'patrol)
       (let* ((patrol (entity/get eid 'patrol))
              (index (entity/get eid 'patrol-index))
              (waypoint (list-ref patrol index))
              (wx (car waypoint))
              (wy (cadr waypoint))
              (dist (entity/distance eid wx wy)))
         (ai/seek eid wx wy)
         (when (< dist 2.0)
           (entity/set! eid 'patrol-index (modulo (+ index 1) (length patrol))))))
      ((eq? behavior 'chase)
       (let ((target (entity/get eid 'target)))
         (when target
           (ai/pursue eid target)))))))

(big-bang
  (on-tick (lambda (state frame)
             (world/step)
             (world/each (lambda (e)
                           (when (eq? (entity/kind e) 'dragonfly)
                             (animate-dragonfly e frame))))
             state))
  (to-draw (lambda (state) #t)))
```

### Spawning the Population

Now we fill the garden.

```scheme
(define (spawn-garden)
  (world/reset!)
  
  ;; Spawn 20 flowers in a meadow
  (let loop ((i 0))
    (when (< i 20)
      (let ((x (+ 5 (* i 1.5)))
            (y (+ 10 (* (dsin (* i 0.5)) 2)))
            (hue (* i 0.05))
            (phase (* i 0.3)))
        (prefab/spawn 'flower x y hue phase))
      (loop (+ i 1))))
  
  ;; Spawn 5 bees
```

## Part 2: The Behavior Layer

Behavior trees (chapter 15) let creatures sense, decide, and act each frame. We'll give each species a `tick` function that runs its brain.

### The Bee's Brain

A bee wants nectar. It wanders until it sees a flower within 5 cells, then seeks it. When it arrives (within 1 cell), it \"feeds\" for 3 seconds (180 frames), then resumes wandering.

```scheme
(define (bee-brain eid frame)
  (let ((nectar (entity/get eid 'nectar))
        (behavior (entity/get eid 'behavior))
        (target (entity/get eid 'target))
        (feed-timer (entity/get-set! eid 'feed-timer 0)))
    
    (cond
      ;; If feeding, decrement timer
      ((> feed-timer 0)
       (entity/set! eid 'feed-timer (- feed-timer 1))
       (when (<= (entity/get eid 'feed-timer) 0)
         (entity/set! eid 'behavior 'wander)
         (entity/set! eid 'target #f)))
      
      ;; If wandering, look for flowers
      ((eq? behavior 'wander)
       (let ((nearest (world/nearest eid 'flower 8.0)))
         (if nearest
             (begin
               (entity/set! eid 'behavior 'seek)
               (entity/set! eid 'target nearest))
             (ai/wander eid 1.0 0.3))))
      
      ;; If seeking, check arrival
      ((eq? behavior 'seek)
       (if (and target (entity/alive? target))
           (let ((dist (entity/distance eid (entity/x target) (entity/y target))))
             (if (< dist 1.5)
                 ;; Arrived: start feeding
                 (begin
                   (entity/set! eid 'behavior 'feed)
                   (entity/set! eid 'feed-timer 180)
                   (entity/set! eid 'nectar (+ nectar 50)))
                 ;; Still traveling
                 (ai/seek eid (entity/x target) (entity/y target))))
           ;; Target lost: resume wander
           (begin
             (entity/set! eid 'behavior 'wander)
             (entity/set! eid 'target #f)))))))

(big-bang
  (on-tick (lambda (state frame)
             (world/step)
             (world/each (lambda (e)
                           (cond
                             ((eq? (entity/kind e) 'flower)
                              (animate-flower e frame))
                             ((eq? (entity/kind e) 'bee)
                              (bee-brain e frame))
                             ((eq? (entity/kind e) 'dragonfly)
                              (animate-dragonfly e frame)))))
             state))
  (to-draw (lambda (state) #t)))
```

### The Dragonfly's Brain

A predator values safety (patrol when alone) and hunger (chase when prey is near).

```scheme
(define (dragonfly-brain eid frame)
  (let ((behavior (entity/get eid 'behavior))
        (target (entity/get eid 'target))
        (hunger (entity/get-set! eid 'hunger 0)))
    
    ;; Hunger grows over time
    (entity/set! eid 'hunger (+ hunger 1))
    
    (cond
      ;; If patrolling and hungry, look for prey
      ((eq? behavior 'patrol)
       (animate-dragonfly eid frame)
       (when (> hunger 300)
         (let ((prey (world/nearest eid 'bee 12.0)))
           (when prey
             (entity/set! eid 'behavior 'chase)
             (entity/set! eid 'target prey)))))
      
      ;; If chasing, pursue and check capture
      ((eq? behavior 'chase)
       (if (and target (entity/alive? target))
           (let ((dist (entity/distance eid (entity/x target) (entity/y target))))
             (ai/pursue eid target)
             (when (< dist 1.0)
               ;; Captured: eat and return to patrol
               (entity/despawn! target)
               (entity/set! eid 'hunger 0)
               (entity/set! eid 'behavior 'patrol)
               (entity/set! eid 'target #f)))
           ;; Prey lost: return to patrol
           (begin
             (entity/set! eid 'behavior 'patrol)
             (entity/set! eid 'target #f)))))))
```

### Time of Day

A `day-phase` that cycles through morning, noon, evening, night (0–1440 frames = 24 seconds at 60fps = 1 \"day\"). Lighting (paint-cell tint) and creature activity shift.

```scheme
            (row (+ y 1))))
        (loop (+ x 1))))))
```

### The Director: Environmental Response

The director (chapter 15) adjusts environmental pressure—wind strength, dragonfly spawn rate, flower growth—based on population health. If bees are thriving, spawn a second dragonfly. If they're nearly extinct, calm the wind and stop predation.

```scheme
  (let ((bee-count (group/count 'bee))
        (dragonfly-count (group/count 'dragonfly))

       (world/wind! (* 0.02 (dsin (* frame 0.005))) 0))
      
      ;; Balanced: maintain

  (on-tick (lambda (state frame)
```

;; appendix-a-bounce-coefficient-field-guide.book.slatl
;; Book of Arcade Games — Appendix A

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(appendix
  :book                "Book of Arcade Games"
  :letter              "A"
  :title               "Bounce Coefficient Field Guide"
  :dialect             "motoi"
  :audience            :kid
  :also-for            :adult
  :content-rating      :G
  :author-lane         "arcade-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"
  :training-eligible   #t
  :confidentiality     "public"
  :book-version        "1.0.0"
  :prose
"`entity/bounce! ent c` sets the restitution coefficient c. This is the
fraction of impact speed that survives a collision with the floor. This
appendix is the table you look up when you want a specific FEEL.

The number c can be any real from 0 to 1 (physical) or above 1
(nonphysical, for game effects). Below is a reference table plus tuning
notes gathered from playtest.

## The table

| c    | Feel                             | Bounces to rest | Example use             |
|------|----------------------------------|-----------------|-------------------------|
| 0.00 | Thud. Zero rebound.              | 0 (sticks)      | Sandbag, mud, wet clay  |
| 0.05 | Barely bounce. Muffled.          | 1               | Beanbag, plush toy      |
| 0.15 | Weak bounce. Soft object.        | 2               | Water balloon           |
| 0.25 | Small dead bounce.               | 3               | Wet tennis ball         |
| 0.35 | Modest bounce.                   | 4               | Old rubber ball         |
| 0.50 | Ordinary bounce.                 | 6               | Playground ball         |
| 0.65 | Springy.                         | 9               | Tennis ball (fresh)     |
| 0.75 | Lively bounce.                   | 12              | Basketball              |
| 0.85 | Very bouncy. Rubbery.            | 20              | Rubber ball, dodgeball  |
| 0.90 | Super-bouncy.                    | 30              | Super-ball              |
| 0.95 | Almost perfect. Long play.       | 50+             | Novelty super-ball      |
| 1.00 | Perfect. Never stops.            | infinite        | Physics-abstraction     |
| 1.05 | Non-physical. Gains energy.      | grows unbounded | Trampoline, chaos toy   |
| 1.20 | Very non-physical.               | wild            | Slapstick game effect   |
| 1.50 | Cartoonish. Rocket-ball.         | leaves screen   | Special effect          |

The bounce-to-rest count assumes dropping from ~200 pixels under
gravity 0.5. Adjust for other conditions.

## Why the numbers

Kinetic energy scales with velocity squared. When a bounce with
coefficient c happens, velocity multiplies by c, so energy multiplies
by c*c. After N bounces, energy is (c^2)^N of original.

For a ball to still be moving at more than 5% of original energy,
(c^2)^N > 0.05, so N < log(0.05) / log(c^2). At c=0.85, that's about
9 bounces before we're below 5%. At c=0.5, about 2. At c=0.95, about
30.

That is why 0.85 feels 'like a real ball' — it plays for about 10
bounces before settling.

## Coefficient by material

Rough real-world rebounds (single bounce onto a hard floor):

| Material        | c (approx) |
|-----------------|------------|
| Steel ball      | 0.60       |
| Marble          | 0.65       |
| Rubber ball     | 0.85       |
| Golf ball       | 0.80       |
| Baseball        | 0.55       |
| Basketball      | 0.75       |
| Water balloon   | 0.15       |
| Egg             | 0.05       |
| Super-ball      | 0.90       |
| Wet cloth       | 0.10       |

Use these when picking a c for a material-authentic feel.

## Interaction with mass and gravity

`entity/bounce!` interacts with `entity/mass!` and `world/gravity!`.

- Higher gravity → bigger impact velocity → same c means longer
  play (more bounces before energy drops below play threshold).
- Higher mass → same velocity but more momentum. Doesn't change
  bounce count, but changes what happens on collision with another
  moving entity.

If your game feels wrong at c=0.85, try tuning gravity or mass first
before adjusting c further.

## Interaction with entity/friction!

`entity/friction!` reduces horizontal velocity during floor contact.
It does not affect vertical bounce. But high friction + high bounce
= ball bounces in place, losing horizontal but not vertical speed.
Weird. Usually you want friction and bounce to LOOSELY correlate:
low bounce = high friction (soft objects); high bounce = low
friction (hard objects).

Rough pairings:

| Bounce | Friction | Effect              |
|--------|----------|---------------------|
| 0.90   | 0.02     | Super-ball feel     |
| 0.75   | 0.05     | Basketball feel     |
| 0.55   | 0.15     | Baseball feel       |
| 0.30   | 0.35     | Beanbag feel        |
| 0.05   | 0.70     | Wet cloth feel      |

## Non-physical values

Values above 1.0 GAIN energy each bounce. They violate conservation
of energy — the ball ends up moving faster than before. Uses:

- **Trampolines and springboards** — you WANT the ball to launch
  higher than the drop. Set c=1.15 to 1.30 on impact with the
  trampoline entity.
- **Slapstick physics toys** — an intentionally chaotic bouncing
  scene where the ball grows louder and wilder as it bounces.
- **Bug-hunt for young programmers** — assign c=1.05 on a ball
  and let the kid discover 'wait, why is it getting faster?' A
  first taste of conservation-of-energy.

Cap c at 1.5 to keep the sim stable. Above that, tunneling and
runaway velocity become likely.

## Common desktop task — the coin flip

A shop's 'flip a coin for a discount' uses c=0.85 for realism.
Spawn the coin at y=20 with initial vy=0. Let it fall, bounce twice,
settle. Random-y-velocity between -1 and +1 on the LAST bounce
determines heads or tails. Deterministic-looking but with the
right amount of unpredictability.

## Ten tuning stories

1. **Rain feels like glass.** You set c=0.15. Balls thud. Try 0.4.
2. **Ball never stops.** c=0.98. Realistic but boring — drop to
   0.85.
3. **Ball leaves screen.** c > 1. Non-physical; make sure that's
   intended.
4. **Ball rolls forever after bouncing.** Bounce ok; friction too
   low. Bump friction from 0 to 0.08.
5. **Playground bouncy castle.** c=0.7 on the ball, c=1.15 on the
   'castle' entity (bouncy surface adds energy). Kids leap higher
   each land.
6. **Ping-pong ball.** c=0.9, mass=0.5, drag=0.05. Balls float
   gently.
7. **Bowling ball.** c=0.05, mass=5, friction=0.2. Rolls, thuds,
   stops.
8. **Peggle-shape.** c=0.75, no floor. Balls ricochet through
   pegs.
9. **Boss-hitbox absorbs.** Boss entity c=0. Player bullets
   despawn on contact instead of bouncing back.
10. **Puddle.** Floor becomes a puddle by lowering bounce to 0.05
    and increasing friction to 0.6. Visual: replace tile sprite.

## Try this

Run this loop with c=0.05, 0.35, 0.65, 0.85, 0.95, 1.05 and observe.

```scheme
(define (bounce-demo c)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.5)
  (world/floor! 240)
  (let ((b (world/spawn 'ball 160 20)))
    (entity/bounce! b c)
    (entity/shape! b 'circle 6)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'ball (entity/x b) (entity/y b) 6 6)
       (paint-text (string-append \"c = \" (number->string c)) 10 10)))))

(big-bang (lambda () (bounce-demo 0.85)))
```

Change the 0.85. Feel it. That is the whole appendix.")

;; appendix-b-layered-collision-cookbook.book.slatl

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(appendix
  :book "Book of Arcade Games"
  :letter "B"
  :title "Layered Collision Cookbook"
  :dialect "motoi"
  :audience :kid
  :also-for :adult
  :content-rating :G
  :author-lane "arcade-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"
  :training-eligible #t
  :confidentiality "public"
  :book-version "1.0.0"
  :prose
"`collision/define-layers!` sorts entities into named bins so the
engine can skip collision checks between bins that don't need to
collide. This cuts collision cost from O(n^2) to something much
smaller AND lets you express game rules cleanly. This appendix is
the recipe file.

## The pattern

```scheme
(collision/define-layers!
 '((layer-name :collides-with (other-layer-name ...))
   ...))
(entity/layer! ent 'layer-name)
```

Every layer lists what it CAN hit. The engine looks up the pair at
collision time and skips if not in the list. Reciprocal? Not
required — 'a collides with b' can be true while 'b collides with a'
is false. But typical usage keeps them symmetric.

## Recipe 1 — Basic shmup

Player, enemy, player-bullet, enemy-bullet.

```scheme
(collision/define-layers!
 '((player       :collides-with (enemy enemy-bullet))
   (enemy        :collides-with (player player-bullet))
   (player-bullet :collides-with (enemy))
   (enemy-bullet  :collides-with (player))))
```

Rules encoded: player takes damage from enemy or enemy-bullet.
Player-bullet kills enemy. No friendly fire. No player-bullet vs
enemy-bullet (bullets pass through each other).

## Recipe 2 — Bullet-vs-bullet cancels

Same as basic, plus bullets can deflect.

```scheme
(collision/define-layers!
 '((player       :collides-with (enemy enemy-bullet))
   (enemy        :collides-with (player player-bullet))
   (player-bullet :collides-with (enemy enemy-bullet))
   (enemy-bullet  :collides-with (player player-bullet))))
```

Now bullets can destroy each other. Kids can 'shoot down' incoming
bullets. Adds a defensive layer to the shmup.

## Recipe 3 — Platformer with pickups

```scheme
(collision/define-layers!
 '((player :collides-with (ground enemy pickup))
   (ground :collides-with (player enemy))
   (enemy  :collides-with (player ground))
   (pickup :collides-with (player))))
```

Enemies walk on ground (won't fall through). Pickups don't interact
with anything except player.

## Recipe 4 — Multi-team fight

Team A vs Team B. Bullets from each team hit the other.

```scheme
(collision/define-layers!
 '((team-a          :collides-with (team-b team-b-bullet))
   (team-b          :collides-with (team-a team-a-bullet))
   (team-a-bullet   :collides-with (team-b))
   (team-b-bullet   :collides-with (team-a))))
```

## Recipe 5 — Racing (no collision between racers)

Racers pass through each other; only interact with the track and
obstacles.

```scheme
(collision/define-layers!
 '((racer    :collides-with (obstacle finish-line))
   (obstacle :collides-with (racer))
   (finish-line :collides-with (racer))))
```

## Recipe 6 — Ghost mode (temporary phase-through)

Player has an invincibility state where they pass through enemies.
Solution: two player layers.

```scheme
(collision/define-layers!
 '((player       :collides-with (enemy enemy-bullet))
   (player-ghost :collides-with ())
   (enemy        :collides-with (player player-bullet))
   (enemy-bullet :collides-with (player))
   (player-bullet :collides-with (enemy))))

;; Switch layer during ghost mode:
(entity/layer! player 'player-ghost)
;; Later, restore:
(entity/layer! player 'player)
```

## Recipe 7 — Environmental layers

Water tiles interact with sinking things; air tiles with flying.

```scheme
(collision/define-layers!
 '((swimmer :collides-with (water shore))
   (flyer   :collides-with (bird shore))
   (walker  :collides-with (shore ground))
   (water   :collides-with (swimmer))
   (bird    :collides-with (flyer))
   (shore   :collides-with (swimmer flyer walker))
   (ground  :collides-with (walker))))
```

Same physics engine; different rules for different creature types.

## Recipe 8 — Debug all-vs-all

Development-time only.

```scheme
(collision/define-layers!
 '((all :collides-with (all))))
```

Then set every entity to layer 'all. See EVERY collision. Useful
when debugging why something isn't hitting.

## Cost model

Roughly: for each entity in a layer, the engine checks against
entities in layers it can hit. With N entities across L layers with
average pair-count K, cost is O(N * K). Well-partitioned layers keep
K small; unpartitioned worlds have K ~ N and cost N^2.

At kid-scale (< 100 entities on screen), the difference is invisible
— everything runs at 60 FPS regardless. At bullet-hell scale (500+
entities), layers matter.

## Reading collisions with layers

`world/collisions` still returns all colliding pairs. Layer filtering
happens BEFORE that list is populated, not on the reading side. So
your `for-each pair` loop is unchanged; it just has fewer pairs to
walk.

## Pitfalls

**Layer defined but not attached.** You wrote the layer-alist but
forgot `entity/layer! e 'name`. Entity uses default layer, doesn't
match the alist rules. Fix: assign layer at spawn.

**Asymmetric layer definition confuses.** 'a hits b' but 'b doesn't
hit a.' The engine has to trigger the pair when EITHER side allows.
Some runtimes require reciprocity. Test both directions of any
new pair.

**All bullets vanish.** Layer for bullets doesn't include ANYTHING
in `:collides-with` list, so bullets have no collisions at all.
Include their targets.

**Layer typo silently fails.** `'plyaer` vs `'player`. The engine
may not warn. Grep your code for consistency.

## The debug-print layer helper

```scheme
(define (print-active-layers)
  (world/each 'all
              (lambda (e)
                (display (entity/kind e))
                (display \" layer: \")
                (display (entity/state e 'layer))
                (newline))))
```

Call once at setup to verify every entity landed on the layer you
intended.

## Rule of thumb

Design your layer alist first, on paper. List every entity type.
Draw arrows for who can collide with whom. Then convert to the
alist. Layer bugs are HARD to debug after the fact; easy to prevent
by drawing.")

(appendix
  :book                "Book of Arcade Games"

  :title               "The Physics Constants Sheet"
  :dialect             "motoi"
  :audience            :kid

  :author-lane         "arcade-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"
