"The one-page tune-from-here sheet. Every arcade game starts by
picking numbers for gravity, mass, friction, drag, and speed cap.
This appendix suggests values that WORK, catalogued by game type.

## world/gravity!

`world/gravity! x y` sets world acceleration in pixels/frame^2.

| Game type              | (world/gravity! x y)       | Feel               |
|------------------------|----------------------------|--------------------|
| Falling-ball demo      | (world/gravity! 0 0.5)     | Playground ball    |
| Slow-fall for aesthetic| (world/gravity! 0 0.15)    | Slow-mo, dreamy    |
| Fast-fall for tension  | (world/gravity! 0 0.9)     | Snappy, brutal     |
| Platformer default     | (world/gravity! 0 0.6)     | Standard jump      |
| Floaty platformer      | (world/gravity! 0 0.35)    | Cosmic feel        |
| Heavy platformer       | (world/gravity! 0 0.85)    | Weight, thump      |
| Space (no gravity)     | (world/gravity! 0 0)       | Frictionless drift |
| Space with attractor   | (world/gravity! 0 0)       | + world/attract!   |
| Tilted-corner rainfall | (world/gravity! 0.2 0.5)   | Sideways drift     |
| Anti-gravity (helium)  | (world/gravity! 0 -0.3)    | Balls float up     |

Rule of thumb: for a game that PRESSURES the player, gravity 0.5-0.7.
For a game that gives them TIME to react, gravity 0.3-0.4.

## entity/mass!

`entity/mass! ent m` sets mass. Default is 1. Mass affects momentum
transfer during collision. It does NOT affect fall speed in a
frictionless world (Galileo).

| Purpose                | (entity/mass! e m)   | Effect                    |
|------------------------|----------------------|---------------------------|
| Default ball           | (entity/mass! b 1)   | Standard behavior         |
| Heavy immovable target | (entity/mass! e 100) | Player pushes weakly      |
| Light bullet           | (entity/mass! b 0.1) | Doesn't disturb hits      |
| Boulder                | (entity/mass! r 5)   | Rolls with real weight    |
| Feather                | (entity/mass! f 0.3) | Wafts, easily deflected   |
| Immovable wall         | (entity/mass! w 999) | Nothing pushes it         |

## entity/friction!

`entity/friction! ent f` sets floor drag. 0 = frictionless surface;
1 = infinite friction (sticks). Actually not that binary in practice.

| Surface           | (entity/friction! e f) |
|-------------------|------------------------|
| Ice               | (entity/friction! e 0.01) |
| Wood floor        | (entity/friction! e 0.05) |
| Carpet            | (entity/friction! e 0.15) |
| Gravel            | (entity/friction! e 0.25) |
| Mud               | (entity/friction! e 0.45) |
| Molasses / glue   | (entity/friction! e 0.75) |

Ice level: friction 0.01, player slides. Grass level: friction 0.15,
player stops normally. Molasses level: friction 0.75, player crawls.
Design levels around friction as much as around geometry.

## entity/drag!

`entity/drag! ent d` sets air drag. Different from friction (which
is floor-based). Drag applies to velocity through the air.

| Purpose                | (entity/drag! e d)  | Effect             |
|------------------------|---------------------|--------------------|
| Space (no drag)        | (entity/drag! e 0)  | Coasts forever     |
| Water (heavy drag)     | (entity/drag! e 0.05)| Slows in air       |
| Underwater             | (entity/drag! e 0.15)| Very slow motion   |
| Normal air             | (entity/drag! e 0.01)| Subtle slowdown    |

For a game where the player must feel WEIGHT of decision, small drag
gives every input importance. In space games use 0.

## entity/max-speed!

`entity/max-speed! ent v` caps velocity. Prevents runaway speeds.

| Purpose             | (entity/max-speed! e v) |
|---------------------|------------------------|
| Player character    | (entity/max-speed! p 4) |
| Fast-runner powerup | (entity/max-speed! p 8) |
| Slow enemy          | (entity/max-speed! e 1) |
| Fast enemy          | (entity/max-speed! e 3) |
| Bullet              | (entity/max-speed! b 8) |
| Boss                | (entity/max-speed! b 2) |

Rule: max-speed of enemies should be < player. Otherwise no escape.
Max-speed of bullets should be > player to guarantee player must dodge.

## entity/gravity-scale!

`entity/gravity-scale! ent k` multiplies world gravity for one entity.

| Purpose                 | (entity/gravity-scale! e k) |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------|
| Default                 | (entity/gravity-scale! e 1)  |
| Bird (light)            | (entity/gravity-scale! e 0.3)|
| Heavy character         | (entity/gravity-scale! e 1.5)|
| Anti-grav               | (entity/gravity-scale! e -1) |
| Jump apex hang          | (entity/gravity-scale! e 0.5) |
| Fast fall               | (entity/gravity-scale! e 1.3) |

The chapter-7 jump uses this variably: 0.7 while rising, 0.4 near
apex, 1.2 while falling.

## The kit — starter values by game type

**Platformer starter:**
```
(world/gravity! 0 0.6)
(entity/mass! player 1)
(entity/friction! player 0.1)
(entity/max-speed! player 4)
(entity/bounce! player 0)
```

**Space shooter starter:**
```
(world/gravity! 0 0)
(entity/mass! ship 1)
(entity/drag! ship 0.01)
(entity/max-speed! ship 5)
```

**Physics puzzle starter:**
```
(world/gravity! 0 0.5)
(entity/friction! box 0.2)
(entity/mass! box 3)
(entity/bounce! box 0.15)
```

**Pinball starter:**
```
(world/gravity! 0 0.4)
(entity/mass! ball 1)
(entity/bounce! ball 0.9)
(entity/friction! ball 0.03)
(entity/max-speed! ball 12)
```

**Racing starter:**
```
(world/gravity! 0 0)   ; top-down
(entity/drag! car 0.03)
(entity/mass! car 2)
(entity/max-speed! car 8)
```

**Falling-object avoid starter:**
```
(world/gravity! 0 0.3)
(entity/gravity-scale! player 0)  ; player doesn't fall
(entity/mass! debris 1)
(entity/bounce! debris 0.2)
```

## Combining constants — the interaction matrix

Some constant pairs conflict:
- High bounce + high friction: ball bounces in place, wastes energy
  horizontally. Fix: correlate them inversely.
- Zero drag + high gravity: entities accelerate to unplayable speeds
  in seconds. Fix: add max-speed cap.
- Zero gravity + high mass: mass doesn't matter (no weight force).
  Fine — mass then only affects collision transfer.
- High gravity-scale + solid enemy: enemy accelerates into ground
  hard, bounces or squashes. Test.

## Playtest cadence

Set your constants. Play for 30 seconds. Change ONE value by ±20%.
Play again. If it's better, keep. If worse, revert. Repeat until
each knob is at its best-of-30-tests value.

Never change two knobs at once. You lose the ability to attribute
change.

## The 12-line tune loop

Here's a live-tune workbench for a bouncing ball:

```scheme
(define g 0.5)
(define b 0.85)
(define f 0.05)
(define (tune-ball)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 g)
  (world/floor! 240)
  (let ((ball (world/spawn 'ball 160 20)))
    (entity/bounce! ball b)
    (entity/friction! ball f)
    (entity/shape! ball 'circle 6)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/pressed? 'up)   (set! g (+ g 0.05)))
       (when (input/pressed? 'down) (set! g (- g 0.05)))
       (when (input/pressed? 'left) (set! b (- b 0.05)))
       (when (input/pressed? 'right)(set! b (+ b 0.05)))
       (world/gravity! 0 g)
       (entity/bounce! ball b)
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'ball (entity/x ball) (entity/y ball) 6 6)
       (paint-text (string-append \"g:\" (number->string g)
                                  \" b:\" (number->string b)) 10 10)))))
(big-bang tune-ball)
```

That is the closed-loop tune. Every physics decision in the book
comes down to numbers from this sheet.")

[book:book-of-arcade-games] [chapter:appendix-d-camera-recipes] [book-type:application]

;; appendix-d-camera-recipes.book.slatl

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(appendix
  :book "Book of Arcade Games"
  :letter "D"
  :title "Camera Recipes"
  :dialect "motoi"
  :audience :kid
  :also-for :adult
  :content-rating :G
  :author-lane "arcade-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"
  :training-eligible #t
  :confidentiality "public"
  :book-version "1.0.0"
  :prose
"Four camera verbs. Twelve recipes. Every arcade camera you'll want.

The verbs:
- `world/camera-follow! target lag dead-w dead-h` — smooth follow
- `world/camera-snap! x y` — instant reposition
- `world/camera-bounds! x y w h` — clamp to rectangle
- `world/camera-shake! magnitude decay` — screen shake
- `world/camera-pan-to x y` — scripted move
- `world/camera` — read current position

## Follow presets

### Twitchy — reflex shooter

```scheme
(world/camera-follow! player 0.5 20 20)
```

Lag factor 0.5 (half-way each frame — fast catch-up). Small deadzone
(20×20) — camera moves almost as soon as player does. Feels precise.

### Smooth — sidescroller

```scheme
(world/camera-follow! player 0.1 60 40)
```

Lag 0.1 (10% each frame — smooth) with a wider deadzone. Player can
strafe within the deadzone without moving the world.

### Cinematic — story game

```scheme
(world/camera-follow! player 0.03 100 60)
```

Very slow lag (3% each frame — 30+ frames to catch up). Huge deadzone.
Player controls a character in a mostly-static frame. Camera moves
only when they leave the pocket.

## Snap presets

### Boss-fight opener

```scheme
(world/camera-snap! boss-x boss-y)
;; Then wait 30 frames, then transition.
(world/after 30 'begin-fight #f)
```

Cinematically snap to the boss to establish presence, hold, then
resume normal follow.

### Two-player midpoint

```scheme
;; Every frame:
(world/camera-snap! (/ (+ (entity/x p1) (entity/x p2)) 2)
                    (/ (+ (entity/y p1) (entity/y p2)) 2))
```

Instant midpoint camera. Combines with dynamic bounds for a
Bounce-tracking effect.

## Bounds presets

### Sidescroller left-lock

```scheme
(world/camera-bounds! 0 0 (* level-tiles 32) 240)
```

Camera can't scroll left of x=0 or right of level width. Standard.

### Vertical shooter

```scheme
(world/camera-bounds! 0 0 320 (* level-height 32))
```

Only vertical scrolling.

### Boss arena — no exit

```scheme
;; When boss fight starts, lock camera to arena rect.
(world/camera-bounds! arena-x arena-y arena-w arena-h)
```

Player can't walk out of frame. Classic boss-arena feel.

## Shake presets

### Light hit

```scheme
(world/camera-shake! 2 0.85)
```

Two-pixel max shake, 85% decay per frame — fades in 3-4 frames.
Barely felt; used for coin pickups.

### Medium hit

```scheme
(world/camera-shake! 5 0.9)
```

Five-pixel, 90% decay. Used for enemy hit, ordinary boss hit.

### Heavy impact

```scheme
(world/camera-shake! 15 0.95)
```

Big shake, slow decay — 12-15 frames. Used for boss phase transition,
big explosion, screen bomb.

### Sustained rumble

```scheme
(world/camera-shake! 3 0.98)
```

Small magnitude, very slow decay — 30+ frames of subtle shake. Used
for approaching monster, engine rumble, earthquake ambient.

## Pan presets

### Cutscene reveal

```scheme
(world/camera-pan-to treasure-x treasure-y)
;; With additional frames-to-target if runtime supports it.
```

Camera smoothly interpolates from current to target over some number
of frames. Great for revealing a new area or event.

### Follow arrow

```scheme
;; Show player where to go by panning to it.
(world/camera-pan-to goal-x goal-y)
(world/after 60 'return-to-player #f)
```

Then return-to-player handler snaps back.

## Common desktop tasks

**Shop item spotlight.** When a customer clicks a product, briefly
pan to zoom on it with `world/camera-pan-to`. Return to grid after 3
seconds. Physics of attention.

**Notification lens.** For a new message alert, `world/camera-shake!
3 0.98` — very subtle. Enough to draw eye without disrupting.

## Camera troubleshooting

**Camera jitters at high player velocity.** Lag too high combined
with fast movement. Increase deadzone or decrease follow rate.

**Camera stops at level edge but player continues.** By design.
Bounds are limiting camera, not player. Player CAN leave the visible
area — decide if that's fine (some games) or add player bounds too.

**Two-player camera excludes P2.** Midpoint camera loses focus if
players spread. Add dynamic bounds that expand with player distance
(see chapter 15).

**Shake never stops.** Shake decay < 1.0 will always terminate.
Check that decay isn't set to 1.0 or higher.

## The debug-camera-print helper

```scheme
(define (paint-camera-info)
  (let ((cam (world/camera)))
    (paint-text (string-append \"cam: \"
                               (number->string (car cam))
                               \", \"
                               (number->string (cadr cam)))
                10 220)))
```

Add to any on-frame while debugging camera behavior. Shows exact
world position each frame. Confirm camera IS where you think.

## Camera as narrative device

Chapters 6 and 12 use camera-shake for FEEL. Chapter 8's tile world
uses camera-follow + bounds for exploration. Chapter 14's cabinet
uses camera-shake on phase transitions for weight. Chapter 15's
two-player uses snap for midpoint.

In every case, the camera is not just showing the game — it is
TELLING the player what to feel. A shake on impact says 'that hit
mattered.' A pan says 'look here.' A lag says 'take a breath.'

Compose your camera as carefully as you compose your physics.")

[book:book-of-arcade-games] [chapter:appendix-e-sprite-cell-palette] [book-type:application]

;; appendix-e-sprite-cell-palette.book.slatl

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(appendix
  :book "Book of Arcade Games"
  :letter "E"
  :title "Sprite Cell Palette"
  :dialect "motoi"
  :audience :kid
  :also-for :adult
  :content-rating :G
  :author-lane "arcade-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"
  :training-eligible #t
  :confidentiality "public"
  :book-version "1.0.0"
  :prose
"Sprites and cells are how you paint characters, enemies, coins, and
everything else that isn't a raw geometric shape. The Motoi runtime
exposes a small sprite library. This appendix covers what you can do
with what's there and how to work around what isn't.

## Verbs

- `paint-cell 'kind x y w h` — paint a named cell at world (x,y)
  with size (w,h). The runtime knows which sprite corresponds to
  'kind based on the game's sprite palette.
- `sprite/rasterize sprite` — convert a sprite to a bitmap. Used
  for pixel-precise hit detection.
- `sprite/address sprite label` — get the (x,y) offset of a named
  point on the sprite (a landmark).
- `sprite/landmarks sprite` — list all named landmarks on a sprite.

## The cell-name convention

Every `paint-cell` call takes a symbol as its first arg. That symbol
names the sprite in the runtime's palette. Conventions:

- `'player` — the main character
- `'enemy` — generic enemy
- `'boss` — boss sprite
- `'bullet` — player bullet
- `'enemy-bullet`, `'boss-bullet` — enemy fire
- `'ground`, `'wall`, `'sky`, `'grass`, `'water` — level tiles
- `'coin`, `'heart`, `'key`, `'star` — pickups
- `'ball`, `'ship`, `'paddle`, `'cannon` — arcade primitives
- `'dot`, `'spark`, `'particle` — small effects

Any symbol works; the runtime maps unknowns to a default filled
rectangle. Kids can invent names.

## Animated sprites via cell rotation

Motoi's sprite lib is small — no `sprite/anim` verb yet (see gap-3
in the architect design). To animate, cycle cell names based on
frame count.

```scheme
;; A walking character: 4 walk-cycle frames.
(define walk-cells '#('walk-0 'walk-1 'walk-2 'walk-3))
(define (paint-walker x y)
  (let ((frame (modulo (world/frame) 24)))
    (paint-cell (vector-ref walk-cells (quotient frame 6)) x y 16 24)))
```

`(quotient frame 6)` gives 0/1/2/3, changing every 6 frames.
`(modulo frame 24)` restarts the cycle every 24 frames. Six frames
per cell at 60 FPS = 100 ms per animation frame — reasonable walk
cycle speed.

For animation while stationary (idle animation), use `tick/sine`:

```scheme
;; A breathing character: subtle 2-frame idle.
(define (paint-breather x y)
  (paint-cell (if (> (tick/sine (* 0.02 (world/frame))) 0)
                  'idle-a
                  'idle-b)
              x y 16 24))
```

## Sprite landmarks — hit points

`sprite/landmarks` returns named points on a sprite. Useful for:

- Muzzle position (where a gun sprite's bullet exits)
- Head-hit-box vs body-hit-box (headshot damage bonus)
- Wheel positions (for a car sprite whose wheels rotate independently)

```scheme
;; Fire bullet from muzzle.
(let* ((muzzle (sprite/address 'ship 'muzzle))
       (mx (car muzzle))
       (my (cadr muzzle)))
  (world/spawn 'bullet (+ (entity/x ship) mx)
                       (+ (entity/y ship) my)))
```

If your sprite doesn't have named landmarks, use an offset by hand:
`(world/spawn 'bullet (entity/x ship) (- (entity/y ship) 8))`.

## Cell size vs entity shape

`entity/shape! e 'rect 16 16` sets the COLLIDER shape (for physics
math). `paint-cell 'kind x y 16 16` sets the VISUAL size. Usually
these match. But you can decouple:

- Visual bigger than collider: a large sprite with a small hit-box.
  Enemy that looks scary but is easy to hit.
- Collider bigger than visual: a small sprite with a large invisible
  hit-box. Enemy that seems small but you get damaged from further
  away.

Play with the ratio to shape difficulty.

## Palette design

For a coherent game, restrict yourself:

- One player color family (blue tones).
- One enemy color family (red tones).
- One pickup color family (yellow/gold tones).
- One environment color family (green/brown tones).

Kids can tell instantly what's what without labels. Chromatic
consistency is 90% of visual game clarity.

## Common desktop tasks

**Shop-product cells.** A shop can register each product category as
a `paint-cell 'product-name` — kids browsing see mini-sprites for
each product. Cortex holds the sprite-per-product palette.

**Custom brand sprite.** A shop's mascot appears throughout its
minigames as a `paint-cell 'shop-mascot`. Same sprite is used as
enemy, hero, or NPC depending on context.

## Pitfalls

**Sprite paints wrong.** Cell name typo. `'plyaer` vs `'player`.
Grep.

**Sprite too big / too small.** `paint-cell` sizing args (w, h)
don't match sprite artwork's native size. Try matching to native
sprite dimensions.

**Sprite doesn't rotate.** `paint-cell` doesn't currently rotate
sprites. Use `entity/pose! e 'angle rad` and hope the runtime honors
it. Otherwise render pre-rotated sprite variants (8 or 16 rotations
in the palette).

**Animation stutters.** Frame-cycle divisor too small. If you
change cells every frame at 60 FPS, animation is too fast to see.
Use `quotient frame 4` or higher.

## Sample paint routines

**Coin flip:**
```scheme
(define (paint-coin-flip x y frame)
  (paint-cell (case (modulo (quotient frame 3) 4)
                ((0) 'coin-face) ((1) 'coin-edge)
                ((2) 'coin-back) ((3) 'coin-edge))
              x y 8 8))
```

**Heart pulse:**
```scheme
(define (paint-pulsing-heart x y frame)
  (let ((size (+ 10 (round (* 2 (tick/sine (* 0.1 frame)))))))
    (paint-cell 'heart x y size size)))
```

**Enemy flash on hit:**
```scheme
(define (paint-enemy e hit-frame)
  (paint-cell (if (< (- (world/frame) hit-frame) 6)
                  'enemy-flash 'enemy)
              (entity/x e) (entity/y e) 12 12))
```

Save the frame of the hit; if within 6 frames, paint the flash
variant.

## The sprite-check tool

At game startup, verify every sprite you use is present in the
palette:

```scheme
(define (verify-sprites needed-names)
  (for-each
   (lambda (name)
     (unless (member name (sprite/landmarks name))
       (display \"WARNING: sprite \")
       (display name)
       (display \" missing\") (newline)))
   needed-names))

(verify-sprites '(player enemy coin ground wall boss))
```

Catches missing-asset bugs before the kid sees a blank rectangle.")

[book:book-of-arcade-games] [chapter:appendix-f-input-timing-windows] [book-type:application]

;; appendix-f-input-timing-windows.book.slatl

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(appendix
  :book "Book of Arcade Games"
  :letter "F"
  :title "Input Timing Windows"
  :dialect "motoi"
  :audience :kid
  :also-for :adult
  :content-rating :G
  :author-lane "arcade-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"
  :training-eligible #t
  :confidentiality "public"
  :book-version "1.0.0"
  :prose
"Feel is timing. The player perceives a game as fair when their
input has a small window of forgiveness. Impossible-to-fail feels
cheap; frame-perfect-or-die feels punishing. The sweet spot is
usually 4-10 frames of slack, invisible to conscious thought but
felt in the thumbs.

This appendix catalogs the timing windows used in real arcade games
and gives you `world/after`-based skeletons for each.

## Coyote time

After walking off a ledge, still-airborne player can jump for N
frames.

```scheme
;; 6-frame coyote time.
(define grounded? #t) (define was-grounded? #t) (define coyote 0)
(when (and was-grounded? (not grounded?)) (set! coyote 6))
(when (> coyote 0) (set! coyote (- coyote 1)))
(when (input/pressed? 'a)
  (when (or grounded? (> coyote 0))
    (entity/set-vel! p (car (entity/vel p)) -12)
    (set! coyote 0)))
(set! was-grounded? grounded?)
```

Recommended: 4-8 frames (0.07-0.13 seconds). Below 4 = harsh. Above
8 = feels like cheating.

## Jump buffer

Pressed jump before landing? Fire on land.

```scheme
;; 8-frame jump buffer.
(define buffer 0)
(when (input/pressed? 'a)
  (if grounded?
      (entity/set-vel! p (car (entity/vel p)) -12)
      (set! buffer 8)))
(when (and grounded? (> buffer 0))
  (entity/set-vel! p (car (entity/vel p)) -12)
  (set! buffer 0))
(when (> buffer 0) (set! buffer (- buffer 1)))
```

Recommended: 6-10 frames. Feels responsive without misfiring.

## Dash cancel

After a dash, N frames of immunity to certain inputs.

```scheme
(define dashing 0)
(define dash-cd 0)   ;; cooldown
(when (input/pressed? 'b)
  (when (= dash-cd 0)
    (entity/set-vel! p (* 8 heading-x) 0)
    (set! dashing 6)
    (set! dash-cd 30)))
(when (> dashing 0) (set! dashing (- dashing 1)))
(when (> dash-cd 0) (set! dash-cd (- dash-cd 1)))
```

6 frames of dash (0.1 sec), 30 frames cooldown (0.5 sec). Player
can't spam dash, but the dash itself is snappy.

## Attack window / combo timing

Chained attacks link if the next input arrives within N frames of
the previous attack's animation start.

```scheme
(define last-attack 0)
(define combo-count 0)
(when (input/pressed? 'a)
  (if (< (- (world/frame) last-attack) 30)
      (set! combo-count (+ combo-count 1))
      (set! combo-count 1))
  (set! last-attack (world/frame))
  (audio/play (case combo-count
                ((1) 'attack-1) ((2) 'attack-2) ((3) 'attack-3)
                (else 'attack-finish))))
```

30 frames = 0.5 sec. If player presses attack again within half a
second, they chain. Combo 4+ triggers finisher.

## Grace period after damage

After taking damage, player is briefly invulnerable.

```scheme
(define invuln 0)
;; On damage:
(when (and enemy-hit? (= invuln 0))
  (entity/damage! p 1)
  (set! invuln 60)   ;; 1 second invincibility
  (world/camera-shake! 5 0.9))
(when (> invuln 0) (set! invuln (- invuln 1)))
```

60 frames (1 sec) is standard 'i-frames' in fighting games. Prevents
combo death after one mistake.

## Input echo / hold detection

Distinguish a tap (short press) from a hold (long press).

```scheme
(define press-frame 0)
(define press-active? #f)
(when (input/pressed? 'a)
  (set! press-frame (world/frame))
  (set! press-active? #t))
(when (and press-active? (not (input/down? 'a)))
  ;; Just released.
  (let ((hold-duration (- (world/frame) press-frame)))
    (cond
      ((< hold-duration 6)  (do-tap))
      ((< hold-duration 30) (do-hold))
      (else                 (do-long-hold))))
  (set! press-active? #f))
```

Under 6 frames = tap. 6-30 = hold. Above = long-hold. Three
distinct actions from one button by measuring release time.

## Double-tap detection

Two taps within N frames.

```scheme
(define last-tap 0)
(when (input/pressed? 'a)
  (if (< (- (world/frame) last-tap) 15)
      (do-double-tap)
      (do-single-tap))
  (set! last-tap (world/frame)))
```

15 frames (0.25 sec) is a reasonable double-click window. Adjustable.

## Charge attack

Hold button N frames for a stronger attack.

```scheme
(define charge 0)
(when (input/down? 'a) (set! charge (+ charge 1)))
(when (and (not (input/down? 'a)) (> charge 0))
  (let ((strength (min 5 (quotient charge 20))))
    (fire-with-strength strength))
  (set! charge 0))
```

Every 20 held frames adds one strength level, capped at 5.

## Rhythm-game timing

Precise beat-locked input windows.

```scheme
;; Beat every 30 frames (2 beats/sec). Window is ±4 frames.
(define (rhythm-hit?)
  (let ((phase (modulo (world/frame) 30)))
    (or (< phase 4) (> phase 26))))

(when (input/pressed? 'a)
  (if (rhythm-hit?)
      (score-hit)
      (score-miss)))
```

4-frame window at 60 FPS = 66 ms — tight but forgiving.

## Common desktop tasks

**Long-press-to-confirm.** A shop's 'delete order' button requires
a hold to fire — prevents accidental clicks. Use hold-detection
above with `hold-duration > 60`.

**Double-click-to-fave.** A shop item can be favorited by double-
clicking. Use double-tap detection.

## Pitfalls

**Coyote fires on stairs.** Every frame the player might briefly
un-ground (stepping between tiles). Add a MINIMUM airborne-frames
check before starting coyote.

**Buffer replays after death.** Clear all input buffers on death
and respawn.

**Charge counter runs during pause menu.** Freeze charge counting
during any state that isn't 'play.

**Combo drops on ONE-frame miss.** Extend combo window by a
frame or two if playtest reveals combo drops too easily.

## The universal window sizes

Committed to memory:

- Frame-perfect (1 frame): only for expert-mode games. Bad default.
- Twitchy (2-3): responsive shooters.
- Comfortable (4-8): most action games. Default.
- Forgiving (9-15): family-friendly. Kids under 10.
- Cinematic (16+): narrative games where input is less about
  precision.

Every timing window in your game should be in one of these bands.
Playtest to pick the band for your audience.

## The one-line test

If your game feels bad, add 4 frames to your coyote and buffer
windows. Play again. Better? Keep. Worse? Revert. Almost every
feel bug is a timing window that's too tight.")

<|repo_name|>motoi-scheme<|file_sep|>scheme-books/book-of-arcade-games/appendix-g-score-combo-formulas.book.slatl
[book:book-of-arcade-games] [chapter:appendix-g-score-combo-formulas] [book-type:application]

;; appendix-g-score-combo-formulas.book.slatl

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(appendix
  :book "Book of Arcade Games"
  :letter "G"
  :title "Score, Combo, Multiplier — Formula Notebook"
  :dialect "motoi"
  :audience :kid
  :also-for :adult
  :content-rating :G
  :author-lane "arcade-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"
  :training-eligible #t
  :confidentiality "public"
  :book-version "1.0.0"
  :prose
"Score = base × combo × difficulty. That's the whole idea. This
appendix expands the shortcut into twelve variations, each drawn
from a different arcade genre.

## The base formula

```
score-per-hit = base * combo-multiplier * difficulty * bonus
```

- `base` — points per hit, varies by target
- `combo-multiplier` — starts at 1, grows with successive hits
- `difficulty` — global scale from level/mode
- `bonus` — situational: air kill bonus, perfect-timing bonus, etc.

Every scoring system in every arcade game is this formula with the
knobs turned differently.

## Variation 1 — Classic (Pac-style)

```scheme
;; Ghost worth 200. Chain 4 ghosts in one power-pill: 200/400/800/1600.
(define ghost-chain 0)
(define (eat-ghost)
  (set! ghost-chain (+ ghost-chain 1))
  (set! score (+ score (* 200 (expt 2 (- ghost-chain 1))))))
```

Powers-of-two scaling. First ghost 200, second 400, fourth 1600.
The rush of the fourth-ghost bite is exponential.

## Variation 2 — Shmup (multi-value targets)

```scheme
;; Small enemy 100; medium 300; large 800; boss 5000.
(define target-values
  '((small . 100) (medium . 300) (large . 800) (boss . 5000)))
(define (kill-target kind)
  (set! score (+ score (* (cdr (assq kind target-values)) combo))))
```

Base score varies by target kind. Combo multiplies uniformly.

## Variation 3 — Tetris-style (line-clear scaling)

```scheme
;; 1 line = 40; 2 = 100; 3 = 300; 4 = 1200. Level multiplies.
(define line-values #(0 40 100 300 1200))
(define (clear-lines n)
  (set! score (+ score (* (vector-ref line-values n) (+ level 1)))))
```

Clearing 4 at once is worth much more than 4 clears of 1. Rewards
strategic play.

## Variation 4 — Rhythm (timing-based)

```scheme
;; Perfect: 100. Great: 60. Good: 30. Miss: 0.
;; Combo grows on hits (perfect/great/good); breaks on miss.
(define (rhythm-hit rating)
  (case rating
    ((perfect) (set! combo (+ combo 1))
               (set! score (+ score (* 100 combo))))
    ((great)   (set! combo (+ combo 1))
               (set! score (+ score (* 60 combo))))
    ((good)    (set! combo (+ combo 1))
               (set! score (+ score (* 30 combo))))
    ((miss)    (set! combo 0))))
```

Combo timing precision is rewarded. Perfect chain = high score.

## Variation 5 — Fighter (damage-scaled)

```scheme
;; Damage dealt = base score. Combo counter increments per hit;
;; combo scale caps at 3.0.
(define (deal-damage dmg)
  (set! combo (+ combo 1))
  (set! score (+ score (* dmg (min 3.0 (+ 1 (* combo 0.1)))))))
```

Every hit worth its damage. Combo cap prevents infinite juggle
scoring.

## Variation 6 — Racing (time-inverse)

```scheme
;; Score = base + (max-time - your-time) * 10.
(define (finish-race your-time max-time)
  (set! score (+ 1000 (* (max 0 (- max-time your-time)) 10))))
```

Faster = higher. Base always awarded for finishing.

## Variation 7 — Puzzle (efficiency-scaled)

```scheme
;; Score = base - (moves-used * 10).
(define (solve-puzzle moves-used)
  (set! score (+ score (max 100 (- 1000 (* moves-used 10))))))
```

Fewer moves = higher score. Min score prevents shame-punishment.

## Variation 8 — Shmup with chain grazing

```scheme
;; Killing an enemy: base score. Grazing (near-miss with bullet):
;; small bonus that MULTIPLIES the next kill.
(define graze-count 0)
(define (graze-bullet)
  (set! graze-count (+ graze-count 1))
  (world/camera-shake! 1 0.9))
(define (kill-enemy)
  (set! score (+ score (* 100 (+ 1 graze-count))))
  (set! graze-count 0))
```

Style bonuses. Getting closer to death = more points if you survive.

## Variation 9 — Beat-em-up (crowd multiplier)

```scheme
;; Base + bonus per enemy currently onscreen.
(define (defeat-enemy)
  (let ((crowd (world/count 'enemy)))
    (set! score (+ score (+ 100 (* 20 crowd))))))
```

Being surrounded = worth more per kill. Rewards daring play.

## Variation 10 — Platformer (time + collectibles)

```scheme
;; End-of-level: base + time bonus + collectibles.
(define (end-level time-left coins-collected)
  (set! score (+ score
                 1000                    ;; base
                 (* time-left 10)         ;; time bonus
                 (* coins-collected 50)))) ;; collectible bonus
```

Multiple axes; player can optimize for speed OR collection.

## Variation 11 — Roguelike (streak multiplier)

```scheme
;; Streak grows each run. Dying resets it. Score at end of run =
;; run-score * streak.
(define run-streak 1)
(define (end-run alive?)
  (if alive?
      (begin (set! score (+ score (* run-score run-streak)))
             (set! run-streak (+ run-streak 1)))
      (set! run-streak 1)))
```

Persistence: winning multiple runs stacks bonuses. Dying resets.

## Variation 12 — Score attack (fixed session)

```scheme
;; Play for 3 minutes. Score all hits. No combo, no multiplier.
;; Just raw count.
(define (score-any-hit)
  (set! score (+ score 100)))
```

Simplest possible: rate * time = total. For pure-reflex practice
modes.

## Formulas with visual scaling

Display side. Bigger score = bigger text. Higher combo = larger
counter.

```scheme
(define (paint-score)
  (let ((size (min 24 (+ 12 (quotient combo 5)))))
    ;; Runtime doesn't have variable text size in the reference, so
    ;; scale via horizontal offset for prominence.
    (paint-text (string-append \"x\" (number->string combo))
                (- 300 (* 4 combo))
                (- 30 (min 20 combo)))))
```

## Display treatments — three grades of score-up feedback

### Understated
Just update the number. Fastest to render, easiest on brain.
Suitable for slow, contemplative games.

### Standard
Update number + 1-pixel camera shake. Enough to notice the hit.

### Explosive
Update number + camera shake proportional to hit value + audio ding
+ number briefly grows 20% before settling. Suitable for shmups,
rhythm games, high-arousal genres.

## Common desktop tasks

**Weekly-goal progress.** Shop owner sets a weekly sales goal. Each
sale = base score. Combo = 2× if within 5 minutes of previous. Total
displayed with mid-week celebration animations at 25%/50%/75%/100%.

**Support-response leaderboard.** Operator team scores: 1 point per
message answered, 2× combo if within 60 sec of receipt, 3× if
answered in shifts back-to-back. Rank displayed on team dashboard.

## The tuning rule

Score numbers should be memorable. Aim for a game where the top
score is a round number (10,000 or 100,000 or 1,000,000). Kids will
brag: 'I got 100k.' They don't brag: 'I got 87,431.' Round numbers
are memes.

Tune your base × combo × difficulty product to make round-number
targets ACHIEVABLE for average players and DIFFICULT to exceed.")

[book:book-of-arcade-games] [chapter:appendix-h-feel-knobs] [book-type:application]

;; appendix-h-feel-knobs.book.slatl

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(appendix
  :book "Book of Arcade Games"
  :letter "H"
  :title "The Feel Knobs"
  :dialect "motoi"
  :audience :kid
  :also-for :adult
  :content-rating :G
  :author-lane "arcade-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"
  :training-eligible #t
  :confidentiality "public"
  :book-version "1.0.0"
  :prose
"Eight knobs, A/B examples for each. Turn them one at a time until
your game feels right. Then you're done.

## Knob 1 — Acceleration

Time from zero to max speed.

**A: instant** — `(entity/set-vel! p (* dir 4) 0)` on button.
Character reaches max speed in one frame. Snappy, twitchy.

**B: eased** — accumulate over 8 frames.
```scheme
(when (input/down? 'right)
  (entity/set-vel! p (min 4 (+ (car (entity/vel p)) 0.5))
                     (cadr (entity/vel p))))
```
Character ramps to max speed. Feels weighty.

**Rule:** action shooters use A; racing sims use B.

## Knob 2 — Deceleration

Time from moving to stopped after button release.

**A: instant** — set velocity to 0 on release.
```scheme
(unless (input/down? 'right) (entity/set-vel! p 0 (cadr (entity/vel p))))
```
Feels precise.

**B: gliding** — decay to zero.
```scheme
(unless (input/down? 'right)
  (entity/set-vel! p (* 0.85 (car (entity/vel p))) (cadr (entity/vel p))))
```
Feels natural.

**Rule:** precision-platformers use A; puzzle-adventures use B.

## Knob 3 — Apex hang

Time spent at top of jump arc.

**A: symmetric** — gravity constant throughout jump. Rise and fall
take equal time.

**B: asymmetric** — `entity/gravity-scale! p 0.5` while vy is near
zero, `1.5` while falling. Hang at top, fall fast.

**Rule:** platformers benefit from B; simulation-style games from A.

## Knob 4 — Coyote time

Frames of jump-forgiveness after leaving ledge.

**A: strict** — 0 frames. Miss the jump = falling.

**B: forgiving** — 6 frames. The kid still lands the jump.

**Rule:** hardcore mode = A; family mode = B. Most games ship with B.

## Knob 5 — Jump buffer

Frames of jump-buffered-for-landing.

**A: strict** — 0 frames. Jump exactly when you land.

**B: forgiving** — 8 frames. Slight pre-press still fires.

**Rule:** always ship with B unless you're building a masocore game.

## Knob 6 — Screen shake

Magnitude scaled to impact.

**A: minimal** — `(world/camera-shake! 1 0.9)` on any hit.
Barely felt.

**B: proportional** — `(world/camera-shake! (* impact-vel 0.3) 0.85)`.
Small hits gentle; big hits BIG.

**Rule:** narrative games use A; action games use B.

## Knob 7 — Sound pitch/volume

Constant vs. variable audio per event.

**A: constant** — same `(audio/play 'hit)` for every hit.

**B: variable** — alternate `(audio/play (if (odd? hit-count) 'hit-a 'hit-b))`. Or scale by hit value.

**Rule:** repetitive events (rain, footsteps) demand B or the ear
fatigues. Unique events (boss death) can be A.

## Knob 8 — Sound volume ducking

Full-volume vs. quiet-during-dialogue.

**A: full-always** — no ducking. Everything at full.

**B: ducked-during-critical** — `(audio/master-volume 0.3)` when
game-important sound plays, restore after.

**Rule:** narrative sections benefit from B. Pure action can stay
at A.

## The tune protocol

Set all knobs to sensible starts (from chapter 6 or Appendix C).
Play the game for 30 seconds. Pick ONE knob you feel is off.
Change it by ±20%. Play again. Better? Keep. Worse? Revert.

Never adjust two knobs at once. You lose signal.

Ten sessions of this = a well-tuned game. Twenty sessions = a
great-tuned game. Fifty = shippable.

## The A/B playtest

Have a friend play your game. Watch. Don't help. Note the moment
they groan or roll their eyes. That's the knob to fix.

```
Your friend jumps.
Your friend jumps AGAIN.
Your friend groans slightly.
```

That's a jump-feel issue. Coyote time too short, buffer too short,
apex too fast. One of those three. Try adjusting each in
isolation.

## Common desktop tasks

**Shop-cursor tuning.** A shop cursor moves via input. Acceleration
knob determines whether the cursor feels 'sticky' (low) or 'floaty'
(high). Different customer segments prefer different tunings.
Consider a settings toggle: 'precise cursor' vs 'smooth cursor.'

**Notification volume.** Sound-ducking knob for notifications: quiet
when the customer is actively browsing; louder when idle. Same
`audio/master-volume` pattern.

## The eight-knob workbench

Chapter 6 shows a live workbench. Here it is in summary:

```scheme
(define knobs (vector 0.5    ; accel-per-frame
                      0.85   ; decel-factor
                      1.5    ; gravity-scale-fall
                      6      ; coyote-frames
                      8      ; buffer-frames
                      5      ; shake-magnitude-base
                      1.0    ; sound-pitch
                      1.0))  ; sound-volume
```

Wire buttons to adjust each. Play with live tuning until you find
what feels right. Then hard-code the values.

## Two rules for shipping

1. Never ship a game where the jump feels bad. Every other bug is
   forgivable; a bad jump is not.
2. Never ship a game where the score display doesn't feel good to
   watch grow. The number is the reward.

If those two are right, the rest can be rough and the game will
still play well.")

[book:book-of-arcade-games] [chapter:appendix-i-reading-world-collisions] [book-type:application]

;; appendix-i-reading-world-collisions.book.slatl

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(appendix
  :book "Book of Arcade Games"
  :letter "I"
  :title "Reading world/collisions Efficiently"
  :dialect "motoi"
  :audience :kid
  :also-for :adult
  :content-rating :G
  :author-lane "arcade-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"
  :training-eligible #t
  :confidentiality "public"
  :book-version "1.0.0"
  :prose
"`world/collisions` returns a list of colliding entity pairs each
frame. Reading it well is 90% of your collision-handling code. Reading
it badly = crashes, double-hits, missed events, and performance
cliffs.

This appendix teaches the patterns that scale.

## The naive walk

```scheme
(for-each
 (lambda (pair)
   (let ((a (car pair)) (b (cadr pair)))
     ;; handle a and b
     ))
 (world/collisions))
```

Works. Two problems:

1. The pair may appear in either order — sometimes (a=player, b=coin),
   sometimes (a=coin, b=player). You need to handle both.
2. If a and b are the same entity across multiple pairs in one frame
   (e.g. player collided with 3 coins), you handle three times.
   Usually fine, sometimes not.

## Pattern 1 — normalize order

Ensure a is always the 'lower-kind' or 'lower-id' partner.

```scheme
(define (normalize-pair pair)
  (let ((a (car pair)) (b (cadr pair)))
    (if (symbol<? (entity/kind a) (entity/kind b))
        (list a b)
        (list b a))))
```

Or by ID:
```scheme
(define (normalize-pair-by-id pair)
  (let ((a (car pair)) (b (cadr pair)))
    (if (< (entity/id a) (entity/id b))
        (list a b)
        (list b a))))
```

Then normalize each pair before dispatching. Simplifies the handler
code — you only handle one order.

## Pattern 2 — dispatch by kind

Group handlers by (kind-a, kind-b) pair.

```scheme
(define collision-handlers
  '((player   coin)  handle-player-coin
    (player   enemy) handle-player-enemy
    (bullet   enemy) handle-bullet-enemy))

(define (dispatch pair)
  (let ((k1 (entity/kind (car pair)))
        (k2 (entity/kind (cadr pair))))
    (let loop ((table collision-handlers))
      (cond
        ((null? table) #f)
        ((and (eq? (caar table) k1) (eq? (cadar table) k2))
         ((cadr table) (car pair) (cadr pair)))
        (else (loop (cddr table)))))))
```

Cleaner than nested `cond`. Every pair-kind gets exactly one handler.
Order-normalize the pair first.

## Pattern 3 — dedupe by frame

Only handle each (a-id, b-id) once per frame.

```scheme
(define handled-this-frame '())

(define (once-per-frame-handler pair)
  (let* ((a (car pair)) (b (cadr pair))
         (key (list (entity/id a) (entity/id b))))
    (unless (member key handled-this-frame)
      (set! handled-this-frame (cons key handled-this-frame))
      (dispatch pair))))

;; At end of frame:
(set! handled-this-frame '())
```

Prevents double-firing for the same collision pair (which can happen
when the runtime returns both orders).

## Pattern 4 — alive guard

Check entities are still alive before handling.

```scheme
(for-each
 (lambda (pair)
   (let ((a (car pair)) (b (cadr pair)))
     (when (and (entity/alive? a) (entity/alive? b))
       (dispatch pair))))
 (world/collisions))
```

A collision may have despawned one partner in an earlier pair this
frame. Trying to process it again = null-pointer.

## Pattern 5 — early-exit on player death

Player died; skip the rest of the frame's collisions.

```scheme
(let ((player-alive? #t))
  (for-each
   (lambda (pair)
     (when player-alive?
       (when (kind-in-pair pair 'player)
         (dispatch-player-collision pair))
       (unless (entity/alive? (find-player))
         (set! player-alive? #f))))
   (world/collisions)))
```

Prevents 'player died 5 times in one frame' bugs.

## Pattern 6 — sort by team

For many-vs-many, group collisions by team.

```scheme
(let ((team-a-hits 0) (team-b-hits 0))
  (for-each
   (lambda (pair)
     (let ((a (car pair)) (b (cadr pair)))
       (cond
         ((and (eq? (entity/team a) 'a) (eq? (entity/team b) 'b))
          (set! team-a-hits (+ team-a-hits 1)))
         ((and (eq? (entity/team a) 'b) (eq? (entity/team b) 'a))
          (set! team-b-hits (+ team-b-hits 1))))))
   (world/collisions))
  ...)
```

Tally, then apply. Prevents ordering bias.

## Pattern 7 — cost accounting

Count how many pairs your frame handles.

```scheme
(let ((count (length (world/collisions))))
  (when (> count 100)
    (display \"Warning: high collision count \")
    (display count) (newline)))
```

If count grows into the thousands, you have a layer problem — too
many entities share too permissive a layer. Split layers, or use
sensors instead of solids for pass-through cases.

## Big-O in kid terms

The runtime uses spatial hashing to keep collision cost near O(n)
in the number of ACTUAL collisions, not O(n^2) in entity count. So:

- 100 entities that don't overlap: ~100 hash lookups per frame.
  Trivial.
- 100 entities all overlapping: 100 * 100 / 2 = 5000 collision
  pairs. Might drop from 60 to 55 FPS at kid-scale hardware.
- 1000 entities with normal spread: still O(1000-ish). Fine.
- 1000 entities all overlapping: catastrophic.

The lesson: layers + sensors + smart level design (entities spread
out) matter more than iterating 'efficiently.'

## Common desktop tasks

**Duplicate-order detection.** A shop's checkout flow needs to know
if a customer clicked 'submit' twice in one second (accidental
double-buy). Same dedupe pattern as collision de-double-hit.

## Debugging with world/collisions

Print every pair for one frame to see what's actually colliding.

```scheme
(define (debug-print-collisions)
  (for-each
   (lambda (pair)
     (display (entity/kind (car pair)))
     (display \" hit \")
     (display (entity/kind (cadr pair)))
     (newline))
   (world/collisions)))
```

Call once from `on-frame` (guarded by a debug flag). See what your
world is doing. Usually reveals a layer bug or a shape-oversize bug.

## The final rule

If your collision code is more than 30 lines, it's probably wrong.
Layers + normalized dispatch + alive-guard should cover 95% of
arcade games. If you have branching per-kind with 20 arms and
nested conditionals, split it into small handlers by kind-pair.")

[book:book-of-arcade-games] [chapter:appendix-j-the-cabinet-loop] [book-type:application]

;; appendix-j-the-cabinet-loop.book.slatl

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(appendix
  :book "Book of Arcade Games"
  :letter "J"
  :title "The Cabinet: Title -> Play -> Game Over Loop"
  :dialect "motoi"
  :audience :kid
  :also-for :adult
  :content-rating :G
  :author-lane "arcade-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"
  :training-eligible #t
  :confidentiality "public"
  :book-version "1.0.0"
  :prose
"Also serves as: 'ten sample tile levels' via the ASCII format from
Chapter 8. Two things a book of arcade games can't ship without.

## Part 1 — The cabinet skeleton

Every arcade game has the same outer loop. Chapter 14 built it.
Here is the skeleton stripped of game-specific parts. Copy this
into any new game.

```scheme
(define game-state 'attract)
(define state-timer 0)

(define (transition new-state)
  (set! game-state new-state)
  (set! state-timer 0)
  (case new-state
    ((play) (init-play))))

(define (init-play)
  (world/reset!)
  ;; your game setup here
  )

(define (game-frame)
  (set! state-timer (+ state-timer 1))
  (paint-clear)
  (case game-state
    ((attract)
     (paint-attract)
     (when (input/pressed? 'a) (transition 'play)))
    ((play)
     (game-play-tick)
     (when (game-over?) (transition 'game-over)))
    ((game-over)
     (paint-game-over)
     (when (> state-timer 180) (transition 'attract)))))

(define (arcade-cabinet) (transition 'attract) (on-frame game-frame))
(big-bang arcade-cabinet)
```

Fill in `paint-attract`, `paint-game-over`, `init-play`,
`game-play-tick`, `game-over?` — you have a full cabinet. Every
game in this book fits this template.

## Part 2 — Ten sample tile levels

Chapter 8's parser maps `#` to solid tile, `.` to air, `P` to
player-spawn, `G` to goal. Here are ten levels you can run today
by dropping them into `parse-level` from chapter 8.

### Level 1 — Straight run

```
'(\"........................\"
  \"........................\"
  \"........................\"
  \"........................\"
  \"........................\"
  \"........................\"
  \"........................\"
  \"........................\"
  \"........................\"
  \"P......................G\"
  \"########################\")
```

Walk. Introduce nothing.

### Level 2 — First gap

```
'(\"........................\"
  \"........................\"
  \"........................\"
  \"........................\"
  \"........................\"
  \"........................\"
  \"........................\"
  \"........................\"
  \"........................\"
  \"P.......................G\"
  \"##########....##########\")
```

Jump a gap. First pressure.

### Level 3 — Rising steps

```
'(\"........................\"
  \"........................\"
  \"........................\"
  \"........................\"
  \"........................\"
  \".................######G\"
  \"..............####......\"
  \"...........####.........\"
  \"........####............\"
  \"P....####...............\"
  \"########################\")
```

Ascending platforms.

### Level 4 — Long jump

```
'(\"........................\"

  \"........................\"
```

Big gap; tests jump distance.

### Level 5 — Ceiling limit

```
'(\"########################\"

  \"........................\"
```

Roof over the player. Jump has a limit.

### Level 6 — Pit maze

```
  \"........................\"
```

Small dropping-through-pits pattern.

### Level 7 — Zigzag

```
  \"........................\"
  \"..####...............####\"
  \"........................\"

  \"########################\")
```

Alternating platforms.

### Level 8 — Tower

```

  \".......................#\"
  \"........................\"
  \"..................######\"
  \"........................\"
  \"..............####......\"
  \"........................\"
  \"........####............\"
  \"........................\"
  \"P...####................\"

```

Climb to a goal.

### Level 9 — Two paths

```
'(\"........................\"
  \"........................\"
  \"........................\"
  \".........####...........\"
  \"........................\"
  \"P......................G\"

  \"........................\"

```

High road or low road. Player picks.

### Level 10 — Ambition

```
'(\"...................######G\"

  \"...............####......\"
  \".............####........\"
  \"...........####..........\"

  \".......####..............\"
  \".....####................\"
  \"...####..................\"
  \"P.####...................\"
  \"##########################\")
```

Long staircase. Practice.

## Loading a level

```scheme
(define levels
  (list level-1 level-2 level-3 level-4 level-5
        level-6 level-7 level-8 level-9 level-10))

(define (load-level n)
  (parse-level (list-ref levels (- n 1))))
```

Play level 1: `(load-level 1)`. Play them in sequence in your
cabinet's game-play-tick.

## Level design principles

- Level 1 introduces the character; teach the primary control.
- Level 2 introduces the primary challenge (gap, enemy, etc).
- Levels 3-6 add one thing each: enemy, pickup, height, hazard.
- Level 7 combines two prior lessons.
- Level 8 introduces a new challenge type.
- Levels 9-10 test synthesis under time pressure.

Ten levels is a pattern-language: introduce, deepen, combine,
challenge. If your game has 40 levels, group into blocks of 10
each; each block starts fresh with a new mechanic.

## Playtest each level

Time yourself. Level 1 should be < 10 seconds. Level 10 should be
30-60 seconds. If any level takes > 2 minutes on first play, it's
too hard for its position in the sequence.

## Sharing levels

Levels are strings. Kids can text each other levels. Print, save,
paste. That's the whole distribution mechanism — no server needed.

Format lets kids read AND write. Kids invent levels by drawing
patterns; they don't need level-editor UI.

## The kid-level test

Give a level to a child. Ask them to read it aloud. If they can
say 'ground, gap, ground, spring, ground, goal,' the format works.
If they say 'a bunch of pound signs,' it doesn't.

"An arcade cabinet without an attract mode is a cabinet nobody
walks up to. When the machine is idle, a recording of the game
plays. The passer-by sees action, imagines themselves playing, drops
in a coin.

Motoi Scheme exposes tape recording and playback:

- `world/tape-record! tape-id` — start recording input to tape-id
- `world/tape-save tape-id path` — save the tape to persistent storage
- `world/tape-replay tape-id-or-path` — play the tape back
- `world/tape-stop! tape-id` — stop recording
- `world/tape-frames tape-id` — get length of recording
- `world/tape-hash tape-id` — checksum for determinism

This appendix wires tapes into an attract mode.

## Basic recording

Start a game, record inputs, save.

```scheme
(define (record-play-session)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/tape-record! 'demo)
  ;; ... your game runs, inputs are captured ...
  (world/spawn 'player 160 210)
  (on-frame
   (lambda ()
     (when (input/down? 'left) ...)
     (when (input/down? 'right) ...)
     ;; ... game logic ...
     )))

;; When done:
(world/tape-stop! 'demo)
(world/tape-save 'demo 'saved-demo)
```

Every input during recording is captured. The tape stores WHAT WAS
PRESSED WHEN, not the resulting game state.

## Playback

```scheme
(define (attract-mode)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/spawn 'player 160 210)
  ;; Same setup as recorded game.
  (world/tape-replay 'saved-demo)
  (on-frame
   (lambda ()
     ;; The tape drives input automatically.
     (world/step)
     (paint-clear)
     (world/each 'player
                 (lambda (p)
                   (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 8 8))))))
```

During replay, `input/down?` and `input/pressed?` return the
recorded values instead of live inputs. Same game, same outcomes,
no player needed.

## Wiring into the cabinet

Chapter 14's cabinet had attract → title → play → game-over →
attract. Now populate attract with tape playback.

```scheme
(define game-state 'attract)
(define state-timer 0)

(define (transition new-state)
  (set! game-state new-state)
  (set! state-timer 0)
  (case new-state
    ((attract)
     (world/reset!)
     (world/tape-replay 'saved-demo))
    ((play)
     (world/reset!)
     (world/tape-record! 'current-play)
     (init-play))))

(define (game-frame)
  (set! state-timer (+ state-timer 1))
  (case game-state
    ((attract)
     ;; Watch the demo. Real-player button press interrupts.
     (game-step-and-paint)
     (when (input/pressed? 'a)     ;; Real player input
       (transition 'play)))
    ((play)
     (game-step-and-paint)
     (when (game-over?)
       (world/tape-stop! 'current-play)
       ;; Optionally: overwrite the demo with this session if score > threshold.
       (when (> current-score demo-threshold)
         (world/tape-save 'current-play 'saved-demo))
       (transition 'game-over)))
    ((game-over)
     (paint-game-over-screen)
     (when (> state-timer 180) (transition 'attract)))))
```

**Nice property:** the attract-mode demo automatically UPGRADES over
time. Every session that scores higher than the previous demo
replaces it. Kids see progressively better demos. The machine
learns to advertise itself.

## Determinism concerns

Tape replay works cleanly only if game outcomes are DETERMINISTIC —
same inputs, same seed → same result. Sources of nondeterminism:

- `world/hash` returns a pseudo-random each call. Seed it at level
  start with the tape's own seed so replay reproduces.
- Frame timing variance in the runtime. Usually the runtime
  handles this — replay locks to logical-frame count, not
  wallclock.
- Cortex writes to persistent storage. If a demo writes, on replay
  it writes again. Guard writes with a `(replay?)` predicate.

## Handling nondeterminism

```scheme
(define (replay-active?)
  (world/tape-frames 'saved-demo) 0)  ; > 0 if replay in progress

(when (input/pressed? 'a)
  (unless (replay-active?)
    (cortex/write 'session-score current-score)))
```

Only write during live play, not during replay.

## Verifying deterministic replay

`world/tape-hash` returns a checksum of world state at each frame.
Compare across runs.

```scheme
(define (checksum-after-frames n)
  (let loop ((i 0))
    (when (< i n) (world/step) (loop (+ i 1))))
  (world/tape-hash 'current-play))

;; Record.
(world/tape-record! 'test)
(let ((hash1 (checksum-after-frames 60)))
  (world/tape-stop! 'test)
  (world/tape-save 'test 'saved)
  ;; Replay.
  (world/reset!)
  (world/tape-replay 'saved)
  (let ((hash2 (checksum-after-frames 60)))
    (if (equal? hash1 hash2)
        (display \"Determinism OK\")
        (display \"Determinism BROKEN\"))))
```

Fails? Find the nondeterministic call and seed it.

## Two-tape shuffle

Store two demos and alternate between them for variety.

```scheme
(define demo-index 0)
(define demos '(saved-demo-1 saved-demo-2))

(define (start-attract)
  (world/tape-replay (list-ref demos demo-index))
  (set! demo-index (modulo (+ demo-index 1) (length demos))))
```

Every attract cycle, next demo. Passers-by see fresh action.

## Common desktop tasks

**Shop tour recorder.** A shop can record its owner's 'ideal tour'
of the product catalog. New visitors see an auto-tour on landing.
Same tape mechanism.

**Onboarding replay.** A new user's first session is recorded. They
can replay it later to see their own progress.

**Bug-report tapes.** When a user reports a bug, ask them to
record the session. The tape reproduces the exact issue for the
developer. Better than 'it happened once, I can't remember what I
did.'

## Pitfalls

**Tape includes real-life pauses.** If the recording paused for
tea, the replay pauses for tea. Use tape-editing (not always
exposed by runtime) or record shorter sessions.

**Replay diverges after N seconds.** Nondeterminism sneaked in.
Debug with `world/tape-hash` checkpoints.

**Tape file huge.** Long sessions can produce large tapes. Cap
recording at 60 seconds for attract mode. Or record only
'interesting' segments.

**Real-player input during replay.** Chapter 14 handles this:
`input/pressed? 'a` from a REAL player interrupts and transitions
to 'play. Otherwise you'd have both replayed and live inputs
fighting each other.

## The 30-second attract loop

Cabinet defaults:

```scheme
(define attract-max-frames (* 60 30))  ; 30 seconds

((eq? game-state 'attract)
 (game-step-and-paint)
 (when (or (input/pressed? 'a) (> state-timer attract-max-frames))
   (if (input/pressed? 'a) (transition 'play) (transition 'title))))
```

30 seconds is the sweet spot: long enough to convey the game,
short enough that a bored bystander sees the loop restart. Then
title screen for 5 seconds. Then attract again.

## Legendary tapes

If you record a player crushing your game (say, 100k+ score), save
that tape as a 'legendary demo' and play it occasionally. Kids
LOVE seeing extraordinary play. Motivates them to try harder.

Save with:
```scheme
(when (> current-score 100000)
  (world/tape-save 'current-play (string->symbol
                                  (string-append \"legend-\"
                                                 (number->string current-score)))))
```

Load a random legendary demo:
```scheme
(let ((legend-tapes (cortex/read 'legend-tapes)))
  (when (pair? legend-tapes)
    (world/tape-replay (list-ref legend-tapes
                                 (modulo (world/hash) (length legend-tapes))))))
```

The game becomes its own museum.")

## 7. Coin-grab (chapter 11)

```scheme
(define sc 0)
(define (coin-grab)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 160 120)))
    (entity/shape! p 'triangle 8) (entity/solid! p #t)
    (let loop ((i 0))
      (when (< i 20)
        (let ((c (world/spawn 'coin (modulo (* i 47) 300)
                              (modulo (* i 71) 200))))
          (entity/shape! c 'circle 5) (entity/sensor! c #t))
        (loop (+ i 1))))

       (when (input/down? 'down)  (entity/move! p 0 3))

       (paint-clear)
       (world/each 'coin (lambda (c) (paint-cell 'coin (entity/x c) (entity/y c) 5 5)))
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 8 8)
```

## Move-and-stop compositions — 6 micro-games (added 2026-07-18)

The twelve games above teach one thing each. This next set teaches
**compositional constraint** — how to hold TWO game rules at once
(move AND stop, spawn AND despawn, animate AND halt). Each example
below is under 30 lines and uses only CORE verbs.

The pattern is uniform: name each constraint, pick the verb for
each, compose them in `on-frame`, verify each constraint independently.

### 13. Move right, stop at edge

Sprite moves right at a constant velocity, then stops when its x
coordinate reaches the right edge of the world.

```scheme
(define (move-stop-right)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 20 120))
        (right-edge 300))
    (entity/shape! p 'rect 12 12)
    (entity/set-vel! p 2 0)         ;; constraint 1: moving right
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (world/step)
       (when (>= (entity/x p) right-edge)   ;; constraint 2: stop at edge
         (entity/set-vel! p 0 0))
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 12 12)))))
(big-bang move-stop-right)
```

Two constraints, held together every frame. Constraint 1: keep
moving. Constraint 2: if we've reached the edge, stop. Both are
checked every tick. Neither drifts.

### 14. Move while key held, stop when released

Sprite moves right ONLY while the right arrow key is held. Releasing
stops it. Uses `input/down?` for held-key detection.

```scheme
(define (move-while-held)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 160 120)))
    (entity/shape! p 'rect 12 12)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (cond
         ((input/down? 'right) (entity/set-vel! p 3 0))   ;; constraint 1: right held
         ((input/down? 'left)  (entity/set-vel! p -3 0))  ;; also left held
         (else                 (entity/set-vel! p 0 0)))  ;; constraint 2: none held → stop
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 12 12)))))
(big-bang move-while-held)
```

The `cond` holds both constraints. If a directional key is down, set
matching velocity. If no key is down (else), zero the velocity. The
sprite stops the frame you release the key.

### 15. Ball rolls, hits wall, stops

Ball starts with velocity, gravity pulls it down, and the world
floor stops its fall. Uses `world/floor!` for the stop-condition.

```scheme
(define (roll-and-stop)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.4)
  (world/floor! 220)                       ;; constraint 2: stop at floor
  (let ((b (world/spawn 'ball 30 30)))
    (entity/shape! b 'circle 6)
    (entity/bounce! b 0)                    ;; no bounce; hits and stops
    (entity/set-vel! b 3 0)                 ;; constraint 1: rolling right
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'ball (entity/x b) (entity/y b) 6 6)))))
(big-bang roll-and-stop)
```

Gravity pulls it down. Rightward velocity moves it sideways. The
floor at y=220 stops downward motion. Bounce coefficient of 0 means
it does not rebound. Two-axis constraint composition, three verbs.

### 16. Thrust and drift, stop when button released

Ship thrusts forward while a button is held; releasing does NOT
instantly stop it (thrust decays through drag). Introduces
`entity/drag!` as the natural decay verb.

```scheme
(define (thrust-drift-stop)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((s (world/spawn 'ship 20 120)))
    (entity/shape! s 'triangle 8)
    (entity/drag! s 0.02)                    ;; constraint 3: friction slows drift
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'a)                ;; constraint 1: thrust while held
         (let ((vx (car (entity/vel s))))
           (entity/set-vel! s (+ vx 0.15) (cadr (entity/vel s)))))
       ;; constraint 2: no explicit stop — drag brings velocity to zero
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'ship (entity/x s) (entity/y s) 8 8)))))
(big-bang thrust-drift-stop)
```

Three constraints layered. Hold 'a' to accelerate. Release and drag
gradually reduces velocity toward zero. No hard-stop — the physics
itself is the halting mechanism.

### 17. Glide to click, stop when arrived

Player character moves smoothly toward a target point set by mouse
click, and stops when it arrives. Uses `motion/move-to` and a
distance check.

```scheme
(define target-x 160)
(define target-y 120)
(define (glide-to-target)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'hero 20 200)))
    (entity/shape! p 'rect 12 12)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)              ;; constraint 1: pick a new target
         (set! target-x (+ 20 (modulo (world/hash) 280)))
         (set! target-y (+ 20 (modulo (world/hash) 200))))
       (motion/move-to p target-x target-y 2) ;; constraint 2: glide toward it
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'target target-x target-y 4 4)
       (paint-cell 'hero (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 12 12)))))
(big-bang glide-to-target)
```

`motion/move-to` is the built-in stop-when-arrived primitive.
Constraint 2 is expressed in a single verb call. Once the sprite is
within one step of the target, `motion/move-to` sets velocity to
zero automatically.

### 18. Enemy patrols between two walls

Enemy oscillates between two x-values, reversing direction each time
it hits a bound. Two constraints: reverse-at-left, reverse-at-right,
both checked every frame.

```scheme
(define (patrol)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((e (world/spawn 'guard 100 120))
        (left-edge 60) (right-edge 260))
    (entity/shape! e 'rect 12 12)
    (entity/set-vel! e 1.5 0)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (world/step)
       (let ((x (entity/x e))
             (vx (car (entity/vel e))))
         (cond
           ((and (<= x left-edge)  (< vx 0))   ;; constraint 1: left bound reached
            (entity/set-vel! e (- vx) 0))
           ((and (>= x right-edge) (> vx 0))   ;; constraint 2: right bound reached
            (entity/set-vel! e (- vx) 0))))
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'guard (entity/x e) (entity/y e) 12 12)))))
(big-bang patrol)
```

Two symmetric constraints. When the guard is at or past the left
edge AND moving left, flip velocity. When at or past the right edge
AND moving right, flip. The AND-with-direction check prevents the
guard from getting stuck at an edge with velocity pushing it back
into the wall.

---

### The pattern: read the prompt, don't drift

Every one of these six games follows the same authoring shape:

1. **Name each constraint.** 'Move right' + 'stop at edge' = two
   constraints. Write them down before you pick verbs.
2. **Pick the verb for each constraint.** `entity/set-vel!` for
   'move.' `entity/x` compared to `right-edge` for 'stop when past
   x=N.' One verb per constraint when possible.
3. **Compose in `on-frame`.** The frame loop is where both
   constraints are checked every tick. Neither drifts because both
   are re-evaluated 60 times a second.
4. **Verify each constraint independently.** Temporarily comment out
   the stop-condition and confirm the sprite moves. Temporarily set
   the velocity to zero and confirm the stop-condition would fire.
   If each works alone, they work together.

If your code starts using verbs you didn't intend — `ai/wander`
instead of `entity/set-vel!` when the prompt said 'move right,' say
— that's DRIFT. Stop, re-read the prompt, restart. The verbs you
need are always the smallest verbs that name the constraint.

See book-of-composition Chapter 16 for the meta-pattern in more
detail. See book-of-scheme Appendix D for the 'move-until-condition'
pattern entry.")

(chapter
  :book             "Book of Arcade Games"
  :chapter-number   null

  :source-path      "authored/2026-07-17/book-fill-lane"
  :status           "book-fill-authored-2026-07-17"
  :audience         "hobbyist + kid"
  :dialect          "motoi"
  :training-eligible true
  :confidentiality "public"
  :prose
"# Appendix — The Verbs Cookbook

Entity-registry verbs — the small crew that manages the collection of live entities as a whole rather than one at a time. Every example verified against `bin/motoi eval`.

---

## Enumerate: `entity/all`

Returns the list of every live entity's id, in creation order. Nullary. Handy for iterating over the world when you need to do something to *every* entity — draw them all, tick them all, count them by kind.

```scheme
(entity/all)                                                     ; => ()
(begin (entity/make 'p1 10 20) (entity/all))                     ; => (\"p1\")
(begin (entity/make 'a 0 0) (entity/make 'b 10 10) (entity/all)) ; => (\"a\" \"b\")
```

Ids are strings. When you call `entity/spawn` (which auto-generates the id) they look like `\"e1\"`, `\"e2\"`; when you call `entity/make` (which takes an explicit id-as-symbol) they preserve the symbol's name as a string. Either way `entity/all` gives you back the strings.

---

## Scratch storage: `entity/ref`

Every entity carries a *scratch map* — a per-entity key/value store for whatever data you want to attach without extending the physics record. `entity/ref id key` reads a value; `entity/set!` (already in the base chapters) writes one. Missing keys return the special symbol `'nan` so a null return does not collide with a legitimate `#f` value.

```scheme
(begin (entity/make 'p1 10 20)
       (entity/set! 'p1 'hp 3)
       (entity/ref 'p1 'hp))
; => 3

(begin (entity/make 'p1 10 20)
       (entity/ref 'p1 'nothing))
; => nan
```

Use scratch for anything the built-in physics does not model — hit points, ammo counts, dialogue state, the entity's favourite colour. Anything a two-line game needs but the shared entity record should not.

---

## Removal: `entity/remove!`

Deletes an entity from the registry. Returns `#t` if the entity existed and got removed, `#f` if the id was already gone or never valid. `entity/remove!` is a *destructive* alias of `entity/despawn!` — same effect, shorter name for people who prefer the register/remove pairing.

```scheme
(begin (entity/make 'p1 10 20)
       (entity/remove! 'p1)
       (entity/all))
; => ()

(entity/remove! 'nonexistent)          ; => #f
```

After removal the id is free — a future `entity/make 'p1 ...` would create a fresh entity under the same name, with no state carried over from the removed one.

---

## Tag removal: `entity/untag!`

`entity/untag! id tag` removes a tag from an entity. Returns `#t` if the tag existed and got removed, `#f` if it was not present. Entities created via `entity/spawn` are auto-tagged with their kind, so you can un-tag them by kind name.

```scheme
(begin (entity/spawn 'hero)
       (entity/untag! \"e1\" 'hero))
; => #t

(entity/untag! \"never-existed\" 'anything)
; => #f
```

Use it when a stateful entity outgrows its group — the pickup that became a projectile, the enemy that turned friendly.

---

## Closing note

Every example in this appendix was checked against `bin/motoi eval` on 2026-07-17. Entity ids are strings once they land in the registry, regardless of whether they came in as symbols.
")

(chapter
