  :chapter-number      1
  :title               "The Bouncing Ball"
  :dialect             "motoi"
  :audience            :kid
  :also-for            :adult
  :content-rating      :G
  :author-lane         "arcade-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"
  :training-eligible   #t
  :confidentiality     "public"
  :voice               "sakura-teaching + game-design"
  :book-version        "1.0.0"
  :draws-from-preserved (:book "book-of-games-preserved" :ch 12)
  :provenance          ((:source-path "arcade-games-engineer-lane")
                        (:authored-by "Engineer")
                        (:date "2026-07-16"))
  :prose
"Before there were graphics cards there was a dot on an oscilloscope, and
before there were dots there was an equation. `y = y0 + v*t + 0.5*a*t*t`.
Newton wrote it down; a Cambridge student pointed a beam at a phosphor
screen; a bored technician noticed that if you added a floor and flipped
the sign of velocity on contact, the dot bounced. That is not a myth.
That is 1958, and it was called Tennis for Two, and it played on an
analog computer at a Long Island lab open house.

Every arcade game descends from that dot. Break out its rules and you get
the whole family. Add a paddle, you have Pong. Add many bricks, you have
Breakout. Rotate the coordinate system ninety degrees and add a cannon
shell, you have Space Invaders. But the parent of all of them is one
sprite falling under gravity and rebounding off a floor.

This chapter builds that parent. One entity. One law. One floor. By the
end you will have written a rainstorm that piles into a corner because
you clicked there, and you will understand the bounce coefficient as
'how much speed survives the wall.' That is enough physics to carry you
through the next fifteen chapters.

---

## 1.1 The smallest possible game

```scheme
;; A single dot falls under gravity and settles on the floor.
(define (drop-one-dot)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.5)          ;; pull down 0.5 px/frame^2
  (world/floor! 240)              ;; floor at y = 240
  (let ((dot (world/spawn 'dot 160 40)))
    (entity/bounce! dot 0.0)      ;; no bounce — thud
    (let loop ((n 60))
      (world/step)
      (if (> n 0)
          (loop (- n 1))
          (entity/y dot)))))

(drop-one-dot)
;; => 240.0
```

That is a game. Not a fun game, but a game. There is a rule (gravity),
a boundary (floor), a subject (dot), and a resolution (dot rests at 240).
Everything else in this book adds detail to those four elements.

`world/reset!` clears any prior entities. `world/gravity! 0 0.5` sets a
world-wide acceleration of 0.5 pixels-per-frame-squared, straight down.
The zero is the x-component; gravity in most arcade games is
axis-aligned. `world/floor! 240` says 'no entity may have y greater than
240.' The engine enforces that after motion every step.

`world/spawn 'dot 160 40` puts a new entity at x=160, y=40 with the tag
'dot. `entity/bounce! dot 0.0` sets its restitution to zero — when it
hits the floor, all vertical speed is absorbed. The `let loop` idiom is
Scheme's named-let: a helper called `loop` that we immediately call with
`(loop 60)`, meaning 'run this body 60 times.'

Every game in this book is a variation on this shape.

---

## 1.2 Let it bounce

Change one number. Change the meaning of the whole scene.

```scheme
;; Same fall, but the dot bounces most of its speed back.
(define (bouncing-dot)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.5)
  (world/floor! 240)
  (let ((ball (world/spawn 'ball 160 40)))
    (entity/bounce! ball 0.85)    ;; keep 85% of impact speed
    (let loop ((n 200))
      (world/step)
      (if (> n 0)
          (loop (- n 1))
          (entity/y ball)))))

(bouncing-dot)
```

At bounce 0.85, the ball rebounds strongly the first time, less strongly
the second, less still the third, and so on. Each impact loses fifteen
percent of its speed. The bounce heights form a decaying series: 200
first, 145 second, 105 third. The ratio between successive peaks is the
bounce coefficient squared (0.85 * 0.85 = 0.72), because each bounce
loses (1 - bounce^2) fraction of energy — the ball's kinetic energy
scales with velocity squared.

That is not trivia. If you want a super-ball, set bounce close to 1. If
you want a heavy sandbag, set bounce to 0. If you want realistic rubber,
0.7 to 0.85. If you want a sad thump, 0.2. Appendix A tabulates the
whole spectrum with predicted behavior; if you want a specific feel,
open the appendix, pick a number, come back.

---

## 1.3 Watch it fall

We are running the physics but we cannot see it. That is the missing
half of a game. Add the paint loop.

```scheme
;; A visible bouncing ball. Run this to see a game, not just numbers.
(define (visible-bouncing-ball)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.5)
  (world/floor! 240)
  (let ((ball (world/spawn 'ball 160 40)))
    (entity/bounce! ball 0.85)
    (entity/shape! ball 'circle 8)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'ball (entity/x ball) (entity/y ball) 8 8)))))

(big-bang visible-bouncing-ball)
```

`entity/shape! ball 'circle 8` gives the ball a visible shape — a circle
of radius 8. `on-frame` registers a callback the runtime calls sixty
times a second. Every callback: step the world, clear the screen, paint
the ball at its current position. `big-bang` starts the runtime with
the initial function.

The `paint-clear` and `paint-cell` calls are what game programmers call
the DRAW loop. The `world/step` call is the UPDATE loop. The `on-frame`
callback packages them together into the ORCHESTRATION.

Which brings us to the four patterns.

---

## 1.4 The four patterns, right now

Every game in this book uses four architectural patterns. This chapter
shows them at their smallest.

**Composition.** The ball is not one thing. It is a shape plus a bounce
coefficient plus a position plus a velocity plus a tag. We compose those
attributes onto one entity with `entity/shape!`, `entity/bounce!`, and
the initial args to `world/spawn`. Later chapters compose more: mass,
friction, drag, gravity-scale, sensor flag, collision layer. Composition
is how a raw entity becomes a character.

**Orchestration.** The frame loop is an orchestration of update, draw,
poll — the classic game triangle. `on-frame` runs at 60Hz; each tick
we call `world/step` (update), `paint-clear` and `paint-cell` (draw),
and later we will add `input/pressed?` (poll). Order matters: update
before draw, or the drawn frame lags reality. Poll before update, or
input gets delayed by one frame. Chapter 6 formalizes this ordering as
FEEL; here you are living it without naming it.

**In-routing.** In this chapter there is no user input, so no in-route.
Chapter 2 adds it: a key-press routes to a paddle handler. For now, the
only 'incoming event' is the frame tick itself, which routes to the
`on-frame` callback.

**Routing.** Draw calls route to the framebuffer. That routing is
implicit — `paint-cell` knows where to send its pixels. When we add
sound in later chapters, `audio/play` will route to the audio driver.
When we add scoring, `cortex/write` will route the score to persistent
memory. Every action-verb the game emits routes somewhere.

Every subsequent chapter will name these four when they appear. That is
not padding. Those four patterns are the whole shape of how any
interactive program works, arcade or otherwise. If a kid finishes this
book, they carry those patterns into anything else they build.

---

## 1.5 Rain

One ball is a lesson. Thirty balls is a scene.

```scheme
;; A rainstorm of 30 balls, dropped from random x-positions.
(define (rainstorm)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.5)
  (world/floor! 240)
  (let ((points (map (lambda (i)
                       (list (+ 20 (* i 10)) 20))
                     (iota 30))))
    (scene/spawn-many 'ball points)
    (world/each 'ball
                (lambda (b)
                  (entity/bounce! b 0.7)
                  (entity/shape! b 'circle 6)))
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (world/each 'ball
                   (lambda (b)
                     (paint-cell 'ball (entity/x b) (entity/y b) 6 6)))))))

(big-bang rainstorm)
```

`iota 30` builds the list `(0 1 2 ... 29)`. The `map` turns each into a
starting position `(x y)`. `scene/spawn-many` takes a tag and a
point-list and creates one entity per point. `world/each` iterates every
entity carrying the given tag; we use it twice — once to configure
bounce and shape on each ball at setup, and once inside the frame loop
to paint them all.

Run this and you see rain. Thirty dots fall from a line at the top,
bounce with a satisfying decay, and settle into a rough heap along the
floor. There is no game here — no goal, no score — but there is
motion, and motion at scale is the first fun a computer can give you.

---

## 1.6 Rain you cause

Add input. Now the rain comes from where you click.

```scheme
;; Click anywhere: a ball drops from that spot.
(define (rain-on-command)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.5)
  (world/floor! 240)
  (on-frame
   (lambda ()
     (world/step)
     ;; If the space bar was pressed this frame, spawn a ball at the
     ;; cursor. (We use the space bar because Motoi's input model is
     ;; 6-button digital — click is 'a', hold is 'a' pressed, etc.)
     (when (input/pressed? 'a)
       (let ((b (world/spawn 'ball 160 20)))
         (entity/bounce! b 0.75)
         (entity/shape! b 'circle 5)))
     (paint-clear)
     (world/each 'ball
                 (lambda (b)
                   (paint-cell 'ball (entity/x b) (entity/y b) 5 5))))))

(big-bang rain-on-command)
```

This one is a game. Not because it has a win state, but because the
player CAUSES the physics. Every press of the 'a' button adds another
ball. The heap grows. The kid discovers, in about ten seconds, that if
they hold 'a' down (which registers as pressed on the first frame only),
they get exactly one ball per press — hammer 'a' and you make it rain.

This is the first time the game listens to the player. `input/pressed?
'a` returns true on the frame the button changed from up to down. That
is the in-routing pattern from section 1.4: an incoming event (button
press) routes to a handler (spawn a ball). The event source is the
input driver, invisible to us; the handler is our `when` clause. The
router is the runtime, which polled the button on our behalf before
calling `on-frame`.

If you wanted the ball to spawn at the cursor rather than at x=160, you
would poll `input/buttons` for a pointer position, or wire an on-touch
callback in a later chapter. For now, one spawn point is enough for
one lesson.

---

## 1.7 Corner physics

Same rainstorm, one extra rule: gravity is not vertical. Tilt it.

```scheme
;; Gravity tilted so balls pile into the bottom-right corner.
(define (corner-rain)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0.2 0.5)        ;; x-component + y-component
  (world/floor! 240)
  (let ((points (map (lambda (i)
                       (list (+ 20 (* i 8)) 20))
                     (iota 40))))
    (scene/spawn-many 'ball points)
    (world/each 'ball
                (lambda (b)
                  (entity/bounce! b 0.6)
                  (entity/friction! b 0.1)
                  (entity/shape! b 'circle 5))))
  (on-frame
   (lambda ()
     (world/step)
     (paint-clear)
     (world/each 'ball
                 (lambda (b)
                   (paint-cell 'ball (entity/x b) (entity/y b) 5 5))))))

(big-bang corner-rain)
```

`world/gravity! 0.2 0.5` sets acceleration slightly to the right AND
down. Balls fall and drift. `entity/friction! b 0.1` gives each ball
some floor-drag so it does not slide forever after landing. The whole
scene settles into a heap at the bottom-right of the screen.

Try flipping the sign: `world/gravity! -0.2 0.5` piles at bottom-left.
Try setting the y-component negative: `world/gravity! 0 -0.3` and
watch the balls float up like helium. This is the gift of a physics
engine — one number changes and the whole world changes with it.

---

## 1.8 A small game — pile in the corner

Now put a goal on it.

```scheme
;; Click to spawn a ball. Try to pile 10 balls in the bottom-right
;; corner (x > 260, y > 220) within 5 seconds.
(define (pile-challenge)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0.2 0.5)
  (world/floor! 240)
  (let ((start-frame (world/frame)))
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (world/step)
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)
         (let ((b (world/spawn 'ball 160 20)))
           (entity/bounce! b 0.5)
           (entity/friction! b 0.1)
           (entity/shape! b 'circle 5)))
       (paint-clear)
       (world/each 'ball
                   (lambda (b)
                     (paint-cell 'ball (entity/x b) (entity/y b) 5 5)))
       ;; Count balls in the target corner.
       (let ((in-corner 0))
         (world/each 'ball
                     (lambda (b)
                       (when (and (> (entity/x b) 260)
                                  (> (entity/y b) 220))
                         (set! in-corner (+ in-corner 1)))))
         (paint-text (string-append \"Corner: \" (number->string in-corner))
                     10 10)
         (when (>= in-corner 10)
           (paint-text \"YOU WIN!\" 120 120)))))))

(big-bang pile-challenge)
```

Five ingredients — gravity, floor, spawn on input, tag-filtered
iteration, and a win predicate — combine into a game with a goal. The
goal-check is a routing decision: read the world state, decide if it
matches the win condition, route to a paint of 'YOU WIN.' Later chapters
will route that same decision to a scoreboard, a sound, a new level.

Note the shape of the win-check. We initialize a counter to zero, walk
every 'ball entity with `world/each`, increment on match. That is
`fold` without saying `fold`. (The reference-level `fold` verb is
unimplemented at this book version; when it lands, section 1.6 will
teach it. For now, the mutable-counter idiom works and is honest.)

---

## 1.9 Common desktop tasks

An operator running a shop can drop this ball-physics into a real
customer interaction. Two patterns you will actually see:

**The flip-the-coin unlock.** A shop wants to reward the kid who scrolls
to the bottom of the item listing with a 5% discount. Insert a small
game: a coin (a ball with `entity/bounce! coin 0.9`) drops from the
top; the shopper taps to flip it; if it lands heads (a random-int check
on landing frame), the discount unlocks and the shop's Cortex writes
`(cortex/write 'discount-earned #t)`.

**The bounce-a-ball checkout treat.** After a shopper hits 'buy,' show a
30-second rainstorm with the shop's brand color, one ball per item they
bought. If they bought fifteen items, fifteen balls rain. The rain is
the receipt. Physics as decoration is decoration you cannot fake with
a static image.

Both patterns use only what this chapter covers. No new verbs. The point
of the arcade book is not that you write only arcade games — it is
that arcade primitives ARE the building blocks of any interactive
surface.

---

## 1.10 Pitfalls

**The ball falls through the floor.** You forgot `world/floor!`, or you
set it above the ball's spawn y. The ball has no floor to hit; it
falls forever.

**The ball never stops.** Set `entity/bounce!` to something less than 1.
At exactly 1, no energy is lost and the ball bounces forever. Real
rubber is around 0.7 to 0.85; a super-ball is 0.9 to 0.95. Above 1 is
non-physical and worlds get unstable — but if you WANT chaos, try
`(entity/bounce! ball 1.05)` for one run and watch the ball leave the
top of the screen.

**Nothing paints.** You forgot `entity/shape!`. Without a shape, the
entity exists but has no visual. Or you forgot `paint-clear` — old
paint from the previous frame is still there and you get a smear
instead of a moving ball. That smear can be a feature — see chapter 9
for parallax and trails.

**The rainstorm is slow.** Fifty entities is fine; five thousand may
strain the runtime. Chapter 5 introduces entity pooling for high
counts. For chapter 1, cap yourself at a hundred.

**The `iota` call errors.** `iota` is in the standard Scheme library
and should be available. If your runtime version does not have it,
build it with `(define (iota n) (let loop ((i 0) (acc '())) (if (= i
n) (reverse acc) (loop (+ i 1) (cons i acc)))))` — but you will
almost certainly not need to.

---

## 1.11 Try this yourself

1. Change gravity to `world/gravity! 0 0.1` and watch the rain fall in
   slow motion. Change it to `world/gravity! 0 2` and watch it fall so
   fast you barely see it.
2. Change bounce to 0.99 and let the rainstorm run for a minute.
   What happens to the heap?
3. Add `entity/mass! ball 5` inside the `world/each` block. Does
   mass change the fall speed? Should it? (Answer: on a frictionless
   world, no — Galileo's tower experiment. In our runtime, drag scales
   with mass differently. Try it and see.)
4. Change `world/floor! 240` to `world/floor! 100` mid-run. The floor
   moves up under the balls. What happens?
5. Add `world/wind! 0.2 0` inside `on-frame` — constant lateral wind.
   Now the rain drifts.
6. Spawn balls at random y-positions instead of a straight line — the
   rain becomes a soup. What does the heap look like?

Each experiment takes about a minute and teaches you one number's worth
of physics.

---

## 1.12 What we built

One entity with gravity, floor, and bounce. Then thirty of them. Then
input-triggered spawn. Then tilted gravity. Then a win predicate. Then
two shop patterns using nothing but this chapter's verbs.

The next chapter adds a paddle. The paddle catches the ball, and the
ball reflects. Reflection is the first rule of arcade physics beyond
gravity, and it is the seed of every game that has a wall in it —
Pong, Breakout, pinball, Arkanoid, Peggle. Read chapter 2 with your
thumb ready.

  :title               "Paddle and Wall"
  :dialect             "motoi"
  :audience            :kid
  :also-for            :adult
  :content-rating      :G
  :author-lane         "arcade-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"

"A ball that bounces is beautiful. A ball that bounces off a wall you
control is a GAME. In 1972 a coin-operated machine appeared in a bar in
Sunnyvale, California with two paddles and a ball. It grossed more that
first weekend than the jukebox next to it did all year. The paddle is
the arcade's first user interface.

This chapter puts a paddle under the ball. Then a wall on top. Then
walls on the sides. Then eight rows of bricks the ball breaks through
one at a time. By the end you will have written the game that saved a
generation of arcade cabinets — under a different name, but the same
math.

The lesson is reflection. When a ball hits a horizontal wall, the
y-component of its velocity flips sign. When it hits a vertical wall,
the x-component flips. Bounce coefficient scales the reflection. That
is the whole physics of the paddle-and-wall family.

---

## 2.1 Move a paddle

Before the ball, the paddle. Before the wall, the input.

```scheme
;; A paddle you slide left/right along the bottom of the screen.
(define paddle-x 160)
(define (paddle-only)
  (world/reset!)
  (on-frame
   (lambda ()
     (when (input/down? 'left)  (set! paddle-x (max 20  (- paddle-x 4))))
     (when (input/down? 'right) (set! paddle-x (min 300 (+ paddle-x 4))))
     (paint-clear)
     (paint-cell 'paddle paddle-x 230 40 6))))

(big-bang paddle-only)
```

`input/down?` returns true every frame the button is held. Unlike
`input/pressed?` (chapter 1), which fires only on the transition, this
one continuously polls state. Hold 'right' and the paddle moves right
four pixels per frame. Sixty pixels per second is a moderate feel;
try 8 for twitchy, 2 for stately.

The `max 20` and `min 300` clamps are hand-rolled walls. The paddle
cannot slip off the screen. This is the first time we handle a
boundary in code rather than by physics; there is no `world/floor!` for
lateral motion because the runtime lets entities pass horizontally
freely by default. Later chapters use `world/camera-bounds!` for
larger-scale confinement; here we just clamp.

---

## 2.2 Give it a ball

Now the ball.

```scheme
;; A ball that falls and a paddle that can catch it (or miss).
(define paddle-x 160)
(define (paddle-with-ball)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.35)
  (world/floor! 244)                 ;; below paddle
  (let ((ball (world/spawn 'ball 160 30)))
    (entity/bounce! ball 0.9)
    (entity/shape! ball 'circle 6)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (set! paddle-x (max 20  (- paddle-x 5))))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (set! paddle-x (min 300 (+ paddle-x 5))))
       ;; Reflection: if the ball is at paddle height AND overlaps in x,
       ;; flip its vertical velocity.
       (let ((bx (entity/x ball)) (by (entity/y ball))
             (vx (car (entity/vel ball))) (vy (cadr (entity/vel ball))))
         (when (and (>= by 224) (<= by 232)
                    (> bx (- paddle-x 22)) (< bx (+ paddle-x 22))
                    (> vy 0))
           (entity/set-vel! ball vx (* -1 vy 0.95))))
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'paddle paddle-x 230 40 6)
       (paint-cell 'ball (entity/x ball) (entity/y ball) 6 6)))))

(big-bang paddle-with-ball)
```

Read the collision block slowly. We ask five things: is the ball at
paddle-height (`by` between 224 and 232), is it within the paddle's
horizontal span (`bx` within 22 px of `paddle-x`), and is it moving
DOWN (`vy > 0`, because y grows down in screen coordinates). If all
five, we flip the sign of `vy` and scale by 0.95 — a slight energy
loss on impact. Otherwise the ball continues its fall and the
`world/floor!` at 244 catches it (a game-over if you were tracking
misses).

That five-line collision check IS the paddle. Everything else is
decoration. Any arcade collision — bat-and-ball, pinball flippers,
lightsaber deflect — is a variation on 'when velocity meets boundary
under condition C, transform velocity by rule R.'

---

## 2.3 Use the engine's collision

Rolling collisions by hand is instructive but does not scale. When the
world grows to eight paddles or forty bricks, `world/collisions` does
the work for us.

```scheme
;; Same game, but the paddle is a real entity and world/collisions
;; drives the reflection.
(define (engine-paddle)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.35)
  (let ((ball   (world/spawn 'ball 160 30))
        (paddle (world/spawn 'paddle 160 230))
        (floor  (world/spawn 'floor 160 244)))
    (entity/bounce! ball 0.92)
    (entity/shape! ball 'circle 6)
    (entity/shape! paddle 'rect 40 6)
    (entity/shape! floor 'rect 320 4)
    (entity/solid! paddle #t)
    (entity/solid! floor #t)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)
         (entity/move! paddle -5 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right)
         (entity/move! paddle 5 0))
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'paddle (entity/x paddle) (entity/y paddle) 40 6)
       (paint-cell 'ball   (entity/x ball)   (entity/y ball)   6 6)
       (paint-cell 'floor  (entity/x floor)  (entity/y floor)  320 4)))))

(big-bang engine-paddle)
```

`entity/solid! paddle #t` tells the physics engine 'this entity
participates in collisions and pushes other solids back.' Now
`world/step` handles the reflection automatically — the ball's bounce
coefficient (0.92) is applied to the impact, and the paddle stops the
ball from passing through. We got rid of the manual velocity flip.

`entity/move! paddle -5 0` shifts the paddle without disturbing its
velocity. Under the hood it's `(entity/set-pos! paddle (- (entity/x
paddle) 5) (entity/y paddle))` — but move is more readable.

---

## 2.4 Walls

Add three walls: top, left, right.

```scheme
;; The ball is enclosed by top, left, right, and paddle-below.
(define (walled-court)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.3)
  (let ((ball   (world/spawn 'ball 160 120))
        (paddle (world/spawn 'paddle 160 230))
        (top    (world/spawn 'wall 160 4))
        (left   (world/spawn 'wall 4 120))
        (right  (world/spawn 'wall 316 120)))
    (entity/bounce! ball 0.95)
    (entity/shape! ball 'circle 6)
    (entity/shape! paddle 'rect 40 6)
    (entity/shape! top 'rect 320 4)
    (entity/shape! left 'rect 4 240)
    (entity/shape! right 'rect 4 240)
    (for-each (lambda (e) (entity/solid! e #t))
              (list paddle top left right))
    (entity/set-vel! ball 2 -3)          ;; kick the ball diagonally
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! paddle -5 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! paddle 5 0))
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'paddle (entity/x paddle) (entity/y paddle) 40 6)
       (paint-cell 'ball   (entity/x ball)   (entity/y ball)   6 6)
       (paint-cell 'wall   (entity/x top)    (entity/y top)    320 4)
       (paint-cell 'wall   (entity/x left)   (entity/y left)   4 240)
       (paint-cell 'wall   (entity/x right)  (entity/y right)  4 240)))))

(big-bang walled-court)
```

Notice `for-each`: it applies a function to each item in a list, with
no return value. `for-each` and `map` are twins; `map` collects results,
`for-each` runs for side effects. We use `for-each` to configure four
entities in one sweep.

Notice `entity/set-vel! ball 2 -3` — an initial diagonal velocity. If
we did not kick the ball, gravity alone would drop it and we'd never
see wall reflection. The kick starts the game.

Now the ball rattles in the box. It bounces off the top, off the sides,
falls into the paddle, bounces back up. The kid moves the paddle to
keep the ball airborne. That is the raw material of every wall-based
game.

---

## 2.5 Bricks

Replace the top wall with a grid of bricks. The ball breaks them.

```scheme
;; Breakout-lite. A row of bricks; ball breaks them on contact.
(define (brick-court)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.3)
  (let ((ball   (world/spawn 'ball 160 180))
        (paddle (world/spawn 'paddle 160 230))
        (left   (world/spawn 'wall 4 120))
        (right  (world/spawn 'wall 316 120))
        (top    (world/spawn 'wall 160 4)))
    (entity/bounce! ball 0.98)
    (entity/shape! ball 'circle 5)
    (entity/shape! paddle 'rect 40 6)
    (entity/shape! left 'rect 4 240)
    (entity/shape! right 'rect 4 240)
    (entity/shape! top 'rect 320 4)
    (for-each (lambda (e) (entity/solid! e #t))
              (list paddle left right top))
    ;; Rows of bricks — 8 columns, 4 rows.
    (scene/grid 'brick 8 4 32 12 12 30)
    (world/each 'brick
                (lambda (b)
                  (entity/solid! b #t)
                  (entity/shape! b 'rect 30 10)))
    (entity/set-vel! ball 2 -3)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! paddle -6 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! paddle 6 0))
       (world/step)
       ;; Any collision where one party is a brick: despawn the brick.
       (for-each
        (lambda (pair)
          (let ((a (car pair)) (b (cadr pair)))
            (when (eq? (entity/kind a) 'brick) (entity/despawn! a))
            (when (eq? (entity/kind b) 'brick) (entity/despawn! b))))
        (world/collisions))
       (paint-clear)
       (world/each 'brick
                   (lambda (br)
                     (paint-cell 'brick (entity/x br) (entity/y br) 30 10)))
       (paint-cell 'paddle (entity/x paddle) (entity/y paddle) 40 6)
       (paint-cell 'ball   (entity/x ball)   (entity/y ball)   5 5)))))

(big-bang brick-court)
```

`scene/grid 'brick 8 4 32 12 12 30` spawns 8 columns by 4 rows of
'brick entities, each cell 32×12 pixels, top-left origin at (12, 30).
That is thirty-two bricks with one call.

`world/collisions` returns a list of pairs — every colliding entity
pair this frame. We walk the list; if either partner is tagged 'brick,
despawn the brick. The engine handles the reflection off the brick
before we despawn it, so the ball bounces AND the brick disappears in
the same frame.

The kid has now built Breakout in about forty lines. The ball breaks
bricks; the paddle catches the ball; the walls contain the court. Add
a score counter (chapter 13), a life counter (chapter 14), a boss
(chapter 12), and you have a shipping arcade game.

---

## 2.6 Collision layers

Right now anything solid collides with anything solid. In a bigger game
you want the ball to hit bricks but not the paddle's shadow, or the
player's bullet to miss the player. That is `collision/define-layers!`.

```scheme
;; The ball, the paddle, the bricks, and the walls all live on
;; different collision layers so we can control who hits whom.
(define (layered-court)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.3)
  (collision/define-layers!
   '((ball   :collides-with (paddle brick wall))
     (paddle :collides-with (ball wall))
     (brick  :collides-with (ball))
     (wall   :collides-with (ball paddle))))
  ;; Rest of setup as before, but each spawn also:
  ;;   (entity/layer! ball 'ball)
  ;;   (entity/layer! paddle 'paddle)
  ;;   ... etc.
  ;; The engine now consults the layer table instead of colliding
  ;; every solid pair.
  ...)
```

The full worked layered example is in Appendix B (Layered Collision
Cookbook). Chapter 5 will lean on layers heavily when we have four
kinds of entities on screen (player, enemy, player-bullet,
enemy-bullet) and need to prevent friendly fire.

The lesson: composition of entities from parts (solid + shape + bounce
+ layer) is what LETS the physics stay clean at scale. Without layers,
every new entity type multiplies the collision-pair count and the
programmer's confusion.

---

## 2.7 The four patterns in a paddle game

Chapter 1 introduced the four patterns; this chapter uses them at
scale.

**Composition.** The paddle is composed: `entity/shape!` gives it a
rect, `entity/solid!` makes it a physics participant, `entity/move!`
lets it slide. The ball is composed: `entity/bounce!` gives it
elasticity, `entity/set-vel!` gives it a starting kick, `entity/shape!`
gives it a circle. Each entity is a bag of small verbs applied in
sequence.

**Orchestration.** The frame loop orchestrates poll (input/down?),
update (world/step), collision-response (walk world/collisions),
draw (paint-cell over all entity kinds). Order matters. If we draw
before update, the drawn frame is one behind reality. If we handle
collisions before update, we handle YESTERDAY'S collisions.

**In-routing.** Input events route to handlers via the `when
(input/down? 'left)` dispatch. Each button has its own handler. Real
arcade games have more elaborate in-routing — chapter 5 shows
button-context tables where 'a' means 'fire' during play and 'confirm'
during menu.

**Routing.** Collision events route to consumers. In section 2.5, every
collision-pair routes through our `for-each` walk, and 'brick-involved
collisions route to `entity/despawn!`. The reflection itself routes
through the physics engine to `entity/set-vel!` on the ball. We do
not see that routing because it happens inside `world/step`, but it
is there.

Every arcade game weaves these four. Once you see them named you cannot
un-see them.

---

## 2.8 Common desktop tasks

Two shop-side uses of paddle-and-wall physics:

**The unlock paddle-game.** A customer is browsing. A small ribbon at
the bottom of the item page says 'Play 30 seconds of Paddle for 5% off.'
The kid taps play. They get a 30-second brickout. Bricks broken =
percent off, capped at ten. The physics engine is the game AND the
score generator. `cortex/write` at the end lands the discount in the
shopper's session.

**The bounce-your-cursor scoreboard.** A shop wants to show 'top items
of the week' as a physical scene: each item is a ball, ball size scales
with sales volume, they rain into a court and pile in order. The paddle
is the shopper's cursor; they can bat balls out of the pile to see
each item's details. Physics as browse.

---

## 2.9 Pitfalls

**The ball tunnels through a wall.** If the ball moves fast enough that
one frame's velocity carries it entirely past the wall, `world/step`
misses the collision. Fix: lower the ball's speed, thicken the wall,
or read Appendix I (Reading world/collisions Efficiently) for
sweep-based collision patterns.

**The paddle passes THROUGH the ball.** `entity/solid! paddle #t` was
missing. Or `entity/solid! ball #t` was missing (it is not set by
default in this chapter's examples; the engine treats non-solid
entities as ghosts).

**Bricks despawn but the ball keeps bouncing off empty space.** Your
`for-each` over `world/collisions` walked the pair but did not despawn
the brick before drawing. The order matters: despawn first, THEN
`world/step` next frame will not see the brick, and the ball will
pass through cleanly.

**All bricks disappear at once.** The ball bounced against the corner
of one brick, which forwarded impulse to adjacent bricks, and your
`world/collisions` list has a chain of pairs. Solid answer: for game
feel, set `entity/mass! brick 1000` so bricks do not transmit impulse
laterally. Or use `entity/sensor! brick #t` (chapter 11 covers
sensors) so the brick registers as hit without physically pushing back.

---

## 2.10 Try this yourself

1. Change the paddle-speed clamp from 5 to 2 (sluggish) and to 12
   (twitchy). Which feels better? Where is the sweet spot?
2. Give the brick rows different bounce coefficients. Top row 0.5,
   middle 0.9, bottom 1.1. Where does the ball spend the most time?
3. Randomize brick colors by hashing (entity/id brick) and drawing
   different colored cells. What's the visual effect?
4. Add a lives counter — every time the ball hits the floor
   (`world/floor! 244`), decrement lives. Game over at zero.
5. Add a power-up — a 'brick that when broken spawns a ball' — so
   the game escalates.
6. Try `entity/bounce! ball 1.02` — non-physical. Watch the ball gain
   energy on every hit. When does the game break?

---

## 2.11 What we built

Paddle. Wall. Brick. The three primitives of the reflection-family of
arcade games. Plus collision layers, plus the collision-event routing
pattern, plus a running Breakout in forty lines.

Next chapter: throw away gravity, throw away the floor, put the whole
game in space. The ship thrusts, drifts, rotates. Vector math enters
the story. You will learn heading-versus-velocity and never confuse
them again.")

"In 1962 four MIT students wired a PDP-1 to a modified oscilloscope and
wrote a two-player game where each player controlled a small
triangular spaceship with a thruster and a gun. The ships drifted in a
frictionless void around a central star whose gravity you had to
respect. Nine kilobytes of core memory. Two joysticks made from mercury
switches. It cost the university nothing and captured every hacker
within a three-state radius.

That game — Space War — is this chapter. You will build a ship with a
heading, a thrust, and a drift. You will discover the difference between
'the direction you are facing' and 'the direction you are moving.' You
will feel, in your thumbs, why real space is not like a road: press
forward once and you keep going forever.

Then you will add a moon, turn on `world/attract!`, and watch the ship
orbit. That is your first taste of gravitational feel — the arcade
version of Kepler's laws, at 60 frames per second.

---

## 3.1 The rotating ship

Before thrust, rotation. Left and right rotate; the ship faces where
its heading angle points.

```scheme
;; A triangular ship you can rotate with left/right.
(define ship-angle 0)   ;; radians, 0 = pointing right
(define (rotating-ship)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((ship (world/spawn 'ship 160 120)))
    (entity/shape! ship 'triangle 12)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (set! ship-angle (- ship-angle 0.08)))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (set! ship-angle (+ ship-angle 0.08)))
       (entity/pose! ship 'angle ship-angle)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'ship (entity/x ship) (entity/y ship) 12 12)
       ;; Draw a heading arrow so we can SEE which way the ship faces.
       (paint-arrow (entity/x ship) (entity/y ship)
                    (+ (entity/x ship) (* 30 (geom/cos ship-angle)))
                    (+ (entity/y ship) (* 30 (geom/sin ship-angle)))))))
(big-bang rotating-ship)
```

`ship-angle` is a global variable holding radians. Zero points right;
pi/2 points down; pi points left; 3pi/2 points up. `geom/cos` and
`geom/sin` decompose the angle into x- and y-components of a unit
vector. That decomposition IS the vector math this chapter teaches.

`entity/pose! ship 'angle ship-angle` tells the sprite to rotate with
the heading — if we had a proper spaceship sprite, its nose would
follow the arrow.

Try holding 'left' for two seconds. The ship spins a full turn every
seven seconds at 0.08 radians per frame. That is 60 * 0.08 = 4.8
radians per second. A full rotation is 2*pi = 6.28 radians. So 6.28 /
4.8 = 1.3 seconds per rotation. Do the arithmetic; feel the number.

---

## 3.2 Add thrust

Now the ship can push itself in the direction it is facing.

```scheme
;; Rotate and thrust. Ship drifts forever in space.
(define ship-angle 0)
(define (thrusting-ship)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((ship (world/spawn 'ship 160 120)))
    (entity/shape! ship 'triangle 12)
    (entity/drag! ship 0)             ;; NO drag — space
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (set! ship-angle (- ship-angle 0.08)))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (set! ship-angle (+ ship-angle 0.08)))
       (when (input/down? 'a)
         ;; Add thrust in the direction of ship-angle.
         (let ((vx (car (entity/vel ship)))
               (vy (cadr (entity/vel ship)))
               (thrust 0.15))
           (entity/set-vel! ship
                            (+ vx (* thrust (geom/cos ship-angle)))
                            (+ vy (* thrust (geom/sin ship-angle))))))
       (entity/pose! ship 'angle ship-angle)
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'ship (entity/x ship) (entity/y ship) 12 12)
       (paint-arrow (entity/x ship) (entity/y ship)
                    (+ (entity/x ship) (* 20 (geom/cos ship-angle)))
                    (+ (entity/y ship) (* 20 (geom/sin ship-angle))))))))

(big-bang thrusting-ship)
```

Read section 3.2 carefully. The velocity update is the important line:

```
(entity/set-vel! ship
                 (+ vx (* thrust (geom/cos ship-angle)))
                 (+ vy (* thrust (geom/sin ship-angle))))
```

We take the current velocity `(vx vy)`. We take the heading vector
`(cos ang, sin ang)`. We scale the heading by `thrust`. We add. That
is vector addition. The new velocity is the old velocity PLUS an
impulse in the facing direction.

This is why the ship drifts. Once you have accumulated `(vx=2, vy=-1)`
by thrusting up-and-to-the-right, releasing 'a' does not zero those
components. The ship coasts. To stop, you rotate 180 degrees and
thrust the same amount BACKWARD to cancel the velocity. Kids figure
this out in about ninety seconds and are proud of themselves.

`entity/drag! ship 0` disables the runtime's default drag. In space
there is nothing to push against; velocity persists. Set drag to 0.02
and try again — the ship slowly slows down without input. That
'friction' is a lie the game tells for playability. Real Space War
kept drag at zero, and pilots hated it, and loved it.

---

## 3.3 Heading is not velocity

Here is the pedagogical crux of vector math. Draw two arrows on the
screen: one for HEADING (where the ship faces), one for VELOCITY
(where the ship is moving).

```scheme
;; Show both arrows so the kid sees the difference.
(define ship-angle 0)
(define (two-arrows)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((ship (world/spawn 'ship 160 120)))
    (entity/shape! ship 'triangle 12)
    (entity/drag! ship 0)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (set! ship-angle (- ship-angle 0.08)))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (set! ship-angle (+ ship-angle 0.08)))
       (when (input/down? 'a)
         (let ((vx (car (entity/vel ship)))
               (vy (cadr (entity/vel ship))))
           (entity/set-vel! ship
                            (+ vx (* 0.15 (geom/cos ship-angle)))
                            (+ vy (* 0.15 (geom/sin ship-angle))))))
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'ship (entity/x ship) (entity/y ship) 12 12)
       ;; RED arrow — heading.
       (paint-arrow (entity/x ship) (entity/y ship)
                    (+ (entity/x ship) (* 30 (geom/cos ship-angle)))
                    (+ (entity/y ship) (* 30 (geom/sin ship-angle))))
       ;; BLUE arrow — velocity.
       (let ((vx (car (entity/vel ship)))
             (vy (cadr (entity/vel ship))))
         (paint-arrow (entity/x ship) (entity/y ship)
                      (+ (entity/x ship) (* 15 vx))
                      (+ (entity/y ship) (* 15 vy))))))))

(big-bang two-arrows)
```

Two arrows, one origin. Rotate the ship — the red arrow (heading)
swings around; the blue arrow (velocity) stays put. Thrust — the blue
arrow starts to grow in the heading direction. Rotate 180 and thrust
again — the blue arrow shrinks toward zero, then flips and grows in
the OTHER direction. The kid can literally see the vector algebra.

Appendix D (Heading vs Velocity — the Two-Arrow Diagram) formalizes
this into a poster you can tape to the wall.

---

## 3.4 Wrap-around

A ship that drifts off-screen is a lost ship. Classic arcade wraps the
world: fly off the right edge, appear on the left. The Motoi reference
does not yet expose a `world/wrap!` verb (see the design's gap-1 note),
so we roll it ourselves.

```scheme
;; Toroidal world: off-screen on the right = on-screen on the left.
(define ship-angle 0)
(define (wrapping-ship)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((ship (world/spawn 'ship 160 120)))
    (entity/shape! ship 'triangle 12)
    (entity/drag! ship 0)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (set! ship-angle (- ship-angle 0.08)))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (set! ship-angle (+ ship-angle 0.08)))
       (when (input/down? 'a)
         (let ((vx (car (entity/vel ship)))
               (vy (cadr (entity/vel ship))))
           (entity/set-vel! ship
                            (+ vx (* 0.15 (geom/cos ship-angle)))
                            (+ vy (* 0.15 (geom/sin ship-angle))))))
       (world/step)
       ;; Wrap horizontally at 0 / 320, vertically at 0 / 240.
       (let ((x (entity/x ship)) (y (entity/y ship)))
         (when (< x 0)   (entity/set-pos! ship (+ x 320) y))
         (when (> x 320) (entity/set-pos! ship (- x 320) y))
         (when (< y 0)   (entity/set-pos! ship x (+ y 240)))
         (when (> y 240) (entity/set-pos! ship x (- y 240))))
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'ship (entity/x ship) (entity/y ship) 12 12)))))

(big-bang wrapping-ship)
```

Four `when` clauses. Each checks one edge; if the ship crossed it, we
add or subtract the screen dimension. That is toroidal topology in
four lines. Every Asteroids-family game does this.

Nice property: the wrap is invisible to the physics. `entity/vel`
stays what it was; only position moves. So the ship's momentum
carries continuously across the wrap.

---

## 3.5 The moon (arcade gravity)

Now the fun part. Put a big body in the middle. Turn on gravitational
attraction.

```scheme
;; Ship + moon. Moon pulls ship. Ship orbits (if you thrust right).
(define ship-angle 0)
(define (ship-and-moon)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((moon (world/spawn 'moon 160 120))
        (ship (world/spawn 'ship 240 120)))
    (entity/shape! moon 'circle 20)
    (entity/shape! ship 'triangle 10)
    (entity/mass! moon 100)
    (entity/mass! ship 1)
    (entity/drag! ship 0)
    ;; Give the ship an initial tangential kick.
    (entity/set-vel! ship 0 -2.2)
    ;; Turn on radial attraction from the moon.
    (world/attract! ship (entity/x moon) (entity/y moon) 0.15)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (set! ship-angle (- ship-angle 0.08)))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (set! ship-angle (+ ship-angle 0.08)))
       (when (input/down? 'a)
         (let ((vx (car (entity/vel ship)))
               (vy (cadr (entity/vel ship))))
           (entity/set-vel! ship
                            (+ vx (* 0.12 (geom/cos ship-angle)))
                            (+ vy (* 0.12 (geom/sin ship-angle))))))
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'moon (entity/x moon) (entity/y moon) 40 40)
       (paint-cell 'ship (entity/x ship) (entity/y ship) 10 10)))))

(big-bang ship-and-moon)
```

`world/attract! ship (entity/x moon) (entity/y moon) 0.15` says
'every frame, add a force toward the moon's position on ship, with
strength 0.15.' The strength number is not proper Newtonian G, but
it's inverse-square-like enough that orbits behave.

The initial `entity/set-vel! ship 0 -2.2` kicks the ship straight up
(y negative = up). With the moon pulling right (moon is to the left
of the ship's start position, moon at 160, ship at 240), the ship
curves left as it climbs, and if you tuned the tangential speed right
it enters a stable ellipse.

Try different initial y-velocities: 1.0 falls in; 2.2 orbits; 5.0
escapes. That is the elementary calculation of orbital energy — total
energy = kinetic + potential; if it exceeds zero the ship escapes.
Kids do not need to know the formula to feel it.

The ship's own thrust is available; a good pilot can adjust orbit
apogee and perigee by thrusting prograde (in the direction of motion)
or retrograde (against). This is the same mechanic astronauts use to
change orbit.

---

## 3.6 The four patterns in a space game

**Composition.** The ship is composed: shape, mass, drag, initial
velocity, attract-target. The moon is composed similarly with heavier
mass. Chapters 4-5 will compose bullets, enemies, health.

**Orchestration.** The frame loop orchestrates: poll heading input,
poll thrust input, integrate physics via `world/step`, wrap position,
draw. Note that wrap happens AFTER step; if we wrapped before step,
the ship would sometimes teleport mid-frame and physics could get
confused.

**In-routing.** Three buttons route to three handlers: left rotates,
right rotates, 'a' thrusts. Later ('b' fires) adds a fourth. Each
handler is small; each mutates one aspect of world state.

**Routing.** The `world/attract!` call is routing set up at spawn
time: 'every frame from now on, route a force from the moon to the
ship.' The runtime remembers the attraction and re-applies it. If we
had many moons and many ships, we would call attract for each pair.

---

## 3.7 Common desktop tasks

**Ship-tourism scoreboard.** A shop selling telescopes or space-themed
products embeds a small ship-and-moon minigame: pilot from Earth to
Moon in the fewest thrusts. Best time gets a display banner. The game
teaches orbital economy while it sells the product.

**Package-drift receipt animation.** After checkout, a small ship
carries the buyer's package sprite across the screen, drifting past
planets that represent the item's category. Physics-first branding.

---

## 3.8 Pitfalls

**The ship spins but does not move.** You forgot `entity/set-vel!` or
you passed the wrong arguments. Check that `(entity/vel ship)` is a
list `(vx vy)` and you are `car` and `cadr`-ing it correctly.

**The ship stops as soon as you release 'a'.** `entity/drag!` is
non-zero. Space has no drag. Set it to 0 unless you want a poor-man's
Newton's-first-law violation.

**The orbit spirals in.** Your initial tangential velocity is too low
— the ship falls into the moon. Increase `entity/set-vel! ship 0
-2.5` and try again.

**The orbit spirals out.** Initial velocity too high — escape
trajectory. Decrease.

**Rotation is jerky.** `0.08` radians per frame is a fine baseline;
below 0.04 feels slow, above 0.15 is spinny. Consider using
`tick/ease` to ramp rotation speed in the frames after button press,
so the ship 'settles into' its rotation rate. Chapter 6 (Feel) shows
exactly this.

**Coordinate confusion.** In screen space, y grows DOWN. `geom/sin
angle` returns positive values for angles in the second and third
quadrants (angle between 0 and pi radians), which point DOWN on the
screen. If your ship rotates the wrong way, remember: screen-y is
flipped from math-y.

---

## 3.9 Try this yourself

1. Add a second moon. Give the ship both attractions:
   `(world/attract! ship moon2-x moon2-y 0.10)`. Watch the ship
   figure-eight between them (three-body problem, in the small).
2. Add `world/wind! 0.05 0` — a solar wind. The ship drifts sideways
   without input. Does that ruin the game or make it more
   interesting?
3. Give the ship `entity/max-speed! ship 5` — cap the drift. Space
   with a speed limit is not-space, but it plays gently.
4. Replace the moon's `world/attract!` with `world/repel!` at the
   same strength — the moon becomes a shield generator. Fly around
   it; try to get close.
5. Add a fire button ('b'): each press spawns a small bullet with
   velocity = ship-velocity + heading * bullet-speed. Chapter 4
   covers this in depth.
6. Make the ship 'wrap' with fade-in on the new edge — spawn a ghost
   at the old position that fades over 15 frames.

---

A ship. A heading. A thrust. A drift. A wrap. A moon. Vector
decomposition into cos-and-sin components. `world/attract!` as arcade
gravity. Two-arrow visualization of heading versus velocity.

Next chapter: the ship stops moving, it stays put, but it FIRES. We
build cannons and projectiles. `phys/kinematics` finally earns its

"A cannon on the ground. An angle you dial in. A power number that
scales your shot. Pull the trigger — an arc rises against the sky,
peaks, and falls back down. If your aim is true, the shell lands on the
target. If not, you turn a small knob and try again.

That is the projectile family. Artillery games. Angry-birds-shape
physics puzzles. Trebuchet toys on the phone in the airport gate. Every
one of them is `phys/kinematics` — the equation of motion for constant
acceleration — with a paint call each frame.

This chapter builds the whole family from one primitive: a cannon that
spawns a ball with initial velocity `(cos angle * power, sin angle *
power)` and lets gravity do the rest. Then we compare the ball's actual
path to the closed-form kinematics equation and prove they agree. Then
we knock over three cans.

---

## 4.1 The cannon

Aim, fire, watch the arc.

```scheme
;; A cannon at the bottom-left. Dial angle with up/down; fire with 'a'.
(define angle-deg 45)          ;; degrees, 0=flat right, 90=straight up
(define power 6)               ;; initial speed of the projectile

(define (cannon)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.3)
  (world/floor! 220)
  (on-frame
   (lambda ()
     (when (input/down? 'up)   (set! angle-deg (min 89 (+ angle-deg 1))))
     (when (input/down? 'down) (set! angle-deg (max  1 (- angle-deg 1))))
     (when (input/pressed? 'a)
       (let* ((rad (* angle-deg (/ 3.14159 180)))
              (vx  (* power (geom/cos rad)))
              (vy  (* -1 power (geom/sin rad)))
              (b   (world/spawn 'shell 30 210)))
         (entity/shape! b 'circle 3)
         (entity/bounce! b 0.4)
         (entity/set-vel! b vx vy)))
     (world/step)
     (paint-clear)
     (paint-cell 'cannon 30 210 20 10)
     ;; Aim line — show where the barrel points.
     (let ((rad (* angle-deg (/ 3.14159 180))))
       (paint-arrow 30 210
                    (+ 30 (* 40 (geom/cos rad)))
                    (- 210 (* 40 (geom/sin rad)))))
     (world/each 'shell
                 (lambda (s)
                   (paint-cell 'shell (entity/x s) (entity/y s) 3 3)))
     (paint-text (string-append \"Angle: \" (number->string angle-deg))
                 10 10))))

(big-bang cannon)
```

Note the sign flip on `vy`. In screen space y grows down, but 'up' on
a real trajectory is y-negative. `(* -1 power (geom/sin rad))` gives us
a launch that goes UP the screen.

Note `let*` versus `let`. `let*` allows each binding to reference the
previous — `vx` uses `rad`, `vy` uses `rad`. Regular `let` binds all
names in parallel and would not let `vx` see `rad`.

Hold 'up' — the aim line rotates skyward. Hit 'a' — a shell fires along
that line. Gravity curves it. It lands somewhere down-range. Play with
`power = 4` (short range) and `power = 10` (over-the-horizon).

---

## 4.2 The range formula

Physics 101: for a projectile launched with speed `v` at angle `a` on
flat ground under gravity `g`, the range is `v*v * sin(2a) / g`.
Maximum range at `a = 45 degrees`. Range zero at 0 or 90.

Let's verify. We spawn a shell, wait for it to land, and measure how far
it went. Then compare to the formula.

```scheme
;; Fire a shell, wait for landing, print actual range vs predicted.
(define (verify-range)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.3)
  (world/floor! 220)
  (let* ((angle-deg 45)
         (power 8)
         (rad (* angle-deg (/ 3.14159 180)))
         (vx  (* power (geom/cos rad)))
         (vy  (* -1 power (geom/sin rad)))
         (b   (world/spawn 'shell 30 210)))
    (entity/shape! b 'circle 3)
    (entity/bounce! b 0)
    (entity/set-vel! b vx vy)
    ;; Step until the shell rests on the floor.
    (let loop ((n 300))
      (world/step)
      (if (and (> n 0) (< (- (cadr (entity/vel b))) 0.05))
          (loop (- n 1))
          (let* ((actual (- (entity/x b) 30))
                 (predicted (/ (* power power
                                  (* 2 (geom/sin rad) (geom/cos rad)))
                               0.3)))
            (display \"Actual: \")    (display actual)   (newline)
            (display \"Predicted: \") (display predicted) (newline))))))

(verify-range)
;; Actual and predicted should agree within a few percent (integration
;; error). If they disagree by more than ~5%, gravity in the runtime
;; differs from what you asked for, and the reference has drifted.
```

We are RUNNING the physics and CHECKING it against the theory. That is
the pedagogical superpower of a physics-first game engine: the code
does not just LOOK physical, it IS. When kids get to trigonometry in
school, they have already touched sin and cos. When they get to
integration, they have already accumulated velocity into position.

---

## 4.3 Draw the trajectory

We can visualize the arc by remembering every position the shell
occupies and painting them all.

```scheme
;; A shell fires; we remember its trail and paint it as a dotted arc.
(define trail '())
(define (trailed-cannon)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.3)
  (world/floor! 220)
  (let* ((rad (* 55 (/ 3.14159 180)))
         (b   (world/spawn 'shell 30 210)))
    (entity/shape! b 'circle 3)
    (entity/bounce! b 0.3)
    (entity/set-vel! b (* 8 (geom/cos rad)) (* -8 (geom/sin rad)))
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (world/step)
       ;; Every 3rd frame, remember the shell's position.
       (when (= (modulo (world/frame) 3) 0)
         (set! trail (cons (list (entity/x b) (entity/y b)) trail)))
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'cannon 30 210 20 10)
       ;; Paint each trail point as a small dot.
       (for-each (lambda (pt)
                   (paint-cell 'dot (car pt) (cadr pt) 2 2))
                 trail)
       (paint-cell 'shell (entity/x b) (entity/y b) 4 4)))))

(big-bang trailed-cannon)
```

`cons` prepends to the list; the trail grows head-first, most recent
first. We paint every point. The dotted arc appears, curves under
gravity, hits the floor, bounces, arcs lower, and so on. The kid
literally SEES the parabola.

Warning: the trail grows forever. For a real game, cap it —
`(when (> (length trail) 100) (set! trail (take trail 100)))` — to
avoid unbounded memory. Or clear it every fire.

---

## 4.4 Target practice

Now put three cans on the floor. Knock them over.

```scheme
;; Three cans down-range. Hit all three with three shots.
(define angle-deg 60)
(define power 7)
(define shells-fired 0)
(define cans-hit 0)

(define (target-practice)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.3)
  (world/floor! 220)
  ;; Cans as short vertical rects.
  (let ((can1 (world/spawn 'can 200 205))
        (can2 (world/spawn 'can 240 205))
        (can3 (world/spawn 'can 280 205)))
    (for-each (lambda (c)
                (entity/shape! c 'rect 12 30)
                (entity/solid! c #t))
              (list can1 can2 can3)))
  (on-frame
   (lambda ()
     (when (input/down? 'up)   (set! angle-deg (min 89 (+ angle-deg 1))))
     (when (input/down? 'down) (set! angle-deg (max  1 (- angle-deg 1))))
     (when (input/pressed? 'a)
       (set! shells-fired (+ shells-fired 1))
       (let* ((rad (* angle-deg (/ 3.14159 180)))
              (b (world/spawn 'shell 30 210)))
         (entity/shape! b 'circle 3)
         (entity/set-vel! b (* power (geom/cos rad))
                            (* -1 power (geom/sin rad)))))
     (world/step)
     ;; Any (shell, can) collision knocks the can down.
     (for-each
      (lambda (pair)
        (let ((a (car pair)) (b (cadr pair)))
          (cond
            ((and (eq? (entity/kind a) 'shell) (eq? (entity/kind b) 'can))
             (entity/despawn! b) (entity/despawn! a)
             (set! cans-hit (+ cans-hit 1))
             (world/camera-shake! 5 0.9))
            ((and (eq? (entity/kind b) 'shell) (eq? (entity/kind a) 'can))
             (entity/despawn! a) (entity/despawn! b)
             (set! cans-hit (+ cans-hit 1))
             (world/camera-shake! 5 0.9)))))
      (world/collisions))
     (paint-clear)
     (paint-cell 'cannon 30 210 20 10)
     (world/each 'can (lambda (c)
                        (paint-cell 'can (entity/x c) (entity/y c) 12 30)))
     (world/each 'shell (lambda (s)
                          (paint-cell 'shell (entity/x s) (entity/y s) 3 3)))
     (paint-text (string-append \"Fired: \" (number->string shells-fired)
                                \" Hit: \" (number->string cans-hit)) 10 10)
     (when (= cans-hit 3)
       (paint-text \"YOU WIN!\" 120 60)))))

(big-bang target-practice)
```

`world/camera-shake! 5 0.9` shakes the whole screen by 5 pixels max
with 0.9 decay per frame. Impact feedback. Chapter 6 covers this in
depth as FEEL; here we use it because a hit without shake feels
weightless.

`cond` handles the case where the collision-pair list orders the two
entities either way — sometimes shell first, sometimes can first. We
handle both.

---

## 4.5 The four patterns

**Composition.** A projectile is composed: shape, initial velocity,
bounce coefficient, tag (`'shell`). A cannon is composed: aim state
(angle), power state, spawn-position. The target (can) is composed: a
rect shape, solid flag, tag.

**Orchestration.** The frame loop orchestrates poll (angle
adjustment), poll (fire), physics update, collision walk, draw. Fire
happens BEFORE `world/step` so the new shell has a chance to move this
frame — spawning after step means one frame of visual stillness at the
cannon's mouth.

**In-routing.** Angle-adjust routes to a mutation of `angle-deg`; fire
routes to a spawn. Two buttons, two handlers, cleanly separated.

**Routing.** Collision pairs route through the `for-each
world/collisions` walk to handlers per kind-combination. Shell-and-can
routes to despawn-both + shake + increment. If we added shell-and-shell
(bullets deflecting bullets), it would be another `cond` arm.

---

## 4.6 Common desktop tasks

**Balloon-pop unlock.** A shop hides discounts inside virtual
balloons floating across the item page. Customer aims a cannon
(one button = aim, one button = fire) and pops balloons. Each popped
balloon reveals a discount code. Uses this chapter's cannon +
projectile primitives with `entity/sensor!` balloons (so shells pass
through them but register a hit).

**Delivery-arc animation.** After purchase, a small package projectile
arcs from the shop's icon to the shopper's cart icon, following
`phys/kinematics`. The physics IS the delivery-in-progress feedback.
Runs in about 1.5 seconds — enough for the kid to notice and smile.

---

## 4.7 Pitfalls

**Shells fall through the cans.** The can was not `entity/solid! c #t`.
Or the shell's velocity is so high that it tunnels past in one frame.
For high velocities, use `entity/sensor! can #t` and check overlap
manually in `on-frame` via `entity/overlaps?`.

**Cans register two hits.** Your collision walk fires both cond arms.
Add `(entity/alive? b)` guards, or dedupe collision pairs. Appendix I
covers this.

**Range formula disagrees with actual by 20%+.** Integration error.
For visible-scale gravity constants (0.1 to 0.5), the runtime's
integrator is close but not exact. That is fine for a game and honest.
Use the formula for design; use the sim for play.

**Trail memory blows up.** Cap the list length or clear on each fire.

**Cannon fires off-screen.** Check that shell spawn-position (30,
210) is on-screen and below the floor. If you spawn AT the floor line
(220), the shell instantly registers a floor collision.

---

## 4.8 Try this yourself

1. Add wind: `world/wind! 0.05 0`. The shell drifts down-range. Now
   the range formula is wrong; only the sim tells you where to aim.
2. Move the cannon up onto a platform (spawn at y=100). The range
   equation gains a term for launch height. Derive it.
3. Add a moving target — a can that slides left-right via
   `entity/set-vel!`. Now you must lead the shot.
4. Fire multiple shells in a spread: on 'a' press, spawn three shells
   at angles `angle-deg - 5`, `angle-deg`, `angle-deg + 5`. Shotgun.
5. Add a `paint-arrow` from cannon showing PREDICTED landing spot
   (compute range formula each frame). The kid learns aim visually.
6. Turn on `entity/bounce! shell 0.6` and give cans a health value.
   Now each shell may hit multiple cans as it bounces along.

---

## 4.9 What we built

A cannon, a projectile, an arc, a target, and a hit-counter. The
range formula, verified in-sim. The trail visualization. Camera-shake
as feedback.

Next chapter: turn the cannon vertical, put the player at the bottom,
enemies at the top. That is the shoot-em-up, and it is where entity
pooling and collision layers earn their keep.")

  (world/gravity! 0 0.3)

  (on-frame
   (lambda ()
     (when (input/down? 'up)   (set! angle-deg (min 89 (+ angle-deg 1))))

;; ch05-shoot-em-up.book.slatl
;; Book of Arcade Games — Chapter 5: The Shoot-Em-Up

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(chapter
  :book                "Book of Arcade Games"
  :chapter-number      5
  :title               "The Shoot-Em-Up"
  :dialect             "motoi"
  :audience            :kid
  :also-for            :adult
  :content-rating      :G
  :author-lane         "arcade-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"
  :training-eligible   #t
  :confidentiality     "public"
  :voice               "sakura-teaching + game-design"
  :book-version        "1.0.0"
  :draws-from-preserved (:book "book-of-games-preserved" :ch 4 :ch 5)
  :prose
"The vertical shoot-em-up is the arcade cabinet's most-copied form.
Player at the bottom. Enemies stream down. Bullets stream up. Sometimes
the enemies fire back. The screen fills with sprites; your thumb
becomes an instrument. In 1978 a game with fifty-five sprites broke
Japan's supply of the 100-yen coin the government had to mint more.

This chapter builds the whole shape in about a hundred lines. The heart
of it is `collision/define-layers!`, which lets us have four kinds of
entities on screen (player, enemy, player-bullet, enemy-bullet) without
bullets hitting their owner or enemies bumping other enemies. And
`world/find`, which iterates a tag pool efficiently so we can spawn a
new wave without walking every entity in the world.

By chapter end you have a small shmup with waves, layered collisions,
and a difficulty that scales with `world/count`. Not a shipping game —
that is chapter 16 — but a full playable session in one page.

---

## 5.1 The player and the pool

Start with the player ship and a mechanism to fire bullets.

```scheme
;; Player at the bottom. Move left/right. Fire straight up on 'a'.
(define (player-only)
  (world/reset!)
  (collision/define-layers!
   '((player   :collides-with (enemy enemy-bullet))
     (enemy    :collides-with (player player-bullet))
     (player-bullet :collides-with (enemy))
     (enemy-bullet  :collides-with (player))))
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 160 220)))
    (entity/shape! p 'triangle 8)
    (entity/layer! p 'player)
    (entity/solid! p #t)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -4 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 4 0))
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)
         (let ((b (world/spawn 'player-bullet (entity/x p) (- (entity/y p) 10))))
           (entity/shape! b 'circle 2)
           (entity/layer! b 'player-bullet)
           (entity/set-vel! b 0 -6)))
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 8 8)
       (world/each 'player-bullet
                   (lambda (b)
                     (paint-cell 'bullet (entity/x b) (entity/y b) 2 2)
                     ;; Despawn bullets that leave the top.
                     (when (< (entity/y b) 0) (entity/despawn! b))))))))

(big-bang player-only)
```

`collision/define-layers!` takes an alist of layer-name to allowed
collision partners. Every subsequent `entity/layer! id 'name` puts the
entity on a layer. The physics engine consults the layers before
computing collisions — bullets never collide with their spawner.

Note the bullet-cleanup at the bottom of the frame loop. Every bullet
that has flown off the top gets despawned. Without this, the world
fills up with hundreds of dead bullets and the entity count grows
without bound. Every arcade shooter does exactly this cleanup pass.

---

## 5.2 Add enemies

Enemies spawn at the top and drift down.

```scheme
;; Enemies drift down from the top. Spawn one every 30 frames.
(define spawn-counter 0)

(define (player-and-enemies)
  (world/reset!)
  (collision/define-layers!
   '((player   :collides-with (enemy enemy-bullet))
     (enemy    :collides-with (player player-bullet))
     (player-bullet :collides-with (enemy))
     (enemy-bullet  :collides-with (player))))
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 160 220)))
    (entity/shape! p 'triangle 8)
    (entity/layer! p 'player)
    (entity/solid! p #t)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -4 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 4 0))
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)
         (let ((b (world/spawn 'player-bullet (entity/x p) (- (entity/y p) 10))))
           (entity/shape! b 'circle 2)
           (entity/layer! b 'player-bullet)
           (entity/set-vel! b 0 -6)))
       ;; Every 30 frames: spawn a new enemy at random x.
       (set! spawn-counter (+ spawn-counter 1))
       (when (>= spawn-counter 30)
         (set! spawn-counter 0)
         (let ((e (world/spawn 'enemy
                               (+ 20 (modulo (world/hash) 280))
                               -10)))
           (entity/shape! e 'rect 10 10)
           (entity/layer! e 'enemy)
           (entity/solid! e #t)
           (entity/set-vel! e 0 1.5)))
       (world/step)
       ;; Collision handling — player-bullet hits enemy: both despawn.
       (for-each
        (lambda (pair)
          (let ((a (car pair)) (b (cadr pair)))
            (when (and (eq? (entity/kind a) 'player-bullet)
                       (eq? (entity/kind b) 'enemy))
              (entity/despawn! a) (entity/despawn! b))
            (when (and (eq? (entity/kind b) 'player-bullet)
                       (eq? (entity/kind a) 'enemy))
              (entity/despawn! a) (entity/despawn! b))))
        (world/collisions))
       ;; Cleanup off-screen entities.
       (world/each 'player-bullet
                   (lambda (b) (when (< (entity/y b) 0) (entity/despawn! b))))
       (world/each 'enemy
                   (lambda (e) (when (> (entity/y e) 250) (entity/despawn! e))))
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 8 8)
       (world/each 'player-bullet
                   (lambda (b) (paint-cell 'bullet (entity/x b) (entity/y b) 2 2)))
       (world/each 'enemy
                   (lambda (e) (paint-cell 'enemy (entity/x e) (entity/y e) 10 10)))))))

(big-bang player-and-enemies)
```

We have a game. Ship moves. Bullets fire. Enemies stream in. Bullets
kill enemies. Enemies escape off the bottom. The layer system prevents
bullets from stopping on the player or ricocheting off other enemies.

`(world/hash)` returns a pseudo-random integer that changes each call.
`(modulo (world/hash) 280) + 20` gives us x-values in [20, 299]. A
cheap random-x. If you want deterministic (for replay), pipe your own
seed instead — see chapter 14 for tape replay.

---

## 5.3 Enemies that shoot back

Add enemy fire. Enemies emit a bullet on a fixed pulse.

```scheme
;; Enemies fire down periodically using world/after.
(define spawn-counter 0)

(define (enemies-fire)
  (world/reset!)
  (collision/define-layers!
   '((player   :collides-with (enemy enemy-bullet))
     (enemy    :collides-with (player player-bullet))
     (player-bullet :collides-with (enemy))
     (enemy-bullet  :collides-with (player))))
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 160 220)))
    (entity/shape! p 'triangle 8)
    (entity/layer! p 'player)
    (entity/hp! p 3)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -4 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 4 0))
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)
         (let ((b (world/spawn 'player-bullet (entity/x p) (- (entity/y p) 10))))
           (entity/shape! b 'circle 2)
           (entity/layer! b 'player-bullet)
           (entity/set-vel! b 0 -6)))
       (set! spawn-counter (+ spawn-counter 1))
       (when (>= spawn-counter 30)
         (set! spawn-counter 0)
         (let ((e (world/spawn 'enemy
                               (+ 20 (modulo (world/hash) 280))
                               -10)))
           (entity/shape! e 'rect 10 10)
           (entity/layer! e 'enemy)
           (entity/solid! e #t)
           (entity/set-vel! e 0 1.5)
           ;; Every enemy fires 60 frames after spawn.
           (world/after 60 'enemy-shoot e)))
       (world/step)
       (for-each
        (lambda (pair)
          (let ((a (car pair)) (b (cadr pair)))
            (cond
              ((and (eq? (entity/kind a) 'player-bullet)
                    (eq? (entity/kind b) 'enemy))
               (entity/despawn! a) (entity/despawn! b))
              ((and (eq? (entity/kind b) 'player-bullet)
                    (eq? (entity/kind a) 'enemy))
               (entity/despawn! a) (entity/despawn! b))
              ((and (eq? (entity/kind a) 'enemy-bullet)
                    (eq? (entity/kind b) 'player))
               (entity/despawn! a)
               (entity/damage! b 1)
               (world/camera-shake! 4 0.9))
              ((and (eq? (entity/kind b) 'enemy-bullet)
                    (eq? (entity/kind a) 'player))
               (entity/despawn! b)
               (entity/damage! a 1)
               (world/camera-shake! 4 0.9)))))
        (world/collisions))
       (world/each 'player-bullet
                   (lambda (b) (when (< (entity/y b) 0) (entity/despawn! b))))
       (world/each 'enemy-bullet
                   (lambda (b) (when (> (entity/y b) 240) (entity/despawn! b))))
       (world/each 'enemy
                   (lambda (e) (when (> (entity/y e) 250) (entity/despawn! e))))
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 8 8)
       (world/each 'player-bullet
                   (lambda (b) (paint-cell 'bullet (entity/x b) (entity/y b) 2 2)))
       (world/each 'enemy-bullet
                   (lambda (b) (paint-cell 'enemy-bullet (entity/x b) (entity/y b) 3 3)))
       (world/each 'enemy
                   (lambda (e) (paint-cell 'enemy (entity/x e) (entity/y e) 10 10)))
       (paint-text (string-append \"HP: \" (number->string (entity/hp! p 0)))
                   10 10)))))
```

`world/after 60 'enemy-shoot e` schedules a callback in 60 frames.
When the runtime fires the `enemy-shoot` event on entity `e`, we
handle it (implicit — the runtime dispatches based on tag name, or you
register a handler; see reference on `world/after`).

For a chapter that keeps its footprint small, we use `world/after` as
a self-firing timer and hook shot-firing by scanning enemies each
frame. A more elaborate treatment would install a per-tag on-fire
handler.

`entity/damage! p 1` decrements the player's hp by 1. When hp reaches
0, the entity is dead (game-over trigger belongs to chapter 14; here
we just track).

---

## 5.4 Entity pooling

At high enemy counts, spawning and despawning entities every few
frames can allocate memory that garbage collection has to reclaim. In
tight arcade action this matters. A pool is a fixed set of entities we
recycle: mark inactive, then reuse on next spawn.

```scheme
;; Simple pool. We pre-spawn 50 bullets at (-100, -100) and toggle
;; alive/dead via entity/set!.
(define (init-bullet-pool)
  (let loop ((i 0) (acc '()))
    (if (= i 50)
        (reverse acc)
        (let ((b (world/spawn 'player-bullet -100 -100)))
          (entity/shape! b 'circle 2)
          (entity/layer! b 'player-bullet)
          (entity/set! b 'alive #f)
          (loop (+ i 1) (cons b acc))))))

(define bullet-pool #f)

(define (spawn-from-pool x y vx vy)
  ;; Find first dead bullet; wake it.
  (let loop ((bs bullet-pool))
    (cond
      ((null? bs) #f)   ;; pool exhausted
      ((not (entity/state (car bs) 'alive))
       (entity/set-pos! (car bs) x y)
       (entity/set-vel! (car bs) vx vy)
       (entity/set! (car bs) 'alive #t))
      (else (loop (cdr bs))))))

(define (release-to-pool b)
  (entity/set-pos! b -100 -100)
  (entity/set-vel! b 0 0)
  (entity/set! b 'alive #f))
```

This is not the only way. For most kid-scale games, allocating and
despawning is fine — the runtime is fast. But knowing the pool
pattern lets you SCALE. If you build a bullet-hell with 500 bullets on
screen and hit a frame-rate drop, come back here.

---

## 5.5 Waves and choreography

The next level of shmup design is coordinated enemy waves.

```scheme
;; A wave spawns 8 enemies in a V-formation, one every 4 frames.
(define (spawn-v-wave center-x)
  (let loop ((i 0))
    (when (< i 8)
      (world/after (* i 4) 'v-spawn
                   (list (+ center-x (* (- i 4) 15))
                         (- -10 (abs (- i 4)) 10)))
      (loop (+ i 1)))))
```

This uses `world/after` as a scheduler: 'four frames from now, fire a
v-spawn event with these parameters.' You would install a handler for
'v-spawn that reads its parameter and calls `world/spawn`. Cleanly:
choreography as data — the wave shape lives in the list of scheduled
events, not in a nested set of ifs.

Real shmups build a whole library of waves this way — line, arc,
spiral, funnel — and pull one at random each round.

---

## 5.6 The four patterns in a shoot-em-up

**Composition.** Every entity in this chapter is composed from small
verbs: shape, layer, solid, hp, velocity, tag. Add or remove a verb
to change kind. The 'player' and 'enemy' entities differ only in
their layer and their solid/sensor flags.

**Orchestration.** The frame loop orchestrates: poll input, spawn
enemies on the spawn-counter, spawn bullets on fire, step physics,
walk collision pairs and dispatch by kind, cleanup off-screen entities,
paint. Order matters HERE more than in earlier chapters — if we did
collision-walk BEFORE step, we'd handle previous frame's collisions.

**In-routing.** Three input handlers (left, right, fire) route to
three player-state mutations. The `world/collisions` list is walked
and routed by the (kind, kind) pair into different handlers. That
routing table is the essence of the shmup's game logic.

**Routing.** Every scheduled `world/after` call routes an event to
its handler in the future. The scheduler IS a router. Sound calls
route to audio; damage routes to hp; despawn routes to entity removal.
Almost every action-verb the shmup emits routes through the runtime
to something.

---

## 5.7 Common desktop tasks

**Balloon-hunt promotion.** Enemies replaced by product-icons floating
across the top of a shop page. Shooter is a virtual arrow. Hit five
in ten seconds = free shipping. Layered collisions ensure you can't
double-count.

**Alert-triage minigame for the operator.** An operator has 30 pending
customer messages. Each message is an enemy drifting down; the
operator clicks the ones to auto-reply and lets the rest fall through
for manual handling. The visualization is a coping game for an
inbox-avalanche.

---

## 5.8 Pitfalls

**Bullets hit their own spawner.** Layer setup incomplete —
`player-bullet` still includes `player` in its collides-with list. Fix
the alist.

**Frame rate craters at 100 enemies.** You are collision-walking a
list of all-pairs, which is O(n^2). For high counts use the pool
pattern and let the engine's broadphase (built into `world/step`) do
the winnowing. Also: check that you are cleaning up dead entities
(off-screen bullets, etc.) each frame.

**Enemy fires immediately on spawn, before moving on-screen.** Your
`world/after 60` handler runs 60 frames after spawn but the enemy is
still at y=-10 when it fires. Add `(when (>= (entity/y e) 0) ...)` to
gate firing.

**Collision-pair fires twice for the same collision.** The pair list
has the same pair in both orders sometimes. Add a hash-set dedupe or
handle only one order in your cond.

**Enemies stream in but never on-screen.** Your spawn y is above
where they can render, OR your enemy velocity is zero. Check
`entity/set-vel!` on spawn.

---

## 5.9 Try this yourself

1. Add a shield powerup: when the player has shield, damage decrements
   shield instead of hp. Shield decays over 10 seconds.
2. Add three enemy variants: fast-weak, slow-tough (2 hp), zigzag
   (velocity flips x every 20 frames).
3. Turn the shooter into an omni-shooter: 'a' fires down, 'b' fires
   up, 'up' fires up-left, 'down' fires up-right. Chapter 15 covers
   two-player; this is one-player two-thumbs.
4. Difficulty scaling: as `world/count 'enemy` grows over 20, add
   spawn-frequency; when it drops, slow spawn. Self-balancing pace.
5. Boss preview: after 30 seconds, spawn one big enemy with 20 hp.
   Chapter 12 covers bosses; this is your first sighting.
6. Screen-clear bomb: 'b' despawns every enemy on-screen and
   `world/camera-shake! 20 0.95`. Use once per life.

---

## 5.10 What we built

A player, a bullet pool, waves of enemies, layered collisions, camera
shake on hit, hp tracking. All in about 100 lines. The core of a shmup
is that small.

Next chapter: the same physics, but we tune FEEL. Same ship — with
deadzone, camera lag, ease-in on rotation, screen-shake calibrated to
impact velocity. Chapter 6 is the polish pass.")

;; Book of Arcade Games — Chapter 6: Feel — Deadzones and Ease

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(chapter
  :book                "Book of Arcade Games"
  :chapter-number      6
  :title               "Feel: Deadzones and Ease"
  :dialect             "motoi"
  :audience            :kid
  :also-for            :adult
  :content-rating      :G
  :author-lane         "arcade-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"
  :training-eligible   #t
  :confidentiality     "public"
  :voice               "sakura-teaching + game-design"
  :book-version        "1.0.0"
