"You have a game. Physics is honest, collisions register, the ship
thrusts, the paddle catches. The kid plays it for five minutes and puts
it down. Your friend's game — same shape, same code density — plays for
an hour. What is the difference?

FEEL. The thousand tiny corrections between raw physics and something a
human enjoys. Camera lag so the ship doesn't jitter. Ease curves so
rotation doesn't snap. Screen-shake sized to impact velocity. Coyote
time so the jump is generous. Input buffers so the fire is responsive.
Sound cued a half-frame before the visual so the ear leads the eye.

This chapter is 90% code that will look almost identical to earlier
chapters — you'll see the ship-with-thrust from chapter 3 twice, side
by side, before and after tuning. The lesson is that FEEL is code. It
is not vibes. It is `tick/ease`, `motion/with-feel`, `world/camera-shake!`
tuned to the right coefficients. Every microsecond has a shape.

We do a before-and-after study on one game so the kid can SEE the
difference. Then we build a knob-tuning workbench that lets you
adjust ten parameters live and feel the change.

---

## 6.1 Before — the raw game

Chapter 3's ship, unpolished.

```scheme
;; Ship + thrust, no polish. Play for 30 seconds. Note how it FEELS.
(define ship-angle 0)
(define (raw-ship)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((ship (world/spawn 'ship 160 120)))
    (entity/shape! ship 'triangle 12)
    (entity/drag! ship 0.01)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (set! ship-angle (- ship-angle 0.10)))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (set! ship-angle (+ ship-angle 0.10)))
       (when (input/down? 'a)
         (let ((vx (car (entity/vel ship)))
               (vy (cadr (entity/vel ship))))
           (entity/set-vel! ship
                            (+ vx (* 0.20 (geom/cos ship-angle)))
                            (+ vy (* 0.20 (geom/sin ship-angle))))))
       (world/step)
       (world/camera-follow! ship 1 0 0)   ;; instant follow — 1.0 factor
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'ship (entity/x ship) (entity/y ship) 12 12)))))

(big-bang raw-ship)
```

Play this. Rotate the ship — it feels snappy but slightly wrong.
Thrust — the camera glued to the ship makes the WORLD look like it
moves, not the ship. Fine for a static shooter; nauseating in a space
game where the ship is the thing.

The rotation is instant. The thrust is instant. The camera is instant.
Everything is instant. That is what earlier chapters teach for
clarity. But instant is not what the human hand wants.

---

## 6.2 After — the polished game

Same game, tuned.

```scheme
;; Same ship, with camera lag, rotation ease, thrust ease, screen shake.
(define ship-angle 0)
(define rot-vel 0)      ;; rotation velocity — accumulates over frames
(define thrust-charge 0) ;; how long 'a' has been held

(define (polished-ship)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((ship (world/spawn 'ship 160 120)))
    (entity/shape! ship 'triangle 12)
    (entity/drag! ship 0.01)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       ;; Rotation with ease — velocity ramps up over 8 frames.
       (cond
         ((input/down? 'left)
          (set! rot-vel (max -0.08 (- rot-vel 0.01))))
         ((input/down? 'right)
          (set! rot-vel (min  0.08 (+ rot-vel 0.01))))
         (else
          ;; No input — decay rotation velocity.
          (set! rot-vel (* rot-vel 0.85))))
       (set! ship-angle (+ ship-angle rot-vel))
       ;; Thrust with charge — hold 'a' longer for more thrust.
       (if (input/down? 'a)
           (set! thrust-charge (min 1.0 (+ thrust-charge 0.08)))
           (set! thrust-charge (* thrust-charge 0.90)))
       (when (> thrust-charge 0.02)
         (let ((vx (car (entity/vel ship)))
               (vy (cadr (entity/vel ship)))
               (thrust (* 0.20 (tick/ease thrust-charge))))
           (entity/set-vel! ship
                            (+ vx (* thrust (geom/cos ship-angle)))
                            (+ vy (* thrust (geom/sin ship-angle))))))
       (world/step)
       ;; Camera with lag — factor 0.08 = smooth follow, deadzone 40x30.
       (world/camera-follow! ship 0.08 40 30)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'ship (entity/x ship) (entity/y ship) 12 12)))))

(big-bang polished-ship)
```

Play THIS one. Rotate — the ship eases into rotation, holds a
constant spin while held, coasts to a stop when released. Thrust — the
first tap gives a small nudge; hold gives a full push. Camera — the
ship can wander within a 40×30 rect at screen center before the camera
begins to move; then the camera catches up smoothly.

Same physics. Same verbs. Different coefficients. Radically different
feel.

`tick/ease x` is a smoothstep — takes a linear 0-to-1 and returns an
S-curve 0-to-1 that starts slow, accelerates through the middle, eases
into 1. It is the single most-used feel primitive in games. Whenever
you have 'a parameter changes over time and abrupt looks bad,' wrap it
in `tick/ease`.

---

## 6.3 The eight knobs

Appendix H tabulates. Here is the shortlist every arcade game tunes.

**1. Acceleration.** How fast do you reach max speed from a standstill?
Small = deliberate; large = twitchy. Fighter jets: large. Trucks:
small.

**2. Deceleration.** How fast do you stop when input releases?
Independent of acceleration! Fast decel = precise. Slow decel = drifty.
Space games tune decel low.

**3. Apex hang.** For jumping games: how long does the player spend
at the top of the arc? `entity/gravity-scale! player 0.7` while
`vy < 0.5` for a hangtime effect. See chapter 7.

**4. Coyote time.** After walking off a ledge, how many frames can the
player still jump? Typically 4-8 frames. See chapter 7 and Appendix F.

**5. Jump buffer.** If the player presses jump N frames BEFORE landing,
buffer the press so it fires on landing. Typically 6-10 frame buffer.

**6. Screen shake.** How much does the screen shake on impact? Scale
with impact velocity. `(world/camera-shake! (* impact-vel 0.3) 0.85)`.
Decay factor 0.85 = 3-4 frame shake; 0.98 = 10+ frames.

**7. Sound pitch.** On impact, `(audio/play 'hit)` at pitch scaled by
impact velocity gives a satisfying variety. Even without pitch control,
alternating between two sounds ('hit1', 'hit2') on successive impacts
reduces monotony.

**8. Sound volume.** Softer sounds for background events, louder for
critical. Use `audio/master-volume` to duck all audio during dialogue.

## 6.4 A knob-tuning workbench

Wire the knobs to buttons so you can tune live.

```scheme
;; A ship you can retune while it flies.
;; 'a' fire; up/down adjust selected knob; left/right change knob.
(define ship-angle 0)
(define rot-vel 0)
(define knob-index 0)
(define knobs (vector 0.01   ; 0: rot-accel
                      0.08   ; 1: rot-max
                      0.85   ; 2: rot-decay
                      0.20   ; 3: thrust-per-frame
                      0.90   ; 4: thrust-decay
                      0.08   ; 5: camera-lag
                      40     ; 6: camera-dead-x
                      30))   ; 7: camera-dead-y
(define knob-names '#(\"rot-acc\" \"rot-max\" \"rot-dec\"
                     \"thr\" \"thr-dec\"
                     \"cam-lag\" \"dead-x\" \"dead-y\"))
(define thrust-charge 0)

(define (tuning-bench)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((ship (world/spawn 'ship 160 120)))
    (entity/shape! ship 'triangle 12)
    (entity/drag! ship 0.01)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       ;; Knob switching.
       (when (input/pressed? 'left)
         (set! knob-index (max 0 (- knob-index 1))))
       (when (input/pressed? 'right)
         (set! knob-index (min 7 (+ knob-index 1))))
       ;; Knob adjustment.
       (when (input/down? 'up)
         (vector-set! knobs knob-index
                      (+ (vector-ref knobs knob-index)
                         (if (< knob-index 5) 0.001 0.5))))
       (when (input/down? 'down)
         (vector-set! knobs knob-index
                      (- (vector-ref knobs knob-index)
                         (if (< knob-index 5) 0.001 0.5))))
       ;; Rotation using knobs.
       (let ((rot-acc (vector-ref knobs 0))
             (rot-max (vector-ref knobs 1))
             (rot-dec (vector-ref knobs 2))
             (thr     (vector-ref knobs 3))
             (thr-dec (vector-ref knobs 4))
             (cam-lag (vector-ref knobs 5))
             (dead-x  (vector-ref knobs 6))
             (dead-y  (vector-ref knobs 7)))
         ;; Rotation.
         (cond
           ((input/down? 'a) (set! rot-vel (min rot-max (+ rot-vel rot-acc))))
           ((input/down? 'b) (set! rot-vel (max (- rot-max) (- rot-vel rot-acc))))
           (else (set! rot-vel (* rot-vel rot-dec))))
         (set! ship-angle (+ ship-angle rot-vel))
         ;; Thrust.
         (set! thrust-charge (* thrust-charge thr-dec))
         ;; (no explicit thrust button in this bench — you're tuning rot)
         (world/step)
         (world/camera-follow! ship cam-lag dead-x dead-y)
         (paint-clear)
         (paint-cell 'ship (entity/x ship) (entity/y ship) 12 12)
         (paint-text (string-append (vector-ref knob-names knob-index)
                                    \": \"
                                    (number->string (vector-ref knobs knob-index)))
                     10 220))))))

(big-bang tuning-bench)
```

The kid selects a knob with left/right, adjusts with up/down, and
watches the ship's behavior change in real time. Turning `rot-acc`
from 0.001 to 0.05 goes from stately to instant. Turning `rot-dec`
from 0.85 to 0.99 makes the ship spin down slowly after release. The
knob values that FEEL right are the ones the kid keeps.

This is how real game designers tune. Get the game running end-to-end,
then spend a week on knobs.

---

## 6.5 motion/with-feel and motion/with-pace

The runtime exposes two feel-shaping primitives worth knowing.

`motion/with-feel target amount` adds micro-jitter to a motion so it
feels alive instead of robotic. Applied to a character's sprite: a
tiny wobble on step, breath-cycle-scale variation.

`motion/with-pace target curve` reshapes the timing of a motion
without changing endpoints. A ball can travel from A to B in the same
duration but with an ease-in, ease-out, or linear pace.

```scheme
;; A ship whose sprite wobbles subtly during coast.
(define (feel-wobble)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((ship (world/spawn 'ship 160 120)))
    (entity/shape! ship 'triangle 12)
    (entity/set-vel! ship 1 0)
    (motion/with-feel ship 0.5)   ;; 0.5-unit wobble
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'ship (entity/x ship) (entity/y ship) 12 12)))))
```

Subtle. The kid may not consciously see it. But turn it off and the
motion feels sterile. That is the wobble's whole job.

---

## 6.6 Impact-scaled shake

Not all impacts deserve the same shake. A tap-collision should not
rattle the screen; a boss-hit should. Scale shake by impact velocity.

```scheme
;; On any collision, shake proportional to impact speed.
(define (impact-scaled-shake)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.3)
  (world/floor! 240)
  (let ((ball (world/spawn 'ball 160 20)))
    (entity/bounce! ball 0.85)
    (entity/shape! ball 'circle 6))
  (on-frame
   (lambda ()
     (world/step)
     ;; Check ball's downward velocity when it touches the floor.
     (world/each 'ball
                 (lambda (b)
                   (when (and (>= (entity/y b) 234)
                              (> (cadr (entity/vel b)) 1.0))
                     (world/camera-shake! (* (cadr (entity/vel b)) 0.5)
                                          0.85))))
     (paint-clear)
     (world/each 'ball
                 (lambda (b) (paint-cell 'ball (entity/x b) (entity/y b) 6 6))))))

(big-bang impact-scaled-shake)
```

The first bounce shakes hard. Subsequent bounces shake less because
velocity has decayed. The screen tells the kid, without words, that
the ball is losing energy.

---

## 6.7 The four patterns for feel

**Composition.** Feel is composed. A polished ship = raw ship +
rotation-ease + thrust-ease + camera-lag + shake. Each layer costs a
few lines. Together they transform the play experience. Composition of
feel-layers is how a game gets great.

**Orchestration.** Order-of-application matters. Poll BEFORE update.
Update BEFORE draw. Apply screen shake to camera AFTER the shot's
impact registers. If you shake before the collision this frame, you
show yesterday's shake for today's hit — subtly wrong.

**In-routing.** Feel affects the in-routing itself. An 8-frame input
buffer changes how buttons ROUTE — a fire pressed 6 frames before
landing still routes to fire, arriving on the landing frame. That
delay is invisible to the player and invaluable to the feel.

**Routing.** Feel routes back out to display (camera shake), audio
(pitch/volume), and sometimes back to input (rumble via haptic
routing). Feel is the OUTBOUND polish on every action.

---

## 6.8 Common desktop tasks

**Shop-cursor deadzone.** In a shop's browsing UI, cursor movement can
be given a small deadzone (0.5 mm equivalent) before scrolling begins.
Kids scrolling on a shaky bus don't accidentally scroll past their
target. Same math as camera deadzone.

**Purchase-confirmation ease.** After 'buy', the button smoothly eases
into a checkmark shape over 12 frames rather than instantly swapping.
The tick/ease call is the same one your ship uses. Physics of UI
transitions is UI FEEL.

---

## 6.9 Pitfalls

**Everything too smooth.** Over-easing makes controls feel sluggish
and unresponsive. There is a bar — too twitchy is uncomfortable, too
smooth is uncomfortable, and the sweet spot is narrow. Playtest.

**Camera shake nauseating.** Shake magnitude scales linearly but
perception is exponential. Cap total shake at 20 pixels. Decay fast.

**Deadzone hides bugs.** A deadzone that suppresses tiny input can
also suppress input from a broken joystick you should be reporting.
Log raw input in dev mode.

**Buffered input replays after death.** If the player dies with 'a'
still in the input buffer, don't fire on respawn. Clear the buffer.

**Feel-tuning goes on forever.** Set a hard cap. Ship the game. Iterate
in a post-release patch. Perfection is the enemy of shipping.

---

## 6.10 Try this yourself

1. Take chapter 2's paddle game. Add rotation-ease-style acceleration
   to paddle movement. Does the game feel better?
2. Add `world/camera-shake!` to the brick game — small shake on brick
   hit, big shake on paddle catch. Where does it feel right?
3. Wire buttons to display 'input echo' — the last 30 frames of button
   state as a scrolling bar. Now you can SEE your own inputs and
   debug feel.
4. Record your play with `world/tape-record!`. Replay it with feel-off
   and feel-on. Note which feels 'more like a game.'
5. Tune the tuning workbench: change knob-adjust rate so precision
   knobs (rot-acc, thr) adjust by 0.001 and coarse knobs (dead-x)
   adjust by 1.
6. Add sound: `(audio/play 'thrust)` while 'a' is held. Volume scales
   with `thrust-charge`.

---

Ease, deadzone, camera lag, impact-scaled shake, tuning workbench.
The eight knobs. `tick/ease` as the workhorse of every feel decision.
`motion/with-feel` and `motion/with-pace` as the polish-layer verbs.

Next chapter: the hardest simple thing in game design. The jump. Slow

"The jump is the hardest simple thing in game design.

You press a button. A character leaves the ground, arcs through the air,
lands. That is one physics equation and two frames of state (grounded,
airborne). And yet: a jump can feel wrong in a hundred different ways.
Too heavy. Too floaty. Too twitchy. Insufficient hangtime at the apex.
Missing coyote time. Missing input buffer. Landing thud not matched to
fall distance. Camera judder on landing. The very best platformers spend
YEARS tuning the jump. Everything else in the game arranges itself
around the character's ability to arc between two platforms and land
where the player expected.

This chapter tunes the jump. We start with the raw physics —
`world/gravity!` + `entity/set-vel!` on 'a' press — and add polish
layer by layer until the jump feels great. Variable jump height by
releasing 'a' early. Slow-float apex via `entity/gravity-scale!`.
Coyote time. Jump buffer. Landing-shake sized to fall speed.

By the end you have a jump you would ship. And you have a template you
can drop into any character game.

---

## 7.1 The naive jump

Press 'a'. Set y-velocity to negative. Done.

```scheme
;; Naive jump: y-velocity to -12 on press. Gravity does the rest.
(define (naive-jump)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.6)
  (world/floor! 220)
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 160 200)))
    (entity/shape! p 'rect 12 16)
    (entity/bounce! p 0)
    (entity/solid! p #t)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -3 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 3 0))
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)
         (entity/set-vel! p (car (entity/vel p)) -12))
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 12 16)))))

(big-bang naive-jump)
```

Play it. The player leaps, arcs, lands. It works. It feels lifeless.

Two problems: every jump goes to the exact same height (you cannot
tap-a for a small hop or hold-a for a big leap), and there is no
generosity — if you press 'a' one frame after walking off a ledge,
tough luck.

We will fix both.

---

## 7.2 Variable jump height

Hold 'a' longer for a higher jump. Release early to cut short.

```scheme
;; Variable jump: release 'a' early cuts the ascent.
(define (variable-jump)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.6)
  (world/floor! 220)
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 160 200)))
    (entity/shape! p 'rect 12 16)
    (entity/bounce! p 0)
    (entity/solid! p #t)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -3 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 3 0))
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)
         (entity/set-vel! p (car (entity/vel p)) -12))
       ;; If ascending AND 'a' not held: cut ascent (fall faster).
       (when (and (not (input/down? 'a))
                  (< (cadr (entity/vel p)) 0))
         (entity/set-vel! p (car (entity/vel p))
                          (* (cadr (entity/vel p)) 0.5)))
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 12 16)))))

(big-bang variable-jump)
```

The block after the jump-press is the whole trick. Every frame we
check: is the player rising (vy < 0), AND is 'a' NOT held? If yes,
halve vy. This effectively terminates the ascent whenever the button
releases.

Tap 'a' quickly: small hop, maybe 15 pixels. Hold 'a' through the
whole ascent: full 60-pixel leap. The single button now has infinite
variability.

Every platformer worth playing has this. Kids feel the difference
within three presses.

---

## 7.3 Apex hang

Gravity should be lower at the top of the arc so the player hangs.
Increase gravity on descent.

```scheme
;; Apex hang: gravity-scale is 0.6 when rising, 1.0 when falling.
(define (hang-jump)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.6)
  (world/floor! 220)
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 160 200)))
    (entity/shape! p 'rect 12 16)
    (entity/bounce! p 0)
    (entity/solid! p #t)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -3 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 3 0))
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)
         (entity/set-vel! p (car (entity/vel p)) -12))
       (when (and (not (input/down? 'a))
                  (< (cadr (entity/vel p)) 0))
         (entity/set-vel! p (car (entity/vel p))
                          (* (cadr (entity/vel p)) 0.5)))
       ;; Apex-hang: dial gravity-scale based on vy.
       (cond
         ((< (cadr (entity/vel p)) -3)
          (entity/gravity-scale! p 0.7))    ;; rising fast — normal
         ((< (cadr (entity/vel p)) 1)
          (entity/gravity-scale! p 0.4))    ;; near apex — float
         (else
          (entity/gravity-scale! p 1.2)))   ;; falling — heavier
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 12 16)))))

(big-bang hang-jump)
```

`entity/gravity-scale! p k` multiplies world gravity for this entity
only. At 0.7 the player is a little floaty; at 0.4 near the apex, they
seem to pause; at 1.2 on descent, they slam back down.

That combination — float up, hang at top, fall fast — is what
distinguishes a good platformer jump from a physical one. Real gravity
is symmetric; game gravity is asymmetric.

---

## 7.4 Coyote time

If the player runs off a ledge, they get a few frames of grace to
still jump. The character 'coyote's — pauses in the air just long
enough to save the button-press. Named after the cartoon that DIDN'T
have this feature.

```scheme
;; Coyote time: 6 frames of jump-grace after leaving the ground.
(define grounded? #t)
(define coyote-frames 0)

(define (coyote-jump)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.6)
  (world/floor! 220)
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 160 200)))
    (entity/shape! p 'rect 12 16)
    (entity/bounce! p 0)
    (entity/solid! p #t)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -3 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 3 0))
       ;; Ground check: are we near the floor?
       (let ((now-grounded? (>= (entity/y p) 212)))
         (when (and grounded? (not now-grounded?))
           ;; Just left the ground — start coyote timer.
           (set! coyote-frames 6))
         (set! grounded? now-grounded?))
       (when (> coyote-frames 0)
         (set! coyote-frames (- coyote-frames 1)))
       ;; Jump if grounded OR within coyote window.
       (when (and (input/pressed? 'a)
                  (or grounded? (> coyote-frames 0)))
         (entity/set-vel! p (car (entity/vel p)) -12)
         (set! coyote-frames 0))
       (when (and (not (input/down? 'a))
                  (< (cadr (entity/vel p)) 0))
         (entity/set-vel! p (car (entity/vel p))
                          (* (cadr (entity/vel p)) 0.5)))
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 12 16)
       (paint-text (if grounded? \"grounded\" \"AIRBORNE\") 10 10)
       (paint-text (string-append \"coyote: \" (number->string coyote-frames))
                   10 20)))))

(big-bang coyote-jump)
```

The kid runs to the edge of the floor, off the edge, and taps 'a'
mid-air. If they are within six frames of leaving, the jump fires.
That is 0.1 seconds — invisible to conscious perception, but the
kid's SUBCONSCIOUS notices, and the game feels 'fair.'

Without coyote time, edges feel punishing. With it, edges feel
generous. Both are the same edge.

---

## 7.5 Jump buffer

If the player presses 'a' shortly BEFORE landing, buffer the press so
it fires on landing.

```scheme
;; Jump buffer: 'a' pressed within 8 frames before landing = fire on
;; land.
(define buffered-jump-frames 0)

(define (buffered-jump)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.6)
  (world/floor! 220)
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 160 200)))
    (entity/shape! p 'rect 12 16)
    (entity/bounce! p 0)
    (entity/solid! p #t)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -3 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 3 0))
       (let ((now-grounded? (>= (entity/y p) 212)))
         (when (input/pressed? 'a)
           (if now-grounded?
               (entity/set-vel! p (car (entity/vel p)) -12)
               (set! buffered-jump-frames 8)))
         ;; If buffered and we JUST landed: fire the buffered jump.
         (when (and now-grounded? (> buffered-jump-frames 0))
           (entity/set-vel! p (car (entity/vel p)) -12)
           (set! buffered-jump-frames 0)))
       (when (> buffered-jump-frames 0)
         (set! buffered-jump-frames (- buffered-jump-frames 1)))
       (when (and (not (input/down? 'a))
                  (< (cadr (entity/vel p)) 0))
         (entity/set-vel! p (car (entity/vel p))
                          (* (cadr (entity/vel p)) 0.5)))
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 12 16)))))

(big-bang buffered-jump)
```

Kids running off a ledge and pressing 'a' juuust before landing feel
respected. The game listens even when they are 'wrong' by strict
timing.

---

## 7.6 Landing shake

Big drops deserve a bigger thud.

```scheme
;; Landing shake sized to fall velocity.
(define was-airborne? #f)

(define (thumpy-jump)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.6)
  (world/floor! 220)
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 160 100)))
    (entity/shape! p 'rect 12 16)
    (entity/bounce! p 0)
    (entity/solid! p #t)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)
         (entity/set-vel! p (car (entity/vel p)) -12))
       (let ((vy (cadr (entity/vel p)))
             (now-grounded? (>= (entity/y p) 212)))
         ;; Just landed?
         (when (and was-airborne? now-grounded?)
           (world/camera-shake! (max 2 (* vy 0.3)) 0.9))
         (set! was-airborne? (not now-grounded?)))
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 12 16)))))

(big-bang thumpy-jump)
```

A small hop lands with barely a shake. A 100-pixel drop shakes the
whole screen. The player intuits WEIGHT from the feedback.

---

## 7.7 Putting it together — the good jump

All the tricks in one player controller.

```scheme
;; The full-featured jump: variable, apex-hang, coyote, buffer, thump.
(define grounded? #t)
(define was-grounded? #t)
(define coyote-frames 0)
(define buffered-jump 0)

(define (great-jump)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.6)
  (world/floor! 220)
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 160 200)))
    (entity/shape! p 'rect 12 16)
    (entity/bounce! p 0)
    (entity/solid! p #t)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -3 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 3 0))
       (set! grounded? (>= (entity/y p) 212))
       ;; Coyote update.
       (when (and was-grounded? (not grounded?))
         (set! coyote-frames 6))
       (when (> coyote-frames 0)
         (set! coyote-frames (- coyote-frames 1)))
       ;; Jump-press: fire if grounded/coyote, else buffer.
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)
         (if (or grounded? (> coyote-frames 0))
             (begin
               (entity/set-vel! p (car (entity/vel p)) -12)
               (set! coyote-frames 0))
             (set! buffered-jump 8)))
       ;; Buffered jump fires on land.
       (when (and grounded? (> buffered-jump 0))
         (entity/set-vel! p (car (entity/vel p)) -12)
         (set! buffered-jump 0))
       (when (> buffered-jump 0)
         (set! buffered-jump (- buffered-jump 1)))
       ;; Variable jump height.
       (when (and (not (input/down? 'a))
                  (< (cadr (entity/vel p)) 0))
         (entity/set-vel! p (car (entity/vel p))
                          (* (cadr (entity/vel p)) 0.5)))
       ;; Apex hang via gravity-scale.
       (cond
         ((< (cadr (entity/vel p)) -3) (entity/gravity-scale! p 0.7))
         ((< (cadr (entity/vel p)) 1)  (entity/gravity-scale! p 0.4))
         (else                          (entity/gravity-scale! p 1.2)))
       ;; Landing thump.
       (when (and (not was-grounded?) grounded?)
         (world/camera-shake!
          (max 2 (* (cadr (entity/vel p)) 0.3)) 0.9))
       (set! was-grounded? grounded?)
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 12 16)))))

(big-bang great-jump)
```

Play this. If you have played any of the classic platformers, you will
recognize the feel: forgiving, expressive, thumpy. About 40 lines
between the raw jump and this one, and every line is one of the eight
knobs from chapter 6.

---

## 7.8 The four patterns in a platformer

**Composition.** The player controller is a stack of small compositions:
gravity, gravity-scale, jump-press-handler, coyote-timer, jump-buffer,
land-shake. Each is a small stateful cell (`grounded?`, `coyote-frames`,
`buffered-jump`, `was-grounded?`) mutated per frame.

**Orchestration.** Order-of-updates matters and is subtle. Update
`grounded?` after physics settles, so the check is accurate. Fire
buffered jump BEFORE variable-height cut, so the cut doesn't
immediately nerf the buffered leap. Landing-shake needs to compare
this frame's grounded to LAST frame's grounded — hence
`was-grounded?`.

**In-routing.** The 'a' button routes to different handlers depending
on state: if grounded, fire jump; if airborne and ascending, cut jump
short (on release); if airborne and 'a' pressed, buffer. One button,
three routes.

**Routing.** Landing routes to camera-shake. Variable-height routes
to velocity. Coyote-timer routes back to input-eligibility. Every
frame is a small router table.

---

## 7.9 Common desktop tasks

**Fetch-decision toy.** A shop with lots of scrollable items presents
a small jump-to-collect: the customer's cursor is a character running
along a row of items; a tap makes them jump to grab an item; hold to
reach higher shelves. The jump curve determines what they can reach.
Playful shopping.

**Timing-check onboarding.** A shop welcoming new users runs a
30-second platformer tutorial as its splash — 'jump across three gaps
to enter.' Kids get in fast. The abandon-rate on 3-gap tutorials is
lower than on 3-tap tutorials, because doing feels better than
watching.

---

## 7.10 Pitfalls

**Player falls through the floor at high fall speed.** Tunneling. The
one-frame delta at terminal velocity exceeds the floor thickness.
Cap fall speed with `entity/max-speed!` or use `entity/gravity-scale!
p 0.5` at high vy to cap gently.

**Jump feels too floaty.** Reduce max jump velocity from -12 to -10,
increase gravity from 0.6 to 0.8. Also check that gravity-scale
returns to 1.2 (or higher) on descent.

**Coyote fires from ceilings.** Your `grounded?` check compares to
floor y=220, but the player may touch a ceiling and register grounded
briefly. Distinguish floor-contact from any-contact via layer-based
collision.

**Buffered jump fires on death.** Clear `buffered-jump` on death or
respawn.

**Apex hang looks weird when player is falling from a standstill.**
The gravity-scale conditional keys off velocity, not intent. If the
player was falling from a jump vs stepping off a platform, the
gravity-scale is the same. Usually fine, but for finicky feel you can
gate hang to 'only after a jump.'

---

## 7.11 Try this yourself

1. Tune max jump velocity from -12 to -8, -14, -20. Find the value
   that feels HEROIC without breaking the game.
2. Add double-jump: on the second press mid-air, if not-yet-double-
   jumped, fire another jump at -9 (weaker second jump).
3. Wall-jump: on collision with a wall while airborne, spring off
   at (5 * heading-x, -8).
4. Dash: 'b' button, sets vx to +/-8 for 6 frames while ignoring
   gravity. Chapter 6's ease applies.
5. Trampoline block: an entity with `entity/bounce! 1.5` that the
   player lands on and gets launched 20% higher.
6. Ledge grab: on collision with the corner of a platform while
   airborne, hold player at that y with `entity/pin!` until 'a' is
   pressed for a mantle-up.

---

## 7.12 What we built

A jump. Variable height. Apex hang. Coyote time. Jump buffer. Landing
shake. The full-featured platformer controller in about 40 lines of
per-frame logic. Every gaming platformer from the last 20 years uses
some subset of these tricks; the great ones use all of them.

Next chapter: leave the fixed screen behind. Build a tile world large
enough that the camera must scroll. Grids, tile-based collision,
level design as data.")

"So far every game has fit on one screen. Chapter 8 breaks out of the
box. A tile world is a grid of small squares — ground, wall, sky —
laid across a canvas larger than the display. The camera pans; the
player walks; the world unfolds under their character's feet.

Tile worlds are how a small computer punches above its weight. Instead
of storing pixels for every part of the map, you store one small
sprite per TYPE of tile and paint them in a grid. A 40x15 map of 32x32
tiles is 600 tiles, which is 1200 bytes of tile-index data, and paints
a 1280x480 pixel world.

This chapter lays out a tile world, walks a character across it, sets
camera bounds so the view stays inside the map, and lets the kid TYPE
a level as a string list and see it come alive. The last part is what
turns 'a game' into 'a game the kid made.'

---

## 8.1 The tile grid

The simplest possible tile world: a ground row.

```scheme
;; A 40-tile-wide ground row across the bottom of a larger world.
(define (ground-row)
  (world/reset!)
  ;; scene/grid 'ground columns rows cell-w cell-h origin-x origin-y
  (scene/grid 'ground 40 1 32 32 0 200)
  (world/each 'ground
              (lambda (t)
                (entity/shape! t 'rect 32 32)
                (entity/solid! t #t)))
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 100 168)))
    (entity/shape! p 'rect 16 32)
    (entity/solid! p #t)
    (entity/gravity-scale! p 1)
    (world/gravity! 0 0.5)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -3 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 3 0))
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)
         (entity/set-vel! p (car (entity/vel p)) -10))
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (world/each 'ground
                   (lambda (t)
                     (paint-cell 'ground (entity/x t) (entity/y t) 32 32)))
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 16 32)))))

(big-bang ground-row)
```

`scene/grid 'ground 40 1 32 32 0 200` says: spawn a grid tagged
'ground, 40 columns × 1 row, tile size 32×32, top-left origin at
(0, 200). Result: 40 tiles side by side at y=200. Each is a real
entity you can query and manipulate.

We iterate the tiles once at setup with `world/each` and mark each
solid. The physics engine now includes them in collision resolution.
The player, also solid, cannot pass through.

The player can walk left and right along the ground and jump. But
they can only see the leftmost 320 pixels of the 1280-pixel world.
Camera time.

---

## 8.2 Camera follow

Move the camera as the player moves.

```scheme
;; The camera follows the player. Now walking right REVEALS the world.
(define (scrolling-world)
  (world/reset!)
  (scene/grid 'ground 40 1 32 32 0 200)
  (world/each 'ground
              (lambda (t) (entity/shape! t 'rect 32 32) (entity/solid! t #t)))
  ;; Add a few 'wall towers.
  (world/spawn 'wall 400 168)
  (world/spawn 'wall 400 136)
  (world/spawn 'wall 700 168)
  (world/spawn 'wall 700 136)
  (world/spawn 'wall 700 104)
  (world/each 'wall
              (lambda (t) (entity/shape! t 'rect 32 32) (entity/solid! t #t)))
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 100 168)))
    (entity/shape! p 'rect 16 32)
    (entity/solid! p #t)
    (world/gravity! 0 0.5)
    (world/camera-follow! p 0.1 60 40)     ;; smooth follow, 60x40 dead
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -3 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 3 0))
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)
         (entity/set-vel! p (car (entity/vel p)) -10))
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (world/each 'ground
                   (lambda (t)
                     (paint-cell 'ground (entity/x t) (entity/y t) 32 32)))
       (world/each 'wall
                   (lambda (t)
                     (paint-cell 'wall (entity/x t) (entity/y t) 32 32)))
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 16 32)))))

(big-bang scrolling-world)
```

`world/camera-follow! p 0.1 60 40` says: follow entity `p` with lag
factor 0.1 (10% of the way each frame — smooth), only re-centering
when the player leaves a 60×40 pixel deadzone. Walk right, the world
slides left under you. Walk back, it slides right.

The paint calls did not change. `paint-cell` takes world coordinates,
and the runtime subtracts the camera position before drawing. The kid
does not have to think about screen-vs-world coordinates — the engine
handles it.

---

## 8.3 Camera bounds

The camera should not scroll past the edge of the world.

```scheme
;; Constrain the camera to a rectangle so you never see 'outside'.
(define (bounded-world)
  (world/reset!)
  (scene/grid 'ground 40 1 32 32 0 200)
  (world/each 'ground
              (lambda (t) (entity/shape! t 'rect 32 32) (entity/solid! t #t)))
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 100 168)))
    (entity/shape! p 'rect 16 32)
    (entity/solid! p #t)
    (world/gravity! 0 0.5)
    (world/camera-follow! p 0.1 60 40)
    ;; World is 40 tiles wide (1280 px) tall enough for jumps up to y=0.
    (world/camera-bounds! 0 0 1280 480)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -3 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 3 0))
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)
         (entity/set-vel! p (car (entity/vel p)) -10))
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (world/each 'ground
                   (lambda (t)
                     (paint-cell 'ground (entity/x t) (entity/y t) 32 32)))
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 16 32)))))

(big-bang bounded-world)
```

At the left edge, camera stops even as the player walks further left
(they leave the deadzone). At the right edge, camera stops. This is
the standard sidescroller camera. It costs one line of code
(`world/camera-bounds!`).

---

## 8.4 Levels as strings

The powerful part: type your level as a string of characters, one
character per tile. Parse it into entities.

```scheme
;; A little level design language.
;;   #  ground/wall
;;   .  air (nothing)
;;   P  player start
;;   G  goal

(define level-1
  '(\"..............................\"
    \"..............................\"
    \"..............................\"
    \"..............................\"
    \"..............#####...........\"
    \"..............................\"
    \"........########..............\"
    \"..............................\"
    \"...##...................######\"
    \"..............................\"
    \"P........................#...G\"
    \"##############################\"))

(define (parse-level lines)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((rows (length lines))
        (player-spawn #f)
        (goal-spawn #f))
    (let loop-r ((row 0))
      (when (< row rows)
        (let ((line (list-ref lines row)))
          (let loop-c ((col 0))
            (when (< col (string-length line))
              (let ((ch (string-ref line col))
                    (x (* col 32))
                    (y (* row 20)))
                (cond
                  ((char=? ch #\\#)
                   (let ((t (world/spawn 'ground x y)))
                     (entity/shape! t 'rect 32 20)
                     (entity/solid! t #t)))
                  ((char=? ch #\\P)
                   (set! player-spawn (list x y)))
                  ((char=? ch #\\G)
                   (set! goal-spawn (list x y))))
                (loop-c (+ col 1)))))
          (loop-r (+ row 1)))))
    (list player-spawn goal-spawn)))

(define (play-level)
  (let* ((spawns (parse-level level-1))
         (player-spawn (car spawns))
         (goal-spawn   (cadr spawns))
         (p (world/spawn 'player (car player-spawn) (cadr player-spawn))))
    (when goal-spawn
      (let ((g (world/spawn 'goal (car goal-spawn) (cadr goal-spawn))))
        (entity/shape! g 'rect 20 20)
        (entity/sensor! g #t)))
    (entity/shape! p 'rect 16 20)
    (entity/solid! p #t)
    (world/gravity! 0 0.5)
    (world/camera-follow! p 0.1 60 40)
    (world/camera-bounds! 0 0 960 240)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -3 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 3 0))
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)
         (entity/set-vel! p (car (entity/vel p)) -8))
       (world/step)
       ;; Check goal collision.
       (for-each
        (lambda (pair)
          (let ((a (car pair)) (b (cadr pair)))
            (when (or (and (eq? (entity/kind a) 'player)
                           (eq? (entity/kind b) 'goal))
                      (and (eq? (entity/kind b) 'player)
                           (eq? (entity/kind a) 'goal)))
              (paint-text \"YOU WIN!\" 120 100))))
        (world/collisions))
       (paint-clear)
       (world/each 'ground
                   (lambda (t)
                     (paint-cell 'ground (entity/x t) (entity/y t) 32 20)))
       (world/each 'goal
                   (lambda (g)
                     (paint-cell 'goal (entity/x g) (entity/y g) 20 20)))
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 16 20)))))

(big-bang play-level)
```

Read the level string. It looks like a picture of the level. That is
the point. The kid can literally SEE the world in the source. Change
a `.` to a `#` and a wall appears. Move `P` to change spawn. Move `G`
to change goal. That IS level design, no editor needed.

`char=?` compares characters. `#\\#` is Scheme's character literal for
'#'. `string-ref` indexes into a string. `list-ref` indexes into a
list. These are R7RS standards; every Motoi runtime has them.

Ten sample levels live in Appendix J (ASCII-to-Tile Level Format).

Eleven lines, twenty-four columns. Three floating platforms, a ground

---

## 8.6 The four patterns in a tile world

**Composition.** A world is composed of tiles. A tile is composed of
shape and solid. A level is composed of tiles arranged by the parser
from a string. Composition happens at three scales: tile, world, game.

**Orchestration.** The frame loop orchestrates: input, physics, tile
paint, entity paint. Tiles are stationary; you could paint them once
to a background buffer and skip re-painting each frame. Optimization
for later.

**In-routing.** Input routes to player movement. The level string
routes to entity spawns via the parser — a static in-routing, done
once at level load. `world/collisions` routes goal-touches to a
win-check.

**Routing.** Paint calls route to the framebuffer, adjusted by the
camera position under the hood. `world/camera-follow!` routes the
player's position to the camera every frame. Tile-load routes strings
to entities.

---

## 8.7 Common desktop tasks

**Shop-as-map.** A shop with lots of product categories can be
represented as a small tile world: each category is a room, walls
between them, doors to open. The kid navigates by walking rather than
clicking. Not for every shop, but for the whimsical ones.

**Save-navigation game.** After a shop sale ends, run a small
'find-your-favorite' minigame: your last three viewed items are goals
at scattered positions; you navigate a tile world to touch them all.
Completion = a bonus coupon.

---

## 8.8 Pitfalls

**Player sinks into the floor.** Your tile shape doesn't match the
grid cell size. Tile is 32×32; you set `entity/shape! t 'rect 32 20`.
Fix: match the shape to the visual.

**Camera stops before the player reaches an edge.** Your camera
bounds are too tight. `world/camera-bounds! 0 0 world-w world-h`
should use the FULL world dimensions.

**Level appears offset.** Your parser uses `(* col 32)` but you spawn
tiles at `y = (* row 20)` — mismatched tile size in x vs y. Use the
same number.

**One giant tile row.** Your loop broke early. Check the `loop-c`
termination condition — you want `<`, not `<=` (or `string-length` +
1, off by one).

**Player warps to spawn but never falls.** Player spawned INSIDE a
tile; the physics resolves by pushing them out (probably up) instantly.
Spawn one tile-row above ground.

---

## 8.9 Try this yourself

1. Add a `C` character for coin. Parse into a sensor entity. Collect

2. Add a `E` character for enemy. Parse into an entity that patrols

3. Add a `S` character for spring. Parse into an entity that on

4. Write your own level. Save it as `my-level.slat` in the same

5. Add a scrolling background parallax layer (chapter 9 will make
   this beautiful).
6. Add a level-select screen: three levels; arrow to pick; 'a' to
   play; on win, back to select.

---

## 8.10 What we built

`scene/grid` for cheap grid-generated worlds. `world/camera-follow!`
+ `world/camera-bounds!` for scrolling. A string-based level format
that a kid can read and write. A goal sensor. Ten sample levels in
Appendix J.

Next chapter: three layers of scrolling background, each at a
different rate. The world gains depth without gaining a Z-axis.")

;; ch09-scrolling-and-parallax.book.slatl
;; Book of Arcade Games — Chapter 9: Scrolling and Parallax

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(chapter
  :book                "Book of Arcade Games"
  :chapter-number      9
  :title               "Scrolling and Parallax"
  :dialect             "motoi"
  :audience            :kid
  :also-for            :adult
  :content-rating      :G
  :author-lane         "arcade-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"
  :training-eligible   #t
  :confidentiality     "public"
  :voice               "sakura-teaching + game-design"
  :book-version        "1.0.0"
  :draws-from-preserved (:book "book-of-games-preserved" :ch 13 :ch 14)
  :prose
"Two-dimensional games learned to feel three-dimensional before there
was a Z-axis. The trick is parallax. When you drive down a road, the
fencepost right next to you flies past your window; the mountain on the
horizon barely moves; the sun in the sky doesn't move at all. Your brain
computes depth from the difference in apparent motion.

Video games discovered this in the mid-1980s. A shoot-em-up with a
starfield background moving at half speed felt vast. A jungle-runner
with grass in front, trees behind, mountains further behind, sky
behind that — each moving at its own rate — felt like flying through
a WORLD, not walking a screen.

This chapter builds a three-layer parallax scene. Foreground grass at
1.0×, mid-hills at 0.5×, distant mountains at 0.2×. The camera pans as
the player runs, and the layers pan at different rates, and the world
gains depth. Same tile grid we built in chapter 8; different rules for
how the background paints.

---

## 9.1 The near layer

Start with just the foreground — camera-follow motion.

```scheme
;; Player runs right; foreground grass follows the camera exactly.
(define (near-only)
  (world/reset!)
  (scene/grid 'ground 60 1 32 20 0 200)
  (world/each 'ground
              (lambda (t) (entity/shape! t 'rect 32 20) (entity/solid! t #t)))
  ;; A row of grass tiles that scroll 1:1 with the camera.
  (scene/grid 'grass 60 1 32 8 0 192)
  (world/each 'grass
              (lambda (t) (entity/shape! t 'rect 32 8)))
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 100 168)))
    (entity/shape! p 'rect 16 32)
    (entity/solid! p #t)
    (world/gravity! 0 0.5)
    (world/camera-follow! p 0.1 60 40)
    (world/camera-bounds! 0 0 1920 240)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -3 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 3 0))
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)
         (entity/set-vel! p (car (entity/vel p)) -10))
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (world/each 'ground
                   (lambda (t)
                     (paint-cell 'ground (entity/x t) (entity/y t) 32 20)))
       (world/each 'grass
                   (lambda (t)
                     (paint-cell 'grass (entity/x t) (entity/y t) 32 8)))
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 16 32)))))

(big-bang near-only)
```

Nothing new — everything scrolls with the camera at rate 1.0×.
Walking right, all tiles slide left across the screen at the same
rate the player moves.

---

## 9.2 Add a slower layer

Now for the depth. We paint hills that scroll at HALF the camera rate.

```scheme
;; Foreground scrolls at 1.0x; mid-hills at 0.5x.
(define (two-layer-parallax)
  (world/reset!)
  (scene/grid 'ground 60 1 32 20 0 200)
  (world/each 'ground
              (lambda (t) (entity/shape! t 'rect 32 20) (entity/solid! t #t)))
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 100 168)))
    (entity/shape! p 'rect 16 32)
    (entity/solid! p #t)
    (world/gravity! 0 0.5)
    (world/camera-follow! p 0.1 60 40)
    (world/camera-bounds! 0 0 1920 240)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -3 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 3 0))
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)
         (entity/set-vel! p (car (entity/vel p)) -10))
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       ;; The camera is at some world position; get x-component.
       (let ((cam-x (car (world/camera))))
         ;; Mid-hills: 5 hill sprites, each 64 wide, at y = 140.
         ;; Their apparent x = world-x - camera-x * 0.5
         ;; So we paint them at (world-x - cam-x * 0.5).
         (let loop ((i 0))
           (when (< i 5)
             (let ((world-hill-x (* i 200))
                   (screen-hill-x (- (* i 200) (* cam-x 0.5))))
               ;; Only paint if visible.
               (when (and (> screen-hill-x -64) (< screen-hill-x 384))
                 (paint-cell 'hill (+ screen-hill-x cam-x) 140 64 40)))
             (loop (+ i 1)))))
       (world/each 'ground
                   (lambda (t)
                     (paint-cell 'ground (entity/x t) (entity/y t) 32 20)))
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 16 32)))))

(big-bang two-layer-parallax)
```

Read the middle-layer paint math carefully.

The camera is at world-x `cam-x`. Normally, an object at world-x `wx`
appears on screen at `wx - cam-x`. But for a parallax layer at rate
0.5, we want the object to appear on screen at `wx - cam-x * 0.5` —
half as much offset. Since `paint-cell` subtracts the camera under the
hood, we PASS a world-x of `screen-x + cam-x` — which becomes
`(wx - cam-x * 0.5) + cam-x = wx + cam-x * 0.5`, so `paint-cell`
displays it at `(wx + cam-x * 0.5) - cam-x = wx - cam-x * 0.5`. That's
the parallax we wanted.

Simpler mental model: 'draw each layer as if the camera moved at
(1 - rate) times its actual speed.'

The mid-hills drift half as fast as the ground. Kids running right
see the hills slide slowly. Their brain interprets: hills are far
away. No Z-axis needed.

---

## 9.3 Three layers

Add distant mountains and sky.

```scheme
;; Three parallax layers: sky (0), mountains (0.2), hills (0.5),
;; plus foreground (1.0).
(define (three-layer-parallax)
  (world/reset!)
  (scene/grid 'ground 60 1 32 20 0 200)
  (world/each 'ground
              (lambda (t) (entity/shape! t 'rect 32 20) (entity/solid! t #t)))
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 100 168)))
    (entity/shape! p 'rect 16 32)
    (entity/solid! p #t)
    (world/gravity! 0 0.5)
    (world/camera-follow! p 0.1 60 40)
    (world/camera-bounds! 0 0 1920 240)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -3 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 3 0))
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)
         (entity/set-vel! p (car (entity/vel p)) -10))
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (let ((cam-x (car (world/camera))))
         ;; Sky — doesn't scroll. Just paint at absolute (0, 0).
         (paint-cell 'sky (+ 160 cam-x) 40 320 80)
         ;; Distant mountains — 5 sprites at 0.2x rate.
         (let loop ((i 0))
           (when (< i 6)
             (paint-cell 'mountain
                         (+ (* i 200) (* cam-x 0.2)) 100 100 60)
             (loop (+ i 1))))
         ;; Mid hills — 5 sprites at 0.5x rate.
         (let loop ((i 0))
           (when (< i 8)
             (paint-cell 'hill
                         (+ (* i 200) (* cam-x 0.5)) 150 80 40)
             (loop (+ i 1))))
         (world/each 'ground
                     (lambda (t)
                       (paint-cell 'ground (entity/x t) (entity/y t) 32 20)))
         (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 16 32))))))

(big-bang three-layer-parallax)
```

Note the simplification: for parallax layers, we pass a world-x of
`(offset) + (cam-x * rate)`. The runtime subtracts cam-x, giving
`(offset - cam-x * (1 - rate))`. When rate is 1.0 (foreground), the
layer moves in perfect step with camera-shift. When rate is 0.5
(mid), half. When rate is 0.2 (distant), one-fifth. When rate is 0
(sky), no motion at all.

Play it. The kid runs right. Ground streams past. Grass tips wave in
front (add wobble via `tick/sine` per tile). Hills roll gently. Distant
mountains barely stir. The sky sits still.

That is depth from motion. It costs perhaps twenty lines of paint code.

---

## 9.4 Parallax within a layer

You can vary parallax rate WITHIN a layer for even more depth cues.
Close mountains at 0.4, far mountains at 0.15. Or clouds at 0.7 (with
independent time-wind) so they drift even when the camera is still.

```scheme
;; Clouds that drift independently of camera motion.
(define cloud-time 0)

(define (moving-clouds)
  (world/reset!)
  (scene/grid 'ground 60 1 32 20 0 200)
  (world/each 'ground
              (lambda (t) (entity/shape! t 'rect 32 20) (entity/solid! t #t)))
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 100 168)))
    (entity/shape! p 'rect 16 32)
    (entity/solid! p #t)
    (world/gravity! 0 0.5)
    (world/camera-follow! p 0.1 60 40)
    (world/camera-bounds! 0 0 1920 240)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (set! cloud-time (+ cloud-time 0.5))
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -3 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 3 0))
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (let ((cam-x (car (world/camera))))
         ;; Three clouds drifting.
         (let loop ((i 0))
           (when (< i 4)
             (let ((cloud-x (modulo (+ (* i 200)
                                        (* cam-x 0.3)
                                        (* cloud-time 0.4))
                                    1920)))
               (paint-cell 'cloud (+ cloud-x cam-x) 60 40 15))
             (loop (+ i 1))))
         (world/each 'ground
                     (lambda (t)
                       (paint-cell 'ground (entity/x t) (entity/y t) 32 20)))
         (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 16 32))))))

(big-bang moving-clouds)
```

The clouds drift right at 0.4 pixels per frame regardless of camera
motion, AND parallax at rate 0.3 with camera. `modulo` wraps them
around the world width so they always have something to show.

---

## 9.5 The four patterns in a scrolling world

**Composition.** Each layer is composed of position + parallax-rate +
paint. Chapter 8's world composition is base-layer only; this chapter
composes multiple parallax layers.

**Orchestration.** Paint order matters. Sky first (backmost). Then
mountains. Then hills. Then ground and entities. Then any UI overlay
last. If you paint in the wrong order, distant things cover close
things and the world looks broken.

**In-routing.** No new input routing.

**Routing.** The critical routing: WHICH cam-x offset each layer sees.
That is a routing table — layer -> parallax rate. Change the table,
change the depth.

---

## 9.6 Common desktop tasks

**Shop-page depth.** A shop's landing page can be a parallax scene:
background 'shop atmosphere' image at 0.2 rate, mid-layer product
categories at 0.6, foreground featured items at 1.0. As the customer
scrolls, the page gets depth. This is not a game — but it IS the same
paint routing.

**Receipt scrolling.** An order confirmation can scroll past like a
side-scroller — the receipt items pass in the foreground, brand imagery
in the mid, sky in back. Physics of a page turn done as parallax.

---

## 9.7 Pitfalls

**Layer flickers on scroll.** Your parallax rate isn't a clean
fraction of pixel positions and rounding causes jitter. Round to
integers per frame: `(round (* cam-x rate))`.

**Distant layer runs out.** Your sprites for the layer don't loop.
Wrap with `modulo` on the world width.

**Player disappears behind mountain.** Paint order — mountain painted
AFTER player. Reverse the order.

**Layer scrolls the wrong way.** You added instead of subtracted.
Parallax means slower motion IN THE SAME direction, not motion in the
opposite direction.

**Performance drops with too many layers.** Cap at 3-4 layers. Paint
only visible sprites (frustum-cull with `when` predicate).

---

## 9.8 Try this yourself

1. Add a fourth layer: fog just in front of the mountains, rate
   0.35, semi-transparent.
2. Add wind: shift the cloud drift with `tick/sine (* frame 0.01)`
   so clouds meander instead of moving in a straight line.
3. Vertical parallax: as the player jumps high, the mountains rise
   slightly. The horizon moves.
4. Time-of-day: swap sky color from blue to orange to purple over
   1000 frames. The parallax pieces don't move, but their palette
   does.
5. Depth-of-field: paint distant layer with smaller sprites and
   dimmer color (via `paint-glow` opposite).
6. A cave scene: everything inverse. Distant walls scroll faster
   than close walls, and near you feels big.

---

## 9.9 What we built

Multi-layer parallax with three rates. Cloud drift independent of
camera. Paint-order awareness. World-width wrapping for infinite
layers.

Next chapter: put enemies in this world that don't just drift — they
REACT. Chase you when close. Run away when hurt. Wander when idle.
Simple AI, arcade-style.")

;; ch10-enemies-that-react.book.slatl
;; Book of Arcade Games — Chapter 10: Enemies That React

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(chapter
  :book                "Book of Arcade Games"
  :chapter-number      10
  :title               "Enemies That React"
  :dialect             "motoi"
  :audience            :kid
  :also-for            :adult
  :content-rating      :G
  :author-lane         "arcade-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"
  :training-eligible   #t
  :confidentiality     "public"
  :voice               "sakura-teaching + game-design"
  :book-version        "1.0.0"
  :draws-from-preserved (:book "book-of-games-preserved" :ch 4 :ch 9)
  :prose
"An enemy that stands still is furniture. An enemy that reacts is a
character. The gap between the two is about fifteen lines of AI code.

Arcade enemies do not need to plan. They do not need utility functions,
minimax, neural nets. They need to LOOK like they are thinking, and
LOOK IS ENOUGH. A goomba that turns around when it reaches a ledge
feels smarter than an enemy that walks off. A ghost that chases you
when close and gives up when far feels alive. That's the whole trick.

This chapter builds five enemy archetypes with the `ai/*` library:
the wanderer, the chaser, the fleer, the patroller, and the ambusher.
Each is 10 to 30 lines. All are runnable. Between them they cover
about 80% of the enemies in any 2D arcade game.

---

## 10.1 The wanderer

Aimless drift with slight direction changes.

```scheme
;; A wandering blob. Doesn't care about the player. Just moves.
(define (wanderer)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((blob (world/spawn 'enemy 100 100)))
    (entity/shape! blob 'circle 8)
    (entity/max-speed! blob 1.5)
    (ai/wander blob 0.05)                ;; slight direction jitter each frame
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'enemy (entity/x blob) (entity/y blob) 8 8)))))

(big-bang wanderer)
```

`ai/wander id amount` sets the entity to steer with random small
direction changes each frame. Amount tunes how erratic — small values
(0.02) look almost purposeful; large values (0.2) look drunk.

`entity/max-speed!` caps velocity. Without it, `ai/wander` can
accelerate the blob past playable speeds.

---

## 10.2 The chaser

Comes toward the player when close; loses interest when far.

```scheme
;; An enemy that chases when within 80 pixels.
(define (chaser)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 160 120))
        (e (world/spawn 'enemy 60 60)))
    (entity/shape! p 'triangle 8)
    (entity/shape! e 'circle 6)
    (entity/max-speed! e 1.2)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -3 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 3 0))
       (when (input/down? 'up)    (entity/move! p 0 -3))
       (when (input/down? 'down)  (entity/move! p 0 3))
       ;; If enemy within 80 px of player: seek. Else wander.
       (if (< (entity/distance e p) 80)
           (ai/seek e p)
           (ai/wander e 0.05))
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 8 8)
       (paint-cell 'enemy (entity/x e) (entity/y e) 6 6)))))

(big-bang chaser)
```

`ai/seek e p` sets `e` to steer toward `p`. Every frame.
`entity/distance a b` is Euclidean distance. Cheap to compute.

Watch the enemy. When you drift close, it starts to home. When you
run past 80 pixels away, it goes back to wandering. That two-line
conditional produces distinct enemy 'moods' the player reads
instantly.

---

## 10.3 The fleer

Low HP? Run.

```scheme
;; Enemy chases when healthy, flees when hurt.
(define (fleer)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 160 120))
        (e (world/spawn 'enemy 60 60)))
    (entity/shape! p 'triangle 8)
    (entity/shape! e 'circle 8)
    (entity/hp! e 3)
    (entity/max-speed! e 1.5)
    ;; Press 'a' to damage the enemy.
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -3 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 3 0))
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)
         (when (< (entity/distance e p) 30)
           (entity/damage! e 1)
           (world/camera-shake! 3 0.9)))
       (if (< (entity/hp! e 0) 2)
           (ai/flee e p)
           (ai/seek e p))
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 8 8)
       (when (entity/alive? e)
         (paint-cell 'enemy (entity/x e) (entity/y e) 8 8))
       (paint-text (string-append \"Enemy HP: \"
                                  (number->string (entity/hp! e 0)))
                   10 10)))))

(big-bang fleer)
```

`ai/flee e p` is the negative of seek — steer away. When the enemy's
hp drops below 2, it panics and runs.

`entity/hp! e 0` with argument 0 READS the current hp without changing
it. If instead you called `entity/hp! e 5` you would SET hp to 5.
(This is a common Motoi-Scheme convention: getter and setter share a
name, disambiguated by argument arity.)

---

## 10.4 The patroller

Walks a fixed path.

```scheme
;; Patrols between (x=40, y=100) and (x=280, y=100).
(define patrol-target 'right)

(define (patroller)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((e (world/spawn 'enemy 40 100)))
    (entity/shape! e 'rect 12 12)
    (entity/max-speed! e 1)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       ;; Decide target end based on current x.
       (cond
         ((and (eq? patrol-target 'right) (> (entity/x e) 275))
          (set! patrol-target 'left))
         ((and (eq? patrol-target 'left)  (< (entity/x e) 45))
          (set! patrol-target 'right)))
       (if (eq? patrol-target 'right)
           (entity/set-vel! e 1 0)
           (entity/set-vel! e -1 0))
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'enemy (entity/x e) (entity/y e) 12 12)))))

(big-bang patroller)
```

Simplest possible AI: a state variable, a switch condition, a velocity
set. No `ai/*` verbs at all. Sometimes the cleanest reactive enemy is
just a `cond`.

You can make patrol paths from lists of waypoints and use
`ai/waypoints` + `ai/follow-path` for more complex routes. The
guarding-a-corridor kind of enemy is this pattern plus a `ai/seek` on
seeing the player.

---

## 10.5 The ambusher

Waits invisible. Springs when the player crosses a line.

```scheme
;; Waits at y=200 (offscreen). When player crosses x=180, springs up.
(define ambush-triggered #f)

(define (ambusher)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 40 120))
        (a (world/spawn 'enemy 180 220)))
    (entity/shape! p 'triangle 8)
    (entity/shape! a 'rect 14 14)
    (entity/max-speed! a 3)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 3 0))
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -3 0))
       (when (and (not ambush-triggered) (> (entity/x p) 180))
         (set! ambush-triggered #t)
         (world/camera-shake! 5 0.9))
       (if ambush-triggered
           (ai/seek a p)
           (entity/set-vel! a 0 0))
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 8 8)
       (when ambush-triggered
         (paint-cell 'enemy (entity/x a) (entity/y a) 14 14))))))

(big-bang ambusher)
```

The ambusher is a trap disguised as an enemy. `ai/seek` doesn't fire
until the trigger. When it does, camera-shake tells the player: THIS
was intentional. You have entered someone's plan.

---

## 10.6 Enemy memory — the blackboard

Enemies benefit from remembering things across frames. Where did they
last see the player? How long since combat? `ai/bb-set!` /
`ai/bb-get` provide per-entity memory (blackboard).

```scheme
;; Enemy remembers last-seen player position. Chases toward it even
;; after losing sight.
(define (memory-enemy)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 160 120))
        (e (world/spawn 'enemy 40 40)))
    (entity/shape! p 'triangle 8)
    (entity/shape! e 'circle 6)
    (entity/max-speed! e 1.5)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -3 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 3 0))
       (when (input/down? 'up)    (entity/move! p 0 -3))
       (when (input/down? 'down)  (entity/move! p 0 3))
       (if (< (entity/distance e p) 100)
           ;; See player: chase directly AND remember.
           (begin
             (ai/bb-set! e 'last-seen-x (entity/x p))
             (ai/bb-set! e 'last-seen-y (entity/y p))
             (ai/seek e p))
           ;; Lost sight: head toward last-seen if remembered.
           (if (ai/bb-has? e 'last-seen-x)
               (let ((lx (ai/bb-get e 'last-seen-x))
                     (ly (ai/bb-get e 'last-seen-y)))
                 (if (< (geom/distance (entity/x e) (entity/y e) lx ly) 5)
                     (ai/wander e 0.05)   ;; arrived — wander
                     (entity/set-vel! e
                                      (* 1.2 (geom/cos
                                              (geom/atan2
                                               (- ly (entity/y e))
                                               (- lx (entity/x e)))))
                                      (* 1.2 (geom/sin
                                              (geom/atan2
                                               (- ly (entity/y e))
                                               (- lx (entity/x e))))))))
               (ai/wander e 0.05)))
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 8 8)
       (paint-cell 'enemy (entity/x e) (entity/y e) 6 6)))))

(big-bang memory-enemy)
```

The enemy chases when it sees you. When it loses sight (>100 px), it
heads toward where it LAST saw you. Reaches that spot, gives up,
wanders. Same reaction sequence as a real guard.

---

## 10.7 The four patterns

**Composition.** Each enemy = shape + max-speed + hp + AI behavior +
blackboard memory. Swap any one to get a different enemy.

**Orchestration.** Per-frame: decide behavior (mode selector), apply
steering (ai/seek/flee/wander), step physics, draw. The mode selector
IS the enemy's brain — often just a `cond` on distance and hp.

**In-routing.** Combat inputs (player attacks) route to
`entity/damage!` which routes to hp change which routes to the mode
selector. Chains all the way through.

**Routing.** Enemies route their intent through the ai/ verbs. `ai/seek`
routes 'go toward this' to the physics engine as continuous force
application. Layered on top of raw velocity control.

---

## 10.8 Common desktop tasks

**Attention-getting scoreboard entity.** A shop's live activity
scoreboard has a small blob that wanders during quiet times and dashes
across the screen when a sale happens. `ai/wander` most of the time,
`ai/seek` a target position (the sale-notification widget) when an
event fires.

**Auto-follow tutorial guide.** A tutorial character that pursues the
customer's cursor as they navigate a shop for the first three visits,
pointing at things. Uses `ai/pursue` (pursue = seek with lookahead)
to feel less lockstep than direct follow.

---

## 10.9 Pitfalls

**Chaser jitters when close.** `ai/seek` doesn't gracefully stop. When
enemy overshoots player, it turns 180, overshoots back. Fix: use
`ai/arrive` instead — same as seek but decelerates near target. Or
switch to `ai/wander` inside 15 px.

**Ambusher fires before player is in position.** Trigger condition
too permissive. Add a compound check: `x > 180 AND y > 100 AND
x-vel > 0`.

**Blackboard grows without bound.** Enemies accumulate keys forever.
Add `ai/bb-del!` to expire old keys.

**All enemies do the same thing at the same time.** Their state is
NOT independent. Check: are you using globals where you should be
using entity blackboard? `patrol-target` in section 10.4 is a global
— fine for one enemy, broken for two. For multi-enemy patrol, store
`patrol-target` on the entity via `ai/bb-set!`.

**Fleer flees INTO a wall.** `ai/flee` steers directly away with no
obstacle avoidance. Add `ai/wall!` around walls, and enemies avoid.

---

## 10.10 Try this yourself

1. Combine chaser + fleer + patroller into ONE enemy with three
   modes. The mode selector: 'default patrol; if player < 80 px,
   chase; if hp < 2, flee.'
2. Give the enemy vision cone: only see player if the vector
   enemy-to-player is within 60 degrees of enemy's facing.
3. Make an enemy that mimics the player's last three inputs (via
   blackboard). It follows your moves on a 10-frame delay.
4. A herd: 20 enemies with wander + weak cohesion + strong separation.
   Move as a group. Chapter 5 of the Simulation book covers this in
   depth.
5. Enemy learns: on each hit, add 1 to a `hits-taken` blackboard
   value; after 5 hits, switch to permanent-flee mode.
6. Sound cues: `audio/play 'growl` when enemy first sees the player
   (transition from wander to seek). One growl per sighting.

---

## 10.11 What we built

Five enemy archetypes: wanderer, chaser, fleer, patroller, ambusher.
Distance + hp mode selectors. Blackboard memory for last-seen. The
`ai/*` steering verbs.

Next chapter: powerups. Coins that magnet to the player. Invincibility
stars. Hearts. Keys. Chapter 11 is where the game gets GENEROUS.")
