;; ch11-powerups-and-pickups.book.slatl
;; Book of Arcade Games — Chapter 11: Powerups and Pickups

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(chapter
  :book                "Book of Arcade Games"
  :chapter-number      11
  :title               "Powerups and Pickups"
  :dialect             "motoi"
  :audience            :kid
  :also-for            :adult
  :content-rating      :G
  :author-lane         "arcade-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"
  :training-eligible   #t
  :confidentiality     "public"
  :voice               "sakura-teaching + game-design"
  :book-version        "1.0.0"
  :prose
"A coin appears. You touch it. Something in you fires a small dopamine
burst. That dopamine is why arcades exist. Every arcade game is a
carefully-timed sequence of small rewards designed to keep you
playing. Coins. Hearts. Stars. Keys. Shields. Weapons. Speed boosts.
Time slows.

This chapter builds the pickup family. Coins that magnet to you when
close. Hearts that restore hp. Invincibility stars that make you glow
and pass through enemies. Keys that unlock doors. Persistent state via
Cortex so the score survives sessions.

The pattern is simple: sensor entity, collision handler, state
mutation. Repeat with variations. By the end you have six pickup types
that compose with everything else in the book.

---

## 11.1 The coin

Touch to collect.

```scheme
;; A coin. You touch it, it disappears, score goes up.
(define score 0)

(define (basic-coin)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.4)
  (world/floor! 220)
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 40 200))
        (c (world/spawn 'coin 240 200)))
    (entity/shape! p 'rect 12 20) (entity/solid! p #t)
    (entity/shape! c 'circle 6) (entity/sensor! c #t)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -3 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 3 0))
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)
         (entity/set-vel! p (car (entity/vel p)) -10))
       (world/step)
       (for-each
        (lambda (pair)
          (let ((a (car pair)) (b (cadr pair)))
            (when (and (eq? (entity/kind a) 'player)
                       (eq? (entity/kind b) 'coin))
              (entity/despawn! b)
              (set! score (+ score 10))
              (world/camera-shake! 1 0.9))
            (when (and (eq? (entity/kind b) 'player)
                       (eq? (entity/kind a) 'coin))
              (entity/despawn! a)
              (set! score (+ score 10))
              (world/camera-shake! 1 0.9))))
        (world/collisions))
       (paint-clear)
       (world/each 'coin
                   (lambda (c) (paint-cell 'coin (entity/x c) (entity/y c) 6 6)))
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 12 20)
       (paint-text (string-append \"Score: \" (number->string score))
                   10 10)))))

(big-bang basic-coin)
```

`entity/sensor! c #t` — a sensor is a collision-registering entity
that does NOT physically block. The player passes through the coin
(doesn't bounce off) but the collision fires. Every pickup uses
sensors.

The tiny camera-shake (1 pixel, 0.9 decay = one-frame twitch) is the
game's kiss. It's imperceptible on paper. In your hand it's the whole
feel.

---

## 11.2 Magnet coins

Coins are more fun when they leap to meet you.

```scheme
;; Coins that gravitate toward the player when within 40 px.
(define score 0)

(define (magnet-coins)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.4)
  (world/floor! 220)
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 40 200)))
    (entity/shape! p 'rect 12 20) (entity/solid! p #t)
    ;; Spawn 8 coins scattered.
    (let loop ((i 0))
      (when (< i 8)
        (let ((c (world/spawn 'coin (+ 60 (* i 30)) (+ 150 (modulo (* i 17) 40)))))
          (entity/shape! c 'circle 5)
          (entity/sensor! c #t))
        (loop (+ i 1))))
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -3 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 3 0))
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)
         (entity/set-vel! p (car (entity/vel p)) -10))
       ;; Magnet: for each coin, if within 40 px, apply attraction.
       (world/each 'coin
                   (lambda (c)
                     (when (< (entity/distance c p) 40)
                       (world/attract! c (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 3))))
       (world/step)
       (for-each
        (lambda (pair)
          (let ((a (car pair)) (b (cadr pair)))
            (when (or (and (eq? (entity/kind a) 'player)
                           (eq? (entity/kind b) 'coin))
                      (and (eq? (entity/kind b) 'player)
                           (eq? (entity/kind a) 'coin)))
              (entity/despawn!
               (if (eq? (entity/kind a) 'coin) a b))
              (set! score (+ score 10))
              (world/camera-shake! 1 0.85))))
        (world/collisions))
       (paint-clear)
       (world/each 'coin
                   (lambda (c) (paint-cell 'coin (entity/x c) (entity/y c) 5 5)))
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 12 20)
       (paint-text (string-append \"Score: \" (number->string score)) 10 10)))))

(big-bang magnet-coins)
```

`world/attract! c (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 3` says 'attract coin c to
the point (player-x, player-y) with strength 3.' The engine keeps
applying that force each frame until you change or clear it.

Coins near you START to leap. The game becomes about MOVEMENT — you
don't need to touch every coin, you need to get CLOSE.

---

## 11.3 Hearts

Restore hp.

```scheme
;; Hearts scattered around; touching restores 1 hp up to max 5.
(define (heart-pickup)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.4)
  (world/floor! 220)
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 40 200)))
    (entity/shape! p 'rect 12 20)
    (entity/solid! p #t)
    (entity/hp! p 2)
    (let loop ((i 0))
      (when (< i 4)
        (let ((h (world/spawn 'heart (+ 80 (* i 60)) 200)))
          (entity/shape! h 'rect 10 10)
          (entity/sensor! h #t))
        (loop (+ i 1))))
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -3 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 3 0))
       (world/step)
       (for-each
        (lambda (pair)
          (let ((a (car pair)) (b (cadr pair)))
            (let ((heart (cond ((eq? (entity/kind a) 'heart) a)
                                ((eq? (entity/kind b) 'heart) b)
                                (else #f))))
              (when heart
                (when (< (entity/hp! p 0) 5)
                  (entity/hp! p (+ (entity/hp! p 0) 1))
                  (entity/despawn! heart)
                  (world/camera-shake! 2 0.9))))))
        (world/collisions))
       (paint-clear)
       (world/each 'heart
                   (lambda (h)
                     (paint-cell 'heart (entity/x h) (entity/y h) 10 10)))
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 12 20)
       (paint-text (string-append \"HP: \" (number->string (entity/hp! p 0)))
                   10 10)))))

(big-bang heart-pickup)
```

Note the trick: touching a heart at max hp does NOT despawn it. The
heart persists for when you actually need it. Small design decision;
massive quality-of-life win.

---

## 11.4 Invincibility star

Timed effect.

```scheme
;; Grab star: 300 frames of invincibility. Star spawns at (200, 200).
(define star-timer 0)

(define (star-pickup)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.4)
  (world/floor! 220)
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 40 200))
        (s (world/spawn 'star 200 200))
        (e (world/spawn 'enemy 280 200)))
    (entity/shape! p 'rect 12 20) (entity/solid! p #t) (entity/hp! p 3)
    (entity/shape! s 'rect 12 12) (entity/sensor! s #t)
    (entity/shape! e 'rect 12 12) (entity/solid! e #t) (entity/max-speed! e 1)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -3 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 3 0))
       ;; Enemy chases if star not active; otherwise stays put.
       (if (> star-timer 0)
           (entity/set-vel! e 0 0)
           (ai/seek e p))
       (world/step)
       (for-each
        (lambda (pair)
          (let ((a (car pair)) (b (cadr pair)))
            (when (or (and (eq? (entity/kind a) 'player)
                           (eq? (entity/kind b) 'star))
                      (and (eq? (entity/kind b) 'player)
                           (eq? (entity/kind a) 'star)))
              (entity/despawn! (if (eq? (entity/kind a) 'star) a b))
              (set! star-timer 300)      ;; 5 seconds at 60 fps
              (world/camera-shake! 4 0.9))
            ;; Player-enemy contact: only damage if NOT invincible.
            (when (and (or (eq? (entity/kind a) 'player)
                           (eq? (entity/kind b) 'player))
                       (or (eq? (entity/kind a) 'enemy)
                           (eq? (entity/kind b) 'enemy))
                       (<= star-timer 0))
              (entity/damage! p 1)
              (world/camera-shake! 5 0.9))))
        (world/collisions))
       (when (> star-timer 0)
         (set! star-timer (- star-timer 1)))
       (paint-clear)
       (world/each 'star
                   (lambda (s) (paint-cell 'star (entity/x s) (entity/y s) 12 12)))
       (paint-cell 'enemy (entity/x e) (entity/y e) 12 12)
       ;; Draw player: sparkly if invincible.
       (if (> star-timer 0)
           (paint-cell 'invincible (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 12 20)
           (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 12 20))
       (paint-text (string-append \"Star: \" (number->string star-timer)) 10 10)
       (paint-text (string-append \"HP: \" (number->string (entity/hp! p 0))) 10 20)))))

(big-bang star-pickup)
```

`star-timer` counts down each frame; while > 0, damage doesn't apply
and the player renders in a different color. When it hits 0, back to
normal. Classic five-second superpower.

---

## 11.5 Cortex — persistent state

Score should survive the browser tab closing.

```scheme
;; Score persists across sessions via Cortex.
(define (persistent-score)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((score (or (cortex/read 'arcade-score) 0)))
    (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 40 200))
          (c (world/spawn 'coin 200 200)))
      (entity/shape! p 'rect 12 20) (entity/solid! p #t)
      (entity/shape! c 'circle 6) (entity/sensor! c #t)
      (on-frame
       (lambda ()
         (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -3 0))
         (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 3 0))
         (world/step)
         (for-each
          (lambda (pair)
            (let ((a (car pair)) (b (cadr pair)))
              (when (or (and (eq? (entity/kind a) 'player)
                             (eq? (entity/kind b) 'coin))
                        (and (eq? (entity/kind b) 'player)
                             (eq? (entity/kind a) 'coin)))
                (entity/despawn! (if (eq? (entity/kind a) 'coin) a b))
                (set! score (+ score 10))
                (cortex/write 'arcade-score score))))
          (world/collisions))
         (paint-clear)
         (world/each 'coin
                     (lambda (c)
                       (paint-cell 'coin (entity/x c) (entity/y c) 6 6)))
         (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 12 20)
         (paint-text (string-append \"Total Score: \" (number->string score))
                     10 10))))))

(big-bang persistent-score)
```

`cortex/read 'arcade-score` returns whatever was last written under
that key, or `#f` if never written. `(or ... 0)` defaults to zero on
first play.

Every coin-pickup, we write back. The score IS the memory. Next
session, `cortex/read` returns the total. The kid's persistence
extends beyond the game session.

---

## 11.6 The four patterns

**Composition.** Every pickup: shape + sensor + tag + optional
per-pickup state. Each pickup is 4 verbs. The powerup catalog is a
composition-shopping list — pick 3, drop them into your game.

**Orchestration.** Frame loop orchestrates spawn (setup),
pickup-collision handling, timer decrement, paint. Pickup effects are
applied inside the collision walk, WHILE the physics step is complete.

**In-routing.** Collision pairs route by (kind-a, kind-b) into
pickup handlers. Each pickup type has its handler; the router picks
by tag.

**Routing.** Pickups route to state: score, hp, timer, or Cortex.
`cortex/write` routes state to persistent storage. Persistence IS
routing across sessions.

---

## 11.7 Common desktop tasks

**Loyalty-point animation.** Every completed purchase spawns a coin
that magnets toward the customer's loyalty-badge icon in the corner.
Physics-first feedback for a real reward accrual.

**Achievement-unlock burst.** When a customer reaches a milestone,
spawn 20 sparkle-entities that scatter from the badge. Cortex persists
the achievement.

---

## 11.8 Pitfalls

**Coin despawns twice.** The collision walk found the pair in both
orders. Add an `entity/alive?` guard.

**Magnet coins fly away.** `world/attract!` strength too high combined
with no `entity/max-speed!`. Cap velocity.

**Star timer resets on second star.** Do you want stacking or refresh?
Depending on design: `(max star-timer 300)` for refresh; `(+ star-timer
150)` for stack.

**Cortex read returns #f.** First-ever run — the key wasn't written
yet. Always `(or (cortex/read 'k) default)`.

**Player passes through everything after grabbing star.** You changed
`entity/solid!` to `#f` for invincibility. Don't; use a soft flag
(star-timer > 0) so physics still works.

---

## 11.9 Try this yourself

1. Add a key pickup. Player carries it (blackboard). Door entity
   opens only if player has key.
2. Speed-boost pickup: `entity/max-speed! p 6` for 200 frames, then
   back to 4.
3. Shrink pickup: `entity/shape! p 'rect 6 10` for 300 frames —
   player fits through smaller gaps.
4. Bomb pickup: on 'b' press, despawn all enemies within 60 px and
   `world/camera-shake! 15`.
5. Score multiplier pickup: for 10 seconds, all coin pickups worth
   2×.
6. High-score leaderboard: Cortex list of last 10 scores. Sort. Show
   top 5 on title screen.

---

## 11.10 What we built

Sensor pickups. Magnet coins. Hearts with max-hp check. Invincibility
star with timer. Cortex persistence. Six patterns; hundreds of possible
combinations.

Next chapter: the big enemy. One boss. Three phases. Bullet-hell
finale. Everything from chapters 4-11 comes together.")

;; Book of Arcade Games — Chapter 12: Bosses

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(chapter
  :book                "Book of Arcade Games"
  :chapter-number      12
  :title               "Bosses"
  :dialect             "motoi"
  :audience            :kid
  :also-for            :adult
  :content-rating      :G
  :author-lane         "arcade-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"

"Every good arcade game ends with a boss. One enemy that survives longer,
patterns you learn by dying, phases that get harder as the fight
progresses. The boss compresses everything you learned in chapters 1-11
into ninety seconds of concentrated challenge.

The trick to a good boss is legibility. The player must be able to LEARN
the boss. Its patterns must be readable — 'ah, when it goes red it
fires an X-cross of bullets.' Random bullet hell is bad boss design;
deterministic-until-you-lose-focus is good boss design. The player fails
because they made a mistake, not because a dice rolled against them.

This chapter builds a three-phase boss: 100 HP; different attack in
each third; phase transition marked with camera-shake and a color
change. The core is a state machine driven by HP thresholds and a
tick-based attack cycle. In under 100 lines.

---

## 12.1 The state machine

Everything about a boss is state. Boss health. Current phase. Attack
cooldown. Sub-attack index. Time-in-phase. Store it all.

```scheme
;; Boss state.
(define boss-phase 1)
(define attack-tick 0)
(define phase-timer 0)
```

Three variables. That's it. Everything else derives from these three
plus `entity/hp!` of the boss.

---

## 12.2 The boss

Spawn, shape, health.

```scheme
(define (boss-and-player)
  (world/reset!)
  (collision/define-layers!
   '((player :collides-with (boss boss-bullet))
     (boss   :collides-with (player player-bullet))
     (player-bullet :collides-with (boss))
     (boss-bullet   :collides-with (player))))
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 160 210))
        (b (world/spawn 'boss   160 40)))
    (entity/shape! p 'triangle 8)  (entity/layer! p 'player)
    (entity/shape! b 'rect 40 40) (entity/layer! b 'boss)
    (entity/hp! p 5) (entity/hp! b 100)
    (entity/solid! p #t) (entity/solid! b #t)
    ...))
```

The boss is 40×40 pixels. Not huge on paper. Huge in feel because it's
the ONLY thing that big on the screen.

---

## 12.3 Phase 1 — Deliberate

Boss wanders slowly, fires single shots every 60 frames.

```scheme
;; Phase 1: single-shot every 60 frames, aimed at player.
(define (phase-1-attack boss player)
  (when (= (modulo attack-tick 60) 0)
    (let* ((dx (- (entity/x player) (entity/x boss)))
           (dy (- (entity/y player) (entity/y boss)))
           (mag (max 0.01 (geom/distance 0 0 dx dy)))
           (vx (* (/ dx mag) 2))
           (vy (* (/ dy mag) 2))
           (bul (world/spawn 'boss-bullet
                             (entity/x boss) (entity/y boss))))
      (entity/shape! bul 'circle 3)
      (entity/layer! bul 'boss-bullet)
      (entity/set-vel! bul vx vy))))
```

`geom/distance` (from the geom library) computes 2D distance. We
normalize the direction (divide by magnitude) then scale to speed 2.
The bullet fires straight at the player's position AT THE MOMENT OF
FIRE.

---

## 12.4 Phase 2 — Aggressive

Boss chases the player. Shots come every 30 frames. Two-way spread.

```scheme
;; Phase 2: chase + 3-shot spread every 30 frames.
(define (phase-2-attack boss player)
  (ai/seek boss player)
  (entity/max-speed! boss 1.5)
  (when (= (modulo attack-tick 30) 0)
    (let ((dx (- (entity/x player) (entity/x boss)))
          (dy (- (entity/y player) (entity/y boss))))
      (let ((base-ang (geom/atan2 dy dx)))
        (for-each
         (lambda (delta)
           (let* ((ang (+ base-ang delta))
                  (bul (world/spawn 'boss-bullet
                                    (entity/x boss) (entity/y boss))))
             (entity/shape! bul 'circle 3)
             (entity/layer! bul 'boss-bullet)
             (entity/set-vel! bul (* 2.5 (geom/cos ang))
                                  (* 2.5 (geom/sin ang)))))
         (list -0.3 0 0.3))))))
```

`geom/atan2 dy dx` returns the angle of the vector (dx, dy). We build
three shots at angles (base-0.3, base, base+0.3) — a cone spread.
Three shots × 30 frame cadence = 6 shots per second. Twitchy.

---

## 12.5 Phase 3 — Bullet Hell

Ring bursts of 12 bullets every 90 frames. Boss stops moving.

```scheme
;; Phase 3: ring burst every 90 frames + boss stationary at top.
(define (phase-3-attack boss player)
  (entity/set-vel! boss 0 0)
  (when (= (modulo attack-tick 90) 0)
    (let loop ((i 0))
      (when (< i 12)
        (let* ((ang (* (/ 6.283 12) i))
               (bul (world/spawn 'boss-bullet
                                 (entity/x boss) (entity/y boss))))
          (entity/shape! bul 'circle 3)
          (entity/layer! bul 'boss-bullet)
          (entity/set-vel! bul (* 2 (geom/cos ang))
                               (* 2 (geom/sin ang))))
        (loop (+ i 1))))))
```

12 bullets in a ring. Player must dodge or hide. Boss stationary makes
positioning matter — approach from the sides during the pause between
bursts.

---

## 12.6 The full fight

Wire it all up.

```scheme
;; Full boss fight — three phases, HP-driven transitions.
(define boss-phase 1)
(define attack-tick 0)

(define (boss-fight)
  (world/reset!)
  (collision/define-layers!
   '((player :collides-with (boss boss-bullet))
     (boss   :collides-with (player player-bullet))
     (player-bullet :collides-with (boss))
     (boss-bullet   :collides-with (player))))
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 160 210))
        (b (world/spawn 'boss   160 40)))
    (entity/shape! p 'triangle 8)  (entity/layer! p 'player)
    (entity/shape! b 'rect 40 40) (entity/layer! b 'boss)
    (entity/hp! p 5) (entity/hp! b 100)
    (entity/solid! p #t) (entity/solid! b #t)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -4 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 4 0))
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)
         (let ((bul (world/spawn 'player-bullet
                                 (entity/x p) (- (entity/y p) 8))))
           (entity/shape! bul 'circle 2)
           (entity/layer! bul 'player-bullet)
           (entity/set-vel! bul 0 -6)))
       ;; Phase-transition detection.
       (let ((hp (entity/hp! b 0)))
         (cond
           ((and (< hp 66) (= boss-phase 1))
            (set! boss-phase 2)
            (world/camera-shake! 10 0.95)
            (audio/play 'phase-shift))
           ((and (< hp 33) (= boss-phase 2))
            (set! boss-phase 3)
            (world/camera-shake! 15 0.97)
            (audio/play 'phase-shift))))
       ;; Attack routing.
       (cond ((= boss-phase 1) (phase-1-attack b p))
             ((= boss-phase 2) (phase-2-attack b p))
             ((= boss-phase 3) (phase-3-attack b p)))
       (set! attack-tick (+ attack-tick 1))
       (world/step)
       ;; Collision handling.
       (for-each
        (lambda (pair)
          (let ((a (car pair)) (bp (cadr pair)))
            (let ((kinds (list (entity/kind a) (entity/kind bp))))
              (cond
                ((or (equal? kinds '(player-bullet boss))
                     (equal? kinds '(boss player-bullet)))
                 (entity/damage! b 1)
                 (entity/despawn!
                  (if (eq? (entity/kind a) 'player-bullet) a bp)))
                ((or (equal? kinds '(boss-bullet player))
                     (equal? kinds '(player boss-bullet)))
                 (entity/damage! p 1)
                 (entity/despawn!
                  (if (eq? (entity/kind a) 'boss-bullet) a bp))
                 (world/camera-shake! 5 0.9))
                ((or (equal? kinds '(boss player))
                     (equal? kinds '(player boss)))
                 (entity/damage! p 1)
                 (world/camera-shake! 8 0.9))))))
        (world/collisions))
       ;; Cleanup off-screen bullets.
       (world/each 'boss-bullet
                   (lambda (bul)
                     (when (or (< (entity/x bul) -10) (> (entity/x bul) 330)
                               (< (entity/y bul) -10) (> (entity/y bul) 250))
                       (entity/despawn! bul))))
       (world/each 'player-bullet
                   (lambda (bul)
                     (when (< (entity/y bul) 0) (entity/despawn! bul))))
       ;; Boss death?
       (when (<= (entity/hp! b 0) 0)
         (paint-text \"VICTORY\" 130 100)
         (world/camera-shake! 20 0.97)
         (audio/play 'victory))
       (paint-clear)
       (when (entity/alive? b)
         (paint-cell (case boss-phase ((1) 'boss1) ((2) 'boss2) ((3) 'boss3))
                     (entity/x b) (entity/y b) 40 40))
       (world/each 'boss-bullet
                   (lambda (bul)
                     (paint-cell 'boss-bullet (entity/x bul) (entity/y bul) 3 3)))
       (world/each 'player-bullet
                   (lambda (bul)
                     (paint-cell 'player-bullet (entity/x bul) (entity/y bul) 2 2)))
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 8 8)
       (paint-text (string-append \"Boss HP: \" (number->string (entity/hp! b 0)))
                   10 10)
       (paint-text (string-append \"You HP: \" (number->string (entity/hp! p 0)))
                   10 20)
       (paint-text (string-append \"Phase: \" (number->string boss-phase))
                   10 30)))))

(big-bang boss-fight)
```

Ninety-second boss fight in one function. Three phases. HP-driven
transitions. Camera-shake and sound cue on phase change. Clean death
scene. That is the arcade boss template.

---

## 12.7 The four patterns for bosses

**Composition.** The boss is composed of health + phase + attack
pattern + physics + shape. Each phase COMPOSES its own attack behavior
from the primitives (spawn bullet, aim, ring-burst).

**Orchestration.** Frame loop orchestrates: player input, phase-
transition check, active-phase attack routine, physics step, collision
walk, cleanup, paint. Phase-transition check MUST come before the
attack routine so the new phase fires immediately.

**In-routing.** HP damage routes to phase-transition check. Player
bullets route to boss damage. Boss bullets route to player damage.
The routing table is a small `cond` on collision-kind pairs.

**Routing.** Every attack routine routes bullets from boss position
to trajectories computed by phase-specific math. `world/camera-shake!`
routes phase-transitions to visual feedback. `audio/play` routes
transitions to audio feedback.

---

## 12.8 Common desktop tasks

**End-of-sale boss.** A shop's month-long clearance ends with a boss
mini-game: destroy the giant discount-flag icon by clicking rapidly.
Three phases of increasing click-required density. Winners get an
extra 10% off.

**Complaint-triage boss.** For an operator, the 'boss' is a difficult
customer message that requires multiple back-and-forth responses. Phase
1: simple response. Phase 2: escalation, more research needed. Phase
3: manager intervention. Same phase-machine, different content.

---

## 12.9 Pitfalls

**Bullets all fire on the same frame.** Multiple `attack-tick` checks
share the same modulo. Give each phase its own timer or use a
staggered offset.

**Boss teleports on phase transition.** You reset boss position on
phase change. Don't; the fight should feel continuous. Only change
BEHAVIOR, not position.

**Player can't damage boss.** Layer setup missing. Check that
`player-bullet` collides with `boss`.

**Bullet count grows unbounded.** Cleanup missing. Every frame, walk
`world/each 'boss-bullet` and despawn those off-screen.

**Boss dies but game continues.** Add a `game/state` transition to
victory-screen. Chapter 14 covers this.

**Phase 3 is unbeatable.** Playtest. Tune bullet count from 12 to 8.
Tune burst frequency from 90 to 120. Tune bullet speed from 2 to 1.5.
Playtest again.

---

## 12.10 Try this yourself

1. Add phase 4: below 10 HP, boss shakes uncontrollably and fires
   both cone AND ring simultaneously.
2. Give boss a shield: unless bullet hits the top-center 20-pixel
   area, damage is 0. Kids learn to aim.
3. Randomize phase-2 attack: 50% cone, 50% chase-and-slam.
4. Add mini-enemies that spawn during phase 3 to distract player.
5. Add a heal drop after each phase transition. Player recovers 1 HP
   between phases.
6. Boss dodge: on player-bullet approach, boss moves ±20 pixels 50%
   of the time. Not always — sometimes lets it through.

---

## 12.11 What we built

A three-phase boss with HP-gated transitions, three attack patterns,
camera-shake feedback, and cleanup. About 100 lines. The template
for every arcade climax.

score doesn't ratchet up? Combo, multiplier, escalation, the number
that grows and grows.")

"Arcade DNA is the scoreboard. The number in the top-right corner is why
you keep playing. Every hit is +100. Two hits in the same 60-frame
window: ×2 multiplier — that hit was worth +200. Three in a row: ×3.
Miss, get hit, wait too long — the multiplier resets and the number
stops growing.

The whole feedback loop is: do a thing, see the number grow, WANT to
do the next thing to keep the number growing. Every arcade cabinet
ever built is a machine for growing that number. The number itself is
free — it's a variable. The magic is in the multiplier, the combo
timer, and how the number is DISPLAYED.

This chapter builds the scoreboard right. Base score. Combo counter
with a decay window. Multiplier that scales visibly with combo.
Number-that-grows visualization with `tick/ease`. Screen-flash on
combo-up. Persistent high score via Cortex.

---

## 13.1 Base score

Every hit is +100.

```scheme
(define score 0)

(define (basic-score)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 160 210)))
    (entity/shape! p 'triangle 8)
    (entity/hp! p 5)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -4 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 4 0))
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)
         (set! score (+ score 100))
         (world/camera-shake! 1 0.9))
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 8 8)
       (paint-text (string-append \"Score: \" (number->string score))
                   10 10)))))

(big-bang basic-score)
```

You press 'a', score grows. That is enough to see the pattern. Now
add combo.

---

## 13.2 The combo counter

Successive hits within a window grow the combo.

```scheme
(define score 0)
(define combo 0)
(define combo-decay-at 0)     ;; frame at which combo resets

(define (combo-score)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 160 210)))
    (entity/shape! p 'triangle 8)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -4 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 4 0))
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)
         (set! combo (+ combo 1))
         (set! combo-decay-at (+ (world/frame) 60))  ;; 1 sec window
         (set! score (+ score (* 100 combo)))
         (world/camera-shake! (min 5 combo) 0.9))
       ;; Combo decay.
       (when (>= (world/frame) combo-decay-at)
         (set! combo 0))
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 8 8)
       (paint-text (string-append \"Score: \" (number->string score)) 10 10)
       (paint-text (string-append \"x\" (number->string combo)) 10 20)))))

(big-bang combo-score)
```

Read the combo logic. Every 'a' press: bump combo, extend the decay
window to 60 frames from now, add `100 * combo` to score. If you
haven't pressed 'a' in a second, combo resets to 0 and the next hit
is worth just 100.

Kid presses 'a' rapidly: 100, 300, 600, 1000, 1500, 2100. Presses
'a' once, waits 2 seconds, presses again: 100, then 100. Same
five inputs, hugely different scores. That's the whole hook.

---

## 13.3 Growing number

The number should GROW when it changes. Not just update — visibly
scale up, then settle.

```scheme
(define score 0)
(define displayed-score 0)     ;; interpolates toward score
(define score-flash 0)          ;; frames of flash

(define (growing-score)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 160 210)))
    (entity/shape! p 'triangle 8)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -4 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 4 0))
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)
         (set! score (+ score 100))
         (set! score-flash 10))
       ;; Displayed-score chases actual score.
       (set! displayed-score
             (+ displayed-score
                (* 0.1 (- score displayed-score))))
       (when (> score-flash 0) (set! score-flash (- score-flash 1)))
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 8 8)
       ;; Score painted big when flashing; normal otherwise.
       (paint-text (string-append \"Score: \"
                                  (number->string (round displayed-score)))
                   10
                   (if (> score-flash 0) 30 10))))))

(big-bang growing-score)
```

Two variables: `score` is the actual, `displayed-score` is the smooth
interpolation. Every frame, `displayed-score` gets 10% closer to
`score`. Hit 'a', score jumps 100, displayed-score smoothly climbs
from 0 to 100 over about 40 frames. That climb IS the dopamine.

The score-flash sets a position offset. When you hit, the text shifts
up 20 pixels for 10 frames, then returns. Subtle, effective. Real
arcade games do this AT SCALE — every hit, the number wobbles, glows,
bounces. Feel is code.

---

## 13.4 The multiplier

Combo doesn't just multiply the score — it multiplies the DISPLAY.
Bigger combo = bigger number on screen.

```scheme
(define score 0)
(define combo 0)
(define combo-decay-at 0)

(define (multiplier-display)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 160 210)))
    (entity/shape! p 'triangle 8)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -4 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 4 0))
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)
         (set! combo (+ combo 1))
         (set! combo-decay-at (+ (world/frame) 60))
         (set! score (+ score (* 100 combo))))
       (when (>= (world/frame) combo-decay-at)
         (set! combo 0))
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 8 8)
       (paint-text (string-append \"Score: \" (number->string score)) 10 10)
       ;; Combo painted increasingly large, right-aligned.
       (when (> combo 0)
         (let ((y-off (- 30 (min combo 20))))
           (paint-text (string-append \"x\" (number->string combo))
                       (- 300 (* 8 (min combo 15))) y-off)))))))
(big-bang multiplier-display)
```

The combo number is painted in a size that grows with combo. At combo
5, subtly bigger. At combo 15, huge. At combo 20+, capped so it
doesn't take over the screen.

Every arcade game does something like this. The number is the reward
AND the punishment — when combo breaks, it disappears from the screen
entirely.

---

## 13.5 High-score persistence

Score should survive the game session.

```scheme
(define score 0)

(define (high-score-tracked)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((high-score (or (cortex/read 'arcade-high) 0))
        (p (world/spawn 'player 160 210)))
    (entity/shape! p 'triangle 8)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -4 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 4 0))
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)
         (set! score (+ score 100))
         (when (> score high-score)
           (set! high-score score)
           (cortex/write 'arcade-high score)))
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 8 8)
       (paint-text (string-append \"Score: \" (number->string score)) 10 10)
       (paint-text (string-append \"High:  \" (number->string high-score))
                   10 20)))))

(big-bang high-score-tracked)
```

When score passes the high-score, we update the display AND persist.
Kid quits, comes back tomorrow: high score persists. The number the
kid is trying to beat is their own past self.

Even better: keep the top 5, not just top 1. Store as a Cortex list.
Show the leaderboard on the title screen (chapter 14).

---

## 13.6 The four patterns

**Composition.** Score display = base score + combo + multiplier +
flash + interpolation. Add or subtract any layer.

**Orchestration.** Frame order: input, score/combo update, decay check,
interpolate displayed-score, paint. Interpolation MUST come after
score update so the interpolation targets the current value.

**In-routing.** Hits route to score-bump handlers. Combo timer routes
frame-tick to decay checker. All routing is state-mutation via `set!`.

**Routing.** Score routes to display (as text). Score also routes to
Cortex (as persistent state). Two routes for one variable.

---

## 13.7 Common desktop tasks

**Shop-progress badge.** Customer completes an action (browse 5 items,
add to wishlist, share). Small score bumps for each; combo bonus if
done in one session. Score routes to a badge on the customer's
profile.

**Support-response streak.** Operator answering customer messages. Each
reply within 60 seconds of receipt = combo. Weekly streak leaderboard
among the operator's team. Score routes to team dashboard.

---

## 13.8 Pitfalls

**Score wraps at max integer.** Motoi Scheme uses bignums; you won't
hit this. But if you display formatted, large numbers get unreadable.
Format as `1.2M` beyond a million.

**Displayed-score never catches up.** Interpolation factor too small.
Try 0.15 or 0.2 for snappier.

**Combo breaks silently.** Kid doesn't know why. Add a visual: on
combo-break, brief red flash of the combo counter, then it vanishes.

**Multiplier resets on death.** By design, mostly. But some players
appreciate keeping their multiplier through respawn. Design choice.

---

1. Cap max combo at 30 with a visual 'MAX!' banner when reached.
2. Add per-enemy score: small enemy 100, medium 300, large 800.
3. Streak bonus: after 10-combo, every point scores +50 as flat bonus.
4. Rank grade: at end of session, compute grade S/A/B/C/D from score.
5. Combo pause: 'b' button freezes decay for 2 seconds. Once per game.
6. Score sharing: on new high score, `paint-text` a share URL that
   encodes the score in a Cortex key.

Base score. Combo with decay window. Multiplier scaling. Interpolated
display. Screen flash on hit. Cortex persistence. All in about 40
lines of scoring logic.

arcade session.")

;; ch14-coin-op-loop.book.slatl
;; Book of Arcade Games — Chapter 14: The Coin-Op Loop

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(chapter
  :book                "Book of Arcade Games"
  :chapter-number      14
  :title               "The Coin-Op Loop"
  :dialect             "motoi"
  :audience            :kid
  :also-for            :adult
  :content-rating      :G
  :author-lane         "arcade-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"
  :training-eligible   #t
  :confidentiality     "public"
  :voice               "sakura-teaching + game-design"
  :book-version        "1.0.0"
  :prose
"A real arcade cabinet doesn't sit idle. It cycles: attract mode →
title screen → press start → play → game over → high score entry →
back to attract mode. The whole life of the machine is a state
machine. When no one is playing, the attract mode plays a demo of the
game to LURE someone to insert a quarter. When someone plays, the
game runs. When they lose, high-score entry captures their initials,
then the machine slips back to attract.

This chapter builds that whole cabinet in about 150 lines. The state
machine is a `game/state` value with transitions driven by
`input/pressed? 'a`. Each state has its own paint and its own logic.
Between states, one moment of blank + reset.

By the end you have a shippable arcade session — everything from title
to leaderboard.

---

## 14.1 States

The cabinet has five states:

- `'attract` — demo playing, waits for start button
- `'title` — title screen with menu
- `'play` — the actual game
- `'game-over` — end screen, brief pause
- `'high-score` — high-score entry

Each has an entry action, a per-frame action, and transitions.

```scheme
(define cabinet-state 'attract)
(define state-timer 0)
```

---

## 14.2 Title screen

Slow breathing animation on 'PRESS START'.

```scheme
(define (paint-title-screen)
  (paint-clear)
  (paint-text \"BALLPIT\" 120 60)
  (paint-text \"the arcade\" 130 80)
  ;; Breathing 'PRESS START' via tick/sine.
  (let* ((phase (* 0.05 (world/frame)))
         (breath (+ 1.0 (* 0.15 (tick/sine phase))))
         (x-offset (round (* breath 130))))
    (paint-text \"PRESS START\" x-offset 140))
  (paint-text \"HIGH: \"
              80 190)
  (paint-text (number->string (or (cortex/read 'arcade-high) 0))
              140 190))
```

`tick/sine phase` returns a sine wave value oscillating between -1
and 1. Multiplied by 0.15 and added to 1.0, gives a factor from 0.85
to 1.15. Times a base position, the text subtly breathes.

Kids read this animation as 'the game is alive, waiting for me.'
Static text feels dead.

---

## 14.3 Play

The actual game — we'll use the small ball-bounce game from chapter 1
for simplicity, but this slot holds whichever chapter's shape you like.

```scheme
(define (init-play)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.4)
  (world/floor! 220)
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 160 200)))
    (entity/shape! p 'triangle 8)
    (entity/solid! p #t))
  (set! current-score 0)
  (set! player-hp 3))

(define current-score 0)
(define player-hp 3)

(define (paint-play)
  (world/step)
  (paint-clear)
  (world/each 'player
              (lambda (p) (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 8 8)))
  (paint-text (string-append \"Score: \" (number->string current-score)) 10 10)
  (paint-text (string-append \"HP: \" (number->string player-hp)) 10 20))
```

Real play code goes here. For a shippable demo, replace with the boss
fight from chapter 12 or the shmup from chapter 5.

---

## 14.4 Game over

Brief pause with the final score.

```scheme
(define (paint-game-over)
  (paint-clear)
  (paint-text \"GAME OVER\" 120 100)
  (paint-text (string-append \"Final: \" (number->string current-score))
              110 130)
  (paint-text (string-append \"Time to attract mode: \"
                             (number->string (max 0 (- 180 state-timer))))
              60 200))
```

180 frames = 3 seconds. Long enough to absorb. Short enough that a
disengaged player doesn't stall.

---

## 14.5 High score entry

If final score beats the top-5 board, capture the player's initials.

```scheme
(define high-score-initials \"AAA\")
(define initial-cursor 0)     ;; which letter (0, 1, 2)

(define (paint-high-score-entry)
  (paint-clear)
  (paint-text \"NEW HIGH SCORE!\" 100 60)
  (paint-text (string-append \"Score: \" (number->string current-score))
              120 90)
  (paint-text \"Enter your initials\" 90 130)
  ;; Draw each of 3 initial letters. Highlight the cursor position.
  (let loop ((i 0))
    (when (< i 3)
      (let ((letter (string (string-ref high-score-initials i)))
            (x (+ 140 (* i 16))))
        (paint-text letter x 160)
        (when (= i initial-cursor)
          (paint-text \"_\" x 165)))     ;; underscore for cursor
      (loop (+ i 1)))))

(define (advance-initial delta)
  (let* ((cur (char->integer (string-ref high-score-initials initial-cursor)))
         (next (+ cur delta))
         (wrapped (cond ((< next 65) 90) ((> next 90) 65) (else next)))
         (str (make-string 3)))
    (string-set! str 0 (string-ref high-score-initials 0))
    (string-set! str 1 (string-ref high-score-initials 1))
    (string-set! str 2 (string-ref high-score-initials 2))
    (string-set! str initial-cursor (integer->char wrapped))
    (set! high-score-initials str)))
```

Up/down cycles through letters A-Z. Left/right moves cursor. 'a' saves
to Cortex leaderboard.

---

## 14.6 The state machine

Wire it all together.

```scheme
(define cabinet-state 'attract)
(define state-timer 0)

(define (transition new-state)
  (set! cabinet-state new-state)
  (set! state-timer 0)
  (when (eq? new-state 'play)
    (init-play)))

(define (arcade-cabinet)
  (transition 'attract)
  (on-frame
   (lambda ()
     (set! state-timer (+ state-timer 1))
     (cond
       ((eq? cabinet-state 'attract)
        ;; Attract mode: play the game silently in background, wait
        ;; for start button. For simplicity we just show the title.
        (paint-title-screen)
        (when (input/pressed? 'a) (transition 'play))
        ;; After 20 seconds of attract, show a demo (chapter 14, App K).
        )
       ((eq? cabinet-state 'title)
        (paint-title-screen)
        (when (input/pressed? 'a) (transition 'play)))
       ((eq? cabinet-state 'play)
        (when (input/down? 'left)
          (world/each 'player (lambda (p) (entity/move! p -4 0))))
        (when (input/down? 'right)
          (world/each 'player (lambda (p) (entity/move! p 4 0))))
        (when (input/pressed? 'a)
          (set! current-score (+ current-score 100)))
        (paint-play)
        ;; Simulated game-over: 30 sec of play, or press 'b'.
        (when (or (> state-timer (* 60 30)) (input/pressed? 'b))
          (transition 'game-over)))
       ((eq? cabinet-state 'game-over)
        (paint-game-over)
        (when (> state-timer 180)
          (if (> current-score (or (cortex/read 'arcade-high) 0))
              (transition 'high-score)
              (transition 'attract))))
       ((eq? cabinet-state 'high-score)
        (paint-high-score-entry)
        (when (input/pressed? 'left)
          (set! initial-cursor (max 0 (- initial-cursor 1))))
        (when (input/pressed? 'right)
          (set! initial-cursor (min 2 (+ initial-cursor 1))))
        (when (input/pressed? 'up)   (advance-initial 1))
        (when (input/pressed? 'down) (advance-initial -1))
        (when (input/pressed? 'a)
          (cortex/write 'arcade-high current-score)
          (cortex/write 'arcade-initials high-score-initials)
          (transition 'attract)))))))

(big-bang arcade-cabinet)
```

Read the `cond` slowly. Each branch handles ONE state. Each branch
paints, polls input, and possibly transitions. Between states, one
frame of setup via `transition`.

`init-play` resets the world. That is the key discipline of a state
machine: each state entry cleans up cleanly. No leftover entities from
the previous game. No leftover state.

---

## 14.7 Attract mode with a demo

The real attract mode plays a demo of the game — recorded input replayed
back at attract time. `world/tape-record!` records inputs; `world/tape-
replay` plays them back. See Appendix K (Tape Replay for Attract Mode)
for the full pattern.

Sketch:

```scheme
;; During play, record.
(world/tape-record! 'demo-play)
;; ... game runs ...
(world/tape-save 'demo-play 'saved-demo)

;; During attract, replay.
(world/tape-replay 'saved-demo)
```

The kid does not immediately see the game. They see A game playing
itself. Muscle memory activates before they realize they're not
playing yet. Then they press start and they ARE playing.

---

## 14.8 The four patterns in a cabinet loop

**Composition.** Each state composes: paint routine + per-frame logic
+ transition condition. Add a new state (e.g. 'options-menu) by
composing a new triple.

**Orchestration.** The frame loop dispatches to the current state
each frame. Each state handles its own per-frame update, poll, paint.

**In-routing.** Input routes to state-specific handlers. 'a' in
attract = start; 'a' in play = fire; 'a' in high-score = save. Same
button, different route per state.

**Routing.** State transitions route via `transition` function. It's
the routing hub. Every transition IS a route from state to state.
Cortex writes route to persistence.

---

## 14.9 Common desktop tasks

**Shop cycle.** A shop's front page could operate as an attract loop:
demo tour → featured items → 'CLICK TO BROWSE' → item detail →
add-to-cart → checkout → thanks → back to demo. Each phase = a state.
Same pattern.

**Support-chat auto-cycle.** For an operator's chat window: idle
attract (rotating tips) → active chat → transcript summary → back to
idle. Chapter 14's shape scales.

---

## 14.10 Pitfalls

**State leaks entities.** `init-play` didn't `world/reset!`. Old boss
still on screen during title.

**Two states fire same frame.** You transitioned mid-cond and the
new state's branch also fires. Use `unless (state-changed)` guard,
or transition-only-on-last-line-of-branch.

**High-score entry saves initials without saving score.** Two Cortex
writes; if either fails, half-state. Wrap in `cortex/transaction!` if
available, or accept the risk for a small game.

**Attract mode too long.** Kids get bored. Cap at 30 seconds; loop
title-then-attract-then-title.

**Game timer runs during pause.** If your state timer counts frames,
it counts during pause menu. Freeze via `game/stop` or gate with
`(unless paused? (set! timer ...))`.

---

## 14.11 Try this yourself

1. Add an options menu — sound on/off, difficulty. State: 'options.
2. Add a credits screen — state: 'credits.
3. Multi-slot save: 3 named save slots. Kid picks which slot at
   title.
4. Difficulty scaling based on high-score history: if the player
   consistently beats top-3, increase enemy count 20%.
5. Achievements: on certain milestones (first boss kill, 10k score),
   flash achievement banner over 60 frames.
6. Cabinet 'coin' — require 3 button presses (as the arcade 'insert
   coin') before play starts. Just for atmosphere.

---

## 14.12 What we built

Five-state cabinet loop. Breathing title. Play. Game over with delay.
High-score entry. Cortex persistence of high score. Transition
discipline that resets cleanly. Full shape of an arcade session.

Next chapter: two players, one screen. Split the input space, split
the camera, share the physics. Local multiplayer.")

;; ch15-two-players-one-screen.book.slatl
;; Book of Arcade Games — Chapter 15: Two Players, One Screen

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(chapter
  :book                "Book of Arcade Games"
  :chapter-number      15
  :title               "Two Players, One Screen"
  :dialect             "motoi"
  :audience            :kid
  :also-for            :adult
  :content-rating      :G
  :author-lane         "arcade-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"
  :training-eligible   #t
  :confidentiality     "public"
  :voice               "sakura-teaching + game-design"
  :book-version        "1.0.0"
  :prose
"Two kids, one screen. Nothing beats it. Not online multiplayer. Not
tournament play. Two humans in the same room, elbows almost touching,
watching the same screen, playing the same game with different
buttons. Sibling rivalry, best-friend teamwork, or the exquisite
tension of a couch fighting game.

Local multiplayer is the arcade's oldest form. Pong shipped as two
paddles. Chapter 15 makes any game two-player by SPLITTING THE INPUT
SPACE.

The trick: player 1 uses ('left, 'right, 'a); player 2 uses ('up,
'down, 'b). Same physics engine, same world, two entities. When the
camera has to frame both players, we introduce dynamic zoom so both
fit in view. When one player wins a round, camera-shake for both.

By chapter end you have a two-player version of any earlier chapter's
game. And you understand that the world is ONE world — two players
are just two entities the world happens to listen to.

---

## 15.1 Two paddles, one ball

The simplest possible two-player game: Pong.

```scheme
;; Two paddles, one ball. Player 1 left/right; Player 2 up/down.
(define (pong)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((p1 (world/spawn 'p1 20 120))
        (p2 (world/spawn 'p2 300 120))
        (ball (world/spawn 'ball 160 120)))
    (entity/shape! p1 'rect 4 30)
    (entity/shape! p2 'rect 4 30)
    (entity/shape! ball 'circle 4)
    (entity/solid! p1 #t) (entity/solid! p2 #t) (entity/solid! ball #t)
    (entity/bounce! ball 1)   ;; perfect bounce
    (entity/set-vel! ball 3 2)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p1 0 -3))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p1 0 3))
       (when (input/down? 'up)    (entity/move! p2 0 -3))
       (when (input/down? 'down)  (entity/move! p2 0 3))
       (world/step)
       ;; Wall bounces (top/bottom).
       (let ((by (entity/y ball)) (vy (cadr (entity/vel ball))))
         (when (and (< by 5) (< vy 0))
           (entity/set-vel! ball (car (entity/vel ball)) (- vy)))
         (when (and (> by 235) (> vy 0))
           (entity/set-vel! ball (car (entity/vel ball)) (- vy))))
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'p1 (entity/x p1) (entity/y p1) 4 30)
       (paint-cell 'p2 (entity/x p2) (entity/y p2) 4 30)
       (paint-cell 'ball (entity/x ball) (entity/y ball) 4 4)))))

(big-bang pong)
```

Read the input handling. Left/right control P1's Y — the paddle moves
UP and DOWN when P1 presses LEFT and RIGHT. That's arbitrary; do
whatever the players agree to. Up/down control P2.

`entity/bounce! ball 1` = perfect bounce, no energy loss. Physics
takes care of paddle reflection. Wall reflection we handle in the
`let` block after `world/step`.

The kids play. One wins a point when the ball flies past the other's
paddle. Add a scoreboard (chapter 13) and you have a full session.

---

## 15.2 Dynamic camera zoom

For a spread-across-the-screen game (racing, brawler), the camera
needs to FRAME both players. When they're close, zoom in. When they
spread apart, zoom out. Cap the zoom limits.

```scheme
;; Two players on a big map. Camera snaps to midpoint, zooms to fit.
(define (dynamic-camera)
  (world/reset!)
  (scene/grid 'ground 40 1 32 20 0 200)
  (world/each 'ground
              (lambda (t) (entity/shape! t 'rect 32 20) (entity/solid! t #t)))
  (let ((p1 (world/spawn 'p1 100 168))
        (p2 (world/spawn 'p2 200 168)))
    (entity/shape! p1 'triangle 8)
    (entity/shape! p2 'triangle 8)
    (entity/solid! p1 #t) (entity/solid! p2 #t)
    (world/gravity! 0 0.5)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p1 -3 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p1 3 0))
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)  (entity/set-vel! p1 (car (entity/vel p1)) -10))
       (when (input/down? 'up)    (entity/move! p2 0 -3))
       (when (input/down? 'down)  (entity/move! p2 0 3))
       (when (input/pressed? 'b)  (entity/set-vel! p2 (car (entity/vel p2)) -10))
       ;; Camera: snap to midpoint. Zoom scales inversely with distance.
       (let* ((mx (/ (+ (entity/x p1) (entity/x p2)) 2))
              (my (/ (+ (entity/y p1) (entity/y p2)) 2))
              (d  (entity/distance p1 p2))
              (zoom (max 0.5 (min 1.5 (/ 200 (+ 100 d))))))
         (world/camera-snap! (- mx 160) (- my 120))
         ;; Zoom would go here if runtime exposes camera-zoom. If not,
         ;; keep-out bounds via camera-bounds! (dynamic).
         (world/camera-bounds! (- mx 200 (* 100 (- 1 zoom)))
                               0
                               (+ mx 200 (* 100 (- 1 zoom)))
                               240))
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (world/each 'ground
                   (lambda (t) (paint-cell 'ground (entity/x t) (entity/y t) 32 20)))
       (paint-cell 'p1 (entity/x p1) (entity/y p1) 8 8)
       (paint-cell 'p2 (entity/x p2) (entity/y p2) 8 8)))))

(big-bang dynamic-camera)
```

Camera midpoint = average of the two positions. Zoom logic based on
distance. Close players see zoomed-in world; distant players see
zoomed-out.

`world/camera-snap!` positions the camera at a specific point. Not the
smooth-follow of chapter 8; two-player often benefits from immediate
snap so neither player suffers camera lag when their opponent moves.

---

## 15.3 Racing

Two ships, side-by-side.

```scheme
;; Race — two ships thrust to the right; first to x=1000 wins.
(define winner #f)

(define (race)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((s1 (world/spawn 'p1 40 100))
        (s2 (world/spawn 'p2 40 140)))
    (entity/shape! s1 'triangle 8)
    (entity/shape! s2 'triangle 8)
    (entity/drag! s1 0.02) (entity/drag! s2 0.02)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (unless winner
         (when (input/down? 'a)
           (entity/set-vel! s1 (+ 0.15 (car (entity/vel s1)))
                            (cadr (entity/vel s1))))
         (when (input/down? 'b)
           (entity/set-vel! s2 (+ 0.15 (car (entity/vel s2)))
                            (cadr (entity/vel s2))))
         ;; Vertical dodge input.
         (when (input/down? 'left)
           (entity/set-vel! s1 (car (entity/vel s1))
                            (- (cadr (entity/vel s1)) 0.5)))
         (when (input/down? 'right)
           (entity/set-vel! s1 (car (entity/vel s1))
                            (+ (cadr (entity/vel s1)) 0.5)))
         (when (input/down? 'up)
           (entity/set-vel! s2 (car (entity/vel s2))
                            (- (cadr (entity/vel s2)) 0.5)))
         (when (input/down? 'down)
           (entity/set-vel! s2 (car (entity/vel s2))
                            (+ (cadr (entity/vel s2)) 0.5)))
         (cond
           ((>= (entity/x s1) 1000) (set! winner 'p1)
                                    (world/camera-shake! 15 0.95))
           ((>= (entity/x s2) 1000) (set! winner 'p2)
                                    (world/camera-shake! 15 0.95))))
       (world/step)
       ;; Camera follows the leading player.
       (let ((leader (if (> (entity/x s1) (entity/x s2)) s1 s2)))
         (world/camera-follow! leader 0.1 60 60))
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'p1 (entity/x s1) (entity/y s1) 8 8)
       (paint-cell 'p2 (entity/x s2) (entity/y s2) 8 8)
       (when winner
         (paint-text (string-append (symbol->string winner) \" WINS!\")
                     130 100))))))

(big-bang race)
```

Two ships, each with their own thruster button. Whoever hits x=1000
first wins. Camera follows the leader — the winning player sees more
of the road ahead, the losing player sees the winner's tail.

Losing feels different from winning. That difference is by DESIGN.

---

## 15.4 Cooperative

Two players share a goal — say, collectively bringing a ball to the
right side of the screen.

```scheme
;; Both players push a ball. It has to reach x=280.
(define (coop-ball)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.4)
  (world/floor! 220)
  (let ((p1 (world/spawn 'p1 40 200))
        (p2 (world/spawn 'p2 80 200))
        (ball (world/spawn 'ball 160 200)))
    (entity/shape! p1 'rect 12 20) (entity/solid! p1 #t)
    (entity/shape! p2 'rect 12 20) (entity/solid! p2 #t)
    (entity/shape! ball 'circle 12) (entity/solid! ball #t)
    (entity/mass! ball 3)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p1 -3 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p1 3 0))
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)
         (entity/set-vel! p1 (car (entity/vel p1)) -10))
       (when (input/down? 'up)    (entity/move! p2 0 -3))
       (when (input/down? 'down)  (entity/move! p2 0 3))
       (when (input/pressed? 'b)
         (entity/set-vel! p2 (car (entity/vel p2)) -10))
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'p1 (entity/x p1) (entity/y p1) 12 20)
       (paint-cell 'p2 (entity/x p2) (entity/y p2) 12 20)
       (paint-cell 'ball (entity/x ball) (entity/y ball) 24 24)
       (paint-cell 'goal 280 200 20 20)
       (when (> (entity/x ball) 275)
         (paint-text \"TEAM WINS!\" 100 100))))))

(big-bang coop-ball)
```

Both players push the ball right. Neither can do it alone — the ball
is heavy (`entity/mass! ball 3`). Push together.

The kids talk more than in a competitive game. That's the coop
signature.

---

## 15.5 The four patterns

**Composition.** Each player = composition of shape + solid + tag +
input-scheme. Two players = two compositions with different input
schemes and different tags.

**Orchestration.** Frame loop orchestrates BOTH players' inputs
before physics step. Order between P1 and P2 doesn't matter (parallel
independent), but both must complete before `world/step`.

**In-routing.** Input events route per player. 'left' routes to P1's
handler; 'up' routes to P2's. That's the whole two-player trick:
routing table with different destinations for each button.

**Routing.** Both players route into the SAME physics engine. Both
players emit into the same paint pipeline. The output layer doesn't
know or care that there are two of them. The world is one world.

---

## 15.6 Common desktop tasks

**Two-operator triage.** Two operators of a shared shop can co-triage
the pending message queue: operator A takes half, operator B takes
half, they alternate for load balance. Same routing pattern, different
'players.'

**Cart-share checkout.** Two friends collaboratively fill one cart —
each of them adds items with their own cursor. Live update. Two
inputs, one shared state.

---

## 15.7 Pitfalls

**Both players push same button.** In a couch setup with two humans
and two controllers, this doesn't happen. In a keyboard setup, key
overlap can. Give players non-overlapping keys.

**Camera excludes a player.** Dynamic zoom saves it. If one player
runs offscreen, the game must decide: lock camera on them (leader-
follow), or wait for slower to catch up (rubber-band). Design choice.

**Score tied.** Design a tiebreaker or accept ties.

**Player 2 has no input at start.** Bug in the input routing table.
Test both players independently.

---

## 15.8 Try this yourself

1. Adapt any earlier chapter's game to two-player. Chapter 5 shmup:
   two ships stacked vertically. Chapter 12 boss: two players
   attacking one boss with pooled HP.
2. Player-vs-player boss: player 1 is the boss with 100 HP, player
   2 is the challenger with 5 HP. Asymmetric roles.
3. Split-screen: divide the display into two 160-wide halves,
   render P1's view left, P2's right. Requires two `world/camera`
   states — beyond this chapter, into rendering appendix territory.
4. Turn-based: only one player has input at a time; 'a' from either
   passes turn. Real chess/checkers pattern.
5. Add AI second player: 'AI thumb' presses buttons based on
   `ai/utility` scoring. Turn a two-player game into single-player
   via AI opponent.
6. Rounds: best-of-three matches. Between rounds, brief scoreboard
   screen. Chapter 14 state machine composes with this.

---

## 15.9 What we built

Pong. Dynamic camera. Racing. Coop. Four two-player shapes. Input
routing by player. Shared physics. Camera-shake for both. Whole game
family from splitting a button table.

Next chapter — the summit. You will build your own arcade game from
scratch using every technique from this book.")

"You have read fifteen chapters. You built a ball, a paddle, a ship, a
cannon, a shmup, a jump, a tile world, a boss. You tuned feel. You
scored. You ran a coin-op loop. You played with a friend on the same
screen.

This chapter is where you make it yours.

The suggested template is a 3-level shoot-em-up with a boss on level
3. Your job is not to copy it. Your job is to build YOUR game. Maybe a
top-down maze runner. Maybe a puzzle platformer. Maybe a two-player
racing brawler. The chapter provides the SKELETON — the cabinet loop,
the state transitions, the persistence — and lets you fill in the

## 16.1 The template

A 3-level shmup with a boss on level 3. Uses everything from chapters
1, 5, 6, 11, 12, 13, 14.

```scheme
;; game.slat — full arcade shmup, ready to define-card.

(define game-state 'attract)
(define state-timer 0)
(define current-level 1)
(define current-score 0)
(define combo 0)
(define combo-decay-at 0)
(define player-hp 3)
(define boss-phase 1)
(define spawn-counter 0)

(define (init-play)
  (world/reset!)
  (collision/define-layers!
   '((player :collides-with (enemy enemy-bullet boss boss-bullet coin))
     (enemy  :collides-with (player player-bullet))
     (boss   :collides-with (player player-bullet))
     (player-bullet :collides-with (enemy boss))
     (enemy-bullet  :collides-with (player))
     (boss-bullet   :collides-with (player))
     (coin :collides-with (player))))
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 160 210)))
    (entity/shape! p 'triangle 8)
    (entity/layer! p 'player)
    (entity/solid! p #t))
  (set! player-hp 3)
  (set! current-score 0)
  (set! combo 0)
  (set! current-level 1))

(define (init-level lvl)
  ;; Clear enemies/bullets; keep player.
  (world/each 'enemy (lambda (e) (entity/despawn! e)))
  (world/each 'boss  (lambda (b) (entity/despawn! b)))
  (world/each 'enemy-bullet (lambda (b) (entity/despawn! b)))
  (world/each 'player-bullet (lambda (b) (entity/despawn! b)))
  (set! spawn-counter 0)
  (set! boss-phase 1)
  (when (= lvl 3)
    (let ((b (world/spawn 'boss 160 40)))
      (entity/shape! b 'rect 40 40)
      (entity/layer! b 'boss)
      (entity/hp! b 100))))

(define (transition new-state)
  (set! game-state new-state)
  (set! state-timer 0)
  (case new-state
    ((play) (init-play) (init-level 1))
    ((next-level)
     (set! current-level (+ current-level 1))
     (if (> current-level 3)
         (transition 'victory)
         (begin (init-level current-level)
                (transition 'play))))))

(define (level-tick p)
  (cond
    ((< current-level 3)
     ;; Levels 1-2: enemy waves.
     (set! spawn-counter (+ spawn-counter 1))
     (let ((spawn-rate (- 40 (* 5 current-level))))
       (when (>= spawn-counter spawn-rate)
         (set! spawn-counter 0)
         (let ((e (world/spawn 'enemy
                               (+ 20 (modulo (world/hash) 280))
                               -10)))
           (entity/shape! e 'rect 10 10)
           (entity/layer! e 'enemy)
           (entity/set-vel! e 0 (+ 1 (* 0.5 current-level)))
           (entity/solid! e #t))))
     ;; Level complete after 30 seconds.
     (when (> state-timer (* 60 30))
       (transition 'next-level)))
    (else
     ;; Level 3: boss phase transitions.
     (world/each 'boss
                 (lambda (b)
                   (let ((hp (entity/hp! b 0)))
                     (cond
                       ((and (< hp 66) (= boss-phase 1))
                        (set! boss-phase 2)
                        (world/camera-shake! 10 0.95))
                       ((and (< hp 33) (= boss-phase 2))
                        (set! boss-phase 3)
                        (world/camera-shake! 15 0.97)))
                     ;; Basic boss shot cadence.
                     (when (= (modulo state-timer (case boss-phase
                                                    ((1) 60)
                                                    ((2) 30)
                                                    ((3) 90))) 0)
                       (let ((bul (world/spawn 'boss-bullet
                                               (entity/x b) (entity/y b))))
                         (entity/shape! bul 'circle 3)
                         (entity/layer! bul 'boss-bullet)
                         (entity/set-vel! bul 0 3)))
                     (when (<= hp 0)
                       (entity/despawn! b)
                       (transition 'victory)))))
     )))

(define (handle-collisions p)
  (for-each
   (lambda (pair)
     (let ((a (car pair)) (b (cadr pair)))
       (let ((kinds (list (entity/kind a) (entity/kind b))))
         (cond
           ((or (equal? kinds '(player-bullet enemy))
                (equal? kinds '(enemy player-bullet)))
            (entity/despawn! (if (eq? (entity/kind a) 'player-bullet) a b))
            (entity/despawn! (if (eq? (entity/kind a) 'enemy) a b))
            (set! combo (+ combo 1))
            (set! combo-decay-at (+ (world/frame) 60))
            (set! current-score (+ current-score (* 100 combo))))
           ((or (equal? kinds '(player-bullet boss))
                (equal? kinds '(boss player-bullet)))
            (entity/despawn! (if (eq? (entity/kind a) 'player-bullet) a b))
            (entity/damage! (if (eq? (entity/kind a) 'boss) a b) 1)
            (set! current-score (+ current-score 200)))
           ((or (equal? kinds '(enemy-bullet player))
                (equal? kinds '(player enemy-bullet))
                (equal? kinds '(boss-bullet player))
                (equal? kinds '(player boss-bullet)))
            (entity/despawn!
             (if (or (eq? (entity/kind a) 'enemy-bullet)
                     (eq? (entity/kind a) 'boss-bullet)) a b))
            (set! player-hp (- player-hp 1))
            (world/camera-shake! 8 0.9))))))
   (world/collisions))
  (when (>= (world/frame) combo-decay-at) (set! combo 0)))

(define (paint-hud)
  (paint-text (string-append \"Score: \" (number->string current-score)) 10 10)
  (paint-text (string-append \"HP: \" (number->string player-hp)) 10 20)
  (paint-text (string-append \"Level: \" (number->string current-level))
              10 30)
  (when (> combo 0)
    (paint-text (string-append \"x\" (number->string combo)) 260 20)))

(define (game-frame)
  (set! state-timer (+ state-timer 1))
  (paint-clear)
  (case game-state
    ((attract)
     (paint-text \"MY ARCADE GAME\" 100 60)
     (paint-text \"PRESS START\"
                 (+ 100 (round (* 15 (tick/sine (* 0.05 state-timer)))))
                 140)
     (paint-text (string-append \"High: \"
                                (number->string
                                 (or (cortex/read 'my-game-high) 0)))
                 110 190)
     (when (input/pressed? 'a) (transition 'play)))
    ((play)
     (let ((p (car (world/find 'player))))
       (when (input/down? 'left)  (entity/move! p -4 0))
       (when (input/down? 'right) (entity/move! p 4 0))
       (when (input/pressed? 'a)
         (let ((bul (world/spawn 'player-bullet
                                 (entity/x p) (- (entity/y p) 8))))
           (entity/shape! bul 'circle 2)
           (entity/layer! bul 'player-bullet)
           (entity/set-vel! bul 0 -6)))
       (level-tick p)
       (world/step)
       (handle-collisions p)
       (world/each 'player-bullet
                   (lambda (b) (when (< (entity/y b) 0) (entity/despawn! b))))
       (world/each 'enemy
                   (lambda (e) (when (> (entity/y e) 250) (entity/despawn! e))))
       (world/each 'enemy-bullet
                   (lambda (b) (when (> (entity/y b) 250) (entity/despawn! b))))
       (when (<= player-hp 0) (transition 'game-over))
       (world/each 'enemy
                   (lambda (e) (paint-cell 'enemy (entity/x e) (entity/y e) 10 10)))
       (world/each 'boss
                   (lambda (b) (paint-cell 'boss (entity/x b) (entity/y b) 40 40)))
       (world/each 'player-bullet
                   (lambda (b) (paint-cell 'bullet (entity/x b) (entity/y b) 2 2)))
       (world/each 'enemy-bullet
                   (lambda (b) (paint-cell 'enemy-bullet (entity/x b) (entity/y b) 3 3)))
       (world/each 'boss-bullet
                   (lambda (b) (paint-cell 'boss-bullet (entity/x b) (entity/y b) 3 3)))
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 8 8)
       (paint-hud)))
    ((game-over)
     (paint-text \"GAME OVER\" 120 100)
     (paint-text (string-append \"Score: \" (number->string current-score))
                 110 130)
     (when (> current-score (or (cortex/read 'my-game-high) 0))
       (cortex/write 'my-game-high current-score))
     (when (> state-timer 180) (transition 'attract)))
    ((victory)
     (paint-text \"YOU WIN!\" 125 90)
     (paint-text (string-append \"Score: \" (number->string current-score))
                 110 120)
     (when (> current-score (or (cortex/read 'my-game-high) 0))
       (cortex/write 'my-game-high current-score))
     (when (> state-timer 240) (transition 'attract)))))

(define (my-arcade-game)
  (transition 'attract)
  (on-frame game-frame))

;; Publish as a card so friends can play from a URL.
(define-card 'my-arcade-game
  :title \"My Arcade Game\"
  :entry my-arcade-game
  :description \"3 levels + boss. Built with Motoi Scheme.\"
  :cortex-keys '(my-game-high))

(big-bang my-arcade-game)
```

Read it end-to-end. Then run it. Then break it. Then remake the parts
you break in your own image.

---

## 16.2 Diagnostic checklist

Before you share the URL, run the play-test:

- Does the first play last more than 30 seconds? If not, level 1 is
  too hard.
- Does level 3 boss die too fast? Too slow? Tune HP.
- Does the score number FEEL good to watch grow? If not, revisit
  chapter 13.
- Does the ship feel snappy? Loose? Revisit chapter 6.
- Does the game over screen let you get back to play in under 5
  seconds? If not, shorten it.
- Does the high score persist? Test by refreshing the page.
- Does 'a' feel like the fire button and not the confirm button
  during the game-over screen? If your accidental confirm sends you
  back to attract, that is a UX bug.

---

## 16.3 Publish

`define-card` in the code above registers the game as a shareable
card. The runtime generates a URL. Copy the URL, send to a friend.
They open it in a browser or in their own Motoi runtime and play.

Their high score writes to their OWN Cortex, not yours. Each player
has their own persistence.

---

## 16.4 The four patterns — a summary

You have seen these sixteen times. This is the last time.

**Composition.** Your whole game is a composition of small verbs.
Player = shape + layer + hp + solid. Enemy = same, different tag.
Boss = same, different HP. Levels = compositions of enemies over
time.

**Orchestration.** Frame loop orchestrates: state-dispatch, input,
spawn, step, collision-walk, cleanup, paint, HUD. Every frame the
same order. That order IS the game.

**In-routing.** Input routes to state-specific handlers. Collisions
route to kind-pair handlers. State transitions route through
`transition`.

**Routing.** Bullets route to physics engine. Score routes to display
AND to Cortex. Camera-shake routes phase transitions to visual
feedback. Every action-verb routes somewhere.

Every arcade game is these four patterns in different arrangements.
So is every simulation. So is every narrative. Once you see them, you
carry them forward.

---

## 16.5 A note to the reader who just built their first arcade game

You did this. Nobody else. The code above is a template; your game is
what you did with it. The tuning is yours. The choices are yours.

When your friends play, they don't see the chapters. They see a game.
That's the whole point.

---

The next book is Book of Simulation Games. Physics is not the game's

automata, particle systems, agents that learn.

Or come back and re-read chapter 6 (feel), chapter 7 (jump), chapter
12 (boss). Every chapter rewards a second pass with new eyes.

Or turn the page. Appendix A tabulates every bounce coefficient you
will ever need. Appendix L has twelve micro-games in thirty lines

You built an arcade game. Go build another.")

"# Appendix C — Solution Shape Guide

Every challenge in this book comes with the same three things: a prompt, an example input/output, and a hint. Your solution — however you write it — should come with the same three things pointed the other way: a summary of what you did, a run that shows it working, and a note on the trade-off you chose.

## The three-part solution

1. **What you did, in one sentence.** Not the code — the shape of the answer. \"I folded over the list.\" \"I built an accumulator and pushed at each step.\" \"I broke it in two by parity.\" One sentence.

2. **A run.** Copy the example input from the challenge. Show the actual output. If it matches, good. If it doesn't, keep working — a solution that produces the wrong answer is not a solution.

3. **The trade-off.** Every solution picks something over something else. Simplicity over speed. Speed over memory. Readability over cleverness. Say which you picked and why. This is the piece that turns a homework answer into an engineering note.

## The four shapes most challenges take

- **Fold** — reduce a list to a single value. ch01, ch07, ch08 lean here.
- **Map+filter** — reshape a list, then drop the parts you don't want. ch02, ch04, ch05.
- **State machine** — a small closure that remembers something between calls. ch03, ch09, ch11.
- **Pipeline** — a chain of verbs where the shape of the data changes at each step. ch06, ch10, ch15.

Most challenges yield to one of these four. When yours doesn't, that's the interesting one — write down what shape it took instead.

## When you fail

ch13 is the whole chapter on this. In brief: the wrong answer is a real fact and worth its own paragraph. Don't erase it. Write down what you thought would happen, what actually happened, and the smallest change that made the difference. That paragraph is worth more than the fix.

## The summit

ch16 asks you to compose several earlier chapters into one program. There is no single right answer. Whatever you build, put the three-part shape above on the outside of it. If someone else reads your solution six months from now and can tell what you did and why, the challenge is complete."
