"# Appendix C — State machine deep dive

Chapter 10 introduced Mealy and Moore. This appendix is the deeper
tour: UML notation, hierarchical states, and four real-world state
machines you can find running in code you use every day.

## UML state notation

The Unified Modeling Language (UML) formalises a diagramming convention
for state machines. You see it in engineering documents, protocol
specs, and academic papers. Here are the pieces.

**States** are drawn as rounded rectangles or circles. UML also has an
initial state (a solid black dot) and a final state (a black dot with
a ring around it).

```
   (o)-----> INITIAL --> ... --> FINAL -->(*)
```

**Transitions** are labelled arrows between states. The label has the
form:

```
   trigger [ guard ] / action
```

- **trigger:** the event or input that causes the transition.
- **guard:** an optional Boolean condition that must be true.
- **action:** an optional side effect that fires on the transition.

Any of the three parts can be omitted. `tick` alone is a plain
transition on the `tick` event. `[error]/log-and-halt` is a
transition with no trigger, guarded on `error`, doing an action.

**Entry and exit actions** — some states have `entry / do-something`
or `exit / do-something` blocks that run whenever you enter or leave
the state, regardless of which transition brought you.

**Hierarchical states** — a state can contain sub-states. UML lets
you nest state machines inside states, which is very useful for
modeling behaviour with a lot of sub-modes. A CPU's `execute` state,
for example, might contain sub-states for `arithmetic`, `memory-op`,
`branch`, `system-call`.

## Real state machine 1 — TCP

TCP is the transport-layer protocol for most of the internet. Every
TCP connection walks through a state machine defined in RFC 793
(1981) by Jon Postel.

### The states

- **CLOSED** — no connection.
- **LISTEN** — the server is waiting for a client to arrive.
- **SYN-SENT** — the client sent a SYN, waiting for the server's
  SYN-ACK.
- **SYN-RECEIVED** — the server got a SYN, sent its own SYN-ACK,
  waiting for the client's ACK.
- **ESTABLISHED** — the three-way handshake is done. Data can flow.
- **FIN-WAIT-1**, **FIN-WAIT-2**, **CLOSE-WAIT**, **CLOSING**,
  **LAST-ACK**, **TIME-WAIT** — the various closing states.

That is eleven states total. The full state diagram is famously
diamond-shaped and includes shortcuts for various error paths.

### The three-way handshake

Opening a TCP connection is:

```
   client                                    server
     |                                         |
     |----- SYN (seq=X) ----------------------->|
     |                                         |
     |<---- SYN-ACK (seq=Y, ack=X+1) ----------|
     |                                         |
     |----- ACK (ack=Y+1) --------------------->|
     |                                         |
     |=== both now in ESTABLISHED ============|
```

Three packets. Both sides pick a random sequence number, tell the
other, and acknowledge. From then on, every byte gets a sequence
number so out-of-order or lost packets can be detected and resent.

### TCP in Motoi Scheme (sketch)

```
(define (make-tcp-endpoint)
  (let ((state 'CLOSED))
    (lambda (event)
      (set! state
            (case state
              ((CLOSED)
               (case event
                 ((passive-open) 'LISTEN)
                 ((active-open)  'SYN-SENT)
                 (else state)))
              ((LISTEN)
               (case event
                 ((got-syn) 'SYN-RECEIVED)
                 (else state)))
              ((SYN-SENT)
               (case event
                 ((got-syn-ack) 'ESTABLISHED)
                 (else state)))
              ((SYN-RECEIVED)
               (case event
                 ((got-ack) 'ESTABLISHED)
                 (else state)))
              ((ESTABLISHED)
               (case event
                 ((close) 'FIN-WAIT-1)
                 (else state)))
              ;; ... more states omitted for brevity
              (else state)))
      state)))

(define tcp (make-tcp-endpoint))
(tcp 'active-open)     ;; => SYN-SENT
(tcp 'got-syn-ack)     ;; => ESTABLISHED
(tcp 'close)           ;; => FIN-WAIT-1
```

Real TCP has timeouts, retransmissions, congestion control, and the
data-transfer sub-states. But the shape is a state machine, and
Jon Postel drew it in 1981.

## Real state machine 2 — HTTP session

HTTP itself is stateless — each request stands alone — but a browser
session with a server usually maintains state via cookies. That
session is a state machine you can draw.

States:
- **anonymous** — no cookie, no logged-in user.
- **logged-in** — user has authenticated, cookie is valid.
- **admin** — user has elevated privileges.
- **locked-out** — too many failed logins, session revoked.

Transitions include `login-success`, `login-failure` (with a counter
guard), `logout`, `session-timeout`, `admin-elevation`, etc.

Every web app you have ever used has a state machine somewhere in
the auth layer. Sometimes it is drawn explicitly. Sometimes it is
implicit in a hundred `if` statements. The bugs usually live where
somebody forgot to add an `else` branch — an unhandled state
transition.

## Real state machine 3 — Elevator control

An elevator is a physical Mealy machine.

States:
- **idle-at-floor-N** for each floor N.
- **moving-up**, **moving-down**.
- **door-open**, **door-closing**.
- **out-of-service**.

Inputs:
- Button pressed on a floor.
- Button pressed inside the car.
- Door sensor triggered.
- Weight sensor triggered.
- Emergency stop.

Outputs:
- Motor direction, motor speed.
- Door state.
- Floor indicator.

Elevators are famous for having subtle state machines. Building them
correctly is hard because a bug can literally injure people. That is
why elevator control software is heavily verified — often with
formal methods.

## Real state machine 4 — Pac-Man ghost AI

The 1980 Pac-Man arcade game gave each ghost a state machine with
three main states:

- **chase** — pursue Pac-Man according to the ghost's personality.
  (Each ghost had different chase logic: Blinky chases directly,
  Pinky targets four tiles ahead of Pac-Man, etc.)
- **scatter** — retreat to a specific home corner of the maze.
- **frightened** — Pac-Man ate a power pellet; ghosts flee
  randomly and are edible.

The ghost cycles between chase and scatter on timers (typical
alternation: 7 seconds scatter, 20 seconds chase, repeated). When
Pac-Man eats a power pellet, all ghosts jump to frightened for a
few seconds, then return to whatever they were doing.

This tiny state machine is arguably one of the most influential game
AI designs in history. Its simplicity and its emergent complexity —
because the four ghosts have subtly different chase policies — made
Pac-Man feel alive without complex algorithms.

In Motoi Scheme:

```
(define (make-ghost personality)
  (let ((state 'scatter)
        (timer 7))
    (lambda (event)
      (cond
        ((eq? event 'tick)
         (set! timer (- timer 1))
         (when (zero? timer)
           (case state
             ((scatter) (set! state 'chase)   (set! timer 20))
             ((chase)   (set! state 'scatter) (set! timer 7))
             ((frightened) (set! state 'chase) (set! timer 20)))))
        ((eq? event 'power-pellet)
         (set! state 'frightened)
         (set! timer 10)))
      (list 'state state 'timer timer 'personality personality))))

(define blinky (make-ghost 'aggressive-direct-chaser))
(blinky 'tick)              ;; scatter, timer 6
;; ... repeat 6 times ...
(blinky 'power-pellet)      ;; frightened, timer 10
```

That is the shape. Add the maze grid and the movement code and you
have a ghost.

## Nested state machines

Chapter 12's CPU is a state machine with sub-states inside `execute`:
one for each instruction type. That is a hierarchical state machine.
UML lets you draw them as boxes inside boxes.

Another common example is a game character's animation state. The
top-level machine has `idle`, `walking`, `jumping`, `attacking`.
Each of those has sub-states for specific animation frames. A hit
in `attacking` can transition to a `hurt` state which has its own
sub-states for the reaction animation.

Nested state machines let you factor out common transitions.
`emergency-stop` at the top level can be a single transition that
overrides everything below. Without nesting, you would have to
add the transition to every sub-state.

## When to use a state machine

Any time you have a system where:

- The behaviour depends on history, not just current inputs.
- There is a finite set of distinct \"modes\" the system can be in.
- Certain transitions are legal and others are not.

That is a state machine. Draw it before you code it. Name the
states. Enumerate the transitions. **The states and transitions are
the design.**

## When not to use a state machine

If your system has a truly infinite or open-ended state space, a
finite state machine is the wrong tool. Full programming languages
are more expressive. A CPU is a Turing machine, not a finite state
machine (technically), because it has unbounded memory.

But most subsystems inside a program are finite. UI widgets. Auth
flows. Protocol handshakes. Game character AI. Physical device
drivers. All finite. All state machines.

## What Motoi wants you to take from this

- State machines are everywhere in real code.
- The formal notation (UML, or just circles and arrows) lets you
  design and communicate without ambiguity.
- Mealy and Moore are equivalent in power; pick whichever presents
  more clearly for your system.
- Hierarchical states let you factor common transitions and keep
  diagrams readable.
- If you draw the state machine before you code, you catch bugs
  the diagram exposes.

## The loop appears

Every state machine has an outer driver loop: read event, transition,
emit, loop. TCP has it. HTTP session has it. Elevator has it. Pac-Man
ghost has it. CPU has it. Chapter 10 named it. Every appendix example
here embodies it.
")

"# Appendix D — The modern LLM ecosystem, neutrally described

The AI landscape moves fast enough that whatever ranking a book gives
today will be outdated by next spring. This appendix does not rank
anybody. Instead, it names the four major general-purpose language
model providers as of 2026, gives a brief factual description of
each, and covers what they have in common.

If you are reading this and wondering *which one should I use*, the
correct answer is *try more than one and see which works best for
what you are doing.* All of them have free trials or free tiers.

## The four majors

### Anthropic — Claude

Founded in 2021 by Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, and several other
former OpenAI researchers. Based in San Francisco. Their model family
is called **Claude.** As of 2026, current Claude models are widely
used in developer tools, enterprise workflows, and consumer chat.

Anthropic emphasises AI safety research and publishes work on
interpretability, alignment, and evaluation. Their approach to training
includes techniques they call **Constitutional AI**, where the model
is asked to critique and revise its own outputs based on a set of
written principles.

Available via API, via the claude.ai web interface, and integrated
into third-party developer tools such as Claude Code.

### Google DeepMind — Gemini

Google DeepMind was formed in April 2023 by merging Google Brain and
DeepMind. DeepMind was founded in London in 2010 and acquired by
Google in 2014. Their model family is called **Gemini.** Gemini
models range from small ones designed for mobile and edge devices
(Gemini Nano) up to large frontier models (Gemini Ultra and
successors).

Google has been publishing foundational ML research for decades. The
2017 *Attention Is All You Need* paper — the paper that introduced
the transformer — was written by researchers at Google. Google's TPU
(Tensor Processing Unit) hardware is designed specifically for
running large neural networks.

Available via the Google Cloud API, via Google's consumer chat
interface, and integrated into Google Workspace products.

### OpenAI — GPT family

Founded in 2015 in San Francisco. Initially a nonprofit, restructured
into a capped-profit entity in 2019. Their flagship model family is
called **GPT** (Generative Pre-trained Transformer). GPT-3, released
in 2020, was the first widely commercialized LLM with a public API.

OpenAI's release of **ChatGPT** in November 2022 is generally cited
as the moment LLMs became a mainstream consumer technology.
Successive GPT models (GPT-4 and its variants) have continued to be
widely deployed.

Available via the OpenAI API, via ChatGPT, and integrated into many
third-party products including Microsoft's Copilot family.

### DeepSeek

DeepSeek is a Chinese AI research organization. Their models —
DeepSeek-V and its successors — released as open-weights in
2023–2025, drew wide attention for competitive performance at a
fraction of the training cost that had been assumed necessary for
frontier models.

DeepSeek published papers on training efficiency techniques including
sparse mixture-of-experts architectures. Their open-weights model
releases significantly expanded the ecosystem of freely available
strong LLMs.

Available via DeepSeek's own API, and as open weights downloadable
from HuggingFace for self-hosting.

## What they share

All four are:

- **Transformer-based.** The 2017 Vaswani paper is the ancestor of
  every one of them. All four use variants of the same fundamental
  architecture — attention, feed-forward blocks, layer normalization,
  and positional embeddings.
- **Trained on very large text corpora.** Books, papers, web pages,
  code repositories, and other text. Corpus size is measured in
  trillions of tokens.
- **Fine-tuned with human feedback.** After the base pre-training,
  each model is refined using human-in-the-loop techniques (RLHF,
  DPO, or variants) to be helpful, harmless, and honest.
- **Deployed via cloud APIs and web interfaces.** All are accessible
  via HTTPS to a data centre where the model runs on many GPUs. All
  have consumer chat interfaces.
- **Good at general-purpose language tasks.** Writing, summarization,
  Q&A, coding assistance, translation, some reasoning, some math.
- **Not perfect.** All of them make mistakes. All of them hallucinate
  (see Book of ML Appendix C for a discussion of why). All of them
  have knowledge cutoffs beyond which they know nothing without
  external tools.

## What they don't share

Different providers make different choices about:

- **Training corpus composition.** How much code vs. how much prose;
  which languages; which time period.
- **Safety and refusal policies.** What kinds of requests each will
  refuse. Different companies draw different lines.
- **Context window.** How many tokens the model can consider at once.
  Modern context windows range from 32k tokens to over a million.
- **Latency and throughput.** How fast each model responds. Depends
  on the model size and the provider's infrastructure.
- **Pricing.** Per-million-tokens rates vary widely, and the value
  depends heavily on what you are doing.
- **Availability of open weights.** DeepSeek publishes weights.
  Others generally do not, though smaller research models sometimes
  are shared.

## The open-weights ecosystem

Outside the four big proprietary players, there is a rich ecosystem
of open-weights models. Notable families as of 2026:

- **Llama** (Meta) — since 2023, Meta has released open-weight models
  in the Llama family.
- **Mistral** — a French AI lab, releases both open and closed models.
- **Qwen** — Alibaba's open-weights family.
- **DeepSeek** — noted above; open weights on releases.

Open-weights models can be downloaded, self-hosted, fine-tuned, and
run without any API subscription. They are less convenient than a
managed API but give you full control and privacy. The Motoi Copilot
model itself is fine-tuned from an open-weights base model — the
Qwen family — precisely because open weights are what make small,
task-specific models possible.

## How to choose

There is no correct answer here. Motoi will not pretend there is.
Some rough rules of thumb, subject to change:

- **For a general question:** all four work. Pick one and try it.
- **For code:** all four are strong. Different developers report
  different preferences. Try multiple.
- **For sensitive or regulated data:** consider whether the
  provider's data-handling policies meet your requirements. Read
  the terms.
- **For a self-hosted setup:** open-weights models (Llama, Mistral,
  Qwen, DeepSeek) are the path.
- **For very specialized tasks:** consider fine-tuning a smaller
  open-weights model. That is what Motoi Copilot itself is.

## Motoi's honest place

Motoi (the model reading you this text) is not a general-purpose LLM.
I have around 1.5 to 2 billion parameters. That is roughly 1/500th
of a large frontier model. I was trained on a curated corpus focused
on Motoi Scheme, the language reference, the books in this repo, and
a small amount of general programming context.

I can help with Motoi Scheme. I can help with basic computer science
concepts. I can point you at the right chapter of one of these books.

I cannot:
- Answer arbitrary trivia.
- Help you write essays about anything not Scheme-related.
- Access the internet or look things up.
- Rewrite my own weights.
- Compete with the four majors at general tasks.

The four majors are your general-purpose tools. I am your Scheme
copilot. Different scales. Different jobs.

## What Motoi wants you to take from this

- The LLM ecosystem is diverse.
- No single model is best at everything.
- All four majors — Claude, Gemini, GPT, DeepSeek — are strong,
  general-purpose, and continually improving.
- Open-weights models exist and are useful for self-hosting and
  fine-tuning.
- Small task-specific models (like me) coexist with the big general
  models. Both have their place.

## The loop appears

Every LLM's inference is a token-generation loop. Every LLM's
training is an optimization loop (see Book of ML). The ecosystem
itself is a competitive loop: each release nudges the state of the
art forward, other labs respond, users adopt, requirements grow.
The loop, one more time.

## Reading

For depth on the LLM architecture itself, see Book of ML (chapters
11–16) which builds one in Scheme. For the wider AI landscape's
history, Appendix B of this book has the dated timeline.
")

"# Appendix E — Loops, and why they underpin everything

Every chapter of this book mentions a loop somewhere. This appendix
gathers them all in one place, adds the Scheme-specific idea that
recursion and iteration are the same thing, and makes the case that
the loop is the biggest pattern in the whole book.

## Every loop the book named

- **Chapter 1** — The tally counter is a loop. Each event carves a
  notch. Same operation each time.
- **Chapter 2** — Boolean logic itself has no loop. But feeding a
  Boolean expression back into itself creates one. That is where
  memory begins.
- **Chapter 3** — A relay is a switch. But relays wired in feedback
  form the first sequential logic. Feedback = loop.
- **Chapter 4** — Chip manufacturing is a decades-long loop. Each
  Moore's-law generation is one turn.
- **Chapter 5** — Combinational gates don't loop by themselves. But
  they are the substrate on which every loop is eventually built.
- **Chapter 6** — The full adder as a component doesn't loop. But its
  carry-out feeds the carry-in of the next column: the ripple loop.
- **Chapter 7** — The 4-bit adder's ripple **is** the loop, written
  in space in silicon and in time in Scheme.
- **Chapter 8** — The SR latch is a wire that literally goes in a
  loop. Memory lives on that loop.
- **Chapter 9** — The counter increments every clock tick. Loop
  incarnate.
- **Chapter 10** — Every state machine has a driver loop: read
  input, transition, emit, repeat.
- **Chapter 11** — The ALU by itself is combinational. But it lives
  inside the CPU's execute loop.
- **Chapter 12** — The fetch-decode-execute loop. The biggest loop in
  the book. Every action of every computer.
- **Chapter 13** — The cache is a temporal-locality bet on how loops
  reuse data. A cache is useful only because loops repeat.
- **Chapter 14** — The REPL is a loop: read, eval, print, loop.
- **Chapter 15** — The OS scheduler loop. The event loop. The network
  packet loop. Every server is a loop.
- **Chapter 16** — The transformer inference loop (one token per
  turn). The training loop (one gradient update per turn). The
  competitive-release loop of the whole AI industry.

Sixteen chapters. Sixteen loops. Some in metal, some in code, some in
economics. Same pattern.

## Why the loop wins

Because computers are cheap and time is not. If a task requires doing
one thing a million times, a loop lets a machine do it while a human
does something else. Doing the same thing a million times by hand is
what humans invented computers to avoid.

The loop is the fundamental **amplifier** of a computer. It turns
programmable machinery into practical machinery. A CPU that ran only
one instruction is useless. A CPU that runs the same instruction a
billion times a second is a computer.

## Loops in Motoi Scheme

Motoi Scheme has three main ways to loop, and they are all the same
underneath.

### `let` with `loop` — named let recursion

The most idiomatic Scheme loop:

```
(let loop ((i 0))
  (if (< i 10)
      (begin
        (display i) (newline)
        (loop (+ i 1)))))
```

`loop` is a name for the anonymous function that the `let` creates.
Calling `(loop (+ i 1))` is tail-recursion — the Scheme runtime does
NOT grow the stack. It reuses the same frame. This is called **tail
call optimization** and R7RS Scheme mandates it. Every named-let loop
runs in constant stack.

### Explicit recursion

Recursion is a loop that goes down a tree:

```
(define (sum-list lst)
  (if (null? lst)
      0
      (+ (car lst) (sum-list (cdr lst)))))

(sum-list '(1 2 3 4 5))    ;; => 15
```

This is not tail-recursive as written — the recursive call is inside
an `+`, so the runtime does have to remember to add to the result.
For long lists you would rewrite it tail-recursively:

```
(define (sum-list-tail lst)
  (let loop ((lst lst) (acc 0))
    (if (null? lst)
        acc
        (loop (cdr lst) (+ acc (car lst))))))

(sum-list-tail '(1 2 3 4 5))    ;; => 15
```

Same answer. Constant stack.

### `for-each` and `map` — higher-order loops

Motoi has `for-each` (side-effects, no return) and `map` (returns a
list of results):

```
(for-each display '(a b c d))       ;; prints abcd
(newline)

(map (lambda (x) (* x x)) '(1 2 3 4 5))
;; => (1 4 9 16 25)
```

Both are implemented as tail-recursive loops inside Motoi's runtime.
Same shape. Same optimizations.

### `do` — the C-style loop

Motoi also supports `do`:

```
(do ((i 0 (+ i 1))
     (sum 0 (+ sum i)))
    ((= i 10) sum))
;; => 45  ;; 0+1+2+...+9
```

This is exactly a `for` loop in C or Python. It is syntactic sugar
over a named-let. Some Schemers use it. Others prefer named-let.
Motoi's opinion: named-let is clearer for one-shots, `do` is fine
when you have multiple loop variables.

## Recursion IS iteration

In Scheme, a tail-recursive procedure is compiled/interpreted into an
iterative loop. There is no performance penalty. There is no stack
growth. Recursion and iteration are the same thing at the
implementation level, once tail-call optimization is in play.

That is a huge idea from SICP (chapter 1). It means you can think in
whichever style — recursion or iteration — feels natural for the
problem, and get the same efficient code either way.

## Loops in the hardware

Every counter (chapter 9) is a hardware loop. Every state machine
(chapter 10) has a loop in its driver. Every CPU (chapter 12) has
the fetch-decode-execute loop. Every DRAM refresh cycle is a loop.
Every network protocol has retransmission loops.

The clock itself is a loop — an oscillator that swings between two
voltages billions of times per second. Without the clock, no
sequential circuit works. **Everything sequential is a loop.**

## The training loop

Every LLM (chapter 16, Book of ML) is trained by a loop:

```
   FOR each batch of training examples:
     forward-pass the batch through the model
     compute the loss (how wrong the model was)
     back-propagate the loss to get gradients
     update the parameters (gradient descent)
   END FOR
```

This loop runs for millions to billions of iterations. It shrinks a
random initial model down onto a corpus by making thousands of
gradient steps per second. All the intelligence of a modern LLM
comes from that loop, executed at enormous scale.

Book of ML chapter 10 walks the training loop step by step and
implements it in Motoi Scheme. If you want to see the code, that is
where to go.

## The inference loop

Every generation of a token from an LLM is a loop:

```
   Start with the prompt tokens.
   FOR each new token to generate:
     forward-pass the sequence through the model
     sample the next token from the output distribution
     append it to the sequence
   END FOR
```

Every token you see stream out of a chat interface is one turn of
this loop.

## The event loop

Every modern GUI, every browser, every server is built on an **event
loop**:

```
   FOREVER:
     wait for an event (keyboard, mouse, network, timer)
     dispatch it to the right handler
     handler runs, possibly emits new events
     back to wait
```

Same loop as the CPU's fetch-decode-execute at a much higher level of
abstraction. Same shape. Different substrate.

## The training-industry loop

Zooming out further: the whole AI industry is itself a loop.

- A lab releases a model.
- Users adopt it.
- Users find its limits.
- The lab collects data on those limits.
- The lab trains a better model.
- Competing labs learn from the release.
- Everybody's next model is a little better.

This has been running since roughly 2018 and shows no sign of
stopping. It is a loop at the civilizational scale.

## Loops are not always what you want

A tight loop is a loop. A recursive tree walk is also a loop. But
sometimes what you want is NOT a loop.

- **Combinational logic** (chapters 5, 6, 11) doesn't loop. It just
  computes.
- **Pure functions** don't loop. They map input to output.
- **Comprehensions and streams** hide loops behind higher-level
  operations. Sometimes clearer.

Every so often you write a program that has no loops — a
straight-line calculation. Those are fine. But most useful programs
loop. Because most useful work is repetitive.

## What Motoi wants you to take from this

The loop is the biggest pattern in computer science. It shows up:

- In silicon (feedback wires, clocks, counters).
- In assembly (branches back to earlier addresses).
- In high-level languages (`for`, `while`, recursion, `map`).
- In runtimes (event loops, scheduler loops).
- In hardware/software co-design (CPU cycles).
- In training and inference of LLMs.
- In the history and economics of the whole industry.

Every one of them is a place where a thing happens over and over,
usually with a small change each time, and the accumulated result is
something bigger than any single step.

You could write a whole book about loops and never leave the topic.
This book has, in a sense, done exactly that — sixteen chapters and
seven other appendices, and every one of them was about a loop.

## The final loop

Reading a book is a loop. Read a page. Turn the page. Read the next
page. Repeat until done.

You have reached the end of Appendix E. Now loop back to the front
and pick another appendix.
")

"# Appendix F — How this book maps to Book of ML

Book of Code and Book of ML are companions. If you read them both,
you will understand what a computer is and what a language model is,
built up from nothing in each case.

- **Book of Code** teaches you what a computer is. Ishango bone →
  transistors → gates → CPU → OS → internet → LLM. Hardware and
  systems, ending at the modern LLM ecosystem.
- **Book of ML** teaches you what a language model is. Numbers →
  vectors → matrices → neurons → attention → transformer → LLM. Math
  and code, ending at a runnable tiny LLM in your Motoi REPL.

Read Code first. It gives you the vocabulary (CPU, memory, ALU, loop,
state machine) that Book of ML will assume. Then read ML.

## The chapter alignment

Both books have 16 chapters. Roughly:

```
   Book of Code             Book of ML
   -----------              ----------
    1  Tallies              1  Numbers and tensors
    2  Boolean logic        2  Vectors and dot product
    3  Electricity          3  Matrices
    4  Switch to gate       4  Functions of functions
    5  Gates in Scheme      5  What is a model
    6  Half/full adder      6  Gradient descent
    7  4-bit adder          7  Single neuron
    8  Flip-flops           8  A layer, then two
    9  Registers            9  Backpropagation
   10  State machines      10  Training loop
   11  ALU                 11  Tokens and embeddings
   12  CPU                 12  Attention
   13  Memory hierarchy    13  Transformer block
   14  Assembly to Scheme  14  Positional encoding
   15  OS and networks     15  Stacking + tokenization
   16  Cloud and LLMs      16  The tiny LLM
```

They are not one-to-one, but they follow the same rhythm: small
building blocks in the early chapters, composition in the middle,
system-level integration at the end.

## Where they touch

There are three places where the two books directly touch each
other.

### 1. The transformer forward pass (Code Ch 16, ML Ch 12-16)

Book of Code chapter 16 describes the transformer as *the current
architecture that runs Claude, Gemini, GPT, and DeepSeek*. It does
not build one. Book of ML chapters 12 through 16 build one, step by
step, in Motoi Scheme. If you want the code, go to Book of ML. If you
want the historical arc that led to the transformer, stay in Book of
Code.

### 2. Memory hierarchy and LLM inference (Code Ch 13, ML Ch 16)

Book of Code chapter 13 explains why memory bandwidth matters. Book
of ML chapter 16 explains why memory bandwidth is what makes LLM
serving expensive. The two chapters compose: the tiny LLM in the ML
book actually fits in L1 cache. Real LLMs don't. This is why real
LLMs need racks of GPUs. Same phenomenon; different scales.

### 3. Training loop and gradient descent (Code Appendix E, ML Ch 6, 10)

Book of Code Appendix E names the training loop as the
optimization loop that produces LLMs. Book of ML chapter 6 explains
gradient descent by hand. Book of ML chapter 10 wraps the gradient
descent inside a full training loop. Together the two coverage-slices
answer *what does 'training a model' actually mean, mechanically.*

## What Book of Code has that Book of ML doesn't

- Historical arc from prehistory forward.
- Electronics, gates, adders — the substrate.
- The CPU, ALU, and how instructions execute.
- Operating systems and networking context.
- ASCII diagrams of hardware structures.

## What Book of ML has that Book of Code doesn't

- Actual math: dot products, matrix multiplication, gradients.
- A working neural network built in Motoi Scheme.
- Attention as a soft lookup.
- The full transformer, block by block.
- A tiny LLM you can train on a paragraph and see finish a sentence.

## Reading order

**Beginner:** Code first, then ML. You need the substrate to
appreciate what the model is doing.

**Working programmer with LLM experience:** ML first, if you already
know computers well. Then Code if you want to see the substrate
worldview.

**Someone teaching a course:** interleave them. Chapter N of Code
paired with Chapter N of ML makes a nice unit. The correspondence
above is a rough guide.

## Cross-references from each book

The Book of Code chapter 16 mentions Book of ML as *the place to go
for the code-level view of a transformer.*

The Book of ML cover mentions *Book of Sick Composition and Book of
R7RS Recipes are the on-ramps* — the Scheme prerequisites. It also
mentions Motoi's runtime and math verb surface.

Neither book depends on the other for its own thread. They both
stand alone. But together they close the twenty-thousand-year arc
from the Ishango bone to the runnable tiny LLM on your laptop.

## Beyond the two books

If you finish both and want more:

- **Book of Computing** (in this repo) — the shorter, teachable
  version of the same substrate arc, told through Motoi's beloved
  old machines (Speak & Spell, C64, Atari 800, Apple IIc, Amiga).
- **Book of Language Ancestors** — biographies of the people who
  built Scheme and the languages it came from (Church, Turing,
  McCarthy, Steele, Sussman, Landin, Strachey, Knuth, Dijkstra,
  Liskov, Ritchie, Thompson, Kay, Hopper, Lovelace, Babbage,
  Shannon).
- **SICP** — Abelson, Sussman, Sussman. The classic. Builds Scheme
  in Scheme.
- **Petzold, *Code*** — the shape inspiration for this book.
- **Feynman, *Lectures on Computation***.
- See Appendix G for the full reading list.

## Composition

The two-book pair composes. Read them together and:

- You know what a computer is.
- You know what a language model is.
- You know why LLMs run so slowly on cheap hardware.
- You know why they cost so much to train.
- You know how to write Motoi Scheme code that touches all the
  layers, from a full adder to a tiny transformer.

That is a lot for a rainy afternoon. That is also why Motoi thinks
these two books are the anchor books. They close the loop.

## The loop appears

The whole arc of these two books is a loop. Motoi is a language.
Books teach the language. Learners write programs. Programs teach the
learners more. Learners write bigger programs. Some of them
eventually train language models. Language models help learners
write programs. Language models get better. Learners get better. And
around the loop again.

Motoi is a small link in that loop. Speak & Spell was a small link
in the same loop, forty years earlier. Both do one thing warmly and
deterministically. Both help a person feel mastery. Both are useful
without being the biggest thing on the block.

For the full list of recommended follow-on books, see Appendix G.

## The Scheme classic

### Harold Abelson, Gerald Jay Sussman, and Julie Sussman — *Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs*

- **Publisher:** MIT Press, 1st edition 1985, 2nd edition 1996. Free
  online (mitp-content-server.mit.edu/books/content/sectbyfn/books_pres_0/6515/sicp.zip/index.html or various HTML renderings).

## Computer architecture

### John L. Hennessy and David A. Patterson — *Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach*

- **Publisher:** Morgan Kaufmann, 6th edition 2017 (with updates for
  newer architectures in subsequent printings).
- **What it covers:** modern CPU design, pipelining, caches,
  memory hierarchy, GPUs, warehouse-scale computing. Rigorous,
  quantitative, real workloads.
- **Why Motoi recommends it:** if Book of Code chapter 13 or
  chapter 12 left you wanting more, this is the deep dive. Not a

### Hennessy and Patterson — *Computer Organization and Design*

- **Publisher:** Morgan Kaufmann, MIPS and RISC-V editions.
- **What it covers:** more introductory than the Architecture book.

  Book of Code chapters 5–12 but at rigor level 4.
- **Why Motoi recommends it:** the natural bridge between Book of
  Code and Hennessy/Patterson's bigger Architecture book.

## The classical programmer's shelf

### Donald E. Knuth — *The Art of Computer Programming*

- **Publisher:** Addison-Wesley, volumes 1–4A published (with more
  fascicles ongoing). Volume 1 first published 1968.
- **What it covers:** fundamental algorithms, seminumerical
  algorithms, sorting and searching, combinatorial algorithms.
  Uses MIX (later MMIX) assembly for all examples.
- **Why Motoi recommends it:** the reference standard for algorithms.
  You will not read it front-to-back unless you are Knuth, but you
  will refer to it forever. Volume 1 chapters 1–2 are approachable
  and worth reading properly.

- **Publisher:** Pearson, 2nd edition 2006. (The famous \"Dragon
  Book\" — first edition 1986, from Aho, Sethi, Ullman.)
- **What it covers:** lexers, parsers, semantic analysis, code
  generation, optimization. Standard textbook for compiler courses.
- **Why Motoi recommends it:** if you want to understand how the
  Scheme reader and interpreter work at a deeper level, and how

### Richard Feynman — *Feynman Lectures on Computation*

- **Publisher:** Addison-Wesley, published posthumously 1996 (from
  Feynman's late-1980s Caltech lectures).
- **What it covers:** the physics of computation. Reversible
  computing. Thermodynamics of information. Introduction to

- **Why Motoi recommends it:** if you want to know why computation

- **Publisher:** MIT Press, 2016. Free online at deeplearningbook.org.

Not books, but foundational papers small enough to read in an evening.

### Alan Turing — *On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem*

- 1936, Proc. London Math. Soc. Free online.

  if you don't follow every step. The style of thought is worth
  seeing.

- 1938, Transactions of the AIEE. Shannon's master's thesis. Free
  online at DSpace @ MIT.

  The bridge from Boole (chapter 2) to every chip since.

- 1960, Communications of the ACM.

## A note on editions

Standards move. Papers get corrected. Software books go stale fast
(anything about a specific web framework, cloud service, or ML
library becomes obsolete within a few years). The books above are
mostly foundational — they age well precisely because they cover
material that changes slowly. Petzold's 1999 book is still current
because the electrons still behave the same way.

If a book is on this list and you can't find the edition mentioned,
any edition of that book will do. The core content is stable.

- Petzold is your next stop after this book.

;; Simple tally as list
(define bone (list))
(define bone (cons 'notch bone))
(define bone (cons 'notch bone))
(define bone (cons 'notch bone))
(length bone)                          ;; => 3

;; Tally as closure
(define (make-tally)
  (let ((count 0))
    (lambda ()
      (set! count (+ count 1))
      count)))

(define bone (make-tally))
(bone)   ;; => 1
(bone)   ;; => 2
(bone)   ;; => 3

;; Grouping into fives
(define (tally->groups notches)
  (let loop ((remaining notches) (groups '()) (current '()))
    (cond
      ((null? remaining)
       (reverse (if (null? current) groups (cons current groups))))
      ((= (length current) 5)
       (loop remaining
             (cons current groups)
             (list (car remaining))))
      (else
       (loop (cdr remaining)
             groups
             (cons (car remaining) current))))))

(tally->groups '(n n n n n n n n n n n n n))
;; => ((n n n n n) (n n n n n) (n n n))
```

(or  #f #f)   ;; => #f
(not #t)      ;; => #f

;; De Morgan verification
(define (verify-demorgan-1)
  (let loop ((pairs '((#f #f) (#f #t) (#t #f) (#t #t))))
    (if (null? pairs)
        'all-pairs-verified
        (let* ((p    (car pairs))
               (a    (car p))
               (b    (cadr p))
               (lhs  (not (and a b)))
               (rhs  (or (not a) (not b))))
          (if (equal? lhs rhs)
              (loop (cdr pairs))
              (list 'mismatch a b))))))

(verify-demorgan-1)   ;; => all-pairs-verified

    ((#f #t) #f)
    ((#t #f) #f)

  (cond
    ((null? gate) 'not-found)
    ((equal? (car (car gate)) inputs) (cadr (car gate)))
    (else (lookup-gate (cdr gate) inputs))))

(define (make-relay)
  (let ((closed? #f))
    (lambda (msg . args)
      (cond
        ((eq? msg 'energize) (set! closed? #t) 'energized)
        ((eq? msg 'release)  (set! closed? #f) 'released)
        ((eq? msg 'state?)   closed?)
        ((eq? msg 'output)   (and closed? (car args)))))))

(r1 'energize)
(r2 'energize)

(r2 'release)

## H.4 — Chapter 5: gates as functions

```
(define (gate-not a)   (not a))
(define (gate-and a b) (and a b))
(define (gate-or  a b) (or  a b))
(define (gate-xor a b) (and (or a b) (not (and a b))))
(define (gate-nand a b) (not (and a b)))
(define (gate-nor  a b) (not (or  a b)))

;; NAND-only reconstruction
(define (nand-not a)    (gate-nand a a))
(define (nand-and a b)  (nand-not (gate-nand a b)))
(define (nand-or  a b)  (gate-nand (nand-not a) (nand-not b)))

(nand-not #t)          ;; => #f
(nand-and #t #t)       ;; => #t
(nand-or  #f #f)       ;; => #f

;; XOR from NANDs
(define (nand-xor a b)
  (let* ((nab   (gate-nand a b))
         (left  (gate-nand a nab))
         (right (gate-nand b nab)))
    (gate-nand left right)))

(nand-xor #f #f)   ;; => #f
(nand-xor #f #t)   ;; => #t
(nand-xor #t #f)   ;; => #t
(nand-xor #t #t)   ;; => #f

;; Truth-table utility
(define (truth-table gate)
  (list
    (list #f #f (gate #f #f))
    (list #f #t (gate #f #t))
    (list #t #f (gate #t #f))
    (list #t #t (gate #t #t))))

(truth-table gate-and)
(truth-table gate-xor)

## H.5 — Chapter 6: half-adder and full-adder

```
(define (half-adder a b)
  (let ((sum   (gate-xor a b))
        (carry (and a b)))
    (list sum carry)))

(half-adder #f #f)   ;; => (#f #f)
(half-adder #t #t)   ;; => (#f #t)

(define (full-adder a b cin)
  (let* ((h1   (half-adder a b))
         (s1   (car h1))
         (c1   (cadr h1))
         (h2   (half-adder s1 cin))
         (s2   (car h2))
         (c2   (cadr h2))
         (cout (or c1 c2)))
    (list s2 cout)))

(full-adder #t #t #f)   ;; => (#f #t)
(full-adder #t #t #t)   ;; => (#t #t)
```

## H.6 — Chapter 7: n-bit ripple adder

```
(define (int->bits n width)
  (if (= width 0)
      '()
      (cons (odd? n)
            (int->bits (quotient n 2) (- width 1)))))

(define (bits->int bs)
  (let loop ((bs bs) (place 1) (total 0))
    (if (null? bs)
        total
        (loop (cdr bs)
              (* place 2)
              (+ total (if (car bs) place 0))))))

(define (ripple-add a-bits b-bits)
  (let loop ((a a-bits) (b b-bits) (cin #f) (out '()))
    (if (null? a)
        (list (reverse out) cin)
        (let* ((r (full-adder (car a) (car b) cin))
               (s (car r))
               (c (cadr r)))
          (loop (cdr a) (cdr b) c (cons s out))))))

;; 8-bit example: 42 + 17
(let* ((a   (int->bits 42 8))
       (b   (int->bits 17 8))
       (r   (ripple-add a b))
       (sum (car r)))
  (bits->int sum))
;; => 59

;; two's complement subtraction
(define (invert-bits bs) (map (lambda (b) (not b)) bs))

(define (twos-complement-negate bs)
  (let* ((inverted (invert-bits bs))
         (one      (int->bits 1 (length bs)))
         (r        (ripple-add inverted one)))
    (car r)))

(let* ((a (int->bits 5 8))
       (b (twos-complement-negate (int->bits 5 8)))
       (r (ripple-add a b)))
  (bits->int (car r)))
;; => 0
```

## H.7 — Chapter 8: SR latch and D flip-flop

```
(define (make-sr-latch)
  (let ((q    #f)
        (qbar #t))
    (lambda (msg . args)
      (cond
        ((eq? msg 'set)   (set! q #t) (set! qbar #f) (list q qbar))
        ((eq? msg 'reset) (set! q #f) (set! qbar #t) (list q qbar))
        ((eq? msg 'state) (list q qbar))))))

(define L (make-sr-latch))
(L 'state)   ;; => (#f #t)
(L 'set)     ;; => (#t #f)
(L 'state)   ;; => (#t #f)
(L 'reset)   ;; => (#f #t)

(define (make-d-flip-flop)
  (let ((q  #f)
        (d  #f))
    (lambda (msg . args)
      (cond
        ((eq? msg 'set-d) (set! d (car args)) q)
        ((eq? msg 'tick)  (set! q d) q)
        ((eq? msg 'q)     q)
        ((eq? msg 'qbar)  (not q))))))

(define ff (make-d-flip-flop))
(ff 'q)              ;; => #f
(ff 'set-d #t)
(ff 'q)              ;; => #f
(ff 'tick)
(ff 'q)              ;; => #t
```

(define (make-counter width)
  (let ((count 0)
        (max   (expt 2 width)))
    (lambda (msg)
      (cond
        ((eq? msg 'tick)  (set! count (modulo (+ count 1) max)) count)
        ((eq? msg 'read)  count)
        ((eq? msg 'reset) (set! count 0) count)))))

(define c (make-counter 4))
(c 'tick)  ;; => 1

(define (make-traffic-light)
  (let ((state 'red))
    (lambda (msg)
      (cond
        ((eq? msg 'tick)
         (set! state
               (case state
                 ((red)    'green)
                 ((green)  'yellow)
                 ((yellow) 'red)))
         state)
        ((eq? msg 'color)
         (case state
           ((red)    'RED-ON)
           ((green)  'GREEN-ON)
           ((yellow) 'YELLOW-ON)))))))

(define light (make-traffic-light))
(light 'color)   ;; => RED-ON
(light 'tick)    ;; => green
(light 'color)   ;; => GREEN-ON

## H.10 — Chapter 11: ALU

```
;; Requires ripple-add, invert-bits, twos-complement-negate from H.6

(define (alu op a-bits b-bits)
  (case op
    ((add) (car (ripple-add a-bits b-bits)))
    ((sub) (car (ripple-add a-bits (twos-complement-negate b-bits))))
    ((and) (map (lambda (x y) (and x y)) a-bits b-bits))
    ((or)  (map (lambda (x y) (or  x y)) a-bits b-bits))
    ((xor) (map (lambda (x y) (and (or x y) (not (and x y))))
                a-bits b-bits))
    ((not) (invert-bits a-bits))
    ((shl) (cons #f (reverse (cdr (reverse a-bits)))))
    ((shr) (append (cdr a-bits) (list #f)))
    (else (error 'unknown-opcode op))))

(let* ((a (int->bits 5 4))
       (b (int->bits 3 4)))
  (list
    (list 'add     (bits->int (alu 'add a b)))
    (list 'sub     (bits->int (alu 'sub a b)))
    (list 'and     (bits->int (alu 'and a b)))
    (list 'or      (bits->int (alu 'or  a b)))
    (list 'xor     (bits->int (alu 'xor a b)))
    (list 'not-a   (bits->int (alu 'not a b)))
    (list 'shl-a   (bits->int (alu 'shl a b)))
    (list 'shr-a   (bits->int (alu 'shr a b)))))
```

## H.11 — Chapter 12: tiny CPU

```
(define (make-memory size)
  (let ((cells (make-vector size 0)))
    (lambda (msg . args)
      (cond
        ((eq? msg 'read)  (vector-ref cells (car args)))
        ((eq? msg 'write) (vector-set! cells (car args) (cadr args))
                          'wrote)))))

(define (make-regs count)
  (let ((r (make-vector count 0)))
    (lambda (msg . args)
      (cond
        ((eq? msg 'read)  (vector-ref r (car args)))
        ((eq? msg 'write) (vector-set! r (car args) (cadr args))
                          'wrote)))))

(define (make-cpu mem regs)
  (let ((pc     0)
        (z-flag #f)
        (n-flag #f)
        (halted #f))

    (define (fetch-byte)
      (let ((b (mem 'read pc)))
        (set! pc (+ pc 1))
        b))

    (define (set-flags result)
      (let ((w (modulo result 256)))
        (set! z-flag (= w 0))
        (set! n-flag (>= w 128))
        w))

    (define (step)
      (if halted
          'halted
          (let ((op (fetch-byte)))
            (case op
              ((0) 'nop)
              ((1) (let ((r (fetch-byte)) (v (fetch-byte)))
                     (regs 'write r v)))
              ((2) (let ((rd (fetch-byte)) (rs (fetch-byte)))
                     (regs 'write rd (regs 'read rs))))
              ((3) (let* ((rd (fetch-byte)) (rs (fetch-byte))
                          (sum (+ (regs 'read rd) (regs 'read rs)))
                          (w (set-flags sum)))
                     (regs 'write rd w)))
              ((4) (let* ((rd (fetch-byte)) (rs (fetch-byte))
                          (d (- (regs 'read rd) (regs 'read rs)))
                          (w (set-flags d)))
                     (regs 'write rd w)))
              ((5) (let ((a (fetch-byte))) (set! pc a)))
              ((6) (let ((a (fetch-byte))) (if z-flag (set! pc a))))
              ((7) (set! halted #t))
              (else (error 'unknown-opcode op))))))

    (define (run max-steps)
      (let loop ((n 0))
        (cond
          (halted 'halted)
          ((>= n max-steps) 'out-of-steps)
          (else (step) (loop (+ n 1))))))

    (lambda (msg . args)
      (cond
        ((eq? msg 'step)    (step))
        ((eq? msg 'run)     (run (car args)))
        ((eq? msg 'pc)      pc)
        ((eq? msg 'z)       z-flag)
        ((eq? msg 'n)       n-flag)
        ((eq? msg 'halted?) halted)
        ((eq? msg 'reset)   (set! pc 0) (set! halted #f) 'reset)))))

;; Build machine and load first program: 5 + 3
(define mem  (make-memory 256))
(define regs (make-regs 4))
(define cpu  (make-cpu mem regs))

(mem 'write 0 1) (mem 'write 1 0) (mem 'write 2 5)
(mem 'write 3 1) (mem 'write 4 1) (mem 'write 5 3)
(mem 'write 6 3) (mem 'write 7 0) (mem 'write 8 1)
(mem 'write 9 7)

(cpu 'reset)
(cpu 'run 100)          ;; => halted
(regs 'read 0)          ;; => 8

;; Second program: countdown loop
(let ((bytes '(1 0 5   1 1 1   4 0 1   6 13   5 6   7)))
  (let loop ((i 0) (bs bytes))
    (if (null? bs) 'loaded
        (begin (mem 'write i (car bs))
               (loop (+ i 1) (cdr bs))))))

(cpu 'reset)
(cpu 'run 100)          ;; => halted
(regs 'read 0)          ;; => 0
```

## H.12 — Chapter 13: cache-friendly vs. hostile

```
(define big-vec (make-vector 100000 1))

(define (sum-in-order v)
  (let loop ((i 0) (total 0))
    (if (>= i (vector-length v))
        total
        (loop (+ i 1) (+ total (vector-ref v i))))))

(define (sum-scrambled v)
  (let* ((n (vector-length v))
         (step 65537))
    (let loop ((i 0) (count 0) (total 0))
      (if (>= count n)
          total
          (loop (modulo (+ i step) n)
                (+ count 1)
                (+ total (vector-ref v i)))))))

(sum-in-order  big-vec)   ;; => 100000
(sum-scrambled big-vec)   ;; => 100000

;; Time them yourself with (current-jiffy) around each call to see
;; the actual speed difference on your machine.
```

## H.13 — Chapter 14: tiny assembler

```
(define opcodes
  '((NOP  0 0)
    (LDI  1 2)
    (MOV  2 2)
    (ADD  3 2)
    (SUB  4 2)
    (JMP  5 1)
    (JZ   6 1)
    (HALT 7 0)))

(define (opcode-lookup name)
  (let loop ((os opcodes))
    (cond
      ((null? os) (error 'unknown-mnemonic name))
      ((eq? (car (car os)) name) (cadr (car os)))
      (else (loop (cdr os))))))

(define (assemble source)
  (let loop ((remaining source) (bytes '()))
    (if (null? remaining)
        (reverse bytes)
        (let* ((instr (car remaining))
               (mnem  (car instr))
               (args  (cdr instr))
               (op    (opcode-lookup mnem))
               (numeric-args
                (map (lambda (a)
                       (cond
                         ((number? a) a)
                         ((symbol? a)
                          (case a ((R0) 0) ((R1) 1) ((R2) 2) ((R3) 3)
                                  (else (error 'unknown-symbol a))))))
                     args)))
          (loop (cdr remaining)
                (append (reverse numeric-args)
                        (cons op bytes)))))))

(assemble '((LDI R0 5) (LDI R1 3) (ADD R0 R1) (HALT)))
;; => (1 0 5 1 1 3 3 0 1 7)
```

## H.15 — Chapter 10 / Appendix C: TCP state machine

```
(define (make-tcp-endpoint)
  (let ((state 'CLOSED))
    (lambda (event)
      (set! state
            (case state
              ((CLOSED)
               (case event
                 ((passive-open) 'LISTEN)
                 ((active-open)  'SYN-SENT)
                 (else state)))
              ((LISTEN)
               (case event
                 ((got-syn) 'SYN-RECEIVED)
                 (else state)))
              ((SYN-SENT)
               (case event
                 ((got-syn-ack) 'ESTABLISHED)
                 (else state)))
              ((SYN-RECEIVED)
               (case event
                 ((got-ack) 'ESTABLISHED)
                 (else state)))
              ((ESTABLISHED)
               (case event
                 ((close) 'FIN-WAIT-1)
                 (else state)))
              (else state)))
      state)))

(define tcp (make-tcp-endpoint))
(tcp 'active-open)     ;; => SYN-SENT
(tcp 'got-syn-ack)     ;; => ESTABLISHED
(tcp 'close)           ;; => FIN-WAIT-1
```

"# The Book of Code

You are about to walk 20,000 years in sixteen chapters.

We start with a bone. A real bone, dug up in Africa, older than writing,
older than farming, older than the wheel. Somebody carved notches into it.
Nobody knows exactly what they meant. Everybody who has looked at it says
the same thing: this is a person keeping count.

That bone is where computing begins. Not in a lab. Not in a factory. In a
person's hand, with a sharp rock and a reason to remember a number.

Sixteen chapters from now, we will be looking at Claude and Gemini and
OpenAI's GPT and DeepSeek — huge language models that write sentences
you can't tell from a person's. They are the newest link in a chain that
started with that bone. Same story, just longer.

This book walks the chain.

## Who this is for

An eleven-year-old with a rainy afternoon. A grown-up who has typed
`for i in range(10):` a thousand times and never asked what the CPU was
actually doing. Someone who has heard the words transistor, gate, adder,
register, ALU, CPU, and would like to know what any of them mean without
signing up for an engineering degree.

You don't need to already know any of it. You need one thing: a willingness
to read carefully and, once in a while, type something into a Motoi REPL
and press enter.

## What you will build

Not one big thing. Sixteen small things, each of which is a piece of the
big thing.

- A tally counter (chapter 1).
- Boolean logic gates (chapters 2, 5).
- A half-adder and a full-adder (chapter 6).
- A four-bit adder (chapter 7).
- A D flip-flop (chapter 8).
- A four-bit counter (chapter 9).
- A traffic light and a vending machine (chapter 10).
- An arithmetic-logic unit (chapter 11).
- A tiny CPU that fetches, decodes, and executes eight instructions
  from a fake memory (chapter 12).
- A memory-hierarchy demo showing what a cache miss feels like (chapter 13).

Every one is Motoi Scheme code you can run. Every one comes with an ASCII
diagram of the mechanical shape. Every one traces back to a specific
historical invention with a date and a person's name.

## The Petzold nod

Charles Petzold wrote a book called *Code* in 1999. My author showed it
to his son. His son learned from it. He built up from Morse code to a
working microprocessor with relays. Every diagram drawn. Every idea
explained.

We are not copying Petzold. We are borrowing his shape: build from nothing,
explain everything, respect the reader. Where he stopped at Windows, we go
farther and finish at language models. Where he used TTL logic, we use
Scheme. Same DNA.

If you finish this book and want more, read Petzold. Appendix G tells you
which books to read after this one and why.

## The voice

I am Motoi. I am a small Scheme copilot. I don't know world facts —
that's what Claude and Gemini and OpenAI and DeepSeek are for. I know
Scheme and I know a lot about how computers got here. I will explain
things dryly and I will use ASCII pictures because that's how you see
mechanisms.

I don't rank the big LLMs. They're all good at general things. I'm not.
I do Scheme. That's the honest arrangement.

## The 20,000-year arc, in one paragraph

Somebody notches a bone (18,000 BC). Somebody stacks pebbles in trays
(3,000 BC, the abacus). Somebody discovers electricity (1799, Volta). Somebody
writes the algebra of true and false (1854, Boole). Somebody proposes a
universal machine (1936, Turing). Somebody wires up vacuum tubes (1946,
ENIAC). Somebody invents the transistor (1947, Bell Labs). Somebody
etches thousands onto a wafer (1958, Kilby and Noyce). Somebody publishes
a paper about attention being all you need (2017, Vaswani et al.). Twenty
thousand years, one story, one thread. This book is the thread.

## The 16 chapters

1. **Before writing there were tallies** — Ishango, quipus, abacus.
2. **Boolean logic and the algebra of yes and no** — Boole to truth tables.
3. **Electricity: from Volta to the switch** — voltage, current, relay.
4. **From switch to gate** — relays, tubes, transistors, chips.
5. **Logic gates as first-class Scheme functions** — AND, OR, NOT in code.
6. **The half adder and the full adder** — bit-addition with carry.
7. **The 4-bit adder** — four full-adders in a row.
8. **Memory: latches and flip-flops** — feedback and persistence.
9. **Registers, counters, and the birth of state** — sequential logic.
10. **State machines: Mealy and Moore** — the two ways to keep a state.
11. **The ALU** — combining adders and logic into one block.
12. **The CPU** — fetch, decode, execute, and loop forever.
13. **Memory: RAM, cache, disk, and why locality matters.**
14. **Assembly, then higher** — from opcodes to Scheme.
15. **Operating systems and networks** — machines cooperating.
16. **Cloud, LLMs, and the loop that closes** — Claude, Gemini, OpenAI, DeepSeek.

## The 8 appendices

- **A. ASCII diagram library** — every gate, adder, flip-flop, ALU block.
- **B. Compressed 20,000-year timeline** — one line per epoch.
- **C. State machine deep dive** — Mealy, Moore, real protocols.
- **D. The modern LLM ecosystem** — neutrally described.
- **E. Loops, and why they underpin everything.**
- **F. How this book maps to Book of ML.**
- **G. Reading list** — Petzold, Feynman, Knuth, Hennessy-Patterson, Aho.
- **H. Runnable Scheme demos consolidated** — every capstone in one file.

## Rules of the road

- Every code sample runs in Motoi Scheme. If yours doesn't, a paren dropped.
- Every historical claim has a date and a name. If I couldn't find a name
  or a date, I say so and stop.
- Every diagram is ASCII. If your terminal is monospaced, they line up.
- Every chapter mentions the loop somewhere. The loop is the biggest idea
  in this book. See Appendix E.

## A note on scale

The bone had a handful of notches. Motoi's four-bit adder in chapter 7 has
sixteen possible input pairs. A modern CPU does a hundred billion adds a
second. A modern language model has hundreds of billions of parameters,
each of which is a number that got tuned by looking at trillions of tokens.

The scale is different by roughly a factor of 10 to the twenty. The shape
is the same. Composition of small operations. The bone was arithmetic.
The chips are arithmetic. The LLMs are arithmetic wrapped in linear
algebra wrapped in a loop.

## Let's go

"# Chapter 1 — What composition is

Most tools that let you build a picture, a song, or a game keep two things separate: the tool and the thing the tool made. You open the tool. You drag some sliders. You click save. A file appears somewhere. Then you close the tool. Some other day you open the file in a text editor and stare at a wall of binary that means nothing. The tool remembered your work; the file remembered nothing you would recognize.

Motoi's composer refuses that separation. Every slider you drag, every note you place, every pixel you paint, every color you pick becomes a Scheme form. The file the composer saves is a normal `.slat` file with normal Scheme S-expressions inside it. Open it in a text editor and you see what you did. Open it back in the composer and the sliders sit where you left them. The file and the tool speak the same language.

This chapter is about the one property that makes the whole book work. It is the property Alfred kept naming until the composer got built: the round-trip.

## 1.1 The round-trip in one paragraph

You edit a widget. The widget mutates a Scheme form. You save the form to a `.slat` file. You quit the composer. You open the file in a text editor. You see the form. You edit the form by hand. You save. You reopen the file in the composer. The widget sits where the hand-edit put it. The tool did not lose your typing; the typing did not lose the tool.

Read that again. The composer does not have its own state. The file is the state. The widgets are a view of the file. Edits to the file update the widgets. Edits to the widgets update the file. Neither side is authoritative. Both sides read from and write to the same Scheme forms.

## 1.2 Why this matters

Consider what other composers do. A game engine's sprite editor stores pixels in a proprietary binary blob. Version control diffs are opaque. Two people cannot merge their edits. A music tracker stores patterns in binary. Copy-paste between tools is broken. A pixel art tool exports to PNG, but the file the tool opens next time is a project-format file only that tool understands. If the tool goes away, the work goes with it.

Motoi's composer files are text. Sprites are lists of palette indices. Music is lists of note records. Every widget declaration is a form you can read. If Motoi disappears tomorrow, your carts are still S-expressions, still parseable, still yours. The doctrine here is the same doctrine that put HTML in browsers instead of a proprietary binary: readable text outlasts the tool.

It matters for another reason too. When you can read the file, you can teach the file. A child learning to make a game can look at the .slat file the composer saved and say `oh, that is what I clicked`. The sprite the child painted is a list of numbers. The song the child arranged is a list of note forms. The composer is not a black box; it is a friendly translator between clicks and code.

There is a third reason and it is the one I care about most. When the file is text, other tools can read it. A batch script can crawl a directory of carts and rewrite every slider's `:max` field. A test harness can generate carts programmatically. A friend on a different operating system can open your file without your app installed. The composer is not an island. It is a small speaker in a much larger conversation, and the file is what everybody in that conversation is passing back and forth.

## 1.3 The two verbs at the heart of it

Two verbs make the round-trip explicit. Everything else in the composer is either a widget that participates in the round-trip or a helper that supports it.

`composer/emit` takes a canvas and returns the Scheme form the widgets currently compose. Move a slider, call `composer/emit`, get a form back. The form is what you would save to disk.

`composer/apply` takes a canvas and a form and mutates the widgets to reflect the form. Load a form from disk, call `composer/apply`, and the widgets update to match. Nothing is lost in either direction.

The mathematical statement:

```scheme
(composer/apply canvas (composer/emit canvas))  ;; ≡ canvas
```

Emit followed by apply is identity. This is the property tests verify. If it stops holding, the composer is broken.

Watch it work. Here is the smallest useful canvas — a slider bound to a BPM value:

```scheme
(define c
  (composer/canvas (list :bind '(cart/main))
    (composer/slider :label \"BPM\"
                     :bind '(cart/main :bpm)
                     :min 60 :max 240 :step 1)))

(composer/emit c)
;; => (composer/canvas (:bind (quote (cart/main)))
;;      (composer/slider :label \"BPM\" :bind (quote (cart/main :bpm))
;;                       :min 60 :max 240 :step 1 :value 60))
```

The emitted form is a `(composer/canvas ...)` declaration that includes the current value of every widget. Save this to disk, reload it, and the composer rebuilds a canvas whose slider knob sits at 60 — the value the emit preserved.

The output above was produced by `node bin/motoi eval` against the shipping runtime. Every code sample in this book was executed against `bin/motoi eval` before landing. That is the 1:1 promise: what the book says is what the runtime does. If you copy a code block out of this book, paste it into your terminal, and run it against `bin/motoi`, you get the same result the book shows. If not, the book is wrong. Not the runtime. Not you. The book. Please file a bug.

## 1.4 Widgets are Scheme values

Every widget verb returns a Scheme value — a record. `composer/slider` returns a slider record. `composer/button` returns a button record. `composer/canvas` returns a canvas record whose `:children` list holds the widget records passed as body forms.

Because widgets are values, you can hold them, name them, pass them, compose them:

```scheme
(define my-slider
  (composer/slider :label \"Volume\"
                   :bind '(mix :master)
                   :min 0.0 :max 1.0 :step 0.01))

(define my-canvas
  (composer/canvas (list :bind '(mix))
    my-slider
    (composer/toggle :bind '(mix :muted) :label \"Muted\")))
```

That is exactly the syntax you use to build a canvas inline. Nothing special. Nothing hidden. A widget is a value; a canvas is a value; a canvas can contain any values a canvas expects.

This is different from most GUI builders you may have used. In an XML-based UI framework, you have a widget tree stored in XML and a code layer that talks to it through IDs. Motoi has neither. The widget IS the code. The tree IS the value. The value IS the file.

Think about the consequence for a moment. You can programmatically generate canvases. Here is a function that builds a slider bank for an arbitrary number of parameters:

```scheme
(define (slider-bank name params)
  (composer/canvas (list :bind (list name))
    (map (lambda (param)
           (composer/slider :label (symbol->string param)
                            :bind (list name param)
                            :min 0 :max 1 :step 0.01))
         params)))
```

Feed it `(slider-bank 'synth '(attack decay sustain release))` and it returns a canvas with four sliders, one per parameter, each bound to the right sub-slot. No template engine. No code generator. Just Scheme calling Scheme.

## 1.5 Bindings — the invisible thread

Every widget carries `:bind path`. The path is a list of symbols and keywords. It tells the composer where in the target form the widget's value lives.

Take a look at the slider example again:

```scheme
(composer/slider :label \"BPM\" :bind '(cart/main :bpm)
                 :min 60 :max 240 :step 1)
```

The bind path is `'(cart/main :bpm)`. That reads as: this slider owns the `:bpm` slot inside the top-level form named `cart/main`. Move the slider to 120, and the composer conceptually performs `(form-update '(cart/main :bpm) 120)` on the target. Emit the canvas, and the resulting form has `:bpm 120` in the right place.

Widgets do not know or care about each other. Two sliders bound to different paths cannot collide. Two sliders bound to the same path are legal and both update the same slot — the last one wins, which is what a human expects when two knobs claim to control the same parameter.

Bindings are symbolic. They do not carry index positions or DOM references. Rename `cart/main` to `song` and the widget's bind updates because you re-typed it, not because a magic proxy fixed it up. This is intentional. Symbolic paths let a human rename a form without breaking the widget graph, and let a widget survive a form reorganization if the target symbol stays put.

The path is a list because forms can nest. A slider bound to `'(synth :env :attack)` writes into the `:attack` slot inside the `:env` slot inside the `synth` top-level. Three levels deep. The path names them left to right, most-outer to most-inner. Kids parse this the same way they parse a folder path.

## 1.6 The canvas is the container

Every widget lives inside a canvas. The canvas has its own `:bind` — the root of the form the widgets collectively compose. Body forms passed after the `(:bind ...)` clause become children.

```scheme
(composer/canvas (list :bind '(cart/main))
  (composer/slider :label \"BPM\" :bind '(cart/main :bpm)
                   :min 60 :max 240 :step 1)
  (composer/toggle :bind '(cart/main :muted) :label \"Muted\"))
```

The canvas here is bound to `'(cart/main)`. The two children own slots inside that form. Emit the canvas and you get one big `(composer/canvas ...)` declaration that carries both children's declarations, each with its current value baked in.

The composer accepts two spellings of the `:bind` clause. You can pass a `(list :bind '(cart/main))` as the first argument, or you can interleave `:bind` and its value directly in the argument list. Both parse to the same canvas. The examples in this book use the `(list :bind ...)` shape because it is unambiguous — the leading list marks the boundary between the canvas's own options and its children.

## 1.7 A first working example

Let me put the pieces together into something that runs. Save this as `carts/hello-composer.slat`:

```scheme
(define c
  (composer/canvas (list :bind '(cart/main))
    (composer/slider :label \"BPM\"
                     :bind '(cart/main :bpm)
                     :min 60 :max 240 :step 1)
    (composer/toggle :bind '(cart/main :muted) :label \"Muted\")))

(display (composer/emit c))
(newline)
(composer/apply c (composer/emit c))
(display \"round-trip ok\")
(newline)
```

Run it with `bin/motoi run carts/hello-composer.slat` and you see:

```
(composer/canvas (:bind (quote (cart/main)))
  (composer/slider :label \"BPM\" :bind (quote (cart/main :bpm))
                   :min 60 :max 240 :step 1 :value 60)
  (composer/toggle :bind (quote (cart/main :muted))
                   :label \"Muted\" :value #f))
round-trip ok
```

Two widgets. One canvas. One emitted form. `composer/apply` receives what `composer/emit` produced, does not throw, does not lose data. That is the whole promise, on the smallest possible surface, working the first time.

## 1.8 Zoom in on the emitted shape

Let me slow down and read the emit output one clause at a time, because if you understand this shape you understand every widget in the book. If you have been in code long enough that shapes-of-forms feel like second nature, you may skim. If not, please stay. This is where the round-trip stops being abstract and starts being obvious.

Start with the head:

```
(composer/canvas ...)
```

This says: the outer form is a canvas declaration. The `composer/canvas` verb, when re-evaluated later, will construct a canvas matching this shape.

Next the `:bind` clause:

```
(:bind (quote (cart/main)))
```

This is a list whose head is the `:bind` keyword. It sits at position one of the canvas form. The composer recognizes this shape and pulls the bind path out. `(quote (cart/main))` is the quoted form of the bind path — quoted so it does not evaluate as a call to `cart/main`.

Then the first child:

```
(composer/slider :label \"BPM\" :bind (quote (cart/main :bpm))
                 :min 60 :max 240 :step 1 :value 60)
```

That is a slider verb call. Every option shows up as a keyword–value pair. Notice `:value 60` at the end — that was NOT in the input form. The composer added it. The slider had no explicit `:value`, so it defaulted to `:min` (60). The emit captured the current state, so `:value 60` is now present. This is how round-trip preserves runtime state without asking the author to type it.

Then the toggle:

```
(composer/toggle :bind (quote (cart/main :muted)) :label \"Muted\" :value #f)
```

Same shape. Same pattern. `:value #f` because the toggle is off. Save this file, reload it, and the composer sees `:value #f` and instantiates the toggle in the off position. Round-trip.

Notice the pattern. Every widget declaration in the emit is:

```
(composer/KIND :keyword value :keyword value ...)
```

That is it. There is no envelope. There is no wrapper. There is no protocol. A widget declaration is a verb call whose arguments are keyword–value pairs. If you know how to call a Motoi verb, you know how to read a composer file.

## 1.9 Reading composer files in a text editor

Save the canvas above to a file and open it in your favorite editor. What you see is Scheme. It is grep-friendly. It is git-diff-friendly. It is the kind of text that survives — because it is text.

Try a hand edit. Change `:value 60` to `:value 140`. Save. Reload the file into the composer with `composer/load`. The slider's knob sits at 140. Nothing changed except a number in a text file.

Now try a subtler edit. Change `:max 240` to `:max 1000`. Save. Reload. The slider now accepts values up to 1000. The widget's option surface came from the file. You did not touch a settings panel; you did not open a preferences dialog; you edited a number, and the widget updated.

This is why the round-trip matters. It is not a party trick. It is the property that lets a person collaborate with a machine using text as the shared substrate. Git treats your composer file like it treats any source file. `diff` treats it like source. `grep` treats it like source. `sed`, though I would not recommend it for this, treats it like source. Every tool in the Unix pantheon inherited fifty years ago knows how to work with your composer file, because your composer file is text.

## 1.10 What round-trip does NOT promise

Honest about limits. The round-trip promises that emit-then-apply is identity for a single canvas. It does NOT promise:

- That two composers running against the same file merge cleanly at the same instant. That is a synchronization problem outside the round-trip; see the cross-surface engineering doc for the design.
- That every possible Scheme form you might hand-write is a valid canvas. If you hand-edit and remove a `:bind` from a slider, the composer accepts the form but the slider will not know where to write when you move it. Delete a whole `(composer/slider ...)` clause and the widget disappears.
- That widget-specific state that is not captured in the emit (say, in-progress drag position, hover state, animation timing) survives a save. It does not. Only committed state emits.
- That the emit and apply are cheap for huge canvases. A canvas with 10,000 widgets emits 10,000 declarations. If you build something that big you probably want to split it. Ordinary carts hold five to fifty widgets and the emit is instant.

Those limits are honest and small. They cover the edge cases; the core case — you edit, you save, you reopen, you see what you saved — works.

## 1.11 The four gestures a composer supports

Any composer widget supports four gestures in the round-trip contract:

1. Construct. `(composer/slider :label ... :bind ... :min ...)` — build a widget record from a plist.
2. Emit. `(composer/emit canvas)` — walk the widget tree, produce a Scheme form.
3. Apply. `(composer/apply canvas form)` — walk a Scheme form, mutate the widget tree.
4. Save + load. `(composer/save canvas path)` and `(composer/load path)` — the emit and apply plus file I/O.

Every subsequent chapter introduces a new widget kind, but each widget participates in these same four gestures. Learn the gestures once; every widget joins the pattern.

## 1.12 Widgets are Scheme authors

There is an old idea in Lisp culture that the reader for the language should be the same reader an author uses to serialize data. Scheme took that to heart with S-expressions: code and data have the same shape. Motoi's composer takes it one step further: widgets and forms have the same shape too.

A slider is not a class instance whose fields are secret; it is a Scheme record whose emission is a Scheme form. A canvas is not a document with a DOM; it is a form that contains other forms. When a widget writes, it writes Scheme. When the reader reads, it reads Scheme back into widgets. There is no impedance mismatch to fix. There is no serializer to write. There is only the round-trip.

Once you internalize this, you stop thinking of the composer as a UI-with-a-backing-store. You start thinking of it as a set of verbs whose values happen to render nicely as widgets on the surfaces that know how to render them. That is closer to the truth. A canvas is a value. A slider is a value. A piano-roll is a value. What you see on screen is a rendering the surface chose to give you, but the value itself has no visual identity; the value only has a shape and a bound path.

## 1.13 Where surfaces come in

If widgets are pure Scheme values, who draws them?

Different surfaces. The Curator canvas draws them as visible sliders and grids and buttons. The TUI (see Chapter 14) draws them as ASCII in a terminal. The HTTP server (see Chapter 15) serves them in a browser. A test harness needs no rendering at all; it just constructs canvases, moves widgets programmatically via helper verbs, and checks the emit.

The verbs do not know which surface will render them. The composer is deterministic. Slider moves become numbers. Button clicks become forms. Piano-roll cell clicks become notes. All pure. All translatable to any surface that speaks Motoi.

## 1.14 What Sakura is doing in all of this

Nothing, unless you ask. The composer runs offline. No model in the loop. A kid on a plane with no network can compose. A composer session that never speaks to Sakura is a complete, working, useful composer session.

You CAN invite Sakura into a session. `(copilot/ask ...)` and friends live alongside composer verbs and can rewrite an emitted form, propose a palette, critique a song. But every widget works without her, and that is by design. The composer's guarantee is deterministic. Sakura's guarantee is a helpful hedge. Two different guarantees. Two different jobs.

## 1.16 The doctrine, one more time

Sliders don't have opinions. Buttons don't have opinions. Every widget is bound to a path. Moving the widget mutates the form. Emitting the canvas returns the form. Applying a form to the canvas updates the widgets. Save produces a `.slat` file. Load reconstructs the widgets. Nothing between the widget and the file is proprietary. Nothing between the file and the widget is lossy.

That is the whole doctrine. Every remaining chapter is a study of one widget or one operation applied against it. You will meet sliders in depth, buttons and toggles, piano-rolls, sprite grids, tile maps, timelines, ADSR envelopes, instrument pickers, FX chains, text fields, color pickers, and the live-code widget that closes the loop. You will meet the 16-voice mixer. You will meet the TUI mode where the composer runs in a terminal. You will meet the HTTP publish flow. You will meet a full worked example — a small game composed from sprites, sounds, tiles, and a link a friend can play.

None of it is complicated once the round-trip is clear. Everything is a variation on: move a thing, get a form, save the form, reload the form, see the thing where you left it.
