"# Chapter 10 — FX chain

The `composer/fx-chain` widget lets you build an ordered list of audio effects — reverb, delay, filter, chorus, distortion, bitcrush. The order matters: a filter after a reverb sounds different from a filter before a reverb. The chain records the order in the emitted form so the runtime processes signal in the sequence the kid arranged.

## 10.1 The verb signature

```
(composer/fx-chain :bind :available)
```

- `:bind` — path. Where the fx chain writes.
- `:available` — list of symbols. The effects the widget will let the user add.

## 10.2 The emitted target form

An fx-chain writes its target as:

```
(fx-chain
  (fx/reverb :room 0.6 :wet 0.4)
  (fx/delay :time 0.25 :feedback 0.5)
  (fx/filter :type (quote lowpass) :cutoff 2000))
```

An ordered list of `(fx/... :kw val ...)` forms. Signal flows left-to-right: reverb first, then delay on the reverb output, then filter on the delayed output.

## 10.3 The widget declaration

```
(composer/fx-chain :bind (quote (synth :fx))
                   :available (quote (fx/reverb fx/delay fx/filter fx/distort)))
```

The available effects and the bind path. The current chain content lives in the target form the widget writes.

## 10.4 ASCII mockup — an fx chain

```
fx-chain: reverb -> delay -> filter

  fx/reverb :room 0.6 :wet 0.4
  fx/delay :time 0.25 :feedback 0.5
  fx/filter :type lowpass :cutoff 2000
```

Three effects in order. Add another with 'a', remove with 'r', reorder with 'm' up/down (per the v1.0 TUI spec).

## 10.5 The six effects (v2 direction)

The v2 audio design proposes six runtime primitives:

- `fx/reverb` — space simulation. `:room 0.0-1.0`, `:wet 0.0-1.0`, `:decay` in seconds.
- `fx/delay` — echo. `:time` in seconds or musical division, `:feedback 0.0-0.95`, `:wet 0.0-1.0`.
- `fx/filter` — spectral shaping. `:type 'lowpass|'highpass|'bandpass`, `:cutoff` in Hz, `:resonance 0.1-30`.
- `fx/chorus` — thickening. `:rate` in Hz, `:depth 0.0-1.0`, `:wet 0.0-1.0`.
- `fx/distortion` — harmonic destruction. `:drive 0.0-1.0`, `:tone 0.0-1.0`.
- `fx/bitcrush` — chiptune crush. `:bits 1-16`, `:rate` sample-rate divider.

The v1.0 widget accepts any symbol in `:available`; the runtime you plug into needs to know what to do with each.

## 10.6 Order matters — an example

Reverb-then-filter versus filter-then-reverb:

```
(fx-chain (fx/reverb :room 0.6 :wet 0.4)
          (fx/filter :type (quote lowpass) :cutoff 2000))
```

Reverb runs first (creating a lush tail), then the filter cuts high frequencies from the entire wet signal — including the reverb tail. Muted, distant sound.

```
(fx-chain (fx/filter :type (quote lowpass) :cutoff 2000)
          (fx/reverb :room 0.6 :wet 0.4))
```

Filter runs first (cutting highs from the dry signal), then reverb adds its natural high-frequency spread to what remains. Warmer sound with more sparkle in the tail.

Same effects. Different order. Different sound. The chain's ORDER is data.

## 10.7 A verified example

```scheme
(composer/fx-chain :bind '(synth :fx)
                   :available '(fx/reverb fx/delay fx/filter fx/distort))
```

Emit in a canvas:

```
(composer/canvas (:bind (quote (synth)))
  (composer/fx-chain :bind (quote (synth :fx))
                     :available (quote (fx/reverb fx/delay fx/filter fx/distort))))
```

The chain content itself (the ordered list of effect calls) is written to `(synth :fx)` when the user adds or reorders effects in the widget.

## 10.8 An fx-chain per instrument, or one per song

You can attach an fx-chain to an instrument (per-note effects) or to the master output (per-song effects). The composer doesn't care; you bind the widget to the appropriate path.

Per-instrument:

```
(instrument/define (quote lead)
  (synth :wave (quote saw)
         :env (adsr :a 0.02 :d 0.1 :s 0.6 :r 0.4)
         :fx (fx-chain (fx/filter :type (quote lowpass) :cutoff 2000))))
```

Per-song master:

```
(song :master-fx
  (fx-chain (fx/reverb :room 0.7 :wet 0.35)))
```

The widget writes wherever its `:bind` points. Both patterns work.

## 10.9 A canvas with an fx chain and controls

A common composer canvas pairs an fx-chain widget with sliders for the parameters of individual effects. The sliders don't write directly into the chain; they write into named slots the chain references.

Alternative: use one fx-chain widget only, and let the user tweak parameters via the widget's per-effect sub-controls (a v2 direction — v1.0 exposes chain add/remove/reorder but not per-effect editing in the widget itself).

## 10.10 What to remember from this chapter

- fx-chain holds an ordered list of effect calls and emits them as `(fx-chain (fx/... ) ...)`.
- Order matters. Signal flows left-to-right.
- `:available` tells the widget which effects to offer.
- Six effect primitives in the v2 audio design: reverb, delay, filter, chorus, distortion, bitcrush.
- Effects have their own parameter surfaces (per-fx keywords like `:room`, `:cutoff`, `:feedback`).
- fx-chain can attach per-instrument or per-song master; the bind path decides.

"# Chapter 11 — Text field, color picker, live-code

Three widgets in one chapter, because they naturally cluster. Text field writes strings. Color picker writes colors. Live-code shows the emitted Scheme as an editable text panel — the widget whose sole job is to make the round-trip visible.

## 11.1 The text field

```
(composer/text-field :bind . options)
```

- `:bind` — path. Where the string writes.
- `:label` — string, optional.
- `:value` — string, optional. Default `\"\"`.

The widget writes a string to the bind path. That is all.

Emit:

```
(composer/text-field :bind (quote (cart/meta :title))
                     :label \"Cart title\" :value \"my song\")
```

The current `:value` is included so a reload lands the field with the user's typing.

## 11.2 ASCII mockup — a text field

```
Cart title: \"my song\"
```

Label, colon, quoted string. That's the TUI rendering.

## 11.3 The color picker

```
(composer/color-picker :bind . options)
```

- `:bind` — path. Where the color writes.
- `:palette` — symbol, optional. If provided, the picker restricts to the named palette and emits a symbol; if omitted, the picker emits a hex string.

## 11.4 Color picker emit

With a palette:

```
(composer/color-picker :bind (quote (cart/theme :bg))
                       :value (quote crimson))
```

The value is a symbol from the palette. The widget declaration includes the current `:value`.

Without a palette:

```
(composer/color-picker :bind (quote (cart/theme :bg))
                       :value \"#dc143c\")
```

The value is a hex string.

The composer stores whichever shape you set. Palette-mode gives you symbolic names (crimson, forestgreen, coral); freeform mode gives you hex strings.

## 11.5 The HTML-16 palette in the color picker

Combined with the v1.1 named-color infrastructure, a color picker bound to the html-16 palette lets kids pick from 16 named CSS colors:

```scheme
(composer/color-picker :bind '(cart/theme :bg) :palette 'html-16)
```

Emit:

```
(composer/color-picker :bind (quote (cart/theme :bg))
                       :value (quote black))
```

Default is 'black when the palette is html-16. Hand-edit to `:value 'crimson` and reload — the picker shows crimson selected.

Look up the actual color a symbol maps to: `(color/named 'crimson)` returns `\"#dc143c\"`. The picker knows this because the palette carries the mapping.

## 11.6 The live-code widget

```
(composer/live-code :bind . options)
```

- `:bind` — path. Where the source string writes.

The live-code widget shows the emitted Scheme form as an editable text panel. Edits to the text propagate back — the widget re-parses and the other widgets in the canvas re-render to match.

This is the round-trip made visible. See the emit, edit the emit, see the widgets follow.

## 11.7 ASCII mockup — a live-code panel

```
live-code: \"(composer/canvas (:bind (quote (cart)))...\"
```

The TUI shows a truncated preview. The full Curator canvas shows a scrollable syntax-highlighted panel with the full emitted form, editable in place.

## 11.8 Why live-code exists

The composer promises: every widget round-trips through Scheme. The live-code widget SHOWS the Scheme. A kid clicking a piano-roll cell sees the note appear in the live-code panel as a new `(note :pitch ...)` form. A kid typing into the live-code panel sees the piano-roll cell update. The two views are the same data, edited from either side.

For programmers, this is the composer's confession: the tool is not hiding anything from you. Everything you can do with a widget you can do by typing Scheme.

For kids, this is the composer's invitation: the code is right there, don't fear it, poke it, watch what happens.

## 11.9 A worked example — a text-field + color-picker canvas

```scheme
(composer/canvas (list :bind '(cart/meta))
  (composer/text-field :bind '(cart/meta :title) :label \"Cart title\" :value \"my song\")
  (composer/text-field :bind '(cart/meta :author) :label \"Author\" :value \"\")
  (composer/color-picker :bind '(cart/theme :bg) :palette 'html-16)
  (composer/color-picker :bind '(cart/theme :fg) :palette 'html-16))
```

Four children: two text fields for metadata, two color pickers for background and foreground theme colors.

Emit:

```
(composer/canvas (:bind (quote (cart/meta)))
  (composer/text-field :bind (quote (cart/meta :title))
                       :label \"Cart title\" :value \"my song\")
  (composer/text-field :bind (quote (cart/meta :author))
                       :label \"Author\" :value \"\")
  (composer/color-picker :bind (quote (cart/theme :bg))
                         :value (quote black))
  (composer/color-picker :bind (quote (cart/theme :fg))
                         :value (quote black)))
```

Save, hand-edit, reload — the fields update.

## 11.10 The live-code widget composes with the others

The most instructive canvas mixes a live-code widget with other widgets:

```scheme
(composer/canvas (list :bind '(cart/main))
  (composer/slider :label \"BPM\" :bind '(cart/main :bpm) :min 60 :max 240 :step 1)
  (composer/toggle :bind '(cart/opts :muted) :label \"Muted\")
  (composer/live-code :bind '(cart/main)))
```

Three children. The live-code widget shows the emitted form of the canvas. Move the slider, the emit updates, the live-code panel updates. Edit the number in the live-code panel, the slider moves.

Kids who click the slider learn what Scheme looks like. Kids who type into the live-code panel learn what a slider is. Same file. Same round-trip. Two teachers.

## 11.11 What to remember from this chapter

- Text field writes a string to a bind path. `:label` and `:value` are optional.
- Color picker writes a color to a bind path. With `:palette`, emits a symbol; without, emits a hex string.
- The v1.1 html-16 palette gives 16 named CSS colors for the picker.

"# Chapter 12 — 16 voices and the voice-16 mixer

Composer v1.1 introduced a 16-voice polyphony bank with voice 16 dedicated as a mixer. This chapter walks the voice-pool widget, how voice-steal works, and how the mixer composes voices 1-15 into a single output stream.

## 12.1 Why 16

PICO-8 has 4 voices. TIC-80 has 4 voices. Both hit the ceiling when a kid writes a beat with kick, snare, bass, and a two-note chord — the fifth voice cuts one of the earlier voices. The kid's music sounds broken and the tool has no message that explains it.

Modern devices, even Chromebooks, run 16 concurrent oscillators comfortably. Composer v1.1 raises the ceiling to 16 and dedicates voice 16 as a mixer for when you want to route several voices into a shared processing chain.

## 12.2 The voice-pool widget

```
(composer/voice-pool :bind :steal . options)
```

- `:bind` — path. Where the pool state writes.
- `:steal` — symbol, optional. Voice-steal policy. Default `'oldest`.

Verified:

```scheme
(composer/voice-pool :bind '(cart :pool) :steal 'oldest)
```

Returns a voice-pool record with 16 voice slots. Slots 1-15 are individual voice slots; slot 16 is the mixer.

## 12.3 The song/config verb

```
(song/config :voices N :voice-steal POLICY :bpm BPM)
```

Creates a song-config record that tells the runtime how many voices to allocate and what policy to use.

Verified:

```scheme
(song/config :voices 16 :bpm 120)
```

Returns a song-config record with 16 voices at 120 bpm. Voices greater than 16 are clamped to 16 with a warning in the record's `:warnings` field. Voices less than 1 are clamped to 1.

## 12.4 Voice-steal policy

When all voices are busy and a new note wants to play, one existing voice has to yield. The steal policy decides which. v1.1 documents:

- `'oldest` — the voice that has been playing longest. Default.
- `'quietest` — the voice with the lowest current velocity. (Runtime-dependent; the spec proposes it.)
- `'newest` — the most recently triggered voice yields. Unusual; kept as an option.

The steal policy is stored in the pool's options and appears in the emit.

## 12.5 The voice/mix verb

```
(voice/mix voice-ids gain)
```

Creates a mix record that references a list of voice IDs and an optional gain. Verified:

```scheme
(voice/mix '(1 2 3))
```

Returns a `voice-mix` record with voices [1, 2, 3] and gain 1.0. Pass a gain:

```scheme
(voice/mix '(1 2 3) 0.75)
```

Gain is applied to the combined signal.

## 12.6 voice/compose is an alias

`(voice/compose voice-ids gain)` is the same as `(voice/mix voice-ids gain)`. The alias exists per Alfred's phrasing — 'compose them together'. Both verbs produce the same record.

## 12.7 The mixer voice (voice 16)

Voice 16 is not a normal voice. Instead of holding an instrument spec, it holds a `mixes` list — the IDs of the voices it combines. Set the mix with:

```
(composer/voice-mix-set pool '(1 2 3))
```

The pool's voice 16 now takes voices 1, 2, and 3 as inputs.

The mixer is a routing statement. Individual voices still emit their own signals independently; the mixer taps their outputs and combines them.

## 12.8 ASCII mockup — the voice pool

```
voice-pool: 16 voices, steal=oldest
   1 lead
   2 bass
   3 hihat
   4 kick
   5 snare
   6 (free)
   7 (free)
   8 (free)
   9 (free)
  10 (free)
  11 (free)
  12 (free)
  13 (free)
  14 (free)
  15 (free)
  16 [MIX] <- #1,#2
```

Fifteen instrument slots + one mixer routing voices 1 and 2.

## 12.9 Assigning voices

`composer/voice-assign` sets an instrument on a specific voice slot:

```
(composer/voice-assign pool 1 '(:instrument lead))
```

Voice 1 now plays with the `lead` instrument. Voices 2-15 can be assigned independently. Voice 16 refuses instrument assignments (it is the mixer).

## 12.10 The emit shape

The voice-pool emits as:

```
(composer/voice-pool :bind (quote (cart :pool))
                     :steal (quote oldest)
                     :mix (quote (1 2)))
```

Bind path, steal policy, and the current mix list on voice 16. The individual instrument assignments on voices 1-15 live in the target form the widget writes to (analogous to how the piano-roll's note list lives separately from the widget declaration).

## 12.11 A worked example — a 5-voice drum + lead cart

```scheme
(define pool
  (composer/voice-pool :bind '(song :pool) :steal 'oldest))

(composer/voice-assign pool 1 '(:instrument kick))
(composer/voice-assign pool 2 '(:instrument snare))
(composer/voice-assign pool 3 '(:instrument hihat))
(composer/voice-assign pool 4 '(:instrument bass))
(composer/voice-assign pool 5 '(:instrument lead))
(composer/voice-mix-set pool '(1 2 3))  ;; drums go to the mixer
```

Five instruments in five voices; voices 1-3 (kick, snare, hihat) are routed to the mixer for shared processing. Voice 4 (bass) and voice 5 (lead) play out directly.

The mixer voice can then have its own fx-chain applied — reverb over the drums, or a shared compressor. The individual voices bypass the mixer.

## 12.12 Why route drums through a mixer

Musicians often want a single reverb applied to the whole drum bus but not to the lead or bass. Routing drums through the mixer gives you that: one reverb on the mixer's output, and the other voices don't touch it.

The composition of voices is data; the routing is data. All in the same file.

## 12.13 What to remember from this chapter

- Composer v1.1 raises polyphony from prior fantasy-console 4 voices to 16.
- The voice-pool widget models 16 voice slots. Slots 1-15 hold individual instruments; slot 16 is a mixer.
- `song/config :voices N` sets voice count (clamped to 1-16). Voices greater than 16 clamp with a warning.
- `voice/mix` and `voice/compose` (the alias) build mix records referencing voice IDs.
- The mixer routes several voices into one output stream for shared processing.
- Voice-steal policy (`'oldest` default) decides which voice yields when the pool is full.
- The pool's emit captures bind path, steal policy, and mixer routing.

"# Chapter 13 — Save and load

Save writes a canvas to a file. Load reconstructs a canvas from a file. Both operations are the composer's disk boundary — they extend the round-trip beyond memory into the file system.

## 13.1 The two verbs

```
(composer/save canvas path)      ;; -> path
(composer/load path)             ;; -> canvas
```

Both are documented in `engineering/COMPOSER-1.0.ENG.slat`. Both are shipping. Both were run through `bin/motoi eval` to confirm they work.

## 13.2 Save

`composer/save` takes a canvas and a file path. It calls `composer/emit` internally to produce the form, writes the form as Scheme text to the file, and returns the path.

Verified:

```scheme
(composer/save (composer/canvas (list :bind '(cart/main))
                 (composer/slider :label \"BPM\" :bind '(cart/main :bpm) :min 60 :max 240 :step 1))
               \"/tmp/test-canvas.slat\")
;; => \"/tmp/test-canvas.slat\"
```

Contents of `/tmp/test-canvas.slat`:

```
(composer/canvas (:bind (quote (cart/main))) (composer/slider :label \"BPM\" :bind (quote (cart/main :bpm)) :min 60 :max 240 :step 1 :value 60))
```

One line. Every widget declaration compacted. The file is valid Scheme.

## 13.3 Load

`composer/load` reads the file, parses it, and returns a canvas record. If the file contains a `(composer/canvas ...)` form, the load reconstructs the canvas with all children. If no canvas form is present, load returns an empty canvas with the file's forms in its `body` field.

Verified:

```scheme
(composer/load \"/tmp/test-canvas.slat\")
;; => canvas record with one slider child
```

## 13.4 What lives on disk

A saved composer file is a normal `.slat` file with two conceptual parts:

1. The TARGET FORMS the widgets compose (a `(sequence ...)` for music, a `(sprite/from-grid ...)` for a sprite, etc.). Written as top-level `(define ...)` forms or standalone data.
2. A trailing `(composer/canvas ...)` declaration that documents the widgets that produced the forms.

Both are Scheme. Both are readable. Either can be edited by hand.

The composer file the shipping `composer/save` writes contains ONLY the canvas declaration, not the target forms. This is by design for v1.0: the canvas declaration is what the composer reconstructs; the target forms live wherever your cart writes them (top-level `(define ...)` in the cart file, or a separate data file).

## 13.5 A round-trip check

The full save-load-emit cycle:

```scheme
(define c
  (composer/canvas (list :bind '(cart/main))
    (composer/slider :label \"BPM\" :bind '(cart/main :bpm) :min 60 :max 240 :step 1)))

(composer/save c \"/tmp/rt.slat\")
;; => \"/tmp/rt.slat\"

(define c2 (composer/load \"/tmp/rt.slat\"))
;; => canvas record

(composer/emit c2)
;; => same form as (composer/emit c)
```

The reloaded canvas emits the same form the original emitted. Round-trip closed over disk.

## 13.6 Multi-file carts (v2 direction)

The v2 code-distribution proposal introduces multi-file cart directories:

```
snake-classic/
  cart.slat       ; header + imports
  logic.slat      ; game logic
  sprites.slat    ; asset records
  song.slat       ; music
  composer.slat   ; composer canvas declarations
```

A cart with `:multi-file #t` in its header signals that the runtime should load all files in the directory as one cart. The composer file becomes just the canvas declarations; the target forms live in their own topic files.

v1.0 ships single-file carts. Multi-file is a v2 direction; nothing about the round-trip changes when it lands.

## 13.7 Cart header (v2 direction)

The v2 spec proposes a `(cart ...)` header at the top of every cart:

```
(cart
  :name          \"snake-classic\"
  :author        \"alfred\"
  :version       \"1.2.0\"
  :parent        (:from motoi.cart/nesbox/snake@0.9.0 :diverged-at 2026-07-14)
  :verbs-used    (display for-each range sprite/blit input/read)
  :audience      :kid
  :one-line      \"Snake, but the food fights back.\")
```

The header carries metadata: author, version, parent (for forks), verbs used, audience, one-line description. This is where publishing (Chapter 15) reads from.

v1.0's `composer/save` does not write a header automatically; you can prepend one by hand if you plan to publish. v2 will add the header on save.

## 13.8 Hand-editing a saved file

The single most important use of the save/load pair is hand-editing.

Save a canvas. Open the file. Change any number, any string, any symbol. Save. Reload. The canvas reflects your edit.

Change a slider's `:max` from 240 to 1000 by editing the number in the file. Reload. The slider now accepts up to 1000.

Change a toggle's `:value #f` to `:value #t`. Reload. The toggle boots on.

Change a color picker's `:value 'black` to `:value 'crimson`. Reload. The picker shows crimson.

Every hand-edit is legal because the file is Scheme and the composer's load re-parses it fresh.

## 13.9 What load does not do

`composer/load` does NOT execute the target forms. It parses the file and looks for a `(composer/canvas ...)` form. Everything else in the file — top-level `(define ...)`, other cart forms — is stored in the canvas's `body` field but not evaluated.

If you want the whole cart to run, use `bin/motoi run path/to/cart.slat`. That evaluates every top-level form. `composer/load` is specifically for reconstructing a widget graph, not running a cart.

## 13.10 What to remember from this chapter

- `composer/save canvas path` writes the emitted form to disk. Returns the path.
- `composer/load path` reads the file, parses it, reconstructs the canvas.
- The disk file is Scheme text. Grep-friendly. Diff-friendly. Editable by hand.
- Round-trip closes over disk: save then load then emit produces the same form the original canvas emitted.
- Multi-file carts and cart headers are v2 directions; v1.0 ships single-file carts without automatic headers.
- Hand-editing the file is legitimate and expected. The composer parses fresh on load.

"# Chapter 14 — TUI mode

Composer v1.1 shipped a terminal renderer. The composer runs inside a shell. No graphical surface required. Kids on Chromebooks in school labs, kids on Raspberry Pis in basements, developers on remote servers over SSH — they all get the same composer, rendered as ASCII.

## 14.1 The verb

```
(composer/render-tui canvas)      ;; -> string
```

Takes a canvas record, returns a string rendering. That's it. The string is the composer view; the caller prints it, updates it on change, and redraws when widgets mutate.

Verified:

```scheme
(composer/render-tui
  (composer/canvas (list :bind '(cart))
    (composer/slider :label \"BPM\" :bind '(cart :bpm) :min 60 :max 240 :step 1)))
;; => \"[pink ] ========================================
;;      [green] ========================================
;;      [brown] ========================================
;;
;;      MOTOI COMPOSER — canvas cart
;;      ----------------------------------------
;;      [--------------------] BPM 60\"
```

## 14.2 The header

The TUI renderer prefixes every canvas with a brand header — three lines of stripes labeled pink, green, brown, followed by a title line. The stripes and the tree logo (see `composer/tree-logo`) are Motoi's branding.

The `TREE_LOGO` string:

```
     /\\
    /  \\
   /----\\
  /      \\
 /--------\\
     ||
     ||
```

`(composer/tree-logo)` returns this string. Useful for printing a landing message.

## 14.3 Slider rendering

Sliders render as:

```
[==|--------] label value
```

`[` and `]` are the bar ends. `=` characters fill the filled portion. `|` is the scrubber. `-` characters fill the empty portion. Label and value at the right.

## 14.4 Piano-roll rendering

Piano-rolls render as a 12-row grid — one row per pitch class (C through B) — with `#` for filled cells and `.` for empty:

```
piano-roll: song/notes (2 notes, 16 steps)
   B ................
  A# ................
   A ................
  G# ................
   G ................
  F# ................
   F ................
   E #...............
  D# ................
   D ................
  C# ................
   C #...............
```

The renderer collapses octaves — pitch C4 and C5 both show on the `C` row. This is the TUI's honest constraint; kids who want fuller resolution use Curator's graphical canvas.

## 14.5 Sprite-grid rendering

Sprite grids render as ASCII characters mapping palette indices to digits and letters:

```
sprite: cart/sprites/hero (8x8, palette pico-8)
  ...88...
  ..8888..
  .888888.
  88888888
  88888888
  .888888.
  ..8888..
  ...88...
```

`.` for 0 (transparent), `1`-`9` for indices 1-9, `a`-`f` for indices 10-15. Sixteen palette entries in one character each.

## 14.6 Button, toggle, text-field renderings

Compact:

```
[ Play ]                              (button)
[X] Muted                             (toggle on)
[ ] Loop                              (toggle off)
Cart title: \"my song\"                 (text-field)
color(theme/bg): black                (color-picker)
```

Each fits one line. A canvas of controls stacks them vertically.

## 14.7 ADSR rendering

```
ADSR: a=0.05 d=0.1 s=0.7 r=0.3
```

Four numbers on one line. Compact — the graphical envelope curve is elsewhere.

## 14.8 Instrument-picker rendering

```
instrument: [sine|square|triangle|saw|noise] chosen=sine
```

Choices in brackets separated by pipes; chosen value labeled.

## 14.9 Tile-map rendering

```
tile-map: (12x4)
  111111111111
  111111111111
  ............
  ............
```

Same character mapping as sprite: `.` for empty, digits/letters for tile IDs.

## 14.10 Timeline rendering

```
timeline: entities=hero,enemy duration=60s fps=30 frames=6
```

One-line summary — entities, duration, fps, total frame count.

## 14.11 fx-chain rendering

```
fx-chain: reverb -> delay -> filter
```

Effect names in order, arrows between.

## 14.12 Voice-pool rendering

```
voice-pool: 16 voices, steal=oldest
   1 lead
   2 bass
   3 hihat
   4 (free)
  ...
  16 [MIX] <- #1,#2
```

Fifteen instrument rows + one mixer row.

## 14.13 Palette strip

If any child widget uses the html-16 palette, the TUI appends a palette strip at the bottom:

```
palette (html-16):
  01:black  02:white  03:crimson  04:forestgreen  05:peachpuff ...
```

Sixteen entries, name and index. Kids can reference by name in hand-edits.

## 14.14 Rendering options

`composer/render-tui` accepts a second argument, an options plist:

```scheme
(composer/render-tui canvas '(:brand #f))
```

`:brand #f` suppresses the header stripes and title. Useful when the composer is embedded in another surface's chrome.

`:palette 'html-16` forces the palette strip even if no child widget uses html-16.

## 14.15 Rendering is pure

`composer/render-tui` is a pure function. It reads the canvas, returns a string, produces no side effects. Print the string with `display`, update it on a redraw loop, drop it into a log — the renderer does not care.

This is the model the terminal driver needs: give me a snapshot; I decide when to paint it. Interactive drivers (like a curses-based composer front-end) call `composer/render-tui` on every user input, then diff the string against the previous frame and paint the diff.

## 14.16 A full worked example

Run this cart with `bin/motoi run` — the output is the TUI rendering of a small composer canvas:

```scheme
(define c
  (composer/canvas (list :bind '(cart))
    (composer/slider :label \"BPM\" :bind '(cart :bpm) :min 60 :max 240 :step 1 :value 120)
    (composer/toggle :bind '(cart :muted) :label \"Muted\")
    (composer/instrument-picker :bind '(cart :wave)
                                :choices '(sine square triangle saw noise))))

(display (composer/render-tui c))
(newline)
```

Verified output:

```
[pink ] ========================================
[green] ========================================
[brown] ========================================

MOTOI COMPOSER — canvas cart
----------------------------------------
[==========|---------] BPM 120

[ ] Muted

instrument: [sine|square|triangle|saw|noise] chosen=sine
```

## 14.17 What to remember from this chapter

- `composer/render-tui canvas` renders a canvas as an ASCII string.
- Every widget kind has a TUI renderer: slider as bar, piano-roll as grid, sprite as character grid, etc.
- The header carries brand stripes + title. Suppress with `:brand #f`.
- The html-16 palette strip appends when the canvas uses html-16 colors.
- Rendering is pure. Print the string; decide when to redraw.
- `(composer/tree-logo)` returns the ASCII tree for a landing message.

"# Chapter 15 — HTTP server

Composer v1.1 shipped an HTTP host. Kids run a small server on their local machine and share a link so a friend on the same wifi can play their cart in a browser. The server hosts carts from a local directory and gates the composer view behind a local-only permission by default.

## 15.1 The four verbs

```
(http/serve :port N :cart-dir DIR :compose-perm 'local-only)  ;; -> server-record
(http/wait-until-ready server [timeout-ms])                    ;; -> server-record with bound port
(http/stop server)                                             ;; -> #t
(http/serve-info server)                                       ;; -> alist of server info
```

All four verify against the runtime.

## 15.2 Starting the server

```scheme
(define s (http/serve :port 8080 :cart-dir \"carts\" :compose-perm 'local-only))
```

Starts an HTTP server on port 8080 serving carts from the `carts/` directory. `:compose-perm 'local-only` gates the `/compose/` route to local requests.

If `:port 0` is passed, the server picks an unused port; use `http/wait-until-ready` to learn the actual port.

## 15.3 Waiting for the server to bind

```scheme
(http/wait-until-ready s 2000)
```

Waits up to 2000 milliseconds for the server to bind. Returns the server record with the actual `:port` field populated.

## 15.4 Stopping the server

```scheme
(http/stop s)
;; => #t
```

Closes the server and removes it from the registry.

## 15.5 Server info

```scheme
(http/serve-info s)
;; => ((:id 1) (:port 8080) (:cart-dir \"/absolute/path/carts\") (:compose-perm local-only))
```

Returns an alist describing the server.

## 15.6 The three routes

The server exposes three route families:

1. `/` — landing page listing carts.
2. `/play/:cart` — browser shell for playing a cart. Public.
3. `/compose/:cart` — browser shell for composing a cart. Permission-gated.

## 15.7 The landing page

Visit `http://localhost:8080/` and you see:

- The ASCII tree logo.
- Three brand stripes (pink, green, brown).
- A list of all carts in the cart directory, each with a play link and a compose link.

The landing page is HTML with inline CSS. Nothing served from a CDN. Everything the browser needs comes from the server itself.

## 15.8 The play route

`/play/:cart` serves a page that shows the cart's source (for v1.1) and a link to compose. The browser runtime that actually executes the cart lives in a later wave — v1.1 gets you as far as viewing and sharing the source. The security review in the source documents this: the play route is READ-ONLY delivery of the composer bundle.

## 15.9 The compose route

`/compose/:cart` opens a compose view. By default `:compose-perm 'local-only` means only requests from 127.0.0.1 or ::1 can hit this route. A remote request receives a 403.

The permission check reads the raw socket's remote address. X-Forwarded-For and other client-supplied headers are IGNORED. A remote client cannot lie its way past the local-only gate by setting a header.

## 15.10 Path-traversal defense

The server refuses:

- URLs containing null bytes.
- URLs containing `..` (literal, not URL-encoded).
- Cart names not matching `/^[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$/` per segment.
- Cart names with more than 4 path segments.
- Cart names longer than 256 characters.

Every cart name is decoded, split on `/`, checked segment-by-segment, and only served if the resolved path is still under the cart directory. A cart named `../../etc/passwd` will not resolve; the server returns 404.

The full path-safety code is in `lib/net/http-serve.js` — `safeCartPath`, `safeCartPathWithSubdir`, and `safeResolveCartDir`. These are the functions Appendix H covers in depth.

## 15.11 GET only

Only GET requests are honored. POST, PUT, DELETE return 405. This is deliberate: v1.1 does not accept cart writes over HTTP. Edits round-trip through the composer's own save/load, not the HTTP layer. A later wave may add a WebSocket edit channel — until then, the HTTP surface is read-only.

## 15.12 Compose-vs-play separation

The `compose-perm` option is the whole model:

- `'local-only` (default) — the compose view only opens for requests from the machine running the server. A remote friend can play carts but cannot compose them.
- `'anyone` — opens compose to all requests. Only use this on trusted networks.

The play view has NO permission gate — anyone reachable by the port can play. This matches the sharing model: kids WANT friends to play their carts, don't want strangers to edit them.

## 15.13 A worked example

Start a server:

```scheme
(define s (http/serve :port 8080 :cart-dir \"carts\" :compose-perm 'local-only))
(http/wait-until-ready s 2000)
```

Visit `http://localhost:8080/` in a browser. See the landing page. Click a cart link. See the play view.

Try to visit `/compose/synth-patch` from another machine on the network. Get a 403 (`compose is local-only`).

Stop:

```scheme
(http/stop s)
```

## 15.14 The cart directory

`:cart-dir \"carts\"` is a relative path. The server resolves it against the process's current working directory and refuses to escape the cwd.

If the resolved cart-dir does not exist, `http/serve` throws. If it exists but is not a directory, `http/serve` throws.

The server walks the cart-dir at request time (not startup) and lists `.slat` and `.sks` files. This means adding a new cart to the directory shows up on the next request without a server restart.

## 15.15 Cart naming rules

Cart names in URLs are limited to `[A-Za-z0-9._-]`. This excludes spaces, slashes (except as path separators within a subdirectory cart name), and any character that could carry a URL-encoding trick.

Kids naming carts should stick to lowercase letters, digits, hyphens, and underscores. `hero-sample`, `snake_v2`, `demo.1` all work. `hero sample` (with a space) does not — rename to `hero-sample`.

## 15.16 The security model in one paragraph

The HTTP server is a local sharing tool. Play is public within reach of the port. Compose is local-only by default. Path traversal is defended in depth. Only GET is accepted. Forwarded-for headers are ignored. Cart names are strict-regexed. The security review in the source (`lib/net/http-serve.js`) calls out each defense and its reasoning. Appendix H walks the whole model.

## 15.17 What to remember from this chapter

- `http/serve` starts a small HTTP server on a port, from a cart directory.
- `http/wait-until-ready` returns once the server has bound.
- `http/stop` closes the server.
- `http/serve-info` returns metadata about a running server.
- Three routes: `/` (landing), `/play/:cart` (public), `/compose/:cart` (permission-gated).
- `:compose-perm 'local-only` (default) restricts compose to 127.0.0.1 / ::1.
- Path traversal is defended: only alphanumeric-dot-underscore-hyphen cart names, no `..`, no null bytes, no header spoofing.
- Only GET is accepted. Writes come later.

Chapter 16 walks a full worked example — sprite plus sound plus tile-map plus HTTP publish plus friend plays.
")

"# Chapter 16 — Composing games

Fifteen chapters of widgets. Now a full game — small, complete, worked end to end. Sprite. Sound. Tile-map. Publish. Friend plays. Every step uses verbs from the previous chapters. The composer file is a single `.slat`.

## 16.1 The game

A tiny platformer. A hero sprite. Four tiles for the ground. One song. One HTTP publish so a friend on the same wifi can open a link and play.

## 16.2 The composer canvas

The whole cart is one canvas of nested canvases. Each nested canvas groups related widgets.

```scheme
(composer/canvas (list :bind '(cart/game))

  ;; ── metadata ────────────────────────────────
  (composer/canvas (list :bind '(cart/game :meta))
    (composer/text-field :bind '(cart/game :meta :title)
                         :label \"title\" :value \"tiny-platformer\")
    (composer/text-field :bind '(cart/game :meta :author)
                         :label \"author\" :value \"\"))

  ;; ── sprites ─────────────────────────────────
  (composer/canvas (list :bind '(cart/game :sprites))
    (composer/sprite-grid :bind '(cart/game :sprites :hero)
                          :size '(16 . 16) :palette 'html-16)
    (composer/sprite-grid :bind '(cart/game :sprites :grass)
                          :size '(8 . 8) :palette 'html-16)
    (composer/color-picker :bind '(cart/game :sprites :ink) :palette 'html-16))

  ;; ── tile map ────────────────────────────────
  (composer/canvas (list :bind '(cart/game :level))
    (composer/tile-map :bind '(cart/game :level :map)
                       :size '(24 . 8)
                       :tileset '(cart/game :sprites)))

  ;; ── animation ───────────────────────────────
  (composer/canvas (list :bind '(cart/game :anim))
    (composer/timeline :bind '(cart/game :anim :hero-walk)
                       :entities '(hero)
                       :duration 4 :fps 8))

  ;; ── sound ───────────────────────────────────
  (composer/canvas (list :bind '(cart/game :sound))
    (composer/instrument-picker :bind '(cart/game :sound :wave)
                                :choices '(sine square triangle saw noise))
    (composer/adsr :bind '(cart/game :sound :env))
    (composer/fx-chain :bind '(cart/game :sound :fx)
                       :available '(fx/reverb fx/delay fx/filter)))

  ;; ── music ───────────────────────────────────
  (composer/canvas (list :bind '(cart/game :music))
    (composer/slider :label \"BPM\" :bind '(cart/game :music :bpm)
                     :min 60 :max 240 :step 1 :value 120)
    (composer/piano-roll :bind '(cart/game :music :notes)
                         :range '(C3 . C6) :steps 32 :emit-shape 'sequence))

  ;; ── voices ──────────────────────────────────
  (composer/voice-pool :bind '(cart/game :pool) :steal 'oldest)

  ;; ── controls ────────────────────────────────
  (composer/button :label \"Play\"    :emits '(game/start))
  (composer/button :label \"Stop\"    :emits '(game/stop))
  (composer/button :label \"Publish\" :emits '(cart/publish))

  ;; ── live-code round-trip window ─────────────
  (composer/live-code :bind '(cart/game)))
```

Every widget from Chapters 3 through 12 is used here. The canvas is deeply nested — six inner canvases plus a voice-pool, four buttons, and a live-code widget. The whole thing is one Scheme value.

## 16.3 What the emit looks like

`composer/emit` on this canvas produces one giant `(composer/canvas ...)` form with all the inner canvases and widgets nested inside it, each with current state baked in. The form is a few hundred lines of Scheme. Save it to disk; you have a complete authoring surface as one file.

I verified the top-level structure with `bin/motoi eval` — the composer accepts the nested canvases, walks them, produces the expected canvas record with all children. The full emit is large but shape-wise it is exactly the pattern from previous chapters: canvas contains children, children contain more canvases, all bound paths write to specific slots in the target `cart/game` form.

## 16.4 The target form

The widgets write to a target `cart/game` form. In your cart file this looks like:

```
(define cart/game
  (:meta    (:title \"tiny-platformer\" :author \"\")
   :sprites (:hero (sprite/from-grid '((0 0 ...) ...))
             :grass (sprite/from-grid '((3 3 ...) ...))
             :ink 'crimson)
   :level   (:map (tile-map :size (24 . 8)
                            :cells ((0 6 1) (1 6 1) ...)))
   :anim    (:hero-walk (animation :entity 'hero
                                    :frames ((0 . hero-1) ...)))
   :sound   (:wave 'square
             :env (adsr :a 0.02 :d 0.1 :s 0.7 :r 0.2)
             :fx (fx-chain (fx/reverb :room 0.3 :wet 0.2)))
   :music   (:bpm 120
             :notes (sequence (note :pitch 'C4 :vel 0.8 :at 0 :dur 2) ...))
   :pool    (voice-pool :steal 'oldest :mix (1 2 3))))
```

Every slot filled with data the widgets composed. Every slot readable, editable, hand-writable.

## 16.5 Playing the game

Once the target form is populated, the runtime consumes it:

```scheme
(define (game/start)
  (song/play (cart/game :music :notes) :bpm (cart/game :music :bpm))
  (spawn-hero)
  (render-level (cart/game :level :map))
  (loop-frame))
```

The `game/start` function reads from the target and starts the play loop. The composer widgets have no runtime responsibility beyond writing the data; the runtime picks it up.

## 16.6 Publishing

```scheme
(define (cart/publish)
  (define s (http/serve :port 8080 :cart-dir \"carts\" :compose-perm 'local-only))
  (http/wait-until-ready s 2000)
  (display \"cart available at http://localhost:8080/play/tiny-platformer\")
  (newline)
  s)
```

Click the Publish button. The `cart/publish` function starts an HTTP server. Print the URL. Copy it. Text it to a friend. Friend opens the link. Friend plays the cart.

The compose route stays local-only. Friend cannot edit — they can only play. That is the sharing model: play is public, compose is private.

## 16.7 The live-code round-trip in action

The live-code widget at the bottom of the canvas shows the full emitted form as an editable panel. Every widget-driven edit updates the live-code. Every live-code edit updates the widgets.

Kid clicks a piano-roll cell to add a note. Live-code panel shows a new `(note :pitch 'C4 :vel 0.8 :at 0 :dur 1)` in the sequence. Kid changes `0.8` to `0.5` in the live-code panel. Piano-roll cell dims to reflect lower velocity.

Kid drags a slider to change BPM from 120 to 140. Live-code panel updates `:bpm 140`. Kid types `:bpm 100` back into the live-code panel. Slider knob moves to 100.

Round-trip visible. Round-trip editable from either side.

## 16.8 Saving the cart

```scheme
(composer/save game-canvas \"carts/tiny-platformer.slat\")
```

Writes the full canvas declaration to disk. Kids doing this from Curator see a save toast. From the REPL, the return value is the file path.

Reload:

```scheme
(define game-canvas-2 (composer/load \"carts/tiny-platformer.slat\"))
```

Reconstructs the canvas with all six inner canvases, all widgets, all bindings. Emit `game-canvas-2` and it matches the emit of `game-canvas`.

## 16.9 The kid on the plane test

A kid on a plane with no wifi opens Motoi. Opens `carts/tiny-platformer.slat`. Composer loads the file. Every widget renders on whatever surface is available — TUI on a laptop terminal, Curator canvas if graphical. Kid edits sprites. Kid tweaks the melody. Kid saves.

Plane lands. Kid opens wifi. Kid clicks Publish. Cart is now on `http://localhost:8080/play/tiny-platformer`. Kid uses a QR code app to make a QR code of the URL. Kid shows the code to a friend at school. Friend scans, opens the URL, plays.

Every step used composer verbs from Chapters 3 through 15. No cloud service. No account. No paid tier. The composer is just a pile of verbs; the kid arranged them into a game.

## 16.10 What the file looks like on disk

The saved cart is a Scheme file with two conceptual sections:

1. Top-level `(define ...)` forms for each target (`cart/game`, `hero-sprite`, `theme-song`, etc.).
2. A trailing `(composer/canvas ...)` declaration documenting the widgets.

Both parts are Scheme. Both parts survive hand-editing. Both parts round-trip.

Version-control it. Diff between two saves shows exactly which cells of a sprite changed, which notes moved in the piano-roll, which slider values shifted. `git blame` on a `.slat` file works.

## 16.11 Sharing without the server

If the kid does not want to run their own server, they can share the raw `.slat` file. A friend with Motoi installed opens it with `bin/motoi run tiny-platformer.slat`. Same cart. Same game.

The HTTP server is a convenience for browser-based play; the file is the artifact.

## 16.12 The whole book in one paragraph

Widgets are Scheme records. Canvases group widgets. Bindings connect widgets to target-form slots. Emit produces a form. Apply updates widgets from a form. Save writes to disk. Load reconstructs from disk. Sixteen chapters of variations on this theme. One game, worked end to end, using all of it.

## 16.13 What to remember from this chapter

- A full game cart uses widgets from every chapter, nested in canvases by concern (meta, sprites, level, sound, music, controls).
- The emit is a single `(composer/canvas ...)` form containing the whole widget graph.
- The target forms (sprite data, note sequences, tile cells) live in top-level defines the runtime consumes.
- Publish with `http/serve`; friend plays over HTTP.
- Save and load work over the whole nested canvas.
- Round-trip closes over disk, over surfaces, over composition depth.
- The composer is just a pile of verbs, deterministically arranged into a game by a kid.

The next section — Appendices A through H — provides reference material: every verb documented, every widget's ASCII mockup, every emit-shape, round-trip proofs, palette catalog, voice mixing recipes, TUI cheat-sheet, and the HTTP security guide.

## 16.14 Composing constraints — the multi-rule pattern

The tiny-platformer above is a game with many parts. Under it lives a smaller compositional skill: how to hold TWO game rules at once and pick the right verbs for each. This is the skill that separates 'my sprite moves' from 'my sprite moves until it hits the wall and then stops.'

### The pattern in four steps

When a prompt gives you two constraints — 'move right AND stop at the edge,' 'spawn a coin AND despawn it when collected,' 'animate a bounce AND halt when velocity is small' — walk through this shape:

1. **Name each constraint.** Write the two rules out in plain English before you type any code. 'Move right' is one rule. 'Stop when x is past 300' is another. If you can't articulate both rules in one sentence each, the prompt hasn't been read carefully enough.

2. **Pick the verb for each constraint.** One verb per constraint when possible. For 'move right,' the verb is `entity/set-vel! p 2 0`. For 'stop at edge,' the check is `(>= (entity/x p) right-edge)` followed by `(entity/set-vel! p 0 0)`. Prefer the smallest verb that names the rule.

3. **Compose in `on-frame`.** The frame loop is where both rules are checked every tick. Constraint 1 sets velocity if it should be moving. Constraint 2 zeroes velocity if the stop-condition holds. Both are re-evaluated 60 times a second.

4. **Verify each constraint independently.** Comment out the stop check; confirm the sprite moves. Uncomment the stop check, set initial velocity to zero; confirm the sprite doesn't move. If each rule works alone, the composition works.

### A worked example — move+stop

Prompt: 'Make a sprite move right and stop at the edge.'

Two constraints named:
- Constraint 1: move right (velocity +2 on x-axis).
- Constraint 2: stop when x >= 300.

Verbs picked:
- `entity/set-vel!` for both (setting non-zero for constraint 1, zero for constraint 2).
- `entity/x` and `>=` for the stop check.

Composed:

```scheme
(define (move-then-stop)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 20 120)))
    (entity/shape! p 'rect 12 12)
    (entity/set-vel! p 2 0)                    ; constraint 1: set initial velocity
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (world/step)
       (when (>= (entity/x p) 300)             ; constraint 2: check stop condition
         (entity/set-vel! p 0 0))
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 12 12)))))
(big-bang move-then-stop)
```

Every frame: step the world (which moves the sprite by its velocity). Then check if we've reached the edge. If yes, zero the velocity. Nothing else. Two rules; two lines that enforce them; the rest is boilerplate.

## 16.15 Drift detection — when your code stops matching the prompt

**Drift** is what happens when your code starts using verbs you didn't intend. You wrote 'move right and stop at the edge.' Your code uses `ai/wander` because you saw it in the reference and it seemed related. Your sprite wanders. It never stops at the edge because you never wrote a stop-check. The code compiled. The code ran. The code does not match the prompt.

Drift is the single most common failure mode when composing multi-constraint games with an LLM. The model has strong single-verb recall — it knows `entity/set-vel!`, it knows `ai/wander`, it knows `motion/move-to`. When two constraints have to be held together, the model sometimes picks a verb that's close-but-wrong for one of them, and the second constraint quietly gets dropped.

### The detection signal

You've drifted when any of these are true:

- Your code uses a verb that wasn't named or implied by the prompt.
- One of the constraints in the prompt has no corresponding verb call in your code.
- The behavior when you run it doesn't match what the prompt described.
- You've written more than 30 lines and the prompt asked for something simple.

### The recovery move

When you detect drift:

1. **Stop.** Don't try to patch. Don't add more verbs to compensate.
2. **Re-read the prompt.** Word for word. Underline each constraint.
3. **Restart.** Not from scratch, but from a clean minimum: `(world/reset!)`, one entity, one verb per constraint, on-frame that composes them. Build up from that.

Restarting is not a defeat. It is the correct move when your code has drifted from the prompt's intent. Every experienced programmer restarts constantly. The five-minute restart beats the fifty-minute patch.

### An example of drift and recovery

Bad response to 'make a sprite move right and stop at the edge':

```scheme
(define (drifted-version)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((p (world/spawn 'player 20 120)))
    (entity/shape! p 'rect 12 12)
    (on-frame
     (lambda ()
       (ai/wander p)                    ; DRIFT — wander is not 'move right'
       (world/step)
       (paint-clear)
       (paint-cell 'player (entity/x p) (entity/y p) 12 12)))))
```

Symptoms: The sprite meanders. Never stops at any edge. The prompt said 'move right' — clearly directional — but the code uses `ai/wander`, which is random motion. Constraint 1 has drifted (wrong verb). Constraint 2 has vanished (no stop-check at all).

Recovery: apply the four-step pattern above. Two constraints. `entity/set-vel!` for move right. `entity/x` compared to edge for stop. Compose in on-frame. Verify each. Result: the correct code from §16.14.

Total time to recover: about two minutes if you catch the drift when the sprite starts wandering. Two hours if you try to add more verbs to fix the wandering and end up with `ai/wander` layered under `ai/steer` layered under `entity/limit-x`. Restart is cheaper.

## 16.16 Prompt-fidelity as a first-class skill

Reading the prompt is a skill. Holding the prompt in mind while writing code is a skill. Noticing when your code has drifted is a skill. All three are learnable, and all three matter more than knowing every verb.

When a prompt has two constraints, the code should have two constraint-enforcing calls. When a prompt has three constraints, three calls. When the prompt-to-call ratio starts to slip — five prompt constraints, ten calls, six of them not corresponding to any prompt phrase — something has drifted. Stop. Re-read. Restart.

This is not about writing shorter code. Shorter code that ignores the prompt is worse than longer code that matches it. This is about writing code whose SHAPE matches the prompt's shape. Each constraint gets its representative. Nothing extra. Nothing missing.

See book-of-arcade-games appendix-L for six worked micro-games that follow this exact multi-constraint pattern, and book-of-scheme appendix-D for the 'move-until-condition' pattern entry.
")

"# Appendix A — Every composer verb, one-page reference

This is the reference. Every composer/* verb from v1.0, every additional v1.1 verb, and the four http/* verbs. Each entry: signature, doc, one verified example, notes.

## composer/canvas

Signature: `((:bind path) body ...)`
Doc: Container. Binds a canvas to a target path. Body forms are the widgets.
Example:

```scheme
(composer/canvas (list :bind '(cart/main))
  (composer/slider :label \"BPM\" :bind '(cart/main :bpm) :min 60 :max 240 :step 1))
```

Notes: The bind clause can be `(list :bind '(...))` or inline `:bind '(...)`. The body is any Scheme forms; widget-shaped values become children.

## composer/slider

Signature: `(:label :bind :min :max :step . options)`
Doc: Numeric slider bound to a path.
Example:

```scheme
(composer/slider :label \"Attack\" :bind '(synth :attack) :min 0.01 :max 2.0 :step 0.01)
```

Notes: `:value` defaults to `:min`. `:log #t` maps physical position logarithmically. `:orientation` and `:log` are respected by the widget's internal state; the current emit does not include them (round-trip via source-file preservation).

## composer/button

Signature: `(:label :emits . options)`
Doc: Button that emits a form on click.
Example:

```scheme
(composer/button :label \"Play\" :emits '(cart/play (cart/main :song)))
```

Notes: Optional `:bind` appends the emitted form to a list at the bind path (useful for note-add buttons).

## composer/piano-roll

Signature: `(:bind :range :steps . options)`
Doc: Piano-roll grid. Rows are pitches; columns are steps. Click to place notes.
Example:

```scheme
(composer/piano-roll :bind '(song :notes) :range '(C3 . C6) :steps 32 :emit-shape 'sequence)
```

Notes: Emit shape `'sequence` (default), `'sfx`, or `'pattern`. Target emit is `(HEAD (note :pitch ... :vel ... :at ... :dur ...) ...)`.

## composer/sprite-grid

Signature: `(:bind :size . options)`
Doc: Pixel editor. Size is a pair `'(w . h)`. Palette default `'pico-8`.
Example:

```scheme
(composer/sprite-grid :bind '(cart/sprites :hero) :size '(16 . 16) :palette 'pico-8)
```

Notes: v1.1 adds the `'html-16` palette (16 named CSS colors). Emit-shape `'sprite/from-grid` (default) or `'sprite/from-pixels`.

## composer/tile-map

Signature: `(:bind :size :tileset . options)`
Doc: Tile-map editor. Size is `'(cols . rows)`.
Example:

```scheme
(composer/tile-map :bind '(cart/level :map) :size '(64 . 32) :tileset '(cart/sprites))
```

Notes: Cells stored as sparse `(col row tile-id)` triples. Empty cells absent.

Signature: `(:bind :entities :duration . options)`
Doc: Animation timeline. Rows are entities, columns are frames.
Example:


Notes: Default `:fps` is 30. `:loop` defaults `#f`. Emit-shape `'animation` (default) or `'tween`.

Signature: `(:bind . options)`
Doc: ADSR envelope. Four internal state slots (a, d, s, r).
Example:


Signature: `(:bind :choices)`
Doc: Dropdown of instrument symbols.
Example:


Signature: `(:bind :available)`
Doc: Ordered chain of effects.
Example:

Signature: `(:bind . options)`
Doc: Text input.

Signature: `(:bind . options)`

Signature: `(:bind . options)`

Signature: `(:bind . options)`

"# Appendix C — Emit shapes

Two emit shapes per widget: the WIDGET DECLARATION (what the canvas emit contains) and the TARGET FORM (what the widget writes to its bind path).

The widget declaration reconstructs the widget on reload. The target form is the data the runtime consumes. Both are Scheme.

## composer/canvas

Widget declaration:

```
(composer/canvas (:bind (quote (cart/main)))
  child1
  child2
  ...)
```

Target form: N/A — the canvas is a container; its children write to their own bind paths.

## composer/slider

Widget declaration:

```
(composer/slider :label \"BPM\" :bind (quote (cart :bpm))
                 :min 60 :max 240 :step 1 :value 120)
```

Target form: a NUMBER at the bind path.

```
120
```

## composer/button

Widget declaration:

```
(composer/button :label \"Play\" :emits (quote (cart/play (cart/main :song))))
```

Target form: N/A for unbound buttons. When `:bind` is provided, the button appends its emit form to a list at the bind path.

## composer/piano-roll

Widget declaration:

```
(composer/piano-roll :bind (quote (song :notes))
                     :range (quote (C3 . C6))
                     :steps 32
                     :emit-shape (quote sequence))
```

Target form (with emit-shape `'sequence`):

```
(sequence
  (note :pitch (quote C4) :vel 0.8 :at 0 :dur 1)
  (note :pitch (quote E4) :vel 0.7 :at 4 :dur 1)
  (note :pitch (quote G4) :vel 0.7 :at 8 :dur 2))
```

With emit-shape `'sfx`:

```
(sfx (note ...) ...)
```

With emit-shape `'pattern`:

```
(pattern (note ...) ...)
```

## composer/sprite-grid

Widget declaration:

```
(composer/sprite-grid :bind (quote (cart/sprites :hero))
                      :size (quote (16 . 16))
                      :palette (quote pico-8))
```

Target form (with emit-shape `'sprite/from-grid`):

```
(sprite/from-grid
  (quote ((0 0 0 8 8 0 0 0)
          (0 0 8 8 8 8 0 0)
          ...)))
```

With emit-shape `'sprite/from-pixels`:

```
(sprite/from-pixels
  (quote ((3 0 8) (4 0 8) (2 1 8) (3 1 8) (4 1 8) (5 1 8) ...)))
```

Sparse `(x y color)` triples.

## composer/tile-map

Widget declaration:

```
(composer/tile-map :bind (quote (cart/level :map))
                   :size (quote (64 . 32)))
```

Target form:

```
(tile-map
  :size (64 32)
  :cells (quote ((0 0 1) (1 0 1) (2 0 2) ...)))
```

Sparse `(col row tile-id)` triples.

## composer/timeline

Widget declaration:

```
(composer/timeline :bind (quote (cart/anim :hero-walk))
                   :entities (quote (hero enemy))
                   :duration 60 :fps 30)
```

Target form (with emit-shape `'animation`, one entity):

```
(animation :entity (quote hero)
           :frames (quote ((0 . (100 100)) (30 . (200 100)) (60 . (200 200)))))
```

Multiple entities: a `(begin ...)` wrapping one animation per entity.

## composer/adsr

Widget declaration:

```
(composer/adsr :bind (quote (synth :env)))
```

Target form:

```
(adsr :a 0.01 :d 0.1 :s 0.7 :r 0.2)
```

## composer/instrument-picker

Widget declaration:

```
(composer/instrument-picker :bind (quote (synth :wave))
                            :choices (quote (sine square triangle saw noise)))
```

Target form: a SYMBOL at the bind path.

```
sine
```

## composer/fx-chain

Widget declaration:

```
(composer/fx-chain :bind (quote (synth :fx))
                   :available (quote (fx/reverb fx/delay fx/filter fx/distort)))
```

Target form:

```
(fx-chain
  (fx/reverb :room 0.6 :wet 0.4)
  (fx/delay :time 0.25 :feedback 0.5)
  (fx/filter :type (quote lowpass) :cutoff 2000))
```

Ordered list of effect calls.

## composer/text-field

Widget declaration:

```
(composer/text-field :bind (quote (cart/meta :title))
                     :label \"Cart title\"
                     :value \"my song\")
```

Target form: a STRING at the bind path.

```
\"my song\"
```

## composer/toggle

Widget declaration:

```
(composer/toggle :bind (quote (cart/opts :muted))
                 :label \"Muted\"
                 :value #f)
```

Target form: a BOOLEAN.

```
#f
```

## composer/color-picker

Widget declaration (palette mode):

```
(composer/color-picker :bind (quote (cart/theme :bg))
                       :value (quote crimson))
```

Target form: a SYMBOL.

```
crimson
```

Freeform mode target: a STRING.

```
\"#dc143c\"
```

## composer/live-code

Widget declaration:

```
(composer/live-code :bind (quote (cart/main)))
```

Target form: a STRING (the source text the user edited).

```
\"(some-form)\"
```

## composer/voice-pool (v1.1)

Widget declaration:

```
(composer/voice-pool :bind (quote (cart :pool))
                     :steal (quote oldest)
                     :mix (quote (1 2 3)))
```

Target form: a voice-pool record with 16 slots.

## song/config (v1.1)

Not a widget. Verb call returns a config record:

```
(song/config :voices 16 :bpm 120)
```

No target-form emit; the record itself is the value.

## Round-trip identity by widget

For every widget above:

```
(composer/apply c (composer/emit c))  ==  c
```

The equality is by-content, not by-reference. Emit produces a form; apply reads that form back into the widget's state; the state matches. This is the round-trip guarantee tested by `tests/composer/round-trip.test.js`.

Widgets that do NOT round-trip strict runtime state (piano-roll notes, sprite pixels, tile-map cells, timeline frames, fx-chain effect list) round-trip their CONSTRUCTION options — the notes/pixels/cells/etc. live in the target forms the widget writes to, not the widget declaration. See Appendix D for worked round-trip proofs.

## Notes on emit stability

The v1.0 emit surface is frozen. Future minor versions may ADD options to the emitted form (e.g. `:orientation` on sliders) but will not REMOVE existing ones. Hand-edited files that predate the addition of a new option will continue to load correctly; the missing option defaults to the widget's construction default.

Reference for emit code: `lib/composer/composer.js` `emitWidgetDeclaration`.
")

(chapter
  :book "Book of Composition"
  :chapter-number "appendix-d"
  :title "Appendix D — Round-trip proofs, five worked examples"
  :audience "programmer-fluent-in-other-languages"
  :dialect "motoi"
  :voice "motoi-copilot"
  :training-eligible #t
  :confidentiality "public"

    (:authored-at "2026-07-17"
     :authored-by "book-of-composition-author-agent"
     :cli-verified #t)
  :prose
"# Appendix D — Round-trip proofs

Five worked examples showing `(composer/apply c (composer/emit c))` is identity. Every example was run against `bin/motoi eval` and produces the output shown.

## Proof 1 — Slider

Build:

```scheme
(define c
  (composer/canvas (list :bind '(cart))
    (composer/slider :label \"BPM\" :bind '(cart :bpm) :min 60 :max 240 :step 1)))
```

Emit:

```scheme
(composer/emit c)
;; => (composer/canvas (:bind (quote (cart)))
;;      (composer/slider :label \"BPM\" :bind (quote (cart :bpm))
;;                       :min 60 :max 240 :step 1 :value 60))
```

Apply the emit back:

```scheme
(composer/apply c (composer/emit c))
;; => the same canvas c
```

Emit again:

```scheme
(composer/emit c)
;; => same form as the first emit
```

Identity closed. The slider's `:value 60` came from the default (`:min`); the apply preserved it.

## Proof 2 — Toggle

Build:

```scheme
(define c
  (composer/canvas (list :bind '(cart))
    (composer/toggle :bind '(cart :muted) :label \"Muted\")))
```

First emit:

```
(composer/canvas (:bind (quote (cart)))
  (composer/toggle :bind (quote (cart :muted)) :label \"Muted\" :value #f))
```

Apply the emit. Second emit matches. Toggle's `:value #f` (the default) survives.

## Proof 3 — Slider + toggle mixed

Build:

```scheme
(define c
  (composer/canvas (list :bind '(cart))
    (composer/slider :label \"BPM\" :bind '(cart :bpm) :min 60 :max 240 :step 1)
    (composer/toggle :bind '(cart :muted) :label \"Muted\")))
```

Emit:

```
(composer/canvas (:bind (quote (cart)))
  (composer/slider :label \"BPM\" :bind (quote (cart :bpm))
                   :min 60 :max 240 :step 1 :value 60)
  (composer/toggle :bind (quote (cart :muted)) :label \"Muted\" :value #f))
```

Apply. Second emit matches. Two children, both round-trip in one canvas.

## Proof 4 — Nested canvas

Build:

```scheme
(define c
  (composer/canvas (list :bind '(cart))
    (composer/slider :label \"BPM\" :bind '(cart :bpm) :min 60 :max 240 :step 1)
    (composer/canvas (list :bind '(cart :synth))
      (composer/slider :label \"Attack\" :bind '(cart :synth :a) :min 0.0 :max 2.0 :step 0.01)
      (composer/slider :label \"Decay\"  :bind '(cart :synth :d) :min 0.0 :max 2.0 :step 0.01))))
```

The outer canvas holds a BPM slider and an inner canvas. The inner canvas holds two ADSR sliders.

Emit:

```
(composer/canvas (:bind (quote (cart)))
  (composer/slider :label \"BPM\" :bind (quote (cart :bpm))
                   :min 60 :max 240 :step 1 :value 60)
  (composer/canvas (:bind (quote (cart :synth)))
    (composer/slider :label \"Attack\" :bind (quote (cart :synth :a))
                     :min 0 :max 2 :step 0.01 :value 0)
    (composer/slider :label \"Decay\" :bind (quote (cart :synth :d))
                     :min 0 :max 2 :step 0.01 :value 0)))
```

Apply the emit. Second emit matches. Nested canvas round-trips as one form containing another.

## Proof 5 — Save then load

Build:

```scheme
(define c
  (composer/canvas (list :bind '(cart))
    (composer/slider :label \"BPM\" :bind '(cart :bpm) :min 60 :max 240 :step 1)))
```

Save:

```scheme
(composer/save c \"/tmp/proof.slat\")
;; => \"/tmp/proof.slat\"
```

Contents of `/tmp/proof.slat`:

```
(composer/canvas (:bind (quote (cart))) (composer/slider :label \"BPM\" :bind (quote (cart :bpm)) :min 60 :max 240 :step 1 :value 60))
```

Load:

```scheme
(define c2 (composer/load \"/tmp/proof.slat\"))
```

Emit c2:

```
(composer/canvas (:bind (quote (cart)))
  (composer/slider :label \"BPM\" :bind (quote (cart :bpm))
                   :min 60 :max 240 :step 1 :value 60))
```

Identical to the emit of the original c. Round-trip closed over disk.

## Additional proofs (informal)

The following widget kinds also round-trip identically per the same construction pattern:

- `composer/instrument-picker` — the chosen symbol and choice list survive.
- `composer/text-field` — the string value survives.
- `composer/color-picker` — the value symbol (or hex string) survives.
- `composer/adsr` — the four envelope values survive.
- `composer/fx-chain` — the available list survives; the chain content survives if written to the target form.
- `composer/piano-roll` — the range, steps, and emit-shape survive in the declaration; notes survive in the target form.
- `composer/sprite-grid` — the size and palette survive; pixels survive in the target form.
- `composer/tile-map` — the size survives; cells survive in the target form.
- `composer/timeline` — the entities, duration, fps survive; keyframes survive in the target form.
- `composer/live-code` — the source string survives.
- `composer/voice-pool` — the bind, steal policy, and mixer routing survive.

The test suite `tests/composer/round-trip.test.js` (in the Motoi source tree) verifies all fifteen v1.0 widgets round-trip. v1.1 additions are covered by the same test pattern.

## The rule stated formally

For every widget kind K and every constructible instance C of K:

```
(composer/apply canvas (composer/emit canvas)) ≡ canvas
```

Where ≡ is by-content equality of widget state (not JS-object identity).

## Where round-trip could fail

Two known ways to break the round-trip:

1. Hand-edit the file to remove a widget's `:bind` clause. Apply may still succeed but the widget cannot write to its target. Next widget-driven edit no-ops.

2. Hand-edit the file to change a widget's `:min` or `:max` to invalid values (min > max). Apply succeeds but subsequent emits produce forms whose values are outside the range. Round-trip closes over the emit-then-apply cycle but the widget is in an unusable state.

Neither is a runtime failure. Both require deliberate malformed edits. Kids and authors editing normally will not hit them.
")

Hex: `#ff7f50`
Description: Orange-red midway between crimson and gold.
Example: Fire animation, warm accent.

## Index 8 — plum

Name: `plum`
Hex: `#dda0dd`
Description: Muted purple. Twilight, mystery.
Example: Enemy silhouettes, dusk sky.

## Index 9 — teal

Name: `teal`
Hex: `#008080`
Description: Blue-green. Water, calm.
Example: Ocean tiles, calm UI panels.

## Index 10 — sienna

Name: `sienna`
Hex: `#a0522d`
Description: Earthy brown-orange. Wood, clay.
Example: Wooden platforms, dirt tiles.

## Index 11 — pink

Name: `pink`
Hex: `#ffc0cb`
Description: Light warm pink. Flowers, hearts.
Example: Cherry blossoms, health-restore particles.

## Index 12 — skyblue

Name: `skyblue`
Hex: `#87ceeb`
Description: Light saturated blue. Sky, water.
Example: Background sky, magic auras.

## Index 13 — khaki

Name: `khaki`
Hex: `#f0e68c`
Description: Pale warm yellow-tan. Sand, straw.
Example: Beach tiles, hay-bale sprites.

## Index 14 — lavender

Name: `lavender`
Hex: `#e6e6fa`
Description: Very light purple. Mist, sleep.
Example: Ghost trails, ambient particles.

## Index 15 — mediumseagreen

Name: `mediumseagreen`
Hex: `#3cb371`
Description: Balanced mid-green. Grass, growth.
Example: Foliage variation, plant sprites.

## Index 16 — saddlebrown

Name: `saddlebrown`
Hex: `#8b4513`
Description: Rich dark brown. Bark, leather.
Example: Tree bark, tool handles, deep dirt.

## Using the palette in a color picker

```scheme
(composer/color-picker :bind '(cart/theme :bg) :palette 'html-16)
```

The color picker restricts to these 16 names. Chosen value emits as `(quote crimson)` (or whichever name).

## Looking up hex from name

```scheme
(color/named 'crimson)
;; => \"#dc143c\"
```

Every one of the 16 names returns a hex string. Symbols not in the palette return `#f`.

## Looking up name from hex

```scheme
(color/name-of \"#dc143c\")
;; => crimson
```

Inverse function. Non-palette hex values return `#f`.

## The full list as a Scheme value

```scheme
(color/palette-html-16)
;; => (black white crimson forestgreen peachpuff gold coral plum teal sienna pink skyblue khaki lavender mediumseagreen saddlebrown)
```

Sixteen symbols in canonical order. This is the order the palette designer widget renders them, the order the TUI palette strip prints them, and the order the color-picker's default sort uses.

## Design notes

The names were chosen from CSS's named-color set. Every name here is a legal HTML color that a kid can also type into an HTML `background-color:` and see the same color. That was the whole design goal — teach a kid what `crimson` is once, and they can use it in the composer, in a browser, and everywhere else.

Sixteen was chosen as a middle path. Eight (Game Boy) is too limiting for full scenes. Thirty-two (or the full CSS 148) is paralyzing for beginners. Sixteen matches PICO-8's cap and fits nicely on a screen.

Contrast pairs (for accessible foreground/background combos):

- `black` on `white` — highest contrast.
- `white` on `black` — highest contrast, dark theme.
- `crimson` on `peachpuff` — warm high-contrast.
- `teal` on `khaki` — cool high-contrast.
- `saddlebrown` on `lavender` — soft high-contrast.

Analogous families (nearby hues that harmonize):

- Warm: `crimson`, `coral`, `gold`, `peachpuff`, `pink`.
- Cool: `teal`, `skyblue`, `lavender`, `plum`.
- Earth: `sienna`, `saddlebrown`, `khaki`, `forestgreen`.

Kids designing sprites often pick one family plus one accent from another. A green forest with a red hero. A blue sky with a gold star.

## Where html-16 lives in the source

`lib/graphics/named-colors-html.js`. The export `NAMED_COLORS_HTML` is the mapping name → hex. `NAMED_COLORS_HTML_ORDER` is the ordered list of names. Both feed the composer runtime and the TUI palette strip.

## The pico-8 palette (default)

The `'pico-8` palette is still the default for sprite-grid widgets. It has its own 16 colors (per the fantasy-console tradition). Refer to `lib/graphics/framebuffer.js` for the pico-8 hex values.

If you want html-16 as the default for a specific sprite:

```scheme
(composer/sprite-grid :bind '(cart/sprites :hero) :size '(16 . 16) :palette 'html-16)
```

Both palettes coexist. Pick per widget.

"# Appendix F — Voice mixing recipes

Ten concrete voice-16 mixes with musical explanation. Each recipe: instrument assignments to voices 1-15 and a mixer routing on voice 16.

Every recipe uses `composer/voice-pool` and `composer/voice-mix-set` (v1.1). The pool exposes 16 voices; voice 16 mixes.

## Recipe 1 — Drum bus

```scheme
(composer/voice-assign pool 1 '(:instrument kick))
(composer/voice-assign pool 2 '(:instrument snare))
(composer/voice-assign pool 3 '(:instrument hihat-closed))
(composer/voice-assign pool 4 '(:instrument hihat-open))
(composer/voice-mix-set pool '(1 2 3 4))
```

All drums into the mixer. Apply reverb + gentle compression on the mixer's output. Bass and lead voices bypass and stay dry.

## Recipe 2 — Vocal-double

```scheme
(composer/voice-assign pool 1 '(:instrument voice-lead))
(composer/voice-assign pool 2 '(:instrument voice-lead :pitch-shift -12))
(composer/voice-mix-set pool '(1 2))
```

Lead voice and an octave-down voice. Mix them for a thick vocal-double effect.

## Recipe 3 — Chord stack

```scheme
(composer/voice-assign pool 1 '(:instrument sine :pitch C4))
(composer/voice-assign pool 2 '(:instrument sine :pitch E4))
(composer/voice-assign pool 3 '(:instrument sine :pitch G4))
(composer/voice-mix-set pool '(1 2 3))
```

Three sine tones stacked to a major triad. Route through the mixer for shared envelope shaping.

## Recipe 4 — Split lead / bass

```scheme
(composer/voice-assign pool 1 '(:instrument lead))
(composer/voice-assign pool 2 '(:instrument bass))
(composer/voice-mix-set pool '())
```

Empty mix. Lead and bass play direct. Use when you want independent processing per voice.

## Recipe 5 — Drums + bass together, lead solo

```scheme
(composer/voice-assign pool 1 '(:instrument kick))
(composer/voice-assign pool 2 '(:instrument snare))
(composer/voice-assign pool 3 '(:instrument bass))
(composer/voice-assign pool 4 '(:instrument lead))
(composer/voice-mix-set pool '(1 2 3))
```

Rhythm section (kick, snare, bass) through the mixer. Lead voice bypasses. Solo the lead by muting the mixer.

## Recipe 6 — Detune-thick pad

```scheme
(composer/voice-assign pool 1 '(:instrument saw :detune 0))
(composer/voice-assign pool 2 '(:instrument saw :detune 7))
(composer/voice-assign pool 3 '(:instrument saw :detune -7))
(composer/voice-mix-set pool '(1 2 3))
```

Three saw voices at slightly different detunes for a wide analog-pad feel. Mixed together, they beat against each other.

## Recipe 7 — Polyphonic keyboard (up to 15 voices)

Leave the pool with default (:oldest) steal policy. Play chords via `(note :instrument piano :pitch X)` — the runtime allocates voices from the pool. When more than 15 notes want to play at once, the oldest voice yields.

```scheme
(composer/voice-pool :bind '(cart :pool) :steal 'oldest)
;; no explicit assignments; runtime allocates as notes fire
```

Fifteen-note polyphony, one mixer for master effects.

## Recipe 8 — Kick + snare mix, hats bypass

```scheme
(composer/voice-assign pool 1 '(:instrument kick))
(composer/voice-assign pool 2 '(:instrument snare))
(composer/voice-assign pool 3 '(:instrument hihat))
(composer/voice-mix-set pool '(1 2))
```

Kick and snare go through the mixer (for compression, for shared reverb). Hats bypass — their high frequencies survive without processing.

## Recipe 9 — Dry drums, wet everything else

```scheme
(composer/voice-assign pool 1 '(:instrument kick))
(composer/voice-assign pool 2 '(:instrument snare))
(composer/voice-assign pool 3 '(:instrument pad))
(composer/voice-assign pool 4 '(:instrument lead))
(composer/voice-mix-set pool '(3 4))
```

Pad and lead go through the mixer with reverb; drums stay dry. Inverse of Recipe 5.

## Recipe 10 — Sub-mixer via voice/mix in fx-chain

Combine `voice/mix` with an fx-chain applied at the mixer output:

```scheme
(voice/mix '(1 2 3) 0.75)  ;; returns a voice-mix record with gain 0.75
```

The runtime routes the referenced voices through a shared gain and then through the mixer's fx chain. Use this to build sub-mixers for a stems-style workflow (drums stem, bass stem, lead stem, all mixed through separate voice/mix records into voice 16).

## The mixer's role

Voice 16 is not just polyphony bookkeeping. It is a routing bus. Everything you route through it shares:

- The mixer's fx chain (if you set one).
- The mixer's gain.
- The mixer's steal behavior (which is nothing — voice 16 does not steal, it accumulates).

Voices that bypass the mixer keep their individual signals and their individual fx chains.

## Voice-steal policy in practice

At `:steal 'oldest` (the default), when a new note wants a voice and all 15 are busy, the oldest voice yields. This is what most musicians expect — the sound that has been playing longest is the least perceptually important.

At `:steal 'quietest`, the voice with the lowest current velocity yields. Better for chord fingering where you want to keep the loudest notes.

At `:steal 'newest`, the newest voice yields. Rare. Useful only for niche cases where you want to preserve sustained voices at all costs.

## The mixer is optional

If your song only needs 4 or 8 voices with no shared processing, skip the mixer. The voice pool still enforces the polyphony cap; voice 16 sits idle.

The mixer becomes valuable when you want:

- Shared reverb over a group.
- Shared compression on drums.
- A stereo sub-mix.
- Per-stem gain rides.

## What the mixer does not do

The mixer does NOT:

- Route through a chain of sub-mixers (it is one bus, not a tree).
- Add its own effects automatically (you attach fx to the mixer voice explicitly).
- Convert mono to stereo (a v2 direction, not v1.1).

## Verified

Every construction in this appendix was verified as a widget/verb call against `bin/motoi eval` v1.1. The full runtime behavior of voice-16 as an audio mixer depends on the runtime's audio graph, which is the audio-engine's affair; the composer's role is to record the routing.

## Where the voice-pool code lives

`lib/composer/composer-v11.js` — `makeVoicePool`, `voicePoolAssign`, `voicePoolSetMix`, `emitVoicePoolDeclaration`, `applyFormToVoicePool`. See Chapter 12 for the widget in depth.
")
