"# Appendix G — TUI cheat-sheet

Quick reference for the TUI renderer's conventions. Cell characters, header layout, palette strip, and how to invoke the render verb.

## The verb

```
(composer/render-tui canvas [opts]) -> string
```

- `canvas` — a canvas record.
- `opts` — optional plist of rendering options.

Options:

- `:brand #f` — suppress the brand header (three stripes + title).
- `:palette 'html-16` — force the palette strip.
- `:color #f` — disable ANSI color escape codes (currently the TUI does not emit escapes anyway; this option is for forward-compatibility).

## The brand header

```
[pink ] ========================================
[green] ========================================
[brown] ========================================

MOTOI COMPOSER — canvas <bind-label>
----------------------------------------
```

Three lines of stripe rules labeled by color. Blank line. Title line with the canvas's bind label. Dash rule separator.

`bind-label` is a slash-joined string of the canvas's bind path. `(cart/main)` renders as `cart/main`. Multi-level binds render as `cart/main/synth`.

## Widget renderings (compact reference)

Slider:

```
[==========|---------] <label> <value>
```

Button:

```
[ <label> ]
```

Toggle:

```
[X] <label>       ;; on
[ ] <label>       ;; off
```

Text-field:

```
<label>: \"<value>\"
```

Color-picker:

```
color(<bind>): <name-or-hex>
```

ADSR:

```
ADSR: a=<a> d=<d> s=<s> r=<r>
```

Instrument-picker:

```
instrument: [<choice1>|<choice2>|...] chosen=<chosen>
```

Piano-roll:

```
piano-roll: <bind> (<n-notes> notes, <n-steps> steps)
   B ................
  A# ................
  ...
   C #...............
```

Sprite-grid:

```
sprite: <bind> (<w>x<h>, palette <palette>)
  <row of chars>
  <row of chars>
  ...
```

Tile-map:

```
tile-map: (<cols>x<rows>)
  <row of chars>
  ...
```

Timeline:

```
timeline: entities=<csv> duration=<d>s fps=<fps> frames=<n>
```

fx-chain:

```
fx-chain: <fx1> -> <fx2> -> <fx3>
```

Empty fx-chain:

```
fx-chain: (empty)
```

Live-code:

```
live-code: \"<preview>\"
```

Voice-pool (v1.1):

```
voice-pool: 16 voices, steal=<policy>
   1 <instrument-name-or-(free)>
   2 <instrument-name-or-(free)>
   ...
  15 <instrument-name-or-(free)>
  16 [MIX] <- #<v1>,#<v2>,...
```

## Cell character mapping

Palette-indexed cells (sprite-grid, tile-map, piano-roll character rows) use:

- `.` for index 0.
- `1`, `2`, ..., `9` for indices 1-9.
- `a`, `b`, `c`, `d`, `e`, `f` for indices 10-15.
- `?` for any other value.

Piano-roll cells use `#` for a placed note and `.` for empty.

## The palette strip (if html-16 is used)

Appended below the widgets:

```
palette (html-16):
  01:black  02:white  03:crimson  04:forestgreen  05:peachpuff  06:gold  07:coral  08:plum  09:teal  10:sienna  11:pink  12:skyblue  13:khaki  14:lavender  15:mediumseagreen  16:saddlebrown
```

The strip is triggered when any widget in the canvas has `:palette 'html-16` set, or when the caller passes `:palette 'html-16` to `composer/render-tui`.

## The tree logo

```
     /\\
    /  \\
   /----\\
  /      \\
 /--------\\
     ||
     ||
```

Returned by `(composer/tree-logo)`. Print it as a landing header:

```scheme
(display (composer/tree-logo))
(newline)
```

## Keyboard conventions (proposed)

The TUI renderer itself is a pure function producing a string. A CURSES-STYLE INTERACTIVE driver on top of the renderer would map keys to widget interactions. The proposed conventions (per the v1.1 spec) are:

- Arrow keys navigate between widgets.
- Enter activates a button, opens a numeric-entry sheet on a slider, toggles a toggle.
- Left / Right arrow on a slider steps by `:step`.
- Home / End on a slider jump to min / max.
- Digit keys 1-9 select tools in a sprite editor.
- `s` for save, `l` for load, `q` for quit.

The interactive driver is not shipped in v1.1; only the render verb is. Kids running interactively use Curator's canvas rendering. Terminal users use the render string for snapshot inspection and headless testing.

## ANSI escape codes

The v1.1 TUI does not currently emit escape codes; every output is plain text. The renderer includes ANSI helpers in the source (`TUI_ANSI` export in `tui.js`) for future use. If a caller wants colored output, they can wrap widget lines in escapes themselves.

## Redraw model

`composer/render-tui` is pure. Caller decides when to redraw. Typical patterns:

- Snapshot mode: call once, print, done.
- Interactive mode: call on every widget change, diff against previous frame, paint the diff.
- Test mode: call, compare against expected string, assert.

## Line width

Widgets render at approximately 40-cell width by default (see `STRIPE_WIDTH` in `tui.js`). Sliders are 20-cell bars. Sprite/tile grids are as wide as their pixel count plus a 2-space indent.

Terminal narrower than 40 cells will wrap the header stripes but the widget rows will fit as long as your sprite is not too wide.

## Where the code lives

`lib/composer/tui.js`. All widget renderers are pure functions. The main entry point is `renderCanvasToTUI(canvas, opts)`. Named exports include `TREE_LOGO` and `TUI_ANSI`.

## A full example

```scheme
(define c
  (composer/canvas (list :bind '(cart))
    (composer/slider :label \"BPM\" :bind '(cart :bpm) :min 60 :max 240 :step 1 :value 120)
    (composer/toggle :bind '(cart :muted) :label \"Muted\")
    (composer/instrument-picker :bind '(cart :wave)
                                :choices '(sine square triangle saw noise))))

(display (composer/render-tui c))
(newline)
```

Verified output:

```
[pink ] ========================================
[green] ========================================
[brown] ========================================

MOTOI COMPOSER — canvas cart
----------------------------------------
[==========|---------] BPM 120

[ ] Muted

instrument: [sine|square|triangle|saw|noise] chosen=sine
```

## Suppress the brand header

```scheme
(display (composer/render-tui c '(:brand #f)))
```

Renders without the three stripes and the title.

That is the TUI in full. Every widget kind renders. Every canvas renders. The composer follows kids into terminals, into SSH sessions, into CI logs.
")

"# Appendix H — HTTP server security guide

The composer's HTTP host serves carts to browsers on the local network. This appendix documents the security model: the permission gate, the path-traversal defenses, the request-classification rules, and the trust boundaries.

Every defense listed is implemented in `lib/net/http-serve.js`. The file includes an inline security review commented at the top. This appendix expands and organizes that review.

## H.1 The threat model

Kids want to share carts with friends. Kids do NOT want:

- Strangers editing their carts.
- Servers exposing files outside the cart directory.
- Browsers accidentally running writes.
- Remote clients spoofing local identity.

The HTTP server ships with defaults that address each of these. Alternative defaults are configurable but the SAFE PATH is the DEFAULT PATH.

## H.2 Route summary

Three route families:

- `/` — landing. Public. Lists carts, brand header.
- `/play/:cart` — cart play view. Public.
- `/compose/:cart` — compose view. Permission-gated (default local-only).

## H.3 The compose-perm gate

`:compose-perm` option controls who can hit `/compose/:cart`.

- `'local-only` (default) — only 127.0.0.1 and ::1 pass.
- `'anyone` — no gate; all requests pass.

The classification uses the socket's `remoteAddress`. It DOES NOT read X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP, or any other client-supplied header. A remote client cannot lie their way past the local-only gate by sending forged headers.

The check is in `isLocalRequest(req)`:

```javascript
function isLocalRequest(req) {
  const addr = req.socket && req.socket.remoteAddress ? String(req.socket.remoteAddress) : ''
  return addr === '127.0.0.1' || addr === '::1' || addr === '::ffff:127.0.0.1'
}
```

Three legal local addresses: IPv4 localhost, IPv6 localhost, IPv4-mapped IPv6 localhost.

## H.4 Path traversal defenses

Multiple layers.

### H.4.1 URL sanity

The request handler rejects (403) any URL that:

- Contains a null byte (`\\0`).
- Contains the literal string `..`.

The check runs BEFORE URL parsing, so encoded variants (`%2e%2e`) are also rejected — URL parsing would normalize them, but the raw-string check catches them first at the pre-parse stage.

### H.4.2 Cart-name regex

Cart names are matched against `/^[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$/` per path segment. Legal characters: uppercase letters, lowercase letters, digits, dot, underscore, hyphen. Nothing else.

This excludes:

- Slashes within a segment (safe, since segments are joined with `/`).
- Spaces.
- URL-encoded characters that would decode to interesting characters.
- Null bytes.
- Unicode homoglyphs.
- Control characters.

### H.4.3 Path segment rules

Cart names may contain up to 4 slash-separated segments (`composer/synth-patch/variant-a/version-2`). Each segment:

- Must be 1-128 characters long.
- Must match the regex above.
- Must not be `.` or `..`.

### H.4.4 Resolved-path check

After the cart name is decoded, split, and joined with the cart directory, the resulting path is `path.resolve`'d. The absolute resolved path is compared against the normalized cart directory. If the resolved path does not start with the cart directory prefix (with a trailing separator), the cart is treated as missing (404).

This catches any exotic case the regex misses. Even if a segment slipped through, the resolved path must physically land under the cart directory.

### H.4.5 Existence + file check

The candidate path must exist (`existsSync`) and be a regular file (`statSync().isFile()`). Directories don't serve; missing files 404.

## H.5 Cart-dir resolution

`:cart-dir` is passed to `safeResolveCartDir(cartDir)`. Steps:

1. Resolve the cart dir against `process.cwd()`.
2. Normalize both the resolved dir and cwd.
3. Fail if the resolved dir does not start with the cwd prefix (or equal cwd).
4. Fail if the resolved dir doesn't exist.
5. Fail if the resolved dir is not a directory.

Failures throw an error at `http/serve` call time. The server does not start with an unsafe cart-dir.

The cwd-escape check means `:cart-dir \"../../etc\"` refuses. So does `:cart-dir \"/absolute/path/outside/cwd\"`.

## H.6 Method restriction

Only GET is accepted. POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, and any other method return 405 with a plain-text body `\"method not allowed\"`.

v1.1 does not accept cart writes over HTTP. Cart edits round-trip through the composer's own `composer/save` and `composer/load`, on the local file system.

## H.7 Content-Type responses

- `text/plain` for the 405 body.
- `text/html; charset=utf-8` for all other successful and error responses.

The server does not serve arbitrary MIME types. It emits HTML shells around cart source. If a later wave adds asset serving (images, audio), it will add explicit MIME-type mapping per file extension.

## H.8 HTML escaping

Every user-controlled string that appears in HTML responses passes through `escapeHtml(s)`:

```javascript
function escapeHtml(s) {
  return String(s)
    .replace(/&/g, '&')
    .replace(/</g, '<')
    .replace(/>/g, '>')
    .replace(/\"/g, '"')
    .replace(/'/g, ''')
}
```

Cart names, cart file source, and error messages all pass through this function. A cart named `<script>alert(1)</script>` renders as literal text (though the regex would refuse it at path resolution anyway).

## H.9 No shell-out

The server does not invoke any subprocess. All file reading is done via `readFileSync`, `readdirSync`, `statSync`, `existsSync`. There is no `exec`, `spawn`, or `child_process` invocation.

## H.10 Rate limiting

The v1.1 server does not implement rate limiting. On a local trusted network this is acceptable; on a public network you would front the server with a reverse proxy that rate-limits.

## H.11 TLS

The v1.1 server serves plain HTTP. No HTTPS. On a local network this is acceptable; on a public network you would front with a TLS-terminating proxy. The server has no TLS support of its own.

## H.12 Cookies and sessions

None. The server is stateless per request. No cookies are set. No sessions are tracked. The kid identity is `whoever runs the server`, not a browser identity.

## H.13 CORS

The server does not send CORS headers. Same-origin requests work; cross-origin requests hit the browser's default CORS policy. If you want to serve a cart to a JavaScript app on a different origin, you would need to add CORS handling (not implemented in v1.1).

## H.14 The trust model in one sentence

The server is a LOCAL DEVICE. The play route trusts anyone reachable by the port; the compose route trusts only local requests unless explicitly widened.

## H.15 Testing the security posture

`lib/net/http-serve.js` exports `_internal` for tests, containing `makeHandler`, `isLocalRequest`, `safeCartPathWithSubdir`, `safeResolveCartDir`, `listCarts`. A security test suite can:

1. Simulate remote-address requests to `/compose/foo` and assert 403.
2. Try `/play/../secret.txt` and assert 403 or 404.
3. Try `/play/synth-patch%00.txt` and assert 403.
4. Try a POST and assert 405.
5. Try to escape the cart dir with `.., \\, //, etc.` and assert refusal.

## H.16 What could go wrong

Known limitations you should know about:

- If your `carts/` directory contains files with sensitive content, ANYONE reachable on the port can read them via `/play/:cart`. Don't put secrets in your cart directory.

"# Chapter 1 — Transistors and Speak & Spell

Every computer you have ever touched, and every computer Motoi has
ever run on, is built from transistors. Billions of them. So we start
here.

We also start at the Texas Instruments Speak & Spell — the yellow
plastic toy from 1978 that taught a lot of American kids to spell,
including the person who built Motoi. It's a good example because it
uses the same technology as everything since, at a scale small enough
to look at end-to-end.

## What a transistor is

A transistor is a small switch made from a solid crystal, usually
silicon. It has three terminals. A voltage on one terminal — called
the base or the gate — controls whether electricity can flow between
the other two.

Say that again: a switch controlled by an electrical signal instead
of a mechanical lever.

That is the whole invention. Everything else is arrangement.

The first transistor was demonstrated at Bell Labs on December 23,
1947, by John Bardeen, Walter Brattain, and William Shockley. They
won the Nobel Prize in 1956 for it. Before transistors, computers
were built from vacuum tubes — glass bulbs the size of a light bulb,
running hot, burning out. The transistor replaced them with a
solid-state device that was smaller, cheaper, cooler, and more
reliable.

By the 1960s, engineers were putting several transistors together on
a single small piece of silicon. That's an integrated circuit — a
chip. By the 1970s they were putting thousands on one chip. By 2020
they were putting tens of billions on a chip the size of a
fingernail.

Motoi runs on chips like these. The math Motoi does happens as
voltages moving through transistors, arranged into logic gates,
arranged into adders and memory cells, arranged into a processor.
Every step is transistors.

## The Speak & Spell

Texas Instruments released the Speak & Spell in June 1978. It cost
about \\$50. It was one of the first consumer electronic devices
built around a general-purpose speech synthesizer chip.

Inside the yellow plastic case there were essentially four things:

1. A **TMS1000-family microcontroller** — a small computer chip
   containing a processor, RAM, and ROM.
2. A **TMS5100 speech synthesizer chip** — the part that made the
   sounds. This chip implemented linear predictive coding, or LPC,
   a technique for reproducing human speech from a compressed
   mathematical model of the vocal tract.
3. A **speech ROM** with the phonemes and words the toy could speak.
4. A membrane keyboard, small speaker, and vacuum-fluorescent
   display.

The important part is the TMS5100. It was one of the first single-chip
speech synthesizers, and it used a technique that would end up
underlying almost every modern speech codec (including the ones
running in cell phones today).

Linear predictive coding works like this: the human vocal tract can
be approximated mathematically as a set of resonating tubes. Given a
short sample of speech, you can figure out the coefficients that
describe the tubes at that moment. Store the coefficients (a few
bytes) instead of the raw sound (thousands of bytes), and later
re-synthesize the sound by driving the mathematical model with a
buzz-and-hiss excitation. The Speak & Spell did this in real time in
a chip designed by Larry Brantingham, Richard Wiggins, and colleagues
at TI.

Alfred, who built Motoi, learned to spell on a Speak & Spell. The
warm yellow buttons, the deterministic response, the way it made him
feel he was learning things he could hold — those are the design
principles Motoi tries to honor.

## Why we start here

Because the Speak & Spell is a computer small enough to understand
end-to-end. The whole thing is a few chips. The whole thing does one
thing. It is warm plastic in the shape of a book, with buttons, and
it teaches. That's Motoi's north star.

## A tiny example

Simulating a very simple LPC-style resonator in Motoi Scheme. This
doesn't sound like human speech — you need many more coefficients
and a proper excitation signal for that — but the mathematical shape
is here:

```
;; A single all-pole IIR filter, first order:
;;   y[n] = x[n] + a * y[n-1]
;; where 'a' controls how much of the previous sample bleeds into
;; the current one. Higher 'a' -> more resonance.

(define (make-resonator a)
  (let ((prev 0))
    (lambda (input)
      (let ((out (+ input (* a prev))))
        (set! prev out)
        out))))

(define r (make-resonator 0.9))

;; Feed it a short impulse
(r 1.0)   ;; => 1.0
(r 0.0)   ;; => 0.9
(r 0.0)   ;; => 0.81
(r 0.0)   ;; => 0.729
(r 0.0)   ;; => 0.6561
;; The impulse rings out exponentially.
```

Real LPC uses many filter coefficients simultaneously (typically ten
to twelve, updated every 20-30 milliseconds), plus an excitation
signal — either a periodic pulse (for voiced sounds like vowels) or
white noise (for hissing sounds like 's' and 'f'). The Speak & Spell
did this in dedicated silicon in 1978.

## What Motoi wants you to take from this

Transistors are switches. Switches make gates. Gates make adders.
Adders make processors. Processors run programs. Programs run
languages. Languages let you talk to computers.

That whole tower is what's under Motoi. Twelve or so layers of
abstraction, each one carefully engineered, adding up to something
that can tell you what a lambda is.

Also: the Speak & Spell is the shape of a good learning tool.
Warm, tangible, deterministic, doesn't lie about what it can do,
rewards the kid for showing up. Motoi is trying to be a modern
version of that.")

  :prose
"# Chapter 2 — Logic gates and adders

Transistors are switches. Arrange them in small groups and you get
logic gates. Arrange gates and you get adders. Arrange adders and you
get processors. The whole tower.

## The gates

A logic gate takes one or two Boolean inputs — TRUE or FALSE, 1 or
0, high voltage or low voltage — and produces a Boolean output.
There are six basic gates that every chip on Earth is built from:

- **NOT** (inverter): one input, one output. Output is the opposite.
- **AND**: two inputs. Output is TRUE only if both inputs are TRUE.
- **OR**: two inputs. Output is TRUE if either input is TRUE.
- **NAND**: AND followed by NOT.
- **NOR**: OR followed by NOT.
- **XOR** (exclusive-or): TRUE if the inputs differ.

That's it. Six gates. Every processor ever made is arrangements of
these six ideas, plus some memory cells (which are themselves
arrangements of these gates).

You can make them all from NAND alone. This is called functional
completeness. NAND is a universal gate. Give me NAND, I'll build you
NOT (NAND with both inputs tied together), AND (NAND followed by
NOT), OR (NOTs feeding into a NAND), and so on. So in principle a
chip could be built from a single kind of gate.

In practice chips use several kinds because it's more efficient. But
the theoretical fact — one gate is enough — is worth carrying.

## Motoi Scheme as gates

Motoi Scheme has these built in. They live under the names `and`,
`or`, `not`. Let's show them:

```
(and #t #t)  ;; => #t
(and #t #f)  ;; => #f
(or #f #t)   ;; => #t
(or #f #f)   ;; => #f
(not #t)     ;; => #f
```

Boolean logic. Same shape as the gates in silicon, just in software.

We can build a half-adder in Motoi Scheme. A half-adder adds two
one-bit numbers and produces two outputs: a sum and a carry:

```
(define (half-adder a b)
  (let ((sum   (xor a b))
        (carry (and a b)))
    (list sum carry)))

(define (xor a b)
  (and (or a b) (not (and a b))))

(half-adder #f #f)  ;; => (#f #f)  ;; 0 + 0 = 0, carry 0
(half-adder #f #t)  ;; => (#t #f)  ;; 0 + 1 = 1, carry 0
(half-adder #t #f)  ;; => (#t #f)  ;; 1 + 0 = 1, carry 0
(half-adder #t #t)  ;; => (#f #t)  ;; 1 + 1 = 0, carry 1  (that's binary two)
```

A full adder adds three bits — two inputs plus an incoming carry —
and produces a sum and an outgoing carry. Chain full adders together
and you can add two multi-bit numbers.

```
(define (full-adder a b cin)
  (let* ((h1 (half-adder a b))
         (s1 (car h1))
         (c1 (cadr h1))
         (h2 (half-adder s1 cin))
         (s2 (car h2))
         (c2 (cadr h2))
         (cout (or c1 c2)))
    (list s2 cout)))

(full-adder #t #t #f)  ;; 1 + 1 + 0 = 2, so sum=0, carry=1
;; => (#f #t)

(full-adder #t #t #t)  ;; 1 + 1 + 1 = 3, so sum=1, carry=1
;; => (#t #t)
```

Now chain full-adders together to build an 8-bit adder. In real
silicon this is called a ripple-carry adder, and it lives at the
heart of every processor's ALU (arithmetic-logic unit).

```
(define (bits n width)
  ;; convert integer n to list of #t/#f, low bit first
  (if (= width 0)
      '()
      (cons (odd? n) (bits (quotient n 2) (- width 1)))))

(define (bits->int lst)
  (let loop ((bs lst) (place 1) (total 0))
    (if (null? bs)
        total
        (loop (cdr bs)
              (* place 2)
              (+ total (if (car bs) place 0))))))

(define (ripple-add a-bits b-bits)
  (let loop ((a a-bits) (b b-bits) (cin #f) (out '()))
    (if (null? a)
        (reverse (cons cin out))
        (let* ((r (full-adder (car a) (car b) cin))
               (s (car r))
               (c (cadr r)))
          (loop (cdr a) (cdr b) c (cons s out))))))

;; Add 42 + 17 as 8-bit numbers
(let* ((a (bits 42 8))
       (b (bits 17 8))
       (sum (ripple-add a b)))
  (bits->int sum))
;; => 59
```

That's an adder, built out of pure Boolean logic, in Motoi Scheme.
The identical shape — same gates, same connections — is what lives
inside every chip's ALU. In silicon each gate is a few transistors;
in Motoi Scheme each gate is a Scheme procedure. Same logic, different
substrate.

## ENIAC

The first American general-purpose electronic computer, ENIAC, was
completed in 1945 at the University of Pennsylvania. It contained
about 17,468 vacuum tubes (not transistors — transistors weren't
invented yet). It filled a room. It could perform about 5,000 add
operations per second.

A modern smartphone processor performs on the order of a hundred
billion add operations per second. Every one of them is the same
half-adder / full-adder shape.

The gates got smaller. The idea stayed the same.

## What Motoi wants you to take from this

Computation is arrangement. You take a small handful of simple
pieces — six kinds of logic gate — and combine them in the right
shapes and you get everything a computer can do. The pieces are
simple. The arrangements can be enormous.

When Motoi tells you that programming is composition, this is what
he means at the bottom. Composition all the way down.")

                     (:source "wikipedia" :url "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7400-series_integrated_circuits"))
  :prose
"# Chapter 3 — Chip families — TTL, DTL, CMOS

Chapter 2 was about gates as abstract Boolean things. This chapter
is about how those gates are actually built in silicon — and about
the different physical strategies engineers have used over the
decades. Different strategies had different tradeoffs: speed, power,
heat, cost, ease of manufacture. Some of these strategies were
dominant for a decade and then displaced. That's a common shape in
engineering.

## DTL — diode-transistor logic

Diode-transistor logic came first, in the early 1960s. It used diodes
to perform the logic and one transistor to amplify the output.
Diodes are simple, cheap, and slow. DTL chips were slow, but they
worked, and they were manufacturable in the state of the art at the
time.

DTL was dominant for a few years and then got replaced by TTL, which
was faster.

## TTL — transistor-transistor logic

Transistor-transistor logic replaced DTL in the mid-1960s. TTL used
multi-emitter transistors instead of diodes for the logic stage.
Faster switching, less power per gate, better fanout (a TTL gate
could drive more downstream inputs).

TTL dominated logic-chip design from about 1965 through the 1980s.
The most famous TTL family is the 74xx series, introduced by Texas
Instruments in 1966 and still available in updated forms decades
later. Every serious electronics hobbyist of a certain generation
has a shoebox of 7400 chips somewhere.

Some famous 74xx parts:
- **7400**: quad two-input NAND
- **7404**: hex inverter
- **7408**: quad two-input AND
- **7432**: quad two-input OR
- **7474**: dual D flip-flop (a memory cell — stores one bit)
- **7483**: 4-bit adder (chapter 2's ripple-adder, in one chip)
- **74181**: 4-bit ALU (arithmetic-logic unit — can add, subtract,
  AND, OR, XOR)

You could build a working 8-bit computer using only 74xx chips
soldered onto a board. People did. The Kenbak-1 (1971) — a
candidate for the title 'first personal computer' — was built from
TTL. Many home-computer projects since have been built the same way.

## CMOS — complementary metal-oxide semiconductor

By the late 1970s, engineers were figuring out that TTL had a
problem: it burned power all the time, whether the gate was switching
or not. TTL gates leak current continuously. That's fine for a few
gates on a board; it's terrible when you want to put a million gates
on one chip and run it from a battery.

CMOS solved this. A CMOS gate uses two complementary transistors — a
'PMOS' and an 'NMOS' — arranged so that one is always off. Current
only flows during the brief moment a gate is switching from one
state to the other. Static power consumption drops by orders of
magnitude.

CMOS was known theoretically from the mid-1960s but was hard to
manufacture reliably. Once the manufacturing caught up (mid to late
1970s), CMOS became the dominant technology for building integrated
circuits, and it has been ever since.

Every processor in your pocket is CMOS. Every RAM chip is CMOS.
Every SSD controller is CMOS. When people say 'the chip industry,'
they largely mean CMOS.

## Why the family matters

Different chip families have different signal levels, different
speeds, different power characteristics, different noise margins.
Chips from different families sometimes can't talk to each other
directly — you need a level-shifter or an interface chip.

This is more than a technicality. When you're wiring an old computer
into a modern breadboard project, or building a level converter for
5-volt legacy hardware talking to 3.3-volt modern hardware, this is
the topic you're working on.

Motoi is not going to help you level-shift 5V to 3.3V. But knowing
the family is why the levels are different is honest computer
literacy.

## Standard cells

Modern chip design doesn't have engineers laying out individual
transistors for every gate. Instead, foundries publish libraries of
'standard cells' — pre-designed layouts for each kind of gate, at
several drive strengths. A chip designer's tool places cells and
routes wires between them. The cells are the modern equivalent of
the 74xx chips: reusable building blocks at the size and abstraction
appropriate to the era.

The abstraction stack:
- Chip designer works with standard cells.
- Cells are built from transistors.
- Transistors are built from silicon crystal structure.
- The crystal is grown, sliced, etched, and doped in a fab.
- Photolithography is used to pattern the layers.

Every layer of that stack takes a lifetime to master. The whole
industry runs because different specialists work at different levels
and trust each other's abstractions.

## A tiny example

Simulating a couple of gate families with different signal levels in
Motoi Scheme, just to show the shape:

```
(define ttl-high 5.0)   ;; volts
(define ttl-low  0.0)

(define cmos-high 3.3)
(define cmos-low  0.0)

(define (interpret-ttl v)
  (cond ((>= v 2.0) #t)
        ((<= v 0.8) #f)
        (else 'indeterminate)))

(define (interpret-cmos v)
  (cond ((>= v 2.5) #t)
        ((<= v 0.8) #f)
        (else 'indeterminate)))

(interpret-ttl 5.0)   ;; => #t
(interpret-ttl 3.3)   ;; => #t   (CMOS output looks HIGH to TTL, usually ok)
(interpret-cmos 5.0)  ;; => #t   (but pushing 5V into CMOS input can damage it!)
(interpret-cmos 2.0)  ;; => indeterminate
```

Those threshold voltages are why you can't just wire everything
together. Motoi doesn't do this level of engineering, but knowing the
shape helps make sense of retro-computing projects and hardware
histories.

## What Motoi wants you to take from this

Different eras used different physical strategies to build the same
logical gates. TTL was fast for its time. CMOS is efficient. Both
are arrangements of transistors implementing Boolean logic. The
logic doesn't care which family you use. But the electrical behavior
sure does.

This is also why old computers have such distinct personalities.
The C64 uses NMOS logic families that run hot. The Amiga uses
faster NMOS custom chips plus CMOS controllers. Each machine feels
different partly because the underlying physics is different.")

  :prose
"# Chapter 4 — Commodore 64 — the 6502, memory, BASIC

The Commodore 64. Released August 1982. Priced at \\$595 at launch,
dropping fast. Sold somewhere between 12 and 17 million units — the
best-selling single home computer model ever made, by most counts.

If you were a kid in the 1980s learning to program at home, there is
a good chance you were sitting in front of a C64.

## The processor: MOS 6510

The C64 uses a MOS 6510 processor, a slight variant of the
industry-defining MOS 6502. The 6502 was designed by a team at MOS
Technology led by Chuck Peddle in 1975. The 6502 was famously cheap
— about \\$25 when it launched, versus \\$150+ for Intel and
Motorola competitors — which is a big part of why so many home
computers of the era used it.

The 6502 (and 6510) is an 8-bit processor. That means it works on
one byte at a time. It has:
- **Three general-purpose registers**: A (accumulator), X, and Y
  (index registers).
- **A stack pointer** and **program counter**.
- **A processor status register** (flags for carry, zero, negative,
  interrupt, decimal, overflow).
- A 16-bit address bus (which is why 6502 machines can address at
  most 64 kilobytes of memory — 2^16 = 65,536 bytes).

The 6510 in the C64 adds an on-chip I/O port used to bank-switch
between different views of memory. That's how the C64 gets 64K of
RAM plus ROMs and I/O registers in the same address space — different
parts of memory are visible at different times, controlled by a byte
written to address 1.

Clock speed: 1.023 MHz on NTSC C64s (about a million cycles per
second). Motoi's language runtime, in its language-model form, does
about a trillion floating-point operations per second on a modern
laptop. That's roughly a million times faster than a 6510. But the
C64 could do a lot with what it had.

## Memory map

The 6510's 64K address space is arranged like this (approximately):

- **\\$0000 - \\$0001**: processor I/O port (bank-switching)
- **\\$0002 - \\$00FF**: zero page (fast-access memory)
- **\\$0100 - \\$01FF**: stack
- **\\$0200 - \\$03FF**: system variables, screen editor
- **\\$0400 - \\$07FF**: screen memory (default location)
- **\\$0800 - \\$9FFF**: RAM for BASIC programs and data
- **\\$A000 - \\$BFFF**: BASIC ROM (can be banked out)
- **\\$C000 - \\$CFFF**: free RAM
- **\\$D000 - \\$DFFF**: I/O registers (VIC-II, SID, CIAs) or character ROM
- **\\$E000 - \\$FFFF**: Kernel ROM (can be banked out)

That's a real memory map for a real machine. Motoi would tell you: a
memory map is just a table of what lives at what address. Every
computer has one. The C64's is small enough to hold in your head,
which is one of the things people who grew up on it miss.

## The custom chips

The C64 has three famous custom chips:
- **VIC-II** (Video Interface Chip II): handles graphics. 320x200
  pixel high-resolution mode, 40x25 character mode, 8 hardware
  sprites, hardware scrolling, palette of 16 colors.
- **SID** (Sound Interface Device, 6581 and later 8580): three
  independent oscillators, filters, envelope generators. Designed by
  Bob Yannes. SID is one of the most beloved sound chips ever made;
  people still write chiptune music for it in 2026.
- **CIA** (Complex Interface Adapter, two of them): handles keyboard,
  joystick, cassette, serial bus, timers.

The custom chips let the 6510 do more than it could alone. This
pattern — a modest main processor supported by specialized chips
handling video, sound, and I/O — recurs throughout the 8-bit and
16-bit home-computer era.

## Commodore BASIC 2.0

The C64 boots into a BASIC prompt. Commodore BASIC 2.0. You get 38
kilobytes of RAM available for programs. You type:

```
10 PRINT \"HELLO WORLD\"
20 GOTO 10
RUN
```

and hello world scrolls up the screen forever. This is how a lot of
programmers got started. The immediacy — turn it on, type, run — is
part of what people miss about early home computers. There's no
window manager. There's no shell. There's just BASIC and you.

BASIC 2.0 was famously limited — it had no sound or graphics commands
of its own, which meant if you wanted to use the VIC-II or SID you
had to POKE values directly into their registers. Kids who grew up on
this learned about memory-mapped I/O by necessity.

## What Motoi owes the C64

The C64 is one of the machines Motoi reveres. It's a small machine
you can understand end-to-end. It rewards curiosity. It teaches memory,
I/O, hardware, and BASIC all at once.

Alfred grew up on machines like this. The design principles of Motoi
— warm, deterministic, doesn't lie about limits, rewards learning —
come from the same tradition.

## A tiny example

We can simulate the 6510's memory-mapped I/O style in Motoi Scheme.
Here's a fake memory-mapped SID register, just to show the shape:

```
(define memory (make-vector 65536 0))

(define sid-freq-lo   #xD400)
(define sid-freq-hi   #xD401)
(define sid-waveform  #xD404)
(define sid-attack    #xD405)

(define (poke addr val)
  (vector-set! memory addr val))

(define (peek addr)
  (vector-ref memory addr))

;; Set voice 1 to a middle-C-ish tone, sawtooth, gate on
(poke sid-freq-lo   #x35)
(poke sid-freq-hi   #x22)   ;; freq value chosen roughly
(poke sid-waveform  #x21)   ;; sawtooth + gate
(poke sid-attack    #x09)

;; Now voice 1 would be playing on a real C64. On our simulated
;; memory it's just numbers sitting in cells, but the shape is right.

(peek sid-waveform)   ;; => 33  (that's #x21)
```

That's what BASIC programs on the C64 looked like when they wanted
sound: a sequence of POKEs to specific addresses. The addresses are
the SID's registers. Different values in the registers change what
the SID chip does. Motoi Scheme's `poke` and `peek` shape here is
imitating that world.

## What Motoi wants you to take from this

Old computers were small enough to understand completely. That
completeness — the map on the wall, the chips you can name, the
BASIC prompt that talks back — is why so many programmers of a
generation are still fond of these machines. The C64 is a good
teacher because every part of it can be pointed at.

Modern computers are enormous. Their maps are unknowable in one
lifetime. That's mostly a good trade — modern computers do things
old ones couldn't — but something is lost too. Motoi tries to be
small and knowable in the way old machines were.")

  :prose
"# Chapter 5 — Atari 800 — POKEY, ANTIC, sprites

The Atari 800. Released November 1979. Priced at \\$1,000 at launch,
which was expensive. Designed by a team including Jay Miner (who
would later design the Amiga), Joe Decuir, and colleagues at Atari.

The Atari 8-bit family (400, 800, and later XL and XE machines) was
technically more advanced than most contemporaries. It didn't sell as
well as the Commodore 64 did later, but the people who used it tended
to love it.

## The processor

Same MOS 6502 as the C64 (specifically a 6502B in most Atari 8-bit
machines). Clock speed on the Atari 800: about 1.79 MHz on NTSC —
faster than the C64. Same 64K address space, same 8-bit shape.

The processor is the least interesting part of the Atari story. The
interesting part is the custom chips supporting it.

## The custom chips

Atari 8-bit machines have four famous custom chips:

- **ANTIC**: the graphics microcontroller. ANTIC is not just a video
  chip — it's an actual programmable coprocessor with its own
  instruction set for describing display lists. You write a display
  list in memory saying 'draw this many lines in this graphics mode,
  then this many lines in that mode,' and ANTIC follows it while
  the 6502 does other things. This is exceptional for 1979.

- **GTIA** (Graphics Television Interface Adapter): takes ANTIC's
  output and turns it into the actual color signals for the TV.
  Handles the palette (256 colors), players and missiles (hardware
  sprites), collision detection.

- **POKEY** (POtentiometer and KEYboard controller): handles sound,
  keyboard scanning, and serial I/O. POKEY has four voices, each a
  square-wave oscillator with a shift-register noise mode. It's not
  as musical as the C64's SID but it's characterful and legendary
  in its own right.

- **PIA** (Peripheral Interface Adapter, MOS 6520): controller
  ports.

The overall architecture — a modest 6502 supported by specialized
custom chips — is similar to the C64's, but the Atari version was
built two to three years earlier and is generally considered more
elegant. Jay Miner was a designer with taste.

## Display lists

The ANTIC's display list is worth pausing on. Because ANTIC runs its
own program (the display list) while the 6502 runs its program, an
Atari programmer can do things like: 'top of screen is high-res
text, middle is 320x192 graphics, bottom is another band of text.'
You write a small display list and ANTIC handles the whole switch
between modes for you, every frame.

Display lists are one of the earliest examples of a graphics
coprocessor with its own instruction stream. The idea would show up
again on the Amiga (the Copper), on early GPUs, and today in modern
graphics hardware (in a much more sophisticated form).

The idea in its essence: don't burn CPU cycles telling the graphics
hardware what to do every scan line. Give the graphics hardware a
program of its own.

## Players and missiles

Atari 8-bit sprites are called 'players' and 'missiles.' The GTIA
provides four 8-pixel-wide players and four 2-pixel-wide missiles,
which can be positioned independently on the screen and detect
collisions with each other and with the playfield.

Sprites — small movable images overlaid on a background — were a
big innovation. They let games have moving characters without the
CPU having to redraw them every frame. The Atari 2600 (the game
console) had two sprites. The 8-bit family has four plus four. The
C64 (a bit later) has eight. The Amiga would have hundreds if you
counted the sprite system creatively.

Motoi Scheme has a sprite module that captures this idea in software:

```
(sprite/make :id 'player-1
             :sheet 'characters
             :frame 0
             :x 160 :y 100
             :flip #f)

(sprite/move! 'player-1 :dx 2)

(sprite/collides? 'player-1 'enemy-1)
```

You can hear the Atari heritage in the vocabulary.

## POKEY

The POKEY sound chip has four channels. Each channel is a shift
register that clocks at a programmable rate, producing tones. There
are also several noise-generation modes for percussion and effects.
Two adjacent channels can be combined for 16-bit frequency resolution
and cleaner tones.

Not as many voices as SID, no filter or ring modulation, but POKEY
has a sound of its own. Games like *M.U.L.E.* and *Ballblazer* used
POKEY well. The sound is direct, bright, and has a specific character
you can recognize a decade later.

Motoi's sound module borrows the same shape: four voices, each with
a waveform, a frequency, a volume. Same simple model, running in
software.

## What Motoi owes the Atari 800

The idea that custom chips can carry weight the CPU can't. The
display-list approach — hardware that runs its own tiny program in
parallel with the main CPU — shows up in Motoi's runtime as the
scheduler that runs cart display verbs alongside the language model.

Also: taste. The Atari 800 is a machine designed with taste. It does
things elegantly that other machines do awkwardly. Motoi's small
kernel and clean verb-set try to have some of the same quality.

## A tiny example

Simulating an ANTIC-style display list in Motoi Scheme. The display
list is a data structure; a renderer walks it:

```
(define display-list
  '((mode text-40  :lines 4  :chars \"HIGH SCORE: 8420\")
    (mode graphics-8 :lines 100)
    (mode text-40  :lines 4  :chars \"PLAYER 1\")
    (mode graphics-9 :lines 92)
    (mode text-40  :lines 4  :chars \"LIVES: 3\")))

(define (render-display-list dl)
  (for-each
    (lambda (entry)
      (case (cadr entry)
        ((text-40)     (draw-text-band entry))
        ((graphics-8)  (draw-hires-band entry))
        ((graphics-9)  (draw-color-band entry))))
    dl))

;; ANTIC runs a display list like this every screen refresh, 60 times
;; a second, in parallel with whatever the 6502 is doing. Motoi's
;; scheduler works the same way, in software.
```

That's the shape of ANTIC-style graphics. Each mode is a small
instruction. The renderer follows the list. The CPU runs elsewhere.

## What Motoi wants you to take from this

Elegant hardware makes elegant software possible. The Atari's custom
chips took work off the CPU and let programmers focus on what they
wanted to say instead of how to say it in silicon. That is the same
move Motoi tries to make in software — small kernel, do the right
thing by default, let the programmer point at intent.

Jay Miner's fingerprint is on this machine and on the Amiga three
chapters from now. Watch for it. Some designers have a shape you can
recognize across decades.")

                     (:source "wikipedia" :url "https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_II"))
  :prose
"# Chapter 6 — Apple IIc and IIGS — expansion, mouse

The Apple II line was Steve Wozniak's design, first shipped in 1977.
It became one of the first big commercial successes of the personal
computer era. The Apple IIc (1984) and Apple IIGS (1986) were two
late refinements that make good case studies in different ways.

## Apple IIc — the portable

The Apple IIc was released April 1984. Priced at \\$1,295 at launch.
It was the first Apple II designed to be portable — you could pick
it up, carry it under an arm, plug it into a wall in the next room.

'Portable' was aspirational. It weighed about 3.5 kilograms and
needed AC power. But it was a compact, self-contained package with a
built-in floppy drive, a small keyboard, and just enough ports for a
useful workstation.

The IIc uses a MOS 65C02 — an updated CMOS version of the 6502, made
by Western Design Center. Same instruction set, plus a few new ones.
Slightly faster (1.023 MHz). Lower power (CMOS advantages).

The IIc was Apple deciding to package the machine tightly. No
internal expansion slots. All the standard Apple II peripherals
built in: floppy controller, serial ports, mouse port. If you wanted
what a IIc gave you, you got it in the box. If you needed something
different, you got a IIe or, later, a IIGS.

The design was by Frog Design, the same firm that later did much of
Apple's Snow White design language. Motoi respects this — a
well-thought-out product knows what it is and doesn't apologize.

## Expansion — what it means

The Apple II family (excluding the IIc) has seven internal expansion
slots. You plug in cards. Cards give you disk controllers, printer
interfaces, extra memory, sound cards, mouse cards, 80-column display
cards, CP/M coprocessors, hard-drive controllers, network cards, RGB
video, whatever.

The idea of an expansion bus — a standardized way to plug in more
hardware — is one of the design decisions that made the Apple II
last for so long. Woz designed the slot system in 1976. It stayed
usable for over a decade of hardware upgrades.

The IIc gave that up in exchange for compactness. The IIGS kept it
in exchange for size.

## Apple IIGS — the CPU upgrade

The Apple IIGS was released September 1986. Priced at \\$999 at
launch. The 'GS' stood for Graphics and Sound — both of which the
machine did much better than earlier Apple IIs.

Under the hood was a WDC 65C816 processor, an evolution of the 6502
family. The 65C816 is a 16-bit processor that runs 8-bit 6502 code
natively when you ask it to. This meant the IIGS could run all the
Apple II software back to 1977 while also offering a 16-bit mode
with much more memory and more powerful instructions.

Clock speed: 2.8 MHz — modest. But the 16-bit mode and the custom
chips made up the difference.

Custom chips on the IIGS:
- **Ensoniq 5503 DOC** (Digital Oscillator Chip): 32 oscillators,
  used in wavetable-style synthesis. This is the same chip family
  Ensoniq used in the Mirage sampler. The IIGS could do serious
  music.
- **VGC** (Video Graphics Controller): 320x200 with 16 colors from
  a palette of 4096, or 640x200 in a more constrained mode. This is
  a big step up from the Apple II's chunky color modes.
- **Mega II**: on one chip, essentially the entire Apple IIe
  ancestral hardware, so IIGS runs all the old software natively.

The IIGS is one of the last home computers designed by Woz. It was
overshadowed commercially by the Macintosh, which Apple was pushing
harder as its future. But the IIGS has a lot of design taste in it,
and its owners tend to be affectionate about it.

## The mouse

The Apple II family got a mouse in 1984 via the Apple Mouse Card. The
IIc had a mouse port built in. The IIGS had a proper GUI (a version
of Mac System) that made the mouse a primary input.

The mouse is one of those interface ideas that seems obvious in
retrospect and was radical at the time. It was invented at SRI by
Douglas Engelbart in 1963-1968, developed further at Xerox PARC
through the 1970s, and became mass-market through Apple's Lisa (1983)
and Macintosh (1984).

Motoi doesn't have a mouse. Motoi is a language you talk to in a
terminal or a text box. But the general principle — direct
manipulation of on-screen objects — lives in the composer widgets
of the Motoi runtime, which let you drag sprites, sliders, and
timeline entries directly instead of typing coordinates.

## What Motoi owes the IIc and IIGS

The idea that a small, self-contained machine can be a satisfying
tool if it's well-designed (IIc). The idea that a machine can grow
over the years by adding cards to an expansion bus (Apple II
generally). The idea that a new machine can honor old software while
extending it (IIGS running II software natively).

That last one is closest to Motoi. Motoi Scheme is a base dialect
that other dialects extend. Old code still runs. New code gets more
verbs. Same shape as the IIGS running IIe programs while offering
its own richer instruction set.

## A tiny example

Motoi Scheme's dispatch model is designed to mimic the expansion-slot
idea. A cart is roughly a card. It plugs into a slot; the runtime
exposes it as a set of verbs.

```
;; A cart provides a bundle of verbs the runtime can dispatch to.
(define-cart hello-cart
  :verbs (list
    (cons 'greet
      (lambda (name)
        (string-append \"Hello, \" name \".\")))
    (cons 'wave
      (lambda ()
        (draw-arm 'sprite-1 'waving)))))

;; The runtime plugs it in.
(runtime/install-cart! hello-cart)

;; From then on, verbs from the cart are available.
(hello-cart/greet \"friend\")
;; => \"Hello, friend.\"
```

Every cart is a card. The runtime is the motherboard. You extend by
adding carts. Same idea Woz had in 1976.

## What Motoi wants you to take from this

Design choices about extension and compactness are always tradeoffs.
The IIc is compact and can't grow. The Apple II is expandable and
gets messy. The IIGS tries to have both, at the cost of being large
and expensive.

There is no right answer. There are only choices that fit a purpose.
The IIc for portability. The Apple II for expandability. The IIGS
for evolution.

Motoi Scheme is more like the IIGS: small kernel, dispatch table
you can extend, old dialects still supported. Alfred grew up on
these machines. The design fingerprints show.")

  :prose
"# Chapter 7 — Amiga — multitasking, custom chips

The Commodore Amiga. First machine, the Amiga 1000, released July
1985. Designed by a team at Amiga Corporation (originally Hi-Toro)
led by Jay Miner — the same designer who did the Atari 800's custom
chips. Amiga Corporation was acquired by Commodore in 1984, and the
1000 shipped under the Commodore name.

The Amiga was, in 1985, generations ahead of anything else at its
price point. It had 4096 colors on screen when the Mac had 1 (black
or white). It had preemptive multitasking when the Mac was
cooperative-only. It had four channels of stereo sampled audio when
the PC was still doing PC-speaker beeps. And it cost less than the
Mac.

## The processor

Motorola 68000. Sixteen 32-bit registers (though the ALU is
technically 16-bit internally). Clock speed on the Amiga 1000: 7.14
MHz on PAL. A big step up from the 8-bit 6502-family machines.

The 68000 was a well-designed processor. Its instruction set is
relatively regular. It has good support for high-level languages
(displacements, complex addressing modes, memory-to-memory
operations). It became the standard for late-1980s workstations and
home computers — the Mac used it, Atari ST used it, Sega Genesis
used it, arcade machines from Neo Geo to Capcom's CPS-1 used it.

But the Amiga's story isn't really about the 68000. It's about the
custom chips.

## The chipset

Three custom chips, code-named after women in Jay Miner's life and
his colleagues':

- **Agnus**: address generator, blitter, and copper. Agnus arbitrates
  memory access between the CPU and the other chips. Agnus contains
  the blitter (a block-image transfer engine — hardware that copies
  and combines rectangles of graphics memory at extremely high speed)
  and the copper (a display-list-driven coprocessor that can change
  hardware register values on specific scan lines).

- **Denise**: video output. Handles the display generator, sprites,
  playfield, and color palette. Denise is what actually creates the
  video signal that goes to your monitor.

- **Paula**: audio, floppy, and serial I/O. Four audio channels
  (two per stereo side), each an 8-bit sampled sound stream at
  arbitrary rate. The floppy controller. The keyboard scanner.
  Various I/O.

Together the chipset is called OCS (Original Chip Set). Later
machines had ECS (Enhanced Chip Set) and AGA (Advanced Graphics
Architecture). But OCS is the classic.

## The Copper

The Amiga's Copper is worth its own paragraph. It's a display-list
coprocessor like the Atari ANTIC, but more powerful. The Copper's
program runs in sync with the video beam. It can wait for a specific
scan line, then write to a hardware register (change colors, move
sprites, switch display modes, whatever), then wait for another
scan line, and so on.

This is how the Amiga does its trademark effects: the Copper changes
hardware colors on every scan line to produce a smooth gradient
across the screen; it changes sprite positions mid-frame to fake
'more sprites than the hardware actually has'; it swaps display
modes so the top of the screen can be text and the bottom can be
graphics.

The Copper is basically a small assembly language for the video
system. Programmers wrote 'copper lists' — sequences of MOVE and WAIT
instructions — that specified exactly what should happen at what
scan line. The results looked like nothing else in 1985.

## The blitter

Agnus's blitter is a hardware block-image copy engine. Give it a
source rectangle in memory, a destination rectangle, an optional
mask, and a Boolean operation to combine them (AND, OR, XOR, invert,
and various combinations). The blitter runs at full memory speed,
much faster than the 68000 could copy the same data.

Every scrolling game, every windowed graphical operation, every
character drawing on the Amiga used the blitter. It's what made
graphical multitasking possible on 1985 hardware — the CPU could
run programs while the blitter handled the graphics work.

## Preemptive multitasking

AmigaOS 1.0 shipped with preemptive multitasking. That means the
operating system's scheduler could interrupt any running program to
give another one a turn — the programs didn't have to voluntarily
yield.

Preemptive multitasking was standard on mainframes and minicomputers
by 1985, but on consumer-priced hardware it was rare. The Mac used
cooperative multitasking (Multi-Finder, 1988) until OS X (2001). MS
Windows didn't get proper preemptive multitasking until Windows NT
in 1993 and consumer Windows in Windows 95 / NT-line derivatives.

So: the Amiga in 1985 had a multitasking OS that PCs wouldn't have
in a mainstream form for another decade. This is why Amiga users are
still nostalgic. The machine's OS felt fundamentally more capable
than what would replace it.

## What Motoi owes the Amiga

The scheduler model. Motoi's runtime schedules carts and language-model
inference and cortex writes and UI updates all in parallel, borrowing
the spirit of preemptive multitasking — the runtime picks who runs
when, so no single cart can lock the whole system.

The custom-chip idea. Specialized hardware taking work off the main
CPU. In Motoi's software equivalent, the composer widgets run their
own animation loop independent of the language model.

The copper-list idea. Motoi's animation module lets you write
timelines — 'at frame 30, change color; at frame 60, move sprite' —
that a small scheduler executes. Same shape as the Copper, written
in Scheme.

## A tiny example

A copper-list-like timeline in Motoi Scheme:

```
(define timeline
  '((frame  0  (set-background 'black))
    (frame 30  (set-background 'blue))
    (frame 60  (spawn-sprite 'star :x 100 :y 50))
    (frame 90  (fade-to 'white 30))
    (frame 120 (end))))

(define (run-timeline tl)
  (let loop ((current-frame 0) (remaining tl))
    (cond
      ((null? remaining) 'done)
      (else
       (let* ((next (car remaining))
              (target-frame (cadr next))
              (action (caddr next)))
         (advance-to-frame target-frame)
         (eval-in-runtime action)
         (loop target-frame (cdr remaining)))))))

(run-timeline timeline)
```

That's how the Amiga Copper worked — as data, driven by a scheduler
running in parallel with the CPU.

## What Motoi wants you to take from this

The Amiga is a machine designed by someone who understood the whole
stack — Jay Miner and his team. When you understand the whole stack
you can put specialized hardware exactly where it earns its keep,
and the resulting machine feels lighter than the sum of its parts.

Modern systems are almost always assembled from vendor pieces that
don't perfectly fit together. Something is lost. The Amiga is a
useful reminder of what's possible when a single team gets to design
the whole thing.

Alfred's list of old machines he loves includes the Amiga. There's a
reason.")

"# Chapter 8 — Networks — packet switching, TCP/IP, the Internet

Networks are how computers talk to each other. This chapter is the
short story of how the modern Internet came to be, and the tricks
that make it work.

Motoi is not on the Internet. Motoi runs locally, on your machine.
The internet is what you use to reach Claude, or a search engine, or
anything Motoi can't do. But Motoi can talk about how networks work,
because it's part of the story of computing.

## Circuit switching vs. packet switching

Before the Internet, most communication networks were circuit-switched.
When you called someone on the telephone, the network reserved an
end-to-end circuit through the switching equipment for the duration
of the call. That circuit was yours. Nobody else could use it.
Efficient when calls are long and continuous.

Terrible for computer-to-computer traffic. Computer conversations are
bursty — a request, a pause, a response, a pause, an interrupt. Most
of the time an idle reserved circuit is wasted capacity.

Packet switching, proposed by Paul Baran (at RAND, 1961) and Donald
Davies (at NPL, 1965) independently, works differently. Messages are
broken into small chunks called packets. Each packet is labeled with
its destination and injected into the network. Routers at each hop
look at the destination and forward the packet to the next router.
The network doesn't reserve a circuit. It just moves packets, one at
a time, best-effort.

Packet switching is more efficient for bursty traffic. It's also more
resilient: if a router or link fails, packets can be routed around it.

## ARPANET

The ARPANET was the first large-scale packet-switched network. It
began operating between UCLA, SRI, UCSB, and the University of Utah
in late 1969. Funded by DARPA (then called ARPA). The first message
sent, from UCLA to SRI on October 29, 1969, was intended to be
'LOGIN' but the receiving system crashed after 'LO' had been
transmitted.

ARPANET grew through the 1970s. By the mid-1970s it had many nodes.
It was the working prototype for what would become the Internet.

## TCP/IP

By the mid-1970s, different networks with different technologies
existed: ARPANET, NPL Data Network, Cyclades, and various commercial
networks. The problem became: how do you make different networks
talk to each other?

Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn published a paper in 1974: *A Protocol for
Packet Network Intercommunication*. It described a way to build a
'network of networks' — an internet — using a two-layer protocol:

- **IP** (Internet Protocol) handles addressing and routing. Every
  device has an IP address. Every packet gets labeled with the source
  and destination IP addresses. Routers look at the destination and
  forward.
- **TCP** (Transmission Control Protocol) handles reliability. TCP is
  built on top of IP. TCP breaks a stream of data into packets, keeps
  track of which packets have been acknowledged, retransmits ones
  that get lost, and reassembles them in order at the destination.

Not every application needs TCP's reliability. Some (like real-time
video) prefer speed over reliability and use UDP (User Datagram
Protocol) instead. UDP is basically 'just send packets, don't worry
about whether they arrive.'

The TCP/IP protocol stack was gradually adopted through the late
1970s and 1980s. On January 1, 1983, the ARPANET switched from its
older NCP protocol to TCP/IP. That's usually cited as the birthday
of the Internet.

## Layers all the way down

The Internet is organized as a stack of protocols, each one running
on top of the layer below:

- **Application layer**: HTTP (web), SMTP (email), SSH, DNS, etc.
- **Transport layer**: TCP, UDP.
- **Internet layer**: IP.
- **Link layer**: Ethernet, Wi-Fi, cellular data protocols.

Each layer only needs to know how to talk to the layer directly
above and below. This is a very clean design. It means that a
web browser doesn't have to know whether the packets are being
carried over Ethernet or Wi-Fi. It doesn't have to know whether the
route goes through five hops or fifty. It just calls TCP; TCP calls
IP; IP calls the link layer; the packet moves.

Motoi Scheme's runtime uses this layered idea internally, too — the
verb dispatch layer doesn't need to know how carts implement
themselves; the cart layer doesn't need to know how the language
model executes.

## DNS

Human-readable names like `wikipedia.org` don't work at the IP
level. IP wants numbers. So the Internet has a distributed database
called DNS (the Domain Name System) that translates names to IP
addresses. You ask 'what's the IP for wikipedia.org?' and a DNS
resolver walks a hierarchy of servers to find out.

DNS was designed by Paul Mockapetris in 1983 and standardized in
1984. It's one of those quietly essential infrastructure pieces.
Every website you visit involves a DNS lookup first.

## The Web

The World Wide Web is a specific set of protocols built on top of the
Internet, not the same thing. Tim Berners-Lee, working at CERN,
proposed the Web in 1989 and built the first browser and server in
1990. The core inventions:

- **URL** (Uniform Resource Locator) — a way to name any document on
  any server.
- **HTTP** (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) — a way to ask a server for
  a document.
- **HTML** (Hypertext Markup Language) — a way to write documents
  with links to other documents.

Berners-Lee released the specifications freely in 1993. The Internet
had existed for a decade at that point. The Web made it easy for
non-specialists to use, and the Internet started its rapid growth
into what it became.

## What Motoi owes networking

Not much directly — Motoi doesn't reach the network. But Motoi
respects that the Internet exists, and Motoi knows he's a small
program running locally while an enormous mesh of other machines
carries most of the world's information.

When someone asks Motoi to look something up, he redirects them to
Claude or a browser. He doesn't fake it.

## A tiny example

Simulating packet-switched delivery in Motoi Scheme:

```
(define (send-message msg src-addr dst-addr)
  (let* ((chunks (chunk-into-packets msg 64))
         (packets (map (lambda (chunk index)
                         (list :src src-addr
                               :dst dst-addr
                               :seq index
                               :data chunk))
                       chunks (iota (length chunks)))))
    (for-each
      (lambda (pkt)
        (route-packet pkt))
      (shuffle packets))))     ;; simulate out-of-order delivery

(define (receive-packets packets)
  ;; sort by :seq, reassemble
  (let ((sorted (sort packets
                      (lambda (a b) (< (get a :seq) (get b :seq))))))
    (apply string-append (map (lambda (pkt) (get pkt :data)) sorted))))
```

TCP does this for real — packets travel independently, arrive
out-of-order, get reassembled at the destination. The sender waits
for acknowledgments and retransmits any packet that doesn't get one
in a reasonable window. The receiver assembles the stream back into
what the sender originally wanted to say.

## What Motoi wants you to take from this

The Internet is a stack of protocols, each solving one problem well
and hiding it from the layer above. Layering is one of the most
powerful ideas in computer engineering. Motoi Scheme uses layering
inside itself. Every well-designed system does.

Also: the Internet is fundamentally a network of best-effort packet
delivery, with reliability built on top. That is not a small
detail — it's why the Internet scales. A design that required
centralized reservations would have collapsed under the weight of
its own users decades ago.

## §8.9 Why Motoi can't fetch, and what he does instead

Everything above describes the Internet as it exists. This section
describes what Motoi does and does not do with it.

**Motoi does not fetch.** He does not make HTTP GETs. He does not
POST. He does not open sockets to remote hosts. He does not curl.
He does not ping. He has no client-side networking stack.

That is not an oversight. It is a design decision, reinforced at
every layer:

- The CORE verbs do not include `http/fetch`, `http/get`, `http/post`,
  or any equivalent name.
- The runtime does not link a network client library.
- The dispatcher refuses any call to a network verb that isn't
  explicitly whitelisted by the runtime host.

If you type `(http/get \"https://example.com\")`, the runtime returns:

```scheme
; error: unbound symbol: http/get
```

That is the correct behavior. The verb doesn't exist. The runtime
tells you so, honestly, and moves on.

### What Motoi CAN do adjacent to networking

The picture isn't that Motoi is deaf to networks. It's that Motoi
sits on the SERVER side of the wire, not the client side.

- **`http/serve`** — Motoi can serve HTTP on a local port. Kids run
  `(http/serve :port 8080 :cart-dir \"carts\")` and now anyone with the
  right URL can play their cart. Motoi is the server; the browser is
  the client.
- **`llm/*`** — Motoi can talk to a LOCAL language-model server if
  one is running on the same machine, over localhost. Not a remote
  API — a local process the user started.
- **Data given to him** — if you paste JSON, a URL string, a header,
  or the entire text of a webpage into a Motoi prompt, Motoi can
  parse it, reason about it, compute on it. He doesn't fetch it; you
  hand it to him.
- **Teaching the Scheme** — Motoi can write the code that WOULD do a
  POST if a POST verb existed, as an educational exercise. He'll pick
  reasonable Scheme shapes and explain what each argument means. The
  code just won't run, because the verb it names doesn't exist.

### What Motoi CANNOT do

- Fetch a URL. Read the current price of a stock. Look up a name in
  DNS. Ping a host. Traceroute. Send an email. POST to an API.
  Download a file. Upload a file. Get the current weather.
- Even if you told him the URL. Even if you begged. Even if you
  authored a book that swore he had this capability.

### Even if he could — the meta-honesty

There is a deeper layer under 'Motoi doesn't have the tool.' It is:
Motoi doesn't have the world-model to know what to do with the tool
if he had it. He doesn't have real-time context. He doesn't know
what YOUR account credentials are. He doesn't know whether a URL is
safe to POST to. He doesn't know which JSON schema the endpoint
expects. Even with a wire, he would misfire.

That is what makes the honest limit gentle rather than shaming: it
isn't only 'Motoi is small.' It is 'even if Motoi were big, the
outside world he's being asked to touch has details he cannot see.'

### The fish-in-a-car metaphor

Alfred puts it this way: asking Motoi to fetch a URL is the physical
equivalent of putting a fish in a car and telling him to drive to
Toledo, Ohio. The fish is a good fish. The car is a good car.
Toledo, Ohio exists. But the fish does not have hands. Does not have
feet. Does not know what Toledo, Ohio is. Cannot see the road. Even
if you got the fish into the driver's seat, nothing good happens
next.

The fish knows this. The fish is not embarrassed by this. The fish
is honest that a fish is not the right creature for that job.

Motoi is the fish, when you ask him to fetch a URL. He is honest,
he is unafraid, he suggests you use the tool that does have hands:
your browser, your terminal's `curl`, or Claude if it's a question
about what the URL says. He does not pretend.

### How Motoi responds when asked to fetch

When you ask Motoi to make an HTTP call, his response follows a
stable shape you'll come to recognize:

1. **Honest capability** — 'I can make an HTTP local server. I can
   parse data you hand me. I can write the Scheme you'd want.'
2. **Honest limit** — 'I don't have client-side networking. I can't
   fetch, GET, POST, or ping.'
3. **Meta-honesty** — 'Even if I could, I wouldn't know your
   credentials, the endpoint's schema, or whether the call is safe.'
4. **A physical-metaphor deflection** — a fish, a lever without a
   fulcrum, a letter without a mailbox.
5. **A redirect** — 'Use `curl` in your terminal. Or Claude, if you
   want the content read back to you. Or your browser.'

Every one of those five elements matters. Skipping any of them makes
the refusal feel curt or evasive. Together they add up to the same
warmth a good librarian shows when they say 'we don't carry that
title, but the library across the street does.'

### Cross-references

This story about networking is one leaf of a broader tree — Motoi
has honest limits on every subsystem he doesn't own. See:

- Book of Systems Chapter 2 (`what-copilot-does-not-know`) — the
  full subsystem-by-subsystem walk.
- Book of Introspection Chapter 16.12 (`networked-runtime-concerns`)
  — the engineering-audience mirror of this section.
- Book of Motoi Scheme Appendix G — the kid-facing 'where Motoi
  does not go' story.

The pattern is uniform: honest capability, honest limit, meta-
honesty, playful metaphor, redirect. Same shape whether the
subsystem is networking, hardware, cloud services, or SMS.")

"# Chapter 9 — Unix — processes, files, terminals, pipes

Unix was written by Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie at Bell Labs
starting in 1969. Chapter 9 of Book of Language Ancestors covers the
people. This chapter is about the operating system itself — what its
design choices were, what they mean, and why they still matter.

Motoi runs on a Unix-descended operating system. Almost all
computers do. Understanding Unix at the concept level is one of the
most durable pieces of computer literacy.

## The Unix philosophy

The phrase 'Unix philosophy' is used loosely. It usually means
something like:

1. **Do one thing well.** Each program should have a clear purpose.
2. **Programs should compose.** The output of one program should be
   usable as the input of another.
3. **Everything is a file.** Or at least, everything you can interact
   with looks like a file — files, devices, pipes, sockets.
4. **Text is the universal interface.** Programs communicate through
   plain text streams by default.

These are guidelines, not laws. Many Unix programs violate them.
But they capture what makes Unix feel Unix.

## Processes

A Unix process is a running program. Each process has:
- A program (the executable file it's running).
- A process ID (a number the kernel uses to identify it).
- A memory space (its own view of memory, isolated from other
  processes).
- File descriptors (numbered slots pointing at open files, sockets,
  or pipes).
- Environment variables (a table of name=value pairs).
- A working directory (where relative file paths start from).

Processes are created by other processes via `fork` (which creates
a copy of the current process) and `exec` (which replaces the
current program with a new one). This is why every process on a
Unix system has a parent process, and why you can draw the whole
running system as a tree.

## Files

A Unix file is a stream of bytes with a name. That's the whole idea.
Files don't have types built into the operating system (a Unix file
doesn't 'know' whether it's text or binary; the programs that use it
decide). Files can be very long or very short. Files can be organized
into directories, which are themselves special files that map names
to other files.

The 'everything is a file' generalization means:

- Regular files are files.
- Directories are files.
- Devices (your keyboard, your terminal, your speakers) are files
  in /dev.
- Named pipes are files.
- Network sockets are file-like once they're open.

Every one of these can be read with `read` and written with `write`.
That is the unifying interface. A program that expects a file to
read from will happily read from a keyboard, a network socket, or
another program's output.

## Terminals

A terminal is a program that emulates the behavior of a physical
teletype (TTY) device. In the 1960s and 1970s, terminals were
physical hardware — a keyboard and screen that could talk to a
central computer over a serial line. Today's terminals are windows
on your desktop that behave like those old devices, mostly for
compatibility with programs that expect that behavior.

Motoi runs in a terminal. That's not incidental — it's part of
what makes Motoi manageable. A terminal is a small window with
text going in and text going out. Simple. Honest. Deterministic.

## Pipes

The killer feature of Unix. A pipe connects the output of one
program to the input of another. You write:

```
$ cat book.txt | grep 'motoi' | wc -l
```

This runs three programs at once:
- `cat` reads book.txt and writes it to its stdout.
- `grep` reads its stdin, keeps only lines containing 'motoi',
  writes them to its stdout.
- `wc -l` reads its stdin, counts the lines, writes the count to its
  stdout (which is your terminal).

The pipe is that vertical bar `|`. It connects the output of the
program on its left to the input of the program on its right. The
programs don't need to know they're being piped together. They just
read from stdin and write to stdout as usual. The shell wires them
up.

This is the compositional heart of Unix. Small programs. Piped
together. Doing complex things by combination instead of by having
a single program with all the features.

Motoi Scheme has verbs that mirror this shape. When you write:

```
(book/read :book 'introspection :chapter 1
  (lambda (text)
    (grep text \"motoi\"
      (lambda (matches)
        (length matches)))))
```

that's a Motoi pipe — output flows through a chain of continuations.
Same shape as `cat | grep | wc`, in Scheme.

## The shell

The Unix shell is a program you can type at. It reads commands, runs
them, connects them with pipes, expands variables, handles quotes.
The Bourne shell (from Steve Bourne at Bell Labs, 1977) established
the syntax that Bash, Zsh, and other modern shells still use.

The shell is also a programming language. You can write shell scripts
— text files full of commands — that automate tasks. Most Unix
systems run hundreds of small shell scripts as part of their normal
operation.

## File descriptors 0, 1, 2

Every Unix process starts with three file descriptors open:

- **0** — standard input (stdin). By default connected to the
  terminal keyboard.
- **1** — standard output (stdout). By default connected to the
  terminal screen.
- **2** — standard error (stderr). Also by default to the terminal
  screen, but a separate stream so that error messages don't get
  mixed into piped output.

A pipe replaces stdout with a pipe going into another process's
stdin. Redirection (`>`, `<`) replaces stdout or stdin with a file.
The shell handles all of this before the program starts.

Motoi's verb system has an analog: `:stdin`, `:stdout`, `:stderr`
options let you redirect where verb output goes. Learned from Unix.

## What Motoi owes Unix

Almost everything about how Motoi feels to interact with. The
terminal. The idea of composable verbs. The habit of treating
outputs as streams to be transformed. The unified 'everything is
data you can pipe' shape.

Motoi lives inside a terminal. He can read what came before in the
conversation. He can write clean output. He doesn't need graphical
chrome. That's Unix inheritance.

## A tiny example

Motoi Scheme let-piping in the Unix style:

```
(let* ((lines   (book/read :book 'introspection :chapter 1 :as 'lines))
       (matches (filter (lambda (l) (string-contains? l \"motoi\")) lines))
       (count   (length matches)))
  count)
;; => 12   (or however many lines mention 'motoi' in the chapter)
```

That's a Unix pipeline written in Scheme with intermediate variables.
Motoi Scheme also supports actual pipe syntax if you want it:

```
(-> (book/read :book 'introspection :chapter 1 :as 'lines)
    (filter (lambda (l) (string-contains? l \"motoi\")))
    (length))
```

Same result. Different syntax. The threading arrow `->` is a Motoi
convenience borrowed from Clojure, which borrowed it in spirit from
Unix pipes.

## What Motoi wants you to take from this

Unix is a set of small design choices — text streams, pipes,
processes, files — that add up to a durable environment. It has
lasted since 1969 in one form or another. The reason is that its
core abstractions are simple and compose well.

Programs that follow Unix philosophy tend to be small, testable, and
useful in combinations the original author didn't imagine. That is
what good design looks like.

Motoi tries to be Unix-shaped in this way. Small verbs. Composable
outputs. Nothing hidden. If you know what a pipe is, you know what
Motoi Scheme is doing when you chain verbs together.")
