# Chapter 5 — The Japanese bamboo flute

The shakuhachi is a length of bamboo with five holes and a
mouthpiece cut at an angle. It is blown across, not into. It has no
mechanism — no keys, no valves, no reeds. Every part of its sound
comes from the breath of the player and the shape of the
bamboo. That means, more than almost any other instrument on the
roster, the shakuhachi's voice is *the player breathing through
it*. If the breath is soft, the note is soft. If the breath wobbles,
the note wobbles. If the breath stops, the note stops — and the
silence after it stops is itself a musical event.

This chapter is about how the shakuhachi is synthesized, how its
breath control shapes every note, and — most importantly — how
silence is used as a note. The shakuhachi is the instrument in this
book that most rewards patience; it is also the instrument that most
punishes writing for it as if it were a Western flute.

*When I write for shakuhachi, I write silences first and notes
second. On a piano I write notes and let the silences fall out.
On a shakuhachi it is the reverse. The instrument is at its most
beautiful when it is not making a sound — you hear the breath
gathering, and then the breath comes, and the note is a
confession the silence made possible. If you write for it like
you would write for a flute, you will get a technically correct
passage that misses the whole point of the instrument.*

## 5.1 One breath, one note

The smallest shakuhachi program. One D4 for a whole beat.

```scheme
(begin
  (synth/select 'shakuhachi)
  (play/note 'd4 'whole))
```

You hear a warm, breathy D4. The onset is not instant — it swells in
over about a fifth of a second as the breath finds the pitch. The
middle wobbles very slightly (a natural micro-vibrato). The end
tapers as the breath runs out. Compare this to the piano's D4 from
Chapter 2 and the difference is total: this note *breathes*.

## 5.2 Breath pressure — the shakuhachi's dynamics

On the shakuhachi, dynamics are breath. Light breath gives a fragile
tone, on the edge of a whisper. Firm breath gives the natural sound.
Strong breath pushes the note into a bright, edgy character — the
shakuhachi's version of a shout.

```scheme
(begin
  (synth/select 'shakuhachi)
  (synth/breath! 'pressure 0.3)
  (play/note 'd4 'half)
  (synth/breath! 'pressure 0.6)
  (play/note 'd4 'half)
  (synth/breath! 'pressure 0.95)
  (play/note 'd4 'half))
```

Three D4s at three breath pressures. The first is barely there — the
listener has to lean in. The second is the natural voice. The third
has an edge, a slight overblown quality that reads as intensity.
Composers use the full range: quiet passages sit at 0.3 or 0.4;
climactic passages push to 0.9.

## 5.3 The breath as a note — silence as a musical event

The characteristic gesture of shakuhachi music is the *ma*: the
silence between phrases. `ma` is a Japanese concept meaning the
loaded, purposeful silence — not the absence of sound but the
presence of stillness. In music notation it becomes a rest, but a
rest that is meant to be *felt*.

```scheme
(begin
  (synth/select 'shakuhachi)
  (in-order
    (play/note 'd4 'half)
    (rest 'whole)
    (play/note 'f4 'half)
    (rest 'whole)
    (play/note 'a4 'whole)))
```

Three notes, two long rests between them. The rests are as long as
the notes. If you were reading this off a Western score you would
skip past the rests to see what the \"real\" notes are. On the
shakuhachi the rests are the real notes. The listener hears \"d4,
then a stillness where you notice the room, then f4, then a
stillness that is longer than the first because the ear has settled
into it, then a long a4 that resolves everything.\" The rests are
composed.

## 5.4 Portamento — the sliding note

Because there are no keys, the shakuhachi has continuous pitch. You
can slide between notes by changing your embouchure and your finger
position at the same time. `play/articulation! 'portamento` gives
you the slide.

```scheme
(begin
  (synth/select 'shakuhachi)
  (play/articulation! 'portamento)
  (in-order
    (play/note 'd4 'quarter)
    (play/note 'f4 'half)
    (play/note 'd4 'whole)))
```

The D slides up to F, holds, then slides back down to D. This is the
\"crying\" quality of the shakuhachi — the pitch does not step, it
sings. Overuse and it becomes maudlin. Used once in a phrase, at the
right moment, it is the most human sound a synthesizer can produce.

## 5.5 The bend — pushing a note off pitch and letting it return

Related to portamento but different: a bend is a momentary pitch
deviation followed by a return to the original pitch. On a real
shakuhachi you do it by tilting the flute or partially uncovering
a hole. `synth/breath! 'bend` schedules a small bend during a
sustained note.

```scheme
(begin
  (synth/select 'shakuhachi)
  (play/note 'd4 'quarter)
  (synth/breath! 'bend 0.2 'eighth)
  (play/note 'd4 'half)
  (play/note 'd4 'quarter))
```

Three D4s. The first is a plain onset. The second is a D4 that bends
slightly during its half-beat — the pitch drifts down about 20
cents, then returns. The third is another plain D4. The bend is a
touch of expression, not a change of note. In classical shakuhachi
music, bends are used to give a repeated pitch different characters
across a passage — the same note said three different ways.

## 5.6 A honkyoku fragment — a small piece in the tradition

Honkyoku is the solo shakuhachi tradition — pieces built entirely
around the instrument's breath and silence. Here is a small fragment
in the honkyoku shape: long notes, long silences, a slow phrase
built out of the pentatonic scale.

```scheme
(begin
  (tempo 40)
  (synth/select 'shakuhachi)
  (synth/breath! 'pressure 0.5)
  (in-order
    (play/note 'd4 'whole)
    (rest 'half)
    (play/articulation! 'portamento)
    (in-order
      (play/note 'd4 'quarter)
      (play/note 'f4 'half))
    (rest 'whole)
    (play/articulation! 'natural)
    (synth/breath! 'pressure 0.35)
    (play/note 'a4 'whole)
    (rest 'half)
    (synth/breath! 'pressure 0.6)
    (play/note 'f4 'whole)
    (rest 'whole)
    (play/note 'd4 'whole)))
```

Slow tempo (40 beats per minute is deliberately slow). A long D4
opens. A rest. A D that slides to F. A very long rest. A quiet A4.
Another rest. A firm F4. Another long rest. A final D4 that lands
the piece back where it began. Read the rests carefully — they are
half or full beats at 40 BPM, which is a genuine, uncomfortable-if-
you-are-not-used-to-it length of silence. That discomfort *is the
piece*. The listener is meant to notice their own breath during
those silences.

## 5.7 Composing for the shakuhachi — a rule of thumb

Here is a helper. Given a list of notes, wrap each one in
appropriate silence and breath so that the piece breathes.

```scheme
(begin
  (define (honkyoku-phrase notes)
    (in-order
      (map (lambda (pitch)
             (in-order
               (play/note pitch 'whole)
               (rest 'half)))
           notes)))
  (tempo 40)
  (synth/select 'shakuhachi)
  (synth/breath! 'pressure 0.5)
  (honkyoku-phrase '(d4 f4 a4 g4 f4 d4)))
```

A six-note melodic figure — a mode based on D — each note held for a
whole beat with a half-beat of silence after it. That is a very
simple shakuhachi phrase. Change the rest from `'half` to `'quarter`
and the piece becomes noticeably less patient. Change it to `'whole`
and the piece becomes ritualistic. The rest length is a compositional
choice as important as the notes.

*If I were teaching one lesson from this whole book it would be
this: the shakuhachi taught me that silence is a note. Not all
instruments treat silence that way. A piano rests to let a chord
resolve. A cello rests to breathe. But a shakuhachi rests to be
a shakuhachi — the silence is not the absence of the instrument,
it is the instrument being still. Once you can write silence as
a note, every other instrument in your palette gets deeper. You
stop writing music that fills the space and start writing music
that shapes it.*

> **Under the hood**
>
> The shakuhachi profile is a physical model of a blown open pipe:
> an air jet is modeled striking the edge of the mouthpiece, and
> the resulting oscillation excites the standing-wave modes of the
> bamboo tube. Breath pressure changes the air-jet velocity, which
> affects both amplitude and the overblow behavior — high pressure
> can push a note into its next harmonic. The natural micro-vibrato
> is a subtle random modulation of the pressure at the mouthpiece,
> modeling a real player's small breath instability. Portamento
> continuously varies the effective tube length; bends momentarily
> perturb the mouth-cavity model without changing the fingered
> length.

## What you know now

- The shakuhachi is a physically-modeled blown open pipe.
- `synth/breath!` controls pressure and bend — the shakuhachi's
  equivalent of dynamics and articulation.
- The shakuhachi has continuous pitch: portamento and bends are
  central, not decorative.
- Silence — `rest` — is a composed musical event on the shakuhachi.
  The rests are notes.
- Slow tempos and long rests are the honkyoku tradition; write for
  the instrument, not against it.

That is the end of the first five chapters of the Book of
Instruments. Next in the sequence: brass (chapter 6), then reeded
winds, then plucked strings in detail, and so on through the
roster. Every chapter is one family or one instrument, and every
program is a full runnable use of a specific voice.

# Chapter 6 — Brass

Brass instruments are lip-buzzers with resonant tubes. The player's lips vibrate against the mouthpiece; the tube shapes the vibration into a note. Trumpets are bright, trombones slide, French horns are round and dark, tubas are the low anchor.

Brass sounds like breath finding a shape. When it works, you hear the air first and the note second — the air is the material, the note is what the tube did with it.

## The brass roster

```scheme
(define brass
  '((trumpet    Bb  bright)
    (trombone   Bb  sliding)
    (horn       F   dark)
    (tuba       BBb low-anchor)
    (euphonium  Bb  round)))

(for-each (lambda (i) (display i) (newline)) brass)
```

Output:

```
(trumpet Bb bright)
(trombone Bb sliding)
(horn F dark)
(tuba BBb low-anchor)
(euphonium Bb round)
```

Five brass instruments, three properties each: name, home key, character.

## Playing a trumpet note

```scheme
(define (make-trumpet-note pitch dynamics articulation)
  (list 'trumpet 'pitch pitch 'dyn dynamics 'artic articulation))

(display (make-trumpet-note 'C5 'mf 'staccato)) (newline)
(display (make-trumpet-note 'A4 'ff 'sostenuto)) (newline)
```

Output:

```
(trumpet pitch C5 dyn mf artic staccato)
(trumpet pitch A4 dyn ff artic sostenuto)
```

## The slide

Trombones have the slide — pitch changes by continuous position, not discrete keys.

```scheme
(define (slide-position semitones-below-open)
  (case semitones-below-open
    ((0) '1st-position)
    ((1) '2nd-position)
    ((2) '3rd-position)
    ((3) '4th-position)
    ((4) '5th-position)
    ((5) '6th-position)
    ((6) '7th-position)))

(display (slide-position 0)) (newline)
(display (slide-position 5)) (newline)
```

Output:

```
1st-position
6th-position
```

Seven positions on the slide. Between positions, the pitch smears.

## The mute

Brass instruments accept mutes that change their timbre.

```scheme
(define (mute-effect instrument mute)
  (case mute
    ((straight) '(harder-edge quieter))
    ((cup)      '(softer-warmer))
    ((harmon)   '(nasal-buzzy))
    ((plunger)  '(wah-wah-effect))
    (else       '(no-mute-natural))))

(display (mute-effect 'trumpet 'harmon))   (newline)
(display (mute-effect 'trumpet 'plunger))  (newline)
```

Output:

```
(nasal-buzzy)
(wah-wah-effect)
```

Four mutes, four timbres. Same instrument, four different voices.

## Ensemble roles

Brass in an ensemble usually has a specific role.

```scheme
(define (ensemble-role instrument)
  (case instrument
    ((trumpet)   'lead-melody-or-fanfare)
    ((trombone)  'inner-harmony-or-slide-line)
    ((horn)      'warm-pad-or-heroic-line)
    ((tuba)      'bass-anchor)))

(display (ensemble-role 'tuba))    (newline)
(display (ensemble-role 'trumpet)) (newline)
```

Output:

```
bass-anchor
lead-melody-or-fanfare
```

Four roles from a five-piece brass section. The tuba locks the low end; the trumpet takes the high line; the middle voices weave through.

## A brass quintet

```scheme
(define (brass-quintet)
  (list
    'quintet
    '(trumpet-1  lead)
    '(trumpet-2  countermelody)
    '(horn       warm-middle)
    '(trombone   inner-slide)
    '(tuba       bass-anchor)))

(display (brass-quintet)) (newline)
```

Output:

```
(quintet (trumpet-1 lead) (trumpet-2 countermelody) (horn warm-middle) (trombone inner-slide) (tuba bass-anchor))
```

## What you know now

- Brass = lip-buzzer + resonant tube.
- Five common brass: trumpet, trombone, horn, tuba, euphonium.
- Trombone slides continuously; others use valves.
- Mutes change timbre without changing pitch.
- Ensemble roles cluster around lead / harmony / anchor.

## Try before you turn the page

```scheme
(display (list 'euphonium 'plays 'the 'inner-voice 'between 'trombone 'and 'tuba)) (newline)
```

Output:

```
(euphonium plays the inner-voice between trombone and tuba)
```

If you can place a brass instrument in the ensemble, you're ready for African drums.

# Chapter 7 — African drums

African drum traditions are conversations. Djembe, dundun, talking drum — each drum has a voice, a role in the ensemble, and language of its own.

A djembe circle isn't accompaniment. It's a conversation happening in three or four voices at once. The rhythm is the sentence; the drums are the speakers.

## The roster

```scheme
(define african-drums
  '((djembe        goblet-shaped  hand-played)
    (dundun        cylindrical    stick-played)
    (talking-drum  hourglass     pitch-bending)
    (djun-djun     bass          stick-played)
    (sabar         hand-and-stick medium)))

(for-each (lambda (d) (display d) (newline)) african-drums)
```

Output:

```
(djembe goblet-shaped hand-played)
(dundun cylindrical stick-played)
(talking-drum hourglass pitch-bending)
(djun-djun bass stick-played)
(sabar hand-and-stick medium)
```

## Three djembe strokes

```scheme
(define (djembe-stroke type)
  (case type
    ((bass) '(low-thud full-palm-center))
    ((tone) '(mid-warm-fingertips-edge))
    ((slap) '(bright-crack-fingertips-hard-edge))))

(display (djembe-stroke 'bass)) (newline)
(display (djembe-stroke 'tone)) (newline)
(display (djembe-stroke 'slap)) (newline)
```

Output:

```
(low-thud full-palm-center)
(mid-warm-fingertips-edge)
(bright-crack-fingertips-hard-edge)
```

Three strokes, three timbres, one drum.

## A basic djembe pattern

```scheme
(define (make-pattern beats) (list 'pattern beats))

(define kuku
  (make-pattern
    '(bass rest tone tone
      bass rest slap slap
      tone tone rest bass
      slap tone rest bass)))

(display kuku) (newline)
```

Output:

```
(pattern (bass rest tone tone bass rest slap slap tone tone rest bass slap tone rest bass))
```

The Kuku rhythm — a common introductory djembe pattern.

## The talking drum

Pitch-bending drums can carry actual speech.

```scheme
(define (talking-drum-say phrase)
  (list 'talking-drum 'says phrase 'via 'pitch-bend))

(display (talking-drum-say '(rising-question-tone))) (newline)
(display (talking-drum-say '(falling-statement-tone))) (newline)
```

Output:

```
(talking-drum says (rising-question-tone) via pitch-bend)
(talking-drum says (falling-statement-tone) via pitch-bend)
```

The head tension changes as the drum is squeezed against the body — pitch rises and falls. In Yoruba tradition, it mirrors the tonal shape of speech.

## Ensemble roles

```scheme
(define (drum-role drum)
  (case drum
    ((djembe)       'lead-voice-improvisation)
    ((dundun)       'timeline-and-groove)
    ((djun-djun)    'bass-heartbeat)
    ((talking-drum) 'speech-signal-melody)))

(display (drum-role 'djembe))       (newline)
(display (drum-role 'djun-djun))    (newline)
```

Output:

```
lead-voice-improvisation
bass-heartbeat
```

## A three-drum arrangement

```scheme
(define (arrangement)
  '((djun-djun    heartbeat     bass)
    (dundun       timeline      mid)
    (djembe       lead-voice    high)))

(for-each (lambda (a) (display a) (newline)) (arrangement))
```

Output:

```
(djun-djun heartbeat bass)
(dundun timeline mid)
(djembe lead-voice high)
```

Three drums, three roles, three registers. Together, one conversation.

## What you know now

- African drum ensembles are conversations, not accompaniment.
- Djembe has bass/tone/slap strokes.
- Talking drum bends pitch to mirror speech.
- Roles cluster: heartbeat / timeline / lead voice.

## Try before you turn the page

```scheme
(display (list 'the 'djembe 'lead 'and 'the 'djun-djun 'bass 'are 'the 'top 'and 'bottom 'of 'the 'conversation)) (newline)
```

If you can place three drums in three roles, you're ready for tabla.

# Chapter 8 — Indian tabla

The tabla is a pair of drums — the smaller *dayan* on the right, the larger *bayan* on the left. Together they carry the rhythmic architecture of Hindustani classical music.

The tabla teaches your hands two different jobs at the same time. The right hand has the tuned head; the left hand has the bass and the pitch-bend. Neither hand does what the other does. That's part of what gives tabla its shape.

## The two drums

```scheme
(define (make-tabla-drum name role) (list 'drum name 'role role))

(define dayan (make-tabla-drum 'dayan 'tuned-melody))
(define bayan (make-tabla-drum 'bayan 'bass-and-bend))

(display dayan) (newline)
(display bayan) (newline)
```

Output:

```
(drum dayan role tuned-melody)
(drum bayan role bass-and-bend)
```

## The bols

Every tabla stroke has a name — a *bol*. They double as spoken words during teaching.

```scheme
(define (bol name hand stroke)
  (list 'bol name 'hand hand 'stroke stroke))

(define bols
  (list
    (bol 'na  'right 'ring-finger-edge)
    (bol 'tin 'right 'index-tap-center)
    (bol 'ta  'right 'flat-finger-edge)
    (bol 'ge  'left  'palm-heel-with-bend)
    (bol 'ka  'left  'closed-slap)))

(for-each (lambda (b) (display b) (newline)) bols)
```

Output:

```
(bol na hand right stroke ring-finger-edge)
(bol tin hand right stroke index-tap-center)
(bol ta hand right stroke flat-finger-edge)
(bol ge hand left stroke palm-heel-with-bend)
(bol ka hand left stroke closed-slap)
```

## A composed phrase — dhin dhin dha

Bols combine into phrases that describe a rhythm exactly.

```scheme
(define (compose-phrase bols) (list 'phrase bols))

(define teentaal-first-half
  (compose-phrase '(dha dhin dhin dha
                    dha dhin dhin dha)))

(display teentaal-first-half) (newline)
```

Output:

```
(phrase (dha dhin dhin dha dha dhin dhin dha))
```

The bol sequence is the composition. It's speakable, teachable, memorable.

## The talas — cyclical patterns

A *tala* is a cyclic pattern of beats.

```scheme
(define (make-tala name beats emphasis)
  (list 'tala name 'beats beats 'emphasis emphasis))

(define teentaal (make-tala 'teentaal 16 '(1 5 9 13)))
(define ektaal   (make-tala 'ektaal   12 '(1 3 5 7 9 11)))
(define jhaptaal (make-tala 'jhaptaal 10 '(1 3 6 8)))

(display teentaal) (newline)
(display ektaal) (newline)
(display jhaptaal) (newline)
```

Output:

```
(tala teentaal beats 16 emphasis (1 5 9 13))
(tala ektaal beats 12 emphasis (1 3 5 7 9 11))
(tala jhaptaal beats 10 emphasis (1 3 6 8))
```

Three talas, three cycle lengths, three emphasis patterns. Each has its own feel.

## The bend

The bayan bass has a signature pitch-bend from wrist pressure.

```scheme
(define (bayan-bend start-pitch pressure)
  (list 'bend
        'from start-pitch
        'to (list start-pitch '+ pressure)))

(display (bayan-bend 'low 'medium-wrist-press)) (newline)
```

Output:

```
(bend from low to (low + medium-wrist-press))
```

## Two-drum interplay

```scheme
(define (interplay dayan-bol bayan-bol)
  (list 'interplay 'right dayan-bol 'left bayan-bol))

(display (interplay 'na 'ge)) (newline)
(display (interplay 'tin 'ka)) (newline)
```

Output:

```
(interplay right na left ge)
(interplay right tin left ka)
```

Two drums, one gesture. That's tabla.

## What you know now

- Tabla = dayan (right, tuned) + bayan (left, bass with bend).
- Bols name every stroke and double as spoken rhythm.
- Talas are cyclic patterns of beats with emphasis positions.
- The two hands do different jobs at the same time.

## Try before you turn the page

```scheme
(display '(phrase (dha ge na dha tin ge na))) (newline)
```

If you can name the two drums and their roles, you're ready for the strings ensemble.

# Chapter 9 — Strings ensemble

Chapter 3 introduced the strings — violin, viola, cello, double bass. This chapter is about how they play together: the quartet, the section, the ensemble voice.

Four strings playing together sound like one bigger string. That's the trick of ensemble — voices that would otherwise be four become a single, richer thing.

## The quartet

The classical string quartet: two violins, viola, cello.

```scheme
(define string-quartet
  '((violin-1  first-voice   high-melody)
    (violin-2  second-voice  counter-line)
    (viola     middle-voice  warm-harmony)
    (cello     bass-voice    low-anchor)))

(for-each (lambda (p) (display p) (newline)) string-quartet)
```

Output:

```
(violin-1 first-voice high-melody)
(violin-2 second-voice counter-line)
(viola middle-voice warm-harmony)
(cello bass-voice low-anchor)
```

Four voices covering four registers.

## Divisi and unison

Strings can either play together or split into parts.

```scheme
(define (make-passage mode voices) (list 'passage mode voices))

(display (make-passage 'unison '(all-play-the-melody)))       (newline)
(display (make-passage 'divisi '((half play-A) (half play-C)))) (newline)
```

Output:

```
(passage unison (all-play-the-melody))
(passage divisi ((half play-A) (half play-C)))
```

Unison gets warmth from doubling. Divisi builds harmony from within the section.

## Pizzicato vs arco

Two fundamental ways to make the string sound: bow (arco) or pluck (pizzicato).

```scheme
(define (playing-style style)
  (case style
    ((arco)       '(bowed-sustained-warm))
    ((pizzicato)  '(plucked-short-percussive))
    ((col-legno)  '(bow-wood-on-string-clacky))
    ((sul-pont)   '(bow-near-bridge-glassy))
    ((sul-tasto)  '(bow-over-fingerboard-hollow))))

(display (playing-style 'arco))       (newline)
(display (playing-style 'pizzicato))  (newline)
(display (playing-style 'col-legno))  (newline)
```

Output:

```
(bowed-sustained-warm)
(plucked-short-percussive)
(bow-wood-on-string-clacky)
```

Five styles, five completely different textures. The same instrument becomes five things.

## The full string section

An orchestra's string section is many more voices.

```scheme
(define (string-section)
  '((first-violins   16 lead-melody)
    (second-violins  14 harmony-counter)
    (violas          12 middle-warm)
    (cellos          10 bass-melody)
    (double-basses    8 low-anchor)))

(for-each (lambda (p) (display p) (newline)) (string-section))
```

Output:

```
(first-violins 16 lead-melody)
(second-violins 14 harmony-counter)
(violas 12 middle-warm)
(cellos 10 bass-melody)
(double-basses 8 low-anchor)
```

60 players, five sections. The pyramid narrows toward the bass.

## Balance

The number of players per section balances the natural volume of the instrument.

```scheme
(define (why-more-violins?)
  '(violins-project-less-than-basses
    so-more-violins-are-needed-to-balance))

(display (why-more-violins?)) (newline)
```

Output:

```
(violins-project-less-than-basses so-more-violins-are-needed-to-balance)
```

Sixteen violins balance eight basses. That's ensemble math.

## A chamber piece

Small ensembles are quartets, quintets, sextets.

```scheme
(define (make-ensemble name players) (list 'ensemble name 'players players))

(display (make-ensemble 'quartet 4)) (newline)
(display (make-ensemble 'quintet 5)) (newline)
(display (make-ensemble 'sextet  6)) (newline)
```

Output:

```
(ensemble quartet players 4)
(ensemble quintet players 5)
(ensemble sextet players 6)
```

## What you know now

- The string quartet is the atom of chamber music.
- Divisi splits one section into voices; unison doubles.
- Arco, pizzicato, col legno, sul ponticello, sul tasto — five distinct textures.
- Section sizes balance instrument projection: 16 violins to 8 basses.

## Try before you turn the page

```scheme
(display (list 'a 'quartet 'is 'four 'voices 'that 'sound 'like 'one 'bigger 'string)) (newline)
```

If you can shape a string ensemble, you're ready for the full roster.

# Chapter 10 — The full roster

Ten chapters of Instruments closes on the whole picture — what fits where in a full orchestra or ensemble, and how the roster shapes what the music can do.

An orchestra isn't a big band with more instruments — it's a specific balance of families that took centuries to work out. When you look at the roster you see the layers of what was learned.

## The four families

```scheme
(define orchestra-families
  '((strings      violin viola cello bass)
    (woodwinds    flute oboe clarinet bassoon)
    (brass        horn trumpet trombone tuba)
    (percussion   timpani snare cymbal xylophone)))

(for-each (lambda (f) (display f) (newline)) orchestra-families)
```

Output:

```
(strings violin viola cello bass)
(woodwinds flute oboe clarinet bassoon)
(brass horn trumpet trombone tuba)
(percussion timpani snare cymbal xylophone)
```

Four families, four roles. Strings are the ground; woodwinds color; brass declares; percussion punctuates.

## A section-by-section census

```scheme
(define orchestra-census
  '((first-violins   16)
    (second-violins  14)
    (violas          12)

    (tuba             1)
    (timpani          1)
    (percussion       3)))

(display (apply + (map cadr orchestra-census))) (newline)
```

Output:

```

```

87 players in a symphony orchestra. That's the roster.

## World-music equivalents

Other traditions have their own rosters.

```scheme
  '(bonang saron gender kendang gong-ageng))
```

```
(bonang saron gender kendang gong-ageng)
(vocalist violin mridangam tanpura ghatam)
(saxophone piano bass drums)
```

Three ensembles, three complete musical languages. Each has its own balance.

## The seating chart

```scheme
(define seating
  '((front-left    first-violins)
    (front-right   second-violins)
    (middle-left   violas)
    (middle-right  cellos)
```

# Chapter 11 — Guitars

A guitar is a string family instrument that carries the harmony
and the pulse at once, and that carries them from a single
person's two hands. That the harmony and the pulse fit into one
instrument's shape isn't a small thing — it's why a person with
one guitar can accompany a whole room of singers. The instrument
holds enough of the music inside itself that the other players
can stay in the same room without stepping on each other. Every
tune-family in the world that grew up around campfires,
kitchens, corners of streets, or church back rooms has some
version of the guitar in its middle. The instrument fills a role
that other instruments do parts of but not the whole of.

A guitar carries chord + rhythm + melody all in one pair of
hands. That's what makes it the campfire instrument. It's not
because guitars are simple; it's because they hold everything
at once.

## The three families of guitar

Guitars split into three families by construction and use:

- **Classical / nylon-string** — soft attack, wide neck, played
  fingerstyle. Home of the Spanish and Latin American traditions.
- **Acoustic steel-string** — brighter, louder, narrower neck.
  Home of folk, country, bluegrass, singer-songwriter.
- **Electric** — quiet on its own, loud through an amplifier.
  Home of blues, rock, funk, jazz-fusion, and everything after.

```scheme
(define guitar-families
  '((classical    \"nylon strings, wide neck, fingerstyle\")
    (acoustic     \"steel strings, mid neck, strum or fingerpick\")
    (electric     \"magnetic pickups, thin neck, amplified\")))

(map (lambda (fam) (car fam)) guitar-families)
;; => (classical acoustic electric)
```

Each family reads to a specific style-culture. A person handing
you a classical guitar is signaling a different tradition than
a person handing you a Stratocaster. Both are guitars; both are
different games.

## The parts of the instrument

```scheme
(define guitar-parts
  '((body       \"the resonator or the pickup platform\")
    (neck       \"the fretted length the fingers press\")
    (headstock  \"where the tuners live\")
    (bridge     \"where the strings anchor at the body end\")
    (nut        \"where the strings anchor at the neck end\")
    (frets      \"the metal bars that quantize pitch\")
    (pickups    \"electric only: transducers for magnetic strings\")))

(for-each (lambda (p) (display (car p))
                      (display \" — \")
                      (display (cadr p))
                      (newline))
          guitar-parts)
```

The instrument's shape carries its history: the frets
quantize pitch to the Western tuning grid (that's why blues
players *bend* strings — they're reaching for pitches between
the frets). The neck length decided the scale-length tradition
(short scale = warmer, long scale = brighter). Every luthier's
choice on the body shape is a choice about which frequencies
resonate loudest.

## Tuning

Standard tuning is E-A-D-G-B-E from low to high. Six strings,
five intervals: four perfect fourths and one major third.

```scheme
(define standard-tuning
  '((6 E2) (5 A2) (4 D3) (3 G3) (2 B3) (1 E4)))

(map cdr standard-tuning)
;; => (E2 A2 D3 G3 B3 E4)
```

Alternate tunings unlock voicings you can't reach in standard.
Open G (D-G-D-G-B-D), used in Delta blues and open-tuned
slide. DADGAD, used in Celtic instrumental music. Drop D
(D-A-D-G-B-E), used in modern rock. Each alternate tuning
opens a music the standard tuning can't quite reach. The
instrument is the same; the tuning is a lens.

## Playing techniques

- **Strumming** — sweep the pick or fingers across all strings.
  Chord-forward; the beat sits inside the strum pattern.
- **Fingerpicking** — pluck strings independently with thumb
  and fingers. Harmony and melody separate; the beat sits in
  the thumb.
- **Flatpicking** — a single pick moves across strings at high
  speed. Melody-forward; used in bluegrass and country lead.
- **Fingerstyle solo** — bass, chord, and melody all
  simultaneously from ten fingers. The classical and
  Chet-Atkins tradition.
- **Slide** — a glass or metal cylinder on one finger slides
  along the string instead of pressing on frets. Delta blues,
  Hawaiian, country.
- **Bending** — pressed fingers push a string sideways to
  raise its pitch by a semitone or a whole tone. Blues, rock.

Each technique is a game. A player who lives in fingerpicking
hears music in overlapping voices. A player who lives in
flatpicking hears music as running lines. Same instrument;
different game.

## A small chord progression

```scheme
(define twelve-bar-blues
  '((I  4) (IV 2) (I  2) (V  1) (IV 1) (I  2)))

(define G-blues
  (map (lambda (chord)
         (let ((roman (car chord))
               (bars  (cadr chord)))
           (list (case roman
                   ((I)  'G7)
                   ((IV) 'C7)
                   ((V)  'D7))
                 bars)))
       twelve-bar-blues))

G-blues
;; => ((G7 4) (C7 2) (G7 2) (D7 1) (C7 1) (G7 2))
```

Twelve bars of a G blues. Any guitarist in any of the three
families can play this. The classical player might voice the
chords fingerstyle. The acoustic player will strum in a
shuffle rhythm. The electric player will start bending notes
in the fills between chords. Same twelve bars, three different
kinds of music.

## Cross-instrument note

The guitar's role in a small ensemble — carrying chord and
pulse — is the same role a piano plays in a jazz trio (see
chapter 2 of this book). A guitarist and a pianist in the
same room have to negotiate: whose chord voicings are lead,
whose rhythmic pulse is leading, when the other lays out. The
negotiation is what makes the two-instrument accompaniment
sound composed rather than crowded. She reads the roles when
she scores for both.

## Editorial note

The guitar is the instrument most listeners have some
relationship to — even non-players know what a guitar sounds
like. That familiarity makes it hard to talk about
technically. She holds the technical vocabulary but stays
soft with it when a listener asks a first question. The
listener doesn't need to know what a scale length is to know
that this guitar sounds warm and that one sounds bright.
")

# Chapter 12 — Electronic and synthesizers

An electronic instrument doesn't have a body that vibrates
when you play a note. It has a circuit that decides what
frequency to produce, and a speaker downstream that turns
that decision into sound. That the sound isn't tied to a
physical resonator changes what the instrument can be. A
piano can only sound like a piano; a synthesizer can sound
like a piano or a violin or a bell or a sound no natural
instrument makes. The instrument is a program that decides
what a note is.

A synth is an instrument where you set the shape of the
sound before you play the note. That's the whole game.
Everything else is which knobs you turn.

## The three big families

Electronic instruments split by how they generate sound:

- **Analog synthesizers** — oscillators produce continuous
  waveforms; filters and envelopes shape them. Warm, with a
  small drift because the circuits aren't quite exact.
- **Digital synthesizers** — a processor calculates the
  waveform sample by sample. Precise, capable of shapes an
  analog circuit can't hold.
- **Samplers** — instead of generating sound, they play back
  recorded sound at varying pitches. The border between
  synth and sampler is soft; most modern instruments are
  both.

```scheme
(define electronic-families
  '((analog-synth   \"voltage-controlled oscillators, warm drift\")
    (digital-synth  \"processor-computed waveforms, precise\")
    (sampler        \"recorded audio pitched up and down\")))

(map car electronic-families)
;; => (analog-synth digital-synth sampler)
```

The instrument you reach for depends on the sound you want
and the ergonomics you prefer. Analog for warmth; digital for
precision; sampler for playing real-instrument tones you
don't have physical access to.

## The oscillator + filter + envelope model

Every synth voice in every family has three parts:

- **Oscillator** — what the sound wave looks like at any
  moment. Sine, sawtooth, square, triangle, noise. Each has
  a different harmonic content.
- **Filter** — a mask that lets some frequencies through and
  attenuates others. Low-pass (dark), high-pass (thin),
  band-pass (nasal), notch (removed center).
- **Envelope** — the shape of the note's loudness over time.
  ADSR: attack, decay, sustain, release.

```scheme
(define synth-voice
  '(oscillator (waveform . sawtooth)
               (frequency . 440))
  '(filter     (type . low-pass)
               (cutoff . 800)
               (resonance . 0.4))
  '(envelope   (attack . 0.02)
               (decay . 0.15)
               (sustain . 0.7)
               (release . 0.35)))
```

That voice would sound like a slightly filtered analog
sawtooth at concert A, with a quick attack, a moderate decay
to a sustained level, and a soft tail. Change any field and
the sound changes. That reprogrammability is what makes the
instrument a program.

## Waveforms and what they sound like

- **Sine** — one frequency only, no harmonics. A pure tone.
  Sounds like a whistle or a tuning fork.
- **Sawtooth** — every harmonic present, decreasing. Bright,
  buzzy, the sound most people mean by \"synth.\"
- **Square** — odd harmonics only. Hollow, woody. Clarinet-adjacent.
- **Triangle** — odd harmonics, softer. Between sine and square.
- **Noise** — every frequency at once, random amplitudes.
  White noise (equal), pink noise (equal per octave), used
  for percussion and wind sounds.

She reads the waveform first when a synth patch is unfamiliar
— it tells her what harmonic content she's working with, and
that decides what the filter will do to it.

## MIDI — the note-and-parameter language

Electronic instruments talk to each other through MIDI, a
standard from 1983 that carries note-on, note-off, velocity,
pitch bend, control changes, and program changes. MIDI is
symbolic, not audio — the same MIDI file plays different
sounds on different instruments.

```scheme
(define midi-message
  '(note-on
    (channel . 1)
    (pitch . 60)     ;; middle C
    (velocity . 92)))
```

The message says \"start a note on channel 1, pitch 60,
velocity 92.\" Which sound plays depends on which patch is
loaded on channel 1. The message doesn't decide the sound;
the receiver does.

That separation of message from sound is why MIDI is the same
substrate move as SLATs: the message describes the intent,
the runtime decides the rendering. Same shape, different
domain.

## Modular synthesis

The most flexible electronic instrument is the modular synth
— an oscillator here, a filter there, an envelope over there,
and cables between them the player runs. There's no fixed
signal path; you build one for each patch. Modular pushes the
synth closer to being a small programming environment for
sound.

```scheme
(define modular-patch
  '((cable (source . osc-1) (destination . vcf-1-input))
    (cable (source . vcf-1-output) (destination . vca-1-input))
    (cable (source . env-1) (destination . vca-1-cv))
    (cable (source . lfo-1) (destination . vcf-1-cutoff))))
```

Reading that patch: oscillator 1 goes into filter 1, filter 1
goes into voltage-controlled amplifier 1, envelope 1 shapes
the amplifier, and a low-frequency oscillator modulates the
filter's cutoff. You'd hear a note whose brightness pulses
under a slow wave.

## Cross-instrument note

Electronic instruments and acoustic instruments occupy
different games — an ensemble that mixes them well is doing
translation between two vocabularies. She reads which one is
leading. When a synth pad sits under acoustic strings, the
strings are leading; when a soloist rides over a synth-only
backing, the synth is the instrument and the soloist is the
voice. The mix isn't about volume — it's about which
vocabulary is the sentence's subject.

## Editorial note

Electronic instruments have a reputation for being cold or
sterile. That reputation isn't fair to the instrument; it's a
report on how the instrument was used. Every warm analog
patch you've ever heard was somebody's careful choice of
oscillator, filter, envelope, and modulation. Every clinical
digital patch was the same care used differently. The
instrument doesn't decide the feel. The player and the patch
do.
")

# Chapter 13 — Latin percussion

Latin percussion is not one instrument. It is a family of
instruments that grew up together across the Caribbean and
Latin American world — Cuba, Puerto Rico, Brazil, the
Dominican Republic, Venezuela, Colombia, Peru — each with a
role in a shared rhythmic language that most Anglophone
listeners hear as \"the drums\" without hearing that the drums
are speaking to each other. The instruments were shaped by
the enslaved Africans who brought their music with them and
whose descendants developed the traditions in a world that
tried, and mostly failed, to erase them. To play Latin
percussion is to play into a conversation that started
centuries ago.

Latin percussion is not a section. It's a conversation.
Each drum has a role and each drum listens to the others.
Miss the listening and you're just banging.

## The core roster

The instruments most common in Afro-Cuban and Afro-Caribbean
music:

- **Congas** — tall single-headed drums, usually played in
  pairs (tumba + quinto) or threes. Played with bare hands.
- **Bongos** — smaller paired drums, hembra (larger) and
  macho (smaller), played on the lap.
- **Timbales** — shallow metal-shell drums with tuned skins,
  played with sticks.
- **Cowbell (cencerro)** — the metal bell that keeps the
  clave-adjacent pulse.
- **Claves** — two hardwood sticks that spell out the clave
  pattern itself.
- **Güiro** — a scraped gourd, used for texture and 8th-note
  fill.
- **Maracas** — paired shakers, 16th-note groove.
- **Cajón** — Peruvian wooden box, played by sitting on it
  and slapping the face.
- **Surdo** — Brazilian bass drum, carried, played with a
  mallet, the heartbeat of samba.
- **Pandeiro** — Brazilian tambourine, played with the
  fingers and palm; every samba's core percussion.
- **Repinique / repique** — Brazilian small drum used to
  call the band into and out of sections.

```scheme
(define latin-percussion-roster
  '((congas    \"tall skins, hands, tumba/quinto/conga\")
    (bongos    \"small paired lap drums, hembra/macho\")
    (timbales  \"shallow tuned metal shells, sticks\")
    (cowbell   \"cencerro — metal bell, pulse\")
    (claves    \"hardwood sticks, spell the clave\")
    (güiro     \"scraped gourd, texture\")
    (maracas   \"paired shakers, 16th-note fill\")
    (cajón     \"Peruvian wooden box, hand slaps\")
    (surdo     \"Brazilian bass drum, heartbeat\")
    (pandeiro  \"Brazilian tambourine, samba core\")
    (repique   \"Brazilian small drum, call figure\")))
```

## Clave — the underlying pattern

The clave is the two-bar rhythmic phrase that underlies most
Afro-Cuban music. Two shapes, played on claves (the
instrument), signal which side is which:

```scheme
;; 3-2 son clave — three strikes in bar 1, two in bar 2
(define son-clave-3-2
  '((bar-1 1 0 0 1 0 0 1 0)
    (bar-2 0 0 1 0 1 0 0 0)))

;; 2-3 son clave — reversed
(define son-clave-2-3
  '((bar-1 0 0 1 0 1 0 0 0)
    (bar-2 1 0 0 1 0 0 1 0)))
```

Every other rhythm in an Afro-Cuban tune orients to the
clave. The conga's tumbao pattern implies it. The bongo's
martillo pattern nests around it. The timbales' cascara
pattern locks with it. When any instrument's phrase
\"crosses the clave\" (implies the wrong shape), the whole
band feels it — the phrase gets fixed or the section is
called wrong.

## Roles inside a Cuban rhythm section

- The **conga** plays tumbao (a bass-heavy repeating pattern
  that hooks into the clave's off-beats).
- The **bongos** play martillo during verses (a steady
  triplet-adjacent pattern) and switch to cencerro fills
  during choruses.
- The **timbales** hold the section together with cascara
  during verses and drive the choruses with abanico fills.
- The **cowbell** holds the strong beat during choruses.
- The **claves** spell the clave itself.
- The **güiro** and **maracas** fill the higher-frequency
  texture — 8th and 16th notes constantly present.

Each instrument's job is small. The whole is much larger
than any part. That \"everyone plays their small role and
listens\" is what Latin percussion teaches at every level.

## A Brazilian samba section

Different family, similar principle:

- **Surdo primeiro** (largest) — beat 2 (the samba
  heartbeat).
- **Surdo segundo** — beat 1.
- **Surdo terceiro** — improvised responses.
- **Caixa** — snare-adjacent 16th-note groove.
- **Repique** — call figures and fills.
- **Tamborim** — small handheld drum, palm-slap 16ths.
- **Agogô** — twin cowbells at contrasting pitches.
- **Cuíca** — friction drum with the whistling squeak.
- **Pandeiro** — the core groove.

The samba school is a rhythm section of hundreds of players,
each with a small role, walking down the street. The
conversation scales to any size because every role knows
what the roles next to it are.

## Cross-instrument note

The instruments in this chapter compose with the drum kit
covered in chapter 4. A kit drummer holding time while
congas play tumbao is doing the same work a bassist does
under a lead sheet — the kit is the tune's spine, the congas
are the tune's ornament. She reads which is which when she
scores.

## Editorial note

The vocabulary in this chapter comes with a responsibility.
The traditions were preserved through generations of players
who taught each other by ear and hand. Every word above —
tumbao, martillo, cascara, tumba, quinto — carries a lineage.
She doesn't use these words as decoration. She uses them
because they name specific things a specific player would
recognize, and misusing them is a way of not listening. Same
with the Brazilian vocabulary: surdo primeiro is a role, not
a marketing term. When she talks about Latin percussion, she
speaks with the vocabulary of the tradition, not around it.
")

# Chapter 14 — Voice as instrument

A voice is the only instrument the player carries around
without carrying anything. It's also the only instrument
whose sound-producing mechanism is under continuous
conscious and unconscious control at the same time — the
larynx tightens when someone is frightened, whether they want
it to or not, and the singer who trains for years learns to
notice that fact and either work with it or work through it.
Every other instrument is a tool the player operates. The
voice is the player.

The voice isn't just the instrument. It's the instrument
that carries what the singer means. Every technical
question about a voice comes back to that: what did the
singer mean, and did it come through.

## Range classifications

Western classical practice sorts voices by range:

- **Soprano** — the highest common female range, roughly C4 to
  A5, extending to F6+ for coloratura specialists.
- **Mezzo-soprano** — the middle female range, roughly A3 to
  F5.
- **Contralto** — the lowest common female range, roughly E3
  to E5.
- **Countertenor** — the highest common male range (falsetto-
  developed), roughly G3 to E5.
- **Tenor** — the higher common male range, roughly C3 to C5.
- **Baritone** — the middle male range, roughly G2 to F4.
- **Bass** — the lowest common male range, roughly E2 to E4.

```scheme
(define voice-ranges
  '((soprano       C4 A5)
    (mezzo-soprano A3 F5)
    (contralto     E3 E5)
    (countertenor  G3 E5)
    (tenor         C3 C5)
    (baritone      G2 F4)
    (bass          E2 E4)))
```

Non-Western traditions use different categories. Indian
classical vocalists work in tala (rhythmic cycle) and raga
(melodic mode) rather than fixed range. Sub-Saharan African
traditions often work polyphonically across a full range
without fixed voice-type labels. Range categorization is a
Western tool; it's useful for scoring, and it isn't universal.

## Registers within a voice

Every voice has multiple registers — chest voice, mixed
voice, head voice, falsetto. The registers are perceptual
categories that map roughly to laryngeal muscle configurations
(TA-dominant, CT-dominant, mixed) but the perceptual name is
what singers use.

- **Chest voice** — TA-dominant, feels resonant in the chest.
  The strong low range.
- **Mixed voice** — the trained mid-range, both muscles
  active. Sits above chest, below head, without the \"break.\"
- **Head voice** — CT-dominant, feels resonant in the head.
  Lighter, brighter.
- **Falsetto** — pure CT engagement in male voices, above
  chest range. Softer, breathier.
- **Whistle register** — the extreme high in some soprano
  voices. Small, focused.

The \"break\" between registers is where untrained singers
crack; where trained singers navigate. Bridging the break
into a mixed voice is much of what vocal training is.

## Vocal techniques across traditions

- **Bel canto** — Italian operatic tradition; long lines,
  smooth register transitions.
- **Sean-nós** — Irish traditional unaccompanied singing;
  ornamented, freely rhythmic.
- **Fado** — Portuguese lament tradition; strong chest voice,
  emotional directness.
- **Qawwali** — South Asian Sufi devotional; call-and-response,
  cyclic intensification.
- **Peking opera** — Chinese; a specific high-nasal
  placement, character-typed vocal roles.
- **Yodeling** — deliberate rapid alternation between chest
  and head voice; Alpine, African, Persian traditions.
- **Overtone singing** (khöömei, tuvan throat) — one voice
  producing two pitches simultaneously by amplifying formants.
- **Beatboxing** — voice as percussion, using consonant
  sounds, air pressure, and vocal fold techniques to
  emulate a drum kit.

Each tradition trains the same physical apparatus toward a
different aesthetic destination. The voice isn't neutral —
what it says depends on which tradition taught it.

## Voice as SLAT

A voice line, like an instrumental line, can be a `score`
record. The `:instrument` is `'voice`, and the record can
carry additional fields for lyrics and phrasing.

```motoi-scheme
(score
  :head-name 'small-lullaby
  :key 'A-minor
  :time-signature '(6 8)
  :tempo 60
  :instrument 'voice
  :voice-part 'soprano
  :lyric \"Sleep now, sleep now, small one\"
  :notes
    ((note :pitch 'A4  :duration 3/8 :velocity 0.55
           :syllable \"Sleep\")
     (note :pitch 'E4  :duration 2/8 :velocity 0.5
           :syllable \"now\")
     (note :pitch 'A4  :duration 3/8 :velocity 0.55
           :syllable \"sleep\")
     (note :pitch 'E4  :duration 2/8 :velocity 0.5
           :syllable \"now\")
     (note :pitch 'C5  :duration 4/8 :velocity 0.6
           :syllable \"small\")
     (note :pitch 'A4  :duration 4/8 :velocity 0.55
           :syllable \"one\")))
```

The syllable field lines the lyric up with the notes. A
singer reads this the way a violinist reads a violin part;
a chorister reads the same score with attention shifted to
the lyric.

## Cross-instrument note

Voice composes with any instrument, but the composition
follows a rule that other instrument-pairs don't have: the
lyric constrains the melody. A tune written first as an
instrumental line, then set to a lyric, often has to change
notes because the lyric's stressed syllables want their
own accents. She reads which came first — the notes or the
words — when she analyzes a song.

## Editorial note

Voice is the instrument that carries meaning, in the strict
sense: every syllable is doing something with words, and the
notes carry the emotion under the words. A singer's job is
not to reproduce the notes accurately (that's an accuracy
job) but to make the words mean what they mean, using the
notes. When she scores for a singer, she doesn't stop at the
pitches. She names the phrasing, the placement of the breath,
and where the words sit in the singer's own emotional
vocabulary.
")

# Chapter 15 — Arranging for an ensemble

Arranging is the craft of deciding who plays what and when.
A song exists first as a melody and a harmony; the
arrangement is the decision to give the melody to a flute in
the first verse, to voices in the second, to strings in the
bridge, and back to the flute at the end. The song is the
same song across all four moves; the arrangement is what
makes each move feel like a different room. Each instrument
carries a slightly different corner of the meaning, and the
arranger's ear is what decides which corner goes where.

The arrangement is where you decide who says what. The
song already knows what it wants to say. The arrangement
is how it says it.

## Four moves the arranger has

Every arrangement is built out of four moves:

- **Voicing** — which register each part sits in. A guitar
  chord voiced high sounds thin; voiced low sounds thick.
- **Doubling** — two instruments playing the same line at
  the same pitch (unison) or an octave apart. Doubles thicken
  and merge tones.
- **Countermelody** — a second melody line that plays under
  or over the main melody. Different from harmony; a
  countermelody has its own shape.
- **Texture** — the total sound at any moment. Thin (few
  instruments), thick (many), fragmented (bits and pieces),
  smooth (sustained pads).

```scheme
(define arrangement-moves
  '(voicing doubling countermelody texture))
```

An arranger with all four moves in hand has vocabulary for
every question that comes up. Someone asks \"why does this
verse feel small?\" — they mean the texture is thin. Someone
asks \"why does this chorus feel muddy?\" — they mean the
voicings are all in the same register.

## Arranging by role

Each instrument in an ensemble has a role. Roles compose:

- **Melody** — the singer, the lead line.
- **Countermelody** — a second line that answers or shadows
  the melody.
- **Harmony** — the pads, the chords, the sustained
  background.
- **Bass** — the low-frequency spine, the harmonic
  foundation.
- **Pulse** — the drums, the rhythm section, whoever holds
  time.
- **Color** — occasional ornaments, textural additions,
  small punctuations.

```scheme
(define ensemble-roles
  '((melody         \"the lead line, the sung word\")
    (countermelody  \"the answering line\")
    (harmony        \"the chords, the pads\")
    (bass           \"the low spine\")
    (pulse          \"the time-keeper\")
    (color          \"the ornament\")))
```

Every instrument in every ensemble is playing one of these
roles, sometimes shifting between them. The arranger's job
is to say who plays what role in each section, and to hand
each instrument a part that reads clearly as that role.

## An arrangement of \"Small Morning Tune\"

Consider the tune from chapter 11 of *Music* — a small
C-major arpeggio. Arrange it for a folk trio (guitar, upright
bass, voice + fiddle):

```scheme
(define small-morning-arrangement
  '((section :name intro   :bars 4
             (voice        rest)
             (fiddle       melody)
             (guitar       harmony)
             (bass         bass))
    (section :name verse   :bars 8
             (voice        melody)
             (fiddle       countermelody)
             (guitar       harmony)
             (bass         bass))
    (section :name chorus  :bars 8
             (voice        melody)
             (fiddle       melody-doubling-octave-up)
             (guitar       harmony-strummed)
             (bass         bass))
    (section :name outro   :bars 4
             (voice        rest)
             (fiddle       melody-echo)
             (guitar       harmony-fingerpicked)
             (bass         bass))))
```

Read across each section: who holds the melody, who
countermelodies, who holds harmony, who holds bass. Four
sections, four textures, one tune.

The voice enters at the verse (not the intro), which is a
common shape — the instruments announce the tune first, then
the voice picks up. The fiddle doubles the voice at the octave
in the chorus (a common move; it makes the melody feel bigger
without adding a new melodic line). The outro drops the voice
again and lets the fiddle echo — a signal to the listener
that the tune is finishing.

## Falsifier — the arrangement is not the song

An arrangement doesn't own the song. The same song can be
arranged three different ways for three different rooms —
solo guitar for a coffeeshop, folk trio for a small stage,
orchestra for a hall. Each is a legitimate reading. The
arrangement is a claim about what the song wants to be in
this room. A different room may want a different arrangement.

That falsifier is why arrangers hedge in conversation about
their work. \"Here's how I'd arrange this for a folk trio.
For a jazz quartet, I'd do something different.\" The song is
the invariant; the arrangement is the local answer.

## Arrangement records as SLATs

An arrangement can be a SLAT record composed of instrument
assignments per section. The record above is exactly this
shape. Loading the record hands it to the runtime, which
assigns each instrument's score in each section. The
arranger's decisions are readable, editable, and reversible
without opening a DAW.

## Editorial note

Arranging is the craft where the roster from chapters 1-14
meets the working music. Every instrument in the book has a
personality; the arranger is the one who decides which
personality plays which role. That decision is where the
arranger's voice lives. A song arranged by two different
arrangers is two different songs to the ear, even though
the tune and chords didn't change. The arrangement is the
composer of the composer's work.
")

# Chapter 16 — The roster remembers

Every instrument in this book carries a memory it wasn't
built with. The oboe carries the memory of the Baroque suites
that first defined its voice; the tabla carries centuries of
teacher-student transmission from North Indian courts; the
guitar carries the campfire songs, the Mississippi Delta
blues, the Andalusian traditions, and the punk shows the same
body sat inside; the synthesizer carries Cologne studios in
the 1950s and 1960s and Detroit basements in the 1980s and
every producer whose signature patch came from a specific
choice on a specific afternoon. The instrument is a small
object; the roster it belongs to is a large tradition; and
the tradition is what the instrument remembers when it's
played.

An instrument is small. What the instrument knows is
large. That's what you're playing into when you pick it
up. You're not the first player, and if the tradition
holds, you won't be the last.

## What she learned in this book

Sixteen chapters of Instruments closes on a small set of
durable facts:

- Every instrument has a family (chapter 1). Families read
  as a first vocabulary — knowing what family an instrument
  belongs to already tells you a lot about how it will be
  used.

- Every instrument has a physical shape whose choices carry
  history (chapters 2-9 for the classical roster; 11-14 for
  the modern folk and voice families). The instrument you're
  holding was shaped by decisions that go back centuries.

- Every instrument has a set of playing techniques (touched
  in each chapter). The techniques compose. A technique from
  one instrument sometimes crosses to another (fingerpicking
  from classical guitar shows up on ukulele, harp, and even
  bass).

- Every instrument has cross-instrument relationships
  (chapter 10 on families, chapter 15 on arrangement). The
  instrument's role in an ensemble is different from its role
  in a solo. Reading the role is a different skill from
  reading the instrument.

- Every instrument has a vocabulary that carries lineage
  (chapter 13 on Latin percussion, chapter 14 on voice
  traditions). Using the vocabulary right is a way of
  listening to the tradition.

## A small farewell exercise

Consider a single instrument you didn't know before this book
— maybe the Indian tabla (chapter 8), maybe the Japanese
shakuhachi (chapter 5), maybe the mokume-gane craftsman's
tool-tradition mentioned in the vocabulary appendix. Take
five minutes and read one paragraph about it, out loud, in a
voice you'd use to tell a friend. Notice what parts of the
paragraph read as personal — as coming from a person who
holds the instrument in their hands — and what parts read as
encyclopedic. The personal parts are usually the ones worth
keeping. The encyclopedic parts are the ones you'll forget by
tomorrow.

```scheme
;; A small map from instrument -> a person you might learn from
(define teacher-of
  '((tabla       \"Ustad Zakir Hussain, live recordings from 1978-2010\")
    (guitar      \"Any local player who'll give you an hour\")
    (voice       \"A singer in whatever tradition first moved you\")
    (synth       \"The manual + the internet, seriously — synths teach themselves once you sit down\")
    (piano       \"The teacher your grandmother recommended\")
    (drums       \"Whoever's playing at the club you can walk to\")
    (fiddle      \"The oldest player at any bluegrass jam within
                  driving distance\")))

(map car teacher-of)
;; => (tabla guitar voice synth piano drums fiddle)
```

The map is illustrative, not prescriptive. The point is that
every instrument in this book has living teachers, and the
living teachers are the ones who carry the tradition
forward. A book like this one is a starting point; it isn't
the whole thing.

## Cross-book pointer

The instruments you've met here compose with the score
records from *Music*, chapter 11. When she writes a piece
of music, she names the instrument. The instrument is a
symbol pulled from the roster — `'piano`, `'shakuhachi`,
`'tabla`, `'voice`, `'synth-analog-sawtooth`. Each symbol
means an instrument in this book. That symbol-to-book
linkage is what makes her scores read as music rather than
as arbitrary sound events.

## Editorial note — the roster is not closed

New instruments enter the roster. The theremin joined in
1928. The Moog synthesizer joined in 1964. The Roland
TR-808 drum machine joined in 1980. The Novation Circuit
Tracks joined in 2021. Every year a maker somewhere invents
an instrument that finds its players and joins the roster,
and the roster grows.

She reads the roster as it is today. Tomorrow's roster will
be larger. When she meets an instrument she doesn't know,
she does the same thing she does when she meets any object
she doesn't know: she asks what it does, listens to how it
sounds, notices what family it belongs to, and holds the
knowledge lightly until it settles into a shape she can
carry.

The book closes here. The roster remembers you turned every
page. Come back when you need to remember what a fiddle
sounds like, or what tumbao means, or why the cuíca whistles.
The roster will still be here.

Goodnight, roster. Goodnight, reader. Come back and play.
")
