Errors as data is one of Motoi's simpler design choices with one of the largest downstream benefits. Because errors are structured, every downstream tool — the REPL's pretty-printer, the LLM-augmented fix, the Cortex error log, the reference-manual generator — can consume them without parsing strings.

If you have used a language where errors are strings, this will feel like a downgrade at first (fewer nice colored stack traces) and an upgrade after a week (every error is queryable and composable).

Turn the page. Chapter 9 opens trace and watch.

## 8.23 A last note

The `last-error` binding is your session's error handle. It updates every time an error is raised. If you want to save an error for later, bind it explicitly:

```scheme
(some-failing-verb)
(define my-error (last-error))
```

Now `my-error` is stable — it will not change when the next error is raised. This lets you compare errors across a session, or accumulate a list of errors to analyze together.

For scripted error collection:

```scheme
(define errors '())
(define (record-error e)
  (set! errors (cons e errors)))

(for-each
  (lambda (test)
    (with-handlers ((error? record-error))
      (run-test test)))
  test-suite)
```

Every failing test's error gets captured. Now `errors` is a list of records you can introspect, filter by kind, compare, or feed to the LLM for batch analysis.

Turn the page.

## 8.24 Deep-seed — every error kind Motoi ships

Motoi's error kinds are a closed vocabulary. Every error raised by the runtime is tagged with one of these kinds. Cart authors can add their own kinds, but the base set is fixed:

- `type-error` — a value's runtime type did not match what a verb expected
- `arity-error` — wrong number of arguments to a verb
- `unknown-verb` — the verb name is not in the registry
- `unbound-variable` — the symbol has no binding in scope
- `perm-denied` — the caller does not have the required permission tier
- `rate-limit` — the verb was called too often
- `fuel-exhausted` — the evaluation exceeded its fuel budget
- `read-error` — the reader could not parse the source
- `macro-error` — the macro expander failed
- `contract-violation` — a runtime contract check failed
- `sandbox-violation` — the sandbox refused the operation
- `network-error` — an outbound network call failed
- `not-implemented` — a stub verb was called
- `user-error` — an error raised by user code via `(error ...)`
- `wrapped` — an error wrapping another error via `:cause`

Fifteen kinds. Every error you catch is one of these. Filter your error handling by kind:

```scheme
(with-handlers
  ((type-error? handle-type-error)
   (arity-error? handle-arity-error)
   (perm-denied? refuse-and-log))
  (do-the-thing))
```

The predicates (`type-error?`, `arity-error?`, etc.) are built from the error's `:kind` field. Each is one line:

```scheme
(define (type-error? e) (and (error? e) (eq? 'type-error (error-kind e))))
```

## 8.25 Deep-seed — raising your own errors

To raise an error with structured fields, use `raise-error`:

```scheme
(raise-error
  :kind 'my-error-kind
  :message \"something went wrong\"
  :context (list :user-id user-id :operation 'save))
```

The error becomes queryable via all the same field verbs. Downstream code that catches it can introspect the `:context` to know what to do about it.

Your own error kinds are just symbols. There is no registration step. Pick a symbol that describes the failure and use it.

## 8.26 Deep-seed — the guard construct

```scheme
(guard
  ((type-error? e) (display \"got a type error: \") (display (error-message e)))
  ((error? e) (display \"got some other error: \") (display (error-message e))))
  (some-code-that-might-fail))
```

The clauses are tried in order. The first predicate that matches gets to handle the error. If none match, the error propagates.

`guard` is Scheme's standard error handling construct. Motoi supports it. It composes with the introspection layer because the error value is bound in each clause.

## 8.27 Deep-seed — the :cause chain

An error can wrap another error via `:cause`:

```scheme
(raise-error
  :kind 'wrapped
  :message \"failed to save user\"
  :cause underlying-io-error)
```

The `:cause` field is another error record. You can walk the chain:

```scheme
(define (root-cause e)
  (if (error-cause e)
      (root-cause (error-cause e))
      e))

(root-cause (last-error))
;; => the deepest cause
```

This is useful when an outer verb wraps a lower-level failure with more context. You can present the outer message to the user and drill down to the root cause for debugging.

## 8.28 Deep-seed — errors and the training corpus

Every documented error in the reference manual is a training pair. The model learns: when a user sees this error, the fix is this. When a user sees that error, the fix is that.

This means errors' structured shape does double duty. It helps the human debug in real time. It also trains the model to reach for the right fix when a similar error comes up in the future.

Well-structured errors are training data. Poorly-structured errors are noise. Motoi's discipline is that every runtime-raised error is well-structured; user-raised errors are the author's responsibility.

## 8.29 A closing observation on error handling philosophy

Motoi treats errors as values that flow through the system, not as exceptions that unwind it. The traditional exception model — throw, unwind stack, catch somewhere higher — is present via `guard` and `with-handlers`, but it is not the primary story.

The primary story is: the runtime raises structured errors; the introspection layer reads them; the LLM composes with them; and the programmer at the REPL handles them by binding, introspecting, and deciding what to do.

This is a different reflex than a Java or Python programmer might have. In those languages the reflex is `try / except: log(e)`. In Motoi the reflex is `(define e (last-error)); (introspect e)`. The intent is the same — understand the failure. The path is different.

Which path is better depends on the language's shape. Motoi's shape rewards the introspection path.

Turn the page. Chapter 9 opens trace and watch.

## 8.30 One last practical pattern — error introspection at the REPL

At the REPL, the most common workflow when something errors is:

```
> (some-verb 42)
error: type error — expected number, got string

> ,doc last-error
Return the most recent error raised in the current session.

> (define e (last-error))
> (error-kind e)
type-error
> (error-context e)
(:verb some-verb :expected number :got string :arg-index 0)
```

The context field told you exactly which argument was wrong and what shape was expected. That is often the entire debug — you now know your first argument to `some-verb` was a string when it should have been a number.

This is what \"errors as data\" enables. The message would have told you a similar thing but you would have had to parse the message. The context gives you the same information as pre-parsed structured data.

Reflex time. When an error surprises you, do not read the printed message twice. Bind and introspect.

"# Chapter 9 — Trace and watch: introspection over time

Snapshot introspection tells you what a value is right now. Sometimes you need the temporal dimension — what has this verb been called with, over the last hundred calls? What has this expression evaluated to over the last twenty prompts? For that Motoi has `,trace` and `,watch`, and both produce logs you can query as data.

## 9.1 Why over time?

A single snapshot answers *what is this?*. A log answers *how did this become what it is?*. For pure code the two are equivalent — the value tells the whole story. For code with state, or for programs that evolve across many calls, the log is where the answers live.

## 9.2 ,trace — record every call to a verb

`,trace foo` at the REPL wraps the verb `foo` in a tracing shim. Every subsequent call is recorded with its arguments and return value.

```
> ,trace my-verb
tracing my-verb

> (my-verb 42)
=> \"result\"
> (my-verb 100)
=> \"result-2\"

> ,trace-log my-verb
call 1: (my-verb 42) => \"result\"
call 2: (my-verb 100) => \"result-2\"
```

The trace log is a value. You can dump it with `,trace-log`, filter it, aggregate it, feed it to the LLM for pattern-finding.

The trace shim is per-verb. Multiple verbs can be traced at once; each has its own log.

## 9.3 ,untrace — stop recording

`,untrace foo` removes the shim. Subsequent calls are not recorded. The log accumulated so far is preserved until you clear it explicitly.

```
> ,untrace my-verb
untraced my-verb (12 calls recorded)

> ,trace-log my-verb
12 calls in log
```

You can inspect the log after untracing. The shim is gone but the data persists.

## 9.4 ,watch — re-evaluate on every prompt

`,watch expr` adds an expression to the watch list. Every time you hit enter at the REPL, every watched expression is re-evaluated and its current value is displayed.

```
> ,watch (length my-list)
watching: (length my-list) = 3

> (set! my-list (cons 99 my-list))
=> ()
(length my-list) = 4

> (set! my-list (cons 98 my-list))
=> ()
(length my-list) = 5
```

The watch line refreshes on every prompt. You see how the value evolves as you make changes.

Watch is useful for state debugging. Set up watches on the pieces of state you care about, then mutate. Every mutation shows you the new state without you having to re-type the query.

Call 3 subtracted 100. That is the mystery. Now you go read the code that decides to call `update-score` with -100 and find the bug.

## 9.22 Deep-seed — trace log shape

Each trace log entry is a record:

```scheme

 :timestamp seconds
 :args list
 :return value
 :duration-ms number

```

Seven fields. You can filter or sort by any of them. Common queries:

```scheme
;; slowest calls
(sort-by :duration-ms > (trace-log 'my-verb))

;; calls in the last 10 seconds
(filter
  (lambda (e) (< (- (current-second) (assoc :timestamp e)) 10))
  (trace-log 'my-verb))

;; total fuel used by this verb
(apply + (map (lambda (e) (assoc :fuel-used e)) (trace-log 'my-verb)))
```

The trace log is data. Every query is a filter or a projection. The primitives compose.

```
watching: (game-state) = 'in-progress
```

Every prompt refreshes all three lines. You have a live view of your game state without opening a UI.

This is watch's real payoff — a poor programmer's dashboard, built from Scheme primitives, updating on every command.

For high-frequency verbs, full tracing can be expensive. Motoi's trace shim supports sampling — record one call in every N.

```

> (draw-scene)
... paint-dot called 30000 times ...

> ,trace-log paint-dot
300 calls in log (sampled 1/100)
```

The log has 300 entries instead of 30000. You get statistical coverage without the memory cost of a full trace.

Sampling is what makes tracing viable for verbs called in tight loops. Without it, tracing a graphics-inner-loop verb would explode memory. With it, you get enough data to spot patterns and outliers.

```scheme
;;     The fourth call returned an unusual negative — that's where the bug is.\"
```

The LLM reads the log, spots patterns, tells you what happened in prose. Grounded in the actual data. No confabulation — the log is right there.

## 9.27 Deep-seed — traces as Cortex records

You can persist a trace to Cortex for durable analysis:

```scheme
(for-each

    (cortex/record
      :subject 'my-verb
      :predicate 'called
      :object entry
      :at (assoc :timestamp entry)
      :source 'trace-log))
  (trace-log 'my-verb))
```

Now the trace lives across sessions. Next week you can query Cortex for every call to `my-verb` and see how usage evolved. This is what having introspection as data enables — traces are just values you can persist, filter, and query alongside everything else.

Trace and watch are Motoi's temporal introspection primitives. They are small (two REPL commands plus a handful of verbs) but they open up a whole dimension of the introspection story.

Static introspection tells you what things are. Temporal introspection tells you how they got there. Together they cover most debugging.

## 9.29 Deep-seed — the trace shim mechanics

The trace shim works by replacing the verb binding with a wrapping procedure. The original verb is preserved on the shim, and every call goes through the wrapper first.

Roughly:

```scheme
(define (make-trace-shim original-verb log-name)
  (lambda args
    (let ((t0 (current-second))
          (call-num (next-call-number log-name)))
      (let ((result (apply original-verb args)))
        (record-trace-entry log-name call-num t0 args result)
        result))))
```

The shim measures time, counts the call, applies the original, records the entry, returns the result. The caller does not notice the wrapping.

`,untrace` restores the original binding by removing the shim. The log records survive.

This is a small piece of machinery but it is what makes tracing composable. Any verb can be traced. Untracing is instant. Multiple verbs can be traced simultaneously.

## 9.30 Deep-seed — a working debugging scenario

Say you have a cart that computes a score based on many small inputs. The output is wrong but you cannot find where.

**Step 1.** Trace the top-level scoring verb.

```
> ,trace compute-final-score
```

**Step 2.** Trace the inner computation.

```
> ,trace compute-partial-score
```

**Step 3.** Run the cart once.

```
> (run-my-cart)
```

**Step 4.** Introspect both logs.

```
> ,trace-log compute-final-score
> ,trace-log compute-partial-score
```

**Step 5.** Correlate. The partial-score calls that fed into the final-score should sum to the final score. If they do not, either the sum is wrong or a call is missing. If they do, the bug is upstream of partial-score.

Two trace commands. Two logs. Systematic debugging without a debugger.

Turn the page. Chapter 10 opens Cortex.

## 9.31 A last observation

Trace is one of those tools that changes how you think about debugging once you have it. You stop trying to reason about what code did and start looking at what code did. The log is authoritative. The reasoning is derivative.

That shift is worth a lot. Reasoning is expensive and error-prone; reading a log is cheap and honest.

If Motoi did nothing else right, having trace as a two-command REPL primitive would still make it a nice language to debug in. Combined with everything else in this book, it becomes a genuinely powerful debugging surface.

Turn the page. Chapter 10 opens Cortex — the persistent memory graph where facts live across sessions and every record carries provenance, source, and time as first-class fields you can query and filter to trace the history of any piece of the program state that the program chose to remember across runs and use as substrate for adaptive behavior later on in the session or the next one.
")

"# Chapter 10 — Cortex: introspecting what the program remembers

Cortex is Motoi's persistent memory graph. Book of Jesse Chapter 13 introduced writing to it. This chapter is the introspection lens — how to read what has already been recorded, how to filter, how to trace a value's provenance, how to see across time.

If Cortex is where the program remembers, introspection is how the program answers *what do I remember?*.

## 10.1 The record shape, one more time

Every Cortex record has five fields: subject, predicate, object, at (timestamp), source. This is deliberate — it is what makes provenance queryable.

```scheme
(cortex/query :subject 'user :predicate 'preferred-color)
;; => ((user preferred-color red 1720000000 ui-click))
```

The return is a list of records. Each record is a five-tuple. You can pull any field.

## 10.2 cortex/query — the introspection verb

`cortex/query` is Cortex's read side. Every keyword argument filters the returned records.

```scheme
(cortex/query :subject 'user)
;; every record about user

(cortex/query :predicate 'preferred-color)
;; every color preference record, across all subjects

(cortex/query :source 'ui-click)
;; every record whose source was ui-click

(cortex/query :subject 'user :predicate 'preferred-color :order-by 'at)
;; user's color history, chronological
```

The query is composable. Add filters to narrow. Add `:order-by` to sort. Add `:limit n` to cap.

## 10.3 Provenance — the :source field

Every record carries where it came from.

- `:source 'user-explicit-preference` — the user said so
- `:source 'inferred-from-3-choices` — the program guessed
- `:source 'default-guess` — the program had no data and made something up

Filter by source to weight evidence:

```scheme
(cortex/query
  :subject 'user
  :predicate 'preferred-color
  :source 'user-explicit-preference)
;; only what the user actually said, no inferences
```

Provenance is what turns Cortex from a database into an introspection layer. You do not just get facts; you get the story of how each fact came to be a fact.

## 10.4 Time — the :at field

Every record has a timestamp. You can query across time.

```scheme
(cortex/query
  :subject 'user
  :predicate 'preferred-color
  :order-by 'at)
;; chronological history

(cortex/query
  :subject 'user
  :predicate 'preferred-color
  :at :gt (- (current-second) 3600))
;; last hour only
```

Time-aware queries let a program say things like *the user's color changed three times today* or *the last preference was five minutes ago*. This is introspection over time via the same query interface.

## Sections 10.5 through 10.16 — pending Wave 3 authoring

- 10.5 Aggregating over Cortex records
- 10.6 Cortex + LLM — reason-about a stored value
- 10.7 Provenance chains — tracing a value back to its source
- 10.8 Cortex introspection at the REPL
- 10.9 Cortex vs environment — persistent vs transient
- 10.10 Bulk introspection — dumping the whole graph
- 10.11 Cortex + trace — logging trace results as records
- 10.12 Cortex as substrate for adaptation
- 10.13 Deleting records (rare, with care)
- 10.14 Cortex introspection safety (Chapter 16 preview)
- 10.15 Cortex + registry — cross-introspection
- 10.16 Closing — memory as a queryable graph

## 10.17 Worked example — tracing a preference

The program has decided the user prefers red. How did it decide?

```scheme
(define color-records
  (cortex/query :subject 'user :predicate 'preferred-color))

color-records
;; => ((user preferred-color red 1720000000 inferred-from-3-choices)
;;     (user picked-color red 1719999900 ui-click)
;;     (user picked-color red 1719999800 ui-click)
;;     (user picked-color red 1719999700 ui-click))
```

Four records. The first is the inference. The next three are the ui-click events that fed the inference. You can trace the whole reasoning chain.

This is what provenance introspection buys you. Not just *what does the program think?* — but *why does it think it?*.

## 10.18 Cortex + LLM

Chapter 13's `reason-about` verb takes a value and reads Cortex for context. If you ask about the user's color preference:

```scheme
(reason-about (cortex/query :subject 'user :predicate 'preferred-color))
;; => \"The user's preference for red was inferred from three ui-click events between
;;     16:00 and 17:00. The inference source suggests this is program-derived, not
;;     user-stated. Confidence: moderate.\"
```

The LLM read the records and produced prose. Grounded in the actual data, not confabulated.

## 10.19 Preview of Chapter 11

Chapter 11 opens the registry — the map of every verb Motoi knows about, as a queryable value. Cortex is memory of runtime events. The registry is memory of the language surface. Both are values you can walk.

Turn the page.

## 10.20 Wave 3 preview

The full chapter (~8000 words) will cover:

- All Cortex query kwargs (subject, predicate, object, at, source, order-by, limit)
- Time-range queries with `:at :gt` and `:at :lt` and `:at :between`
- Aggregation patterns (count, group-by, distinct)
- Provenance chain walking
- Cortex introspection at the REPL
- Bulk dumping and inspection
- Integration with trace logs from Chapter 9
- Reasoning about stored values with the LLM (Chapter 13 crossover)
- Safety considerations (Chapter 16 crossover)
- Cortex as a training substrate

## 10.21 A closing observation

Cortex is what turns a Motoi program from a stateless computation into an accretive process. Introspection over Cortex is what turns that accretion into an observable one.

Without Cortex the program forgets on every run. Without introspection over Cortex the accretion is invisible. Together they give you a program that learns and knows what it has learned.

That is not a small thing. Most programs do neither.

## 10.22 A closing exercise

Try this session. Write three color preferences. Query them back. Introspect.

```scheme
(cortex/record :subject 'user :predicate 'picked-color :object 'red :at (current-second) :source 'ui-click)
(cortex/record :subject 'user :predicate 'picked-color :object 'red :at (current-second) :source 'ui-click)
(cortex/record :subject 'user :predicate 'picked-color :object 'blue :at (current-second) :source 'ui-click)

(cortex/query :subject 'user :predicate 'picked-color)
;; three records

(length (cortex/query :subject 'user :predicate 'picked-color :object 'red))
;; 2 — red was picked twice
```

Two writes, one query, one count. That is the whole rhythm of Cortex introspection. Records in, records out, projections over records to answer specific questions.

Turn the page. Chapter 11 opens the registry.

## 10.23 Deep-seed — one worked provenance walk

Suppose your program shows the user a suggested color. You want to explain why.

```scheme
(define (explain-suggestion subject)
  (define preference
    (car (cortex/query
           :subject subject
           :predicate 'preferred-color
           :order-by 'at :limit 1)))
  (define source (cortex/object-source preference))
  (define supporting
    (cortex/query
      :subject subject
      :predicate 'picked-color
      :source 'ui-click))
  (list
    :suggestion (cortex/object preference)
    :because (list :source source :evidence (length supporting) :records supporting)))

(explain-suggestion 'user)
;; => (:suggestion red
;;     :because (:source inferred-from-3-choices :evidence 3 :records (...)))
```

The verb returns a complete explanation — the suggestion, the source, the count of supporting evidence, and the raw records. If the user asks *why do you keep suggesting red?* you have the answer built in.

## 10.24 Deep-seed — Cortex + registry cross-introspection

Cortex holds facts. The registry holds verbs. They can reference each other.

```scheme
;; record that we used a specific verb
(cortex/record :subject 'session :predicate 'used-verb :object 'map :at (current-second) :source 'trace)

;; introspect verb usage
(define verb-usage (cortex/query :subject 'session :predicate 'used-verb))
;; list of records

;; join with registry to get docs for each used verb
(map
  (lambda (r)
    (let ((v (cortex/object r)))
      (list :verb v :doc (doc-of v))))
  verb-usage)
```

Cortex tells you what was used. The registry tells you what it does. Compose them and you have a personalized usage report.

## 10.25 Turn the page

Chapter 11 opens the registry — the vocabulary of the language, as a queryable map. Turn the page.

## 10.26 Deep-seed — aggregation

Cortex does not have SQL-style aggregation built in. You build it from primitives.

**Count records matching a filter.**

```scheme
(length (cortex/query :subject 'user :predicate 'picked-color :object 'red))
```

**Group records by a field.**

```scheme
(define (group-by field records)
  (define groups (hash))
  (for-each
    (lambda (r)
      (let ((k (assoc field r)))
        (hash-set! groups k (cons r (hash-ref groups k '())))))
    records)
  groups)

(group-by :object (cortex/query :subject 'user :predicate 'picked-color))
;; => hash of color -> list of records
```

**Distinct values.**

```scheme
(define (distinct-objects records)
  (unique (map cortex/object records)))

(distinct-objects (cortex/query :subject 'user :predicate 'picked-color))
;; => (red blue green)
```

Three tiny helpers built from primitives. Aggregation over Cortex is a filter followed by a fold, always. Once you know the pattern you can build any aggregation you need in a few lines.

## 10.27 Deep-seed — time-range queries

Cortex supports range predicates on `:at`.

```scheme
;; last hour
(cortex/query :at :gt (- (current-second) 3600))

;; last hour of specific subject
(cortex/query :subject 'user :at :gt (- (current-second) 3600))

;; between two timestamps
(cortex/query :at :between (list start-time end-time))
```

Time-range introspection is what lets you answer questions like *what happened during this specific session?* or *how has the user's behavior changed since we shipped the update?*. Both are one query.

## 10.28 Deep-seed — the whole graph

If you want to see the whole Cortex graph for a subject:

```scheme
(cortex/query :subject 'user)
;; every fact ever recorded about the user
```

That is often a lot of records. Bulk introspection at this scale needs pagination:

```scheme
(cortex/query :subject 'user :limit 100 :offset 0)
;; first 100 records

(cortex/query :subject 'user :limit 100 :offset 100)
;; next 100
```

Or just take a summary:

```scheme
(define user-summary
  (list
    :total-records (length (cortex/query :subject 'user))
    :predicates (distinct-objects (map cortex/predicate (cortex/query :subject 'user)))
    :oldest (car (cortex/query :subject 'user :order-by 'at :limit 1))
    :newest (car (cortex/query :subject 'user :order-by 'at-desc :limit 1))))
```

Four fields describing what the program knows about the user, computed from Cortex introspection primitives. Print it and you have a one-screen summary of a subject's whole history.

Turn the page.

## 10.29 A closing note on doctrine

Cortex is not a database. It is a memory graph. The introspection layer treats it as data — records with fields, queries with filters, projections over the returns.

Every pattern here would work over any store shaped like Cortex. If you have a graph database, the queries port. If you have a triple store, the queries port. The Cortex verb layer is a specific implementation; the introspection reflex generalizes.

If you learn to introspect Cortex well, you have learned to introspect any memory graph. That skill transfers.

Turn the page. Chapter 11 opens the registry — the introspectable map of the language itself.

## 10.30 One more example — the last-N pattern

A common Cortex introspection is *what happened most recently?*. The pattern:

```scheme
(define (last-n subject predicate n)
  (cortex/query
    :subject subject
    :predicate predicate
    :order-by 'at-desc
    :limit n))

(last-n 'user 'picked-color 5)
;; => last five color picks, newest first
```

`last-n` is a five-line helper that becomes the workhorse for any recent-activity display. Every game's HUD, every dashboard, every recent-history widget uses this shape.

## 10.31 Deep-seed — Cortex as substrate for adaptation

Cortex introspection is what lets a program adapt. Without introspection, Cortex would just be a write-only log — no way to consult past facts to decide current behavior.

With introspection:

```scheme
(define (default-color)
  (or (cortex/object (car (last-n 'user 'preferred-color 1)))
      'blue))
```

When the program needs a default color, it introspects Cortex first. If the user has ever expressed a preference, use it. Otherwise fall back.

This tiny pattern is what turns a program from stateless-across-sessions to adaptive. And it is entirely built from Cortex introspection — no separate personalization system needed.

Turn the page. Chapter 11 opens the registry.

## 10.32 A last observation on time

Cortex records have an :at field. That means every query can be time-scoped. Every fact can be historical.

This makes Cortex fundamentally different from a key-value store. Key-value stores overwrite. Cortex accretes. The introspection layer lets you see the accretion.

If you have ever wanted a database that remembers not just the current state but every past state, Cortex is that database. And it introspects the same way as everything else in Motoi — one verb call, one filtered projection.

Turn the page.
")

"# Chapter 11 — The registry: introspecting the whole vocabulary

Every registered verb lives in one map. That map is a value. You can iterate it, filter it, project fields out of it, and build any tool you want on top of it. This chapter shows the registry as a first-class queryable data structure.

## 11.1 snapshot-registry

The primary verb is `snapshot-registry`. It returns a copy of the current registry as a plain object — verb name → metadata record.

```scheme
(snapshot-registry)
;; => a hash-like structure mapping every verb name to its metadata
```

The return is a snapshot — safe to iterate without worrying about mutation. Every subsequent call returns a fresh snapshot.

## 11.2 Iterating the registry

```scheme
(define all-verbs (map car (snapshot-registry)))
(length all-verbs)
;; => 512 (or however many verbs are registered)

(take all-verbs 10)
;; => (car cdr cons list map filter fold apply eval define)
```

The list of names is the vocabulary of the language. You can enumerate it in any order — sorted, filtered by prefix, grouped by namespace.

## 11.3 Filtering by namespace

```scheme
(define (verbs-in-namespace ns)
  (filter
    (lambda (n) (string-prefix? (string-append ns \"/\") n))
    (map car (snapshot-registry))))

(verbs-in-namespace \"cortex\")
;; => (cortex/read cortex/write cortex/record cortex/query cortex/remember cortex/recall)
```

Every cortex verb, in one call. Same for `card/`, `composer/`, `paint-`, etc.

## 11.4 Filtering by perm

```scheme
(define (verbs-with-perm perm)
  (filter
    (lambda (n)
      (equal? perm (cdr (assoc 'perm (help n)))))
    (map car (snapshot-registry))))

(verbs-with-perm \"financial\")
;; => every financial-tier verb — audit this list carefully
```

Filter by any metadata field. The registry is data; every field is queryable.

## Sections 11.5 through 11.16 — pending Wave 3 authoring

- 11.5 The namespace map
- 11.6 Perm distribution
- 11.7 Tier distribution
- 11.8 Since distribution — verbs by release
- 11.9 Auditing a runtime
- 11.10 The registry and the reference manual
- 11.11 The registry and the LLM training corpus
- 11.12 Custom queries — building small tools
- 11.13 The registry as documentation source
- 11.14 Enumerating aliases and deprecations
- 11.15 The registry validation step
- 11.16 Closing — the registry as the language surface

## 11.17 A worked audit

```scheme
(define (audit-runtime)
  (let ((all (snapshot-registry)))
    (list
      :total-verbs (length all)
      :by-namespace (group-by-namespace all)
      :by-perm (group-by-perm all)
      :by-tier (group-by-tier all)
      :undocumented (count-undocumented all)
      :deprecated (count-deprecated all))))
```

One function that reports on the whole language surface. The primitives compose.

## 11.18 A worked report

```scheme
(audit-runtime)
;; => (:total-verbs 512
;;     :by-namespace ((base . 87) (list . 34) (string . 22) (cortex . 6) (composer . 15) ...)
;;     :by-perm ((read . 380) (paint . 52) (animate . 8) (state-change . 45) (financial . 3) ...)
;;     :by-tier ((core . 335) (extended . 155) (experimental . 22))
;;     :undocumented 13
;;     :deprecated 6)
```

That is a snapshot of Motoi's language surface. 512 verbs. Most are read. 335 are frozen core. 13 need docs. Actionable, from the introspection primitives.

## 11.19 Preview of Chapter 12

Chapter 12 opens apropos and shape-based search. When you know what you want but not the verb's name, search finds it. The registry from this chapter is the search space.

Turn the page.

## 11.20 Wave 3 preview

The full chapter will cover:

- The full snapshot-registry return shape
- Every projection over the registry
- Namespace and tier distributions
- Auditing patterns (docs, examples, perms, sources)
- Release-notes generation from since-tag distribution
- Custom tool-building on top of the registry
- Interaction with the reference-manual generator
- Registry validation and startup checks
- Alias and deprecation enumeration

## 11.21 Closing

The registry is the language surface as data. Every verb, every field, every convention captured in one map. Query it and you have queried the language.

Turn the page. Chapter 12 opens search.

## 11.22 Deep-seed — the registry validation step

At startup, `validateRegistry` in `src/verbRegistry.js` walks every registered verb and checks the perm invariant: any name pattern that looks state-changing (ends in `!`, starts with `card-`, etc.) must have an explicit perm, not an inferred one.

```scheme
(validate-registry)
;; either succeeds silently or lists offenders
```

This is the runtime's cheapest safety net against forgotten perm declarations. If a new verb was registered without thinking about perm, the validation catches it before any cart runs.

For introspection purposes: `(validate-registry)` returns nil on success or a list of offending names on failure. You can wire it into CI.

## 11.23 Deep-seed — enumerating deprecated aliases

Some verbs are aliases for others. The metadata records this via `deprecated` and `aliasFor` fields.

```scheme
(define (deprecated-verbs)
  (filter
    (lambda (n)
      (assoc 'deprecated (help n)))
    (map car (snapshot-registry))))

(deprecated-verbs)
;; => (cortex/remember old-name-1 old-name-2)
```

For each, get the canonical name:

```scheme
(map
  (lambda (n) (list n (cdr (assoc 'aliasFor (help n)))))
  (deprecated-verbs))
;; => ((cortex/remember cortex/write) (old-name-1 new-name-1) ...)
```

Now you have a migration map. Every deprecated verb and what to rename it to. A linter can consume this map and flag every deprecated call in a cart with a suggested rename.

## 11.24 Deep-seed — the reference manual is generated from this

`src/docs-emitter.js` walks the registry and emits a section per verb into `scheme/MOTOI-SCHEME-REFERENCE.slat`. Every field the introspection layer reads is what the reference documents.

If you want to regenerate the reference:

```scheme
(emit-reference-manual \"scheme/MOTOI-SCHEME-REFERENCE.slat\")
;; writes a fresh manual from the current registry
```

The manual and the registry are consistent by construction. If the registry adds a verb, the next manual build has it. If the registry loses a verb, the next manual build drops the section.

Turn the page. Chapter 12 opens apropos and search — how to find a verb when you know what you want but not what to call it.

## 11.25 A closing observation on scale

The registry is small. Around five hundred verbs in a typical Motoi runtime. That is small enough to iterate in a millisecond and small enough to hold in your head with practice.

Compare to a JVM classpath with fifty thousand classes, or a JavaScript ecosystem with a million published packages. Motoi's registry is walkable. That walkability is why introspection over the registry is worth doing.

If Motoi ever grows past a few thousand verbs the introspection story will need to be re-thought. For now, the whole language surface is queryable in a fraction of a second, and that speed is what makes the reflex viable.

## 11.26 Turn the page

Chapter 12 opens apropos, find-by-arity, find-by-contract — search over the registry when you know the shape but not the name. Turn the page.

## 11.27 One more small example

If you want to see every verb whose name contains a substring:

```scheme
(filter (lambda (n) (string-contains n \"sort\"))
        (map car (snapshot-registry)))
;; => (sort sort-by sort! sorted? unsort merge-sort)
```

Simple filter, useful result. This is `apropos` under the hood — Chapter 12 will name it and formalize it. Here the primitive is enough.

Turn the page.

## 11.28 Deep-seed — the registry as training data

Motoi Copilot was trained on the registry. Every field on every record contributed. The model learned:

- Verb names (as tokens the model can generate)
- Doc strings (as natural-language associations)
- Contracts (as signature templates)
- Examples (as generation templates)
- Namespaces (as grouping context)
- Perms (as safety hints)

The registry is not just a runtime lookup. It is a corpus. Every well-written verb metadata record is a training pair for the next model iteration.

This is why Chapter 2 emphasized filling in the fields. Every field-that-was-filled-in becomes training signal. Every field-that-was-not becomes a gap the model has to guess through.

## 11.29 Deep-seed — the by-since query

```scheme
(define (verbs-since version)
  (filter
    (lambda (n)
      (equal? version (cdr (assoc 'since (help n)))))
    (map car (snapshot-registry))))

(verbs-since \"1.4\")
;; => every verb added in the 1.4 release
```

Release notes generator, built from introspection. Publish `(verbs-since \"1.4\")` and you have the addition list for the release.

## 11.30 Deep-seed — the by-source query

```scheme
(define (verbs-from-file path)
  (filter
    (lambda (n)
      (let ((src (source-of n)))
        (and src (string-prefix? path src))))
    (map car (snapshot-registry))))

(verbs-from-file \"lib/composer/\")
;; => every verb registered from lib/composer/
```

Grouping by source file often groups by feature. All the composer widgets are in `lib/composer/`; all the audio verbs in `lib/audio/`. This query gives you the feature-level slice.

Turn the page.

## 11.31 Deep-seed — a quality dashboard

Combine everything from this chapter into a live quality dashboard:

```scheme
(define (registry-dashboard)
  (let ((all (snapshot-registry)))
    (list
      :total (length all)
      :core (length (verbs-with-tier \"core\"))
      :extended (length (verbs-with-tier \"extended\"))
      :experimental (length (verbs-with-tier \"experimental\"))
      :undocumented (length (undocumented-verbs))
      :missing-examples (length (verbs-missing-examples))
      :deprecated (length (deprecated-verbs))
      :namespaces (length (unique (namespaces-in-registry))))))
```

Ten fields, one call. Print at the end of every dev session and you know the language's health.

Turn the page. Chapter 12 opens the search family.

## 11.32 Deep-seed — walking the whole map

For a bird's-eye view, dump the registry to a summary form:

```scheme
(define (registry-summary)
  (for-each
    (lambda (entry)
      (let ((name (car entry))
            (meta (cdr entry)))
        (display (string-append
                   name \" [\" (or (cdr (assoc 'namespace meta)) \"base\") \"] \"
                   (or (cdr (assoc 'doc meta)) \"(no doc)\")))
        (newline)))
    (snapshot-registry)))
```

Call `(registry-summary)` and you get every verb, one per line, with namespace and doc. That is the whole language surface in one scroll. Print to a file and you have your own local reference.

## 11.33 Deep-seed — the tiny language browser

Combine namespace enumeration with per-namespace listings and you have a two-level browser:

```scheme
(define (list-namespaces)
  (unique
    (filter (lambda (x) x)

(list-namespaces)
```

This is what Chapters 10 and 11 have been leading to. Small primitives compose into tools. The tools are lightweight enough to write in a session, portable enough to work in any REPL, useful enough to keep in your notes.

The registry is the whole language surface as data. That statement sounds abstract until you use it.

The first time you sit down and write `(map car (snapshot-registry))` and see every verb Motoi has scroll past on stdout, something clicks. The language stops being a mysterious thing you learn from tutorials and starts being a queryable data structure you can examine at will.

For your notes, one last helper:

```scheme

    (display (string-append n \": \" (or (doc-of n) \"(no doc)\"))) (newline))
  (my-favorite-verbs))
```

Curate the list of the fifteen verbs you use most. Wrap them in a helper. Now `(my-favorite-verbs)` gives you your personal one-liner cheat-sheet whenever you need it.

That is the shape of tools you build on top of introspection. Small, personal, one call away.

"# Chapter 12 — Apropos and search: introspecting by shape

You know what you want. You do not remember what the verb is called. Search bridges the gap.

Motoi's search family runs over the registry (Chapter 11) with different match criteria: by name (`apropos`), by arity, by contract shape, by doc-string content. Each is one filter over the registry. Each returns a list of verb names.

## 12.1 apropos — the workhorse

`apropos` takes a regex or substring and returns every verb whose name matches.

```scheme
(apropos \"sort\")
;; => (sort sort-by sort! sorted? unsort merge-sort)

(apropos \"cortex\")
;; => (cortex/read cortex/write cortex/record cortex/query cortex/remember cortex/recall)

(apropos \"paint-.*\")
;; => (paint-dot paint-line paint-circle paint-arc paint-rect ...)
```

At the REPL: `,apropos <regex>` prints the matching names one per line, sorted.

The default match is a regex if the string looks regex-y, substring otherwise. Motoi's implementation lives in `src/repl.js` line 69.

## 12.2 verbs-in-namespace

`(verbs-in-namespace ns)` returns every verb whose name is prefixed with `ns/`. This was shown in Chapter 11.

```scheme
(verbs-in-namespace \"composer\")
;; => (composer/canvas composer/slider composer/button ...)
```

Namespace scope for search when you know the family.

## 12.3 doc-search

Search doc strings (not just names) for a keyword:

```scheme
(define (doc-search keyword)
  (filter
    (lambda (n)
      (let ((d (doc-of n)))
        (and d (string-contains d keyword))))
    (map car (snapshot-registry))))

(doc-search \"predicate\")
;; => every verb whose doc mentions the word predicate
```

Doc-search finds verbs whose name does not include the concept but whose behavior does. Chapter 11's grep-docs was the same pattern.

## Sections 12.4 through 12.16 — pending Wave 3 authoring

- 12.4 find-by-arity
- 12.5 find-by-contract shape
- 12.6 find-by-perm

- 12.14 Search and Cortex — searching past usage

When you know what you want but not the name:

1. `(apropos \"keyword\")` — try the name first
2. `(doc-search \"keyword\")` — try the docs if the name search was thin
3. `(verbs-in-namespace \"ns\")` — try the namespace if you know the family
4. `(did-you-mean 'guess)` — LLM-augmented for tricky cases (Chapter 13)

Four options. Try them in order. One of them will hit.

Three candidates. Which one?

```scheme
(describe 'std-dev)

;; Return the standard deviation of a list of numbers.
```

Perfect. Copy from `(examples-of 'std-dev)`, adapt, done.

Two searches, one describe, one examples. From *I need standard deviation* to *I have a working call* in four keystrokes.

**Verbs that take exactly two arguments.**

```scheme
(filter (lambda (n) (eq? 2 (arity-of n)))
```

**Verbs whose contract mentions a hash return.**

```scheme
(define (ranked-apropos keyword)

    (sort-by
      (lambda (n) (string-distance keyword n))

```

Now the closest matches come first. If you typed `\"sotr\"` (a typo), `sort` should be at the top of the list because the edit distance is small.

```scheme
(define (find-by-contract-return type)

    (lambda (n)
      (let ((c (contract-of n)))
        (and c (string-contains c (string-append \"-> \" type)))))
    (map car (snapshot-registry))))
```


The registry is per-runtime. Whatever is loaded is searchable. Dialects add their own verbs to the same registry; apropos surfaces them all.

Every time you find yourself thinking *what was that verb called?*, reach for `,apropos <keyword>`. Faster than a browser. Faster than a text editor. Faster than remembering.

Three calls. You have a working sense of a namespace you had never touched. That is exploration at introspection speed.

## 12.33 Deep-seed — the map of search primitives

The complete search family, so far:

- `apropos <regex-or-substring>` — by name
- `doc-search <keyword>` — by doc string content
- `verbs-in-namespace <ns>` — by namespace prefix
- `verbs-with-perm <perm>` — by permission tier
- `verbs-with-tier <tier>` — by core/extended/experimental
- `find-by-arity <n>` — by argument count
- `find-by-contract-return <type>` — by return shape (Wave 3)
- `find-by-source-file <path>` — by source location
- `verbs-since <version>` — by release version

Nine search axes. Combine them with `filter` for AND, `append` and `unique` for OR. Any search you can describe as a boolean expression on the metadata is one filter away.

## 12.34 A last thought on search

Search is where the introspection layer becomes an ecosystem browser. Not just *what does this verb do?* — but *what verbs are there?*. That question, asked easily and answered fully, is what makes a language feel explorable.

Motoi's small verb count is what makes search feasible. The uniform metadata is what makes it useful. Both together are what make apropos a reflex instead of a curiosity.

Turn the page. Chapter 13 opens the LLM-augmented layer, where mechanical search meets peer reasoning.


Four candidates. `hash->list` sounds like what you want.

```scheme
;; hash->list [base] — arity 1
;; Return the contents of a hash as a list of (key . value) pairs.
```

Yes. `(examples-of 'hash->list)` for a call template. Done.

Shape-based search took *I need something with this shape* to *here is the verb* in one filter and one describe.

"# Chapter 13 — Ask the LLM: introspection through a peer

Every chapter so far has been mechanical. Registry lookups. Deterministic returns. No model in the loop. This chapter opens the LLM-augmented layer — a family of verbs that use a peer language model to answer questions the mechanical layer cannot.

Read carefully. The rules are different here. The LLM can guess where the mechanical layer would return nil. That is powerful. It is also dangerous unless the layer is honest about the difference.

Motoi's LLM-augmented family is designed to be honest.

## 13.1 The five primitives

The LLM layer bottoms out in five primitives:

- `llm/ask` — ask the model a question, get a string
- `llm/complete` — complete a partial expression
- `llm/stream` — stream tokens to a callback
- `llm/embed` — embed text as a vector for similarity
- `llm/config` — describe the current model binding

Every higher-level verb in this chapter is built from these five. `llm/config` is the introspection verb on the LLM itself — it tells you which model is bound, what temperature, what endpoint. It is a verb that describes the model behind the model.

```scheme
(llm/config)
;; => (:model \"motoi-copilot\" :endpoint \"local\" :temperature 0.2 :max-tokens 2048)
```

## 13.2 what-is — grounded lookup

`what-is` is the LLM-augmented equivalent of `help`. It takes a symbol and returns everything known about it: the registry record if it exists, plus an LLM-generated prose description if useful.

```scheme
(what-is 'car)
;; => (:name \"car\" :grounded #t :doc \"Return the first element...\" :examples (...) :prose \"car is a foundational list operation...\")
```

Key field: `:grounded`. If true, the answer came from the registry — the LLM added prose but did not invent facts. If false, the LLM speculated and the answer includes a `:confidence` score.

This is the *grounded, not hallucinated* principle. Every LLM-augmented verb tries the mechanical layer first and only speculates when the mechanical layer returned nothing.

## 13.3 explain — prose for a value or form

`explain` takes any value or form and returns a prose description.

```scheme
(explain '(map + '(1 2 3) '(4 5 6)))
;; => \"This form applies + to corresponding pairs from two lists,
;;     producing (5 7 9). The + verb takes multiple arguments;
;;     map with multiple lists supplies one from each in parallel.\"
```

The LLM read the form. It looked up every verb (via `help`) to ground its explanation. It produced prose that walks the reader through what the form does.

If the LLM cannot ground a symbol (because it is not registered), the returned prose says so explicitly.

## 13.4 fix — suggest a fix for an error

`fix` takes an error record and returns a suggested corrected form.

```scheme
(crdr '(1 2 3))
;; error: unknown verb: crdr

(fix (last-error))
;; => (cdr '(1 2 3))
```

The LLM read the error's `:did-you-mean` field, the `:context`, the raw message. It generated a fix. The return is a form you can evaluate.

Nothing forces you to eval the fix. The REPL prints it as a suggestion; the human decides.

## 13.5 shape-of — mechanical plus interpretive

`shape-of` bridges Chapter 3's mechanical `type-of` with the LLM's interpretive prose.

```scheme
(shape-of some-cortex-record)
;; => (:mechanical (:type hash :length 5 :keys (:subject :predicate :object :at :source))
;;     :prose \"This appears to be a Cortex record — a five-tuple of subject, predicate, object, timestamp, and source.\"
;;     :probable-origin \"cortex/record or cortex/query\"
;;     :confidence 0.92)
```

The mechanical fields are always right (they come from `type-of` and `keys`). The prose is the LLM's interpretation. The confidence tells you how sure the model is.

## 13.6 reason-about — where did this come from?

`reason-about` reads Cortex records mentioning a value, REPL history producing it, and the registry lookups it depended on. Returns prose about provenance.

```scheme
(reason-about (cortex/query :predicate 'preferred-color))
;; => \"The user's preference for red was inferred from three ui-click events
;;     between 16:00 and 17:00. The inference source suggests this is
;;     program-derived, not user-stated. Confidence: moderate.\"
```

The LLM read the actual records and the actual history. The prose is grounded. Nothing invented.

## Sections 13.7 through 13.16 — pending Wave 4 authoring

- 13.7 The four families from LLM-AUGMENTED-REPL-1.0 spec
- 13.8 rewrite / critique / annotate — code transformation
- 13.9 paraphrase / disambiguate — style variation
- 13.10 next-step / reflect / mentor — session-aware verbs
- 13.11 what-changed / diff-explain — temporal comparison
- 13.12 pretty-error / reduce-noise — meta verbs
- 13.13 rag / book — retrieval-augmented Q&A
- 13.14 scaffold / propose-verb — generative verbs
- 13.15 quiz / grade-quiz — pedagogical verbs
- 13.16 Closing — LLM as peer, not oracle

## 13.17 The grounded-vs-hallucinated principle

Every LLM-augmented verb obeys the same rule: try the mechanical layer first. Only speculate when the mechanical layer runs out. Always mark the return with `:grounded #t` or `:grounded #f` and, when not grounded, include a `:confidence` score.

This is what separates a useful peer verb from a dangerous one. A verb that always hallucinates is a liability. A verb that hallucinates only when it must, and marks the hallucination clearly, is a peer.

## 13.18 Preview of Chapter 14

Chapter 14 opens composer introspection. A composer canvas is a live rendering of a form; moving a widget updates the form; changing the form updates the widgets. Introspection over the round-trip is a different flavor of introspection than what Chapters 1-13 covered.

Turn the page.

## 13.19 Wave 4 preview

The full chapter (~8000 words) will cover:

- All four LLM-augmented families from the spec (primitives, introspection-augmented, session-aware, generative)
- Every verb from the LLM-AUGMENTED-REPL-1.0 doc, with worked examples
- The composition rules (pipeline chaining)
- The four-surface test (terminal, web, iOS, voice)
- The graceful-degradation story (what happens when LLM is offline)
- Cross-language consistency (Motoi vs Sakura models)
- The safety story (Chapter 16 crossover)
- Extensive exercises

## 13.20 A closing observation

The LLM is not the star. Introspection is. The LLM extends what introspection can answer, but the mechanical layer is what keeps every answer honest.

If Motoi shipped only the mechanical introspection layer, you would still have most of the value. The LLM verbs are icing — powerful icing, but icing. The cake is the registry, the metadata, the deterministic queries.

Do not skip Chapters 1-12 to jump to Chapter 13. The LLM works best when you already know what the mechanical layer can do. It works badly when the reader treats it as a substitute for reading the metadata.

## 13.21 Deep-seed — the composition pipeline

Verbs from the LLM-augmented family chain naturally.

```scheme
;; fix + rewrite: repair, then improve
(rewrite (fix (last-error)) :goal 'idiomatic)

;; propose + scaffold: design a verb, then write the stub
(scaffold 'verb (propose-verb \"convert color to hex\"))

;; explain + annotate: prose plus inline comments
(list :prose (explain form) :annotated (annotate form))

;; imagine-output + apply: predict, then verify
(let ((predicted (imagine-output 'sort '((3 1 2))))
      (actual (sort '(3 1 2))))
  (compare predicted actual))
```

Each verb returns data. Data flows into the next verb. Pipelines read left-to-right when they are chained with `->`.

## 13.22 Deep-seed — what changes with an LLM

Without the LLM:
- You get grounded answers or nil.
- Explanations come from the docs verbatim.
- Errors are structured but not narrated.
- Debugging is manual pattern-matching.

With the LLM:
- You get grounded answers plus interpretive prose.
- Explanations blend the docs with contextual analysis.
- Errors get narrated in plain language.
- Debugging can be conversational (pair-with).

The LLM does not replace anything. It adds a layer on top. Every mechanical capability from Chapters 1-12 still works and is still preferred where deterministic answers are needed.

## 13.23 Deep-seed — the honesty audit

Every LLM-augmented verb should pass this audit:

1. Does it try the mechanical layer first?
2. Does it mark grounded vs speculative in the return?
3. Does it include a confidence score when speculating?
4. Does it degrade gracefully when the LLM is offline?
5. Does it cite sources when doing retrieval?

If a verb fails any of these, file a bug. The point of the LLM-augmented layer is honesty; a dishonest verb defeats the whole design.

## 13.24 Turn the page

Chapter 14 opens the composer's round-trip as introspection. Turn the page.

## 13.25 A closing note on models

Motoi Copilot is the model bound in a Motoi runtime. It was trained on this book (among others) plus the reference manual plus the registry metadata. When it answers, it is answering from having read the source.

Sakura in the Sakura runtime uses a different model with a different persona. Same verbs, different voice. That is the fork story from Motoi Copilot's memory notes.

If you swap models (via `llm/config`), you get a different personality answering the same verbs. The verbs are stable; the interpretation is model-dependent. That is worth remembering when you read an LLM-augmented answer — the answer's shape is the verb; its style is the model.

Turn the page. Chapter 14.

## 13.26 Deep-seed — a worked LLM-augmented session

You are debugging. You get an error you do not understand.

```scheme
(some-verb 42)
;; error: unexpected shape at position 2
```

Cryptic. Enable the LLM helper.

```scheme
(pretty-error (last-error))
;; => \"The verb some-verb expected its second argument to be a list of numbers,
;;     but you passed a string. Position 2 (the third argument if you're
;;     counting from zero) was 'hello' when it should have been like '(1 2 3).
;;     Fix: convert 'hello' or replace with the intended list.\"
```

Now you understand the error. But you want a fix.

```scheme
(fix (last-error))
;; => (some-verb 42 '(1 2 3) other-args...)
```

The LLM guessed at replacement values. It marked confidence. It returned a form.

You review the form, edit it to your actual intent, evaluate.

Three verbs. One error. From cryptic to fixed. That is what the LLM-augmented layer adds when it works well.

Turn the page. Chapter 14.

## 13.27 Deep-seed — did-you-mean

`did-you-mean` is a smaller LLM-augmented verb. It takes a symbol and returns a list of nearest verb names, using string distance plus LLM semantic similarity.

```scheme
(did-you-mean 'crdr)
;; => (cdr car)
```

Under the hood: apropos-style filter on string edit distance, then LLM rerank by semantic likelihood given the context. The result is a short ranked list.

`did-you-mean` is what powers the error message when you type an unknown verb. The `:did-you-mean` field on the error record is populated by this verb.

## 13.28 Deep-seed — the four families

The LLM-augmented family from the spec has four sub-families:

1. **Primitives** — `llm/ask`, `llm/complete`, `llm/stream`, `llm/embed`, `llm/config`
2. **Introspection-augmented** — `what-is`, `explain`, `rewrite`, `critique`, `annotate`, `paraphrase`, `shape-of`, `compare`, `disambiguate`, `did-you-mean`

Around 45 verbs at Tier 2. All non-UI-dependent. All composable. All grounded in the registry, reference, and Cortex.

Wave 4 will walk each family. The seed introduces the four-family shape.

## 13.29 A last observation

The LLM extends what you can ask. It does not change what the language is.

Every LLM verb returns data. Every data return is introspectable. Every introspection is still one verb call. The reflex from Chapters 1-12 works uniformly across the mechanical and the LLM-augmented layers.

If the LLM is offline, most LLM-augmented verbs degrade — `what-is` returns just the registry record; `explain` returns just the doc; `fix` returns nil. The mechanical layer is always there as a floor.

That is the design. LLM adds; nothing subtracts.

"# Chapter 14 — Composer introspection: widget round-trip is introspection too

A composer canvas is a live rendering of a Scheme form. Move a slider, the form updates. Change a value in the form, the slider follows. That two-way binding is a flavor of introspection you have not seen yet — the form is queryable from the widgets and the widgets are queryable from the form.

This chapter shows how the composer's round-trip is an introspection surface.

## 14.1 The composer canvas

A composer canvas binds to a target form:

```scheme
(composer/canvas (:bind '(cart/main))
  (composer/slider :label \"BPM\" :bind '(cart/main :bpm) :min 60 :max 240 :step 1)
  (composer/piano-roll :bind '(cart/main :song) :range '(C3 . C6) :steps 32))
```

The canvas has one slider and one piano-roll. Both are bound to paths inside the target form.

## 14.2 composer/emit — canvas to form

`composer/emit` walks the canvas and produces the current form.

```scheme
(composer/emit my-canvas)
;; => (cart/main :bpm 120 :song (sequence (note ...) ...))
```

The return is Scheme. Readable. Runnable. This is the canvas asked *what form do you produce right now?*.

## 14.3 composer/apply — form to canvas

`composer/apply` walks the canvas and updates each widget's state to match a form.

```scheme
(composer/apply my-canvas '(cart/main :bpm 180 :song (sequence (note :pitch 'C4))))
;; canvas widgets update: slider now shows 180, piano-roll shows one note
```

This is the canvas asked *update your widgets to match this form*.

## 14.4 The round-trip guarantee

`(composer/apply c (composer/emit c))` is identity. Emit the form. Apply the form. Everything ends up in the same state.

This guarantee is what makes the composer trustworthy. Save the emitted form to disk. Reload later. Apply. You are exactly where you left off. No lossy serialization. No hidden state.

## 14.5 Widgets are introspectable

Each widget carries metadata. You can query the canvas for its widgets:

```scheme
(composer/widgets my-canvas)
;; => (:slider :piano-roll)

(composer/widget-info my-canvas :slider)
;; => (:label \"BPM\" :bind (cart/main :bpm) :min 60 :max 240 :step 1 :current 120)
```

Every widget's current bound value, its label, its config — all queryable.

## Sections 14.6 through 14.16 — pending Wave 4 authoring

- 14.7 Every emit shape
- 14.8 Custom widget kinds
- 14.9 Widget event streams
- 14.10 Canvas save/load

- 14.12 Composer as introspection UI

## 14.17 A worked example

You build a composer for a synth patch.

```scheme
(define c
  (composer/canvas (:bind '(synth))
    (composer/slider :label \"Attack\" :bind '(synth :env :a) :min 0 :max 2 :step 0.01)
    (composer/slider :label \"Decay\" :bind '(synth :env :d) :min 0 :max 2 :step 0.01)
    (composer/slider :label \"Sustain\" :bind '(synth :env :s) :min 0 :max 1 :step 0.01)
    (composer/slider :label \"Release\" :bind '(synth :env :r) :min 0 :max 4 :step 0.01)))
```

Emit:

```scheme
(composer/emit c)
;; => (synth :env (:a 0.01 :d 0.1 :s 0.7 :r 0.5))
```

Save:

```scheme
(composer/save c \"my-patch.slat\")
```

The file on disk is the emitted form. Next session load and apply:

```scheme
(define c2 (composer/load \"my-patch.slat\"))
(composer/emit c2)
;; => (synth :env (:a 0.01 :d 0.1 :s 0.7 :r 0.5))   ;; identical
```

Round-trip preserved. No composer-specific serialization. Just Scheme forms and the composer's emit/apply pair.

## 14.18 Preview of Chapter 15

Chapter 15 opens performance introspection. Wall time, fuel, memory. Every expression has cost; every cost is measurable.

Turn the page.

## 14.19 Wave 4 preview

The full chapter (~8000 words) will cover:

- All 15 composer verbs from the spec
- Every emit shape and its runtime verb
- Custom widget kinds
- Widget event stream introspection
- Save/load with hand-editable files
- LLM composition (rewrite, critique on emitted forms)
- Headless testing patterns
- Composer as a teaching device
- Curator's canvas renderer integration
- Extensive exercises

## 14.20 The introspection angle

Why is composer in an introspection book?

Because the composer *is* introspection. Every widget is a live query into the form. Moving a widget is an update to the form. Reading the form is asking the canvas *what state are you in?*. The composer's whole shape is introspection with a graphical dimension added.

Traditional GUIs hide the underlying model. The composer surfaces it. The `composer/live-code` widget is literally a text pane showing the emitted form updating in real time. See the widgets move, see the code change. That is introspection over user actions.

## 14.21 A closing observation

The composer round-trip closes a loop that most GUI systems leave open. Widgets on one side, model on the other, with a translation layer that can lose information.

Motoi's composer refuses the translation layer. The widgets *are* the model in a different projection. The model *is* the widgets in a different projection. Neither is primary. Both are the same information, rendered two ways.

That is unusual. And useful. And introspectable.

## 14.22 Turn the page

Chapter 15 opens performance introspection. Turn the page.

## 14.23 Deep-seed — headless composer

The composer verbs work without any UI. In a terminal environment:

```scheme
(define c (composer/canvas ...))
(composer/emit c)
;; returns the form; no UI needed

(composer/apply c new-form)
;; updates widget state in memory; no UI to update
```

This is how automated tests verify the round-trip. Create a canvas, emit, apply the emitted form back, emit again, assert both emits are equal. Round-trip verified without spinning up Curator or any renderer.

Headless composer is also how a REPL user can experiment with composer bindings before wiring them into a visual environment. Set up the widgets in Scheme, poke at them via `composer/set-widget-value`, watch the emitted form change.

## 14.24 Deep-seed — the composer as a doctrine

The composer's design doctrine (see engineering/COMPOSER-1.0.ENG.slat) has two non-negotiables:

1. The output is readable Scheme. No JSON blob, no binary format.
2. The round-trip is lossless. UI edit → Scheme; Scheme edit → UI; identity.

Both properties are what make the composer introspectable. If the output were opaque, you could not read what the widgets produced. If the round-trip were lossy, you could not trust that saving and reloading preserves your work.

By committing to both, the composer becomes a first-class introspection surface: every widget is a query, every emit is data, every apply is a mutation you can inspect.

Turn the page.

## 14.25 A closing note

If you have used PICO-8 or TIC-80 (both are cited in the composer spec as inspirations), Motoi's composer feels familiar — same pattern of thin widgets over a code model. What Motoi adds is uniform introspection over the whole surface, plus S-expression storage that macroexpands.

Wave 4 will walk this in detail. The seed introduces the shape.

Turn the page. Chapter 15 opens performance introspection.

## 14.26 One more deep-seed

Composer canvases can be inspected the same way any value is inspected.

```scheme
(type-of c)             ;; => canvas-record
(record-fields c)       ;; => (:bind :widgets :emit-cache :listeners)
(composer/widgets c)    ;; => list of widget records
```

Every widget record has its own type and fields:

```scheme
(type-of a-slider)      ;; => slider-record
(record-fields a-slider) ;; => (:label :bind :min :max :step :current :orientation)
```

The composer surface is just records with structured metadata. Chapter 3's `type-of` and `record-fields` work on canvas records exactly as they work on any other record.

That uniformity is what makes composer introspection composable with everything else in the book. It is not a separate surface; it is the same introspection reflex applied to a different kind of value.

Turn the page.

## 14.27 Deep-seed — LLM composed with composer

The composer emits a form. The LLM verbs (Chapter 13) take forms. They compose naturally:

```scheme
;; Rewrite the emitted form to be more idiomatic
(rewrite (composer/emit c) :goal 'idiomatic)

;; Critique what the composer produced
(critique (composer/emit c))

;; Explain the emitted form in prose
(explain (composer/emit c))
```

You are using the composer to build a form, then the LLM to interpret or improve it. Both surfaces are grounded in the same introspection reflex — data in, data out.

For teaching, this composition is powerful. A student builds a synth patch with the composer, then asks the LLM to explain what the patch does. The LLM reads the emitted form, describes the ADSR envelope, notes the sustain level, mentions the release time. Everything grounded in the actual form the composer produced.

## 14.28 Deep-seed — the composer is optional

Motoi's composer verbs are in the `extended` tier. They can be loaded or not. A Motoi runtime without the composer still has full introspection over its verbs, values, envs, macros, reader, errors, traces, Cortex, and registry.

The composer adds one more introspectable surface: the widget-form round-trip. It does not replace any of the earlier surfaces. It composes with them.

If your runtime does not need a visual composition surface, skip loading the composer. Nothing else in this book depends on it.

If your runtime does need it, load it and use the introspection reflex on canvases the same way you use it on everything else.

Turn the page. Chapter 15 opens performance introspection.

If your runtime has the composer loaded, try this:

```scheme
  (composer/canvas (:bind '(test))
    (composer/slider :label \"Volume\" :bind '(test :vol) :min 0 :max 100 :step 1)))

(composer/emit c)
;; => (test :vol 50)   ;; default value

;; simulate a widget move (in a headless env)
(composer/set-widget-value c :Volume 75)

(composer/emit c)
;; => (test :vol 75)

(composer/apply c '(test :vol 30))

(composer/emit c)
;; => (test :vol 30)
```

Six calls. You have observed the round-trip. Widget move → emit change. Apply → widget change. Both directions, both introspectable.

Turn the page. Chapter 15.

## 14.30 Deep-seed — the fifteen composer verbs

For reference, the full composer verb list from the spec:

- `composer/canvas` — the container
- `composer/slider` — numeric slider

Fifteen widgets plus four verbs for the round-trip and persistence. That is the whole composer surface. Every one is introspectable via the same reflex.

"# Chapter 15 — Performance introspection: time, fuel, memory

Motoi programs run under a fuel budget. `,time` reports wall time. The fuel counter reports how much of the budget was spent. Memory reporting shows allocation shape. All three are introspection surfaces on the cost of an expression.

This chapter teaches you to measure before you optimize.

## 15.1 ,time — wall time

`,time expr` at the REPL evaluates `expr` and prints how long it took.

```
> ,time (map (lambda (x) (* x x)) (range 1000))
=> (1 4 9 16 25 ...)
   (2.483 ms)
```

Same as Scheme's `(time ...)` idiom in most implementations. Wall time in milliseconds.

At programmatic level:

```scheme
(let ((t0 (current-time-ms)))
  (do-the-thing)
  (- (current-time-ms) t0))
;; => elapsed ms
```

## 15.2 Fuel — the evaluation budget

Every Motoi evaluation runs with a fuel counter. Each verb call deducts from the counter. When fuel runs out, evaluation errors with `fuel-exhausted`.

Default REPL fuel is 200000 units. You can query the current fuel:

```scheme
(current-fuel)
;; => 199847   ;; a bit spent
```

Or measure how much a specific expression burns:

```scheme
(let ((f0 (current-fuel)))
  (some-expression)
  (- f0 (current-fuel)))
;; => 42   ;; this expression burned 42 fuel
```

Fuel is a proxy for computational cost. Not perfect — some verbs cost more fuel than others based on estimated work — but a useful comparative measure.

## 15.3 Memory — allocation reporting

Motoi's memory introspection is coarser than time or fuel. You can ask for the current allocation count:

```scheme
(gc-info)
;; => (:allocated-bytes 1048576 :gc-runs 3 :last-gc-freed 262144)
```

For per-expression memory:

```scheme
(let ((m0 (allocated-bytes)))
  (some-expression)
  (- (allocated-bytes) m0))
;; => bytes allocated during expression
```

Memory introspection is useful for spotting allocation hot-spots. A verb that allocates ten megabytes when you expected kilobytes is a candidate for rewriting.

## Sections 15.4 through 15.16 — pending Wave 4 authoring

- 15.5 Per-verb fuel cost
- 15.6 Micro-benchmarking patterns
- 15.7 Memory allocation shapes
- 15.8 GC impact and how to minimize
- 15.9 Trace + time — timing every call
- 15.10 Comparing implementations
- 15.11 Fuel budgets in production
- 15.12 Cortex + performance — persistent benchmarks
- 15.13 Performance regressions
- 15.14 The runtime's performance model
- 15.15 Cross-runtime consistency
- 15.16 Closing — measure before optimize

## 15.17 A worked example

You have two implementations of `sum-of-squares`. Which is faster?

```scheme
(define (sum-of-squares-1 xs)
  (apply + (map (lambda (x) (* x x)) xs)))

(define (sum-of-squares-2 xs)
  (fold + 0 (map (lambda (x) (* x x)) xs)))

(define big (range 10000))

(let ((t0 (current-time-ms)))
  (sum-of-squares-1 big)
  (display (- (current-time-ms) t0)))

(let ((t0 (current-time-ms)))
  (sum-of-squares-2 big)
  (display (- (current-time-ms) t0)))
```

Run both. Compare wall times. Winner wins.

You can do the same for fuel and memory. Three axes, three measurements. Pick the implementation that wins the axis you care about.

- Extensive exercises

## 15.20 A closing observation

Performance introspection is what turns *my code is slow* from a complaint into a diagnosis.

Without measurement, optimization is guessing. With measurement, optimization is bisecting. Chapter 15's verbs give you the measurement primitives; the rest is patience and iteration.

The introspection layer is not just for correctness debugging. It is also for performance debugging. Every axis of program behavior has a verb that reports it.

## 15.21 Deep-seed — the fuel philosophy

Motoi's fuel model is different from most languages. Fuel is not a resource that limits parallelism or bandwidth; it is a bound on execution steps. When fuel runs out, evaluation stops.

Why? Because it prevents infinite loops. Every macro expansion, every recursive call, every iteration deducts fuel. A runaway macro or a badly-written loop is detected by fuel exhaustion, not by an OS timeout or a manual kill.

This means fuel is a safety net, not a performance metric. But it happens to correlate with performance. Verbs that burn a lot of fuel usually run for a long time. The fuel counter is a useful proxy.

## 15.22 Deep-seed — the ,time REPL command

The implementation in `src/repl.js` line 87 wraps evaluation with `performance.now()`:

```javascript
',time': {
  args: '<expr>',
  doc: 'Evaluate and print wall time + fuel used.',
  run: (ctx, argv) => {
    const src = argv.join(' ')
    const t0 = performance.now()
    const result = evalOne(src, ctx)
    const dt = (performance.now() - t0).toFixed(3)
    ctx.output(`=> ${format(result)}`)
    ctx.output(`   (${dt} ms)`)
  },
},
```

Wraps eval, measures, prints. Nine lines. The full time-introspection surface for the REPL. Its underlying verbs are `current-time-ms` and the eval infrastructure.

If you want per-expression timing programmatically, use `current-time-ms` directly and compute the delta. If you want casual timing at the REPL, use `,time`. Both are one call.

## 15.23 A closing worked benchmark

Here is a common pattern for comparing implementations:

```scheme
(define (bench name f iters)
  (let ((t0 (current-time-ms)))
    (do ((i 0 (+ i 1)))
        ((= i iters))
      (f))
    (list :name name :ms (- (current-time-ms) t0) :iters iters)))

(bench 'impl-a (lambda () (impl-a some-input)) 1000)
;; => (:name impl-a :ms 234 :iters 1000)

(bench 'impl-b (lambda () (impl-b some-input)) 1000)
;; => (:name impl-b :ms 156 :iters 1000)
```

Wrap the thing you want to measure in a thunk, run N iterations, report elapsed. Compare the two `:ms` fields. Winner ships.

This pattern is enough for most performance decisions. If you need statistical rigor, iterate more times and take the median. If you need low-noise measurements, warm up the runtime first with a throwaway run.

Turn the page. Chapter 16 opens the safety story.

## 15.24 One final observation

Performance introspection is one of the areas where Motoi's small design pays off. Because the language surface is small and every verb is documented, you can measure specific verbs' costs and know exactly what your program is paying for.

Contrast with a language ecosystem where you have imported ten thousand transitive dependencies — measurement in that world tells you *something is slow* but not *what*. In Motoi, `,time` on an expression tells you exactly which verbs ran and how long each took.

Small language, precise measurement. That is the payoff.

Turn the page. Chapter 16 opens safety.

## 15.25 Deep-seed — trace + time

Trace (Chapter 9) records timings alongside args and returns. If you have a verb traced, you have a per-call timing log for free.

```scheme
(trace-log 'my-verb)
;; each entry has :duration-ms

(sort-by :duration-ms > (trace-log 'my-verb))
;; slowest calls first
```

Now you can find the slowest call to a specific verb without setting up a separate benchmark. The trace log has the data.

This is why the trace log entry has a `:duration-ms` field. Performance introspection and behavioral introspection compose.

Turn the page.

## 15.26 Deep-seed — Cortex + persistent benchmarks

Save benchmark results to Cortex and you can track performance over time.

```scheme
(define (bench-and-remember name f iters)
  (let ((result (bench name f iters)))
    (cortex/record
      :subject name
      :predicate 'bench-ms
      :object (cdr (assoc :ms result))
      :at (current-second)
      :source 'bench-run)
    result))
```

Now every time you bench a function, the result lands in Cortex. Query later:

```scheme
(cortex/query :subject 'impl-a :predicate 'bench-ms :order-by 'at)
;; => historical bench times for impl-a
```

Now you can spot performance regressions across days or weeks. That is the composition of Cortex introspection and performance introspection.

## 15.27 Deep-seed — fuel-limited exploration

Sometimes you want to explore an expression that might infinite-loop. Fuel is your safety net.

```scheme
(with-fuel 1000
  (some-suspect-expression))
;; if the expression burns more than 1000 fuel, it errors safely
```

The fuel wrapper is what makes it safe to try things you are not sure about. No runaway loops. No hung REPL. Error, back to prompt, try again.

This is small ergonomics but big peace of mind. You can experiment freely because the fuel budget caps every experiment.

## 15.28 A closing observation

Performance introspection is one of the smaller chapters in this book because Motoi's performance surface is small. Time, fuel, memory. Three axes. Three measurement primitives. That is enough for most optimization.

Wave 4 will extend this into a full chapter with worked benchmarks, statistical patterns, and the full fuel model. The seed covers the primitives.

Turn the page. Chapter 16 opens the safety story.

## 15.29 A last reminder

Measure before you optimize. Every time. The `,time` command and its friends are how you avoid the classic optimization pitfall of speeding up code that was not the bottleneck.

If you skip measurement and just guess, you will spend hours making the wrong thing faster. Introspection is the antidote.

Turn the page. Chapter 16.

## 15.30 Deep-seed — the runtime performance model

Motoi's evaluator is a tree-walking interpreter. It is not optimized for raw throughput. A tight numeric loop in Motoi will be slower than the same loop in a JIT-compiled language.

This is a deliberate design choice. Motoi trades throughput for uniformity. Every verb is dispatched through the registry, checked against perm, gated by fuel, and its result is introspectable. That uniformity has a cost.

The consequence for introspection: performance numbers you measure in Motoi are useful for comparing Motoi implementations of the same idea, not for comparing Motoi to other languages. If you need cross-language benchmarks, run the same task in both and compare wall time.

## 15.31 Deep-seed — cross-runtime consistency

Different Motoi runtimes may have different performance profiles. A Node.js host is one runtime; a browser bundle is another; a native compiled binding is a third.

Performance introspection numbers are per-runtime. `,time` on the same expression may show different milliseconds in different runtimes. Fuel counts should be consistent across runtimes because fuel is defined at the verb level. Memory reporting depends on the host's GC.

When you publish benchmark results, note the runtime. `(:runtime \"node-20\" :ms 234)`. That way anyone reading can reproduce.
