"# Chapter 16 — Safe introspection: perm, sandbox, and what shouldn't leak

Every chapter so far has been about what you can see. This chapter is about what you cannot — deliberately, honestly, by design.

Not all introspection is safe. Reading a verb's perm tier is safe. Reading a runtime secret environment variable is not. Reading a Cortex record you wrote is safe. Reading a stranger's cart's private state is not. Motoi's introspection surface draws the line and this chapter shows where.

## 16.1 The perm boundary

Every verb has a perm tier (Chapter 2). The dispatcher checks the caller's perm against the verb's requirement before allowing the call.

Introspection verbs are all `read` tier. That is deliberate — they only observe. But *what they observe* is bounded by what the runtime chooses to expose.

The registry snapshot returns metadata, not implementation. The metadata does not include the verb's actual function body, just its name, doc, contract, and pointer to source. If you want the body, you go read source; the runtime does not hand you the function.

Similarly, `snapshot-registry` returns a copy, not the live registry. Mutating the returned object does not affect the runtime's registry. This is a read-only projection.

## 16.2 Runtime redaction

A runtime can redact fields before returning them from introspection. Sensitive fields — source pointers pointing at proprietary code, doc strings referencing internal systems, examples exposing credentials — can be stripped.

```scheme
(source-of 'some-private-verb)
;; => nil    ;; runtime redacted the source pointer
```

The introspection layer is honest about the redaction — you get nil, not a fake pointer. If a field is nil where you expected a value, either the field was never populated or the runtime is redacting.

## 16.3 The never-introspectable mark

A cart author can mark specific values as never-introspectable. The runtime respects the mark — introspection verbs return an opaque placeholder.

```scheme
(define secret (make-opaque-value my-actual-secret))
(type-of secret)
;; => opaque

(shape-of secret)
;; => (:mechanical (:type opaque) :prose \"This value has been marked as never-introspectable by its creator.\")
```

The type is `opaque`. The mechanical fields are minimal. The LLM's prose is honest — the value cannot be introspected because someone said so.

## Sections 16.4 through 16.11 — pending Wave 4 authoring

## 16.12 Networked runtime concerns (subsystem-limit awareness for the engineering audience)

Every earlier section in this chapter is about what the runtime EXPOSES safely — the perm tiers, redaction, opaque values, the sandbox. This section is about what the runtime does NOT expose because the underlying subsystem is not present at all.

The distinction matters for auditors. A missing subsystem is not a bug in the introspection layer; it is a feature of the runtime. Introspecting for a subsystem that isn't there should return a specific, honest signal — not silence, not a fake stub, not a fabricated value.

### 16.12.1 The subsystem-presence protocol

For each of the fourteen subsystems Motoi does not natively include, the runtime exposes a small introspection surface:

```scheme
(system/has? 'networking)      ; => #f    (Motoi cannot fetch)
(system/has? 'shell)           ; => #f    (no exec/system escape)
(system/has? 'gps)             ; => #f    (no geolocation sensor)
(system/has? 'llm-remote)      ; => #f    (no cloud LLM API)
(system/has? 'http-serve)      ; => #t    (LOCAL server IS present)
(system/has? 'llm-local)       ; => #t/#f (depends on runtime host)
```

`system/has?` returns a boolean. `#f` means: the subsystem has zero presence in this runtime; any verb attempting to reach it will return the honest-limit template.

`(system/limit-info 'networking)` returns the full metadata record:

```scheme
(system/limit-info 'networking)
;; => (:subsystem \"networking\"
;;     :present #f
;;     :adjacent-capability \"http/serve — Motoi as LOCAL server\"
;;     :canonical-refusal-template \"honest-capability + honest-limit +
;;       meta-honesty + fish-in-car-metaphor + redirect-to-curl-or-Claude\"
;;     :redirect-targets (\"curl\" \"user-terminal\" \"claude\" \"sakura\")
;;     :book-crossref \"book-of-computing/08 §8.9\"
;;     :systems-crossref \"book-of-systems/02 networking section\")
```

The introspection layer does not lie about what's present. If `system/has?` returns `#f`, no clever Scheme can talk the runtime into calling that subsystem.

### 16.12.2 The fourteen subsystems

Enumerate what's tracked, for audit completeness:

- `networking` — client-side HTTP (fetch, POST, socket to remote).
- `filesystem-external` — read/write outside the sandbox.
- `shell` — `system(cmd)`, exec, subprocess.
- `external-api` — Etsy, Shopify, Stripe, third-party services.
- `llm-remote` — GPT-4/Claude/Gemini via cloud API.
- `hardware` — GPIO, serial, USB, robotics, reactor control.
- `database-sql` — Postgres, MySQL, SQLite, Mongo.
- `cloud-deploy` — AWS/GCP/Fly/Vercel deploys.
- `gps` — geolocation sensor read.
- `camera-mic-capture` — device media capture initiation.
- `email-sms-notify` — SMTP, Twilio, push notifications.
- `date-time-external` — timezone DB lookup, NTP sync.
- `file-download-upload` — wire file transfer.
- `install-package` — npm, pip, apt-get, brew execution.

For each, `system/has?` returns `#f` and `system/limit-info` returns the full metadata record. This is the engineering-audience-friendly enumeration of what the sandbox mechanics in §16.5 (Wave 4) will formalize.

### 16.12.3 Auditing a cart for subsystem-presumption

When you review a cart, run:

```scheme
(define cart-verbs (extract-verb-calls my-cart))
(define assumed-subsystems
  (map (lambda (v) (assoc 'requires-subsystem (help v)))
       cart-verbs))
(define missing
  (filter (lambda (s)
            (and s (not (system/has? (cdr s)))))
          assumed-subsystems))

missing
;; => list of (verb requires-subsystem) pairs where the subsystem is
;;    absent from this runtime
```

If `missing` is non-empty, the cart assumes a subsystem this runtime does not have. Either:
(a) the cart cannot run here — reject or warn the user, or
(b) the cart has a graceful fallback and will surface the honest-limit template at that verb call.

This audit runs at cart-load time in most host configurations.

### 16.12.4 The honest-limit response as introspectable behavior

When user code (or an LLM authoring code) attempts to call a verb from a missing subsystem, the runtime does NOT throw an unrecoverable error. It emits a structured error record you can inspect:

```scheme
(define result (try (http/get \"https://example.com\")))

result
;; => (:kind subsystem-unavailable
;;     :subsystem networking
;;     :verb-attempted http/get
;;     :honest-limit-template \"Motoi does not have client-side networking.
;;       He can serve HTTP locally. He cannot fetch.\"
;;     :adjacent-capability \"http/serve\"
;;     :redirect \"curl in user's terminal, or Claude, or Sakura for
;;       business-side wire\")
```

The error record's `:kind` is `subsystem-unavailable` — not `unbound-symbol`, not `perm-denied`, not `runtime-error`. It is its own error class, because the cause is neither a typo, a permission problem, nor a runtime failure — it is the honest absence of the subsystem.

This lets code and LLMs handle the case cleanly:

```scheme
(cond
  ((eq? (:kind result) 'subsystem-unavailable)
   (display (:honest-limit-template result))
   (display \"\\nTry: \")
   (display (:redirect result)))
  ((eq? (:kind result) 'perm-denied)
   ;; a different case — perm rejected, not subsystem missing
   ...)
  (else
   (process-result result)))
```

### 16.12.5 Why this is not the same as a perm-denied refusal

Perm-denied is: 'You do not have permission to call this verb.'
Subsystem-unavailable is: 'This verb has no implementation in this runtime.'

They are distinct concerns:

- Perm-denied is a SANDBOX or POLICY refusal. The verb exists; you're not allowed to call it. Might work in a different runtime with a different perm set.
- Subsystem-unavailable is a WORLD-BOUND refusal. The verb has no implementation to call. Even with maximum perms, calling it does nothing.

Introspection must report them separately or an auditor cannot reason about what the cart actually needs. `system/has?` reports subsystem presence; the perm system reports permission. Both are queryable, both are auditable, neither substitutes for the other.

### 16.12.6 Why the honest-limit template is uniform

The honest-limit template that fires for every missing subsystem has a uniform five-element shape:

1. Honest capability (what Motoi CAN do adjacent to this)
2. Honest limit (what he CAN'T)
3. Meta-honesty (even if he could, he might not know the right move)
4. Playful physical metaphor
5. Redirect (who or what has the capability)

The uniformity IS a safety feature. When users and LLMs see the same shape every time they hit a subsystem wall, they learn the shape and stop pushing on the wall. They start using the redirect. Inconsistency in the refusal shape would train the user to prompt harder.

This is analogous to Wave 6's crisis-refusal-template consistency: the template stays constant so people learn to recognize it. Same doctrine, different leaf.

- Book of Computing Chapter 8, §8.9 — networking-specific version.
- Book of Systems Chapter 2 — the systematic subsystem walk for the operator audience.
- Book of Motoi Scheme Appendix G — the kid-facing version.
- Motoi safety refusals (see Book of Reason if it exists in your tree, or the motoi-safety-refusals doctrine) — a distinct system; subsystem-limits are ADDITIVE to safety refusals, not replacements.

## 16.17 The three principles

Motoi's safety-of-introspection story rests on three principles:

**Principle one: no covert exposure.** If introspection cannot show you a field, the runtime returns nil or an opaque placeholder — never a fabricated value. The reader can always tell what is present versus absent.

**Principle two: opt-in transparency.** By default, every verb's metadata is fully introspectable. To make something private, the author marks it. There is no accidental exposure of things that were marked private; there is no accidental hiding of things that were meant to be public.

**Principle three: the sandbox is authoritative.** If the runtime is sandboxed, the sandbox has the final say on what can be introspected. Cart authors cannot override the sandbox's redactions.

## 16.18 A worked example

You are running a stranger's cart in a sandboxed runtime.

```scheme
(help 'their/private-verb)
;; => (:name \"their/private-verb\" :doc \"[redacted]\" :contract \"[redacted]\" :source nil ...)
```

The sandbox has redacted the interesting fields. You know the verb exists (name is present). You do not know what it does (doc is redacted). You cannot go read source (source is nil).

This is honest. The sandbox told you what it hid. You can decide to run the cart or not, given that private verbs are opaque.

## 16.19 The last preview

The book ends here. Introspection is a superpower. Motoi trusts you to use it without leaking through it.

## 16.21 The honesty principle, one more time

Every field the introspection layer returns is honest. If it says a verb exists, it exists. If it says a field is nil, the field is nil. If it says a value is opaque, the value is opaque. There are no false negatives, no false positives, no misleading returns.

This is what makes introspection trustworthy. If you cannot trust the returns, the whole surface collapses. Motoi trades some flexibility for that trust — the runtime cannot silently expose secrets and cannot silently hide things — and the trade is worth it for a language that wants to be introspected freely.

## 16.22 A closing observation

Introspection and safety compose the same way every other pair in this book composes. Small primitives. Uniform metadata. Explicit fields. The safety story is not a separate system; it is the same introspection layer, with a few extra fields (`:redacted`, `:opaque`, `:confidentiality`) that mean something specific.

Learn to read those fields the same way you learned to read the doc field. When you see nil where a value was expected, ask why. Sometimes the field was never populated. Sometimes the runtime redacted. Sometimes the value is opaque by design. All three are honest returns; you just have to know which is which.

## 16.23 The book closes

Sixteen chapters. Every question you can ask about a Motoi program has a verb that will answer it — unless the answer would leak something the runtime chose to protect, in which case the runtime tells you honestly that the answer is unavailable.

That is the whole introspection surface.

Turn to the appendices for reference material, cheat sheets, and worked examples of the patterns from throughout the book.

## 16.24 Deep-seed — the sandbox model

Motoi's dispatcher (`src/dispatch.js`) checks every verb call against the caller's perm tier. If the caller does not have the required perm, the call errors with `perm-denied`.

The sandbox is stricter — it can also add allow-lists (only these specific verbs) and deny-lists (never these), regardless of perm.

Introspection verbs are all `read` tier. In most sandboxes they are allowed. But a paranoid sandbox can deny even introspection — for example, refusing `snapshot-registry` if it does not want the cart to enumerate the whole verb space.

If introspection is denied, the introspection verbs error like any other perm-denied verb. The error record's `:kind` is `perm-denied`. You can catch it and adjust behavior.

## 16.25 Deep-seed — Cortex confidentiality

Cortex records can carry a `:confidentiality` field:

```scheme
(cortex/record
  :subject 'user
  :predicate 'ssn
  :object \"123-45-6789\"
  :at (current-second)
  :source 'user-input
  :confidentiality 'personal-data)
```

When another verb queries Cortex, the runtime checks the querier's perm against the record's confidentiality. If the querier does not have `personal-data` perm, the record is filtered out.

This means introspection over Cortex is also perm-gated. `cortex/query` respects confidentiality. You do not accidentally expose personal data by listing every record about a user.

## 16.26 Deep-seed — the audit pattern

If you are running a cart and want to know what it introspected during a session, you can trace the introspection verbs themselves:

```scheme
(,trace help)
(,trace snapshot-registry)
(,trace cortex/query)

(run-the-cart)

(,trace-log help)
;; every help call the cart made
```

Now you know exactly what the cart looked at. If it snooped your Cortex records unnecessarily, or introspected verbs it should not have needed, the log tells you.

This is defense-in-depth. Perm-gating stops the cart from calling verbs it should not; tracing tells you what it did call. Together they give you visibility into introspection-as-surveillance.

Turn to the appendices.

## 16.27 The closing rhythm

The book is done. Sixteen chapters. Eight appendices to follow.

Every verb from the book is one call away. Every reflex from the book gets stronger with practice. Every question you have about your own Motoi programs has an introspection verb that will answer it.

Introspection is a superpower. Now you have it. Use it well.

Turn to Appendix A.

## 16.28 A last note for the reader

You have finished reading Book of Introspection. Or at least the parts that were written in Wave 1. Wave 2 through 4 will fill in the seeded chapters and appendices.

Regardless of which wave you are reading in, the shape of the book is the same. Chapters 1-4 are the foundations. Chapters 5-7 are the runtime layers. Chapters 8-12 are the value-side surfaces. Chapters 13-16 are the extended and safety layers.

Whichever chapter you close on, you have more introspection reflex than you started with. Every reflex serves you every time you write a Motoi program from now on.

Turn to the appendices for reference.

## 16.29 The final closing

Book of Introspection ends here. The appendices are reference material and worked examples. Read them for the specific patterns you need; skim them for orientation.

Onward to Appendix A — the SLAT schema of a verb record, field by field.

## 16.30 One more time

Every question you can ask about a Motoi program has a verb that will answer it — subject to the safety limits this chapter drew — and every verb is one call away, and every call composes with the next, and every composition is data you can further introspect. That is the shape of the language and the shape of this book.

Onward to the appendices.

## 16.31 Deep-seed — the eight perm tiers, one more time

For the closing, the perm vocabulary in one place:

- `read` — pure observation. Every introspection verb, every query, every projection is here. Safe by default.
- `paint` — visual side effects only. Draw a dot, place a glyph. No state mutation.
- `animate` — motion or RAF tween. Runs at full or half substrate power; skipped at quarter or paused.
- `state-change` — moves cards, focuses UI, opens/closes something. First tier that persists across the current frame.
- `destructive` — deletes data, transfers ownership. Irreversible operations.
- `financial` — money moves. Requires cart-manifest declaration.
- `network` — outbound network call. Requires cart-manifest declaration and possibly per-endpoint approval.
- `personal-data` — reads or writes user PII. Requires user consent flow.

Eight tiers. Every verb has one. Every caller has a set. Dispatch is a match: caller's set must contain the verb's requirement.

## 16.32 Deep-seed — auditing your own cart

Before you publish a cart, audit its perm usage:

```scheme
(define my-cart (read-slat-file \"my-cart.slat\"))
(define calls (extract-verb-calls my-cart))
(define perms
  (unique (map (lambda (n) (cdr (assoc 'perm (help n)))) calls)))

perms
;; => (\"read\" \"paint\" \"animate\" \"state-change\")
```

Your cart requires these four perms. Declare them in the cart's manifest. Do not declare more than you need — the sandbox will grant only what you declare, and asking for `financial` when you do not use it makes users suspicious.

## 16.33 Closing exercise

Try this on a cart file (any cart):

```scheme
(define cart (read-slat-file \"path/to/cart.slat\"))
(define verbs (extract-verb-calls cart))
(define sensitive
  (filter
    (lambda (n)
      (member (cdr (assoc 'perm (help n)))
              '(\"financial\" \"personal-data\" \"destructive\" \"network\"))))
    verbs))

sensitive
;; => any verb the cart uses with a sensitive perm
```

If sensitive is empty, the cart is low-risk. If it is not, review each entry and decide whether the cart's use of that verb is legitimate.

That is auditing at introspection speed. One filter, one review. No security scanner needed.

## 16.34 Turn to Appendix A

Book of Introspection ends. The appendices are next. Turn the page.

"# Appendix A — Reference-manual anatomy: the SLAT schema of a verb record

Every verb record in the reference manual is a SLAT s-expression with a fixed field set. This appendix documents the schema. Use it as a reference when reading or generating records.

## A.1 The full schema

```scheme
(verb
  :name          string              ;; required — the verb's registered name
  :doc           string              ;; one-sentence imperative description
  :contract      string              ;; signature, e.g. \"(pair) -> any\"
  :arity         integer-or-list     ;; N, or (min max), or 'variadic
  :examples      list                ;; list of (:level :code) records
  :namespace     string-or-nil       ;; e.g. \"cortex\", or nil for base
  :tier          string              ;; \"core\" | \"extended\" | \"experimental\"
  :perm          string              ;; closed vocabulary of 8 tiers
  :atom          string-or-nil       ;; fine-grained category grouping
  :source        string-or-nil       ;; path:line pointing at impl
  :since         string-or-nil       ;; version when verb was added
  :confirm       boolean             ;; dispatcher gate
  :rateLimit     string-or-nil       ;; e.g. \"1/30s\"
  :schema        function-or-nil     ;; validator: (args) -> #t or error-string
  :idempotent    boolean             ;; dispatcher dedupes when true
  :powerTier     string              ;; \"always\" | \"paint\" | \"animate\" | \"full-power\"
  :chip          string-or-nil       ;; auto-emit chip kind
  :deprecated    boolean             ;; if true, prefer :aliasFor
  :aliasFor      string-or-nil       ;; canonical name this aliases
  :examples-arc  string-or-nil       ;; optional pedagogical arc description
)
```

Twenty fields. The first eleven are what `help` returns. The next eight are dispatcher-facing. `:examples-arc` is optional metadata for teaching context.

## A.2 Field-by-field

### :name

Required. String. The name the verb is registered under. This is what the dispatcher looks up when a caller invokes the verb. Also what `help` and every other introspection verb use as the primary key.

Convention: lowercase, hyphens between words, optional namespace prefix with `/`. Examples: `car`, `map`, `cortex/query`, `card/open`, `composer/piano-roll`.

### :doc

String. One sentence in imperative mood ending in a period. This is the primary human-readable description.

Style: `\"Return the first element of a pair.\"` Not `\"Returns...\"` (present-continuous is dispreferred). Not `\"A function that returns...\"` (frame is unnecessary).

If a verb has no doc, `doc-of` returns nil and the reader has no summary. Every published verb should have a doc.

### :contract

String. A signature mini-language description of the verb's shape.

Grammar (informal):
- `(a b c) -> d` — takes three args of shapes a, b, c; returns shape d
- `(a b?)` — b is optional
- `(a ...)` — variadic in a
- `(:key val)` — keyword-plist argument
- `X | Y` — union type

The mini-language is not enforced at runtime. It documents the intended shape.

### :arity

Integer, list, or symbol. Encodes argument count.

- Integer N — takes exactly N arguments
- List `(min max)` — takes between min and max
- Symbol `'variadic` — takes any number

Used by the dispatcher for arity-mismatch errors.

### :examples

List of records. Each record is a plist with `:level` and `:code`.

- `:level` — one of `novice`, `intermediate`, `expert`
- `:code` — a runnable Scheme expression as a string

Ideally three examples per verb, one per level. Feeds the LLM training corpus.

## A.3 Namespace, tier, perm, atom

### :namespace

Optional string. Prefix grouping the verb belongs to. Examples: `\"cortex\"`, `\"card\"`, `\"composer\"`, `\"paint\"`. Nil for base verbs without a prefix.

### :tier

String. One of `\"core\"`, `\"extended\"`, `\"experimental\"`.

- `core` — frozen, never changes
- `extended` — stable but not yet trained on; may evolve
- `experimental` — may change name or arity

### :perm

String. Closed vocabulary:

- `read` — pure observation
- `paint` — visual side effects only
- `animate` — motion or RAF tween
- `state-change` — moves UI or persists state
- `destructive` — deletes or transfers
- `financial` — money moves
- `network` — outbound network call
- `personal-data` — reads/writes user PII

Enforced by the dispatcher.

### :atom

Optional string. Fine-grained category for reference-manual TOC grouping. Examples: `\"paint-primitive\"`, `\"synth-note\"`, `\"card-lifecycle\"`. Nil for verbs in the general pool.

## A.4 Source, since

### :source

Optional string. Format `path:line`. Path is relative to runtime root. Line is 1-indexed.

Manually maintained; may drift when implementations move within a file.

### :since

Optional string. Version tag when the verb was added. Examples: `\"1.0\"`, `\"1.4\"`, `\"1.5-experimental\"`.

Useful for release notes generation and durability audits.

## A.5 Dispatcher fields

### :confirm

Boolean. If true, dispatcher requires the caller to have set `caller.confirmed` before allowing the call. Used for verbs that need explicit user confirmation (e.g., destructive operations).

### :rateLimit

Optional string. Format `<count>/<duration>` like `\"1/30s\"` or `\"10/min\"`. Dispatcher tracks call frequency per caller and refuses if the rate is exceeded.

### :schema

Optional function `(args) -> #t | error-string`. Called by dispatcher before the verb runs. Returns `#t` to pass, an error message string to reject.

Runtime type-check hook. Not populated for most verbs.

### :idempotent

Boolean. If true, dispatcher dedupes recent calls — a second call with the same args within a short window returns the cached result without re-invoking the verb.

Useful for verbs that are pure functions of their input and expensive to compute.

### :powerTier

String. Substrate power gate. One of `always`, `paint`, `animate`, `full-power`.

- `always` — runs at any substrate tier
- `paint` — runs at full/half/quarter; skip at paused
- `animate` — runs at full/half; skip at quarter/paused
- `full-power` — runs only at full

Defaults derived from `:perm` if not specified.

### :chip

Optional string. Auto-emit chip kind on successful dispatch. One of `paint.applied`, `motion.applied`, `look.changed`.

Zero per-verb code — the dispatcher emits one chip envelope per accepted call when this is set.

## A.6 Alias and deprecation

### :deprecated

Boolean. If true, the verb still works but is not the preferred name. Doc typically prefixed with `[deprecated]`.

### :aliasFor

Optional string. If this verb is an alias, the canonical name it points to.

Together: `:deprecated #t :aliasFor \"cortex/write\"` means \"this verb still works but you should use cortex/write instead.\"

## A.7 Optional and reserved fields

### :examples-arc

Optional string. Pedagogical context — a paragraph describing how the examples build on each other.

Used by teaching-oriented reference-manual renderers. Not part of the base introspection surface.

### Reserved fields

The following field names are reserved for future use and should not be added to verb records:

- `:body` — the implementation function (never stored, always fetched from source)
- `:tests` — test suite reference (planned, not yet standard)
- `:complexity` — algorithmic complexity annotation (planned)
- `:examples-generated` — LLM-generated examples that supplement `:examples`

## A.8 A worked SLAT record

Here is a complete verb record as SLAT:

```scheme
(verb
  :name        \"map\"
  :doc         \"Apply a procedure to each element of one or more lists, returning a new list of results.\"
  :contract    \"(procedure list ...) -> list\"
  :arity       variadic
  :examples
  ((:level novice       :code \"(map (lambda (x) (* x 2)) '(1 2 3))\")
   (:level intermediate :code \"(map + '(1 2 3) '(10 20 30))\")
   (:level expert       :code \"(map (lambda (kv) (cons (car kv) (* (cdr kv) 2))) alist)\"))
  :namespace   \"base\"
  :tier        \"core\"
  :perm        \"read\"
  :atom        \"list-op\"
  :source      \"src/base.js:77\"
  :since       \"1.0\"
  :confirm     #f
  :rateLimit   nil
  :idempotent  #t
  :powerTier   \"always\"
  :chip        nil
  :deprecated  #f
  :aliasFor    nil)
```

This is what the reference manual emits for `map`. Every verb has this same shape, with values that vary.

## A.9 Reading a record

Given a record, the reading workflow is:

1. **Read :doc.** One-sentence understanding.
2. **Read :contract.** Signature shape.
3. **Read :arity.** Argument count confirmation.
4. **Read :examples.** Working call templates.
5. **Read :perm.** Trust check.
6. **Read :tier.** Durability check.
7. **Read :source if needed.** Implementation reference.

Skim in order. Stop when you have what you need. Most calls stop at step 4.

## A.10 Generating a record

If you are registering a new verb, produce a record with at minimum these fields:

- `:name` (required)
- `:doc` (culturally required)
- `:contract` (culturally required)
- `:arity` (culturally required)
- `:examples` (at least one novice)
- `:perm` (required for state-changing verbs; inferred for reads)

The other fields are optional but recommended. `:namespace`, `:tier`, `:source`, `:since` all improve the introspection experience for downstream readers.

## A.11 The reference manual generator

`src/docs-emitter.js` walks the registry and emits one section per verb in this schema. The manual and the registry are consistent by construction — the manual is a rendering of the registry, not a separate authoring source.

To regenerate the manual after adding a verb:

```scheme
(emit-reference-manual \"scheme/MOTOI-SCHEME-REFERENCE.slat\")
```

The manual updates. No drift.

## A.12 A field-quality checklist

For every verb you register:

- [ ] `:name` is unique in the registry
- [ ] `:doc` is imperative, one sentence, ends in period
- [ ] `:contract` accurately describes the intended shape
- [ ] `:arity` matches what the impl accepts
- [ ] `:examples` has at least one novice level
- [ ] `:perm` is explicit if the verb changes state
- [ ] `:namespace` is present if the verb has a prefix
- [ ] `:tier` is set (defaults to extended if unclear)
- [ ] `:source` points at the registration line
- [ ] `:since` records when the verb was added

Ten items. If your registration passes all ten, the verb is well-documented.

## A.13 The schema is stable

The field set has been frozen since Motoi 1.0. New fields (like `:powerTier`, `:chip`) have been added as additive extensions. Existing fields have not changed shape.

This stability matters because tools built on the schema keep working across releases. If you built a linter that reads `:perm`, that linter will still work in Motoi 2.0 because `:perm` is not going anywhere.

## A.14 A note on non-verb records

The reference manual also contains records for:

- Special forms (`define`, `lambda`, `let`, etc.) — these have a subset of the fields
- Macros — these have the verb schema plus a `:macro #t` marker
- Reader syntax (`#t`, `#f`, quote, etc.) — minimal records with `:reader-syntax #t`

The verb schema is the base; other kinds are variants that add or omit fields as needed.

## A.15 Conclusion

The verb record schema is the alphabet the whole introspection layer is spelled in. Every field has a purpose. Every purpose has a consumer (REPL, reference manual, LLM training corpus, cart audit tools).

Fill in the fields. Every verb, every time. The reader on the other end will thank you.

## A.16 Field reference — one-line summary

- `:name` — registered name
- `:doc` — one-sentence description
- `:contract` — signature string
- `:arity` — integer/list/variadic
- `:examples` — tiered example list
- `:namespace` — prefix grouping
- `:tier` — core/extended/experimental
- `:perm` — permission tier
- `:atom` — fine-grained category
- `:source` — path:line
- `:since` — version tag
- `:confirm` — dispatcher confirmation
- `:rateLimit` — call frequency cap
- `:schema` — argument validator
- `:idempotent` — dedupe recent calls
- `:powerTier` — substrate power gate
- `:chip` — auto-emit chip kind
- `:deprecated` — alias-only flag
- `:aliasFor` — canonical name
- `:examples-arc` — pedagogical context

Twenty fields. That is the whole verb record. Everything else in the introspection layer is a projection over these twenty.

## A.17 Compatibility notes

Older Motoi runtimes (pre-1.4) may not have `:powerTier` or `:chip`. Introspection over those fields returns nil. New tools should tolerate nil returns for these newer fields.

If you are writing a tool that must run across runtime versions, defensive coding is required:

```scheme
(or (cdr (assoc 'powerTier meta)) \"always\")
;; safe default if the field is missing
```

## A.18 SLAT rendering

When the reference manual renders a verb record as SLAT, the field order matches this appendix's schema. Reading the manual, you see fields in a predictable order every time.

When you author a verb record for the registry, order does not matter — the registry is a map, not a list. But for readability in source, follow the schema order.

## A.19 The end

That is the schema. Twenty fields. One record per verb. One consistent shape across the whole language surface.

Next: Appendix B — a printable cheat-sheet of introspection verbs.

## A.20 Field-by-field examples

Because concrete examples cement understanding, here is one worked record per field with commentary.

**`:name`** — for `cortex/query`, the name is `\"cortex/query\"`. The slash is part of the name. Every character between the quotes is significant.

**`:doc`** — for `cortex/query`, `\"Query Cortex records. Kwargs: :subject :predicate :object :at :source :order-by.\"` Notice: imperative (\"Query\"), one sentence, ends in period, names the kwargs.

**`:contract`** — for `cortex/query`, `\"(:subject? :predicate? :object? :at? :source? :order-by?) -> list\"`. All kwargs are optional (marked with `?`). Returns a list of records.

**`:arity`** — for `cortex/query`, `variadic` because kwargs mean any number of `:key value` pairs.

**`:examples`** — for `cortex/query`, a list like:
```scheme
((:level novice :code \"(cortex/query :subject 'user)\")
 (:level intermediate :code \"(cortex/query :subject 'user :predicate 'preferred-color)\")
 (:level expert :code \"(cortex/query :subject 'user :predicate 'preferred-color :order-by 'at)\"))
```

**`:namespace`** — `\"cortex\"`. The prefix before the slash.

**`:tier`** — `\"core\"`. Frozen. Will not rename.

**`:perm`** — `\"read\"`. Pure observation of Cortex records.

**`:atom`** — `\"cortex-io\"`. Groups with `cortex/read` and `cortex/write`.

**`:source`** — `\"lib/ai/cortex-io.js:121\"`. The line in the file where the verb is registered.

**`:since`** — `\"1.0\"`. Has been there since day one.

## A.21 More on the schema fields not covered above

Every field in the schema has a purpose. If you did not know why a field exists, this section clarifies.

**`:confirm`** exists because some verbs are destructive enough that they should require the caller to have set a confirmation flag. Deleting cards, publishing to platforms, sending payments — these are the kinds of things where accidental invocation is bad. The dispatcher checks `:confirm` and if true refuses to run unless `caller.confirmed` is set.

**`:rateLimit`** exists because some verbs make network calls or expensive computations. Rate-limiting prevents accidental spam. The format is `count/duration` where duration can be `s` (seconds), `min` (minutes), `hr` (hours), or `day`.

**`:schema`** is optional argument validation. A verb can attach a function that inspects its arguments before running. If the function returns anything other than `#t`, the dispatcher raises an error with that value as the message.

**`:idempotent`** is a performance hint. If a verb is a pure function of its input and expensive, marking it idempotent lets the dispatcher cache recent calls and skip re-invocation. Idempotence must be true; if the verb has hidden state, marking it idempotent will produce stale caches.

**`:powerTier`** gates against substrate power state. The substrate has a live power level (full, half, quarter, paused). A verb with `:powerTier animate` will be skipped when the substrate is at quarter or paused. This is how Motoi keeps animation loops from burning battery when the tab is backgrounded.

**`:chip`** is a display-tier convenience. If set, the dispatcher emits a small event envelope after successful dispatch. Chips are how UIs get real-time feedback that things happened without every verb needing to know about the UI.

## A.22 The manifest of what is and is not in the record

The verb record contains metadata. It does not contain:

- The implementation function itself (that lives in the source file)
- Tests (planned but not yet standard)
- Change history (git handles that)
- Author information (unless explicitly in the doc)
- Deployment status (managed elsewhere)

The record is intentionally lean. Everything on it is what a reader would want when they call `(help 'foo)`. Everything not on it is either tooling concern or living somewhere else with its own lifecycle.

## A.23 SLAT vs JSON

The reference manual emits SLAT. Some tooling around Motoi may render it as JSON for external consumers. The two are isomorphic — every SLAT record maps to a JSON object with matching keys.

For internal Motoi tools, prefer SLAT. It macroexpands, it reads with source positions, it composes with the rest of the language.

For external tools (documentation sites, syntax highlighters, third-party editors), JSON is fine. `slat->json` and `json->slat` are the converters.

## A.24 A parting note

The verb record schema is old, in Motoi terms. It was set in the 1.0 release and has not changed in shape since. Every extension has been additive.

That stability is what lets you build tools on the schema without worrying about breakage. Every verb you introspect today has the same shape as every verb you will introspect in five years, minus additive fields that will only expand the answer, never change its interpretation.

Twenty fields. Same shape. Every verb. That is the schema.

## B.16 The five reflexes

Boiled down to five habits:

1. **Ask before guessing.** `(help 'foo)` before you guess what foo does.
2. **Describe before assuming.** `(type-of value)` before you assume the shape.
3. **Expand before debugging.** `(macroexpand form)` before you debug a macro use.
4. **Query before scrolling.** `(cortex/query ...)` or `(apropos ...)` before you scroll.
5. **Introspect before fixing.** `(last-error)` before you edit the code that erred.

## B.17 Common compositions

```
;; enumerate + describe
(map describe (verbs-in-namespace \"cortex\"))

;; filter by shape
(filter (lambda (n) (= 2 (arity-of n))) (map car (snapshot-registry)))

;; introspect a value
(let ((v (some-verb)))
  (list :type (type-of v) :length (and (list? v) (length v))))

;; walk env chain
(define (walk e) (if e (cons (env-vars e) (walk (env-parent e))) '()))
(walk (current-env))

;; trace a session
(,trace my-verb)
(run-session)
(trace-log 'my-verb)
```

Five patterns. Every one is a couple of primitives combined. Compose freely.

## B.25 Extended prose — why each verb earns its place

For a reader who wants to understand the shape of the cheat-sheet, not just memorize it, this section explains why each verb category matters.

The verb-metadata section (B.1) exists because verbs are the primary units of the language. Every question you might ask about a piece of Motoi code starts with a verb. Being able to describe, doc, contract, arity, source, and examples any verb is the foundational reflex. Without these seven verbs, you are guessing.

The value-shape section (B.2) exists because values are the second primary units. Every computation produces values; every debugging session inspects values. Knowing the runtime type, the length, the keys, the fields — this is the difference between reading a printed result and understanding it.

The predicates (B.3) exist for conditional dispatch. When your code needs to branch on a value's shape, predicates give you the boolean checks. They are the counterpart to `type-of` — one returns a symbol, the other returns a yes/no.

The env section (B.4) exists because scope is a real thing and can be walked. Most languages hide scope; Motoi exposes it. When a closure's behavior surprises you, walking its captured env tells you what it captured.

The macro section (B.5) exists because macros generate code. Without seeing the generated code, you cannot debug the generation. `macroexpand` is the microscope.

The reader section (B.6) exists because the interpreter operates on forms, not strings. The reader is the strings-to-forms step. When you want to metaprogram, you go through the reader.

The errors section (B.7) exists because failures are informative. An error record has more data than an error message. Introspecting the record is faster than parsing the message.

The trace and watch section (B.8) exists because sometimes you need the temporal dimension. A snapshot is a moment; a trace is a story.

The Cortex section (B.9) exists because programs remember. Reading what a program remembers is as fundamental as reading what it computes now.

The registry section (B.10) exists because the language surface is itself a value. Iterating it, filtering it, projecting fields — these operations turn the language into a queryable data structure.

The search section (B.11) exists because you cannot remember every verb name. Search bridges the gap between what you want and what to call it.

The LLM-augmented section (B.12) exists because sometimes mechanical introspection runs out and a peer verb can go further. Grounded, honest, always distinguishing what the registry knows from what the model guesses.

The composer section (B.13) exists because widgets are a live projection of forms. Introspecting a canvas is introspecting the form the widgets produce.

The performance section (B.14) exists because measurement precedes optimization. Time, fuel, memory — three axes, three verbs each.

The REPL section (B.15) exists because sugar matters. Meta-commands are shortcuts; the underlying verbs are the reality.

The five reflexes (B.16) are the whole book distilled to five habits. If you build these five reflexes, the book has done its job.

The compositions (B.17) show that the primitives combine. Five verbs, five patterns, infinite variations.

The verbatim reference (B.20) is the copy-paste layer. When you need the exact call form, it is there.

## B.26 The cheat-sheet as pedagogy

A cheat-sheet like this one is meant to be a scaffold, not a crutch. The intent is that you consult it often at first, less over time, and eventually not at all — because the verbs have moved from the paper on your desk to the muscle memory in your fingers.

If a cheat-sheet is doing its job well, you outgrow it. That is the goal. Print this page. Use it for a week. Come back to check the syntax of a verb you forget. Come back less often. Eventually stop looking. That is what proficiency looks like.

## B.27 A closing observation

The introspection surface is small enough to fit on one sheet of paper. That is remarkable. Most language reference sheets run to dozens of pages because the language surface is enormous. Motoi's introspection surface is 30-40 verbs, and they compose enough that a reader who has memorized 15 of them can express queries that would take hundreds of API calls in another language.

Small language, deep introspection, one sheet.

Onward to Appendix C, where a 40-line REPL extension demonstrates every verb this sheet listed in a working project.

## B.28 An expanded task-index

For finding the right verb quickly, indexed by the task you are doing:

**\"I want to know what a verb does.\"** — `(describe 'foo)` or `(doc-of 'foo)`.

**\"I want to see a working example of a verb.\"** — `(examples-of 'foo)`.

**\"I want to see the source code of a verb.\"** — `(source-of 'foo)` gives you the pointer.

**\"I want to check what a value's runtime type is.\"** — `(type-of value)`.

**\"I want to see the keys of a hash.\"** — `(keys hash)`.

**\"I want to see what bindings are in the current scope.\"** — `(env-vars (current-env))`.

**\"I want to see what a macro expanded to.\"** — `(macroexpand '(macro-use args))`.

**\"I want to see what my last error was.\"** — `(last-error)`.

**\"I want to know why the program remembers something.\"** — `(cortex/query ...)` with provenance.

**\"I want to enumerate every verb in a namespace.\"** — `(verbs-in-namespace \"ns\")`.

**\"I want to search for a verb by keyword.\"** — `(apropos \"keyword\")`.

**\"I want to time an expression.\"** — `,time <expr>` or `(current-time-ms)` deltas.

**\"I want the LLM to explain a value.\"** — `(explain value)` or `(shape-of value)`.

**\"I want to audit a cart's permissions.\"** — filter registry by `:perm` (see B.9 and B.10 combined).

Fourteen tasks, fourteen answers. Every one is one or two verbs. That is the practical shape of the surface.

## B.30 One final reference — the verb dispatch model

Because it comes up in every appendix, one more explanation of how the introspection layer works under the hood.

When you call `(help 'car)`, this happens:

1. `car` is parsed as a symbol.
2. `help` is looked up in the current environment — it is a registered verb.
3. The `help` verb's implementation is called with the symbol `car` as its argument.
4. The implementation converts `car` to its name string `\"car\"`.
5. The implementation looks up `\"car\"` in the registry via `getVerbMeta`.
6. The registry returns the metadata object.
7. `help` shapes the metadata into a plist and returns it.
8. The REPL prints the plist.

Eight steps. All standard verb dispatch plus a registry lookup. Introspection is not a special path in the runtime — it is a regular verb that happens to consult metadata.

Same for `describe`, `type-of`, `source-of`, and every other introspection primitive. They are all verbs. They all go through dispatch. They all return data. They all compose.

## B.31 The universal claim

Every introspection question in Motoi is answered by a verb that consults the registry or the runtime state and returns data. No verb requires a special mode. No verb writes to disk unless it says it does. No verb bypasses the dispatcher's perm check.

Uniform, honest, composable. That is the introspection layer.

"# Appendix C — Building a ,help command from scratch: 40-line REPL extension

This appendix builds a custom REPL meta-command from scratch. When you finish, you will have a working example of how the REPL's introspection surface is assembled out of the primitives from Chapters 1-4. The pattern generalizes — you can write your own meta-commands for any query the introspection layer supports.

## C.1 The goal

Build a `,my-help` meta-command that:

1. Takes a verb name as argument
2. Prints the verb's name, doc, arity, contract, and first example
3. Colors the output (if the terminal supports it)
4. Handles the not-found case gracefully

Total: about 40 lines of Scheme. All built on introspection primitives.

## C.2 The plan

The REPL's meta-command dispatch table lives in `src/repl.js`. Each meta-command is an object with `args`, `doc`, and `run` fields. Adding a new one is a matter of registering a new entry.

Motoi's REPL exposes a `register-meta-command` verb for this purpose. If your runtime does not expose it, you can achieve the same by defining the verb in Scheme and calling it manually.

## C.3 Step 1 — the core function

Start with the introspection call:

```scheme
(define (fetch-verb-info name)
  (help name))
```

That returns the metadata record. Now we need to format it.

## C.4 Step 2 — the formatter

```scheme
(define (format-verb-info meta)
  (if (not meta)
      (string-append \"unknown verb: \" (symbol->string name))
      (let ((name (or (cdr (assoc 'name meta)) \"???\"))
            (doc (or (cdr (assoc 'doc meta)) \"(no doc)\"))
            (contract (or (cdr (assoc 'contract meta)) \"(no contract)\"))
            (arity (or (cdr (assoc 'arity meta)) \"(no arity)\"))
            (first-example
             (let ((exs (cdr (assoc 'examples meta))))
               (and exs (not (null? exs))
                    (cdr (assoc :code (car exs)))))))
        (string-append
          name \" — \" doc \"\\n\"
          \"contract: \" contract \"\\n\"
          \"arity:    \" (any->string arity) \"\\n\"
          (or (and first-example (string-append \"example:  \" first-example)) \"\")))))
```

Fifteen lines. Handles the not-found case. Extracts each field with `assoc`. Falls back to defaults when a field is missing. Concatenates with newlines for readability.

## C.5 Step 3 — the meta-command wrapper

```scheme
(define my-help-command
  (lambda (ctx argv)
    (let ((name (car argv)))
      (if (not name)
          (ctx-output ctx \"usage: ,my-help <verb>\")
          (ctx-output ctx (format-verb-info (help name)))))))
```

Six lines. Takes the REPL context and the parsed argv. Checks for the required argument. Calls `format-verb-info` on the result of `help`. Prints via the context's output handler.

## C.6 Step 4 — registration

```scheme
(register-meta-command \",my-help\"
  :args \"<verb>\"
  :doc \"Custom help formatter using introspection primitives.\"
  :run my-help-command)
```

Four lines. Names the command. Describes the args. Describes what it does. Points at the run function.

## C.7 The full extension

Combined:

```scheme
;; my-help-command.slat — custom REPL meta-command
;; 40 lines of Motoi Scheme demonstrating the introspection layer

(define (fetch-verb-info name)
  (help name))

(define (any->string x)
  (cond
    ((string? x) x)
    ((symbol? x) (symbol->string x))
    ((number? x) (number->string x))
    (else (with-output-to-string (lambda () (display x))))))

(define (format-verb-info meta name-str)
  (if (not meta)
      (string-append \"unknown verb: \" name-str)
      (let ((name (or (cdr (assoc 'name meta)) name-str))
            (doc (or (cdr (assoc 'doc meta)) \"(no doc)\"))
            (contract (or (cdr (assoc 'contract meta)) \"(no contract)\"))
            (arity (or (cdr (assoc 'arity meta)) \"(no arity)\"))
            (first-example
             (let ((exs (cdr (assoc 'examples meta))))
               (and exs (not (null? exs))
                    (cdr (assoc :code (car exs)))))))
        (string-append
          name \" — \" doc \"\\n\"
          \"contract: \" contract \"\\n\"
          \"arity:    \" (any->string arity) \"\\n\"
          (if first-example
              (string-append \"example:  \" first-example)
              \"\")))))

(define my-help-command
  (lambda (ctx argv)
    (let ((name (car argv)))
      (if (not name)
          (ctx-output ctx \"usage: ,my-help <verb>\")
          (ctx-output ctx (format-verb-info (help name) name))))))

(register-meta-command \",my-help\"
  :args \"<verb>\"
  :doc \"Custom help formatter using introspection primitives.\"
  :run my-help-command)
```

Forty lines exactly. A complete, working REPL extension.

## C.8 Usage

Load the extension into your REPL:

```
> (load \"my-help-command.slat\")
=> registered ,my-help

> ,my-help map
map — Apply a procedure to each element of one or more lists, returning a new list of results.
contract: (procedure list ...) -> list
arity:    variadic
example:  (map (lambda (x) (* x 2)) '(1 2 3))

> ,my-help nonexistent
unknown verb: nonexistent
```

Works. Handles the good case and the not-found case.

## C.9 Extension patterns

Once you have the pattern, you can build any number of custom meta-commands. Some ideas:

**,doc-all namespace** — print every verb's doc for a namespace.

```scheme
(define doc-all-command
  (lambda (ctx argv)
    (let ((ns (car argv)))
      (for-each
        (lambda (n)
          (ctx-output ctx (string-append n \": \" (or (doc-of n) \"(no doc)\"))))
        (verbs-in-namespace ns)))))

(register-meta-command \",doc-all\"
  :args \"<namespace>\"
  :doc \"Print every verb's doc in a namespace.\"
  :run doc-all-command)
```

**,by-perm perm** — enumerate verbs by permission tier.

```scheme
(define by-perm-command
  (lambda (ctx argv)
    (let ((perm (car argv)))
      (for-each
        (lambda (n)
          (ctx-output ctx n))
        (verbs-with-perm perm)))))

(register-meta-command \",by-perm\" :args \"<perm>\" :doc \"...\" :run by-perm-command)
```

**,mine** — print your favorite verbs (customized).

```scheme
(define (my-favorite-verbs)
  '(map filter fold cons car cdr display describe help apropos))

(define mine-command
  (lambda (ctx argv)
    (for-each
      (lambda (n) (ctx-output ctx (describe n)))
      (my-favorite-verbs))))

(register-meta-command \",mine\" :args \"\" :doc \"Print my favorite verbs.\" :run mine-command)
```

Every extension is a wrap around a Scheme function that uses the introspection primitives. Ten lines each, often less.

## C.10 The teaching value

This appendix is here for a specific reason: to show that the REPL's introspection surface is not magic. It is built out of the same primitives you have been reading about. If you can call `help` and `apropos` and format their returns, you can extend the REPL to expose whatever queries you find useful.

Motoi's design encourages this. Every REPL command in `src/repl.js` is thirty lines or less. Each is a thin wrap over the introspection primitives. If Motoi shipped a meta-command you wish worked differently, write a replacement in your own Scheme file.

## C.11 A more ambitious extension

For a taste of what is possible, here is a meta-command that produces a full dashboard.

```scheme
(define (dashboard-command ctx argv)
  (let ((all (map car (snapshot-registry))))
    (ctx-output ctx \"=== Motoi Runtime Dashboard ===\")
    (ctx-output ctx (string-append \"Total verbs: \" (number->string (length all))))
    (ctx-output ctx (string-append \"Core: \" (number->string (length (verbs-with-tier \"core\")))))
    (ctx-output ctx (string-append \"Extended: \" (number->string (length (verbs-with-tier \"extended\")))))
    (ctx-output ctx (string-append \"Experimental: \" (number->string (length (verbs-with-tier \"experimental\")))))
    (ctx-output ctx (string-append \"Undocumented: \" (number->string (length (verbs-missing-doc)))))
    (ctx-output ctx (string-append \"Financial-perm verbs: \" (number->string (length (verbs-with-perm \"financial\")))))
    (ctx-output ctx (string-append \"Networking verbs: \" (number->string (length (verbs-with-perm \"network\")))))))

(register-meta-command \",dashboard\" :args \"\" :doc \"Runtime dashboard.\" :run dashboard-command)
```

Now `,dashboard` at the REPL prints a runtime summary. Every metric comes from introspection primitives. No new backend needed.

## C.12 The permissions to know about

When registering a new meta-command, the runtime treats it as a read-only helper. It does not require any special perm tier. The meta-command dispatch layer runs at read tier by default.

If your custom meta-command does something more than read (like writing files or making network calls), the underlying verbs it uses will enforce their own perms. The meta-command layer is transparent to perm checks.

## C.13 The name conflict rule

If you register a meta-command with a name that already exists, the runtime warns and takes the last-registered version. To be safe, prefix your custom commands with initials or a project name:

```scheme
(register-meta-command \",dg-help\" ...)  ;; dg = my initials
```

Avoids conflicts with anything Motoi might add later.

## C.14 The extension file convention

Save your custom commands in `.slat` files under `~/.motoi/extensions/`. Motoi's REPL loads every `.slat` file in that directory at startup. Your custom commands become available in every session.

This is how a working Motoi user builds up a personal REPL — a few extensions in the extensions directory, all loaded automatically, all using the same introspection primitives the built-in commands use.

## C.15 What you have built

Forty lines. A working REPL meta-command. A pattern that generalizes. A demonstration that the introspection layer is programmable.

More importantly: a working example of the reflex the book has been teaching. Introspection primitives → useful tool. That is the shape.

- `,find-slow <verb-pattern>` — trace verbs matching a pattern, run a script, print the slowest calls
- `,who-uses <verb>` — grep all loaded carts for callers of a verb

Every one is under 20 lines. All built on introspection primitives.

## C.17 The general shape

Every REPL extension has this shape:

```scheme
(define (my-command ctx argv)
  (let ((result <some-introspection-query>))
    (<format-and-output ctx result>)))

(register-meta-command \",name\"
  :args \"<args>\"
  :doc \"description\"
  :run my-command)
```

Two blocks. The command function; the registration call. Everything specific to your extension is in the function.

## C.18 The maintenance story

Custom meta-commands are your responsibility to keep working. If Motoi adds a new field to the metadata record, your command using the old field set still works — the new field is additive. If Motoi renames a field (rare), your command breaks and you update it.

The runtime does not version meta-commands. If you have twenty custom commands and Motoi ships an update that removes a primitive you were using, you find out at REPL startup. The runtime reports the error and continues without the broken command.

Keep your extensions in version control so you can roll back if needed.

## C.19 A closing observation

The REPL is a Motoi program. So is every command in it. So is every extension you write. The whole tool is built out of the same verbs you write your carts with.

That uniformity is what makes extending it approachable. You do not need to learn a plugin API. You do not need to fork the runtime. You write a Scheme file that calls introspection verbs and registers a meta-command. Done.

## C.21 Deep-seed — the pattern in general

The pattern from this appendix is more general than REPL meta-commands. Any Motoi tool that uses introspection has this shape:

1. Query the runtime via introspection primitives (help, apropos, cortex/query, etc.).
2. Format the result for the target consumer (terminal, file, UI, API).
3. Register the tool at whatever layer (REPL meta-command, verb, cart) makes sense.

You can build:

- Documentation site generators (query registry, emit HTML)
- Cart auditors (query cart's called verbs, cross-reference with perms)
- Test-suite generators (query registry, emit test cases from examples)
- Curriculum builders (query namespace, emit lesson SLAT files)
- Metadata linters (query registry, flag missing fields)

Every one is a Scheme file that uses the introspection primitives and formats the results. Every one is small — usually under 100 lines.

## C.22 The build lesson

Motoi's introspection layer was designed to be built on. It is not a closed system exposed only to internal tools. It is open, uniform, and small enough to compose into any tool a programmer needs.

If you find yourself thinking *the REPL doesn't do X*, write a meta-command that does X. The pattern is in this appendix. The primitives are in the book. The result is yours.

Onward to Appendix D.

## C.23 Deep-seed — walkthrough of the reference REPL implementation

For completeness, here is how Motoi's built-in `,help` command is implemented in `src/repl.js`:

```javascript
',help': {
  args: '<verb>',
  doc: 'Print help for a verb (name, doc, contract, examples, source).',
  run: (ctx, argv) => {
    const name = argv[0]
    if (!name) return ctx.output('usage: ,help <verb>')
    const meta = help(name)
    if (!meta) return ctx.output(`unknown verb: ${name}`)
    printHelp(ctx, meta)
  },
},
```

Ten lines of JavaScript. Argument check. Metadata lookup. Not-found check. Format-and-print via a helper.

The `printHelp` helper is another twenty or so lines that formats the record with labels for each field. Add them together and you have thirty lines for the built-in `,help`.

Motoi's REPL is minimalist by design. Every command is thirty lines or less. That's why extending it is so approachable — the base is small.

## C.24 Deep-seed — combining primitives creatively

Once you internalize the pattern, you start seeing opportunities for creative combinations. For example, a `,graph` command that shows the call graph of a verb:

```scheme
(define (call-graph name)
  ;; walk the source of `name`, extract every verb it calls, recurse
  (let loop ((frontier (list name))
             (seen (set-empty)))
    (if (null? frontier)
        (list->set seen)
        (let* ((current (car frontier))
               (rest (cdr frontier))
               (calls (verb-calls-in-source current)))
          (loop (append rest (filter (lambda (c) (not (set-member? seen c))) calls))
                (set-add seen current))))))
```

A `verb-calls-in-source` helper walks the source of a verb (using `source-of` + read-file) and extracts every symbol in call position. Filter by whether the symbol is a registered verb, and you have the call graph.

Not built-in. Not standard. But composable from primitives, and useful when you want to see what verbs depend on what other verbs.

## C.25 Deep-seed — a summary generator

Another useful extension: a session summary that prints what happened.

```scheme
(define (session-summary-command ctx argv)
  (let ((history-length (length (repl-history)))
        (cortex-writes (length (cortex/query :at :gt (session-start-time))))
        (errors (length (session-errors))))
    (ctx-output ctx (string-append \"Session summary:\\n\"
                                    \"  \" (number->string history-length) \" prompts evaluated\\n\"
                                    \"  \" (number->string cortex-writes) \" Cortex records written\\n\"
                                    \"  \" (number->string errors) \" errors raised\"))))
```

Run at end of session, print a summary. That is Chapter 13's `reflect` verb in miniature — a session summary built from introspection primitives.

## C.26 The extensibility principle

Every layer of Motoi is extensible via the same pattern: query primitives, format the result, register the extension. The REPL is the most visible example, but the same pattern works for:

- Reference-manual renderers (query registry, emit SLAT sections)
- Cart audit tools (query cart, check against registry)
- Runtime dashboards (query state, format as UI)
- Training-corpus generators (query registry, emit training pairs)

Every one of these is a Scheme program. Every one uses the introspection primitives. Every one is customizable by rewriting the format-and-register logic.

## C.27 A final observation

Motoi's introspection layer is not designed just for reading. It is designed for building. The primitives are meant to be composed into tools. The reference REPL is an example, not a limit.

Write your own tools. That is what the primitives are for.

Onward to Appendix D.

## C.28 One more deep-seed

A meta-command that summarizes the LLM-augmented family (Chapter 13):

```scheme
(define (llm-family-command ctx argv)
  (let ((verbs (filter (lambda (n) (string-prefix? \"llm/\" n))
                       (map car (snapshot-registry)))))
    (for-each
      (lambda (n) (ctx-output ctx (describe n)))
      verbs)))
```

Five lines. Prints every `llm/*` verb with its description. Useful when you want to know what LLM primitives are available.

## C.29 The larger design

Meta-commands are a small piece of Motoi's larger design of everything-is-a-verb. The REPL is not a special surface with its own API; it is a Motoi program that dispatches verbs based on line input. Meta-commands are just verbs with a shortcut syntax. The pattern is uniform.

That uniformity is why extending Motoi is approachable. You do not learn a plugin API; you write Scheme.

Onward to Appendix D.

## C.30 A final worked example — the tiered examples printer

If you want a meta-command that shows just the examples of a verb in a nice tiered layout:

```scheme
(define (tiered-examples-command ctx argv)
  (let* ((name (car argv))
         (meta (help name)))
    (if (not meta)
        (ctx-output ctx (string-append \"unknown verb: \" name))
        (let ((exs (cdr (assoc 'examples meta))))
          (if (null? exs)
              (ctx-output ctx (string-append name \" has no examples\"))
              (begin
                (ctx-output ctx (string-append \"Examples for \" name \":\"))
                (for-each
                  (lambda (ex)
                    (let ((level (cdr (assoc :level ex)))
                          (code (cdr (assoc :code ex))))
                      (ctx-output ctx (string-append
                                        \"  [\" (symbol->string level) \"] \"
                                        code))))
                  exs)))))))

(register-meta-command \",tex\"
  :args \"<verb>\"
  :doc \"Print tiered examples for a verb.\"
  :run tiered-examples-command)
```

Twenty lines. Full command. Handles all edge cases. Reuses introspection primitives.

Usage:

```
> ,tex map
Examples for map:
  [novice] (map (lambda (x) (* x 2)) '(1 2 3))
  [intermediate] (map + '(1 2 3) '(10 20 30))
  [expert] (map (lambda (kv) (cons (car kv) (* (cdr kv) 2))) alist)
```

Clean output. Custom formatting. Yours to modify.

That reflex is what makes the REPL yours, not Motoi's.

```scheme
(define (recent-verbs-command ctx argv)
  (let* ((n (if (null? argv) 20 (string->number (car argv))))
         (calls (extract-verb-calls (last-n-history n)))
         (counts (frequency-of calls)))
    (for-each
      (lambda (pair)
        (ctx-output ctx (string-append
                          (number->string (cdr pair))
                          \" \" (car pair))))
      (sort-by cdr > counts))))
```

Ten lines. Now `,recent-verbs 20` prints the twenty most-used verbs from your last twenty prompts, with counts. Your own usage report at a keystroke.

## C.33 The final closing

Extensions are the point. Motoi's introspection layer is worth exactly as much as the tools you build on it. Every tool you build sharpens your relationship with the language.

Onward to Appendix D — introspection at boundaries you did not draw yourself but must still be able to describe with confidence and reasonable safety in production carts.
")

"# Appendix D — Introspection at the boundary: foreign values, sidecars, sockets

Not every value in Motoi is native. Values cross boundaries — from foreign function interfaces, from network sockets, from sidecar processes, from disk. This appendix shows how to describe values you did not create, and where introspection stops being able to help.

## D.1 What is a boundary value?

A boundary value is a value that entered the Motoi runtime from outside. Common sources:

- **File reads** — bytes from disk parsed into strings or forms
- **Network reads** — bytes from a socket
- **Foreign function calls** — return values from JavaScript, Python, Rust bindings
- **Sidecar processes** — output from spawned subprocesses
- **User input** — REPL prompts, form fields, voice
- **Cortex reads from previous sessions** — records written by past runs

Every boundary value has less introspection than a native one because the runtime did not create it and does not know its full history.

## D.2 The introspection story for boundary values

For a value that came from outside, `type-of` still works — the runtime knows the shape of what it received. `length`, `keys`, `record-fields` all work on the structural level.

What does not work automatically:

- Provenance beyond \"came from that boundary\"
- Source location (there is no Motoi source)
- Contract (unless the boundary annotated the value)
- Semantic interpretation (the runtime just sees bytes shaped into a value)

For those, you need to introspect the boundary itself, not just the value.

## D.3 Foreign function values

Motoi can call JavaScript, Python, or native functions through a foreign function interface. The return value comes back as a Motoi value, but its origin is the foreign function.

```scheme
(define result (foreign/call \"my-js-function\" 42))
(type-of result)
;; => hash    ;; Motoi shape

(foreign/origin result)
;; => (:kind ffi :language javascript :function \"my-js-function\" :args (42))
```

`foreign/origin` is a boundary introspection verb. It returns metadata about where the value came from, if the runtime tracked it.

Not every foreign value has origin metadata — the runtime tracks it only when the FFI was configured to. For raw FFI calls with no tracking, `foreign/origin` returns nil.

## D.4 Sidecar processes

A sidecar is a subprocess spawned by Motoi that speaks a protocol over stdin/stdout. Motoi's runtime has sidecar helpers for common protocols.

```scheme
(define sidecar (sidecar/start \"my-tool\"))
(sidecar/type sidecar)
;; => (:kind subprocess :cmd \"my-tool\" :pid 12345 :protocol json)

(define result (sidecar/call sidecar (list :op 'compute :input 42)))
(type-of result)
;; => hash    ;; parsed from JSON

(foreign/origin result)
;; => (:kind sidecar :sidecar 12345 :op compute :args (:input 42))
```

The sidecar itself is introspectable — you can see its pid, its command, its protocol. Values returned through the sidecar can carry origin metadata pointing back at the specific call.

## D.5 Socket values

Data arriving through a network socket is the most opaque boundary. The runtime knows only that bytes arrived; it does not know their intended shape.

```scheme
(define sock (socket/connect \"example.com\" 8080))
(socket/info sock)
;; => (:kind socket :remote \"example.com:8080\" :protocol tcp :status open)

(define data (socket/read sock 1024))
(type-of data)
;; => string    ;; raw bytes
```

To make sense of the data you have to parse it. The introspection layer treats it as a string until you parse. After parsing:

```scheme
(define parsed (parse-json data))
(type-of parsed)
;; => hash
(foreign/origin parsed)
;; => (:kind socket :remote \"example.com:8080\" :read-at 1720000000)
```

The origin traces back to the socket. This is useful for debugging — if a value has unexpected shape, `foreign/origin` tells you where it entered the program.

## D.6 File values

Files are the friendliest boundary. Reading a file gives you a string; parsing gives you forms. Both are fully introspectable.

```scheme
(define contents (read-file \"data.txt\"))
(type-of contents)
;; => string
(length contents)
;; => 1024

(foreign/origin contents)
;; => (:kind file :path \"data.txt\" :read-at 1720000000)
```

If you parsed the file:

```scheme
(define forms (parse contents :filename \"data.txt\"))
(length forms)
;; => 12
(form-pos (car forms))
;; => (:filename \"data.txt\" :line 1 :column 1)
```

Now the forms carry file position metadata (Chapter 7). You can trace any form back to its source location.

## Sections D.7 through D.16 — pending Wave 4 authoring

- D.7 The FFI protocol
- D.8 Sidecar lifecycle introspection
- D.9 Socket state and error introspection
- D.10 Cortex boundary — cross-session values
- D.11 Voice input as a boundary
- D.12 Web request boundaries
- D.13 Bindings inspection for foreign values
- D.14 Redaction at the boundary
- D.15 The trust boundary
- D.16 Closing — where introspection stops

## D.17 The trust boundary

Boundary values require judgment. A value that entered from a trusted source (your own file, your own sidecar) can usually be trusted. A value from an untrusted source (a network socket, a user input) should be validated before use.

Introspection helps here:

```scheme
(define user-input (repl-read))
(type-of user-input)
;; => string

(if (contract-satisfied? '(a b c) user-input)
    (do-something-with user-input)
    (raise-error :kind 'invalid-input :context (list :got user-input)))
```

`contract-satisfied?` checks whether a value matches a contract shape. For boundary values, always check before using.

## D.18 The opaque case

Sometimes a boundary value is truly opaque. A binary blob from a network socket. A handle to a foreign resource. A closure returned from FFI. Introspection can only tell you it exists and what type it is.

```scheme
(define handle (native/get-resource))
(type-of handle)
;; => opaque    ;; runtime does not know its shape
(shape-of handle)
;; => (:mechanical (:type opaque) :prose \"This value is a handle to a native resource. It cannot be introspected further.\")
```

Opaque is honest. The runtime does not pretend to know more than it does.

## D.19 A worked example

You are wiring a Motoi cart to a JavaScript library through FFI. The library returns hash objects. You want to make sure your cart handles them correctly.

```scheme
(define result (foreign/call \"js-lib.compute\" input))
(type-of result)
;; => hash
(keys result)
;; => (:status :data :error)

(cond
  ((equal? \"success\" (hash-ref result :status))
   (process (hash-ref result :data)))
  (else
   (handle-error (hash-ref result :error))))
```

Standard boundary handling. Introspect the shape, branch on the fields, extract the data.

## D.20 A closing observation

Introspection is honest about boundaries. It does not pretend to know what it does not know. When a value came from outside, the introspection layer reports what it can (type, shape) and marks the rest as opaque or unknown.

That honesty is what makes the introspection layer trustworthy at boundaries. You cannot be misled by fabricated origin info; if the origin is unknown, the return is nil, not a guess.
