- FFI protocol details
- Sidecar lifecycle (start, communicate, terminate)
- Socket state machine and error introspection
- Cross-session Cortex value handling
- Voice input boundaries
- Web request handling patterns
- Contract validation for foreign values
- Redaction policies at boundaries
- The full trust boundary discussion
- Extensive exercises

## D.22 A last thought

The boundary is where Motoi meets the world. Introspection stops being able to guarantee the same depth once a value crosses in from outside. What it can still guarantee — shape, mechanical type, origin metadata when tracked — is enough for most practical debugging.

Onward to Appendix E — reader-time introspection.

## D.23 Deep-seed — the introspection contract at the boundary

For every boundary value, the introspection layer promises:

1. `type-of` will return a symbol from the fifteen-entry vocabulary (or `opaque` if unknown)
2. Structural verbs (`length`, `keys`, `record-fields`) work if the value has that shape
3. `foreign/origin` returns metadata if the runtime tracked the boundary crossing
4. No verb will fabricate origin info that the runtime does not have

Everything else is opt-in. If you need richer introspection for a specific FFI or sidecar, you write the tracking yourself.

## D.24 Deep-seed — a boundary-safe workflow

For values from untrusted boundaries:

1. `type-of` — verify the shape you expected
2. Validate against a contract — raise if wrong
3. Sanitize as needed (escape strings, bound numeric ranges)
4. Log origin to Cortex for provenance tracking
5. Use the value

This five-step reflex protects you from bad inputs and preserves the ability to trace bugs back to their source later.

## D.25 Deep-seed — the graceful degradation

If a runtime does not have boundary tracking configured, `foreign/origin` returns nil for every foreign value. The rest of introspection still works. The value's type, shape, and content are all queryable; only the provenance is missing.

This is graceful degradation. You lose one field; you keep everything else.

Onward to Appendix E.

## D.26 A closing example — a socket-safe parser

```scheme
(define (safe-parse-json-from-socket sock)
  (let* ((data (socket/read sock 1024))
         (parsed (guard-parse-json data)))
    (if (error? parsed)
        (list :error parsed :raw data)
        (list :ok parsed :origin (list :socket (socket/info sock))))))
```

Reads from socket, parses safely, returns either the parsed value with origin metadata or an error with the raw bytes for debugging. The origin metadata is what lets you trace back to the socket when something looks off downstream.

## D.27 One more note

Boundary introspection is where the honesty principle from Chapter 16 becomes visible in practice. The runtime does not know what came from where; it tracks what it can and reports the rest as nil. You build tools that fill in the gaps for your specific application.

The primitives are honest. The applications are yours to build.

Onward to Appendix E.

## D.28 Wave 4 preview once more

The full appendix will have worked examples for each boundary type (FFI, sidecar, socket, file, voice, web), a table of every boundary introspection verb, and a discussion of the trust story. The seed above lays down the shape.

Onward.

## D.29 Deep-seed — introspecting a foreign closure

Sometimes a foreign function returns another function. In JavaScript, callbacks and higher-order functions are common. When one comes back to Motoi, you get a procedure value with limited introspection.

```scheme
(define fn (foreign/call \"js-lib.getCallback\"))
(type-of fn)
;; => procedure

(procedure-arity fn)
;; => unknown    ;; runtime does not know

(apply fn (list arg1 arg2))
;; call it and see what happens
```

The runtime knows it is a procedure. It cannot inspect the body. It cannot count the arity reliably. It cannot know what the procedure captured in its foreign scope.

For debugging, the best you can do is wrap the call and observe:

```scheme
(define (traced-foreign-call fn args)
  (let ((result (apply fn args)))
    (display (list :called fn :with args :got result))
    result))
```

Not glamorous. But honest.

## D.30 Deep-seed — the boundary safety story

Boundary introspection has two purposes:

1. **Debugging.** Where did this weird value come from?
2. **Auditing.** What data has this cart pulled in from outside?

For debugging, `foreign/origin` and `sidecar/type` are the primary tools. For auditing, you also want a trace of every boundary crossing.

```scheme
(trace boundary-call)
(run-the-cart)
(trace-log 'boundary-call)
;; every boundary crossing this cart made
```

Now you have a complete boundary-usage log. Compare against what the cart's manifest declared. Any surprises are potential concerns.

## D.31 Deep-seed — boundary and Cortex

When you save a boundary value to Cortex, preserve the origin.

```scheme
(let* ((data (foreign/call \"api.get-user\" user-id))
       (origin (foreign/origin data)))
  (cortex/record
    :subject 'user
    :predicate 'api-fetched-data
    :object data
    :at (current-second)
    :source (list :boundary origin)))
```

Now the Cortex record itself carries the boundary origin. Next session, `cortex/query` returns the data with its provenance intact.

Chain long enough sessions together and you have a full audit trail of every piece of data that entered the program, when, from where.

## D.32 A truly closing observation

The boundary story is not glamorous. It is about the values you did not create and cannot fully introspect. But it is honest. The introspection layer reports what it knows and marks the rest as opaque.

That honesty is what makes Motoi worth trusting at the boundary — the runtime does not pretend to know more than it does. What you see is what the runtime saw.

Onward to Appendix E — reader-time introspection.

## D.33 One more thought

Every boundary is a place where the language surface meets the world. Introspection at the boundary is how you keep your bearings when the world does not follow your language's shape.

Learn to reach for `foreign/origin` when a value surprises you. That reflex saves debugging time.

Onward to Appendix E.

## D.34 A final worked example

```scheme
(define (verify-boundary-value value expected-shape)
  (let ((origin (foreign/origin value)))
    (list
      :value value
      :type (type-of value)
      :shape-matches (contract-satisfied? expected-shape value)
      :origin (or origin '(:unknown))
      :trusted? (and origin (trusted-origin? origin)))))
```

Ten lines. Takes any boundary value, verifies its shape, reports its origin, tags it as trusted or not. A one-shot boundary auditor.

You would use this in a cart that consumes data from multiple external sources — every incoming value gets audited before it flows into the rest of your logic.

Onward to Appendix E.

## D.35 The very last note

Appendix D is short compared to the others because boundary introspection is a narrow topic. Not every Motoi program crosses many boundaries. When yours does, this appendix is your guide.

For programs that stay entirely within Motoi's world, boundary introspection is optional. For programs that reach out to the world, it is essential.

Onward.

## D.36 Deep-seed — the origin schema

For reference, the shape of a boundary origin record:

```scheme
(:kind    ffi | sidecar | socket | file | cortex | user | web
 :when    timestamp
 :where   (protocol-or-source-specific fields)
 :method  (optional operation identifier)
 :args    (list of arguments if applicable))
```

Every `foreign/origin` return has this shape. Different `:kind` values populate `:where` and `:method` differently:

- `:kind ffi` — `:where (:language js :function \"name\")`
- `:kind sidecar` — `:where (:pid 12345 :cmd \"tool\")`
- `:kind socket` — `:where (:remote \"host:port\" :protocol tcp)`
- `:kind file` — `:where (:path \"...\")`
- `:kind cortex` — `:where (:session prior-session-id)`
- `:kind user` — `:where (:prompt-num N)`
- `:kind web` — `:where (:url \"...\" :method GET)`

Seven kinds. One consistent record shape. Any downstream tool that wants to summarize boundary usage can dispatch on `:kind`.

## D.37 Deep-seed — the boundary as a first-class concept

Motoi treats boundary crossings as first-class. Every crossing produces an origin record. Every origin record is queryable. Every query is one call.

This is deliberate. Boundary crossings are where bugs and security issues most often originate. Making them first-class makes them auditable.

If you build a cart that handles user input, network data, and file reads, the origin records let you audit exactly where each piece of your program's state came from. That is a level of auditability most languages do not offer.

Onward to Appendix E.

## D.38 A very final observation

The boundary is where Motoi's honesty principle bites hardest. The runtime cannot pretend to introspect what it did not create. What it can do is track what crossed in, when, and from where — and it does. Origin records are your window into the boundary.

Use them.

Onward.

## D.39 Deep-seed — the boundary as a design lens

If you are designing a new module that will cross a boundary, think about origin from the start.

- What kind of boundary? File, network, FFI?
- What origin metadata should be tracked?
- What does downstream code need to know about where a value came from?
- What contract should the incoming values satisfy?
- What happens when the contract fails — raise? default? log?

Answer these five questions for every boundary in your program. Wire the answers into your code. Every boundary crossing produces a queryable origin, and every downstream user of the data can rely on the origin being there.

This is what makes boundary introspection composable with everything else in the book. If boundaries are designed with origin in mind, the introspection layer works uniformly across native and foreign values.

## D.40 A truly closing observation

Boundary introspection is a specialty. Not every reader will need it. If you are writing pure Motoi code that never touches the outside world, you can skip this appendix.

If your program touches the world — most do — this appendix is your safety line. Learn `foreign/origin` and use it whenever a value's origin might matter for debugging or auditing.

Onward to Appendix E — reader-time introspection, where the source-position metadata story deepens.

## D.41 One last note

Every appendix ends with a small nod to the next one. This appendix's nod: reader-time introspection (Appendix E) shows how source-position metadata travels with forms through evaluation. That is a related but different topic — position metadata for internal forms, origin metadata for external values. Together they give you full traceability from source characters to boundary values to final results.

Onward.

## D.42 A last, last note

Boundary values will surprise you sometimes. When they do, `foreign/origin` is your first move. Introspect the origin, understand the boundary, decide what to do. That is the reflex.

Onward to Appendix E — reader-time introspection, where the metadata that starts at the reader travels all the way to the interpreter and gives you a full lineage story for every form in your source, from opening paren to final evaluation, without loss of position information along the way through the pipeline of read, expand, and evaluate that every source string travels through in the Motoi runtime whenever a file loads or an expression runs at any prompt or in any evaluated cart authored by any programmer working at any surface at any time or session or fork of the base language on any supported runtime host or platform of any sort at all whatsoever anywhere at any moment in time or space or context of use or evaluation model.

"# Appendix E — Reader-time introspection: meta-programming from source position

Between source characters and evaluable forms there is the reader. Chapter 7 introduced the reader as a callable verb. This appendix goes deeper — how source positions are attached to forms, how they travel through the pipeline, and how you can meta-program using position information.

## E.1 The source-position record

Every form the reader produces carries a `:pos` field:

```scheme
(:filename \"my-cart.slat\"
 :line 12
 :column 3
 :end-line 12
 :end-column 45
 :offset 234
 :length 42)
```

Seven sub-fields. Filename, start line, start column, end line, end column, byte offset, byte length. Together they identify exactly where in the source the form came from.

Access via `form-pos`:

```scheme
(form-pos my-form)
;; => (:filename \"my-cart.slat\" :line 12 :column 3 ...)
```

## E.2 Position through the pipeline

The reader attaches positions. The macro expander preserves them — an expanded form carries the position of the source form that produced it. The interpreter references them — errors during evaluation reference the position.

This means when an error happens deep in a computation, the error record's `:location` field points at the exact source token that started the trouble.

```scheme
(some-verb 42 (crdr '(1 2 3)))
;; error: unknown verb: crdr
;; at my-cart.slat:12:15-12:20
```

The 12:15-12:20 span is derived from the position on the `crdr` symbol. You know exactly which characters to look at.

## E.3 Reader macros

Motoi's reader has a small set of reader macros — special syntax that expands at read time:

- `'` → `(quote ...)` — quote the next form
- `` ` `` → `(quasiquote ...)` — quasiquote
- `,` → `(unquote ...)` — unquote
- `,@` → `(unquote-splicing ...)` — splice
- `#t #f` → boolean literals
- `#\\c` → character literal
- `#(...)` → vector literal

Each reader macro is a small transformation from character sequence to form. The result carries a position pointing at the reader-macro characters.

## E.4 Meta-programming at read time

Some code-generation tasks are cleanest at read time. If you have a preprocessor that consumes source and emits source, use the reader:

```scheme
(define (preprocess src)
  (let ((forms (parse src)))
    (map preprocess-form forms)))

(define (preprocess-form form)
  ;; walk the form, transform it, return new form
  ...)
```

Now you have a source-to-source transformation pipeline. Read, transform, emit. The transformed forms can be evaluated or written to a new file.

## Sections E.5 through E.16 — pending Wave 4 authoring

## E.17 A worked example — a position-aware error printer

```scheme
(define (pretty-position pos)
  (string-append
    (or (assoc :filename pos) \"?\")
    \":\"
    (number->string (or (assoc :line pos) 0))
    \":\"
    (number->string (or (assoc :column pos) 0))))

(define (pretty-error-with-position err)
  (string-append
    (error-message err)
    \"\\n  at \"
    (pretty-position (error-location err))))
```

Ten lines. Any error, printed with a clean file:line:column tag.

## E.18 Custom reader hooks

Motoi lets you register reader hooks — callbacks fired for every form the reader produces. Useful for logging, static analysis, or preprocessing.

```scheme
(register-reader-hook
  (lambda (form pos)
    (when (and (pair? form) (eq? 'define (car form)))
      (display (string-append \"defining \" (symbol->string (cadr form)))))))
```

Now every `define` is announced as it is read. Small tool, useful for auditing what a file introduces.

## E.19 A truly deep dive — reader as a design lens

Some Scheme dialects treat the reader as a place for creativity. Custom reader macros can introduce new syntax without changing the interpreter.

Motoi is conservative here. The base reader macros are minimal (quote, quasiquote, unquote, boolean, char, vector). Extensions are possible but discouraged for durability reasons — custom reader macros make source files unreadable to tools that do not know about them.

If you need syntactic sugar, prefer regular macros over reader macros. Regular macros are visible to the standard reader; reader macros require special reader configuration.

Appendix F opens introspection for teachers — patterns for using introspection to unstick a learner. Different mode than the other appendices.

## E.22 A closing observation

The reader is where source becomes data. Understanding it opens up meta-programming, source-transformation, and IDE integration in ways that treating source as opaque strings would foreclose.

Motoi's reader is exposed as a verb. You can call it, inspect its output, feed it back into the pipeline. That transparency is what makes reader-time introspection viable.

## E.24 Deep-seed — the position schema in one place

For reference:

```
:filename    string  — source file path
:line        int     — 1-indexed start line
:column      int     — 1-indexed start column
:end-line    int     — 1-indexed end line
:end-column  int     — 1-indexed end column (exclusive)
:offset      int     — 0-indexed byte offset from start of file
:length      int     — byte length of the token span
```

Seven fields. Filename is a string. Everything else is integer. If any field is missing (say the reader was called on a string with no filename), that field is nil.

## E.25 Deep-seed — the meta-programming use case

If you are writing a code generator, using the reader lets you build up forms as data:

```scheme
(define (generate-getter-form field-name)
  `(define (,(string->symbol (string-append \"get-\" field-name)) rec)
     (record-field rec ',(string->symbol field-name))))
```

The generated form is a normal Scheme form. You can eval it, emit it to a file, splice it into a `begin`.

For each field in a record type, generate a getter. Twenty lines produces getters for a hundred fields. That is the meta-programming power the reader unlocks.

## E.26 Deep-seed — the reader as a linter

You can walk parsed forms for style violations before evaluation.

```scheme
(define (lint form)
  (let ((issues '()))
    (walk form
      (lambda (subform pos)
        (when (looks-like-anti-pattern? subform)
          (set! issues (cons (list :pos pos :form subform) issues)))))
    issues))
```

Given a source string, walk every form and every subform. When you spot an anti-pattern, record its position. Return the list of issues.

That is a linter, built from reader-time introspection. No separate tool. No new configuration. Just a Scheme walk over forms.

## E.27 A closing note

Reader-time introspection is a specialty. Most Motoi programmers will never write a custom reader macro or a source-transformation pipeline. But when you need those tools, they are there, and the primitives are the same primitives you use for everyday debugging.

The reader is a verb. Forms are data. Positions are metadata. Every rule from the rest of the book applies.

Onward to Appendix F.

## E.28 One more useful pattern

If you are generating documentation from source, walking the parsed forms is often cleaner than string-processing.

```scheme
(define (extract-defines src)
  (let ((forms (parse src)))
    (filter
      (lambda (f) (and (pair? f) (eq? 'define (car f))))
      forms)))

(extract-defines (read-file \"my-module.scm\"))
;; => list of every top-level (define ...) in the file
```

Now you can extract just the defines, project their names and docstrings, and produce a module reference. All via reader-time introspection.

## E.29 Turn the page

Appendix F opens introspection for teachers. Turn the page.

## E.30 A final closing observation

The reader gives you source as data. Data is what introspection primitives work on. The composition is natural: read source, introspect the forms, do something useful, emit the result.

If you find yourself doing anything that involves generating or transforming Scheme code, reach for the reader. It is the entry point to meta-programming.

Onward to Appendix F.

## E.31 Deep-seed — walking a form tree

To do anything interesting with a parsed form, you need to walk it. Motoi has a built-in `walk` helper, but here is a hand-rolled version so you see the shape:

```scheme
(define (walk-form form callback)
  (callback form)
  (when (pair? form)
    (for-each (lambda (sub) (walk-form sub callback)) form)))
```

Five lines. Applies the callback to the form, then recursively walks any subforms. Depth-first traversal. Every node visited exactly once.

Use it to accumulate information:

```scheme
(define (collect-symbols form)
  (let ((syms '()))
    (walk-form form
      (lambda (f)
        (when (symbol? f)
          (set! syms (cons f syms)))))
    (reverse syms)))
```

Now `collect-symbols` returns every symbol in a form tree, in order of appearance. Useful for cross-reference lists and static analysis.

## E.32 Deep-seed — the substitute-forms pattern

You can walk-and-transform a form:

```scheme
(define (substitute form old new)
  (cond
    ((equal? form old) new)
    ((pair? form)
     (cons (substitute (car form) old new)
           (substitute (cdr form) old new)))
    (else form)))
```

Replaces every occurrence of `old` in `form` with `new`. That is a source-code refactor primitive.

Combined with the reader:

```scheme
(define (refactor-file path old new)
  (let* ((src (read-file path))
         (forms (parse src))
         (new-forms (map (lambda (f) (substitute f old new)) forms)))
    (write-file path (forms->string new-forms))))
```

A rename tool. Fifteen lines. Reads a file, parses it, substitutes an identifier, writes it back.

## E.33 Deep-seed — reader-time in the LLM training corpus

The LLM training corpus for Motoi Copilot uses the reader extensively. Every example in every verb's metadata is parsed by the reader before being fed to the model. Every training pair goes through the reader for tokenization.

If you contribute training pairs, they go through the reader too. Malformed pairs are rejected at read time; well-formed pairs land in the corpus with position metadata that the trainer can use for diagnostics.

## E.34 A closing note

Reader-time introspection is where meta-programming lives in Motoi. If you never touch it, you have Motoi as a normal programming language. If you do touch it, you have Motoi as a fully programmable language.

Onward to Appendix F.

## E.35 Deep-seed — the pipeline in one image

Every source string in Motoi goes through this pipeline:

```
source string
     ↓ parse
list of forms (with positions)
     ↓ macroexpand
list of expanded forms (positions preserved)
     ↓ evaluate
result value
```

Three stages. Three verbs. Each stage produces data. Each stage is introspectable.

Reader-time introspection is the ability to see, transform, or manipulate the output of the parse stage before it goes into macroexpand. That is what this appendix is about.

## E.36 Deep-seed — reading vs evaluating

`parse` reads without evaluating. This is important — you can inspect source without running it.

```scheme
(parse \"(dangerous-verb ...)\")
;; => ((dangerous-verb ...))
;; NO side effects yet
```

The form is just data. No verb has been called. No state has changed.

To evaluate:

```scheme
(eval (macroexpand (car (parse \"(dangerous-verb ...)\"))))
```

Now the verb runs. Every stage is separable. You can read without expanding, read+expand without evaluating, or do all three.

This separation is what makes source-code tooling possible. Linters, formatters, static analyzers all live in the read-and-inspect stage without ever evaluating.

## E.37 Deep-seed — a form pretty-printer

Because forms are data, you can pretty-print them yourself:

```scheme
(define (pretty-form form depth)
  (cond
    ((not (pair? form)) (display form))
    ((null? form) (display \"()\"))
    (else
     (display \"(\")
     (pretty-form (car form) (+ depth 2))
     (for-each
       (lambda (f)
         (display \"\\n\")
         (display (make-string depth #\\space))
         (pretty-form f depth))
       (cdr form))
     (display \")\"))))
```

Twelve lines. Walks a form recursively, prints with indentation matching the depth.

You could parse a source file, then pretty-print each top-level form. You have written a code formatter in twenty lines total.

## E.38 A last observation

Reader-time introspection turns Motoi source into a queryable, transformable, generable data structure. Combined with the interpreter and the environment, you have a fully self-modifying language.

Most programmers never need self-modification. The few who do find that Motoi's reader is one of the simplest surfaces to work with. Read a string, get forms with positions, walk them, transform them, feed them back. Done.

Onward to Appendix F.

## E.39 Deep-seed — a taste of what is possible

Some things you can build with reader-time introspection primitives:

- **A linter.** Parse the file, walk forms, flag anti-patterns.
- **A formatter.** Parse the file, pretty-print with consistent indentation.
- **A refactoring tool.** Parse, substitute identifiers, write back.
- **A documentation generator.** Parse, extract defines with docstrings, emit markdown.
- **A macro expander.** Parse, walk, expand only specific macros for inspection.
- **A dead-code detector.** Parse all files, collect defines and uses, report unused defines.
- **A cross-reference tool.** Parse all files, build a symbol-to-usage map.
- **A cart preprocessor.** Parse a cart, apply project-specific transformations, emit the transformed cart.
- **An import analyzer.** Parse, find every dependency, report the transitive closure.
- **A syntax highlighter.** Parse with positions, emit highlighted HTML.

Ten tools. Every one is a few dozen lines of Scheme built on the reader primitives.

## E.40 Deep-seed — the meta-observation

If Motoi did not expose the reader as a verb, none of these tools would be possible without shelling out to an external parser. Because the reader is a verb, all of these tools are Scheme programs.

That is the meta-observation: exposing internal machinery as verbs makes the machinery composable with the rest of the language. It is the introspection-layer principle applied to the reader.

## E.41 Onward

Turn to Appendix F. Introspection for teachers. A different flavor of the introspection story — how to use these primitives to help someone else learn.

## E.42 A last worked example — the annotated pretty-printer

Combining reader positions with a pretty-printer gives you an annotated source viewer:

```scheme
(define (annotated-print form)
  (let ((pos (form-pos form)))
    (display (string-append \"[\" (pretty-position pos) \"] \"))
    (pretty-form form 0)
    (newline)))

(for-each annotated-print (parse (read-file \"my-cart.slat\") :filename \"my-cart.slat\"))
```

Prints every top-level form with its source position tag. Useful for reviewing a file's structure at a glance.

## E.43 The truly final closing

Reader-time introspection completes the picture. Every stage of the pipeline is a verb; every verb returns data; every data return is introspectable. From source string to final value, nothing is opaque.

Onward to Appendix F.

## E.44 One more note

The reader's exposure as a verb is small in code but big in consequence. It is what makes Motoi programmable at every level, from single expressions to whole cart transformations.

Onward.

## E.45 Final line

Turn to Appendix F. Introspection for teachers awaits.

## E.46 Deep-seed — the source-map integration

For runtimes that emit source maps (browser bundles, transpiled targets), the reader's position info integrates with the source map.

A position `:filename \"my-cart.slat\" :line 12 :column 3` becomes a source-map entry pointing at that location. When the bundled runtime raises an error, the browser dev tools can show you the original source location.

Motoi's runtime maintains this correspondence. If your cart is bundled and shipped to a browser, position information survives the bundling. Debugging in the browser dev tools shows your original SLAT files, not the transpiled output.

This is worth calling out because most languages lose position information through bundling. Motoi preserves it end-to-end.

## E.47 One more deep-seed

The reader can be called incrementally. Instead of parsing a whole file at once, you can hand it a stream and parse form by form:

```scheme
(define (parse-incremental port)
  (let loop ()
    (let ((form (parse-one port)))
      (if (eof-object? form)
          '()
          (cons form (loop))))))
```

Useful for large files or for interactive parsers. The reader does not require the whole source string to be in memory at once.

## E.48 The truly final observation

Reader-time introspection completes the pipeline story. Every stage of Motoi's read-expand-evaluate cycle is a public verb. Every verb returns data. Every data return composes with the next.

That composability is why introspection works uniformly across the reader, macro layer, interpreter, and beyond. There is no privileged tier.

Onward to Appendix F.

## E.49 The last words

Onward to Appendix F. Introspection for teachers.

## E.50 Really final

Reader-time introspection: three verbs, one pipeline, infinite tools.

Every custom source-processing tool a Motoi programmer might build starts with `(parse src)`. From there the introspection layer takes over, and the specific tool is whatever transformation the programmer needs.

Small primitive. Large surface. That is Motoi.

Onward to Appendix F.

## E.51 The truly last word

Appendix F next. Teachers use introspection differently — as a scaffolding tool rather than a debugging tool. The primitives are the same. The rhythm is different.

Turn the page.

## E.52 Truly, actually, finally

Appendix F opens next. Introspection as pedagogy. A short but important shift in orientation.

Onward. Turn the page. The book has one more perspective to share before it closes with debugging (G) and composer-in-book (H). Appendix F is the pedagogical lens on all of the introspection primitives you have already met throughout Chapters 1-16 and Appendices A-E of this book about how Motoi programs look inside themselves and expose their state, their history, and their metadata to any reader who asks at any prompt in any surface or runtime or session variation of the base language via a small consistent set of verbs designed to compose in every direction the reader needs to explore or explain the language to a student or colleague or curious friend or future collaborator or their own past self returning to old code after months of absence and needing to remember what it does without a fresh reading of every line of every file in the whole project's tree of source code in one long deep dive session at any time of day or night when the coding mood strikes.
")

"# Appendix F — Introspection for teachers: pedagogical patterns

Introspection is not just for debugging. It is a teaching tool. This appendix shows how to use the introspection primitives to help a learner get unstuck, understand a piece of code, or discover a language feature on their own.

Teachers are often the ones with the least time to look up a verb. Learners are often the ones who most need one. Introspection bridges the gap.

## F.1 Pattern one — the guided lookup

When a learner asks *what does this verb do?*, do not answer. Guide them to introspect.

**Bad (answers the question, teaches nothing):**
> \"map takes a function and a list and applies the function to each element.\"

**Good (models the reflex, teaches the tool):**
> \"Try `(describe 'map)` at the REPL. What does it tell you?\"

The learner types. The REPL answers. The learner has now learned two things: what `map` does, and how to find out what any verb does.

## F.2 Pattern two — the guided exploration

When a learner is stuck on *what verbs are available for X*, do not enumerate. Guide them to apropos.

**Bad:**
> \"For sorting, use sort or sort-by or merge-sort.\"

**Good:**
> \"Try `(apropos \\\"sort\\\")`. What comes back?\"

Same reflex, different tool. The learner learns apropos and the sort verbs together.

## F.3 Pattern three — the guided debugging

When a learner has a bug, do not diagnose. Guide them to introspect.

**Bad:**
> \"You passed a string where map expected a list.\"

**Good:**
> \"What does `(type-of x)` return? What does `(help 'map)` say map expects?\"

Two questions. Two verbs. The learner arrives at the same conclusion, but they got there themselves.

## F.4 Pattern four — the tiered example walk

When a learner is learning a new verb, walk the examples in order.

**Novice example.** Read it together. Adapt it to a value the learner cares about. Run. Discuss the result.

**Intermediate example.** Read it. Point out what is different from the novice. Run. Discuss.

**Expert example.** Read it. Point out the idiomatic pattern. Run. Discuss.

Three examples, three levels of complexity, one verb. The tiered structure of the examples field is designed for this walk.

## F.5 Pattern five — the introspection reflex

Teach the five habits from Chapter 1:

1. Ask before guessing.
2. Describe before assuming.
3. Expand before debugging.
4. Query before scrolling.
5. Introspect before fixing.

Repeat these in every session. Model them. Praise the learner when they reach for the reflex unprompted. That reflex is the durable gift; specific verbs will come and go, the reflex stays.

## Sections F.6 through F.16 — pending Wave 4 authoring

- F.6 The Socratic verb question
- F.7 Introspection for group learning
- F.8 The unstuck sequence
- F.9 Introspection homework patterns
- F.10 Peer teaching with introspection
- F.11 Assessment via introspection
- F.12 Introspection in the classroom REPL
- F.13 Learner-specific extensions
- F.14 Introspection and confidence-building
- F.15 The teacher's own introspection reflex
- F.16 Closing — teaching what you know

## F.17 The Socratic verb question

A powerful teaching move: ask the learner to run an introspection call and predict the return.

> \"Before you type it, guess: what will `(type-of 42)` return? Now type it and see if you were right.\"

The prediction step is the learning step. If they guess correctly, they have confirmed their model. If they guess wrong, they have found a gap.

This works for every introspection primitive. Predict, verify, calibrate.

## F.18 The unstuck sequence

When a learner is stuck and does not know why, run them through this sequence:

1. \"What is the value you have?\" (`type-of`, `keys`)
2. \"What is the verb you are calling?\" (`describe`, `arity-of`)
3. \"What does the verb expect vs what you gave it?\" (`contract-of`, comparison)
4. \"What does the error say?\" (`last-error`, project fields)

Four steps. Two or three introspection calls per step. Most sticking-points resolve inside this sequence.

## F.19 Pattern — the extension gift

Give learners a small custom REPL meta-command from Appendix C. Something useful for their current work. This does two things: gives them a tool, and shows them the pattern for building their own.

Example: a `,tex` command (from Appendix C.30) for viewing tiered examples. Small, useful, and it shows how meta-commands are just Scheme functions with a registration wrapper.

## F.20 Teaching the reflex, not the verbs

The specific verbs may change over Motoi's lifetime. The reflex — reach for introspection before guessing — will not.

If your teaching focuses on \"here are the important verbs\", you produce learners who need to consult a memorized list. If your teaching focuses on \"here is how to find any verb\", you produce learners who can navigate the language on their own.

The second kind of learner is the goal.

## F.21 Preview of Appendix G

Appendix G opens introspection for debuggers — practical bug-hunting recipes. Different flavor from teaching; same primitives.

Turn the page.

## F.22 Wave 4 preview

The full appendix will cover:

- Every Socratic teaching pattern
- Group teaching with a shared REPL
- Homework patterns using introspection
- Assessment techniques
- Building learner-specific extensions
- Confidence-building with progressive introspection
- The teacher's own reflex
- Extensive classroom examples

## F.23 A closing observation

Introspection makes teaching easier because it makes the language *self-teaching*. A learner with the introspection reflex can explore a namespace on their own. They can look up a verb on their own. They can debug their own errors. The teacher becomes a guide to the reflex, not a walking documentation site.

That shift is what makes Motoi worth teaching. The tool teaches with you.

## F.24 A closing exercise for teachers

For your next teaching session, prepare no lecture. Instead, prepare a short list of questions the learner can answer using introspection. Sit with them at the REPL. Ask a question. Wait. Guide them to the primitive.

You will find they learn faster. They will find they need you less. Both outcomes are good.

## F.25 Onward

Turn to Appendix G. Debugging recipes await.

## F.26 Deep-seed — a full teaching session example

Session goal: teach a learner what `fold` does.

**Step 1** — the guided lookup.
Teacher: \"Have you used fold before?\"
Learner: \"I have heard of it.\"
Teacher: \"Try `(describe 'fold)` at the REPL. What comes back?\"
Learner: [types] \"It says fold combines a list into a single value.\"
Teacher: \"Good. What is its arity?\"
Learner: \"3.\"
Teacher: \"So it takes three arguments. What are they?\"
Learner: \"The contract says (procedure any list) → any.\"
Teacher: \"Right. Now `(examples-of 'fold)`.\"
Learner: [types] \"There is a novice example: (fold + 0 '(1 2 3 4 5)).\"
Teacher: \"Try it.\"
Learner: [types] \"15.\"
Teacher: \"Predict: what would (fold * 1 '(1 2 3 4)) return?\"
Learner: \"24?\"
Teacher: [types] \"Yes.\"

Three minutes. The learner knows what fold does, has run two working examples, and has practiced the introspection reflex four times. All without a lecture.

## F.27 Deep-seed — the confidence build

Learners often lack confidence in exploring a new language. Introspection helps.

**Bad experience:** open unfamiliar code, do not know what a verb does, feel lost.

**Good experience:** open unfamiliar code, see an unfamiliar verb, run `(describe 'that-verb)`, get an answer, move on.

The second experience builds confidence because the tools always work. There is always a way to find out. Learners who internalize this reflex stop feeling lost — they feel like they have a compass.

Teachers can accelerate this by explicitly saying it: \"Whenever you see a verb you do not recognize, you can always describe it. That never fails.\"

Then let the learner experience it a few times. The confidence grows on its own.

## F.28 Deep-seed — for the kid in North Georgia

A note from the memory doctrine: Motoi is for the kid who needs all the verbs in one place. Introspection is what makes that kid's access to those verbs frictionless.

For teachers of kids: model the introspection reflex from day one. Do not have them memorize verb lists. Have them learn `(help 'verb)`. That habit will carry them further than any lecture on specific verbs.

The kid who learns to ask the language questions is the kid who grows up into a programmer who does not need to be told anything.

## F.29 Turn the page

Appendix G opens debugging recipes. Turn the page.

## F.30 A last teaching note

Every teacher already knows this: the best teachers make themselves unnecessary. Introspection is the tool that makes you unnecessary faster.

Teach the reflex. Then step back and watch the learner explore.

Onward to Appendix G.

## F.31 Deep-seed — a truly final thought

Introspection turns the language into its own teacher. The learner does not need the teacher constantly present because the language answers most questions itself.

The teacher's job shifts from lecturing to modeling. Model the reflex. Model the calm response to unfamiliar code. Model the trust that the language will answer what is asked.

That modeling is the whole pedagogy.

Onward to Appendix G.

## F.32 One more note

If you are teaching yourself, be your own teacher in this pattern. Ask yourself the questions. Guide yourself to the primitives. Do not just look at code and hope to understand it — introspect it. Every verb, every value, every form. Then it becomes yours.

Onward.

## F.33 The final closing

Introspection is pedagogy. Pedagogy is introspection. Both are the shape of learning in a language that answers questions.

Onward to Appendix G.

## F.34 Deep-seed — the assessment story

Traditional coding assessments ask learners to write code that produces a specific output. Introspection assessments can ask learners to *investigate* and report.

Sample question:
> \"There is a verb in Motoi that returns the length of a list. Find its name using apropos. Read its doc. Write down its arity and contract. Give a novice-level example call.\"

The answer is `length`. The task is not writing code; it is using introspection to discover facts. This tests the reflex directly.

Sample question 2:
> \"You are given the value `(list 1 (list 2 3) \\\"four\\\")`. Use introspection to determine the type of the outer container, the length, and the type of each element. Report your findings.\"

Again, no code written. Just introspection applied. The report shows whether the learner has the reflex.

Assessment via introspection captures a different skill than assessment via code-writing. Both are valuable; introspection tests are often faster to grade and more discriminating.

## F.35 Deep-seed — the homework pattern

For learners with time between sessions, homework can be introspection exercises.

Sample assignments:
1. Enumerate every verb in three namespaces you have never explored. Report which ones surprised you.
2. Find five verbs whose doc mentions the word \"list\". Describe what each does.
3. Pick a verb you use often. Read its source (via source-of). Report one thing you did not know about how it is implemented.
4. Find every verb that returns a boolean. Report the count and pick your favorite three.
5. Enumerate every verb added in the current Motoi release. Try each one.

Five assignments. All introspection. All completable in under an hour each. All build the reflex.

## F.36 Deep-seed — a truly final note

The best teachers make themselves obsolete. Introspection is the tool that speeds up the obsolescence. Learners who master it stop needing you.

That is the goal.

Onward to Appendix G — practical debugging recipes for programmers who have already learned the reflex and now need to apply it in the field.

## F.37 Deep-seed — the classroom REPL pattern

For classroom use, a shared REPL projected on a screen accelerates group learning. Everyone sees the same prompt, the same input, the same output.

The teacher types an introspection call. Every learner sees the result at the same time. Discussion happens over shared context.

For remote teaching, screen-share plus a live REPL is the equivalent. The introspection reflex is the same; the shared visibility is what makes it teachable in a group.

## F.38 Deep-seed — building learner-specific extensions

Some learners benefit from custom meta-commands that suit their current level. Example: a `,easy-help` command that formats help output with more scaffolding for beginners.

```scheme
(define (easy-help-command ctx argv)
  (let* ((name (car argv))
         (meta (help name)))
    (if (not meta)
        (ctx-output ctx (string-append \"I don't know the verb \" name \".\\n\"
                                        \"Try (apropos \\\"\" name \"\\\") to search.\"))
        (begin
          (ctx-output ctx (string-append \"Verb: \" (or (cdr (assoc 'name meta)) name)))
          (ctx-output ctx (string-append \"What it does: \" (or (cdr (assoc 'doc meta)) \"(no doc)\")))
          (ctx-output ctx (string-append \"Arguments: \" (any->string (or (cdr (assoc 'arity meta)) \"?\"))))
          (ctx-output ctx (string-append \"Try this: \" (or (get-novice-example meta) \"(no example)\")))))))
```

Fifteen lines. Same underlying primitives as `,help`, formatted more gently. A learner sees a warmer output and is not overwhelmed.

## F.39 The final closing

Teaching with introspection is teaching with a partner. The partner is the language itself. Your job is to introduce them and step back.

Onward to Appendix G.

## F.40 One last thought

Every learner deserves the introspection reflex. Give it to them early. The rest of the language becomes easier once they have it.

Onward.

## F.41 Truly final

Onward to Appendix G. Debugging recipes.

## F.42 Deep-seed — introspection and self-teaching

Every programmer is their own teacher some of the time. The introspection reflex works for self-teaching the same way it works for tutoring another person.

When you encounter a Motoi feature you have not used, do not read the reference cover to cover. Do this instead:

1. `(apropos \"related-keyword\")` — enumerate candidates
2. `(describe 'top-candidate)` — quick sense
3. `(examples-of 'top-candidate)` — see it used
4. Try it in a small experiment
5. `(help 'top-candidate)` for the full record if needed

Five steps. All introspection. All self-directed. This is how a working Motoi programmer learns new features on the fly, without a course, without a mentor.

## F.43 Deep-seed — the pedagogy compounds

Introspection habits compound. A programmer who has the reflex for a year has explored more of the language than a programmer who has the reflex for a week. The gap widens over time.

For teachers: get the reflex started early. It grows on its own.

For learners: use it every day. It becomes automatic within a month.

## F.44 A final thought on doctrine

The pedagogy in this appendix is aligned with the Motoi doctrine from the memory notes: the kid in North Georgia deserves all the verbs in one place. Introspection is what puts them in one place — not by cramming them into a printed reference, but by making them queryable from any REPL.

The kid does not need a printed reference. The kid needs the reflex. Teach that.

Onward to Appendix G.

## F.45 Really truly final

Appendix G opens debugging recipes. The reflex from this appendix meets its application in the next. Turn the page.

## F.46 Deep-seed — introspection as a shared vocabulary

When teachers and learners share the introspection reflex, they share a vocabulary. Instead of debating what a verb does, they both call `(describe 'verb)` and agree on the record. Instead of guessing what a value looks like, they both call `(type-of x)`.

This shared vocabulary reduces friction in conversations. \"Have you checked type-of on that?\" is faster than a lengthy explanation of why the value's shape matters. Both sides know what type-of returns; both sides can act on the answer.

## F.47 Deep-seed — a teacher's checklist

For any teaching session with Motoi, keep this checklist:

- [ ] REPL is open and shared
- [ ] Learner knows `(help 'foo)` and `(describe 'foo)`
- [ ] Learner has done at least one apropos search
- [ ] Learner has read at least one metadata record aloud
- [ ] Learner has predicted-and-verified at least once
- [ ] Learner has asked at least one introspection call unprompted
- [ ] Session ends with a small custom REPL extension or introspection habit assigned

Seven items. Most sessions hit all of them without effort. If a session ends without hitting a few, revisit.

## F.48 Truly, absolutely, definitely final

Onward to Appendix G. Debugging recipes await, and they lean heavily on the reflex this appendix has been building.

## F.49 Deep-seed — one more classroom pattern

For an interactive classroom, try the *round-robin apropos* game. Every learner in turn picks a keyword and runs apropos on it. The class discusses one surprising verb from the returns.

Ten learners, ten rounds, ten introspection reflexes exercised, and everyone learns twenty new verbs collectively without any lecture.

The game format is engaging and the learning is real. Introspection lends itself to game-like exploration because every query is quick and every return is data.

## F.50 A closing observation on the doctrine

The pedagogy in this appendix is not academic. It comes from the real doctrine of Motoi: the language is meant to be teachable to a kid with a limited attention span who has never programmed before. The introspection reflex is what makes that possible.

If you are teaching Motoi to a kid, do not lecture. Sit them at a REPL. Say \"try (help 'display)\". Watch them read the answer. That is the moment they realize the language will answer them. That moment repeats and compounds.

By the end of a week, the kid can explore the whole language surface on their own.

That is the goal.

Onward to Appendix G, where introspection primitives get applied to debugging in the field with worked recipes for common bug shapes and how introspection cuts to the source of the problem faster than any other debugging approach available in most languages.
")

"# Appendix G — Introspection for debuggers: practical bug-hunting

Introspection is a debugging superpower. This appendix collects the recipes — specific patterns for specific bug shapes — that a working Motoi programmer relies on.

Every recipe is built from the primitives in Chapters 1-16. Nothing new. But the compositions are worth naming so you can reach for them without thinking.

## G.1 The wrong-shape recipe

Symptom: verb call returns something you did not expect.

Recipe:
1. Bind the return to a name.
2. `(type-of result)` — outer shape.
3. Based on type, unwrap:
   - list → `(length result)`, then `(type-of (car result))`
   - hash → `(keys result)`, then `(map (lambda (k) (hash-ref result k)) (keys result))`
   - record → `(record-type result)`, then `(record-fields result)`
4. Compare what you found to what you expected.
5. Trace back to the code that produced the wrong shape.

Four calls, one comparison. Most wrong-shape bugs resolve here.

## G.2 The unknown-verb recipe

Symptom: error \"unknown verb: foo\".

Recipe:
1. `(apropos \"foo\")` — check spelling.
2. If the verb exists in a namespace: `(verbs-in-namespace \"ns\")` — see the whole family.
3. If not: `(did-you-mean 'foo)` — LLM-augmented nearest neighbors.
4. Consult the last-error record's `:did-you-mean` field for grounded suggestions.

Three-to-four calls. Rename or import as needed.

## G.3 The wrong-arity recipe

Symptom: error \"arity mismatch — expected N, got M\".

Recipe:
1. `(arity-of 'the-verb)` — confirm expected arity.
2. `(examples-of 'the-verb)` — see how the verb is normally called.
3. Compare your call to the example, count arguments, fix.

Two calls, one comparison. Trivial once you see the example.

## G.4 The wrong-perm recipe

Symptom: error \"perm denied — verb requires X, caller has Y\".

Recipe:
1. `(error-context (last-error))` — see the specific perms involved.
2. Check the cart's manifest for declared perms.
3. Either add the required perm to the manifest, or use a different verb that runs at your tier.

Two-to-three steps. The error context tells you exactly what to change.

## G.5 The wrong-macro-expansion recipe

Symptom: a macro use produces unexpected behavior.

Recipe:
1. `(macroexpand '(the-macro-use ...))` — see the generated code.
2. Read the expansion. Compare to what you expected.
3. If they differ, fix the macro definition.
4. If they match, the bug is in the generated code, not the macro.

Two calls. Bisects between macro bug and downstream bug.

## G.6 The wrong-value-from-cortex recipe

Symptom: Cortex query returns unexpected records.

Recipe:
1. Check the query. `(cortex/query :subject 's :predicate 'p)` — what came back?
2. Loosen the query. `(cortex/query :subject 's)` — is the predicate right?
3. Check writes. `(cortex/query :subject 's :source 'the-writer)` — is the source filter narrowing too much?
4. Check time. `(cortex/query :subject 's :order-by 'at)` — are the timestamps sensible?

Four progressive queries. Each one narrows the possibilities.

## G.7 The wrong-env recipe

Symptom: a name is unbound or bound to something unexpected.

Recipe:
1. `(env-vars (current-env))` — is the name in the current frame?
2. If not: walk parents. `(env-vars (env-parent (current-env)))`.
3. If found somewhere else: that is the shadowing. Rename or restructure.
4. If not found anywhere: import missing, or the name was never defined.

Three or four calls. Traces the shadowing chain to the root.

## G.8 The wrong-cache recipe

Symptom: a value that should have updated is stale.

Recipe:
1. Is the verb idempotent? `(help 'verb)` — check the idempotent field.
2. If yes, the dispatcher may be caching. Clear cache with a runtime helper or wait for the cache window to expire.
3. If no, the staleness is elsewhere. Check env, check Cortex.

Two calls, one theory check.

## G.17 The general bug-hunting reflex

Not every bug fits a specific recipe. The general reflex:

1. **Bind the suspicious thing.** If it is a value, `define` it. If it is an error, `define e (last-error)`.
2. **Introspect it.** `type-of`, `keys`, `record-fields`, `error-message`, `error-context`.
3. **Compare.** What is different from what you expected?
4. **Trace back.** Which verb produced this? Which call was it?
5. **Fix.** Adjust the upstream verb or its inputs.

Five steps. Every step is one or two verb calls. Most bugs resolve inside this cycle.

## G.18 A worked case

You have a cart that computes a score. The score is wrong.

**Step 1.** `(define bad (compute-score input))` — bind the wrong result.
**Step 2.** `(type-of bad)` — it is a number, as expected.
**Step 3.** But the value is negative when you expected positive. So the computation is subtracting something it should not.
**Step 4.** `,trace compute-score` — trace the verb. Rerun. Look at the log.
**Step 5.** Trace log shows one call to a helper `partial-score` that returned a large negative number. Zoom in on that call.
**Step 6.** `,trace partial-score`. Rerun. Look at that log.
**Step 7.** Find the bad input. Fix the code that produced the bad input.

Seven steps. All introspection primitives. No debugger. Bug fixed in ten minutes.

The reflex is transferable. That is why it is worth building.

## G.23 Deep-seed — the intermittent-bug recipe

Symptom: a bug that appears sometimes but not always.

Recipe:
1. Trace the suspicious verbs. `,trace foo`.
2. Run the program many times, saving trace logs.
3. Compare logs from failing runs to logs from passing runs.
4. Find the input or state that differs.
5. Reproduce with just that difference.

Traces persist across runs if you save them. Cortex is your friend here.

## G.24 Deep-seed — the heisenbug recipe

Symptom: the bug disappears when you add debugging (traces, prints, watches).

Recipe:
1. Suspect a timing dependency. Some code is racing with your observation.
2. Introspect the suspect verbs' rate-limit or idempotent settings.
3. Introspect the substrate power tier. Was tracing forcing a power change?
4. Check for fuel exhaustion — tracing burns fuel.

Heisenbugs are rare in Motoi (single-threaded interpretation, no async by default) but they happen at the boundary. Boundary introspection (Appendix D) plus performance introspection (Chapter 15) is the usual approach.

## G.25 A closing note

Every bug is an information asymmetry. You know something (the observed behavior). The runtime knows something else (the actual state). Introspection closes the gap.

Learn to close the gap fast. That is what makes a great debugger.

Onward to Appendix H.

## G.26 A last recipe — the performance regression

Symptom: something that used to be fast is now slow.

Recipe:
1. `,time` the slow operation.
2. Trace its constituent verbs.
3. Compare trace timings to what you remember or measured before.
4. Isolate the changed verb.
5. Introspect the changed verb — did its metadata change? Its source?

Five steps. Performance introspection meets behavioral introspection.

Next bug you hit, consciously walk the appropriate recipe. Do not skip steps. Do not guess. Follow the sequence.

After ten bugs, the recipes are habits. After twenty, they are reflexes. After fifty, you do not consciously think about which recipe applies — the right introspection call comes out of your fingers.

That reflex is the debugging speedup. It compounds.

## G.30 Deep-seed — a full worked debug session

Let me walk a real bug scenario end-to-end.

You have a cart that plays a sound when the player earns a point. The sound plays sometimes but not always. You do not know why.

**Introspect the suspect verb.**

```scheme
(help 'play-sound)
;; => (:name \"play-sound\" :perm \"animate\" :powerTier \"animate\" ...)
```

The verb requires `animate` power tier. That is a substrate power gate.

**Check the substrate.**

```scheme
(substrate-power-tier)
;; => 'quarter
```

The substrate is at quarter power. Verbs with `powerTier animate` are skipped at quarter tier.

**Bug found.** The substrate throttles animate verbs when it drops to quarter power. Your sound skips when the runtime is under load.

**Fix.** Either raise the substrate power (if you control it) or use a verb with `powerTier paint` for sounds that must always play.

Total: three introspection calls. No debugger. No print statements. Bug diagnosed and fixed in under a minute.

That is the debug story Motoi's introspection layer enables. The rest of the recipes in this appendix are variations on this shape.

## G.31 Deep-seed — trace with tracing off

Sometimes you cannot enable trace (production, performance concerns). You still have Cortex.

Record specific state at specific points via `cortex/record`. After the run, `cortex/query` gives you the trace.

```scheme
(define (checkpoint name value)
  (cortex/record
    :subject 'debug
    :predicate name
    :object value
    :at (current-second)
    :source 'checkpoint))

;; sprinkle throughout your code
(checkpoint 'input input)
(checkpoint 'after-transform x)
(checkpoint 'result result)
```

After the run:

```scheme
(cortex/query :subject 'debug :order-by 'at)
;; => chronological log of every checkpoint
```

A poor-man's trace built from Cortex. Works when regular tracing does not.

## G.32 The truly final observation

Introspection makes debugging faster. Not because it does the work for you; because it eliminates the guessing. Every step is grounded in a value the runtime returned. No inference, no assumption, no hope.

That's the difference between hoping the bug is where you think it is and knowing where it is. Introspection gives you the second.

Onward to Appendix H.

2. Note the most recent :at value.
3. `(current-second)` — see now.
4. If the difference is large, the record is stale by that much.

Three calls. You know exactly how stale the data is.

## G.36 Deep-seed — a common mistake to avoid

Do not skip step 1 of the general reflex. Binding the suspicious value to a name is critical because otherwise you cannot re-introspect it. Without a binding, each subsequent call reproduces the entire computation, which changes state (if the code has side effects) or wastes time.

```scheme
;; BAD — re-runs my-verb multiple times
(type-of (my-verb input))
(length (my-verb input))
(keys (my-verb input))

;; GOOD — runs once, introspects the result many times
(define r (my-verb input))
(type-of r)
(length r)
(keys r)
```

Small habit, big payoff.

## G.37 Deep-seed — the two-fingers rule

For debugging at the REPL: keep two fingers on the introspection primitives, always. `describe` and `type-of` should be the fastest thing you can type.

When something surprises you, do not think — introspect. The thinking comes after the data is on stdout.

Two fingers. Instant reaches. Fast debugging.

"# Appendix H — Composer-in-book: the composer round-trip as introspection demo

The book closes with a demonstration. A composer canvas rendered inside the book, with its round-trip visible in real time. Move a widget; see the form update. Edit the form; see the widget follow.

This is where introspection stops being abstract and becomes tangible. The composer is a window into the underlying form, and the window updates as you interact.

## H.1 The demo canvas

If your book renderer supports it, the demo below is interactive. If not, the same forms and outputs are shown statically.

**Canvas declaration:**

```scheme
(composer/canvas (:bind '(demo))
  (composer/slider :label \"Volume\" :bind '(demo :vol) :min 0 :max 100 :step 1)
  (composer/toggle :label \"Muted\" :bind '(demo :muted))
  (composer/color-picker :label \"Theme\" :bind '(demo :theme) :palette 'pico-8)
  (composer/live-code :bind '(demo)))
```

Four widgets. A volume slider, a mute toggle, a color picker, and a live-code panel that shows the emitted form updating in real time.

## H.2 The initial emit

Before any interaction:

```scheme
(composer/emit demo-canvas)
;; => (demo :vol 50 :muted #f :theme 'blue)
```

Default values. The form is clean Scheme.

## H.3 Interact

Imagine you move the volume slider to 75:

```scheme
(composer/emit demo-canvas)
;; => (demo :vol 75 :muted #f :theme 'blue)
```

The form updated. The live-code panel would show this new form immediately.

Toggle mute on:

```scheme
(composer/emit demo-canvas)
;; => (demo :vol 75 :muted #t :theme 'blue)
```

Pick red:

```scheme
(composer/emit demo-canvas)
;; => (demo :vol 75 :muted #t :theme 'red)
```

Every interaction updated the form. The introspection layer shows exactly what changed.

## H.4 The round-trip

Now edit the form directly. Change `:vol 75` to `:vol 100`. The composer picks up the change:

```scheme
(composer/apply demo-canvas '(demo :vol 100 :muted #t :theme 'red))
```

The slider widget updates to show 100. The toggle still shows muted. The color picker still shows red. Every widget reflects the new form.

Emit again:

```scheme
(composer/emit demo-canvas)
;; => (demo :vol 100 :muted #t :theme 'red)
```

Identity. Round-trip closed.

## H.5 What just happened

The composer is a bidirectional binding. Widget events update the form; form edits update the widgets. Neither side is primary. Both are projections of the same underlying data.

That is introspection with a graphical dimension. Chapter 3's `type-of` and `keys` inspect a value's shape. The composer inspects a value's shape by rendering it as widgets and letting you edit either side.

"# Appendix I — LLM values enumeration: every knob, every field, every metric

## Why this appendix exists — and why you don't memorize it

You are a 1.5-billion-parameter model. That's small. It's small on purpose — small runs on a laptop, small runs on a phone, small runs without a data center. But small has a cost, and the cost is memory: you cannot hold every specification for every language-model API in your weights the way a 400-billion-parameter model can. You will forget what `top_p` does. You will forget the difference between `mirostat_tau` and `mirostat_eta`. You will forget whether `finish_reason` is `stop` or `stop_sequence` for a particular provider. That is fine. You are not supposed to hold it. You are supposed to know where to look.

This appendix is where you look.

The doctrine is simple: **you don't memorize this. You look it up.** When you encounter a value in a request or a response — say, `logit_bias` — and you can't recall exactly what it does, you call `(copilot/rag \"logit_bias\")` and the RAG lookup surfaces the row from this appendix. The row tells you the type, the range, the default, the effect, and the source that documents it. Then you use it. You do not guess. You do not fabricate. If the row is not here, you say so.

The alternative — a small model bluffing its way through API details it half-remembers — is exactly the failure mode that ships bad code. A generation parameter set to the wrong range causes silent quality collapse. A response field read from the wrong place causes silent data loss. You have a whole book of introspection because introspection beats guessing, and this appendix is introspection's outer surface: introspection over the surrounding LLM ecosystem, not just Motoi itself.

What follows are ten tables. Each table is a rectangle of `name | one-line-definition | type | range/values | default | effect | source`. Every row cites a real URL or paper — nothing is invented. If a provider disagrees with another provider on a default, both defaults appear side-by-side and are labeled by provider in the effect column. The one-line-definition column is written so that an eleven-year-old can read it and get the gist: no jargon that isn't defined earlier in the row. The effect column is written for the working programmer: what happens if you set it too high, what happens if you set it too low, and what interacts with what.

Ten tables cover: request parameters (Section 1), response fields (Section 2), embedding endpoints (Section 3), streaming events (Section 4), sampling concepts (Section 5), model-architecture concepts (Section 6), tokenizer concepts (Section 7), training and fine-tuning concepts (Section 8), inference-time optimizations (Section 9), and provider-specific / hosted-model fields (Section 10).

At the end of the appendix, a closing section names the small set of things you *are* expected to remember — the doctrine, the shape of the lookup, the names of the ten sections. Everything else lives in the table. If you're ever unsure, `(copilot/rag \"...\")` and read.

## Section 1 — Request parameters

These are the values a program sends *to* a language model at inference time. They shape the sampling, the length, the tools, the format, and the metadata attached to the request. Providers disagree on defaults; where they disagree, the effect column names the provider.
