| ignore_eos | keep generating past the end-of-sequence token | boolean | true or false | false | vLLM/others; useful for capacity benchmarks; will produce garbage past EOS | https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/api/vllm/sampling_params/ |
| skip_special_tokens | omit special tokens from decoded output | boolean | true or false | true | vLLM/HF; false shows BOS/EOS/control tokens in the output string | https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/api/vllm/sampling_params/ |
| bad_words | strings the model must never produce | array of strings | any list | none | vLLM; hard filter at generation time; costs a small amount of speed | https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/api/vllm/sampling_params/ |
| think | request explicit reasoning-mode output | boolean or string | true/false, or `low`/`medium`/`high` | false | Ollama; models with reasoning support emit a separate `thinking` field | https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md |
| format | force output into a machine-shaped format | string or object | `json` or a JSON schema | none | Ollama-style constrained decoding; equivalent to response_format elsewhere | https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md |
| images | base64-encoded images for multimodal requests | array of strings | list of base64 blobs | none | for vision-capable models only; each blob is one image | https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md |

## Section 2 — Response fields (chat completion)

These are the values a language model sends *back*. They describe what was produced, how much it cost, and why the generation stopped.

| name | one-line-definition | type | range/values | default | effect | source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| id | opaque unique id for this completion | string | provider-specific | assigned by server | log this for support tickets and audit trails | https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat-streaming/streaming |
| object | tag identifying the response shape | string | `chat.completion`, `chat.completion.chunk`, `list`, etc. | fixed | lets clients dispatch on shape without parsing everything | https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat-streaming/streaming |
| created | Unix timestamp when the response was created | integer | seconds since epoch | assigned by server | for ordering and logging; not for billing rounds | https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat-streaming/streaming |
| model | the exact model id that produced this response | string | any registered model | echoes the request | may differ from the request when the provider aliases (e.g., `-latest`) | https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat-streaming/streaming |
| system_fingerprint | hash of the runtime configuration | string | provider hex string | assigned | if this changes between calls with the same seed, reproducibility can drift | https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat-streaming/streaming |
| choices | array of completions (one per requested output) | array | length = n from request | none | index into it; typical case is length 1 | https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat-streaming/streaming |
| choices[].index | position of this choice in the choices array | integer | 0+ | 0 | matches the n from the request; stable across streamed chunks | https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat-streaming/streaming |
| choices[].message | the completed message when not streaming | object | `{role, content, tool_calls?, refusal?}` | present when stream=false | on streamed responses, use `delta` instead | https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat-streaming/streaming |
| choices[].message.role | role of the message the model produced | string | usually `assistant` | `assistant` | tool responses have `tool`; system rarely | https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat-streaming/streaming |
| choices[].message.content | the text the model produced | string or null | any text; null if tool_calls only | none | primary payload; may be empty when the model only calls tools | https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat-streaming/streaming |
| choices[].message.tool_calls | list of tool invocations the model wants | array | list of `{id, type, function: {name, arguments}}` | none | arguments is a JSON string, not an object; parse it yourself | https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat-streaming/streaming |
| choices[].message.refusal | reason string when the model declined | string or null | any text, or null | null | present when policy rejected the request; content is null in that case | https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat-streaming/streaming |
| choices[].finish_reason | why the generation ended | string | `stop`, `length`, `tool_calls`, `content_filter`, `function_call` | one of these | `stop` = natural end; `length` = hit max_tokens; `content_filter` = blocked | https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat-streaming/streaming |
| choices[].logprobs | log-probabilities attached to the output | object or null | `{content: [{token, logprob, top_logprobs}, ...]}` | null unless requested | present only when the request set logprobs=true | https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/chat/subresources/completions/methods/create |
| usage | how many tokens were used | object | `{prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, total_tokens}` | present on non-stream | on streaming, appears only in the last chunk | https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat-streaming/streaming |
| usage.prompt_tokens | tokens consumed by the request | integer | 0+ | counted server-side | includes system+user+tool messages and tool schemas | https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat-streaming/streaming |
| usage.completion_tokens | tokens the model produced | integer | 0+ | counted server-side | includes tool-call arguments; does not include reasoning tokens (see below) | https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat-streaming/streaming |
| usage.total_tokens | prompt + completion | integer | 0+ | sum of the above | primary billing number; multiply by per-model rate | https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat-streaming/streaming |
| usage.reasoning_tokens | tokens spent on reasoning (o1-style models) | integer | 0+ | present on reasoning models | billed but not visible in content; can dwarf visible completion tokens | https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/chat/subresources/completions/methods/create |
| usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens | prompt tokens served from cache | integer | 0+ | 0 if no cache hit | discount tier; large speed and cost win on repeated prefixes | https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/chat/subresources/completions/methods/create |
| done | Ollama's flag that generation finished | boolean | true or false | false during stream, true at end | mirrors the finish_reason concept in Ollama | https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md |
| done_reason | why an Ollama generation ended | string | `stop`, `length`, `load`, `unload` | present when done=true | Ollama's equivalent of finish_reason | https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md |
| response | Ollama's full text field on /api/generate | string | any text | empty if streamed | on stream, per-chunk `response` accumulates | https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md |
| context | Ollama's opaque prior-conversation encoding | array of integers | token ids | none | pass back on next request to continue; Ollama-specific | https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md |
| total_duration | wall-clock time for the whole response | integer | nanoseconds | measured | Ollama; includes load time and eval time | https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md |
| load_duration | time spent loading the model | integer | nanoseconds | measured | Ollama; nonzero on first call after model change | https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md |
| prompt_eval_count | Ollama's prompt token count | integer | 0+ | measured | equivalent to prompt_tokens | https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md |
| prompt_eval_duration | time evaluating the prompt | integer | nanoseconds | measured | divide count by duration to get prompt throughput | https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md |
| eval_count | Ollama's completion token count | integer | 0+ | measured | equivalent to completion_tokens | https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md |
| eval_duration | time generating the completion | integer | nanoseconds | measured | divide count by duration to get generation throughput | https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md |

## Section 3 — Embedding endpoints

Embeddings turn text into vectors. The request/response shapes are simpler than chat, but they have their own knobs.

| name | one-line-definition | type | range/values | default | effect | source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| model | which embedding model to use | string | any registered embedding model | none (required) | different models produce different-dimensional vectors; not interchangeable | https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/embeddings/methods/create |
| input | the text (or list of texts) to embed | string or array of strings or array of arrays of integers | any text; batching supported | none (required) | batch = one request, one vector each; also accepts pre-tokenized ids | https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/embeddings/methods/create |
| encoding_format | how vectors are returned on the wire | string | `float` or `base64` | `float` | base64 is smaller over the network but you have to decode client-side | https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/embeddings/methods/create |
| dimensions | reduce the returned vector's dimensionality | integer | 1 to the model's native dim | native dim | some models support Matryoshka truncation; smaller = cheaper storage | https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/embeddings/methods/create |
| user | opaque end-user id | string | any string | none | same as chat; used for abuse detection | https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/embeddings/methods/create |
| data | array of embedding records in the response | array | length = number of inputs | assigned | order matches the input order | https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/embeddings/methods/create |
| data[].embedding | the actual vector | array of floats (or base64 string) | length = dimensions | assigned | float32 by default; unit-norm depending on model | https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/embeddings/methods/create |
| data[].index | position of this embedding matching the input | integer | 0+ | assigned | needed when inputs are batched | https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/embeddings/methods/create |
| data[].object | tag; always `embedding` for this endpoint | string | `embedding` | fixed | for shape dispatch by clients | https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/embeddings/methods/create |
| usage.prompt_tokens | tokens read from the input | integer | 0+ | counted server-side | embeddings have no completion tokens; only prompt | https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/embeddings/methods/create |
| usage.total_tokens | same as prompt_tokens for embeddings | integer | 0+ | equal to prompt_tokens | included for symmetry with chat responses | https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/embeddings/methods/create |
| embedding | Ollama's single-vector field on /api/embeddings | array of floats | length = model dim | assigned | Ollama's minimal shape; no batching in classic endpoint | https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md |
| truncate | Ollama flag: truncate long inputs to fit | boolean | true or false | true | false = error if input exceeds model max | https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md |
| normalize | return unit-length vectors | boolean | true or false | model-dependent | if you want cosine similarity, normalize on either request or response | https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md |
| pooling | how token-level vectors are combined into one | string | `mean`, `cls`, `last-token` | model-dependent | mean = average across tokens; cls = first token; last-token = last | https://huggingface.co/docs/text-generation-inference/en/index |
| input_type | hint about whether input is a query or a document | string | `query`, `document`, or a task label | none | some models produce asymmetric embeddings; hint matters for retrieval quality | https://huggingface.co/docs/text-generation-inference/en/index |

## Section 4 — Streaming events

When `stream=true`, the response is a series of small chunks over server-sent events. Each chunk mirrors the non-streaming shape but with a `delta` field instead of `message`.

| name | one-line-definition | type | range/values | default | effect | source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| event | SSE event type prefix (rarely used on OpenAI chat) | string | `data`, custom names | `data` | most implementations only emit `data:` lines with JSON bodies | https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/chat/subresources/completions/streaming-events |
| data | the JSON body of one streamed chunk | string (JSON) | one chunk per line | assigned | each `data:` line contains a full chunk object; parse independently | https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/chat/subresources/completions/streaming-events |
| [DONE] | sentinel marker on the last SSE line | string | `data: [DONE]` | fixed | signals end-of-stream; not JSON; stop reading after this | https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat-streaming/streaming |
| chunk.id | id shared across all chunks of one response | string | provider-specific | assigned once | lets clients group chunks into one completion | https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat-streaming/streaming |
| chunk.object | tag; `chat.completion.chunk` for chat streams | string | fixed | fixed | disambiguates from non-stream responses | https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat-streaming/streaming |
| chunk.created | timestamp; identical across chunks | integer | seconds since epoch | assigned | doesn't advance per chunk | https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat-streaming/streaming |
| chunk.model | model id | string | any | assigned | echoes across chunks | https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat-streaming/streaming |
| chunk.system_fingerprint | runtime config hash | string | provider-specific | assigned | same across chunks; may change between calls | https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat-streaming/streaming |
| chunk.choices | array of per-choice deltas | array | usually length 1 | present | one entry per requested n | https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat-streaming/streaming |
| chunk.choices[].index | which choice this chunk belongs to | integer | 0+ | 0 | groups chunks per parallel completion | https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat-streaming/streaming |
| chunk.choices[].delta | the incremental piece of the message | object | `{role?, content?, tool_calls?, refusal?}` | present until last | first chunk usually has role; then content chunks; then empty | https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/chat/subresources/completions/streaming-events |
| delta.role | role token, sent on the first chunk only | string | `assistant` | `assistant` | absent after the first chunk | https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/chat/subresources/completions/streaming-events |
| delta.content | text fragment for this chunk | string | any short string | none | concatenate across chunks to reconstruct the full message | https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/chat/subresources/completions/streaming-events |
| delta.tool_calls | partial tool call info | array | list of tool-call fragments | none | tool call arguments stream as JSON string fragments; concatenate before parsing | https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/chat/subresources/completions/streaming-events |
| chunk.choices[].finish_reason | present only on the final content chunk | string or null | `stop`, `length`, `tool_calls`, `content_filter`, or null | null | last non-empty chunk carries this; then [DONE] follows | https://platform.openai.com/docs/api-reference/chat-streaming/streaming |
| chunk.usage | usage stats; final chunk only | object | `{prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, total_tokens}` | absent from mid-stream chunks | request `stream_options.include_usage=true` to receive it | https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/chat/subresources/completions/streaming-events |
| stream_options.include_usage | request usage stats in stream | boolean | true or false | false | if true, adds a final chunk with usage before [DONE] | https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/chat/subresources/completions/streaming-events |
| Ollama chunk | per-token JSON message, not SSE | object | `{model, created_at, response, done}` | streamed via HTTP chunked transfer | Ollama uses newline-delimited JSON, not SSE | https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md |
| Ollama chunk.response | text fragment | string | short string | assigned | concatenate across chunks | https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md |
| Ollama chunk.done | end-of-stream flag | boolean | true or false | false until end | final chunk has done=true and full metrics | https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md |

## Section 5 — Sampling concepts

These are not request fields but the theory that shapes what the request fields mean. A model outputs a probability distribution over next tokens; sampling is how you pick one.

| name | one-line-definition | type | range/values | default | effect | source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| logits | raw pre-softmax scores the model emits per candidate token | array of floats | any real numbers | model output | sampling operates on these; higher = more likely; range varies by model | https://towardsdatascience.com/decoding-strategies-in-large-language-models-9733a8f70539/ |
| softmax | function that turns logits into probabilities summing to 1 | function | probabilities in [0, 1] | applied unconditionally | `p_i = exp(logit_i / T) / sum_j exp(logit_j / T)` where T is temperature | https://towardsdatascience.com/decoding-strategies-in-large-language-models-9733a8f70539/ |
| temperature scaling | dividing logits by T before softmax | scalar knob | 0+ | 1.0 (identity) | T<1 sharpens the distribution; T>1 flattens it; T=0 = deterministic argmax | https://medium.com/data-science/temperature-scaling-and-beam-search-text-generation-in-llms-for-the-ml-adjacent-21212cc5dddb |
| greedy decoding | always pick the argmax token | strategy | none | equivalent to temperature=0 | fast, deterministic, prone to loops; the strictest form of sampling | https://towardsdatascience.com/decoding-strategies-in-large-language-models-9733a8f70539/ |
| argmax | pick the token with the highest logit | operation | none | applied when greedy | ignores all other tokens; same as temperature=0 and top_k=1 | https://towardsdatascience.com/decoding-strategies-in-large-language-models-9733a8f70539/ |
| top-k truncation | zero out all but the k highest-probability tokens | strategy | k >= 1 | k=40 (llama.cpp) | fixed cutoff; can be too permissive when the head is peaky | https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/tools/server/README.md |
| nucleus sampling (top_p) | keep the smallest set with cumulative prob >= p | strategy | p in (0, 1] | p=0.95 (llama.cpp) | adapts to entropy: small set on confident tokens, wider on uncertain ones | https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/chat/subresources/completions/methods/create |
| min-p sampling | keep tokens with prob >= p * top_prob | strategy | p in [0, 1] | p=0.05 (llama.cpp) | relative threshold; more robust than fixed top_p across confidence levels | https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/tools/server/README.md |
| typical sampling | keep tokens whose surprise is close to average surprise | strategy | p in (0, 1] | disabled at p=1 | tightens around 'typical' behavior; reduces both flat and peaky failures | https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/tools/server/README.md |
| tail-free sampling | cut where the sorted-probs' second derivative peaks | strategy | z in (0, 1] | disabled at z=1 | data-driven cutoff; no fixed threshold needed | https://github.com/ollama/ollama/blob/main/docs/api.md |
| Mirostat | adaptive sampler that targets a fixed output entropy | strategy | tau, eta | tau=5.0, eta=0.1 | reduces both repetition and incoherence; overrides top_k/top_p/typical | https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.14966 |
| repetition penalty | multiplicative logit adjustment on already-seen tokens | penalty | value >= 0 | 1.0 (off) | value > 1 discourages repeats; value < 1 encourages them | https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/api/vllm/sampling_params/ |
| presence penalty | flat penalty for any token that appeared once | penalty | in [-2, 2] | 0.0 | additive to logits; encourages topic diversity without discouraging any word extra | https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/chat/subresources/completions/methods/create |
| frequency penalty | penalty proportional to token count | penalty | in [-2, 2] | 0.0 | grows with each repeat; more targeted than presence penalty | https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/chat/subresources/completions/methods/create |
| beam search | keep the top B partial sequences and expand each step | strategy | beam width B | B=1 = greedy | expensive; high quality on constrained tasks; produces generic text on open ones | https://towardsdatascience.com/decoding-strategies-in-large-language-models-9733a8f70539/ |
| length penalty | during beam search, scale the score by length^alpha | scalar | typically 0.6 to 1.5 | 1.0 | discourages very short beams from winning by log-prob accident | https://huggingface.co/docs/text-generation-inference/en/index |
| contrastive search | penalize tokens that look too similar to prior hidden states | strategy | alpha, k | alpha=0.6, k=4 | pushes for coherence + diversity; slower than sampling | https://towardsdatascience.com/decoding-strategies-in-large-language-models-9733a8f70539/ |
| speculative decoding | small draft model proposes k tokens, big model verifies | strategy | k | k=5 to 10 | 2-3x decode speedup when acceptance rate is high; zero quality loss | https://vllm.ai/blog/2025-09-05-anatomy-of-vllm |
| DRY sampling | penalize continuations that would extend a repeated n-gram | strategy | multiplier, base, length | multiplier=0 (off) | targets long verbatim repeats without harming natural repetition | https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/tools/server/README.md |
| XTC | randomly drop the top choice with small probability | strategy | probability, threshold | probability=0 (off) | inject creativity by giving second-best a chance | https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/tools/server/README.md |
| logit_bias | additive adjustment to specific tokens' logits before sampling | mechanism | per-token adjustment in [-100, 100] | none | -100 effectively bans; +100 effectively forces | https://developers.openai.com/api/reference/resources/chat/subresources/completions/methods/create |
| grammar-guided decoding | mask logits so only grammar-valid tokens are sampled | mechanism | GBNF or JSON schema | none | guarantees output conforms; some quality cost from mask | https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/tools/server/README.md |

## Section 6 — Model architecture concepts

These are not runtime knobs — they're baked into the model file. You can't change them at inference time, but you'll see them in model cards and config.json files.

| name | one-line-definition | type | range/values | default | effect | source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| parameters | total learned scalar values in the model | integer | millions to trillions | model-dependent | 1.5B = small (phone-ready); 70B = big; 400B = frontier | https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.08295 |
| layers | number of transformer blocks stacked | integer | ~12 (small) to ~96 (large) | model-dependent | more layers = more capacity but slower per-token | https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.08295 |
| hidden_dim | width of each token's internal vector (a.k.a. d_model) | integer | 512 to 12288+ | model-dependent | wider = more capacity per token; scales quadratically with attention cost | https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.08295 |
| attention heads | how the attention operation is split into parallel views | integer | 8 to 128 | model-dependent | more heads = finer-grained attention patterns; each head is d_model/n_heads wide | https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.08295 |
| kv heads | key/value heads shared across query heads (GQA/MQA) | integer | 1 to n_heads | usually 8 for GQA | fewer = smaller KV cache, faster decode, small quality loss | https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245 |
| head_dim | dimension per attention head | integer | 64 to 256 | usually 64 or 128 | hidden_dim / n_heads; smaller heads = more heads for the same width | https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.08295 |
| ffn_dim | width of the feed-forward layer inside each block | integer | 2 to 8 times hidden_dim | usually 4x hidden_dim | dominant parameter cost; SwiGLU variants use different ratios | https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.08295 |
| vocab_size | number of distinct tokens the model can emit | integer | 32000 to 256000 | model-dependent | bigger vocab = fewer tokens per word but bigger embedding matrix | https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.08295 |
| context_length | maximum tokens the model can attend over | integer | 2048 to 2000000 | model-dependent | prompt + output must fit; longer = more memory for KV cache | https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.08295 |
| sliding window | attention only over the last W tokens | integer | 512 to 32768 | model-dependent | trades long-range attention for memory/speed; some models mix layers | https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.09834 |
| RoPE base (theta) | base frequency for rotary positional embedding | number | 10000, 500000, 1000000+ | 10000 (classic), 500000+ (long-context) | higher base = supports longer sequences; needs matched training | https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.08295 |
| positional encoding type | how the model represents token position | string | `absolute`, `sinusoidal`, `RoPE`, `ALiBi` | model-dependent | RoPE dominates modern models; ALiBi extrapolates without training | https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.08295 |
| activation function | nonlinearity inside the feed-forward layer | string | `GELU`, `ReLU`, `SwiGLU`, `GeGLU` | model-dependent | SwiGLU is common in modern LLMs; small quality gain over GELU | https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.08295 |
| normalization | how layer inputs are rescaled | string | `LayerNorm`, `RMSNorm` | RMSNorm in modern LLMs | RMSNorm skips the mean; slightly faster, matches quality | https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.04167 |
| norm_epsilon | small constant added to variance for numerical stability | number | 1e-5 to 1e-6 | usually 1e-5 or 1e-6 | prevents divide-by-zero; smaller = less bias, more risk of NaN | https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.04167 |
| tied embeddings | whether input embedding = output projection weights | boolean | true or false | often true in small models | saves parameters; small quality cost in very large models | https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.08295 |
| MoE (mixture of experts) | route each token through a subset of experts | boolean or count | number of experts | none in dense models | active params << total params; big quality per active FLOP | https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.09834 |
| experts_per_token | number of experts a token activates | integer | 1 to 8 | 2 in most MoE | trades quality for speed; more experts = more compute per token | https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.09834 |
| dtype (weights) | the numeric type weights are stored in | string | `float32`, `float16`, `bfloat16`, `int8`, `int4` | bf16 for training; smaller for inference | smaller dtype = less memory, some quality cost | https://mljourney.com/quantization-techniques-for-llm-inference-int8-int4-gptq-and-awq/ |
| tokenizer type | which subword algorithm the model uses | string | `BPE`, `SentencePiece`, `WordPiece`, `Tiktoken` | BPE dominates modern LLMs | must use the same tokenizer as training or output is garbage | https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/tokenizer_summary |

## Section 7 — Tokenizer concepts

The tokenizer sits between text and the model. It converts a string into a list of integer token ids, and back. Its choices shape everything downstream: cost, context usage, and quality on non-English text.

| name | one-line-definition | type | range/values | default | effect | source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

## Section 8 — Training and fine-tuning concepts

These are the knobs you set when you train (or fine-tune) a model. You don't touch them at inference — but you must know what a model card tells you when it names them.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| learning rate | step size for each parameter update | number | 1e-6 to 1e-3 | 1e-4 to 5e-5 for fine-tuning | too high = divergence; too low = slow convergence | https://mbrenndoerfer.com/writing/cosine-learning-rate-schedule-decay-restarts-warmup |

## Section 9 — Inference optimizations

At serving time, the same model file can be run faster or slower depending on which of these tricks are enabled.

| name | one-line-definition | type | range/values | default | effect | source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| KV cache | store past key/value tensors so decode only computes new tokens | mechanism | on/off | on | without it, every new token re-computes attention over all prior tokens (quadratic) | https://vllm.ai/blog/2025-09-05-anatomy-of-vllm |
| PagedAttention | manage KV cache in fixed-size blocks (OS-style paging) | mechanism | on/off | on in vLLM | eliminates fragmentation; enables much higher batch sizes | https://vllm.ai/blog/2025-09-05-anatomy-of-vllm |
| prefix caching | reuse KV cache across requests sharing a prefix | mechanism | on/off | on in modern servers | huge speedup for common system prompts; requires exact byte-match on prefix | https://vllm.ai/blog/2025-09-05-anatomy-of-vllm |
| continuous batching | admit new requests into a running batch step-by-step | mechanism | on/off | on in vLLM, TGI | eliminates head-of-line blocking; near-optimal GPU utilization | https://vllm.ai/blog/2025-09-05-anatomy-of-vllm |
| static batching | fix the batch, run to completion together | mechanism | on/off | uncommon now | wastes cycles waiting for the longest sequence in the batch | https://vllm.ai/blog/2025-09-05-anatomy-of-vllm |
| speculative decoding | draft model proposes tokens; big model verifies in one pass | mechanism | on/off | off by default | 2-3x decode speedup at high acceptance; no quality loss | https://vllm.ai/blog/2025-09-05-anatomy-of-vllm |
| draft model | the small model used for speculation | model | 100M to 1B typical | small model paired to target | must share tokenizer; higher agreement = higher speedup | https://vllm.ai/blog/2025-09-05-anatomy-of-vllm |
| flash attention | IO-aware, kernel-fused exact attention | kernel | on/off | on where supported | 2-4x faster attention, same math; enables longer contexts | https://arxiv.org/pdf/2501.01005 |
| tensor parallelism | shard weight matrices across GPUs | strategy | 2, 4, 8 | 1 (single GPU) | linear speedup with GPU count until interconnect saturates | https://vllm.ai/blog/2025-09-05-anatomy-of-vllm |
| pipeline parallelism | split layers across GPUs | strategy | 2, 4, 8 | 1 | helps when a single GPU can't fit the model; adds latency | https://vllm.ai/blog/2025-09-05-anatomy-of-vllm |
| quantization at inference | run with int8/int4 weights | technique | int8, int4, fp8 | fp16 | smaller memory footprint; faster on tensor cores that support the dtype | https://mljourney.com/quantization-techniques-for-llm-inference-int8-int4-gptq-and-awq/ |
| chunked prefill | split long-prompt prefill across steps | mechanism | on/off | on in vLLM 0.6+ | improves latency of interleaved short requests | https://vllm.ai/blog/2025-09-05-anatomy-of-vllm |
| sliding-window inference | drop KV cache entries older than W tokens | mechanism | on/off | model-dependent | bounds memory in long contexts; some quality cost on very long recall | https://arxiv.org/pdf/2508.09834 |
| GQA (grouped-query attention) | share KV heads across query heads | architecture | 1 to n_heads | 8 groups common | shrinks KV cache proportionally to n_heads/n_kv_heads | https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245 |
| MQA (multi-query attention) | one KV head shared by all query heads | architecture | 1 kv head | uncommon standalone | maximum KV cache shrink; more quality loss than GQA | https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245 |
| RoPE scaling | stretch positional embeddings past training length | technique | linear, YaRN, dynamic | none | extends context at inference without retraining; quality varies | https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.08295 |
| context extension | any method that lets a model handle longer inputs than trained | umbrella | RoPE scaling, chunked, sliding | model-dependent | usually cheaper than retraining but with tradeoffs | https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.08295 |

| name | one-line-definition | type | range/values | default | effect | source |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

## What the model IS expected to remember — and what belongs in this appendix

You do not memorize the tables above. You never will and you should not try. Instead, hold the following short list in your working weights, and let RAG hold the rest.

**Hold in weights.** The doctrine: you look values up rather than guessing. The names of the ten sections in this appendix so you know which one to query. The shape of a lookup row: `name | one-line-definition | type | range | default | effect | source`. The core intuition that sampling means turning a distribution into a token, that temperature scales the sharpness, that top_p / top_k / min_p / mirostat are all different ways to trim the tail, that a KV cache is what makes decoding fast, and that fine-tuning changes weights while RAG (Cortex) changes context without changing weights. The habit of citing the source you found.

**Look up.** Every default value. Every exact range. Every provider-specific field name. Every response-shape field. Every training hyperparameter that isn't part of your daily inference vocabulary. If a program asks about `mirostat_tau`, `dry_penalty_last_n`, `chunk.usage`, `LoRA rank`, or `x-ratelimit-remaining-tokens`, you look. If it asks about `logit_bias` at a hostile-token level, you look. If it asks how to constrain a JSON response across three different providers, you look.

There is one hard rule under all of this. **If a row is not in this appendix and you cannot verify a source, say so.** Do not fabricate. Do not guess a default. Do not paraphrase a paper you have not been trained on. The failure mode of a small model is over-confident hallucination, and the whole point of this appendix is that you do not have to hallucinate: you have the lookup table, and the lookup table has sources. Use it.

That is the appendix. Read a row when you need it, forget it after you use it, come back and read the row again. That is what the appendix is for.")

"# Appendix J — LLM x Introspection

Introspection asks the language a question. The language answers with a record — a shape, a docstring, a source hint. The LLM does not add to that record. It reads it. Then it turns the record into prose a human can hold in their head faster than they can parse an alist.

That is the whole shape of this appendix. Every combination below has an introspection verb producing a mechanical answer and an LLM verb producing a human-shaped answer. The two never contradict, because the LLM is not free-associating. It is looking at the same alist you see and writing a paragraph about it.

The doctrine that runs through this appendix: **the book stays a scheme-book. Cortex knows the book exists and points the model at it via `(copilot/rag ...)`. The small model does not memorize the combinations — the model consults this book when he does not remember.**

The combinations here are not a memorization target. They are a lookup surface. When the model is asked to help a programmer with a task that requires both metadata and prose — 'explain what this verb does in three sentences and give me a novice example' — the model consults this appendix and finds the recipe. He does not have to have seen every combination in training. He has to have seen enough of them to know that the shape is compositional.

Fifteen combinations follow. Each is a scenario, a form, an expected result, and a note about why the combination composes cleanly. A summary table closes the appendix.

## Why these combinations matter

A verb metadata record is machine-readable. It is not human-readable at the speed a human wants. `help` returns nine fields; `describe` collapses them to one paragraph. Neither is enough on its own for the kinds of questions a programmer actually asks.

'What does map do?' — the human wants prose. `describe` gives it.
'What does map return when the list is empty?' — the human wants prose grounded in the contract. `describe` does not give this. `(copilot/explain (help 'map))` does.
'Rewrite this function to be more idiomatic.' — the human wants a form back. `rewrite` gives it.
'What am I looking at?' — the human wants shape and description together. `shape-of` gives it.

The LLM does not replace introspection. It renders introspection into human-fit prose. Every combination in this appendix has that shape.

## The retrieval-augmentation contract

When the small model looks up a combination in this book, he is not memorizing it. He is retrieving it. The contract is:

  1. The model does not invent verbs.
  2. The model does not invent field names.
  3. The model does not invent contracts.
  4. When asked something the book covers, the model cites the book.
  5. When asked something the book does not cover, the model says so.

This appendix documents fifteen combinations. In production the model will encounter dozens more. The training corpus teaches the model the shape of a combination — verb + verb + optional glue — so that new combinations at inference time are compositional rather than memorized."

     :expected-output  "((:type . \"alist\") (:length . 4) (:keys . (:name :age :role :active?)) (:what-you-see . \"A user profile record.\") (:probable-origin . \"Likely from a (cortex/query :kind 'user) call.\") (:common-uses . (\"Feed to (render-profile ...)\" \"Serialize with (slat/write ...)\")))"
     :why-it-composes  "shape-of is one verb that runs both surfaces — the mechanical type-of and the LLM's prose. The record has fields the terminal can print row-by-row and fields the web IDE can render as headers.")

   (combination-5
     :scenario         "Programmer wants to critique a description she wrote of a verb, comparing it to what the model would write given the same metadata."
     :form             "(copilot/critique (describe 'map))"
     :expected-output  "((:severity . 'low) (:kind . 'unclear) (:location . 'closing) (:message . \"The paragraph mentions map's arity but not the higher-order case.\") (:suggestion . \"Add a sentence: 'map with multiple lists pairs elements pointwise.'\"))"
     :why-it-composes  "describe returns a paragraph (string). critique accepts a form or a string. The critique alist points at parts of the paragraph the model finds thin.")

   (combination-6
     :scenario         "Programmer wants to know what a macro will expand to before she calls it. She uses macroexpand-1 (an introspection verb) and hands the result to explain (an LLM verb)."
     :form             "(copilot/explain (macroexpand-1 '(when p x y)))"
     :expected-output  "\"The when macro expands to an if with a begin. (when p x y) becomes (if p (begin x y) #f). This is a Scheme convention — when guards a side-effecting sequence.\""
     :why-it-composes  "macroexpand-1 is deterministic and mechanical; explain adds interpretive prose. The two together teach macro semantics from the actual expansion, not from a mnemonic.")

   (combination-7
     :scenario         "Programmer wants a unified answer for a symbol — 'tell me everything you know about map'."
     :form             "(copilot/what-is 'map)"
     :expected-output  "((:from-registry . (help 'map)) (:from-reference . (reference/lookup 'map)) (:from-llm . \"map is Scheme's core higher-order function...\") (:confidence . 0.98) (:sources . (\"src/base.js:412\" \"reference/motoi/map\")))"
     :why-it-composes  "copilot/what-is composes three lookups (registry, reference, LLM). If the first two succeed, the LLM prose is a bonus. If they fail, the LLM prose carries a :confidence field so the human knows to verify.")

   (combination-8
     :scenario         "Programmer wrote a function without a docstring; she asks the model to propose one based on the source."
     :form             "(copilot/ask \"Write a docstring for this function.\" :context (source-of 'compute-median))"
     :expected-output  "\"Return the median of a non-empty list of numbers. If the list has even length the median is the mean of the two middle elements. Sorts the input; does not mutate it. Contract: (list-of-number) -> number.\""
     :why-it-composes  "source-of returns the definition; copilot/ask takes prose questions with context. The model reads the code and writes what it does.")

   (combination-9
     :scenario         "Programmer wants to inspect a closure — see the bindings it captured — and get an LLM narration of what the closure is likely for."
     :form             "(copilot/explain (env-of my-closure))"
     :expected-output  "\"This closure captured three bindings: threshold=0.5, direction='up, and hits=#(...). It looks like a running-tally callback for a signal detector — threshold gates, direction filters, hits accumulates.\""
     :why-it-composes  "env-of returns an alist of captured names. copilot/explain names the pattern the alist looks like from experience with common closure shapes.")

   (combination-10
     :scenario         "Programmer wrote a complex expression and wants two views side by side — the annotated form and a prose walk-through."
     :form             "(list :annotated (copilot/annotate form) :prose (copilot/tell-story form))"
     :expected-output  "((:annotated . (let ((x 1)) ;; bind x to 1\\n  (+ x 2))) (:prose . \"First we bind x to the number 1. Then we compute x + 2, which returns 3.\"))"
     :why-it-composes  "annotate returns a form with inline comments; tell-story returns prose. Both draw from the same introspective reading of the form. The list is a value; a surface renders each key however it likes.")

   (combination-11
     :scenario         "Programmer sees a name in unfamiliar code and wants to know which verb it refers to. did-you-mean turns a typo into a ranked list; explain narrates the top hit."
     :form             "(copilot/explain (car (did-you-mean 'crdr)))"
     :expected-output  "\"cdr — returns everything but the first element of a pair. Contract: (pair) -> any. You likely meant this; 'crdr' is a common typo where a d and r got transposed.\""
     :why-it-composes  "did-you-mean returns a ranked list of candidate verbs. car extracts the top hit. explain narrates its metadata. Three-verb pipeline; each step is compositional.")

   (combination-12
     :scenario         "Programmer wants to test whether her mental model of a verb matches the model's. imagine-output predicts; apply verifies; compare surfaces the gap."
     :form             "(let ((predicted (copilot/imagine-output 'sort '((3 1 2))))\n      (actual (sort '(3 1 2))))\n  (copilot/compare predicted actual))"
     :expected-output  "((:structural-diff . 'identical) (:semantic-diff . 'identical) (:when-they-diverge . \"Only diverges if sort's comparator is non-default.\"))"
     :why-it-composes  "imagine-output is grounded in the verb's contract (from the registry). apply runs the verb. compare highlights any gap. All three read the same metadata; only apply also executes.")

     :scenario         "Programmer wants to know all the verbs in a namespace and the LLM's summary of what the namespace is for."
     :form             "(copilot/explain (filter (lambda (v) (starts-with? (car v) \"cortex/\")) (all-verbs)))"
     :expected-output  "\"cortex/* is Motoi's persistent-memory namespace. It contains read, write, record, and query — a minimal set for storing facts and retrieving them by key or by predicate match.\""
     :why-it-composes  "all-verbs enumerates the registry; filter narrows to a namespace; explain summarizes the filtered list. The LLM sees names + docs; prose follows from the names, no invention required.")

   (combination-14
     :scenario         "Programmer sees a stale error record and wants to know what it means without re-triggering the error."
     :form             "(copilot/pretty-error (last-error))"

     :why-it-composes  "last-error is an introspection verb — it returns the last raised error record. pretty-error is an LLM verb that narrates the record. The record carries :message :location :context; the narration puts them in a sentence a beginner can read.")

   (combination-15
     :scenario         "Programmer wants a novice example of a verb generated on demand — the reference has three but she wants a fresh one aimed at what she is doing now."
     :form             "(copilot/build-example 'fold :level 'novice :context 'summing-a-list)"
     :expected-output  "\"(fold + 0 '(1 2 3 4)) => 10 — fold takes an operator (+), a starting value (0), and a list. It threads the operator through the list, starting from 0, and returns the final accumulated value.\""
     :why-it-composes  "build-example reads the verb's contract from the registry and generates a runnable example. The :context option biases the generation without inventing signature — the model still respects (fold f init list).")

   (combination-16
     :scenario         "Programmer wants the model to walk through evaluation step by step for teaching."
     :form             "(copilot/step '(let ((x 1) (y 2)) (+ x y)))"

     :why-it-composes  "step is an LLM verb that produces a structured trace — each step has a form, an environment snapshot, and a pedagogical note. The introspection here is over the evaluation itself; the LLM adds the annotations, the runtime supplies the actual step transitions.")

     :scenario         "Programmer opens a verb and wants a paragraph description AND the source location AND a runnable example in one call."
     :form             "(let ((meta (help 'reduce)))\n  (list :prose (copilot/explain meta)\n        :source (docof 'reduce)\n        :example (copilot/build-example 'reduce :level 'intermediate)))"
     :expected-output  "((:prose \"reduce is a left-fold with the initial value being the first element of the list. Contract: (procedure list) -> any. Arity 2.\") (:source \"Return the accumulated result of applying proc across the list, starting from the first element.\") (:example (reduce + '(1 2 3 4 5))))"
     :why-it-composes  "Three verbs composed in a let-binding. Each verb contributes one field. The list value can be rendered as a card in an IDE, three lines in a REPL, or a single spoken paragraph in a voice interface.")

     :scenario         "Programmer wants to know if a verb has ever been called in this session and get prose about the pattern of calls."

The dominant pattern is doubling — (map (lambda (x) (* x 2)) some-list). If this is a hot path, a specialized double-list verb might be worth extracting.\""
     :why-it-composes  "call-history is a session-aware introspection verb. reason-about is an LLM verb that reads a value's history and writes about the pattern. The two combine to turn a numeric log into a narrative recommendation.")

   (combination-19
     :scenario         "Programmer wants to name an anonymous let-binding. name-of reads the shape and proposes."
     :form             "(let ((it (map (lambda (x) (* x x)) (range 10))))\n  (copilot/name-of it))"
     :expected-output  "'squares-of-ten-integers"
     :why-it-composes  "The anonymous binding it is a value. name-of reads its shape (a list of ten squared integers) and proposes a symbol. The programmer can rebind: (define squares-of-ten-integers it).")

   (combination-20
     :scenario         "Programmer wants a paragraph explaining WHY a verb was designed a certain way — reads the contract, the doc, and the surrounding module doc together."

     :expected-output  "\"cortex/write takes a value directly because the memory store is meant to be simple — a key-value alist backed by a SLAT file. A builder would complicate the interface for no gain; the value passed is already the shape stored. cortex/read symmetrically returns the stored value.\""
     :why-it-composes  "Three introspection sources become context for one LLM question. The model does not free-associate a design rationale — it grounds the answer in the metadata of the verbs and the module.")

   (combination-21
     :scenario         "Programmer suspects a verb's contract is wrong. She asks the model to critique the contract itself given the source."
     :form             "(copilot/critique (list :contract (typeof 'compute-median) :source (source-of 'compute-median)))"
     :expected-output  "((:severity . 'medium) (:kind . 'contract-mismatch) (:location . 'contract) (:message . \"Contract says (list-of-number) -> number but the source does not check for the empty list — an empty list would divide by zero.\") (:suggestion . \"Amend contract to (non-empty-list-of-number) -> number, or add an empty-list guard in the source.\"))"
     :why-it-composes  "typeof and source-of are both introspection verbs. critique reads them together and reports mismatches. The value returned is a critique record; a surface can render it as a lint warning.")

     :scenario         "Programmer wants a summary of every LLM-augmented verb in the current registry, to teach a workshop."

  :prose
"# Appendix K — LLM x Cortex

Cortex is what the program remembers. It survives the REPL closing. It survives the machine rebooting. Every write to Cortex is a fact the program can consult next time. Every query is a way of asking 'what did I know before?'

The LLM is what the program can reason about the memory with. Cortex tells the model what happened; the model tells the human what it means. Cortex refuses to hallucinate — it either has a record or it does not. The LLM fills the gap by paraphrasing, summarizing, or asking a follow-up question.

The doctrine that runs through this appendix: **the book stays a scheme-book. Cortex knows the book exists and points the model at it via `(copilot/rag ...)`. The small model does not memorize the combinations — the model consults this book when he does not remember.**

The combinations below fall into three shapes: **LLM writes to Cortex** (save an insight the model produced), **LLM reads from Cortex** (ground an answer in what the program already knows), and **LLM reconciles Cortex** (when a new fact disagrees with a stored one, the model decides what to do). All twenty combinations follow one of those three shapes.

## Cortex is small and simple, on purpose

Cortex in Motoi is deliberately spare — four verbs (`cortex/read`, `cortex/write`, `cortex/record`, `cortex/query`). The store is a SLAT file at `~/.motoi/cortex.slat`. Values are plain data — numbers, strings, symbols, lists, alists. There is no schema. There is no query language beyond keyword-arg exact match. There are no indexes. Reads and writes are O(records).

That simplicity is not a limitation for LLM composition — it is the enabling constraint. Because Cortex speaks in plain data, the LLM sees plain data. Because the LLM sees plain data, it can reason about the memory without a wrapper library. Every combination in this appendix is a small pipe from Cortex-verb output to LLM-verb input, or the reverse.

A richer memory graph is possible (Sakura layers `sakura/fact-add` and `sakura/fact-query` on top for atomic-facts per-verb annotations, and Curator adds an atlas layer for cross-object relationships). Motoi keeps the base small. Everything below composes with all three tiers because the shape stays the same: records in, records out.

## Why Cortex plus LLM matters

A language without persistent memory forgets everything every session. A language with persistent memory but no LLM remembers exactly what you wrote and returns it verbatim. A language with both remembers, and also can talk about what it remembers.

'What color does the user prefer?' — Cortex has a record. `cortex/read :key 'preferred-color` returns it.
'Why does the user prefer that color?' — Cortex may not have a stored reason. `(copilot/reason-about (cortex/query :subject 'user :predicate 'preferred-color))` narrates what the program knows, and honestly says when it does not know a reason.
'Save this insight for later.' — LLM produces an explanation; `cortex/write :key 'why-user-prefers-blue :value ...` persists it.
'Two records disagree — which is right?' — `(copilot/critique (cortex/query :key 'preferred-color))` returns the conflict and a suggestion.

Cortex is the archive. LLM is the librarian. They compose.

## The retrieval-augmentation contract, again

The small model does not memorize what is in Cortex — Cortex is per-session, per-user, mutable. What the model memorizes is the shape of Cortex verbs. When asked to consult memory, the model calls `(cortex/query ...)` or `(cortex/read ...)`. When asked to save an insight, the model calls `(cortex/write ...)` or `(cortex/record ...)`. Everything else is data.

That is the same shape as the book. The book is not memorized either. `(copilot/rag q)` looks the book up when needed, cites it in the answer, and does not invent. Cortex + book together form the RAG surface. The model is small; the surface is large; the composition works because the model consults instead of remembers.

## The atomic-facts overlap (for Sakura-parallel readers)

Motoi keeps Cortex simple — read, write, record, query. Sakura's dialect adds atomic-facts (per-verb annotations stored per-user). This appendix uses the Motoi four; the Sakura variant of this appendix substitutes `sakura/fact-add` and `sakura/fact-query` in places, but the shape of the composition is identical. Every combination in this appendix has a Sakura mirror.

Twenty combinations follow."

  :combinations
  ((combination-1
     :scenario         "Programmer asks a question the LLM should answer using her personal preferences stored in Cortex."
     :form             "(copilot/ask \"What's a good chart type for this data?\" :context (cortex/query :subject 'user :predicate 'preferred-visualization))"
     :expected-output  "\"Given you usually prefer bar charts for categorical data (per your Cortex preferences), and this is categorical, I recommend a bar chart.\""
     :why-it-composes  "cortex/query returns a list of matching records; ask takes prose questions with :context. The model reads the records and grounds its recommendation. If Cortex has no records, the model says 'I don't have any stored preferences for you' rather than inventing one.")

   (combination-2
     :scenario         "Programmer wants to save an explanation the LLM just produced so a later session can consult it."
     :form             "(cortex/write :key 'why-my-cart-caches-x :value (copilot/explain '(define x (memoize compute-heavy))))"
     :expected-output  "#t  ;; write succeeded"
     :why-it-composes  "explain returns a string; cortex/write takes a key and any value. The LLM's prose becomes a stored fact indexed by a memorable key. Next session she calls (cortex/read :key 'why-my-cart-caches-x) and gets the paragraph back.")

   (combination-3
     :scenario         "Programmer wants RAG scoped to a specific set of Cortex facts, not the whole memory."
     :form             "(copilot/rag \"What programming style should I use in this cart?\" :cortex-scope '(:predicate 'preferred-style :subject 'this-project))"
     :expected-output  "((:answer \"Based on stored preferences for this project (idiomatic Scheme, no macros unless necessary, small verbs), I'd write it in that style.\") (:sources ((:from 'cortex :key 'preferred-style :subject 'this-project))))"
     :why-it-composes  "rag normally searches all Cortex + reference + books. The :cortex-scope option narrows the retrieval to matching records. The answer cites its sources. The model grounds recommendations in stored facts.")

   (combination-4
     :scenario         "Programmer wants to record a long-term insight — a lesson the LLM helped extract."
     :form             "(cortex/record :kind 'lesson :topic 'error-handling :insight (copilot/explain '(when (null? result) (fail 'garbled))) :date (current-time))"
     :expected-output  "#t  ;; record appended to Cortex's __records__ collection"
     :why-it-composes  "cortex/record takes keyword-arg records; explain returns the prose. The record joins Cortex's queryable collection. Later a query like (cortex/query :kind 'lesson :topic 'error-handling) surfaces every stored lesson on the topic.")

   (combination-5
     :scenario         "Programmer stored a fact yesterday; today the LLM was about to hallucinate a different answer. She asks the model to check Cortex first."
     :form             "(let ((stored (cortex/read :key 'preferred-editor-width)))\n  (if stored\n      (copilot/ask \"Format this code respecting my preferred width.\" :context stored :value some-code)\n      (copilot/ask \"Format this code.\" :value some-code)))"
     :expected-output  "\";; formatted at 96 columns per your Cortex preference\\n(define ...)\""
     :why-it-composes  "cortex/read returns #f when the key is missing. The if branch chooses between grounded prompt (has stored preference) and generic prompt (no preference). This is the read-your-writes pattern for LLM prompting.")

   (combination-6
     :scenario         "Programmer wants the model to summarize everything Cortex knows about a subject in prose."
     :form             "(copilot/explain (cortex/query :subject 'ongoing-refactor))"
     :expected-output  "\"Cortex has seventeen records about the ongoing refactor. The gist: extraction of the auth module started July 3, three verbs migrated by July 10, tests passing since July 12, blocker on July 14 about circular imports, resolved by July 15 with a shim. Current state: waiting on your review of PR-42.\""
     :why-it-composes  "cortex/query returns a list. explain reads the list and writes a summary. The prose is grounded in the records; the dates and verbs come from the records verbatim.")

   (combination-7
     :scenario         "Programmer wants to know when Cortex disagrees with itself — the same key was written twice with different values."
     :form             "(copilot/critique (cortex/query :subject 'preferred-language))"
     :expected-output  "((:severity . 'medium) (:kind . 'conflict) (:message . \"Two records for :preferred-language. On July 10 you wrote 'scheme; on July 15 you wrote 'clojure. No later write to resolve.\") (:suggestion . \"Call (cortex/write :key 'preferred-language :value 'scheme) or (:value 'clojure) to disambiguate; the newer wins by default but the LLM should not assume.\"))"
     :why-it-composes  "cortex/query surfaces the conflict; critique reads a list and reports issues. Conflict is a first-class critique :kind. The programmer decides how to resolve.")

   (combination-8
     :scenario         "Programmer wants to persist a Cortex-scoped RAG answer so next session's read is instant."
     :form             "(let ((answer (copilot/rag \"How does fold handle empty lists?\")))\n  (cortex/write :key 'fold-empty-list-behavior :value answer))"
     :expected-output  "#t"
     :why-it-composes  "rag returns a record with :answer and :sources. cortex/write stores it. Later calls to (cortex/read :key 'fold-empty-list-behavior) return the whole record — answer plus provenance.")

   (combination-9
     :scenario         "Programmer wants a next-step recommendation grounded in what the current session has done, plus what Cortex remembers about past sessions."
     :form             "(copilot/next-step :context (cortex/query :subject 'current-project :since '30-days-ago))"
     :expected-output  "(((:form (test-idea 'compute-median)) (:reason \"You wrote compute-median twenty minutes ago and Cortex shows you usually add tests within an hour.\")) ((:form (scaffold 'chapter :book 'introspection :number 12)) (:reason \"Cortex shows chapter 11 landed yesterday; you tend to author one chapter per day.\")))"
     :why-it-composes  "next-step normally reads session history; :context option lets Cortex records enrich the read. The recommendations are grounded in patterns Cortex has recorded.")

   (combination-10
     :scenario         "Programmer wants the model to detect a stale Cortex record — one that hasn't been touched in weeks and might be outdated."
     :form             "(copilot/reason-about (filter (lambda (r) (> (- (current-time) (assq :ts r)) (days 30))) (cortex/query)))"
     :expected-output  "\"Six records in Cortex are over thirty days old and haven't been read since. Three look like meaningful preferences (:preferred-editor-width, :preferred-language, :author-name). Three look like stale project state — old branch names, old machine IDs, an old API endpoint. Consider (cortex/prune ...) on the stale three.\""
     :why-it-composes  "cortex/query with no args returns everything; the filter narrows by age; reason-about narrates why the model thinks each is stale or not.")

   (combination-11
     :scenario         "Programmer wants a Cortex-backed quiz — the model quizzes her on facts from her own Cortex."
     :form             "(copilot/quiz 'preferences :from (cortex/query :subject 'user))"
     :expected-output  "((:question \"What editor width did you prefer as of last month?\") (:expected-shape 'number) (:hints (\"You wrote it as :preferred-editor-width.\")))"
     :why-it-composes  "quiz takes a topic; :from option lets it draw from Cortex. The programmer's answers get graded against her own stored facts.")

  :closing-prose
"Cortex remembers. The LLM summarizes what Cortex remembers. Neither replaces the other. The programmer moves between them fluidly — asking the model to persist what it just told her, asking it to reason about what was persisted a month ago, asking it to reconcile when new and old disagree.

The book stays a scheme-book. Cortex is where per-user, per-project facts live; the book is where the durable teaching lives. Together they are the retrieval surface the small model consults when he does not remember. He remembers the verbs; he consults Cortex and the book for the facts.

## When the LLM should not touch Cortex

Three cases where a well-behaved model refuses to compose:

  1. **Cortex is empty.** No records for the queried key. The model must not fabricate a value. Return #f or a not-found record and let the caller ask the user.
  2. **Cortex has one record, but it is stale.** The record has a :ts field older than a session-appropriate threshold. The model surfaces the age and asks whether to trust it.
  3. **Cortex has two conflicting records.** The model does not silently pick one. It surfaces the conflict as a critique record. The programmer resolves.

The general rule: the LLM never invents a Cortex fact, never picks a winner in a conflict, and never treats staleness as absence. All three are first-class outcomes with named shapes. Every combination in this appendix respects these.

For the LLM x Introspection pair, see Appendix J. For the meta-question of what the model can and cannot be expected to remember (which is really a question about what needs to be in weights versus what needs to be in Cortex versus what needs to be in the book), see Appendix N."

"# Appendix L — Completions x Modules

A completion is a partial answer. The user typed some characters; the system offers the words that could follow. This appendix is about what happens when the completion surface knows about the module system — which verbs are exported by which module, which modules are imported into the current cart, which are available on disk but not yet imported.

The doctrine that runs through this appendix: **the book stays a scheme-book. Cortex knows the book exists and points the model at it via `(copilot/rag ...)`. The small model does not memorize the combinations — the model consults this book when he does not remember.**

A completion without module awareness is a bag of names. It returns every verb the registry knows about, sorted by string distance. That works when there are 300 verbs. When the runtime has 1,200 verbs across 80 modules and the current cart imports only three of them, an unfiltered completion is noise. Module awareness turns noise into signal.

The verbs in this appendix live in two namespaces: `completions/*` (the completion surface) and the module system (`import`, `export`, `module`, `provides`, `uses`, `available-modules`). The introspection verbs from earlier chapters — `all-verbs`, `help`, `namespace-of` — round out the palette.

## Why completions plus modules matters

Type `co` at a REPL prompt with a naive completion. You get: `car`, `cdr`, `cons`, `compose`, `copilot/ask`, `copilot/complete`, `copilot/rewrite`, `cortex/read`, `cortex/write`, `cortex/query`, `count`, `count-if`, and thirty more. Twelve of those are useless to you right now because you have not imported the modules they live in. The completion is technically correct and practically wrong.

Module awareness fixes this. If the current cart declares `(import (motoi cortex))` but not `(import (motoi copilot))`, then `co` completes to `car`, `cdr`, `cons`, `count`, `count-if`, `cortex/*`. The `copilot/*` names are elided because they are not in scope. The completion returns what the programmer can actually call without adding an import.

But a good completion surface goes one step further. If `co` is typed and no imported module provides a match, the surface offers module suggestions: 'no local match; the copilot module provides copilot/ask, copilot/rewrite, copilot/critique — want to (import (motoi copilot))?' The completion becomes a discovery tool.

Fifteen combinations follow. They cover: scope-aware completion, cross-module completion (author-scoped, cart-scoped, project-scoped), completion for imports themselves (what modules exist?), and completion for the meta-verbs of the module system (what does export mean? what does provides return?).

## Terminology

- **Registered verb:** a verb the runtime knows about. Might not be imported into the current env.
- **Imported verb:** a verb the current cart's env has bound. Callable without qualification.
- **Available module:** a module the runtime has discovered on disk, not necessarily imported.
- **Loaded module:** a module whose top-level has been evaluated. All its exports are on the registry.
- **In-scope name:** a name callable from the current prompt without qualification. The intersection of loaded-module exports and current-env bindings.

Completion works on any of these layers depending on the option passed.

## The completion / module axis

Every completion query in this appendix answers one of five questions:

  1. **What can I call right now?** (in-scope names only)
  2. **What could I call if I imported the module?** (registered but not in scope)
  3. **What modules exist that I have not touched?** (available but not loaded)
  4. **Where does this name come from?** (module of origin for a specific verb)
  5. **What comes after this fragment?** (prefix + fragment-shape match, scoped to any of the above)

A completion surface that answers all five smoothly feels like the language is helping. A completion surface that answers only the first feels like the language is guessing. The verbs in this appendix cover all five, and their compositions cover the interesting corners — cart-scoped, author-scoped, contract-scoped, deprecated-aware, popularity-ranked.

## Why the module system matters for a small model

The small model does not have to remember every module's exports. He remembers that (module-exports (motoi cortex)) returns the exports, and he calls the verb when a user asks 'what verbs does the cortex module have?' The alternative — memorizing every export of every module — would balloon the training corpus and go stale the moment a new module ships.

This is the retrieval-augmentation contract at work. Verb names are stable and small enough to memorize; module contents are large and volatile and must be consulted. The book documents the query patterns. Cortex points the model at the book when the model needs a query pattern he has not used before."

| 5 | completions/at-point       | (author scope)         | cross-cart      |
| 6 | (none)                     | available-modules      | disk            |
| 7 | completions/missing-import | providing-modules      | discovery       |
| 8 | (none)                     | module-exports         | module surface  |
| 9 | completions/at-point       | (Cortex rank)          | frequency-ranked |
|10 | (none)                     | providing-modules      | disambiguation  |
|11 | completions/at-point       | (namespace-prefix)     | namespace       |
|12 | completions/import-suggestions | (popularity rank)  | trust-biased    |
|13 | completions/by-contract    | (contract intro)       | shape-matched   |
|14 | completions/at-point       | (import-form)          | import mode     |
|15 | completions/at-point       | (deprecated? filter)   | maturity        |

Every completion combination pairs a name-narrowing operation with a module-system introspection operation. The result is a name list that respects the programmer's actual context — not a bag of every registered verb."

  :closing-prose
"Completions plus modules turn a noisy autocompleter into a guide. The programmer types three characters and gets back verbs she can actually call, plus discovery hints for verbs one import away. The composition is the whole point — completions without module awareness are surface-agnostic and useful; completions with module awareness are scoped and actionable.

The book stays a scheme-book. Cortex tells the model that this appendix exists and points him here when he needs the recipe for a completion query he has not seen before. The model does not memorize all fifteen combinations. He memorizes the shape: completion-verb + module-verb + optional Cortex rank = scoped completion.

Two verbs cited in this appendix are proposed but not yet in the registry: `completions/by-contract` (combination 13) and `completions/missing-import` (combination 7). Both are natural compositions of existing verbs (`all-verbs` + contract filter; `providing-modules` + env-check) and should ship in the next completion-surface build lane. Every other verb is already registered as of the reference date.

## A worked completion session

Here is a small session showing the composition in real time. The programmer is writing a music cart; she has typed (import (motoi music)) at the top but nothing else yet.

```
> (completions/at-point \"no\" :context 'in-scope)
=> (note note/off note/on note/tag)

> (completions/import-suggestions 'reverb)
=> (((:name . fx/reverb) (:from-module . (motoi music fx)) (:import-form . (import (motoi music fx))))
    ((:name . reverb/preset) (:from-module . (motoi music fx)) (:import-form . (import (motoi music fx)))))

> (import (motoi music fx))
=> #t

> (completions/at-point \"re\" :context 'in-scope)
=> (rest reverb/preset)

> (completions/by-contract :input '(note) :output 'note :context 'in-scope)
=> (note/off note/on transpose-note)
```

Five queries, four verbs total, one import. The programmer moved from empty-scope-plus-hint to a full working palette in a minute of typing. Every query returned only what she could act on. That is the point.

## Sakura's parallel — same shape, different vocabulary

Sakura's dialect layer adds `card/*` and `shop/*` and `artifact/*` namespaces. The completion + module composition works the same way: type 'ca' at the Sakura REPL, get a card/* completion scoped to the imported dialect modules, get import suggestions for card/* verbs from modules not yet imported. Every combination in this appendix has an obvious Sakura mirror.

The one difference: Sakura's namespaces are richer (card, shop, radio, cine, flower, afford, ai-sidecar, cortex). Completion by namespace prefix (combination 11) is more useful in Sakura because the namespaces cluster tighter. Otherwise the shapes are identical.

For LLM x Introspection see Appendix J. For LLM x Cortex see Appendix K. For the meta-question of what the small model can be expected to remember versus consult, see Appendix N."

  :closes-with "See Appendix M next.")
