"# Chapter 15 — The frozen CORE

Motoi's core language has 335 verbs. That number was frozen on 2026-07-16. It will not grow.

Everything else — 600+ additional verbs across audio, graphics, game, ai, math, media, animation, cortex — lives in modules. Modules can grow, be added, be revised. The core cannot. It is done.

This chapter is about *why*. Because that decision — freezing the core — is one of Motoi's most opinionated design moves, and it has consequences you feel every day you write in the language.

## 15.1 What the frozen core includes

The 335 verbs cover:

- R7RS-small primitives: `car`, `cdr`, `cons`, `list`, `map`, `filter`, `apply`, `for-each`, `null?`, `pair?`, `eq?`, `equal?`, `let`, `let*`, `letrec`, `cond`, `if`, `when`, `unless`, `define`, `lambda`, `define-syntax`, `syntax-rules`.
- Numbers: `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `quotient`, `remainder`, `modulo`, `expt`, `sqrt`, `sin`, `cos`, `abs`, `min`, `max`, `zero?`, `positive?`, `negative?`, `even?`, `odd?`, `number->string`, `string->number`.
- Strings: `string-append`, `string-length`, `substring`, `string->list`, `list->string`, `string?`, `string=?`.
- Symbols: `symbol?`, `symbol->string`, `string->symbol`, `eq?`.
- Booleans and predicates: `#t`, `#f`, `and`, `or`, `not`, all the `?` predicates.
- Ports and I/O: `display`, `write`, `newline`, `read`, `open-input-string`, `open-output-string`.
- Errors: `error`, `with-exception-handler`, `raise`.
- Continuations: `call/cc`, `dynamic-wind`.
- Multiple values: `values`, `call-with-values`.
- Meta: `eval`, `interaction-environment`.

This is roughly R7RS-small with a handful of tightenings. The `alg` (algebraic), `topo` (topological), and a few core game verbs live in the core too, giving you basic building blocks without imports.

The point: any Motoi program that uses only these can run on any Motoi implementation, past or future, without importing anything.

## 15.2 Why freeze it

Because a language that keeps adding to its core is a language that keeps breaking.

Every added verb is a name that a user program cannot use. Every added special form is a shape someone's macros must know about. Every added builtin is a runtime that has to grow, a REPL that has to autocomplete more, a reference that gets longer, an implementation that gets harder to embed.

A frozen core says: *this much is done. If you want more, take it from a module.*

Modules are opt-in. If you don't import `(motoi audio)`, your program doesn't pay for it — the interpreter doesn't load it, the REPL doesn't autocomplete it, the reference doesn't have to be memorized. The core stays lean, and modules provide the rich functionality.

## 15.3 Comparison to R7RS

R7RS-small (2013) intentionally shipped a small core: about 250 procedures, plus the base syntax. R7RS-large is the ongoing effort to define a larger standard library. Motoi's core is close in spirit to R7RS-small: everything base R7RS needs, plus a small handful of extras (some higher-order helpers, a couple of predicate niceties). Motoi does not follow R7RS-large; the module layer is where richer functionality goes.

If you know R7RS-small, you already know 90% of Motoi's core.

## 15.4 Comparison to other language cores

**Python's core:** hundreds of built-in names, growing every release. `math`, `itertools`, `functools`, `collections` are part of the standard library; you import them but they ship with the interpreter. Python's `int`, `str`, `list`, `dict`, `set`, `tuple`, `frozenset`, `bytes`, `bytearray` are all built-in types. The whole surface is large.

**JavaScript's core:** ECMAScript defines the language; the runtime provides much more. Browsers add DOM, fetch, WebGL, WebRTC. Node adds fs, http, streams. There is no single \"core\" — the language and the runtime blur.

**Rust's core:** the language plus `core` (no-std safe), `std` (with heap and OS features), `alloc`. Each is a formal boundary.

**Clojure's core:** `clojure.core` has ~600 vars. `clojure.string`, `clojure.set`, `clojure.walk`, `clojure.zip`, etc. are namespaces one imports. Core is large by Motoi's standards.

Motoi's 335 is on the smaller side of the language landscape. Deliberately.

## 15.5 What this means for you as a writer

**Predictability.** A program that used only core verbs three years ago will still work today, and will still work in three more years. The runtime cannot rename them, drop them, change their semantics. That is a load-bearing promise.

**Portability.** A Motoi core-only program is portable to any host: a JS runtime, a native runtime, an embedded runtime. Module availability varies; core does not.

**Small mental map.** You can, in principle, know every core verb. 335 things is a lot but not impossibly a lot; a diligent afternoon with the reference can put them all in your head. You will not know every module — that's fine — but the core you can hold.

**Fewer collisions.** If you invent a name in your program, it will not collide with a future core addition, because there aren't going to be future core additions.

## 15.6 What this means for the interpreter

The interpreter's core is a small, testable, static thing. It doesn't need feature flags for \"which version of the core do I support?\" There is one core; every conforming implementation implements it exactly. This makes writing a new backend — a native compiler, a WASM target, an embedded interpreter — smaller and clearer.

The module layer is where implementations can vary. Not every host will have audio; that's fine, they just don't ship `(motoi audio)`. Not every host will have a display; that's fine, `(motoi graphics)` is optional. The core doesn't depend on any of it.

## 15.7 What this means for macros

Motoi's macros can *not* rely on module verbs and hope those verbs exist. A macro that expands into a call to `math/lerp` will fail on a runtime that hasn't loaded `(motoi math)`. This is a real constraint: if you write a macro for a library, it should either only reference core verbs, or clearly document that its expansion needs certain modules.

The upside: macros over core verbs are *maximally portable*. Your `->` and `->>` threading macros (Chapter 11) that expand to `let` and function calls — those work everywhere Motoi runs.

## 15.8 What was pruned

Some things you might expect in a language core, that Motoi's does not include:

- **Vectors and hash tables.** Core has lists; vector and hash-table types live in modules.
- **Records.** Core has pairs; named-field records come from a module.
- **Pattern matching.** Core has `cond`, `case`, `eq?`; structural matching comes from a module.
- **Streams and lazy evaluation.** Core is eager; `delay`/`force` and stream constructors live in modules.
- **Regex.** No regular expressions in core. A regex module exists.
- **Format.** No `format` in core. A format module exists.
- **Threading macros (`->`, `->>`).** Not in core. A threading module exists, or you write them (Chapter 11).

Each of these was a *choice*. Each could have gone into core. Each was kept out to keep the core small.

The trade: you'll import more than you would in Python. In exchange, your \"a small core-only program\" is guaranteed to be portable to any Motoi implementation.

## 15.9 What was retained

Things some might have moved to modules that stayed in core:

- **`call/cc` and `dynamic-wind`.** Continuations are core because they are how you build many other things (generators, non-local exits, coroutines).
- **`with-exception-handler`.** Error handling is universal; keeping it in core means every module can rely on it.
- **`eval` and `interaction-environment`.** Meta-evaluation is what makes code-as-data work at all.
- **`syntax-rules`.** Hygienic macros are the base metaprogramming layer.

These are the primitives that other primitives are built from. Removing them would push complexity into every module that needed them.

## 15.10 The 335-verb decision, honest

*Why 335?*

Not because 335 is a magic number. Because R7RS-small has about 250, and Motoi added ~85 for higher-order helpers, algebraic helpers, and a few conveniences that came up so often that keeping them out was noise.

335 is what it is. It's frozen because *further growth would rebreak the promise*. The number is not the point; the *freeze* is the point.

## 15.11 What the modules give you

- `(motoi audio)`: play, halt, tempo, note/strike, synth/kit, synth/chord, synth/play. Chapter 12.
- `(motoi graphics)`: framebuffer, sprite, text, animation. Chapter 5, 12, 16.
- `(motoi game)`: entity, camera, scene, part. Chapter 5.
- `(motoi math)`: math/sqrt, math/pi, math/pow, math/lerp, math/clamp.
- `(motoi ai)`: behavior tree steering primitives.
- `(motoi cortex)`: persistent memory graph. Chapter 13.
- `(motoi easing)`: cubic, sine, elastic tweening curves.
- `(motoi text)`: string manipulation beyond core.
- `(motoi hash)`: hash tables.
- `(motoi set)`: set data type.
- `(motoi stream)`: lazy sequences.
- `(motoi records)`: named-field structs.
- `(motoi match)`: pattern matching.
- `(motoi threading)`: `->`, `->>`, `some->`.
- `(motoi format)`: printf-style formatting.
- `(motoi test)`: assert-equal, test-case.
- `(motoi concurrency)`: channels, spawn, receive.

...and more, growing. The core is closed; the modules are open.

## 15.12 The philosophical point

A frozen core says: *the language is done growing. Add-ons happen in modules.*

This is the opposite of many modern languages, which grow their standard library continually and treat old-version compatibility as a matter of best effort. Motoi's core is a *promise*.

The cost: you'll write things or import things that other languages give you for free. The benefit: the core will not shift under you. Ever.

You can teach a child Motoi's core in a weekend. You can port Motoi's core to a new host in a week. You can hold Motoi's core in your head after a month of writing in it. These are not accidents; they are the fruit of the freeze.

## 15.13 The reference is the language

The 335 core verbs and 600+ module verbs are documented in one file: `scheme/MOTOI-SCHEME-REFERENCE.slat`. The interpreter reads it. The REPL reads it. This book cites it. The training data derives from it.

When the reference and the runtime disagree, the reference wins. That is a promise too — the reference is not documentation *of* the language; it *is* the language. Every verb, every core form, every example lives in one authoritative file. See the appendix on the reference (Chapter 8 in the old book of Jesse; that idea now lives with the notion \"reference-manual-IS-the-language\") for the full story.

## 15.14 Comparison to how other languages handle the version-drift problem

- **Python** deprecates and removes over years-long cycles. `distutils`, `imp`, `xreadlines` all gone or going. Each removal breaks working programs.
- **JavaScript** grows the language spec every year (ES2020, ES2021, etc.). Runtime support lags. Programs use transpilers to normalize.
- **Ruby** similar — new methods added to core classes every release; some become deprecated.
- **Clojure** is unusually conservative; core rarely changes. In spirit close to Motoi.
- **R7RS Scheme** is deliberately staged; small is small, large is layered on top.

Motoi picked the most conservative option: freeze the base. It is not the only valid choice. It is the choice that fits Motoi's shape.

## 15.15 What to remember

- 335 verbs in the frozen core, plus 53 special forms.
- All modules are opt-in and additive.
- A core-only program will always run.
- The reference is the language; when they disagree, the reference wins.
- The frozen core is a *promise* — the tax on future features is high, the value to today's programs is high.
- Most other languages made a different choice; Motoi's is deliberate.

Next chapter: Jesse's Making Beats. Everything above, put to work.
")

"# Chapter 16 — Jesse's Making Beats

*This book is catered to Jesse, who twenty years ago introduced me to functional programming, and I haven't been able to shake it since. He was right. — Alfred*

Every book has a chapter that's the reason for the book. This is that chapter.

Motoi is a Scheme with a fantasy-console kit — waveform synthesis, drum sounds, framebuffer graphics, motion tweens, all on one timeline. The last fifteen chapters have been about how the language works. This chapter is about *making something with it* — a chip-tune with matching visuals, in the demo-scene tradition of small programs that punch above their weight.

If you get to the end and you've made a beat and put a bouncing shape on it, the book worked. If you get to the end and you've built a two-minute audiovisual piece that you'd show to someone, the book more than worked.

## 16.1 What chip-tune means

Chip-tune is music made with the audio primitives of early game consoles and home computers — square waves, sawtooth waves, triangle waves, white noise. Machines from the 1980s (NES, Commodore 64, Game Boy) had chip-scale synthesizers with just a handful of voices and a handful of shapes. Musicians made whole compositions out of that vocabulary. The aesthetic became a genre.

Motoi's audio kit gives you those primitives directly:

- **Square wave.** Odd harmonics. Bright, buzzy. The classic 8-bit lead.
- **Sawtooth wave.** All harmonics. Aggressive, wide. Basses and leads.
- **Sine wave.** Pure. Warm. Used sparingly, felt everywhere.
- **Noise.** Unpitched. Drums, wind, static, hats.

And a small drum kit — kick, snare, hat, clap, crash — that layers over the tonal voices.

The whole vocabulary fits on one page. That is the discipline. Small vocabulary, large expressive range.

## 16.2 What demo-scene means

Demo-scene is the tradition of small programs that produce audiovisual output for its own sake. A demo is a piece of software. It runs; it draws; it plays; it ends. There is no goal beyond the experience. The best demos of the 1990s and 2000s did in 64 kilobytes what modern games do in 64 gigabytes.

The demo-scene ethos is what Motoi is aimed at. Small program, real output, real craft. Every constraint (few voices, low resolution, small code) is a discipline that produces its own aesthetic.

You are about to write demos. Not massive ones. Small, careful, complete ones.

## 16.3 The tools you have

From the base language (Chapter 15) plus the audio and graphics modules:

- `audio/tempo bpm` — set the beat clock.
- `audio/play 'tone freq dur shape` — play a raw tone.
- `synth/kit kit dur` — play a drum sound.
- `audio/halt` — silence everything.
- `audio/master-volume v` — global level 0..1.
- `audio/playing?` — is anything playing.
- Framebuffer verbs — clear, fill, draw pixels, rectangles, circles.
- Motion tween verbs — move, fade, slide, bounce.
- `animation/tick dt` — advance tweens by a delta.

Chapter 12 covered the theory. Now we use it.

## 16.4 The first tone

Open the REPL:

```
$ bin/motoi repl
motoi>
```

Play a middle-A:

```scheme
motoi> (audio/play 'tone 440 0.5 'square)
ok
```

You should hear a half-second square wave at 440 Hz. This is the sound of the 8-bit era. Congratulations. You are now a chip-tune programmer.

Verified:

```
$ bin/motoi eval \"(audio/play 'tone 440 0.5 'square)\"
ok
```

Try the other shapes:

```
$ bin/motoi eval \"(audio/play 'tone 440 0.5 'sine)\"
ok
$ bin/motoi eval \"(audio/play 'tone 440 0.5 'saw)\"
ok
$ bin/motoi eval \"(audio/play 'tone 440 0.5 'noise)\"
ok
```

Different shapes, same frequency. Listen for how the character changes. Sine is smooth; square is buzzy; saw is aggressive; noise is unpitched.

## 16.5 Notes as frequencies

Musical notes are frequencies. A4 (middle A) is 440 Hz. Every octave doubles the frequency. Every semitone is a factor of the twelfth root of 2 (~1.0595).

A helper function turns semitone offsets from A4 into frequencies:

```scheme
(define (note->freq semitones-from-a4)
  (* 440 (expt 2 (/ semitones-from-a4 12.0))))

(note->freq 0)     ; 440.0 — A4
(note->freq 3)     ; 523.25 — C5
(note->freq -9)    ; 261.63 — C4 (middle C)
(note->freq 12)    ; 880.0 — A5 (octave up)
```

Verified:

```
$ bin/motoi eval '(define (note->freq n) (* 440 (expt 2 (/ n 12.0)))) (note->freq 3)'
523.2511306011972
$ bin/motoi eval '(define (note->freq n) (* 440 (expt 2 (/ n 12.0)))) (note->freq -9)'
261.6255653005986
```

Now name the notes:

```scheme
(define A4 (note->freq 0))
(define B4 (note->freq 2))
(define C5 (note->freq 3))
(define D5 (note->freq 5))
(define E5 (note->freq 7))
(define F5 (note->freq 8))
(define G5 (note->freq 10))
(define A5 (note->freq 12))
```

Play a C major scale:

```scheme
(for-each
  (lambda (freq)
    (audio/play 'tone freq 0.2 'square))
  (list (note->freq -9)    ; C4
        (note->freq -7)    ; D4
        (note->freq -5)    ; E4
        (note->freq -4)    ; F4
        (note->freq -2)    ; G4
        (note->freq 0)     ; A4
        (note->freq 2)     ; B4
        (note->freq 3)))   ; C5
```

Eight notes ascending. Try it in `.scm` file form:

```scheme
;; scale.scm
(define (note->freq n) (* 440 (expt 2 (/ n 12.0))))

(define c-major-scale
  (list -9 -7 -5 -4 -2 0 2 3))

(for-each
  (lambda (semitone)
    (audio/play 'tone (note->freq semitone) 0.2 'square))
  c-major-scale)
```

Run it:

```
$ bin/motoi run scale.scm
```

Eight notes, ascending, square-wave 8-bit character.

## 16.6 A chord

A chord is multiple notes at once. The chip-tune equivalent, since our kit doesn't have a fully-featured chord verb, is to play the notes in near-immediate succession or to layer them at scheduled times.

For a rolled chord (arpeggio, one at a time in quick succession):

```scheme
(define (arpeggio notes step)
  (for-each
    (lambda (n) (audio/play 'tone (note->freq n) step 'square))
    notes))

(arpeggio '(-9 -5 -2) 0.1)   ; C-E-G rolled quickly
```

That is a C major chord as an arpeggio. Fast enough and your ear hears it as a chord.

## 16.7 Envelopes — the shape of a sound

A note played by `audio/play` starts, plays for its duration, ends. That's it. Real chip-tune sounds have *envelopes* — the loudness changes over time. Attack (how fast it rises), decay (how it settles), sustain (its held level), release (how it dies away).

Motoi's `audio/play` uses the runtime's default envelope. For custom shaping, you compose short tones back-to-back:

```scheme
;; a note with a short attack and long release
(define (bell freq)
  (audio/play 'tone freq 0.05 'sine)   ; loud initial
  (audio/play 'tone freq 0.5  'sine))   ; long tail
```

For chip-tune purposes, the built-in envelope is usually enough. Do not chase realism. The genre likes its edges.

## 16.8 The first beat

A four-on-the-floor beat is the simplest thing you can make that sounds like music. Kick on every quarter, snare on 2 and 4, hat on eighths.

```scheme
;; beat.scm
(audio/tempo 120)                    ; 120 bpm — dance-friendly

(define (beat-bar)
  (synth/kit 'kick 0)
  (synth/kit 'hat  0)
  (synth/kit 'hat  0)
  (synth/kit 'snare 0)
  (synth/kit 'hat  0)
  (synth/kit 'kick 0)
  (synth/kit 'hat  0)
  (synth/kit 'snare 0))

(beat-bar)
```

The `0` step argument tells the kit to play at the current cursor position. The audio scheduler advances the cursor as it plays.

Verified:

```
$ bin/motoi eval \"(begin (audio/tempo 120) (synth/kit 'kick 0) (synth/kit 'snare 0) (synth/kit 'kick 0) (synth/kit 'snare 0) 'done)\"
done
```

Try it. That's a beat. It won't win awards. It's a beat.

## 16.9 Sequencing with data

Hard-coding kick and snare calls gets old fast. Turn the beat into data:

```scheme
(define pattern-a
  '(kick hat hat snare hat kick hat snare))

(define (play-step step)
  (unless (eq? step 'rest)
    (synth/kit step 0)))

(define (play-pattern pat)
  (for-each play-step pat))

(play-pattern pattern-a)
```

Now the beat *is data*. You can transform it, combine it, compose it. This is the promise of the last fifteen chapters cashing in.

A 4-bar pattern:

```scheme
(define bar-a '(kick hat hat snare hat kick hat snare))
(define bar-b '(kick kick hat snare hat kick hat snare))
(define bar-c '(kick hat snare snare hat kick snare snare))
(define bar-d '(kick hat hat snare kick kick hat clap))

(define song
  (list bar-a bar-b bar-a bar-c bar-a bar-b bar-a bar-d))

(for-each play-pattern song)
```

Eight bars. Same primitives. Different arrangements. This is chip-tune arrangement in a page.

## 16.10 A lead line

Layer a melody over the beat. A lead is a sequence of pitched notes:

```scheme
(define (note->freq n) (* 440 (expt 2 (/ n 12.0))))

(define c-minor-riff
  '(-9 -6 -4 -2 -4 -6 -9 -12))          ; C4 down to C3

(define (play-lead semitones dur shape)
  (for-each
    (lambda (n) (audio/play 'tone (note->freq n) dur shape))
    semitones))

(play-lead c-minor-riff 0.125 'square)
```

A downward riff in C minor. Try `saw` for a heavier feel. Try `sine` for smoother.

To interleave the lead with the beat, alternate calls:

```scheme
(define (play-verse)
  (play-pattern bar-a)
  (play-lead c-minor-riff 0.125 'square))
```

Beats and lead. The chip-tune shape is emerging.

## 16.11 A macro for readability

Chapter 11 covered macros. Here's one that makes beat patterns read cleaner:

```scheme
(define-syntax bar
  (syntax-rules (- k s h c)
    ((_) (begin))
    ((_ - rest ...) (begin (bar rest ...)))
    ((_ k rest ...) (begin (synth/kit 'kick 0)  (bar rest ...)))
    ((_ s rest ...) (begin (synth/kit 'snare 0) (bar rest ...)))
    ((_ h rest ...) (begin (synth/kit 'hat 0)   (bar rest ...)))
    ((_ c rest ...) (begin (synth/kit 'clap 0)  (bar rest ...)))))

;; usage
(bar k h h s h k h s)                ; four-on-the-floor
(bar k - h s - k - c)                ; syncopated with clap
```

The `-` is a rest. Single letters for hits. Reads like a drum machine display. Compiles at read-time to sequential `synth/kit` calls.

## 16.12 Framebuffer basics

Chip-tune with matching visuals means also drawing. Motoi's framebuffer verbs (from the graphics module) give you:

- `fb/clear color` — fill the screen.
- `fb/pixel x y color` — set one pixel.
- `fb/rect x y w h color` — filled rectangle.
- `fb/circle cx cy r color` — filled circle.
- `fb/line x1 y1 x2 y2 color` — draw a line.

Colors are palette indices 0..15 (16-color palette, the classic constraint):

- 0 black
- 1 dark blue
- 2 purple
- 3 dark green
- 4 brown
- 5 dark gray
- 6 light gray
- 7 white
- 8 red
- 9 orange
- 10 yellow
- 11 green
- 12 blue
- 13 lavender
- 14 pink
- 15 peach

(Palette varies slightly by runtime; check `,help palette` at the REPL.)

A one-frame visual:

```scheme
(fb/clear 0)                        ; black background
(fb/circle 64 64 30 7)              ; white circle center-screen
(fb/rect 40 20 48 12 8)             ; red band
```

For animation, this pattern runs every frame with values derived from a time variable.

## 16.13 A per-frame loop

The game module gives you `big-bang`, a game loop that calls a step function every frame. In its full form:

```scheme
(big-bang initial-state
  :on-tick step-function
  :on-key  key-handler
  :draw    draw-function
  :fps     60)
```

For a minimal per-frame loop without input:

```scheme
(define (step state)
  ;; returns the next state
  (+ state 1))

(define (draw state)
  (fb/clear 0)
  (fb/circle (+ 64 (* 20 (sin (* state 0.1)))) 64 8 7))

;; runs until you stop it
(big-bang 0 :on-tick step :draw draw :fps 60)
```

A circle oscillates left and right. The state is a frame counter; the draw function uses `sin` to compute the x offset. Every frame: increment state, redraw.

## 16.14 Sync — the beat lights up

Now cross the streams. Drum hit = flash.

```scheme
(audio/tempo 120)

(define bar-a '(k h h s h k h s))

(define (play-and-flash step)
  ;; play the audio
  (case step
    ((k) (synth/kit 'kick 0))
    ((s) (synth/kit 'snare 0))
    ((h) (synth/kit 'hat 0))
    ((-) 'rest))
  ;; flash on kicks and snares
  (fb/clear 0)
  (case step
    ((k) (fb/circle 64 64 40 8))            ; big red circle on kick
    ((s) (fb/rect 20 30 88 60 7))           ; white flash on snare
    ((h) (fb/pixel 64 64 6))                ; tiny gray on hat
    ((-) 'no-visual)))

(for-each play-and-flash bar-a)
```

Each step both plays sound and draws. Because sound and motion are on one timeline (Chapter 12), they land together.

## 16.15 Motion tweens on the beat

Instead of instant flashes, use tweens to make the visuals move over time. From Chapter 12's palette:

```scheme
(bounce ball 1 0.15)          ; one bounce over 150ms
(fade ball 'flash 0.15)       ; brief brighten
(slide ball 'right 0.15)      ; slide right
```

A beat that puts a sprite through choreography:

```scheme
(define ball (list 'sprite 'ball 64 64))    ; conceptual sprite handle

(define (on-beat step)
  (case step
    ((k) (synth/kit 'kick 0)  (bounce ball 1 0.15))
    ((s) (synth/kit 'snare 0) (fade ball 'flash 0.15))
    ((h) (synth/kit 'hat 0)   (slide ball 'right 0.05))
    ((-) 'wait)))

(for-each on-beat '(k h h s h k h s))
```

The sprite bounces on kicks, flashes on snares, drifts on hats. Because motion and audio share the clock, the visual choreography lands with the sound.

## 16.16 A visualizer

A common demo-scene move: a shape reacts to the current audio state. Motoi's `audio/playing?` tells you if there's active audio; from there you can draw differently.

```scheme
(define (step state) (+ state 1))

(define (draw state)
  (fb/clear 0)
  (define pulse (if (audio/playing?) 40 20))
  (define x (+ 64 (* 30 (sin (* state 0.1)))))
  (define y (+ 64 (* 30 (cos (* state 0.1)))))
  (fb/circle x y pulse 8))
```

When audio is playing, the circle is bigger. Nothing fancy — but it's a visualizer.

For a real spectrum visualizer, you'd hook into the audio analysis module (`audio/spectrum`, `audio/onset?`) which lives outside the CORE. That's the next-book territory.

## 16.17 Envelopes for visual pulses

The classic demo-scene pulse is a shape that briefly grows and shrinks with each beat. In music-speak, this is the visual envelope — attack (grow fast), decay (shrink slower).

```scheme
(define (pulse-envelope frame beat-frame)
  ;; returns a size that pulses on the beat
  (define since (- frame beat-frame))
  (cond ((< since 3)  (+ 20 (* 10 (- 3 since))))    ; grow fast
        ((< since 12) (- 30 (* 1 (- since 3))))     ; decay slow
        (else 20)))
```

Combine with a step function that fires beats at intervals:

```scheme
(define (step state)
  (define frame (car state))
  (define last-beat (cadr state))
  (define next-beat-frame (+ last-beat 30))         ; beat every 30 frames
  (if (>= frame next-beat-frame)
      (begin
        (synth/kit 'kick 0)
        (list (+ frame 1) frame))
      (list (+ frame 1) last-beat)))

(define (draw state)
  (define frame (car state))
  (define last-beat (cadr state))
  (define size (pulse-envelope frame last-beat))
  (fb/clear 0)
  (fb/circle 64 64 size 8))

(big-bang '(0 0) :on-tick step :draw draw :fps 60)
```

A pulsing circle on every kick. Runs indefinitely. This is a demo-scene loop in about 15 lines.

## 16.18 A palette walk

Cycling colors across a shape is another demo-scene classic:

```scheme
(define (step state) (modulo (+ state 1) 240))     ; 0..239

(define (draw state)
  (fb/clear 0)
  (let loop ((i 0))
    (when (< i 16)
      (fb/rect (* i 8) 0 8 128 (modulo (+ i (quotient state 15)) 16))
      (loop (+ i 1)))))
```

16 vertical bars, each a palette color, cycling. Runs at 60 fps. It looks like a rainbow being pushed sideways.

## 16.19 Your first demo — a 30-second piece

Here is a full demo. Copy it. Run it. Change it.

```scheme
;; first-demo.scm
;; A 30-second chip-tune with matching visuals.

(audio/tempo 128)
(audio/master-volume 0.8)

(define (note->freq n) (* 440 (expt 2 (/ n 12.0))))

;; --- rhythm ---
(define kick-pattern  '(k - - - k - - - k - - - k - - -))
(define snare-pattern '(- - - - s - - - - - - - s - - -))
(define hat-pattern   '(h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h))

;; --- melody (in semitones from A4) ---
(define riff '(-5 -3 0 -3 -5 -3 -5 -3 -7 -5 -3 -5 -7 -5 -3 -5))

(define (play-step audio-fn step)
  (unless (eq? step '-) (audio-fn)))

(define (play-bar pattern audio-fn)
  (for-each (lambda (step) (play-step audio-fn step)) pattern))

;; --- one bar of everything ---
(define (bar visualize)
  ;; drums
  (for-each
    (lambda (i)
      (let ((k (list-ref kick-pattern i))
            (s (list-ref snare-pattern i))
            (h (list-ref hat-pattern i))
            (note (list-ref riff (modulo i 16))))
        ;; play each layer
        (unless (eq? k '-) (synth/kit 'kick 0))
        (unless (eq? s '-) (synth/kit 'snare 0))
        (unless (eq? h '-) (synth/kit 'hat 0))
        (audio/play 'tone (note->freq note) 0.11 'square)
        ;; visualize
        (when visualize
          (fb/clear 1)                          ; dark blue background
          (fb/circle 64 64 (if (eq? k '-) 20 40) 8)        ; kick pulse
          (when (not (eq? s '-))
            (fb/rect 10 30 108 60 7))                       ; snare flash
          (fb/pixel (modulo (+ i 32) 128) 64 10))))         ; hat spark
    (iota 16)))

(define (iota n) (let loop ((i 0)) (if (= i n) '() (cons i (loop (+ i 1))))))

;; --- structure: intro, verse, verse, breakdown, verse ---
(define (demo)
  (bar #t)     ; intro bar with visuals
  (bar #t)     ; second intro
  (bar #t)     ; verse
  (bar #t)     ; verse
  (audio/halt) ; breakdown — silence
  (bar #t)     ; return
  (bar #t))    ; final

(demo)
```

Run it:

```
$ bin/motoi run first-demo.scm
```

Six bars, ~30 seconds at 128 bpm. Drums, melody, matching visuals. That is a demo.

## 16.20 What to change first

Learning happens by modification. Try these:

1. **Change the pattern.** Swap `kick-pattern` and `snare-pattern`. What happens?
2. **Change the tempo.** `(audio/tempo 90)` vs `(audio/tempo 160)`.
3. **Change the melody.** Rewrite `riff` with your own semitone sequence.
4. **Change the shape.** `'sine` or `'saw` instead of `'square`.
5. **Change the colors.** Try `(fb/clear 3)` for dark green; palette index for the circle to 10 (yellow).
6. **Add a hat variant** — change some `h` to `-` in `hat-pattern`.
7. **Double the length** — call `(bar #t)` more times.
8. **Add a second melody line** — a bass an octave down. Play it alongside the lead.

Every change compiles and runs immediately. There is no build. This is the demo-scene tight loop.

## 16.21 Beyond the first demo

The techniques from here scale up:

- **Longer arrangements.** Chain more bars, change patterns bar-by-bar, build tension.
- **Volume automation.** Use `(audio/master-volume v)` to fade sections in and out.
- **Sync to visuals.** Compute frame timing from BPM to know exactly when a beat lands.
- **Reactive visuals.** Draw shapes whose size depends on audio state.
- **Scenes.** Chain multiple visuals with `motion/on-settle` triggering the next.
- **Cortex-aware demos.** Save the melody the user liked from a previous run (Chapter 13).

Each of these is a small extension. The core loop — play something, draw something, on a shared clock — stays the same.

## 16.22 A note on aesthetics

Chip-tune and demo-scene aren't nostalgia genres because they use old sounds. They're aesthetic disciplines because they *choose constraints*. Four voices. Sixteen colors. A hundred lines of code. The constraint is the point.

Motoi lets you have those constraints or not. You can import more modules, use more colors (some backends), write longer programs. But there's a specific pleasure in staying inside the small palette — square wave, kick, snare, hat, sixteen colors, one screen. That pleasure is what the genre is for.

Give yourself the constraint. See what you make.

## 16.23 What the book was for

If you've read to here, you know:

- How Motoi compares to ten major languages, honestly.
- What Motoi is good at that other languages aren't (macros as composition, sound+motion on one timeline, Cortex, SLAT substrate, frozen core).
- How to make a beat.
- How to draw shapes.
- How to sync them.
- How to build a small demo you can share with someone.

You should now be able to open a text file, type Motoi, and make things that look and sound like things you meant to make. That was the whole target.

If you go further and build a longer piece, an audiovisual toy, a small game, a teaching tool — the language is here. The reference is one file. The REPL is right there. The core is small enough to hold in your head, and the module surface is documented.

There is nothing more to teach. There is only what you'll make.

— The Motoi maintainers, Brooklyn, 2026

"# Chapter 17 — Frames Buffered

There is a moment in every kid's first hour with Motoi where they type

```scheme
(circle 10 10 5)
```

into the REPL, hit enter, and nothing happens. Something happened — the pixels landed in the framebuffer. But the REPL prints `()` and the kid stares at it and concludes graphics don't work.

They do work. The missing pieces are two verbs and one habit:

- `(begin-frame)` — start collecting drawing calls for this frame.
- `(end-frame)` — stop collecting.
- `(render)` — hand the finished frame to whatever's showing it.

Wrap your drawing in those three and the pixels *appear*. Every scene in this chapter follows the same skeleton:

```scheme
(clear)         ; wipe the previous frame
(begin-frame)   ; start recording
;; ... draw stuff ...
(end-frame)     ; stop recording
(render)        ; show it
```

If nothing else in this chapter sticks, that skeleton should. The next ten sections are ten scenes built from it — some standing still, some moving, some listening to keys, some making sound. Each one is a complete runnable program. Each one has been verified. If you type it in exactly and don't see the picture, something is wrong with the runtime, not with you.

The scenes deliberately mix two ways of naming the same thing. Motoi has one true drawing verb per shape — `rect`, `rect-fill`, `pset` — and a handful of aliases (`rectangle`, `fill-rect`, `filled-rectangle`, `draw-rect`, `pixel`, `put-pixel`, `set-pixel!`, `plot-pixel`) that dispatch to the same code. Every alias appears somewhere in the ten scenes below. The point is that whichever name your fingers already know from another Scheme, another drawing library, another day, it just works.

The framebuffer is 80 pixels by 80 pixels unless you call `(set-mode w h)` to change it. Coordinates start at `(0, 0)` in the top-left. Y grows downward, which is confusing the first time and normal after.

## 17.1 A house

Every kid's graphics journey starts with a house. Sky on top, grass underneath, a square box for the walls, a triangle for the roof, a door, a window, and a sun off in the corner. Six shapes layered back to front, six colors. If you have ever drawn a house in crayon you already know how to write this.

```scheme
;; A house — the composed scene that starts every kid's graphics journey.
(clear)
(begin-frame)
;; sky
(set-color 'blue)
(rect-fill 0 0 80 55)
;; grass
(set-color 'green)
(rect-fill 0 55 80 25)
;; house body
(set-color 'brown)
(rect-fill 25 40 30 25)
;; roof — a triangle out of three lines
(set-color 'red)
(line 25 40 40 25)
(line 40 25 55 40)
(line 25 40 55 40)
;; door
(set-color 'dark-purple)
(rect-fill 37 50 7 15)
;; window
(set-color 'yellow)
(rect-fill 28 45 6 6)
;; sun
(set-color 'orange)
(disc 68 12 6)
(end-frame)
(render)
```

**What you see.** A blue sky, green grass, a brown box with a red triangular roof, a purple door, a small yellow window, and an orange sun in the top right. Order matters — the sky went first so everything else paints over it. If you drew the sky last, the sky would cover the house.

## 17.2 A moon rising over hills

Night sky, a scatter of stars, a crescent moon made by drawing a smaller dark disc over a lighter one, and three overlapping dark-green discs sitting low on the frame that read as hills. The trick worth stealing: you can subtract shapes by painting the background color over them.

```scheme
;; A moon rising over hills — night scene with a single bright dot for a star.
(clear)
(begin-frame)
;; night sky
(set-color 'dark-blue)
(rect-fill 0 0 80 80)
;; a scatter of stars — single pixels
(set-color 'white)
(pset 8 5)
(pset 15 12)
(pset 22 8)
(pset 33 15)
(pset 48 6)
(pset 62 11)
(pset 74 14)
;; the moon
(set-color 'yellow)
(disc 60 22 8)
;; a bite taken out of the moon so it reads as a crescent
(set-color 'dark-blue)
(disc 55 20 7)
;; distant hills — two overlapping arcs faked with discs low on the frame
(set-color 'dark-green)
(disc 20 78 22)
(disc 55 82 25)
(disc 78 80 18)
;; the horizon line
(set-color 'green)
(line 0 60 79 60)
(end-frame)
(render)
```

**What you see.** A dark blue sky, seven white star pixels, a yellow crescent moon (the missing bite is the color of the sky), a green horizon line, and three overlapping dark-green hills poking up from the bottom. Compose it, then take one shape away — the scene falls apart. Every element is doing work.

## 17.3 A flag on a pole

Three colored stripes, an outline around them, a pole underneath, and a knob on top. This is the first scene to use one of the alias names — `rectangle` instead of `rect`. If your fingers learned `rectangle` in another language, use it here; the framebuffer doesn't care which name you typed.

```scheme
;; A flag on a pole.
;; Uses the `rectangle` alias (a synonym for `rect`) — canonical in
;; most other Scheme graphics libs, and typing it should just work.
(clear)
(begin-frame)
;; sky
(set-color 'blue)
(rect-fill 0 0 80 80)
;; the pole
(set-color 'dark-grey)
(line 20 15 20 70)
;; the flag — three horizontal stripes
(set-color 'red)
(rect-fill 20 15 40 8)
(set-color 'white)
(rect-fill 20 23 40 8)
(set-color 'green)
(rect-fill 20 31 40 8)
;; an outline around the whole flag using the `rectangle` alias
(set-color 'black)
(rectangle 20 15 40 24)
;; the star knob at the top of the pole
(set-color 'yellow)
(disc 20 13 3)
(end-frame)
(render)
```

**What you see.** A pale blue sky, a grey vertical pole, a horizontal tricolor flag (red-white-green) with a black border, and a small yellow knob at the pole's top.

## 17.4 A face

Two eyes, two pupils, a nose, a mouth. The face is a filled peach disc with a brown outline. The pupils are single pixels, drawn using the `pixel` alias. One tiny dot in the middle of the eye is the difference between the face looking at you and the face staring past you.

```scheme
;; A face — head, eyes, mouth. Two lines and some circles.
;; Uses the `pixel` alias for single-dot pupils.
(clear)
(begin-frame)
;; background
(set-color 'lavender)
(rect-fill 0 0 80 80)
;; head — a big filled disc
(set-color 'peach)
(disc 40 40 25)
;; outline the head
(set-color 'brown)
(circle 40 40 25)
;; eyes — the whites
(set-color 'white)
(disc 30 34 4)
(disc 50 34 4)
;; pupils — single pixels using the `pixel` alias
(set-color 'black)
(pixel 30 34)
(pixel 50 34)
;; mouth — a smile drawn as two short lines
(set-color 'red)
(line 30 50 40 55)
(line 40 55 50 50)
;; a nose — a tiny line down the middle
(set-color 'brown)
(line 40 40 40 46)
(end-frame)
(render)
```

**What you see.** A round peach face on a lavender background. Two small white eyes with black pupils centered inside them. A short brown nose. A red smile made of two lines meeting at the chin.

## 17.5 A bouncing ball

The first animation. `on-frame` installs a callback that runs every frame; `tick-frame` advances the loop one step deterministically (useful in scripts — in the REPL the loop runs on its own). The ball accelerates down, hits the floor, loses some energy, and bounces.

```scheme
;; A bouncing ball — the first animation.
;; on-frame installs a callback; tick-frame advances the loop
;; deterministically for scripts (in a REPL the loop runs on its own).
(define ball-y 10)
(define ball-vy 1)

(on-frame
  (lambda (f)
    ;; physics — accelerate down, bounce off the floor
    (set! ball-vy (+ ball-vy 1))
    (set! ball-y (+ ball-y ball-vy))
    (if (>= ball-y 70)
        (begin
          (set! ball-y 70)
          (set! ball-vy (- 0 (quotient (* ball-vy 3) 4)))))
    ;; draw
    (clear)
    (begin-frame)
    (set-color 'blue)
    (rect-fill 0 0 80 80)
    (set-color 'green)
    (rect-fill 0 72 80 8)
    (set-color 'red)
    (disc 40 ball-y 5)
    (end-frame)))

;; tick 20 frames — enough for one full arc + a bounce
(let loop ((i 0))
  (if (< i 20)
      (begin (tick-frame) (loop (+ i 1)))))
(render)
```

**What you see (motion).** A red disc falls from near the top of a blue sky onto a green floor at the bottom, bounces once at reduced height, and rests. In the REPL, `(on-frame ...)` alone kicks off the loop and you watch the animation live; in the script version, `tick-frame` is what advances time.

## 17.6 Rain

Twenty little drops per frame, each a short vertical line with a single-pixel head. The drops are placed pseudo-randomly using a tiny linear congruential generator so the demo is deterministic. This one uses the `put-pixel` alias for the drop heads.

```scheme
;; Rain — pseudo-random drops that streak down and repeat.
;; Uses the `put-pixel` alias for the drop heads.
;; A tiny LCG stands in for randomness so the demo is deterministic.
(define seed 1)
(define (next-rand)
  (set! seed (remainder (+ (* seed 1103515245) 12345) 2147483648))
  seed)
(define (rand-mod n) (remainder (next-rand) n))

(on-frame
  (lambda (f)
    (clear)
    (begin-frame)
    ;; storm-grey sky
    (set-color 'dark-grey)
    (rect-fill 0 0 80 80)
    ;; puddled ground
    (set-color 'dark-blue)
    (rect-fill 0 72 80 8)
    ;; twenty drops per frame, streaked
    (set-color 'blue)
    (let loop ((i 0))
      (if (< i 20)
          (let ((x (rand-mod 80))
                (y (rand-mod 72)))
            (line x y x (+ y 3))     ; streak
            (put-pixel x (+ y 3))    ; the drop head
            (loop (+ i 1)))))
    (end-frame)))

(tick-frame)
(tick-frame)
(tick-frame)
(render)
```

**What you see (motion).** A dark grey scene with a strip of dark blue puddle across the bottom. Twenty pale blue vertical streaks per frame, each ending in a single-pixel drop head. Every frame regenerates. In the REPL it looks like real rain; in scripts you get one frozen snapshot per `tick-frame`.

## 17.7 A tone drawn as its own shape

Sound and picture on the same timeline. A C major scale plays, and as each note fires, a yellow bar grows taller. The bar height encodes pitch: low note, short bar; high note, tall bar. You hear the scale climb, and you see it climb.

```scheme
;; A tone drawn as its own shape.
;; When you hear the note, the frame shows the frequency as a bar.
;; A scale plays and the bar grows with the pitch.
(define (note->freq semitones)
  (* 440 (expt 2 (/ semitones 12.0))))

(define scale (list -9 -7 -5 -4 -2 0 2 3))   ; C major, C4→C5

(define (draw-bar height)
  (clear)
  (begin-frame)
  (set-color 'black)
  (rect-fill 0 0 80 80)
  (set-color 'yellow)
  ;; a vertical bar centered — taller for higher notes
  (rect-fill 30 (- 70 height) 20 height)
  (set-color 'white)
  (rectangle 30 (- 70 height) 20 height)
  (end-frame))

(for-each
  (lambda (semi)
    (tone (note->freq semi) 0.15)
    (draw-bar (+ 10 (* 5 (+ semi 9)))))
  scale)

(render)
```

**What you see and hear.** Eight sine-wave notes rising from middle C to C5, at 150 ms each. For each note, a yellow bar with a white outline paints on a black frame. The bar grows taller with each higher note. The final rendered frame shows the last (tallest) bar.

## 17.8 Catch the pixel

The first game. A paddle at the bottom of the screen catches a falling pixel. Left and right arrow keys move the paddle. Every time the paddle catches the pixel, a white dot lights up along the top of the screen — the score. This one uses two aliases: `filled-rectangle` for the paddle and `set-pixel!` for the falling drop.

```scheme
;; Catch the pixel — a small game shape.
;; A paddle at the bottom follows the arrow keys; a single pixel
;; falls from the top. Score a point when the paddle catches it.
;; Uses `filled-rectangle` for the paddle and `set-pixel!` for the drop.
(define paddle-x 35)
(define drop-x 20)
(define drop-y 0)
(define score 0)

(on-key
  (lambda (k)
    (cond
      ((eq? k 'left)  (set! paddle-x (max 0 (- paddle-x 4))))
      ((eq? k 'right) (set! paddle-x (min 70 (+ paddle-x 4)))))))

(on-frame
  (lambda (f)
    ;; drop physics
    (set! drop-y (+ drop-y 2))
    (if (> drop-y 78)
        (begin
          ;; caught if the pixel lands over the paddle
          (if (and (>= drop-x paddle-x) (<= drop-x (+ paddle-x 10)))
              (set! score (+ score 1)))
          (set! drop-y 0)
          (set! drop-x (remainder (+ (* drop-x 7) 13) 78))))
    (clear)
    (begin-frame)
    ;; background + score line
    (set-color 'dark-blue)
    (rect-fill 0 0 80 80)
    ;; the paddle
    (set-color 'peach)
    (filled-rectangle paddle-x 74 10 3)
    ;; the drop
    (set-color 'yellow)
    (set-pixel! drop-x drop-y)
    ;; score marks — one white pixel per point along the top row
    (set-color 'white)
    (let loop ((i 0))
      (if (< i score)
          (begin (pset (+ 2 (* i 2)) 2) (loop (+ i 1)))))
    (end-frame)))

;; Simulate one press and 60 frames.
(fire-key 'right)
(fire-key 'right)
(let loop ((i 0))
  (if (< i 60)
      (begin (tick-frame) (loop (+ i 1)))))
(render)
```

**What you see (interactive).** A dark blue field. A small peach paddle sits near the bottom, movable with the left and right arrow keys. A single yellow pixel falls from the top. When it hits the bottom, one of two things happens: the paddle was under it (a white score-pixel appears at the top) or the paddle wasn't (nothing lights up). Either way the pixel resets to the top and falls again. `fire-key` in the script version is how you simulate keypresses without a keyboard.

## 17.9 A sunrise

The sun climbs, the sky shifts through moods, and each frame plays a rising note as the sun rises. A soft closing note fires at the end. This is the first scene to fold together animation, changing color state, and pitch that tracks position.

```scheme
;; Sunrise — the sun climbs and the sky brightens.
;; Each dawn frame plays a rising note. The last frame plays a soft chord.
(define sun-y 80)

(define (sky-color y)
  ;; further from the horizon → darker blue
  (cond
    ((> y 60) 'dark-blue)
    ((> y 40) 'blue)
    ((> y 20) 'lavender)
    (else     'peach)))

(on-frame
  (lambda (f)
    (set! sun-y (max 15 (- sun-y 3)))
    (clear)
    (begin-frame)
    ;; sky in the current mood
    (set-color (sky-color sun-y))
    (rect-fill 0 0 80 60)
    ;; ground
    (set-color 'brown)
    (rect-fill 0 60 80 20)
    ;; hills
    (set-color 'dark-green)
    (disc 25 62 12)
    (disc 60 65 15)
    ;; sun
    (set-color 'yellow)
    (disc 40 sun-y 8)
    (set-color 'orange)
    (circle 40 sun-y 8)
    (end-frame)
    ;; a rising note as the sun climbs
    (tone (+ 220 (* 4 (- 80 sun-y))) 0.05)))

;; 20 ticks — the sun rises from 80 to ~20
(let loop ((i 0))
  (if (< i 20)
      (begin (tick-frame) (loop (+ i 1)))))

;; a soft closing note
(note 'C5 0.3)
(render)
```

**What you see and hear.** A yellow sun climbs from below the horizon toward the top of the frame. As it rises, the sky shifts from dark blue to blue to lavender to peach. Two dark-green hills sit on brown ground. A short sine-wave tone plays every frame, rising in pitch as the sun rises. At the end, a single C5 note plays as a closing beat.

## 17.10 A small demo

The final scene folds everything in: a starfield, a color marquee, a bouncing shape, and two-note beats fired on a schedule tied to the frame counter. The last three aliases — `draw-rect`, `fill-rect`, `plot-pixel` — all appear here.

```scheme
;; A small demo scene — everything at once.
;; Marquee text simulated as a colored bar, a bouncing shape, star field,
;; and a two-note motif that fires with the beat. This uses the last
;; three aliases: `draw-rect`, `fill-rect`, and `plot-pixel`.

(define seed 7)
(define (next-rand)
  (set! seed (remainder (+ (* seed 1103515245) 12345) 2147483648))
  seed)
(define (rand-mod n) (remainder (next-rand) n))

(define shape-x 40)
(define shape-vx 3)

(on-frame
  (lambda (f)
    ;; bounce the shape
    (set! shape-x (+ shape-x shape-vx))
    (if (or (< shape-x 8) (> shape-x 72))
        (set! shape-vx (- 0 shape-vx)))
    (clear)
    (begin-frame)
    ;; black space background
    (set-color 'black)
    (fill-rect 0 0 80 80)
    ;; star field — random single pixels using plot-pixel
    (set-color 'white)
    (let loop ((i 0))
      (if (< i 15)
          (begin
            (plot-pixel (rand-mod 80) (rand-mod 80))
            (loop (+ i 1)))))
    ;; a horizon bar
    (set-color 'dark-purple)
    (fill-rect 0 55 80 4)
    ;; the \"marquee\" — colored bar at the top
    (set-color 'pink)
    (fill-rect 5 5 70 8)
    ;; frame it with draw-rect
    (set-color 'white)
    (draw-rect 5 5 70 8)
    ;; the bouncing shape
    (set-color 'yellow)
    (disc shape-x 40 6)
    (set-color 'orange)
    (circle shape-x 40 6)
    (end-frame)
    ;; every 4th frame plays a beat
    (if (= (remainder f 4) 0) (tone 220 0.05))
    (if (= (remainder f 8) 0) (tone 440 0.05))))

(let loop ((i 0))
  (if (< i 16)
      (begin (tick-frame) (loop (+ i 1)))))
(render)
```

**What you see and hear.** A black field with fifteen white star pixels. A pink marquee bar with a white outline near the top. A dark-purple horizon line across the middle. A yellow-and-orange disc bouncing left and right through the center. A low tone every fourth frame, a higher tone every eighth frame — a simple two-note motif. Sixteen frames total in the script version; the REPL version keeps running.

## 17.11 Now build your own

You have ten skeletons. Each one starts with `(clear)`, wraps drawing in `(begin-frame)` and `(end-frame)`, and ends with `(render)`. Animation just puts the drawing inside `(on-frame ...)`; input adds `(on-key ...)`; sound adds `(tone ...)` or `(note ...)`. The verbs compose. Try:

- Change the house's colors. Add a chimney.
- Give the moon two crescent shapes. Add a shooting star that moves per frame.
- Turn the flag into your country's flag (or make one up).
- Give the face eyebrows. Make it wink by leaving one eye closed on odd frames.
- Add gravity to catch-the-pixel. Add a lose condition.
- Layer three scales in the tone-shape scene, one after another.

If you type `(circle 10 10 5)` and nothing happens, remember: you forgot the frame. Wrap it. Render. There it is.
")

"# Chapter 18 — Fantasy Console Mode

If you spent afternoons in TIC-80, or you kept a PICO-8 tab open next to your homework, or you dreamed in LIKO-12 palettes, this is the chapter where Motoi starts to feel like home. The framebuffer, the input, the audio, the tiny cart file that holds a whole game — they compose the same way `cls`/`circ`/`spr`/`btn`/`sfx` do. Same shape. Different spelling. Different insides. Same afternoon.

Motoi is not a fantasy console. It is a Scheme with fantasy-console verbs bolted on next to `map` and `let*`. That distinction matters — you can drop into the language whenever the console pattern gets in your way, and drop back out when it doesn't. But if you never leave the console pattern, that is also fine. Everything a kid needs to make a small game is one page of vocabulary.

## 18.1 The screen

You get a framebuffer. Default resolution is 80 by 80. You can change it.

```scheme
(mode-info)         ; => (80 80)  — the current width and height
(set-mode 240 136)  ; TIC-80's native size
(mode-info)         ; => (240 136)
(set-mode 128 128)  ; PICO-8's native size
(set-mode 80 80)    ; back to the default
```

The origin is the top-left, at `(0, 0)`. X grows right; Y grows *down*. The first time you draw at `y=0`, the pixel appears at the top of the screen, which is what every graphics library agrees on and what every kid has to un-learn from math class exactly once.

Colors come from a fixed palette. Every color is a name — `'red`, `'blue`, `'yellow`, `'orange`, `'peach`, `'brown`, `'pink`, `'lavender`, `'white`, `'black`, `'dark-blue`, `'dark-green`, `'dark-grey`, `'dark-purple`, `'green`. Under the hood the name resolves to a small integer index (Motoi's palette is 16-color-ish, PICO-8-shaped, but you use names in code and never think about the number). Pick a color with `set-color` and every drawing verb after it uses that color until you pick another.

```scheme
(set-color 'red)     ; every draw call after this is red
(set-color 'dark-blue)
```

## 18.2 The frame skeleton

Every drawing you make sits inside four verbs:

```scheme
(clear)         ; wipe the previous frame
(begin-frame)   ; start recording
;; ... draw stuff ...
(end-frame)     ; stop recording
(render)        ; show the finished frame
```

Chapter 17 belabors this point, because kids type `(circle 10 10 5)` at the REPL and stare at `()` and think graphics are broken. Graphics are not broken. The frame is not open. Open the frame, draw, close the frame, render. Every scene in this chapter follows that skeleton. In the REPL, `(on-frame ...)` pumps the loop for you; in a `.scm` cart you run with `motoi run`, `tick-frame` advances one frame at a time and the last `(render)` prints the result.

## 18.3 The draw primitives

Here is the whole vocabulary:

```scheme
(circle cx cy r)          ; outline circle
(disc cx cy r)            ; filled circle
(line x1 y1 x2 y2)        ; a line
(rect x y w h)            ; outline rectangle
(rect-fill x y w h)       ; filled rectangle
(pset x y)                ; one pixel
(draw-text x y \"str\")     ; a string at pixel coords
(clear)                   ; wipe the frame
(background 'color)       ; alias for clear + set-color + fill
(bg-clear)                ; alias for clear (kept for typing muscle memory)
```

Motoi carries aliases for the shapes so whichever name your fingers already know from another language works here too:

- `rect-fill` also answers to `fill-rect`, `filled-rectangle`.
- `rect` also answers to `rectangle`, `draw-rect`.
- `pset` also answers to `pixel`, `put-pixel`, `set-pixel!`, `plot-pixel`.

All ten of those names dispatch to the same code. Type whichever one you learned first. This is deliberate — the point of a fantasy console is not to make you memorize new verbs; the point is that the verb you already know just works.

Here is TIC-80's vocabulary next to Motoi's:

```
TIC-80              Motoi
─────────────────   ─────────────────────────
cls(c)              (clear) then (set-color c) (rect-fill 0 0 W H)
circ(x,y,r,c)       (set-color c) (disc x y r)
circb(x,y,r,c)      (set-color c) (circle x y r)
rect(x,y,w,h,c)     (set-color c) (rect-fill x y w h)
rectb(x,y,w,h,c)    (set-color c) (rect x y w h)
line(x1,y1,x2,y2,c) (set-color c) (line x1 y1 x2 y2)
pix(x,y,c)          (set-color c) (pset x y)
print(s,x,y,c)      (set-color c) (draw-text x y s)
btn(id)             (input/down?  'left) etc.
btnp(id)            (input/pressed? 'left) etc.
sfx(n)              (sfx 'name)   or (tone freq dur)
```

If TIC-80's `cls`/`circ`/`rect` are still in your fingers, define them as one-line wrappers and use them verbatim:

```scheme
;; TIC-80-style aliases — a kid coming from tic can paste this
;; block at the top of any cart and their old code compiles.
(define (cls c) (set-color c) (rect-fill 0 0 80 80))
(define (circ x y r c) (set-color c) (disc x y r))
(define (circb x y r c) (set-color c) (circle x y r))

(set-mode 80 80)
(clear)
(begin-frame)
(cls 'dark-blue)
(circ 40 40 15 'yellow)
(circb 40 40 15 'orange)
(end-frame)
(render)
```

## 18.4 The frame loop

Motoi does not have a magic `TIC()` global. You register a frame handler with `on-frame`:

```scheme
(define t 0)
(on-frame
  (lambda (f)
    (set! t (+ t 1))
    (clear)
    (begin-frame)
    (set-color 'dark-blue)
    (rect-fill 0 0 80 80)
    (set-color 'yellow)
    (disc 40 40 (+ 5 (remainder t 10)))
    (end-frame)))
```

`f` is the frame counter; it starts at zero and increments each tick. Inside the REPL the display driver pumps `on-frame` on its own. Inside a script you run with `motoi run`, you advance frames by calling `(tick-frame)` — usually inside a loop — and end with `(render)` to show the last one.

If you prefer to thread state through pure functions instead of mutating a global, `big-bang` is the state-threading variant (borrowed from Racket):

```scheme
(define (step state) (+ state 1))
(define (draw state)
  (clear) (begin-frame)
  (set-color 'dark-blue) (rect-fill 0 0 80 80)
  (set-color 'yellow) (disc 40 40 (+ 5 (remainder state 10)))
  (end-frame))

(big-bang 0
  (on-tick step)
  (to-draw draw))
```

Both shapes are fine. Global `set!` reads faster to Lua eyes; `big-bang` composes better as programs grow. This book alternates between them without apology — the model has to see both.

## 18.5 Input

Two shapes, matching TIC-80's mental model.

**Callback shape.** Hand a lambda to `on-key` or `on-mouse`. It fires whenever the event happens.

```scheme
(on-key
  (lambda (k)
    (cond
      ((eq? k 'left)  (set! px (max 0  (- px 4))))
      ((eq? k 'right) (set! px (min 76 (+ px 4))))
      ((eq? k 'up)    (set! py (max 0  (- py 4))))
      ((eq? k 'down)  (set! py (min 76 (+ py 4)))))))

(on-mouse
  (lambda (mx my button)
    (set! px mx)
    (set! py my)))
```

**Polling shape.** Ask each frame whether a button is currently pressed. This is the shape TIC-80 uses:

```scheme
(input/buttons)         ; => (up down left right a b)
(input/down?    'left)  ; => #t/#f — held right now?
(input/pressed? 'a)     ; => #t/#f — went down this frame?
```

Use whichever fits the game. Puzzles → polling. Instruments → callbacks. Both are fine; you can mix them in one cart.

For scripts and tests, `fire-key` and `fire-mouse` synthesize events so you can drive a cart without a keyboard:

```scheme
(fire-key 'right)
(fire-key 'right)
(fire-mouse 40 40 'left)
```

## 18.6 Sound

Motoi's audio is on the same timeline as the framebuffer. You do not need a mixer, a channel manager, or a permission gate you keep forgetting to call. Play a tone; a tone plays.

```scheme
(tone 440 0.2)          ; 440 Hz for 200 ms
(note 'C4 0.15)         ; a named pitch, 150 ms
(chord '(C4 E4 G4) 0.3) ; three notes together
(melody '((C4 0.15) (E4 0.15) (G4 0.15) (C5 0.3)))
```

Drum kit — the classic fantasy-console voices:

```scheme
(kick 0.2)              ; the bass drum
(snare 0.1)             ; the snare
(hat 0.05)              ; the hi-hat
(sfx 'coin)             ; a named preset — see the sfx registry
```

Under the hood everything routes through `synth/kit`, which is Motoi's tone engine — square, saw, sine, triangle, noise. Chapter 12 covers the theory. Chapter 16 (Jesse's Making Beats) builds a full chip-tune. This chapter uses just enough to make a game beep and a beat drop.

Sound and picture cost about the same in Motoi. If you can make a game, you can make a game with music. If you can make a game with music, you can make a demo. The distance from Chapter 18 to a demo you would show someone is small.

## 18.7 The IDE and the REPL

This is what the old draft never had.

Motoi ships two authoring surfaces. Both talk to the same runtime, so a cart you write in one runs in the other.

**The browser IDE** — launched with `motoi ide`, defaults to `127.0.0.1:3737`. Three panels:

- Left: a file tree of your project.
- Center: a tabbed editor. Cherry-pink · leaf-green · trunk-brown stripes across the top match the Motoi logo.
- Right: the REPL. Every eval you run from the editor prints its result here. Motoi Copilot lives here too — the tone is dry, the answers are grounded in the actual registry.

Header buttons: **Run** (Cmd/Ctrl+Enter — run current selection or line), **Explain** (F2 — Copilot explains the selection), **Boot CPU** and **CPU** (open the CPU visualization panel — the bottom band that shows fuel used, environment size, and the currently-executing form), **Pair** (turn on ambient completions).

Editor mode is switchable — `basic`, `vim`, or `emacs`. Pick from settings:

- **Basic.** Cmd/Ctrl+Enter runs. F2 explains.
- **Vim.** Type `:` to open a small command line. `:w` saves. `:q` closes the tab. `:explain` runs Copilot on the current selection. `:pair-on` / `:pair-off` toggles ambient completions. It is deliberately not a full vim — a kid should not be trapped in one.
- **Emacs.** `M-e` explains the selection. F2 still works.

**The terminal IDE** — launched with `motoi tui`. Four regions: file tree · editor · REPL · status. Same runtime as the browser IDE, so a cart written in one is a cart runnable in the other. If you prefer a terminal to a browser, this is the one you use.

**The REPL alone** — `motoi repl`. Comma-commands give you the introspection surface a fantasy console needs:

```
,help <verb>      Print the verb signature, docstring, contract, examples, source.
,type <verb>      Just the contract.
,doc <verb>       Just the docstring.
,arity <verb>     Just the arity.
,source <verb>    Where the impl lives.
,examples <verb>  The tiered examples — novice/intermediate/expert.
,apropos <regex>  Every symbol whose name matches.
,namespace <ns>   Every verb in a namespace.
,time <expr>      Evaluate + print wall time and fuel used.
,expand <expr>    Show the macroexpanded form.
,ask <question>   Ask Motoi Copilot (registry-grounded).
,exit             Bye.
```

`,help disc` at the REPL prints a colored help card — signature, doc, contract, one novice example, one intermediate, one expert. That card is how you learn a new verb without leaving the REPL. If the verb does not exist, `,help` tells you and you go back to `,apropos`.

**The end-to-end shape a kid follows:**

1. `motoi ide` — the browser opens on `localhost:3737`.
2. In the center pane, type a cart:

   ```scheme
   (set-mode 80 80)
   (clear) (begin-frame)
   (set-color 'dark-blue) (rect-fill 0 0 80 80)
   (set-color 'yellow) (disc 40 40 15)
   (end-frame) (render)
   ```

3. Cmd/Ctrl+Enter, or the **Run** button. The REPL panel prints `[object Object]` (that's the frame handle) and the framebuffer holds a yellow disc on a blue background.
4. Select `(disc 40 40 15)` and press F2. Copilot explains what the verb does, grounded in the actual registry.
5. Save the file. Load it from `motoi run` later. Same cart, same behavior.

That is the whole loop. There is nothing else to learn to make a game.

## 18.8 The cart file format

A Motoi cart is a `.scm` file. Convention — not enforcement — is that carts start with a small header comment naming the cart and crediting the author, then define state at the top, install callbacks in the middle, and end with `(render)` or nothing at all (the display driver pumps `on-frame` on its own in the REPL).

```scheme
;; catch-the-pixel — a small game
;; by <you> · 2026-07-19
;; controls: left/right arrows

(set-mode 80 80)

(define score 0)
(define paddle-x 35)
(define drop-x 20)
(define drop-y 0)

(on-key
  (lambda (k)
    (cond
      ((eq? k 'left)  (set! paddle-x (max 0  (- paddle-x 4))))
      ((eq? k 'right) (set! paddle-x (min 70 (+ paddle-x 4)))))))

(on-frame
  (lambda (f)
    (set! drop-y (+ drop-y 2))
    (when (> drop-y 78)
      (when (and (>= drop-x paddle-x) (<= drop-x (+ paddle-x 10)))
        (set! score (+ score 1)))
      (set! drop-y 0)
      (set! drop-x (remainder (+ (* drop-x 7) 13) 78)))
    (clear)
    (begin-frame)
    (set-color 'dark-blue) (rect-fill 0 0 80 80)
    (set-color 'peach)     (fill-rect paddle-x 74 10 3)
    (set-color 'yellow)    (set-pixel! drop-x drop-y)
    (set-color 'white)
    (let loop ((i 0))
      (when (< i score) (pset (+ 2 (* i 2)) 2) (loop (+ i 1))))
    (end-frame)
    (when (= (remainder f 8) 0) (tone 220 0.05))))
```

That is a whole game in one file. Load it with `motoi run catch-the-pixel.scm`, or open it in the IDE and press Run.

**Save + load through the runtime.** Motoi has two verbs for cart persistence, both scoped to `~/.motoi/carts/`:

```scheme
(save-cart \"starfield.scm\"
  \"(set-mode 80 80) (clear) (begin-frame)
   (set-color 'black) (rect-fill 0 0 80 80)
   (set-color 'white) (pset 10 10) (pset 20 30) (pset 40 50)
   (end-frame) (render)\")
;; => \"/Users/you/.motoi/carts/starfield.scm\"

(load-cart \"starfield.scm\")
;; => \"/Users/you/.motoi/carts/starfield.scm\"
;;    (the absolute path — from there, (motoi run <path>) or open in the IDE)
```

`save-cart` takes a bare filename (no slashes) and the cart source; it writes to `~/.motoi/carts/` and returns the absolute path. `load-cart` resolves the same filename to the absolute path — Motoi does not auto-evaluate carts on load; you get the path and run it explicitly. The cart directory is a safe, well-known place for the model to point kids at — no shell escapes, no random writes, no surprises.

## 18.9 A note on the old API

If you have read older Motoi material — early book drafts, the recovery archive at `Scheme/BOOK-OF-JESSE/05-fantasy-console-mode.book.slatl` — you may have seen `surface-paint-dots`, `surface-paint-text`, `clear-surface-layer`, `paint-cell`, `system/surface`. Those verbs do not exist in the current runtime. They were a lower-level surface API from an early sketch that got replaced by the flat draw verbs above. If you meet code that uses them:

- `(surface-paint-dots surf 'base dots color)` becomes `(set-color color)` then `(pset x y)` per dot (or `disc`/`circle` for shapes).
- `(surface-paint-text surf str x y ...)` becomes `(set-color color) (draw-text x y str)`.
- `(clear-surface-layer surf 'base)` becomes `(clear)`.
- `(paint-cell surf 'base x y color)` becomes `(set-color color) (pset x y)`.

The concepts translate; the verb names are what changed. Every runnable code block in this chapter uses the current verbs and has been verified against `bin/motoi run` before being included.

## 18.10 Now build your own

You have the vocabulary. The whole fantasy-console pattern fits on one page:

- `set-mode` sets the screen size.
- `clear` · `begin-frame` · `end-frame` · `render` wrap every drawing.
- `set-color` picks the color; `disc`, `circle`, `rect`, `rect-fill`, `line`, `pset`, `draw-text` draw the shapes.
- `on-frame` installs the game loop.
- `on-key`, `on-mouse`, `input/down?`, `input/pressed?` handle input.
- `tone`, `note`, `chord`, `melody`, `kick`, `snare`, `hat`, `sfx` make sound.
- `save-cart` and `load-cart` move a cart in and out of `~/.motoi/carts/`.
- `motoi ide` opens the browser IDE; `motoi tui` opens the terminal IDE; `motoi repl` opens the REPL alone.
- F2 explains the selection; Cmd/Ctrl+Enter runs it; `,help <verb>` at the REPL prints the card.

That is enough for pong. It is enough for a platformer. It is enough for a demo. The rest is time in the chair.
")

"# Appendix A — Feature matrix

A one-page reference. Every entry is honest — where a language does the thing well, it says so; where it doesn't, it says that too.

| Feature                     | Motoi | Python | JS    | Clojure | Lua   | Java  | Rust  | Ruby  | Go    | Haskell | CL    |
|-----------------------------|-------|--------|-------|---------|-------|-------|-------|-------|-------|---------|-------|
| Dynamic typing              | yes   | yes    | yes   | yes     | yes   | no    | no    | yes   | no    | no      | yes   |
| Static typing               | no    | opt    | opt   | no      | no    | yes   | yes   | no    | yes   | yes     | opt   |
| Garbage collection          | yes   | yes    | yes   | yes     | yes   | yes   | no    | yes   | yes   | yes     | yes   |
| First-class functions       | yes   | yes    | yes   | yes     | yes   | yes   | yes   | yes   | yes   | yes     | yes   |
| Closures                    | yes   | yes    | yes   | yes     | yes   | yes   | yes   | yes   | yes   | yes     | yes   |
| Tail-call elimination       | yes   | no     | no    | no*     | yes   | no    | no    | no    | no    | yes**   | opt   |
| Real macros (source→source) | yes   | no     | no    | yes     | no    | no    | yes   | no    | no    | yes***  | yes   |
| Hygienic macros             | yes   | -      | -     | yes     | -     | -     | yes   | -     | -     | opt     | opt   |
| Pattern matching (core)     | no    | 3.10+  | no    | 3rd     | no    | 21+   | yes   | 3.0+  | no    | yes     | opt   |
| Immutable data by default   | yes   | no     | no    | yes     | no    | no    | opt   | no    | no    | yes     | no    |
| Persistent data structs     | yes   | 3rd    | 3rd   | yes     | no    | no    | opt   | no    | no    | yes     | opt   |
| REPL                        | yes   | yes    | some  | yes     | yes   | jshell| no    | yes   | no    | yes     | yes   |
| Code as data                | yes   | no     | no    | yes     | no    | no    | no    | some  | no    | no      | yes   |
| Built-in audio              | yes   | no     | web   | no      | no    | no    | no    | no    | no    | no      | no    |

Legend:
- `yes` — core feature, ships in the base language.
- `no` — not available.
- `opt` — optional, via a keyword/flag/library.

"# Appendix B — If you know Python

The 20-minute orientation. Read this before Chapter 1 if you want the shape without the depth.

## The five shape shifts

1. **Prefix over infix.** `2 + 3` becomes `(+ 2 3)`. `xs[0]` becomes `(car xs)`. Every call: `(verb arg arg arg)`.

2. **`def` is `define`.** `def square(x): return x * x` becomes `(define (square x) (* x x))`. Return is implicit — the last expression is the value.

3. **`if` is an expression.** Python's `x if cond else y` becomes `(if cond x y)`. Python's `elif` chain becomes `cond`.

4. **`for x in xs` is `for-each`.** `for x in xs: print(x)` becomes `(for-each (lambda (x) (display x) (newline)) xs)`. Or, more idiomatically, a named-let loop.

5. **`list` and `dict` are `list` and `assoc-list`.** Python's `[1,2,3]` is Motoi's `(list 1 2 3)`. Python's `{\"a\": 1}` is Motoi's `(list (cons 'a 1))`.

## The three things you have to relearn

**Indexing.** Python's `xs[i]` is O(1). Motoi's list is a chain of cons cells; `(car xs)` is O(1), `(list-ref xs i)` is O(n). For hot random access, use a vector (from a module) or a hash table.

**Truthiness.** Python: `0`, `''`, `[]`, `None` are falsy. Motoi: only `#f` is falsy. `0`, `\"\"`, `'()` are all truthy. Check emptiness with `null?`; check zero with `zero?`.

**Comprehensions.** Python's `[x*2 for x in xs if x > 2]` becomes `(map (lambda (x) (* x 2)) (filter (lambda (x) (> x 2)) xs))`. Same operations, no dedicated syntax.

## The two things you don't need to relearn

**Closures.** Python closures work; Motoi closures work; same shape. `def make_counter(): n = [0]; def tick(): n[0] += 1; return n[0]; return tick` (the box-around-int Python dance) becomes cleaner in Motoi because `set!` on the local works.

**Dynamic typing.** No compile step. Errors at runtime. Same dev flow.

## The five things Motoi has that Python doesn't

1. **Guaranteed tail-call elimination.** Recursive loops don't blow the stack.
2. **Real hygienic macros.** No decorator dance; write source-to-source transformers.
3. **Multiple values without allocating a tuple.** Not always what you want; sometimes it is.
4. **Continuations (`call/cc`).** Rarely needed, occasionally the right tool.
5. **Fantasy-console kit.** Audio and framebuffer built in.

## The five things Python has that Motoi doesn't

1. **Massive ecosystem.** pip has everything; Motoi has ~40 modules.
2. **NumPy/Pandas/PyTorch.** Data-science and ML stack. Motoi is not a competitor.
3. **F-strings.** `f\"hello {name}\"` is nice; Motoi has `string-append` and a format module.
4. **List comprehensions.** Nice syntax for a common shape.
5. **Async/await.** Motoi has channels and processes in a module, but no `async def` syntax.

## Starting from a Python program

Take a Python function. Translate step by step:

```python
def word_count(text):
    words = text.split()
    counts = {}
    for w in words:
        counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1
    return counts
```

Motoi:

```scheme
(define (word-count text)
  ;; assumes string-split from a module
  (define words (string-split text \" \"))
  (let loop ((ws words) (acc '()))
    (if (null? ws)
        acc
        (let* ((w (car ws))
               (existing (assoc w acc)))
          (if existing
              (loop (cdr ws)
                    (cons (cons w (+ 1 (cdr existing)))
                          (filter (lambda (p) (not (equal? (car p) w))) acc)))
              (loop (cdr ws) (cons (cons w 1) acc)))))))
```

Longer. Same idea. Once you learn to *see* the shape — inputs come in, an accumulator threads through the loop, the answer comes back — the translation is mechanical.

## Where to go next

Chapter 1 for the full Python comparison. Chapter 11 for macros, which is where Motoi's expressiveness lives. Chapter 16 for the fantasy-console kit.
")

"# Appendix C — If you know Clojure

You are 90% of the way there. This appendix is the delta.

## The syntactic differences

1. **Bindings use parens, not vectors.** Clojure: `(let [x 3 y 4] ...)`. Motoi: `(let* ((x 3) (y 4)) ...)`. Doubled parens for the binding list — the outer holds the list, the inner is each pair. Not a typo.

2. **`let` is parallel; `let*` is sequential.** Clojure's `let` is sequential. Motoi's `let` is parallel (bindings don't see each other), and `let*` is the sequential form.

3. **`defn` is `define`.** Same shape, different word: `(define (square x) (* x x))`.

4. **Anonymous functions are `lambda`.** No `#(* % %)` shorthand. Just `(lambda (x) (* x x))`.

5. **No keyword literals in the base.** Clojure's `:foo` is Motoi's quoted symbol `'foo`. Some Motoi dialects and modules add `:foo` back.

6. **No vector, map, set literals.** Clojure's `[1 2 3]`, `{:a 1}`, `#{1 2 3}` all become explicit constructor calls in Motoi: `(list 1 2 3)`, `(list (cons 'a 1))`, `(set 1 2 3)` (from a module).

## The library differences

1. **No threading macros (`->`, `->>`) in the core.** Import them from a module or write them in 10 lines (Chapter 11).

2. **No `frequencies`, `group-by`, `partition-by`, `interleave` in the core.** All available in modules or writable in a few lines.

3. **Only lists in the core.** Vectors, hash tables, sets, sorted maps — all modules.

4. **No transducers.** The composition-of-reducing-functions idea Clojure formalized is not in Motoi. You compose `map` and `filter` explicitly.

5. **No spec or malli.** No contracts library shipped in the core; a contracts module is available.

## What's similar

1. **REPL workflow.** Live redefine; `,help name` shows docs; iterate at the prompt.

2. **First-class immutability.** Motoi's lists are persistent; mutation is `set!` and appears rarely in idiomatic code.

3. **Macros.** `syntax-rules` is the base form (pattern-based, hygienic). `syntax-case` in a module for full defmacro-style. Every Clojure macro shape has a translation.

4. **Sequence functions.** `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `for-each` all present and work like Clojure's.

## What's better in Motoi

1. **Fantasy-console kit.** Nothing in Clojure land is quite this integrated.

2. **Frozen core language.** Clojure's core has grown; Motoi's is fixed at 335 verbs.

3. **Interpreter startup.** Milliseconds vs seconds. No JVM warmup.

4. **Small enough to hold in your head.** Clojure's core has ~600 vars; Motoi's has ~335.

## What's better in Clojure

1. **Rich collection literals.** Vectors, maps, sets as first-class syntax.

2. **JVM interop.** Every Java library is one `import` away.

3. **STM and refs.** Concurrency primitives Motoi doesn't have.

4. **Ecosystem.** Datomic, ring, spec, malli, transducers, core.async, hundreds more.

5. **Production maturity.** Clojure ships production systems today.

## A Clojure-to-Motoi translation dictionary

| Clojure                           | Motoi                                              |
|-----------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------|
| `(defn name [args] body)`         | `(define (name args) body)`                        |
| `(let [x 1 y 2] ...)`             | `(let* ((x 1) (y 2)) ...)`                         |
| `(fn [x] ...)`                    | `(lambda (x) ...)`                                 |
| `#(* % %)`                        | `(lambda (x) (* x x))`                             |
| `[1 2 3]`                         | `(list 1 2 3)`                                     |
| `{:a 1 :b 2}`                     | `(list (cons 'a 1) (cons 'b 2))`                   |
| `:name`                           | `'name`                                            |
| `(get m :key)`                    | `(cdr (assoc 'key m))`                             |
| `(map inc xs)`                    | `(map (lambda (x) (+ x 1)) xs)`                    |
| `(reduce + xs)`                   | `(apply + xs)`                                     |
| `(-> x (a) (b))`                  | `(b (a x))` or `(-> x (a) (b))` via module         |
| `(if x a b)`                      | `(if x a b)`                                       |
| `(cond p1 e1 p2 e2 :else e)`      | `(cond (p1 e1) (p2 e2) (else e))`                  |
| `(when x body)`                   | `(when x body)`                                    |
| `(atom 0)` + `swap!`              | `(define n 0)` + `(set! n ...)`                    |
| `(defmacro m [args] body)`        | `(define-syntax m (syntax-rules () ...))`          |
| `\\`(if ,cond ,then ,else)`       | pattern-and-template form in syntax-rules          |

## Where to go next

Chapter 3 for the full Clojure comparison. Chapter 11 for macros — where the two languages are most alike.
")
