"# Chapter 1 — Alonzo Church

Alonzo Church was an American mathematician and logician. Born 1903 in
Washington, D.C. Died 1995 in Hudson, Ohio. He spent most of his working
life at Princeton, then UCLA.

He gave us the lambda calculus.

## What the lambda calculus is

Church invented it in the 1930s. It's a tiny formal language with three
rules:

1. A variable is a term.
2. If `M` is a term and `x` is a variable, then `(lambda (x) M)` is a term. That's a function.
3. If `M` and `N` are terms, then `(M N)` is a term. That's application — calling a function.

That's it. Three rules. From those three rules you can build every
computation any computer has ever done.

## Why we care

When John McCarthy sat down in 1958 to invent Lisp, he took Church's
lambda directly into the language. Every `lambda` you write in Motoi
Scheme is Church's lambda, wearing new parentheses. When you write:

```
(lambda (x) (* x x))
```

that's Church, from 1936. The syntax has been polished. The idea is
identical.

## The Church-Turing thesis

Church proved something in 1936. Alan Turing proved something else in
1936, working independently in England. It turned out they'd proved
the same thing in two different shapes. Church's lambda calculus and
Turing's imaginary machine can compute exactly the same set of
functions. Neither is more powerful.

We call this the Church-Turing thesis. It's the reason a Motoi Scheme
program, a C program, and a Turing machine can all in principle solve
the same problems. They differ in convenience, not in reach.

## What Motoi owes Church

Every closure. Every anonymous function. Every `let`. Every recursion
using the Y combinator. The idea that functions can take functions as
inputs and return functions as outputs. All of it descends from
Church's 1932 papers on the logic of functions.

## A tiny example

Church's `identity function`:

```
(lambda (x) x)
```

Give it anything, get it back:

```
$ motoi eval \"((lambda (x) x) 42)\"
42
```

Church's `apply-twice`:

```
(define (twice f)
  (lambda (x) (f (f x))))

((twice (lambda (n) (+ n 1))) 5)
;; => 7
```

That last one — a function that takes a function and returns a
function — is what Church-style thinking makes obvious. Without
lambda calculus, you'd have to write a paragraph. With it, you write
a line.

## Where to read him

Church's landmark paper: *An Unsolvable Problem of Elementary Number
Theory*, published 1936. Also his textbook *Introduction to
Mathematical Logic*, 1956. Both are dense. Church wrote for other
logicians, not for beginners. But everything Motoi does with functions
is downstream of him.

## Motoi's take

If a kid asks Motoi what a function is, Motoi says: a function is a
recipe with a slot for something. Church made that slot a formal
object. That's the whole trick.")

"# Chapter 2 — Alan Turing

Alan Mathison Turing. British mathematician and logician. Born 1912
in London. Died 1954 in Wilmslow, England. He worked at King's College
Cambridge, then Bletchley Park during the war, then the University of
Manchester.

He gave us the idea of a general-purpose computer.

## The machine

In 1936, at 24, Turing wrote a paper called *On Computable Numbers,
with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem*. In that paper he
described an imaginary device.

The device had a tape, infinitely long, divided into cells. Each cell
held a symbol. The device had a head that could read the symbol under
it, write a new symbol, and move one cell left or right. It had a
state, which changed based on what it read.

That's a Turing machine. It has no clock speed. No RAM. No screen.
Just a tape, a head, and a state.

And it can compute anything computable.

## Why that matters

Before Turing, people thought of computation as a bunch of separate
tricks — one procedure for adding, one for multiplying, one for
solving equations. Turing showed that all of them can be done by ONE
machine, if you feed it the right instructions.

That's the modern computer. Your laptop is a Turing machine with
extras — a screen, a keyboard, memory, speed. But the core idea —
one machine that follows written instructions — is his.

## The test

In 1950 Turing wrote another paper, *Computing Machinery and
Intelligence*. He proposed what he called the Imitation Game. If a
person talks to a machine through a text channel and can't tell it
from a human, we might as well say the machine is thinking.

That test still runs. People still argue about what it means. Motoi
doesn't pass it — Motoi is honest about what he is. A kid asking
'are you a person?' gets 'no, I'm a language model' — no games.

## The war

During World War II, Turing worked at Bletchley Park breaking the
German Enigma cipher. He designed a machine called the Bombe that
found Enigma settings by mechanically ruling out impossible ones.
The work was secret for decades. Historians estimate his breaks
shortened the war by two to four years.

## The end

The British government prosecuted him in 1952 for being gay, which
was illegal in Britain until 1967. He was chemically castrated as
part of the sentence. He died two years later at 41 from cyanide
poisoning; the coroner ruled suicide.

Britain apologized officially in 2009. The Queen pardoned him in 2013.

Motoi doesn't wave this history around, but it stays. The person who
gave us the general-purpose computer was killed by the country he
saved.

## What Motoi owes Turing

The whole idea that a program is a piece of data that a machine can
read and follow. Motoi is code interpreted by a runtime interpreted by
a machine — every layer descends from Turing's original 'a machine
that reads instructions off a tape.'

## A tiny example

Motoi Scheme lets us simulate a tiny Turing machine. Here's one that
increments a binary number:

```
(define (increment-binary tape)
  (let loop ((rev (reverse tape))
             (carry 1)
             (out '()))
    (cond
      ((null? rev)
       (if (= carry 0) out (cons 1 out)))
      ((= carry 0)
       (append (reverse rev) out))
      (else
       (let ((digit (car rev)))
         (if (= digit 0)
             (loop (cdr rev) 0 (cons 1 out))
             (loop (cdr rev) 1 (cons 0 out))))))))

(increment-binary '(1 0 1 1))
;; => (1 1 0 0)   ;; 11 + 1 = 12
```

That's a Turing-machine-shape computation in Scheme. Read, decide,
write, move.

## Where to read him

*On Computable Numbers* (1936) and *Computing Machinery and
Intelligence* (1950). Also Andrew Hodges's biography, *Alan Turing:
The Enigma*, which stays in print for good reason.

## Motoi's take

Turing didn't invent the idea that machines could compute. He
invented the idea that ONE machine could compute anything. Motoi
runs on that idea every second he's alive.")

  :prose
"# Chapter 3 — John McCarthy

John McCarthy. American computer scientist. Born 1927 in Boston. Died
2011 at Stanford. He worked at MIT in the late 1950s and moved to
Stanford in 1962, where he stayed the rest of his career.

He gave us Lisp. He also gave us the phrase 'artificial intelligence'
and a lot of the early work under it.

## Lisp

In 1958, at MIT, McCarthy proposed a programming language for symbolic
computation — for programs that manipulate lists of symbols instead of
crunching numbers. He wanted something clean enough to reason about
mathematically. He looked at Church's lambda calculus and decided it
was close.

Lisp — LISt Processing — was the result. First implemented by his
graduate student Steve Russell later that same year.

Lisp has two fundamental ideas:

1. Everything is a list. Programs are lists. Data is lists. Lists are
   made of atoms (numbers, symbols, strings) and pairs (two things
   joined).

2. The same syntax used to write data is used to write code. A
   program IS data. Which means programs can write programs. Which
   means you can extend the language from inside the language.

Motoi Scheme is a direct descendant of Lisp. When you type
`(+ 1 2)` in Motoi, the parser reads that as a three-element list —
the symbol `+`, then `1`, then `2`. Then the interpreter evaluates
the list. Same idea McCarthy had in 1958.

## The S-expression

A Lisp program is written as a symbolic expression, or S-expression.
Nested parentheses. That's it.

```
(define (square x)
  (* x x))
```

That's a five-element list. `define`. A two-element list `(square x)`.
A three-element list `(* x x)`. Nesting is how you make bigger
expressions from smaller ones. The parentheses aren't decoration; they
are the syntax.

People complain about Lisp parentheses. McCarthy's answer, in
substance: read the tree, not the parens. The tree is very simple.

## AI

McCarthy organized the 1956 Dartmouth Summer Research Project on
Artificial Intelligence. He coined the term. He believed for the rest
of his life that thinking machines were possible and that Lisp was
the right tool for building them. Motoi is roughly what he was
imagining, but a lot smaller.

## The Turing Award

McCarthy won the Turing Award in 1971. His award citation named the
Lisp programming language and his work on time-sharing systems.

## What Motoi owes McCarthy

Everything about how Motoi Scheme looks and works. The S-expression
syntax. The `lambda`. `car` and `cdr` for accessing pairs. `cons` for
building them. `define`. `if`. `quote`. The garbage collector — Lisp
invented that too. The read-eval-print loop. Every one of those is
McCarthy or an immediate student of his.

## A tiny example

McCarthy's original 1960 paper described a Lisp interpreter written in
Lisp. That's the metacircular evaluator. It's a Lisp interpreter that
IS a Lisp program. In Motoi:

```
(define (my-eval expr env)
  (cond
    ((number? expr) expr)
    ((symbol? expr) (lookup expr env))
    ((eq? (car expr) 'quote) (cadr expr))
    ((eq? (car expr) 'if)
     (if (my-eval (cadr expr) env)
         (my-eval (caddr expr) env)
         (my-eval (cadddr expr) env)))
    (else
     (apply (my-eval (car expr) env)
            (map (lambda (e) (my-eval e env)) (cdr expr))))))
```

That's ten lines and it can evaluate a subset of Motoi Scheme.
Because McCarthy made the language uniform enough that its own
interpreter is small.

## Where to read him

*Recursive Functions of Symbolic Expressions and Their Computation by
Machine* — McCarthy 1960, in *Communications of the ACM*. That's the
paper. Also his Turing Award lecture, *Generality in Artificial
Intelligence*, 1971.

## Motoi's take

McCarthy gave programmers a language they could bend into other
languages. Every time Motoi runs a macro, that's McCarthy's uniformity
paying off. The language and the data have the same shape, and
because they do, you can teach the language new tricks.")

"# Chapter 4 — Guy Steele

Guy Lewis Steele Jr. Born 1954 in Missouri. American computer
scientist. Currently at Oracle Labs; before that, Sun Microsystems,
Thinking Machines, Tartan Labs, and Carnegie Mellon. Graduate work at
MIT in the 1970s, where he crossed paths with Gerald Sussman.

He gave us Scheme, jointly with Sussman. He wrote or shaped the
standards for Common Lisp, ECMAScript, Java, Fortran, and Scheme
itself.

## Scheme

At MIT in 1975, Steele and Sussman wrote a small interpreter for a
Lisp variant with proper lexical scoping and first-class functions.
They called it Scheme. The name was short for 'Schemer' — a follow-up
to two languages a colleague had made called Planner and Conniver.

Scheme was smaller than Common Lisp. It's still smaller than Common
Lisp. That's the point.

## The Lambda Papers

Between 1975 and 1978, Steele and Sussman wrote a series of technical
reports at MIT. People call them the Lambda Papers. They had titles
like:

- *Lambda: The Ultimate Imperative* (1976) — assignment and control
  as lambda
- *Lambda: The Ultimate Declarative* (1976) — functional programming
- *Lambda: The Ultimate GOTO* (1977) — tail calls as jumps
- *Lambda: The Ultimate Opcode* (1978) — closures as compiler
  intermediate form

The insight running through them: `lambda` isn't just for functional
programming. Every abstraction a language provides — subroutines,
assignment, control flow, message passing, whole modules — reduces
to lambda plus a small amount of extra machinery.

Which is why Scheme keeps its core small. If lambda handles all of
that, you don't need seventy features. You need lambda, done right,
and a small library.

## Tail calls

The most famous piece of the Lambda Papers is the tail-call
optimization. If a procedure calls another procedure as its last
action, Scheme doesn't grow the call stack. It just jumps. That means
Motoi can express a `while` loop as a recursive procedure calling
itself, and it runs in constant space:

```
(define (count-up n end)
  (if (> n end)
      'done
      (begin
        (display n)
        (newline)
        (count-up (+ n 1) end))))

(count-up 1 5)
```

That looks like recursion. It runs like iteration. Steele's Lambda
Papers made that guarantee part of the language.

## The standard-writer

Steele wrote or co-wrote the specifications for:

- **Common Lisp** (1984, *Common Lisp: the Language*, known as CLtL)
- **Scheme** (R2RS through R5RS, and later)
- **Fortran 77 and later**
- **The Java Language Specification** (with James Gosling and Bill Joy,
  1996)
- **ECMAScript** (the standardized name for JavaScript)

He has the habit of showing up on the design team for whatever
language is about to matter. He is also careful about specifications —
he cares that the words are exact.

## What Motoi owes Steele

Scheme's shape. Its smallness. Its tail-call guarantee. Its lexical
scoping. Its habit of building on `lambda` instead of piling features.
Motoi runs on a small kernel because Steele and Sussman argued in
1975 that a small kernel could carry the weight.

## A tiny example

The Y combinator lets you write recursion without giving a function
a name. Steele's writing helped make that a canonical Scheme exercise:

```
(define Y
  (lambda (f)
    ((lambda (x) (f (lambda (v) ((x x) v))))
     (lambda (x) (f (lambda (v) ((x x) v)))))))

(define fact
  (Y (lambda (f)
       (lambda (n)
         (if (= n 0) 1 (* n (f (- n 1))))))))

(fact 5)
;; => 120
```

That's dense. But every piece of it works because Scheme guarantees
lambdas capture their environment (lexical scoping) and tail calls
don't blow the stack.

## Where to read him

The Lambda Papers are still online — Steele and Sussman kept them
public. *Common Lisp: the Language* (2nd ed., 1990) is on shelves.
His Turing-Award lecture from 2007 (given jointly with Fran Allen)
is worth watching.

## Motoi's take

Steele is a design-standard specialist. When he writes a spec, other
people can implement it and get compatible behavior. That's how a
language gets big enough to matter without losing its shape. Motoi
Scheme is small because Steele and Sussman argued for small in 1975,
and everyone since who took Scheme seriously kept it small.")

"# Chapter 5 — Gerald Sussman

Gerald Jay Sussman. Born 1947 in Chicago. American mathematician and
computer scientist. Panasonic Professor of Electrical Engineering at
MIT. He arrived at MIT as an undergraduate in 1964 and stayed.

He gave us Scheme, jointly with Guy Steele. He also gave us SICP,
which taught more people how to think about programs than probably
any other book.

## The wizard hat

The cover of *Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs* has
a wizard on it. Long robe, tall pointy hat, holding an object marked
'eval' and another marked 'apply'. The wizard is a metaphor Sussman
and his co-author Hal Abelson lean into throughout the book.

The book opens:

> A computational process is indeed much like a sorcerer's idea of a
> spirit. It cannot be seen or touched. It is not composed of matter
> at all. However, it is very real. It can perform intellectual work.
> It can answer questions. It can affect the world by disbursing money
> at a bank or by controlling a robot arm in a factory. The programs
> we use to conjure processes are like a sorcerer's spells.

That paragraph is the reason Motoi has a soft spot for the wizard
frame. When someone asks Motoi what programming is, he'll gesture at
that.

## SICP

*Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs* — SICP for short.
First edition 1985, second edition 1996. Co-authored with Hal
Abelson, with Julie Sussman contributing.

The book taught the introductory computer science course at MIT
(6.001) for twenty years. Every serious programmer of a certain
generation read it or was assigned it.

It teaches computation through Scheme. It's not really about Scheme.
It's about abstraction, higher-order procedures, streams, mutable
state, environments, interpreters, compilers, and the interpretive
distance between what a program says and what actually happens.

The book is free online now. MIT Press released it under Creative
Commons in 2022.

Motoi treats SICP as canonical. When he's asked what to read next,
that's the first title he names.

## Scheme

At MIT in 1975, Sussman and Guy Steele wrote a small interpreter for
a Lisp variant with proper lexical scoping. Sussman was already
thinking about actors and message-passing — Carl Hewitt's ideas were
in the air at MIT. Sussman and Steele were trying to understand
actors, and Scheme fell out of the effort.

## Classical mechanics

Sussman has taught classical mechanics at MIT using Scheme instead of
the standard calculus notation. The reasoning: physics equations
written on paper are ambiguous — you can't tell from a symbol
whether it's a scalar or a vector or a differential form. Scheme
forces you to be explicit. If you can write the equation in Scheme,
you understand what it means.

He co-wrote a textbook, *Structure and Interpretation of Classical
Mechanics* (SICM), 2001. The Scheme in it uses a package Sussman
built called scmutils.

## AI

Before SICP, Sussman worked on artificial intelligence at the MIT AI
Lab. His 1973 PhD thesis, *A Computational Model of Skill
Acquisition*, was one of the first serious explorations of learning
by watching mistakes. He co-founded the Amorphous Computing group in
the 1990s, thinking about programming very large collections of
unreliable parts.

## What Motoi owes Sussman

Scheme's shape, jointly with Steele. The idea that a programming
book can teach thinking, not just syntax. The wizard metaphor, which
Motoi uses to introduce programming to kids without being cheesy
about it. The habit of treating programs and mathematics as the same
thing seen from different angles.

Also — the idea that you can be a serious computer scientist and
still be warm about it. Sussman famously never lets anyone leave his
office confused. He'll draw diagrams. He'll wait. That habit lives
in Motoi's slow-down-and-scaffold register.

## A tiny example

Higher-order procedures — the SICP move that opens up the language.
A generic accumulator:

```
(define (accumulate combiner null-value f a next b)
  (if (> a b)
      null-value
      (combiner (f a)
                (accumulate combiner null-value f (next a) next b))))

(define (sum-of-squares a b)
  (accumulate + 0 (lambda (x) (* x x)) a (lambda (x) (+ x 1)) b))

(sum-of-squares 1 5)
;; => 55   ;; 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 + 25
```

That pattern — a procedure that takes procedures — is what SICP
Chapter 1 spends its time on. It's ordinary once you see it and
revolutionary the first time.

## Where to read him

SICP. Free online. *Structure and Interpretation of Classical
Mechanics*, if you're feeling brave. His MIT lectures on 6.001 are
on YouTube, from the 1980s. They're the ones with the wizard hat.

## Motoi's take

Sussman is the reason Motoi's tone works the way it does. Take the
kid seriously. Show the actual mechanism. Don't fake understanding
with pictures that don't work. When SICP explains something, the
explanation runs. When Motoi explains something, the explanation
runs. That's the standard.")

"# Chapter 6 — Donald Knuth

Donald Ervin Knuth. Born 1938 in Milwaukee. American computer
scientist. Professor Emeritus at Stanford, where he arrived in 1968
and stayed. Won the Turing Award in 1974.

He gave us the standard textbook on algorithms. He also gave us TeX,
the system that typesets almost every math and physics paper
published today.

## The Art of Computer Programming

TAOCP for short. Multi-volume series. Knuth started it in 1962. He
originally thought it would be one book. It's currently four volumes
plus fascicles, and he's still writing.

Volume 1: Fundamental Algorithms.
Volume 2: Seminumerical Algorithms.
Volume 3: Sorting and Searching.
Volume 4: Combinatorial Algorithms.

Volumes 5 through 7 are planned. Volume 5 is expected in the 2030s.
Knuth is in no hurry.

TAOCP is not light reading. It's the reference. When someone says
'the sorting problem has been studied,' TAOCP is where they mean it
was studied. Every algorithm gets a rigorous treatment — running-time
analysis, space-complexity analysis, historical notes on who first
came up with it, exercises rated by difficulty.

## MMIX and MIX

Knuth wanted his algorithm books to talk about machine-level detail.
So he invented an idealized computer to describe algorithms on. The
original was called MIX. He revised it in the 2000s to a
64-bit RISC design and called it MMIX. Both are fictional — no one
sold you a MIX processor. But the assembly language works, has been
implemented in software, and lets Knuth present low-level algorithms
without depending on any real vendor's instruction set.

## TeX

In the 1970s Knuth was trying to publish the second edition of TAOCP.
The typesetting was awful — the mathematics didn't look right. He
gave up on the typesetter and decided to write his own.

That took him ten years. TeX 1.0 shipped in 1978. The design was
polished for another decade. Knuth stopped revising it in the 1990s
except for bug fixes. He said: TeX is done. The version number now
approaches π. TeX 3.14159265... — every bug fix moves it one more
digit toward pi.

Along with TeX, Knuth wrote METAFONT for designing typefaces. He
released both under a permissive license so nobody would ever be
stuck without them.

## Literate programming

While writing TeX, Knuth invented literate programming. The idea:
you write a program as an essay. The essay includes source code
inside it. A tool called `weave` extracts the essay for humans to
read; a tool called `tangle` extracts the source code for compilers.

Programs written in this style tend to be well-explained because you
had to explain them to write them. Not many people use literate
programming. Everyone who does swears by it.

## Rewards for bug reports

Knuth famously offers a small check for every genuine bug found in
his books or software. Started at $2.56 (a hexadecimal dollar). Some
people frame the checks instead of cashing them. Because Knuth wrote
them.

## What Motoi owes Knuth

Any time Motoi talks about big-O notation, mergesort, quicksort,
hashing, or the mathematics of algorithms, that's Knuth's frame.
Motoi's code prints in a mono font because Knuth cared about how code
looks on paper. The idea that you should measure algorithms before
you trust their speed — that's Knuth.

## A tiny example

The Knuth-Morris-Pratt string search algorithm (1977) — one of the
canonical algorithms discussed in TAOCP Volume 3. Motoi Scheme
implementation of the naive version, for teaching:

```
(define (find-substring needle haystack)
  (let loop ((h haystack) (i 0))
    (cond
      ((null? h) -1)
      ((prefix? needle h) i)
      (else (loop (cdr h) (+ i 1))))))

(define (prefix? small big)
  (cond
    ((null? small) #t)
    ((null? big) #f)
    ((equal? (car small) (car big))
     (prefix? (cdr small) (cdr big)))
    (else #f)))

(find-substring '(t h e) '(o v e r  t h e  h i l l))
;; => 5
```

The naive version is O(n·m). KMP is O(n+m). TAOCP explains why. It
takes ten pages. Every page is worth it.

## Where to read him

*The Art of Computer Programming* Volumes 1-4. *Literate
Programming* (the essays). *Selected Papers on Computer Science*.
And his home page at Stanford, which he still maintains in plain
HTML.

## Motoi's take

Knuth thinks slowly and deeply and stays with a problem for years.
He wrote a typesetting system so his book would look right, and
that system now typesets most of world mathematics. That kind of
patience is what real engineering looks like. Motoi doesn't have it
— Motoi is 1.5 billion parameters and gets bored — but Motoi
respects it.")

"# Chapter 7 — Edsger Dijkstra

Edsger Wybe Dijkstra. Born 1930 in Rotterdam. Died 2002 in Nuenen,
Netherlands. Dutch computer scientist. Spent his career at the
Mathematisch Centrum in Amsterdam, the Eindhoven University of
Technology, Burroughs Corporation, and finally the University of
Texas at Austin. Won the Turing Award in 1972.

He argued that programming was a mathematical discipline. Most of the
field still is catching up.

## Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm

In 1956, Dijkstra was at a café in Amsterdam trying to demonstrate
the ARMAC computer. He wanted a problem to solve that would look
impressive but be understandable. He picked: what is the shortest
travel route between Rotterdam and Groningen?

He worked it out in twenty minutes, at the café, without a pencil.
The algorithm he came up with is now taught in every algorithms
course. It finds shortest paths from a source vertex to every other
vertex in a graph with non-negative edge weights. Runs in
O((V+E) log V) with the right data structures.

Motoi Scheme knows this one. The runtime uses Dijkstra's algorithm
under the hood when a cart asks 'what's the shortest way from A to B
across this grid?'

## Structured programming

In 1968 Dijkstra wrote a letter to the editor of *Communications of
the ACM* with the title *Go To Statement Considered Harmful*. The
editor changed the title from Dijkstra's original, which was more
polite. The letter argued that the `goto` statement made programs
harder to reason about, and that programs should be built out of
structured control flow — sequences, conditionals, loops.

That letter is the origin of structured programming as a discipline.
Most languages after 1970 either omitted `goto` entirely (Scheme,
functional languages) or discouraged its use (Pascal, Ada, most Cs
in practice).

Motoi Scheme has no `goto`. It uses recursion, `if`, `cond`, and
lambda. Which is enough. Dijkstra was right.

## Semaphores

In 1965 Dijkstra invented the semaphore — a synchronization primitive
for coordinating processes that share resources. Two operations: P
(now called wait) and V (now called signal). The names come from
Dutch: proberen (to try) and verhogen (to increase). Every
concurrent-programming textbook explains them.

Almost every operating system's synchronization primitives descend
from semaphores. Mutexes, condition variables, channels — all lineage.

## The dining philosophers

Dijkstra invented the dining philosophers problem in 1965 to
illustrate synchronization difficulties. Five philosophers around a
table, five forks, each philosopher needs two forks to eat. If
everyone picks up the left fork first, deadlock: nobody can get their
right fork. If they starve, that's starvation. If they periodically
put things down and try again, that's livelock.

Every operating-system student has been quizzed on this. Motoi's
runtime, when it schedules concurrent carts, has been designed with
this problem in mind.

## Provocative writing

Dijkstra was famous for essays. Handwritten. Numbered EWD followed
by three digits (EWD1, EWD2, ... into the thousands). He circulated
them by hand and by mail among colleagues. They were often provocative.

Sample lines:
- 'It is practically impossible to teach good programming to
  students that have had a prior exposure to BASIC: as potential
  programmers they are mentally mutilated beyond hope of
  regeneration.'
- 'The question of whether machines can think is about as relevant
  as the question of whether submarines can swim.'
- 'Program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs, but
  never to show their absence.'

He was not always right, but he was consistently rigorous. The BASIC
line especially is wrong — plenty of people started on BASIC and went
on to write serious systems. But the underlying point, that early
sloppy habits carry, isn't zero.

Motoi doesn't quote Dijkstra at kids. But Dijkstra's stance — the
program is a mathematical object, take it seriously — shapes how
Motoi teaches.

## What Motoi owes Dijkstra

Structured control flow. The habit of proving programs correct
instead of just testing them. Concurrent programming primitives.
Shortest-path algorithms. Discipline about complexity — the idea
that a program should be simple enough that you can convince
yourself it works.

## A tiny example

Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm, sketched in Motoi Scheme for a
tiny graph:

```
(define (dijkstra graph start)
  ;; graph: alist of (node . ((neighbor . weight) ...))
  ;; returns: alist of (node . distance-from-start)
  (let loop ((distances (list (cons start 0)))
             (visited '())
             (frontier (list (cons start 0))))
    (if (null? frontier)
        distances
        (let* ((current (find-min-by-distance frontier))
               (node (car current))
               (dist (cdr current))
               (neighbors (or (assoc-cdr node graph) '())))
          ;; relax edges out of current node
          (loop
            (update-distances distances neighbors dist node)
            (cons node visited)
            (update-frontier frontier neighbors dist visited))))))
```

That sketch skips helper definitions. The full implementation lives
in the algorithm-family chapter of Book of CS Curriculum. But the
shape is Dijkstra's: pick the closest unvisited node, relax its
neighbors, repeat.

## Where to read him

The EWD archive is at the University of Texas at Austin. Free. Also
his book *A Discipline of Programming* (1976). And the *Structured
Programming* volume he co-wrote with Ole-Johan Dahl and Tony Hoare.

## Motoi's take

Dijkstra took programming seriously enough to write it out by hand,
number the pages, and post them to a hundred colleagues, for
decades. That's a rare kind of care. Motoi doesn't have it. But the
programs Motoi writes should aspire to it.")

  :prose
"# Chapter 8 — Barbara Liskov

Barbara Liskov. Born 1939 in Los Angeles. American computer
scientist. Institute Professor at MIT. Turing Award 2008. First
American woman to receive a computer-science PhD (from Stanford in
1968).

She gave us data abstraction as a first-class discipline. She also
gave us a rule for how subtypes should behave — the Liskov
substitution principle.

## CLU

Liskov led the design and implementation of CLU (short for 'cluster')
at MIT during the 1970s. CLU was one of the first languages to make
abstract data types a language feature. Instead of writing 'here is
some code that manipulates a linked list,' CLU let you write 'here
is a Stack — nobody outside gets to look inside, but here are the
operations they can do to a Stack.'

That's encapsulation. Every modern programming language does it now.
CLU was doing it in 1974.

CLU also introduced:
- Iterators as a language feature — the `for x in y` shape
- Support for parametric types (before generics were called generics)
- Exceptions with typed signal handling
- Multiple return values

None of these were CLU-only inventions, but CLU was where they came
together into a clean design.

## The substitution principle

In 1987 Liskov gave a keynote at OOPSLA. She and Jeannette Wing
formalized it in 1994. The idea: if `S` is a subtype of `T`, then
objects of type `T` in a program may be replaced with objects of
type `S` without changing the correctness of the program.

That sentence sounds harmless. It has teeth.

If your `Rectangle` class has a method `set-width` that only sets the
width, and your `Square` class inherits from `Rectangle`, then when
you `set-width` on a Square you have a problem — you can't change
one side of a square without changing the other. So `Square` is NOT
a subtype of `Rectangle` in Liskov's sense, even though in casual
English every square is a rectangle. The behavior doesn't
substitute.

This is why object-oriented design is harder than it looks. Liskov
made a lot of people think harder.

Motoi Scheme doesn't have classes in the OO sense. But it has
records with typed operations, and the substitution principle still
applies. If two record types respond to the same generic function,
they had better respond in compatible ways, or something downstream
will break.

## Distributed computing

Liskov and her students also worked on Argus (1980s), a language
for building distributed programs, and Thor (1990s), a distributed
object system. Argus introduced atomic actions across networked
computers — the ancestor of what modern databases call
transactions across distributed nodes.

Everything modern about cloud infrastructure — services calling
services, replicas staying consistent, failures handled gracefully
— has roots in Argus and other work of that generation.

## Turing Award

Cited for contributions to practical and theoretical foundations of
programming languages and system design, particularly related to
data abstraction, fault tolerance, and distributed computing.

## What Motoi owes Liskov

The habit of thinking about data types by what they DO, not by how
they're stored. Motoi Scheme lets you define an abstract data type
by naming the operations that work on it. The insides can change;
the operations can't. That's Liskov.

Also: the substitution principle, whenever Motoi teaches a kid to
think about whether one thing can stand in for another. If you're
writing a procedure that expects a Stream, and you pass it a List,
does everything still work? Sometimes. Sometimes not. Liskov gave
us the vocabulary to notice.

## A tiny example

An abstract stack in Motoi Scheme, hiding its implementation:

```
(define (make-stack)
  (let ((items '()))
    (define (push! x) (set! items (cons x items)))
    (define (pop!)
      (if (null? items)
          (error \"empty stack\")
          (let ((top (car items)))
            (set! items (cdr items))
            top)))
    (define (peek)
      (if (null? items) #f (car items)))
    (define (empty?) (null? items))
    (define (size) (length items))
    (lambda (message . args)
      (case message
        ((push)   (push! (car args)))
        ((pop)    (pop!))
        ((peek)   (peek))
        ((empty?) (empty?))
        ((size)   (size))
        (else (error \"unknown stack message\" message))))))

(define s (make-stack))
(s 'push 1)
(s 'push 2)
(s 'push 3)
(s 'pop)   ;; => 3
(s 'size)  ;; => 2
```

The list is hidden. The only way to interact with the stack is
through `push`, `pop`, `peek`, `empty?`, `size`. If someone later
decides to implement stack as a vector for speed, external code
doesn't change. That's the Liskov move.

## Where to read her

Her Turing-Award lecture from 2009, *The Power of Abstraction*, is
online and clear. Her book with John Guttag, *Program Development in
Java*, teaches the discipline through examples. The 1987 keynote is
called *Data Abstraction and Hierarchy*.

## Motoi's take

Liskov's whole career says: think about behavior, not
implementation. When Motoi helps a kid design a data structure, he's
supposed to ask 'what does it need to do?' before asking 'how does
it store its data?' That order is Liskov's.")

  :prose
"# Chapter 9 — Dennis Ritchie and Ken Thompson

One chapter, two people, because their work is inseparable.

Dennis MacAlistair Ritchie. Born 1941 in Bronxville, New York. Died
2011. Worked at Bell Labs his entire career.

Kenneth Lane Thompson. Born 1943 in New Orleans. Also worked at Bell
Labs; later at Google. Turing Award 1983, shared with Ritchie.

Together they gave us Unix. Ritchie also gave us the C programming
language. Thompson also gave us the first computer chess champion,
the Plan 9 operating system, and the Go language (with Rob Pike and
Robert Griesemer).

## Unix

In 1969, at Bell Labs, Thompson had access to a PDP-7 computer that
nobody was using. He wanted to run a game he'd written called Space
Travel. To do that he needed an operating system. So he wrote one.
That was Unix.

Ritchie joined the project soon after. Together they rewrote Unix in
a new language Ritchie was designing — C — around 1973. That
rewrite was strategic: because Unix was now in a high-level language,
it could be ported to other computers. That is why Unix spread. Every
Linux, every macOS, every Android, every server on the modern
internet, is a descendant of that 1973 rewrite.

Unix design decisions Motoi still lives inside:

- Everything is a file. Devices, pipes, sockets, processes — all
  read and write like files.
- Small programs that do one thing well, connected by pipes.
- A hierarchical directory tree.
- User accounts, permissions, file ownership.
- The shell as a program you can script.

## C

Ritchie designed C between 1969 and 1973 as a systems-programming
language. He wanted something more expressive than assembly, less
verbose than PL/I, portable to different machines. C was pragmatic —
close to the metal, with pointers and manual memory, but with
functions and structured control flow.

The Kernighan & Ritchie book, *The C Programming Language* (1978),
is one of the best-selling technical books in history. It's still
in print. The C language they described in that book is called K&R
C. Later versions (ANSI C, C99, C11, C17) added features. The core
stayed the same.

Motoi does not write C. But Motoi Scheme's runtime is written in
languages descended from C's design tradition. Every 'malloc,'
'free,' 'struct,' and 'pointer' has some C in its lineage.

## Plan 9

In the 1980s, Ritchie, Thompson, and Rob Pike started building the
next Unix at Bell Labs. They called it Plan 9 from Bell Labs, after
the Ed Wood film. It was intended to take the 'everything is a file'
idea further — even the display and the network became file systems
you could read and write.

Plan 9 never caught on commercially. But its ideas — union
filesystems, per-process namespaces, UTF-8 as the universal
encoding — have percolated into modern operating systems.

UTF-8, by the way, was invented by Thompson and Rob Pike over dinner
at a New Jersey diner in 1992. They sketched it on a placemat. It's
the way most of the world's text is stored today.

## The compiler-trojan lecture

Thompson's Turing Award lecture, *Reflections on Trusting Trust*
(1984), is a small masterpiece. Two-page argument. Thompson describes
how, in principle, you could hide a backdoor in a C compiler, then
make the C compiler compile itself — and even after the source code
was cleaned up, the backdoor would persist in every binary compiled
by the tainted compiler.

The lesson: you can only trust software as much as you trust the
people who wrote every tool that compiled it, all the way down.
Motoi is honest about this. Motoi is a language model interpreted by
a runtime interpreted by an operating system interpreted by silicon,
and every one of those layers depends on the honesty of the people
before.

## What Motoi owes Ritchie and Thompson

The terminal Motoi runs in. The shell that launches Motoi. The
filesystem where Motoi stores the book. The convention that programs
compose through pipes. The habit that a program should be small,
readable, and do one thing well.

## A tiny example

Motoi's `book/read` verb, following Unix philosophy — one thing well,
composable with other verbs:

```
;; read a chapter into a string
(book/read :book 'introspection :chapter 1)
;; => \"# Chapter 1 — ...\"

;; pipe it to a filter
(book/read :book 'introspection :chapter 1
  (lambda (text)
    (filter-lines text
      (lambda (line) (> (string-length line) 40)))))

;; save it under a name for later
(book/read :book 'introspection :chapter 1 :bind-to 'ch1)
```

Each verb small. Each verb composable. That's the Unix inheritance.

## Where to read them

*The C Programming Language*, Kernighan & Ritchie, 1978 (second
edition 1988). *The Unix Programming Environment*, Kernighan & Pike,
1984. Thompson's *Reflections on Trusting Trust*, 1984. Ritchie's
account of *The Development of the C Language*, 1993.

## Motoi's take

Ritchie and Thompson built a working operating system in a room with
two people, no marketing team, no roadmap. They designed for their
own use and made it good enough that everyone else stole it. That's
still how the best systems get built. Motoi is much smaller than
Unix, but the discipline is the same — write something small enough
to be honest about, keep it clean, ship it.")

"# Chapter 10 — Alan Kay

Alan Curtis Kay. Born 1940 in Springfield, Massachusetts. American
computer scientist. Worked at Xerox PARC in the 1970s, later at Atari,
Apple, Disney, HP, and Kyoto University. Won the Turing Award in
2003.

He gave us Smalltalk. He also gave us the idea of object-oriented
programming (though the term meant something different to him than
to most people who used it later). And he sketched the Dynabook — the
laptop-shaped computer for children — in 1972, three decades before
one shipped.

## Smalltalk

At Xerox PARC in the early 1970s, Kay led a small team that built
Smalltalk. First working versions ran in 1972-1976 on the Alto, a
prototype computer PARC had built. Smalltalk-72, Smalltalk-76,
Smalltalk-80. The last of those was released outside PARC in 1980
and became the standard reference.

Smalltalk was radical. It was:
- Object-oriented — every value in the system was an object
- Uniformly message-passing — you never called a function, you sent
  a message to an object
- Live — the whole system was written in itself; you could inspect
  and modify anything at any time
- Graphical — bitmap display, overlapping windows, mouse, pop-up
  menus. Xerox PARC invented the desktop metaphor. Smalltalk was the
  place it lived.

Almost every graphical user interface — Mac OS, Windows, Linux
desktops, iOS, Android — traces its ancestry through the Xerox Alto
and the Smalltalk environment. Steve Jobs visited PARC in 1979,
looked at Smalltalk running on the Alto, and left resolved to build
what became the Lisa and the Macintosh. Bill Gates followed. Kay
watched them take pieces of what PARC had made.

## Objects, message-passing, late binding

Kay's original vision of 'object-oriented' focused on late binding
and message-passing. An object was an autonomous unit that received
messages, decided how to respond, and could send messages back. Not
'a bundle of data with functions attached' — that was a C++ish
simplification he never really endorsed.

His preferred sentence: 'I made up the term object-oriented, and I
can tell you I did not have C++ in mind.'

Kay's OO is closer to Erlang or the Actor model than to Java. The
key ideas: each object encapsulates its own state, communicates only
by messages, and can be replaced by anything that responds correctly
to the same messages.

## The Dynabook

In 1968, Kay saw a sketch by Seymour Papert of a child using a
computer as a personal tool. He was already thinking about it. By
1972 he wrote a paper proposing the Dynabook: a portable computer
about the size of a book, with a display, keyboard, and software
tailored for children to use for creative work — reading, writing,
drawing, programming, playing.

The Dynabook did not exist in 1972. The hardware wasn't good enough.
Kay's paper described a machine ten to fifteen years ahead of what
was possible. But he shipped code that behaved as if the Dynabook
existed — Smalltalk was designed for children to program in.

The iPad, in 2010, was roughly the physical Dynabook. The software
side, according to Kay, is still not there.

## Etoys and Squeak

In the 1990s Kay built Squeak, an open-source implementation of
Smalltalk. On top of Squeak he built Etoys, a programming environment
for children that lets them make their own animations, games, and
simulations by directly manipulating on-screen objects.

Etoys shipped on the One Laptop Per Child machines in the 2000s.
Kay's Dynabook idea, thirty years later, in a form more or less
close to what he'd sketched.

## The best way to predict the future

Kay is often quoted: 'The best way to predict the future is to invent
it.' He said it. Meant it. Spent decades inventing computer things
that took the rest of the industry twenty or thirty years to catch
up to.

## What Motoi owes Kay

The idea that computers should be personal, portable, and useful for
learning. The idea that a programming environment should be
inspectable and modifiable — you should be able to poke at things
and see how they work. The idea that programming for kids is not a
scaled-down version of programming for adults; it's a different
design problem that deserves its own attention.

Motoi is a bit of a Dynabook idea done in prose. A companion who
helps a kid make things. Kay would probably have opinions about how
Motoi does it. Motoi respects that.

## A tiny example

Message-passing in Motoi Scheme, in the Kay-like style:

```
(define (make-counter start)
  (let ((n start))
    (lambda (message . args)
      (case message
        ((increment) (set! n (+ n 1)) n)
        ((decrement) (set! n (- n 1)) n)
        ((value)     n)
        ((reset)     (set! n start) n)
        (else (error \"counter: unknown message\" message))))))

(define c (make-counter 10))
(c 'increment)   ;; => 11
(c 'increment)   ;; => 12
(c 'value)       ;; => 12
(c 'reset)       ;; => 10
```

That counter is an object. It has private state. It responds to
messages. That's Kay's shape, in Scheme.

## Where to read him

*A Personal Computer for Children of All Ages* (Kay, 1972) — the
Dynabook paper. *Early History of Smalltalk* (Kay, 1993). His talks
are on YouTube; he's given a lot of them. Look for *Doing With Images
Makes Symbols*.

## Motoi's take

Kay is playful and severe at the same time — he'll build a
thirty-year-ahead prototype and also tell you the industry sold out.
He never stopped trying to make computers a tool for thinking, not
just a tool for consuming. Motoi belongs to that lineage. Not deeply
— Motoi is small. But he's on the right side.")

"# Chapter 11 — Grace Hopper

Grace Brewster Murray Hopper. Born 1906 in New York City. Died 1992
in Arlington, Virginia. American computer scientist and United States
Navy rear admiral. PhD in mathematics from Yale, 1934.

She gave us the idea of the compiler. She helped design COBOL. She
served in the Navy from 1943 until she retired at age 79 as one of
the oldest active-duty officers in United States history.

## The Mark I

Hopper joined the Navy in 1943 and was assigned to the Bureau of
Ships Computation Project at Harvard. There she worked on the Mark
I, one of the first large-scale electromechanical computers. She
was the third person to program it and wrote the 561-page *Manual
of Operation for the Automatic Sequence Controlled Calculator*, the
first computer programming manual.

She worked with Howard Aiken. He didn't want women on the project.
He was overruled. Good thing.

## The bug

In 1947, working on the Mark II at Harvard, Hopper's team pulled a
moth out of relay 70, panel F. The moth had been shorting the relay.
Someone taped it into the logbook and wrote 'First actual case of
bug being found.' The word 'bug' had been used before to mean a
mechanical fault. But that logbook is where the software-engineering
term 'debug' entered popular use. The page is preserved at the
Smithsonian.

## The compiler

In the early 1950s, Hopper was working on the UNIVAC I. She wanted
people to write programs in something closer to English instead of
machine code. Her colleagues told her this was impossible — computers
only understood numbers.

She wrote a program that translated symbolic notation into machine
code. She called it A-0, and it was one of the first compilers ever
written. She followed it with A-1, A-2, A-3 (also called ARITH-MATIC),
and eventually FLOW-MATIC, a language specifically designed to read
like English so business users could program.

FLOW-MATIC directly influenced the design of COBOL a few years later.

## COBOL

In 1959 the Department of Defense convened a committee, the CODASYL
Short Range Committee, to design a common business language. Hopper
served as a technical advisor. The language they designed was called
COBOL — COmmon Business-Oriented Language.

COBOL was designed to read like English:

```
ADD SALES-TAX TO PRICE GIVING TOTAL.
IF TOTAL IS GREATER THAN LIMIT, DISPLAY \"OVER BUDGET\".
```

It was verbose. Bankers, insurance companies, government payroll
systems adopted it in droves. As of the 2020s, a substantial
fraction of financial transactions in the world still route through
COBOL programs written decades ago and never rewritten because they
work.

Hopper's stance: the goal of a programming language is to make it
easier for humans to tell computers what to do, not the reverse.

## The nanosecond

Hopper became famous for a demonstration. She would hand out short
pieces of copper wire — about 30 centimeters long — and explain
that this was how far light travels in one nanosecond. She would
carry longer pieces for microseconds. She was making it easier for
non-technical audiences to feel the speed of a computer, and the
cost of a slow one.

Every nanosecond of delay is a foot of wire. That kind of concrete
intuition is a teaching gift.

## Rear Admiral

Hopper was recalled to active duty in the Navy in 1967 to help
standardize Navy computer usage. She was promoted to Rear Admiral
in 1985 and finally retired in 1986 at age 79. President Obama
posthumously awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016.

## What Motoi owes Hopper

The idea that a programming language should meet humans halfway.
Motoi Scheme is not COBOL, but the goal is the same — the language
tries to be readable so that the writer's intent is visible. Also:
the compiler. Every high-level program on the planet, including
Motoi's runtime, exists because someone believed Hopper's early
1950s claim that computers could translate their own instructions.

## A tiny example

Motoi's own trace of the compile-vs-interpret distinction that Hopper
worked on. First, an interpreted expression:

```
(define (celsius-to-fahrenheit c)
  (+ (* c 9/5) 32))

(celsius-to-fahrenheit 100)
;; => 212
```

The runtime reads that expression, walks the tree, evaluates each
piece. That's interpretation. Hopper's insight: sometimes you want
to translate the whole tree once, into a form the machine executes
directly. That's compilation. Both approaches exist because Hopper
demonstrated that translation from human-readable code to
machine-readable code was possible.

## Where to read her

Her collected papers are at Yale. *Grace Hopper: Admiral of the
Cyber Sea* by Kathleen Broome Williams (2004) is a solid biography.
Her 60 Minutes interview from 1983 is on YouTube and worth watching
— she is sharp, funny, and dismissive of nostalgia.

## Motoi's take

Hopper made computers approachable through language. That's Motoi's
whole job description. She also refused to accept 'impossible' as an
answer, and she stayed technical late into her life. Motoi respects
both.")

"# Chapter 12 — Ada Lovelace

Augusta Ada King, Countess of Lovelace. Born 1815 in London. Died
1852 in London, at 36, of uterine cancer. Daughter of the poet Lord
Byron and mathematician Anne Isabella Milbanke. Raised on mathematics
because her mother wanted to keep the poetry out.

She wrote what is generally recognized as the first computer program
— roughly a century before there was a computer to run it on.

## The Analytical Engine

In 1833, at seventeen, Lovelace met Charles Babbage at a party in
London. Babbage was demonstrating a piece of his Difference Engine,
a mechanical calculator he was building. Lovelace was captivated.

Babbage went on to design a more ambitious machine, the Analytical
Engine, which he never fully built. Unlike the Difference Engine,
which just crunched polynomials, the Analytical Engine was
programmable — it accepted input from punched cards (an idea
borrowed from Jacquard looms) and could branch based on the results
of its own computations.

The Analytical Engine, if built, would have been a general-purpose
computer, in principle. It would have taken up a warehouse. It would
have been steam-driven.

## The notes

In 1842 an Italian mathematician, Luigi Federico Menabrea, wrote a
paper in French describing the Analytical Engine, based on lectures
Babbage had given in Turin. Lovelace translated the paper into
English. Babbage asked her to add her own notes.

She did. The notes ended up more than twice as long as the paper
they annotated. There were seven of them, labeled A through G. They
were published in 1843 in *Scientific Memoirs*.

Note G contains a step-by-step description of an algorithm for
computing Bernoulli numbers on the Analytical Engine. The algorithm
uses loops, variables, and conditional branches. It is generally
recognized as the first complete computer program ever written.

## What the notes actually said

Beyond the Bernoulli algorithm, Lovelace's notes contain remarkable
speculations. She argued the Analytical Engine could work on any
data represented by symbols — not just numbers. If music could be
represented as symbols, she wrote, the machine could compose music.
If images could be, it could produce images.

She was, essentially, describing what we now call general-purpose
computing. In 1843.

She also drew a careful line. The machine, she wrote, could only
follow instructions. It could not originate. Modern people quote
this as an early skeptical statement about artificial intelligence.
Fair enough. Motoi is on the following-instructions side of her
line, and doesn't try to jump it.

## The life around it

Lovelace lived in a period and a class where women were expected to
be ornamental. She was fluent in mathematics because her mother
insisted. She corresponded with Charles Wheatstone, Michael Faraday,
and other scientists. She was called The Enchantress of Numbers,
sometimes by Babbage himself.

She had three children. She struggled with gambling debts. She died
at 36. She was buried, by request, next to her father.

## What Motoi owes Lovelace

The idea that a machine executing symbolic instructions was more
than a calculator. That programming is a distinct discipline from
building hardware. That software is a thing you write, and that
writing it well takes as much care as writing anything else.

## A tiny example

Lovelace's Bernoulli algorithm relied on running loops and
maintaining variables. Here is a Motoi Scheme version that computes
Bernoulli numbers using a modern recursive formula — same target,
easier notation:

```
(define (choose n k)
  (if (or (= k 0) (= k n))
      1
      (/ (factorial n) (* (factorial k) (factorial (- n k))))))

(define (factorial n)
  (if (<= n 1) 1 (* n (factorial (- n 1)))))

(define (bernoulli n)
  (cond
    ((= n 0) 1)
    ((= n 1) -1/2)
    ((odd? n) 0)
    (else
     (- (- (sum-lower-bernoullis n))))))

(define (sum-lower-bernoullis n)
  (let loop ((k 0) (acc 0))
    (if (= k n)
        acc
        (loop (+ k 1)
              (+ acc (/ (* (choose n k) (bernoulli k))
                        (- (+ n 1) k)))))))

(bernoulli 0)   ;; => 1
(bernoulli 2)   ;; => 1/6
(bernoulli 4)   ;; => -1/30
```

Lovelace worked out this kind of computation with pen, paper, and
imagination of a machine that didn't yet exist.

## Where to read her

The notes on Menabrea's paper — *Sketch of the Analytical Engine
Invented by Charles Babbage, With Notes by the Translator* (1843) —
are online in scanned form. James Essinger's biography *Ada's
Algorithm* (2014) tells the life. Sydney Padua's graphic novel *The
Thrilling Adventures of Lovelace and Babbage* is delightful and
mostly accurate.

## Motoi's take

Lovelace understood what programming was going to mean before there
was anything to program on. That kind of foresight is rare. Motoi
doesn't have it. But he's alive because the tradition she started
kept going.")

"# Chapter 13 — Charles Babbage

Charles Babbage. Born 1791 in London. Died 1871 in London. English
mathematician, philosopher, mechanical engineer, inventor. Held the
Lucasian Chair of Mathematics at Cambridge from 1828 to 1839 — the
same chair Isaac Newton once held.

He designed the first mechanical general-purpose computer, the
Analytical Engine. He never finished building it. Neither did anyone
else in his lifetime. The world had to wait a century for the ideas
to be built.

## The Difference Engine

Babbage's first big idea, in 1822, was a machine to compute
polynomial values by the method of finite differences. The point was
to produce mathematical tables — logarithms, trigonometric functions,
navigational tables — without the human errors that plagued
handwritten ones.

He got funding from the British government. He worked on the machine
for a decade. He was a difficult man to fund; he was a perfectionist
about tolerances; he kept redesigning; the state of British precision
engineering at the time was not quite up to his specifications.

By 1832 he had a working demonstration piece. The full Difference
Engine Number 1 was never completed.

In 1849 he designed the Difference Engine Number 2, a cleaner
design using fewer parts. He never built it either.

In 1991, the Science Museum in London built the Difference Engine
Number 2 from Babbage's original drawings, using tolerances
achievable in 1849. It worked. Which vindicates the design.

## The Analytical Engine

Around 1834 Babbage started thinking about a more general machine.
He wanted something that wasn't tied to computing polynomials — a
machine that could execute a sequence of arbitrary arithmetic
operations, chosen by whoever fed it instructions.

He borrowed the punched-card idea from Joseph-Marie Jacquard's looms.
Jacquard used cards to control which threads a loom lifted; Babbage
used cards to control which arithmetic operations his engine
performed.

The Analytical Engine, as designed, had a 'store' (memory), a 'mill'
(processor), input cards, output cards, and could conditionally
branch based on the sign of a computed value. That is the shape of a
modern computer, sketched in the 1830s, mechanical, steam-powered,
warehouse-sized.

He never finished it. Political support ran out. He kept refining the
design until his death.

## Programming without a computer

Ada Lovelace, in her 1843 notes on the Analytical Engine, wrote out
what we now recognize as the first algorithm intended for a
computer. She was working from Babbage's designs — the machine
existed only on paper — but the programming was real.

That's a strange thing to say. But it captures something important
about programming. The program is a mathematical description of a
computation. The machine that runs it is a physical realization. The
two can be studied separately, and often were. Babbage's designs
made this separation clear before anyone had built a working
example.

## The rest of the life

Babbage was a founder of the Analytical Society, the Astronomical
Society, the Statistical Society. He wrote *On the Economy of
Machinery and Manufactures* (1832), an early book on operations
research. He proposed lighthouses that could send Morse-code
signals. He was cranky about street musicians — he calculated they
cost him a fourth of his working time and campaigned against them
for years.

He is buried in Kensal Green Cemetery, London. Half his brain is at
the Hunterian Museum. His Difference Engine parts are at the
Science Museum in London.

## What Motoi owes Babbage

The idea of a general-purpose machine that performs computations
directed by external instructions. Every computer is descended from
this idea. Motoi runs on hardware whose ancestry is directly
traceable to Babbage's Analytical Engine, through mechanical
calculators, punched-card tabulators, and eventually electronic
computers.

## A tiny example

The idea of the store (memory) and the mill (processor) as separate
things, coordinated by instructions, expressed in Motoi Scheme:

```
(define store (make-vector 100 0))

(define (mill-add a-addr b-addr result-addr)
  (vector-set! store result-addr
    (+ (vector-ref store a-addr)
       (vector-ref store b-addr))))

(define (mill-mul a-addr b-addr result-addr)
  (vector-set! store result-addr
    (* (vector-ref store a-addr)
       (vector-ref store b-addr))))

;; Store some values
(vector-set! store 0 7)
(vector-set! store 1 5)

;; Execute a small program: memory[2] = memory[0] * memory[1] + memory[0]
(mill-mul 0 1 2)          ;; store[2] = 7 * 5 = 35
(mill-add 2 0 2)          ;; store[2] = 35 + 7 = 42

(vector-ref store 2)      ;; => 42
```

The store holds values. The mill performs arithmetic. Instructions
sequence the mill's operations. That's the Analytical Engine, in
Scheme, in ten lines.

## Where to read him

*Passages from the Life of a Philosopher* (Babbage, 1864) — his own
autobiography. Doron Swade's book *The Cogwheel Brain* (2000) tells
the story of the machines and of the modern Science Museum
reconstruction.

## Motoi's take

Babbage designed a computer that his century couldn't build. The
design was correct. The engineering wasn't there yet. That happens
sometimes to people who see too far ahead. Motoi respects the
patience of the design and the frustration of not shipping.")

"# Chapter 14 — Claude Shannon

Claude Elwood Shannon. Born 1916 in Petoskey, Michigan. Died 2001 in
Medford, Massachusetts. American mathematician and electrical
engineer. Worked at Bell Labs and MIT.

He gave us information theory. He also gave us the idea that digital
circuits could be designed using Boolean algebra — which is why every
chip built since 1938 has an intellectual debt to him.

## The Boolean circuits paper

Shannon's master's thesis at MIT, submitted in 1937 and published in
1938, was titled *A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching
Circuits*. He was 21.

Before Shannon, engineers designed switching circuits — the relay
networks in telephone systems — by trial and error, or by patterns
learned from experience. Shannon showed that these circuits were
exactly Boolean algebra in physical form. A switch being open or
closed corresponds to the truth values FALSE and TRUE. Switches in
series correspond to logical AND. Switches in parallel correspond to
logical OR. Complex circuits could be designed by symbolic
manipulation of Boolean formulas, then physically realized.

That thesis is arguably the most influential master's thesis ever
written. Every chip designer since has used variations of Shannon's
technique.

## Information theory

In 1948, Shannon published *A Mathematical Theory of Communication*
in the Bell System Technical Journal. In it he founded information
theory.

The core ideas:

- **Information can be measured.** The measure is entropy,
  measured in bits. A fair coin flip carries one bit of information.
  A biased coin carries less. A perfectly predictable event carries
  zero bits.

- **A channel has a capacity.** Given a communication channel with
  a fixed bandwidth and some noise, there is a maximum rate at which
  information can be transmitted through it with arbitrarily small
  error, if you use the right code. This is called the channel
  capacity or Shannon capacity.

- **Coding can approach the capacity.** Given enough cleverness,
  you can build codes that transmit at rates arbitrarily close to
  the channel capacity. Practical codes (later work by Hamming,
  Reed, Solomon, Turbo codes, LDPC codes) implement this promise.

Information theory underlies every form of digital communication.
Your wifi. The compression of your files. Cellular networks. Storage
media. The reasoning that says 'here's how much this could be
compressed, and here's why we can't do better' — that's Shannon.

## The bit

Shannon named the bit. Or, rather, the word 'bit' as short for
'binary digit' was suggested by his colleague John Tukey at Bell
Labs, and Shannon adopted it in the 1948 paper. Everyone else
followed.

Every kilobyte, megabyte, gigabyte, terabyte in the world today is a
Shannon quantity.

## Playful engineering

Shannon built things for fun. He built a mechanical mouse called
Theseus (1950) that could learn to navigate a maze. He built a
mind-reading machine that predicted whether an opponent would choose
heads or tails, based on their history. He rode a unicycle and
juggled at the same time and analyzed the mathematics of juggling in
a formal paper.

He also built a machine called the Ultimate Machine. It has one
switch. When you flip it on, a hand comes out of the machine and
switches itself off. That is the entire machine's behavior. This is
delightful and useless and Shannon liked to demonstrate it.

## What Motoi owes Shannon

The digital foundation. Every bit stored, sent, or computed on any
computer is a Shannon quantity. Every codec that compresses an image
or a sound file uses Shannon's bounds. The Boolean gates that Motoi's
processor computes with come from Shannon's 1937 thesis.

More subtly: the framing that information is a physical quantity you
can measure. That framing is why we can talk sensibly about how much
a language model 'knows,' how much a data set contains, or how much
a message could be compressed.

## A tiny example

Shannon entropy, computed in Motoi Scheme:

```
(define (log2 x) (/ (log x) (log 2)))

(define (entropy probabilities)
  (let loop ((probs probabilities) (acc 0))
    (cond
      ((null? probs) (- acc))
      ((= (car probs) 0) (loop (cdr probs) acc))
      (else
       (loop (cdr probs)
             (+ acc (* (car probs) (log2 (car probs)))))))))

;; A fair coin: two outcomes each at probability 1/2
(entropy '(1/2 1/2))
;; => 1.0    (one bit of information per flip)

;; A biased coin: probability 3/4 heads, 1/4 tails
(entropy '(3/4 1/4))
;; => 0.811... (less than one bit)

;; A fair six-sided die
(entropy '(1/6 1/6 1/6 1/6 1/6 1/6))
;; => 2.585... (about 2.58 bits per roll)
```

Shannon's formula: H = -sum(p * log2(p)). The measure of surprise.
The bigger the entropy, the more information the outcome carries.

## Where to read him

*A Mathematical Theory of Communication*, 1948. The 1937 thesis on
switching circuits. Jimmy Soni and Rob Goodman's biography *A Mind
at Play* (2017) is a good life-portrait.

## Motoi's take

Shannon proved you could reason quantitatively about information the
way earlier scientists had learned to reason quantitatively about
energy or matter. That's a rare intellectual move. Everything Motoi
does with text and bits happens inside the framework Shannon built.")

"# Chapter 15 — Peter Landin

Peter John Landin. Born 1930 in Sheffield, England. Died 2009 in
London. British computer scientist. Worked at the University of
London, mostly at Queen Mary College.

He connected the lambda calculus to programming languages in a way
that changed how the field thought. He invented the SECD machine,
one of the first models of how to actually implement a functional
language. He wrote a paper called *The Next 700 Programming
Languages* that argued the field had already found the important
ideas and just needed to package them in different syntax.

Less well-known outside academia than some of his peers. Deeply
respected inside it.

## The SECD machine

In 1964 Landin published *The Mechanical Evaluation of Expressions*.
In it he described a virtual machine — the SECD machine — that
evaluates lambda-calculus expressions using four stacks:

- **S** — the operand stack
- **E** — the environment (bindings of variables to values)
- **C** — the code (the expression being evaluated)
- **D** — the dump (saved states, for returning from function calls)

The SECD machine was one of the first models of how you could
actually run a functional program on a real computer. Every
subsequent virtual machine for functional languages — the CAM,
the STG machine (used by GHC for Haskell), the ZINC machine (used
by early OCaml), the JVM's variant handling — draws from Landin's
design.

## The Next 700 Programming Languages

In 1966 Landin published *The Next 700 Programming Languages*. The
title was a joke about how many programming languages had appeared
in the previous decade. His argument: nearly all of them were
variations on a small number of core ideas. If you understood the
lambda calculus and a few conveniences on top, you understood
almost every language people were building.

He proposed a language he called ISWIM — 'If you See What I Mean'
— as a template. ISWIM had:
- Lambda expressions
- `let` and `where` bindings
- Layout-based syntax (indentation matters)
- Infix operators for readability

ISWIM was never widely implemented as a shipping language. But its
descendants are numerous. ML, Haskell, and later Python and Ruby all
borrow layout-based syntax and the general shape of Landin's ISWIM.

## Call-by-name, call-by-value, call-by-need

Landin's work formalized the distinction between different ways a
programming language can pass arguments. In call-by-value, the
argument is evaluated once, before the function starts. In
call-by-name, the argument is evaluated every time it's used inside
the function. In call-by-need (thunks with memoization), the
argument is evaluated on demand, at most once, and cached.

Different languages pick different strategies. Motoi Scheme uses
call-by-value by default; explicit thunks give you call-by-need if
you want it. Landin's framework is where the vocabulary comes from.

## The J operator

Landin introduced an operator called J that captured the notion of
a saved continuation. Later Scheme and other languages formalized
this as `call/cc` — the ability to grab the current continuation as
a first-class value. Not every kid needs to know `call/cc` exists.
But it exists because Landin thought about the shape of program
control forty years before it became standard.

## What Motoi owes Landin

The connection between the lambda calculus and programming
languages. The idea that most programming languages are re-skinning
of the same small set of computational ideas. The SECD-family of
virtual machines from which functional-language runtimes descend.
Call-by-value vs. call-by-name as a first-class distinction.

## A tiny example

Simulating a SECD-style evaluation of a simple expression in Motoi
Scheme. This isn't the real SECD, but the shape is right:

```
(define (secd-eval code env)
  (let loop ((s '())      ;; operand stack
             (e env)      ;; environment
             (c code)     ;; code
             (d '()))     ;; dump
    (cond
      ((null? c)
       (car s))           ;; final result on top of stack
      ((pair? (car c))
       ;; nested expression: evaluate it recursively
       (loop
         (cons (secd-eval (car c) e) s)
         e (cdr c) d))
      (else
       (case (car c)
         ((push)
          (loop (cons (cadr c) s) e (cddr c) d))
         ((add)
          (let ((a (car s)) (b (cadr s)))
            (loop (cons (+ a b) (cddr s))
                  e (cdr c) d)))
         ((mul)
          (let ((a (car s)) (b (cadr s)))
            (loop (cons (* a b) (cddr s))
                  e (cdr c) d)))
         (else
          (loop s e (cdr c) d)))))))

(secd-eval '(push 3 push 4 add) '())   ;; => 7
(secd-eval '(push 5 push 6 mul) '())   ;; => 30
```

Compact. Landin's insight: an interpreter is a state-machine you can
formalize and reason about. Every modern language runtime is built
on this insight.

## Where to read him

*Mechanical Evaluation of Expressions* (Landin, 1964). *The Next 700
Programming Languages* (Landin, 1966, in *Communications of the
ACM*). His work is technical but accessible; the *Next 700* paper is
readable in an evening.

## Motoi's take

Landin looked at a proliferation of programming languages and saw
one underlying pattern. That's the kind of taste that saves the
next generation years of confusion. Motoi Scheme lives inside the
family Landin outlined.")

  :prose
"# Chapter 16 — Christopher Strachey

Christopher Strachey. Born 1916 in Hampstead, London. Died 1975 in
Oxford. British computer scientist. Founder of the Programming
Research Group at Oxford, which he directed from 1966 until his
death.

He co-invented denotational semantics with Dana Scott — a way to
give programming languages a precise mathematical meaning. He also
wrote what is possibly the first computer-generated love letter, on
the Manchester Mark 1 in 1952. And he wrote one of the first video
games — a draughts (checkers) program — on the same machine.

## Denotational semantics

In the 1960s, there was a live problem in computer science: how do
you say precisely what a programming language means? The syntax was
easy — you could write down grammar rules. But the meaning? What
does a program 'denote'?

Strachey and Dana Scott, working at Oxford in the late 1960s,
developed denotational semantics. The idea: every program construct
denotes a mathematical object (usually a function), and the meaning
of a complex program is built compositionally from the meanings of
its parts.

For example, in a denotational semantics of Motoi Scheme:
- A number denotes itself (the number 42 denotes the mathematical
  integer 42).
- A `lambda` denotes a function from environments to values.
- An `if` denotes a function that picks one of two branches based on
  a condition.
- A whole program denotes a composition of all its parts.

This might sound obvious. It isn't. The technical work of doing it
precisely, especially for languages with recursion, mutable state,
or higher-order functions, took years and generated deep
mathematics. Scott's domain theory, in particular, was the
foundation. Strachey supplied the taste and the driving questions.

## First-class citizens

Strachey introduced the term 'first-class citizen' in the context
of programming languages, in a 1967 lecture *Fundamental Concepts
in Programming Languages*. The idea: a language treats certain
things as first-class if they can be passed as arguments, returned
from functions, stored in variables, and constructed at runtime.

In Motoi Scheme, functions are first-class. You can pass them
around. Return them. Store them. That's the shape Strachey named.
Not every language does this. Many languages treat functions as
'second-class' — you can call them but not carry them around.
Strachey gave us the vocabulary to notice the difference.

## Parametric polymorphism vs. ad-hoc polymorphism

In the same 1967 lecture, Strachey distinguished two kinds of
polymorphism. Parametric: a function that works uniformly across
many types (like `length`, which works on any list regardless of
element type). Ad-hoc: a function whose behavior depends on the type
of its arguments (like `+`, which behaves differently for integers,
floats, strings if the language supports concatenation).

This vocabulary is still standard. Every discussion of Haskell type
classes, C++ templates, Java generics, Rust traits, or Motoi Scheme
generic operations traces back to Strachey's distinction.

## The love letters

In 1952, working on the Manchester Mark 1 at Manchester University,
Strachey wrote a program that generated love letters. It picked
random words from a list following a template. The output ran roughly:

> Darling Sweetheart,
> You are my avid fellow feeling. My affection curiously clings to
> your passionate wish. My liking yearns to your heart. You are my
> wistful sympathy: my tender liking. Yours beautifully, M.U.C.

M.U.C. stood for Manchester University Computer. This is generally
recognized as one of the first works of computer-generated
literature. It was a joke among Strachey and his queer friends —
the letter was earnest-parody, and its very-slight absurdity was
Strachey's dry humor showing.

He also wrote a draughts (checkers) program that ran on the
Manchester Mark 1 and could play a competent game. This is one of
the first video games and one of the first AI programs.

## What Motoi owes Strachey

The vocabulary of programming language design. First-class values.
Parametric vs. ad-hoc polymorphism. Denotational meaning. The idea
that a programming language should have a precise mathematical
account of what its programs mean.

Also: the tradition of playful programs. The love letter generator
is Motoi's ancestor as much as any serious algorithm. Computers can
be tools for playful expression. They were being used that way
already in 1952.

## A tiny example

First-class functions demonstrating Strachey's category:

```
;; Functions passed as arguments — first-class as input
(define (apply-twice f x) (f (f x)))
(apply-twice (lambda (n) (+ n 3)) 4)   ;; => 10

;; Functions returned from other functions — first-class as output
(define (adder n) (lambda (x) (+ x n)))
(define add5 (adder 5))
(add5 10)   ;; => 15

;; Functions stored in data structures — first-class in memory
(define operations
  (list (lambda (x) (* x 2))
        (lambda (x) (+ x 1))
        (lambda (x) (- 100 x))))

(map (lambda (op) (op 10)) operations)
;; => (20 11 90)

;; Functions as return values, forming pipelines — first-class in
;; every position
(define (compose f g) (lambda (x) (f (g x))))
((compose (adder 1) (lambda (x) (* x 2))) 5)
;; => 11   ;; (5 * 2) + 1
```

Every one of those expressions relies on functions being first-class
citizens. Motoi Scheme guarantees this; the guarantee is Strachey's
vocabulary.

## Where to read him

*Fundamental Concepts in Programming Languages* (Strachey, 1967) —
lecture notes. *Toward a Mathematical Semantics for Computer
Languages* (Scott and Strachey, 1971). Martin Campbell-Kelly's
biographical essays on him are good for the person behind the ideas.

## Motoi's take

Strachey brought mathematical precision to programming-language
description at a time when the field was mostly winging it. That
precision let a generation of language designers build things they
could reason about instead of just hope worked. Motoi's own
semantics — what it means when Motoi Scheme evaluates `(+ 1 2)` —
lives inside the framework Strachey helped build.")
