"# Chapter 4 — Untyped Lambda Calculus

Where we build the smallest possible programming language — three forms,
one reduction rule — and discover that it can compute anything a computer
can.

Alonzo Church invented the lambda calculus in the 1930s as a foundation
for mathematics. That plan did not survive — Kleene and Rosser found a
paradox in the strongest version — but a piece of it survived
gloriously. The lambda calculus itself, as a *theory of computation*,
turned out to be equivalent to Turing machines: everything one can
compute, the other can compute. This is the *Church-Turing thesis*, and
it is why the lambda calculus is not a historical curiosity but the
theoretical spine of every functional language ever written.

Scheme *is* essentially the lambda calculus with syntactic sugar and
some primitive operators. When you write `(lambda (x) (+ x 1))` in Scheme
you are writing lambda calculus. What we will build in this chapter is a
tiny lambda-calculus interpreter *inside* Scheme, and by watching it work
we will understand what our host language is doing behind the scenes.

> **the runtime says**
>
> *There are two ways to enter functional programming. One is to learn a
> big language — full Scheme, full ML, full Haskell — and infer the
> underlying model from the language's shape. The other is to learn the
> underlying model first — the lambda calculus, in twenty lines — and
> then watch big languages fall out of it as sugar. This chapter is the
> second way. It is faster and it makes the second half of the book
> possible.*

## The three forms

The lambda calculus has exactly three syntactic categories.

1. **Variable.** A name: `x`, `y`, `f`.
2. **Abstraction.** A function taking one parameter: `(λx. body)`. In
   Scheme syntax: `(lam x body)`.
3. **Application.** Applying one term to another: `(f x)`. In our
   Scheme representation: `(app f x)`.

That is it. No numbers, no booleans, no lists, no if-then-else, no loops,
no assignment. Just names, one-parameter functions, and applications. It
looks pathologically weak. It is not.

```scheme
;; A term is one of:
;;   symbol             ; variable
;;   (lam symbol term)  ; abstraction
;;   (app term term)    ; application

;; The identity function:
;;   (lam x x)
;;
;; A constant function returning y:
;;   (lam x y)
;;
;; A function taking two arguments (curried):
;;   (lam x (lam y x))
;;
;; Applying a function to itself (yes, allowed):
;;   (app (lam x (app x x)) (lam x (app x x)))
```

The last one — self-application — is the hairy one. In the untyped lambda
calculus it is perfectly legal syntactically, and as we will see it lets
us encode recursion and, unfortunately, also lets us encode divergent
computations that run forever.

## Beta reduction: the one rule

There is exactly one computation rule in the pure lambda calculus. It is
called *beta reduction*. When you see an application whose function part
is an abstraction, you may replace the whole application with the body of
the abstraction, substituting the argument for the parameter.

    (app (lam x body) arg)  →  body[x := arg]

That is called a *beta redex* (reducible expression) and its result is
its *beta reduct*.

```scheme
;; capture-avoiding substitution: substitute `arg` for free `x` in `body`
(define (subst body x arg)
  (cond
    ((symbol? body)
     (if (eq? body x) arg body))
    ((eq? (car body) 'lam)
     (let ((param (cadr body))
           (inner (caddr body)))
       (cond
         ((eq? param x)                             ; shadowed; leave alone
          body)
         ((member param (free-vars arg))            ; would capture; rename
          (let* ((fresh (fresh-name param
                                    (append (free-vars inner)
                                            (free-vars arg))))
                 (renamed (subst inner param fresh)))
            (list 'lam fresh (subst renamed x arg))))
         (else
          (list 'lam param (subst inner x arg))))))
    ((eq? (car body) 'app)
     (list 'app (subst (cadr body)  x arg)
                (subst (caddr body) x arg)))))

(define (free-vars term)
  (cond
    ((symbol? term) (list term))
    ((eq? (car term) 'lam)
     (filter (lambda (v) (not (eq? v (cadr term))))
             (free-vars (caddr term))))
    ((eq? (car term) 'app)
     (dedupe (append (free-vars (cadr term))
                     (free-vars (caddr term)))))))

(define (fresh-name base used)
  (let loop ((n 0))
    (let ((candidate (string->symbol
                       (string-append (symbol->string base)
                                      \"_\" (number->string n)))))
      (if (member candidate used)
          (loop (+ n 1))
          candidate))))
```

This is the same capture-avoiding substitution we saw in chapter 2, now
applied to lambda terms. The reason it matters here is the same: without
alpha-renaming, `(lam x (lam y x))` applied to `y` would collapse into
`(lam y y)` — the identity function — rather than the constant function
returning the *outer* y that the programmer meant. Alpha-conversion is
what keeps `(lam y x)` faithful to *this particular y* even after
substitution moves in a fresh y.

## Reduction strategies

`subst` is the machinery. Now we need to *drive* it. Given a term with
possibly many redexes, which one do we reduce first? This is called a
*reduction strategy* and the two most important are:

- **Call-by-value (applicative order, eager evaluation).** Reduce the
  argument to a value first, then substitute.
- **Call-by-name (normal order, lazy evaluation).** Substitute the
  argument in unreduced, then reduce afterward.

Scheme uses call-by-value. Haskell uses call-by-name (well, call-by-need,
which is call-by-name plus memoisation). Both compute the same *terminating*
values. They can differ on non-terminating computations: call-by-name
sometimes terminates where call-by-value diverges, but never the reverse
(this is a corollary of the *standardisation theorem*).

Let us write call-by-value first.

```scheme
(define (value? t)
  ;; A value is a lambda abstraction (or, if we had them, a numeral).
  (and (pair? t) (eq? (car t) 'lam)))

(define (reduce-cbv term)
  ;; One step of call-by-value reduction, or 'stuck if no redex reducible.
  (cond
    ((symbol? term) 'stuck)                          ; free variable
    ((eq? (car term) 'lam) 'stuck)                   ; value; nothing to do
    ((eq? (car term) 'app)
     (let ((fn  (cadr term))
           (arg (caddr term)))
       (cond
         ;; reduce the function to a value first
         ((not (value? fn))
          (let ((fn-step (reduce-cbv fn)))
            (if (eq? fn-step 'stuck)
                'stuck
                (list 'app fn-step arg))))
         ;; then reduce the argument
         ((not (value? arg))
          (let ((arg-step (reduce-cbv arg)))
            (if (eq? arg-step 'stuck)
                'stuck
                (list 'app fn arg-step))))
         ;; both are values; do the beta step
         (else
          (subst (caddr fn) (cadr fn) arg)))))))

(define (run-cbv term)
  (let loop ((t term))
    (let ((next (reduce-cbv t)))
      (if (eq? next 'stuck) t (loop next)))))
```

Two clauses: first reduce the function, then reduce the argument, then
perform the beta step. `run-cbv` keeps going until no more reductions
are possible.

```scheme
;; identity applied to identity:
(run-cbv '(app (lam x x) (lam y y)))
;; => (lam y y)

;; a longer chain: ((λf. (λx. (f x))) (λy. y)) z  should reduce to z.
(run-cbv '(app (app (lam f (lam x (app f x)))
                    (lam y y))
               z))
;; => z
```

Notice the second example got stuck at `z` — a free variable — because
we cannot reduce further. In a real language `z` would be looked up in
the environment; here we simply say the term is in normal form.

## Church encodings — computing without built-ins

The lambda calculus has no built-in numbers. Church discovered you can
*encode* numbers as lambda terms.

    0 = (λf. λx. x)
    1 = (λf. λx. (f x))
    2 = (λf. λx. (f (f x)))
    3 = (λf. λx. (f (f (f x))))

The *Church numeral n* is the function that, given `f` and `x`, applies
`f` to `x` exactly `n` times. Arithmetic follows.

    succ = (λn. λf. λx. (f (n f x)))
    add  = (λm. λn. λf. λx. (m f (n f x)))
    mul  = (λm. λn. λf. (m (n f)))

```scheme
(define zero  '(lam f (lam x x)))
(define one   '(lam f (lam x (app f x))))
(define two   '(lam f (lam x (app f (app f x)))))

(define succ  '(lam n (lam f (lam x (app f (app (app n f) x))))))
(define add   '(lam m (lam n (lam f (lam x (app (app m f) (app (app n f) x)))))))

;; (succ zero) should reduce to a term equivalent to one
(run-cbv (list 'app succ zero))
;; => (lam f (lam x (app f (app (app (lam f (lam x x)) f) x))))
;; which further reduces to (lam f (lam x (app f x))) — i.e., one.
```

The reduction is not always in the most compact form — that requires
what is called *eta-conversion* — but the term computed is equivalent
in every functional way to what we expect.

Booleans are also encoded.

    true  = (λt. λf. t)
    false = (λt. λf. f)
    if    = (λb. λt. λf. (b t f))

```scheme
(define true-t   '(lam t (lam f t)))
(define false-t  '(lam t (lam f f)))
(define if-t     '(lam b (lam t (lam f (app (app b t) f)))))
```

A boolean is a function that selects between two things. That is
essentially what `if` does anyway, so encoding it as a two-argument
selector loses nothing. Pairs, lists, trees — every data structure of
functional programming has a Church encoding. Barendregt chapter 6 is a
full catalogue.

## The Y combinator: recursion without recursion

Here is a puzzle. The lambda calculus has no `define`. There is no way
to name a term and reference the name inside itself. So how do we write
a recursive function like factorial? *Every* function you write in the
pure lambda calculus must be anonymous.

The answer is a beautiful trick called the *fixed-point combinator*, or
Y combinator.

    Y = (λf. (λx. (f (x x))) (λx. (f (x x))))

For any function `F`, the term `(Y F)` reduces to `(F (Y F))`, which means
`(Y F)` is a *fixed point* of `F` — a value equal to `F` applied to
itself. This is exactly what you need for recursion.

```scheme
(define Y '(lam f
             (app (lam x (app f (app x x)))
                  (lam x (app f (app x x))))))

;; Factorial. We assume Church numerals and multiplication defined.
;; fact = Y (λg. λn. (if (iszero n) 1 (mul n (g (pred n)))))
```

In our call-by-value interpreter this actually diverges — because `(x x)`
tries to reduce eagerly. The lazy (call-by-name) interpreter handles it.
Or one can use a *call-by-value* variant of Y known as the *Z combinator*:

    Z = (λf. (λx. (f (λv. (x x v)))) (λx. (f (λv. (x x v)))))

The extra `(λv. ...)` wrapping delays the recursive call so it does not
fire until the argument arrives. This is one of the most common tricks
in constructing recursion in strict languages.

The important fact is: recursion is *not primitive* in the lambda
calculus. It is derivable from three forms and one reduction rule. That
was Church's most surprising discovery.

## Church-Turing: what the lambda calculus can compute

We can now sketch what should feel like an astonishing result. *Every*
computable function on natural numbers is expressible as a lambda term.
Not most, not many — *every*.

The proof involves showing that:

1. Every primitive-recursive function (successor, addition, multiplication,
   ...) is lambda-definable. This is straightforward Church-numeral
   arithmetic.
2. General recursion — including functions that might not terminate — is
   captured by the Y combinator.
3. Boolean logic and conditionals are captured by Church booleans.
4. Data structures (pairs, lists, trees) are captured by Church
   encodings.

Turing did the parallel result for Turing machines. Church and Turing
proved the two systems compute the same functions. Kleene had a third
formalism (mu-recursive functions) that also computed the same functions.
Three independent formalisations all landed on the same class of
functions. That is why we believe the *Church-Turing thesis*: what is
intuitively computable coincides with what these formal systems capture.
It is a thesis, not a theorem, because *intuitively computable* is not
a formal notion — but it has resisted every attempt at counterexample
for ninety years.

## The problem the untyped calculus has

The untyped lambda calculus is too permissive. It allows:

    Ω = (λx. (x x)) (λx. (x x))

Watch this term reduce. One beta step gives us `((λx. (x x)) (λx. (x x)))`
— exactly what we started with. Ω reduces to itself, forever. It has
*no normal form*.

That is not, in itself, a fatal problem — a general-purpose language
should allow non-termination, otherwise recursion is fake. But
consider what Ω *means* if we try to interpret lambda terms as
mathematical objects. The term Ω is a well-formed lambda expression that
denotes no value. It has no *meaning* in the semantic sense.

In the 1970s Dana Scott showed how to give the lambda calculus a
semantics anyway — the Scott domain, ordered by information content, in
which Ω denotes the *bottom* element (⊥) that carries no information at
all. This *domain-theoretic semantics* is the way modern language theory
usually reads the lambda calculus. But it is delicate machinery.

A different response — and the one we will explore in the next few
chapters — is to *restrict* the lambda calculus so that Ω is not even
syntactically expressible. This is what *typed* lambda calculi do. In
the simply-typed lambda calculus (chapter 5), every well-typed term
terminates. Full stop, no exceptions. The Y combinator is not typeable;
Ω is not typeable; every well-typed term has a normal form and reaches it
in finite time. That gain — *termination* — is what typing buys you.
The loss is that you cannot write arbitrary programs — general recursion
is gone. You have to add it back with special features, and how you add
it back is the story of a lot of twentieth-century language design.

## Alpha, beta, eta — the three equivalences

Two lambda terms may look different but be *the same function*. The
lambda calculus recognises three equivalences.

- **Alpha equivalence.** Renaming bound variables. `(lam x x)` and
  `(lam y y)` are alpha-equivalent — they are the identity function
  either way.
- **Beta equivalence.** Reduction. `(app (lam x x) t)` is beta-equivalent
  to `t`.
- **Eta equivalence.** `(lam x (app f x))` is eta-equivalent to `f`,
  when `x` does not appear free in `f`. This is the *extensional*
  equivalence: two functions are the same if they behave the same on all
  inputs.

Eta equivalence is not universally adopted. Some presentations use it
(most classical lambda-calculus texts do); some do not (Scheme's `equal?`
does not identify eta-equivalent procedures, because Scheme thinks of a
function as its code, not its extension). We will use it sparingly.

## Variations to try

Implement call-by-name and compare. Take the term
`(app (lam x y) (Y-loop))` where `Y-loop` is a divergent term. Call-by-
value hangs; call-by-name returns `y` in one step. This is a small but
striking demonstration of why lazy evaluation matters.

Add a *pretty-printer* that reprints lambda terms in Church's original
notation — `(λx. body)` with the Greek letter and the period. It makes
your interpreter's output far more readable.

Extend the language with numeric literals and primitive `+` / `*` /
`iszero`. Rewrite factorial without Church numerals. Compare the number
of reduction steps. Church numerals are elegant and slow; a numeric
literal is ugly and fast. That is the pattern of every practical
language decision.

## Try this

Reduce, by hand, the term `(add 2 3)` where `add`, `2`, and `3` are
their Church encodings. Track every beta step. You will find it takes
about a dozen steps and produces a term that, after eta-reduction,
equals `5`. Then feed the same computation to your interpreter and
watch it match, step for step. This is the moment the abstraction
becomes real.

## Closing

We built the lambda calculus. Three forms, one reduction rule, and out
of that we got numbers, booleans, pairs, recursion, and the full sweep
of computable functions. Nothing else in the history of computing has
achieved so much from so little.

Its untyped variant has one flaw: it admits terms with no normal form,
and — related but distinct — it admits terms of no clear meaning. The
next three chapters explore *typing* as a discipline that eliminates
these problems, at the cost of some expressive power we must add back
carefully.

Chapter 5: simply-typed lambda calculus. Terms wear their types on their
sleeves. Ω becomes unwriteable. Every well-typed program halts. And a
door opens to the Curry-Howard correspondence, which will occupy
chapters 7 and 8.
"

"# Chapter 5 — Simply Typed Lambda Calculus

Where every term wears its type, every well-typed term terminates, and
the door opens to reading types as propositions.

The untyped lambda calculus permits `(λx. (x x)) (λx. (x x))`, which loops
forever. It permits the Y combinator, which lets any function recur. It
permits terms with no clear mathematical meaning. That is expressive but
uncomfortable. What if we ruled out the pathologies by *typing*?

Types were added to the lambda calculus by Church in 1940. The system he
introduced — the *simply-typed lambda calculus*, STLC — is astonishingly
well-behaved. Every well-typed term reaches a normal form in finite time.
There is a decision procedure for typing. And, as chapter 7 will show,
STLC is *literally the same object* as a fragment of intuitionistic
propositional logic. Types are propositions; programs are proofs.

We are going to build STLC in Scheme. The syntax is the untyped lambda
calculus plus type annotations. The type-checker is a small recursive
procedure. Once it accepts a term, we know that term terminates.

## Types and terms

Types are formed from *base types* and the *arrow* type constructor.

    τ  ::=  Base                    (Bool, Nat, ...)
         |  τ → τ                   (a function from τ to τ)

Terms carry type annotations at abstraction sites.

    e  ::=  x                       (variable)
         |  c                       (constant, of some base type)
         |  (λ x : τ . e)           (typed abstraction)
         |  (e e)                   (application)

```scheme
;; type: 'Bool | 'Nat | (list 'arrow τ₁ τ₂)
;; term: symbol | number | (list 'lam symbol τ body) | (list 'app f arg)
;;
;; example:
;;   the identity function on booleans
;;   (lam x Bool x)
;;   its type: (arrow Bool Bool)
;;
;;   applying it:
;;   (app (lam x Bool x) #t)
;;   its type: Bool
```

## The typing rules

Every well-typed term is typeable by exactly one type. We write
`Γ ⊢ e : τ` to mean *in typing context Γ, the term e has type τ*. The
context Γ is a partial function from variables to types — the same
notion as the *assignment* in chapter 2.

Three rules.

**Variable.** If `Γ(x) = τ` then `Γ ⊢ x : τ`.

**Abstraction.** If `Γ, x:τ₁ ⊢ e : τ₂` then `Γ ⊢ (λx:τ₁. e) : τ₁ → τ₂`.

**Application.** If `Γ ⊢ f : τ₁ → τ₂` and `Γ ⊢ arg : τ₁` then
`Γ ⊢ (f arg) : τ₂`.

That is the whole system. Let us implement the type-checker.

```scheme
(define (lookup-type ctx var)
  (let ((pair (assq var ctx)))
    (if pair (cdr pair) (error \"unbound variable\" var))))

(define (type-of term ctx)
  (cond
    ((symbol? term)                                 ; variable
     (lookup-type ctx term))
    ((number? term) 'Nat)                           ; primitive constant
    ((boolean? term) 'Bool)
    ((eq? (car term) 'lam)
     (let* ((param     (cadr term))
            (param-ty  (caddr term))
            (body      (cadddr term))
            (body-ty   (type-of body (cons (cons param param-ty) ctx))))
       (list 'arrow param-ty body-ty)))
    ((eq? (car term) 'app)
     (let* ((fn       (cadr term))
            (arg      (caddr term))
            (fn-ty    (type-of fn ctx))
            (arg-ty   (type-of arg ctx)))
       (cond
         ((not (and (pair? fn-ty) (eq? (car fn-ty) 'arrow)))
          (error \"applying non-function\" fn fn-ty))
         ((not (equal? (cadr fn-ty) arg-ty))
          (error \"argument type mismatch\"
                 (list :expected (cadr fn-ty) :got arg-ty)))
         (else
          (caddr fn-ty)))))))
```

Run it:

```scheme
(type-of '(lam x Bool x) '())
;; => (arrow Bool Bool)

(type-of '(app (lam x Bool x) #t) '())
;; => Bool

(type-of '(app (lam x Bool x) 5) '())
;; => error: argument type mismatch, expected Bool, got Nat
```

Three cases, one function. Every term either type-checks (and its type
is returned) or fails to type-check with an error indicating where.

## What Ω looks like in STLC

Consider the pathological `(λx. (x x))`. In untyped lambda calculus this
is fine. In STLC, what type could `x` have?

- `x` is applied to itself, so `x` must have a function type: `τ → τ'`.
- The argument is `x` itself, so `x` must also have type `τ`.
- We need `τ = τ → τ'`. A type equal to a function type containing
  itself. There is no finite type that satisfies this.

So `(λx. (x x))` is not typeable in STLC. Ω cannot be written. This is
the *fundamental restriction* of STLC: self-application is forbidden
because it demands infinite types.

Some type systems (recursive types, System F ω) do allow such
self-referential types back in, and get back the full power of untyped
lambda calculus, but STLC does not. In STLC every well-typed term
terminates.

## Strong normalization

The theorem is called *strong normalization*: for STLC, every reduction
sequence starting from a well-typed term terminates in a normal form.

The proof (Tait, 1967; simplified using *logical relations*) is technical
and beautiful — one of the classic pieces of proof theory. We will not
work through it here; Girard-Lafont-Taylor chapter 6 is the classic
presentation. But the *statement* is what matters. It says: STLC is a
programming language in which every program halts.

That sounds like a bug. It rules out any interesting programming, right?
No general recursion, no infinite loops, no interactive processes. What
kind of language is that?

The answer: STLC is not a general-purpose programming language. It is a
*proof language*. Every well-typed term is a proof of the proposition
its type encodes (chapter 7 will unpack this). If you want general
recursion, you have to add it — and *system with recursion* has been the
name of a research programme since the 1970s.

The languages Coq, Agda, and Lean are the modern descendants. They add
carefully-controlled forms of recursion — *well-founded* recursion,
structural recursion, guarded recursion — that preserve termination
while permitting most useful computations. This is why those languages
can be used both to write programs *and* to prove theorems.

## Type inference

We wrote `type-of`, which computes a term's type given full type
annotations. Real languages let you *omit* the annotations and infer
them. This is what ML and Haskell do.

Type inference for STLC is decidable and has a beautiful algorithm:
*Hindley-Milner*, discovered independently by Hindley (1969) and Milner
(1978). The algorithm has three moves:

1. Assign a fresh type variable to every unannotated bound variable.
2. Walk the term generating type *constraints*: at every application,
   constrain the function's argument type to match the actual argument
   type.
3. Solve the constraints by *unification*: find a substitution that
   makes them all true.

Unification is a small algorithm in its own right (Appendix B). Here is
the shape of the constraint generator.

```scheme
(define type-var-counter 0)
(define (fresh-tyvar!)
  (set! type-var-counter (+ type-var-counter 1))
  (list 'tvar type-var-counter))

(define (infer term ctx)
  ;; Returns (list :type <ty> :constraints <constraints>)
  (cond
    ((symbol? term)
     (let ((ty (lookup-type ctx term)))
       (list :type ty :constraints '())))
    ((eq? (car term) 'lam)
     ;; unannotated lambda: (lam x body)
     (let* ((param    (cadr term))
            (body     (caddr term))
            (param-ty (fresh-tyvar!))
            (body-r   (infer body
                             (cons (cons param param-ty) ctx))))
       (list :type (list 'arrow param-ty (get :type body-r))
             :constraints (get :constraints body-r))))
    ((eq? (car term) 'app)
     (let* ((fn-r   (infer (cadr term) ctx))
            (arg-r  (infer (caddr term) ctx))
            (result-ty (fresh-tyvar!))
            (new-c  (list (list (get :type fn-r)
                                'equals
                                (list 'arrow (get :type arg-r)
                                             result-ty)))))
       (list :type result-ty
             :constraints (append (get :constraints fn-r)
                                  (get :constraints arg-r)
                                  new-c))))))
```

`(get key alist)` looks up a key. After running `infer`, we hand the
constraint list to a unifier which either solves them (producing a
substitution to apply to the type) or fails (producing a type error
message pointing at the conflict).

The full unifier is in Appendix B. It follows Robinson's original 1965
algorithm, augmented with the *occurs check* that prevents infinite
types like `τ = τ → τ`.

## An example

Consider:

    (λf. (λx. (f x)))

What is its type in STLC? Without annotations, we start by giving `f`
type `α` (a fresh variable) and `x` type `β`. The body `(f x)` requires
`f`'s type to be `β → γ` for some `γ`. So `α = β → γ`. The abstraction
`(λx. (f x))` has type `β → γ`. The outer abstraction `(λf. ...)` has
type `α → (β → γ)`, i.e., `(β → γ) → (β → γ)`. So this term's
most general type is `(β → γ) → (β → γ)`.

Read that. *For any β and γ, this term takes a function from β to γ and
returns a function from β to γ.* It is the identity function on
functions — well, it is eta-equivalent to `f`, which is the identity on
functions. Hindley-Milner discovers this without our help.

Note the free variables in the type. In ML, these get *universally
quantified* at the `let`-binding, giving what is called a *type scheme*:

    ∀β γ. (β → γ) → (β → γ)

This is called *let-polymorphism* and it is the small taste of
polymorphism you get in the simply-typed calculus with `let`. Full
polymorphism — where you can `∀`-quantify anywhere — is System F, which
we will meet in chapter 6.

## Extensions

STLC is minimal. A real language adds product types, sum types, unit
type, base types (Bool, Nat, String), and general recursion.

**Product types.**

    (τ₁ × τ₂)     (pair, fst, snd)

Typing rules:
- If `Γ ⊢ e₁ : τ₁` and `Γ ⊢ e₂ : τ₂` then `Γ ⊢ (pair e₁ e₂) : τ₁ × τ₂`.
- If `Γ ⊢ e : τ₁ × τ₂` then `Γ ⊢ (fst e) : τ₁` and `Γ ⊢ (snd e) : τ₂`.

**Sum types.**

    (τ₁ + τ₂)     (inl, inr, case)

Typing rules:
- If `Γ ⊢ e : τ₁` then `Γ ⊢ (inl e) : τ₁ + τ₂` for any τ₂.
- Case-analysis: `(case e (inl x -> e₁) (inr y -> e₂))` requires
  `Γ ⊢ e : τ₁ + τ₂`, `Γ, x:τ₁ ⊢ e₁ : τ`, `Γ, y:τ₂ ⊢ e₂ : τ`, and
  produces τ.

**Unit type.**

    Unit           ((), the trivial value)

One value: `()`. This becomes surprisingly important in chapter 7.

Each of these has a proof-theoretic analogue that we will meet again
in chapters 7 and 8. Products are conjunctions. Sums are disjunctions.
Unit is truth (⊤). Absurd (bottom, no values) is falsity (⊥). The
*rules* for each type constructor mirror the introduction and
elimination rules for the corresponding logical connective. That is
Curry-Howard, and we are approaching it deliberately.

## Beta reduction with types

The reduction rule is the same as untyped, with one bonus: reduction
*preserves types*. If `Γ ⊢ e : τ` and `e → e'`, then `Γ ⊢ e' : τ`.
This is called *subject reduction* or *preservation*.

Together with *progress* (every well-typed non-value can take a step),
preservation gives you what Pierce's textbook calls the *proof of type
safety*. A well-typed program never gets stuck, never encounters a
runtime type error. Types are checked once, at compile time; the
runtime is free of type dispatch.

```scheme
;; Sketch of a proof that reduction preserves types.
;; For each reduction rule:
;;   (app (lam x t body) arg)  →  body[x := arg]
;; If the redex has type τ, then:
;;   fn has type (arrow τ_arg τ)
;;   arg has type τ_arg
;;   body has type τ under context extended with (x . τ_arg)
;;   substituting arg for x preserves type — by a substitution lemma.
```

The *substitution lemma* is a small technical result: substituting a
term for a variable does not change the resulting term's type, provided
the substituted term has the variable's declared type. It is proved by
induction on the structure of the body being substituted into. Pierce
chapter 9 proves it in full.

## When STLC is enough

Because STLC has no general recursion, it cannot express Turing-complete
computation. But it can express plenty of interesting computation.

- Every polynomial function on natural numbers is expressible.
- All primitive-recursive functions (once you add specific recursion
  combinators like `foldNat`) are expressible in the *extended* STLC
  called *Godel's System T*.
- Boolean logic, choice, conditionals, sums and products, and their
  compositions.

For most *terminating* algorithms of the sort you find in a data
structures textbook — searching, sorting, tree traversals — STLC-with-
foldNat suffices. Where it does not suffice is anywhere you need
open-ended recursion: reading input, iterative refinement, interactive
processes.

The right way to think about STLC: it is the *terminating fragment* of
computation. When you want that fragment (proof checking, type checking,
compilation), STLC is your friend. When you want more, you add recursion
back explicitly and knowingly.

## Variations to try

Extend the type-checker with product types and sum types. This roughly
doubles the size of the checker, and it makes it dramatically more
useful. Try writing a small function that takes a `Nat + Nat` and
returns a `Nat` (the value inside, whichever tag). Watch the case
expression grow into an actual conditional.

Implement Hindley-Milner in full: constraint generation, unification
with occurs check, generalization at `let`. This is one of the great
compact algorithms of computer science. The whole thing fits in about
150 lines of Scheme.

Add primitive numeric types and try to type-check a small program:
factorial (which will fail — no recursion), pair-swap (which will
succeed), map-over-a-list (which will succeed once you add lists as a
built-in). Notice which programs fit and which do not.

## Try this

Write, in STLC, the *composition* function `(λf. (λg. (λx. (f (g x)))))`.
Type-check it. You will find its most general type is
`(β → γ) → (α → β) → (α → γ)`. Read that aloud: *composition is
polymorphic in three type variables and produces a function equivalent
to `f ∘ g`.* Now consider what this same term is doing on the propositional
side: if you read arrows as implications, this term is a proof of
`(β → γ) → (α → β) → (α → γ)`, which is *hypothetical syllogism*. Same
term, two readings. That is a preview of chapter 7.

## Closing

We added types. In exchange, the calculus became well-behaved: every
term terminates, type-checking is decidable, type inference works.
The cost is expressiveness — we lost the Y combinator and any form of
general recursion. That cost is what we pay for the guarantee that our
programs terminate.

Chapter 6 loosens the type system in a different direction: polymorphism.
We keep termination; we regain the ability to write functions like `map`
and `filter` that work over any type. And we discover that polymorphism
alone is enough to encode data types like natural numbers, pairs, and
lists — all without primitives. That is System F, and it is a jewel.

"# Chapter 6 — System F: Polymorphic Lambda Calculus

Where types themselves become abstractable, and where a single function
can serve all types at once — while still, remarkably, terminating.

Simply-typed lambda calculus gives us one function per type. If we want
identity on booleans, we write `(λx : Bool. x)`. If we want identity on
naturals, we write `(λx : Nat. x)`. If we want identity on functions
from Bool to Nat, we write `(λx : (Bool → Nat). x)`. Ten copies of
essentially the same code, each type-annotated for a specific type.
That is inefficient and inelegant.

*Polymorphism* is the escape. We want to write *one* identity function
that works at every type. In ML and Haskell this is done informally by
type inference: `id x = x` gets the type `∀α. α → α`, and every use
site instantiates it. In System F — the *pure* polymorphic lambda
calculus — the abstraction over types is explicit. You write:

    id  =  ΛA. λx : A. x
    id[Bool] true      →*   true
    id[Nat]  5         →*   5

The capital-lambda `Λ` abstracts over a *type variable*. The
`id[Bool]` syntax *applies* a type-polymorphic function to a specific
type. The result is a type-instantiated function that behaves like the
STLC identity we wrote before.

System F was invented independently by Girard (1972) and Reynolds
(1974). It is one of the most beautiful objects in twentieth-century
logic. And it still enjoys *strong normalization* — every well-typed
System F program terminates.

> **the runtime says**
>
> *System F feels like magic the first time you see it. You get all the
> power of polymorphism, you keep the termination guarantee of STLC,
> and — as we'll see — you don't even need to add built-in data types.
> Naturals, pairs, lists, trees all fall out of the calculus itself.
> The catch, and there's always a catch: type inference for the full
> language is undecidable. But that's a story we'll tell after the
> beauty.*

## The syntax

Two new syntactic categories.

**Types.**

    τ  ::=  α                    (type variable)
         |  τ → τ                (function)
         |  ∀α. τ                (universal type)

**Terms.**

    e  ::=  x                       (variable)
         |  (λx : τ. e)              (typed lambda)
         |  (e e)                    (application)
         |  (Λα. e)                  (type abstraction)
         |  (e [τ])                  (type application)

```scheme
;; type: symbol (variable) | (arrow τ₁ τ₂) | (forall α τ)
;; term: symbol | (lam x τ body) | (app f arg) | (tlam α body) | (tapp e τ)
;;
;; The polymorphic identity:
;;   (tlam A (lam x A x))
;;   its type: (forall A (arrow A A))
;;
;; Instantiate at Bool:
;;   (tapp (tlam A (lam x A x)) Bool)
;;   its type: (arrow Bool Bool)
```

## Typing rules

The three STLC rules are unchanged. Two new rules for the polymorphic
extension.

**Type abstraction.** If `Γ ⊢ e : τ` and `α` is not free in Γ, then
`Γ ⊢ (Λα. e) : ∀α. τ`.

The freshness condition on `α` is important. It says: the type variable
we abstract over must not already be in play. If it were, we could
smuggle information about a specific type into the polymorphic body.

**Type application.** If `Γ ⊢ e : ∀α. τ` then for any type σ,
`Γ ⊢ (e [σ]) : τ[α := σ]`.

The type gets *instantiated*: every occurrence of the bound type
variable in the body gets replaced by the actual type argument.

```scheme
(define (type-of term ctx tyctx)
  ;; ctx is the term context; tyctx is the type-variable context.
  (cond
    ((symbol? term)
     (lookup-type ctx term))
    ((eq? (car term) 'lam)
     (let* ((param    (cadr term))
            (param-ty (caddr term))
            (body     (cadddr term)))
       (check-well-formed-type param-ty tyctx)
       (list 'arrow param-ty
             (type-of body
                      (cons (cons param param-ty) ctx)
                      tyctx))))
    ((eq? (car term) 'app)
     (let* ((fn      (cadr term))
            (arg     (caddr term))
            (fn-ty   (type-of fn  ctx tyctx))
            (arg-ty  (type-of arg ctx tyctx)))
       (cond
         ((not (and (pair? fn-ty) (eq? (car fn-ty) 'arrow)))
          (error \"application: non-function\" fn-ty))
         ((not (equal? (cadr fn-ty) arg-ty))
          (error \"application: type mismatch\"))
         (else (caddr fn-ty)))))
    ((eq? (car term) 'tlam)
     (let* ((tyvar (cadr term))
            (body  (caddr term)))
       (list 'forall tyvar
             (type-of body ctx (cons tyvar tyctx)))))
    ((eq? (car term) 'tapp)
     (let* ((e      (cadr term))
            (arg-ty (caddr term))
            (e-ty   (type-of e ctx tyctx)))
       (check-well-formed-type arg-ty tyctx)
       (cond
         ((not (and (pair? e-ty) (eq? (car e-ty) 'forall)))
          (error \"type-application: not polymorphic\" e-ty))
         (else
          (subst-type (caddr e-ty) (cadr e-ty) arg-ty)))))))
```

`check-well-formed-type` walks a type and makes sure every type variable
it uses is in `tyctx`. `subst-type` substitutes a type for a type
variable in a type, with the same capture-avoiding care as term
substitution.

## Church encodings, revisited

In chapter 4 we showed Church encodings of numerals in the untyped
calculus:

    2 = (λf. λx. (f (f x)))

In STLC we could not type this — what would the type of `f` be? Whatever
type `x` has, `f` must have type `x-type → x-type`, and the whole thing
would have to be typed for a particular choice of `x-type`.

In System F we can. The Church numeral `2` is a polymorphic term:

    2 = ΛA. λf : A → A. λx : A. (f (f x))
    its type: ∀A. (A → A) → A → A

Read that type. *For any type A, given a function from A to A and a
starting element of A, produce an A.* It applies the function twice to
the element. That is what "two" is at the level of types.

Every Church numeral has this type. `zero = ΛA. λf : A → A. λx : A. x`.
`succ = λn : Nat_Church. ΛA. λf : A → A. λx : A. (f (n [A] f x))`.

```scheme
(define Nat-Church '(forall A (arrow (arrow A A) (arrow A A))))

(define zero-F
  '(tlam A (lam f (arrow A A) (lam x A x))))

(define succ-F
  '(lam n (forall A (arrow (arrow A A) (arrow A A)))
     (tlam A
       (lam f (arrow A A)
         (lam x A
           (app f
                (app (app (tapp n A) f) x)))))))

(type-of zero-F '() '())
;; => (forall A (arrow (arrow A A) (arrow A A)))

(type-of succ-F '() '())
;; => (arrow (forall A (arrow (arrow A A) (arrow A A)))
;;           (forall A (arrow (arrow A A) (arrow A A))))
```

Read the type of `succ-F`. It takes a Nat-Church and returns a
Nat-Church. All well-typed. All terminating.

## Encoding pairs and sums

Pairs.

    Pair(A, B)  =  ∀R. (A → B → R) → R
    (pair a b)  =  ΛR. λk : A → B → R. (k a b)
    fst         =  ΛA. ΛB. λp : Pair(A,B). (p [A] (λa : A. λb : B. a))

A pair is a function that takes a *continuation* and applies it to the
two components. The type says: *for any result type R, if you give me a
function that takes A and B and produces R, I will produce R for you.*
By choosing different continuations we can extract the first component,
the second component, or any function of both.

Sums (A + B).

    Sum(A, B)  =  ∀R. (A → R) → (B → R) → R
    inl        =  ΛA. ΛB. λa : A. ΛR. λk₁. λk₂. (k₁ a)
    inr        =  ΛA. ΛB. λb : B. ΛR. λk₁. λk₂. (k₂ b)
    case       =  ΛA. ΛB. ΛR. λs : Sum(A,B). λk₁. λk₂. (s [R] k₁ k₂)

A sum is a function that takes *two* continuations — one for each side
— and applies the appropriate one. The tags `inl` and `inr` remember
which side they came from and dispatch accordingly.

This pattern generalises. Every algebraic data type (list, tree, natural
number, expression tree) has a *Church encoding* — an encoding as a
polymorphic function that consumes its data by taking a continuation
for each constructor case. The technical term is *fold encoding*, and
the Church encoding is the fold's function type.

Lists:

    List(A)  =  ∀R. R → (A → R → R) → R
    nil      =  ΛA. ΛR. λnil-case : R. λcons-case : A → R → R. nil-case
    cons     =  ΛA. λx : A. λxs : List(A).
                  ΛR. λnil-case : R. λcons-case : A → R → R.
                    (cons-case x (xs [R] nil-case cons-case))

`List(A)` is the type of a *fold* over an A-valued list: given a base
value for `nil` and a combining function for `cons`, produce the fold
result. `nil` returns the base case; `cons x xs` calls the combining
function on `x` and the recursively computed fold of `xs`.

This is why System F is such a beautiful theory: **it needs no primitive
data types**. Everything is a lambda term. And every one of these terms
terminates.

## Strong normalization for System F

The theorem is the same as STLC's: every well-typed System F term
reduces to a normal form in finite time. The proof (Girard 1972) is
strictly harder than for STLC — it requires a technique called
*candidates of reducibility* or *reducibility candidates* — because
polymorphic instantiation can produce arbitrarily complex terms. But
the theorem holds.

This is a startling result. Consider: I can Church-encode arbitrary
data types. I can Church-encode fold operations that traverse those
data types. I can compose these into arbitrarily complex programs. And
*every one of those programs terminates*. How can this be, given that
System F is so expressive?

The answer is that System F is expressive but not Turing-complete. Every
System F program corresponds to a proof in second-order intuitionistic
propositional logic (chapter 7 makes this precise). Every proof is
finite. Therefore every program is finite in its execution.

To get general recursion back, you must add it to System F as a
primitive. This is what Coq and Agda do — they extend System F with
inductive types and well-founded recursion, giving up strong
normalization for general recursion but bounding recursion in ways that
still guarantee termination for structurally-recursive definitions.

## Type inference is undecidable

Here is the catch. Type inference for the full System F is
*undecidable* (Wells, 1994). This means: given an untyped term, there
is no algorithm that always determines whether it has a System F type
and, if so, what its most general type is.

This is why ML and Haskell do not use full System F. They use
*prenex polymorphism* — polymorphism restricted to the outermost level
of a type — where inference *is* decidable (Hindley-Milner). Prenex
polymorphism gives up expressiveness (you cannot have a function that
takes a polymorphic function as an argument, for example) in exchange
for full type inference.

Higher-rank polymorphism — allowing `∀` inside function arguments —
requires the programmer to add annotations at those points. GHC Haskell
supports higher-rank types with an extension; you write `forall a. a ->
a` explicitly at a function argument's type, and inference works within
each rank.

The moral: full polymorphism is a design tension between expressiveness
and inference. You can have one or the other, not both.

## Existential types

System F has a hidden dual to `∀`: *existential types*, written `∃α. τ`.
An existential type describes a value where *some* type α is used
internally but the outside world does not know which type.

    ∃α. (α, α → Int)

Read this as: *there exists a type α and a pair whose first component
has type α and whose second component is a function from α to Int.*
This is the type of an *abstract data type*: a hidden representation
plus operations on it.

Existentials do not need to be added as primitives; they can be encoded
in System F using universals. The encoding is:

    ∃α. τ  ≡  ∀R. (∀α. τ → R) → R

An existential is a function that takes a continuation which is
polymorphic in α, and applies it. This encoding is what enables abstract
data types in polymorphic languages like ML — every ADT is fundamentally
an existential in disguise.

The Church-encoded pattern shows up over and over in System F. Data
becomes function; concrete becomes abstract; the two are unified by
polymorphism.

## Beyond System F: Fω and dependent types

System F can be extended in two directions:

- **System Fω.** Allow *type functions* — types that themselves take
  types as arguments. Now `List` is not a type-family but a type-level
  function: `List : ★ → ★`. You have kinds (types of types) and can do
  type-level programming.
- **Dependent types.** Allow types to depend on *values*. A vector of
  length 3 becomes a genuinely different type from a vector of length
  4. This is what Coq, Agda, and Idris implement.

Both of these extend the correspondence between programs and proofs into
richer logics. Chapter 7 explores this correspondence at the STLC/System F
level; the higher extensions are homes for another book.

## Variations to try

Write a `map` function in System F. Its type should be `∀A. ∀B. (A → B)
→ List(A) → List(B)`. Notice how the polymorphism does its work: the
same code processes lists of any element type into lists of any other
element type.

Encode Peano naturals as a Church-numeral-alternative: `Nat = ∀A. A →
(Nat → A) → A` (roughly). This is the *Scott encoding*, which supports
`case` and `pred` in constant time — Church numerals require linear time
for `pred`. Compare the two encodings on the same operations.

Sketch how *existential types* enable a *counter* module: a type that
hides its internal representation but exposes `new : Int → Counter`,
`incr : Counter → Counter`, `read : Counter → Int`. The internal
representation could be an integer, a list of ticks, a stateful record —
the type keeps you honest about not peeking inside.

## Try this

Take Church-encoded `succ` and Church-encoded `2` from earlier in this
chapter. Type-check `(succ 2)` and reduce it by hand to normal form. It
takes about a dozen beta and type-application steps. The result should
be a term equivalent to the Church numeral 3. Every step preserves the
type — that is subject reduction — and the whole reduction terminates
in finite time — that is strong normalization. Two theorems, one
computation.

## Closing

System F is polymorphic lambda calculus. Types abstract over types.
Data structures are Church-encoded polymorphic functions. Strong
normalization holds. Type inference is undecidable in full generality,
but the *checking* problem (does this annotated term have this type?)
is straightforward.

We now have three lambda calculi in hand: untyped, simply-typed, and
polymorphically-typed. Each has trade-offs. Untyped is
Turing-complete but has meaningless terms. STLC is well-behaved but
weak. System F is well-behaved and strong but requires more annotation.

Chapter 7 changes the frame. Instead of thinking of these as
*programming languages*, we start thinking of them as *proof systems*.
Every type is a proposition. Every well-typed term is a proof of the
proposition its type expresses. This is the Curry-Howard correspondence,
and it is one of the deepest connections in twentieth-century thought.
"

"# Chapter 7 — Constructive Logic and the Curry-Howard Correspondence

Where types are propositions, programs are proofs, and computing is
proving. The single most beautiful discovery in twentieth-century logic
and its consequences for how we think about mathematics.

Two histories, running in parallel from the 1930s. One is the history of
*proof theory*: Gentzen's natural deduction, intuitionistic logic (of
Brouwer and Heyting), formal systems for constructive proof. The other
is the history of *lambda calculus* and *type theory*: Church's typed
lambda calculus, Curry's combinators, later Girard's and Reynolds's
System F.

Around 1969 Howard, and independently Curry (much earlier), noticed:
these are the same object. Every proof rule of intuitionistic
propositional logic is a term-construction rule of simply-typed lambda
calculus. Every proof is a program. Every program is a proof. Types are
propositions. Not analogous — *the same object under different names*.

That correspondence has three names: *Curry-Howard*, *the propositions-
as-types principle*, *the proofs-as-programs principle*. It is the same
thing. And once you see it, you cannot unsee it. Every proof you write
is code; every well-typed program is proof of a theorem.

> **the runtime says**
>
> *This is the chapter where the book pivots. Everything before was
> preparation — logic on one side, lambda calculus on the other. Once
> you see they are the same, half the field of programming-language
> theory rearranges around it. Constructive mathematics is not a small
> corner of mathematics; it is the fragment that maps onto computation.
> If you were going to remember one chapter, remember this one.*

## The correspondence at a glance

Here is the whole thing, in one table.

    Propositional connective       Type constructor
    ----------------------------------------------------
    proposition P                  type P
    A ∧ B (conjunction)            A × B (product)
    A ∨ B (disjunction)            A + B (sum)
    A → B (implication)            A → B (function)
    ⊤ (truth)                      Unit
    ⊥ (falsity)                    Empty
    ¬A (negation)                  A → Empty
    proof of P                     program of type P
    proof composition              function composition
    proof by cases                 pattern matching / case-analysis
    modus ponens                   function application
    conditional proof              function definition

That is the whole correspondence. Every row is a real, verifiable,
formal statement. Read the second column as *if you have a program of
type P, you have a proof of proposition P*.

Let me unpack the most important cases.

## Conjunction ↔ Product

A proof of `(A ∧ B)` is a pair: a proof of A and a proof of B. That is
a value of type `A × B`.

    (conj-intro pa pb)  ↔  (pair pa pb)      : A × B
    (conj-elim-l p)     ↔  (fst p)           : A
    (conj-elim-r p)     ↔  (snd p)           : B

To *use* a conjunction is to project out one component. That is
`fst`/`snd`. To *build* a conjunction is to pair the components. That
is `pair`. Exactly the introduction and elimination rules of chapter 3.

```scheme
;; The proof: A ∧ B → B ∧ A.
;; As a program: (λp : A × B. (pair (snd p) (fst p))) : A × B → B × A
;;
;; Read this as a proof:
;;   Assume you have p : A × B.
;;   Get snd p : B and fst p : A.
;;   Pair them: (pair (snd p) (fst p)) : B × A.
;;   Discharge the assumption:  (λp. ...) : (A × B) → (B × A).
;;
;; That is a proof that conjunction is commutative.
```

## Disjunction ↔ Sum

A proof of `(A ∨ B)` is either a proof of A tagged with `inl` or a
proof of B tagged with `inr`. That is a value of type `A + B`.

    (disj-intro-l pa)  ↔  (inl pa)                   : A + B
    (disj-intro-r pb)  ↔  (inr pb)                   : A + B
    (disj-elim d f g)  ↔  (case d (inl x. f) (inr y. g))  : C

To *build* a disjunction is to tag a proof of one side. To *use* one is
to case-analyse and provide proofs of the goal in each case. Exactly
the disjunction rules of natural deduction.

## Implication ↔ Function type

A proof of `A → B` is a function taking a proof of A and producing a
proof of B.

    (impl-intro (assume A) (prove B))  ↔  (λx : A. body : B)
    (impl-elim f a)                     ↔  (f a)

Modus ponens is function application. Conditional proof is function
definition. This is the correspondence in its cleanest form.

```scheme
;; A tiny theorem: (A → B) → (B → C) → A → C  (hypothetical syllogism)
;; As a program (function composition):
;;   (λf : A → B. λg : B → C. λx : A. (g (f x)))
;;
;; If you have a proof of A → B, a proof of B → C, and a witness of A,
;; then chaining them gives you a witness of C.
```

## Universal quantification ↔ Dependent function

For predicate logic we need one more.

    (forall x : A. P x)  ↔  Π (x : A). P x
    (forall-intro proof-body)  ↔  (λx : A. body)
    (forall-elim p t)          ↔  (p t)

A proof of a universally-quantified statement is a function from the
domain to a proof of the body. The type `Π (x : A). P x` is a
*dependent function type*: the return type depends on the input value.

This is where the correspondence *deepens* — you now need dependent
types (not just simple types) to represent predicates. This is Martin-
Löf type theory (1984); it is what Coq and Agda implement.

    (exists x : A. P x)  ↔  Σ (x : A). P x

Existentially-quantified statements correspond to *dependent pairs* —
the first component is the witness, the second is a proof about it.
The dual to a dependent function type.

## The empty type: no proofs of falsity

The falsity connective ⊥ corresponds to the *empty type* — a type with
no values. If you had a value of the empty type, you could produce a
value of any other type from it (*ex falso quodlibet*), which is exactly
the elimination rule for falsity in natural deduction.

    ⊥        ↔  Empty
    absurd   ↔  (λx : Empty. anything)

Negation is *implication into falsity*.

    ¬A       ↔  A → Empty

A proof of `¬A` is a function that turns any purported proof of A into
a proof of falsity — that is, a function that can never actually be
invoked (unless A has no proofs, i.e., is false).

```scheme
;; A proof of ¬(A ∧ ¬A) — the *law of non-contradiction*.
;; As a program:  (λp : A × (A → Empty). ((snd p) (fst p))) : (A × (A → Empty)) → Empty
;;
;; Read: If you had a proof of A and a proof of ¬A, you could apply the
;; second to the first, yielding a value of the empty type. So the
;; supposition (A × ¬A) leads to Empty; therefore ¬(A ∧ ¬A).
```

## The correspondence changes what proof means

Now for the deep part. In classical logic, `(A ∨ ¬A)` is a *tautology* —
the law of the excluded middle. You can prove it by walking a truth
table: either A is true or A is false, either way `(A ∨ ¬A)` is true.

But under Curry-Howard, a proof of `(A ∨ ¬A)` would be a value of type
`A + (A → Empty)`. That value would need to be either `(inl a)` for
some proof `a : A`, or `(inr f)` for some function `f : A → Empty`.

*How do we produce such a value in general?* We would need to know, for
any A, whether A is true (and produce a proof) or false (and produce a
refutation). But for many propositions, we do not know. Are there
infinitely many twin primes? We do not know. Is the Riemann hypothesis
true? We do not know. If `A ∨ ¬A` is a tautology, we should have a
proof of `RH ∨ ¬RH`. But we do not — because neither `inl(proof of RH)`
nor `inr(refutation of RH)` is a term we can write.

*The law of the excluded middle is not constructively valid.*

That is the observation Brouwer made in 1907 and Heyting formalized in
1930. Intuitionistic (constructive) logic drops the excluded middle. A
proof of `A ∨ B` really is a proof of one of them, not a proof by cases
of the negation. This is what constructive mathematicians insist on,
and it is what Curry-Howard makes precise: constructive proofs are
programs.

## What you lose without excluded middle

You lose double-negation elimination. In classical logic,
`¬¬A → A` is a tautology. In intuitionistic logic it is not. To prove
A, having a proof of ¬¬A is *not enough*; you need to actually construct
A. From ¬¬A you can only conclude ¬¬A.

You lose proof by contradiction *for positive statements*. Classical:
*assume ¬A, derive ⊥, conclude A*. Intuitionistic: this technique
gives you ¬¬A, not A. To conclude A you need a direct construction.

You lose the equivalence `P → Q  ≡  ¬P ∨ Q`. In classical logic these
are the same. In intuitionistic logic, `¬P ∨ Q` is stronger — it lets
you decide upfront which disjunct holds.

The upshot: intuitionistic logic is more demanding. It asks *for a
construction*, not just *for a proof by contradiction*. The proofs it
produces are computationally meaningful.

## What you gain without excluded middle

You gain the *disjunction property*: if `A ∨ B` is provable, then either
A is provable or B is provable. Classical logic does not have this
property (excluded middle is provable but neither disjunct is
necessarily provable for a given A).

You gain the *existence property*: if `∃x. P x` is provable, then there
exists a *specific* term t such that `P t` is provable. Classical logic
does not have this — you can prove existence non-constructively.

You gain *computational content*: every proof is a program. Every proof
of `A → B` is a function you can run. Every proof of `∃x. P x` is a
witness x plus a proof that P(x). This is the whole reason Curry-Howard
matters for computer science: constructive proofs *are executable
programs*. Extract the algorithm from the proof; you get correct-by-
construction software.

## Classical logic under Curry-Howard

You can add classical reasoning to constructive logic by adding an
axiom: excluded middle, or double-negation elimination, or Peirce's law.
On the type side, adding excluded middle corresponds to adding an
operator called `callcc` — *call with current continuation* — which is
a control operator familiar to Scheme programmers.

*Classical logic is constructive logic plus continuations.*

Griffin (1990) proved this: adding call/cc to STLC gives you a term
that has type equivalent to Peirce's law, which is a classical tautology
not provable in intuitionistic logic. Every classical proof corresponds
to a program with control operators.

This is deep. It says: continuations are what classical logic *is*,
computationally. When you use call/cc, you are using classical
reasoning about your program's control flow.

## Program extraction

A significant industrial use of Curry-Howard: *program extraction*.
You prove a theorem in Coq or Agda. The proof, being a program, can be
compiled and run. If the theorem was *for every input x, there exists
an output y such that P(x, y)*, the extracted program takes x and
returns y — with a mathematical guarantee that P(x, y) holds.

Real systems built this way include the *seL4* microkernel (proved
correct in Isabelle), the *CompCert* C compiler (proved correct in
Coq), and pieces of the Coq system itself. The proofs and the code are
literally the same object.

## A worked correspondence: currying

Currying — the trick of turning a two-argument function into a chain of
one-argument functions — is on the program side.

    curry : ((A × B) → C) → (A → B → C)

On the proof side, this type is a *theorem*: `(A ∧ B → C) → (A → B → C)`.
That is one of De Morgan's laws (sort of; the implication version).
Currying is a proof of it, and the proof is exactly the function.

```scheme
;; The proof:
(define (curry f) (lambda (a) (lambda (b) (f (list a b)))))
```

Uncurrying goes the other way.

    uncurry : (A → B → C) → ((A × B) → C)

Same proof, other direction. Currying and uncurrying are inverse
functions, and together they show that `A × B → C` and `A → B → C` are
*isomorphic types* — meaning the corresponding propositions are
*equivalent* in intuitionistic propositional logic. Currying's classical
statement is proved, constructively, by writing the function.

## When you meet a proof, ask: what does it compute?

This is a habit worth cultivating. Whenever you see a theorem statement,
convert it to a type and imagine what program that type is. Whenever
you see a proof, imagine what algorithm the proof extracts.

Sometimes the algorithm is trivial: a proof of `P → P` extracts to the
identity function. Sometimes the algorithm is deep: a proof of
Ramsey's theorem extracts to an algorithm that finds monochromatic
subgraphs. Kleene's *realizability* interpretation makes this fully
precise: every constructive proof has an implicit program lurking
inside it.

Once you have the habit, you look at classical mathematics differently.
Some proofs *do not extract* — they use excluded middle in an
essential way and the resulting theorem is *non-constructive*. Other
proofs *do extract* even though they look classical; the constructive
core is buried but present.

## What Curry-Howard is not

Curry-Howard is *not* the claim that all mathematics is constructive.
Classical mathematicians reason non-constructively all the time, and the
theorems they prove are perfectly good theorems (assuming excluded
middle is a valid inference, which most of the mathematical world does).

Curry-Howard is *not* the claim that programming is proving. Most
programming is not typed with sufficient precision to correspond to
interesting theorems. When you write `(let ((x 5)) ...)`, you are
proving nothing beyond the trivial theorem that Nat is inhabited.

Curry-Howard *is* the observation that there is a fragment of
mathematics — constructive proof — and a fragment of programming —
typed lambda calculus — that are literally the same thing. Programs are
proofs of their types. Types are propositions. When you refine the
correspondence far enough (Martin-Löf type theory, homotopy type
theory), you get a whole new foundation for mathematics that is
essentially computational.

## Variations to try

Take the classical theorem *if not(all A are B) then some A is not B*.
This is a De Morgan's law: `¬(∀x. Bx) → (∃x. ¬Bx)`. Try to write a
Scheme function of the corresponding type. You cannot — this direction
of De Morgan is classically valid but *constructively invalid*. The
converse `(∃x. ¬Bx) → ¬(∀x. Bx)` you *can* write.

Write, in Scheme, a proof (program) of `(P → (Q → R)) → ((P × Q) → R)`.
This is currying's dual and is constructively valid.

## Try this

Pick a theorem from a math textbook — anything intuitionistic will do.
Rewrite its statement as a type. Then try to write a Scheme function
that inhabits that type. If you succeed, you have proved the theorem
constructively. If you fail, ask why. Often the reason is that the
theorem needed excluded middle in the proof — and now you know
something about the theorem that a purely classical training never
told you.

## Closing

Curry-Howard is the discovery that logic and computation are the same
thing. Types are propositions. Programs are proofs. Constructive proof
extracts to executable programs. Classical proof requires continuations.

We now have the framework to make the deep unification that runs
through the rest of this book. Chapter 8 walks through several
worked correspondences in detail — the theorems, the types, the
programs, side by side. Chapters 9-12 explore extensions and other
correspondences: modal logic with types, temporal logic with types,
linear logic with types, category theory as logic.

The whole tower rests on this chapter. If it clicked, keep going. If
not, re-read; a lot of the field became easier once this idea landed.
"

"# Chapter 8 — Propositions as Types, Worked

Where we walk through five worked examples of the Curry-Howard
correspondence — theorem, type, term — in enough detail that the
correspondence stops being an abstraction and becomes a habit.

Chapter 7 laid out the correspondence. This chapter picks five theorems
of intuitionistic logic and writes their corresponding programs, one
by one, watching how the proof structure and the code structure line
up move for move. By the end, the two-way translation should feel
mechanical.

## Example 1: The identity theorem

The theorem: `P → P`. *Anything implies itself.*

The proof, in natural deduction:

    Assume P.
    Discharge: therefore P → P.

The type: `P → P`. The program:

```scheme
(define (id x) x)
;; type:  P → P  for any P
```

The Scheme function `id` is exactly the proof. Assume `x : P`; return
it as a witness of P; discharge the assumption to get a function of
type `P → P`. Read the code as a proof: given a proof of P (namely x),
return a proof of P (namely x). The proof is that boring.

That is the correspondence at its simplest. The identity function is
the identity theorem.

## Example 2: Hypothetical syllogism

The theorem: `(P → Q) → (Q → R) → P → R`. *Implication is transitive.*

Natural deduction proof:

    Assume f : P → Q.
    Assume g : Q → R.
    Assume x : P.
    From f and x, by modus ponens: (f x) : Q.
    From g and (f x), by modus ponens: (g (f x)) : R.
    Discharge x: (P → R).
    Discharge g: (Q → R) → (P → R).
    Discharge f: (P → Q) → (Q → R) → (P → R).

The program:

```scheme
(define (compose f g) (lambda (x) (g (f x))))
;; type:  (P → Q) → (Q → R) → P → R
```

Function composition *is* the proof of hypothetical syllogism. Every
time you compose two functions, you are silently proving a theorem of
implicational logic. This is the reason function composition feels
mathematically inevitable — it is inevitable in exactly the same way
transitivity is inevitable in ordering.

## Example 3: Commutativity of conjunction

The theorem: `P ∧ Q → Q ∧ P`. *And is commutative.*

Natural deduction proof:

    Assume p : P ∧ Q.
    Apply conj-elim-l: (fst p) : P.
    Apply conj-elim-r: (snd p) : Q.
    Apply conj-intro: (pair (snd p) (fst p)) : Q ∧ P.
    Discharge p: (P ∧ Q) → (Q ∧ P).

The program:

```scheme
(define (swap p)
  (cons (cdr p) (car p)))
;; type:  (P × Q) → (Q × P)
```

Reordering the elements of a pair is a proof of the commutativity of
conjunction. When you write `swap` in a data-processing pipeline you
are quietly using this theorem. When you cannot easily *avoid* using
`swap`, you can conclude that your data type has a genuine order that
matters — the type is not really a symmetric conjunction.

## Example 4: Distribution of conjunction over disjunction

The theorem: `P ∧ (Q ∨ R) → (P ∧ Q) ∨ (P ∧ R)`. *And distributes over or.*

This is where the correspondence gets interesting because there is a
*case analysis*.

Natural deduction proof:

    Assume p : P ∧ (Q ∨ R).
    From p by conj-elim-l: (fst p) : P.
    From p by conj-elim-r: (snd p) : Q ∨ R.
    Case-analyse (snd p):
      Case (inl q):  q : Q; so (pair (fst p) q) : P ∧ Q;
                     so (inl (pair (fst p) q)) : (P ∧ Q) ∨ (P ∧ R).
      Case (inr r):  r : R; so (pair (fst p) r) : P ∧ R;
                     so (inr (pair (fst p) r)) : (P ∧ Q) ∨ (P ∧ R).
    Discharge p.

The program:

```scheme
(define (distribute p)
  (let ((a  (car p))
        (qr (cdr p)))
    (cond
      ((eq? (car qr) 'inl)
       (cons 'inl (cons a (cdr qr))))
      ((eq? (car qr) 'inr)
       (cons 'inr (cons a (cdr qr)))))))
;; type: P × (Q + R)  →  (P × Q) + (P × R)
```

Case-analysis in the proof becomes a `cond` in the program. Every branch
of the `cond` produces a value on one side of the sum. The tags 'inl
and 'inr in our representation mark which side of the disjunction we
are in. The program is a proof by cases; the code just makes the
cases explicit.

## Example 5: De Morgan (one direction)

The theorem: `¬P ∧ ¬Q → ¬(P ∨ Q)`. *If both are false, then their
disjunction is false.*

Reminder: `¬X` corresponds to `X → Empty`.

Natural deduction proof:

    Assume p : ¬P ∧ ¬Q.
    Assume d : P ∨ Q. (We aim to derive ⊥ from these two.)
    Case-analyse d:
      Case (inl x): x : P. Combine with (fst p) : ¬P — that is
                    (fst p) : P → Empty. Apply to x: ((fst p) x) : Empty.
      Case (inr y): y : Q. Combine with (snd p) : ¬Q. Apply to y:
                    ((snd p) y) : Empty.
    Discharge d: (P ∨ Q) → Empty, i.e., ¬(P ∨ Q).
    Discharge p: (¬P ∧ ¬Q) → ¬(P ∨ Q).

The program:

```scheme
(define (demorgan-fwd p)
  (lambda (d)
    (cond
      ((eq? (car d) 'inl) ((car p) (cdr d)))     ; (fst p) applied to x : P
      ((eq? (car d) 'inr) ((cdr p) (cdr d))))))  ; (snd p) applied to y : Q
;; type:  (¬P × ¬Q) → ¬(P ∨ Q)
;;     = (P → Empty) × (Q → Empty) → (P + Q) → Empty
```

The pattern is the same as before. Case-analysis becomes `cond`, and
each case invokes the appropriate refutation function. The program
never actually produces anything in Empty (it cannot, Empty has no
values); it demonstrates the emptiness by showing that whichever case
we are in, we could produce something in Empty if only the premise were
truthful.

Note the other direction of De Morgan — `¬(P ∨ Q) → ¬P ∧ ¬Q` — is also
constructively valid. But the *other* De Morgan pair — going between
`¬(P ∧ Q)` and `¬P ∨ ¬Q` — only holds *one way* constructively:
`¬P ∨ ¬Q → ¬(P ∧ Q)` is fine, but `¬(P ∧ Q) → ¬P ∨ ¬Q` is not. It
requires the excluded middle. Try to write the program for the second
direction and you will get stuck exactly where the classical proof uses
LEM.

## The pattern: proof structure = code structure

Every one of these five examples had the same shape:

- Assumptions become function arguments (`λx. ...`).
- Conjunction becomes pair (`cons`, `car`, `cdr`).
- Disjunction becomes tagged sum with case-analysis (`cond` on the tag).
- Application of an implication becomes function application.
- Introduction of an implication becomes function definition.

The proof is *literally the same object* as the program. Not analogous,
not similar — the same object. The two representations differ only in
whether you write `(cons a b)` or `(pair-intro a b)`, `λx.body` or
`(assume x; body; discharge x)`. They are notational variants.

## The Kolmogorov interpretation

There is an older name for this: the *Brouwer-Heyting-Kolmogorov*
interpretation, or *BHK*. It predates Curry-Howard by decades and gives
the reading directly.

- A proof of `A ∧ B` is a pair (proof of A, proof of B).
- A proof of `A ∨ B` is a tagged proof: either of A or of B, with the
  tag showing which.
- A proof of `A → B` is a construction that turns any proof of A into
  a proof of B.
- A proof of `∀x. P(x)` is a construction that, given any x in the
  domain, produces a proof of P(x).
- A proof of `∃x. P(x)` is a pair (witness x, proof of P(x)).
- A proof of `⊥` does not exist.
- A proof of `¬A` is a construction that, given any proof of A, produces
  a proof of ⊥.

Read that list and compare it to the type constructors in a functional
language. They line up perfectly. Kolmogorov's interpretation *is*
Curry-Howard, expressed as a philosophy of proof rather than as a
correspondence with types. Which came first depends on whom you ask;
in any case, the ideas landed on top of one another and lasted.

## Where the correspondence extends

We have seen Curry-Howard for intuitionistic propositional logic and
simply-typed lambda calculus. There are richer correspondences for
richer systems.

- **First-order intuitionistic logic** ↔ **dependent type theory
  (Martin-Löf)**. Quantifiers become dependent products (Π) and
  dependent sums (Σ). This is the basis of Agda and Idris.
- **Second-order intuitionistic logic** ↔ **System F**. Quantifiers over
  propositions become quantifiers over types.
- **Classical propositional logic** ↔ **lambda calculus with control
  operators** (call/cc). Griffin's 1990 correspondence.
- **Modal S4** ↔ **staged computation / metaprogramming**. Davies-
  Pfenning 1996.
- **Linear logic** ↔ **linear type systems** (Wadler 1990, Bierman 1994).
  Girard's linear logic corresponds to type systems where every value is
  used exactly once — the foundation of ownership types in Rust, of
  session types in concurrent languages.
- **Modal logic (temporal, epistemic)** ↔ **effect types / capability
  types**. Modern research (2010s+) has developed correspondences with
  many industrial type systems.

The pattern that emerges: nearly every interesting logic has a
computational correspondent. Chapter 9 will explore modal logic
directly. Chapter 11 will explore linear logic. The idea that types
are propositions is a wedge that opens many doors.

## Where the correspondence does not extend (obviously)

Some logics resist. Second-order *classical* logic corresponds to
something, but that something is not as clean. Modal logic with
non-normal modalities can be hard to find a type-theoretic reading
for. Substructural logics (relevance, affine) each have their own
correspondence but the details are delicate.

The trend: give a logic a Kripke semantics (worlds and accessibility
relations) and there is *usually* a computational correspondence to
some form of *staged* or *distributed* or *effectful* computation.

## Homotopy type theory: types are spaces

The most surprising modern extension: *homotopy type theory* (HoTT), a
research programme launched around 2010 and consolidated in the
Univalent Foundations project (Voevodsky et al., 2013). HoTT reads
types not just as propositions but as *homotopy types* — as spaces up
to continuous deformation. Two types are *equivalent* if they are
homotopy-equivalent as spaces. Every proof is a path in the space.

This has led to a new foundation for mathematics with *univalence* as
an axiom (isomorphic types are equal) and to fully mechanised proofs of
theorems in synthetic homotopy theory. It is beautiful and unfinished
research. You do not need it for programming, but you should know it
exists as the current frontier of Curry-Howard.

## Extracting a program from a proof

One of the industrial uses of the correspondence: prove a theorem in a
proof assistant, then extract the proof as executable code.

Consider the theorem: *for every list, there exists a sorted permutation
of that list.* In Coq/Agda this is:

    ∀ (l : List A) . ∃ (m : List A) . (Sorted m ∧ Permutation l m)

A proof of this theorem, mechanically extracted to Scheme, would be a
function `sort : List A → List A` with a *guarantee* that the output is
a sorted permutation of the input.

The extraction machinery: given a proof term, walk through it and drop
the parts of the term that only carry proof information (not
computational information). What remains is the computational content —
the algorithm. Coq has an `Extraction` tactic that does this and can
produce OCaml, Haskell, or Scheme code. The extracted code is *provably
correct* — it satisfies the theorem it was extracted from.

Real deployed systems built this way exist. CompCert extracts to OCaml.
Fiat Cryptography extracts to C. Each is correct-by-construction: the
algorithm's correctness was proved as a theorem, and the executable
code is the proof term.

## Try this

Take the theorem `((P → Q) → P) → P` (Peirce's law). This is *classically*
valid but not *constructively* valid. Try to write a Scheme function of
its type. You will get stuck. The place you get stuck is exactly where
classical proof used excluded middle. Notice the stuck point; it is a
diagnostic of what non-constructive reasoning would need.

Take the theorem `P → ¬¬P`. Write the program. It should type-check as
`P → (P → Empty) → Empty`. The trick: given a proof of P and a proof of
¬P, apply the second to the first. Simple. Notice you *cannot* prove
the reverse `¬¬P → P` in the same style; that direction requires
excluded middle.

Prove associativity of pairing: `(A × B) × C → A × (B × C)`. Then
prove its reverse. Then compose them. What do you get? A pair of
functions that witnesses the *isomorphism* of the two associations of
conjunction. Isomorphism at the type level is equivalence at the
proposition level.

## Closing

Five worked examples. Every proof becomes a program by direct
translation. Every program of a certain type is a proof of the
corresponding theorem.

This is not merely elegant. It has industrial consequences: it lets
proof assistants extract executable programs from proofs. It has
foundational consequences: it lets us build constructive mathematics
on programming. It has pedagogical consequences: it lets us teach
proof theory by teaching typed programming, and vice versa.

Chapters 9-12 explore where the correspondence goes: modal logic
becomes staged programming, temporal logic becomes protocol
verification, linear logic becomes resource-typed programming, and
category theory becomes a language of composition that unifies all
of these under a single algebraic frame.
"
