"# Chapter 9 — Modal Logic: Necessity, Possibility, and Kripke Worlds

Where we add two operators — *necessarily* and *possibly* — and
discover that the same trick supports reasoning about time, knowledge,
obligation, and program correctness.

Modal logic is what you get when you enrich propositional logic with
*modes* — operators that qualify truth. The two classic modes are
alethic:

- `□P` — *necessarily P*, P is true in every possibility.
- `◇P` — *possibly P*, P is true in some possibility.

These operators do not fit into truth-functional propositional logic
because their truth depends not just on P's truth but on *which
possibilities exist and how they relate*. That extra structure — the
possibility space — is what modal semantics captures.

The modern semantics was invented by Kripke in the late 1950s. Modal
logic became suddenly rigorous, testable, and useful. Today it
underlies epistemic reasoning (knowledge, belief), temporal reasoning
(before/after), deontic reasoning (obligation, permission), and formal
verification of concurrent systems (invariants, liveness).

We will build a small modal-logic engine in Scheme. The engine has two
parts: a *Kripke frame* (worlds and relations) and an *evaluator* that
tells you whether a modal formula is true at a given world.

> **the runtime says**
>
> *The move from propositional to modal logic is like the move from
> propositional to predicate: you gain a whole dimension of expressive
> power for the cost of some formal machinery. Where predicate logic
> lets you talk about many objects at once, modal logic lets you talk
> about many possibilities at once. Once you have both, most of the
> reasoning humans actually do is expressible.*

## Kripke frames

A *Kripke frame* is a pair (W, R) where:

- W is a non-empty set of *worlds*.
- R is a binary *accessibility relation* on W. `w R w'` means *from w
  you can see w'*.

A *Kripke model* adds an interpretation: a function V that assigns to
each atomic proposition the set of worlds in which it is true.

```scheme
(define example-frame
  '((:worlds (w1 w2 w3))
    (:accessible ((w1 w2) (w1 w3) (w2 w2) (w3 w3)))
    (:valuation
     ((P . (w1 w2))
      (Q . (w2 w3))))))
```

Three worlds; w1 can see w2 and w3; w2 can see itself; w3 can see
itself. P is true at w1 and w2; Q is true at w2 and w3.

## Semantics: truth at a world

The truth of a modal formula is *relative to a world*. Write
`M, w ⊨ φ` for *φ is true at world w in model M*.

    M, w ⊨ P             iff  w ∈ V(P)                          [atomic]
    M, w ⊨ ¬φ            iff  not (M, w ⊨ φ)
    M, w ⊨ (φ ∧ ψ)       iff  (M, w ⊨ φ) and (M, w ⊨ ψ)
    M, w ⊨ (φ ∨ ψ)       iff  (M, w ⊨ φ) or  (M, w ⊨ ψ)
    M, w ⊨ (φ → ψ)       iff  if (M, w ⊨ φ) then (M, w ⊨ ψ)
    M, w ⊨ (□φ)          iff  for all w' with w R w': (M, w' ⊨ φ)
    M, w ⊨ (◇φ)          iff  there exists w' with w R w' and (M, w' ⊨ φ)

The two new clauses are the interesting ones. `□φ` at w means every
world reachable from w satisfies φ. `◇φ` at w means some world
reachable from w satisfies φ.

```scheme
(define (accessible-worlds w frame)
  (map cadr
       (filter (lambda (edge) (eq? (car edge) w))
               (cdr (assq :accessible frame)))))

(define (holds-atomic p w frame)
  (let ((valuation (cdr (assq :valuation frame))))
    (member w (cdr (assq p valuation)))))

(define (eval-modal phi w frame)
  (cond
    ((symbol? phi)
     (holds-atomic phi w frame))
    ((eq? (car phi) 'not)
     (not (eval-modal (cadr phi) w frame)))
    ((eq? (car phi) 'and)
     (and (eval-modal (cadr phi)  w frame)
          (eval-modal (caddr phi) w frame)))
    ((eq? (car phi) 'or)
     (or  (eval-modal (cadr phi)  w frame)
          (eval-modal (caddr phi) w frame)))
    ((eq? (car phi) 'implies)
     (or (not (eval-modal (cadr phi) w frame))
         (eval-modal (caddr phi) w frame)))
    ((eq? (car phi) 'box)
     (every (lambda (w2) (eval-modal (cadr phi) w2 frame))
            (accessible-worlds w frame)))
    ((eq? (car phi) 'diamond)
     (any (lambda (w2) (eval-modal (cadr phi) w2 frame))
          (accessible-worlds w frame)))))
```

Ten lines of semantics. Run it.

```scheme
(eval-modal '(box P) 'w1 example-frame)
;; => #t iff P holds at every world w1 can see: w2 and w3.
;;    P holds at w2 (yes) and at w3 (no). So (box P) is #f at w1.

(eval-modal '(diamond P) 'w1 example-frame)
;; => #t (P holds at w2, and w1 can see w2).

(eval-modal '(box (or P Q)) 'w1 example-frame)
;; => #t (at w2, P holds; at w3, Q holds; so (P ∨ Q) holds at both).
```

That last is illustrative. `(□(P ∨ Q))` is true at w1 because every
world accessible from w1 satisfies at least one of P and Q. But `(□P ∨ □Q)`
is false at w1 — neither P nor Q holds at every accessible world. Modal
distribution over disjunction fails.

## Modal axioms and the systems K, T, S4, S5

Modal logic is not a single logic — it is a *family* of logics, each
determined by which axioms hold. The base system is called **K**, after
Kripke. K contains only:

- All propositional tautologies.
- `K axiom: □(P → Q) → (□P → □Q)`  (distribution of box over implication).
- `Necessitation rule: if ⊢ P then ⊢ □P`  (theorems are necessary).

That is the base. Depending on what you want to model, you strengthen K
with more axioms.

- **T = K + □P → P**. What is necessary is actual. Corresponds to
  reflexive frames (`w R w` for all w). *Alethic modal logic.*
- **S4 = T + □P → □□P**. Iterated necessity is necessity. Corresponds to
  reflexive + transitive frames. *Epistemic reasoning about a persistent
  knower.*
- **S5 = S4 + ◇P → □◇P**. If something is possible, that possibility
  itself is necessarily possible. Corresponds to reflexive + transitive
  + symmetric frames (i.e., equivalence relations). *Metaphysical
  necessity; logical omniscience.*

These correspondences are called *Sahlqvist correspondence theorems*
and they are one of the deepest results in modal logic: certain axioms
correspond exactly to certain frame properties.

```scheme
(define (reflexive? frame)
  (every (lambda (w)
           (member w (accessible-worlds w frame)))
         (cdr (assq :worlds frame))))

(define (transitive? frame)
  (let ((worlds (cdr (assq :worlds frame))))
    (every (lambda (w)
             (every (lambda (u)
                      (every (lambda (v)
                               (implies (and (member u (accessible-worlds w frame))
                                             (member v (accessible-worlds u frame)))
                                        (member v (accessible-worlds w frame))))
                             worlds))
                    worlds))
           worlds)))

(define (symmetric? frame)
  (let ((worlds (cdr (assq :worlds frame))))
    (every (lambda (w)
             (every (lambda (u)
                      (implies (member u (accessible-worlds w frame))
                               (member w (accessible-worlds u frame))))
                    worlds))
           worlds)))
```

If your frame is reflexive, T holds. If reflexive and transitive, S4
holds. If reflexive, transitive, and symmetric, S5 holds. Design your
frame; know your logic.

## Epistemic reading

The most fruitful modern application is *epistemic modal logic*, where
`□φ` reads *the agent knows φ*.

- T says: what you know is true. (You cannot know a falsehood.)
- S4 says: what you know, you know that you know. (Positive
  introspection.)
- S5 says: what you *do not* know, you know that you do not know.
  (Negative introspection.)

S5 is the logic of an idealized omniscient reasoner who has perfect
introspection. Real humans do not satisfy S5 — we do not always know
what we do not know. But S5 is a useful *model*, and much of computer
science's reasoning about *distributed knowledge* uses it (Fagin,
Halpern, Moses, Vardi — *Reasoning About Knowledge*, 1995).

With multiple agents (Alice, Bob), you have multiple modalities:
`K_alice φ`, `K_bob φ`, etc. Now you can express:

- `K_alice (K_bob P)` — Alice knows that Bob knows P.
- `K_alice (¬K_bob P)` — Alice knows that Bob does not know P.
- `¬K_alice (K_bob P)` — Alice does not know whether Bob knows P.

Adding a *common knowledge* modality `C_G` — φ is common knowledge
among group G — is famously subtle: `C_G φ` means everyone knows φ,
everyone knows that everyone knows φ, and so on ad infinitum. Cryptographic
protocols use exactly this notion of common knowledge to reason about
what an adversary can and cannot infer.

## Deontic reading

`□φ` reads *it is obligatory that φ*, and `◇φ` reads *it is permitted
that φ*. Deontic modal logic.

- `¬◇P ↔ □¬P`: what is not permitted is forbidden.
- `□P → ¬□¬P` (deontic D): if you must do P, you may not be required to
  do not-P. Rules out contradictory obligations.

Deontic logic captures the structure of *systems of rules* — legal
codes, contracts, policies. It is useful because it makes contradictions
in rule systems explicit: if a policy demands both P and ¬P, the deontic
formulas capture that inconsistency.

## Program correctness

`□P` can be read *P holds throughout the program's execution* and `◇P`
as *P eventually holds*. This is a very small taste of *temporal logic*,
which we treat in chapter 10.

More directly, modal logic underlies *Hoare logic*: `{P} c {Q}` means
*if P holds before c executes, Q holds after*. This can be recast
modally as `[c] (P → Q)`, where `[c]` is a modality parameterized by
the program c. This is *dynamic logic* (Pratt, 1976).

## Composition: multiple modalities

Real reasoning often needs several modalities at once.

- Time + knowledge: *Alice knows now that Bob will know tomorrow.*
- Space + obligation: *Everyone in this building must wear a mask.*
- Belief + counterfactual: *If Alice had known, she would have acted.*

Each modality is a separate operator with its own accessibility
relation, and formulas can nest them arbitrarily. The engine we built
above generalises: index the frame with a *set* of accessibility
relations, one per modality, and add cases to the evaluator.

## Canonical models and completeness

For each of K, T, S4, S5, there is a completeness theorem: the axioms
prove exactly the formulas that are semantically valid in the
corresponding class of frames. The classic proof technique is the
*canonical model construction*: build a model whose worlds are
maximally-consistent sets of formulas, define accessibility so that
w R w' iff every `□φ` in w has φ in w'. Show that a formula is true at
w iff it is in w. Instant completeness.

The full development is Blackburn-de Rijke-Venema, chapters 4-5. It is
a beautiful piece of proof theory.

## Bisimulation

Two modal models are *bisimilar* if there is a relation between their
worlds preserving atomic truths and matching accessibility both ways.
Bisimilar worlds satisfy the same modal formulas — bisimulation is the
appropriate notion of *sameness* for modal models.

This matters computationally. If two systems (say two concurrent
processes) are bisimilar, they satisfy the same modal temporal
properties — every safety and liveness property that holds of one holds
of the other. Bisimulation-based process algebras (CCS, CSP, pi-
calculus) use this equivalence as their notion of behavioral
equality.

```scheme
;; A sketch: two worlds w and w' are bisimilar (relative to a relation R)
;; iff they agree on all atomic propositions and for every world u
;; accessible from w, there is a world u' accessible from w' with (u,u') in R
;; (and vice versa).
```

## Kripke and constructive modal logic

Modal logic has a *constructive* variant: intuitionistic modal logic.
The correspondence extends — modal S4 corresponds to *staged
computation*, where `□P` is *a computation that produces P at a later
stage*. This is the Davies-Pfenning 1996 correspondence and it
underlies modern research on multi-stage languages, macro systems, and
metaprogramming.

The pattern: every modality gives rise to a computational effect. Boxed
values are *stage-portable* values. Diamond-values are *possible*
values in some non-deterministic sense. The type-theoretic reading of
modality is one of the currently most active corners of the
Curry-Howard programme.

## Variations to try

Extend the frame with multiple modalities — one for each of two agents,
say. Now the syntax includes `(K-alice φ)` and `(K-bob φ)`. Rewrite the
evaluator to handle both. Then encode a *common knowledge* modality as
the fixed point of *everyone-knows*: `C φ = φ ∧ E φ ∧ E(E φ) ∧ ...`.
The full common-knowledge modality does not terminate on infinite
models; on finite models the fixed-point iteration converges. Try it
on a two-agent puzzle.

Build a *model checker*: given a frame and a formula, report the set of
worlds where the formula is true. This is essentially the evaluator
run at every world, collected. It is the seed of what real model
checkers do for temporal logic (chapter 10).

## Try this

Set up a Kripke frame with three worlds, w1 = *rainy*, w2 = *sunny*,
w3 = *snowy*, and accessibility that models weather transitions (say,
rainy → sunny, sunny → rainy or snowy, snowy → snowy). Add an atomic
proposition *outdoor-activity-possible* true at sunny only. Ask
questions: at w1, is `◇ outdoor-activity-possible` true (yes)? At w3,
`□ outdoor-activity-possible` (definitely not)? Play with the frame;
add new worlds; adjust the relation. This is what modal logic feels
like once you internalise it — a semantic sandbox for reasoning about
possibilities.

## Closing

Modal logic adds two operators to propositional logic and gains a
whole dimension of expressive power. Frames-and-relations semantics
gives it precise meaning. The axiom systems K, T, S4, S5 correspond
exactly to frame properties. Applications span knowledge, obligation,
time, and program verification.

Chapter 10 zooms in on one of these applications: temporal logic, where
worlds are moments in time, accessibility is *time-after*, and we can
formally verify properties like *once the system enters this state, it
never leaves*. This is what model checkers do, and it has caught real
bugs in real critical systems.
"

"# Chapter 10 — Temporal Logic and Little Model Checkers

Where worlds become moments in time, and where a small algorithm
verifies that a system does the right thing forever.

Modal logic, as chapter 9 set up, has worlds and an accessibility
relation. Interpret the worlds as *moments in time* and the relation as
*is a possible next moment*, and you get *temporal logic*.

Temporal logic was invented by Arthur Prior in the late 1950s. Amir
Pnueli's 1977 paper *The Temporal Logic of Programs* opened the door to
computer science, and the field of *model checking* took off in the
1980s. Today, temporal-logic model checkers routinely verify hardware
designs, communication protocols, cryptographic proofs, and
distributed algorithms. They catch bugs no test suite would find, and
they have saved billions of dollars by catching design flaws before
silicon was cut.

We are going to build a *very* small temporal-logic model checker in
Scheme. It handles a fragment of *Linear Temporal Logic* (LTL). It
takes a finite-state transition system and a formula and answers *does
every execution of the system satisfy the formula?*.

## Two flavours: linear vs branching time

There are two schools.

**Linear-time logic (LTL)** treats time as a single unbranching line.
Every state has exactly one next state. Formulas talk about the sequence
of states along that line. Pnueli's original setting.

**Branching-time logic (CTL, CTL*)** treats time as a tree. Every state
can branch into multiple possible futures. Formulas can talk about
*all* futures or *some* future. Clarke-Emerson's original setting.

The two are incomparable in expressive power: some things one can say
that the other cannot. LTL is arguably more intuitive; CTL is more
computationally tractable in some ways. Modern model checkers usually
support both.

We will implement LTL for its intuitive shape. CTL is a straightforward
adaptation once the pattern is clear.

## LTL operators

Standard propositional connectives, plus:

- `X φ` — *next*, φ holds at the next moment.
- `F φ` — *finally* (or *eventually*), φ holds at some future moment.
- `G φ` — *globally* (or *always*), φ holds at every future moment.
- `φ U ψ` — *until*, φ holds until at some point ψ holds.

The dualities:

- `F φ = true U φ`
- `G φ = ¬ F ¬ φ`

So you could get away with `X` and `U` alone; the others are shorthand.

Read informally:

- `G (request → F response)` — *whenever a request is issued, a response
  eventually comes*. Liveness.
- `G ¬ (writer_1 ∧ writer_2)` — *never two writers active at once*.
  Safety.
- `¬ (F crash)` — *never crashes*. Equivalent to `G ¬ crash`.

Every reactive-system correctness property is expressible in this
language or a small extension of it.

## Transition systems

A finite-state transition system is:

    S = (states, initial-states, transitions, labelling)

Where:
- states is a finite set;
- initial-states ⊆ states;
- transitions ⊆ states × states (the *next-state* relation);
- labelling maps each state to a set of atomic propositions that hold there.

```scheme
(define elevator-system
  '((:states        (floor-1 floor-2 floor-3))
    (:initial       (floor-1))
    (:transitions   ((floor-1 floor-2) (floor-2 floor-1) (floor-2 floor-3)
                     (floor-3 floor-2)))
    (:labels        ((floor-1 . (at-1 not-moving))
                     (floor-2 . (at-2 not-moving))
                     (floor-3 . (at-3 not-moving))))))
```

Three states, six transitions. A tiny elevator that moves between
floors 1, 2, and 3 but does not skip floors.

## LTL semantics

LTL is interpreted over *paths* — infinite sequences of states
respecting the transition relation. Write `π = s_0, s_1, s_2, ...` for
a path, and `π_i` for `s_i, s_{i+1}, ...` — the suffix starting at
position i.

    π ⊨ P            iff  P is in labelling(s_0)
    π ⊨ ¬ φ          iff  not (π ⊨ φ)
    π ⊨ φ ∧ ψ        iff  (π ⊨ φ) and (π ⊨ ψ)
    π ⊨ X φ          iff  π_1 ⊨ φ
    π ⊨ F φ          iff  there exists i ≥ 0 with π_i ⊨ φ
    π ⊨ G φ          iff  for all i ≥ 0, π_i ⊨ φ
    π ⊨ φ U ψ        iff  there exists i ≥ 0 with π_i ⊨ ψ and
                          for all 0 ≤ j < i: π_j ⊨ φ

A *system* satisfies a formula if *every path from every initial state*
satisfies it. This *for-all-paths* is what makes model checking hard —
you must consider every execution.

## Checking safety properties directly

A *safety property* asserts that *something bad never happens*: `G ¬
bad`. To check this, we enumerate reachable states and verify none
satisfy `bad`. Simple graph search.

```scheme
(define (reachable-states system)
  (let ((initial (cdr (assq :initial system)))
        (edges   (cdr (assq :transitions system))))
    (let loop ((frontier initial)
               (visited  '()))
      (if (null? frontier)
          visited
          (let* ((s (car frontier))
                 (new-visited (if (member s visited)
                                  visited
                                  (cons s visited)))
                 (successors (map cadr
                                  (filter (lambda (e)
                                            (and (eq? (car e) s)
                                                 (not (member (cadr e) new-visited))))
                                          edges))))
            (loop (append (cdr frontier) successors) new-visited))))))

(define (atomic-holds? state atomic-prop system)
  (let ((labels (cdr (assq :labels system))))
    (member atomic-prop (cdr (assq state labels)))))

(define (check-safety system atomic-prop)
  ;; True iff atomic-prop is FALSE at every reachable state.
  (every (lambda (s) (not (atomic-holds? s atomic-prop system)))
         (reachable-states system)))
```

Run it:

```scheme
(check-safety elevator-system 'at-4)
;; => #t  ; the elevator never reaches floor 4 (it does not exist)

(check-safety elevator-system 'at-2)
;; => #f  ; the elevator does reach floor 2.
```

This is the seed of model checking. Real checkers do this over billions
of states using symbolic techniques (BDDs, SAT). Our version handles
tens of states, which is plenty for a book.

## Checking full LTL: the automaton approach

For the full temporal fragment we need a smarter technique. The
classical approach:

1. Translate the formula ¬φ into a *Buchi automaton* — a finite
   automaton over infinite words that accepts exactly the sequences
   satisfying ¬φ.
2. Take the product of this automaton with the transition system.
3. Check whether the product has an accepting infinite path (a cycle
   passing through an accepting state).

If yes, the system has a path violating φ. If no, φ holds.

The full Buchi construction is intricate — it fills a chapter of
Baier-Katoen. Our small checker will handle a fragment: formulas of the
form `G φ` and `F φ` where φ is propositional. These cover most safety
and simple liveness properties and are checkable with modest algorithms.

```scheme
(define (eval-ltl-simple formula system)
  ;; Handles: propositional | (G prop) | (F prop) | (not prop)
  (cond
    ((symbol? formula)                             ; atomic proposition
     (every (lambda (s) (atomic-holds? s formula system))
            (cdr (assq :initial system))))
    ((eq? (car formula) 'G)
     ;; Every reachable state satisfies the inner formula.
     (every (lambda (s) (atomic-holds? s (cadr formula) system))
            (reachable-states system)))
    ((eq? (car formula) 'F)
     ;; Some reachable state satisfies the inner formula.
     (any (lambda (s) (atomic-holds? s (cadr formula) system))
          (reachable-states system)))
    ((eq? (car formula) 'not)
     (not (eval-ltl-simple (cadr formula) system)))))

(eval-ltl-simple '(G not-moving) elevator-system)
;; => #t (every state has not-moving in its labelling).

(eval-ltl-simple '(F at-3) elevator-system)
;; => #t (floor-3 is reachable).
```

Real LTL is much richer than this, but the shape of the checker is
right: reduce the formula to statements about the reachable-state graph
and answer them by search.

## Fairness

One of the subtle points in temporal-logic verification: *fairness*
assumptions. Without them, many verifications fail on infinite paths
that get *stuck* on transitions that would take them to accepting
states. A *fair* path is one that visits every enabled transition
infinitely often. Model checkers let you specify fairness conditions:

- *Strong fairness on transition t*: if t is enabled infinitely often,
  it is taken infinitely often.
- *Weak fairness on t*: if t is continuously enabled from some point
  on, it is taken eventually.

Modelling systems with fairness lets you say *the scheduler is fair*,
which is required for most liveness proofs of concurrent systems.

## What real model checkers verify

Modern tools like SPIN, NuSMV, TLA+, and mCRL2 have found bugs in:

- Cache coherence protocols in hardware.
- Communication protocols (TCP, cryptographic key exchange).
- Distributed consensus algorithms (Paxos, Raft).
- Bus arbiters in embedded systems.
- Elevator controllers, traffic light systems, medical device firmware.

The pattern: model your system as a finite-state (or bounded-state)
machine; write correctness properties as temporal-logic formulas; run
the checker; get back either *satisfied* or *counter-example trace*.
The counter-example is the killer feature — the tool does not just say
*your system is broken*, it shows you *the exact sequence of events
that leads to the failure*.

## State explosion

The bane of model checking. A system with n components each having 10
possible internal states has 10^n global states. At n=20 that is 10^20
states — beyond direct enumeration.

The response has been decades of research on how to represent large
state spaces symbolically:

- **BDDs (Binary Decision Diagrams).** Compact canonical representation
  of boolean functions. Enables reachability computation over sets of
  states rather than individual states.
- **SAT-based model checking.** Encode the model-checking problem as a
  SAT instance and hand it to a modern SAT solver.
- **Abstraction.** Replace the system with a smaller *abstract* system
  that over-approximates its behaviour. Verify the abstract system; if
  correct, done; if incorrect, refine the abstraction.
- **Compositional reasoning.** Decompose the system into components,
  verify each in isolation with assumptions about the others, then
  combine.

These techniques let modern checkers handle systems with 10^100 or more
states routinely. The scale is genuinely impressive.

## LTL vs. CTL: a small comparison

The classic distinction. In LTL, path quantifiers are implicit — every
formula is evaluated over paths. In CTL, path quantifiers are explicit:
`A φ` (for all paths) and `E φ` (for some path).

- LTL `G F P` — *P holds infinitely often on every path*.
- CTL `A G (E F P)` — *from every reachable state, some future has P*.

The first is a global liveness property. The second is a *reactivity*
property saying we can always still reach P. These are different, and
LTL can express the first but not the second, while CTL can express
the second but not the first. CTL* combines both.

## Model checking as proof

There is a correspondence lurking here too: model checking corresponds
to constructive proof, and finding a counter-example corresponds to
extracting a falsifying witness. A trace showing violation is a proof
of `¬ φ`, and its structure carries computational content.

Some modern proof assistants use this: build a Buchi automaton for the
negation of your property, do the emptiness check, and get either a
proof of the property or an executable counter-example. This unifies
model checking with theorem proving under the Curry-Howard umbrella.

## Variations to try

Extend `eval-ltl-simple` to handle the `X` (next) operator by picking a
single successor of the current state. This requires walking the
transition graph rather than the reachable-states set.

Implement `until`: `(φ U ψ)` holds iff there is a path prefix where φ
holds throughout and eventually ψ becomes true. This requires exploring
paths rather than just states.

Build a *counter-example* returner: instead of just `#t`/`#f`, when a
property fails, return the sequence of states that witness the failure.
This is the single feature that makes real model checkers so useful.

## Try this

Model a two-process mutual-exclusion protocol as a transition system.
State encodes each process's phase (thinking, waiting, critical). Add
the transitions of your favourite mutex algorithm — Peterson's, Lamport's
bakery, or your own. Encode the safety property (no two in critical at
once) and the liveness property (every waiter eventually enters
critical). Run your checker. If it says safety fails, look at the
counter-example. Many first-attempt mutex algorithms fail on the
liveness property; only after a fairness assumption is added do they
verify. This is a very hands-on way to feel why fairness matters.

## Closing

Temporal logic is modal logic where the modality is *time*. It lets us
state and check reactive-system correctness properties. Small model
checkers verify small systems directly; large model checkers use
symbolic techniques to verify vast state spaces. The counter-example
extraction makes model checking practically useful.

Chapter 11 shifts to a very different logic: *linear logic*. Where
classical logic treats propositions as timeless truths that can be
reused freely, linear logic treats propositions as *resources* that are
consumed by use. This turns out to be exactly what you need to reason
about memory, capabilities, protocols, and concurrent messaging.

"# Chapter 11 — Linear Logic: Resources That Get Used

Where propositions are no longer eternal truths but resources — used
once, consumed by inference — and where a hidden structural rule that
we always took for granted turns out to be optional.

In classical logic, if you have a proof of P, you can use it as many
times as you like. You can prove P; then prove Q from P; then prove R
from P too; then prove S from Q and R; and P is still available at the
end. That is called the *structural rule of contraction*: a hypothesis
may be duplicated. There is a dual rule, *weakening*: an unused
hypothesis may be discarded.

Linear logic drops both. If you have a proof of P, you must use it
exactly once. No duplication, no discarding. This makes propositions
behave like *resources*: cake once eaten cannot be eaten again, dollar
spent cannot be spent again, message once received cannot be received
again.

Girard invented linear logic in 1987 as a decomposition of intuitionistic
logic. It has been enormously influential in computer science: it
underlies Rust's ownership types, session types for concurrency, the
semantics of quantum computing, and much of category-theoretic
semantics. It is also mathematically beautiful in its own right — a
constellation of new connectives whose interactions form a small
algebraic garden.

> **the runtime says**
>
> *Linear logic changed how I think about ordinary reasoning. Once you
> notice that classical logic silently allows you to use assumptions
> multiple times, you start seeing the trick everywhere. A recipe
> assumes flour once, but the reasoning about it uses the fact 'we
> have flour' three or four times. Linear logic makes the resource
> flow explicit. Sometimes that is what you want (money, memory,
> messages). Sometimes it is not (truths, definitions, laws). The
> value is in being able to choose.*

## The connectives

Linear logic has more connectives than classical logic. The connectives
of classical `∧` and `∨` each split into two, based on how they treat
resources.

**Multiplicatives:**

- `A ⊗ B` (*tensor*, *of course*) — *have both A and B, use each once*.
- `A ⅋ B` (*par*, hard to translate) — dual to tensor; combine two things
  in a parallel/complementary way.

**Additives:**

- `A & B` (*with*) — *you may choose either A or B; the other becomes
  unavailable*.
- `A ⊕ B` (*plus*) — *one of A or B is provided; you do not know which*.

**Implication:** `A ⊸ B` (*lollipop*) — *consume an A to produce a B*.

**Exponentials:** `!A` (*of course*, *bang*) — *A can be duplicated,
discarded, treated classically*. `?A` (*why not*) — dual.

That is nine connectives (counting bang and why-not) versus classical's
five. It looks like a lot, but each has a clear role.

## The multiplicative distinction

Tensor and with both have a *dual* to their classical counterparts.
Tensor `A ⊗ B` means *I have exactly one A and exactly one B, and I
will use each once*. With `A & B` means *I have the ability to produce
either A or B on demand, but only one of them, and using one loses the
other*.

Compare:

- I have `20 dollars ⊗ movie ticket`: I have both, I can use both,
  they are independent.
- I have `20 dollars & movie ticket`: I have the *option* of taking
  one or the other. I can pick the twenty or pick the ticket, but not
  both.

Classical logic conflates these. Linear logic separates them and reveals
the structure.

Similarly for `⅋` and `⊕`: `A ⅋ B` is a *combined* thing that lets you
work with A and B together in parallel; `A ⊕ B` is an *anonymous* thing
that is one of them without your knowing which.

## Linear implication

`A ⊸ B` is *linear implication*: consume one A to produce one B. Compare:

- `A → B` (classical): you may use the argument as many times as you want.
- `A ⊸ B` (linear): you must use the argument exactly once.

Multiplication of natural numbers is linear-implied by addition:
`Nat ⊸ Nat ⊸ Nat` fits addition (consume two numbers, produce one). It
does not fit multiplication in the same way, because multiplication
uses its arguments multiple times inside the definition. To type
multiplication linearly you need `!Nat ⊸ !Nat ⊸ Nat` — the arguments
must be *reusable* (banged).

## The bang: recovery of classical reasoning

The exponential `!A` lets you recover classical reasoning locally. `!A`
means *A that can be used as many times as needed*. It supports:

- **Contraction:** `!A ⊸ (!A ⊗ !A)` — a banged thing can be duplicated.
- **Weakening:** `!A ⊸ 1` — a banged thing can be discarded.

So classical logic is a sublogic of linear logic: everywhere in
classical logic where you would duplicate a hypothesis, you introduce
a bang. Every classical proof translates to a linear proof.

This makes linear logic a *refinement*: it does not lose classical
expressive power, it *reveals* the structural moves that classical
logic makes silently.

## Encoding linear reasoning in Scheme

Let us encode a simple linear-logic proof checker. The key data
structure is a *multiset* of assumptions — we track *how many copies*
of each formula we have, and every rule application either consumes
copies or produces them.

```scheme
;; A context is a list of formulas (with multiplicity — repeats matter).
;; Consuming a formula removes one copy; producing adds one.

(define (remove-one x xs)
  (cond ((null? xs) 'not-found)
        ((equal? (car xs) x) (cdr xs))
        (else (let ((rest (remove-one x (cdr xs))))
                (if (eq? rest 'not-found)
                    'not-found
                    (cons (car xs) rest))))))

(define (consume-from ctx formulas)
  ;; Remove one copy of each formula in formulas; return new ctx or 'stuck.
  (if (null? formulas)
      ctx
      (let ((ctx2 (remove-one (car formulas) ctx)))
        (if (eq? ctx2 'not-found)
            'stuck
            (consume-from ctx2 (cdr formulas))))))
```

Now some linear-logic rules.

- **Tensor introduction.** From two proofs — one with context Γ₁
  producing A, one with context Γ₂ producing B — obtain a proof with
  context Γ₁ ∪ Γ₂ producing A ⊗ B. Contexts are disjoint; they don't
  share resources.

- **Tensor elimination.** From a proof of A ⊗ B and a proof of C in a
  context extended with fresh A and fresh B, obtain a proof of C in
  the combined context.

- **Lollipop introduction.** From a proof of B in context Γ, x:A (using
  the resource x exactly once), obtain a proof of A ⊸ B in context Γ.

- **Lollipop elimination.** From a proof of A ⊸ B in context Γ and a
  proof of A in context Δ, obtain a proof of B in Γ ∪ Δ.

```scheme
(define (check-linear proof)
  ;; A proof is (rule conclusion context children ...)
  ;; We check locally that each rule consumes and produces correctly.
  (case (car proof)
    ((assumption)
     ;; A single formula in the context; the conclusion matches.
     (equal? (cadr proof) (list (caddr proof))))
    ((tensor-intro)
     (let* ((concl (cadr proof))
            (l (list-ref proof 3))
            (r (list-ref proof 4)))
       (and (check-linear l)
            (check-linear r)
            (equal? concl (list 'tensor (proof-concl l) (proof-concl r)))
            (equal? (caddr proof)
                    (append (proof-ctx l) (proof-ctx r))))))
    ((lollipop-intro)
     (let* ((concl (cadr proof))
            (child (list-ref proof 3)))
       (and (check-linear child)
            (equal? (car concl) 'lollipop)
            (equal? (caddr concl) (proof-concl child))
            ;; child's context includes one extra assumption of A
            (equal? (proof-ctx child)
                    (cons (cadr concl) (caddr proof))))))
    ;; ...
    (else 'unknown-rule)))
```

The checker is more intricate than the classical one because it must
track resource consumption exactly. But the shape is familiar.

## The programming correspondence

Under Curry-Howard, linear logic corresponds to *linear type systems*
— type systems that track how many times each value is used.

- `A ⊗ B` — a pair of *independent* values, each used once.
- `A ⊸ B` — a function that consumes its argument once (a linear
  function).
- `!A` — an *unrestricted* value, freely duplicable.

This is the type system Rust implements (with some variations). Every
value in Rust has an *owner*; passing a value transfers ownership; the
old owner cannot use it anymore. This is linear typing. Rust adds
*borrowing* — the ability to temporarily lend a value without
transferring ownership — but the linear structure is the foundation.

Session types (Honda 1993, Honda-Vasconcelos-Kubo 1998) extend this to
concurrent protocols: a channel's type describes the sequence of sends
and receives that must happen on it, using linear connectives to
enforce that each send matches exactly one receive.

## Applications: garbage collection, protocols, quantum

**Garbage collection.** In a linearly-typed language, memory management
is trivial — each value has exactly one path of use, so you know when
to deallocate it without runtime tracing. Rust and Cyclone were both
designed around this observation.

**Protocol correctness.** Session types verify that concurrent
processes exchange messages in the agreed order and never deadlock.
This is what tools like SessionKotlin and Multiparty Session Types
research aim at.

**Quantum computing.** Quantum states cannot be duplicated (the *no-
cloning theorem* is a physical fact). Linear types are the *right*
type discipline for quantum programming languages, because they
enforce no-cloning at compile time. Languages like Quipper and Q# use
linear typing for exactly this reason.

**Petri nets.** A very old model of concurrent systems (Petri, 1962)
turns out to have exactly linear-logic semantics. Every Petri net
computation is a linear-logic proof. This connection was clarified in
the 1990s and it unified two previously separate research fields.

## Categorical semantics: *-autonomous categories

Linear logic has a beautiful categorical semantics: it is the internal
logic of *-autonomous categories (Barr, 1979). In these categories,
every object A has a *dual* A*, and the two multiplicative connectives
(tensor and par) are related by A ⅋ B = (A* ⊗ B*)*.

The additive connectives (with and plus) correspond to products and
coproducts. The exponentials (bang and why-not) correspond to a certain
kind of comonad.

We will meet categorical semantics more properly in chapter 12; for
now, the point is that linear logic has a categorical interpretation
that ties it into every other categorical structure in mathematics —
and this is one reason it feels so *right* to computer scientists who
care about clean semantic foundations.

## Substructural cousins

Linear logic is one member of a family of *substructural* logics —
logics that drop or restrict the structural rules.

- **Relevance logic.** Drops weakening. Every hypothesis must be *used*
  (relevant to the conclusion), but you can use it multiple times.
- **Affine logic.** Drops contraction. Every hypothesis is used *at
  most* once (may be discarded).
- **Linear logic.** Drops both. Every hypothesis is used *exactly*
  once.
- **Ordered logic.** Drops the *exchange* rule too. Hypotheses have an
  order that must be respected. Used for reasoning about sequences,
  DNA strings, and word order in linguistics.

Each has computational correspondents. Rust is affine (values may be
dropped). Linear-typed lambda calculi are linear. Ordered logics show
up in bio-informatics and computational linguistics.

## What linear logic makes visible

Once you learn to see the world through linear-logic eyes, you notice
resource-flow patterns everywhere.

- Money is linear. A dollar spent is not still yours.
- Memory is linear. A byte overwritten is gone.
- Attention is linear. A conversation you did not have this evening
  was not stored for later.
- Physical objects are linear. A cake eaten is not still cake.
- Cryptographic secrets are effectively linear. Once used to sign a
  message, a nonce should not be reused; once compromised, a key
  should be rotated.

Classical logic silently duplicates these things when it reasons. Linear
logic tracks them explicitly. For domains where the physical resource
metaphor matters (payment systems, memory allocators, cryptographic
protocols), linear typing gives you compile-time guarantees that
classical typing cannot.

## Variations to try

Extend the linear-logic proof checker with additive connectives (with
and plus). Note carefully: `with-intro` requires *the same context* on
both branches (you *choose* which to produce, but the resources you
would have needed are the same either way); `plus-intro` picks one
branch and consumes only that branch's resources.

Implement a small session-typed channel: a channel with type
`Send(Int) ; Receive(String) ; End`. The type says: first send an
integer, then receive a string, then close the channel. Write the
sender and receiver, using linear typing to ensure the channel is used
exactly according to its type.

Sketch a Petri net for a simple producer-consumer system. Verify that
its firing sequences correspond to linear-logic proofs. This is a
concrete way to see the linear-logic ↔ Petri-net correspondence.

## Try this

Take an ordinary program you wrote — anything with mutation, or with
memory allocation, or with cryptographic operations. Trace through it
with linear-logic eyes: at every step, ask *which values are being
consumed and which are being duplicated?* You will find places where
you *thought* you were being careful but were actually implicitly
copying. This exercise is what taught many people in the 1990s why
Rust's borrow checker was going to be worth the syntactic overhead.

## Closing

Linear logic makes resource flow visible. It drops the structural rules
that classical logic silently uses, and it introduces new connectives
whose interactions form a delicate algebraic structure. Under
Curry-Howard it corresponds to linear type systems, session types, and
the semantics of quantum computing.

"# Chapter 12 — Category Theory as Logic

Where composition itself becomes the primitive, and where a small set
of abstract laws organises logic, computation, and much of modern
mathematics under a single frame.

Category theory was invented by Eilenberg and Mac Lane in 1945 to
formalise the notion of *natural transformation* between algebraic
structures. It has since become the *lingua franca* of modern
mathematics — algebraic geometry, algebraic topology, homological
algebra, and, of particular interest here, mathematical logic.

The connection to logic runs deep. Lawvere (1963) showed that theories
can be seen as categories. Lambek (1968) showed that typed lambda
calculi are the *internal languages* of certain kinds of categories.
Every logic we have met in this book has a categorical semantics; every
computational model has a categorical semantics; and these semantics
compose in elegant, uniform ways.

This chapter is a *light touch*. Full category theory is a book of its
own (Awodey's; Mac Lane's). We will lay down the definitions, motivate
them, and show how they organise what we have already learned.

> **the runtime says**
>
> *Category theory has a reputation for being obscure. It is not.
> It is the most elementary mathematics you can do — objects and
> arrows and composition, that is the entire subject — and the reason
> it feels obscure is that the payoff comes only after you have
> patiently accepted its abstractions. Once you have, the payoff is
> substantial: every mathematical structure you know starts speaking
> a common language.*

## The definition

A *category* consists of:

- A collection of *objects*.
- For each pair of objects (A, B), a collection of *arrows* (or
  *morphisms*) from A to B, written `Hom(A, B)`.
- For each object A, an *identity arrow* `id_A : A → A`.
- A *composition* operation: given arrows `f : A → B` and `g : B → C`,
  there is a composed arrow `g ∘ f : A → C`.

Two axioms:

- **Identity.** `id_B ∘ f = f = f ∘ id_A` for every `f : A → B`.
- **Associativity.** `(h ∘ g) ∘ f = h ∘ (g ∘ f)`.

That is a category. Objects. Arrows. Identity. Composition. Two axioms.

Examples abound.

- **Set.** Objects are sets; arrows are functions; composition is
  function composition.
- **Grp.** Objects are groups; arrows are group homomorphisms.
- **Top.** Objects are topological spaces; arrows are continuous maps.
- **Vect.** Objects are vector spaces; arrows are linear maps.
- **Cat.** Objects are (small) categories; arrows are *functors*
  (structure-preserving maps between categories).
- **Types-of-a-language.** Objects are types; arrows are terms of type
  `A → B`. This is the categorical view of a programming language.

```scheme
;; Encoding a small category in Scheme.
;;
;; category:
;;   :objects   (list of object names)
;;   :arrows    (list of arrow descriptors: (:src :tgt :name))
;;   :identity  (function: object -> arrow name)
;;   :compose   (function: (arrow, arrow) -> arrow name, or 'not-composable)

(define (compose-arrows cat f g)
  ;; g ∘ f  (f goes first)
  ((cdr (assq :compose cat)) f g))
```

## Functors: maps between categories

A *functor* F : C → D is a *structure-preserving* map between categories.
It sends:

- each object A of C to an object F(A) of D;
- each arrow `f : A → B` in C to an arrow `F(f) : F(A) → F(B)` in D;

subject to two laws:

- `F(id_A) = id_{F(A)}` (preserves identities);
- `F(g ∘ f) = F(g) ∘ F(f)` (preserves composition).

Functors are how you *translate* between mathematical universes. Every
translation you have ever seen in mathematics — homology (from
topological spaces to abelian groups), fundamental group (from pointed
spaces to groups), free construction (from sets to groups) — is a
functor.

In programming, functors show up as *type constructors* with a `map`
operation. `List` is a functor: given a function `A → B`, it produces
a function `List(A) → List(B)`. Same for `Option`, `Tree`, `Map`, and so
on. Every generic container is a functor.

```scheme
;; The list functor's map:
(define (list-fmap f xs)
  (map f xs))

;; The option functor's map:
(define (option-fmap f opt)
  (cond
    ((eq? (car opt) 'none) '(none))
    ((eq? (car opt) 'some) (list 'some (f (cadr opt))))))
```

## Natural transformations: maps between functors

Given two functors F, G : C → D, a *natural transformation* η : F ⇒ G is
a family of arrows `η_A : F(A) → G(A)`, one for each object A of C,
satisfying a *naturality* condition: for every arrow `f : A → B`,
`G(f) ∘ η_A = η_B ∘ F(f)`.

Naturality means: the transformation *does not depend on the specific
object*; it works uniformly across the whole category.

A classical example: for lists, `reverse` is a natural transformation
from `List` to `List`. The naturality condition says: reversing after
mapping f is the same as mapping f after reversing. That is a
mathematically precise way to say *reverse does not care what is
inside the list, only how the list is structured*.

Category theory takes natural transformations very seriously — they
are, in a sense, what category theory was invented to make precise.

## Products and coproducts

In a category, a *product* of two objects A and B is an object A × B
together with two arrows `p₁ : A × B → A` and `p₂ : A × B → B` (the
*projections*) such that for any object C with arrows `f : C → A` and
`g : C → B`, there is a *unique* arrow `⟨f, g⟩ : C → A × B` with
`p₁ ∘ ⟨f, g⟩ = f` and `p₂ ∘ ⟨f, g⟩ = g`.

That is a *universal property*. It defines A × B not by what it *is*
but by how it *behaves*. Any object satisfying the universal property
of a product is (up to unique isomorphism) *the same* product.

The dual concept — *coproduct* — reverses the arrows. A + B has arrows
*into* it (called *injections*), and given any C with arrows *out of*
A and *out of* B, there is a unique arrow *out of* A + B.

In Set, product is Cartesian product; coproduct is disjoint union. In
Grp, product is direct product; coproduct is *free product*. In Top,
product is product topology; coproduct is disjoint union with
topology-summed. Every specific mathematical universe has its own
notion; the universal property picks out the right one.

**Categorical logic:** products correspond to *conjunctions*, coproducts
to *disjunctions*. Under Curry-Howard, this is exactly the semantics
we saw in chapter 7. Conjunction is a product in the category of
propositions-and-proofs; disjunction is a coproduct.

## Exponentials: the internal Hom

An *exponential* B^A in a category is an object such that arrows
`C → B^A` correspond naturally to arrows `C × A → B`. That is
currying at the categorical level: `Hom(C × A, B) ≅ Hom(C, B^A)`.

An exponential is an object that *internalises* the arrow-set. In Set,
`B^A` is the set of functions from A to B. In categories that have
exponentials (called *Cartesian closed categories*), the notion of
*function type* is definable internally.

**Categorical logic:** an exponential B^A corresponds to the
*implication* A → B. Cartesian closed categories are exactly the
categorical semantics of the simply-typed lambda calculus. This is the
Lambek-Scott theorem (1986): STLC and Cartesian closed categories are
the *same object*, up to change of notation.

## Adjunctions: the deepest categorical notion

Two functors F : C → D and G : D → C are *adjoint* (with F left
adjoint to G) if there is a natural isomorphism

    Hom_D(F(A), B) ≅ Hom_C(A, G(B))

for every A in C and B in D. Mac Lane wrote that *adjoint functors
arise everywhere*, and it is true. Nearly every meaningful pair of
mathematical constructions is an adjunction.

Examples:

- **Free-forgetful adjunction.** The functor that takes a set to the
  free group generated by it is left adjoint to the functor that
  forgets the group structure and remembers only the underlying set.
- **Product-projection.** The diagonal functor A → (A, A) is left
  adjoint to the product functor.
- **Existential-substitution.** Existential quantification is left
  adjoint to substitution; universal quantification is right adjoint
  to substitution. This is Lawvere's celebrated observation.

The pattern that emerges: every *natural* mathematical construction is
adjoint to some other construction. Learning to see adjunctions is what
separates a category theorist from someone who has just memorised the
definitions.

## Monads

A *monad* is an endofunctor T : C → C equipped with two natural
transformations:

- `η : Id ⇒ T` (unit)
- `μ : T ∘ T ⇒ T` (join)

subject to two coherence laws (the *monad laws*).

Monads structure *computational effects*. In programming, the *List*
monad models nondeterminism (a value that could be any of several).
The *Option* (or *Maybe*) monad models partiality (a value that might
be absent). The *State* monad models mutable state. The *IO* monad
models input/output. Each is defined by picking an endofunctor and
providing `η` and `μ`.

Kleisli composition — the composition of monadic actions — lets you
chain effectful computations. Every do-notation in Haskell or F# is
sugar for monadic composition.

Monads are how modern functional languages control effects. The
categorical formulation makes precise what an effect *is* — a
structured way of enriching pure computation with side-information.

```scheme
;; The Option monad's bind (Kleisli composition operator):
(define (option-bind opt f)
  (cond
    ((eq? (car opt) 'none) '(none))
    ((eq? (car opt) 'some) (f (cadr opt)))))

;; Chain: (bind (some 3) (λx. (bind (some 4) (λy. (some (+ x y))))))
;; => (some 7)
```

## Topoi: categorical universes of mathematics

A *topos* is a category with a great deal of structure — it has all
finite limits and colimits, exponentials, and a *subobject classifier*
Ω that plays the role of the truth-value type. Topoi are, in a strong
sense, *categorical universes*: much of set theory can be developed
inside any topos.

The most important topoi:

- **Set** itself.
- **Sheaves on a topological space X.** The internal logic is an
  intuitionistic logic that depends on X.
- **The effective topos.** Its internal logic captures computability.
- **The realizability topos.** Internal logic captures constructive
  proof with computational content.

For each topos, the *internal logic* is a specific kind of higher-order
intuitionistic logic. Working *inside* a topos, you use ordinary
mathematical language, but the truth-values are those of the topos —
not necessarily bivalent.

This is what makes topos theory important for logic: it provides
concrete non-classical universes where the excluded middle fails, and
lets you *do mathematics* inside them.

## Categorical semantics of the logics we have seen

Here is the summary table.

    Logic                            Categorical semantics
    --------------------------------------------------------------------
    Simply-typed lambda calculus     Cartesian closed category
    Intuitionistic propositional     Bicartesian closed category
    Linear logic                     *-autonomous category
    Modal S4                         Category with a comonad
    First-order intuitionistic       Locally-Cartesian-closed category
                                     with existential and universal quantifier structure
    Dependent type theory            Locally-Cartesian-closed category (with more)
    Homotopy type theory              (∞,1)-topos

Each row is a research subject. But the pattern holds. Category theory
gives every logic a home; each logic gives category theory a language.

## Applications: what category theory buys you

Practically speaking, categorical thinking in programming shows up as:

- **Programming to interfaces, not implementations.** The universal
  property of a construction determines it up to isomorphism; you can
  swap implementations freely.
- **Free constructions.** The free monoid, free monad, free algebra —
  each is a construction with a universal property that generates the
  minimum structure needed. Understanding freeness lets you factor
  code cleanly.
- **Duality.** Every construction has a dual (reverse the arrows). Once
  you know one construction, you know its dual for free.
- **Composition laws.** Categorical laws (functor laws, monad laws)
  give you *equational reasoning* about programs: refactorings that
  are guaranteed to preserve behaviour.
- **Semantics.** When you need to know what a construction *means*, its
  categorical semantics tell you. Denotational semantics, effect
  systems, and program equivalences are all built on categorical
  foundations.

Milewski's *Category Theory for Programmers* is a friendly walk through
these applications for working programmers.

## Variations to try

Implement in Scheme the *list monad*: `unit x = (list x)` and
`bind xs f = (apply append (map f xs))`. Verify the monad laws by
running them on small examples.

Encode the *Reader monad*: `Reader R A = R → A`. Its bind chains
computations that all read from the same environment. This is the
essence of dependency injection.

Sketch the *free monoid* on a set A: it is the type of lists of A, with
`nil` as identity and concatenation as multiplication. Verify that any
function from A to a monoid B extends uniquely to a monoid homomorphism
from `List A` to B. That is the *universal property* of the free
monoid, in code.

## Try this

Take a piece of code you have written with error handling — try/catch,
Option types, Result types. Rewrite it using the Option monad's bind.
Watch the nested case-analysis collapse into a linear chain of
monadic operations. The code becomes noticeably shorter and clearer.
That is what monadic structuring buys you, and it is why monads went
from an obscure category-theoretic notion in the 1960s to a standard
technique in modern functional programming.

## Closing

Category theory is composition, promoted to the level of primitive.
Every construction is an object; every meaningful map is an arrow;
every meaningful *comparison of maps* is a natural transformation.
Under this frame, logics become categories, computations become
functors, and effects become monads.

The chapter has been a light touch — the full development requires a
book. But you now know what to *ask* about a mathematical structure:
what are its objects? what are its arrows? what universal properties
does it satisfy? and which other categories does it map into?

Chapter 13 changes register again. We turn from formal correspondence
to a genuinely different logic: *non-monotonic reasoning*. Where
classical logic never revises a conclusion in the face of new
information, non-monotonic logic revises constantly — and turns out to
model much of ordinary human inference.
"

"# Chapter 13 — Non-Monotonic and Default Logic

Where we drop a property of classical reasoning that turns out never to
have been true of ordinary human reasoning, and where the resulting
logics model exactly the moves people make when they revise beliefs on
new information.

Classical logic has a property called *monotonicity*: adding premises
never invalidates conclusions. If Γ ⊢ φ then Γ ∪ {ψ} ⊢ φ, for any ψ.
Once a theorem is proved from a theory, it stays proved as the theory
grows.

This is not how human reasoning works. Consider:

- *Tweety is a bird.* Therefore, tentatively, Tweety flies.
- *Tweety is a penguin.* Therefore, tentatively, Tweety does not fly.
- *Tweety is a superheroic penguin from a comic.* Therefore Tweety
  flies after all.

Each new fact reverses the previous conclusion. This is *non-monotonic
reasoning* — reasoning where adding information can invalidate old
conclusions.

Non-monotonic logic was invented in the late 1970s by AI researchers
trying to formalise commonsense reasoning. McCarthy's *circumscription*
(1980), Reiter's *default logic* (1980), and Moore's *autoepistemic
logic* (1985) were the three founding formalisms. They differ in
detail but share the same insight: real reasoning uses defaults that
can be overridden.

> **the runtime says**
>
> *This is the chapter where formal logic starts to resemble how
> reasoning actually feels. When I look at a puzzle, I make provisional
> assumptions, work with them, and revise as new information arrives.
> Classical logic pretends none of this happens. Non-monotonic logic
> admits it and gives it structure. If I ever have to explain to
> someone why my earlier answer was wrong, non-monotonic reasoning is
> the vocabulary I reach for.*

## The Tweety problem

The problem that launched the field: encode our knowledge that *birds
typically fly* while allowing that *penguins are birds that do not fly*.

In classical logic, the natural encoding runs into trouble.

    (forall ?x (implies (bird ?x) (flies ?x)))       ; birds fly
    (forall ?x (implies (penguin ?x) (bird ?x)))     ; penguins are birds
    (forall ?x (implies (penguin ?x) (not (flies ?x))))  ; penguins do not fly

    (penguin Tweety)

From these we derive:

    (bird Tweety)
    (flies Tweety)         ; from rule 1
    (not (flies Tweety))   ; from rule 3

A contradiction. The classical logician's response: strengthen rule 1
to *(forall ?x (implies (and (bird ?x) (not (penguin ?x))) (flies ?x)))*.
But then when we learn Tweety is a wounded bird (also a non-flyer), we
must strengthen again. And again for baby birds, birds in cages, dead
birds, birds coated in tar. The classical encoding requires enumerating
every exception in the antecedent of the rule.

## Default rules

Reiter's default logic replaces the classical rule with a *default
rule*:

    bird(x) : flies(x)
    ----------------------
         flies(x)

Read: *if bird(x) holds, and it is consistent to assume flies(x), then
conclude flies(x).* The middle line — the *justification* — says the
conclusion may be adopted as long as it does not contradict what we
already know.

For Tweety-the-penguin, the default fires initially. Then we learn
`(not (flies Tweety))`. This makes `flies(Tweety)` inconsistent with
our known facts, so the default no longer fires. The conclusion is
withdrawn.

Formally, a default is a triple (prerequisite, justifications, conclusion).
An *extension* of a default theory is a maximal consistent set of
formulas that can be derived by treating the classical facts and firing
consistent defaults.

Default theories may have zero, one, or multiple extensions. Multiple
extensions correspond to genuine ambiguity in the theory. This is a
feature — real commonsense knowledge is often ambiguous.

## Encoding it

```scheme
;; A default: (prerequisite (justifications ...) conclusion)
;; A default theory: (classical-facts defaults)

(define tweety-theory
  '(:classical
    ((penguin Tweety)
     (forall ?x (implies (penguin ?x) (bird ?x)))
     (forall ?x (implies (penguin ?x) (not (flies ?x)))))
    :defaults
    ((bird ?x) ((flies ?x)) (flies ?x))))

;; Compute the extension by fixed-point iteration:
;;   Start with the classical facts.
;;   For each default whose prerequisite holds and whose justifications
;;     are consistent with the current set, fire it — add its conclusion.
;;   Repeat until no new default fires.

(define (compute-extension theory)
  (let* ((facts (cdr (assq :classical theory)))
         (defaults (cdr (assq :defaults theory))))
    (let loop ((current facts))
      (let ((next (add-fireable-defaults current defaults)))
        (if (equal? next current)
            current
            (loop next))))))

(define (add-fireable-defaults facts defaults)
  (fold-left
    (lambda (acc d)
      (if (and (prerequisite-holds? (car d) acc)
               (all-consistent? (cadr d) acc)
               (not (member (caddr d) acc)))
          (cons (caddr d) acc)
          acc))
    facts
    defaults))
```

`prerequisite-holds?` is a classical inference check (does the fact
follow from the current beliefs?). `all-consistent?` is the delicate
piece: it must check that each justification is consistent with the
current beliefs, which in general is undecidable. Practical
implementations use restricted forms (*normal* defaults, where
prerequisite = justification = conclusion, are decidable).

## Circumscription

McCarthy's approach. Given a theory, *circumscribe* a predicate — assume
it holds *only where the theory requires it to hold*, and false
otherwise. This is a *closed-world assumption* on that predicate.

    (bird Tweety)                    ; Tweety is a bird
    (bird Woody)                     ; Woody is a bird

Circumscribing *abnormal*: assume `abnormal(x)` is false for every x
not explicitly abnormal. Then:

    (forall ?x (implies (and (bird ?x) (not (abnormal ?x))) (flies ?x)))

For Tweety, no explicit assertion of abnormality, so circumscription
gives `not(abnormal Tweety)`, so we conclude `flies Tweety`. Later,
learning that penguins are abnormal, we retract: penguins get abnormal
by an explicit rule, and their non-flight becomes provable.

Circumscription is a *model-preference* semantics — it selects a
particular model (or class of models) as the *intended* model of the
theory. Formally: a model M is *preferred* if there is no other model
M' with strictly less extension of the circumscribed predicate.

## Autoepistemic logic

Moore's approach. Add a modal operator *L* meaning *the agent believes*.
The formula `Lφ` reads *I believe φ*. Then:

    (forall ?x (implies (and (bird ?x) (not (L (not (flies ?x))))) (flies ?x)))

Read: *if x is a bird and I do not believe x does not fly, then x flies.*
This is *introspective* — the rule refers to the agent's own belief
state. Extensions of the theory are *stable expansions* — fixpoints
under introspection.

Autoepistemic logic is closely related to the *stable model semantics*
of logic programming, which is what modern *answer set programming*
systems (Clingo, DLV) use. Every non-monotonic logic here has industrial
descendants; the field did not go away, it went underground into
practical tools.

## Belief revision

A separate but related field: *belief revision*. Given a set of beliefs
B and a new belief φ, how do you *revise* B to accommodate φ, especially
when φ contradicts what you already believe?

The AGM postulates (Alchourron-Gardenfors-Makinson, 1985) axiomatise
rational belief revision:

1. **Closure.** The revised belief set is closed under logical
   consequence.
2. **Success.** The new belief is in the revised set.
3. **Inclusion.** The revision does not add beyond the original plus
   the new.
4. **Vacuity.** If the new belief is consistent with the old, the
   revision is just the union.
5. **Consistency.** The revision is consistent if the new belief is.
6. **Extensionality.** Equivalent new beliefs produce equivalent
   revisions.

The AGM postulates were adopted broadly and have descendants in
database theory (integrity constraints), diagnostic reasoning
(consistency-based diagnosis), and knowledge base updates.

## Argumentation frameworks

Dung's *argumentation frameworks* (1995) provide another take. An
argumentation framework is a graph whose nodes are *arguments* and
whose edges represent *attack* — one argument attacks another. A set
of arguments is *acceptable* if it is internally consistent and each
argument in it is defended (all attackers are attacked back).

Different notions of *acceptable* give different semantics: *grounded*,
*preferred*, *stable*, *complete*. Each corresponds to a way of
extracting a coherent position from a network of conflicting arguments.

This framework has applications in legal reasoning (arguments for and
against a verdict), scientific reasoning (evidence for and against a
hypothesis), and social AI (recommender systems that explain
themselves).

## Applications to abduction

Non-monotonic reasoning provides one of the natural homes for
*abduction* — inference to the best explanation. Chapter 15 will develop
the runtime's reasoning routes; abduction is one of them. The pattern is:

- Observe a fact E that is not entailed by the current theory.
- Consider possible explanations H₁, H₂, ..., Hₙ such that each H_i,
  added to the theory, would entail E.
- Prefer the H_i that best fits — is most consistent with the rest of
  the theory, is simplest, has the most prior support.
- Adopt H_i tentatively, subject to revision.

This is exactly non-monotonic reasoning in an abductive dress. The
*best explanation* is provisional and defeasible; new evidence may
overturn it. Formal frameworks for abduction (Poole 1988; Kakas-Kowalski-
Toni 1992) are built on top of non-monotonic logics.

## The frame problem

Non-monotonic reasoning was invented largely to solve the *frame
problem* in AI — the problem of specifying what does *not* change
when an action is performed. When I move a chair, the position of the
chair changes, but the color does not, and the temperature of the
room does not, and the phase of the moon does not. Enumerating all the
non-changes is impossible.

The default-logic solution: default rules that say *properties do not
change unless there is a rule saying they change*. This is called
*inertia* or *persistence*, and it captures commonsense reasoning about
actions.

Real AI planning systems (STRIPS, PDDL, action-language descendants)
all rely on some form of the frame axiom / inertia default. Non-
monotonic logic is why these systems can be built at all — the frame
problem was fatal to first-generation AI, and the non-monotonic
response is what let planning become tractable again.

## Diagnostic reasoning

*Consistency-based diagnosis* (Reiter 1987): given a device
specification and observed symptoms that contradict the specification,
find the minimal sets of components whose *abnormality* would restore
consistency. Each such set is a *diagnosis*.

The formulation is directly non-monotonic. Components are assumed
normal by default; observations override the default; the diagnostic
task is to find the smallest override that explains the observations.

Real deployed systems (particularly in aircraft avionics and industrial
process control) use consistency-based diagnosis. The math is
non-monotonic reasoning; the implementation is often SAT- or SMT-based.

## Non-monotonic and constructive: an uncomfortable pair

Non-monotonic reasoning does not sit easily with the Curry-Howard
correspondence we developed in chapter 7. A constructive proof produces
a witness; a non-monotonic conclusion is provisional and may not
correspond to any construction at all.

Efforts to bridge the two have taken decades. *Reflective* proof
systems (Konolige 1988; McDermott-Doyle 1980) allow non-monotonic
rules within a modal logic. *Well-founded* semantics for logic programs
(Van Gelder-Ross-Schlipf 1991) gives a constructive semantics to
non-monotonic negation. But full unification remains open — the two
frameworks have different flavors, and translating between them costs
you either soundness or expressiveness.

The practical stance: use classical/constructive reasoning where you
need guarantees; use non-monotonic reasoning where you need
commonsense inference; be explicit about which mode you are in.

## Variations to try

Implement Reiter's default logic more fully. Handle multiple extensions
by returning a *list* of possible extensions rather than a single one.
Try it on the classic *Nixon diamond*: Nixon is a Quaker (defaults to
pacifist) and a Republican (defaults to non-pacifist). Two extensions —
pacifist Nixon, non-pacifist Nixon — with no way to prefer one.

Encode a small *inheritance network* with defaults: Fido is a dog, dogs
are mammals, mammals have four legs *by default*, Fido has three legs
*explicitly*. Show that the explicit fact overrides the default.

Sketch belief revision AGM-style. Given a starting belief set and a
sequence of new beliefs, some of which contradict the old, produce the
revised belief set after each. Explore what happens when you receive
contradictory new beliefs.

## Try this

Take a real conversation you had recently where your view *changed*
during the conversation. Model it as a sequence of non-monotonic
updates. What was the initial belief? What new information came in?
Which of your prior conclusions had to be withdrawn? Which defaults
had you been using implicitly? This is the exercise that made
non-monotonic reasoning stick for me the first time: it maps directly
onto how ordinary thinking feels when it is going well.

## Closing

Non-monotonic reasoning drops the classical property that adding
premises preserves conclusions. Default logic, circumscription, and
autoepistemic logic are three founding formalisms. Belief revision and
argumentation frameworks are close relatives. Diagnosis, abduction, and
the frame problem are practical applications.

Chapter 14 continues the theme of *inference under uncertainty*:
probabilistic reasoning, fuzzy logic, and how the runtime's confidence-
grade system fits into these formalisms. Where non-monotonic logic
withdraws conclusions on new information, probabilistic reasoning
updates conclusions *quantitatively* — Bayesian updating is the
mathematical spine of both.
