"# Chapter 10 — The training loop

Everything the last four chapters set up gets used here. Forward
pass, loss, backward pass, parameter update. Do that many times on
many examples. That is training. Change the data, change the
architecture, change the loss, but the loop shape is the same
whether you are fitting a line or training GPT-4.

## The loop, in words

```
initialize parameters (randomly)
repeat many times:
  pick some examples
  forward: compute predictions from current parameters
  loss: compute how wrong the predictions are
  backward: compute the gradient of the loss with respect to every parameter
  update: parameter := parameter - learning_rate * gradient
stop when the loss is small enough (or you run out of time)
```

Every trained model in the world went through this loop. Big models
have more data, more parameters, and more sophisticated update rules
(Adam, AdamW), but the loop is exactly this shape.

## Problem 1 — Train a single neuron to fit y = 2x + 1

We did this in chapter 6 with finite-difference gradients. Now let's
do it with analytic backprop. Same result, faster, cleaner.

```
;; Data: pairs (x, y) where y = 2x + 1 with a little noise
(define data
  (list (cons -2.0 -3.0)
        (cons -1.0 -1.0)
        (cons  0.0  1.0)
        (cons  1.0  3.0)
        (cons  2.0  5.0)))

;; Model: y_pred = w*x + b
;; Loss: (y_pred - y_true)^2

(define (train-step w b lr example)
  (define x (car example))
  (define y-true (cdr example))
  (define y-pred (+ (* w x) b))
  ;; Backprop:
  (define dL-dy (* 2 (- y-pred y-true)))
  (define dL-dw (* dL-dy x))
  (define dL-db dL-dy)
  ;; Update:
  (list (- w (* lr dL-dw))
        (- b (* lr dL-db))))

(define (train-epoch w b lr data)
  (fold (lambda (example params)
          (train-step (car params) (cadr params) lr example))
        (list w b)
        data))

(define (mean-loss w b data)
  (define (sq p)
    (let ((y-pred (+ (* w (car p)) b))
          (y-true (cdr p)))
      (* (- y-pred y-true) (- y-pred y-true))))
  (/ (reduce + 0 (map sq data)) (length data)))

(define final
  (let loop ((w 0.0) (b 0.0) (epoch 0))
    (if (> epoch 200)
        (list w b (mean-loss w b data))
        (let ((next (train-epoch w b 0.05 data)))
          (loop (car next) (cadr next) (+ epoch 1))))))

(display final)
;; => approximately (2.0 1.0 ~0)
```

The neuron converged. Starting from `w=0, b=0`, after 200 epochs
(passes through the data), the parameters are essentially the true
`w=2, b=1` and the loss is essentially zero.

Read the code:

- `train-step` takes one example, computes gradients, updates.
- `train-epoch` folds `train-step` over the whole data list.
- The outer loop runs 200 epochs.
- `mean-loss` at the end tells us how well we did.

## Problem 2 — Batching

In problem 1 we updated after every example (called stochastic
gradient descent, or SGD). The gradient from one example is noisy.
Averaging gradients over a batch of examples smooths the noise.

Batch gradient descent:

```
(define (batch-gradient w b batch)
  (define n (length batch))
  (define (grads example)
    (let ((x (car example)) (y-true (cdr example)))
      (let ((y-pred (+ (* w x) b)))
        (let ((dL-dy (* 2 (- y-pred y-true))))
          (list (* dL-dy x) dL-dy)))))
  (define all (map grads batch))
  (define sum-dw (reduce + 0 (map car all)))
  (define sum-db (reduce + 0 (map cadr all)))
  (list (/ sum-dw n) (/ sum-db n)))

(define (batch-train w b lr batch)
  (define g (batch-gradient w b batch))
  (list (- w (* lr (car g)))
        (- b (* lr (cadr g)))))

(define data
  (list (cons -2.0 -3.0) (cons -1.0 -1.0)
        (cons  0.0  1.0) (cons  1.0  3.0) (cons 2.0 5.0)))

(define result
  (let loop ((w 0.0) (b 0.0) (n 0))
    (if (> n 500)
        (list w b)
        (let ((next (batch-train w b 0.1 data)))
          (loop (car next) (cadr next) (+ n 1))))))

(display result)
;; => approximately (2.0 1.0)
```

Same answer as SGD but the loss curve is smoother. In practice
mini-batches (10-256 examples) balance smoothness against speed.

## Problem 3 — Training a two-layer network on non-linear data

Now let's train the multi-layer perceptron from chapter 8. Target:
fit `y = x^2` on some data points. A linear model cannot do this.
A network with ReLU and a hidden layer can.

```
(define (relu x) (if (> x 0) x 0))
(define (relu-grad u) (if (> u 0) 1 0))

;; Two-layer network: 1 input, H hidden, 1 output
(define H 8)

;; Random initialization
(define (init-vec dim)
  (map (lambda (_) (- (* (random) 0.5) 0.25)) (iota dim)))

(define W1 (map (lambda (_) (init-vec 1)) (iota H)))    ;; H x 1
(define b1 (init-vec H))
(define W2 (list (init-vec H)))                          ;; 1 x H
(define b2 (init-vec 1))

;; Forward pass: returns (u1, h, y)
(define (forward W1 b1 W2 b2 x)
  (define u1 (map (lambda (row bi) (+ (vec/dot (vec/make row) (listx))) bi))
                  W1 b1))
  (define h  (map relu u1))
  (define y  (+ (vec/dot (vec/make (car W2)) (vec/make h)) (car b2)))
  (list u1 h y))

;; Backward: computes gradients for all parameters
(define (backward W1 b1 W2 b2 x y-true)
  (define fwd (forward W1 b1 W2 b2 x))
  (define u1 (car fwd))
  (define h  (cadr fwd))
  (define y  (caddr fwd))
  (define dL-dy (* 2 (- y y-true)))
  ;; y = W2·h + b2  -> dL/dW2[i] = dL-dy * h[i], dL/db2 = dL-dy
  (define dL-dW2 (list (map (lambda (hi) (* dL-dy hi)) h)))
  (define dL-db2 (list dL-dy))
  (define dL-dh (map (lambda (w2i) (* dL-dy w2i)) (car W2)))
  ;; h = relu(u1)  -> dL/du1[i] = dL-dh[i] * relu'(u1[i])
  (define dL-du1 (map (lambda (dh u) (* dh (relu-grad u))) dL-dh u1))
  ;; u1 = W1·x + b1 (each u1[i] = W1[i][0]*x + b1[i])
  (define dL-dW1 (map (lambda (du) (list (* du x))) dL-du1))
  (define dL-db1 dL-du1)
  (list dL-dW1 dL-db1 dL-dW2 dL-db2))

;; Update
(define (vec-update v grads lr)
  (map (lambda (vi gi) (- vi (* lr gi))) v grads))

(define (row-update rows grads lr)
  (map (lambda (r g) (vec-update r g lr)) rows grads))

;; Data
(define data
  (map (lambda (i)
         (let ((x (/ (- i 5) 2.5)))
           (cons x (* x x))))
       (iota 11)))
;; x from -2 to 2 in steps of 0.4, y = x^2

;; Training loop
(define lr 0.03)

(let loop ((W1 W1) (b1 b1) (W2 W2) (b2 b2) (epoch 0))
  (if (> epoch 3000)
      (begin
        (display \"final loss: \")
        (display
          (/ (reduce +
                     0
                     (map (lambda (p)
                            (let ((y (caddr (forward W1 b1 W2 b2 (car p)))))
                              (* (- y (cdr p)) (- y (cdr p)))))
                          data))
             (length data)))
        (newline))
      (let inner ((rem data) (W1 W1) (b1 b1) (W2 W2) (b2 b2))
        (if (null? rem)
            (loop W1 b1 W2 b2 (+ epoch 1))
            (let* ((example (car rem))
                   (grads (backward W1 b1 W2 b2 (car example) (cdr example)))
                   (dW1 (car grads))
                   (db1 (cadr grads))
                   (dW2 (caddr grads))
                   (db2 (cadddr grads)))
              (inner (cdr rem)
                     (row-update W1 dW1 lr)
                     (vec-update b1 db1 lr)
                     (row-update W2 dW2 lr)
                     (vec-update b2 db2 lr)))))))
;; final loss: something small (< 0.05 typically, depending on random init)
```

The network learned to approximate `y = x^2` on the training data.
The ReLU units bent the input space; the output layer summed them into
a curve. This is the smallest interesting neural network training in
Motoi Scheme.

Read the code carefully. It has all the pieces: forward pass, loss,
backward pass with chain rule, and parameter update. Nothing else.
Everything else in this book is more of the same, arranged
differently.

## Problem 4 — Overfitting

If you train a large network on a small dataset, it may memorize the
training examples rather than learning the underlying pattern. The
training loss goes to zero. The loss on held-out (test) data is
large. That is overfitting.

```
;; If your training data has 5 points and your network has 50
;; parameters, the network has enough capacity to hit every training
;; point exactly and do nothing sensible in between.
```

The fix: more data, or a smaller model, or regularization (a penalty
in the loss that discourages large parameters), or dropout (randomly
zeroing hidden units during training). Real ML is largely about
managing this trade-off.

For a language model, overfitting means memorizing the training
corpus rather than learning language patterns. Big models trained
on huge corpora have a hard time overfitting because there is too
much data to memorize. Small models on small corpora overfit like
mad.

## Problem 5 — When to stop

Training does not stop 'automatically.' You choose when. Two
strategies.

**Fixed number of epochs.** Train for a preset number of passes over
the data. Simple, predictable.

**Early stopping.** Keep a held-out validation set. Train and track
loss on the validation set. When the validation loss stops decreasing
(or starts increasing), stop. That is the moment the model started
to overfit.

Modern practice is early stopping with a patience of a few epochs:
stop after N consecutive epochs of no validation improvement.

## Capstone — Training loop template

A complete training loop as a template you can reuse. Not for any
particular model — a scaffold.

```
;; Given:
;;   init-params  -> parameters
;;   forward params x -> prediction
;;   loss params batch -> scalar
;;   backward params batch -> gradient
;;   update params gradient lr -> new params
(define (train init-params forward loss backward update data lr epochs)
  (let loop ((params init-params) (epoch 0))
    (if (>= epoch epochs)
        params
        (let ((g (backward params data)))
          (let ((new-params (update params g lr)))
            (when (= (modulo epoch 100) 0)
              (display \"epoch \") (display epoch)
              (display \" loss \") (display (loss new-params data))
              (newline))
            (loop new-params (+ epoch 1)))))))
```

This shape works for any model. Change `forward`, `backward`, and
`update` to match the architecture. The loop shell is invariant.

## Why this matters

You now know how to train. From random weights, through many small
updates, to a model that fits data. This is the mechanism that
produces every trained model in the world. Chapters 11-15 build the
architecture of a language model. Chapter 16 trains it with the loop
you just learned.

## What's next

Chapter 11 is where the language part of language models begins. We
have to turn words into vectors. That is what tokens and embeddings
are for. Once we have vectors, all the machinery from chapters 2-10
applies directly.
")

"# Chapter 11 — Tokens and embeddings

Language is symbols. Networks eat numbers. The bridge between them
is embeddings — a table that maps each symbol to a vector of numbers.
Once every symbol has a vector, the vector arithmetic from chapters
2-10 applies to language.

This chapter builds that bridge in three pieces:

1. Tokenization — split text into symbols.
2. A vocabulary — number the symbols.
3. An embedding table — associate each numbered symbol with a
   learnable vector.

## Problem 1 — Tokenize on whitespace

The simplest tokenizer splits on spaces. Not great for real language
(no punctuation handling, no subword) but a fine starting point.

```
(define (whitespace-tokenize text)
  ;; string-split is in Motoi's r7rs completions
  (string-split text \" \"))

(display (whitespace-tokenize \"the cat sat on the mat\"))
;; => (\"the\" \"cat\" \"sat\" \"on\" \"the\" \"mat\")
```

Six tokens. Notice 'the' appears twice — the tokenizer produces a
sequence, not a set. Order matters. The model will use position to
know that the second 'the' comes after 'cat sat on the.'

## Problem 2 — A vocabulary from a corpus

The vocabulary is the set of distinct tokens the model knows about.
Every token in it gets a number (its index). Tokens not in the
vocabulary become an 'unknown' symbol.

```
(define (build-vocab tokens)
  ;; Return an alist: token -> id
  (define (add-unique acc tok)
    (if (assoc tok acc)
        acc
        (cons (cons tok (length acc)) acc)))
  (reverse (fold add-unique '() tokens)))

(define corpus
  (whitespace-tokenize \"the cat sat on the mat and the mat sat still\"))

(display (build-vocab corpus))
;; => ((\"the\" . 0) (\"cat\" . 1) (\"sat\" . 2) (\"on\" . 3)
;;     (\"mat\" . 4) (\"and\" . 5) (\"still\" . 6))
;; 7 unique tokens
```

The vocabulary maps each distinct word to a numeric id. `'the'` gets
0. `'cat'` gets 1. And so on. Real vocabularies for language models
have between 30,000 and 100,000 entries.

## Problem 3 — Token to id, id to token

Two lookups. Given a token, get its id. Given an id, get the token
back. Both are needed at training time (token→id for input) and
inference (id→token for output).

```
(define vocab (build-vocab (whitespace-tokenize \"the cat sat on the mat\")))

(define (tok->id tok)
  (let ((entry (assoc tok vocab)))
    (if entry (cadr entry) -1)))    ;; -1 = unknown  (see note below)

(define (id->tok id)
  (let loop ((rest vocab))
    (cond ((null? rest) \"[UNK]\")
          ((= (cadr (car rest)) id) (car (car rest)))
          (else (loop (cdr rest))))))

(display (tok->id \"cat\"))     ;; => 1
(display (id->tok 3))            ;; => \"on\"
(display (tok->id \"llama\"))    ;; => -1  (not in vocab)
```

`assoc` is a linear search. For real vocabs you'd use a hash table
(chapter 3 of Book of R7RS Recipes covers `make-hash-table`). The
idea is the same, just faster.

Note about Motoi's alist convention. Motoi's `cons` produces proper
lists rather than R5RS-style dotted pairs, so a vocab entry built as
`(cons \"cat\" 1)` is the two-element list `(\"cat\" 1)`, not the
dotted pair `(\"cat\" . 1)`. The key is `(car entry)`, and the value
is `(cadr entry)`. Same shape as any other alist, just a different
accessor for the value. If you copy code from an R7RS book that uses
`(cdr entry)` to get the value, remember to swap in `cadr` for Motoi.

## Problem 4 — One-hot encoding

The most naive way to turn a token into a vector: a vector of length
vocab-size, all zeros except a 1 at the token's index. This is called
one-hot.

```
(define vocab (build-vocab (whitespace-tokenize \"a b c d e\")))
(define vocab-size (length vocab))

(define (one-hot id)
  (vec/make
    (map (lambda (i) (if (= i id) 1 0))
         (iota vocab-size))))

(display (one-hot 0))    ;; => vector (1 0 0 0 0)
(display (one-hot 2))    ;; => vector (0 0 1 0 0)
```

One-hot vectors are correct but wasteful. In a vocab of 50,000, every
token is a 50,000-dimensional vector that is mostly zero. And more
important: one-hot vectors carry no meaning — the vectors for 'cat'
and 'kitten' are as orthogonal as those for 'cat' and 'kilowatt.'

Embeddings fix both problems.

## Problem 5 — The embedding table

An embedding table is a matrix of shape (vocab-size, embed-dim). Row
i is the embedding vector for token id i. Looking up a token becomes:
'fetch row i.' No matrix multiplication needed — direct indexing.

```
(define vocab-size 7)
(define embed-dim 4)

;; Random init — every token gets a random 4-dim vector at start
(define (random-vec dim)
  (vec/make (map (lambda (_) (- (* (random) 0.4) 0.2))
                 (iota dim))))

(define embedding-table
  (map (lambda (_) (random-vec embed-dim)) (iota vocab-size)))

(define (embed id) (list-ref embedding-table id))

(display (embed 0))    ;; embedding of token 0 — a 4-dim vector
(display (embed 3))    ;; embedding of token 3 — a different 4-dim vector
```

The embedding for each token is a vector in 4-dimensional space.
Initially those vectors are random and meaningless. During training,
gradient descent updates them so tokens used in similar contexts end
up in similar directions. That is the miracle: the embeddings LEARN
meaning by pushing similar-context tokens closer together.

## Problem 6 — A tokenized sentence as a sequence of embeddings

```
(define sentence \"the cat sat\")
(define vocab (build-vocab (whitespace-tokenize \"the cat sat on the mat\")))
(define vocab-size (length vocab))
(define embed-dim 4)

(define embedding-table
  (map (lambda (_)
         (vec/make (map (lambda (_) (- (* (random) 0.4) 0.2))
                        (iota embed-dim))))
       (iota vocab-size)))

(define (tok->id tok)
  (let ((entry (assoc tok vocab)))
    (if entry (cadr entry) -1)))

(define (embed-sentence text)
  (map (lambda (tok) (list-ref embedding-table (tok->id tok)))
       (whitespace-tokenize text)))

(display (embed-sentence sentence))
;; => a list of 3 vectors of dim 4
```

A sentence has become a matrix — one row per token, one column per
embedding dimension. This is the shape the transformer eats. Every
subsequent chapter operates on this shape.

## Problem 7 — Learning embeddings by co-occurrence (word2vec sketch)

The classic word2vec trick: train an embedding table so that words
that appear near each other have similar embeddings. The loss:
predict the surrounding context from the center word. Backprop
through the prediction updates the center word's embedding.

We won't implement full word2vec here — chapter 16's tiny LLM learns
its embeddings the same way, as part of the whole model. But the
core observation is: embeddings are just parameters. The training
loop from chapter 10 updates them by gradient descent, exactly like
it updates the network weights.

Mikolov et al. 2013 showed that trained embeddings capture stunning
patterns: `king - man + woman ≈ queen`. Vector arithmetic on words
matches semantic arithmetic. The embedding space encodes meaning as
geometry. That was one of the most important results in NLP in the
last twenty years.

## Capstone — Similarity search in an embedding space

Build a tiny vocabulary with hand-set embeddings. Show that words we
consider similar are close in cosine distance.

```
(define vocab
  (list (list \"cat\"    (list 0.8 0.2 0.1 0.0))
        (list \"kitten\" (list 0.7 0.3 0.1 0.0))
        (list \"dog\"    (list 0.7 0.1 0.2 0.0))
        (list \"car\"    (list 0.0 0.1 0.8 0.2))
        (list \"truck\"  (list 0.1 0.0 0.7 0.3))
        (list \"book\"   (list 0.0 0.0 0.0 0.9))))

(define (cosine a b)
  (/ (vec/dot a b) (* (vec/norm a) (vec/norm b))))

(define query (cadr (assoc \"cat\" vocab)))

(for-each (lambda (entry)
            (display (car entry))
            (display \" -> similarity \")
            (display (cosine query (cadr entry)))
            (newline))
          vocab)
;; cat    -> 1.0
;; kitten -> 0.98
;; dog    -> 0.94
;; car    -> 0.11
;; truck  -> 0.13
;; book   -> 0.00
```

Cat is closest to kitten and dog. Cat is nearly orthogonal to book.
The geometry of the embedding space captures a notion of similarity.
When you look up an embedding, you get semantic content — not just
an index.

Real embeddings are learned, not hand-crafted. But the shape is the
same: high-dimensional vectors, similar contexts → similar
directions, cosine to compare.

## Why this matters

Embeddings are the ground floor of every language model. Every token
in every prompt goes through an embedding lookup before anything
else happens. The embedding table is one of the biggest parameter
groups in a language model — for a 50,000 vocab with 768-dim
embeddings, the table alone has 38.4 million parameters. Learning
good embeddings is a large part of what training does.

## What's next

Chapter 12 introduces attention. The transformer's core mechanism.
Given a sequence of embedded tokens, produce a new sequence where
each position is a weighted mixture of the others. The weights are
computed by soft lookup — a dot-product comparison of query and key
vectors. Attention is what let language models get big.
")

"# Chapter 12 — Attention as a soft-lookup

Here we are. Attention is the mechanism that let language models get
big. Transformers use it. GPT uses it. Every modern LLM uses it. The
math is not that hard. The intuition is even simpler.

Attention is a soft-lookup in a table. You have a question (a query)
and a bunch of table rows (each with a key and a value). You compare
the query to every key. Rows whose key is more similar to the query
get more of their value in the answer. Rows whose key is dissimilar
contribute little.

Note: 'soft' means every row contributes at least a little, weighted
by similarity. A 'hard' lookup (like `list-ref`) picks exactly one
row. Attention is soft because gradient descent needs a smooth
function, not a discrete pick.

## The recipe

Given a query `q` (a vector), a list of keys `k1, k2, ..., kn` (also
vectors), and a list of values `v1, v2, ..., vn` (also vectors):

1. **Score** — compute `q · k1`, `q · k2`, ..., `q · kn`. These are
   the raw similarity scores. Larger score = more similar.
2. **Scale** — divide each score by `sqrt(d_k)` where `d_k` is the
   dimension of the key vectors. This keeps the softmax stable when
   the dimension is large.
3. **Softmax** — convert scores into positive weights that sum to 1.
4. **Weighted sum** — the output is `w1 * v1 + w2 * v2 + ... + wn * vn`.

That is scaled dot-product attention. Vaswani et al. 2017.

## Problem 1 — Softmax

Softmax turns a list of any numbers into a list of positive numbers
that sum to 1. It emphasizes the largest inputs. It is smooth (has a
gradient everywhere), which is why we can backprop through it.

```
softmax(x)[i] = exp(x[i]) / sum(exp(x[j]))
```

A subtle point: `exp` can overflow for large inputs. Standard
practice is to subtract the max before exponentiating. Same result,
no overflow.

```
(define (softmax xs)
  (define m (fold (lambda (a b) (if (> a b) a b)) (car xs) (cdr xs)))
  (define exps (map (lambda (x) (math/exp (- x m))) xs))
  (define s (reduce + 0 exps))
  (map (lambda (e) (/ e s)) exps))

(display (softmax (list 1 2 3)))
;; => (0.0900... 0.2447... 0.6652...)
;; sum = 1.0
```

The largest input (3) gets the largest weight (0.66). The smallest
(1) gets the smallest weight (0.09). All weights are positive, and
they sum to 1. That is what softmax buys you: a probability
distribution over the inputs.

## Problem 2 — Attention on tiny hand-picked vectors

Let's do one full attention step by hand. Three tokens. Each has a
query, a key, and a value. We take the query of token 0 and use it
to attend over the keys and values of all three.

```
;; Three tokens, each with query, key, value. All 2-dimensional.
(define q0 (list 1.0 0.0))
(define k0 (list 1.0 0.0))
(define k1 (list 0.9 0.1))
(define k2 (list 0.0 1.0))
(define v0 (list 10 20))
(define v1 (list 30 40))
(define v2 (list 50 60))

;; Step 1: scores. Query dot each key.
(define scores
  (list (vec/dot q0 k0) (vec/dot q0 k1) (vec/dot q0 k2)))
;; scores = (1.0, 0.9, 0.0)

;; Step 2: scale by sqrt(d_k). Here d_k = 2, so divide by sqrt(2).
(define scaled (map (lambda (s) (/ s (math/sqrt 2))) scores))
;; ~ (0.707, 0.636, 0.0)

;; Step 3: softmax.
(define (softmax xs)
  (define m (fold (lambda (a b) (if (> a b) a b)) (car xs) (cdr xs)))
  (define exps (map (lambda (x) (math/exp (- x m))) xs))
  (define s (reduce + 0 exps))
  (map (lambda (e) (/ e s)) exps))

(define weights (softmax scaled))
;; e.g. (0.421, 0.393, 0.186)

;; Step 4: weighted sum of values.
(define output
  (vec/add (vec/scale v0 (car weights))
    (vec/add (vec/scale v1 (cadr weights))
             (vec/scale v2 (caddr weights)))))

(display weights)
(display output)
;; weights: (0.421 0.393 0.186)
;; output: mostly a mix of v0 and v1 (their keys aligned with q0),
;;         plus a smaller mix of v2 (its key was orthogonal to q0).
```

That is scaled dot-product attention on one query. The output is
NOT a copy of any single value vector. It is a MIX, weighted by how
similar each key was to the query. That is what 'soft' means.

## Problem 3 — Attention as a function

Wrap it up. Given a query vector, a list of key vectors, and a list
of value vectors (all same length), return the attention output.

```
(define (softmax xs)
  (define m (fold (lambda (a b) (if (> a b) a b)) (car xs) (cdr xs)))
  (define exps (map (lambda (x) (math/exp (- x m))) xs))
  (define s (reduce + 0 exps))
  (map (lambda (e) (/ e s)) exps))

(define (attention q keys values)
  (define d-k (vec/dim (car keys)))
  (define scale (math/sqrt d-k))
  (define scores
    (map (lambda (k) (/ (vec/dot q k) scale)) keys))
  (define weights (softmax scores))
  ;; weighted sum: fold vec/add over the scaled values
  (fold vec/add
        (vec/scale (car values) 0)   ;; start with zero vector of same dim
        (map (lambda (w v) (vec/scale v w)) weights values)))

(define q (list 1 0))
(define keys (list (list 1 0)) (list 0 1))))
(define values (list (list 100 0)) (list 0 100))))

(display (attention q keys values))
;; q is aligned with keys[0], so output is close to values[0].
;; Something like a vector near (85, 15) or similar.
```

`attention` in one call. Reusable. The transformer will call this
once per query, once per position, once per attention head. Many
times over. But each individual call is just this.

## Problem 4 — Multi-query attention

In a real transformer, you don't attend from one query — you attend
from EVERY position at once. Each token's query attends over every
other token's key and value. That is a matrix of queries times a
matrix of keys.

```
;; queries: list of query vectors (one per position)
;; keys, values: same
(define (multi-attention queries keys values)
  (map (lambda (q) (attention q keys values)) queries))

(define qs (list (list 1 0))
                 (list 0 1))))
(define ks (list (list 1 0))
                 (list 0 1))))
(define vs (list (list 10 20))
                 (list 30 40))))

(display (multi-attention qs ks vs))
;; Two output vectors, one per query.
;; Query 0 attends mostly to k0, so its output is mostly v0 -> (10, 20).
;; Query 1 attends mostly to k1, so its output is mostly v1 -> (30, 40).
;; Actual numbers are close to but not exactly those (softmax spreads a little).
```

Same attention verb, called once per query. In real transformers this
is done with matrix multiplications for speed, but the semantics is
exactly the loop above.

## Problem 5 — Where do the queries, keys, values come from?

Not from thin air. Each is a linear projection of the token's
embedding.

```
;; For each position i:
;;   x[i] = embedding of token at position i
;;   q[i] = W_q * x[i]     (Q projection)
;;   k[i] = W_k * x[i]     (K projection)
;;   v[i] = W_v * x[i]     (V projection)
```

`W_q`, `W_k`, `W_v` are learned matrices. They are what the model
trains. Given the token embeddings and the three matrices, you
produce the queries, keys, and values, then run scaled dot-product
attention.

```
(define (matvec rows v)
  (map (lambda (r) (vec/dot r v)) rows))

;; Assume x is a token embedding (vector).
;; W-q, W-k, W-v are lists of vectors (rows) — the projection matrices.
(define (project-qkv W-q W-k W-v x)
  (list
    (vec/make (matvec W-q x))
    (vec/make (matvec W-k x))
    (vec/make (matvec W-v x))))

;; Given a list of embeddings, produce lists of queries, keys, values.
(define (all-qkv W-q W-k W-v embeddings)
  (define triples (map (lambda (x) (project-qkv W-q W-k W-v x))
                       embeddings))
  (list (map car triples)
        (map cadr triples)
        (map caddr triples)))
```

Three learned matrices per attention head. Times many heads. Times
many layers. That is where a lot of the parameters in a transformer
come from.

## Problem 6 — Multi-head attention (concept)

One attention head learns one 'kind' of relationship — maybe
subject-to-verb, or noun-to-adjective. Real transformers have many
heads working in parallel, each with its own Q/K/V matrices. Their
outputs are concatenated and re-projected.

```
;; For H heads, run attention H times, each with its own W_q, W_k, W_v.
;; Concatenate the H output vectors per position.
;; Project through a final W_o matrix back to the model dimension.
```

In chapter 16 our tiny LLM has ONE head to keep things readable. Real
GPT models have anywhere from 12 to 128 heads per layer. Same
attention verb, just called more times.

## Capstone — A one-head attention block that runs

Full attention block. Take a list of token embeddings. Project to
queries, keys, values. Run attention. Return a list of output vectors.

```
(define (softmax xs)
  (define m (fold (lambda (a b) (if (> a b) a b)) (car xs) (cdr xs)))
  (define exps (map (lambda (x) (math/exp (- x m))) xs))
  (define s (reduce + 0 exps))
  (map (lambda (e) (/ e s)) exps))

(define (matvec rows v) (map (lambda (r) (vec/dot r v)) rows))

(define (attention q keys values)
  (define d-k (vec/dim (car keys)))
  (define scale (math/sqrt d-k))
  (define scores (map (lambda (k) (/ (vec/dot q k) scale)) keys))
  (define weights (softmax scores))
  (fold vec/add
        (vec/scale (car values) 0)
        (map (lambda (w v) (vec/scale v w)) weights values)))

(define (attention-block W-q W-k W-v embeddings)
  (define qs (map (lambda (x) (vec/make (matvec W-q x))) embeddings))
  (define ks (map (lambda (x) (vec/make (matvec W-k x))) embeddings))
  (define vs (map (lambda (x) (vec/make (matvec W-v x))) embeddings))
  (map (lambda (q) (attention q ks vs)) qs))

;; Try it: 3 tokens, 2-dim embeddings, W_q W_k W_v are identity-like
(define embs (list (list 1 0))
                   (list 0 1))
                   (list 1 1))))
(define I2 (list (list 1 0)) (list 0 1))))

(display (attention-block I2 I2 I2 embs))
;; Three output vectors, each a soft mix of the three inputs weighted
;; by how similar their key (input) is to the query (input).
```

You just built a scaled dot-product attention block. Feed it token
embeddings, and it produces a new sequence where each position is a
soft mixture of all positions weighted by learned similarity. That is
attention. That is the transformer's magic ingredient. There is no
more. It's just a soft lookup.

## Why this matters

Attention is what gave language models their scaling behavior.
Recurrent networks (RNNs) processed tokens one at a time — you had
to wait for token 999 before you could look at token 1000. Attention
compares every token to every other token in ONE step (per layer).
That parallelism is why transformers train fast on GPUs. That
parallelism is what made GPT-3 possible.

## What's next

Chapter 13 wraps attention into a transformer block. Attention plus a
feed-forward network plus skip connections plus layer normalization.
That block, stacked N times, is a transformer. Then in chapter 14 we
handle position (attention has no notion of order) and masking (the
model shouldn't peek at the future during training).
")

"# Chapter 13 — A transformer block

A transformer BLOCK is not the whole transformer. It is one unit,
one 'floor' of the tower. A full transformer stacks N of these blocks
on top of each other (12 for a small model, 96 for GPT-3). Each block
has the same structure. The stack does more or less computation
depending on how tall it is.

A block has four ingredients wired together:

1. **Attention** (from chapter 12).
2. **A feed-forward network** (from chapter 8 — two-layer MLP).
3. **Residual connections** (add the input back to the output — skip
   connections).
4. **Layer normalization** (rescale so activations stay in a healthy
   range).

Every real transformer has all four. Skip any and training breaks
or gets much slower.

## The block structure

Here is the shape, in pseudocode:

```
input: x        (a sequence of embeddings, shape (seq_len, embed_dim))

output_1 = LayerNorm(x + Attention(x))
output_2 = LayerNorm(output_1 + FeedForward(output_1))
return output_2
```

The `x + Attention(x)` and `output_1 + FeedForward(output_1)` are
the residual connections. You compute a transformation, then add the
INPUT back in. That way if the transformation learned to do
'nothing', the block is still the identity — no harm done.

## Problem 1 — Layer normalization

Layer norm takes a vector and shifts + scales it so the mean is 0 and
the variance is 1, then applies a learned per-dimension gain and
bias.

```
;; Given a vector, subtract mean, divide by stddev, then apply gamma and beta.
(define (layernorm v gamma beta)
  (define d (vec/dim v))
  (define components (map (lambda (i) (vec/ref v i)) (iota d)))
  (define mean (/ (reduce + 0 components) d))
  (define centered (map (lambda (x) (- x mean)) components))
  (define variance (/ (reduce + 0 (map (lambda (c) (* c c)) centered)) d))
  (define stddev (math/sqrt (+ variance 0.00001)))   ;; 0.00001 for numerical safety
  (define normalized (map (lambda (c) (/ c stddev)) centered))
  (map (lambda (i)
         (+ (* (list-ref normalized i) (list-ref gamma i))
            (list-ref beta i)))
       (iota d)))

(define v (list 1 2 3 4 5))
(define gamma (list 1 1 1 1 1))   ;; no scaling
(define beta (list 0 0 0 0 0))    ;; no shift

(display (layernorm v gamma beta))
;; A vector with mean 0 and stddev 1.
;; components: something like (-1.41 -0.71 0 0.71 1.41)
```

Layer norm keeps activations from exploding or vanishing as the
signal passes through many layers. It is applied to each token's
embedding independently — not across the whole sequence.

`gamma` and `beta` are LEARNED. Every layernorm has its own gamma
and beta vectors, trained by gradient descent like everything else.
Usually initialized to gamma=1, beta=0.

## Problem 2 — Feed-forward network

The FF part of a transformer block is exactly a 2-layer MLP with
ReLU (or GELU in some models) between the two linear layers. The
hidden dimension is usually 4x the embed dimension.

```
;; Feed-forward: input dim d, hidden dim 4d, output dim d
;; f(x) = W2 * relu(W1 * x + b1) + b2

(define (matvec rows v) (map (lambda (r) (vec/dot r v)) rows))
(define (relu-vec v)
  (vec/make (map (lambda (i)
                   (let ((x (vec/ref v i)))
                     (if (> x 0) x 0)))
                 (iota (vec/dim v)))))

(define (feed-forward W1 b1 W2 b2 x)
  (define hidden (relu-vec (vec/make (map + (matvec W1 x) b1))))
  (vec/make (map + (matvec W2 hidden) b2)))

;; Example: d=2, hidden=8
(define embed-dim 2)
(define hidden-dim 8)

(define (rand-vec n) (vec/make (map (lambda (_) (- (* (random) 0.3) 0.15)) (iota n))))
(define W1 (map (lambda (_) (rand-vec embed-dim)) (iota hidden-dim)))
(define b1 (map (lambda (_) 0.0) (iota hidden-dim)))
(define W2 (map (lambda (_) (rand-vec hidden-dim)) (iota embed-dim)))
(define b2 (map (lambda (_) 0.0) (iota embed-dim)))

(define x (list 1.0 -0.5))
(display (feed-forward W1 b1 W2 b2 x))
;; => a 2-vector (some transformed version of x)
```

FF is applied INDEPENDENTLY per token position. Each token's embedding
goes through the same feed-forward network. No mixing between
positions in the FF layer — that mixing already happened in attention.

## Problem 3 — Residual connections

Given input `x` and a transformation `T`, the residual output is
`x + T(x)`. Very simple.

```
(define (residual x transform)
  (vec/add x (transform x)))
```

Why does this matter? Two reasons.

**Gradient flow.** In a very deep network, gradients have to
backpropagate through many layers. Without residuals, the gradient
gets multiplied by many small numbers and vanishes. With residuals,
the gradient can flow around the transformation — the '+ x' path
preserves the original signal.

**Identity default.** With residuals, if a layer learns to do
nothing (weights near zero), the block is still the identity. Adding
more layers can't hurt — only help. Without residuals, an untrained
layer can DAMAGE the signal.

He et al. 2015 (ResNets) showed residuals were the key to training
very deep networks. Vaswani et al. 2017 kept them in the transformer
and they've been there ever since.

## Problem 4 — Put it together — a full block

Now compose. Attention + residual + layernorm. FF + residual +
layernorm. That is one transformer block.

```
;; Assume these are already defined:
;;   (attention-block W-q W-k W-v embeddings)
;;   (feed-forward W1 b1 W2 b2 x)
;;   (layernorm v gamma beta)

(define (transformer-block
          W-q W-k W-v          ;; attention projections
          W1-ff b1-ff W2-ff b2-ff  ;; feed-forward
          gamma1 beta1         ;; layernorm after attention
          gamma2 beta2         ;; layernorm after feed-forward
          embeddings)
  ;; 1. Attention with residual and layernorm
  (define attn-out (attention-block W-q W-k W-v embeddings))
  (define after-attn
    (map (lambda (x a) (layernorm (vec/add x a) gamma1 beta1))
         embeddings attn-out))
  ;; 2. Feed-forward with residual and layernorm
  (define ff-out
    (map (lambda (x) (feed-forward W1-ff b1-ff W2-ff b2-ff x)) after-attn))
  (define after-ff
    (map (lambda (x f) (layernorm (vec/add x f) gamma2 beta2))
         after-attn ff-out))
  after-ff)
```

Read the block. Two sub-blocks. Each is: apply transformation, add
the input back, layer-normalize. First sub-block does attention.
Second sub-block does feed-forward. Both have residuals. Both are
layer-normed.

## Problem 5 — Pre-norm vs post-norm

Above I did LayerNorm AFTER adding the residual (post-norm). Modern
transformers (GPT-2 onward) do LayerNorm BEFORE the transformation
(pre-norm):

```
;; Pre-norm variant:
;;   attn_out = x + Attention(LayerNorm(x))
;;   final   = attn_out + FeedForward(LayerNorm(attn_out))
```

Pre-norm trains more stably. Post-norm (as in the original 2017
paper) requires more careful learning-rate schedules. Both work; both
are still used. Our chapter 16 tiny LLM will use pre-norm because it
is easier to get right.

## Problem 6 — Parameter count of a block

For an embed dimension d, hidden dimension 4d, one attention head:

- Attention projections: 3 matrices of shape (d, d) plus 3 bias
  vectors = 3d^2 + 3d parameters.
- Feed-forward: (d, 4d) matrix + 4d bias + (4d, d) matrix + d bias
  = 8d^2 + 5d parameters.
- Two layernorms: 2 * 2d = 4d parameters.

Total: 11d^2 + 12d.

For d=768 (BERT-base): 11 * 589824 + 12 * 768 ≈ 6.5 million per
block. Twelve blocks: ~78 million. Plus the embedding table
(~24 million) plus the output projection (~24 million). BERT-base
was ~110 million total. Numbers check out.

For d=12288 (GPT-3): 11 * 150 million + 12 * 12288 ≈ 1.66 BILLION per
block. Ninety-six blocks: ~159 billion. Plus embeddings. GPT-3 was
175 billion. Same math, just bigger tensors.

## Capstone — Run a whole block on a small sequence

Assemble the full block and run it. We won't train — that is
chapter 16. But we can verify the shapes work end to end.

```
;; Small dimensions for a runnable demo.
(define d 4)     ;; embed dim
(define ff-hidden 8)
(define seq-len 3)

(define (rand-vec n) (vec/make (map (lambda (_) (- (* (random) 0.2) 0.1)) (iota n))))

;; Attention projections
(define W-q (map (lambda (_) (rand-vec d)) (iota d)))
(define W-k (map (lambda (_) (rand-vec d)) (iota d)))
(define W-v (map (lambda (_) (rand-vec d)) (iota d)))

;; Feed-forward
(define W1-ff (map (lambda (_) (rand-vec d)) (iota ff-hidden)))
(define b1-ff (map (lambda (_) 0.0) (iota ff-hidden)))
(define W2-ff (map (lambda (_) (rand-vec ff-hidden)) (iota d)))
(define b2-ff (map (lambda (_) 0.0) (iota d)))

;; Layernorms — gamma=1, beta=0
(define gamma1 (map (lambda (_) 1.0) (iota d)))
(define beta1  (map (lambda (_) 0.0) (iota d)))
(define gamma2 (map (lambda (_) 1.0) (iota d)))
(define beta2  (map (lambda (_) 0.0) (iota d)))

;; Sequence: three token embeddings
(define embeddings
  (list (rand-vec d) (rand-vec d) (rand-vec d)))

(define out
  (transformer-block W-q W-k W-v
                     W1-ff b1-ff W2-ff b2-ff
                     gamma1 beta1
                     gamma2 beta2
                     embeddings))

(display (length out))
;; => 3   (one output vector per input token)
(display (vec/dim (car out)))
;; => 4   (each output vector has the same dim as the input)
```

The block returned three vectors of dimension 4 from three input
vectors of dimension 4. The shape is preserved — that is the point
of the residuals. You can stack these blocks any number of times and
the shapes still line up.

## Why this matters

The transformer block is the modular unit that made deep language
models tractable. Stack 12 of them and you have BERT. Stack 96 of
them and you have GPT-3. Every block does the same thing: mix
information across positions (attention), transform per-position
(feed-forward), and add layer norm and residuals to keep gradients
flowing. You have built the atomic unit. In chapter 16 we stack a
couple and train.

## What's next

Chapter 14 solves two problems attention has:

1. **No sense of order.** Attention treats a sequence like a set —
   swap positions and the output is the same. That is fine for a bag
   of words but terrible for language, where 'dog bites man' and
   'man bites dog' mean different things. Positional encoding fixes
   this.

2. **Peeking at the future.** In a causal (next-token-prediction)
   language model, position `i` must not see positions `> i`. Causal
   masking enforces this during training. Otherwise the model just
   copies the answer and doesn't learn.
")

"# Chapter 14 — Positional encoding and causal masking

Attention has two problems we glossed over. This chapter fixes them.

**Problem 1.** Attention treats a sequence like a set. If you shuffle
the token embeddings before feeding them to attention, the outputs
just shuffle by the same permutation. That means the model has no
idea what order the tokens came in. 'Dog bites man' and 'man bites
dog' would be indistinguishable — same tokens, different meaning.

**Problem 2.** During training we want to teach the model to predict
the next token given the previous ones. If we feed the whole
sequence into attention, position i can 'see' positions i+1, i+2,
etc. — the answer is right there. The model would learn nothing.

Positional encoding solves problem 1. Causal masking solves problem 2.

## Positional encoding — giving the model a sense of order

The idea: add a position-dependent vector to each token embedding
BEFORE it goes into the attention layers. Position 0 gets one vector.
Position 1 gets a different one. The model can then look at the sum
and figure out both 'what token is this' and 'where in the sequence
is it.'

The original transformer used SINUSOIDAL positional encoding. Each
dimension of the position vector is a sine or cosine of position at
a different frequency:

```
PE(pos, 2i)   = sin(pos / 10000^(2i/d))
PE(pos, 2i+1) = cos(pos / 10000^(2i/d))
```

Where pos is the position (0, 1, 2, ...) and i is the dimension
index. Different dimensions oscillate at different rates. Low
dimensions oscillate slowly (they encode which 'chapter' of the
sequence). High dimensions oscillate fast (they encode fine position).

## Problem 1 — Sinusoidal positional encoding

```
(define (sinusoidal-pos pos d)
  ;; Return a d-dim vector encoding position pos.
  (vec/make
    (map (lambda (i)
           (let ((exponent (/ (* 2 (quotient i 2)) d)))
             (let ((angle (/ pos (math/pow 10000 exponent))))
               (if (even? i) (math/sin angle) (math/cos angle)))))
         (iota d))))

(display (sinusoidal-pos 0 4))
;; => (sin(0/1) cos(0/1) sin(0/100) cos(0/100))
;; => (0 1 0 1)

(display (sinusoidal-pos 1 4))
;; => (sin(1) cos(1) sin(0.01) cos(0.01))
;; => (~0.841 ~0.540 ~0.01 ~1.0)

(display (sinusoidal-pos 10 4))
;; => (sin(10) cos(10) sin(0.1) cos(0.1))
;; => (~-0.544 ~-0.839 ~0.0998 ~0.995)
```

Different positions produce different vectors. Adjacent positions are
similar in the slow dimensions, different in the fast dimensions. The
model can learn to read these.

## Problem 2 — Add positional encoding to embeddings

Very simple. Element-wise addition.

```
(define (add-positions embeddings)
  (define d (vec/dim (car embeddings)))
  (define seq-len (length embeddings))
  (map (lambda (i emb)
         (vec/add emb (sinusoidal-pos i d)))
       (iota seq-len)
       embeddings))

;; If your token embeddings are tok-embs, feed
;; (add-positions tok-embs) to the transformer instead.
```

That is the entire positional-encoding step. Token embeddings +
position encoding = position-aware embeddings. The transformer layers
never need to know about position specifically — the information is
baked into the vectors.

## Learned vs sinusoidal

Modern transformers (BERT, GPT) often use LEARNED positional
embeddings — just an embedding table indexed by position, updated by
gradient descent like everything else. Same shape as token
embeddings, learned in the same way. Slightly better empirical
performance; more parameters. Both work.

A newer alternative — RoPE (rotary positional encoding) used by
Llama and others — encodes position via rotations applied inside the
attention. It generalizes better to sequences longer than the model
was trained on. For our tiny LLM, sinusoidal or a small learned
table are fine.

## Causal masking — no peeking at the future

Now the training-time problem. When we train a language model, the
task is 'given tokens 0..i, predict token i+1.' If attention at
position i can see positions i+1, i+2, etc., the model can just copy
the answer.

The fix is to MASK OUT future positions in the attention. Specifically,
before the softmax, we set the scores for future positions to
negative infinity. After softmax, those positions have weight zero.
The model literally cannot see them.

```
;; A causal mask matrix M for sequence length n:
;;   M[i][j] = 0 if j <= i
;;   M[i][j] = -infinity if j > i
;; Add M to the scores BEFORE softmax.

(define (causal-mask-value i j)
  (if (<= j i) 0 -10000000000.0))    ;; -10000000000.0 acts as -infinity for float practice

(define (masked-attention q keys values i)
  (define d-k (vec/dim (car keys)))
  (define scale (math/sqrt d-k))
  (define raw-scores (map (lambda (k) (/ (vec/dot q k) scale)) keys))
  (define masked-scores
    (map (lambda (score j) (+ score (causal-mask-value i j)))
         raw-scores
         (iota (length raw-scores))))
  (define weights (softmax masked-scores))
  (fold vec/add
        (vec/scale (car values) 0)
        (map (lambda (w v) (vec/scale v w)) weights values)))
```

At position i, all future positions get score -10000000000.0 added. `exp(-10000000000.0)`
is essentially zero. After softmax, all future positions have weight
zero. Only positions 0..i contribute to the output.

## Problem 3 — Verify masking works

Verify by counting nonzero attention weights.

```
(define (softmax xs)
  (define m (fold (lambda (a b) (if (> a b) a b)) (car xs) (cdr xs)))
  (define exps (map (lambda (x) (math/exp (- x m))) xs))
  (define s (reduce + 0 exps))
  (map (lambda (e) (/ e s)) exps))

(define q (list 1 0))
(define keys (list (list 1 0))
                   (list 0 1))
                   (list 1 1))
                   (list 0 0))))

;; From position 1: can see positions 0 and 1, not 2 or 3.
(define d-k 2)
(define raw-scores (map (lambda (k) (/ (vec/dot q k) (math/sqrt d-k))) keys))
(define masked (map (lambda (s j) (if (<= j 1) s -10000000000.0))
                    raw-scores (iota 4)))
(display (softmax masked))
;; => (some positive, some positive, ~0, ~0)
;; Positions 2 and 3 got weight ~0 as required.
```

Read the output. The first two weights are nonzero (positions 0 and 1
are allowed). The last two are essentially zero (positions 2 and 3
are masked). Position 1's attention literally cannot see the future.

## Problem 4 — Training with causal masking

During training we feed a whole sequence into the model. The model
produces a sequence of predictions — position i's prediction of what
token comes next. We compare each prediction to the actual next
token, sum the losses, backpropagate.

The masking ensures that position i's prediction only used positions
0..i to produce it. So the loss at position i measures 'given the
first i+1 tokens, how well did the model predict token i+2.' Summed
over all positions, this trains the model on many next-token
predictions in parallel — one per position in the sequence. Very
efficient use of the data.

```
;; Pseudo-training-step:
;;   input_tokens = [t0, t1, t2, ..., tn]
;;   embeddings = [embed(t0), ...] + positional_encoding
;;   hidden = transformer_blocks(embeddings, with causal mask)
;;   logits = project hidden to vocab dimension
;;   for each position i:
;;     loss_i = cross-entropy(logits[i], t[i+1])
;;   total_loss = sum of loss_i
;;   backprop and update
```

Every token except the last one contributes to training. That is
what a next-token-prediction language model learns from.

## Problem 5 — Bidirectional models don't mask

BERT and its family use BIDIRECTIONAL attention — no causal mask.
Every position can see every other position. They train on a
different task: mask out some tokens and predict them from the
surrounding context (masked language modeling). Both directions
matter for that task.

GPT and its family use CAUSAL attention. Only left-to-right. That
makes them natural next-token predictors and text generators.

Our tiny LLM in chapter 16 is causal — we want to generate text.

## Capstone — Position-aware causally-masked attention

Combine everything from this chapter into one working attention
call.

```
(define (softmax xs)
  (define m (fold (lambda (a b) (if (> a b) a b)) (car xs) (cdr xs)))
  (define exps (map (lambda (x) (math/exp (- x m))) xs))
  (define s (reduce + 0 exps))
  (map (lambda (e) (/ e s)) exps))

(define (sinusoidal-pos pos d)
  (vec/make
    (map (lambda (i)
           (let ((exponent (/ (* 2 (quotient i 2)) d)))
             (let ((angle (/ pos (math/pow 10000 exponent))))
               (if (even? i) (math/sin angle) (math/cos angle)))))
         (iota d))))

(define (add-positions embeddings)
  (define d (vec/dim (car embeddings)))
  (define seq-len (length embeddings))
  (map (lambda (i emb) (vec/add emb (sinusoidal-pos i d)))
       (iota seq-len) embeddings))

(define (causal-masked-attention embeddings W-q W-k W-v)
  (define positioned (add-positions embeddings))
  (define d (vec/dim (car positioned)))
  (define scale (math/sqrt d))
  (define (matvec rows v) (map (lambda (r) (vec/dot r v)) rows))
  (define qs (map (lambda (x) (vec/make (matvec W-q x))) positioned))
  (define ks (map (lambda (x) (vec/make (matvec W-k x))) positioned))
  (define vs (map (lambda (x) (vec/make (matvec W-v x))) positioned))
  ;; For each position i, compute masked attention
  (map (lambda (i q)
         (let* ((raw (map (lambda (k) (/ (vec/dot q k) scale)) ks))
                (masked (map (lambda (s j) (if (<= j i) s -10000000000.0))
                             raw (iota (length ks))))
                (weights (softmax masked)))
           (fold vec/add
                 (vec/scale (car vs) 0)
                 (map (lambda (w v) (vec/scale v w)) weights vs))))
       (iota (length qs)) qs))

;; Try it on a random small sequence
(define d 4)
(define I (list (list 1 0 0 0))
                (list 0 1 0 0))
                (list 0 0 1 0))
                (list 0 0 0 1))))
(define embs (list (list 0.5 0.1 0.2 0.3))
                   (list 0.3 0.6 0.1 0.0))
                   (list 0.1 0.2 0.7 0.0))))

(display (causal-masked-attention embs I I I))
;; Three output vectors of dim 4.
;; Position 0: only saw position 0 (its output is close to its own value projection)
;; Position 1: saw positions 0 and 1
;; Position 2: saw positions 0, 1, 2
```

Position matters. Future is hidden. This is the exact attention
mechanism used in every GPT-family model. In chapter 16 we wire it
into a small transformer and train it on a paragraph of text.

## Why this matters

Position and masking are what turn a bag-of-vectors attention
mechanism into a proper sequence model. Without position, the model
can't distinguish word orders. Without causal masking, the training
is trivial (the model can copy the answer). Both are one-line fixes
that change the model qualitatively.

## What's next

Chapter 15 covers two more prerequisites for chapter 16's tiny LLM:
stacking multiple transformer blocks (deep networks) and tokenizing
sensibly (BPE — byte-pair encoding). Then chapter 16 assembles the
whole thing.
")

"# Chapter 15 — Stacking blocks and tokenization

Two final pieces before chapter 16 assembles the tiny LLM.

**Stacking.** A single transformer block is one 'floor' of the tower.
Real models stack many blocks — 12 for BERT-base, 96 for GPT-3. This
chapter shows how to stack them and why deeper is usually better up
to a point.

**Tokenization.** Whitespace tokenization (chapter 11) is fine for
demonstration but fails at scale — rare words become 'unknown,'
compound words don't split, punctuation is a mess. Real language
models use subword tokenization. The most common algorithm is Byte
Pair Encoding (BPE), which we build here in a small form.

## Stacking blocks

Stacking is just function composition. Each block takes a sequence
of vectors and returns a sequence of vectors of the same shape.
Compose them.

```
(define (stacked-transformer blocks embeddings)
  (fold (lambda (block acc) (block acc))
        embeddings
        blocks))
```

`blocks` is a list of block functions. Each is a closure over its
own weights. We fold — apply them one at a time in sequence.

## Problem 1 — Two stacked blocks

Not runnable end-to-end here because the block functions need many
weight matrices, but the shape.

```
;; Assume make-block builds a full transformer block (chapter 13) as
;; a closure. Then stacking is trivial.

(define block1 (make-block ...weights1...))
(define block2 (make-block ...weights2...))
(define block3 (make-block ...weights3...))

(define transformer
  (lambda (embeddings)
    (block3 (block2 (block1 embeddings)))))

;; Or as a fold:
(define transformer
  (lambda (embeddings)
    (fold (lambda (b acc) (b acc))
          embeddings
          (list block1 block2 block3))))
```

Read the shape. The output of block1 becomes the input to block2.
Same for block2 → block3. Since blocks preserve the (seq_len,
embed_dim) shape, they can be stacked arbitrarily.

## Why deeper helps

Each block can mix information across positions ONCE (in its
attention layer) and transform per-position ONCE (in its feed-forward
layer). With more blocks, information can flow further and be
transformed more times.

Empirically: a 1-block transformer is decent at short local patterns.
A 12-block transformer is much better at longer-range dependencies. A
96-block transformer can hold context over thousands of tokens. This
is one reason GPT-3 was so much more capable than smaller models.

More depth = more compute per token, more parameters to train, more
data required. Depth is not free. The sweet spot depends on data
budget and hardware.

## Tokenization — beyond whitespace

Whitespace tokenization has three problems:

1. **Vocabulary explosion.** Every distinct word is a distinct token.
   In English there are hundreds of thousands of distinct words if you
   count all forms and typos.

2. **Unknown words.** Any word not seen during training becomes an
   [UNK] token. Rare technical terms, new slang, foreign names — all
   [UNK].

3. **Morphology loss.** 'run,' 'runs,' 'running' are three separate
   tokens with no shared representation. The model has to learn each
   independently.

Subword tokenization fixes all three. Common words stay whole. Rare
words split into pieces. New words are ALWAYS representable as a
sequence of subword pieces.

## Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) — the algorithm

Sennrich et al. 2015 adapted BPE (originally a compression algorithm)
for text tokenization. The idea:

1. Start with a vocabulary of individual characters.
2. Count all pairs of adjacent tokens in the training corpus.
3. Find the most common pair. Merge it into a new token.
4. Repeat until vocabulary reaches desired size.

At tokenization time you apply the merges in the same order.

## Problem 2 — BPE training on a tiny corpus

Build a mini-BPE trainer. Not efficient — pedagogical.

```
(define (split-word s)
  ;; 'cat' -> ('c' 'a' 't' '</w>')
  (append
    (map (lambda (i) (string (string-ref s i)))
         (iota (string-length s)))
    (list \"</w>\")))

(define corpus
  (list \"cat\" \"cats\" \"car\" \"cars\" \"bar\" \"bat\"))

(define pieces
  (map split-word corpus))
;; -> ((c a t </w>) (c a t s </w>) (c a r </w>) ...)

(define (pairs-in tokens)
  ;; return list of adjacent pairs
  (if (or (null? tokens) (null? (cdr tokens)))
      '()
      (cons (list (car tokens) (cadr tokens))
            (pairs-in (cdr tokens)))))

(define (count-pairs word-lists)
  (define all-pairs (apply append (map pairs-in word-lists)))
  ;; return an alist pair -> count
  (fold (lambda (p acc)
          (let ((existing (assoc p acc)))
            (if existing
                (map (lambda (e) (if (equal? (car e) p)
                                     (cons p (+ (cdr e) 1))
                                     e)) acc)
                (cons (cons p 1) acc))))
        '()
        all-pairs))

(define (max-pair counts)
  (car (fold (lambda (e best) (if (> (cdr e) (cdr best)) e best))
             (car counts) (cdr counts))))

(display (max-pair (count-pairs pieces)))
;; => the most common pair, e.g. (\"c\" \"a\") -- because c and a appear
;; adjacent in cat, cats, car, cars.
```

Given the most common pair, we merge it. Every occurrence of that
pair in the corpus becomes a single token. Then we recount and
repeat.

## Problem 3 — Apply a merge

```
(define (apply-merge pair word)
  ;; Replace every occurrence of the pair with the merged token
  (define merged (string-append (car pair) (cadr pair)))
  (let loop ((rem word) (out '()))
    (cond ((null? rem) (reverse out))
          ((and (pair? rem) (pair? (cdr rem))
                (equal? (car rem) (car pair))
                (equal? (cadr rem) (cadr pair)))
           (loop (cddr rem) (cons merged out)))
          (else (loop (cdr rem) (cons (car rem) out))))))

(display (apply-merge (list \"c\" \"a\")
                      (list \"c\" \"a\" \"t\" \"</w>\")))
;; => (\"ca\" \"t\" \"</w>\")
```

After the merge, 'ca' is one token. Now we can find the next most
common pair — probably (ca t) — and merge again to get 'cat.' After
enough merges, common English words are single tokens; rare words
split into subword pieces.

## Problem 4 — BPE training loop

Put it together. Train BPE to build a vocabulary of size N.

```
(define (train-bpe corpus target-vocab-size)
  ;; corpus: list of words (strings)
  ;; return: list of merges applied in order
  (let loop ((pieces (map split-word corpus))
             (merges '())
             (n 0))
    (if (>= n target-vocab-size)
        (reverse merges)
        (let* ((counts (count-pairs pieces))
               (best (if (null? counts) #f (max-pair counts))))
          (if (or (not best) (null? counts))
              (reverse merges)
              (loop (map (lambda (word) (apply-merge best word)) pieces)
                    (cons best merges)
                    (+ n 1)))))))

(display (train-bpe (list \"cat\" \"cats\" \"car\" \"cars\") 5))
;; => a list of ~5 merges, ordered by count
;; e.g. ((\"c\" \"a\") (\"ca\" \"t\") (\"ca\" \"r\") ...)
```

The merges are stored in ORDER. At tokenization time we apply them
in the same order. That way 'ca' is always merged before 'cat,'
which is important for consistency.

## Problem 5 — Tokenize with a trained BPE

Given a word and a list of merges, apply the merges in order.

```
(define (tokenize-bpe merges word)
  (let loop ((tokens (split-word word)) (rest merges))
    (if (null? rest)
        tokens
        (loop (apply-merge (car rest) tokens) (cdr rest)))))
```

Feed a new word (never seen in training), and BPE produces a
tokenization — always representable because character-level tokens
are in the base vocabulary.

## For our tiny LLM

BPE is overkill for chapter 16. Our tiny LLM will use a fixed
whitespace vocabulary on a very small corpus, because the goal is to
show the mechanics of the model, not to fight the tokenizer. In real
GPTs, BPE (or its close relatives WordPiece and SentencePiece) is
essential.

## Why this matters

Stacking is the mechanism by which transformers get 'deep.' More
blocks = more transformation capacity = better model up to some
limit set by data and compute. Tokenization is how symbols enter and
exit the model — without a decent tokenizer, everything downstream
is corrupted. Both are foundational, both usually taken for granted,
both worth doing once by hand to see.

We store the whole model as a list. That way we can pass it through

;; b2 : D
