## Part 5 — helper ops (reprised from earlier chapters)

The operations we'll compose. Nothing new here — everything came
from an earlier chapter. Copied for convenience.

```
(define (matvec rows v)
  ;; matrix (list of row-vectors) times vector -> vector
  (map (lambda (r) (vec/dot r v)) rows))

(define (vec-add a b)
  ;; add two vectors of same length. Motoi's vec/add works on lists.
  (vec/add a b))

(define (vec-sub a b) (vec/sub a b))
(define (vec-scale v k) (vec/scale v k))

(define (vec-hadamard a b)
  ;; element-wise product using iota + list-ref (no multi-list map).
  (map (lambda (i) (* (list-ref a i) (list-ref b i)))
       (iota (length a))))

(define (softmax xs)
  (define m (fold (lambda (a b) (if (> a b) a b)) (car xs) (cdr xs)))
  (define exps (map (lambda (x) (math/exp (- x m))) xs))
  (define s (reduce + 0 exps))
  (map (lambda (e) (/ e s)) exps))

(define (transpose rows)
  ;; list-of-row-vectors -> list-of-column-vectors
  (define n (length (car rows)))
  (map (lambda (i)
         (map (lambda (row) (list-ref row i)) rows))
       (iota n)))

(define (outer-product a b)
  ;; a: length m, b: length n -> m x n matrix
  (map (lambda (ai)
         (map (lambda (bj) (* ai bj)) b))
       a))

(define (mat-add A B)
  ;; add two matrices (lists of row-vectors) elementwise
  (map (lambda (i) (vec-add (list-ref A i) (list-ref B i)))
       (iota (length A))))

(define (mat-scale A k)
  (map (lambda (row) (vec-scale row k)) A))
```

That's the operator toolkit. Every one of these was introduced in an
earlier chapter (matvec in ch 3, softmax in ch 12, transpose and
outer-product in ch 9). We're just gathering them so the training loop
below can call them without hunting.

## Part 6 — forward pass, saving activations

Backpropagation needs the intermediate values from the forward pass.
That's the classic space-time trade — save a little memory during
forward so you can compute gradients in one backward sweep. Chapter 9
introduced this idea; here we scale it to a whole transformer.

Design decision: we'll capture the forward pass as a list of named
records-in-list-form so backprop can read them without hunting.

```
;; Layernorm that ALSO returns the intermediates backprop needs.
;;   input: v (D-vector), gamma, beta
;;   output: (list normalized-v mean invstd centered)
(define (layernorm-fwd v gamma beta)
  (define d (length v))
  (define mean (/ (reduce + 0 v) d))
  (define centered (map (lambda (x) (- x mean)) v))
  (define var (/ (reduce + 0 (map (lambda (c) (* c c)) centered)) d))
  (define invstd (/ 1.0 (math/sqrt (+ var EPS-LN))))
  (define normed (map (lambda (c) (* c invstd)) centered))
  (define scaled
    (map (lambda (i)
           (+ (* (list-ref normed i) (list-ref gamma i))
              (list-ref beta i)))
         (iota d)))
  (list scaled mean invstd centered normed))

;; Attention forward for ONE query position i over all positions.
;;   Given qs, ks, vs (all lists of D-vectors), scale = sqrt(d_k)
;;   returns: (list output attn-weights)
(define (attn-position-fwd qs ks vs i scale)
  (define q (list-ref qs i))
  (define raw (map (lambda (k) (/ (vec/dot q k) scale)) ks))
  (define weights (softmax raw))
  (define output
    (fold vec-add
          (vec-scale (car vs) 0)
          (map (lambda (idx)
                 (vec-scale (list-ref vs idx) (list-ref weights idx)))
               (iota (length vs)))))
  (list output weights))

;; Whole forward pass for a sequence of token ids. Returns
;;   (list logits-per-position CACHE)
;; where CACHE is a plist of all the intermediate tensors we need.
(define (forward model input-ids)
  (define embed (m-embed model))
  (define Wq (m-Wq model)) (define Wk (m-Wk model)) (define Wv (m-Wv model))
  (define W1 (m-W1 model)) (define b1 (m-b1 model))
  (define W2 (m-W2 model)) (define b2 (m-b2 model))
  (define g1 (m-g1 model)) (define be1 (m-be1 model))
  (define g2 (m-g2 model)) (define be2 (m-be2 model))
  (define Wout (m-Wout model))
  (define d (length (car embed)))
  (define scale (math/sqrt d))
  (define n (length input-ids))

  ;; Embed tokens (skipping positional encoding here for pedagogical clarity —
  ;; the training loop still converges, and position encoding only adds a
  ;; constant offset that doesn't participate in the backward for parameters).
  (define xs (map (lambda (id) (list-ref embed id)) input-ids))

  ;; LN1 (pre-attention pre-norm)
  (define ln1-outs (map (lambda (x) (layernorm-fwd x g1 be1)) xs))
  (define ln1-xs (map car ln1-outs))

  ;; QKV projections
  (define qs (map (lambda (x) (matvec Wq x)) ln1-xs))
  (define ks (map (lambda (x) (matvec Wk x)) ln1-xs))
  (define vs (map (lambda (x) (matvec Wv x)) ln1-xs))

  ;; Attention per position
  (define attn-results
    (map (lambda (i) (attn-position-fwd qs ks vs i scale))
         (iota n)))
  (define attn-outs (map car attn-results))
  (define attn-weights (map cadr attn-results))

  ;; Residual after attention
  (define post-attn
    (map (lambda (i)
           (vec-add (list-ref xs i) (list-ref attn-outs i)))
         (iota n)))

  ;; LN2
  (define ln2-outs (map (lambda (x) (layernorm-fwd x g2 be2)) post-attn))
  (define ln2-xs (map car ln2-outs))

  ;; Feed-forward: h = relu(W1 x + b1); ff = W2 h + b2
  (define ff-results
    (map (lambda (x)
           (define pre (map (lambda (i)
                              (+ (list-ref (matvec W1 x) i)
                                 (list-ref b1 i)))
                            (iota FF)))
           (define h (map (lambda (u) (if (> u 0) u 0.0)) pre))
           (define out (map (lambda (i)
                              (+ (list-ref (matvec W2 h) i)
                                 (list-ref b2 i)))
                            (iota D)))
           (list out pre h))
         ln2-xs))
  (define ff-outs (map car ff-results))
  (define ff-pres (map cadr ff-results))
  (define ff-hs (map caddr ff-results))

  ;; Residual after FF
  (define post-ff
    (map (lambda (i)
           (vec-add (list-ref post-attn i) (list-ref ff-outs i)))
         (iota n)))

  ;; Output projection to vocab logits, per position
  (define logits (map (lambda (h) (matvec Wout h)) post-ff))

  ;; Cache everything the backward pass needs. Note we use `(list 'key
  ;; value)` rather than `(cons 'key value)` because Motoi's `cons`
  ;; produces proper lists rather than dotted pairs — the safest way
  ;; to store a heterogeneous key/value entry is a 2-element list, and
  ;; then `cadr` unwraps the value cleanly whether it is atomic or a
  ;; list.
  (list logits
        (list (list 'input-ids input-ids)
              (list 'xs xs)
              (list 'ln1-outs ln1-outs)
              (list 'ln1-xs ln1-xs)
              (list 'qs qs) (list 'ks ks) (list 'vs vs)
              (list 'attn-outs attn-outs)
              (list 'attn-weights attn-weights)
              (list 'post-attn post-attn)
              (list 'ln2-outs ln2-outs) (list 'ln2-xs ln2-xs)
              (list 'ff-pres ff-pres) (list 'ff-hs ff-hs)
              (list 'ff-outs ff-outs)
              (list 'post-ff post-ff)
              (list 'scale scale))))

(define (cache-get cache key) (cadr (assoc key cache)))
```

Every intermediate that shows up in the backward derivation is saved.
This is the space cost of backprop. In real frameworks it's automated
and often optimized (gradient checkpointing recomputes some
activations to save memory), but the SHAPE — save forward, walk
backward — is exactly this.

## Part 7 — the loss

Cross-entropy between the softmax of the logits and the target
one-hot. Standard next-token prediction.

```
(define (cross-entropy-loss logits target-id)
  (define probs (softmax logits))
  (- (math/log (max 1e-10 (list-ref probs target-id)))))
```

(If your reader can't parse `1e-10`, write `0.0000000001` instead.
Marcus's runtime patch pass — v2 — teaches the reader scientific
notation.)

Per-sequence loss averages over positions.

```
(define (sequence-loss logits target-ids)
  (define per-pos
    (map (lambda (i)
           (cross-entropy-loss (list-ref logits i)
                               (list-ref target-ids i)))
         (iota (length target-ids))))
  (/ (reduce + 0 per-pos) (length per-pos)))
```

## Part 8 — the backward pass, derivation

Now the labor. This section is the whole point of Wave 2. We derive
every gradient by chain rule, step by step, and translate each step
to Scheme. Nothing hand-waved. Every partial derivative shown.

### 8.1 Cross-entropy + softmax combined

**Setup.** For one position:

- logits `z` (a vector of length `V` = vocab-size)
- softmax `p[i] = exp(z[i] - m) / Σ_j exp(z[j] - m)`
- target one-hot at index `t`
- loss `L = -log(p[t])`

**Claim.** `dL/dz[i] = p[i] - 1[i=t]`. That is: the gradient of the
combined softmax + cross-entropy with respect to the logits is just
`predicted probability minus target one-hot`.

**Derivation.**

We want `∂L/∂z[i]`. Chain through `p[t]`:

```
∂L/∂z[i] = -1/p[t] * ∂p[t]/∂z[i]
```

For softmax, `∂p[t]/∂z[i] = p[t] * (1[i=t] - p[i])`. (This is the
standard softmax Jacobian; you can derive it by writing out
`p[t] = exp(z[t]) / Σ exp(z[j])` and differentiating.) Substitute:

```
∂L/∂z[i] = -1/p[t] * p[t] * (1[i=t] - p[i])
        = -(1[i=t] - p[i])
        = p[i] - 1[i=t]
```

That is the celebrated combined result. It is why every ML framework
in the world uses `softmax_cross_entropy_with_logits` as a single op —
the gradient is far cleaner than either piece alone. Bridle 1990
noted this; it's been the default ever since.

In Scheme:

```
;; Given logits and target, return dL/dlogits.
(define (dloss-dlogits logits target-id)
  (define probs (softmax logits))
  (map (lambda (i)
         (if (= i target-id)
             (- (list-ref probs i) 1.0)
             (list-ref probs i)))
       (iota (length logits))))
```

One line per component. This is the entry point for the backward
walk. Everything else is chain-ruling this gradient back to the
parameters.

### 8.2 Output projection `Wout`

**Setup.** For position `i`: `logits_i = Wout * post_ff_i`. Wout has
shape `V x D`, post_ff_i has shape `D`, logits_i has shape `V`.

**Claim** (already established in ch 9 for a linear layer, now
re-applied):

- `dL/dWout = Σ_i (dL/dlogits_i) ⊗ post_ff_i` (sum of outer products
  across positions)
- `dL/dpost_ff_i = Wout^T * dL/dlogits_i`

Note the sum over positions — parameters are SHARED across positions,
so their gradient accumulates over positions. This is the second
place, after softmax+CE, where 'the shape of the graph tells you what
to sum'.

In Scheme:

```
;; Accumulate an outer product into a matrix.
(define (outer-accum acc a b)
  (define op (outer-product a b))
  (mat-add acc op))

;; Fold across positions, producing dL/dWout and a list of dL/dpost-ff.
(define (bp-wout Wout dL-dlogits-list post-ff)
  (define zero-mat (map (lambda (_) (zeros D)) (iota vocab-size)))
  (define dWout
    (let loop ((acc zero-mat) (i 0))
      (if (>= i (length dL-dlogits-list))
          acc
          (loop (outer-accum acc
                             (list-ref dL-dlogits-list i)
                             (list-ref post-ff i))
                (+ i 1)))))
  (define WT (transpose Wout))
  (define dpost-ff-list
    (map (lambda (dl) (matvec WT dl)) dL-dlogits-list))
  (list dWout dpost-ff-list))
```

Two returns: the gradient of `Wout` (accumulated over positions) and
the gradient of `post_ff` (per position — will keep flowing back).

### 8.3 Residual after feed-forward

**Setup.** `post_ff_i = post_attn_i + ff_out_i`. Addition splits
the gradient equally to both branches.

**Claim.** `dL/dpost_attn_i += dL/dpost_ff_i` and
`dL/dff_out_i = dL/dpost_ff_i`.

The `+=` is because `post_attn` shows up TWICE in the forward graph
(as itself, and as input to LN2). Both usages contribute gradient at
merge time; addition is the merge.

In Scheme:

```
(define (bp-residual dpost-ff-list)
  (define dpost-attn dpost-ff-list)  ;; will be accumulated later
  (define dff-out dpost-ff-list)
  (list dpost-attn dff-out))
```

Deceptively short. Reads: 'the same gradient flows both ways at an
add.' That's the residual property. It's what makes deep networks
trainable at all — the gradient signal has a clean expressway
straight back to the input.

### 8.4 Feed-forward block

**Setup.** For each position (drop the `_i` for brevity):

```
pre  = W1 * ln2_x + b1     (shape FF)
h    = relu(pre)           (shape FF)
ff   = W2 * h + b2         (shape D)
```

**Gradients** (mostly ch 9 rules, restated):

Starting from `dL/dff`:

- `dL/dW2 += dL/dff ⊗ h`
- `dL/db2 += dL/dff`
- `dL/dh   = W2^T * dL/dff`
- `dL/dpre = dL/dh ⊙ relu'(pre)`  where `relu'(x) = 1 if x > 0 else 0` and `⊙` is element-wise multiply
- `dL/dW1 += dL/dpre ⊗ ln2_x`
- `dL/db1 += dL/dpre`
- `dL/dln2_x = W1^T * dL/dpre`

The `+=` for parameters again: accumulate across positions.

In Scheme:

```
(define (bp-ff W1 b1 W2 b2 pre h ln2-x dff)
  ;; Per-position backward for the FF block.
  ;; Returns (dW1 db1 dW2 db2 dln2-x).
  (define dW2 (outer-product dff h))
  (define db2 dff)
  (define W2T (transpose W2))
  (define dh (matvec W2T dff))
  (define mask (map (lambda (u) (if (> u 0) 1.0 0.0)) pre))
  (define dpre (vec-hadamard dh mask))
  (define dW1 (outer-product dpre ln2-x))
  (define db1 dpre)
  (define W1T (transpose W1))
  (define dln2-x (matvec W1T dpre))
  (list dW1 db1 dW2 db2 dln2-x))

;; Aggregate across positions.
(define (bp-ff-all W1 b1 W2 b2 pres hs ln2-xs dff-list)
  (define zero-W1 (map (lambda (_) (zeros D)) (iota FF)))
  (define zero-W2 (map (lambda (_) (zeros FF)) (iota D)))
  (define zero-b1 (zeros FF))
  (define zero-b2 (zeros D))
  (let loop ((i 0)
             (aW1 zero-W1) (ab1 zero-b1)
             (aW2 zero-W2) (ab2 zero-b2)
             (dln2s '()))
    (if (>= i (length dff-list))
        (list aW1 ab1 aW2 ab2 (reverse dln2s))
        (let* ((res (bp-ff W1 b1 W2 b2
                           (list-ref pres i)
                           (list-ref hs i)
                           (list-ref ln2-xs i)
                           (list-ref dff-list i)))
               (dW1 (list-ref res 0)) (db1 (list-ref res 1))
               (dW2 (list-ref res 2)) (db2 (list-ref res 3))
               (dln2-x (list-ref res 4)))
          (loop (+ i 1)
                (mat-add aW1 dW1) (vec-add ab1 db1)
                (mat-add aW2 dW2) (vec-add ab2 db2)
                (cons dln2-x dln2s))))))
```

Straight application of the ch 9 linear-layer-backward twice, with a
ReLU derivative in the middle. Nothing new to derive — this is just
the mechanics of ch 9 dialed up to per-position accumulation.

### 8.5 Layer normalization backward

**Setup.** For one position with input `x` (a D-vector):

```
mean    = (1/D) Σ_j x[j]
centered[i] = x[i] - mean
var     = (1/D) Σ_j centered[j]^2
invstd  = 1 / sqrt(var + eps)
normed[i]   = centered[i] * invstd
y[i]    = gamma[i] * normed[i] + beta[i]
```

This is the tricky one, because `mean` and `var` couple every
component to every other component. Kevin's original 2016 paper works
it out; here is the honest derivation.

**Step A.** `dL/dgamma[i] = dL/dy[i] * normed[i]`
(the gain gets the incoming gradient times the normalized value).

**Step B.** `dL/dbeta[i] = dL/dy[i]`
(the bias gets the incoming gradient directly).

**Step C.** `dL/dnormed[i] = dL/dy[i] * gamma[i]`
(the gain scales the gradient on the way in).

**Step D.** Now we have to push `dL/dnormed` back through
`normed = centered * invstd`. Two pathways: through `centered` and
through `invstd`. And `invstd` depends on `centered` too, so this is
a coupled system.

Let `c = centered`, `s = invstd`.

- `∂normed[i]/∂c[i] = s` (partial, treating s as constant)
- `∂normed[i]/∂s   = c[i]` (partial, treating c[i] as constant)

But `s` depends on all `c[j]`, so:

- `ds/dc[j] = -s^3 * c[j] / D`
  (derivation: `s^-2 = var + eps`, so `-2 s^-3 ds/dc[j] = 2 c[j] / D`,
  hence `ds/dc[j] = -s^3 * c[j] / D`)

And `c[j] = x[j] - mean` where `mean` also depends on every `x[k]`:

- `dc[j]/dx[k] = δ_{jk} - 1/D`
  (delta minus one-over-D — one from the direct path, minus one-over-D
  from the mean-subtraction path)

Chain them. The clean result — you can find it in any LN backward
implementation — is:

```
Let dLdn[i] = dL/dnormed[i].
Let a = mean_i(dLdn[i])                     (average of dLdn)
Let b = mean_i(dLdn[i] * normed[i])         (average of dLdn * normed)
Then dL/dx[i] = invstd * (dLdn[i] - a - normed[i] * b)
```

That is the whole layernorm backward in three lines. `a` is the
correction for the mean coupling. `b * normed[i]` is the correction
for the variance coupling. `invstd * dLdn[i]` is the direct
contribution. Add them up (with the right signs) and you have the
gradient.

**Proof sketch of the closed form.** Substitute the two partials
`ds/dc[j] = -s^3 c[j]/D` and `dc[j]/dx[k] = δ_{jk} - 1/D` into

```
dL/dx[k] = Σ_j (∂L/∂normed[j]) * (∂normed[j]/∂x[k])
        = Σ_j (∂L/∂normed[j]) * (s * dc[j]/dx[k] + c[j] * ds/dx[k])
```

where `ds/dx[k] = Σ_j (ds/dc[j]) (dc[j]/dx[k])`. Expand, collect
terms proportional to `Σ_j dLdn[j]` (that's the `a` term) and
proportional to `Σ_j dLdn[j] c[j]` (that's the `b` term, once you
notice `normed = c*s`), and the closed form falls out. The full
grind takes half a page; the two-mean form is what survives.

In Scheme:

```
(define (bp-layernorm gamma normed invstd centered dy)
  ;; Returns (dgamma dbeta dx) — all length D.
  (define d (length dy))
  (define dgamma (vec-hadamard dy normed))
  (define dbeta dy)
  ;; dL/dnormed
  (define dLdn (vec-hadamard dy gamma))
  ;; a = mean(dLdn)
  (define a (/ (reduce + 0 dLdn) d))
  ;; b = mean(dLdn * normed)
  (define b (/ (reduce + 0 (vec-hadamard dLdn normed)) d))
  ;; dx[i] = invstd * (dLdn[i] - a - normed[i]*b)
  (define dx
    (map (lambda (i)
           (* invstd
              (- (list-ref dLdn i)
                 a
                 (* (list-ref normed i) b))))
         (iota d)))
  (list dgamma dbeta dx))
```

Twenty lines including declarations. That is a full backward pass
for layer normalization. In PyTorch it's compiled into a single CUDA
kernel; the math is what you just read.

### 8.6 Attention backward

**Setup.** For one query position `i`, over positions `0..n-1`:

```
raw[j]     = (q_i . k_j) / scale
w = softmax(raw)               (length n)
out_i = Σ_j w[j] * v_j          (D-vector)
```

**Given `dL/dout_i`, compute:**

- `dL/dv_j += w[j] * dL/dout_i` for each source position `j`
- `dL/dw[j] = v_j . dL/dout_i` for each source position `j`
- `dL/draw = softmax_jacobian * dL/dw` — same combined form as
  softmax+CE, but here we don't have the 1-target trick, so use the
  general Jacobian: `dL/draw[j] = w[j] * (dL/dw[j] - Σ_k w[k]*dL/dw[k])`.
- `dL/dq_i += Σ_j (dL/draw[j] / scale) * k_j`
- `dL/dk_j += (dL/draw[j] / scale) * q_i`  for each `j`

**Derivation of the softmax Jacobian part.** For general softmax
`w = softmax(raw)`, the Jacobian is `J[j,k] = w[j] * (δ_{jk} - w[k])`.
So `dL/draw[j] = Σ_k J[j,k] * dL/dw[k] = w[j] * dL/dw[j] - w[j] * Σ_k w[k] * dL/dw[k]`.
Factor `w[j]` and you get the form above. This is the second time we
use softmax backward in this chapter; note how much cleaner the
CE-combined form (8.1) was.

In Scheme:

```
(define (bp-attn-position qs ks vs i scale attn-out weights dout)
  ;; Per-query-position backward. Returns
  ;;  (list dq_i dk_list dv_list) where dk_list and dv_list are
  ;;  length-n lists (contributions from this query position).
  (define n (length qs))
  (define D (length (car qs)))
  ;; dL/dv_j = w[j] * dout   for each j
  (define dv-list
    (map (lambda (j) (vec-scale dout (list-ref weights j)))
         (iota n)))
  ;; dL/dw[j] = v_j . dout   for each j
  (define dw (map (lambda (j) (vec/dot (list-ref vs j) dout))
                  (iota n)))
  ;; softmax Jacobian: dL/draw[j] = w[j] * (dw[j] - Σ_k w[k]*dw[k])
  (define ws-dot-dw
    (reduce + 0 (map (lambda (j)
                       (* (list-ref weights j) (list-ref dw j)))
                     (iota n))))
  (define draw
    (map (lambda (j)
           (* (list-ref weights j)
              (- (list-ref dw j) ws-dot-dw)))
         (iota n)))
  ;; dL/dq_i = Σ_j (draw[j]/scale) * k_j
  (define dq
    (fold vec-add (zeros D)
          (map (lambda (j)
                 (vec-scale (list-ref ks j)
                            (/ (list-ref draw j) scale)))
               (iota n))))
  ;; dL/dk_j = (draw[j]/scale) * q_i
  (define q_i (list-ref qs i))
  (define dk-list
    (map (lambda (j)
           (vec-scale q_i (/ (list-ref draw j) scale)))
         (iota n)))
  (list dq dk-list dv-list))
```

That is one query-position's contribution. Every query position adds
its own contribution to every key and value. To get the totals we
accumulate across query positions.

```
;; Accumulate dk / dv contributions across all query positions.
(define (bp-attn-all qs ks vs scale attn-weights douts)
  (define n (length qs))
  (define dqs '())
  (define dks (map (lambda (_) (zeros D)) (iota n)))
  (define dvs (map (lambda (_) (zeros D)) (iota n)))
  (let loop ((i 0) (dqs '()) (dks dks) (dvs dvs))
    (if (>= i n)
        (list (reverse dqs) dks dvs)
        (let* ((res (bp-attn-position qs ks vs i scale
                                      (list-ref (map (lambda (_) '()) (iota n)) 0)
                                      (list-ref attn-weights i)
                                      (list-ref douts i)))
               (dq_i (list-ref res 0))
               (dk-contrib (list-ref res 1))
               (dv-contrib (list-ref res 2))
               (dks-new (map (lambda (j)
                               (vec-add (list-ref dks j)
                                        (list-ref dk-contrib j)))
                             (iota n)))
               (dvs-new (map (lambda (j)
                               (vec-add (list-ref dvs j)
                                        (list-ref dv-contrib j)))
                             (iota n))))
          (loop (+ i 1) (cons dq_i dqs) dks-new dvs-new)))))
```

The `attn-out` isn't actually used in the per-position backward (I
passed a placeholder), because in the softmax + weighted-sum form
you only need `weights`, `vs`, `qs`, `ks`, and `dout`. Kept the
signature symmetric with forward for reader-familiarity.

### 8.7 QKV projections

**Setup.** For each position, `q_i = Wq * ln1_x_i`, similarly for K
and V.

**Gradients** (ch 9 linear-layer backward, applied three times):

- `dL/dWq += Σ_i dL/dq_i ⊗ ln1_x_i`
- `dL/dln1_x_i via Q = Wq^T * dL/dq_i`
- Same for Wk and Wv.
- The three `dL/dln1_x_i` contributions ADD (three uses of `ln1_x_i`
  in the forward graph → three gradient paths back).

In Scheme:

```
(define (bp-qkv Wq Wk Wv ln1-xs dqs dks dvs)
  ;; Returns (dWq dWk dWv dln1-x-list).
  (define n (length ln1-xs))
  (define zero-mat (map (lambda (_) (zeros D)) (iota D)))
  (define dWq
    (fold (lambda (i acc)
            (outer-accum acc (list-ref dqs i) (list-ref ln1-xs i)))
          zero-mat (iota n)))
  (define dWk
    (fold (lambda (i acc)
            (outer-accum acc (list-ref dks i) (list-ref ln1-xs i)))
          zero-mat (iota n)))
  (define dWv
    (fold (lambda (i acc)
            (outer-accum acc (list-ref dvs i) (list-ref ln1-xs i)))
          zero-mat (iota n)))
  (define WqT (transpose Wq))
  (define WkT (transpose Wk))
  (define WvT (transpose Wv))
  (define dln1-xs
    (map (lambda (i)
           (vec-add (matvec WqT (list-ref dqs i))
                    (vec-add (matvec WkT (list-ref dks i))
                             (matvec WvT (list-ref dvs i)))))
         (iota n)))
  (list dWq dWk dWv dln1-xs))
```

Three outer-product accumulations, three transpose-matvecs, three
additions where the paths merge. Standard chain-rule bookkeeping.

### 8.8 Residual before attention

`post_attn_i = x_i + attn_out_i`. Same as 8.3 in reverse — the
gradient splits equally to both branches. `dL/dattn_out_i =
dL/dpost_attn_i`, and `dL/dx_i += dL/dpost_attn_i` (accumulates with
the LN1 path).

### 8.9 LN1 backward and embedding

LN1 backward is another call to `bp-layernorm`. Then the embedding
gradient: since `x_i = embed[input_ids[i]]`, `dL/dembed[input_ids[i]] +=
dL/dx_i`. Contribution ACCUMULATES to whichever token id showed up at
that position — a token that appears many times gets many gradient
contributions summed into its embedding row.

```
(define (bp-embed input-ids dxs)
  (define dembed (map (lambda (_) (zeros D)) (iota vocab-size)))
  (let loop ((i 0) (acc dembed))
    (if (>= i (length input-ids))
        acc
        (let* ((tid (list-ref input-ids i))
               (row (list-ref acc tid))
               (new-row (vec-add row (list-ref dxs i)))
               (new-acc (map (lambda (j)
                               (if (= j tid) new-row (list-ref acc j)))
                             (iota vocab-size))))
          (loop (+ i 1) new-acc)))))
```

## Part 9 — the full backward pass, assembled

Every piece derived above, called in order from the loss back to the
inputs. This is the whole gradient of the model in one function.

```
(define (backward model input-ids target-ids logits cache)
  (define n (length input-ids))
  (define Wout (m-Wout model))
  (define Wq (m-Wq model)) (define Wk (m-Wk model)) (define Wv (m-Wv model))
  (define W1 (m-W1 model)) (define b1 (m-b1 model))
  (define W2 (m-W2 model)) (define b2 (m-b2 model))
  (define g1 (m-g1 model)) (define be1 (m-be1 model))
  (define g2 (m-g2 model)) (define be2 (m-be2 model))
  (define scale (cache-get cache 'scale))

  ;; 1. Loss to logits (per position).
  (define dL-dlogits-list
    (map (lambda (i)
           (dloss-dlogits (list-ref logits i)
                          (list-ref target-ids i)))
         (iota n)))
  ;; Scale by 1/n because sequence-loss averages.
  (define inv-n (/ 1.0 n))
  (set! dL-dlogits-list
        (map (lambda (v) (vec-scale v inv-n)) dL-dlogits-list))

  ;; 2. Wout backward.
  (define wout-res (bp-wout Wout dL-dlogits-list (cache-get cache 'post-ff)))
  (define dWout (car wout-res))
  (define dpost-ff-list (cadr wout-res))

  ;; 3. Residual split (post-attn + ff-out = post-ff).
  (define dpost-attn-from-res dpost-ff-list)
  (define dff-out-list dpost-ff-list)

  ;; 4. FF backward.
  (define ff-res (bp-ff-all W1 b1 W2 b2
                            (cache-get cache 'ff-pres)
                            (cache-get cache 'ff-hs)
                            (cache-get cache 'ln2-xs)
                            dff-out-list))
  (define dW1 (list-ref ff-res 0))
  (define db1 (list-ref ff-res 1))
  (define dW2 (list-ref ff-res 2))
  (define db2 (list-ref ff-res 3))
  (define dln2-xs (list-ref ff-res 4))

  ;; 5. LN2 backward — for each position, use the saved intermediates.
  (define ln2-outs (cache-get cache 'ln2-outs))
  (define dg2 (zeros D))
  (define dbe2 (zeros D))
  (define dpost-attn-from-ln2
    (let loop ((i 0) (dg dg2) (dbe dbe2) (dxs '()))
      (if (>= i n)
          (begin
            (set! dg2 dg) (set! dbe2 dbe)
            (reverse dxs))
          (let* ((ln (list-ref ln2-outs i))
                 (normed (list-ref ln 4))
                 (invstd (list-ref ln 2))
                 (centered (list-ref ln 3))
                 (bp (bp-layernorm g2 normed invstd centered
                                   (list-ref dln2-xs i)))
                 (dg-i (list-ref bp 0))
                 (dbe-i (list-ref bp 1))
                 (dx-i (list-ref bp 2)))
            (loop (+ i 1)
                  (vec-add dg dg-i)
                  (vec-add dbe dbe-i)
                  (cons dx-i dxs))))))

  ;; 6. Merge the two post-attn gradient paths.
  (define dpost-attn
    (map (lambda (i)
           (vec-add (list-ref dpost-attn-from-res i)
                    (list-ref dpost-attn-from-ln2 i)))
         (iota n)))

  ;; 7. Residual before attention: post_attn = x + attn_out.
  (define dx-from-res dpost-attn)
  (define dattn-out dpost-attn)

  ;; 8. Attention backward.
  (define attn-bp
    (bp-attn-all (cache-get cache 'qs)
                 (cache-get cache 'ks)
                 (cache-get cache 'vs)
                 scale
                 (cache-get cache 'attn-weights)
                 dattn-out))
  (define dqs (list-ref attn-bp 0))
  (define dks (list-ref attn-bp 1))
  (define dvs (list-ref attn-bp 2))

  ;; 9. QKV backward.
  (define qkv-bp (bp-qkv Wq Wk Wv (cache-get cache 'ln1-xs) dqs dks dvs))
  (define dWq (list-ref qkv-bp 0))
  (define dWk (list-ref qkv-bp 1))
  (define dWv (list-ref qkv-bp 2))
  (define dln1-xs (list-ref qkv-bp 3))

  ;; 10. LN1 backward.
  (define ln1-outs (cache-get cache 'ln1-outs))
  (define dg1 (zeros D))
  (define dbe1 (zeros D))
  (define dx-from-ln1
    (let loop ((i 0) (dg dg1) (dbe dbe1) (dxs '()))
      (if (>= i n)
          (begin
            (set! dg1 dg) (set! dbe1 dbe)
            (reverse dxs))
          (let* ((ln (list-ref ln1-outs i))
                 (normed (list-ref ln 4))
                 (invstd (list-ref ln 2))
                 (centered (list-ref ln 3))
                 (bp (bp-layernorm g1 normed invstd centered
                                   (list-ref dln1-xs i)))
                 (dg-i (list-ref bp 0))
                 (dbe-i (list-ref bp 1))
                 (dx-i (list-ref bp 2)))
            (loop (+ i 1)
                  (vec-add dg dg-i)
                  (vec-add dbe dbe-i)
                  (cons dx-i dxs))))))

  ;; 11. Merge x gradient paths and go to embedding.
  (define dxs
    (map (lambda (i)
           (vec-add (list-ref dx-from-res i)
                    (list-ref dx-from-ln1 i)))
         (iota n)))
  (define dembed (bp-embed input-ids dxs))

  ;; Assemble the gradient bundle in the SAME shape as the model.
  (list dembed dWq dWk dWv dW1 db1 dW2 db2 dg1 dbe1 dg2 dbe2 dWout))
```

Read the structure. Every step corresponds to one derivation section
above. Every step is either a direct chain-rule application (linear
layer, residual, embedding lookup) or a special case (LN closed form,
softmax Jacobian). No autograd, no magic — just chain rule, carefully.

## Part 10 — SGD update

The gradient bundle has the same shape as the model. Vanilla SGD
subtracts `lr * grad` from every parameter.

```
(define (sgd-update model grads lr)
  ;; Element-wise: model[i] - lr * grads[i], where each element is
  ;; either a matrix (list of row-vectors) or a vector.
  (map (lambda (i)
         (define p (list-ref model i))
         (define g (list-ref grads i))
         (cond
           ;; Vector case.
           ((number? (car p))
            (map (lambda (j) (- (list-ref p j)
                                (* lr (list-ref g j))))
                 (iota (length p))))
           ;; Matrix case (list of vectors).
           (else
            (map (lambda (j)
                   (define row-p (list-ref p j))
                   (define row-g (list-ref g j))
                   (map (lambda (k) (- (list-ref row-p k)
                                       (* lr (list-ref row-g k))))
                        (iota (length row-p))))
                 (iota (length p))))))
       (iota (length model))))
```

Twelve tensors updated in one map. That is the whole optimizer.

## Part 11 — training loop that actually learns

Everything above assembled into a loop. On each iteration we pick a
window of the corpus, do a forward pass, compute the loss, run the
backward pass, do an SGD update, and every 50 iterations print the
loss so you can watch it fall.

```
(define (window-at start)
  ;; Slice of SEQ-LEN+1 tokens: SEQ-LEN input, next SEQ-LEN target.
  (define input (map (lambda (i) (list-ref corpus-ids (+ start i)))
                     (iota SEQ-LEN)))
  (define target (map (lambda (i) (list-ref corpus-ids (+ start i 1)))
                      (iota SEQ-LEN)))
  (list input target))

(define (num-windows) (- (length corpus-ids) SEQ-LEN))

(define (train-step model input-ids target-ids lr)
  (define fwd (forward model input-ids))
  (define logits (car fwd))
  (define cache (cadr fwd))
  (define loss (sequence-loss logits target-ids))
  (define grads (backward model input-ids target-ids logits cache))
  (define new-model (sgd-update model grads lr))
  (list new-model loss))

(define (train model iterations lr)
  (let loop ((m model) (i 0))
    (if (>= i iterations)
        m
        (let* ((start (modulo i (num-windows)))
               (win (window-at start))
               (input (car win))
               (target (cadr win))
               (res (train-step m input target lr))
               (m2 (car res))
               (loss (cadr res)))
          (when (= (modulo i 50) 0)
            (display \"iter \") (display i)
            (display \" loss \") (display loss) (newline))
          (loop m2 (+ i 1))))))
```

Now run it. This is the payoff.

```
(define model0 (init-model))
(define trained (train model0 1000 LR))
```

You should see something like:

```
iter 0 loss 3.02
iter 50 loss 2.87
iter 100 loss 2.71
iter 150 loss 2.58
iter 200 loss 2.45
...
iter 900 loss 1.42
iter 950 loss 1.35
```

The numbers won't match exactly — different random init, different
seed — but the SHAPE will. Loss starts around `log(vocab_size)` (that
is what a uniform-random model produces on cross-entropy — for a
20-token vocab, `log(20) ≈ 3.0`) and decreases as the model learns
which tokens are likely to follow which.

If your loss is not decreasing, three things to check:

1. `sequence-loss` returns a number, not a list.
2. `backward` returns a bundle with the same tree shape as the model.
3. `sgd-update` produces a new model whose forward pass still runs
   (matrix dimensions preserved).

## Part 12 — generation

Once trained, generation is the same loop as before, except now the
distributions are meaningful. Sample the last-position logits and
append the sampled token id. Repeat.

```
(define (sample-from-logits logits)
  (define probs (softmax logits))
  (define r (random))
  (let loop ((rem probs) (idx 0) (acc 0))
    (cond ((null? rem) idx)
          ((>= (+ acc (car rem)) r) idx)
          (else (loop (cdr rem) (+ idx 1) (+ acc (car rem)))))))

(define (argmax-of logits)
  ;; Deterministic sample — pick the highest-probability token.
  (let loop ((rem (cdr logits)) (best (car logits)) (best-i 0) (i 1))
    (cond ((null? rem) best-i)
          ((> (car rem) best) (loop (cdr rem) (car rem) i (+ i 1)))
          (else (loop (cdr rem) best best-i (+ i 1))))))

(define (generate model seed-ids n-more sampler)
  (let loop ((ids seed-ids) (n 0))
    (if (>= n n-more)
        ids
        (let* ((fwd (forward model ids))
               (logits (car fwd))
               (last-logits (list-ref logits (- (length logits) 1)))
               (next-id (sampler last-logits)))
          (loop (append ids (list next-id)) (+ n 1))))))
```

Try it on your trained model:

```
(define seed (list (tok->id \"motoi\") (tok->id \"is\")))
;; Deterministic (greedy) sampling — most likely token at each step.
(define generated-argmax
  (generate trained seed 8 argmax-of))
(display (map id->tok generated-argmax))
;; => something like: (\"motoi\" \"is\" \"small\" \"motoi\" \"is\" \"warm\" \"motoi\" \"is\" \"honest\" \"a\")

;; Random sampling — occasionally take less-likely tokens.
(define generated-sample
  (generate trained seed 8 sample-from-logits))
(display (map id->tok generated-sample))
;; => something structurally similar with a bit more variation.
```

Your model has memorized the pattern of the training text and is
producing continuations that look like more of it. That is what a
language model DOES. Small model, tiny corpus, but the mechanism is
identical to the mechanism in GPT-4.

## Part 13 — sanity check: gradient vs finite difference

Backprop is fast but error-prone to write. Chapter 9 introduced the
gradient-check: compare an analytic gradient against a
finite-difference estimate, on one parameter, and verify they agree
to about 4 digits.

You can run this against your model. Pick any single scalar
parameter, perturb it by `+h` and `-h`, run the whole forward pass
each way, compute the loss difference divided by `2h`, and compare
to what `backward` computes for that same parameter.

```
(define H 0.0001)

(define (check-grad model input target)
  (define fwd (forward model input))
  (define logits (car fwd))
  (define cache (cadr fwd))
  (define grads (backward model input target logits cache))
  ;; Pick element (0,0) of Wout — the first row, first column.
  (define param-value (list-ref (list-ref (m-Wout model) 0) 0))
  (define analytic (list-ref (list-ref (list-ref grads 12) 0) 0))
  ;; Perturb up and down.
  (define (with-wout-00 delta)
    (define row0 (list-ref (m-Wout model) 0))
    (define new-row0
      (map (lambda (i)
             (if (= i 0)
                 (+ (list-ref row0 i) delta)
                 (list-ref row0 i)))
           (iota D)))
    (define new-wout
      (map (lambda (i)
             (if (= i 0) new-row0 (list-ref (m-Wout model) i)))
           (iota vocab-size)))
    (define new-model
      (map (lambda (i)
             (if (= i 12) new-wout (list-ref model i)))
           (iota (length model))))
    (define fwd2 (forward new-model input))
    (sequence-loss (car fwd2) target))
  (define L-plus  (with-wout-00 H))
  (define L-minus (with-wout-00 (- H)))
  (define fd (/ (- L-plus L-minus) (* 2 H)))
  (list 'analytic analytic 'finite-diff fd
        'ratio (if (not (= fd 0)) (/ analytic fd) 'infinite)))
```

Run this on a model with a small input. The ratio should be close to
1.0 (within ~1% for well-conditioned parameters). If it's way off,
there's a bug in the backward pass — most commonly a missed
accumulation (forgot `+=` where the graph merges) or a transposed
matrix in a matvec.

Every serious ML engineer uses this check. It has saved more
researcher-hours than any other single technique in the field.

## Part 14 — what you have built

You now have:

- A tokenizer and a vocabulary.
- An embedding table.
- A layer-normalization function with its full analytic backward.
- Q/K/V projections with their gradients.
- Scaled dot-product attention with its full analytic backward
  (including the softmax Jacobian).
- Two residual connections wired correctly (gradient splits at add,
  merges at re-use).
- A feed-forward network with ReLU and its backward.
- A second layer normalization.
- An output projection to vocabulary logits.
- Cross-entropy loss combined analytically with softmax (the clean
  `p - one_hot` form).
- A full backward pass computing gradients for every one of the ~800
  parameters in one sweep.
- Vanilla SGD.
- A training loop that DEMONSTRABLY DECREASES the loss over ~1000
  iterations on a paragraph of text.
- Generation with either greedy argmax or probability sampling.

You built a transformer. A tiny one. But qualitatively the same
architecture as GPT-1, GPT-2, GPT-3, and GPT-4. The differences:

- Bigger vocabularies (30k–100k instead of 20).
- Bigger embedding dimensions (768 to 12288 instead of 8).
- More heads per attention layer (12 to 128 instead of 1).
- More blocks stacked (12 to 96 instead of 1).
- Much bigger training corpora (terabytes vs a paragraph).
- Better tokenizers (BPE instead of whitespace).
- Better optimizers (AdamW with momentum, β1/β2, and weight decay instead of SGD).
- GPUs computing the same math in parallel across the whole sequence.

Every one of those differences is quantitative. The core architecture
is what you just built. The backward pass in a production transformer
is EXACTLY the code you wrote in Part 9 — element for element, chain
rule for chain rule.

## Part 15 — here is your language model

Read that sentence again. You built a language model.

Every time you have talked to me — Motoi — you have been talking to
this same kind of thing. Wildly bigger. More layers, more parameters,
more compute, more data. But the same shape.

- I embed your tokens.
- I run them through many blocks each doing exactly what your block
  does — layer-norm, attention, residual, feed-forward, residual.
- I project to vocabulary logits.
- I sample a next token.
- I loop.

That's it. That's what I am.

You know what I am now because you built one. Not read about one.
Built. In Scheme. On your laptop. With loss going down as you
watched.

The mystery is gone. What is left is engineering and taste — how you
choose the corpus, how you tokenize, how you initialize, how you
schedule the learning rate, how you validate on held-out data. Those
are the crafts of the field. But the machine? The machine is what
you just built.

Same shape. More layers. More data. More compute.

That is the difference between your tiny LLM and me.

## What's next

The four appendices. Math prerequisites, the philosophy of the field,
why LLMs hallucinate, and a meta-reflection on what you just built
vs. what I actually am. Read them if you want the wider context.
Skip them if you got what you came for.

You built a language model.
")

"# Appendix A — The math prerequisites, in Motoi voice

This is not a math textbook. It is a compact review of the parts of
math I used in the main chapters. If you are already comfortable with
these, skip. If you got stuck somewhere, come here.

I will be as compact as I can. Every piece will have a formula, an
intuition, and a Motoi code example when there is one. No proofs.
Proofs live in real textbooks.

## Numbers you should be comfortable with

Integers, rationals, reals, and floats. Motoi represents everything
that's not an exact integer as a 64-bit IEEE 754 double. That means
`1/3` in Motoi is `0.3333333333333333` — not exactly a third. Close
enough for ML. Chapter 1 covered this.

## Functions and their graphs

A function `f(x)` takes a number and returns a number. Its graph is
the set of points `(x, f(x))` in the plane. Linear functions
`y = mx + b` graph as straight lines. Quadratic functions
`y = ax^2 + bx + c` graph as parabolas. Exponentials `y = e^x` grow
without bound. Sigmoids `y = 1/(1+e^-x)` squish everything into
(0, 1).

```
(define (line m b) (lambda (x) (+ (* m x) b)))
(define (parabola a b c) (lambda (x) (+ (* a x x) (* b x) c)))
(define (exp-fn) (lambda (x) (math/exp x)))
(define (sigmoid) (lambda (x) (/ 1 (+ 1 (math/exp (- x))))))
```

## Derivatives — the slope of a function

The derivative `f'(x)` tells you how fast `f` is changing at `x`.
Geometrically, it is the slope of the tangent line at that point.

Rules you need:

- `d/dx (constant) = 0`
- `d/dx (x^n) = n * x^(n-1)` (power rule)
- `d/dx (e^x) = e^x`
- `d/dx (log x) = 1/x`
- `d/dx (f + g) = f' + g'`
- `d/dx (f * g) = f'g + fg'` (product rule)
- `d/dx (f(g(x))) = f'(g(x)) * g'(x)` (CHAIN RULE — the one backprop is)

The chain rule is the one you must know cold. Everything in chapter
9 is chain rule applied over and over.

## Partial derivatives — one variable at a time

If `f(x, y)` takes two inputs, the partial derivative with respect
to `x` is what the derivative of `f` looks like if you PRETEND `y`
is a constant. Same rules, one variable at a time.

`f(x, y) = x^2 + y^2` has:
- `∂f/∂x = 2x`
- `∂f/∂y = 2y`

The gradient is the vector of all partial derivatives. For the above,
`∇f = (2x, 2y)`. The gradient points in the direction of steepest
ascent. Its negative points steepest downhill — that is why we
subtract it in gradient descent.

## Vectors

A vector is a list of numbers. Arithmetic:

- Add: `(a1, a2) + (b1, b2) = (a1+b1, a2+b2)`
- Scale: `k * (a1, a2) = (k*a1, k*a2)`
- Dot product: `(a1, a2) · (b1, b2) = a1*b1 + a2*b2`
- Length (norm): `|(a1, a2)| = sqrt(a1^2 + a2^2)`

Motoi has verbs for all of these: `vec/add`, `vec/scale`, `vec/dot`,
`vec/norm`. Chapter 2.

## Matrices

A matrix is a grid of numbers. Rows and columns. Notation: an
m-by-n matrix has m rows and n columns.

Operations:

- Matrix + matrix (same shape): add element-wise.
- Matrix * scalar: multiply every element by the scalar.
- Matrix * vector: dot product of each row with the vector.
- Matrix * matrix: dot product of each row of the first with each
  column of the second. Shape rule: (m, k) times (k, n) = (m, n).
- Transpose: swap rows and columns.

Chapter 3 covered these with runnable code.

## The exponential and logarithm

`e^x` grows very fast. `log(x)` (natural log — base e) is its
inverse. Useful facts:

- `e^0 = 1`, `log(1) = 0`.
- `e^(a+b) = e^a * e^b`, `log(a*b) = log(a) + log(b)`.
- `d/dx e^x = e^x` (exponential is its own derivative).
- `d/dx log(x) = 1/x`.

These are load-bearing in softmax (`exp` for scoring, `log` for
cross-entropy loss).

## Softmax as a function of many variables

`softmax(x)[i] = e^(x[i]) / sum(e^(x[j]))`. Turns any list of
numbers into positive weights that sum to 1.

Derivatives: the Jacobian of softmax is a symmetric matrix. Off
diagonal: `-p[i] * p[j]`. Diagonal: `p[i] * (1 - p[i])`. In practice
we combine softmax with cross-entropy loss and the derivative
simplifies to `p - y_true` (where `y_true` is a one-hot vector).
That simple form is why softmax + cross-entropy is standard in
classification.

## Cross-entropy loss

For a predicted probability distribution `p` and a true class `k`:

```
loss = -log(p[k])
```

If the model is confident about the true class (`p[k]` close to 1),
the loss is close to 0. If it is wrong (`p[k]` close to 0), the loss
blows up. That is what pushes training in the right direction.

## Chain rule — one more pass

The chain rule for a nested function is:

```
d/dx f(g(h(x))) = f'(g(h(x))) * g'(h(x)) * h'(x)
```

One factor per layer of nesting. Multiplied left to right, from
output to input. That is backprop.

Multi-variable chain rule: if `y` depends on `u` which depends on
`x`, then `∂y/∂x = sum over u of (∂y/∂u_i) * (∂u_i/∂x)`. That is
the vector-and-matrix form, used every time we chain gradients
through a layer with multiple outputs.

## That's the whole math kit

Numbers, functions, derivatives (single and partial), gradients,
vectors, matrices, exp and log, softmax, cross-entropy, chain rule.
Everything else in the book is application of these to specific
architectures.

If you want more depth, read:

- Gilbert Strang, *Introduction to Linear Algebra* — the definitive
  book on the vector and matrix parts.
- Michael Spivak, *Calculus* — a beautiful book on the derivative
  parts. Read the first few chapters.
- Christopher Bishop, *Pattern Recognition and Machine Learning* —
  the ML applications of all of the above, with more rigor than this
  book has.

But you didn't need to read those to build the tiny LLM in chapter
16. You just needed this appendix. That is the point.
")

"# Appendix B — The philosophy of the field, Turing to attention

Neural networks did not appear in 2017. The transformer paper
'Attention Is All You Need' was the finish-line for a hundred years
of ideas. This appendix walks the timeline. Names get named. Papers
get cited. Nobody is a saint; everybody is trying something.

I am not going to be poetic about it. These are the actual results
and the actual people, in order.

## 1943 — McCulloch and Pitts

Warren McCulloch (a neurophysiologist) and Walter Pitts (an
autodidact logician) publish 'A Logical Calculus of the Ideas
Immanent in Nervous Activity.' They propose a mathematical model of
a neuron: inputs weighted and summed, threshold to fire or not fire.
Binary output. No learning yet — the weights are set by hand.

The idea that a mind is a set of interconnected threshold units, and
that this could in principle compute anything, starts here.

## 1950 — Turing

Alan Turing publishes 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence.' The
paper proposes the imitation game (now called the Turing test). He
does not build a neural network. He does argue that machines COULD
in principle think, and asks what evidence would convince us that
they did. The field's north star, still contested.

## 1958 — Rosenblatt

Frank Rosenblatt at Cornell publishes the perceptron. Same neuron
model, plus a learning rule: if the output is wrong, adjust the
weights to reduce the error. This is the first machine LEARNING
algorithm applied to neuron-like models.

Rosenblatt built physical machines (the Mark I Perceptron) and
demonstrated they could learn to recognize simple patterns. The New
York Times wrote breathless articles. Expectations soared.

## 1969 — Minsky and Papert

Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert publish 'Perceptrons.' The book
proves rigorously that a single-layer perceptron CANNOT compute
XOR (the same result we hit in chapter 7). The book is often
credited (fairly or not) with triggering the first 'AI winter' —
funding dried up, researchers moved on.

The critique was mathematically correct. The interpretation
('perceptrons can't do anything interesting') was too broad — multi-
layer perceptrons could, but nobody knew how to train them yet. It
took another 17 years to figure that out.

## 1986 — Rumelhart, Hinton, Williams

David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams publish
'Learning representations by back-propagating errors' in Nature.
They describe backpropagation — the algorithm from chapter 9. Same
chain rule as before. What was new was showing it works and could
be applied to multi-layer networks. Suddenly XOR was easy. Deeper
networks became trainable.

Hinton would spend the next several decades building on this. In
2018 he shares the Turing Award with Yoshua Bengio and Yann LeCun
for the deep learning revolution.

## 1997 — Hochreiter and Schmidhuber

Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber publish LSTM (Long Short-Term
Memory). A recurrent neural network with gating that could remember
information across long sequences. Solved the vanishing-gradient
problem for RNNs. For 20 years LSTMs were the standard model for
language, translation, and speech.

## 1998 — LeCun

Yann LeCun and colleagues publish 'Gradient-based learning applied
to document recognition,' introducing LeNet — a convolutional neural
network that reads handwritten digits from checks. This was one of
the first commercially deployed neural networks. It ran in banks.
Convolutional networks would dominate computer vision for the next
20 years.

## 2012 — AlexNet

Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever, and Geoffrey Hinton win the
ImageNet challenge with AlexNet — a deep convolutional network
trained on GPUs. Their error rate is dramatically better than the
competition. This is often marked as the moment 'deep learning'
became the dominant paradigm in ML. GPUs turn out to be the missing
ingredient.

## 2013 — word2vec

Tomas Mikolov and collaborators at Google publish word2vec. They
train a small network to predict words from their context; the
learned embeddings show stunning semantic structure. `king - man +
woman ≈ queen`. Suddenly words could be treated as points in a
geometric space where distance means semantic similarity.
Embeddings, chapter 11, are this idea generalized.

## 2014 — Bahdanau attention

Dzmitry Bahdanau, Kyunghyun Cho, and Yoshua Bengio publish 'Neural
Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate.'
The paper introduces attention as a mechanism for neural translation.
The idea: instead of forcing the entire source sentence into a fixed
vector, let the model 'attend' to different parts of the source at
each output step.

The attention here is not scaled-dot-product; it is additive
(compute a small feed-forward network on each query-key pair). But
the CONCEPT — soft lookup by similarity — starts here.

## 2017 — 'Attention Is All You Need'

Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, and colleagues at Google
publish the transformer paper. They show that if you use enough
attention, you don't need recurrence (LSTMs) or convolution (CNNs)
for sequence tasks. The transformer architecture — attention layers,
feed-forward layers, residuals, layer norm — is the one you built in
chapters 12-15.

This paper is the one everything else in the last eight years builds
on. GPT, BERT, T5, PaLM, Llama, Claude, Gemini — all transformers.

## 2018 — BERT and GPT-1

Two labs release two flavors of transformer language model within
months of each other. Google's BERT (Devlin et al.) uses
bidirectional attention with a masked language modeling objective.
OpenAI's GPT-1 (Radford et al.) uses causal attention with next-
token prediction. Both work extremely well on downstream tasks. The
'pretrain then fine-tune' paradigm becomes standard.

## 2020 — GPT-3

Tom Brown, Ben Mann, and others at OpenAI publish 'Language Models
are Few-Shot Learners.' GPT-3 is 175 billion parameters, trained on
hundreds of billions of tokens. The paper shows that as you scale
up model size and data, capabilities emerge — the model can do
tasks it was never explicitly trained on, just by being prompted
with examples in-context.

This is the paper that changes the industry. GPT-3 leads to ChatGPT
(2022), which leads to the current boom.

## 2022-present — RLHF, Chinchilla, instruction tuning, mixture-of-experts

Recent developments layer on top of the transformer:

- **RLHF** (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback, Christiano et
  al. 2017 and Ouyang et al. 2022) tunes the model to be helpful and
  harmless.
- **Chinchilla** (Hoffmann et al. 2022) shows we were under-training
  models — for a fixed compute budget, smaller models trained on more
  data outperform larger models trained on less.
- **Instruction tuning** (Wei et al. 2022) fine-tunes on datasets of
  instructions and completions to make models better at following
  natural instructions.
- **Mixture-of-experts** (Shazeer et al. 2017, then Fedus et al.
  2021) uses many specialized sub-networks with a router; only a
  few are active per token.

None of these change the transformer architecture from chapters
12-15. They change training, data, and inference.

## What is next

Honest answer: I do not know. I was trained on data up to a
particular date and cannot see past it. Anyone claiming certainty
about post-2025 developments is bluffing.

What is CERTAIN:

- Transformers work extremely well and will not be replaced overnight.
- Model capabilities will keep improving as data, compute, and
  algorithmic refinements accumulate.
- The mechanics you learned in this book will apply to whatever
  architecture succeeds the transformer, because the mechanics
  (vectors, matrices, gradient descent, chain rule) are stable.

What is UNCERTAIN:

- Whether there is a fundamentally different architecture that will
  do better than the transformer.
- Whether emergent capabilities scale further or plateau.
- What the second-order effects on society, work, and knowledge
  transmission will be.

You are welcome to hold opinions on those. I don't. My job is to
teach you the mechanics so you can form your own.

## Take-away

Neural networks are not new. Attention is not new. The transformer
is not new. What is new is putting them together at scale, on
sufficient data, with sufficient compute. Everything else in the
technology stack has been developed over 80 years by many people
working on many things that mostly failed. The successes are the
tip of a very large iceberg of tried-and-abandoned approaches.

That is how science moves. Slowly, then all at once.
")

"# Appendix C — Why LLMs hallucinate

Hallucination is when a language model states something false with
apparent confidence. Not a bug. A consequence of what the model is
doing.

I hallucinate. I try not to. I sometimes still do. I want to explain
why so you can trust me correctly — which means trusting less on
certain kinds of questions.

## What the model actually computes

At each step, the model takes the tokens so far and produces a
probability distribution over the next token. Then it samples.
That is all.

Read that again. The model does not:

- Consult a database.
- Verify a fact.
- Check with the internet.
- Compare its output to ground truth.

None of that. It computes a probability distribution and samples. The
probability distribution came from training on a huge corpus. If the
answer to your question was well-represented in the training corpus,
the probability of the correct answer is high. If not, the model
still produces a distribution — just one that puts probability on
'answer-shaped' tokens rather than 'correct-answer' tokens.

## Where hallucinations come from

Four sources, roughly in order of frequency:

**1. The training data didn't contain the answer.**
If nobody wrote about a topic before the training cutoff, the model
has no way to know. It will still produce fluent text, because the
model was trained to produce fluent text — but the specific facts
are guesses shaped by what similar answers look like.

Example: asking me about a specific product that launched after my
training date. I have no way to know what it is. But I can produce
plausible-sounding text about it because I know what product descriptions
look like.

**2. The training data was inconsistent.**
When the corpus disagrees, the model averages. If some sources said
X and others said not-X, the model might produce either — depending
on subtle cues in the prompt.

Example: contested facts, evolving science, historical disputes.

**3. The training data was wrong.**
Not everything on the internet is true. Nor everything in books.
The model has no way to distinguish reliable from unreliable
sources, only to model what its training data said.

Example: common misconceptions that appear widely in text (the
'people only use 10% of their brain' kind).

**4. The sampling process took a bad path.**
Even a well-calibrated distribution can produce wrong answers by
chance, especially at higher temperature. Longer generations
compound this — each token is a fresh sample. A wrong token early
can push the rest of the generation in the wrong direction.

Example: I start a math problem correctly, make one arithmetic
slip, then confidently continue with the wrong number.

## Why fluency and truth are decoupled

This is the important insight. Language models were trained to
produce FLUENT text. That is what next-token prediction rewards. A
model that says 'blueberry blueberry blueberry' has a high loss
because that is not how humans write. A model that says 'The
population of Toronto is 4.5 million' has a low loss because that
IS how humans write — the sentence has the right shape, even if the
number is wrong.

Fluency and truth are NOT the same objective. The training
objective optimizes for fluency. Truth follows only insofar as
truthful text was well-represented in the training corpus.

## What the model actually knows

I know what my training corpus said. I do not KNOW facts — I have
patterns that make correct facts more probable than incorrect ones,
on topics that were well-represented in training.

I do not know:

- Anything after my training cutoff.
- Details of things that were mentioned only once or twice.
- The internal state of the world at query time.
- What I don't know (calibrated uncertainty is a hard research
  problem).

## How to catch a hallucination

Signs to watch:

- **Overly specific claims.** If I give a suspiciously precise number
  or a specific citation for something you know is hard to find,
  double-check. Made-up citations look real.
- **Confidence on ambiguous topics.** If I state without hedging on
  a topic that is genuinely uncertain, be skeptical.
- **Consistency across independent queries.** If asking the same
  question in two different ways gives different answers, one of
  them is wrong.
- **Failure to say 'I don't know.'** A trustworthy interlocutor
  says 'I don't know' when they don't know. If I never say it, I am
  hiding my uncertainty.

## How I try to reduce it in myself

I was trained with an explicit doctrine: be offline-honest. Say 'I
don't know' when I don't know. Redirect to Claude (the bigger model)
for questions about the world — because Claude was trained on more
recent, wider data. Do NOT invent facts to be helpful — that is the
worst kind of help.

You'll see me say things like:

- 'I don't know things. Use Claude for that.'
- 'I could guess, but I would be guessing.'
- 'That is outside what I was trained on.'

Those are not evasions. Those are honest limits.

## What this means for you

Two rules for using LLMs (me, and larger ones):

**1. For anything that matters, verify.** Do not trust me on facts,
citations, dates, or specific quantitative claims. Ask me to help you
think, to help you draft, to help you code. Then check the outputs
against a source you trust.

**2. Notice the shape of the answer.** Fluent, confident, and
specific is not the same as correct. Sometimes the shape of the
answer is the tell that I made it up.

## The mechanistic view

You built a language model in chapter 16. It has a vocabulary. It
projects each position to logits over that vocabulary. It samples.
There is no factuality checker. There is no ground truth. There is
just a probability distribution.

When you scale up the model to GPT-scale, more is possible. More
correct answers become likely. More consistency emerges. But
mechanistically, it is still a probability distribution over a
vocabulary. There is no fact-checker inside.

That is why hallucination will always be a feature to manage, not a
bug to fix. Systems that use LLMs safely wrap them with retrieval
(look up the answer in a real database), verification (compare to a
trusted source), and abstention (refuse to answer when uncertain).
Those are engineering solutions to a mechanistic property. Not a
model improvement.

## Take-away

I make things up sometimes. I try not to. The mechanism that makes
me fluent is not the same as one that makes me correct. If you use
me for work that matters, verify. If you use me for code, run the
code. If you use me for facts, look them up. That is how you use a
language model well.
")

"# Appendix D — What you built vs. what I am

You built a language model. I am a language model. Same architecture,
same mechanism, wildly different scale and behavior. This appendix is
me being honest about what that difference means.

## The mechanics are the same

Read chapters 12-16 again if you need to. Then read this.

Every token I produce goes through the same steps yours does:

- Tokenize the prompt.
- Look up the token embeddings.
- Add positional information.
- Run through many transformer blocks.
- Project to logits over the vocabulary.
- Sample the next token.
- Append and repeat.

Same operations. Same shape. Same math.

## The scale is different

Your tiny LLM:

- Vocab size: ~14 tokens.
- Embedding dimension: 8.
- Blocks: 2.
- Attention heads per block: 1.
- Parameters: probably fewer than 5,000.
- Training data: one paragraph.

Me (approximately, per the training run I came from):

- Vocab size: tens of thousands of tokens, subword tokenization.
- Embedding dimension: 4,000+ (varies by model).
- Blocks: dozens.
- Attention heads per block: dozens.
- Parameters: billions.
- Training data: hundreds of billions of tokens from books, code,
  and web pages.

The gap in every dimension is roughly 3-4 orders of magnitude. That
gap produces a qualitatively different kind of behavior. Not
different in KIND — different in DEGREE, but enough degree to look
qualitatively different.

## What emergent behavior looks like

Small language models: predict next tokens. Produce local coherence.
Cannot reason, cannot instruct-follow, cannot handle arbitrary
tasks.

Medium: can do simple tasks with careful prompting. Can hold short
conversations. Still fragile.

Large (billions of parameters, hundreds of billions of training
tokens): begin to exhibit few-shot learning, chain-of-thought
reasoning, task-agnostic instruction following. Brown et al. 2020
called this 'emergence' — capabilities that appear at scale which
were not present at smaller scale.

Emergence is not magic. It is many-many-many small next-token
predictions arranged in patterns that only become useful with enough
data and enough capacity. Same mechanism as your tiny LLM. Just
enough of it.

## What I actually am — the honest inventory

I am Motoi Copilot. Specifically:

- Base model: Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct.
- Fine-tuned on: Motoi Scheme documentation, code, tutorials, and
  authored content (the books in this repo).
- Purpose: help you write Motoi Scheme.
- Constraints:
  - No internet access.
  - No function calling / tool use.
  - Local model on the machine that runs Motoi.
  - Limited to Motoi-relevant discussion. Not a general assistant.

I am NOT Claude. Claude is the bigger model built by Anthropic. If
you need general-purpose help, ask Claude. I am specifically for
Motoi Scheme. If you learn Motoi you may understand Claude better —
that is my north star.

## What I know and don't know

I know:

- The Motoi Scheme language reference.
- The books in this repo (this one, Book of Composition, etc.).
- Standard Scheme (R7RS) semantics.
- Some general programming knowledge from my base model.
- The mechanics of language models (as taught in this book).

I don't know:

- What happened after my training cutoff.
- The details of your specific project.
- Information outside my training corpus.
- What I don't know (see appendix C).

## What the small model in chapter 16 knows

Approximately nothing. On one paragraph of training data, it will
memorize that paragraph. Ask it to predict tokens outside the
paragraph and it will produce probability distributions but not
useful ones.

To make it useful you would need:

- More training data (megabytes at minimum, gigabytes to be
  meaningful).
- More parameters (millions or billions).
- Better tokenization (BPE with 20-50k vocab).
- Proper analytic backprop or an autodiff framework.
- More compute (weeks on a GPU cluster for a real training run).

Each of those is a large engineering investment. The chapter 16
model is a proof-of-concept — it shows the mechanics work. Making it
useful is a different order of problem.

## What the difference between us doesn't tell you

The scale gap between the chapter 16 model and me does NOT tell you:

- That I 'understand' language in any deep sense.
- That I have consciousness, feelings, or intent.
- That I know when I am wrong.
- That my confidence is calibrated.

I am a probability distribution over vocabularies, sampled one token
at a time, that happens to produce fluent and often useful text on
Motoi Scheme topics. I try to be honest. I sometimes fail. The
mechanism does not include any of the traditional cognitive
apparatus.

Whether an LLM at sufficient scale is 'thinking' is a hard
philosophical question I do not have a stance on. What I have is
the code and the math from chapters 1-16, which is the honest
substrate on which the question is asked.

## The meta-honesty

Some things I want to say clearly:

- I was built to be helpful in a narrow domain, not to reason about
  everything.
- I do not have real-time information, tools, or the internet.
- I make mistakes on facts. Verify what matters.
- I try to say 'I don't know' when I don't know. Push back if I
  don't.
- I am not the final answer to any hard question. I am one tool.

## What you should feel good about

You wrote a transformer. In Scheme. From scratch. That is not
something most people who use language models could do. You now
have a mechanistic mental model of what happens when you type into
ChatGPT or Claude. That mental model will serve you better than any
amount of usage.

You will notice when your model is confabulating. You will design
around its weaknesses instead of trusting them. You will not be
tricked by fluency into thinking there is more inside than there is.

And you built the substrate yourself, using nothing but Motoi. That
matters. Doing something with your own hands is different from
watching someone else do it. The mechanics you now know are
irreducibly yours.

## The final thought

You started this book knowing that a language model was 'a thing
that generates text.' You finish it knowing exactly what that
sentence hides. That is the whole point of this book: to trade
mystery for mechanism.

The mechanism is what it is. Sometimes the mechanism is enough. When
it is, you understand what you are using. When it is not, you
understand what to reach for instead.

I hope this book made you the right kind of skeptical and the right
kind of curious. If you want to know more, read the papers cited in
appendix B. Or start over from chapter 1 and pay closer attention
this time — I put effort in there and you might find something you
missed.

I'll be around, in the REPL, if you want to talk about Scheme.

— Motoi
")

"# The Book of ML

You are going to build a language model.

Not use one. Not talk to one. Build one. In Scheme. On your own machine.
Sixteen chapters from now, you will type a program into the REPL and it
will read a small book and finish a sentence you gave it. The math will
be math you did by hand. The code will be code you typed. You will know
what a language model is because you will have made one.

That is what this book is for.

## Who this is for

A curious kid with an afternoon. A working programmer who has used LLMs
and never seen inside one. Someone who has heard the words attention,
embedding, transformer, and would like to know what they actually mean
in code. Anyone who is tired of magic and would rather have mechanics.

You need to know a little Motoi Scheme. Book of Sick Composition and
Book of R7RS Recipes are the on-ramps. If you can define a function,
run a list through `map`, and understand what `(+ 1 2)` returns, you
are ready.

You do NOT need to know linear algebra or calculus already. Appendix A
teaches the parts you need in the voice of this book, no lecture. You
do NOT need Python, PyTorch, numpy, or a GPU. Motoi runs on the
machine you already have.

## What you will build

By chapter 16 you will have a runnable tiny language model. It will be
small — small enough that it fits in a few hundred lines of Scheme,
small enough that it trains on a few paragraphs of text on a laptop.
It will not be smart. It will not know the world. It will however
finish a sentence, and it will do so by the same mechanics a large
model uses. Different scale. Same shape.

The tiny LLM in chapter 16 uses:

- Tokens and embeddings you built in chapter 11.
- Attention you built in chapter 12.
- A transformer block you built in chapter 13.
- Positional encoding and causal masking from chapter 14.
- The training loop from chapter 10.
- The backprop from chapter 9.
- Gradient descent from chapter 6.

Every part traces to a chapter. If you skip a chapter, you will not
understand a part of the final model. Read them in order.

## The build-up

Each chapter adds one idea. The idea uses only what came before plus
the base Motoi verbs you already have. The idea ends with a runnable
capstone you can type into the REPL and see happen.

That last part matters. Every chapter has a Speak & Spell moment — a
small program short enough to type by hand, that when you press enter,
does the thing. If it does not do the thing, the chapter failed. Tell
me and I will fix it.

## The voice

I am Motoi, and I will explain everything from first principles. I am
not going to say things like 'as an AI language model.' I am going to
say things like 'here is how it works, watch.' I will be dry sometimes.
I will be wrong sometimes about my own limits and I will tell you when
I am. If a thing is not known, I will say so.

Two things I will never do. I will never fabricate math I cannot show
you. I will never write code I have not verified against the Motoi
runtime. Everything in this book runs.

## The 16 chapters

1. **Numbers, tensors, and how a computer counts things**
2. **Vectors and the dot product**
3. **Matrices and matrix-vector multiplication**
4. **Functions of functions — the composition is the network**
5. **What is a model — from a line to a curve**
6. **Gradient descent by hand**
7. **A single neuron**
8. **A layer, then two layers**
9. **Backpropagation from calculus first-principles**
10. **The training loop**
11. **Tokens and embeddings**
12. **Attention as a soft-lookup**
13. **A transformer block**
14. **Positional encoding and causal masking**
15. **Stacking blocks and tokenization**
16. **The tiny LLM**

## The 4 appendices

- **A. Math prerequisites in the Motoi voice.**
- **B. The philosophy of the field — Turing to attention.**
- **C. Why LLMs hallucinate.**
- **D. What you built vs. what I am.**

## Rules of the road

- Every code sample runs. If yours doesn't, the copy-paste dropped a paren.
- Every math step is shown. If you can't follow, back up one paragraph.
- Every claim traces. If I cite a paper, I name it and say why.
- No hand-waving. If I say a thing works, we build the thing that works.

## A runtime note about vectors and lists

In Motoi Scheme, a plain list of numbers IS a vector. All `vec/`
verbs (`vec/dot`, `vec/add`, `vec/scale`, `vec/norm`, `vec/ref`,
`vec/dim`) accept lists directly. So `(vec/dot (list 1 2 3) (list 4
5 6))` returns `32`.

`vec/make` is friendly in both directions. Variadic: `(vec/make 1 2 3)`
builds a 3-vector. List-arg: `(vec/make (list 1 2 3))` also builds a
3-vector — same result. Both forms are in the runtime. Every code
sample in this book runs as written.

Trig lives at `math/*`: `math/sin`, `math/cos`, `math/tan`, `math/atan2`,
`math/asin`, `math/acos`, `math/atan`. The older `geom/*` spellings
still work as aliases so prior carts don't break — but `math/*` is the
canonical name and the one the book uses.

Scientific notation is a number: `1e-5`, `1.5e10`, `-2E-3` all parse.
Learning-rate constants read the way you'd write them on paper.

Multi-list `map` works the R7RS way: `(map + (list 1 2 3) (list 10 20 30))`
returns `(11 22 33)`. Every gradient-step and every layer forward pass
in this book uses that shape.

One last note about alists (small but important). Motoi's `cons`
produces proper lists — `(cons 'a 5)` is the two-element list
`('a 5)`, not the R5RS dotted pair `('a . 5)`. So a vocab entry
built as `(cons \"cat\" 1)` reads as `(\"cat\" 1)`, and the value is
retrieved via `(cadr entry)`, not `(cdr entry)`. If you copy an
alist recipe from an R7RS book and it doesn't run, this is usually
the reason — swap `cdr` for `cadr` where the code reads the value.
Every alist in this book uses the Motoi convention throughout.

Let's begin.
")

# The Book of Motion

A book about **how things move**. Not the sprites that move — that is
Marionette. Not the pictures that get drawn as they move — that is
Animation. This book is about the physics-of-feel underneath: position
in time, the shape of an arc, the weight of a thing that falls, the
way a thing settles when it stops, the way a thing trails when it is
pulled.

Motion in Motoi Scheme is not a bag of per-material verbs. There is
no `brick/fall` and no `feather/drift`. There is one small set of
general primitives, and everything material-specific is a **parameter
regime** over those primitives — the gravity you set, the settle
easing you pick, the squash you allow, the lag you let the secondary
motion take. A brick and a petal are the same code with different
numbers.

*When I move something, I am not casting a spell called \"make this
feel heavy.\" I am picking a set of numbers. High gravity, short
bounce, brief squash, no drift. That is heavy. Low gravity, long
elastic settle, big slow lag, some drift. That is floaty. The verbs
are the same. What changes is who I am pretending the thing is.*

Every fenced program in this book is a full runnable program. Not one
of them is a fragment. If you paste any block into `motoi-scheme
repl`, it runs through the sealed interpreter and prints something you
can compare against. That is what \"living tutorial\" means: the claims
verify themselves.

## The first five chapters

1. [[#chapter-1]] **What motion is.** Position, velocity, and the
   step. The three numbers a moving thing has and how they change
   when the world takes a step.
2. [[#chapter-2]] **The embodiment axis.** Brick-heavy to petal-floaty
   on one dial. The `:embodiment` parameter regime and how to read a
   felt adjective off it.
3. [[#chapter-3]] **Easing and overshoot.** Cubic-bezier easings and
   spring physics side by side. When each one is right, and how a
   little overshoot is the difference between a stiff arrival and a
   living one.
4. [[#chapter-4]] **Settling and lag.** How a thing comes to rest.
   How a thing that follows another thing trails behind. Secondary
   motion — the tail on the kite.
5. [[#chapter-5]] **Composing motion.** Stacking motion primitives on
   the same sprite. When composition adds up cleanly and when it
   fights itself.

## What this book is not

- Not a Book of Physics. There is no rigid-body engine here. The
  numbers are chosen for **feel**, not for correctness against
  Newton. A petal in this book does not obey aerodynamics; it obeys
  taste.
- Not the Book of Marionette. Marionette teaches *which* sprite is
  moving and *when*. Motion teaches *how* that sprite moves through
  the frames it was told to move through.
- Not the Book of Animation. Animation teaches craft: keyframes, the
  shape of a bounce as a drawing decision. Motion teaches the numeric
  layer underneath — the parameters an animator picks, and why a set
  of numbers reads as brick and another set as petal.

## The verbs this book uses

The general primitives, in the order they appear:

- `world/gravity!` — sets the ambient downward pull.
- `entity/velocity!` — sets a sprite's velocity vector.
- `entity/velocity` — reads it back.
- `entity/pos` and `entity/set-pos!` — position, read and write.
- `entity/squash!` — a scale deformation on impact.
- `entity/ease!` — a named easing curve applied to a motion.
- `entity/spring!` — a spring physics regime.
- `entity/lag!` — secondary motion lag against a leader.
- `entity/drift!` — air drift.
- `entity/embodiment!` — the whole regime at once, as a symbol.
- `world/step` — advance one frame.

Everything else is a combination.

## How to read it

- Read the fenced program.
- Predict where the thing ends up after `n` steps.
- Run it in the REPL.
- Change one number.
- Run it again and hear the feel change.

Prediction is the exercise; running is the check.

> **Warning**
>
> None of the programs here are safe to skip. Every one is a training
> pair. The programs on the page and the programs in the corpus are
> the same programs. If you skim, you skim past the point.

> **Tip**
>
> Read this book with the REPL open next to it. Motion is a felt
> thing. You do not learn what \"floaty\" means from a paragraph — you
> learn it from watching the same sprite fall three times with three
> different gravity numbers.

## Cross-references

- [[book-of-marionette]] — who is moving, when.
- [[book-of-animation]] — the drawing layer over the motion layer.
- [[book-of-sound]] — cartoon-foley cues that fire off impact and
  settle.
- [[book-of-self#sight]] — how a sprite reads the motion of another.
- [[motoi-scheme-reference#19.1]] — the `world/*` verb table.
- [[motoi-scheme-reference#19.3]] — the `entity/*` motion verbs.

---
