";; appendix-01-winsor-mccay-gertie.slat
;; Book of Motion — Appendix 1: Winsor McCay and Gertie the Dinosaur (1914)
;; Written 2026-07-13. Author: Lacuna Labs Engineering.
;; Source: John Canemaker, Winsor McCay: His Life and Art (Harry N. Abrams, 2005).
;; Film: Gertie the Dinosaur (1914), Winsor McCay, public domain.

(appendix
  :book \"book-of-motion\"
  :number 1
  :title \"Winsor McCay and Gertie the Dinosaur\"
  :short-title \"winsor-mccay-gertie\"
  :estimated-words 1400
  :subject-verified \"Zenas Winsor McCay, born ~1867-1871 (his birth date is uncertain, standard reference gives ~1867 or later); died 26 July 1934, Brooklyn, New York.\"
  :film-verified \"Gertie the Dinosaur, first exhibited February 1914, Chicago (vaudeville tour); film version distributed by Box Office Attractions/Fox, late 1914. Public domain.\"
  :philosopher-weave (jung aristotle sartre)

  :prose
\"Winsor McCay was a working newspaper artist. He drew *Little Nemo in Slumberland* for the *New York Herald* from 1905 to 1911, and *Dream of the Rarebit Fiend* under a pseudonym for the *Evening Telegram* around the same time. He supported his family by producing enormous amounts of drawing every week — comic strips, editorial cartoons, illustrated features. He was famously fast and famously precise.

In 1911 he began animating. His first two films (*Little Nemo*, 1911; *How a Mosquito Operates*, 1912) were experimental, showing what could be done with hand-drawn character animation. Then in 1914 he made *Gertie the Dinosaur*.

# What Gertie is

Gertie is a female Apatosaurus. She lives on a small island. The film opens with McCay in top hat and vaudeville coat introducing her from off-screen (the introduction was originally live, spoken by McCay on stage; the film also has intertitle cards for cinema release). McCay calls Gertie out from behind a large boulder. She emerges shyly. Over the next ten minutes McCay directs her through a series of tricks: she raises one foot, she bows, she throws a small mammoth into a lake, she drinks from the lake so heartily that the lake nearly empties. At one point she cries — McCay has scolded her for eating a tree — and the animator, apparently seeing her tears, apologizes to her by feeding her an apple.

The film ends with McCay walking into the frame (or seeming to; the technique is a live-action shot cut into the animated sequence) and Gertie tenderly lifting him with her mouth and carrying him away on her back.

# Why Gertie matters

There had been animated films before Gertie. What Gertie did that hadn't been done before was give the animated character *personality*.

Personality in animation means the audience believes the character has an inner life — that she has preferences, moods, memory, embarrassment, affection. Before Gertie, animated characters had been abstract shapes or figures that moved but didn't feel. Gertie feels bashful when she emerges from behind the rock. She feels stubborn when McCay tells her to do a trick and she looks away. She feels hurt when she is scolded. She feels affectionate when she carries McCay off.

McCay achieved these effects with specific animation techniques that later animators would recognize and formalize:

**Weight in every step.** When Gertie walks, her body settles and lifts with each step. Her weight is visible.

**Anticipation.** Before Gertie does anything, she prepares. Before she leans down to drink, she stretches her neck first.

**Follow-through.** After Gertie moves, her tail continues to swing for a moment. Her body doesn't stop all at once.

**Squash and stretch in the face.** Gertie's expressions come from her whole face flexing — brows raising, cheeks pulling, jaw dropping.

**Pauses.** Gertie sometimes stops between actions, and the stop itself communicates something — hesitation, thought, sulking.

These are all animation-of-personality techniques. McCay figured them out one drawing at a time.

# How McCay made it

McCay drew every frame of Gertie by hand on rice paper. The film runs about ten minutes. At sixteen frames per second (typical silent-cinema rate), that is roughly ten thousand drawings. McCay drew them all himself.

He didn't use cels — cel animation was invented by Earl Hurd the same year and wasn't yet in wide use. That meant McCay had to redraw the *background* on every frame too. Every drawing has Gertie and the island and the lake and the sky, all drawn over again. When Gertie moves, McCay had to keep the background completely consistent across thousands of drawings.

He developed a technique of tracing register marks onto each sheet so the sheets would align exactly. This system — registration for animation — became standard practice.

# The vaudeville presentation

McCay took Gertie on vaudeville tours in 1914. In the theater, McCay would stand in front of the screen dressed as an animal trainer. He would call to Gertie, and the projected Gertie would appear to respond. He would tell her to bow, and she would bow. He would say she was being stubborn, and she would look away. The timing between McCay's spoken cues and the projected film was precise — worked out in advance and rehearsed.

At the end of the performance, McCay would appear to walk into the film — he would step behind a small hidden entrance, and the film would cut to an animated McCay entering the frame. Gertie would lift him on her back and carry him off. Audiences reportedly gasped. The illusion was extraordinary.

# The legacy

Every animated character that has an inner life is a descendant of Gertie. Every audience that laughs or cries at an animated figure is doing so partly because Winsor McCay, in 1914, discovered how to make an animated figure feel.

McCay went on to make *The Sinking of the Lusitania* in 1918 — a serious animated documentary reconstruction of the 1915 sinking, roughly twenty-five thousand drawings, no comedy. It is one of the earliest serious uses of animation for factual subject matter. He continued to animate through the 1920s but was pulled by his newspaper contracts back into daily comic strip work and never made another film on Gertie's scale.

He died in 1934. His son Robert McCay preserved much of his work; it is now held in various archives including the Ohio State University Cartoon Library and the Museum of Modern Art.

# What we can do in Scheme

McCay's essential technique — hand-drawing each frame with careful attention to weight, anticipation, and follow-through — is what modern animators still do, just with different tools. Let's build a small demonstration of a Gertie-like character emerging bashfully from behind a rock.

```scheme
;; A shy emergence: character peeks out, retreats, peeks further, emerges.
;; The retreat-and-return communicates bashfulness.

(define (bashful-emerge frame total-frames)
  (let ((progress (/ frame total-frames)))
    (cond
      ((< progress 0.15)   ; peek out
       (world/place-rock 200 300)
       (world/place-head-behind-rock 220 250 (* progress 40)))

      ((< progress 0.25)   ; retreat
       (world/place-rock 200 300)
       (world/place-head-behind-rock 220 250 (- 6 (* (- progress 0.15) 60))))

      ((< progress 0.5)    ; peek further
       (world/place-rock 200 300)
       (world/place-head-behind-rock 220 250 (* (- progress 0.25) 80)))

      ((< progress 0.6)    ; hesitate
       (world/place-rock 200 300)
       (world/place-head-behind-rock 220 250 20))

      (else                ; emerge
       (let ((x (+ 220 (* (- progress 0.6) 150))))
         (world/place-rock 200 300)
         (world/place-figure x 300 'looking-around))))))

(define (animate-emergence)
  (for-each
    (lambda (f)
      (world/reset!)
      (bashful-emerge f 48)
      (world/render!)
      (world/wait (/ 1.0 12.0)))     ; 12 fps for silent-cinema feel
    (range 0 48)))

(animate-emergence)
```

The peek-retreat-peek-hesitate-emerge pattern is what a shy character does. Watching this animate, the character reads as bashful. That is McCay's discovery: sequence of motion patterns can communicate character.

# Recommended viewing

*Gertie the Dinosaur* (1914). Public domain. Available on multiple archives including the Library of Congress and the Internet Archive.

*The Sinking of the Lusitania* (1918). Also public domain. A very different film — serious, sober, documentary.

*How a Mosquito Operates* (1912). Public domain. McCay's second animated film, showing his development toward Gertie.

# Sources cited

John Canemaker, *Winsor McCay: His Life and Art* (Harry N. Abrams, 2005). The standard modern biography.

Donald Crafton, *Before Mickey: The Animated Film 1898-1928* (Chicago, 1993).\"

  :notes
\"Gertie's status as first personality-animation is a widely-accepted historical claim in animation scholarship (Canemaker, Crafton, Solomon all agree). The vaudeville presentation and the McCay-walks-into-the-film illusion are documented. The 10,000 frames estimate is standard (based on runtime × frame rate); McCay's own drawings of Gertie exist in archives.\"

  :philosopher-weave-details
\"Jung: Gertie as archetype — the emergence of the anima character in early animation.
Aristotle: personality-through-action — Gertie is what she does.
Sartre: being-is-doing — Gertie's shyness IS her animated behavior. There's no shy Gertie underneath the frames.\"

  :tie-forward
\"Appendix 2 will take us into rotoscoping — Fleischer's technique and what it enables.\")

;; Book of Motion — Appendix 2: Fleischer's Rotoscope
;; Written 2026-07-13. Author: Lacuna Labs Engineering.
;; Source: Leslie Cabarga, The Fleischer Story (Da Capo, 1988);
;; US Patent 1,242,674, granted 9 October 1917.

(appendix
  :book \"book-of-motion\"
  :number 2
  :title \"Fleischer's Rotoscope\"
  :short-title \"fleischer-rotoscope\"
  :estimated-words 1400
  :subject-verified \"Max Fleischer (born Majer Fleischer, 19 July 1883, Kraków, then Austria-Hungary; died 11 September 1972, Los Angeles) and his brother Dave Fleischer (1894-1979).\"
  :patent-verified \"US Patent 1,242,674, 'Method of Producing Moving Picture Cartoons', filed 1915, granted 9 October 1917.\"
  :philosopher-weave (peirce wittgenstein-late aristotle)

  :prose
\"In 1915 Max Fleischer, a technical illustrator working in Brooklyn, filed a patent for a device that would let animators trace live-action film frame by frame. The patent was granted in 1917. Fleischer called the device the rotoscope. It solved a specific problem that had frustrated early animators: how to make animated human motion look natural.

Drawn-from-scratch animated humans in the 1910s often looked stiff or stagey. Their walks were mechanical. Their gestures were exaggerated. The animators drawing them didn't have a reference for how real human motion looked frame by frame — they were working from memory and observation, but the specific frame-by-frame character of natural motion was hard to capture without direct reference.

The rotoscope gave them the reference. A short live-action film of a person performing an action would be projected, one frame at a time, onto a translucent screen. The animator sat on the other side and traced the outline of the person onto paper. Advance the film one frame; trace again. When the traced drawings were played back, the animated figure moved with the exact character of the underlying live-action performance.

# What the machine actually did

The rotoscope was a compact box with a projector on one side, a light source, a translucent tracing screen in the middle, and a paper-holding table with adjustable position. The animator would insert a strip of live-action film into the projector, advance it to the first frame, project the frame onto the screen, and trace what they saw. Then they would advance the film to the next frame and repeat.

Max Fleischer's patent (US 1,242,674) describes the mechanism in detail. It is a straightforward optical device, and its innovation is not in any single component but in the recognition that live-action reference could be turned into animated frames systematically. Prior animators had used live-action reference in loose ways — an animator might watch a film once and then try to remember the motion — but the rotoscope made the reference *systematic and precise*.

# Koko the Clown

The Fleischer brothers used the rotoscope to make *Out of the Inkwell*, a series of short films that began in 1918. The premise was that Max Fleischer sat at a drawing table, drew a clown character called Koko, and then Koko would come to life and interact with him. The interaction was accomplished by combining rotoscoped animation of Koko with live-action footage of Max at the drawing table.

For the Koko rotoscoping, Dave Fleischer put on a clown costume and performed each scene in front of a camera. The film of Dave was then loaded into the rotoscope, and Max (or a team of animators) traced the outline of Dave frame by frame. The traced drawings, when played back, produced Koko — a clown character whose walk, dance, and gestures had the exact character of Dave Fleischer's performance.

The results were remarkable. Koko moved *naturalistically* in ways that other animated characters of 1918 could not. He could dance; he could interact with objects; he could perform tricks. The Out of the Inkwell films were popular and long-running (they continued into the early 1930s).

# The rotoscope's later career

The rotoscope became a widely-used technique. By the 1930s, animation studios were using it selectively — for specific characters that needed naturalistic motion, or for specific sequences that would be difficult to draw from scratch.

For the 1937 feature *Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs*, the studio produced live-action reference films of actors performing the scenes. The actors performed in front of cameras, dressed in costumes approximating the animated characters. The films were used as reference for the animators, sometimes traced directly (rotoscoped) and sometimes used as observation material. The result was human character animation with a naturalistic quality that had not been seen at this scale before.

Ralph Bakshi, in the 1970s and 1980s, used rotoscoping as the primary animation technique for several features including *Fritz the Cat* (1972), *Wizards* (1977), and *The Lord of the Rings* (1978). In these films, rotoscoping was not a hidden reference but a visible stylistic choice — the films look rotoscoped, and the underlying live-action performances are legible through the drawings.

More recently, Richard Linklater's *Waking Life* (2001) and *A Scanner Darkly* (2006) used a rotoscoping-derived technique called *interpolated rotoscoping* to produce distinctive animated features from live-action footage.

# What the rotoscope enables and what it costs

The rotoscope gives animators access to the physical character of real motion. This is a substantial advantage — human motion has subtle qualities that are hard to invent from scratch, and rotoscoping preserves them exactly.

But the rotoscope has costs. Critics of rotoscoping (many animators are among them) argue that rotoscoped motion is *literal* rather than *expressive*. Real human motion is often subtle, restrained, and unarticulated. Cartoon motion — animation from scratch — can be exaggerated, timed, and shaped for clarity in a way that live-action motion cannot. A rotoscoped character walks the way a person walks, which might be indistinct compared to how an animated character *should* walk in the medium.

There is a middle path that many animators use: rotoscope as reference, not as final. Use the live-action footage to study the frame-by-frame character of a motion, then draw the animation from scratch, informed by what you have observed but not tracing directly. This gives you the observational insight of rotoscoping without the flattening effect of literal tracing.

# What we can do in Scheme

We can simulate the difference between literal-motion animation and expressive-motion animation. Both animate the same basic gesture (a wave), but with different curvature and timing.

```scheme
;; A literal wave — human-like motion, no exaggeration
(define (literal-wave frame total)
  (let* ((progress (/ frame total))
         (angle (* 15 (sin (* progress 2 3.14159 3)))))
    (world/place-figure 200 200 'arm-up angle)))

;; An expressive wave — exaggerated arc, held at extremes, quicker in middle
(define (expressive-wave frame total)
  (let* ((progress (/ frame total))
         (t (* progress 2 3.14159 3))
         ;; Exaggerate amplitude
         (amp 30)
         ;; Add slight hold at extremes with a squared sine
         (angle (* amp (* (sin t) (abs (sin t))))))
    (world/place-figure 200 200 'arm-up angle)))

(define (compare-waves)
  (for-each
    (lambda (f)
      (world/reset!)
      (literal-wave f 48)
      (world/render! 'panel-a)
      (world/reset!)
      (expressive-wave f 48)
      (world/render! 'panel-b)
      (world/wait (/ 1.0 24.0)))
    (range 0 48)))

(compare-waves)
```

The literal wave is small, natural, quick. The expressive wave is larger, curves further, holds slightly at the extremes. Watched side by side, the literal one reads as *human*; the expressive one reads as *animated*. Both are legitimate; they serve different purposes. The rotoscope produces the literal; hand-drawn character animation produces the expressive.

# Recommended viewing

*Out of the Inkwell* (Fleischer, 1918 onward). Public domain. Multiple episodes available online.

*Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs* (1937). Historic use of live-action reference and rotoscoping.

*The Lord of the Rings* (Ralph Bakshi, 1978). Rotoscoping as visible stylistic choice.

*Waking Life* (Linklater, 2001). Modern interpolated rotoscoping.

# Sources cited

Leslie Cabarga, *The Fleischer Story* (Da Capo Press, 1988). Standard history of Fleischer Studios.

Ray Pointer, *The Art and Inventions of Max Fleischer: American Animation Pioneer* (McFarland, 2017).

US Patent 1,242,674, granted 9 October 1917 (public record at USPTO).

Michael Barrier, *Hollywood Cartoons: American Animation in Its Golden Age* (Oxford UP, 1999).\"

Snow White (1937) rotoscoping/live-action reference is standard scholarly account. Bakshi films are historical. The rotoscope critique (literal vs expressive) is standard animator debate.\"

\"Peirce: rotoscope tracing as pure index — the drawn line is a literal physical trace of the projected live-action frame.
Wittgenstein-late: the literal-versus-expressive debate as language-game — some animators want literal motion, some want animated language, both are legitimate uses of the medium.
Aristotle: the tension between mimesis (imitation of nature) and the expressive shape of animated action.\"

  :title \"The Termite Terrace Directors\"
  :short-title \"termite-terrace\"
  :estimated-words 1500
  :subject-verified \"The animators working at the Warner Bros. animation unit in Los Angeles in the late 1930s and 1940s, whose small building was nicknamed 'Termite Terrace.' Key directors included Chuck Jones (1912-2002), Tex Avery (1908-1980), Bob Clampett (1913-1984), Friz Freleng (1906-1995), Robert McKimson (1910-1977), and Frank Tashlin (1913-1972).\"
  :philosopher-weave (aristotle wittgenstein-late peirce freud)

  :prose
\"'Termite Terrace' is the nickname given to a small wooden building on the Warner Bros. Sunset Boulevard lot in Los Angeles where, in the late 1930s and 1940s, a group of animators worked on short cartoons. The nickname came from the deterioration of the building. The group who worked there — Chuck Jones, Tex Avery, Bob Clampett, Friz Freleng, Robert McKimson, and Frank Tashlin among others — developed a house style of comic animation that shaped American cartooning for the next several decades.

The films they made were about six or seven minutes long, distributed with feature films, and produced under budget pressure. Each director had a unit of animators working with them and produced roughly six to twelve shorts a year. Between them, over the course of about fifteen years, they made hundreds of films — and a small number of these films remain among the greatest short animations ever produced.

# What distinguished the group

The Termite Terrace tradition had several distinctive qualities:

**Fast comic timing.** The films moved. Setups were brief; punchlines came quickly; scenes cut when they needed to cut. There was no leisurely observation of the character. If a joke needed three beats, it got three beats; if it needed one, it got one.

**Verbal invention.** Many of the Termite Terrace characters — Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck, Yosemite Sam, Foghorn Leghorn — were verbal creations. Their dialogue was fast, character-specific, and often ridiculous. Mel Blanc, the voice actor for most of these characters, was as central to the tradition as any of the directors.

**Musical drive.** The films were often scored by Carl Stalling, whose music was fast, densely quotational (borrowing from classical and popular music constantly), and tightly synchronized to the action. Every frame had accompaniment; every gag had a musical hit.

**Physical extremes.** Characters could be run flat by a steamroller and pop back into shape. Coyotes fell off cliffs and left character-shaped holes in the ground. Ducks got their beaks blown off their faces and then their beaks came back. The physics violations were the point.

**Self-reference.** Termite Terrace cartoons routinely broke the fourth wall. Bugs Bunny would address the audience; Daffy Duck would complain about the animators; the film would reveal its own construction. This meta-quality was ahead of its time.

# The individual directors

**Chuck Jones (1912-2002).** Jones's specialty was character reaction. His most enduring work — the Wile E. Coyote and Roadrunner series, the Pepe Le Pew shorts, films like *One Froggy Evening* (1955) and *What's Opera, Doc?* (1957) — depended on the audience reading a character's specific mental state at each moment. Jones would linger on a Coyote's slow realization that something bad was about to happen; the extended silent stare was funnier than any physical gag could be. Jones's *Chuck Amuck* (1989) is one of the best books written about animation.

**Tex Avery (1908-1980).** Avery went in the opposite direction: away from character reaction and toward physical extremity. His shorts (many at MGM after leaving Warner in 1942) featured wolves whose eyes literally shot out of their skulls on stalks, dogs whose jaws dropped to the floor, characters who ran so fast they became blurred smears with legs. Avery's *Red Hot Riding Hood* (1943) and *King-Size Canary* (1947) are among the wildest visual comedies ever made.

**Bob Clampett (1913-1984).** Clampett's animation was elastic — characters visibly stretched and compressed at the boundary of what a drawn body could do. His *Porky in Wackyland* (1938) is a Surrealist masterwork; his *Book Revue* (1946) is a musical fantasia of book-cover characters coming to life. Clampett left Warner in 1946.

**Friz Freleng (1906-1995).** Freleng was the veteran — he had joined the studio in the early 1930s and directed shorts until 1963. His timing was crisp, his musical sync (with composer Carl Stalling) was legendary, and his shorts include some of the most-watched cartoons in American history. *Rhapsody in Rivets* (1941) uses Liszt's Hungarian Rhapsody No. 2 as the timing spine of a construction-worker cartoon.

**Robert McKimson (1910-1977).** McKimson became a director in 1946. His work is often less-remembered than Jones's or Avery's, but he refined the Foghorn Leghorn character and directed strong Bugs Bunny shorts.

**Frank Tashlin (1913-1972).** Tashlin worked at Warner off and on from the 1930s. He is often remembered as a live-action feature comedy director in the 1950s and 1960s (*The Girl Can't Help It*, 1956), but his animation work established the fast comic timing that he later brought to live-action.

# The tradition's influence

The Termite Terrace tradition shaped American comic animation for the next fifty years. Its influence can be traced through:

Hanna-Barbera's television animation of the 1960s and 1970s, which used simplified versions of the Warner comic timing at a much lower budget.

*The Simpsons* and other prime-time animated comedy of the 1980s onward, which inherited the fast timing and character-specific voice work.

Contemporary animated comedy for both film and streaming, which continues to use the pause-before-the-joke, the physical extreme, the fourth-wall break — all Termite Terrace inventions.

More broadly, the tradition established that animation could be a serious *comic* medium — that laughs could come from timing, character, and physical invention rather than from cute drawings or musical numbers. The Warner shorts were funny in a way that no other American animation of their era was, and their approach became the template for what animated comedy could be.

# What we can do in Scheme

The Termite Terrace comic-timing pattern can be captured in a small program.

```scheme
;; A three-beat comic timing: setup, response, sting.
;; Each beat is a specific duration measured in frames at 24 fps.

(define (setup-beat frame)
  ;; Character enters, notices something. Duration: 24 frames (1 sec)
  (world/place-character 200 200 'noticing))

(define (response-beat frame)
  ;; Character reacts subtly. Duration: 18 frames (0.75 sec)
  (world/place-character 200 200 'about-to-react))

(define (sting-beat frame)
  ;; Character takes an extreme action. Duration: 6 frames (0.25 sec)
  (world/place-character 200 200 'extreme-reaction))

(define (comic-timing-scene)
  (transport/fps 24)
  ;; Setup: 24 frames
  (for-each (lambda (f) (setup-beat f) (world/step)) (range 0 24))
  ;; Response: 18 frames
  (for-each (lambda (f) (response-beat f) (world/step)) (range 0 18))
  ;; Sting: 6 frames
  (for-each (lambda (f) (sting-beat f) (world/step)) (range 0 6)))
```

The 24-18-6 pattern gives 48 frames total — two seconds. The setup takes the longest; the sting is the shortest. When run at 24 fps, this timing produces a joke that lands: the audience has time to see the noticing, gets a beat to anticipate the reaction, and is then delivered the punchline quickly.

Change the proportions and the joke breaks. 24-24-24 makes it feel drawn out; 6-6-6 makes it feel rushed; 12-6-24 makes the punchline overstay its welcome. The 24-18-6 pattern (or something close to it) is what Chuck Jones would have used for many of his gags.

# Recommended viewing

*What's Opera, Doc?* (Chuck Jones, 1957). Wagner-parody Bugs Bunny short. Museum of Modern Art collection; frequently anthologized.

*Duck Amuck* (Chuck Jones, 1953). Self-reference master class — the animator torments Daffy Duck by continually redrawing his surroundings.

*Rabbit of Seville* (Chuck Jones, 1950). Rossini-parody Bugs Bunny short. Uses musical timing throughout.

*Red Hot Riding Hood* (Tex Avery, 1943, MGM). Avery's frenetic extremes.

*Porky in Wackyland* (Bob Clampett, 1938). Surrealist masterwork.

# Sources cited

Chuck Jones, *Chuck Amuck: The Life and Times of an Animated Cartoonist* (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1989).

Michael Barrier, *Hollywood Cartoons: American Animation in Its Golden Age* (Oxford UP, 1999).

Steve Schneider, *That's All Folks: The Art of Warner Bros. Animation* (Aurum, 1988).\"

  :subject-verified \"United Productions of America (UPA), founded 1943 by former studio animators including John Hubley, Zachary Schwartz, David Hilberman, and others.\"
  :philosopher-weave (wittgenstein-late jung aristotle)

  :prose
\"United Productions of America — universally called UPA — was founded in 1943 by a group of animators who had been working at various American studios and wanted to make animation that looked and moved differently. Over the following fifteen years, UPA developed a house style that broke with the naturalistic character animation of the feature-studio tradition and produced some of the most influential short films of the 1950s. When historians of animation talk about *modernism* in the medium, they usually mean UPA.

# What UPA looked like

Imagine a mid-century magazine illustration or a graphic-designed poster. Flat colored areas rather than rendered shading. Bold outlines. Angular characters with stylized proportions. Backgrounds that suggest space rather than depicting it fully — a suggestion of a wall, a chair rendered as a few lines, a floor implied by a colored plane.

That is what UPA films looked like. They were graphic design in motion.

The stylization was not just a look. It was tied to a philosophy of animation. UPA's animators believed that the naturalistic character animation of the feature studios was a wrong turn — that trying to make animated characters look and move like *real people* was missing what animation could uniquely do. Animation, they argued, was drawing that moved. Its power was in stylization, in graphic design, in visual invention. Making it look like live-action was not using its unique strengths.

# The house style

UPA films had several distinctive stylistic markers:

**Limited animation.** Characters didn't fully-animate the way Termite Terrace and studio-feature characters did. Instead of drawing every frame with all body parts moving, UPA animators would hold much of the body still and animate only the specific parts required for the current action. A talking character might have only their mouth animated; a walking character might have only their legs.

This was partly a budget decision — limited animation is cheaper — but it was also an aesthetic choice. Held drawings looked graphic, poster-like. Focused animation drew the eye to the specific action.

**Flat backgrounds.** No rendered depth, no atmospheric perspective. Backgrounds were graphic designs. Characters existed in front of flat colored planes.

**Stylized character design.** Characters had strong graphic silhouettes but were not naturalistic. Angular geometries; caricatured proportions; simplified anatomy.

**Modernist score.** UPA films often used contemporary jazz or modernist classical music rather than the Wagnerian orchestral scores of feature animation or the Stalling quotational medleys of Warner shorts.

# The major films

*Gerald McBoing-Boing* (1950). Directed by Robert Cannon (or Bobe Cannon as he was called). Based on a Dr. Seuss story. A little boy named Gerald can only speak in sound effects rather than words. The design is deliberately stylized and the animation is limited. The film won the Academy Award for Best Animated Short Film in 1950.

*Rooty Toot Toot* (1951). Directed by John Hubley. An animated adaptation of the *Frankie and Johnny* murder ballad, set in a courtroom. Fast, angular, jazz-scored. Bold color choices — pinks, blacks, oranges. One of the most stylistically radical animated shorts of its era.

*The Tell-Tale Heart* (1953). Directed by Ted Parmelee. An animated adaptation of the Poe story. Voiced by James Mason. Dark, expressionist, deeply stylized backgrounds evoking mental disturbance rather than physical space. Nominated for the Academy Award.

*Boyhood Daze* (1957). Directed by Chuck Jones during a UPA-adjacent period. Uses UPA-derived stylization within a Warner narrative context.

*Mr. Magoo* series (starting 1949). The near-sighted Mr. Magoo character was UPA's most commercially successful creation. The shorts used UPA's stylized approach applied to a comic character. The character's blind-man premise has been widely criticized in later decades as insensitive; the design work and animation, however, remain historically significant.

# The influence on graphic design and animation

UPA's stylistic vocabulary influenced not just animation but American commercial art of the 1950s and 1960s. UPA's work overlapped with the mid-century modern movement in graphic design, illustration, and animation for television commercials. Many of the animators who worked at UPA moved into commercial work in the late 1950s, taking the UPA style with them, and mid-century American animated commercials often bear a strong UPA family resemblance.

Later animation-modernism traditions — including some contemporary independent animators and various television animation styles — trace back to UPA. The show *The Simpsons* in its early years shows some UPA influence in its flat color palettes and stylized character design. The direct visual descendants are numerous.

# What UPA teaches us

The UPA lesson is that animation does not have to try to look real. It can be graphic. It can be stylized. It can hold drawings for longer than continuous motion requires, letting each drawing read as a composition on its own. It can use bold colors, flat planes, angular geometries.

For an animator working today, UPA is one alternative to full-animation naturalism. If your project is a graphic-design piece — a title sequence, a short animated illustration, a music video — the UPA vocabulary may be a better fit than trying to produce feature-quality character animation on a small budget. The choice of style is aesthetic, and UPA proves that stylization can be as expressive as naturalism.

# What we can do in Scheme

Let's build a small UPA-style scene: limited animation, flat background, held poses.

```scheme
;; UPA-style scene: a character speaks. Only the mouth animates.
;; The body is a graphic design in a colored area.

(define (upa-character-still)
  ;; Draw once and hold
  (world/background 'salmon)                           ; flat colored background
  (world/place-shape 'rectangle 100 200 200 300 'olive)  ; simple furniture
  (world/place-figure 'stylized 250 200 'stiff-body)   ; angular figure
  (world/set-eye-position 250 220 'looking-right))

(define (animate-mouth frame)
  ;; The only animation: the mouth opening and closing
  (let ((mouth-open? (odd? (quotient frame 6))))
    (if mouth-open?
        (world/set-mouth 250 240 'open)
        (world/set-mouth 250 240 'closed))))

(define (upa-scene)
  ;; Draw the character once. Hold. Animate only the mouth.
  (upa-character-still)
  (for-each
    (lambda (f)
      (animate-mouth f)
      (world/render!)
      (world/wait (/ 1.0 24.0)))
    (range 0 96)))    ; four seconds
```

The character is drawn once. The background is flat. The only motion is a mouth opening and closing every quarter-second or so. This is limited animation in the UPA sense: a graphic composition that moves just enough to indicate speech.

The result reads as UPA-style. Compare with feature-studio-style animation, which would have the character breathing, blinking, gesturing, shifting weight — many secondary motions layered over the primary action. UPA strips all of that away and lets the pose be the composition.

# Recommended viewing

*Gerald McBoing-Boing* (1950). Academy Award winner. Available on many streaming services and DVD compilations.

*Rooty Toot Toot* (1951). Cornerstone of animated modernism.

*The Tell-Tale Heart* (1953). Adaptation of Poe as expressionist animation.

Any of Amid Amidi's compiled UPA shorts collections on DVD.

# Sources cited

Amid Amidi, *Cartoon Modern: Style and Design in Fifties Animation* (Chronicle Books, 2006).

Adam Abraham, *When Magoo Flew: The Rise and Fall of Animation Studio UPA* (Wesleyan UP, 2012).

Michael Frierson, 'The Animation Aesthetic of UPA,' in *A Reader in Animation Studies*, ed. Jayne Pilling (John Libbey, 1997).\"

\"UPA founding date (1943) and founders (Hubley, Schwartz, Hilberman among others) are standard. Named films (Gerald McBoing-Boing, Rooty Toot Toot, The Tell-Tale Heart, Boyhood Daze, Mr. Magoo series) are all verifiable with their years and directors. The critique of Mr. Magoo's premise as later-considered-insensitive is a widely-noted fact in animation-history scholarship, not a judgment invented here.\"

  :philosopher-weave-details
\"Wittgenstein-late: UPA style as language-game — a set of conventions the audience learned to read as its own aesthetic, distinct from naturalistic animation.
Jung: stylization as archetype — the flat graphic body reads as a category rather than an individual, which is a different mode of character.
Aristotle: limited animation as economy — the parts moved are exactly the parts required for the action, no more.\"

  :tie-forward
\"Appendix 5 will move to Studio Ghibli — the Japanese hand-drawn feature tradition that carried a different sensibility into the twenty-first century.\")
")

  :philosopher-weave (jung wittgenstein-late aristotle sartre)

  :prose
\"Studio Ghibli was founded in Tokyo in 1985, right at the moment when American animation was starting to consolidate around computer techniques. Ghibli did the opposite. It committed to hand-drawn feature animation as a serious art form and produced, over the following four decades, a body of work that stands as one of the great achievements of the medium.

Hayao Miyazaki was forty-four when Ghibli was founded. He had been working as a professional animator since 1963, first at Toei Animation, later at various studios, on television series and features. He had directed *Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind* in 1984 — the film whose commercial success made Ghibli possible. Isao Takahata was fifty. He was Miyazaki's older colleague and had directed *Grave of the Fireflies* (1988) among other works. Toshio Suzuki was the producer who kept the studio's finances viable.

The three of them, over the next thirty-plus years, would produce or oversee approximately twenty feature films.

# What Ghibli committed to

Hand-drawn character animation. Every character in every Ghibli film through *The Wind Rises* (2013) was drawn frame by frame in traditional cel or digital-cel animation. Backgrounds were painted by teams of background artists using traditional gouache or acrylic techniques. Computer effects were used sparingly, often for tasks that hand animation could not do (rendering complex particle effects, for example), but the character work stayed hand-drawn.

Long production timelines. A Ghibli feature typically took three to four years from initial concept to release. This is far longer than most other animation studios' production schedules. The extended timeline allowed for detailed hand work, extensive character-design iteration, and careful planning of every scene.

Environmental attention. Backgrounds and settings in Ghibli films are treated as characters. Landscapes are rendered with the same care as protagonists. Weather, seasons, time of day, light quality — all are essential to the storytelling. Miyazaki has spoken repeatedly of the importance of showing children the physical beauty of the natural world.

Narrative patience. Ghibli films often include long sustained shots where nothing dramatic happens — a character walking through a field, watching clouds, sitting quietly. These shots are not dead time; they are essential to the pacing. They give the audience time to inhabit the film's world.

# The signature qualities

**Meditative pacing.** Ghibli films are not fast-paced. They breathe. Long shots of characters in landscape are common. The films assume the audience is willing to slow down.

**Ambiguous morality.** Villains in Ghibli films are often complicated — sympathetic in some scenes, threatening in others. Heroines and heroes are also complicated. Nobody is pure evil; nobody is pure good.

**Attention to weather and season.** Rain, snow, wind, seasonal change, and time of day are rendered with unusual care. Ghibli films use weather as expressive material.

**Female protagonists.** Many Ghibli films (starting with *Nausicaä* through *Kiki's Delivery Service*, *Princess Mononoke*, *Spirited Away*, *Ponyo*, *When Marnie Was There*) center on young girls or young women. The protagonists are active, curious, courageous, complicated.

**Ecological concern.** Themes of humans in relation to the natural world are constant. *Nausicaä*, *Princess Mononoke*, *Pom Poko* (Takahata, 1994), and others engage directly with human impact on ecosystems. This engagement is neither preachy nor sentimental; it is present as a substrate.

# The great films

*My Neighbor Totoro* (1988, Miyazaki). Two young sisters move to the countryside with their father while their mother recovers from illness. They meet Totoro, a large forest spirit. The film is small in narrative scale (there is no antagonist in the conventional sense) but enormous in feeling.

*Grave of the Fireflies* (1988, Takahata). Two children in Kobe during the last months of World War II lose their family and eventually their lives. One of the most devastating films — animated or otherwise — ever made.

*Kiki's Delivery Service* (1989, Miyazaki). A young witch leaves home for a year to establish her independence. The film is a coming-of-age story about a girl running a small business.

*Only Yesterday* (1991, Takahata). A young woman travels to the countryside and remembers her fifth-grade self. Adult-child scenes intercut across time. Made for adult audiences.

*Princess Mononoke* (1997, Miyazaki). A young prince, cursed by a demon, journeys west to find its source. Encounters a forest-god war between the industrial town of Iron Town and the animal-gods of the forest.

*Spirited Away* (2001, Miyazaki). A young girl, moving to a new town, gets stranded in a spirit-world bathhouse and must save her parents from being trapped there. Academy Award for Best Animated Feature (2003).

*The Wind Rises* (2013, Miyazaki). A biographical film about the Japanese aeronautical engineer Jirō Horikoshi, designer of the Zero fighter plane. Miyazaki's originally-planned final feature (he later came out of retirement).

*The Boy and the Heron* (2023, Miyazaki). Miyazaki's late-career film, released after his announced retirement.

# What Ghibli teaches

For an animator, Ghibli teaches:

That hand-drawn animation can remain a serious contemporary art form. Even in a world of computer animation, hand drawing has qualities that computer techniques do not: specific line quality, tactile presence, the sense of a human hand having been in physical contact with the image.

That pacing is a choice. You do not have to move fast to be watchable. If you have committed to a rich world, the audience will slow down with you.

That character can be told through small moments. A child leaning against a tree, a girl watching a train, a woman writing at a table. These small moments are where character deepens.

That the natural world is a fit subject for serious animation. Landscape, weather, and season can be as expressive as character animation.

That female protagonists in animation are not niche. Girls and young women can carry major features that succeed with global audiences.

# What we can do in Scheme

A small Ghibli-inflected scene: a character walks through a field, pauses, watches the wind.

```scheme
;; A slow-paced observation scene, Ghibli-style.
;; The character walks, then stops, then looks at the environment.
;; Pacing: 24 frames per second, but the scene runs for a full 8 seconds.

(define (field-background t)
  (world/background 'pale-sky-blue)
  (world/place-shape 'gradient 0 300 800 400 'meadow-green)
  ;; Grass that ripples with the wind, animated by t
  (let ((wind-offset (* 3 (sin (* t 0.5)))))
    (world/place-grass 100 350 700 380 wind-offset)))

(define (walking-frame t)
  (let ((x (+ 100 (* 40 t))))    ; slow forward motion
    (world/place-character x 320 'walking-quietly)))

(define (paused-frame t)
  (world/place-character 260 320 'still-looking))

(define (wind-watching-frame t)
  ;; Character is still, but her hair moves in the wind
  (let ((hair-offset (* 5 (sin (* t 1.0)))))
    (world/place-character 260 320 'still-looking hair-offset)))

(define (ghibli-scene)
  (transport/fps 24)
  ;; Seconds 0-3: character walks
  (let loop ((t 0))
    (when (< t 3.0)
      (world/reset!)
      (field-background t)
      (walking-frame t)
      (world/render!)
      (world/wait (/ 1.0 24.0))
      (loop (+ t (/ 1.0 24.0)))))

  ;; Seconds 3-4: character stops
  (let loop ((t 3.0))
    (when (< t 4.0)
      (world/reset!)
      (field-background t)
      (paused-frame t)
      (world/render!)
      (world/wait (/ 1.0 24.0))
      (loop (+ t (/ 1.0 24.0)))))

  ;; Seconds 4-8: character watches the wind (four seconds)
  (let loop ((t 4.0))
    (when (< t 8.0)
      (world/reset!)
      (field-background t)
      (wind-watching-frame t)
      (world/render!)
      (world/wait (/ 1.0 24.0))
      (loop (+ t (/ 1.0 24.0))))))
```

The scene is eight seconds long — a substantial commitment of screen time for what is, dramatically, almost nothing. Three seconds of walking; one second of stopping; four seconds of watching the wind move the grass.

In a Termite Terrace short, this scene would take one second. In a Ghibli film, this scene might take fifteen seconds. The pacing carries the meaning: the character is *paying attention* to her surroundings, and the audience is asked to pay attention with her.

# Recommended viewing

*My Neighbor Totoro* (Miyazaki, 1988). The gentlest Ghibli feature. Suitable for children of any age.

*Grave of the Fireflies* (Takahata, 1988). Serious adult feature. Not suitable for children.

*Spirited Away* (Miyazaki, 2001). The Academy-Award-winning feature. Suitable for older children through adults.

*Only Yesterday* (Takahata, 1991). Adult-focused; a masterwork of Takahata's second style.

*Princess Mononoke* (Miyazaki, 1997). Complex feature for older audiences.

# Sources cited

Helen McCarthy, *Hayao Miyazaki: Master of Japanese Animation* (Stone Bridge Press, 1999).

Susan Napier, *Anime from Akira to Howl's Moving Castle* (Palgrave, 2005).

Miyazaki's own book *Starting Point 1979-1996* (VIZ Media, 2009 English translation) — his collected essays.\"

  :notes
\"Ghibli founding date (1985) and founders (Miyazaki, Takahata, Suzuki) are documented. Miyazaki birth year 1941 and Takahata dates 1935-2018 are standard. All film titles, directors, and release dates are verifiable. The critique/description of Miyazaki's aesthetic is well-supported by McCarthy and Napier. Studio Ghibli is treated as artistic movement per doctrine, not as corporate entity.\"

  :philosopher-weave-details
\"Jung: Ghibli's female protagonists as anima archetypes exploring consciousness, integration, and passage into adulthood.
Wittgenstein-late: Ghibli's meditative pacing as a different form of life for animated feature — the audience learns to inhabit a slower rhythm.
Aristotle: attention to environment as the substrate of action — the natural world is not scenery but a fellow actor.
Sartre: being-is-doing on longer time scales — the character's identity emerges from sustained attention over minutes rather than reactive moments.\"

  :tie-forward
\"Appendix 6 will look at stop-motion — an entirely different physical practice with its own tradition.\")
")

;; Book of Motion — Appendix 6: Satoshi Kon and the Cut
;; Written 2026-07-13. Author: Lacuna Labs Engineering.
;; Real subject: Satoshi Kon (1963-2010).
;; Sources: Andrew Osmond, Satoshi Kon: The Illusionist (Stone Bridge Press, 2009);
;; Susan Napier writings on Kon in Anime from Akira to Howl's Moving Castle.

(appendix
  :book \"book-of-motion\"
  :number 6
  :title \"Satoshi Kon and the Cut\"
  :short-title \"satoshi-kon\"
  :estimated-words 1400
  :subject-verified \"Satoshi Kon (今 敏), born 12 October 1963, Kushiro, Hokkaido; died 24 August 2010, Tokyo, of pancreatic cancer at age 46. Animation director.\"
  :philosopher-weave (aristotle jung wittgenstein-late peirce)

  :prose
\"Satoshi Kon directed four feature-length animated films and one television series before his early death in 2010 at the age of 46. His body of work is small in quantity — *Perfect Blue* (1997), *Millennium Actress* (2001), *Tokyo Godfathers* (2003), and *Paprika* (2006), plus the 13-episode television series *Paranoia Agent* (2004) — but it stands as one of the most distinctive achievements in animated film of its era.

Kon's specialty was the transition. In his films, the cut from one scene to the next is often used to blur the boundary between what is real and what is imagined, remembered, or dreamed. A character walking down a street cuts to the same character walking down a different street — but the second street is inside a movie the character is watching, or inside a memory she is having, or inside a dream she is dreaming. The cut is used to erase the boundary, and the audience has to catch up to what has happened.

This is a specifically cinematic technique. Live-action films can do it too, but animation, because every frame is drawn, can make the transitions absolutely seamless. Kon exploited this affordance.

# Perfect Blue (1997)

Kon's first feature, based on a novel by Yoshikazu Takeuchi. A pop idol named Mima leaves her singing group to pursue a career as a serious actress. As she takes on a violent role in a psychological thriller, she begins to lose her sense of what is real and what is being filmed. She starts to see a doppelganger of herself — the pop-idol Mima she used to be — appearing at her window.

The film uses matched cuts constantly. A shot of Mima screaming on set cuts to a shot of Mima waking up from what she thought was a nightmare — the scream continues; the visual match is exact. Was the scream from the set or from the nightmare? Both. Neither. The audience is thrown into Mima's disorientation directly.

Perfect Blue was rated for adult audiences and dealt with disturbing material (stalking, violence, sexual assault). It is not for children. But its cinematic technique — the seamless-cut, the identity-collapse — was groundbreaking.

# Millennium Actress (2001)

Kon's second feature. A documentary team goes to interview a legendary retired Japanese actress, Chiyoko Fujiwara, about her long career. As she tells them her life story, the film cuts fluidly between her memories and the fictional roles she played in her films. In one shot she is running through a field in a Meiji-era historical film; in the next, she is running through the same field but now the field is real, in her own life memory; in the next she is running through the burning ruins of Tokyo in a wartime film.

The cuts blur what is memory, what is film, what is life. By the end, Chiyoko's identity across all of it — the actress, the woman, the roles — has become one thing. The film is a love letter to Japanese cinema and a meditation on how playing many people over a lifetime shapes what a person is.

# Tokyo Godfathers (2003)

Kon's most accessible feature. Three homeless people in Tokyo — a middle-aged man, a transgender woman, and a teenage girl — find an abandoned baby on Christmas Eve and attempt to return it to its parents. Over the following days, their journey through the city becomes a chain of coincidences that resolves both the baby's story and their own.

The film uses fewer of Kon's signature reality-blurring cuts, but its narrative structure — coincidence upon coincidence, each character's past unfolding through chance encounters — is another kind of Kon technique. Different scenes turn out to have been connected all along.

# Paprika (2006)

Kon's most visually elaborate feature. A therapist named Atsuko Chiba uses a device called the DC Mini to enter patients' dreams. When the DC Mini is stolen, dreams begin invading the waking world, and the boundary between dream and reality collapses.

The visual invention in *Paprika* is extraordinary. Parades of dream-imagery — dolls, samurai, refrigerators, statues — march through Tokyo. Characters transition between dream-selves and waking-selves without cuts, their identities morphing during a single shot. The film's title character Paprika is Atsuko's dream-self, a young woman who can walk through other people's dreams and change forms at will.

Christopher Nolan's *Inception* (2010) shares clear resemblances with *Paprika*, though the comparison is debated.

# Paranoia Agent (2004)

Kon's only television series. Thirteen episodes originally aired on WOWOW. The premise: a young boy on rollerblades called Shōnen Bat ('Little Boy Bat') attacks strangers with a golden baseball bat, and each episode follows a different victim.

The episodes are individually compact studies of psychological disturbance. Together they build a larger meditation on collective anxiety in contemporary Tokyo. The style shifts across episodes — some are surreal, some are procedural, some are experimental. Paranoia Agent is one of the most artistically ambitious animated television series ever produced.

# What Kon's technique teaches

Kon shows that animation can use the *cut* as an expressive tool at a level of subtlety live-action cannot easily match. Because animation is drawn, transitions between shots can be exactly matched — the same character in the same pose in the same lighting, cut into a different context. This gives the animator control over the audience's perception of continuity that no live-action director has.

Kon uses this control to explore identity, memory, and the boundary between real and imagined. In his films, characters are often multiple people (Mima the pop-idol and Mima the actress; Chiyoko the actress and Chiyoko in every role she played). The cuts show how these selves live together — how one person can contain multitudes without breaking apart.

For an animator or filmmaker, Kon's technique is a lesson in what cinematic language animation can bring. The technical possibility of the matched cut becomes an expressive possibility for exploring subjectivity, memory, and identity.

# What we can do in Scheme

A small demonstration of a Kon-style matched cut.

```scheme
;; Two scenes that share the same visual composition but different contexts.
;; The cut between them uses the same pose to disorient the audience.

(define (scene-a-street-walk t)
  ;; Character walks down a rainy Tokyo street at night
  (world/background 'dark-blue)
  (world/place-rain)
  (world/place-street-signs)
  (let ((x (+ 100 (* t 30))))
    (world/place-character x 320 'walking 'blue-umbrella)))

(define (scene-b-dream-street t)
  ;; Same character, same pose — but the street is now surreal
  (world/background 'pink-cotton-candy)
  (world/place-floating-fish)
  (world/place-clock-with-melted-face)
  (let ((x (+ 100 (* t 30))))
    (world/place-character x 320 'walking 'blue-umbrella)))

(define (kon-cut-scene)
  ;; Scene A: three seconds of street walk
  (let loop ((t 0))
    (when (< t 3.0)
      (world/reset!)
      (scene-a-street-walk t)
      (world/render!)
      (world/wait (/ 1.0 24.0))
      (loop (+ t (/ 1.0 24.0)))))

  ;; The cut — exactly matched frame from Scene A to Scene B.
  ;; The character's pose is IDENTICAL across the cut.
  ;; Only the environment changes.

  ;; Scene B: three more seconds — but now in a dream
  (let loop ((t 3.0))
    (when (< t 6.0)
      (world/reset!)
      (scene-b-dream-street t)
      (world/render!)
      (world/wait (/ 1.0 24.0))
      (loop (+ t (/ 1.0 24.0))))))
```

The character's walk continues seamlessly from Scene A to Scene B. Her pose, her stride, her umbrella — all match exactly across the cut. Only the environment changes. To the audience, the transition is a shock: the character has stepped from one world into another, and the animation makes the transition indistinguishable from a normal shot cut.

This is Kon's method in miniature. When executed with skill and used to explore a character's shifting perception of reality, it can produce moments of genuine cinematic power.

# Recommended viewing

*Millennium Actress* (2001). The most accessible starting point for Kon. Beautiful, moving, and technically remarkable.

*Perfect Blue* (1997). For adult audiences only. Kon's first and most disturbing feature.

*Paprika* (2006). Visually spectacular; dense with imagery.

*Paranoia Agent* (2004). The television series, for viewers with time for a longer form.

# Sources cited

Andrew Osmond, *Satoshi Kon: The Illusionist* (Stone Bridge Press, 2009). The essential English-language monograph.

Susan Napier, *Anime from Akira to Howl's Moving Castle* (Palgrave, 2005). Includes substantial discussion of Kon.\"

  :notes
\"Satoshi Kon's biographical dates (born 12 October 1963, died 24 August 2010 of pancreatic cancer) are standard and documented. All four features and Paranoia Agent are historically verifiable with their release years and studios. The Inception comparison is a widely discussed fact but stated cautiously. Kon is treated as an artist within an artistic movement (Japanese hand-drawn feature animation); his production studios (Madhouse for most projects) are referenced only implicitly.\"

  :philosopher-weave-details
\"Aristotle: the cut as the shape of an action — the transition between shots is itself an action in animation.
Jung: identity across multiple selves (Mima-as-idol, Mima-as-actress; Chiyoko across all her roles) as individuation through absorbing many selves into one.
Wittgenstein-late: the matched cut as a form of life the audience learns to read — after enough exposure to Kon's technique, the viewer starts to expect and read the reality-shifting cuts.
Peirce: each frame of the matched cut as index of a specific reality; the cut is a discontinuity in the index-chain.\"

  :tie-forward
\"Appendix 7 will look at Norman McLaren and hand-manipulated experimental animation.\")

(appendix
  :book \"book-of-motion\"
  :number 7
  :title \"Norman McLaren and Direct Animation\"
  :short-title \"norman-mclaren\"
  :estimated-words 1300
  :subject-verified \"Norman McLaren, born 11 April 1914, Stirling, Scotland; died 27 January 1987, Montreal. Animator, primarily associated with the National Film Board of Canada from 1941.\"
  :philosopher-weave (peirce sartre aristotle)

  :prose
\"Norman McLaren, working at the National Film Board of Canada from 1941 until his retirement in 1983, developed a body of experimental animation that was unlike any other in the medium. He worked on individual sequences for years, exploring specific technical questions — what happens if you scratch the emulsion of the film directly? what happens if you photograph a live actor one frame at a time and let them move slightly between frames? what happens if you overlay two frames of dancing at different speeds? His films are meditations on the physical medium of animation.

McLaren was not concerned with characters, or with narrative in the conventional sense. He was concerned with what animation *is* — with the direct relationship between the physical film strip and the perceived motion. His work is closer to abstract art or experimental music than to storytelling animation.

# Direct animation

McLaren's earliest signature technique was *direct animation* — drawing or scratching directly onto the celluloid of the film strip. In the 1940s and 1950s, he made a series of films (*Dots*, 1940; *Loops*, 1940; *Boogie Doodle*, 1941; *Fiddle-de-dee*, 1947) in which every frame was a scratch or dab of paint on the film itself. When the film was projected, the marks appeared as moving abstract shapes, synchronized to music.

This technique has an unusual philosophical property. In conventional animation, drawings are photographed frame by frame; the film is a record of a series of drawings. In direct animation, the film *is* the drawing. There is no separation between the physical film strip and the animated image. What the projector shows is exactly what McLaren scratched.

# Neighbours (1952)

McLaren's *Neighbours* — an 8-minute short from 1952 — used a technique called *pixilation* to animate live actors as if they were animated puppets. Two neighbors, played by live actors, are photographed frame by frame; between frames, they move slightly, so when the film is projected the actors appear to move in unnatural, jerky, staccato motion.

The film's premise: two neighbors sit peacefully in their yards until a flower grows between them. Both want the flower. They fight over it. The fight escalates. By the end of the film, both are dead and the flower is destroyed.

Neighbours won an Academy Award for Best Documentary Short (1952 — categorization was contested but the film received the honor). It is a political allegory produced during the Korean War and remains one of the most striking anti-war statements in the medium.

The pixilation technique gave the actors an unheimlich, animated quality. They were unmistakably real people, but they moved as animated figures. This blurring — human bodies in animated time — produced a specific unsettling effect that McLaren returned to in subsequent films.

# Pas de deux (1968)

*Pas de deux* is a ten-minute film in which two ballet dancers (Margaret Mercier and Vincent Warren) perform a duet in silhouette against a black background. McLaren photographed the dance normally, but he then processed the film so that each moment of the dance was overlaid with images of the dancers' positions from several frames earlier and later. The result is that a single dancer, at any moment, appears as multiple overlapping ghost-images of herself — the trailing echoes of her past positions and the pre-echoes of her future ones.

The effect is astonishing. A dancer performing a lift is preceded and followed by multiple translucent versions of herself, each in a slightly different position. When she moves, all her ghosts move with her, each with its own lag or lead. The film is like watching a dance while also seeing every phase of its motion trailing behind and reaching ahead.

*Pas de deux* is often shown to animation students as an example of what can be done at the boundary between live-action and animated technique. It uses live dance as its material but treats time itself as animation.

# What McLaren's work teaches

McLaren teaches that animation is a medium of *time manipulation*. The frame is not just a drawing to be advanced twenty-four times a second; the frame is a moment that can be scratched, overlaid, delayed, doubled, and combined with adjacent moments to produce effects that only animation can produce.

For animators working with digital tools today, McLaren's work is a reminder that the *physical properties of the medium* — whatever the current medium is — are themselves expressive material. In McLaren's era, the physical medium was 35mm film, and he scratched it, painted on it, exposed it multiple times. Today the physical medium is often digital pixels, layers, and shaders, and the same experimental spirit applies: what happens if you manipulate the digital medium directly? What can be shown by working *with the medium* rather than through it?

McLaren's technical papers, published as internal National Film Board documents in the 1950s and 1960s, are still studied by experimental animators. His combination of technical curiosity and aesthetic seriousness set a standard that later independent animators — the Quay Brothers, Jan Švankmajer, Jodie Mack — have continued in their different ways.

# What we can do in Scheme

A small demonstration of overlaid-time animation (the *Pas de deux* trick).

```scheme
;; Given a sequence of frames, produce a new sequence where each frame is
;; overlaid with the frames a few positions before and after.

(define (overlaid-frame all-frames index)
  (let* ((n (length all-frames))
         (indices (list (max 0 (- index 6))
                        (max 0 (- index 3))
                        index
                        (min (- n 1) (+ index 3))
                        (min (- n 1) (+ index 6))))
         (frames (map (lambda (i) (list-ref all-frames i)) indices))
         (alphas '(0.2 0.4 1.0 0.4 0.2)))
    (world/reset!)
    (for-each
      (lambda (frame alpha)
        (world/place-frame frame :alpha alpha))
      frames alphas)
    (world/render!)))

(define (overlaid-time-animation frames)
  (transport/fps 24)
  (for-each
    (lambda (i)
      (overlaid-frame frames i)
      (world/wait (/ 1.0 24.0)))
    (range 0 (length frames))))
```

Each frame in the output is the center frame at full opacity, overlaid with the frames 3 and 6 positions before and after at reduced opacity. When the animation plays, the current moment is always visible clearly, but ghostly versions of adjacent moments trail behind and lead ahead. This is a Scheme approximation of McLaren's technique.

The result would be that any motion in the original animation — a walk, a jump, a wave — would appear surrounded by translucent echoes of itself. Time becomes visible.

# Recommended viewing

*Neighbours* (1952). Available from the National Film Board of Canada online archive.

*Pas de deux* (1968). Also available from NFB online.

*Blinkity Blank* (1955). Direct animation scratched onto film.

*A Chairy Tale* (1957). Live-action pixilation, this time with a chair as the antagonist.

Many of McLaren's films are freely viewable at nfb.ca (National Film Board of Canada archive).

# Sources cited

Terence Dobson, *The Film Work of Norman McLaren* (John Libbey Publishing, 2007). Standard critical monograph.

National Film Board of Canada, Norman McLaren archive. Includes technical notes, correspondence, and films.

Donald McWilliams, ed., *Norman McLaren: On the Creative Process* (National Film Board of Canada, 1991). Collection of McLaren's own writings on his technique.\"

  :notes
\"McLaren's biographical dates (1914-1987) and NFB tenure (1941-1983) are standard and verifiable. All named films (Dots, Loops, Boogie Doodle, Fiddle-de-dee, Neighbours, Pas de deux, Blinkity Blank, A Chairy Tale) exist and are documented. Neighbours won an Academy Award in 1953 for the 1952 film year — the categorization confusion is noted honestly. NFB online archive is real and does host these films for public viewing.\"

  :philosopher-weave-details
\"Peirce: direct animation as pure index — the scratches on the film ARE the physical trace of the animator's hand; there is no representation-of, only the mark itself.
Sartre: McLaren's practice as commitment to a specific medium — the animator IS what they do to the film strip.
Aristotle: time-manipulation as the animator's true material — animation is the shape of an action through time, and McLaren treated the time-shape as the primary compositional element.\"

  :tie-forward
\"The final appendix will look at contemporary independent animation and where the medium is going.\")
")

  :prose
\"Stop-motion animation is a specific physical practice. A three-dimensional object — a puppet, a clay figure, a manipulated real-world scene — is photographed. The object is moved a small amount. Another photograph is taken. Repeat many thousands of times. When the sequence of photographs is played back, the object appears to move on its own.

This is a very old technique. Georges Méliès used stop-motion for special effects in the 1890s and 1900s. Willis O'Brien pioneered stop-motion for feature films with *The Lost World* (1925) and *King Kong* (1933). Ray Harryhausen carried O'Brien's tradition into the 1950s and 1960s with a series of adventure and fantasy features (*Jason and the Argonauts*, 1963; *The 7th Voyage of Sinbad*, 1958). Every one of the mythological creatures in those films was a small puppet, animated one frame at a time.

# Ray Harryhausen and the fantastic

Harryhausen (1920-2013) called his work *Dynamation*. His technique combined stop-motion puppets with live-action footage: the puppets were animated against a rear-projected film of live actors, so the finished shot showed puppets and actors interacting as if they were in the same space. In *Jason and the Argonauts*, the famous skeleton fight took Harryhausen four months to animate — seven skeletons versus three actors, each skeleton moving independently, all synchronized to the live actors' sword-fight choreography.

Harryhausen worked mostly alone. His puppets were small — a foot or two tall. He built them from wire armatures with foam-rubber musculature and painted latex skin. He animated them by moving each puppet incrementally between exposures. A single day of work produced perhaps a few seconds of finished animation.

# The Aardman tradition

Peter Lord and David Sproxton founded Aardman Animations in Bristol, England, in 1972. Aardman developed a distinctive style using plasticine (a modeling clay) for figures and elaborate physical sets. Their television shorts of the 1980s — including *Creature Comforts* (1989), directed by Nick Park — established the studio's approach, and Park's *Wallace and Gromit* series (starting with *A Grand Day Out*, 1989) brought Aardman to worldwide attention.

Aardman's technique involves molding plasticine figures with movable armatures inside, photographing them one frame at a time, and adjusting facial expressions by hand for each frame. Each character's face is often replaced with a slightly different sculpted version for each dialogue-frame, giving the specific plasticine-fingermark quality that Aardman films are famous for. If you look closely at a Wallace and Gromit shot, you can often see the thumbprints in Wallace's face — small marks left by the animator's fingers pressing the clay into the required expression.

Aardman later made features (*Chicken Run*, 2000; *Wallace & Gromit: The Curse of the Were-Rabbit*, 2005; *Flushed Away*, 2006) and continues to produce stop-motion work into the 2020s.

# Laika and the American revival

Laika, based in Portland, Oregon and founded in 2005 as a stop-motion feature studio, has continued the practice at feature scale in the 2010s. Their films *Coraline* (2009), *ParaNorman* (2012), *The Boxtrolls* (2014), *Kubo and the Two Strings* (2016), and *Missing Link* (2019) use stop-motion combined with computer techniques for elements that would be too difficult to build physically (large-scale environmental effects, some crowd shots, digital replacement of visible armatures).

Laika's puppets are highly engineered. Each character has an armature designed for specific ranges of motion, sculpted faces printed with 3D printers so that dozens of subtly different facial expressions can be swapped in per shot, and rigging systems that hold the puppet in position between exposures. A Laika feature typically takes four to five years to produce.

# The Quay Brothers and Jan Švankmajer

At the more experimental end of stop-motion is the tradition of dark, surreal, symbol-heavy animation exemplified by the American twin brothers Stephen and Timothy Quay (working from London since the 1970s) and by the Czech animator Jan Švankmajer.

The Quays' films — *Street of Crocodiles* (1986), *The Comb* (1990), *In Absentia* (2000) among many others — use stop-motion of dolls, mannequins, dust, hair, screws, and other found objects. Their work has a specific atmosphere: unsettling, tactile, dreamlike. They are more influenced by Central European visual traditions than by American animation.

Švankmajer (born 1934), working from Prague since the 1960s, uses stop-motion of live actors, meat, clay, and everyday objects. His films (*Dimensions of Dialogue*, 1982; *Alice*, 1988; *Faust*, 1994) are politically and psychologically complex, often engaging with childhood, appetite, and totalitarianism. He is one of the most important experimental filmmakers of the second half of the twentieth century.

Both the Quays and Švankmajer show that stop-motion can be adult, complex, and deeply psychological — a medium capable of representing what other techniques cannot.

# What stop-motion has that other techniques don't

Stop-motion has specific qualities that computer animation and hand-drawn animation cannot easily replicate.

**Physical light on physical objects.** Stop-motion puppets are real objects in real space. When light falls on them, it falls with the specific physical character of real light: shadows, reflections, subsurface scattering through translucent materials. This gives stop-motion a tactile presence that hand-drawn animation cannot fully achieve and that computer animation must expensively simulate.

**Materiality.** The puppets have weight, texture, and physical mass. When they interact with other objects, they push against them. The physical interactions have a substance that drawn interactions lack.

**Fingerprints of the animator.** Because the puppets are handled by human animators, they carry marks of that handling — thumbprints in clay, wear patterns in fabric, small distortions in silhouette from being manipulated. These marks give stop-motion its characteristic hand-made quality.

**Time-heaviness.** Stop-motion is slow to produce. A minute of finished animation might take a week or two of work. This slowness is often visible in the final work — the pacing, the deliberateness, the sense that every frame was earned.

For an animator, the choice to use stop-motion is a choice for these qualities. It is not the fastest or the cheapest technique, but it produces effects that other techniques struggle to achieve.

# What we can do in Scheme

We cannot really do stop-motion in Scheme — the technique requires physical objects and cameras. But we can simulate its rhythmic characteristics.

```scheme
;; Stop-motion animation typically runs at 12 or 24 fps but each frame is a
;; discrete, held pose — no in-between motion blur. We can simulate this by
;; using stepped positions rather than continuous motion.

(define (stop-motion-step t total-time discrete-frames)
  ;; Given continuous time t, snap it to one of the discrete frames.
  (let* ((frame-duration (/ total-time discrete-frames))
         (frame-index (floor (/ t frame-duration))))
    (/ frame-index discrete-frames)))

(define (stop-motion-walk duration)
  (let ((discrete-frames 12))    ; 12 discrete poses across the walk
    (let loop ((t 0))
      (when (< t duration)
        (let* ((discrete-t (stop-motion-step t duration discrete-frames))
               (x (+ 100 (* discrete-t 400))))
          (world/reset!)
          (world/place-puppet x 300 'walking-pose (floor (* discrete-t 12)))
          (world/render!)
          (world/wait (/ 1.0 24.0))
          (loop (+ t (/ 1.0 24.0))))))))

(stop-motion-walk 3.0)
```

The character moves in discrete 'stepped' positions rather than continuously. When played back, the motion has the specific staccato character of stop-motion — the character appears to jump from one held pose to the next, with no smooth transition between. This is what stop-motion actually looks like on screen, and it is part of its charm: the visible discreteness of the frames makes the medium's physical practice legible.

# Recommended viewing

*Jason and the Argonauts* (1963). Harryhausen's skeleton fight.

*Wallace & Gromit: The Wrong Trousers* (Nick Park, 1993). Aardman's most complete early masterpiece.

*Coraline* (Henry Selick, 2009). Laika's first feature; a serious dark fantasy for children.

*Kubo and the Two Strings* (Travis Knight, 2016). Laika at its most ambitious.

*Street of Crocodiles* (Quay Brothers, 1986). Twenty minutes of dark, tactile, sound-designed stop-motion.

*Dimensions of Dialogue* (Švankmajer, 1982). One of the most technically inventive short animated films ever made.

# Sources cited

Ken A. Priebe, *The Advanced Art of Stop-Motion Animation* (Cengage Learning, 2011).

Peter Lord and Brian Sibley, *Cracking Animation: The Aardman Book of 3-D Animation* (Thames & Hudson, 1998; later editions).

Julius Wiedemann, ed., *Animation Now!* (Taschen, 2004). Overview of contemporary independent animation.

Michael Brooke, *The Quay Brothers* (Illuminations Films documentary, 2000).\"

\"All named individuals (Harryhausen, Peter Lord, David Sproxton, Nick Park, Quay Brothers, Švankmajer, Willis O'Brien, Méliès) and studios (Aardman, Laika) are historically documented with their films and dates. King Kong (1933) O'Brien attribution is standard. Jason and the Argonauts (1963) Harryhausen skeleton fight is famous and documented. All films cited are widely-verifiable via their studios' or directors' filmographies. Aardman and Laika treated as artistic movements rather than corporate entities; specific film credits (directors) attributed correctly.\"

  :philosopher-weave-details
\"Aristotle: stop-motion as an action executed through many small acts, each a physical intervention.
Sartre: the animator's being is the puppet's being — the puppet moves because the animator moved it, in a very direct sense.
Peirce: the puppet on film as index — the physical trace of the animator's hand is captured directly on the film.
Wittgenstein-late: stop-motion as a distinct language-game the audience learns to read — the stepped motion is not a flaw but a feature the medium teaches its viewers to enjoy.\"
