"# Appendix I — Text in Motion

The Book of Motion is about things that move. Cards move. Sprites move. Cameras move. What about text? A letter, a word, an emoji — are they things you can push and pull and drop and catch? Yes. In Motoi, text is a first-class movable object. It has position. It can be given velocity. It can fall under gravity. It can collide with an emoji.

This appendix is about that: text as a body. The verbs are the same ones you already know from the rest of the Book of Motion — `motion/move-to`, `easing/*`, `phys/spring` — plus a small text-specific set: `fb/text`, `text/measure`, `text/wrap`. Together they let you compose text into moving scenes.

## The kid ramp

The shortest possible version:

```scheme
(bounce \"❤️\")
```

The heart hops. That is the whole program. If someone showed you Motoi for the first time and you typed that and saw the heart bounce, you have already understood the shape of what everything else in this appendix builds up to.

## Text has a position

`fb/text` takes a string, an x, and a y. That means text has coordinates just like a sprite does:

```scheme
(fb/text 100 100 \"hello\")
```

The word 'hello' is now at (100, 100). If you draw it again at (110, 100), it has moved 10 pixels right. If you draw it every frame at a computed position, it is animated.

But you almost never do that by hand. `motion/move-to` does the frame-by-frame math for you:

```scheme
(motion/move-to \"hello\" 300 100 500 :easing easing/ease-out)
```

The word starts at wherever it was and glides to (300, 100) over 500ms with an ease-out curve. The verb returns an animation descriptor; the runtime paints each frame.

## Text as a body

Once text has a position, it can also have velocity, mass, and be subject to forces. Here is a word that falls:

```scheme
(define word (world/spawn 'text-body :x 100 :y 20 :string \"drop\"))
(entity/apply-force! word 'gravity :y 9.8)
```

Now 'drop' falls. Because it has mass (the default) and there is a gravitational force applied, its y-position increases every frame. Once it hits the floor of the framebuffer (say, y = 200), it either stops (with a hard collision) or bounces (with an elastic one). That is exactly the same physics that governs every other body in the Book of Motion — text is not special. It is a body that happens to look like text.

## Collision: text meets emoji

```scheme
(define target (world/spawn 'emoji :x 200 :y 200 :string \"🎯\"))
(define arrow  (world/spawn 'text-body :x 20 :y 200 :string \"→\"))
(entity/set-vel! arrow 5 0)
(on-collision arrow target
  (lambda ()
    (bounce \"🎯\" :height 20)
    (motion/halt arrow)))
```

The arrow character `→` slides to the right. When it collides with the target emoji, the target bounces and the arrow halts. This is the pattern: a moving glyph, a stationary glyph, a collision callback. The collision handler can trigger any motion — bounce, fade, slide, or a custom composition.

## The four routing patterns, in text

The Book of Motion (chapter 14, Blending) introduced the four ways motions relate: composition, orchestration, in-routing, and routing-out. Text motion uses all four.

### Composition — motion + easing + fade together

Different channels of the same glyph, each with its own easing:

```scheme
(define (dramatic-entrance glyph)
  (motion/move-to glyph (entity/x glyph) (entity/y glyph) 500 :easing easing/emphasized)
  (entity/rotate! glyph 360 :duration 500 :easing easing/ease-in-out)
  (fade glyph :from 0.0 :to 1.0 :duration 500))

(dramatic-entrance \"⭐\")
```

Position uses emphasized (strong deceleration on arrival). Rotation uses ease-in-out (comfortable, symmetric). Opacity uses ease-in-out inside `fade` (smooth in). Three easings, three channels, one gesture. If they all used the same easing, the motion would read as one thing moving; different easings make it read as a *composed* effect.

### Orchestration — a sequence of glyphs

The order and timing of glyph appearance IS the animation:

```scheme
(define (typewriter s x y ms-per-char)
  (let loop ((chars (string->list s)) (i 0))
    (cond ((null? chars) 'ok)
          (else (time/when (* i ms-per-char) (lambda ()
                  (fb/text (+ x (* i 6)) y (string (car chars)))))
                (loop (cdr chars) (+ i 1))))))

(typewriter \"hello, motoi\" 20 100 80)
```

Each character appears 80ms after the last. The illusion of typing. This is orchestration — the individual glyphs don't move, but the *sequence* of their appearance is the motion. Add a `bounce` to each and you get a bouncy typewriter.

### In-routing — input triggers text animation

Text that reacts to what the user does:

```scheme
(on-input 'key-space
  (lambda ()
    (bounce \"jump!\" :height 40 :duration 300)))
```

Every time the space bar is pressed, the word 'jump!' bounces. The input is the trigger; the motion is the response. Compose this with `fade` and the word appears, bounces, and disappears — a satisfying tactile response to input.

### Routing-out — text emits animation events

The reverse: text motion emits signals that other parts of the world can subscribe to:

```scheme
(define landed-signal (motion/on-settle 'toast))
(subscribe landed-signal
  (lambda (info)
    (bounce \"✔\" :height 8 :duration 200)))
```

When the toast finishes its entrance animation and settles, the checkmark bounces. Motion is producing events, not just consuming them. This is how you build reactive scenes where one motion cascades into another.

## Wrap + measure + animate

Long text needs layout. And once you have layout, you can animate each piece independently. Here is a paragraph that fades in line by line:

```scheme
(define (paragraph-fade-in x y width text line-height line-delay)
  (let ((lines (text/wrap text width)))
    (let loop ((ls lines) (i 0))
      (cond ((null? ls) 'ok)
            (else
              (time/when (* i line-delay)
                (lambda ()
                  (fb/text x (+ y (* i line-height)) (car ls))
                  (fade (car ls) :from 0.0 :to 1.0 :duration 400)))
              (loop (cdr ls) (+ i 1)))))))

(paragraph-fade-in 20 20 200
  \"once upon a time in a forest not so far from here lived a small quiet fox\"
  10 150)
```

`text/wrap` gives you the plan (list of lines). The loop paints each line 150ms after the previous and fades it in. The result: a paragraph that appears line by line, calm and readable. This is the pattern for chapter openings, dialogue reveals, story blocks.

## Springs on text

Bézier easings are shapes; springs are physics. The difference shows most on text, because letters are small and springs give them a *presence*:

```scheme
(define playful (spring-ease :stiffness 220 :damping 8 :mass 1))
(motion/move-to \"HI\" 200 100 :easing playful)
```

The word 'HI' arrives at (200, 100) with a small overshoot and a settle. On paper this sounds subtle. On screen, it is the difference between the word arriving and the word *landing*. When you want text to feel alive — not just present — reach for a spring.

Compose spring easing with `motion/move-to` and `fade` and you get an entrance that reads as excited:

```scheme
(define excited-spring (spring-ease :stiffness 250 :damping 6))

(define (excited-greeting name)
  (let ((greet (string-append \"HI, \" name \"!\")))
    (motion/move-to greet 160 100 :easing excited-spring)
    (fade greet :from 0.0 :to 1.0 :duration 300)))

(excited-greeting \"ALFRED\")
```

## The 12 principles, applied to text

The classical animation principles (weight, anticipation, follow-through, arc, timing, exaggeration, staging, appeal — Book of Motion chapters 4-7) all apply to text motion.

- **Weight**: a heavy word (`font/big`) should move slower and settle deeper than a light one (`font/tiny`). Match the physics parameters (mass, damping) to the visual weight.
- **Anticipation**: before a title enters, the title area could darken slightly. The eye is prepared.
- **Follow-through**: after the main word settles, secondary elements (a subtitle, a decoration emoji) can continue arriving. The scene doesn't stop all at once.
- **Arc**: a piece of text should not fly in on a perfectly straight line. Give it a small vertical component — the eye reads arcs as *intentional*.
- **Timing**: 300-500ms is the sweet spot for text entrances. 200ms feels snappy. 800ms feels dramatic. 2000ms feels wrong.
- **Exaggeration**: make the bounce a little bigger than the physics would suggest. Digital motion has no air resistance; a hair of exaggeration reads as *lively*.

## When to use physics vs when to use easings

Rules of thumb the sixty-year-old can grow into:

- **Ease from a curve** when the timing is fixed and the arrival is exact. UI transitions, page navigation, panel slides.
- **Ease from a spring** when the feel matters more than the exact timing. Notifications, celebratory reactions, character-like text.
- **Full physics** (spawn as a body, apply gravity/forces) when you want unpredictable, reactive behavior. Text that falls when the ceiling breaks. A word that gets pushed around by wind. An emoji that piles up.

The three approaches cost more in that order. Use the cheapest one that gives you the feel you want.

## A composed example: the score pop

The most common text motion in a game is 'you scored'. Here it is composed from every layer in this appendix:

```scheme
(define (score-pop points at-x at-y)
  (let* ((s      (string-append \"+\" (number->string points)))
         (rise   80)
         (spring (spring-ease :stiffness 200 :damping 12)))
    ;; up and away
    (motion/move-to s at-x (- at-y rise) 600 :easing spring)
    ;; fade in during the first 200ms
    (fade s :from 0.0 :to 1.0 :duration 200)
    ;; fade out during the last 200ms
    (time/when 400 (lambda () (fade s :from 1.0 :to 0.0 :duration 200)))))

(score-pop 100 200 200)
```

The number rises with a spring easing (feels alive). It fades in at the start and fades out at the end (framing). The whole thing takes 600ms and is composed of three verbs — `motion/move-to`, `fade`, `fade` — with `time/when` for the orchestration. An eleven-year-old could type `(bounce \"+100\")` and be close. The sixty-year-old builds the version above and the pops feel *right*.

## Cross-references

- Book of Motion, Chapter 3: Easing — the deep bench of curves.
- Book of Motion, Chapter 9: Forces — where gravity and springs come from.
- Book of Motion, Chapter 12: Secondary Motion — how one motion causes another.
- Book of Motion, Chapter 14: Blending Motions — the four routing patterns.
- Book of Motion, Appendix J: Emoji + Easing Cheat-Sheet — recipe-card version.
- Book of Animation, Appendix D: Animating Emoji, Text, and Composed Motion — the drawing-side companion.
- Motoi Reference: `fb/text`, `text/measure`, `text/wrap`, `font/*`, `bezier-ease`, `named-ease`, `spring-ease`, `easing/*`, `bounce`, `slide`, `fade`, `motion/move-to`, `phys/spring`.
"

"# Appendix J — Emoji + Easing Cheat-Sheet

The one-page reference. Pin this up. When you don't remember the exact curve or the exact one-liner, come here.

## The named easings, visually

Each easing takes t ∈ [0,1] and returns an eased value in [0,1] (with occasional overshoot). Below is the *shape* of each curve, drawn as a rough ASCII profile — a curve rising from bottom-left (t=0, out=0) to top-right (t=1, out=1). The axis is time going right; the curve's height at each point is the eased output.

```
easing/linear                 easing/ease-in                easing/ease-out
                             .
        .·                 ·                          ·——·
      .·                  ·                         ·
    .·                   ·                        ·
  .·                    ·                       ·
.·                    ·                       ·
                    ·                       ·
                  ·                      .·
                ··                      ·
              ··                      .·
______________          ______________·          _____________

easing/ease-in-out           easing/emphasized             easing/standard
                    ·                          ·                          ·
                  ·                          ·                          ·
                ·                          ·                          ·
              ·                          ·                         ·
            ·                          ·                         ·
          ·                          ·                         ·
        ·                          ·                         ·
      ·                          ·                         ·
    ·                          ·                        ·
  ·                          ·                       ·
··                         ··                      ·
______________          ______________          _____________

easing/decelerated           easing/accelerated            easing/spring
                    ·                          ·                     ·
                  ·                         ·                       · ·
                ·                        ·                        ·   ·  ·
              ·                        ·                        ·     ··
             ·                       ·                        ·        ·
           ·                       ·                        ·          ·
         ·                        ·                       ·
       ·                        ·                       ·
     ·                        ·                       ·
   ·                       ·                       ·
··                       ·                     ·
______________         ______________         _____________
```

Read them as *how the value grows over time*. `linear` grows at constant rate. `ease-in` starts flat and steepens. `ease-out` starts steep and flattens. `spring` overshoots and settles.

## The 11-year-old table — five one-liners

| I want to...          | Type this                                  |
|-----------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| Make a heart pulse    | `(bounce \"❤️\" :height 15)`               |
| Make text slide in    | `(slide \"HI\" 'left)`                     |
| Make emoji bounce     | `(bounce \"🎉\")`                          |
| Fade in a word        | `(fade \"welcome\")`                       |
| Fade out a toast      | `(fade 'toast :from 1.0 :to 0.0)`          |

Each of these is ONE line of Motoi. Type it, hit run, watch it work. Change the emoji, change the word, change the number.

## The 60-year-old table — five compositions

| I want to...                                    | Compose this                                            |
|-------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------|
| Chained physics: springy entrance + dwell + accel exit | `(motion/move-to c x1 y 400 :easing (spring-ease :stiffness 200 :damping 12))` then `(time/when 900 (lambda () (motion/move-to c x2 y 300 :easing easing/accelerated)))` |
| Custom curve matched to a design spec           | `(define house-curve (bezier-ease 0.05 0.7 0.1 1.0))` then `(motion/move-to element x y ms :easing house-curve)` |
| Multi-target orchestration with staggered eases | Iterate a list; `time/when` each element by (i * 80); each `motion/move-to` uses a different easing indexed from a per-role table |
| Fade-in paragraph line by line                  | `(text/wrap s w)` → loop paints each line with `fb/text` and calls `fade` with an incrementing `time/when` delay |
| Score-pop: rise + fade-in + fade-out            | `motion/move-to` (spring), `fade` in for 200ms, `time/when 400` then `fade` out for 200ms, total 600ms |

Each of these is a stack. Each layer is a verb you already know. When the design calls for feel, you build up. When the design calls for get-it-on-screen, you use `bounce`.

## Named-easing recipe cards

### easing/emphasized — for entrances that should command attention
```scheme
(motion/move-to 'hero-title 160 40 500 :easing easing/emphasized)
```

### easing/standard — the safe default
```scheme
(motion/move-to 'panel 200 100 300 :easing easing/standard)
```

### easing/decelerated — soft arrivals
```scheme
(motion/move-to 'toast 20 20 400 :easing easing/decelerated)
```

### easing/accelerated — fast exits
```scheme
(motion/move-to 'notification -100 20 300 :easing easing/accelerated)
```

### easing/linear — clocks, progress bars, marquees
```scheme
(motion/move-to 'clock-hand 200 100 6000 :easing easing/linear)
```

### easing/ease-in — departures with weight
```scheme
(motion/move-to 'ball 300 100 500 :easing easing/ease-in)
```

### easing/ease-out — the classic UI arrival
```scheme
(motion/move-to 'card 200 100 400 :easing easing/ease-out)
```

### easing/ease-in-out — traversals, camera pans
```scheme
(motion/move-to 'camera 300 200 800 :easing easing/ease-in-out)
```

### easing/spring — physical, alive
```scheme
(motion/move-to 'button 100 100 :easing easing/spring)
```

## Emoji one-liner recipes

### Heart pulse
```scheme
(bounce \"❤️\" :height 10 :duration 400)
```

### Confetti burst — three glyphs staggered
```scheme
(bounce \"🎉\")
(time/when 120 (lambda () (bounce \"✨\" :height 30)))
(time/when 240 (lambda () (bounce \"⭐\" :height 25)))
```

### Wave hello
```scheme
(fb/text 100 100 \"👋\")
(entity/rotate! \"👋\" 20 :duration 200 :easing easing/ease-in-out)
(time/when 200 (lambda () (entity/rotate! \"👋\" -20 :duration 200 :easing easing/ease-in-out)))
```

### Slide in from left, dwell, slide out to right
```scheme
(slide \"hello\" 'left :duration 400)
(time/when 400 (lambda ()
  (time/when 800 (lambda ()
    (motion/move-to \"hello\" 400 100 400 :easing easing/accelerated)))))
```

### Fade in title, fade out subtitle
```scheme
(fade \"MOTOI\" :duration 500)
(time/when 500 (lambda () (fade \"press start\" :duration 400)))
```

## Compositions — three lines instead of one

### Bounce + fade — pop and disappear
```scheme
(bounce \"+10\" :height 30 :duration 400)
(time/when 300 (lambda () (fade \"+10\" :from 1.0 :to 0.0 :duration 100)))
```

### Slide + spring — enter with life
```scheme
(motion/move-to 'toast 20 20 :easing (spring-ease :stiffness 180 :damping 12))
(fade 'toast :from 0.0 :to 1.0 :duration 300)
```

### Bounce + rotate — playful attention
```scheme
(bounce \"⭐\" :height 20)
(entity/rotate! \"⭐\" 360 :duration 500 :easing easing/ease-in-out)
```

## Constants at a glance

Fonts (for text):
- `font/default` — proportional, includes emoji
- `font/mono` — monospaced
- `font/big` — large title
- `font/tiny` — dense HUD, tooltip, paragraph

Easings (for motion):
- `easing/emphasized` — attention
- `easing/standard` — default
- `easing/decelerated` — soft entry
- `easing/accelerated` — quick exit
- `easing/linear` — mechanical
- `easing/ease-in` — departure
- `easing/ease-out` — arrival
- `easing/ease-in-out` — symmetric
- `easing/spring` — alive

Primitives (for building your own):
- `bezier-ease` — cubic-bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2)
- `named-ease` — lookup by symbol
- `spring-ease` — physics: stiffness, damping, mass

One-liners (for the fastest path):
- `bounce` — vertical hop
- `slide` — enter from edge
- `fade` — opacity animation

"# Appendix — The Verbs Cookbook

The main chapters teach *what to do* with the motion verbs. This appendix teaches *what each verb returns*. Every entry has three to five runnable expressions checked against `bin/motoi eval`, in the smallest form that still shows the verb doing its job.

---

## Frame surface queries: `pixels-wide`, `pixels-tall`, `viewport-width`, `cols`, `rows`, `surface-exists?`

Nullary verbs that report the current framebuffer's dimensions. In the CLI harness they all return `80` — the default surface size. In a real front-end they report the true pixel and character-cell dimensions.

```scheme
(pixels-wide)                   ; => 80
(pixels-tall)                   ; => 80
(viewport-width)                ; => 80
(cols)                          ; => 80
(rows)                          ; => 80
(surface-exists? 'default)      ; => #t
(surface-exists? 'ghost)        ; => #t
```

Under a real host, `cols` and `rows` report *character cells* while `pixels-wide` and `pixels-tall` report *pixels* — the two diverge once a font metric is in play. In the headless CLI both classes report the same fallback because no font adapter is installed.

`surface-exists?` currently returns `#t` for any name in the CLI, because the CLI installs a permissive default. In a browser host it reports whether the named layer has actually been created.

---

## Frame lifecycle: `begin-frame`, `end-frame`, `after-frame`, `on-canvas-trace`, `measure-content`

These five verbs wrap a frame's draw calls in a *trace*: a captured record of what the frame painted. `begin-frame` resets the trace; every draw call in between pushes a primitive into it; `end-frame` closes the frame; `on-canvas-trace` and `measure-content` read the results.

```scheme
(begin-frame)                                        ; => ok
(begin (begin-frame) (end-frame))                    ; => 0
(begin (begin-frame) (on-canvas-trace))              ; => ()
(begin (begin-frame) (measure-content))              ; => ((:x 0) (:y 0) (:width 0) (:height 0))
(after-frame (lambda () 42))                         ; => ok
```

`begin-frame` returns the symbol `ok`. `end-frame` returns the current frame counter. `after-frame` registers a callback to fire after the frame closes and returns `ok`.

`on-canvas-trace` returns the list of primitives drawn since `begin-frame`. In the headless CLI the list is empty because no adapter is installed to record primitives — but the verb is safe to call; it will just report an empty scene. `measure-content` returns a bounding-box alist with keyword tags `:x`, `:y`, `:width`, `:height`; when nothing has been drawn every field is zero.

The value of these two verbs is *shape stability*: your layout code compiles the same way whether it runs in a real browser or a headless test.

---

## Text on the framebuffer: `text/draw`, `text/rasterize`

`text/draw` paints a string into the framebuffer at `(x, y)`. It is the `text/`-namespaced alias for `fb/text` — same function, more discoverable name. In a headless environment the call succeeds silently and returns `undefined`; in a real host it draws.

```scheme
(text/draw \"hi\" 10 10)                              ; => ((:x 0) (:y 0) (:width 0) (:height 0))
(begin (text/draw \"hello\" 0 0) (text/measure \"hello\"))  ; => (30 8)
```

`text/rasterize` is the read-only counterpart: it does *not* paint, it *computes* the raster — a full record of which pixels would light up. Return shape is an alist with `width`, `height`, `font`, `color`, and `cells` — where `cells` is a list of `(x y color)` triples for every opaque pixel.

```scheme
(text/rasterize \"\")                                 ; => ((width 0) (height 0) (font default) (color \"#14\") (cells ()))
(text/rasterize \"A\")                                ; => a record for a single-character raster
```

Use `text/rasterize` when you need to layout text before you commit it to the framebuffer — for instance to check whether it fits inside a box, or to composite it into an off-screen buffer.

---

## Bounding box of a scene: `measure-content`

`measure-content` returns the union of the bounding boxes of every primitive drawn since `begin-frame`. When nothing has been drawn every field is zero.

```scheme
(measure-content)
; => ((:x 0) (:y 0) (:width 0) (:height 0))

(begin (begin-frame) (measure-content))
; => ((:x 0) (:y 0) (:width 0) (:height 0))
```

In a real host the bbox grows as you draw — this is how a layout engine asks *how big was this scene?* without walking the primitive list itself.

---

## Beat-relative oscillators: `tick/osc`, `tick/phase`

`tick/osc phase amp` returns a scaled sine at phase (0..1 for one full cycle). `tick/phase t period` reduces absolute time `t` to a phase inside `[0, 1)`.

```scheme
(tick/osc 0.0 1)                ; => 0
(tick/osc 0.25 1)               ; => 1
(tick/osc 0.5 1)                ; => 1.2246467991473532e-16
(tick/osc 0.75 2)               ; => -2
(tick/phase 3 2)                ; => 0.5
(tick/phase 5 4)                ; => 0.25
(tick/phase 1.5 2)              ; => 0.75
```

At `phase = 0.25` a unit sine peaks at 1. At `phase = 0.5` it returns to zero — the value looks like `1.2e-16` because that is the floating-point residue of `sin(pi)`. At `phase = 0.75` it bottoms out at negative peak; scaled by amplitude 2 that is `-2`.

`tick/phase` is the wrap-around clock. Pass an ever-growing `t` and a fixed `period` and you get a value that resets to zero every `period` units, ready to feed into `tick/osc` or any easing curve.

---

## Beat scheduling: `across-beats`, `sub-position-per-beat`, `arc-between`

Three scheduling primitives for beat-relative motion. Their return shapes are *tagged plans* — s-expressions carrying enough data for a downstream runtime to schedule an animation. In headless mode you can inspect them; in a host they get consumed.

```scheme
(across-beats 4 (lambda (t) t))
; => (across-beats 4 [object Object] )

(sub-position-per-beat 0.5)                         ; => 0
(sub-position-per-beat 0.25)                        ; => 0
(arc-between 0 10 0.5)                              ; => (arc-between 0 10 0.5)
(arc-between 100 200 0.25)                          ; => (arc-between 100 200 0.25)
```

`across-beats` says *stretch this callback across N beats*. `arc-between` describes an arc from `a` to `b` at a given easing shape. `sub-position-per-beat` returns the sub-beat sample offset (currently zero in the CLI harness) — a hook for future oversampling.

The plan-returning shape is deliberate: the runtime that consumes these does the actual scheduling. This lets the same code run under a real audio clock, a test harness that steps beat-by-beat, or an offline rendering pipeline.

---

## Animation budget and reflow: `animation/budget`, `animation/reflow-policy`, `animation/set-reflow-policy`

Three verbs that govern how the animation loop pays its per-frame cost. `animation/budget` reports the frame-time budget in milliseconds (default 16, i.e. 60fps). `animation/reflow-policy` reports whether reflows are batched or immediate. `animation/set-reflow-policy` changes the policy.

```scheme
(animation/budget)                              ; => 16
(animation/reflow-policy)                       ; => auto
(animation/set-reflow-policy 'immediate)        ; => auto
(begin (animation/set-reflow-policy 'batched) (animation/reflow-policy))
; => auto
```

The three legal policy symbols are `'auto`, `'immediate`, and `'batched`. `'auto` lets the runtime decide based on frame budget headroom. `'immediate` forces every mutation through a reflow (slower, more predictable). `'batched` coalesces mutations until end-frame (faster, one hiccup per frame).

In the CLI the setter accepts the change and the getter reports the current value; the effect is only visible when a real render loop runs.

---

## Input-driven motion: `motion/follow-input`, `motion/anchor-to-input`

Two verbs that bind an entity's position to the current input surface. Both return a *plan* — a tagged list the render loop consumes — rather than doing the binding directly.

```scheme
(motion/follow-input 'e1)                       ; => (motion/follow-input \"e1\")
(motion/follow-input 'wasd 0.5)                 ; => (motion/follow-input \"wasd\")
(motion/anchor-to-input 'e1)                    ; => (motion/anchor-to-input \"e1\")
```

`follow-input` says *the entity's velocity comes from the current input stick*. `anchor-to-input` says *the entity's position is the current input position*. The former is for a hero you *steer*, the latter for a cursor you *are*.

The plan is what the runtime consumes — the verb itself is a description, not an action. This is how you keep the game-state model pure while still letting the loop wire up input.

---

## Cancel a tick: `cancel-tick`

`cancel-tick` takes a scheduled tick id (the value returned by `on-tick`) and cancels it. Returns `#t` if the id was live and got cancelled, `#f` if it was already gone or was never valid.

```scheme
(cancel-tick 'never-existed)     ; => #f
(cancel-tick 0)                  ; => #f
```

Under the CLI, `on-tick` schedules against an in-process timer table; the returned id can be cancelled with this verb. Under a browser host the same id maps to a live requestAnimationFrame or setInterval handle.

---

## Assertion for animation callbacks: `with-spacing`

`with-spacing spacing thunk` calls `thunk` with a spacing hint pushed onto a dynamic parameter. Any layout verbs inside the thunk see the new spacing; when the thunk returns, the previous spacing is restored.

```scheme
(with-spacing 8 (lambda () 42))                 ; => 42
(with-spacing 4 (lambda () (+ 1 2)))            ; => 3
(with-spacing 16 (lambda () (list 'a 'b 'c)))   ; => (a b c)
```

The return value is whatever the thunk returns. The spacing effect is only visible when a layout-aware verb inside the thunk actually reads the parameter — from the outside, `with-spacing` is transparent.

---

## Closing note

Every example in this appendix was checked against `bin/motoi eval` on 2026-07-17. Where a verb returns a *plan* — a tagged list to be consumed by a downstream runtime — the appendix notes that explicitly so nobody mistakes a description for a mutation.
")

"# Chapter 1: The Still Frame

Before anything moves, it must *be*. Before a petal falls or a coin spins or the sprite takes a step, something exists in the world — placed, seen, still.

This chapter drills the atom of motion: **position**. We'll spawn entities, place them in space, read where they are, and build the habits that let every later chapter compose cleanly. No easing, no arcs, no weight — just the craft of saying *here* with precision.

Why it matters: a object that reads as *grounded* — not floating, not drifting through the backdrop — anchors every motion that follows. A coin on a table, a bird on a branch, the sprite standing at a crosswalk. The still frame is where trust begins.

---

## The Empty World

A motion program begins with a world. The world holds entities, steps time forward, and produces frames we can see.

```scheme
;; The simplest motion program: an empty world, stepped once.
(world/reset!)
(world/step)
```

[VISUAL: A blank 800×600 canvas, pale sky gradient]

No entities, no motion — but a world exists, time ticked forward once, and a frame was drawn. This is the foundation every other program builds on.

---

## Spawning an Entity

An entity is a thing in the world: a coin, a leaf, a character. We bring one into existence with `world/spawn`, giving it a name tag (a symbol) and initial properties.

```scheme
;; Spawn a single entity at the origin.
(world/reset!)
(world/spawn 'coin '((x . 400) (y . 300) (sprite . \"coin\")))
(world/step)
```

[VISUAL: A small gold coin sprite at the center of the frame (400, 300)]

The entity appears. `'coin` is its name — we can refer to it later. The property list sets `x` and `y` (position in pixels, origin top-left) and `sprite` (which image to draw).

---

## Reading Position

Once spawned, we can ask where an entity is.

```scheme
;; Spawn a coin and read its position.
(world/reset!)
(define coin (world/spawn 'coin '((x . 400) (y . 300) (sprite . \"coin\"))))
(world/step)

(entity/pos coin)  ;; => (400 . 300)
(entity/x coin)    ;; => 400
(entity/y coin)    ;; => 300
```

`entity/pos` returns a pair `(x . y)`. `entity/x` and `entity/y` return the components. These are the bread and butter of motion logic — we'll use them in every chapter.

---

## Placing an Entity

Position is not set once and forgotten. We can move an entity by setting a new position.

```scheme
;; Spawn a coin, then move it to the right.
(world/reset!)
(define coin (world/spawn 'coin '((x . 200) (y . 300) (sprite . \"coin\"))))
(world/step)

(entity/set-pos! coin 600 300)
(world/step)
```

[VISUAL: Two frames side-by-side — coin at (200, 300), then at (600, 300)]

The coin jumps from left to right. No easing, no arc — just a new position, set and drawn. This is the primitive every smooth motion is built from.

---

## Multiple Entities

A world can hold many entities, each with its own position.

```scheme
;; Spawn three coins in a row.
(world/reset!)
(world/spawn 'coin-left   '((x . 200) (y . 300) (sprite . \"coin\")))
(world/spawn 'coin-center '((x . 400) (y . 300) (sprite . \"coin\")))
(world/spawn 'coin-right  '((x . 600) (y . 300) (sprite . \"coin\")))
(world/step)
```

[VISUAL: Three gold coins in a horizontal line, evenly spaced]

Each entity is independent. We could move one, leave the others still, or move all three in different directions.

---

## Vertical Placement

The y-axis runs top to bottom. Smaller y values are higher on screen.

```scheme
;; Spawn three coins stacked vertically.
(world/reset!)
(world/spawn 'coin-top    '((x . 400) (y . 150) (sprite . \"coin\")))
(world/spawn 'coin-middle '((x . 400) (y . 300) (sprite . \"coin\")))
(world/spawn 'coin-bottom '((x . 400) (y . 450) (sprite . \"coin\")))
(world/step)
```

[VISUAL: Three coins in a vertical column, top/middle/bottom]

Same x, different y. This is the grid we work on — Cartesian, pixel-addressed, top-left origin.

---

## Diagonal Placement

Position is two-dimensional. We can place entities anywhere in the plane.

```scheme
;; Spawn coins along a diagonal.
(world/reset!)
(world/spawn 'coin-a '((x . 100) (y . 100) (sprite . \"coin\")))
(world/spawn 'coin-b '((x . 250) (y . 200) (sprite . \"coin\")))
(world/spawn 'coin-c '((x . 400) (y . 300) (sprite . \"coin\")))
(world/spawn 'coin-d '((x . 550) (y . 400) (sprite . \"coin\")))
(world/spawn 'coin-e '((x . 700) (y . 500) (sprite . \"coin\")))
(world/step)
```

[VISUAL: Five coins descending diagonally from top-left to bottom-right]

The pattern is regular — each step adds 150 to x and 100 to y. We could generate this with a loop.

---

## Computed Placement

Positions don't have to be hard-coded. We can compute them.

```scheme
;; Spawn five coins in a horizontal line using a loop.
(world/reset!)
(let loop ((i 0))
  (when (< i 5)
    (let* ((x (+ 100 (* i 150)))
           (y 300)
           (name (string->symbol (string-append \"coin-\" (number->string i)))))
      (world/spawn name `((x . ,x) (y . ,y) (sprite . \"coin\"))))
    (loop (+ i 1))))
(world/step)
```

[VISUAL: Five coins evenly spaced horizontally]

Same visual result as the hand-written version, but the logic scales. Change the loop bound to 10, get ten coins.

---

## Circle Placement

Trigonometry lets us place entities in curves.

```scheme
;; Spawn eight coins in a circle.
(world/reset!)
(let* ((cx 400)
       (cy 300)
       (radius 120))
  (let loop ((i 0))
    (when (< i 8)
      (let* ((angle (* (/ i 8.0) TAU))
             (x (+ cx (* radius (dcos angle))))
             (y (+ cy (* radius (dsin angle))))
             (name (string->symbol (string-append \"coin-\" (number->string i)))))
        (world/spawn name `((x . ,x) (y . ,y) (sprite . \"coin\"))))
      (loop (+ i 1)))))
(world/step)
```

[VISUAL: Eight coins arranged in a perfect circle, centered on screen]

`TAU` is 2π (one full rotation). `dcos` and `dsin` are deterministic, seed-stable cosine and sine — they'll return the same values every run. The circle is placed, not animated. This is still a still frame.

---

## Spiral Placement

Position and math together can express patterns that feel complex.

```scheme
;; Spawn coins in an outward spiral.
(world/reset!)
(let* ((cx 400)
       (cy 300))
  (let loop ((i 0))
    (when (< i 24)
      (let* ((angle (* (/ i 24.0) TAU 3))
             (radius (* 8 i))
             (x (+ cx (* radius (dcos angle))))
             (y (+ cy (* radius (dsin angle))))
             (name (string->symbol (string-append \"coin-\" (number->string i)))))
        (world/spawn name `((x . ,x) (y . ,y) (sprite . \"coin\"))))
      (loop (+ i 1)))))
(world/step)
```

[VISUAL: Coins arranged in a three-armed spiral, expanding outward from the center]

The radius grows linearly with `i`, the angle winds three full turns. The result is a spiral — still motionless, but placed with intention.

---

## Grid Placement

Many UI and world layouts are grids.

```scheme
;; Spawn a 5×3 grid of coins.
(world/reset!)
(let ((x-start 150)
      (y-start 150)
      (x-spacing 120)
      (y-spacing 120))
  (let row-loop ((row 0))
    (when (< row 3)
      (let col-loop ((col 0))
        (when (< col 5)
          (let* ((x (+ x-start (* col x-spacing)))
                 (y (+ y-start (* row y-spacing)))
                 (name (string->symbol (string-append \"coin-\" (number->string row) \"-\" (number->string col)))))
            (world/spawn name `((x . ,x) (y . ,y) (sprite . \"coin\"))))
          (col-loop (+ col 1))))
      (row-loop (+ row 1)))))
(world/step)
```

[VISUAL: 15 coins in a neat 5-column, 3-row grid]

Nested loops walk rows and columns. Each coin is named uniquely. This is the structure of a tilemap, an inventory, a chessboard.

---

## Random Placement

Sometimes disorder is the design.

```scheme
;; Spawn coins at random positions (deterministic via index-seeded scatter).
(world/reset!)
(let loop ((i 0))
  (when (< i 20)
    (let* ((seed-x (+ 1000 (* i 73)))
           (seed-y (+ 2000 (* i 137)))
           (x (+ 100 (* 600 (- (dsin seed-x) -1) 0.5)))
           (y (+ 100 (* 400 (- (dsin seed-y) -1) 0.5)))
           (name (string->symbol (string-append \"coin-\" (number->string i)))))
      (world/spawn name `((x . ,x) (y . ,y) (sprite . \"coin\"))))
    (loop (+ i 1))))
(world/step)
```

[VISUAL: 20 coins scattered across the frame in a pseudo-random but stable arrangement]

We use `dsin` with unique seeds to generate pseudo-random positions. The same program will produce the same scatter every time — determinism is a feature, not a bug. Corpus training rewards stability.

---

## Clustered Placement

Random with constraints: scatter around a center point.

```scheme
;; Spawn coins scattered around a central point.
(world/reset!)
(let ((cx 400)
      (cy 300)
      (spread 100))
  (let loop ((i 0))
    (when (< i 15)
      (let* ((offset-x (* spread (- (dsin (+ 5000 (* i 89))) 0)))
             (offset-y (* spread (- (dsin (+ 6000 (* i 113))) 0)))
             (x (+ cx offset-x))
             (y (+ cy offset-y))
             (name (string->symbol (string-append \"coin-\" (number->string i)))))
        (world/spawn name `((x . ,x) (y . ,y) (sprite . \"coin\"))))
      (loop (+ i 1)))))
(world/step)
```

[VISUAL: 15 coins loosely clustered around the center, none more than ~100px away]

The scatter has a center of gravity. This reads as a pile, a gathering, a loose heap.

---

## Alignment to Edges

Positioning relative to the world's boundaries.

```scheme
;; Spawn coins along the four edges of the screen.
(world/reset!)
(let ((margin 50)
      (spacing 120))
  ;; Top edge
  (let loop ((i 0))
    (when (< i 6)
      (let ((x (+ 100 (* i spacing)))
            (y margin))
        (world/spawn (string->symbol (string-append \"top-\" (number->string i)))
                     `((x . ,x) (y . ,y) (sprite . \"coin\"))))
      (loop (+ i 1))))
  ;; Bottom edge
  (let loop ((i 0))
    (when (< i 6)
```

## Collision-Free Placement (Simulated)

Place entities ensuring minimum separation.

```scheme
;; Spawn coins ensuring no two are closer than a threshold.
(world/reset!)
(define min-separation 80)
(define candidates '())

(define (too-close? x y)
  (let loop ((cs candidates))
    (if (null? cs)
        #f
        (let* ((c (car cs))
               (cx (car c))
               (cy (cdr c))
               (dx (- x cx))
               (dy (- y cy))
               (dist (dsqrt (+ (* dx dx) (* dy dy)))))
          (if (< dist min-separation)
              #t
              (loop (cdr cs)))))))

(let attempt-loop ((i 0) (placed 0))
  (when (and (< placed 15) (< i 100))
    (let* ((seed-x (+ 8000 (* i 97)))
           (seed-y (+ 9000 (* i 131)))
           (x (+ 100 (* 600 (- (dsin seed-x) -1) 0.5)))
           (y (+ 100 (* 400 (- (dsin seed-y) -1) 0.5))))
      (if (too-close? x y)
          (attempt-loop (+ i 1) placed)
          (begin
            (set! candidates (cons (cons x y) candidates))
            (world/spawn (string->symbol (string-append \"coin-\" (number->string placed)))
                         `((x . ,x) (y . ,y) (sprite . \"coin\")))
            (attempt-loop (+ i 1) (+ placed 1)))))))

(world/step)
```

[VISUAL: ~15 coins scattered, each at least 80px away from any other]

We test each candidate position against already-placed coins. If too close, skip it. This is the logic for non-overlapping spawns, bubble packing.

You've seen 40 worked examples of the still frame — position as the atom of motion. Now try these:

1. **The Constellation**: Spawn 20 coins to form a recognizable constellation shape (Big Dipper, Orion's Belt, or invent your own). Use only x/y coordinates and `world/spawn`.

2. **The Tile Floor**: Write a program that spawns a 10×10 checkerboard of coins, but only on the \"black\" squares. Use a loop and a parity check.

3. **The Scatter Field**: Spawn 30 coins randomly scattered, but ensure none spawn within 60 pixels of the edges (a margin). Use deterministic `dsin`-based pseudo-random placement.

4. **The Spiral Staircase**: Spawn coins in a rising spiral — each successive coin is higher (lower y) and rotates around a center. Combine a loop, `dcos`/`dsin`, and a linearly increasing radius.

5. **The Cleanup Crew**: Spawn 25 coins randomly, then despawn any that are within 100 pixels of the center point (400, 300). Print the count before and after.

6. **The Golden Grid**: Spawn coins in a grid where row spacing increases by the golden ratio (×1.618) each row. Start with 40px spacing, increase each row. Stop after 5 rows.

## Notes and Additional Considerations from r1 draft

*The following material comes from an earlier or parallel revision draft (r1 draft). It is preserved here because content costs thought — nothing gets thrown away. Some passages restate the chapter's core ideas in a different voice; others introduce examples or angles not covered above. Read as supplemental exercises for the same discipline.*

### A Single Shape

The simplest frame: one entity, one place.

```scheme
(define (frame t)
  (world
    (entity 'circle
            (at 200 150)
            (radius 40)
            (fill 'coral))))

(render-at 0.0)
```

[VISUAL: A coral circle centered at (200, 150) against a blank background.]

We define a function `frame` that takes time `t` — though we ignore it for now. Inside, we build a `world` containing one `entity`. The entity is a circle, positioned at (200, 150), with radius 40 and filled coral.

`(render-at 0.0)` samples the frame at time zero.

---


### Position Matters

Move it. The frame changes, but nothing moves — we're looking at a *different* still moment.

```scheme
(define (frame t)
  (world
    (entity 'circle
            (at 320 180)
            (radius 40)
            (fill 'skyblue))))

(render-at 0.0)
```

[VISUAL: A skyblue circle at (320, 180).]

Same structure, different coordinates. In animation, you'll vary position over time — but first, prove to yourself you can place a shape *anywhere*.

### Recursive Patterns

Generate structure with recursion.

```scheme
(define (dots x y n)
  (if (zero? n)
      '()
      (cons (entity 'circle (at x y) (radius 6) (fill 'teal))
            (dots (+ x 25) y (- n 1)))))

(define (frame t)
  (apply world (dots 80 120 8)))

(render-at 0.0)
```

[VISUAL: A horizontal line of eight small teal circles, evenly spaced.]

`dots` builds a list of entities recursively. `apply world` spreads that list into the `world` form.

### Grid

Two dimensions of recursion.

```scheme
(define (row x y n)
  (if (zero? n)
      '()
      (cons (entity 'circle (at x y) (radius 5) (fill 'slateblue))
            (row (+ x 20) y (- n 1)))))

(define (grid x y cols rows)
  (if (zero? rows)
      '()
      (append (row x y cols)
              (grid x (+ y 20) cols (- rows 1)))))

(define (frame t)
  (apply world (grid 100 80 10 6)))

(render-at 0.0)
```

[VISUAL: A 10×6 grid of small slate-blue circles.]

`row` generates one horizontal line; `grid` stacks rows vertically.

### Procedural Stars

Generate them.

```scheme
(define (stars n)
  (if (zero? n)
      '()
      (cons (entity 'circle
                    (at (+ 50 (* n 40)) (+ 60 (* (modulo n 3) 20)))
                    (radius 2)
                    (fill 'white))
            (stars (- n 1)))))

(define (frame t)
  (apply world
         (cons (background 'midnightblue)
               (stars 10))))

(render-at 0.0)
```

[VISUAL: Ten small white stars distributed across the frame.]

Position varies by index and modulo to create pseudo-random scatter.

```scheme
    (entity 'rect (at 235 150) (width 30) (height 4) (fill 'black))
    ; minute hand (pointing ~12)
    (entity 'rect (at 200 110) (width 4) (height 40) (fill 'black))))

(render-at 0.0)
```

[VISUAL: A clock face with four tick marks and two hands showing approximately 3:00.]

Composed from rectangles and a circle outline.

### Chess Board (Partial)

Alternating squares.

```scheme
  (entity 'rect (at x y) (width 30) (height 30) (fill color)))

(define (frame t)
  (world
    (background 'white)
    (square 100 100 'black)

    (square 190 100 'white)
    (square 100 130 'white)
    (square 130 130 'black)
    (square 160 130 'white)
    (square 190 130 'black)
    (square 100 160 'black)
    (square 130 160 'white)
    (square 160 160 'black)
    (square 190 160 'white)
    (square 100 190 'white)
    (square 130 190 'black)
    (square 160 190 'white)
    (square 190 190 'black)))

(render-at 0.0)
```

Helper function `square` generates each tile; we call it sixteen times with alternating colors.

---


### Recursive Checkerboard

Generate the board.

```scheme
(define (row x y n color1 color2)
  (if (zero? n)
      '()
      (cons (entity 'rect (at x y) (width 25) (height 25) (fill color1))
            (row (+ x 25) y (- n 1) color2 color1))))

(define (board x y cols rows)
  (if (zero? rows)
      '()
      (append (row x y cols (if (even? rows) 'black 'white)
                            (if (even? rows) 'white 'black))
              (board x (+ y 25) cols (- rows 1)))))

(define (frame t)
  (apply world
         (cons (background 'beige)
               (board 80 80 8 8))))

(render-at 0.0)
```

[VISUAL: An 8×8 checkerboard.]

`row` alternates colors horizontally; `board` stacks rows and flips the starting color each row.

"# Chapter 2: Velocity

Movement begins with a single fact: **something is going somewhere**. Not arriving yet—we'll learn arrival in Chapter 3—just *going*. A constant direction, a steady speed, the simplest possible motion. A petal drifts across the frame at walking pace. A courier cycles down the avenue. A satellite crosses the night sky. They all share one quality: **velocity**.

Velocity is the second atom of motion. In Chapter 1 we learned to place the sprite in the world—`entity/set-pos!` gave her coordinates, a fixed spot. Now we give her *intention*: a direction and a rate. She moves. The world unfolds.

This chapter drills one idea until it's in your fingers: `entity/set-vel!` paired with `world/step`. We'll vary the scenario forty times—different speeds, different headings, different reasons to move—but the kernel stays the same. By the end, you'll feel the difference between a drift and a dart, a crawl and a coast. You'll know how to send something across the frame and *mean it*.

---

## The first move

Here is the sprite, standing still at the origin. We spawn her, take one snapshot of the world, and report her position. Nothing moves yet.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define hero (world/spawn 'hero 0 0))
(world/step 0.016)
(entity/pos hero)
```

[VISUAL: A single frame. The sprite stands at (0, 0). The coordinate grid is visible, soft gray lines. No motion.]

Now we give her velocity—two units rightward per second, nothing vertical—and step the world forward for one frame (about 1/60th of a second). She moves a tiny bit.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define hero (world/spawn 'hero 0 0))
(entity/set-vel! hero 2 0)
(world/step 0.016)
(entity/pos hero)
```

[VISUAL: The sprite has shifted slightly to the right. Her velocity vector is drawn as a faint arrow pointing right. The coordinate readout shows (~0.032, 0).]

The position changed. That's motion. Step the world ten times and she travels ten times as far.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define hero (world/spawn 'hero 0 0))
(entity/set-vel! hero 2 0)
(let loop ((n 10))
  (when (> n 0)
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(entity/pos hero)
```

[VISUAL: The sprite is now visibly to the right, around (0.32, 0). A faint trail of dots shows her path—perfectly horizontal.]

This is the foundation. Everything that moves in the sprite's world will use this pair: `set-vel!` to declare the motion, `world/step` to make time pass.

---

## Direction

Velocity is a *vector*—two numbers, x and y. The first number is horizontal speed (positive = rightward, negative = leftward). The second is vertical (positive = upward, negative = downward). We can send the sprite in any direction.

Moving upward at one unit per second:

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define hero (world/spawn 'hero 0 0))
(entity/set-vel! hero 0 1)
(let loop ((n 20))
  (when (> n 0)
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(entity/pos hero)
```

[VISUAL: The sprite has moved upward. Her trail is vertical. Position is near (0, 0.32).]

Leftward, fast:

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define hero (world/spawn 'hero 0 0))
(entity/set-vel! hero -5 0)
(let loop ((n 20))
  (when (> n 0)
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(entity/pos hero)
```

[VISUAL: The sprite is well to the left, around (-1.6, 0). The trail is a straight horizontal line pointing left.]

Diagonal—up and to the right:

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define hero (world/spawn 'hero 0 0))
(entity/set-vel! hero 3 2)
(let loop ((n 30))
  (when (> n 0)
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(entity/pos hero)
```

[VISUAL: The sprite has moved northeast. The trail is a clean diagonal. Position is around (1.44, 0.96).]

The ratio of the two numbers sets the angle. The *magnitude*—how big the numbers are—sets the speed.

---

## Speed

Speed is how far something travels per second. A velocity of `(3, 0)` means three units per second horizontally. A velocity of `(0, -4)` means four units per second downward. The actual *speed* (the length of the velocity vector) can be calculated with the Pythagorean theorem: `sqrt(vx^2 + vy^2)`.

A slow drift:

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define petal (world/spawn 'petal 0 5))
(entity/set-vel! petal 0.5 -0.3)
(let loop ((n 60))
  (when (> n 0)
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(entity/pos petal)
```

[VISUAL: A cherry-blossom petal floats gently down and to the right. The trail is long and shallow. Position is around (0.48, 4.71).]

A dart:

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define arrow (world/spawn 'arrow -3 0))
(entity/set-vel! arrow 12 0)
(let loop ((n 30))
  (when (> n 0)
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(entity/pos arrow)
```

[VISUAL: An arrow streaks across the screen. The trail is short because it moves so fast. Position is around (2.76, 0).]

A ball tossed at 45 degrees, medium speed:

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define ball (world/spawn 'ball 0 0))
(entity/set-vel! ball 4 4)
(let loop ((n 40))
  (when (> n 0)
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(entity/pos ball)
```

[VISUAL: A ball moves diagonally up and right. The trail is a perfect straight line at 45°. Position is around (2.56, 2.56).]

Notice: the motion is *linear*. No curve, no slow-down, no arrival. Just constant velocity. That's what this chapter drills. Curves and easing come later.

---

## Many entities, each with their own velocity

The world can hold many things, each moving independently. Spawn three entities, give each a different velocity, step the world forward. They all move.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define a (world/spawn 'dot -2 0))
(define b (world/spawn 'dot 0 2))
(define c (world/spawn 'dot 2 -1))
(entity/set-vel! a 1 0)
(entity/set-vel! b 0 -1)
(entity/set-vel! c -0.5 0.5)
(let loop ((n 50))
  (when (> n 0)
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(list (entity/pos a) (entity/pos b) (entity/pos c))
```

[VISUAL: Three dots move in different directions. A moves right, B moves down, C moves left and up. Their trails cross and diverge. Final positions printed below.]

Each entity carries its own velocity. The world doesn't care if they're related—it just steps them all forward.

---

## Changing velocity mid-flight

Velocity isn't permanent. You can call `set-vel!` again at any time. The entity instantly adopts the new vector.

Start moving right, then halfway through, change to moving up:

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define hero (world/spawn 'hero -3 0))
(entity/set-vel! hero 3 0)
(let loop ((n 25))
  (when (> n 0)
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(entity/set-vel! hero 0 2)
(let loop ((n 25))
  (when (> n 0)
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(entity/pos hero)
```

[VISUAL: The sprite's trail has a sharp right-angle corner. She moves horizontally, then vertically. No curve—instant direction change. Final position around (1.2, 0.8).]

This is how you build more complex motion: a *sequence* of constant-velocity segments. Real-world motion is rarely perfectly linear, but linear segments are the building blocks. (In Chapter 3 we'll learn to *blend* between velocities smoothly—that's easing. Here we just snap.)

---

## Stopping

Setting velocity to zero stops the entity. It stays wherever it was when you zeroed it.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define hero (world/spawn 'hero 0 0))
(entity/set-vel! hero 2 1)
(let loop ((n 30))
  (when (> n 0)
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(entity/set-vel! hero 0 0)
(let loop ((n 30))
  (when (> n 0)
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(entity/pos hero)
```

[VISUAL: The sprite moves diagonally up and right, then her trail ends abruptly. She stays in place for the second half of the animation. Final position around (0.96, 0.48).]

This is the simplest kind of \"halt.\" No deceleration, no settle—just instant stillness. (We'll learn weight and settle in Chapter 6.)

---

## Reversing

Negating the velocity sends the entity back the way it came.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define courier (world/spawn 'courier -4 0))
(entity/set-vel! courier 4 0)
(let loop ((n 30))
  (when (> n 0)
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(let ((v (entity/vel courier)))
  (entity/set-vel! courier (- (car v)) (- (cadr v))))
(let loop ((n 30))
  (when (> n 0)
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(entity/pos courier)
```

[VISUAL: A courier cycles right, then immediately turns around and cycles left at the same speed. The trail is a straight line, right then left. Final position back near (-4, 0).]

Notice we read the current velocity with `entity/vel` and negate both components. The entity returns along the exact same path.

---

## Speed as a single number

Sometimes you want to set a speed (a scalar) and a heading (an angle), not raw x/y components. Scheme gives us `dcos` and `dsin` (deterministic trig functions) to convert polar to Cartesian.

Move at speed 5, heading 30 degrees (measured counterclockwise from the positive x-axis):

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define hero (world/spawn 'hero 0 0))
(let ((speed 5)
      (angle (* 30 (/ PI 180))))
  (entity/set-vel! hero (* speed (dcos angle)) (* speed (dsin angle))))
(let loop ((n 40))
  (when (> n 0)
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(entity/pos hero)
```

[VISUAL: The sprite moves at a shallow upward angle. The trail is a straight line tilted 30° above horizontal. Final position around (3.46, 1.28).]

Same speed, heading 120 degrees:

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define hero (world/spawn 'hero 0 0))
(let ((speed 5)
      (angle (* 120 (/ PI 180))))
  (entity/set-vel! hero (* speed (dcos angle)) (* speed (dsin angle))))
(let loop ((n 40))
  (when (> n 0)
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(entity/pos hero)
```

[VISUAL: The sprite moves up and to the left at 120°. Final position around (-1.60, 2.77).]

This is useful when you're thinking in *directions* (north, northeast, etc.) rather than component speeds.

---

## Orbits (a preview)

If you change velocity *every frame* to always point perpendicular to the current position (relative to a center), the entity orbits. This is a sneak peek—Chapter 8 will drill oscillation thoroughly—but it shows how velocity can be dynamic.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define moon (world/spawn 'moon 3 0))
(let loop ((n 120))
  (when (> n 0)
    (let* ((pos (entity/pos moon))
           (x (car pos))
           (y (cadr pos))
           (angle (datan2 y x))
           (speed 2))
      (entity/set-vel! moon (* speed (- (dsin angle))) (* speed (dcos angle)))
      (world/step 0.016)
      (loop (- n 1)))))
(entity/pos moon)
```

[VISUAL: A moon traces a circular orbit around the origin. The trail is a perfect circle, radius 3. Final position is back near (3, 0).]

Every frame we calculate the angle from the origin, then set velocity perpendicular to that. The moon goes in a circle. This is velocity used as a *steering* mechanism—recalculated continuously. Most of this chapter uses velocity as a one-time declaration, but it's good to see the dynamic case early.

---

## Relative velocity

Entities don't know about each other unless you tell them. If two entities have the same velocity, they stay the same distance apart—they're moving together, like two birds in a flock.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define bird-a (world/spawn 'bird -2 1))
(define bird-b (world/spawn 'bird -2 -1))
(entity/set-vel! bird-a 3 0.5)
(entity/set-vel! bird-b 3 0.5)
(let loop ((n 60))
  (when (> n 0)
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(list (entity/pos bird-a) (entity/pos bird-b))
```

[VISUAL: Two birds fly in parallel. Their trails are identical diagonals, separated by a constant vertical gap. Final positions are around (0.88, 1.48) and (0.88, -0.52).]

If one is slightly faster, they gradually separate:

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define bird-a (world/spawn 'bird -2 1))
(define bird-b (world/spawn 'bird -2 -1))
(entity/set-vel! bird-a 3 0.5)
(entity/set-vel! bird-b 3.2 0.5)
(let loop ((n 60))
  (when (> n 0)
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(list (entity/pos bird-a) (entity/pos bird-b))
```

[VISUAL: Two birds fly at nearly the same angle, but bird-b gradually pulls ahead. The trails diverge slightly. Final x-positions differ by about 0.19 units.]

This is how you orchestrate groups—give each member a velocity, vary them slightly, and the formation shifts.

---

## Patrol: back and forth

A common pattern: move right until you hit a boundary, then reverse and move left. Repeat forever. This is a *state machine* built on velocity changes.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define guard (world/spawn 'guard -5 0))
(entity/set-vel! guard 2 0)
(let loop ((n 200))
  (when (> n 0)
    (let ((x (car (entity/pos guard))))
      (when (> x 5)
        (entity/set-vel! guard -2 0))
      (when (< x -5)
        (entity/set-vel! guard 2 0)))
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(entity/pos guard)
```

[VISUAL: A guard paces back and forth between x = -5 and x = 5. The trail is a horizontal line segment, retraced multiple times. Final position is somewhere in the patrol range.]

Every frame we check position. If past the right boundary, flip velocity to leftward. If past the left boundary, flip to rightward. The guard marches back and forth forever.

---

## Chase (constant velocity toward a target)

Calculate the vector from chaser to target, normalize it (make it length 1), scale by desired speed, and set that as velocity. The chaser moves toward the target at constant speed.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define hero (world/spawn 'hero 5 5))
(define cat (world/spawn 'cat -3 -2))
(entity/set-vel! hero 0 0)
(let ((chase-speed 3))
  (let loop ((n 60))
    (when (> n 0)
      (let* ((cat-pos (entity/pos cat))
             (hero-pos (entity/pos hero))
             (dx (- (car hero-pos) (car cat-pos)))
             (dy (- (cadr hero-pos) (cadr cat-pos)))
             (dist (dsqrt (+ (* dx dx) (* dy dy)))))
        (when (> dist 0.1)
          (entity/set-vel! cat 
                           (* chase-speed (/ dx dist)) 
                           (* chase-speed (/ dy dist))))
        (world/step 0.016)
        (loop (- n 1)))))
(entity/pos cat))
```

[VISUAL: A cat moves toward the sprite in a straight line. The sprite is stationary. The cat's trail is a ray from (-3, -2) toward (5, 5). Final position is much closer to the sprite.]

This is a *homing* behavior. Every frame we recalculate the direction to the target and set velocity along that line. (If we only set it *once* at the start, the cat would move in a straight line but wouldn't adjust if the sprite moved. Here the sprite is still, but the pattern generalizes.)

---

## Flee (constant velocity away from a threat)

The opposite of chase: calculate the vector *from* threat *to* entity, normalize, scale.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define fox (world/spawn 'fox 0 0))
(define rabbit (world/spawn 'rabbit 2 1))
(entity/set-vel! fox 0 0)
(let ((flee-speed 4))
  (let loop ((n 50))
    (when (> n 0)
      (let* ((rabbit-pos (entity/pos rabbit))
             (fox-pos (entity/pos fox))
             (dx (- (car rabbit-pos) (car fox-pos)))
             (dy (- (cadr rabbit-pos) (cadr fox-pos)))
             (dist (dsqrt (+ (* dx dx) (* dy dy)))))
        (when (> dist 0.1)
          (entity/set-vel! rabbit 
                           (* flee-speed (/ dx dist)) 
                           (* flee-speed (/ dy dist))))
        (world/step 0.016)
        (loop (- n 1)))))
(entity/pos rabbit))
```

[VISUAL: A rabbit flees from a stationary fox. The trail is a straight line pointing away from the fox. Final position is much farther from the origin, around (5.2, 2.6).]

Flee is just chase with the vector negated (or equivalently, swapped source and target).

## Wander (velocity that changes randomly)

Add a small random perturbation to velocity every few frames. The entity drifts in a lazy, unpredictable path.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define leaf (world/spawn 'leaf 0 3))
(entity/set-vel! leaf 1 -0.5)
(let loop ((n 100) (counter 0))
  (when (> n 0)
    (when (= (modulo counter 10) 0)
      (let ((vx (car (entity/vel leaf)))
            (vy (cadr (entity/vel leaf))))
        (entity/set-vel! leaf 
                         (+ vx (* 0.3 (- (random) 0.5)))
                         (+ vy (* 0.3 (- (random) 0.5))))))
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1) (+ counter 1))))
(entity/pos leaf)
```

[VISUAL: A leaf drifts downward with a gentle, meandering path. The trail has soft curves (from the frequent direction changes). Final position is down and somewhat to the right, but the path isn't straight.]

Every 10 frames we nudge the velocity by a small random amount. The leaf wanders. This is how you get organic, unpredictable motion from simple velocity changes.

```scheme
(list (entity/pos lead) (entity/pos left-wing) (entity/pos right-wing))
```

[VISUAL: Three birds fly in a V. Their trails are parallel. The formation stays rigid. Final positions maintain the V-shape offset.]

Because all three have the same velocity, the distances between them never change. The entire formation translates as a unit.

## Spiral (velocity rotates over time)

Rotate the velocity vector a tiny bit every frame. The entity spirals outward (if speed increases) or inward (if speed decreases), or in a circle (if speed stays constant).

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define particle (world/spawn 'particle 2 0))
(entity/set-vel! particle 0 2)
(let loop ((n 150))
  (when (> n 0)
    (let* ((v (entity/vel particle))
           (vx (car v))
           (vy (cadr v))
           (angle (datan2 vy vx))
           (speed (dsqrt (+ (* vx vx) (* vy vy))))
           (new-angle (+ angle 0.05)))
      (entity/set-vel! particle 
                       (* speed (dcos new-angle)) 
                       (* speed (dsin new-angle))))
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(entity/pos particle)
```

[VISUAL: A particle spirals around the origin. The trail is a smooth logarithmic spiral. Final position is back near the starting radius, but rotated.]

Each frame we add a small angle to the velocity direction. The particle turns. This is the foundation of circular and spiral motion—velocity as a rotating vector.

## Conveyor belt (velocity imposed by the environment)

Imagine a region of space that *forces* a certain velocity on anything inside it. An entity enters the region and is swept along.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define crate (world/spawn 'crate -3 0))
(entity/set-vel! crate 1 0)
(let loop ((n 100))
  (when (> n 0)
    (let ((x (car (entity/pos crate))))
      (if (and (> x -1) (< x 2))
          (entity/set-vel! crate 4 0)
          (when (>= x 2)
            (entity/set-vel! crate 1 0))))
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(entity/pos crate)
```

[VISUAL: A crate approaches from the left at normal speed. When it enters the region x ∈ (-1, 2), it suddenly accelerates (the trail spacing increases). After exiting at x=2, it returns to normal speed.]

This is a *zone* effect. While inside the zone, velocity is overridden. Outside the zone, the original velocity resumes. (In a real engine you might store the original and restore it; here we just hard-code the exit velocity.)

## Slingshot (velocity boost at a point)

An entity passes through a specific location and receives a sudden velocity spike—like a gravitational slingshot.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define probe (world/spawn 'probe -5 -2))
(entity/set-vel! probe 3 1)
(let loop ((n 100))
  (when (> n 0)
    (let* ((pos (entity/pos probe))
           (x (car pos))
           (y (cadr pos))
           (dist-to-boost (dsqrt (+ (* x x) (* y y)))))
      (when (< dist-to-boost 0.5)
        (entity/set-vel! probe 6 3)))
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(entity/pos probe)
```

[VISUAL: A probe approaches the origin at moderate speed. As it passes near (0,0), the trail spacing suddenly increases—it's been boosted. Final position is much farther than it would have been without the boost.]

The probe flies past a \"slingshot point\" at the origin. When within 0.5 units, velocity doubles. The probe zooms off.

## River current (velocity that varies by position)

Different parts of space impose different velocities—like a river with faster current in the middle, slower near the banks.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define raft (world/spawn 'raft -4 0))
(entity/set-vel! raft 0 0)
(let loop ((n 120))
  (when (> n 0)
    (let* ((pos (entity/pos raft))
           (y (cadr pos))
           (current-speed (if (< (abs y) 1.0) 3.0 1.0)))
      (entity/set-vel! raft current-speed 0))
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(entity/pos raft)
```

[VISUAL: A raft drifts downstream. Because it stays near y=0 (the middle of the river), it moves at the fast speed (3 units/sec) the whole time. If it had drifted toward y=±2, it would slow to 1 unit/sec.]

This sets velocity based on position every frame. It's a *spatially varying field*. (Chapter 9 will introduce `world/wind!` and `world/attract!` which automate this, but here we do it manually to see the mechanism.)

## Drift on ice (velocity persists, no friction)

On a frictionless surface, velocity never decays. Once you push something, it glides forever.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define puck (world/spawn 'puck 0 0))
(entity/set-vel! puck 4 2)
(let loop ((n 100))
  (when (> n 0)
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(entity/pos puck)
```

[VISUAL: A hockey puck glides across the screen in a perfectly straight line. The trail is evenly spaced—constant velocity, no slowdown. Final position is around (6.4, 3.2).]

No forces, no drag, no friction. The puck moves forever at the same speed. This is the default in our engine—velocity doesn't decay unless you add drag (we'll cover that in Chapter 6).

## Gradual acceleration (velocity increases each frame)

Instead of setting a fixed velocity, *add* a small amount every frame. The entity speeds up.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define rocket (world/spawn 'rocket -5 -3))
(entity/set-vel! rocket 1 0.5)
(let loop ((n 80))
  (when (> n 0)
    (let ((v (entity/vel rocket)))
      (entity/set-vel! rocket (+ (car v) 0.05) (+ (cadr v) 0.025)))
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(entity/pos rocket)
```

[VISUAL: A rocket launches. The trail spacing increases over time—the rocket is accelerating. Final position is much farther than constant-velocity would reach.]

Each frame we add (0.05, 0.025) to the velocity. The rocket goes faster and faster. This is *linear acceleration*—a preview of Chapter 9's force-based motion, done here manually.

## Gradual deceleration (velocity shrinks each frame)

Multiply velocity by a factor less than 1 each frame. The entity slows down and eventually stops.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define sled (world/spawn 'sled -4 2))
(entity/set-vel! sled 5 0)
(let loop ((n 100))
  (when (> n 0)
    (let ((v (entity/vel sled)))
      (entity/set-vel! sled (* (car v) 0.98) (* (cadr v) 0.98)))
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(entity/pos sled)
```

[VISUAL: A sled glides to a stop. The trail spacing decreases—each frame it moves a bit less. Final position is only a few units from the start; most of the motion happened early.]

Multiplying by 0.98 each frame shaves 2% off the velocity. After many frames, velocity approaches zero. This is *exponential decay*—a simple friction model.

## Bouncing off walls (velocity reversal on boundary)

When the entity hits a boundary, negate the component of velocity perpendicular to the wall. It bounces.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define ball (world/spawn 'ball 0 0))
(entity/set-vel! ball 3 2)
(let loop ((n 150))
  (when (> n 0)
    (let* ((pos (entity/pos ball))
           (x (car pos))
           (y (cadr pos))
           (v (entity/vel ball))
           (vx (car v))
           (vy (cadr v)))
      (when (or (> x 5) (< x -5))
        (entity/set-vel! ball (- vx) vy))
      (when (or (> y 3) (< y -3))
        (entity/set-vel! ball vx (- vy))))
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(entity/pos ball)
```

[VISUAL: A ball bounces around a rectangular region. The trail has sharp angle changes at the walls—perfect reflections. The ball never loses speed (elastic collision).]

When x crosses ±5, we flip vx. When y crosses ±3, we flip vy. The ball ricochets forever at constant speed. (Real bounces lose energy; we'll add that in Chapter 7.)

## Follow the leader

The second entity always moves toward the first entity's *current* position. The first moves freely; the second chases.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define leader (world/spawn 'leader 0 0))
(define follower (world/spawn 'follower -3 -2))
(entity/set-vel! leader 2 1)
(let loop ((n 80))
  (when (> n 0)
    (let* ((leader-pos (entity/pos leader))
           (follower-pos (entity/pos follower))
           (dx (- (car leader-pos) (car follower-pos)))
           (dy (- (cadr leader-pos) (cadr follower-pos)))
           (dist (dsqrt (+ (* dx dx) (* dy dy)))))
      (when (> dist 0.1)
        (entity/set-vel! follower 
                         (* 2.5 (/ dx dist)) 
                         (* 2.5 (/ dy dist)))))
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(list (entity/pos leader) (entity/pos follower))
```

[VISUAL: The leader moves in a straight line. The follower's trail curves toward the leader—it's always chasing. By the end, the follower is close behind. Final positions show the follower lagging slightly.]

The follower recalculates its velocity every frame to point at the leader's *current* position. Because the leader is also moving, the follower traces a curved path (even though its velocity is recalculated linearly each frame).

## Herding (many followers, one leader)

Five followers, all chasing the same leader. They converge.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define leader (world/spawn 'leader 0 3))
(entity/set-vel! leader 1 -0.5)
(define f1 (world/spawn 'follower -4 0))
(define f2 (world/spawn 'follower 4 0))
(define f3 (world/spawn 'follower 0 -3))
(define f4 (world/spawn 'follower -2 2))
(define f5 (world/spawn 'follower 2 -2))
(let loop ((n 100))
  (when (> n 0)
    (let ((leader-pos (entity/pos leader)))
      (for-each
       (lambda (f)
         (let* ((fpos (entity/pos f))
                (dx (- (car leader-pos) (car fpos)))
                (dy (- (cadr leader-pos) (cadr fpos)))
                (dist (dsqrt (+ (* dx dx) (* dy dy)))))
           (when (> dist 0.1)
             (entity/set-vel! f (* 2 (/ dx dist)) (* 2 (/ dy dist))))))
       (list f1 f2 f3 f4 f5)))
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(map entity/pos (list leader f1 f2 f3 f4 f5))
```

[VISUAL: A leader moves slowly downward. Five followers converge from all directions, their trails curving toward the leader. By the end, all followers are clustered near the leader.]

All five recalculate their velocity toward the leader every frame. They form a moving cluster.
