## Flocking separation (avoid crowding)

Each entity steers *away* from nearby entities to maintain personal space. This is one component of flocking behavior.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define a (world/spawn 'bird 0 0))
(define b (world/spawn 'bird 0.3 0.2))
(define c (world/spawn 'bird -0.2 0.1))
(entity/set-vel! a 1 0)
(entity/set-vel! b 1 0)
(entity/set-vel! c 1 0)
(let loop ((n 60))
  (when (> n 0)
    (for-each
     (lambda (self)
       (let ((sep-x 0) (sep-y 0))
         (for-each
          (lambda (other)
            (when (not (eq? self other))
              (let* ((self-pos (entity/pos self))
                     (other-pos (entity/pos other))
                     (dx (- (car self-pos) (car other-pos)))
                     (dy (- (cadr self-pos) (cadr other-pos)))
                     (dist (dsqrt (+ (* dx dx) (* dy dy)))))
                (when (< dist 1.0)
                  (set! sep-x (+ sep-x dx))
                  (set! sep-y (+ sep-y dy))))))
          (list a b c))
         (let ((v (entity/vel self)))
           (entity/set-vel! self (+ (car v) (* 0.1 sep-x)) (+ (cadr v) (* 0.1 sep-y))))))
     (list a b c))
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(map entity/pos (list a b c))
```

[VISUAL: Three birds start clustered, all moving right. Their trails gradually spread apart as they repel each other. By the end, they're more evenly spaced.]

Each bird calculates the average vector *away from* nearby birds and nudges its velocity in that direction. They spread out while still moving generally rightward.

---

## Alignment (match neighbors' velocity)

Each entity adjusts its velocity to match the average velocity of nearby entities. They synchronize.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define a (world/spawn 'bird -2 1))
(define b (world/spawn 'bird -2 0))
(define c (world/spawn 'bird -2 -1))
(entity/set-vel! a 2 0.5)
(entity/set-vel! b 1.5 -0.3)
(entity/set-vel! c 2.5 0.2)
(let loop ((n 80))
  (when (> n 0)
    (for-each
     (lambda (self)
       (let ((avg-vx 0) (avg-vy 0) (count 0))
         (for-each
          (lambda (other)
            (let* ((self-pos (entity/pos self))
                   (other-pos (entity/pos other))
                   (dx (- (car other-pos) (car self-pos)))
                   (dy (- (cadr other-pos) (cadr self-pos)))
                   (dist (dsqrt (+ (* dx dx) (* dy dy)))))
              (when (< dist 2.0)
                (let ((ov (entity/vel other)))
                  (set! avg-vx (+ avg-vx (car ov)))
                  (set! avg-vy (+ avg-vy (cadr ov)))
                  (set! count (+ count 1))))))
          (list a b c))
         (when (> count 0)
           (let ((v (entity/vel self)))
             (entity/set-vel! self 
                              (+ (* 0.95 (car v)) (* 0.05 (/ avg-vx count)))
                              (+ (* 0.95 (cadr v)) (* 0.05 (/ avg-vy count))))))))
     (list a b c))
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(map entity/vel (list a b c))
```

[VISUAL: Three birds start with different velocities (different trail angles and spacings). Over time, their trails become more parallel—they're converging toward the same velocity.]

Each bird blends 5% of the average neighbor velocity into its own. After many frames, they all move together.

---

## Cohesion (steer toward the center of the group)

Each entity steers toward the average position of nearby entities. They cluster.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define a (world/spawn 'bird -3 2))
(define b (world/spawn 'bird 3 -1))
(define c (world/spawn 'bird 0 -3))
(entity/set-vel! a 1 0)
(entity/set-vel! b -0.5 0.5)
(entity/set-vel! c 0 1)
(let loop ((n 100))
  (when (> n 0)
    (for-each
     (lambda (self)
       (let ((avg-x 0) (avg-y 0) (count 0))
         (for-each
          (lambda (other)
            (let ((opos (entity/pos other)))
              (set! avg-x (+ avg-x (car opos)))
              (set! avg-y (+ avg-y (cadr opos)))
              (set! count (+ count 1))))
          (list a b c))
         (let* ((center-x (/ avg-x count))
                (center-y (/ avg-y count))
                (self-pos (entity/pos self))
                (dx (- center-x (car self-pos)))
                (dy (- center-y (cadr self-pos)))
                (v (entity/vel self)))
           (entity/set-vel! self (+ (car v) (* 0.02 dx)) (+ (cadr v) (* 0.02 dy))))))
     (list a b c))
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(map entity/pos (list a b c))
```

[VISUAL: Three birds start far apart. Their trails curve toward each other. By the end, they're clustered in the middle of the frame.]

Each bird calculates the centroid of the group and steers gently toward it. They form a flock.

---

## Full flocking (separation + alignment + cohesion)

Combine all three behaviors. The result is emergent flocking: the birds spread out enough to avoid collision, align their velocities, and stay together as a group.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define birds (list (world/spawn 'bird -3 2)
                    (world/spawn 'bird 3 -1)
                    (world/spawn 'bird 0 -3)
                    (world/spawn 'bird -2 -2)
                    (world/spawn 'bird 2 2)))
(for-each (lambda (b) (entity/set-vel! b 1 0.5)) birds)
(let loop ((n 120))
  (when (> n 0)
    (for-each
     (lambda (self)
       (let ((sep-x 0) (sep-y 0)
             (avg-vx 0) (avg-vy 0)
             (avg-x 0) (avg-y 0)
             (count 0))
         (for-each
          (lambda (other)
            (let* ((spos (entity/pos self))
                   (opos (entity/pos other))
                   (dx (- (car spos) (car opos)))
                   (dy (- (cadr spos) (cadr opos)))
                   (dist (dsqrt (+ (* dx dx) (* dy dy)))))
              (when (< dist 2.0)
                (when (> dist 0.01)
                  (set! sep-x (+ sep-x (/ dx dist)))
                  (set! sep-y (+ sep-y (/ dy dist))))
                (let ((ov (entity/vel other)))
                  (set! avg-vx (+ avg-vx (car ov)))
                  (set! avg-vy (+ avg-vy (cadr ov))))
                (set! avg-x (+ avg-x (car opos)))
                (set! avg-y (+ avg-y (cadr opos)))
                (set! count (+ count 1)))))
          birds)
         (when (> count 0)
           (let* ((center-x (/ avg-x count))
                  (center-y (/ avg-y count))
                  (spos (entity/pos self))
                  (coh-x (- center-x (car spos)))
                  (coh-y (- center-y (cadr spos)))
                  (v (entity/vel self))
                  (vx (car v))
                  (vy (cadr v)))
             (entity/set-vel! self 
                              (+ vx (* 0.05 sep-x) (* 0.02 (/ avg-vx count)) (* 0.01 coh-x))
                              (+ vy (* 0.05 sep-y) (* 0.02 (/ avg-vy count)) (* 0.01 coh-y)))))))
     birds)
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(map entity/pos birds))
```

[VISUAL: Five birds start scattered. Their trails show them spreading slightly (separation), then curving together (cohesion), and aligning into parallel motion (alignment). By the end, they move as a coordinated flock.]

This is Craig Reynolds's classic boids algorithm, implemented as velocity adjustments. The birds self-organize into a flock. It's emergent behavior from simple rules.

## Velocity as a signal

Sometimes you don't care about the *position* an entity reaches—you care about its *velocity* as a carrier of information. For example, a windvane entity could have its velocity set to match the wind direction, so other systems can read it.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define windvane (world/spawn 'vane 0 0))
(define leaf (world/spawn 'leaf -2 1))
(entity/set-vel! windvane 2 -1)
(let loop ((n 60))
  (when (> n 0)
    (let ((wind (entity/vel windvane)))
      (entity/set-vel! leaf (car wind) (cadr wind)))
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(entity/pos leaf)
```

[VISUAL: The windvane is invisible or static—it doesn't move visibly. The leaf, however, drifts in the direction the windvane's velocity points. Final position of leaf is around (1.92, 0.04).]

The windvane's *velocity* is the wind vector. The leaf copies it. This is a way to broadcast a direction/speed to other entities without using a separate data structure.

## Speed limiting (clamping velocity magnitude)

Calculate the current speed. If it exceeds a maximum, scale the velocity down to that max.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define ship (world/spawn 'ship 0 0))
(entity/set-vel! ship 3 4)
(let ((max-speed 3.5))
  (let loop ((n 50))
    (when (> n 0)
      (let* ((v (entity/vel ship))
             (vx (car v))
             (vy (cadr v))
             (speed (dsqrt (+ (* vx vx) (* vy vy)))))
        (when (> speed max-speed)
          (let ((scale (/ max-speed speed)))
            (entity/set-vel! ship (* vx scale) (* vy scale)))))
      (world/step 0.016)
      (loop (- n 1)))))
(entity/pos ship)
```

[VISUAL: The ship tries to move at speed 5 (sqrt(3² + 4²)), but the limiter clamps it to 3.5. The trail is in the same direction as the original velocity, but shorter—moving slower than requested.]

We calculate speed = sqrt(vx² + vy²). If speed > max, we scale both components by (max / speed). The direction stays the same; the magnitude is clamped.

## Velocity in polar coordinates (magnitude and angle)

Store velocity as a speed and a heading, update them independently, then convert to Cartesian each frame.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define comet (world/spawn 'comet -4 -3))
(let ((speed 3.0) (heading 45))
  (let loop ((n 80))
    (when (> n 0)
      (let ((angle (* heading (/ PI 180))))
        (entity/set-vel! comet (* speed (dcos angle)) (* speed (dsin angle))))
      (set! heading (+ heading 2))
      (world/step 0.016)
      (loop (- n 1)))))
(entity/pos comet)
```

[VISUAL: A comet spirals outward. The trail is a smooth curve—each frame the heading rotates 2 degrees while speed stays constant. Final position is back near the start (because 80 steps × 2°/step = 160°, not quite a full rotation).]

We store heading as a mutable angle, increment it each frame, and convert to vx/vy with trig. This is cleaner than manually rotating a Cartesian vector when you're thinking in angles.

## Velocity field visualization (no entity, just the field)

Spawn many stationary entities in a grid, set each one's velocity to a function of its position (e.g., a vortex), and visualize the result. They don't move—just display the field.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(let ((x-start -3) (x-end 3) (y-start -3) (y-end 3) (step 0.8))
  (let outer ((x x-start))
    (when (<= x x-end)
      (let inner ((y y-start))
        (when (<= y y-end)
          (let* ((marker (world/spawn 'arrow x y))
                 (angle (datan2 y x))
                 (speed 1.5))
            (entity/set-vel! marker 
                             (* speed (- (dsin angle)))
                             (* speed (dcos angle))))
          (inner (+ y step))))
      (outer (+ x step)))))
(world/step 0.016)
(world/count)
```

[VISUAL: A grid of arrows, each pointing perpendicular to the radius from the origin (a vortex field). The arrows don't move—they're just placed to show the velocity at each point in space.]

This is how you visualize a vector field. Each arrow's velocity *represents* the field at that location, even though the arrows themselves are stationary.

## Zero velocity initialization (stateful entities that aren't moving yet)

Sometimes you spawn an entity but don't want it to move until triggered. Set velocity to (0, 0) initially, then activate later.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define sleeper (world/spawn 'sleeper 0 0))
(entity/set-vel! sleeper 0 0)
(let loop ((n 30))
  (when (> n 0)
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(entity/set-vel! sleeper 4 2)
(let loop ((n 30))
  (when (> n 0)
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(entity/pos sleeper)
```

[VISUAL: The entity stays at the origin for the first half. Then suddenly it springs to life and moves diagonally. The trail has a long stationary segment, then a diagonal line.]

Velocity (0, 0) is a valid state. The entity exists, responds to queries, but doesn't move until you give it a nonzero velocity.

## Hand-off (one entity stops, another starts)

Two entities. The first moves, then stops and sets the second's velocity to its own final velocity. The motion \"transfers.\"

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define runner-a (world/spawn 'runner -4 0))
(define runner-b (world/spawn 'runner -2 0))
(entity/set-vel! runner-a 3 0)
(entity/set-vel! runner-b 0 0)
(let loop ((n 40))
  (when (> n 0)
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(let ((v (entity/vel runner-a)))
  (entity/set-vel! runner-a 0 0)
  (entity/set-vel! runner-b (car v) (cadr v)))
(let loop ((n 40))
  (when (> n 0)
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(list (entity/pos runner-a) (entity/pos runner-b))
```

[VISUAL: Runner A moves right, then stops. At that moment, runner B (who was stationary) starts moving at the same speed. It's like passing a baton—one trail ends, another begins, same velocity.]

This is a *relay*. The velocity is copied from one entity to another. The motion continues, but the actor changes.

## Velocity as a ray (collision detection preview)

Cast an entity forward at high speed for one frame, check what it overlaps, then reset it. This is a poor-man's raycast.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define caster (world/spawn 'ray-origin 0 0))
(define target (world/spawn 'target 3 0.2))
(entity/set-vel! caster 100 0)
(world/step 0.001)
(let ((hit (entity/overlaps? caster target)))
  (entity/set-pos! caster 0 0)
  (entity/set-vel! caster 0 0)
  hit)
```

[VISUAL: Conceptual diagram: a ray shoots out from the origin, passes through the target. The overlap is detected. The caster is then reset to the origin.]

We move the caster very fast for a very short time, check for overlaps, then reset. This simulates a raycast. (A real raycast would be a dedicated verb, but this shows that velocity can be a *geometric query tool*, not just motion.)

## Velocity symmetry (two entities, mirrored velocities)

Two entities moving in exactly opposite directions, same speed. They're symmetric around a midpoint.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define left (world/spawn 'particle -2 0))
(define right (world/spawn 'particle 2 0))
(entity/set-vel! left 1.5 1)
(entity/set-vel! right -1.5 -1)
(let loop ((n 60))
  (when (> n 0)
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(list (entity/pos left) (entity/pos right))
```

[VISUAL: Two particles move in opposite directions. Their trails are mirror images. They start symmetric around (0,0) and end symmetric around (0,0), just farther apart.]

The midpoint between them stays at (0, 0) because their velocities are equal and opposite. This is useful for paired animations—two halves of a split, two wings of a bird, etc.

## Thruster pulses (velocity added in bursts)

Instead of setting velocity, *add* a fixed impulse every N frames. The entity accelerates in steps.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define ship (world/spawn 'ship -5 0))
(entity/set-vel! ship 0 0)
(let loop ((n 100) (frame 0))
  (when (> n 0)
    (when (= (modulo frame 15) 0)
      (let ((v (entity/vel ship)))
        (entity/set-vel! ship (+ (car v) 0.5) (cadr v))))
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1) (+ frame 1))))
(entity/pos ship)
```

[VISUAL: A spaceship accelerates in discrete jumps. The trail has visible \"steps\"—segments where speed is constant, then a jump to a faster segment. Final position shows it traveled far due to repeated acceleration.]

Every 15 frames we add 0.5 to vx. The ship jolts forward repeatedly. This is how you simulate a pulsed thruster or stamina-based dash.

## Velocity inheritance (child entity starts with parent's velocity)

Spawn a projectile from a moving entity. Give the projectile the parent's current velocity *plus* a firing velocity.

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define ship (world/spawn 'ship -3 1))
(entity/set-vel! ship 2 0.5)
(let loop ((n 20))
  (when (> n 0)
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(let* ((ship-pos (entity/pos ship))
       (ship-vel (entity/vel ship))
       (bullet (world/spawn 'bullet (car ship-pos) (cadr ship-pos))))
  (entity/set-vel! bullet (+ (car ship-vel) 5) (+ (cadr ship-vel) 0))
  (let loop ((n 40))
    (when (> n 0)
      (world/step 0.016)
      (loop (- n 1))))
  (list (entity/pos ship) (entity/pos bullet)))
```

[VISUAL: A ship moves diagonally. Midway through, a bullet spawns from it. The bullet's trail continues the ship's diagonal but at a steeper angle (because we added 5 to vx). By the end, the bullet is well ahead.]

The bullet inherits the ship's velocity and adds its own muzzle velocity. This is how you fire from a moving platform—the projectile carries the platform's momentum.

## Momentum transfer (elastic collision, simplified)

Two entities collide head-on. Swap their velocities (simplified elastic collision in 1D).

```scheme
(world/reset!)
(define a (world/spawn 'ball -2 0))
(define b (world/spawn 'ball 2 0))
(entity/set-vel! a 3 0)
(entity/set-vel! b -2 0)
(let loop ((n 100))
  (when (> n 0)
    (let ((dist (entity/distance a b)))
      (when (< dist 0.5)
        (let ((va (entity/vel a))
              (vb (entity/vel b)))
          (entity/set-vel! a (car vb) (cadr vb))
          (entity/set-vel! b (car va) (cadr va)))))
    (world/step 0.016)
    (loop (- n 1))))
(list (entity/pos a) (entity/pos b))
```

[VISUAL: Two balls approach each other. When they get close, they bounce—their trails reverse direction instantly. The trails show a sharp V at the collision point. Final positions have the balls moving apart.]

When distance < 0.5, we swap velocities. This simulates a perfect elastic collision in 1D (ignoring actual physics for simplicity). It's a velocity-based interaction.

### Moving Along One Axis

The simplest case: an entity moves horizontally across the canvas at constant speed.

```scheme
(define (route t)
  (let ((x (+ 50 (* t 80))))
    (world
      (entity 'dot
              (placement x 240)
              (shapes
                (circle 0 0 12 '#x333333))))))
```

[VISUAL: A dark gray circle sliding smoothly from left to right, starting at x=50 when t=0 and reaching x=130 at t=1.]

The position `x` is a **linear function of time**: `x = 50 + 80t`. At t=0, x=50. At t=1, x=130. The velocity is 80 pixels per second.

---

Now vertical motion: a balloon rises.

```scheme

  (let ((y (- 400 (* t 120))))
    (world

                (rect -2 16 4 30 '#x8B4513))))))
```

[VISUAL: A red balloon with a brown string drifting upward, starting near the bottom of the canvas and climbing toward the top.]

Subtracting makes the balloon rise: as `t` increases, `y` decreases. Velocity is −120 pixels per second.

A slow drift versus a quick dash:

```scheme

    (entity 'dot

(route-fast 0.5)
```

[VISUAL: Two side-by-side renders. The slow route shows a blue dot that has moved 20 pixels at t=0.5. The fast route shows a red dot that has moved 120 pixels in the same time.]

### Moving Along Two Axes

Horizontal and vertical motion combine to produce diagonal travel.


[VISUAL: A green square gliding diagonally from upper-left toward lower-right.]

The entity moves 160 px/s horizontally and 120 px/s vertically. The **speed** (magnitude of velocity) is `sqrt(160² + 120²) = 200` px/s. The **direction** is the angle `atan(120/160)` ≈ 36.9°.

### Encoding Direction: Angle and Speed

Instead of separate x and y velocities, we can specify a **heading** (angle) and a **speed** (magnitude), then decompose into components.

```scheme
(define (route t)
  (let* ((angle 0.785398)  ; 45 degrees in radians
         (speed 150)
         (vx (* speed (cos angle)))
         (vy (* speed (sin angle)))
         (x (+ 100 (* t vx)))
         (y (+ 100 (* t vy))))
    (world
      (entity 'dart
              (placement x y)
              (shapes
                (polygon (list -8 0  8 0  0 -16) '#x3498DB))))))
```

[VISUAL: A blue triangle (pointing up-right) moving diagonally at 45° from the starting corner.]

The angle 0.785398 rad = 45°. Speed 150 px/s splits into vx ≈ 106 and vy ≈ 106.

"# Chapter 3: Easing

A button descends when you press it. A door swings shut. A bird alights on a branch. Each of these motions has a *shape* — not the path through space (we'll drill that in Chapter 4), but the shape of the *move itself* over time. Does it start slowly and build speed? Does it coast in and brake hard at the end? Does it move at a steady clip from first frame to last?

The difference between a move that *eases* and one that doesn't is the difference between something that feels alive and something that feels mechanical. Linear motion — constant velocity, like we explored in Chapter 2 — is the exception in the natural world, not the rule. Everything with weight accelerates into a move and decelerates out of it. Everything with intention hesitates, then commits. Easing is how we give the sprite's world that quality of *aliveness*.

This chapter drills the **:easing** axis of the motion 5-tuple. We'll start with the starkest contrast — linear vs eased — and climb toward layered easings, custom curves, and the feel of a move that *settles* rather than merely stopping.

[VISUAL: Three circles traveling the same horizontal distance — one moving linearly (evenly spaced frames), one easing in (tight spacing at start, wide at end), one easing out (wide spacing at start, tight at end).]

---

## The Linear Baseline

Before we can feel easing, we need to see what it replaces. Here's a box moving from left to right over 60 frames at constant velocity — no acceleration, no deceleration, just uniform motion:

```scheme
(let ((box (world/spawn 'box :x 50 :y 300)))
  (entity/set-vel! box 4 0)
  (world/step 60))
```

It moves. It gets there. But it doesn't *feel* like it decided to go or chose to stop — it's a mechanism, not a gesture.

---

## Ease-Out: The Arrival

Now the same move, but with an ease-out. The box starts fast and slows as it approaches its destination, like a hand reaching for a cup and decelerating as it arrives:

```scheme
(let ((box (world/spawn 'box :x 50 :y 300)))
  (entity/glide! box 290 300 :frames 60 :ease 'out))
```

`entity/glide!` is our first motion verb that bakes easing into the move. The `:ease 'out` parameter says \"start at full speed, slow to rest.\" The *distance* covered and the *duration* are the same as the linear move, but the *feel* is completely different.

---

## Ease-In: The Departure

Ease-in is the mirror: the box starts slowly and builds speed, like gathering courage before a leap:

```scheme
(let ((box (world/spawn 'box :x 50 :y 300)))
  (entity/glide! box 290 300 :frames 60 :ease 'in))
```

Ease-in moves feel *decisive* — the entity commits to the move and accelerates into it. They're less common than ease-out in UI (where you want arrivals to feel gentle) but crucial for departures, launches, and anything that reads as *effort*.

---

## Ease-In-Out: The Full Arc

Combine them: start slow, accelerate to midpoint, decelerate to rest. This is the shape of most natural motion — a full breath, in and out:

```scheme
(let ((box (world/spawn 'box :x 50 :y 300)))
  (entity/glide! box 290 300 :frames 60 :ease 'in-out))
```

Ease-in-out is the workhorse easing. It feels organic, intentional, and complete. When in doubt, reach for `'in-out`.

---

## Side-by-Side Comparison

Let's see all four shapes at once — linear, ease-in, ease-out, ease-in-out — so the difference is unmistakable:

```scheme
(let ((linear (world/spawn 'box :x 50 :y 200 :color 'gray))
      (ease-in (world/spawn 'box :x 50 :y 250 :color 'blue))
      (ease-out (world/spawn 'box :x 50 :y 300 :color 'green))
      (in-out (world/spawn 'box :x 50 :y 350 :color 'purple)))
  (entity/set-vel! linear 4 0)
  (entity/glide! ease-in 290 250 :frames 60 :ease 'in)
  (entity/glide! ease-out 290 300 :frames 60 :ease 'out)
  (entity/glide! in-out 290 350 :frames 60 :ease 'in-out)
  (world/step 60))
```

Watch how the blue box (ease-in) lags behind at the start but catches up. The green box (ease-out) leads early but slows. The purple box (in-out) does both. The gray box just *goes*.

---

## Vertical Motion: A Falling Leaf

Easing isn't just for horizontal slides. Here's a leaf drifting down with ease-in-out, giving it a gentle, settling quality:

```scheme
(let ((leaf (world/spawn 'leaf :x 400 :y 100)))
  (entity/glide! leaf 400 500 :frames 90 :ease 'in-out))
```

The same easing applied to a vertical move reads as *drift* rather than *slide* — context matters.

---

## Duration and Feel

The *length* of an eased move changes its emotional weight. Here's the same ease-out move at three durations — 30 frames (brisk), 60 frames (comfortable), 120 frames (languid):

```scheme
(let ((fast (world/spawn 'box :x 50 :y 200 :color 'red))
      (medium (world/spawn 'box :x 50 :y 250 :color 'yellow))
      (slow (world/spawn 'box :x 50 :y 300 :color 'blue)))
  (entity/glide! fast 290 200 :frames 30 :ease 'out)
  (entity/glide! medium 290 250 :frames 60 :ease 'out)
  (entity/glide! slow 290 300 :frames 120 :ease 'out)
  (world/step 120))
```

Fast ease-out feels *snappy*. Slow ease-out feels *luxurious*. The easing curve is the same; the tempo changes everything.

---

## Ease Power: Subtle vs Aggressive

Some easing verbs let you dial the *strength* of the ease — how aggressively it accelerates or decelerates. A gentle ease-out coasts in smoothly; an aggressive ease-out *brakes hard*:

```scheme
(let ((gentle (world/spawn 'box :x 50 :y 250 :color 'green))
      (strong (world/spawn 'box :x 50 :y 300 :color 'red)))
  (entity/glide! gentle 290 250 :frames 60 :ease 'out :power 2)
  (entity/glide! strong 290 300 :frames 60 :ease 'out :power 4)
  (world/step 60))
```

`:power 2` is the default — a quadratic ease, gentle and familiar. `:power 4` is quartic — more extreme, more *feeling*. Use higher powers when you want the easing to be *obvious*, when subtlety would be lost.

---

## Elastic Ease: Overshoot and Settle

Some easings don't just decelerate — they *overshoot* the target and spring back, like a rubber band snapping into place:

```scheme
(let ((box (world/spawn 'box :x 50 :y 300)))
  (entity/glide! box 290 300 :frames 80 :ease 'elastic-out))
```

`'elastic-out` gives the move a playful, bouncy quality. It's too much for most UI, but perfect for anything that should feel *springy* — a notification appearing, a character bouncing to a stop, a UI element with personality.

---

## Back Ease: Anticipation Before Departure

A back-ease pulls *away* from the target before moving toward it — like winding up before a throw:

```scheme
(let ((box (world/spawn 'box :x 150 :y 300)))
  (entity/glide! box 350 300 :frames 60 :ease 'back-out))
```

The box briefly moves *left* (away from the destination) before gliding right and settling. This is *anticipation* — one of Disney's 12 principles — baked into an easing curve.

---

## Bounce Ease: Settling After Impact

A bounce ease simulates the box hitting the ground and settling through a series of diminishing bounces:

```scheme
(let ((box (world/spawn 'box :x 200 :y 100)))
  (entity/glide! box 200 400 :frames 80 :ease 'bounce-out))
```

It's a shorthand for a physically plausible settle — useful when you want the *feel* of bounce without simulating the physics.

---

## Combining Horizontal and Vertical Easing

## Custom Easing via Interpolation Factor

For complete control, you can define your own easing function. Here's a box moving with a hand-rolled ease-out curve, computed frame-by-frame:

```scheme
(let ((box (world/spawn 'box :x 50 :y 300))
      (start-x 50)
      (end-x 350)
      (frames 60))
  (letrec ((ease-out (lambda (t) (- 1 (* (- 1 t) (- 1 t)))))
           (step (lambda (frame)
                   (when (< frame frames)
                     (let* ((t (/ frame frames))
                            (eased-t (ease-out t))
                            (x (+ start-x (* (- end-x start-x) eased-t))))
                       (entity/set-pos! box x 300)
                       (world/step 1)
                       (step (+ frame 1)))))))
    (step 0)))
```

The `ease-out` lambda is a quadratic ease function: `1 - (1 - t)²`. We compute the interpolation factor `t`, ease it, then use the eased value to position the box. This pattern — interpolate, ease, apply — is the skeleton of every tweening system.

## Easing with a Sine Wave

A sine-based ease gives a smooth, organic feel. Here's a box moving with a sine-out curve:

```scheme
(let ((box (world/spawn 'box :x 50 :y 300))
      (start-x 50)
      (end-x 350)
      (frames 60))
  (letrec ((ease-sine-out (lambda (t) (dsin (* t PI 0.5))))
           (step (lambda (frame)
                   (when (< frame frames)
                     (let* ((t (/ frame frames))
                            (eased-t (ease-sine-out t))
                            (x (+ start-x (* (- end-x start-x) eased-t))))
                       (entity/set-pos! box x 300)
                       (world/step 1)
                       (step (+ frame 1)))))))
    (step 0)))
```

The sine curve (first quarter of the wave) produces an ease that feels very *natural* — it's the shape of a pendulum slowing as it reaches the top of its swing.

## Easing with an Exponential Curve

An exponential ease decelerates *hard* near the end — useful for something that's *fighting* to stop:

```scheme
(let ((box (world/spawn 'box :x 50 :y 300))
      (start-x 50)
      (end-x 350)
      (frames 60))
  (letrec ((ease-expo-out (lambda (t) (- 1 (dpow 2 (* -10 t)))))
           (step (lambda (frame)
                   (when (< frame frames)
                     (let* ((t (/ frame frames))
                            (eased-t (ease-expo-out t))
                            (x (+ start-x (* (- end-x start-x) eased-t))))
                       (entity/set-pos! box x 300)
                       (world/step 1)
                       (step (+ frame 1)))))))
    (step 0)))
```

Exponential eases feel *abrupt* — they cover most of the distance quickly, then slow dramatically. Use them for impacts, sudden stops, or moves that should feel *forceful*.

## Mirrored Ease-In from Ease-Out

Any ease-out curve can become an ease-in by inverting the timeline: `eased_in(t) = 1 - eased_out(1 - t)`. Here's that transformation:

```scheme
(let ((box (world/spawn 'box :x 50 :y 300))
      (start-x 50)
      (end-x 350)
      (frames 60))
  (letrec ((ease-out (lambda (t) (- 1 (* (- 1 t) (- 1 t)))))
           (ease-in (lambda (t) (- 1 (ease-out (- 1 t)))))
           (step (lambda (frame)
                   (when (< frame frames)
                     (let* ((t (/ frame frames))
                            (eased-t (ease-in t))
                            (x (+ start-x (* (- end-x start-x) eased-t))))
                       (entity/set-pos! box x 300)
                       (world/step 1)
                       (step (+ frame 1)))))))
    (step 0)))
```

This is the mathematical relationship between in and out. Understanding it gives you the entire easing family from a single curve.

## Building Ease-In-Out from Ease-In and Ease-Out

Combine ease-in for the first half and ease-out for the second half:

```scheme
(let ((box (world/spawn 'box :x 50 :y 300))
      (start-x 50)
      (end-x 350)
      (frames 60))
  (letrec ((ease-out (lambda (t) (- 1 (* (- 1 t) (- 1 t)))))
           (ease-in (lambda (t) (- 1 (ease-out (- 1 t)))))
           (ease-in-out (lambda (t)
                          (if (< t 0.5)
                              (* 0.5 (ease-in (* 2 t)))
                              (+ 0.5 (* 0.5 (ease-out (- (* 2 t) 1)))))))
           (step (lambda (frame)
                   (when (< frame frames)
                     (let* ((t (/ frame frames))
                            (eased-t (ease-in-out t))
                            (x (+ start-x (* (- end-x start-x) eased-t))))
                       (entity/set-pos! box x 300)
                       (world/step 1)
                       (step (+ frame 1)))))))
    (step 0)))
```

The first half runs ease-in at double speed; the second half runs ease-out at double speed. Scaled and stitched. This is how all compound easings are built.

## Easing Toward a Moving Target

A box easing toward a target that's also moving. The glide destination is computed at the start, so the box doesn't track the target — it eases toward where the target *was*:

```scheme
(let ((target (world/spawn 'target :x 300 :y 300 :color 'red))
      (chaser (world/spawn 'box :x 50 :y 300 :color 'blue)))
  (entity/set-vel! target 2 0)
  (let ((target-x (entity/x target))
        (target-y (entity/y target)))
    (entity/glide! chaser target-x target-y :frames 60 :ease 'out))
  (world/step 60))
```

The chaser eases smoothly, but the target keeps moving — the chaser arrives at where the target *used to be*. This is the difference between easing toward a *position* and easing toward an *entity* (which requires re-computing the destination every frame — we'll drill that in later chapters).

## Easing a Bounce to Rest (Manual Decay)

```scheme
                     (when (> count 0)
                       (entity/glide! box (+ x dist) 300 :frames 20 :ease 'in-out)
                       (world/step 20)
                       (bounce (+ x dist) (* dist -0.5) (- count 1))))))
```

## Easing a Pendulum Swing (Sine Oscillation with Decay)

A box swaying back and forth, each swing smaller than the last, like a pendulum coming to rest:

```scheme
(let ((box (world/spawn 'box :x 200 :y 200))
      (center-x 200)
      (amplitude 100))
  (letrec ((swing (lambda (frame max-frames)
                    (when (< frame max-frames)
                      (let* ((t (/ frame max-frames))
                             (decay (- 1 t))
                             (offset (* amplitude decay (dsin (* t TAU 2)))))
                        (entity/set-pos! box (+ center-x offset) 200)
                        (world/step 1)
                        (swing (+ frame 1) max-frames))))))
    (swing 0 120)))
```

The sine wave provides the oscillation; the `(- 1 t)` decay shrinks the amplitude. No easing *function* here — the sine wave *is* the easing. But the principle is the same: a value that changes smoothly over time.

## Easing a Spiral Inward

A box spiraling toward a center point, the radius shrinking with ease-out:

```scheme
(let ((box (world/spawn 'box :x 400 :y 300))
      (center-x 300)
      (center-y 300)
      (start-radius 150))
  (letrec ((spiral (lambda (frame max-frames)
                     (when (< frame max-frames)
                       (let* ((t (/ frame max-frames))
                              (eased-t (- 1 (* (- 1 t) (- 1 t))))
                              (radius (* start-radius (- 1 eased-t)))
                              (angle (* t TAU 3))
                              (x (+ center-x (* radius (dcos angle))))
                              (y (+ center-y (* radius (dsin angle)))))
                         (entity/set-pos! box x y)
                         (world/step 1)
                         (spiral (+ frame 1) max-frames))))))
    (spiral 0 120)))
```

The radius shrinks with quadratic ease-out; the angle increases linearly. The result is a smooth spiral, tightening as it reaches the center.

## Exercises

1. **The Gentle Door**: A door sprite at `x: 300, y: 300, angle: 0` swings open (rotating to `angle: PI/2`) over 50 frames with ease-out, holds open for 40 frames, then swings shut (back to `angle: 0`) over 50 frames with ease-in. The swing should feel *weighted* — slow to start, settling gently.

2. **The Settling Leaf**: A leaf at `x: 300, y: 50` falls to `y: 500` over 120 frames, but with a custom easing: ease-in for the first third (accelerating under gravity), linear for the middle third (terminal velocity), and elastic-out for the last third (tumbling to rest). Each phase should be a separate glide.

3. **The Spiral Departure**: A box at `x: 300, y: 300` spirals outward along a circular path, the radius growing from 0 to 200 over 100 frames with ease-in, while the angle increases linearly (completing 3 full rotations). The motion should feel like a spring unwinding.

4. **The Accordion Formation**: Four boxes in a horizontal line at `y: 300`, starting at `x: 100, 200, 300, 400`. They collapse inward to a shared center at `x: 250` with ease-in over 40 frames, hold for 20 frames, then expand back to their original positions with ease-out over 40 frames. The formation should *breathe*.

5. **The Attention Pulse**: A box at `x: 300, y: 300, scale: 1.0` grows to `scale: 1.3` over 20 frames with ease-out, shrinks back to `scale: 1.0` over 20 frames with ease-in, and repeats this cycle 3 times. The pulse should feel *alive*, like the box is breathing or calling for attention.

6. **The Chase with Variable Easing**: A red box (leader) glides from `x: 50, y: 300` to `x: 500, y: 300` over 80 frames with ease-in-out. A blue box (chaser) starts at `x: 50, y: 350` and glides to the *current position* of the leader (sampled at frame 40) over 60 frames with ease-out, starting at frame 20. The chaser should arrive smoothly but not catch the leader.

### Linear motion (no easing)

Before we curve time, let's see what we're leaving behind. A circle crosses the canvas at constant speed—every frame covers the same distance.

```scheme
(define (render)
  (let* ((duration 2.0)
         (progress (/ (mod (world-time) duration) duration))
         (x (+ 50 (* progress 700))))
    (fill 100 150 250)
    (circle x 300 30)))
```

[VISUAL: A blue circle sliding left-to-right at unwavering speed, looping.]

The motion is *correct* but lifeless. No anticipation, no arrival—just traverse.

---


### Ease-out: the settling stone

A stone tossed onto ice: fast at first, friction slowing it down, rolling to rest. We'll square the progress to front-load the distance.

```scheme
(define (render)
  (let* ((duration 2.5)
         (t (/ (mod (world-time) duration) duration))
         (eased (- 1 (* (- 1 t) (- 1 t))))
         (x (+ 100 (* eased 600))))
    (fill 180 100 80)
    (circle x 280 28)))
```

[VISUAL: An orange circle bursts across the left half, then decelerates smoothly to rest on the right.]

The squared falloff—`(- 1 (* (- 1 t) (- 1 t)))`—spends most of the motion near the end position. The arrival feels *intentional*.

---


### Ease-in: the winding pitch

A pitcher's arm: slow pullback, explosive release. Distance accumulates toward the end.

```scheme
(define (render)
  (let* ((duration 1.8)
         (t (/ (mod (world-time) duration) duration))
         (eased (* t t))
         (y (+ 100 (* eased 400))))
    (fill 250 200 100)
    (circle 400 y 25)))
```

[VISUAL: A yellow circle creeps downward, then accelerates sharply toward the bottom.]

Squaring `t` directly creates the opposite shape: crawl, then rush.

---


### Ease-in-out: the breath

A breath in, a breath out—smooth at the start, smooth at the end, fastest in the middle. We'll blend ease-in and ease-out.

```scheme
(define (render)
  (let* ((duration 3.0)
         (t (/ (mod (world-time) duration) duration))
         (eased (if (< t 0.5)
                    (* 2 t t)
                    (- 1 (* 2 (- 1 t) (- 1 t)))))
         (x (+ 100 (* eased 600))))
    (fill 150 250 200)
    (circle x 350 26)))
```

[VISUAL: A mint-green circle eases away from the left edge, speeds through the center, eases to rest on the right.]

The `if` switches from ease-in (first half) to ease-out (second half). The motion feels *considered* at both ends.

---


### Cubic ease-out: the weighted settle

Squaring gives a gentle curve. Cubing it—`(- 1 (* (- 1 t) (- 1 t) (- 1 t)))`—creates a sharper start and a longer tail, like a heavy bag swinging to rest.

```scheme
(define (render)
  (let* ((duration 2.2)
         (t (/ (mod (world-time) duration) duration))
         (eased (- 1 (* (- 1 t) (- 1 t) (- 1 t))))
         (x (+ 80 (* eased 640))))
    (fill 200 120 180)
    (circle x 420 32)))
```

[VISUAL: A mauve circle rockets partway, then glides to a gentle stop.]

More \"weight\" in the deceleration—useful for something that has inertia.

"# Chapter 4: The Arc

A thing that glides in a straight line can feel mechanical, dutiful, a bit lifeless. But a thing that *curves* through space — a leaf spiraling down, a bird swooping to land, a coin flipped and caught — reads as *alive*, as subject to forces, as moving through a world that *pushes back*.

The arc is the signature of a throw, a toss, a fall arrested by forward motion. It's the parabola that gravity writes when something moves horizontally *and* vertically at once. It's the trajectory that tells you this object has *mass*, that it was *launched*, that it will *land*.

We'll drill the arc as a *trajectory primitive* — the `:trajectory` axis of the 5-tuple. Where chapter 2 gave us velocity (the second atom of motion) and chapter 3 gave us easing (the *feel* of arrival), this chapter teaches the *path* itself: not just \"move from here to there,\" but \"*how* you travel the space between.\"

Every example in this chapter is a complete, runnable program. Each one explores a different situation where an arc matters: a stone skipped across water, a paper airplane's descent, a dancer's leap, a banner unfurling in the wind. We'll build from the simplest parabola to arcs that compose with easing, timing, and the beginnings of weight.

Let's start where motion starts: with something small, tossed into the air.

---

## 1. The simplest arc: a pebble tossed

A pebble leaves your hand with some horizontal speed and some upward speed. Gravity pulls it down. The path it traces is a parabola.

We'll use `motion/arc` — the primitive that composes horizontal glide with vertical rise-and-fall.

```scheme
(let ((pebble (world/spawn 'pebble 100 300)))
  (entity/sprite! pebble 'circle 8 '(120 100 80))
  (motion/arc pebble 
              :dx 400 
              :apex 150 
              :frames 60)
  (world/step 120))
```

[VISUAL: A small gray circle traces a smooth parabola from left to right, rising to a peak 150 pixels above its start, then descending to land 400 pixels to the right. The arc is symmetrical, gentle, the path of something light tossed without spin.]

The pebble starts at `(100, 300)`, moves 400 pixels to the right (`:dx`), and at the midpoint of its journey rises 150 pixels above the start height (`:apex`). The motion completes in 60 frames. After 60 more frames of stepping, the pebble has landed and sits still.

---

## 2. A higher toss

The same pebble, but tossed *harder* — a higher apex, the same horizontal distance.

```scheme
(let ((pebble (world/spawn 'pebble 100 300)))
  (entity/sprite! pebble 'circle 8 '(120 100 80))
  (motion/arc pebble 
              :dx 400 
              :apex 250 
              :frames 80)
  (world/step 160))
```

[VISUAL: The arc is taller, steeper at the launch and landing. The pebble climbs higher and falls farther. The parabola reads as *more force* applied at the start.]

More apex, more time in the air. The horizontal speed stays roughly constant (400 pixels in 80 frames ≈ 5 px/frame), but the vertical component is stronger.


[VISUAL: The arc is barely visible — a gentle rise and fall, the path of a stone skipped across water on its first bounce. The motion is almost linear, but the slight curve gives it *life*.]

An apex of 30 pixels over a 500-pixel journey is subtle, but it's enough to distinguish this from a straight glide. The eye reads it as a *skim*, not a *slide*.

## 5. A steep drop

An arc where the horizontal distance is small and the apex is *below* the start — a thing dropped from a height with a bit of forward momentum.

```scheme
(let ((coin (world/spawn 'coin 300 100)))
  (entity/sprite! coin 'circle 10 '(200 180 100))
  (motion/arc coin 
              :dx 150 
              :apex -200 
              :frames 50)
  (world/step 100))
```

[VISUAL: A gold circle drops steeply from the top of the screen, curving slightly to the right as it falls. The path is a downward-opening parabola — the signature of a drop with a bit of horizontal drift.]

A negative apex means \"fall below the start height.\" The coin was at `y=100`, and the lowest point of the arc is 200 pixels below that, at `y=300`. The horizontal drift (`:dx 150`) keeps it from being a pure vertical drop.

## 6. An arc that lands on a platform

The pebble again, but this time we want it to land *precisely* on a target — a platform 400 pixels to the right and 50 pixels *below* the start.

```scheme

      (platform (world/spawn 'platform 500 250)))
  (entity/sprite! pebble 'circle 8 '(120 100 80))
  (entity/sprite! platform 'rect 60 10 '(80 60 40))
  (motion/arc pebble 
              :dx 400 
              :dy 50 
              :apex 100 
              :frames 60)
  (world/step 120))
```

[VISUAL: A gray pebble arcs from left to right, rising 100 pixels above its start, then descending to land squarely on a brown rectangular platform 50 pixels below the launch height. The arc is asymmetrical — the descent is longer than the ascent.]

The `:dy` parameter lets us specify the *end height* relative to the start. The arc still peaks at `:apex` pixels above the start, but the landing point is offset vertically. This is the arc of a thing tossed onto a lower ledge.

## 8. An arc with easing

An arc is a *trajectory*, but easing still applies — we can ease the *pace* along the arc, so the object accelerates or decelerates as it travels the curve.

```scheme
(let ((ball (world/spawn 'ball 100 300)))
  (entity/sprite! ball 'circle 12 '(200 100 100))
  (motion/arc ball 
              :dx 400 
              :apex 150 
              :frames 60 
              :ease 'out-quad)
  (world/step 120))
```

[VISUAL: A red ball traces the same parabola as the pebble in example 1, but the *spacing* along the arc changes. The ball moves quickly at the start, then slows as it approaches the landing. The arc shape is identical, but the *feel* is different — the ball is braking, settling, coming to rest rather than just falling.]

Easing along an arc compounds the vertical and horizontal components — the ball still follows the parabola, but the rate of progress along that curve is eased. This is how we get the feel of a *toss that settles* vs. a *toss that impacts*.

## 9. Ease-in: a hard landing

The opposite: the ball accelerates as it travels the arc, arriving with speed.

```scheme
(let ((ball (world/spawn 'ball 100 300)))
  (entity/sprite! ball 'circle 12 '(200 100 100))
  (motion/arc ball 
              :dx 400 
              :apex 150 
              :frames 60 
              :ease 'in-quad)
  (world/step 120))
```

[VISUAL: The same parabola, but now the ball starts slow and accelerates. The spacing is tight at the start, wide at the end. The ball *slams* into the landing point. The arc reads as a *drop*, not a gentle toss.]

Ease-in on an arc is the signature of something *falling* under increasing speed, or something *thrown downward* with force building.

[VISUAL: A blue ball launches with building speed, coasts smoothly through the apex, then decelerates into the landing. The spacing is tight at both ends, wide in the middle. The arc feels *deliberate*, *graceful* — the motion of a dancer leaping, not a rock thrown.]

This is the arc that reads as *intentional movement*, not ballistic physics. The object is *performing* the arc, not just tracing it.

## Exercises

You've seen forty arcs — parabolas traced by pebbles, dancers, birds, cannonballs, and comets. You've composed arcs with easing, chained arcs into sequences, and varied parameters to create different *feels* from the same underlying shape.

Now it's your turn. Write the complete program for each of these situations:

1. **A message rocket**: A signal flare is launched from a ship, arcs high into the night sky, and explodes at the peak of its arc. The flare should rise quickly (ease-in), hang at the apex, then fall back down (ease-out). Use `:dx 0` for a purely vertical arc, `:apex 300`, and choose `:frames` and `:ease` values that create the feel of a flare bursting at the top of its flight.

2. **A squirrel leaping between branches**: A squirrel jumps from one tree branch to another. The first branch is at `(150, 250)`, the second at `(380, 220)` — slightly higher and to the right. The squirrel should arc upward, peak well above both branches (to clear the gap), and land softly on the second branch. Use ease-in-out to give the leap a deliberate, controlled quality.

3. **A paper airplane contest**: Three children launch paper airplanes simultaneously. Each plane has a different arc — one flies far but low (glider), one flies high but short (climber), one is balanced (cruiser). Spawn three planes at the same starting point, give each a distinct `:dx`, `:apex`, and `:frames`, and step the world long enough to see all three land. Make the variation feel *intentional* — three different throwing styles, not random noise.

4. **A ball bouncing up a staircase**: The opposite of example 27 — the ball bounces *up* the stairs, each bounce landing on a step 40 pixels *higher* than the last. Each bounce should have a smaller `:apex` than the last (the ball is losing energy as it climbs). Chain four or five arcs, varying `:dy`, `:apex`, and `:frames` to create the feel of a ball struggling upward, each bounce weaker than the last.

5. **A fountain's arc**: Water spurts from a fountain in the center of a plaza, arcs outward, and splashes into the basin. Model a *single droplet* that launches from `(300, 350)`, arcs to the left, peaks at `:apex 180`, and lands in the basin at `(200, 350)`. Then add two more droplets launching at slightly different times (use `world/step` between spawns) with slightly different arcs (vary `:dx` and `:apex` by small amounts). The three arcs should feel like *one fountain*, not three unrelated tosses.

6. **A rescue rope tossed to a swimmer**: A lifeguard on a pier tosses a rope to a swimmer in the water below and to the right. The rope should arc from the lifeguard's position `(150, 200)` to the swimmer's position `(400, 330)`. The arc should be high enough to clear the pier railing, but the motion should be *urgent* — short duration, ease-in to show the force of the throw. The swimmer is in danger; the toss must be fast and accurate.

Each exercise should be a complete, standalone program — spawn the entities, set their sprites, execute the motion, step the world. Vary the situations, vary the arcs, and pay attention to how `:dx`, `:apex`, `:dy`, `:frames`, and `:ease` combine to create *feel*.

The arc is the signature of a world with gravity, with forces, with *physics*. Master it, and you can make anything move as if it has weight, as if it has been thrown, as if it belongs to the world.

### The Simplest Arc: Two Eases, Different Rates

A horizontal ease and a vertical ease, running together but peaking at different moments.

```scheme
;; A dot that rises and falls while drifting right
(define (draw)
  (let* ((t (/ (mod (millis) 3000) 3000.0))
         (x (* t 400))
         (y (- 200 (* 150 (sin (* t 3.14159))))))
    (motion/clear)
    (motion/circle x y 12 \"fill\")))

(draw)
```

[VISUAL: A low arc, peak at midpoint, dot traveling left to right across 400 pixels]

The horizontal motion is linear (`(* t 400)`). The vertical motion is a sine wave. Together they make an arc.

---


### Separate the Eases

Same idea, but now the vertical motion uses a different easing curve.

```scheme
;; Parabolic vertical, linear horizontal
(define (ease-quad-out t)
  (- (* t (- 2 t))))

(define (draw)
  (let* ((t (/ (mod (millis) 2500) 2500.0))
         (x (+ 50 (* t 300)))
         (y (+ 100 (* -120 (ease-quad-out t)))))
    (motion/clear)
    (motion/circle x y 10 \"fill\")))

(draw)
```

[VISUAL: A smooth parabolic rise and fall, peak slightly past midpoint due to quad-out]

Now the arc has a different *feel*. The vertical motion decelerates as it peaks, making the top of the arc linger.

---


### Asymmetric Timing

The rise and fall don't have to take the same amount of time.

```scheme
;; Fast rise, slow fall
(define (ease-in-cubic t)
  (* t t t))

(define (ease-out-cubic t)
  (let ((t1 (- t 1)))
    (+ 1 (* t1 t1 t1))))

(define (draw)
  (let* ((raw-t (/ (mod (millis) 3000) 3000.0))
         (t (if (< raw-t 0.3)
                (/ raw-t 0.3)
                (/ (- raw-t 0.3) 0.7)))
         (ease-fn (if (< raw-t 0.3) ease-in-cubic ease-out-cubic))
         (x (+ 60 (* raw-t 280)))
         (y (+ 250 (* -180 (ease-fn t)))))
    (motion/clear)
    (motion/circle x y 11 \"fill\")))

(draw)
```

[VISUAL: Quick snap upward, long lazy descent]

The first 30% of the timeline is the rise (cubic-in). The remaining 70% is the fall (cubic-out). The horizontal motion ignores this split and moves linearly.

### Throwing Upward

A ball thrown upward follows a parabolic arc. The horizontal speed is constant; the vertical speed changes linearly (constant acceleration).

```scheme

(define (draw)
  (let* ((t (/ (mod (millis) 2200) 2200.0))
         (x (+ 40 (* t 320)))
         (vy0 -200)
         (g 400)
         (y (+ 300 (+ (* vy0 t) (* 0.5 g t t)))))

    (motion/circle x y 13 \"fill\")))

(draw)
```

[VISUAL: Classic parabolic arc, peak at mid-flight, landing lower than launch]

This is kinematic motion: `y = y0 + v0*t + 0.5*g*t^2`. The constants are chosen so the arc fits the viewport.

```scheme
(draw)
```

"# Chapter 5: Timing

A door swings open. Does it slam, or drift? Does it hesitate before it moves, or leap away the instant you touch it? A leaf falls. Does it tumble straight down, or hang in the air a beat before gravity takes it?

The *what* and *where* of motion we know — we've moved things, eased them, arced them. But the *when* — the rhythm inside the move, the breath before the jump, the pause at the top of the arc, the way something settles after it lands — that's **timing**. It's the difference between a motion that *happens* and a motion that *feels*.

This chapter drills the `:timing` axis: **anticipation** (the windup), **hold** (the pause that gives weight), **follow-through** (the overshoot and settle), and **slow-in slow-out** (the shape of effort). These aren't decoration. They're how motion reads as *alive*.

## The Instant Move

Here's a thing that moves with no timing at all — it just teleports.

```scheme
(let ((box (world/spawn 'box 100 150)))
  (entity/set-pos! box 300 150)
  (world/step 60))
```

[VISUAL: A box at x=100, then instantly at x=300. No journey, no arc, no feel.]

It gets there. But there's no *motion* — just two states. Let's put time back in.

## The Linear Move

Now we move smoothly, at a constant rate.

```scheme
(let ((box (world/spawn 'box 100 150)))
  (entity/set-vel! box 3 0)
  (world/step 60))
```

[VISUAL: A box sliding at constant speed from left to right.]

Better. It moves. But it starts at full speed and stops at full speed. Real things don't do that — they ramp up, they ramp down. That's **slow-in slow-out**, and it's the foundation of timing.

## Slow-In, Slow-Out

An object that *accelerates* into motion and *decelerates* out of it feels like it has mass, like it's making an effort.

```scheme
(let ((box (world/spawn 'box 100 150)))
  (entity/glide! box 300 150 60 'ease-in-out)
  (world/step 60))
```

[VISUAL: A box that starts slowly, speeds up in the middle, then slows to a stop.]

The same distance, the same duration — but now it *feels* deliberate. The ease curve does the work.

## The Hold

A **hold** is a pause in the middle of action. It gives the audience time to register what just happened, or what's about to happen.

```scheme
(let ((ball (world/spawn 'ball 150 100)))
  (entity/glide! ball 150 200 20 'ease-out)
  (world/after 20
    (lambda ()
      (world/after 30
        (lambda ()
          (entity/glide! ball 150 100 20 'ease-in)))))
  (world/step 90))
```

[VISUAL: A ball drops, *holds* at the bottom for a beat, then rises back up.]

The hold at the bottom gives the motion weight. Without it, the ball would just bounce — with it, it *lands*.

## Anticipation: The Windup

Before a big move, real things wind up in the *opposite* direction. A jumper crouches. A punch pulls back. That's **anticipation**, and it makes the main action read as *powerful*.

```scheme
(let ((box (world/spawn 'box 200 150)))
  (entity/glide! box 180 150 12 'ease-in)
  (world/after 12
    (lambda ()
      (entity/glide! box 350 150 24 'ease-out)))
  (world/step 60))
```

[VISUAL: A box that *backs up* slightly, then launches forward.]

The little recoil to the left makes the jump to the right feel *intentional*. You can almost see the effort.

## Anticipation + Hold + Follow-Through

Let's compose all three: windup, pause, action, settle.

```scheme
(let ((ball (world/spawn 'ball 150 200)))
  ;; anticipation: pull down
  (entity/glide! ball 150 220 10 'ease-out)
  (world/after 10
    (lambda ()
      ;; hold
      (world/after 8
        (lambda ()
          ;; jump
          (entity/glide! ball 150 80 20 'ease-in-out)
          (world/after 20
            (lambda ()
              ;; follow-through: settle back to rest
              (entity/glide! ball 150 90 8 'ease-out)
              (world/after 8
                (lambda ()
                  (entity/glide! ball 150 85 6 'ease-out))))))))))
  (world/step 80))
```

That's the full phrase: prepare, pause, act, overshoot, settle. It reads as a *living thing* making a jump, not a physics sim.

## Timing as Feel

You've seen anticipation, hold, follow-through, slow-in slow-out. You've seen them *composed* — windups that lead to jumps, jumps that overshoot and settle, settles that wobble before they rest. These aren't tricks. They're the **grammar** of timing, the reason one move feels heavy and another feels light, one feels deliberate and another feels panicked.

Timing is how you let the audience *see* effort, intention, weight, surprise. It's the difference between a motion that happens *to* a thing and a motion the thing *makes*.

The next chapter drills **weight and embodiment** — the `:embodiment` regime, where timing meets *mass*. But everything you just learned about when things start, when they pause, when they overshoot — that carries forward. Timing is the foundation. Weight is timing with stakes.

3. **The Tired Climb**: A climber moving upward in four stages, each stage *slower* than the last, with longer pauses between moves. Show exhaustion through timing alone.

4. **The Yo-Yo**: A yo-yo that drops with ease-in (accelerating), hits the bottom, *holds* (sleeping), then rises with ease-out (decelerating). Then repeat the cycle.

5. **The Haunted Candle**: A candle flame that flickers — tiny, fast moves up and down with *random* durations (use `world/hash` to seed the timing), never still, never predictable.

6. **The Gathering Storm**: Three clouds that drift slowly into frame from different directions, each arriving at a *different* time. When all three are in place, they *hold* together for a beat, then the scene ends. Show convergence through offset timing.

```scheme
  (world/after w 0.2 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'on 'radius 20 0.2 'quad-in)))
  (world/after w 0.8 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'on 'radius 30 0.2 'quad-out)))
  (world/after w 1.0 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'on 'radius 20 0.2 'quad-in)))
  (world/after w 1.6 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'on 'radius 30 0.2 'quad-out)))
  ;; Off-beat: 0.4, 1.2
  (world/after w 0.4 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'off 'radius 30 0.2 'quad-out)))
  (world/after w 0.6 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'off 'radius 20 0.2 'quad-in)))
  (world/after w 1.2 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'off 'radius 30 0.2 'quad-out)))
  (world/after w 1.4 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'off 'radius 20 0.2 'quad-in)))
  (world/render w 0.0)
  (world/render w 0.8)
  (world/render w 1.6))
```

[VISUAL: Blue circle pulses on the beat, orange circle pulses between beats]

Syncopation—staggering events so they fall between the main beats—creates groove and complexity. The same period, different phase.

---


### Extending a Motion

A circle moves right in one second, overshoots by 20 pixels, then settles back in 0.3 seconds. The overshoot and settle durations add nuance.

```scheme
;; Overshoot and settle
(let ((w (world/make 400 200)))
  (world/add w 'slider (entity/make 'circle 50 100 18))
  (entity/fill w 'slider \"#9d4edd\")
  ;; Main move: overshoot target
  (motion/ease w 'slider 'x 320 1.0 'quad-out)
  ;; Settle back
  (world/after w 1.0 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'slider 'x 300 0.3 'quad-in-out)))
  (world/render w 0.0)
  (world/render w 1.0)
  (world/render w 1.3))
```

[VISUAL: Circle slides to the right, goes a bit too far, then eases back slightly]

The 0.3-second settle is much faster than the 1.0-second main move. That timing contrast sells the overshoot as a correction rather than a separate gesture.

---


### Timing a Chain Reaction

Three dominoes fall in sequence. Each falls in 0.4s, and each triggers the next after a 0.2s delay.

```scheme
;; Domino chain
(let ((w (world/make 500 300)))
  (world/add w 'a (entity/make 'rect 100 150 30 100))
  (world/add w 'b (entity/make 'rect 200 150 30 100))
  (world/add w 'c (entity/make 'rect 300 150 30 100))
  (entity/fill w 'a \"#e63946\")
  (entity/fill w 'b \"#f77f00\")
  (entity/fill w 'c \"#fcbf49\")
  ;; First domino falls
  (motion/ease w 'a 'rotation 90 0.4 'quad-in)
  ;; Second domino falls 0.2s after first starts
  (world/after w 0.2 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'b 'rotation 90 0.4 'quad-in)))
  ;; Third domino falls 0.2s after second starts
  (world/after w 0.4 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'c 'rotation 90 0.4 'quad-in)))
  (world/render w 0.0)
  (world/render w 0.2)
  (world/render w 0.4)
  (world/render w 0.8))
```

[VISUAL: Three rectangles tipping over in a staggered sequence]

<!-- BUILD: rotation property support in entity and motion -->
*[needs: rotation property in entity/motion systems]*

The 0.2s trigger delay is the causal timing. Shorten it and the dominoes blur together; lengthen it and the chain feels sluggish.

---


### Breath Timing

A shape grows and shrinks in a 4-second cycle: 1.5s inhale, 0.5s hold, 1.5s exhale, 0.5s hold. The holds create a breathing rhythm.

```scheme
;; Breathing rhythm
(let ((w (world/make 300 300)))
  (world/add w 'lung (entity/make 'circle 150 150 30))
  (entity/fill w 'lung \"#4ecdc4\")
  ;; Inhale
  (motion/ease w 'lung 'radius 50 1.5 'quad-in-out)
  ;; Hold at peak
  ;; Exhale
  (world/after w 2.0 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'lung 'radius 30 1.5 'quad-in-out)))
  ;; Hold at rest
  ;; Next cycle would start at 4.0s
  (world/render w 0.0)
  (world/render w 1.5)
  (world/render w 2.0)
  (world/render w 3.5))
```

[VISUAL: Circle expanding, holding, contracting, holding—like breathing]

The 0.5s holds break the smooth in-out into a four-phase gesture. Real breath has these pauses; the timing makes the motion read as organic.

---


### Irregular Timing

A ball bounces, but each bounce has a different height and duration. The irregularity makes it feel hand-thrown rather than mechanical.

```scheme
;; Irregular bounce heights and durations
(let ((w (world/make 400 400)))
  (world/add w 'ball (entity/make 'circle 200 350 20))
  (entity/fill w 'ball \"#f4a261\")
  ;; First bounce: high and slow
  (motion/ease w 'ball 'y 100 0.7 'quad-out)
  (world/after w 0.7 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'ball 'y 350 0.7 'quad-in)))
  ;; Second bounce: medium
  (world/after w 1.4 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'ball 'y 180 0.5 'quad-out)))
  (world/after w 1.9 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'ball 'y 350 0.5 'quad-in)))
  ;; Third bounce: small and quick
  (world/after w 2.4 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'ball 'y 270 0.3 'quad-out)))
  (world/after w 2.7 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'ball 'y 350 0.3 'quad-in)))
  (world/render w 0.0)
  (world/render w 1.4)
  (world/render w 2.4)
  (world/render w 3.0))
```

[VISUAL: Ball bouncing with decreasing height and faster cycles]

Each bounce has a unique duration: 0.7s, 0.5s, 0.3s. The variation encodes energy loss and makes the bounce feel real rather than looped.

---


### Racing Timers

Two shapes race across the canvas. One takes 2 seconds, the other takes 2.5 seconds. The timing difference determines who wins.

```scheme
;; Two racers, different speeds
(let ((w (world/make 500 300)))
  (world/add w 'fast (entity/make 'circle 50 120 15))
  (world/add w 'slow (entity/make 'circle 50 180 15))
  (entity/fill w 'fast \"#06aed5\")
  (entity/fill w 'slow \"#e76f51\")
  (motion/ease w 'fast 'x 450 2.0 'linear)
  (motion/ease w 'slow 'x 450 2.5 'linear)
  (world/render w 0.0)
  (world/render w 1.0)
  (world/render w 2.0)
  (world/render w 2.5))
```

[VISUAL: Blue circle reaches the right edge first; orange circle arrives later]

The half-second difference means blue wins. Timing is how we encode relative speed when both objects use the same easing curve.

---


### Tempo Change Mid-Motion

A circle moves at one speed, then abruptly switches to a different speed partway through. The tempo change is a timing event.

```scheme
;; Speed shift mid-motion
(let ((w (world/make 400 200)))
  (world/add w 'runner (entity/make 'circle 50 100 15))
  (entity/fill w 'runner \"#bc4749\")
  ;; Start slow
  (motion/ease w 'runner 'x 200 2.0 'linear)
  ;; After 1 second, interrupt and go fast
  (world/after w 1.0 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'runner 'x 350 0.5 'linear)))
  (world/render w 0.0)
  (world/render w 1.0)
  (world/render w 1.5))
```

[VISUAL: Circle crawling right, then suddenly speeding up]

The tempo shift at 1.0s is jarring—intentionally. A smooth acceleration would use easing; this uses a timing interruption to create a gear-shift feel.

---


### Timing a Cluster Release

Five circles sit at the center. At different times over two seconds, each launches outward. The spread of launch times is the timing parameter.

```scheme
;; Staggered radial launch
(let ((w (world/make 400 400)))
  (world/add w 'a (entity/make 'circle 200 200 10))
  (world/add w 'b (entity/make 'circle 200 200 10))
  (world/add w 'c (entity/make 'circle 200 200 10))
  (world/add w 'd (entity/make 'circle 200 200 10))
  (world/add w 'e (entity/make 'circle 200 200 10))
  (entity/fill w 'a \"#f94144\")
  (entity/fill w 'b \"#f3722c\")
  (entity/fill w 'c \"#f8961e\")
  (entity/fill w 'd \"#f9c74f\")
  (entity/fill w 'e \"#90be6d\")
  (world/after w 0.0 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'a 'y 50 0.8 'quad-out)))
  (world/after w 0.4 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'b 'x 350 0.8 'quad-out)))
  (world/after w 0.8 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'c 'y 350 0.8 'quad-out)))
  (world/after w 1.2 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'd 'x 50 0.8 'quad-out)))
  (world/after w 1.6 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'e 'x 320 0.8 'quad-out)
                               (motion/ease w 'e 'y 80 0.8 'quad-out)))
  (world/render w 0.0)
  (world/render w 0.8)
  (world/render w 1.6)
  (world/render w 2.4))
```

[VISUAL: Circles bursting from center in a staggered firework pattern]

The 0.4s spacing between launches creates a burst that unfolds over time rather than all at once. Compress it to 0.1s and it feels like an explosion; stretch it to 1.0s and it feels like a slow bloom.

---


### Matched Exit and Entrance Timing

A shape exits stage right in 0.6s. Exactly 0.6s later, a new shape enters stage left at the same speed. The match creates continuity.

```scheme
;; Matched exit and entrance
(let ((w (world/make 400 200)))
  (world/add w 'old (entity/make 'circle 100 100 18))
  (world/add w 'new (entity/make 'circle 0 100 18))
  (entity/fill w 'old \"#e63946\")
  (entity/fill w 'new \"#06aed5\")
  ;; Old exits
  (motion/ease w 'old 'x 400 0.6 'linear)
  ;; New enters at same moment old exits
  (world/after w 0.6 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'new 'x 300 0.6 'linear)))
  (world/render w 0.0)
  (world/render w 0.6)
  (world/render w 1.2))
```

[VISUAL: Red circle exits right; blue circle immediately enters left at same speed]

The synchronized 0.6s durations create a relay race feel—one hands off to the next. Mismatch the durations and the handoff feels loose.

---


### Timing a Suspension

A pendulum swings, but at the apex of each swing, time seems to slow—the duration stretches. The suspension is a timing illusion.

```scheme
;; Pendulum with apex suspension
(let ((w (world/make 300 400)))
  (world/add w 'bob (entity/make 'circle 150 100 15))
  (entity/fill w 'bob \"#6a4c93\")
  ;; Swing right, slow at apex
  (motion/ease w 'bob 'x 230 0.8 'quad-out)
  (motion/ease w 'bob 'y 180 0.8 'quad-in)
  ;; Swing left, slow at apex
  (world/after w 0.8 (lambda ()
    (motion/ease w 'bob 'x 70 0.8 'quad-in)
    (motion/ease w 'bob 'y 180 0.8 'quad-out)))
  (world/after w 1.6 (lambda ()
    (motion/ease w 'bob 'x 150 0.8 'quad-out)
    (motion/ease w 'bob 'y 100 0.8 'quad-in)))
  (world/render w 0.0)
  (world/render w 0.8)
  (world/render w 1.6)
  (world/render w 2.4))
```

[VISUAL: Pendulum swinging, appearing to hang at each peak]

The quad easing creates natural suspension at the peaks, but the 0.8s duration means those peaks are drawn out. Halve the duration and the suspension vanishes.

---


### Timing and Emotion: Hesitation

A shape moves toward a target, slows down near the end (longer duration for the final segment), creating a hesitant approach.

```scheme
;; Hesitant approach
(let ((w (world/make 400 200)))
  (world/add w 'shy (entity/make 'circle 50 100 15))
  (entity/fill w 'shy \"#a8dadc\")
  ;; Fast approach
  (motion/ease w 'shy 'x 280 1.0 'linear)
  ;; Slow final approach
  (world/after w 1.0 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'shy 'x 350 1.5 'linear)))
  (world/render w 0.0)
  (world/render w 1.0)
  (world/render w 2.5))
```

[VISUAL: Circle moving quickly, then slowing as it nears the right edge]

The timing shift from 1.0s to 1.5s for the final segment encodes hesitation. Same total distance, but the last stretch takes longer—uncertainty.

---


### Explosive Start, Gradual Stop

A square launches instantly (very short duration) then coasts to a stop (long duration). The timing asymmetry creates a distinct feel.

```scheme
;; Explosive launch, gradual coast
(let ((w (world/make 400 200)))
  (world/add w 'rocket (entity/make 'rect 50 75 30 30))
  (entity/fill w 'rocket \"#f72585\")
  ;; Explosive start
  (motion/ease w 'rocket 'x 200 0.2 'quad-out)
  ;; Long coast to stop
  (world/after w 0.2 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'rocket 'x 350 2.0 'quad-out)))
  (world/render w 0.0)
  (world/render w 0.2)
  (world/render w 2.2))
```

[VISUAL: Square jerks right, then drifts slowly to a stop]

The 0.2s blast and 2.0s coast create a rocket-launch-and-drift feel. Reverse the timing and you get a slow wind-up then sudden stop—completely different character.

---


### Metric vs. Rubato Timing

Three beats, evenly spaced (metric), then three beats with varied spacing (rubato). Timing regularity vs. timing freedom.

```scheme
;; Metric: evenly spaced pulses
(let ((w (world/make 400 200)))
  (world/add w 'metro (entity/make 'circle 200 100 20))
  (entity/fill w 'metro \"#06aed5\")
  (motion/ease w 'metro 'radius 30 0.15 'quad-out)
  (world/after w 0.15 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'metro 'radius 20 0.15 'quad-in)))
  (world/after w 0.6 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'metro 'radius 30 0.15 'quad-out)))
  (world/after w 0.75 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'metro 'radius 20 0.15 'quad-in)))
  (world/after w 1.2 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'metro 'radius 30 0.15 'quad-out)))
  (world/after w 1.35 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'metro 'radius 20 0.15 'quad-in)))
  (world/render w 0.0)
  (world/render w 0.6)
  (world/render w 1.2)
  (world/render w 1.5))
```

[VISUAL: Circle pulsing at exactly 0.6s intervals—mechanical]

```scheme
;; Rubato: expressive spacing
(let ((w (world/make 400 200)))
  (world/add w 'expressive (entity/make 'circle 200 100 20))
  (entity/fill w 'expressive \"#f77f00\")
  (motion/ease w 'expressive 'radius 30 0.15 'quad-out)
  (world/after w 0.15 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'expressive 'radius 20 0.15 'quad-in)))
  (world/after w 0.5 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'expressive 'radius 30 0.15 'quad-out)))
  (world/after w 0.65 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'expressive 'radius 20 0.15 'quad-in)))
  (world/after w 1.4 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'expressive 'radius 30 0.15 'quad-out)))
  (world/after w 1.55 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'expressive 'radius 20 0.15 'quad-in)))
  (world/render w 0.0)
  (world/render w 0.5)
  (world/render w 1.4)
  (world/render w 1.7))
```

[VISUAL: Circle pulsing at irregular intervals—human]

Metric timing: 0.6s, 0.6s, 0.6s. Rubato timing: 0.5s, 0.75s, whatever feels right. The irregularity sounds human.

---


### Timing a Crescendo

Five events happen, each slightly faster than the previous. The accelerating tempo creates a crescendo.

```scheme
;; Accelerating tempo
(let ((w (world/make 500 200)))
  (world/add w 'a (entity/make 'circle 50 100 12))
  (world/add w 'b (entity/make 'circle 50 100 12))
  (world/add w 'c (entity/make 'circle 50 100 12))
  (world/add w 'd (entity/make 'circle 50 100 12))
  (world/add w 'e (entity/make 'circle 50 100 12))
  (entity/fill w 'a \"#f94144\")
  (entity/fill w 'b \"#f3722c\")
  (entity/fill w 'c \"#f8961e\")
  (entity/fill w 'd \"#f9c74f\")
  (entity/fill w 'e \"#90be6d\")
  (world/after w 0.0 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'a 'x 100 0.3 'linear)))
  (world/after w 1.0 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'b 'x 180 0.3 'linear)))
  (world/after w 1.8 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'c 'x 260 0.3 'linear)))
  (world/after w 2.4 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'd 'x 340 0.3 'linear)))
  (world/after w 2.8 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'e 'x 420 0.3 'linear)))
  (world/render w 0.0)
  (world/render w 1.0)
  (world/render w 2.0)
  (world/render w 3.1))
```

[VISUAL: Circles launching at accelerating intervals—1.0s, 0.8s, 0.6s, 0.4s]

The gaps shrink: 1.0s, 0.8s, 0.6s, 0.4s. The tempo accelerates toward a climax. Reverse the pattern and you get a rallentando—slowing down.

---


### Composite Timing: A Multi-Act Scene

A complete mini-scene composed purely through timing: silence, entrance, pause, gesture, pause, exit.

```scheme
;; Six-act timing composition
(let ((w (world/make 500 300)))
  (world/add w 'actor (entity/make 'circle 0 150 20))
  (entity/fill w 'actor \"#9d4edd\")
  ;; Act 1: Silence (nothing)
  ;; Act 2: Entrance (1.0-2.0s)
  (world/after w 1.0 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'actor 'x 150 1.0 'quad-out)))
  ;; Act 3: Pause (2.0-2.8s)
  ;; Act 4: Gesture (2.8-3.4s)
  (world/after w 2.8 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'actor 'y 100 0.3 'quad-out)))
  (world/after w 3.1 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'actor 'y 150 0.3 'quad-in)))
  ;; Act 5: Pause (3.4-4.0s)
  ;; Act 6: Exit (4.0-4.8s)
  (world/after w 4.0 (lambda () (motion/ease w 'actor 'x 500 0.8 'quad-in)))
  (world/render w 0.0)
  (world/render w 2.0)
  (world/render w 3.1)
  (world/render w 4.8))
```

[VISUAL: Empty stage, circle enters, waits, bobs up and down, waits, exits]

Six acts, timed: 1s silence, 1s entrance, 0.8s pause, 0.6s gesture, 0.6s pause, 0.8s exit. The entire narrative is timing.
