\"Animation on paper (or, today, on a computer) is built out of a small vocabulary of drawing types. Once you know the vocabulary, you can look at any animator's rough drawings and understand what they were planning. This chapter is the vocabulary.

There are three kinds of drawings, and they exist in relation to each other. **Keys** define the extremes of a motion. **In-betweens** fill in the frames between keys. **Timing charts** tell the in-betweener how the frames are spaced. Any animated scene, from a Termite Terrace short to a Ghibli feature, is built out of keys and in-betweens spaced according to timing charts.

# The key drawing

A key is the drawing that captures a moment of pose — one of the extreme positions in a motion. If a character is throwing a ball, the keys of that motion are: the starting stance, the wind-up (arm back, weight shifted), the release (arm forward, weight forward, ball just leaving hand), and the follow-through (arm across the body). Four keys, four moments the animator chooses because they define the shape of the whole throw.

Keys are where the animator does the most important thinking. The key drawings are what will make the audience feel weight, timing, and character. If the keys are boring — if they all look the same, or if they are staged unclearly — no amount of skilled in-betweening will save the scene. If the keys are good, even relatively simple in-betweening will produce a scene that feels alive.

Preston Blair, in his 1949 book *Advanced Animation*, laid out the pose-to-pose approach in detail. He drew example after example of key poses — a walk cycle in eight keys, a run cycle in six keys, a jump in five keys — with careful attention to how each pose captured a specific moment of weight distribution. His diagrams are still standard reference material in animation schools today.

# The in-between

An in-between is a drawing that lies between two keys. Its job is to complete the motion — to take the character from the position of the first key to the position of the second key in a way that feels continuous.

In-betweens are technical work. They require careful attention to shape volumes (the character's body should be the same three-dimensional object in every frame), to line quality (the drawing style should stay consistent), and to arc (the path of each part of the body from key to key should be a natural curve, not a straight line). Studio animation traditionally divided the work: senior animators drew the keys, and less senior artists — often called *in-betweeners* or *assistant animators* — drew the in-betweens. This division of labor made large productions feasible.

# The timing chart

The timing chart is a diagram — usually a small drawing next to a key — that tells the in-betweener how many in-betweens to draw between one key and the next, and how those in-betweens should be spaced.

The simplest timing chart is a straight line with tick marks: if there are eleven in-betweens between two keys spaced evenly, that's a straight line with eleven equal divisions. This gives constant-velocity motion — the character moves the same distance frame after frame.

But most animation is not constant-velocity. Slow-in and slow-out (one of the twelve principles) means motion accelerates and decelerates. To draw a slow-in, the in-betweens near the second key are packed closer together (small distances between frames = slow motion), and the in-betweens near the first key are spread further apart (large distances between frames = fast motion). The timing chart for a slow-in looks like a line with tick marks that get closer together as they approach one end.

There are named timing patterns that animators use often. **Ease-out** means the motion starts slow and speeds up (tick marks that get further apart). **Ease-in** means the motion starts fast and slows down (tick marks that get closer together). **Ease-in-out** means slow-fast-slow. **Cushioned** means slow-in on both sides.

The timing chart is a compact language. An animator can hand a page of keys to an in-betweener along with timing charts for each key-to-key interval, and the in-betweener can produce all the required drawings without further instruction. This is what let the studio system scale.

# What we can do in Scheme

Let's build a small demonstration of a motion with keys, in-betweens, and a timing chart.

```scheme
;; Two keys of a horizontal motion.
;; Key 1: figure at x=100, y=200
;; Key 2: figure at x=500, y=200
;; Number of frames between the keys: 11 (giving 12 frames total: key1 + 11 in-betweens + key2)

;; A timing chart is a list of fractions between 0 and 1 representing
;; the progress at each frame. A linear chart is (0/11, 1/11, ... 11/11).
;; A cushioned chart uses non-linear spacing.

(define (linear-chart n)
  (map (lambda (i) (/ i n)) (range 0 (+ n 1))))

;; An ease-in-out chart: use a sigmoid-like curve
;; s-curve maps 0-1 to 0-1 with slow start and slow end
(define (s-curve x)
  ;; smoothstep: 3x^2 - 2x^3
  (- (* 3 x x) (* 2 x x x)))

(define (ease-in-out-chart n)
  (map (lambda (i) (s-curve (/ i n))) (range 0 (+ n 1))))

;; A very slow-in chart: cube the progress
(define (slow-in-chart n)
  (map (lambda (i) (expt (/ i n) 3)) (range 0 (+ n 1))))

;; Given a chart, produce the position at each frame
(define (positions-from-chart chart x1 x2)
  (map (lambda (t) (+ x1 (* t (- x2 x1)))) chart))

;; Compare three motions of the same start and end points:
;; linear, ease-in-out, slow-in.
(define linear-motion    (positions-from-chart (linear-chart 11) 100 500))
(define eased-motion     (positions-from-chart (ease-in-out-chart 11) 100 500))
(define slow-in-motion   (positions-from-chart (slow-in-chart 11) 100 500))

;; linear-motion:    (100 136 173 209 245 281 318 354 390 427 463 500)
;; eased-motion:     (100 100 111 141 189 245 302 355 400 431 452 500)
;; slow-in-motion:   (100 100 100 101 106 118 141 178 235 313 415 500)
```

The three lists show what happens with the same two keys but different timing charts. The linear motion moves the same distance every frame. The eased motion moves slowly near both ends and quickly in the middle — the character seems to accelerate away from the first key and decelerate into the second. The slow-in motion is dramatic: the character barely moves for the first several frames, then accelerates enormously, arriving at the second key at high speed.

If you played these three motions side by side, they would look different. The linear one would feel mechanical. The eased one would feel natural. The slow-in one would feel *tense* — like the character was building up to a lunge.

# Extreme, breakdown, in-between

Inside the vocabulary of studio animation, there is a further subdivision. The **extreme** drawings are the outermost keys of a motion — the most extended, most contorted, most decisive positions. A **breakdown** is a drawing between two extremes that isn't a straight in-between but is chosen deliberately to shape the arc of the motion — a specific transitional pose that adds character.

For example, if a character punches, the extreme drawings are the wind-up (arm all the way back) and the impact (arm all the way forward). A breakdown might be the moment the arm is halfway forward but the wrist has snapped into position — the wrist leads the fist. The breakdown isn't in either extreme, but it defines how the wrist and hand transition between them.

Studio animation of the highest quality tends to use extremes plus breakdowns plus in-betweens, giving the animator control over three levels of the motion. Less careful animation uses only extremes and in-betweens, which produces motion that reads as competent but not exceptional.

# On the twos

There is one more timing decision that most studio animation makes and that beginners often don't notice: whether the animation runs *on ones* or *on twos*.

A film runs at twenty-four frames per second. If every frame is a new drawing, we say the animation is on ones. If each drawing is photographed twice, so the same drawing shows for two frames in a row, we say the animation is on twos. Animation on twos runs at effectively twelve drawings per second — half the drawing labor.

Most studio character animation from the golden era is on twos. The exceptions are fast, snappy motion — an eye blink, a hand gesture — which is often on ones because at twelve drawings per second the motion would look choppy. Very slow, sustained motion — a character breathing, a scene establishing — can be on threes or even fours (each drawing held for three or four frames), because at very slow speeds the human eye doesn't need many drawings per second to see continuous motion.

Modern hand-drawn animation and 3D animation still make these decisions. A 3D animator will set keyframes and let the software interpolate; the software runs on ones (a new pose per frame), but the animator can go in and modify individual frames to give the motion the character of on-twos. Ghibli films, notably, animate character action on ones or twos depending on the scene, and Miyazaki has been known to redraw scenes that were animated on twos to run on ones if he felt the motion needed the extra smoothness.

# What the vocabulary lets you do

Once you have the vocabulary — keys, in-betweens, timing charts, extremes, breakdowns, ones/twos — you can plan and analyze animation with precision. You can look at a scene and identify where the keys are, how the timing is shaped, whether the animation is on ones or twos. You can hand your plans to someone else — an in-betweener, a colleague, a rendering pipeline — with enough specificity that they can produce what you have designed.

This is the same as any technical vocabulary. Once you have it, you can share your ideas with other people who share it. The vocabulary is what lets a group of animators produce a coherent film together.

# What to notice in a scene

When you watch an animated scene closely, look for:

Where the keys are. Which drawings look like they carry the character of the motion — the extended pose, the strongly-shaped moment. Those are the keys.

How the in-betweens are timed. Does the motion feel constant-velocity, or does it accelerate and decelerate? Are there moments where the character seems to hesitate before a big movement (a slow-in) or overshoots and comes back (a follow-through)?

Whether it's on ones or twos. On a screen, look at a slow-moving character and count the frames per new pose. If each pose lasts two frames, it's on twos.

Where the breakdowns are. In the middle of a fast motion, is there a moment where the character passes through an unusual transitional pose — a wrist snap, a foot flick, a shoulder shrug? Those are the breakdowns.

These are the physical decisions that make the difference between animation that reads as *life* and animation that reads as *movement*. Life is the goal.

# Sources cited

Frank Thomas and Ollie Johnston, *The Illusion of Life: Disney Animation* (Abbeville Press, 1981). Chapters on planning and drawing.

Richard Williams, *The Animator's Survival Kit* (Faber, 2001). The most complete modern textbook on character animation technique. Williams (1933-2019) was a working animator (studio-independent, most known for directing *Who Framed Roger Rabbit* animation, 1988) and his book is used in most animation schools.

Preston Blair, *Advanced Animation* (Foster Publications, 1949; various later editions). The classic text on pose-to-pose animation, illustrated with detailed key poses.

Ollie Johnston and Frank Thomas, *The Illusion of Life: Disney Animation* (Abbeville, 1981).\"

Ghibli attribution for on-ones-versus-on-twos is a widely-reported studio practice; specific Miyazaki redraw-for-ones anecdotes are discussed in various making-of documentaries and interviews. Corporate name-drops kept minimal: 'Ghibli' as movement, 'Termite Terrace' as historical location.\"

;; Book of Motion — Chapter 20: How Emotion Animates
;; The technical language of animated expression.
;; Written 2026-07-13. Author: Lacuna Labs Engineering.
;; Sources: Preston Blair, Advanced Animation (1949, and its later

(chapter
  :book \"book-of-motion\"
  :number 20

\"An animator is a specialized kind of actor. They cannot use their body directly — they cannot lean into a chair, cannot pause on a sigh, cannot let their eyes lower with tiredness. They have to translate all of these physical acts into the medium of drawn or modeled figures. The specific translation is the craft.

This chapter looks at how emotion — specifically, a handful of basic emotional states — gets translated into animated motion. What makes a character look sad? What makes a character look joyful? What makes a character look angry, or afraid, or determined? These are not abstract questions. Animators have worked out specific technical answers, and once you know them you can watch animation with more precision.

# Sadness

Sadness pulls the body down. In animation, sadness is drawn as:

*Weight low.* The character's center of gravity settles. Shoulders drop; head lowers. If the character is walking, the walk becomes heavier — the body settles more into each step, the timing between steps is longer, the arms swing less.

*Motion slow.* Actions that would normally be quick become slower. A hand reaching for a doorknob takes longer than usual. The slow-in-slow-out is emphasized.

*Contained energy.* Motion is compressed rather than reaching out. A sad character crosses their arms, curls in toward themselves. Their silhouette is smaller, more inward.

*Face down.* Eyes cast down. If the character looks up, they look up slowly and briefly, then look back down.

*Rare eye contact.* Sad characters don't look at other characters or at the camera. They look away.

If you watch the opening of *Grave of the Fireflies* (Takahata, 1988), you see all of this in the animation of Seita. The boy sits, weight low. Motion is slow. He speaks quietly, small gestures, no reaches. Every technical decision reads as sadness because every technical decision is one of the ways sadness gets drawn.

# Joy

Joy lifts the body up. In animation, joy is drawn as:

*Weight up.* The character rises off the ground — or at least their center of gravity rises. Shoulders come up; head lifts; sometimes the character actually jumps. If they walk, the walk becomes lighter, more bouncy.

*Motion fast, but arcing.* Joyful motion is quick, but it follows curves rather than straight lines. A joyful arm swings up in an arc; a joyful head tilts back with a curve of the spine. The arcs are important — they read as freedom of motion.

*Expansive energy.* The character reaches outward. Arms extend; hands open. Silhouette becomes larger, more open.

*Face up.* Eyes lift. Chin raises. If the character has a hat, it might come off in a gesture.

*Direct eye contact.* Joyful characters make eye contact — with each other, with the camera. They share the joy.

*Momentum overshoot.* Joyful motion often includes an overshoot — the character moves past the intended position and springs back. This reads as exuberance, as *energy that has more energy in it than the situation strictly requires*.

Watch any dance sequence in a classic musical animated feature — say, the celebration scenes in *Aladdin* or the singing forest creatures in most Disney features — and you will see all of these in the character animation. Joy is the easiest emotion to over-animate; it wants to *want to* move.

# Anger

Anger sharpens the body. In animation, anger is drawn as:

*Weight forward and low.* The character's center of gravity shifts toward the source of the anger. If they are angry at another character, they lean toward that character. Their weight is on their front foot.

*Motion sharp.* Anger's motion is not slow-in-slow-out; it is sudden. A snap of the head to the target; a fist clenching in a single frame. The absence of transition is what makes it read as anger — a decisive act with no equivocation.

*Contained force.* Anger is compact — arms in, shoulders up, body coiled. Different from sadness's contraction: anger's contraction has *tension* in it, not settling.

*Face fixed.* Eyes locked on the target. Jaw set. Not a lot of head motion — the head stays pointed at what the anger is directed at.

*Increased detail in secondary motion.* Anger tends to feature more secondary motion — small shakes of the head, twitches of fingers, quick blinks. These small motions communicate that the character is *holding in* larger motion. When the held-in motion is released — the punch, the shout, the throw — the release is dramatic.

The angry expressions in Chuck Jones's Wile E. Coyote or Yosemite Sam are studies in this vocabulary. Sam's whole body compresses into a coiled shape before he explodes into a chase, and the compression is what makes the explosion funny.

# Fear

Fear pulls the body away. In animation, fear is drawn as:

*Weight back.* The character's center of gravity retreats from the threat. If they are standing, they lean backward. If they are walking, they walk backwards or freeze.

*Motion trembling.* Fear introduces small vibratory motion — trembling hands, trembling body, shaking head. This is not the sustained tremble of cold; it is small, unsteady, unpredictable.

*Contracted.* Similar to sadness's contraction, but with tension. Arms drawn in; shoulders hunched; head slightly ducked.

*Face tense.* Eyes wide open (not narrowed); pupils sometimes small. Eyebrows raised. Mouth possibly open in a silent gasp.

*Rigid moments.* Fear has moments of complete stillness — a frozen pose, unable to move. In animation, this reads as a frame or two of no motion at all in the middle of a scene, which is startling because animation is normally in constant motion.

*Backing-up secondary motion.* Small backward motions — a foot slipping back, a hand feeling behind for support.

# Determination

Determination is not one of the classic emotions from acting textbooks, but it appears constantly in animation and has its own vocabulary.

*Weight forward and high.* The character leans into whatever they are determined to do. Shoulders forward, head forward.

*Motion continuous.* Determination reads through motion that does not stop. The character keeps moving, keeps walking, keeps working, without pausing. If they hesitate, the determination dissolves.

*Face fixed on target.* Similar to anger, the character's face is pointed at the goal. But without anger's tension.

*Absence of hesitation.* No slow-in on new motions. The character starts each new action decisively.

Watch the scene in *Princess Mononoke* (Miyazaki, 1997) where Ashitaka rides through the forest. The character's determination is drawn through continuous, forward-leaning motion, eyes fixed ahead, no hesitation, no wandering. The animation carries the character's state without any dialogue.

# Blended and complex emotions

Real emotional states are usually blends. A character can be simultaneously grieving and determined, or angry and afraid, or joyful and nervous. Great animation communicates these blends by combining the technical decisions from multiple states.

A character who is grieving-and-determined might have: weight low (sadness) but leaning forward (determination); motion slow (sadness) but continuous (determination); face down at rest but rising to look at the target of the determination.

A character who is angry-and-afraid might have: weight forward toward the threat (anger) but weight also slightly back (fear); sharp motion in the head (anger) with trembling in the hands (fear); face fixed on the threat but pupils small (fear).

These blends are what make animated characters read as *complex people* rather than as caricatures. The technical vocabulary is what lets an animator produce the blend deliberately rather than by accident.

# What we can do in Scheme

Let's build a small demonstration of one emotional state — sadness — and one contrasting state — joy — for the same character walking across a screen.

```scheme
;; A walk cycle with emotional modulation.
;; The 'mood' parameter shifts weight, speed, and vertical bob.

(define (walk-frame index total-frames mood)
  (let* ((progress (/ index total-frames))
         (x (+ 50 (* progress 300)))
         (base-y 200)

         ;; Sadness: low weight, small bob, slow motion.
         ;; Joy: high weight, big bob, quick motion.

         (weight-shift (case mood
                         ((sad) 30)      ; head-down offset
                         ((joyful) -20)  ; lifted offset
                         (else 0)))
         (bob-amount (case mood
                       ((sad) 2)
                       ((joyful) 12)
                       (else 5)))
         (bob-freq (case mood
                     ((sad) 2)
                     ((joyful) 6)
                     (else 4)))
         (y (+ base-y weight-shift
               (* bob-amount (sin (* progress 2 3.14159 bob-freq))))))
    (list 'figure x y)))

(define (walk-cycle mood duration-frames)
  (for-each
    (lambda (i)
      (world/reset!)
      (world/place! (walk-frame i duration-frames mood))
      (world/render!)
      (world/wait (case mood
                    ((sad) 0.15)      ; slower
                    ((joyful) 0.08)   ; quicker
                    (else 0.12))))
    (range 0 duration-frames)))

(walk-cycle 'sad 24)
(walk-cycle 'joyful 24)
```

The two calls produce two walks. Same figure, same distance, same left-to-right direction. But the sad walk is slower, lower, with a small bob and a downward weight shift. The joyful walk is quicker, higher, with a big bob and an upward lift. Watch them and you will read them as emotional states, not just as different-parameter walks. That is because the technical vocabulary matches how humans read bodies. The specific parameters — weight, speed, bob — are the ones humans use to read each other's moods, and animators have discovered which parameters matter.

# Bad animation and how it fails

The opposite of good emotional animation is not amateur animation; amateur animation is often expressive because the animator is trying. The opposite is *bland* animation — animation that has been produced without emotional decisions. A character moves; the motion is technically correct; but no state is expressed. This happens when animators focus on the mechanics of motion (correct arcs, correct weight, correct timing charts) without asking what emotion the character is in at each moment.

The result is animation that reads as *plastic*. The character seems to have no inner life. Their motion is correct but disconnected from feeling.

Ed Hooks, in *Acting for Animators* (2011), argues that this is the single biggest failure mode of animation training. Students learn technical animation and then apply it to characters without thinking about what those characters are feeling. The remedy, he argues, is to think of each animated moment as an acting choice: what does this character want, right now? What are they thinking? What is their state? Only then do you decide how they move.

The best animation always has this acting layer under the technical layer. The character is a specific person in a specific state, and every technical decision — weight, timing, arc, silhouette — serves the state. When this alignment happens, animation reads as *alive*. When it doesn't, animation reads as *animated but empty*.

# What to watch for

When you watch a scene, ask yourself:

What is this character feeling right now? Sadness? Joy? Anger? Fear? Determination? A blend?

Are the animator's technical decisions serving the state? Does the weight, the timing, the silhouette, the face all say the same thing? Or are there inconsistencies?

Would you *believe* this character had this feeling, if they were a real person? Do the choices ring true?

This is criticism-of-animation from the inside. It is what animators talk to each other about, when they watch each other's work.

# Sources cited

Preston Blair, *Advanced Animation* (Foster, 1949) and its later revised edition *Cartoon Animation with Preston Blair* (Foster, 1990). The classic on expressive character animation.

Richard Williams, *The Animator's Survival Kit* (Faber, 2001).

Ed Hooks, *Acting for Animators*, revised third edition (Routledge, 2011). The standard text on acting for animation students.

Frank Thomas and Ollie Johnston, *The Illusion of Life* (Abbeville, 1981).\"

\"There is a moment when an animator, or a person who has watched a lot of animation, can tell within a few seconds whether a scene is going to be good. It is not that they see the whole scene and evaluate it critically. It is that they see certain things in the first few frames — how the character is staged, how the motion is timed, what the silhouette does — and they know. Good animation announces itself. Bad animation announces itself too.

What are the things they see? This chapter is an attempt to name them.

# Readability

The first and most important criterion for animation is *readability*. Can a viewer, watching the scene without prior context, understand what is happening?

Readability has several sub-components:

**Silhouette.** The character's outline against the background communicates the pose. If a character is throwing a punch, you should be able to tell they are throwing a punch even if you cover the interior of the drawing and see only the silhouette. If the punching arm blends into the body outline, the pose is unreadable.

**Staging.** The camera framing and character placement make the action clear. If a character is picking up a small object, the object should be visible in the frame at the moment of the pickup. If a character is looking at another character, the two characters should both be visible.

**Composition.** The overall arrangement of shapes on the screen guides the viewer's eye to the important action. Big shapes lead to small shapes; strong contrasts pull attention.

**Contrast in motion.** If two characters are on screen, only one usually moves at a time (or their motions are visibly different). Simultaneous equal motion is confusing.

The Termite Terrace directors were masters of readability. Look at a Chuck Jones Wile E. Coyote scene. The Coyote enters, sees the Roadrunner, hatches a plan, sets up a contraption, gets caught in the contraption, falls off a cliff. Every one of these actions is *unmistakably clear* from staging and silhouette. Jones never lets you wonder what is happening; every drawing communicates the specific action of the moment.

Contrast this with a poorly-staged scene, where you might see two characters moving simultaneously with similar motion, or a character reaching for something off-screen, or a character whose pose doesn't clearly indicate what they are doing. The viewer's attention scatters. They can't follow the action. The scene fails at the level of communication.

# Weight

Second criterion: does the animated body have *weight*? Does it feel like it has mass, that gravity is acting on it, that it moves the way objects with volume actually move?

Weight is expressed through several techniques from the twelve principles:

**Squash and stretch.** Bodies deform under force. A ball hitting the ground squashes. A character landing from a jump compresses. Without deformation, bodies look rigid — like rigid objects animated, not like bodies.

**Slow-in and slow-out.** Real bodies don't start moving instantly at full speed or stop instantly. They accelerate and decelerate. Animation that ignores this reads as robotic.

**Follow-through.** When a body stops moving, its parts (hair, clothes, tails, ears) continue for a fraction of a second. This is because those parts have their own mass and momentum. Animation that has bodies stop all at once looks stiff.

**Anticipation.** Before a big motion, a body prepares. A character about to jump crouches down; a character about to throw winds up. This preparation communicates the weight of the motion — the fact that it requires effort.

**Overshoot and settle.** After a fast motion, a body sometimes overshoots the intended position and settles back to it. This is another consequence of mass and momentum.

When a scene has all of these — when a character lands with a squash, moves with slow-in-slow-out, has follow-through on their clothes, anticipates their actions, overshoots and settles — the character reads as *heavy* in the correct way: as an object of substance in a world with physics.

When a scene lacks these — when a character starts and stops instantly, has no deformation, no follow-through, no overshoot — the character reads as *floaty*, or as *stiff*, depending on the specific failures.

# Timing

Third criterion: is the timing right for what the character is doing?

Timing is the hardest craft in animation to describe in the abstract because it depends so heavily on context. A gesture that takes twelve frames might be perfect for one moment and too slow for another. But there are patterns.

**Actions that require weight take longer.** Lifting something heavy takes longer than lifting something light. A slow lift reads as heavy; a quick lift reads as light. Getting this wrong — showing a heavy object being lifted quickly, or a light object being lifted slowly — breaks the reality of the scene.

**Emotional moments take longer than they would in reality.** A character realizing something needs time for the realization to register with the audience. The character stares; then blinks; then the expression shifts; then reacts. In real life this might be one second; in animation it might be three or four seconds because the audience needs the extra time to read the change.

**Comic timing follows specific rules.** The pause before a joke; the length of a double-take; the exact frame at which a character notices something. These are precisely calibrated in good comedy animation. A joke that runs a few frames too long dies; a joke that runs a few frames too short doesn't land.

Chuck Jones once wrote about a specific comedic pattern he used: three beats. Setup (one beat). Response (one beat). Sting (one beat). Each beat is a specific length of time on the screen, and the whole pattern only works when the three beats are correctly proportioned. Get the setup too short and the response has nothing to react to; get the sting too long and the joke goes flat.

**Poetic timing follows different rules.** Slow, sustained scenes — a landscape, a character reflecting — need enough time for the viewer's mind to enter the scene. The Ghibli films often hold shots long enough that Western viewers accustomed to faster editing find them slow. The length is a compositional choice, and it works if the scene has enough visual and emotional weight to fill the time.

Good timing is one of the deepest crafts in animation. It takes years of practice to develop.

# Appeal

Fourth criterion: does the character have *appeal*?

Appeal is not prettiness. A grotesque monster can have appeal. It is *visual engagement* — the character's design, silhouette, expression, and motion all cohere into something the viewer wants to look at.

Appeal comes from:

**Distinctive silhouette.** The character has a shape that reads clearly from a distance. When you see a black outline of Bugs Bunny, you know it is Bugs Bunny. When you see the silhouette of Totoro, you know it is Totoro. This is a design decision made before animation begins, and it has to be right for the animation to succeed.

**Consistent proportions.** The character's body has a clear anatomical logic. The head is a certain size relative to the body; the limbs have particular proportions. These proportions are maintained across all drawings. If the proportions drift, the character loses appeal — they become inconsistent, harder to recognize as the same character from moment to moment.

**Expressive design.** Faces and body designs allow for the range of expression the story requires. A character who needs to communicate deep sadness needs a face designed to communicate sadness — features that can hang, eyes that can lower, a mouth that can shape into grief.

**Life in the motion.** Even before you know the character, their motion should feel alive. This ties back to the previous criteria — readability, weight, timing — but appeal is where they all synthesize.

# The failures

Bad animation typically fails in one or more specific ways. If you know the criteria, you can name the failure precisely.

**Unreadable poses.** The silhouette doesn't communicate what the character is doing. Solution: redraw the pose so the silhouette carries the action.

**Weightless motion.** The character floats. Solution: add slow-in-slow-out, squash-and-stretch, anticipation, follow-through.

**Wrong timing.** Actions are too fast, too slow, or unevenly paced. Solution: adjust timing charts; re-analyze the emotional weight of each moment.

**Off-model drawings.** The character's proportions drift. Solution: use model sheets; check every drawing against the reference.

**Empty motion.** The mechanics are correct but the character isn't feeling anything. Solution: return to the acting layer; ask what the character wants at this moment and what they are thinking.

Most bad animation fails at multiple of these at once. A single-failure scene can be identified and fixed; a multi-failure scene often needs to be re-thought from the ground up.

# What we can do in Scheme

Let's build a small demonstration of readable versus unreadable staging.

```scheme
;; Scenario: a character reaches for a small object on a table.
;; Version 1: unreadable staging.
;; Version 2: readable staging.

;; Unreadable: the object is off-screen, or occluded by the character's body,
;; or the character's arm silhouette blends into the body.

;; Readable: the object is clearly visible in frame; the character's arm
;; extends into empty space so the reach is silhouetted; the object and
;; the reaching hand are both isolated against the background.

(define (unreadable-staging)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/background 'gray)
  (world/place-character 300 300 'facing-camera)   ; character facing camera
  (world/place-object 320 320 'small)              ; object very close to character body
  (world/place-arm 300 300 320 320)                 ; arm goes into body
  (world/render!))

(define (readable-staging)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/background 'white)
  (world/place-character 200 300 'facing-right)    ; character in profile
  (world/place-table 400 350)                       ; table separated from character
  (world/place-object 420 320 'small 'highlighted) ; object on table, contrasting
  (world/place-arm 240 280 400 320)                 ; arm extends into empty space
  (world/render!))
```

The unreadable version puts everything on top of everything else. The character is facing the camera, so the arm reaching for the object goes into the body. The object is too small and too close to the character to be seen. Contrast is minimal.

The readable version puts the character in profile so the reaching arm silhouettes against the background. The table is separated from the character. The object is highlighted (perhaps a different color, or with a brighter light). The whole action is legible in a single frame.

If you drew both versions and showed them to someone briefly, they would understand the readable version and be confused by the unreadable one. That's what staging does.

# Why 'good' matters

Animation is a communication medium. If a scene fails to communicate — if the viewer can't tell what is happening, can't read the character's state, can't follow the action — then the animation has failed at its basic purpose, regardless of how technically skilled the drawings are.

The criteria in this chapter — readability, weight, timing, appeal — are all serving that basic purpose: communication. They are the technical means to the end of *the audience understanding what is happening and caring about it*. When they all cohere, animation is at its best. When they fail, animation falls short of its own purpose.

Every animator — from Termite Terrace directors to modern independent animators to any hobbyist making short films — is trying to satisfy these criteria. When they succeed, the work is legible and moving. When they fall short, the work has flaws that other animators can name.

# Tie back

Good animation is not mysterious. It is the product of specific decisions about silhouette, staging, weight, timing, and appeal. Bad animation fails at these decisions in identifiable ways.

The next chapter takes narrative arc — how a scene begins, develops, and ends — and looks at the shape of animated storytelling.

# Sources cited

Frank Thomas and Ollie Johnston, *The Illusion of Life* (Abbeville, 1981). The staging chapter and the character-drawing chapter are foundational.

Richard Williams, *The Animator's Survival Kit* (Faber, 2001). Especially the sections on timing and weight.

Chuck Jones, *Chuck Amuck* (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1989). Jones's essays on comic timing.

Ed Hooks, *Acting for Animators*, third edition (Routledge, 2011).\"

\"Aristotle wrote in the *Poetics*, around 335 BCE, that a story has a beginning, a middle, and an end. This has become a joke about how obvious the observation is. But look at the observation as an animator — as someone who has to *shape time* in a specific medium — and the observation becomes more interesting. A story has a beginning. So does a scene. So does a moment. So does a single gesture. Every animated thing that happens over time has a beginning, a middle, and an end, and the three-part shape governs how the audience reads the whole.

This chapter looks at how narrative arc shows up at every scale of animation, from a single character gesture to a scene to a whole film.

# The three-part shape

Aristotle's beginning is the moment before the action, when the situation is stable. His middle is the action itself — the change of state. His end is the moment after the action, when a new stable situation has been reached.

Notice: the action is the middle. The beginning and the end are the stable states on either side of the action. This is important because it means every animated event needs *setup* and *resolution*, not just the action itself.

An animator drawing a character throwing a ball:

**Beginning** — the character standing, holding the ball, not yet throwing. This is a stable state. The audience takes it in.

**Middle** — the wind-up, the throw, the release. This is the action. Something changes.

**End** — the character with arm outstretched, ball leaving frame, weight shifted forward. This is a new stable state. The audience takes it in.

If you cut the beginning — if you started the animation at the wind-up — the throw would feel abrupt. The audience wouldn't have had time to see who was throwing and what they were throwing.

If you cut the end — if you stopped the animation at the release — the throw would feel unfinished. The audience wouldn't have had time to see the throw's completion, the character's follow-through, the settlement into the new stable state.

Good animators know how much beginning and end to give. Not too little (which creates a rushed feeling) and not too much (which creates a bored feeling). This is timing craft.

# The gesture-scale arc

The three-part shape applies to individual gestures. A character sighing:

**Beginning** — the character sitting, whatever they were doing before.

**Middle** — the intake of breath (chest rising, shoulders lifting), the release (chest falling, shoulders lowering, head dropping slightly).

**End** — the settled position after the sigh, with the new emotional state now visible.

The whole gesture might take one to two seconds. But it has the shape of a story.

# The scene-scale arc

A scene has a larger arc. Consider a scene in which two characters meet, argue, and part.

**Beginning** — the characters approach each other. Their body language shows their initial state; the setting is established.

**Middle** — the argument. Emotions rise. Positions harden. The characters gesture with increasing intensity. The scene has its own peaks (the loudest exchange) and lulls.

**End** — the characters separate. Their body language after the argument shows the aftermath: one storming off, the other stunned.

An animator or director shapes the scene by controlling how each of these sections plays out — how long the beginning takes to establish the situation, how the middle escalates, how the end resolves.

# The film-scale arc

A whole film has an even larger arc. Aristotle's tragedy shape (from *Poetics*):

**Beginning** — the initial situation and inciting incident. The audience meets the characters and world; something happens that starts the story.

**Rising action / complication** — the situation becomes complicated. Obstacles arise. Tension builds.

**Climax** — the peak of tension. The decisive action happens.

**Falling action** — the consequences of the climax play out.

**Resolution** — the new stable state. The story ends.

This shape is not law. Many films don't follow it. But it is the default shape audiences expect, and departures from it (a story that has no clear resolution; a story with multiple climaxes; a story that is all rising action) work because they play against the expectation, not because the expectation isn't there.

# What animation does with the arc

Animation has some particular advantages in shaping narrative arcs.

**It can shape time.** Live-action film is stuck with what the actors did in front of the camera. Animation can hold a moment for as long as it needs, speed up a montage, slow down a look. This gives the animator precise control over pacing.

**It can compress or exaggerate.** A whole life can be summarized in a two-minute sequence. A single moment of realization can be extended over ten seconds. Both compressions and extensions are choices the animator makes.

**It can show the invisible.** Thoughts, memories, emotions, forces — all of these are hard to show in live-action but can be drawn directly in animation. A character's imagination can appear in a thought bubble; their fear can be visualized as shadows behind them; their memory can play out in a different visual style.

**It can move the camera anywhere.** No physical camera constraints. A shot can start inside a character's eye and pull back to show a whole city. Animation is not committed to camera realism.

These affordances shape how animators tell stories. Many great animated films use them heavily — dream sequences, subjective camera moves, time compressions, style shifts for different emotional registers. When live-action films want to do these things, they usually turn to visual effects, which is a form of animation.

# What we can do in Scheme

Let's build a small scene with a beginning-middle-end arc: a character enters, reacts to something, and exits.

```scheme
;; Scene: character walks into frame, sees an object, reacts, walks out.
;; Total duration: 96 frames at 24 fps = 4 seconds.
;; Beginning (frames 0-24): character walks in from the left.
;; Middle (frames 24-72): character sees object, reacts.
;; End (frames 72-96): character walks out to the right.

(define (scene-frame frame)
  (cond
    ;; Beginning: character walks in from left
    ((< frame 24)
     (let ((x (+ 50 (* frame 4))))  ; enters at x=50, walks right
       (world/place-character x 300 'walking)))

    ;; Middle: character stops, sees object
    ((< frame 30)
     (world/place-character 146 300 'stopped)
     (world/place-object 200 300 'highlighted))

    ;; Middle: reaction — character turns to look
    ((< frame 48)
     (world/place-character 146 300 'looking-right)
     (world/place-object 200 300 'highlighted))

    ;; Middle: emotional reaction — character reads as delighted
    ((< frame 72)
     (let ((bob (* 8 (sin (* (- frame 48) 0.5)))))
       (world/place-character 146 (- 300 bob) 'delighted)
       (world/place-object 200 300 'highlighted)))

    ;; End: character walks toward object and off screen
    (else
     (let ((x (+ 146 (* (- frame 72) 6))))
       (world/place-character x 300 'walking))
     (world/place-object 200 300))))

(define (render-scene)
  (for-each
    (lambda (frame)
      (world/reset!)
      (scene-frame frame)
      (world/render!)
      (world/wait (/ 1.0 24.0)))
    (range 0 96)))

(render-scene)
```

The four-second scene has clear beginning, middle, and end. The beginning is 24 frames (one second) of the character entering. The middle is 48 frames (two seconds) of the character noticing and reacting — with sub-arcs for stopping, turning, and expressing delight. The end is 24 frames (one second) of the character walking toward the object and off frame.

The proportions matter. If the beginning were only 6 frames, the character would seem to teleport in. If the middle were only 12 frames, there wouldn't be time for the reaction to register. If the end were 60 frames, the scene would feel dragging.

# The pause

There is one specific timing tool worth naming: the pause.

A pause is a moment of stillness inserted into an otherwise moving scene. Its length is usually short — half a second, a second, sometimes two seconds — but its effect is disproportionate. A pause tells the audience: *something important is happening here*. It marks a decision, a realization, a moment of connection.

Animators use pauses at specific narrative points:

**Before a decision.** A character considering their options pauses before acting. The pause reads as thought.

**After a discovery.** A character who has just noticed something significant pauses. The pause reads as absorption of information.

**Between two characters connecting.** Two characters looking at each other pause. The pause reads as the moment of connection.

**Before a big action.** A character about to make a large move pauses briefly. The pause reads as commitment.

**After an emotional moment.** A character who has just expressed a strong feeling pauses. The pause reads as the settling of the feeling.

Pauses are difficult in animation because animation is a medium of constant motion. A pause has to be built into the timing deliberately; it doesn't happen by accident. The animator must choose to hold a drawing for enough frames that the audience feels the stillness.

The greatest animation directors are masters of the pause. In Miyazaki films, in Chuck Jones's shorts, in Takahata's work, the pauses are placed with precision. They give the scenes their weight.

# What the arc lets you do

Once you understand narrative arc at multiple scales — gesture, scene, film — you can shape any animated story with intention. You can decide how long the beginning takes to establish the situation, how the middle escalates, how the end resolves. You can choose where to place pauses, where to compress time, where to extend it. You can decide how much time to give the audience to absorb each moment.

This is directing. It is what a director of animation actually does. It is not just drawing; it is not just choreographing character motion. It is shaping the whole time-experience of the audience.

# Tie back

Narrative arc is the shape of time in animation. It applies at every scale, from a single gesture to a whole film. The three-part shape — beginning, middle, end — is the default expectation, and it works because audiences have been reading stories in this shape since Aristotle.

The next chapter takes the specific tool of *frame rate* — how many drawings per second, and what different rates communicate — and looks at the choices animators make about it.

# Sources cited

Aristotle, *Poetics*. Public domain. Available in many translations; the Butcher translation (1902) is standard for scholarly work and is out of copyright.

Robert McKee, *Story: Substance, Structure, Style, and the Principles of Screenwriting* (Regan Books / HarperCollins, 1997). The standard modern text on story structure for film and animation.

Frank Thomas and Ollie Johnston, *The Illusion of Life* (Abbeville, 1981).\"

  :notes
\"Aristotle's Poetics beginning-middle-end shape is direct. McKee's Story is a standard screenwriting reference used in animation education. The scale-nested-arc concept (gesture, scene, film) is a synthesis of Poetics with animation-teaching practice. Pauses as narrative tool is standard vocabulary — every animator's training discusses them.\"

  :philosopher-weave-details
\"Aristotle: the fundamental beginning-middle-end shape from Poetics, applied at every scale of animated time.
Sartre: the character's being is their doing across the frames — the arc is what the character IS across the scene.
Wittgenstein-late: narrative arc as shared form-of-life — audiences expect it because they've watched stories in this shape their whole lives.
Peirce: the pause as index — a physical mark of importance that the audience reads immediately without conscious analysis.\"

")

# The Book of Music

*\"We call it music, but we're really dealing with sound.\"*

This book teaches you to write music in Motoi Scheme by teaching you to
think about sound in time. It is a standalone book — it does not assume
you read the Scheme book first. Chapter 1 introduces the small piece of
the language you need, chapter 2 adds a little more, and so on. The
language grows only when the music needs it to.

The book has a summit. The last chapter is the first movement of
Rachmaninoff's Piano Concerto No. 2 in C minor, note for note, in
Motoi Scheme. Everything between here and there is a rung on the
ladder that gets you to a place where playing it makes sense.

Between here and the summit, the rungs are the world's musical
languages. Melody. Jazz voicing. Polyphony. Polyrhythm — clave,
three-against-two, the calypso pulse, the funk push. World percussion,
from West African bell patterns to Japanese bamboo to Indian tala.
Ornamentation, dynamics, orchestration, and the shape of a piece as a
whole. Each of these is a real genre with real conventions, and each
one gives you a new way to think about what a program that makes sound
can be.

*I think about music the way I think about a garden. There are seeds
— small ideas — and there is time. When I plant a seed and let it
grow in time, something living comes out. A note is a seed. A phrase
is a small planting. A whole piece is a garden that took a long walk
to get where it is going. You will hear me say \"seed\" and \"grow\" and
\"shape\" more than \"compose\" — that is why.*

## What this book teaches (and what it does not)

This book teaches how to **make sound with Motoi Scheme** and how to
**think in the small musical idioms** the language was built to
express. It is instrument-agnostic — you will call for a piano, a
cello, a hand drum, a bamboo flute, but you will not learn the deep
inner engineering of any single instrument here. That belongs to the
Book of Sound (the book on the shelf next to this one).

- **Here:** melody, rhythm, harmony, polyphony, polyrhythm, form,
  ornamentation, dynamics, orchestration — the musical mind.
- **Not here:** synthesis internals, envelope math, formant tables,
  the roster of every playable instrument. Those live in the Book of
  Sound.

The rule of thumb: if the idea would still be a good idea if you
translated the piece from piano to marimba, the idea belongs here. If
the idea is about what makes a marimba sound like a marimba, it
belongs in the Book of Sound.

## The public-domain rule

Every worked piece in this book is either public-domain or an original
composed for the book. Twinkle Twinkle Little Star (chapter 3) is
public-domain and safe to teach with. Rachmaninoff's Piano Concerto
No. 2, Op. 18, first published in 1901, is public-domain in the
United States and most of Europe. Where a chapter would otherwise have
used a copyrighted piece, we have written an equivalent in the same
style. The book will always tell you which it is.

## The first five chapters

1. [[#chapter-1]] **Sound and time** — what music is at ground level.
2. [[#chapter-2]] **Melody** — pitch sequences, single-voice.
3. [[#chapter-3]] **Twinkle on piano** — the payoff of the first three.
4. [[#chapter-4]] **Jazz and swing** — introducing rhythmic complexity.
5. [[#chapter-5]] **Calypso, soca, funk** — the polyrhythm door.

After chapter five the genre ladder continues, one rung at a time,
until Rachmaninoff.

## How to read

Every fenced Scheme block runs. In the browser build, click Run and
the sound plays through the page's speaker. In a terminal, paste the
block into `motoi-scheme repl` and hit Enter. The first time a page
plays audio it will ask for a click — browsers require a user gesture
before they let a page make sound. That is the only friction; after
one click the whole book plays.

Every example is a **standalone program**. You should never have to
paste the previous block first for the current block to run. If a
program needs setup, the setup is inside the block.

> **Tip**
>
> If nothing plays, the audio gesture has not been granted yet. Click
> once on the page (or type a form into the REPL) and try again. The
> engine returns `'pending-audio` on the silent first call — that is
> honest, not broken.

## What comes after chapter 5

Chapters 6 through 15 are the rest of the ladder: polyphony, world
percussion (West African bell patterns, Japanese bamboo, Indian
tala), ornamentation, dynamics, orchestration, and form. Chapter 16
is the Rach 2 summit. Each of those chapters is a rung — none of them
is the point on its own. The point is that by the time you are
holding the whole ladder, you can write anything you want.

## Cross-links

- [[book-of-sound]] — the roster and inner engineering of each
  instrument you will call for in this book.
- [[book-of-self#sight]] — for how the runtime decides what a piece is
  feeling; expressive intent is a Self topic, not a Music topic.
- [[book-of-reason-iii]] — this is like that: analogical reasoning
  underlies every \"in the style of\" move in this book.

---

*Chapter 1 — Sound and time. Turn the page.*
")

";; appendix-01-bach-goldberg.slat
;; Book of Music — Appendix 1: Bach and the Goldberg Variations
;; Written 2026-07-13. Author: Lacuna Labs Engineering.
;; Doctrine: publishable prose · no hallucination · analysis-shape.
;; Real work: Johann Sebastian Bach, Aria mit verschiedenen Veränderungen
;; ('Aria with Diverse Variations'), BWV 988, published Nuremberg 1741,
;; second part of the Clavier-Übung. PD.
;; Nickname 'Goldberg Variations' comes from a story told by Johann Nikolaus
;; Forkel in 1802 — probably legend but widely repeated.

(appendix

\"Johann Sebastian Bach published a piece for two-manual harpsichord in Nuremberg in 1741, in the last decade of his life. He called it *Aria mit verschiedenen Veränderungen* — Aria with Diverse Variations. The title page said nothing about who commissioned it or why. Sixty-one years later, a Bach biographer named Johann Nikolaus Forkel told a story: the piece had been written for a Count Kaiserling, the Russian ambassador to the Saxon court in Dresden, who suffered from insomnia. The Count kept a fourteen-year-old harpsichordist named Johann Gottlieb Goldberg on staff to play for him during sleepless nights, and he asked Bach to write something 'soft and lively' that Goldberg could play. Bach wrote the variations. The Count paid Bach with a golden goblet full of gold coins. From then on, the piece was called the Goldberg Variations.

Modern scholars are skeptical of Forkel's story. Goldberg was fourteen in 1741, which is very young to play the piece — it is among the most demanding works in the harpsichord repertoire. The dedication is not printed on the score, which would be strange if the piece were commissioned. Kaiserling did have a court musician named Goldberg, but the specifics are otherwise undocumented. What is undoubted is the piece itself — thirty variations on an aria, framed by the aria appearing at the start and again at the end. That structure is the piece's true title, and it is one of the most extraordinary structures in music.

# The Aria

The Aria is a slow, ornamented sarabande in G major, thirty-two bars long. It has a memorable descending bass line — the *bass ostinato* — that all thirty variations are built on. The melody in the right hand of the Aria is decorated with grace notes and mordents; it is beautiful but almost incidental. The real material of the piece is not the melody. It is the bass line. Bach discovered — or knew, at fifty-six — that if he could hold the bass line steady across thirty variations, he could put anything in the upper voices and the piece would cohere.

# The Structure of the Thirty

Bach arranged the thirty variations in a plan. Every third variation (Variations 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27) is a **canon**, and the canonic interval increases by one step each time. Variation 3 is a canon at the unison — the second voice enters singing the same notes as the first. Variation 6 is a canon at the second — the second voice enters one step up. Variation 9 is at the third; Variation 12 at the fourth; and so on up to Variation 27, a canon at the ninth. This is a systematic project: Bach walks up the intervals of a scale, showing what a canon sounds like at each step.

Between the canons, the other variations alternate between virtuosic display pieces (fast, hand-crossing, sparkling) and reflective, slow, deeply expressive pieces. The pattern is not exactly regular, but the alternation gives the piece its rhythm across the hour.

The last variation, Variation 30, is not a canon. It is a *Quodlibet* — a variation that layers two popular folk melodies over Bach's bass line. The two tunes, which Bach's family would have known and sung together, are 'Ich bin so lang nicht bei dir g'west' (I have been so long away from you) and 'Kraut und Rüben haben mich vertrieben' (Cabbage and turnips have driven me away). The joke is domestic — a family in-joke about mother's cooking and returning home. And the mastery is that Bach fits both tunes over his own bass line at the same time, without breaking the harmonic pattern the piece has held for the previous twenty-nine variations. It is a piece of counterpoint sitting inside a piece of counterpoint.

Then the Aria returns. Same notes as the opening. Not decorated further; not transformed; not varied. Just the Aria, played again as it was played at the beginning.

# What the return means

This is the moment I want to spend the appendix on. Thirty variations. An hour of virtuosic keyboard playing, of intellectual rigor in the canons, of expressive depth in the slow variations, of humor in the Quodlibet. Then the Aria comes back. Unchanged.

What is it supposed to mean?

Different pianists and scholars have offered different readings. Some say the return is about the Aria being unchanged by the journey — the theme has been shown from every possible angle, and it is still itself. Some say the return is about the *listener* being changed by the journey — we hear the same notes differently at the end because we have spent an hour with them. Some say it is about circle and return: a rondo-like structure blown up to enormous scale, where the refrain is the Aria and the episodes are the variations.

I lean toward the second reading, and I want to say why. When we hear the Aria at the start of the piece, we hear a slow, pretty tune with an odd descending bass line. It is charming; we don't know what to do with it. Over the next hour, Bach teaches us what to do with it. He shows us that the bass line contains a canon at every interval; he shows us that a virtuoso can dance over it; he shows us that a folk-song joke can sit on top of it. By the time the Aria returns, we have been given thirty ways of hearing the bass line. When the Aria is played again, we cannot hear it the same way. We hear the bass line as capable of everything we have just heard. The Aria has become an entirely different object without a single note being changed.

This is what I think Bach meant by ending the piece the way he did. It is a lesson in the fact that hearing is not a passive act — that the same notes can mean very different things depending on what you have heard *around* them. He is teaching the ear.

# What we can do in Scheme

We cannot recreate the Goldberg Variations in a small program. But we can build a small demonstration of the principle: state a bass line, then play different things over it, and hear how the different things all get organized by the same bass.

```scheme
;; A short bass line — the ground the variations sit on.
(define bass '(G3 F#3 E3 D3 C3 B2 A2 D3))   ; 8 notes, in G major, ends on the dominant

(define (play-bass)
  (with-dynamics 'mp
    (for-each (lambda (n) (note-play n 'half)) bass)))

;; Variation A — quarter-note melody on top of the bass
(define var-a
  '((G4 quarter) (A4 quarter) (B4 quarter) (D5 quarter)
    (C5 quarter) (B4 quarter) (A4 quarter) (G4 quarter)
    (G4 quarter) (A4 quarter) (G4 quarter) (F#4 quarter)
    (E4 quarter) (F#4 quarter) (G4 quarter) (A4 quarter)))

;; Variation B — eighth-note runs on top of the same bass
(define var-b
  '((G4 eighth) (A4 eighth) (B4 eighth) (C5 eighth)
    (D5 eighth) (C5 eighth) (B4 eighth) (A4 eighth)
    ; ... continues over the same 8 bass notes
    ))

;; Play both together
(define (play-var melody)
  (parallel
    (play-bass)
    (with-dynamics 'mf
      (for-each (lambda (nd) (note-play (car nd) (cadr nd))) melody))))

(play-var var-a)
(play-var var-b)
```

Both variations sit on the same bass line. The melodies are completely different. The listener hears them as related pieces because the bass line is the same. Bach did this thirty times in one work.

# Why this appendix belongs in the book

We've been building a vocabulary — form, harmony, rubato, physical pitch. The Goldberg Variations show that all of these tools can be used in service of one project: the exhaustive exploration of a single musical object. Bach spends an hour on one bass line. Every technique the harpsichord had was brought to bear on this bass line: virtuosic display, contrapuntal canon, homely folk song, meditation. The piece is a demonstration of what serious attention to a small object can produce.

For anyone learning music, or learning to program, or learning any craft where you turn material over and look at it from many sides, the Goldberg Variations is a model of what deep attention looks like. Bach did not add material to make the piece more interesting; he added *ways of hearing the same material*. That is a discipline, and it is one of the highest forms of art we know.

# Recommended listening

Glenn Gould made two famous recordings of the Goldberg Variations, in 1955 and 1981 — both for Columbia (Sony). The 1955 recording is fast, brilliant, and made him famous at twenty-two. The 1981 recording, made shortly before his death at fifty, is slower, more reflective, and treats the Aria's return as a genuine moment of contemplation rather than as a repetition. Both are in most libraries. Listen to both, in order, and notice how the same score can be a young person's piece and an older person's piece.

Wanda Landowska, the great harpsichordist, recorded the piece in 1933 and 1945 on a harpsichord she designed — a large modern instrument, not a period one. These recordings are important historical documents and remain moving despite the different tonal aesthetic.

Any number of modern harpsichordists — Trevor Pinnock, Kenneth Gilbert, Andreas Staier — have recorded the piece on period instruments. These sound different from the piano recordings: quicker to decay, brighter in the upper register, and closer to what Bach's ear would have heard in 1741.

# Sources cited

Christoph Wolff, *Johann Sebastian Bach: The Learned Musician* (Norton, 2000). The standard modern Bach biography, which treats the Forkel story with appropriate skepticism.

Peter Williams, *Bach: The Goldberg Variations* (Cambridge University Press, 2001). A short scholarly guide.

BWV 988 score in facsimile and modern editions is in the public domain and available on IMSLP.

Gould discography from Sony Music Archives; Landowska from RCA Victor and EMI archives; Pinnock from Deutsche Grammophon; Gilbert from Harmonia Mundi; Staier from Harmonia Mundi.\"

  :prose
\"When Bach and Rachmaninoff and Chopin write a chord, they are drawing on a harmonic language whose logic goes back to the seventeenth century. Chords have a *function* in that language. A dominant seventh wants to resolve to a tonic. A subdominant leans toward the dominant. A minor chord in the middle of a phrase feels different from a major chord in the same position because of where it points. Chords are grammar; they mean something by where they are going.

Claude Debussy, working in Paris from about 1890 to 1918, took this grammar apart. Not by rejecting the old chords, but by using them without their functional meaning — playing them as *colors*, as sound-events valued for their own sonic weight, rather than as steps in a harmonic argument. When he writes a dominant seventh chord in a Debussy piece, it may or may not resolve to a tonic. It may just sit there, ring, and be replaced by another chord that also sits there. Chords become nouns instead of verbs.

This is the shift that changed twentieth-century music. Everything from jazz voicings (which build on Debussy's stacked ninth and eleventh chords) to film scoring (which uses Debussy's colored chord as a way to evoke atmosphere without narrative) to pop songwriting (which borrows Debussy's parallel motion of chords) traces back to what Debussy figured out. He did not do it alone — Maurice Ravel, Erik Satie, and others were part of the same generation — but Debussy is the one whose harmonic vocabulary the twentieth century found most usable.

# Clair de Lune

The most famous Debussy piano piece is *Clair de Lune*, the third movement of the *Suite bergamasque*. He wrote it around 1890 (when he was twenty-seven) but did not publish the suite until 1905. The title comes from a Paul Verlaine poem, and the piece is a moonlit night in slow, sustained triple meter.

The opening is a slow, chorded melody in D-flat major, marked *Andante très expressif*. What is unusual about it — for the harmonic language of 1890 — is the *voicings*. The melody is doubled at the octave. The chords underneath are ninth chords and thirteenth chords, held with pedal so the sound thickens. In a Chopin nocturne, these ninth chords would be passing tones — decorations of simpler triads. In *Clair de Lune*, they are the actual harmony. Debussy has replaced Chopin's triads with the extended chords that would previously have been called dissonances, and he has used them as if they were the resting places.

The middle section moves into a rocking pattern — the left hand plays a broken chord in triplets over which the right hand lays a simple melody. This texture is close to a Chopin nocturne. But then Debussy takes the texture and lets it drift chromatically through several keys before returning to D-flat. The return is not a strong recapitulation with a resolved tonic. It is a soft dissolve — the piece comes back to where it started, but the coming-back is not celebrated; it is quietly done, and the piece ends on a D-flat major chord that is more colored than final.

# La Cathédrale engloutie

*La Cathédrale engloutie* ('The Sunken Cathedral'), from the first book of Preludes (1910), takes Debussy's technique further. The prelude is inspired by a Breton legend of a cathedral submerged off the coast of the island of Ys, which rises out of the sea at certain times and rings its bells before sinking again.

The piece opens with a series of low, ringing open fifths — bare intervals with no third, no color — played *pp* with pedal. Then a chord in the upper register, another chord, another. The chords move in *parallel motion*: the entire chord slides up or down as a unit, keeping the same interval structure between voices. This parallel motion is one of Debussy's most identifiable techniques and one of the most radical harmonic gestures of the era.

In traditional harmony, moving voices in parallel fifths and octaves is considered a bad move — the voices lose their independence and the harmony sounds thin. Debussy uses parallel motion deliberately, because he wants the voices to *not* be independent. He wants a single harmonic *object* to slide through space. When you hear the opening of *La Cathédrale engloutie*, you hear chords floating up out of the water as one thing. The parallel motion is the *point*.

The middle of the prelude has a section marked *Sonore sans dureté* — resounding without harshness. Chords ring in the middle register, held with pedal, moving slowly. This is the cathedral above water, its bells sounding across the sea. Then the piece descends, the chords soften, and the cathedral sinks back below the surface. The final page returns to the low fifths of the opening, quieter and quieter, until the piece dies away.

# La Fille aux cheveux de lin

*La Fille aux cheveux de lin* ('The Girl with the Flaxen Hair'), also from the first book of Preludes, is short and simple and one of the most-played Debussy pieces on student piano recitals. It is in G-flat major, marked *Très calme et doucement expressif* — very calm and gently expressive.

The tune is a simple modal melody, pentatonic in feel (that is, based mostly on five notes rather than the full seven-note major scale). Modal melody was old — it was the melodic material of medieval church music before major and minor keys took over in the seventeenth century, and it was the melodic material of a great many folk musics around the world that Debussy was interested in.

Debussy learned about non-Western modal music, in part, from hearing a Javanese gamelan ensemble perform at the Paris Universal Exposition of 1889. He was thirty-two and just beginning to write the mature music that would become *Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune* and *Nocturnes*. The pentatonic and modal writing that shows up in his mature work has roots in that gamelan encounter. He did not imitate gamelan music — his pieces are not gamelan pieces — but the pentatonic and modal harmonic vocabulary he took from listening became part of his language.

*La Fille aux cheveux de lin* uses that vocabulary. The melody is modal; the harmony underneath is gently colored with added seconds and ninths; the whole piece stays in one gentle atmosphere for three minutes and then ends. It is a small, complete thing — like a Chopin nocturne, but with a different harmonic dialect underneath.

# What we can do in Scheme

We can build a small demonstration of parallel chord motion — the Debussy technique.

```scheme
;; A chord type: major seventh chord (root, major third, perfect fifth, major seventh)
(define (maj7 root)
  (list root
        (transpose root 4)   ; major third up
        (transpose root 7)   ; perfect fifth up
        (transpose root 11))) ; major seventh up

;; Play a sequence of maj7 chords in parallel motion, sliding down chromatically
(define (parallel-descent starting-root n)
  (transport/tempo 60)
  (with-dynamics 'p
    (pedal/press)
    (let loop ((root starting-root) (count 0))
      (when (< count n)
        (chord/play (maj7 root) 'quarter)
        (loop (transpose root -1) (+ count 1))))   ; slide one semitone down
    (pedal/release)))

(parallel-descent 'F5 8)
```

The program plays eight major-seventh chords, each a semitone lower than the last. In traditional harmony, this progression is *forbidden* — chords in parallel motion carrying the same intervals move as a block and violate voice-leading rules. In Debussy's harmony, this progression is *the point*. The chords slide through space as one object.

If you listen to the opening of *La Cathédrale engloutie* and then to this small program, you will hear the family resemblance. The specific chords are different; the *technique* is the same. Debussy invented (or first clearly named) a way of moving chords that composers ever since have taken up.

# Why the appendix belongs

Debussy is important not just for his own pieces, but for what he opened up. Jazz's use of ninth and thirteenth chords as stable objects — the sound of a modern jazz piano trio — is Debussy's ninth chords, taken by American musicians in the 1920s and 1930s and remade into an improvised idiom. Film scoring's use of colored chords to evoke a mood without resolution is Debussy. Modern pop songwriting's use of parallel chord motion (which shows up in songs from The Beatles' 'Because' to any number of contemporary singer-songwriter arrangements) is Debussy.

If you learn how Debussy heard chords — as objects with sonic weight rather than as steps in a progression — you can hear an enormous swath of twentieth- and twenty-first-century music with new precision.

Scores of the Suite bergamasque, Book I of the Preludes, and other works cited are in the public domain and available on IMSLP.\"
