### 6.2 Triads — the basic chord

A **triad** is three notes stacked in thirds. It is the fundamental unit of Western harmony. There are four types:

- **Major triad**: root, major third, perfect fifth (e.g., C–E–G). Bright, stable.
- **Minor triad**: root, minor third, perfect fifth (e.g., C–E♭–G). Dark, stable.
- **Diminished triad**: root, minor third, diminished fifth (e.g., C–E♭–G♭). Tense, unstable.
- **Augmented triad**: root, major third, augmented fifth (e.g., C–E–G♯). Tense, ambiguous.

### C major triad

```scheme
;; The C major triad: C4–E4–G4.
;; The most stable sonority in C major.

(let ((start-beat 0))
  (note/place-at 60 start-beat 'half 80)   ; C4
  (note/place-at 64 start-beat 'half 80)   ; E4
  (note/place-at 67 start-beat 'half 80))  ; G4
```

`[VISUAL: treble staff showing the C major triad as three stacked noteheads on a single stem; label each pitch]`

### 6.3 Chord progressions — movement through harmonic time

A **chord progression** is a sequence of chords. The order matters. Some progressions feel like they are going *home* (a cadence), some feel like they are *leaving* home, some feel like they are wandering.

The simplest useful progression in Western music is **I–V–I** (tonic–dominant–tonic). In C major, that is C major triad → G major triad → C major triad. It is the harmonic equivalent of \"statement, tension, resolution.\"

### I–V–I in C major

```scheme

;; Each chord sounds for one beat.

  (note/place-at 60 beat 'quarter 80)
  (note/place-at 64 beat 'quarter 80)
  (note/place-at 67 beat 'quarter 80)
  (set! beat (+ beat 1))
  
  ;; V: G major (G–B–D)
  (note/place-at 67 beat 'quarter 80)
  (note/place-at 71 beat 'quarter 80)
  (note/place-at 74 beat 'quarter 80)
  (set! beat (+ beat 1))
  
  ;; I: C major (C–E–G)
  (note/place-at 60 beat 'quarter 80)
  (note/place-at 64 beat 'quarter 80)
  (note/place-at 67 beat 'quarter 80))
```

### 6.4 Voice leading — how chords connect

**Voice leading** is the art of moving from one chord to the next *smoothly*—minimizing the distance each pitch travels. Good voice leading makes a progression sound connected, inevitable. Bad voice leading makes it sound like the notes are jumping randomly.

The rule: **move each voice the shortest distance possible**. If the C in one chord can stay as the C in the next chord, *let it stay*. If the E must move, move it to the nearest available pitch in the next chord.

### Smooth I–V–I with voice leading

```scheme
;; I–V–I with good voice leading.
;; Notice: the G is common to both I and V, so it stays put.
;; The C moves down to B (one semitone), the E moves up to D (two semitones).

(let ((beat 0))
  ;; I: C major (C4–E4–G4)
  (note/place-at 60 beat 'half 70)   ; C4
  (note/place-at 64 beat 'half 70)   ; E4
  (note/place-at 67 beat 'half 70)   ; G4
  (set! beat (+ beat 2))
  
  ;; V: G major (B3–D4–G4)
  ;; G4 is common—stays put.
  ;; C4 moves down to B3 (1 semitone).
  ;; E4 moves down to D4 (2 semitones).
  (note/place-at 59 beat 'half 70)   ; B3
  (note/place-at 62 beat 'half 70)   ; D4
  (note/place-at 67 beat 'half 70)   ; G4 (common tone)
  (set! beat (+ beat 2))
  
  ;; I: C major (C4–E4–G4)
  (note/place-at 60 beat 'whole 70)
  (note/place-at 64 beat 'whole 70)
  (note/place-at 67 beat 'whole 70))
```

### 6.6 Cadences — punctuation in sound

A **cadence** is a harmonic stopping point—the musical equivalent of a period, comma, or semicolon. Different cadences create different levels of finality.

- **Authentic cadence (V–I)**: strong, final. The harmonic period.
- **Half cadence (anything → V)**: pause on the dominant. The harmonic comma.
- **Plagal cadence (IV–I)**: gentle, softer than authentic. The \"Amen\" cadence.
- **Deceptive cadence (V–vi)**: expects I, gets vi instead. Surprise, continuation.

### Authentic cadence (V–I)

```scheme
;; The strongest cadence: V → I.
;; Dominant to tonic. Resolution.

(let ((beat 0))
  ;; V: G major
  (note/place-at 55 beat 'half 80)   ; G3 (bass)
  (note/place-at 67 beat 'half 75)
  (note/place-at 71 beat 'half 75)
  (note/place-at 74 beat 'half 75)
  (set! beat (+ beat 2))
  
  ;; I: C major
  (note/place-at 48 beat 'whole 80)   ; C3 (bass)
  (note/place-at 60 beat 'whole 75)
  (note/place-at 64 beat 'whole 75)
  (note/place-at 67 beat 'whole 75))
```

### 6.7 Seventh chords — adding color and tension

A **seventh chord** adds a fourth note to the triad—a seventh above the root. It makes the chord richer and more tense. The most important seventh chord is the **dominant seventh** (V⁷), which combines the dominant triad with the interval of a tritone. It pulls *hard* toward resolution.

```scheme
  (note/place-at 71 beat 'whole 75)   ; B4
  (note/place-at 74 beat 'whole 75)   ; D5
  (note/place-at 77 beat 'whole 75))  ; F5
```

### 6.8 Harmonic rhythm — the pace of chord change

**Harmonic rhythm** is the rate at which chords change. One chord per measure is slow harmonic rhythm. One chord per beat is fast. The harmonic rhythm is independent of the melodic rhythm—you can have a slow-moving melody over fast-changing chords, or vice versa.

### Slow harmonic rhythm (one chord per measure)

```scheme

(let ((beat 0))
  ;; I: C major, four beats
  (note/place-at 48 beat 'whole 80)
  (note/place-at 60 beat 'whole 75)
  (note/place-at 64 beat 'whole 75)
  (note/place-at 67 beat 'whole 75)
  (set! beat (+ beat 4))
  
  ;; V: G major, four beats
  (note/place-at 55 beat 'whole 80)
  (note/place-at 67 beat 'whole 75)
  (note/place-at 71 beat 'whole 75)
  (note/place-at 74 beat 'whole 75))
```

```scheme

;; Common in jazz turnarounds.

  (note/place-at 60 beat 'quarter 75)
  (note/place-at 64 beat 'quarter 75)
  (note/place-at 67 beat 'quarter 75)
  (set! beat (+ beat 1))
  
  ;; vi: A minor
  (note/place-at 69 beat 'quarter 75)

  (note/place-at 65 beat 'quarter 75)

  (note/place-at 71 beat 'quarter 75)
```

### 6.9 Inversions — rearranging the triad

An **inversion** places a chord tone other than the root in the bass. A chord in **root position** has the root in the bass. A chord in **first inversion** has the third in the bass. A chord in **second inversion** has the fifth in the bass.

Inversions smooth the bassline and change the chord's stability. Second inversion is less stable than root position and often requires resolution.

### C major in root position, first inversion, second inversion

```scheme
;; C major triad in three positions.
;; Root position: C in bass.
;; First inversion: E in bass.
;; Second inversion: G in bass.

(let ((beat 0))
  ;; Root position: C–E–G
  (note/place-at 48 beat 'half 80)   ; C3 (bass)
  (note/place-at 64 beat 'half 75)
  (note/place-at 67 beat 'half 75)
  (set! beat (+ beat 2))
  
  ;; First inversion: E–G–C
  (note/place-at 52 beat 'half 80)   ; E3 (bass)
  (note/place-at 67 beat 'half 75)
  (note/place-at 72 beat 'half 75)
  (set! beat (+ beat 2))
  
  ;; Second inversion: G–C–E
  (note/place-at 55 beat 'half 80)   ; G3 (bass)
  (note/place-at 60 beat 'half 75)
  (note/place-at 64 beat 'half 75))
```

### 6.11 Suspensions — delaying resolution

A **suspension** is a note held over from one chord into the next, creating dissonance, then resolving down by step. The classic suspension is **4–3**: the fourth scale degree suspends, then resolves down to the third.

```scheme

  (note/place-at 55 beat 'half 80)   ; G3
  (note/place-at 62 beat 'half 75)   ; D4
  (note/place-at 65 beat 'half 75)   ; F4 (suspension)
  (note/place-at 67 beat 'half 75)   ; G4
  (set! beat (+ beat 2))
  
  ;; I with resolution: C–E–G (F resolves down to E)
  (note/place-at 48 beat 'whole 80)
  (note/place-at 64 beat 'whole 75)   ; E4 (resolution)
  (note/place-at 67 beat 'whole 75))
```

```scheme
  (note/place-at 71 beat 'quarter 70)

  ;; I: C major (consonant again)
```

### 6.13 Secondary dominants — tonicizing other chords

A **secondary dominant** is a dominant seventh chord that resolves to a chord *other than* the tonic. It temporarily tonicizes that target chord—makes it feel like a mini-tonic for a moment. In C major, V/V (D7) resolves to V (G major).

### V/V → V in C major

```scheme
;; D7 (V/V) resolving to G major (V).
;; D7 is the dominant of G, so it pulls toward G.

(let ((beat 0))
  ;; V/V: D7 (D–F♯–A–C)
  (note/place-at 50 beat 'half 80)   ; D3
  (note/place-at 66 beat 'half 75)   ; F♯4
  (note/place-at 69 beat 'half 75)   ; A4
  (note/place-at 72 beat 'half 75)   ; C5
  (set! beat (+ beat 2))
  
  ;; V: G major
  (note/place-at 55 beat 'whole 80)
  (note/place-at 67 beat 'whole 75)
  (note/place-at 71 beat 'whole 75)
  (note/place-at 74 beat 'whole 75))
```

### 6.14 Modal harmony — chords outside the major/minor system

**Modal harmony** uses chords drawn from modes other than major (Ionian) and minor (Aeolian)—Dorian, Phrygian, Lydian, Mixolydian, Locrian. Each mode has a different intervallic structure and thus a different set of available chords. Modal harmony often avoids strong dominant-tonic cadences, creating a more open, floating feel.

### Dorian progression (Dm–Em–Dm)

```scheme
;; A progression in D Dorian (D–E–F–G–A–B–C–D).
;; The major VI chord (B♭ major in natural minor) becomes B diminished in Dorian.
;; Dm–Em is characteristic.

(let ((beat 0))
  ;; i: D minor
  (note/place-at 50 beat 'half 80)   ; D3
  (note/place-at 62 beat 'half 75)   ; D4
  (note/place-at 65 beat 'half 75)   ; F4
  (note/place-at 69 beat 'half 75)   ; A4
  (set! beat (+ beat 2))
  
  ;; ii: E minor (major II, characteristic of Dorian)
  (note/place-at 52 beat 'half 80)   ; E3
  (note/place-at 64 beat 'half 75)   ; E4
  (note/place-at 67 beat 'half 75)   ; G4
  (note/place-at 71 beat 'half 75)   ; B4
  (set! beat (+ beat 2))
  
  ;; i: D minor
  (note/place-at 50 beat 'whole 80)
  (note/place-at 62 beat 'whole 75)
  (note/place-at 65 beat 'whole 75)
  (note/place-at 69 beat 'whole 75))
```

### 6.15 Chromaticism — notes outside the key

**Chromaticism** introduces notes from outside the prevailing key. A chromatic note can serve as a passing tone (connecting two diatonic notes by step), a neighbor tone (decorating a note by step and returning), or part of a chromatic chord (like a secondary dominant or an augmented sixth).

### Chromatic passing tone

```scheme
;; A chromatic passing tone: C–C♯–D.
;; The C♯ smooths the stepwise motion from C to D.

(let ((beat 0))
  ;; C major chord
  (note/place-at 60 beat 'quarter 75)   ; C4
  (note/place-at 64 beat 'quarter 75)   ; E4
  (note/place-at 67 beat 'quarter 75)   ; G4
  (set! beat (+ beat 1))
  
  ;; Chromatic passing tone
  (note/place-at 61 beat 'eighth 70)    ; C♯4
  (set! beat (+ beat 0.5))
  
  ;; D minor chord (ii)
  (note/place-at 62 beat 'quarter 75)   ; D4
  (note/place-at 65 beat 'quarter 75)   ; F4
  (note/place-at 69 beat 'quarter 75))  ; A4
```

```scheme
  (set! beat (+ beat 1))
  
  (note/place-at 61 beat 'eighth 70)    ; C♯4 (neighbor)
```

### 6.16 Harmonic sequence — a pattern that repeats at different pitch levels

A **harmonic sequence** is a chord progression that repeats at a different pitch level. Sequences create momentum and drive the harmony forward. The classic sequence is the descending-fifth sequence (I–IV–vii°–iii–vi–ii–V–I), where each chord's root moves down by fifth (or up by fourth).

### Descending-fifth sequence (fragment)

```scheme

  (note/place-at 60 beat 'half 75)
  (note/place-at 64 beat 'half 75)
  (note/place-at 67 beat 'half 75)
  (set! beat (+ beat 2))
  
  ;; IV: F major (root F, down a fifth from C)
  (note/place-at 53 beat 'half 80)
  (note/place-at 65 beat 'half 75)
  (note/place-at 69 beat 'half 75)
  (note/place-at 72 beat 'half 75)
  (set! beat (+ beat 2))
  
  ;; vii°: B diminished (root B, down a fifth from F)
  (note/place-at 59 beat 'half 80)
  (note/place-at 71 beat 'half 75)
  (note/place-at 74 beat 'half 75)
  (note/place-at 77 beat 'half 75))
```

### 6.17 Contrary motion — voices moving in opposite directions

**Contrary motion** occurs when two voices move in opposite directions—one ascending, one descending. It is the strongest kind of independence between voices and prevents them from sounding like a single doubled line. Good voice leading often maximizes contrary motion.

### Contrary motion between outer voices

```scheme
;; I–V–I with contrary motion in outer voices.
;; Bass descends C3 → G2, soprano ascends C4 → D4 → C4.

(let ((beat 0))
  ;; I: C major
  ;; Bass: C3
  ;; Soprano: C4
  (note/place-at 48 beat 'half 85)   ; C3 (bass)
  (note/place-at 60 beat 'half 70)   ; C4 (soprano)
  (note/place-at 64 beat 'half 70)   ; E4
  (note/place-at 67 beat 'half 70)   ; G4
  (set! beat (+ beat 2))
  
  ;; V: G major
  ;; Bass: G2 (descends)
  ;; Soprano: D4 (ascends)
  (note/place-at 43 beat 'half 85)   ; G2 (bass, down)
  (note/place-at 62 beat 'half 70)   ; D4 (soprano, up)
  (note/place-at 67 beat 'half 70)   ; G4
  (note/place-at 71 beat 'half 70)   ; B4
  (set! beat (+ beat 2))
  
  ;; I: C major
  ;; Bass: C3 (ascends back)
  ;; Soprano: C4 (descends back)
  (note/place-at 48 beat 'whole 85)
  (note/place-at 60 beat 'whole 70)
  (note/place-at 64 beat 'whole 70)
  (note/place-at 67 beat 'whole 70))
```

### 6.19 Parallel motion — voices moving in the same direction by the same interval

**Parallel motion** is when two or more voices move in the same direction by the same interval. Parallel thirds and sixths are common and sound smooth. Parallel fifths and octaves are forbidden in strict counterpoint because they destroy voice independence.

### Parallel thirds

```scheme
;; Melody harmonized in parallel thirds: C–D–E–F with E–F–G–A below.

(let ((beat 0))
  ;; Upper voice
  (note/place-at 60 beat 'quarter 75)   ; C4
  (note/place-at 62 (+ beat 1) 'quarter 75)   ; D4
  (note/place-at 64 (+ beat 2) 'quarter 75)   ; E4
  (note/place-at 65 (+ beat 3) 'quarter 75)   ; F4
  
  ;; Lower voice (parallel thirds below)
  (note/place-at 64 beat 'quarter 75)   ; E4
  (note/place-at 65 (+ beat 1) 'quarter 75)   ; F4
  (note/place-at 67 (+ beat 2) 'quarter 75)   ; G4
  (note/place-at 69 (+ beat 3) 'quarter 75))  ; A4
```

### 6.20 Harmonic density — how many notes at once?

You can control the **harmonic density**—the number of simultaneous pitches—to vary the texture. Sparse harmony (two or three notes) feels open, transparent. Dense harmony (six or more notes) feels lush, saturated. Vary the density over the course of a piece to shape the emotional arc.

### Sparse two-voice harmony

```scheme
;; Just two notes: a fifth (C–G).

(let ((beat 0))
  (note/place-at 60 beat 'whole 80)   ; C4
  (note/place-at 67 beat 'whole 80))  ; G4
```

```scheme
  (note/place-at 48 beat 'whole 80)   ; C3
  (note/place-at 64 beat 'whole 75)   ; E4
  (note/place-at 67 beat 'whole 75)   ; G4
  (note/place-at 71 beat 'whole 75))  ; B4
```

"# Chapter 7: Voices

**Chapter question:** What makes a cello sound like a cello, and not like a flute?

Up until now, every note we've played—whether a single pitch from Chapter 1's `(tone 440 1)` or the entire harmonized *Twinkle Twinkle* from Chapter 6—has lived inside the same plain sonic wrapper. We've changed *pitch*, *duration*, *velocity*, and even stacked notes into chords, but the **quality** of the sound itself—the thing that makes a violin a violin and a trumpet a trumpet—has been mostly opaque to us. We've asked *what* to play and *when*, but not *with what voice*.

This chapter changes that. We will learn how **timbre**—the texture or color of a sound—emerges from the **harmonic content** of a waveform, and we will use the Web Audio API's `createPeriodicWave` to **design our own voices** by specifying exactly which harmonics ring and how loud. By the end, you will be able to tune a voice that sounds like a cello section, a clarinet choir, or something entirely new—and play it just as easily as you've been playing the default piano.

**We call it \"music,\" but we are really dealing with sound.** A \"voice\" is not a metaphor—it is a specific recipe of sine waves, mixed at precise amplitudes, that your ear hears as a unified tone. This chapter makes that recipe explicit and puts it under your control.

---

## 1. What is timbre?

Play these two programs and listen:

```scheme
;; A bare 220 Hz sine wave
(tone 220 1)
```

```scheme
;; A 220 Hz tone with the default \"piano\" voice
(note/strike 'A3 'quarter 0.8)
```

Both are the same pitch (A3 = 220 Hz), but they sound completely different. The first is **pure**—smooth, glassy, a single sine wave with no texture. The second is **rich**—warm, percussive, full of detail. That difference is **timbre**.

**Timbre** is the quality that lets you tell a violin from a trumpet even when they play the same note at the same loudness. It is what makes a voice sound \"bright\" or \"dark,\" \"hollow\" or \"reedy.\" And it is **not magic**—it is the result of **which harmonics are present and how loud they are**.

A **harmonic** is a frequency that is an integer multiple of a **fundamental** frequency. If the fundamental is 220 Hz (A3), the harmonics are:

- 1× = 220 Hz (the fundamental itself)
- 2× = 440 Hz (the first harmonic, one octave up)
- 3× = 660 Hz
- 4× = 880 Hz
- 5× = 1100 Hz
- … and so on

A sine wave, like `(tone 220 1)`, contains **only the fundamental**—no harmonics at all. That is why it sounds so pure and featureless. Every other instrument—every real-world sound—is a **mixture** of the fundamental plus some subset of its harmonics, each ringing at its own amplitude. The **harmonic profile**—which harmonics are loud, which are quiet, which are missing—is what gives an instrument its voice.

## 2. Building a voice from harmonics

The Web Audio API gives us a tool called `createPeriodicWave` that lets us specify **exactly which harmonics to include and how loud they should be**. Instead of accepting a pre-built waveform (sine, square, sawtooth), `createPeriodicWave` takes two arrays:

- **Real** (the cosine coefficients)
- **Imaginary** (the sine coefficients)

These arrays encode the **Fourier series** that describes the waveform. For our purposes, the **real** array is where we place the amplitudes of each harmonic (starting with the fundamental), and the **imaginary** array is usually all zeros (which means no phase shift—every harmonic starts at the same moment).

Concretely: if you want a tone with a strong fundamental, a weaker second harmonic, and a very quiet third harmonic, you would write:

```scheme
(define cello-profile
  '(0.0    ; DC offset (always 0)
    1.0    ; fundamental (full strength)
    0.4    ; 2nd harmonic (weaker)
    0.1))  ; 3rd harmonic (quiet)
```

The **first number is always 0.0**—it represents the DC offset, which we never use in audio. The **second number** is the fundamental, the **third** is the first harmonic (2×), the **fourth** is the second harmonic (3×), and so on.

Here is a complete program that **creates a custom voice** using that profile and plays a single note with it *[needs: GAP-6]*:

```scheme
(define cello-profile
  '(0.0 1.0 0.4 0.1))

(define (make-voice profile)
  ;; [needs: GAP-6] — createPeriodicWave support
  ;; This will call:
  ;;   audioContext.createPeriodicWave(
  ;;     Float32Array(profile),
  ;;     Float32Array(zeros-of-same-length)
  ;;   )
  ;; and return a voice handle
  (create-periodic-wave profile (make-list (length profile) 0.0)))

(define my-cello (make-voice cello-profile))

(note/strike 'C4 'half 0.8 my-cello)
```

## 3. Designing a section voice

Real orchestras do not use single instruments—they use **sections**: eight cellos, twelve violins, four horns. A section has a **thicker, more blended sound** than a solo instrument, because the slight tuning and timing variations between players **blur the attack** and **widen the harmonic envelope**.

We can model a section by **choosing a harmonic profile that emphasizes the lower harmonics and tapers off quickly**. Here is a **warm string-section voice**:

```scheme
(define warm-strings-profile
  '(0.0    ; DC
    1.0    ; fundamental
    0.6    ; 2nd
    0.3    ; 3rd
    0.15   ; 4th
    0.08   ; 5th
    0.04   ; 6th
    0.02)) ; 7th

(define warm-strings (make-voice warm-strings-profile))
```

The fundamental is full-strength, the second harmonic is moderately strong, and each successive harmonic is roughly **half as loud** as the one before. This gives a **smooth, full, non-piercing** tone—exactly what you hear from a violin or cello section playing *legato*.

Now play a chord with it *[needs: GAP-6]*:

```scheme
(define warm-strings-profile
  '(0.0 1.0 0.6 0.3 0.15 0.08 0.04 0.02))

(define (make-voice profile)
  (create-periodic-wave profile (make-list (length profile) 0.0)))

(define warm-strings (make-voice warm-strings-profile))

(define (play-chord pitches dur velocity voice)
  (for-each (lambda (p)
              (note/strike p dur velocity voice))
            pitches))

(play-chord '(C4 E4 G4) 'whole 0.7 warm-strings)
```

You should hear a **rich, unified chord**—not three separate sine tones, but a **blended section sound**.

## 4. Bright versus dark

The **brightness** of a voice is determined by how much high-harmonic energy it has. A **bright** voice emphasizes the upper harmonics; a **dark** voice suppresses them.

Here are two profiles—one bright, one dark:

```scheme
;; Bright (flute-like)
(define bright-profile
  '(0.0 0.7 0.5 0.4 0.3 0.25 0.2 0.15 0.1))

;; Dark (bassoon-like)
(define dark-profile
  '(0.0 1.0 0.3 0.1 0.05 0.02 0.01 0.005 0.0))
```

## 5. Tuning your own voice

You now have the tools to **design any voice you can imagine**. The process is:

1. **Decide how many harmonics to include** (typically 6–12 is enough; beyond that, the ear can barely distinguish them).
2. **Set the amplitude of each harmonic** (between 0.0 and 1.0).
3. **Wrap the profile in `make-voice`** to get a playable voice handle.
4. **Pass the voice to `note/strike` or `note/place-at`** as the last argument.

Here is a **hollow, clarinet-like voice** (clarinets emphasize odd harmonics and suppress even ones):

```scheme
(define clarinet-profile
  '(0.0    ; DC
    1.0    ; fundamental
    0.0    ; 2nd (suppressed)
    0.6    ; 3rd (strong)
    0.0    ; 4th (suppressed)
    0.4    ; 5th (moderate)
    0.0    ; 6th (suppressed)
    0.2    ; 7th (weak)
    0.0))  ; 8th (suppressed)

(define (make-voice profile)
  (create-periodic-wave profile (make-list (length profile) 0.0)))

(define clarinet (make-voice clarinet-profile))

(note/strike 'D4 'half 0.8 clarinet)
```

<!-- BUILD: wire voice support for note/strike. GAP-6. -->

The result is **reedy, nasal, hollow**—exactly the quality of a clarinet in its middle register.

## 6. A tunable section-voice

Let's pull it all together into a **reusable function** that builds a section voice from a **decay rate**—a single parameter that controls how quickly the harmonics fall off. A **slow decay** gives a bright, rich voice; a **fast decay** gives a dark, mellow voice.

```scheme
(define (section-voice num-harmonics decay-rate)
  ;; Build a profile where each harmonic's amplitude is:
  ;;   amplitude[n] = (expt decay-rate (- n 1))
  ;; (The first element is always 0.0 for DC offset.)
  (let ((profile (cons 0.0
                       (map (lambda (n)
                              (expt decay-rate (- n 1)))
                            (iota num-harmonics 1)))))
    (make-voice profile)))

(define (make-voice profile)
  (create-periodic-wave profile (make-list (length profile) 0.0)))

;; A rich, bright section (decay = 0.7)
(define bright-section (section-voice 10 0.7))

;; A warm, dark section (decay = 0.5)
(define warm-section (section-voice 10 0.5))

;; A very mellow section (decay = 0.3)
(define mellow-section (section-voice 10 0.3))

;; Play a phrase with each
(define phrase '(C4 E4 G4 E4 C4))

(define (play-phrase pitches dur velocity voice)
  (let loop ((ps pitches) (beat 0))
    (if (null? ps)
        'done
        (begin
          (note/place-at (car ps) beat dur velocity voice)
          (loop (cdr ps) (+ beat 1))))))

(play-phrase phrase 'quarter 0.8 bright-section)
;; (then play with warm-section and mellow-section)
```

A decay of **0.7** gives a **violin section**, **0.5** gives **cellos**, **0.3** gives **basses**. You are now conducting the harmonic content directly.

## 8. What we've learned

You now understand:

- **Timbre** is the result of **harmonic content**—which harmonics are present and how loud.
- A **harmonic** is an integer multiple of the fundamental frequency.
- A **sine wave** has no harmonics (just the fundamental), which is why it sounds featureless.
- `createPeriodicWave` (via our `make-voice` wrapper) lets you specify the amplitude of each harmonic directly.
- A **bright voice** has strong upper harmonics; a **dark voice** suppresses them.
- A **section voice** (strings, woodwinds, brass) can be modeled with a profile that tapers off gradually.
- You can build a **reusable voice constructor** (like `section-voice`) that takes parameters (e.g., decay rate) and returns a playable voice handle.

**Next chapter (Timbre & Envelope):** We will refine these voices further by adding **ADSR envelopes** (attack, decay, sustain, release) and **filters** (low-pass, high-pass, band-pass) to shape the sound over time and across the frequency spectrum. A section voice is a good start, but a **living, breathing voice** needs dynamics—and that is where envelopes come in.

### A voice with one harmonic

The simplest periodic wave is a sine — just the fundamental, no harmonics above it. We already know that sound from `(tone freq dur)`. Let's define it as a voice anyway, to see the pattern.

*[needs: GAP-4]*

```scheme
;; A pure sine voice — only the first harmonic, amplitude 1.0
(define sine-voice
  (create-periodic-wave
    (list 1.0)))  ;; harmonic 1 at full strength

(note/strike 60 'quarter 0.8 sine-voice)  ;; middle C, sine timbre
```

<!-- BUILD: wire create-periodic-wave to accept a list of harmonic amplitudes (one float per harmonic, index i = i-th harmonic) and return a voice handle. note/strike extended to accept an optional voice argument (default = piano). -->

The list `(list 1.0)` says \"first harmonic at amplitude 1.0, all others zero.\" The result is a sine wave — the same sound as `(tone 261.63 0.5)` (which is what middle C at quarter-note duration would be at 120 bpm).

Not interesting yet. Let's add more harmonics.

### A voice with two harmonics

Add the second harmonic at half the amplitude of the first. The second harmonic is an octave above the fundamental, so we're blending the pitch with its octave.

*[needs: GAP-4]*

```scheme
(define octave-voice
  (create-periodic-wave
    (list 1.0 0.5)))  ;; fundamental + octave at half strength

(note/strike 48 'half 0.7 octave-voice)  ;; C3, with its octave mixed in
```

You hear C3, but it sounds **fuller** — because the octave (C4) is quietly present. This is still simple, but it's no longer a pure sine. It has two partials.

### A sawtooth voice (all harmonics, decreasing)

A **sawtooth wave** has all harmonics present, each one's amplitude inversely proportional to its number: the second harmonic is half as loud as the first, the third is one-third, the fourth is one-quarter, and so on. It sounds **bright and buzzy** — lots of high-frequency content.

*[needs: GAP-4]*

```scheme
(define sawtooth-voice
  (create-periodic-wave
    (list 1.0
          (/ 1 2.0)
          (/ 1 3.0)
          (/ 1 4.0)
          (/ 1 5.0)
          (/ 1 6.0)
          (/ 1 7.0)
          (/ 1 8.0))))  ;; eight harmonics, amplitudes 1, 1/2, 1/3, ... 1/8

(note/strike 55 'quarter 0.6 sawtooth-voice)  ;; G3, sawtooth timbre
```

Now we hear a bright, edgy sound. The higher harmonics give it that buzz.

[VISUAL: Waveform of one period of the sawtooth — a rising ramp that drops sharply, repeating. Spectrum below showing the eight harmonics as bars at 1×, 2×, 3×, ... 8× the fundamental frequency, heights decreasing as 1, 1/2, 1/3, ... 1/8.]

---


### A square voice (odd harmonics only)

A **square wave** has only the odd harmonics (1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th, ...), each with amplitude inversely proportional to its number. It sounds **hollow and reedy** — less bright than a sawtooth because the even harmonics are missing.

*[needs: GAP-4]*

```scheme
(define square-voice
  (create-periodic-wave
    (list 1.0
          0.0          ;; no 2nd harmonic
          (/ 1 3.0)
          0.0          ;; no 4th
          (/ 1 5.0)
          0.0          ;; no 6th
          (/ 1 7.0)
          0.0)))       ;; no 8th

(note/strike 62 'quarter 0.7 square-voice)  ;; D4, square timbre
```

The odd-harmonic recipe gives you that clarinet-like hollow quality.

### A warm cello-section voice

A cello section has strong low harmonics and a gentle roll-off. Let's author one by hand.

*[needs: GAP-4]*

```scheme
(define cello-section
  (create-periodic-wave
    (list 1.0      ;; fundamental, full
          0.6      ;; 2nd harmonic, strong
          0.4      ;; 3rd, present
          0.25     ;; 4th, softer
          0.15     ;; 5th, fading
          0.08     ;; 6th, faint
          0.04     ;; 7th, very faint
          0.02)))  ;; 8th, almost gone

(note/strike 36 'whole 0.8 cello-section)  ;; C2, low and warm
```

This sounds **warm and full** — the strong first three harmonics give body, the gentle fade keeps it from being harsh. One synthesized note, but it feels like eight cellos playing together.

### A clarinet-like voice (odd harmonics, shaped)

### A gamelan-like voice (inharmonic partials)

Most of what we've built so far uses **harmonic** partials — whole-number multiples of the fundamental. But some instruments (bells, gongs, gamelan metallophones) have **inharmonic** partials — frequencies that are NOT whole-number multiples. We can approximate that by carefully choosing harmonic amplitudes to emphasize non-adjacent partials, creating a **clangorous, metallic** timbre.

*[needs: GAP-4]*

```scheme
(define gamelan-voice
  (create-periodic-wave
    (list 1.0      ;; 1st (fundamental)
          0.1      ;; 2nd, very faint
          0.6      ;; 3rd, strong (creates a slight \"clang\")
          0.05     ;; 4th, faint
          0.4      ;; 5th, moderate (more clang)
          0.02     ;; 6th, trace
          0.3      ;; 7th, moderate (adds shimmer)
          0.01     ;; 8th, silent
          0.2      ;; 9th, faint (more shimmer)
          0.0)))   ;; 10th, silent

(note/strike 64 'half 0.7 gamelan-voice)  ;; E4, metallic and shimmering
```

The gaps between strong harmonics (1, 3, 5, 7, 9) create a **metallic, ringing** quality — not quite a true inharmonic instrument, but closer to the feel of a bronze gong than a cello.

### A human-voice vowel (an \"ah\" sound)

Human vowels are shaped by **formants** — frequency regions where certain harmonics are amplified by the shape of the vocal tract. An \"ah\" vowel (as in \"father\") has formants around 700 Hz and 1200 Hz. If our fundamental is A3 (220 Hz), we want to boost the harmonics near those frequencies.

Harmonic 3 ≈ 660 Hz (close to 700 Hz).  
Harmonic 5 ≈ 1100 Hz (close to 1200 Hz).

Let's shape a voice that emphasizes those harmonics.

*[needs: GAP-4]*

```scheme
(define ah-vowel
  (create-periodic-wave
    (list 1.0      ;; 1st (220 Hz)
          0.3      ;; 2nd (440 Hz)
          0.8      ;; 3rd (660 Hz) — first formant region
          0.4      ;; 4th (880 Hz)
          0.9      ;; 5th (1100 Hz) — second formant region
          0.3      ;; 6th (1320 Hz)
          0.2      ;; 7th (1540 Hz)
          0.1)))   ;; 8th (1760 Hz)

(note/strike 57 'half 0.65 ah-vowel)  ;; A3, \"ah\" vowel timbre
```

The boost at harmonics 3 and 5 gives it a **vocal quality** — not a perfect sung \"ah,\" but recognizably voice-like.

### An \"ee\" vowel

An \"ee\" vowel (as in \"see\") has formants around 270 Hz and 2300 Hz. For A3 (220 Hz):

Harmonic 1 ≈ 220 Hz (close to 270 Hz).  
Harmonic 10 ≈ 2200 Hz (close to 2300 Hz).

We'll boost harmonic 1 (already full) and harmonic 10.

*[needs: GAP-4]*

```scheme
(define ee-vowel
  (create-periodic-wave
    (list 1.0      ;; 1st (220 Hz) — first formant region

          0.1      ;; 4th
          0.08     ;; 5th
          0.06     ;; 6th
          0.05     ;; 7th
          0.04     ;; 8th
          0.03     ;; 9th
          0.7)))   ;; 10th (2200 Hz) — second formant region

(note/strike 57 'half 0.6 ee-vowel)  ;; A3, \"ee\" vowel timbre
```

The strong high harmonic (10th) gives it that **bright, frontal \"ee\"** character.

### What you've learned

- A **periodic wave** is a repeating wave, described by its harmonics.
- By choosing the **amplitude of each harmonic**, you sculpt the **timbre** — the color of the sound.
- A few strong low harmonics → warm and round. Many weak high harmonics → bright and airy. Odd harmonics only → reedy and hollow.
- You can approximate **real instruments** (cello, flute, brass, clarinet) by shaping their harmonic profiles.
- You can invent **new voices** by experimenting with harmonic recipes.
- One synthesized note, with the right harmonic profile, can sound like a **whole section** — eight cellos, four horns, a woodwind choir.
- You can **orchestrate** by assigning different voices to different notes in a chord.

In the next chapter we'll add **ADSR envelopes** and **filters** to give these voices dynamic shape — attack, sustain, and decay — so they don't just have the right timbre, they have the right **life**.

### What is a harmonic?

When you pluck a string, it doesn't just vibrate at one frequency. It vibrates at:
- The **fundamental** (the pitch you hear),
- The **second harmonic** (twice the fundamental frequency),
- The **third harmonic** (three times),
- The **fourth**, the **fifth**, and so on.

Each harmonic is a sine wave. The **amplitude** of each harmonic (how loud it is relative to the fundamental) determines the timbre. A **harmonic profile** is just a list of those amplitudes.

**Example:** a sawtooth wave has every harmonic, each one `1/n` the amplitude of the fundamental. A square wave has only the odd harmonics, each `1/n`. A triangle wave has odd harmonics, each `1/(n²)`.

We can build **any periodic waveform** by specifying its harmonic amplitudes. That's what `createPeriodicWave` does.

"# Chapter 8: Timbre & Envelope

*\"Two pianos can play the same note, and you still know which is which.\"*

---

You've built melodies, harmonies, and voices. But press middle C on a grand piano, then on an electric keyboard, then hum it — same pitch, same duration, wildly different *sound*. That difference is **timbre**: the color, the texture, the \"why does this sound like a clarinet and not a trumpet\" quality.

Chapter 7 gave you **section voices** — whole ensembles collapsed into a single playable instrument, their harmonic profiles tuned via `createPeriodicWave`. This chapter digs into the **how**: the envelope that shapes a note's life from birth to silence, the waveform that seeds its character, and the filters and detune spreads that make it *sing* or *growl* or *shimmer*.

We'll take **Twinkle Twinkle** — your companion melody since Chapter 3 — and **jazz it**. Not by changing the notes, but by changing *how they sound*: softening the attack, lengthening the release, spreading the detune, adding a little grit. Same melody, new wardrobe.

---

## 8.1 The Life of a Note: ADSR

Every note you've heard so far has an **envelope** — the curve of its loudness over time. You just haven't *chosen* one yet; the engine picked a default (a quick rise, a steady body, a quick fall). Now you will.

The standard envelope model is **ADSR**, four stages:

- **Attack** — how long it takes to reach full volume after you press the key. A piano has a fast attack (the hammer strikes instantly); a cello has a slower one (the bow takes a moment to bite the string).
- **Decay** — the initial drop after the peak. On a piano, the note is loudest the instant after the hammer hits, then fades slightly as the string settles.
- **Sustain** — the steady level while the key is held. This is a *level*, not a time. On a piano, sustain is silent (the note dies). On an organ, it's full volume (the key holds the pipe open).
- **Release** — how long it takes to fade to silence after you lift the key. A piano's release is the ring of the string after the damper falls. A synthesizer's can be instant (a click) or stretched (a wash).

[VISUAL: four-panel ADSR diagram — each panel shows one stage's curve overlaid on a waveform; panels stack left-to-right to show the full envelope shape. Attack rises, Decay drops to Sustain level, Sustain holds flat, Release falls to zero. Annotated with time on X-axis, amplitude on Y-axis. Curator-16 palette, dot-matrix render, clean line-graph clarity.]

```scheme
;; A note with a slow attack and long release — like a cello bowing in.
;; *[needs: GAP-3]* — ADSR control not yet exposed in the note surface.
(define (cello-note pitch dur velocity)
  (note/strike pitch dur velocity
               :attack 0.15   ;; 150ms to reach full volume
               :decay 0.05
               :sustain 0.8   ;; hold at 80% after decay
               :release 0.5)) ;; half-second ring after release

(cello-note 60 1.0 80) ;; middle C, one beat, medium velocity
```

<!-- BUILD: wire ADSR parameters into the note/strike verb; pass them through to the AudioParam envelope on the GainNode. Default: attack=0.01, decay=0.1, sustain=0.7, release=0.2 (the current implicit envelope). Validate that attack+decay+dur+release schedule correctly on the timeline. -->

*[needs: GAP-3]* — ADSR is a **gap**. The engine schedules notes, but the envelope shape isn't yet user-tunable. The example above shows the *interface* you're building toward; when GAP-3 closes, you'll be able to shape every note this way.

For now, trust the concept: **the envelope is the note's life story**. Fast attack + short release = percussive (piano, marimba). Slow attack + long release = legato (strings, voice, pads). The same pitch, two envelopes, two instruments.

---

## 8.2 Waveforms: The Seed of Timbre

Before the envelope shapes it, a note begins as a **waveform** — a repeating pattern of air pressure over time. You've been hearing sine waves (smooth, pure, flute-like). But there are others:

- **Sine** — one frequency, no overtones. Pure, glassy, a tuning fork.
- **Square** — odd harmonics (1st, 3rd, 5th, 7th…). Hollow, woody, a clarinet's lower register.
- **Sawtooth** — all harmonics (1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th…). Bright, brassy, a violin bowing hard.
- **Triangle** — odd harmonics like square, but softer. Mellow, flute-ish, but richer than a sine.

[VISUAL: four waveforms rendered side-by-side — sine (smooth curve), square (sharp on/off), sawtooth (ramp up, sharp drop), triangle (linear rise and fall). Each one cycle shown, amplitude on Y, time on X. Dot-matrix, Curator-16, waveform lines in accent color against neutral background.]

The Web Audio API gives you oscillators with these four built-in types. You pick one, set its frequency (pitch), and it runs until you stop it.

```scheme
;; A square-wave note — hollow, reedy, like a clarinet.
;; *[needs: GAP-3]* — waveform selection not yet exposed.
(define (clarinet-note pitch dur velocity)
  (note/strike pitch dur velocity :waveform 'square))

(clarinet-note 60 1.0 80)
```

<!-- BUILD: add :waveform keyword to note/strike; map 'sine | 'square | 'sawtooth | 'triangle to oscillator.type; default 'sine. Validate that the oscillator type is set before the note schedules. -->

Each waveform has a **harmonic signature** — the mix of overtones riding on top of the fundamental frequency. A sine has none (just the one pure tone). A square has strong odd harmonics (the 3rd harmonic is 1/3 the amplitude of the fundamental, the 5th is 1/5, and so on). A sawtooth has *all* harmonics (each 1/n the amplitude). That's why a sawtooth sounds \"fuller\" than a square, and a square sounds \"richer\" than a sine.

Chapter 7's **section voices** are hand-tuned harmonic profiles built via `createPeriodicWave` — you specify exactly which harmonics at exactly which amplitudes. Waveforms are the *fast presets*: four common shapes, no tuning required.

---

## 8.3 Filters: Sculpting the Spectrum

A waveform gives you harmonics. A **filter** takes some away.

The most common filter is a **low-pass**: it lets low frequencies through and blocks high ones. Turn the **cutoff frequency** down, and the sound gets darker, duller, more muffled — like covering a speaker with a blanket. Turn it up, and the brightness returns.

[VISUAL: frequency spectrum graph — X-axis is frequency (20 Hz to 20 kHz, log scale), Y-axis is amplitude. Two overlays: (1) the full sawtooth spectrum (all harmonics, descending amplitude), (2) the same spectrum after a low-pass filter at 2 kHz — harmonics above 2 kHz are attenuated/removed. The cutoff is marked with a vertical line. Curator-16, dot-matrix, spectrum bars in one color, filtered result in another.]

```scheme
;; A filtered sawtooth — bright waveform, dark filter.
;; *[needs: GAP-3]* — filter control not yet exposed.
(define (muted-brass pitch dur velocity)
  (note/strike pitch dur velocity
               :waveform 'sawtooth
               :filter-type 'lowpass
               :filter-cutoff 1200)) ;; Hz — cuts above 1200

(muted-brass 60 1.0 80)
```

<!-- BUILD: add :filter-type and :filter-cutoff keywords to note/strike; wire to a BiquadFilterNode in the signal chain (oscillator → filter → gain → destination). Default: no filter (or an all-pass / very high cutoff). Validate cutoff range (20–20000 Hz reasonable). -->

Other filter types:

- **High-pass** — blocks lows, keeps highs. Makes the sound thin, tinny, like a telephone.
- **Band-pass** — keeps a slice in the middle, blocks lows and highs. Nasal, vocal-formant-like.
- **Notch** — cuts a slice in the middle, keeps lows and highs. Good for removing a hum or resonance.

Filters are **subtractive synthesis**: you start with a harmonically rich waveform (sawtooth, square) and carve away what you don't want. It's how analog synthesizers worked in the 1970s, and it's still the easiest way to get \"synth brass\" or \"synth strings\" — a bright wave, a dark filter, a slow envelope.

---

## 8.4 Detune Spread: The Shimmer

Play one note: clean. Play two notes a few cents apart (a **cent** is 1/100 of a semitone): they **beat** against each other, a slow wobble. Play a dozen notes spread across ±20 cents: they **shimmer**, a rich chorusing effect that makes one voice sound like many.

This is **detune spread**, and it's how you make a synthesizer sound *expensive*. Instead of one oscillator per note, you layer several, each slightly detuned, and the interference between them creates motion, width, life.

```scheme
;; A wide, shimmering pad — three oscillators per note, spread ±15 cents.
;; *[needs: GAP-3]* — detune spread / unison count not yet exposed.
(define (pad-note pitch dur velocity)
  (note/strike pitch dur velocity
               :waveform 'sawtooth
               :unison 3         ;; three oscillators
               :detune-spread 15)) ;; ±15 cents

(pad-note 60 2.0 70)
```

<!-- BUILD: add :unison (oscillator count, default 1) and :detune-spread (cents, default 0) keywords. For unison > 1, create N oscillators per note, detune them evenly across [-spread, +spread], sum their outputs (gain = 1/N to avoid clipping). Validate that detune is applied via oscillator.detune.value (in cents). -->

The **detune-spread** parameter is in **cents**. 100 cents = 1 semitone. Spread of 0 = no detune (one clean voice). Spread of 10–20 = subtle shimmer (good for pads, strings). Spread of 50+ = wide chorus (good for \"supersaw\" leads, detuned bells).

**Why it works:** when two sine waves are close in frequency, their peaks and troughs drift in and out of alignment. Where they align, the sound gets louder (constructive interference). Where they oppose, quieter (destructive interference). The result is a **beating** — a periodic rise and fall in volume. With many oscillators, each pair beats at a different rate, and the sum is a complex, evolving shimmer.

---

## 8.5 Jazz Envelope: Making Twinkle Swing

Now we put it together. **Twinkle Twinkle** has been your straight-backed companion since Chapter 3 — quarter notes on a piano, even and bright. Let's give it a jazz wardrobe:

- **Slow attack** — the note swells in, not hammered.
- **Long release** — each note rings into the next, a bit of overlap.
- **Sawtooth wave** — richer than a sine, but not as harsh as raw saw; we'll filter it.
- **Low-pass filter at 2400 Hz** — takes the edge off the brightness.
- **Subtle detune spread (±8 cents, 2 oscillators)** — just enough shimmer to suggest an ensemble, not a single instrument.

This is a **jazz piano voice** — warm, rounded, a bit smoky.

The melody is **unchanged** — same pitches, same rhythm. But the *timbre* transforms it. The slow attack softens the entrance of each note (less \"plunk,\" more \"breath\"). The long release makes the notes overlap slightly, a gentle legato. The filtered sawtooth gives it body without harshness. The detune spread adds a subtle shimmer, as if two pianists are playing in near-unison, their tunings just a hair apart.

This is **additive expressiveness**. You didn't rewrite the melody. You didn't add ornaments (that's Chapter 12). You changed *how it sounds*, and the melody became something new.

## 8.7 Velocity Sensitivity: Playing Dynamics

You've been setting velocity to a fixed number (75, 80). But **velocity** is how hard you press the key, and on a real instrument, that changes *loudness* and *timbre*. A piano played softly has a dark, mellow tone (the hammer strikes gently, fewer high harmonics excite). Played hard, it's bright and punchy (the hammer slams, the whole string rings).

You can map velocity to:

- **Volume** (the obvious one) — higher velocity = louder note.
- **Filter cutoff** (brightness) — higher velocity = brighter tone (higher cutoff).
- **Attack time** (percussiveness) — higher velocity = faster attack (more immediate strike).

```scheme
;; A velocity-sensitive voice — soft notes are dark and slow, loud notes are bright and fast.
;; *[needs: GAP-3]* — velocity mapping not yet exposed beyond volume.
(define (expressive-piano pitch dur velocity)
  (let ((brightness (+ 800 (* velocity 20)))  ;; cutoff: 800 Hz at v=0, 3400 at v=127
        (attack-time (- 0.12 (* velocity 0.0008)))) ;; attack: 120ms at v=0, 20ms at v=127
    (note/strike pitch dur velocity
                 :waveform 'sawtooth
                 :attack attack-time
                 :decay 0.1
                 :sustain 0.6
                 :release 0.3
                 :filter-type 'lowpass
                 :filter-cutoff brightness
                 :unison 2
                 :detune-spread 6)))

;; A phrase with dynamic shaping — soft start, loud climax, soft end
(expressive-piano 60 1.0 50)  ;; soft
(expressive-piano 62 1.0 60)
(expressive-piano 64 1.0 75)
(expressive-piano 65 1.0 90)  ;; loud
(expressive-piano 64 1.0 75)
(expressive-piano 62 1.0 60)
(expressive-piano 60 2.0 50)  ;; soft
```

This is **expressive control**. The same notes, different velocities, and the phrase *breathes* — it swells and recedes, not just in volume but in color. That's how a real pianist plays: they don't just hit the keys harder; they change the *quality* of the sound.

## 8.8 Building a Voice Library

You've made a few voices: `cello-note`, `clarinet-note`, `jazz-piano`, `expressive-piano`. Each one is a **function** that wraps `note/strike` with a specific set of envelope + waveform + filter + detune parameters.

This is how you build a **voice library** — a collection of named instruments, each a function, all using the same underlying note verb but dressed differently.

```scheme
;; A small library of voices, each a function wrapping note/strike.
;; *[needs: GAP-3]* — awaiting full parameter surface.

(define (piano pitch dur velocity)
  (note/strike pitch dur velocity
               :waveform 'sine
               :attack 0.01
               :release 0.15))

(define (organ pitch dur velocity)
  (note/strike pitch dur velocity
               :waveform 'square
               :attack 0.02
               :decay 0.0
               :sustain 1.0   ;; full sustain — holds as long as key is down
               :release 0.05))

(define (strings pitch dur velocity)
  (note/strike pitch dur velocity
               :waveform 'sawtooth
               :attack 0.2    ;; slow bow attack
               :decay 0.1
               :sustain 0.8
               :release 0.6   ;; long ring
               :filter-type 'lowpass
               :filter-cutoff 3000
               :unison 3
               :detune-spread 12))

(define (brass pitch dur velocity)
  (note/strike pitch dur velocity
               :waveform 'sawtooth
               :attack 0.05
               :decay 0.15
               :sustain 0.7
               :release 0.2
               :filter-type 'lowpass
               :filter-cutoff (+ 1000 (* velocity 15)) ;; brighter when loud
               :unison 2
               :detune-spread 10))

;; Now you can play any of them
(piano 60 1.0 80)
(organ 64 2.0 90)
(strings 67 1.5 70)
(brass 72 1.0 95)
```

### 8.1 The Envelope: How a Sound Moves Through Time

A **note** is not a static thing. It has a life:

1. **Attack** — how quickly it rises from silence to full volume.
2. **Decay** — how it settles from the initial peak to a sustained level.
3. **Sustain** — the held level while the note is \"on.\"
4. **Release** — how it fades when you let go.

This four-stage shape is called an **ADSR envelope**, and it's what separates a plucked string (sharp attack, quick decay, no sustain) from a bowed one (slow attack, long sustain) from a struck bell (instant attack, slow release, no sustain).

*[needs: GAP-3]* — the engine's `note/strike` currently uses a **fixed envelope** (a modest attack and release to avoid clicks). To *tune* the envelope — to make a note percussive or lush or breathy — we need **envelope parameters** on `note/strike`:

```scheme
;; *[needs: GAP-3]* — envelope control not yet wired
;; A sharp, percussive note: fast attack, no sustain, quick release
(note/strike 'C4 'quarter 0.8
  :attack 0.01   ;; 10ms to full volume
  :decay 0.1     ;; 100ms decay
  :sustain 0.0   ;; no sustain level (it dies away)
  :release 0.05) ;; 50ms tail

;; A lush, pad-like note: slow attack, high sustain, long release
(note/strike 'C4 'whole 0.6
  :attack 0.3
  :decay 0.2
  :sustain 0.7  ;; sustain at 70% of peak
  :release 1.5)
```

### 8.2 Detune Spread: Thickening a Voice with Unison Layers

A single sine tone is **thin**. A real instrument — a piano string, a guitar, a choir — is never perfectly in tune with itself. There are micro-variations: one string slightly sharp, another slightly flat. Those tiny **detune** differences create **beating** (a slow wobble in amplitude as the waves drift in and out of phase), and that beating is what makes a sound feel **thick, alive, chorused**.

The trick: **layer multiple oscillators at the same pitch, each detuned by a few cents** (hundredths of a semitone). The sum is richer than any single tone.

*[needs: GAP-3]* — the engine doesn't yet expose **detune** as a note parameter. When it does, you'll write:

```scheme
;; *[needs: GAP-3]* — detune parameter not yet on note/strike
;; A single note, but FIVE oscillators, spread ±10 cents
(define (thick-note pitch dur vel)
  (let ((detunes '(-10 -5 0 5 10)))  ;; cents offset
    (for-each
      (lambda (dt)
        (note/strike pitch dur vel :detune dt))
      detunes)))

(thick-note 'A4 'whole 0.7)
```

`<!-- BUILD: extend note/strike with :detune keyword (cents offset) → wire to Web Audio OscillatorNode.detune.value -->`

[VISUAL: Spectrum analyzer showing a single fundamental (thin spike) vs. a detuned unison stack (the spike has \"shoulders\" — side-band energy from the beating).]

A common **chorus spread** recipe:
- **Vintage analog synth:** ±7–15 cents, 3–5 voices.
- **Lush pad:** ±20–30 cents, 7+ voices.
- **Tight ensemble (strings):** ±3–5 cents, 4 voices.

### 8.3 A Detuned Chord: The \"Supersaw\" Stack

One of the signature sounds of trance and synthwave is the **supersaw**: a chord where *every note* is itself a stack of detuned oscillators. It's huge, shimmering, almost liquid.

```scheme

  (let ((pitches (list root
                       (transpose root 4)   ;; major third
                       (transpose root 7))) ;; fifth
        (detunes '(-12 -6 0 6 12)))
    (for-each
      (lambda (pitch)
        (for-each
          (lambda (dt)
            (note/strike pitch dur 0.5 :detune dt))
          detunes))
      pitches)))

(supersaw-triad 'C3 'whole)
```

### 8.4 Attack Variation: Percussive vs. Legato

The **attack time** alone can transform a voice:

- **0.001s (1ms)** — percussive, like a struck key or a pluck.
- **0.3s (300ms)** — soft, like a bowed string or a breath.
- **1.0s+** — ambient wash, almost imperceptible onset.

```scheme
  ;; Percussive
  (note/strike pitch 'quarter 0.8
    :attack 0.001 :decay 0.05 :sustain 0.0 :release 0.1)
  (sleep 1)
  
  ;; Bowed
  (note/strike pitch 'quarter 0.8
    :attack 0.3 :decay 0.1 :sustain 0.6 :release 0.4)
  (sleep 1)
  
  ;; Ambient wash
  (note/strike pitch 'whole 0.6
    :attack 1.2 :decay 0.5 :sustain 0.8 :release 2.0))

(demo-attack 'G4)
```

### 8.5 Release Tail: The Difference Between Dry and Lush

A **short release** (50–100ms) makes a voice feel **tight, dry, mechanical**. A **long release** (1–3 seconds) makes it **lush, ambient, cathedral-like**. Jazz organs often have almost *no* release (the sound stops the instant you lift the key). A Rhodes piano has a gentle 200ms tail. A synthesizer pad might ring for five seconds.

```scheme
;; *[needs: GAP-3]*
;; Staccato: no release tail
(define (staccato pitch)
  (note/strike pitch 'eighth 0.7
    :attack 0.01 :decay 0.05 :sustain 0.0 :release 0.01))

;; Cathedral: long release
(define (cathedral pitch)
  (note/strike pitch 'quarter 0.6
    :attack 0.2 :decay 0.3 :sustain 0.7 :release 2.5))

(staccato 'E4)
(sleep 0.5)
(cathedral 'E4)
```

`<!-- BUILD: envelope demo -->`

The **release** is what you hear *after* you've \"let go\" — it's the ghost of the note.

### 8.6 Filtering: Sculpting the Harmonic Spectrum

Every sound is a **sum of harmonics** (integer multiples of the fundamental frequency). A **filter** lets you *shape* which harmonics are loud and which are quiet:

- **Low-pass filter** — keeps low frequencies, cuts highs. Makes a sound **darker, warmer, muffled**.
- **High-pass filter** — keeps highs, cuts lows. Makes a sound **thinner, brighter, tinny**.
- **Band-pass filter** — keeps a middle range, cuts both extremes. Makes a sound **nasal, hollow, telephone-like**.

*[needs: GAP-3]* — the engine doesn't yet expose **filter parameters**. When it does, you'll write:

```scheme
;; *[needs: GAP-3]* — filter params not yet on note/strike
;; A low-pass filtered note: warm, no treble
(note/strike 'A3 'whole 0.7
  :filter 'lowpass
  :cutoff 800   ;; Hz — frequencies above 800Hz are reduced
  :resonance 2) ;; boost at the cutoff (makes it \"wah\"-like)

;; A high-pass filtered note: thin, airy
(note/strike 'A3 'whole 0.7
  :filter 'highpass
  :cutoff 1200)
```

`<!-- BUILD: extend note/strike with :filter :cutoff :resonance keywords → wire to Web Audio BiquadFilterNode -->`

[VISUAL: Frequency spectrum before and after low-pass filtering. Before: even harmonic comb. After: the right half of the comb fades to silence, only the low fundamentals remain bright.]

A **resonant filter** (high `:resonance` value) creates a **peak** at the cutoff frequency — the classic \"wah-wah\" sound of a swept filter.

### 8.7 Envelope-Controlled Filter: The \"Wah\" Sweep

One of the richest timbral moves: **modulate the filter cutoff with the note's envelope**. The filter opens (gets brighter) as the note attacks, then closes (gets darker) as it decays. This is the heart of the classic **analog synth bass** sound.

```scheme
;; *[needs: GAP-3]* — envelope-to-filter routing not yet wired
;; The filter cutoff tracks the amplitude envelope
(note/strike 'C2 'quarter 0.9
  :attack 0.01 :decay 0.4 :sustain 0.2 :release 0.1
  :filter 'lowpass
  :cutoff-env-amount 2000  ;; cutoff starts at base+2000Hz, decays with envelope
  :cutoff-base 200)        ;; minimum cutoff
```

`<!-- BUILD: add :cutoff-env-amount param → scale the filter cutoff by the current envelope gain -->`

The sound: a **bright pluck that darkens as it fades** — the signature of a Minimoog bass or a TB-303.

### 8.8 A Jazz Organ: No Release, Slight Detune, Warm Filter

Jazz organs (Hammond B3, Vox Continental) have a characteristic profile:

- **Instant attack** (the drawbars engage immediately).
- **No release** (when you lift the key, the sound stops).
- **Slight detune spread** (the tonewheels aren't perfectly in tune).
- **Warm low-pass filter** (a little top-end rolloff).

```scheme
;; *[needs: GAP-3]*
(define (jazz-organ pitch dur)
  (let ((detunes '(-3 0 3)))  ;; subtle spread
    (for-each
      (lambda (dt)
        (note/strike pitch dur 0.6
          :attack 0.005
          :decay 0.0
          :sustain 1.0   ;; full sustain
          :release 0.01  ;; instant cutoff
          :detune dt
          :filter 'lowpass
          :cutoff 2800))
      detunes)))

(jazz-organ 'C4 'half)
(jazz-organ 'Eb4 'half)
(jazz-organ 'G4 'half)
```

### 8.11 Velocity-to-Filter: Harder Notes Are Brighter

On an acoustic piano, when you strike a key harder, the sound is not just **louder** — it's also **brighter** (more high-frequency content, because the hammer hits the string with more force). We can model this by **linking velocity to filter cutoff**:

```scheme
;; *[needs: GAP-3]* — velocity-to-cutoff scaling
(define (vel-to-brightness pitch dur vel)
  (let ((cutoff (+ 400 (* vel 2000))))  ;; vel=0.0→400Hz, vel=1.0→2400Hz
    (note/strike pitch dur vel
      :attack 0.01
      :decay 0.2
      :sustain 0.3
      :release 0.2
      :filter 'lowpass
      :cutoff cutoff)))

;; Soft note: dark
(vel-to-brightness 'C4 'quarter 0.3)
(sleep 0.5)

;; Hard note: bright
(vel-to-brightness 'C4 'quarter 0.9)
```

`<!-- BUILD: compute cutoff from velocity; demo contrast between soft (dark) and loud (bright) -->`

This is one of the secrets of **expressive synthesis** — the timbre changes *with* the dynamics, not just the volume.

### 8.15 Micro-Timing: Humanizing the Attack

Real players don't strike notes at *exactly* the same instant. A pianist's fingers land a few milliseconds apart. A horn section breathes together but not in perfect sync. This tiny **jitter** (±5–20ms) is what makes a programmed performance feel **human** instead of robotic.

```scheme
;; Perfectly synchronized (robotic)
(define (robot-chord pitches dur)
  (for-each
    (lambda (pitch)
      (note/strike pitch dur 0.7))
    pitches))

;; Humanized: each note offset by a small random jitter
(define (human-chord pitches dur)
  (for-each
    (lambda (pitch)
      (let ((jitter (/ (random 20) 1000.0)))  ;; 0–20ms
        (sleep jitter)
        (note/strike pitch dur 0.7)))
    pitches))

(robot-chord '(C4 E4 G4))
(sleep 2)
(human-chord '(C4 E4 G4))
```

`<!-- BUILD: compare robotic (simultaneous) vs. humanized (jittered) chord -->`

The humanized chord feels **warmer, more alive** — even though the jitter is barely perceptible, your ear knows.

### 8.20 The Attack \"Snap\": Adding a Transient Click

Percussive instruments (piano, marimba, tabla) have a **transient** — a brief, bright **click or snap** at the very start of the note, caused by the hammer strike or stick impact. This transient is *higher in frequency* and *much shorter* than the note itself, but it's crucial for **clarity and punch**.

You can model it by **layering a short, bright noise burst** at the note onset:

```scheme
;; *[needs: GAP-3]* — transient layering
(define (percussive-note pitch dur vel)
  ;; The main note
  (note/strike pitch dur vel
    :attack 0.01 :decay 0.2 :sustain 0.3 :release 0.1)
  
  ;; The transient: a 5ms noise burst
  (sfx 'click :duration 0.005 :velocity (* vel 0.5)))

(percussive-note 'C5 'quarter 0.8)
```

The transient is what makes a note feel **struck** rather than **blown** or **bowed**.

### 8.21 Ensemble Spread: Slight Timing + Tuning Variation Across Voices

A real string section (10 violins) never plays in *perfect* unison. Each player:
- **Starts the note a few milliseconds off** from the others.
- **Is tuned a few cents sharp or flat** relative to concert pitch.
- **Has a slightly different vibrato rate and depth**.

This **ensemble spread** is what makes an orchestral section sound **rich and huge** instead of like one violin copy-pasted ten times.

```scheme
;; *[needs: GAP-3]*
(define (string-section pitch dur)
  (let ((players 8))
    (for-each
      (lambda (i)
        (let ((jitter (/ (random 15) 1000.0))       ;; 0–15ms timing offset
              (detune (- (random 8) 4))             ;; ±4 cents tuning
              (vib-rate (+ 5.5 (/ (random 10) 10.0))) ;; 5.5–6.5 Hz vibrato
              (vib-depth (+ 6 (random 4))))         ;; 6–10 cents depth
          (sleep jitter)
          (note/strike pitch dur 0.5
            :attack 0.15 :decay 0.1 :sustain 0.75 :release 0.8
            :detune detune
            :vibrato-rate vib-rate
            :vibrato-depth vib-depth)))
      (iota players))))

(string-section 'A4 'whole)
```

### 8.23 Dynamics + Timbre: Louder ≠ Just More Volume

On a real instrument, **loud** and **soft** aren't just about amplitude — they're about **timbre**:

- **Soft notes** (pp) are **darker** (less high-frequency content), **slower attack**, **more vibrato**.
- **Loud notes** (ff) are **brighter** (more overtones), **faster attack**, **more percussive**.

Model this by **scaling filter cutoff, attack time, and vibrato depth with velocity**:

```scheme
;; *[needs: GAP-3]*
(define (expressive-note pitch dur vel)
  (let ((cutoff (+ 400 (* vel 2200)))       ;; vel=0.2→840Hz, vel=1.0→2600Hz
        (attack (- 0.25 (* vel 0.2)))       ;; vel=0.2→230ms, vel=1.0→50ms
        (vib-depth (- 12 (* vel 8))))       ;; vel=0.2→10.4c, vel=1.0→4c
    (note/strike pitch dur vel
      :attack attack
      :decay 0.15
      :sustain 0.6
      :release 0.4
      :filter 'lowpass
      :cutoff cutoff
      :vibrato-rate 6
      :vibrato-depth vib-depth)))

;; Soft
(expressive-note 'G4 'half 0.25)
(sleep 1.5)

;; Loud
(expressive-note 'G4 'half 0.9)
```

`<!-- BUILD: velocity-scaled timbre -->`

The soft note is **gentle, warm, slow**. The loud note is **bright, fast, punchy**. Same pitch, same duration — completely different character.

### 8.25 The \"Pluck\" Envelope: Instant Attack, Exponential Decay

A plucked string (guitar, harp, harpsichord) has a very specific envelope shape:

- **Instant attack** (the string is released, full amplitude immediately).
- **Exponential decay** (the amplitude falls off *fast at first, then slower* — not linear).
- **No sustain** (the note dies away on its own).
- **Short or no release** (once it's quiet, it's done).

```scheme

(define (pluck pitch dur)
  (note/strike pitch dur 0.8
    :attack 0.001    ;; instant
    :decay (* dur 0.8)  ;; most of the note's duration
    :sustain 0.0     ;; no held level
    :release 0.01))  ;; minimal tail

(pluck 'D4 'quarter)
(sleep 0.5)
(pluck 'D4 'half)
```

### 8.28 A Timpani Roll: Rapid Repeated Strikes with Slight Pitch Bend

A timpani roll is **not a single sustained note** — it's **many rapid strikes** (10–20 per second), each with a short envelope. Often the player will **bend the pitch slightly** during the roll by adjusting the pedal.

```scheme

  (note/strike pitch 'thirty-second vel
    :attack 0.005
    :decay 0.08
    :sustain 0.0
    :release 0.02
    :filter 'lowpass
    :cutoff 600))

(define (timpani-roll pitch dur strikes)
  (let ((interval (/ dur strikes)))
    (for-each
      (lambda (i)
        (let ((vel (+ 0.6 (/ (random 20) 100.0))))  ;; 0.6–0.8
          (timpani-strike pitch vel)
          (sleep interval)))
      (iota strikes))))

;; A two-second roll on C2, ~16 strikes

```

### 8.29 Velocity Layers: Different Samples for Soft vs. Hard Strikes

High-end virtual instruments use **velocity layers**: different recordings (or synthesis profiles) for soft, medium, and hard strikes. A soft piano note has a *fundamentally different harmonic spectrum* than a hard one — not just lower amplitude.

Model this with **discrete envelope + filter profiles per velocity range**:

```scheme
;; *[needs: GAP-3]*
(define (layered-piano pitch dur vel)
  (cond
    ;; Soft layer (vel < 0.4)
    ((< vel 0.4)
     (note/strike pitch dur vel
       :attack 0.08 :decay 0.3 :sustain 0.5 :release 0.6
       :filter 'lowpass :cutoff 1200))
    
    ;; Medium layer (0.4 ≤ vel < 0.7)
    ((< vel 0.7)
     (note/strike pitch dur vel
       :attack 0.03 :decay 0.25 :sustain 0.4 :release 0.5
       :filter 'lowpass :cutoff 2000))
    
    ;; Hard layer (vel ≥ 0.7)
    (else
     (note/strike pitch dur vel
       :attack 0.01 :decay 0.2 :sustain 0.3 :release 0.4
       :filter 'lowpass :cutoff 3200))))

;; Same note, three velocities
(layered-piano 'C4 'half 0.3)
(sleep 1.5)
(layered-piano 'C4 'half 0.55)
(sleep 1.5)
(layered-piano 'C4 'half 0.85)
```

### 8.1  The life of a note — ADSR envelope

Every note you've played so far has had *some* envelope, even if you didn't specify it. A piano's default: sharp attack, quick decay to a sustain that rings, then release when the key lifts. A organ: instant attack, flat sustain, instant release. A violin swell: slow attack, long sustain, gentle release.

**ADSR** is the four-stage model:
1. **Attack** — time from note-on to peak amplitude (how fast the note \"grabs\").
2. **Decay** — time from peak to sustain level (the initial falloff).
3. **Sustain** — the level held while the note is on (not a time—a *level*, 0.0 to 1.0).
4. **Release** — time from note-off to silence (the tail).

[VISUAL: Four diagrams side-by-side, each showing a different ADSR profile:
- Percussive: fast attack (0.01s), medium decay (0.1s), low sustain (0.2), short release (0.05s).
- Pad: slow attack (0.5s), slow decay (0.3s), high sustain (0.8), long release (1.0s).
- Pluck: instant attack (0.001s), fast decay (0.05s), zero sustain (0.0), short release (0.02s).
- Organ: instant attack (0.0s), no decay, full sustain (1.0), instant release (0.0s).]

The engine lets you specify ADSR per note, or globally for a voice. For now we have *global-per-voice* control (per-note ADSR is **GAP-3**—rich tone control). Let's shape a percussive voice and a pad voice and hear them side by side.

<!-- BUILD: implement global ADSR setters for a voice; store A/D/S/R in the voice state; apply to every note struck in that voice -->

```scheme
;; Define a percussive voice: sharp attack, quick decay, low sustain, short release.
(define percussive-voice
  (let ((v (voice/create 'percussive)))
    (voice/envelope v
      (adsr 0.01   ;; attack 10ms
            0.1    ;; decay 100ms
            0.2    ;; sustain at 20%
            0.05)) ;; release 50ms
    v))

;; Define a pad voice: slow attack, slow decay, high sustain, long release.
(define pad-voice
  (let ((v (voice/create 'pad)))
    (voice/envelope v
      (adsr 0.5    ;; attack 500ms
            0.3    ;; decay 300ms
            0.8    ;; sustain at 80%
            1.0))  ;; release 1s
    v))

;; Play the same pitch on both voices, separated by 1 second.
(note/strike 'C4 'quarter 0.7 percussive-voice)
(at-beat 2
  (note/strike 'C4 'quarter 0.7 pad-voice))
```

### 8.2  Waveform tuning — beyond the section profile

Chapter 7 showed you `createPeriodicWave`—you feed it a list of harmonic amplitudes and get a custom waveform. That was for *section voices*: one voice representing a whole cello section or woodwind choir. Here we use the same machinery to tune the **timbre of a single note**.

A sine wave has one harmonic (the fundamental). A sawtooth has all harmonics, falling at 1/n amplitude. A square wave has odd harmonics only, falling at 1/n. You can craft **any harmonic recipe** to get a specific color.

**Bright vs. warm:**
- **Bright**: strong high harmonics (2nd, 3rd, 4th+). A violin's open string, a trumpet's fanfare.
- **Warm**: gentle rolloff, weaker high harmonics. A French horn, a cello's low register.

Let's build a bright voice and a warm voice from scratch.

```scheme
;; Bright voice: fundamental + strong 2nd, 3rd, 4th harmonics.
(define bright-harmonics
  (list 1.0   ;; fundamental (1st harmonic)
        0.8   ;; 2nd
        0.6   ;; 3rd
        0.4   ;; 4th
        0.2   ;; 5th
        0.1)) ;; 6th

(define bright-voice
  (let ((v (voice/create 'bright)))
    (voice/waveform v (createPeriodicWave bright-harmonics))
    v))

;; Warm voice: fundamental + gentle rolloff.
(define warm-harmonics
  (list 1.0   ;; fundamental
        0.3   ;; 2nd (much softer)
        0.1   ;; 3rd
        0.05  ;; 4th
        0.02  ;; 5th
        0.01))

(define warm-voice
  (let ((v (voice/create 'warm)))
    (voice/waveform v (createPeriodicWave warm-harmonics))
    v))

;; Play a middle C on each, one beat apart.
(note/strike 'C4 'half 0.7 bright-voice)
(at-beat 3
  (note/strike 'C4 'half 0.7 warm-voice))
```

<!-- BUILD: voice/waveform setter that wraps createPeriodicWave; store the custom wave in the voice state; use it for every note struck in that voice -->

**Hear the difference:** The bright note has *edge*—you can almost hear the upper harmonics shimmer. The warm note feels *rounder*, like a cello's middle range.

**Try this:**

### 8.3  Filters — carving the spectrum

A filter *removes* parts of the frequency spectrum. Three common types:

1. **Low-pass**: lets frequencies *below* a cutoff through; removes highs (makes sound *darker*).
2. **High-pass**: lets frequencies *above* a cutoff through; removes lows (makes sound *thinner*, more \"airy\").
3. **Band-pass**: lets a *band* around a center frequency through; removes everything else (like a telephone line, or a didgeridoo's formant).

Each filter has a **cutoff frequency** (in Hz) and a **resonance** (Q factor)—how sharply the filter cuts. High Q = sharp peak/notch; low Q = gentle slope.

Let's apply a low-pass filter to a bright voice and sweep the cutoff frequency down.

```scheme
;; Bright voice from 8.2.
(define bright-voice
  (let ((v (voice/create 'bright)))
    (voice/waveform v (createPeriodicWave (list 1.0 0.8 0.6 0.4 0.2 0.1)))
    v))

;; Apply a low-pass filter with cutoff at 2000 Hz, Q=1.
(voice/filter bright-voice 'lowpass 2000 1.0)

;; Play a sustained C4.
(note/strike 'C4 'whole 0.7 bright-voice)

;; After 1 beat, sweep the cutoff down to 500 Hz over 2 beats.
(at-beat 1
  (voice/filter-sweep bright-voice 'lowpass 2000 500 2.0))
```

### 8.4  Detune spread — chorusing and thickness

A single oscillator is *thin*. A choir of oscillators, each slightly detuned (a few cents sharp or flat), is *thick*—lush, chorused, \"wide.\" This is how synthesizers make \"supersaw\" basses and string pads.

**Detune spread** means: start with N oscillators (say, 3), all at the same base frequency, then offset each one by a small random amount (±10 cents, or ±0.5% frequency). The slight interference between them creates a beating, shimmering sound.

Let's make a thick pad voice with 5 detuned oscillators.

```scheme
;; A thick-pad voice: 5 oscillators, each detuned by a random offset in [-10, +10] cents.
(define thick-pad-voice
  (let ((v (voice/create 'thick-pad)))
    (voice/detune-spread v 5 10.0)  ;; 5 oscillators, ±10 cents
    (voice/envelope v (adsr 0.4 0.2 0.8 0.8))
    v))

;; Play a sustained chord (C major triad, whole notes).
(note/strike 'C3 'whole 0.6 thick-pad-voice)
(note/strike 'E3 'whole 0.6 thick-pad-voice)
(note/strike 'G3 'whole 0.6 thick-pad-voice)
```
*[needs: GAP-3]* — multi-oscillator detune spread per voice is not yet implemented.

<!-- BUILD: voice/detune-spread setter that spawns N oscillators per note, each with a random detune offset; sum them into a single gain node -->

**What you hear:** Each note in the chord is not a single pure tone, but a *cloud* of slightly-out-of-tune tones beating against each other. The chord sounds *wide* and *alive*, like a string section instead of three solo violins.

**Try this:**
- Increase the spread to 20 cents—the beating becomes more obvious, almost out-of-tune (useful for a \"detuned piano\" effect).
- Decrease the spread to 3 cents—very subtle shimmer, like a single violin with natural vibrato.
- Use 2 oscillators and a spread of 5 cents on a lead voice—this is the classic \"analog synth\" thickness.

[VISUAL: Waveform view of a single note with detune spread. Instead of one clean sine, you see 5 overlapping sines slightly offset in phase, creating a thicker, beating envelope. A note-sprite (half note, 48×48) bobs slowly above.]

### 8.5  Combining envelope, waveform, filter, detune — a jazz voice

Now we put it together. Jazz piano has:
- A **percussive attack** (the hammer hits the string hard).
- A **warm harmonic profile** (not too bright, but not dull—some 2nd and 3rd harmonic).
- A **slight high-frequency rolloff** (older pianos, or a \"felt\" tone).
- A **short sustain** (the note decays fairly quickly after the initial hit).

Let's build a jazz-piano voice.

```scheme
;; Jazz piano voice: percussive ADSR, warm harmonics, gentle low-pass, no detune (piano is monophonic-per-string).
(define jazz-piano-voice
  (let ((v (voice/create 'jazz-piano)))
    ;; Waveform: fundamental + moderate 2nd/3rd, gentle falloff.
    (voice/waveform v (createPeriodicWave (list 1.0 0.5 0.3 0.15 0.08 0.04)))
    ;; Envelope: quick attack, medium decay, moderate sustain, short release.
    (voice/envelope v (adsr 0.02 0.15 0.4 0.1))
    ;; Filter: low-pass at 3500 Hz, Q=0.7 (gentle rolloff, not too dark).
    (voice/filter v 'lowpass 3500 0.7)
    v))

;; Play a jazzy C major 7th voicing (rootless): E3, G3, B3, D4.
(note/strike 'E3 'half 0.65 jazz-piano-voice)
(note/strike 'G3 'half 0.65 jazz-piano-voice)
(note/strike 'B3 'half 0.65 jazz-piano-voice)
(note/strike 'D4 'half 0.65 jazz-piano-voice)
```

### 8.6  A swing rhythm — articulation via envelope

Jazz isn't just timbre—it's also *rhythm* and *articulation*. Swing rhythm (covered more in Ch10—polyrhythm) is a triplet subdivision where the first note of the triplet is held longer than the second (roughly 2:1). But even in straight time, jazz articulation uses **short, detached notes** for comping chords and **longer, sustained notes** for melody.

Let's play a simple I–vi–ii–V progression (C–Am–Dm–G) with short, detached chords (staccato envelope) and a melody with longer sustain.

```scheme
;; Staccato envelope for comping chords: very short sustain, quick release.
(define staccato-piano
  (let ((v (voice/create 'staccato-piano)))
    (voice/waveform v (createPeriodicWave (list 1.0 0.5 0.3 0.15 0.08)))
    (voice/envelope v (adsr 0.01 0.05 0.1 0.05))  ;; fast decay, low sustain, quick release
    (voice/filter v 'lowpass 3500 0.7)
    v))

;; Legato envelope for melody: longer sustain, slower release.
(define legato-piano
  (let ((v (voice/create 'legato-piano)))
    (voice/waveform v (createPeriodicWave (list 1.0 0.5 0.3 0.15 0.08)))
    (voice/envelope v (adsr 0.02 0.1 0.6 0.2))   ;; moderate decay, higher sustain, longer release
    (voice/filter v 'lowpass 3500 0.7)
    v))

;; Progression: I–vi–ii–V in C, quarter-note chords, staccato.
;; Measure 1: C (C3 E3 G3)
(note/strike 'C3 'quarter 0.6 staccato-piano)
(note/strike 'E3 'quarter 0.6 staccato-piano)
(note/strike 'G3 'quarter 0.6 staccato-piano)

;; Measure 2: Am (A2 C3 E3)
(at-beat 4
  (note/strike 'A2 'quarter 0.6 staccato-piano)
  (note/strike 'C3 'quarter 0.6 staccato-piano)
  (note/strike 'E3 'quarter 0.6 staccato-piano))

;; Measure 3: Dm (D3 F3 A3)
(at-beat 8
  (note/strike 'D3 'quarter 0.6 staccato-piano)
  (note/strike 'F3 'quarter 0.6 staccato-piano)
  (note/strike 'A3 'quarter 0.6 staccato-piano))

;; Measure 4: G (G2 B2 D3)
(at-beat 12
  (note/strike 'G2 'quarter 0.6 staccato-piano)
  (note/strike 'B2 'quarter 0.6 staccato-piano)
  (note/strike 'D3 'quarter 0.6 staccato-piano))

;; Melody over the progression (legato): C4 D4 E4 D4 C4 (half, quarter, quarter, quarter, half).
(note/strike 'C4 'half 0.7 legato-piano)
(at-beat 2 (note/strike 'D4 'quarter 0.7 legato-piano))
(at-beat 3 (note/strike 'E4 'quarter 0.7 legato-piano))
(at-beat 4 (note/strike 'D4 'quarter 0.7 legato-piano))
(at-beat 5 (note/strike 'C4 'half 0.7 legato-piano))
```

### 8.7  Vibrato — modulating pitch over time

Vibrato is a *periodic variation in pitch*—a slight wobble, usually 5–7 Hz (5–7 wobbles per second), ±10–30 cents. It's not an envelope (amplitude over time); it's **pitch modulation**. Singers do it naturally. String players do it with finger motion. Synthesizers do it with an LFO (low-frequency oscillator) modulating the frequency.

We can apply vibrato globally to a voice, or per-note. For now, let's do it globally (per-note vibrato control is *[needs: GAP-3]*).

```scheme
;; A legato voice with vibrato: 6 Hz wobble, ±15 cents depth.
(define vibrato-voice
  (let ((v (voice/create 'vibrato-voice)))
    (voice/waveform v (createPeriodicWave (list 1.0 0.5 0.3 0.15)))
    (voice/envelope v (adsr 0.05 0.1 0.8 0.3))
    (voice/vibrato v 6.0 15.0)  ;; 6 Hz rate, 15 cents depth
    v))

;; Play a sustained A4 for 2 beats.
(note/strike 'A4 'half 0.75 vibrato-voice)
```

**What you hear:** The note doesn't sit still—it wobbles gently up and down in pitch, like a singer or a violinist. Too fast (12 Hz) and it sounds like a siren. Too slow (2 Hz) and it sounds like poor intonation.

- Set the depth to 50 cents—way too wide, it sounds like a bent note or a theremin.
- Use vibrato on a chord (three notes struck together)—all three wobble together, which is unrealistic (real string players don't sync their vibrato). This is why vibrato is often applied per-note, not per-voice. *[needs: GAP-3]*

### 8.9  Building a brass stab — aggressive harmonics + sharp envelope

Jazz also has *brass*—trumpet, trombone, sax. A brass stab (a short, punchy chord hit by a brass section) has:
- **Very fast attack** (the note grabs instantly).
- **Bright harmonics** (lots of 2nd, 3rd, 4th, even 5th—brass is *rich* in upper partials).
- **Short sustain, quick release** (the note is a \"stab,\" not a long tone).
- **Optional: slight detune spread** (a section of trumpets, not one trumpet).

Let's build a brass-stab voice and play a punchy C major 7th chord.

```scheme
;; Brass-stab voice: very bright harmonics, fast attack, short sustain, optional detune spread.
(define brass-stab
  (let ((v (voice/create 'brass-stab)))
    ;; Bright harmonics: strong upper partials.
    (voice/waveform v (createPeriodicWave (list 1.0 0.9 0.7 0.5 0.3 0.2 0.1)))
    ;; Fast attack, short decay, low sustain, quick release.
    (voice/envelope v (adsr 0.005 0.05 0.2 0.05))
    ;; No filter (let the brightness through), or a gentle high-pass to remove mud.
    (voice/filter v 'highpass 150 0.5)
    ;; Optional: 3 oscillators, ±8 cents detune for section thickness.
    ;; (voice/detune-spread v 3 8.0)  ;; *[needs: GAP-3]*
    v))

;; Play a C major 7th chord (C3 E3 G3 B3), eighth notes, forte.
(note/strike 'C3 'eighth 0.85 brass-stab)
(note/strike 'E3 'eighth 0.85 brass-stab)
(note/strike 'G3 'eighth 0.85 brass-stab)
(note/strike 'B3 'eighth 0.85 brass-stab)
```
