### What polyrhythm is (and what it isn't)

**Polyphony** (Ch9) gave you independent melodic lines — each voice has its own pitches, its own contour, its own direction. They sound together, but each sings its own tune.

**Polyrhythm** gives you independent **metric subdivisions** — each voice has its own way of slicing time. One voice subdivides a measure into three equal parts. Another subdivides the same measure into two. Both are *right*, both are *steady*, and when they sound together, you hear a rhythmic texture richer than either alone.

**A simple duple beat** (two pulses per measure) **and a simple triple beat** (three pulses per measure) **are not polyrhythmic by themselves**. Polyrhythm happens when both subdivisions run **in the same span of time** — when three beats fit in the same duration as two beats, so the attacks fall on different fractional positions of the measure and weave together.

The most famous example is **3-against-2**: three notes in the time of two. Play two quarter-notes in one hand, three eighth-note triplets in the other, and you have a classic polyrhythmic cell.

[VISUAL: A two-staff score, one measure. Top staff: two quarter-notes (simple duple). Bottom staff: a triplet bracket over three eighth-note triplets (simple triple). Both span the same measure. Vertical lines show where attacks align (downbeat and end) and where they do not (the middle attacks are offset). The note-sprites on the triplet staff bop faster than the note-sprites on the duple staff, illustrating the different subdivision rates.]

Polyrhythm is everywhere once you listen for it — in African drumming (where multiple bell patterns and hand-drum cycles layer), in Latin clave (the five-stroke pattern that contradicts the pulse), in calypso and soca (where the bass drum walks in one time and the hi-hat ticks in another), in funk (where the snare backbeat, the hi-hat shuffle, and the kick drum syncopation each subdivide the groove differently). It's the grain of the rhythm, the way interlocking pulses give a beat its **feel**.

We call it **polyrhythm** when the subdivisions are steady and maintain their own independent metric logic. We call it **cross-rhythm** when one line's accents contradict another's downbeats, making you hear the pulse in two places at once. Both are in scope for this chapter.

### The simplest polyrhythm: 2-against-3 (the hemiola)

Let's start with the **hemiola** — a 2-against-3 pattern so common it has a Renaissance name.

Set the tempo steady. Play three notes evenly spaced across two beats. Then play two notes evenly spaced across the same two beats. Layer them.

```scheme
(transport/tempo 80)

(define (hemiola-three)
  ;; Three evenly-spaced notes across two beats
  (let ((span 2.0)) ;; two beats total
    (for-each
     (lambda (i)
       (note/strike 60 0.3 0.6) ;; middle C, short
       (wait (/ span 3)))
     '(0 1 2))))

(define (hemiola-two)
  ;; Two evenly-spaced notes across two beats
  (let ((span 2.0))
    (for-each
     (lambda (i)
       (note/strike 64 0.3 0.7) ;; E, slightly louder
       (wait (/ span 2)))
     '(0 1))))

;; Play them in sequence, then together
(hemiola-three)
(wait 0.5)
(hemiola-two)
(wait 0.5)
;; Now together
(base/at-beat 0
  (hemiola-three)
  (hemiola-two))
```

Below, a staff render: top line three notes with a triplet bracket, bottom line two notes, both spanning two beats.]

You hear the three-stream as a gentle triplet lilt. You hear the two-stream as a steady duple walk. Together, they interlock — the downbeat aligns, the end aligns, but the middle attacks are offset, and that offset is what makes it *groove*.

### The clave: a rhythmic anchor

The **clave** is a five-stroke rhythmic pattern from Afro-Cuban music. It's not a polyrhythm by itself, but it *contradicts* the pulse — it accents beats that aren't downbeats, making you hear the measure in two different ways at once. When you layer a steady bass pulse underneath, the clave becomes a **cross-rhythm** — the clave's accents and the bass's downbeats are independent metric worlds.

The **son clave** (in 4/4) has strokes on: beat 1, the \"and\" of beat 2, beat 4, beat 1 of the next measure, the \"and\" of beat 2 of the next measure. (That's the 3-2 son clave — three strokes in the first measure, two in the second.)

We'll use `(sfx 'woodblock)` for the clave and a low kick for the bass pulse.

```scheme
(transport/tempo 96)

(define (son-clave-3-2)
  ;; 3-2 son clave: two measures
  ;; Measure 1: beat 1, and-of-2, beat 4
  ;; Measure 2: beat 1, and-of-2
  (sfx 'woodblock) (wait 1.0)   ;; beat 1
  (wait 0.5) (sfx 'woodblock) (wait 0.5) ;; and-of-2
  (wait 1.0)                     ;; beat 3 (silent)
  (sfx 'woodblock) (wait 1.0)   ;; beat 4
  ;; Measure 2
  (sfx 'woodblock) (wait 1.0)   ;; beat 1
  (wait 0.5) (sfx 'woodblock) (wait 0.5) ;; and-of-2
  (wait 2.0))                    ;; beats 3-4 (silent)

(define (bass-pulse-two-bars)
  ;; Steady kick on every beat for two measures
  (for-each
   (lambda (i)
     (sfx 'kick)
     (wait 1.0))
   '(0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7)))

(base/at-beat 0
  (son-clave-3-2)
  (bass-pulse-two-bars))
```

Bottom staff (kick): eight quarter-note kicks, one per beat. The clave's attacks align with some kicks (downbeats) and fall between others (offbeats), creating the cross-rhythmic tension.]

### A calypso groove: bass, rimshot, and cowbell

Calypso (and its faster cousin, soca) is built on layered polyrhythm. The bass drum walks in a steady pattern. The rimshot (or side-stick) ticks on the offbeats. The cowbell or agogô plays a syncopated two-bar phrase that contradicts both. Each layer subdivides time differently, and together they lock into a groove that feels effortless but is rhythmically dense.

Let's build a two-measure calypso cell.

```scheme
(transport/tempo 108)

(define (calypso-bass)
  ;; Bass drum: quarter-note walk, but skip beat 2 of each measure
  ;; Measure 1: 1, (2 silent), 3, 4
  ;; Measure 2: 1, (2 silent), 3, 4
  (sfx 'kick) (wait 1.0)   ;; beat 1
  (wait 1.0)                ;; beat 2 silent
  (sfx 'kick) (wait 1.0)   ;; beat 3
  (sfx 'kick) (wait 1.0)   ;; beat 4
  (sfx 'kick) (wait 1.0)   ;; beat 1 (m2)
  (wait 1.0)                ;; beat 2 silent
  (sfx 'kick) (wait 1.0)   ;; beat 3
  (sfx 'kick) (wait 1.0))  ;; beat 4

(define (calypso-rimshot)
  ;; Rimshot on the \"and\" of every beat (eighth-note offbeats)
  (for-each
   (lambda (i)
     (wait 0.5)
     (sfx 'rimshot)
     (wait 0.5))
   '(0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7))) ;; eight beats total (two measures)

(define (calypso-cowbell)
  ;; Cowbell: syncopated two-bar pattern
  ;; beats: 1, and-of-2, 3, and-of-4, and-of-1(m2), 3(m2), 4(m2)
  (sfx 'cowbell) (wait 1.0)   ;; 1
  (wait 0.5) (sfx 'cowbell) (wait 0.5) ;; and-of-2
  (sfx 'cowbell) (wait 1.0)   ;; 3
  (wait 0.5) (sfx 'cowbell) (wait 0.5) ;; and-of-4
  ;; Measure 2
  (wait 0.5) (sfx 'cowbell) (wait 0.5) ;; and-of-1
  (wait 1.0)                   ;; 2 silent
  (sfx 'cowbell) (wait 1.0)   ;; 3
  (sfx 'cowbell) (wait 1.0))  ;; 4

(base/at-beat 0
  (calypso-bass)
  (calypso-rimshot)
  (calypso-cowbell))
```

### A funk backbeat: layered syncopation

Funk is built on **syncopation** — accenting the offbeats, especially the \"and\" of beat 2 and the \"and\" of beat 4. When you layer a syncopated snare, a straight kick, and a shuffle hi-hat, you get a groove where every layer subdivides differently.

Let's build a one-measure funk cell with kick, snare, and hi-hat.

```scheme

  ;; Kick on 1, and-of-2, 3
  (sfx 'kick) (wait 1.0)   ;; 1
  (wait 0.5) (sfx 'kick) (wait 0.5) ;; and-of-2
  (sfx 'kick) (wait 2.0))  ;; 3, then wait through 4

(define (funk-snare)
  ;; Snare on 2, and-of-3
  (wait 1.0)               ;; 1 silent
  (sfx 'snare) (wait 1.0)  ;; 2
  (wait 0.5) (sfx 'snare) (wait 0.5) ;; and-of-3
  (wait 1.0))              ;; 4 silent

(define (funk-hihat-shuffle)
  ;; Hi-hat: shuffle eighth-notes (swing feel, not straight)
  ;; Play on 1, and-of-1 (delayed), 2, and-of-2 (delayed), etc.
  ;; Simplified: straight eighths for now *[needs: swing timing]*
  (for-each
   (lambda (i)
     (sfx 'hihat-closed)
     (wait 0.5))
   '(0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7)))

(base/at-beat 0
  (funk-kick)
  (funk-snare)
  (funk-hihat-shuffle))
```

Let's go dense: **seven notes in the time of four beats**. Septuplets are rare in Western music but common in some African and Balkan traditions. They create a rolling, lopsided feel — like the rhythm is tumbling forward, never quite settling.

```scheme
       (wait (/ span 7)))

   (lambda (i)
     (note/strike 65 0.3 0.6) ;; higher F
     (wait 1.0))
   '(0 1 2 3)))

(base/at-beat 0
  (septuplet-layer)
  (four-beat-anchor-low))
```

### Layering multiple polyrhythms: a percussion ensemble

Now let's combine several polyrhythmic cells into a single ensemble. We'll layer:

1. A **steady bass pulse** (quarter-notes, the anchor).
2. A **triplet hi-hat** (three notes per beat, creating a 3-against-4 feel with the bass).
3. A **clave pattern** (cross-rhythmic, five strokes over two measures).
4. A **shaker** playing straight sixteenths (the finest subdivision, filling every gap).

Each layer is rhythmically independent. Together, they create a dense, polyrhythmic groove.

```scheme

  ;; Quarter-note kick for two measures
  (for-each
   (lambda (i)
     (sfx 'kick)
     (wait 1.0))
   '(0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7)))

(define (ensemble-triplet-hihat)
  ;; Triplet hi-hat: three notes per beat, two measures = 24 notes
  (for-each
   (lambda (i)
     (sfx 'hihat-closed)
     (wait (/ 1.0 3))) ;; one beat divided into three
   (make-list 24 #t)))

(define (ensemble-clave)
  ;; 3-2 son clave (as before)
  (sfx 'woodblock) (wait 1.0)
  (wait 0.5) (sfx 'woodblock) (wait 0.5)
  (wait 1.0)
  (sfx 'woodblock) (wait 1.0)
  (sfx 'woodblock) (wait 1.0)
  (wait 0.5) (sfx 'woodblock) (wait 0.5)
  (wait 2.0))

(define (ensemble-shaker)
  ;; Sixteenth-note shaker for two measures = 32 notes
  (for-each
   (lambda (i)
     (sfx 'shaker)
     (wait 0.25))
   (make-list 32 #t)))

(base/at-beat 0
  (ensemble-bass-two-bars)
  (ensemble-triplet-hihat)
  (ensemble-clave)
  (ensemble-shaker))
```

### A two-measure soca groove: bass, rim, cowbell, and shaker

Soca (the faster, modern descendant of calypso) builds on the same polyrhythmic foundation but pushes the tempo and adds more syncopation. Let's build a two-measure soca cell with four layers:

1. **Bass drum**: steady quarters on 1, 3, 4 (each measure).
2. **Rim**: offbeat eighths (on the \"and\" of every beat).
3. **Cowbell**: a syncopated two-bar phrase.
4. **Shaker**: continuous sixteenths.

```scheme

(define (soca-bass)
  ;; Bass on 1, 3, 4 (both measures)
  (sfx 'kick) (wait 2.0)   ;; 1, skip 2
  (sfx 'kick) (wait 1.0)   ;; 3
  (sfx 'kick) (wait 1.0)   ;; 4
  (sfx 'kick) (wait 2.0)   ;; 1 (m2), skip 2
  (sfx 'kick) (wait 1.0)   ;; 3
  (sfx 'kick) (wait 1.0))  ;; 4

(define (soca-rim)
  ;; Rim on every offbeat (and-of-1, and-of-2, and-of-3, and-of-4, both measures)
  (for-each
   (lambda (i)
     (wait 0.5)
     (sfx 'rimshot)
     (wait 0.5))
   '(0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7)))

(define (soca-cowbell)
  ;; Syncopated cowbell: 1, and-of-1, 3, and-of-4 (m1), and-of-2, 4 (m2)
  (sfx 'cowbell) (wait 0.5)   ;; 1
  (sfx 'cowbell) (wait 1.5)   ;; and-of-1
  (sfx 'cowbell) (wait 1.5)   ;; 3
  (wait 0.5) (sfx 'cowbell) (wait 0.5) ;; and-of-4
  ;; Measure 2
  (wait 1.5) (sfx 'cowbell) (wait 0.5) ;; and-of-2
  (wait 1.0)                   ;; 3 silent
  (sfx 'cowbell) (wait 1.0))  ;; 4

(define (soca-shaker)
  ;; Continuous sixteenths for two measures
  (for-each
   (lambda (i)
     (sfx 'shaker)
     (wait 0.25))
   (make-list 32 #t)))

(base/at-beat 0
  (soca-bass)
  (soca-rim)
  (soca-cowbell)
  (soca-shaker))
```

### Cross-rhythm: shifting the downbeat

A **cross-rhythm** is a polyrhythmic pattern where one layer's accents fall on another layer's offbeats, making you hear the downbeat in two different places. The simplest example is a **3-against-4 cross-rhythm**, where a three-beat pattern repeats across four-beat measures, so the three-beat pattern's \"downbeat\" shifts on every repetition.

Let's build a two-measure example where a three-beat motif repeats four times, cycling through different beat positions in the 4/4 grid.

```scheme
(transport/tempo 96)

(define (three-beat-motif start-beat)
  ;; A three-beat rhythmic motif: note on 1, note on 2, note on 3
  ;; Each note is a short chime
  (base/at-beat start-beat
    (note/strike 72 0.2 0.5) (wait 1.0)   ;; beat 1 of motif
    (note/strike 74 0.2 0.5) (wait 1.0)   ;; beat 2 of motif
    (note/strike 76 0.2 0.5)))            ;; beat 3 of motif

(define (cross-rhythm-bass)
  ;; Steady bass on beats 1, 3 of both measures (anchoring 4/4)
  (for-each
   (lambda (beat)
     (base/at-beat beat
       (sfx 'kick)))
   '(0 2 4 6))) ;; beats 1, 3 (m1), 1, 3 (m2)

;; Play the three-beat motif starting on beat 0, 3, 6, 9 (wrapping)
;; That's four repetitions of a three-beat cycle across two 4/4 measures
(three-beat-motif 0)
(three-beat-motif 3)
(three-beat-motif 6)
;; (three-beat-motif 9 would be in measure 3, omitted for two-bar scope)

(cross-rhythm-bass)
```

Top staff: a three-note melodic motif (pitches C5-D5-E5) repeats three times, starting on beats 0, 3, 6 (so the motif's \"downbeat\" shifts relative to the measure). Bottom staff: kick on beats 1, 3 (both measures). The motif's attacks align with the kick on beat 0 and beat 6, but on beat 3 the motif's second note aligns with the kick, creating a cross-rhythmic shift.]

<!-- BUILD: runnable cross-rhythm example with three-beat motif repeating across 4/4 measures and bass anchoring 1,3; verify motif starts at t=0,3,6 and bass hits t=0,2,4,6 -->

The motif is steady — it always plays three notes in a row, one beat apart. But because it starts on beat 0, then beat 3, then beat 6, its **phase** shifts relative to the 4/4 measure. The ear hears the motif's \"downbeat\" moving — first it aligns with the measure's downbeat (beat 0), then it starts on beat 3 (the measure's third beat), then on beat 6 (the second measure's third beat). This is cross-rhythm: the pattern's internal pulse contradicts the meter's pulse.

### 4-against-3: the inverse hemiola

We started with 3-against-2 (hemiola). Now let's do **4-against-3** — four notes in the time of three beats. This is the inverse: instead of triplets against a duple grid, we have a quadruple subdivision against a triple grid.

```scheme
(transport/tempo 90)

(define (four-against-three-layer)
  ;; Four notes across three beats
  (let ((span 3.0))
    (for-each
     (lambda (i)
       (note/strike 60 0.2 0.5) ;; middle C
       (wait (/ span 4)))
     '(0 1 2 3))))

(define (three-beat-anchor)
  ;; Three steady beats (quarter-notes in 3/4, or three beats in any meter)
  (for-each
   (lambda (i)
     (note/strike 67 0.3 0.6) ;; G
     (wait 1.0))
   '(0 1 2)))

(base/at-beat 0
  (four-against-three-layer)
  (three-beat-anchor))
```

The four-note attacks fall on fractional beats (0, 0.75, 1.5, 2.25), weaving against the three-beat grid. The four-note layer's note-sprites bop at a faster rate (four divisions per three beats).]

The 4-against-3 feel is **looser** than 3-against-2 — the four-note layer feels like it's pulling ahead, subdividing the beat more finely than the three-beat anchor. ### A polyrhythmic canon: the same melody in two meters

A **polyrhythmic canon** layers the same melody in two different metric subdivisions — one voice plays it in duple time, another in triple time, so the melody unfolds at different rates and the two voices interlock polyrhythmically.

Let's take a simple four-note melody (C-D-E-C) and play it twice: once with each note lasting one beat (four beats total), and once with each note lasting two-thirds of a beat (triplet feel, so the whole melody fits in 8/3 beats ≈ 2.666... beats).

```scheme
(transport/tempo 84)

(define melody-pitches '(60 62 64 60)) ;; C D E C

(define (melody-duple)
  ;; Each note lasts one beat (four beats total)
  (for-each
   (lambda (pitch)
     (note/strike pitch 0.4 0.6)
     (wait 1.0))
   melody-pitches))

(define (melody-triple)
  ;; Each note lasts 2/3 beat (triplet feel, total = 8/3 beats)
  (for-each
   (lambda (pitch)
     (note/strike pitch 0.3 0.5)
     (wait (/ 2.0 3)))
   melody-pitches))

(base/at-beat 0
  (melody-duple)
  (melody-triple))
```

Bottom staff: the same melody in quarter-notes (each note one beat, total four beats). Both voices start on beat 0 (C aligns), but then the triplet voice moves faster, so the second note (D) in the triplet voice sounds before the second note in the duple voice, and the two voices diverge and then re-converge near the end (both land on the final C, but offset slightly). The melody is the same, but the rhythmic grid is different, creating a polyrhythmic canon.]

The two voices sing the **same tune**, but because one moves in duple time and the other in triple time, they diverge and then re-align in a **phase-shifting** pattern. This is a canon in **rhythm** as much as in pitch.

### Polyrhythm as structure: a two-section piece

Polyrhythm doesn't have to be confined to a single groove. You can **structure an entire piece** around polyrhythmic cells, shifting from one texture to another.

Let's write a two-section piece:

- **Section A**: a sparse 3-against-2 hemiola (just two layers, lots of space).
- **Section B**: a dense 4-against-3 groove with bass, hi-hat, and cowbell (three layers, tighter).

Each section lasts four measures.

```scheme
(transport/tempo 100)

;; Section A: sparse 3-against-2 hemiola
(define (section-a-three)
  ;; Three notes per two beats, four measures = 8 beats = 12 notes
  (for-each
   (lambda (i)
     (note/strike 55 0.3 0.4) ;; low G
     (wait (/ 2.0 3)))
   (make-list 12 #t)))

(define (section-a-two)
  ;; Two notes per two beats, four measures = 8 beats = 4 two-beat pairs = 8 notes
  (for-each
   (lambda (i)
     (note/strike 67 0.4 0.5) ;; higher G
     (wait 1.0))
   (make-list 8 #t)))

(define (section-a)
  (base/at-beat 0
    (section-a-three)
    (section-a-two)))

;; Section B: 4-against-3 with bass, hi-hat, cowbell
(define (section-b-bass)
  ;; Kick on 1, 3 (four measures = 16 beats, kick on every other beat)
  (for-each
   (lambda (i)
     (sfx 'kick)
     (wait 2.0))
   (make-list 8 #t)))

(define (section-b-hihat)
  ;; Four notes per three beats, repeating
  ;; Four measures of 4/4 = 16 beats; 16 beats = (16/3)*4 = 21.33... notes
  ;; Simplified: four-per-three pattern for 12 beats (three measures), then fill fourth measure
  (for-each
   (lambda (i)
     (sfx 'hihat-closed)
     (wait (/ 3.0 4)))
   (make-list 20 #t)))

(define (section-b-cowbell)
  ;; Syncopated cowbell: custom pattern across four measures
  ;; beats 1, and-of-2, 4, and-of-2(m2), 3(m3), and-of-4(m4)
  (sfx 'cowbell) (wait 1.5)
  (sfx 'cowbell) (wait 2.5)
  (sfx 'cowbell) (wait 1.5)
  (sfx 'cowbell) (wait 2.5)
  (sfx 'cowbell) (wait 1.5)
  (sfx 'cowbell) (wait 2.5))

(define (section-b)
  (base/at-beat 0
    (section-b-bass)
    (section-b-hihat)
    (section-b-cowbell)))

;; Play section A, then section B
(section-a)
(wait 8.0) ;; four measures at tempo 100 = 8 beats
```

### A polyrhythmic phrase: melody and counter-melody in different meters

Let's layer a melody in 4/4 with a counter-melody in 6/8 (or, equivalently, a counter-melody that subdivides the same span into six beats while the melody subdivides it into four). The two melodies interlock polyrhythmically.

```scheme
(transport/tempo 96)

(define melody-4 '(60 62 64 65)) ;; C D E F (one note per beat, four beats)
(define counter-6 '(67 65 64 62 60 58)) ;; G F E D C A# (six notes, triplet feel)

(define (melody-in-4)
  (for-each
   (lambda (pitch)
     (note/strike pitch 0.4 0.6)
     (wait 1.0))
   melody-4))

(define (counter-in-6)
  ;; Six notes in the same span as four beats
  (for-each
   (lambda (pitch)
     (note/strike pitch 0.3 0.5)
     (wait (/ 4.0 6))) ;; four beats divided into six
   counter-6))

(base/at-beat 0
  (melody-in-4)
  (counter-in-6))
```

The two melodies start together (C and G on beat 0) and end together (F and A# near beat 4, slightly offset), but in between they diverge — the six-note line moves faster and creates a 6-against-4 (or 3-against-2) polyrhythmic texture. The note-sprites on the top staff bop in steady quarter-time; on the bottom staff, faster (six-fold subdivision).]

### Tuplets nested in polyrhythm: quintuplets over triplets

Let's go deep: layer **quintuplets** (five notes in the time of four beats) over **triplets** (three notes per beat, so twelve notes in four beats). The two layers subdivide time in completely different ways — five-fold vs. three-fold — creating a dense, tangled polyrhythmic texture.

```scheme
(transport/tempo 88)

(define (quintuplet-line)
  ;; Five notes across four beats
  (let ((span 4.0))
    (for-each
     (lambda (i)
       (note/strike 62 0.2 0.4) ;; D
       (wait (/ span 5)))
     '(0 1 2 3 4))))

(define (triplet-line)
  ;; Three notes per beat, four beats = 12 notes
  (for-each
   (lambda (i)
     (note/strike 69 0.2 0.5) ;; A
     (wait (/ 1.0 3)))
   (make-list 12 #t)))

(base/at-beat 0
  (quintuplet-line)
  (triplet-line))
```

The quintuplet note-sprites bop at a five-fold rate; the triplet note-sprites at a faster twelve-fold rate. The texture is dense and intricate.]

### A polyrhythmic ostinato: a repeating cell in 7/8 over 4/4

An **ostinato** is a repeating rhythmic or melodic pattern. When you layer an ostinato in one meter (say, 7/8 — seven eighth-notes per measure) over a bass line in another meter (4/4 — eight eighth-notes per measure), the ostinato's \"downbeat\" shifts on every repetition, creating a **phasing** polyrhythmic texture.

Let's write a seven-note ostinato (one pitch per eighth-note, total duration = 7 eighths = 3.5 beats) and repeat it four times over a steady 4/4 bass (which lasts 16 beats total). The ostinato will phase through the 4/4 grid.

```scheme
(transport/tempo 104)

(define ostinato-pitches '(60 62 64 65 67 69 71)) ;; C D E F G A B (7 notes)

(define (ostinato-7)
  ;; Seven notes, each an eighth-note (0.5 beats), total = 3.5 beats
  (for-each
   (lambda (pitch)
     (note/strike pitch 0.2 0.5)
     (wait 0.5))
   ostinato-pitches))

(define (ostinato-repeated)
  ;; Repeat the ostinato four times (4 * 3.5 = 14 beats)
  (for-each
   (lambda (i)
     (ostinato-7))
   '(0 1 2 3)))

(define (bass-4-4)
  ;; Steady bass on beats 1, 3 for four measures (16 beats total)
  (for-each
   (lambda (i)
     (sfx 'kick)
     (wait 2.0))
   (make-list 8 #t)))

(base/at-beat 0
  (ostinato-repeated)
  (bass-4-4))
```

The ostinato **phases** through the 4/4 grid — it starts aligned with the downbeat, then shifts by half a beat on each repetition. After four repetitions, it's shifted by 14 beats total (3.5 * 4 = 14), which is not a multiple of 4, so the pattern never fully re-aligns with the 4/4 measure structure. This is **metric phasing** — a polyrhythmic technique where a repeating pattern drifts through a different metric framework.

### Polyrhythm as orchestration: different sections in different meters

You can use polyrhythm to **orchestrate** an ensemble — assign different sections to different meters, so each section subdivides time in its own way.

Let's write a short ensemble piece where:

- **Strings** play a melody in 4/4 (steady quarter-notes).
- **Woodwinds** play a counter-melody in 6/8 (triplet feel, six notes per four beats).
- **Brass** play a bass line in 3/4 (three notes per four beats, creating a hemiola feel).

All three sections sound together, each in its own meter, creating a **polymetric texture**.

```scheme

(define (strings-4-4)
  ;; Melody in 4/4: four quarter-notes
  (for-each
   (lambda (pitch)
     (note/strike pitch 0.5 0.6)
     (wait 1.0))
   '(60 62 64 65))) ;; C D E F

(define (woodwinds-6-8)
  ;; Counter-melody in 6/8: six notes in four beats
  (for-each
   (lambda (pitch)
     (note/strike pitch 0.3 0.5)
     (wait (/ 4.0 6)))
   '(67 69 71 72 71 69))) ;; G A B C B A

(define (brass-3-4)
  ;; Bass line in 3/4: three notes in four beats
  (for-each
   (lambda (pitch)
     (note/strike pitch 0.6 0.7)
     (wait (/ 4.0 3)))
   '(48 52 55))) ;; low C E G

(base/at-beat 0
  (strings-4-4)
  (woodwinds-6-8)
  (brass-3-4))
```

The three sections interlock, creating a polymetric texture where each voice moves in its own metric world. The note-sprites on each staff bop at different rates (quarter-note, triplet, hemiola), visually reinforcing the polyrhythmic/polymetric structure.]

### A polyrhythmic round: canon with phase-shifted entries

A **round** (Ch9) is a canon where each voice enters at a different time but sings the same melody. A **polyrhythmic round** adds a twist: each voice sings the melody in a different **subdivision**, so the voices interlock polyrhythmically as well as canonically.

Let's write a three-voice round where:

- **Voice 1** sings a four-note melody in quarter-notes (one note per beat).
- **Voice 2** sings the same melody in triplet eighths (three notes per two beats, so the melody lasts 8/3 beats).
- **Voice 3** sings the same melody in dotted eighths (each note 0.75 beats, so the melody lasts 3 beats).

All three voices sing the same pitches, but at different rates, and they enter at different times (staggered by one beat).

```scheme
(transport/tempo 96)

(define melody '(60 64 67 72)) ;; C E G high C

(define (voice-1)
  ;; Quarter-notes (one beat per note)
  (for-each
   (lambda (pitch)
     (note/strike pitch 0.4 0.6)
     (wait 1.0))
   melody))

(define (voice-2)
  ;; Triplet subdivision: each note 2/3 beat
  (for-each
   (lambda (pitch)
     (note/strike pitch 0.3 0.5)
     (wait (/ 2.0 3)))
   melody))

(define (voice-3)
  ;; Dotted eighth subdivision: each note 0.75 beat
  (for-each
   (lambda (pitch)
     (note/strike pitch 0.35 0.55)
     (wait 0.75))
   melody))

;; Stagger entries: voice 1 at beat 0, voice 2 at beat 1, voice 3 at beat 2
(base/at-beat 0 (voice-1))
(base/at-beat 1 (voice-2))
(base/at-beat 2 (voice-3))
```

\"There is a story Rachmaninoff told about himself, in a small book of memories dictated to a friend, that I keep coming back to. In 1897 his First Symphony was performed for the first time, and it was a disaster — the conductor was drunk, the strings were ragged, the young composer heard his careful writing turn into noise. He walked out of the hall and did not compose anything meaningful for almost three years. He drank. He gave piano lessons he didn't want to give. Friends worried.

His aunt, Varvara Satina, brought him in the winter of 1900 to see a doctor named Nikolai Dahl. Dahl was a hypnotherapist and an amateur violist, which is a lovely combination. He sat Rachmaninoff in a chair and he said, in effect, the same sentence every day for four months: 'You will begin to write your concerto. You will work with great facility. The concerto will be of excellent quality.' Rachmaninoff wrote later that he did not fully believe it, but he liked Dahl, and he liked being told, and he began.

The second movement came first, in the summer of 1900. Then the third. Then, finally, the first — which is the movement everyone thinks of when they think of Rach 2, the one that opens with those eight enormous piano chords swelling out of silence like a bell tolled inside your ribcage. He finished the whole thing in the spring of 1901 and premiered it complete in Moscow on the 27th of October that year, playing the piano part himself while Alexander Siloti conducted. He dedicated the score to Dahl. That dedication is printed on the title page of every edition of the Op. 18 you will ever pick up. If you find an old score at a used shop and it says 'A Monsieur N. Dahl,' you are holding a fragment of a specific kindness done to one man over a hundred and twenty-five years ago.

I tell you all of this because when we listen to the piece — really listen, not as background but as an object to look at — the story is *inside the music*. Not in a program-notes way, where you know something about the composer and it colors what you hear. In a stronger way. The concerto is built out of the fact that a person who could not write music began again. Every phrase is an argument, first with silence and then with itself, that a beginning is possible.

Let's look at it.

# The opening — the argument with silence

The first movement is marked *Moderato*, in C minor, four-four. There is no orchestral introduction. The piano begins alone. What it plays is a series of eight chords, each one held long enough to hear the next one gather. The first four chords are F minor, F minor, F minor, F minor — the same chord, but each played with more notes underneath, so the *sound* thickens. Then a shift: G minor. Then Bb major, D-flat major, C major. Then a great crashing arrival on F minor again. All of this happens over about twenty seconds of played time. The dynamic marking climbs from *piano* (soft) to *fortissimo* (very loud) across those eight chords. It is the sound of someone who has not spoken in a long time deciding to speak.

Then the orchestra enters, and the piano turns from speaker into accompanist — it plays a rolling, wave-like figure in triplets while the strings sing the main theme. This is *the* Rach 2 theme, and if you have heard the piece even once, this is the melody your body remembers. It is in C minor. It moves down more than up. It is patient — a quarter note, a quarter note, a half note, a quarter, a quarter, a half — and it doesn't hurry, because the whole point is that it was almost never written and now here it is, so it takes its time.

# What the shape *is*

There is a form for a first movement of a concerto, called **sonata form**, that has been in use since the middle of the eighteenth century. It has three big sections and I will name them:

**Exposition.** Two themes are stated — a first theme in the home key (C minor, for us), and a second theme in a related key (in this concerto, E-flat major — the relative major, the sunny sibling of C minor).

**Development.** The composer takes the themes apart and works them over — fragments, transpositions, combinations. This is where the piece *thinks*. The home key comes and goes. Tension gathers.

**Recapitulation.** Both themes return, this time both in the home key or nearby, and the piece finds its way back to where it started, but changed.

Sonata form is not a mould you pour music into. It is a shape people learned to hear over a couple of centuries — a shape that a listener finds their place in. When you hear a second theme in a new key, some part of your musical mind marks the location. When it comes back later in the home key, you feel the return before you can name what has returned. Composers who use sonata form are trusting that their listener has the shape in their body, and they play with the trust.

Rachmaninoff, writing in 1900, is very late to sonata form — a century and a half after Haydn worked it out, half a century after Brahms was writing symphonies that still used it. He is using an old shape. But he is putting inside it a theme (the C minor rolling melody, the E-flat major second theme) that could not have been written earlier, because it uses a Romantic-era harmonic language that took decades to develop.

# The second theme

The second theme arrives about two and a half minutes into the movement. The piano plays it — a long, singing melody in E-flat major, a key that sounds warm and open after the brooding C minor. In some editions the tempo marking eases here to *un poco meno mosso* (a little less busy). The melody has a slight upward reach at the start of each phrase and a settling downward at the end. If you are listening for it, you can hear the piece take a breath.

This second theme is one of the most-borrowed tunes in classical music. Frank Sinatra recorded a song called 'Full Moon and Empty Arms' in 1946 that is this theme with lyrics. Eric Carmen's 'All by Myself' from 1975 quotes the same melody. When people who have never listened to a concerto say they know Rach 2, this is usually the phrase they mean. It has been converted into a pop song at least four times in the last century, which tells us something about what a tune has to *do* to be that portable: it has to be sing-able in one breath, memorable after one hearing, and open enough at the top and bottom that a lyricist can fit words into its arch.

# What we can do with it in Scheme

Let's make a small program that plays the opening eight chords. Not to replace the piece — no eight lines of code will do that — but to make the shape touchable. We'll use the vocabulary from Chapter 6 (harmony) and Chapter 13 (dynamics).

```scheme
;; Rachmaninoff Piano Concerto No. 2, Op. 18
;; Movement I: Moderato, opening 8 chords (piano solo, unaccompanied)

(define (rach2-opening)
  (transport/tempo 66)  ; ~66 bpm — a slow, deliberate Moderato

  ;; Chord 1: F minor, piano, held for a whole note
  (with-dynamics 'p
    (chord/play '(F2 Ab2 C3 F3) 'whole))

  ;; Chord 2: F minor, thicker, mezzo-piano
  (with-dynamics 'mp
    (chord/play '(F2 Ab2 C3 F3 Ab3) 'whole))

  ;; Chord 3: F minor, thicker still, mezzo-forte
  (with-dynamics 'mf
    (chord/play '(F2 Ab2 C3 F3 Ab3 C4) 'whole))

  ;; Chord 4: F minor, fortissimo, full — the peak of the swell
  (with-dynamics 'f
    (chord/play '(F2 Ab2 C3 F3 Ab3 C4 F4) 'whole))

  ;; The harmonic shift begins — G minor
  (with-dynamics 'f
    (chord/play '(G2 Bb2 D3 G3 Bb3 D4 G4) 'whole))

  ;; Bb major
  (with-dynamics 'ff
    (chord/play '(Bb2 D3 F3 Bb3 D4 F4 Bb4) 'whole))

  ;; Db major — the great expansion
  (with-dynamics 'ff
    (chord/play '(Db2 F2 Ab2 Db3 F3 Ab3 Db4) 'whole))

  ;; C major arrival — the dominant of F minor, preparing the theme
  (with-dynamics 'fff
    (chord/play '(C3 E3 G3 C4 E4 G4 C5) 'whole)))
```

If you run that, you will not have Rachmaninoff. You will have a small demonstration of the harmonic ladder the opening climbs — F minor thickening, then a walk through G minor, Bb major, Db major, and arriving on C major. The C major at the end is the *dominant* of F minor, which means it is the chord that traditionally leads back to F minor. But here, at the very moment we expect F minor, the orchestra enters in C minor — the *actual* home key — and we realize the opening was setting us up. All eight chords were a kind of question, and the entrance of the orchestra was the answer.

That trick — expectations set up in one key, resolved in another — is a Romantic-era harmonic move that Rachmaninoff loved. It works on the listener because the ear has learned to expect resolution, and the composer knows that.

# Why the concerto lands

Here is what I think is true about Rach 2 as an object — as a piece you can pick up, turn over, put down.

The concerto is a story of an entrance. The opening chords are the story of a man walking back to the piano after almost three years of silence. The rolling triplets that follow are the story of accompaniment — the composer's own hands, playing under the orchestra's melody, doing the *work of holding up* the tune that everyone remembers. The second theme is the story of warmth after cold, E-flat after C minor. The development is the story of thinking things through. The recapitulation is the story of return.

None of this is program music. There are no signposts in the score that say 'this is where I was ill' or 'this is where I got better.' Rachmaninoff never claimed the piece was autobiographical in that direct way. But the dedication to Dahl is real, printed on every score, and the timing is real — 1900 into 1901, right after Dahl's treatment. And the *sound* of the piece — its willingness to be beautiful, its patience, its return to warmth — matches the story so cleanly that when you know both, you cannot un-know them together.

I think this is what the philosopher-lens people would call a **case of a work being both about itself and about the moment of its making**. It is not that the concerto describes the depression and the recovery. It is that the concerto *is what a recovery sounded like*, in one man's hands, once, in 1900. The concerto and the recovery are the same object. You cannot separate them without breaking both.

# What to listen for

If you have never heard Rach 2 all the way through, here is what I'd notice:

The first movement, *Moderato*. Listen for the eight opening chords. Listen for how the piano enters as accompanist, not soloist. Listen for the second theme in E-flat — the one Sinatra sang. Listen for the development section, where the themes get pulled apart and worked on. Listen for the recapitulation, and notice whether the return of the first theme feels the same or different.

The second movement, *Adagio sostenuto* in E major. This is the slow movement — the movement Rachmaninoff wrote first, in the summer of 1900, when Dahl's treatment was still fresh. It opens with the strings modulating quietly from C minor to E major over about eight bars, and then the piano enters with a long, singing melody. It stays slow. It does not hurry. If the first movement is the argument with silence, the second is what silence sounds like when it becomes friendly.

The third movement, *Allegro scherzando*, in C minor moving to C major. This is fast, virtuosic, joyful. There is a moment near the end when the second theme of the third movement — a big, sweeping melody that the pop world has borrowed less than the first movement's E-flat tune, but only just — returns in C major, at full volume, and the piano and orchestra ride it home. The piece ends in C major. The C minor of the opening has been won over.

# Tie back

I told you at the top: every phrase in this concerto is an argument that a beginning is possible. That is what I hear in the eight opening chords, in the patience of the C minor theme, in the warmth of the E-flat second theme, in the way the third movement ends in C major.

There is a small, useful thing about form-as-meaning that this piece teaches. It is not that the composer felt something and then encoded it. It is that the *shape* — sonata form, three movements, C minor to C major — was already there in the tradition, and Rachmaninoff put himself into the shape and let the shape do some of the work. The shape carries the meaning because generations of composers have used it to carry that kind of meaning. When we hear a sonata-form first movement in C minor, we already half-expect a recapitulation and a resolution. We already half-know we are being told a story of return. The composer's job is to make the story *specific*.

Rachmaninoff, in 1900 and 1901, made the story of return specific to one man, one doctor, one dedication, one set of chords. And because he made it that specific — with Dahl's name on the score, with a melody that would not have been possible ten years earlier — the return became something everyone else could feel too. That is a strange thing. It is the strange thing music does. The more particular the composer is, the more everyone can find themselves inside the shape.

If you are just starting to listen to classical music and you want a piece to begin with, this is a good one. It is not too long. It has famous tunes you will already know. It has structure you can follow. And it is, at its heart, a story about beginning again after not being able to — which is a story a great many people need to hear, and which the piece will tell you as many times as you want to press play.

# Sources cited in this chapter

Sergei Rachmaninoff, *Recollections* as dictated to Oskar von Riesemann (Macmillan, 1934). The Dahl treatment story is told by Rachmaninoff himself here.

Sergei Bertensson and Jay Leyda, *Rachmaninoff: A Lifetime in Music* (New York University Press, 1956). Full biographical account, standard reference; contains the primary correspondence around Op. 18.

Grove Music Online, entry 'Rachmaninoff, Serge' (article by Robert Threlfall and Geoffrey Norris), for dates and works list.

International Music Score Library Project (IMSLP), which hosts the complete score of Op. 18 in the public domain and can be consulted for any measure-by-measure claim in this chapter.\"

;; Book of Music — Chapter 11a (bridge): Form as Meaning
;; Written 2026-07-13. Author: Lacuna Labs Engineering.
;; Doctrine: publishable prose · no hallucination · analysis-shape.
;; A short bridge chapter framing what \"form as meaning\" means before we
;; dive into Rach 2, Chopin, forms, pitch, tempo. This is the philosophical
;; anchor for chapters 11-15.

  :book \"book-of-music\"
  :number \"11a-bridge\"
  :title \"Form as Meaning\"
  :short-title \"form-as-meaning\"
  :estimated-words 1800
  :philosopher-weave (peirce jung wittgenstein-late aristotle)

  :prose
\"Before we go into the specific pieces of the next five chapters — a concerto, a set of nocturnes and a waltz, three classical formal shapes, the physics of pitch, the art of timing — I want to name something that sits under all of them. It's a simple idea, but a load-bearing one, and once you have it in your ear you cannot hear music the same way.

The idea is: **form is not decoration. Form is what a piece means.**

I don't mean this poetically. I mean it structurally. When Rachmaninoff writes a concerto in sonata form and ends the third movement in C major after starting the first in C minor, the C-minor-to-C-major arc is not a container for the meaning. It *is* the meaning. When Chopin writes a nocturne that states a plain melody, moves through a middle section, and returns with the melody decorated, the return-decorated is what the piece is about. When Bach writes thirty variations on a small aria, and the whole hour-long journey ends with the aria unchanged from where it started, the journey-and-return is the piece's whole argument.

If you take those forms away — if you play only the themes, only the melodies, only the notes stripped of their formal position — you have kept some of the material and lost most of the meaning. Music is not the notes. Music is the notes arranged in a shape that a listener can find their place in over time.

# What kinds of meaning form carries

There are a few different kinds of meaning that musical form can carry, and I want to name them so we notice them when they arrive in the next chapters.

**Return meaning.** When a theme comes back, it means something. The listener has been away from it — through a middle section, through a development, through several minutes of music — and its return says: *here we are again, but changed*. In a Chopin nocturne, the return is often decorated, and the decoration says *I have thought about you*. In a Rachmaninoff concerto, the return is in the home key after a long journey away, and it says *we have come back*. Return is the oldest formal move in music. It is why refrains work in songs, why choruses work in pop, why cadences work in classical: return is a form of arrival, and arrival is a form of meaning.

**Contrast meaning.** When a new theme arrives in a new key, it means something. The change of harmonic color creates the sense of a new place, a new mood, a new thought. In sonata form the second theme in a contrasting key is not just decoration; it is the argument that the first theme was not the whole story. Contrast opens up the space of what the piece can say.

**Development meaning.** When a theme gets pulled apart — fragmented, transposed, combined with other material — it means something. The composer is *thinking* on the theme, showing us what the theme can become, testing its limits. Development is the intellectual work of a piece. When it lands well, we feel that we have watched an idea grow.

**Duration meaning.** How long a section lasts is a kind of meaning. A slow movement that takes twelve minutes is saying *this material deserves this time*. A brisk finale that takes four minutes is saying *this is the release, don't overstay*. Great composers know how long to hold a mood; the length itself is expressive.

**Proportion meaning.** How the sections balance each other is a kind of meaning. If a first movement is fifteen minutes and a slow movement is twelve, they are structurally comparable. If a slow movement is three minutes and a finale is fifteen, the piece has a different weight distribution and a different feel. The proportions are part of the composition.

# Why this is not just theory

You do not need to know any of this in order to enjoy music. Millions of people listen to Rach 2 and love it without being able to name sonata form. Millions of people love Chopin without knowing what rubato is. Musical enjoyment does not require musical analysis.

But if you are trying to *hear* what a piece is doing — if you want to understand why one nocturne feels sadder than another, why one concerto feels like it argues for something and another feels like it just plays with sound — the concept of form-as-meaning is the door in. Once you have it, you can start noticing.

You start noticing when a piece returns to its opening key and feels resolved. You start noticing when a middle section modulates far away and doesn't come back for a while. You start noticing when a variation set stays on the same theme for so long that the theme becomes an old friend by the end. You start noticing what a piece is *shaped like*, not just what it sounds like moment to moment.

And once you notice, you can talk to other listeners about what they hear. You can say: *listen to the second theme in the recapitulation, it's in a different key than I expected*. You can say: *this variation is a change of mode, not just a change of ornament*. You can say: *the slow movement is the emotional center of the whole piece — the outer movements circle it*. Musical talk becomes possible, and musical friendships become possible, and eventually musical love becomes deeper than it was when you started.

# What the next chapters do with this

The next five chapters will take this idea into specific pieces.

Chapter 11 is Rachmaninoff's Second Piano Concerto — a piece whose *form* is the meaning: the return from silence, the C-minor-to-C-major arc, the dedication to the doctor who helped the composer begin again.

Chapter 12 is Chopin's Op. 18 waltz and three of his nocturnes — pieces where the small form (rondo, single-mood nocturne with decorated return) carries as much weight as the large form does in a symphony.

Chapter 13 names the three big classical forms — sonata form, rondo, theme and variations — as three different answers to the question of how a piece can be one thing and also many things.

Chapter 14 gets under the notes themselves: pitch as frequency, interval as ratio, the harmonic series as the physical substrate of consonance. The physics under the forms.

Chapter 15 is about time: tempo and rubato, and what it means for a performer to shape time inside a piece. The moment-to-moment experience under the forms.

Then Chapter 16 (already in the book) is the concerto synthesis — where all of it comes together on Rach 2 as a full composed programmatic performance.

Read them in that order and by the end you will have a working vocabulary for form-as-meaning. Then, if you want, listen to whatever piece you have been meaning to listen to, and see if it opens up.

# Tie back

Form is meaning. Not container, meaning. When we look at a piece of music, we are looking at an arrangement of sound over time whose *shape* carries a large fraction of what the piece is about. The next chapters will show this in specifics. Keep the idea in your ear and see what happens.\"

  :notes

Wittgenstein-late: form as language-game — the shared conventions that let a listener understand what a return or a modulation means.
Aristotle: form as the shape of a musical action — beginning, middle, end.
Jung: form as archetype — the underlying pattern that carries meaning across centuries.
Nothing named in prose.\"

  :tie-forward
\"Chapter 11 is Rachmaninoff's Second Piano Concerto — a piece where form IS the meaning.\")

  :prose
\"John Field, an Irish pianist working in St. Petersburg, invented the word 'nocturne' as a title for a piano piece around 1812. He published his first three of them in 1814. They were slow, songful, single-mood pieces — a right hand carrying a melody, a left hand rolling underneath in wide arpeggios that sustained the harmony like the pedal of a hurdy-gurdy. Chopin, born in 1810 in a village outside Warsaw, heard Field's nocturnes when he was a student and understood the form immediately. He wrote twenty-one nocturnes of his own between roughly 1830 and 1846. When people say 'nocturne' now, they usually mean a Chopin nocturne. The form is Field's; the sound is Chopin's.

I want to look at three of the nocturnes and one waltz in this chapter, because taken together they show something about what a small piano piece can hold — how a single mood, over three to seven minutes, can be built and released and returned to. This is different work from what Rachmaninoff did in the last chapter. Rach 2 is an arc across forty minutes. A Chopin nocturne is a night, sustained.

# The waltz — Op. 18 in E-flat major

Let's start with the waltz, because it is more famous than any of the nocturnes and it will teach us how Chopin thinks about form.

The Grande Valse Brillante in E-flat major, Opus 18, was published in 1834, when Chopin was twenty-four. He had left Warsaw in 1830 for what was meant to be a concert tour and become, by an accident of history — the November Uprising against Russian rule broke out weeks after he left, and by the time it was crushed he was permanently in exile — a Paris resident. Op. 18 is his first published waltz. He dedicated it to a Miss Laura Horsford, one of his English piano students; the dedication is on the title page of the first edition.

The piece is in a form called **rondo**, which is one of the oldest forms in Western music. A rondo has a refrain — the main tune — that keeps coming back, with contrasting episodes between the returns. The pattern is A-B-A-C-A, or A-B-A-C-A-B-A, or some longer chain. The A theme is the piece's home; the episodes are journeys out and back.

Op. 18's A theme is the tune everyone knows: an eight-bar phrase in E-flat major, the melody dancing up and coming back down, marked *Vivo* (lively). Chopin repeats it. Then he goes into a B episode in a slightly lower register — the tune is different but the mood is similar, still elegant, still dance-like. Then the A theme returns. Then a C episode, more dramatic, moving into new harmonic territory. Then A again. Then a D episode, quieter, with a leftward-leaning phrase in the melody that seems almost to hesitate. Then A. Then a coda that keeps threatening to end and doesn't, until finally it does, on an E-flat major chord with the top note ringing out.

The whole piece is about five minutes. Its form is legible in about one hearing. That is part of the point. A waltz has to be dance-able, in principle — even if nobody will actually dance to it, the listener has to feel the *possibility* of dance in the rhythm. Chopin's waltzes are almost never actually danceable at their real tempo (they are too fast, too free), but they preserve the shape of the dance, and the listener feels the ghost of the ballroom.

# The first nocturne — Op. 9 No. 2 in E-flat major

Now the nocturnes. Op. 9 is a set of three, published in 1832 when Chopin was twenty-two, dedicated to Madame Marie Pleyel. The second of the three is the one most people know — the E-flat major nocturne, marked *Andante*, in twelve-eight time.

Twelve-eight is a rocking meter — twelve eighth-notes to a bar, grouped into four groups of three. It feels like a boat on gentle water. The left hand plays a wide, slow-rolling arpeggio pattern — bottom note, middle chord, middle chord, all across the twelve — while the right hand sings a melody above. The melody is a simple three-note descending idea that immediately embellishes itself: a turn, a small run, a trill. Chopin marks it *dolce* (sweet) at the start, and *espressivo* (expressively) a few bars in.

The tune is fourteen bars long, and then it repeats — but the second time, Chopin decorates the melody. Where the first time had a plain quarter note, the second time has a scale in thirty-second notes running up to the same landing. Where the first time had a simple leap, the second time fills the leap in with an ornament. This is a Chopin habit: *the repeat is the elaboration*. The listener remembers the plain version, and the elaborated version reads over the plain one like handwriting over pencil.

That habit is central to how the nocturnes work. They are almost all built from a short melodic idea, stated plainly and then decorated on return. The decorations feel improvised — as if the pianist were making them up on the spot — but they are precisely notated in the score, sixty-fourth notes stacked in complicated groups over the 12/8. Chopin was known in Paris for playing in a way that made the audience think he was improvising, and the nocturnes preserve that quality in ink.

# The second nocturne — Op. 27 No. 2 in D-flat major

Op. 27 is a pair, published in 1836, dedicated to Countess d'Appony. The second of the two, in D-flat major, is often held up (by people who make lists of such things) as one of the most beautiful pieces of solo piano music ever written. I would not argue with them.

D-flat major has five flats. It sits far from the ear's home. It is the enharmonic equivalent of C-sharp major, and pianists who look at it complain about the fingerings because the black keys and white keys form patterns that lie awkwardly under the hand. But the sound of D-flat major is warm and slightly veiled — the black-key pentatonic figures in the melody sit naturally, and the wide left-hand arpeggios roll out across the low register with a resonance that C major, one semitone up, cannot quite match.

The tune is six bars long. It begins with a rising sixth, held, and then it settles down. Chopin marks it *Lento sostenuto* — slow, sustained — and *dolce*. The right hand sings; the left hand rolls a low D-flat arpeggio across the whole bar, with the pedal held so that all the notes ring together. The pedal is doing enormous work here. In classical piano writing before Chopin, the pedal was used sparingly, mostly for effect. Chopin used it as a coloring instrument, held for whole bars, releasing only when the harmony changed. The nocturnes are unplayable without pedal, in a strong sense: the notes are correct without it, but the *sound* is missing.

The Op. 27 No. 2 grows in intensity as it goes. The middle section moves through several keys, brings the left hand up higher on the piano so the two hands are closer together, and lets the melody stretch into longer phrases. Then the opening tune returns, decorated with a long, flowing run in the right hand that spans almost the whole keyboard. Then it fades. Then it ends on a D-flat major chord, high, quiet, held with pedal until the sound dies.

# The third nocturne — Op. 48 No. 1 in C minor

The C minor nocturne, Op. 48 No. 1, published in 1841, is different from the other two. It has a middle section that is not a dreamy contrast; it is a chorale, marked *Poco più lento* (a little slower), moving in solid block chords, sounding like a hymn played in a huge stone church. Then the opening tune returns, but now agitated — the left hand has taken on a fast triplet pattern, the melody is being interrupted by chords that stab in from underneath. The mood has darkened.

The C minor nocturne is one of the few Chopin nocturnes that leaves the single-mood territory of the genre. Field's nocturnes and most of Chopin's early ones are one atmosphere sustained. This one has three: the opening lament, the chorale middle, the agitated return. It ends in C minor, quietly, but the memory of the chorale is still in the room. Some pianists — Vladimir Horowitz recorded it in the 1960s, Arthur Rubinstein in the 1930s and again in the 1960s — treat it almost as a small tone poem, with the middle section arriving as a vision and the return as the vision troubling the original mood.

# What the small piece can hold

Rachmaninoff wrote a concerto in three movements that argued a big argument — beginning again after silence — across forty minutes. Chopin wrote pieces that were five to seven minutes long and used the small span to sustain one atmosphere so completely that the listener falls all the way into it.

Both approaches are legitimate. Neither is superior. What Chopin taught the piano was that a small form could be as serious as a large one, if the composer went deep enough into the material. His nocturnes are studied by every serious pianist for the same reason they are played at wedding receptions and used in film scores: they are teachable and singable and moving at once. That is not an easy combination.

# What we can do in Scheme

Let's build a small version of a nocturne's texture. Not a specific piece — the actual nocturnes are more complex than a short program can honestly represent — but the *texture*: right hand melody, left hand rolling arpeggio in twelve-eight, sustained by the pedal.

```scheme
;; A nocturne-texture study in E-flat major, 12/8 meter
;; Right hand: simple melody
;; Left hand: rolling arpeggio pattern
;; Pedal: held per bar, released on harmony change

(define eflat-major '(Eb Bb G))         ; tonic chord
(define bb7        '(Bb F Ab D))        ; dominant seventh
(define cm         '(C Eb G))           ; relative minor
(define ab-major   '(Ab C Eb))          ; subdominant

(define (nocturne-left-hand chord octave)
  ;; twelve eighth-notes: bass, middle-chord × 5 across a 12/8 bar
  (let ((bass (list-ref chord 0))
        (mid  (cdr chord)))
    (list
      (note (string->symbol
              (string-append (symbol->string bass)
                             (number->string octave))) 'eighth)
      (chord/play mid 'eighth)
      (chord/play mid 'eighth)
      (chord/play mid 'eighth)
      (chord/play mid 'eighth)
      (chord/play mid 'eighth))))

(define (nocturne-melody)
  (list
    (note 'Eb5 'dotted-quarter)   ; the anchor
    (note 'F5  'eighth)
    (note 'G5  'quarter)
    (note 'Bb5 'eighth)
    (note 'G5  'dotted-quarter)   ; settle back
    (note 'F5  'eighth)
    (note 'Eb5 'half)))

(define (nocturne-bar chord)
  (pedal/press)
  (parallel
    (nocturne-melody)
    (nocturne-left-hand chord 2))
  (pedal/release))

(define (nocturne-opening)
  (transport/tempo 60)
  (transport/meter 12 8)
  (with-dynamics 'p
    (nocturne-bar eflat-major)
    (nocturne-bar bb7)
    (nocturne-bar cm)
    (nocturne-bar ab-major)
    (nocturne-bar eflat-major)))
```

That program will not sound like Chopin. It has none of Chopin's ornamentation, none of his voice-leading care, none of his pedal artistry. What it has is the *shape* of the texture: the left hand rolls, the right hand sings, the pedal holds. If you take that shape and hand it to someone who has spent years learning to voice a melody over an accompaniment, you have the physical substrate that a nocturne is played on.

# Why this matters for the book

We are learning what music does, and one of the things it does is *hold a mood without hurrying*. The nocturne is the small form that holds. A great nocturne performance is thirty percent notes and seventy percent time — how long you wait, how much you breathe between phrases, how gently you release each chord. This is what pianists mean by *rubato*, which we will look at properly in Chapter 15. The nocturnes are the school of rubato. If you want to hear what a musician means when they say a phrase is 'played free,' listen to a great pianist take the opening of Op. 9 No. 2 or Op. 27 No. 2 and notice how the melody does not sit on the beat — how it enters a little late, arrives a little early, leans forward and pulls back — while the left hand keeps steady time underneath.

Rubato is one of the hardest musical qualities to notate. Chopin's scores mark it with *tempo rubato* at the start of certain passages, but he doesn't specify how much or where. The performer has to *find* it. Two great pianists playing the same nocturne make almost different pieces. That is not a bug of the form; it is the form.

# Tie back

Field invented the nocturne as a title. Chopin made it into a place. When we speak of a piece being 'like a Chopin nocturne,' we are saying something specific — that the piece sits in one mood, uses a right-hand melody over a wide left-hand accompaniment, feels improvised but is written out, and treats the small form as capable of holding as much weight as the large one.

The next chapter will look at three of the forms that hold weight in the *large* — sonata form, rondo, and theme and variations. We have already met sonata form (Rach 2's first movement) and rondo (Chopin's Op. 18 waltz). The chapter will name what we have already heard.

Alan Walker, *Fryderyk Chopin: A Life and Times* (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 2018). Standard modern biography.

For the Field origin of the term 'nocturne': see Grove entry above and Nicholas Temperley, *John Field* (Cambridge University Press, 1988).

Scores of Op. 9, Op. 18, Op. 27, and Op. 48 are all in the public domain and available on IMSLP.\"

Peirce: the nocturne as icon of a night (resemblance), of a mood (index), and of the genre (symbol).

\"In the last two chapters we have met three big musical shapes without naming them: Rachmaninoff's first movement was in sonata form, Chopin's Op. 18 waltz was a rondo, and the elaborate returns in Chopin's nocturnes hinted at a third shape called theme and variations. This chapter is where we stop and name them. Not so we can pin the pieces down like specimens, but so we can *hear* them when they arrive — so a listener can find their place in a piece the way a reader finds their place in a book.

There are three of them. There are more than three classical forms; there are also many baroque forms (fugue, ritornello, dance-suite) and many modern forms (through-composed, arch, moment form) and many non-Western forms that don't fit any of these words. But if you learn these three, you can navigate roughly two hundred years of Western classical music — from about 1750 to about 1900 — with a sense of where you are at any moment. That is worth the hour.

# Sonata form

The name is misleading. 'Sonata form' is not the form of a sonata (a sonata is a multi-movement piece for one or two instruments). It is the form used in the *first movement* of most sonatas, symphonies, string quartets, and concertos from about 1750 to about 1900. It could just as fairly be called 'first-movement form' or 'exposition-development-recapitulation form.' It got its name in the nineteenth century, from music theorists looking back at Haydn and Mozart's practice and giving it a label.

Here is the shape, in three parts, with the language a listener might use:

**Exposition** — the composer presents two themes. The first theme is in the piece's home key (say, C minor). It usually has a distinct character — often bold, energetic, or brooding, depending on the piece. Then there's a transition, which shifts to a new key. Then the second theme arrives in that new key (often the relative major, so E-flat major if the home key was C minor; or the dominant, so G major if the home key was C major). The second theme has a contrasting character — often more lyrical, more singing, more relaxed. The exposition ends with a closing section that stays in the new key and settles down. In a classical-era sonata the whole exposition is usually repeated once before moving on.

**Development** — this is where the composer *works on* the material. The themes get pulled apart into fragments; the fragments get transposed into different keys, combined with each other, rhythmically altered. The home key is deliberately avoided. Harmonic tension builds. The listener starts to feel *away from home*.

**Recapitulation** — both themes return, but now both in the home key. The first theme comes back where you expect it, in the home key it started in. The transition is rewritten so that instead of leading to a new key, it stays in the home key. The second theme therefore arrives in the home key — the same tune the exposition had, but now cast in the tonic. The closing material returns, also in home key. The piece feels resolved.

Sometimes there is a **coda** — a little tail after the recapitulation, extending and confirming the home key.

The whole shape is a departure and return. The exposition sets up a home and then travels; the development wanders far; the recapitulation returns home; the coda closes the door.

Why does this work on a listener who does not know the theory? Because it uses two facts about how the ear listens:

The ear notices when a new key arrives, even if the listener can't name it. Something changes in the color of the sound.

The ear remembers the home key from the opening and feels satisfaction when it returns.

Composers who used sonata form were trusting these two things about the ear. Haydn wrote roughly 106 symphonies, most of them with sonata-form first movements. Mozart wrote 41. Beethoven wrote 9, all with sonata-form first movements. By the time Brahms wrote his four symphonies in the 1870s and 1880s, the form was so worn into the shared listening ear that Brahms could play with it — delaying a recapitulation, disguising the return of the second theme — and the listener would *feel* the play without needing to be told.

Rachmaninoff, in 1900, was working in a form that was over a hundred and fifty years old. He wrote inside it as inside a room he knew.

# Rondo

If sonata form is a big journey with two themes and a lot of thinking, rondo is a small journey with one theme that keeps coming home.

The shape is a refrain (A) alternating with episodes (B, C, D...). Something like:

A — B — A — C — A — D — A

or

A — B — A — C — A — B — A

Each A is the refrain: the tune the piece is built around. Each letter that isn't A is a contrasting episode, in a different key or mood. The refrain returns after each episode, sometimes lightly varied, sometimes exactly as before.

Rondo is older than sonata form. Its ancestors are in baroque dance suites (the *rondeau*) and in medieval song forms (the refrain-verse pattern). By the classical era it was often used for the last movement of a sonata, symphony, or concerto — the finale — because its cyclical shape and repeated refrain make it feel celebratory and dance-like. You know where you are because you keep coming home.

Chopin's Op. 18 waltz is a rondo. Mozart's Piano Sonata in C major, K. 545 — the piece most kids play in their second year of lessons — has a rondo finale. The finale of Beethoven's Piano Concerto No. 5 (the 'Emperor') is a rondo. The finale of Rachmaninoff's Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini is a modified rondo.

The rondo trick that great composers use is this: when the refrain comes back the last time, they change something small — a new orchestration, a new dynamic level, a small harmonic swerve — that makes the last return *land differently* from the earlier ones. The audience has been trained by the repetitions to expect the same thing; the composer honors the expectation and undercuts it at the same time.

# Theme and variations

The third form is the oldest of the three by centuries, and in some ways the simplest. You state a theme. Then you play the theme again, changed. Then again, changed differently. Then again. And again. The theme is the same on every pass — it has the same phrase structure, usually the same harmonic outline, often the same length — but the surface (melody, texture, tempo, mode, register) is different each time.

The variation set has been used since the sixteenth century. In Elizabethan England a whole book called *My Ladye Nevells Booke* (1591) is full of virginal variations by William Byrd. In the baroque, Bach's Goldberg Variations (published 1741) is an aria followed by thirty variations followed by the aria again. In the classical era, Mozart wrote variation sets on popular songs; Beethoven's Diabelli Variations (1823) is a monumental set of thirty-three variations on a small waltz theme sent to him by the publisher Anton Diabelli, who had asked fifty composers each to write a single variation. Beethoven wrote thirty-three.

The variation form asks a different question from sonata form. Sonata form asks *how do we go somewhere and come back?* Variation form asks *how much can we say about the same thing?*

Some standard techniques inside a variation set:

**Melodic elaboration.** The theme's melody gets decorated with runs, trills, and ornaments while the harmonic structure stays the same. This is the technique Chopin uses inside a single nocturne when the tune returns embellished.

**Rhythmic transformation.** The theme's melodic notes get replaced with different rhythmic patterns while the pitches stay. A theme in quarter notes becomes a theme in triplets, or in dotted rhythms, or in syncopations.

**Change of mode.** A theme in major becomes the same theme in the parallel minor (or vice versa). The tune is instantly recognizable but its emotional temperature is inverted.

**Change of texture.** A theme played as a simple melody becomes the same theme as a fugue, or a chorale, or a chase between two voices.

**Change of tempo.** A brisk theme becomes a slow one, or vice versa.

**Change of register or instrument.** A theme played by piano becomes a theme played by orchestra, or the same instrument in a different register.

The best variation sets use these tools to reveal something the theme itself did not know. Bach's Goldberg thirtieth variation — the *Quodlibet* — layers two popular folk songs of Bach's day over the theme's bass line, so the same harmonic ground is holding up three different melodies at once. Beethoven's Diabelli Variations turn the modest waltz theme into philosophies of humor, of grief, of joy, of fugue, of parody, of transcendence, one after the other, over the course of nearly an hour.

# What we can do in Scheme

Let's write a small theme and one variation.

```scheme
;; Theme: 'Twinkle Twinkle Little Star' — the tune we grew up with,
;; which is also 'Ah! Vous dirai-je, maman', which Mozart used
;; for his K. 265 variations. In C major, 4/4.

(define twinkle-theme
  '((C4 quarter) (C4 quarter) (G4 quarter) (G4 quarter)
    (A4 quarter) (A4 quarter) (G4 half)
    (F4 quarter) (F4 quarter) (E4 quarter) (E4 quarter)
    (D4 quarter) (D4 quarter) (C4 half)))

(define (play-theme melody)
  (transport/tempo 120)
  (with-dynamics 'mf
    (for-each (lambda (note-and-duration)
                (note-play (car note-and-duration)
                           (cadr note-and-duration)))
              melody)))

;; Variation 1: the same tune, but each quarter note filled in
;; with a run of four sixteenth-notes going up.
;; (The 'melodic elaboration' technique.)

(define (fill-quarter-with-run note-symbol)
  ;; Turn a quarter-note into a four-sixteenth arpeggio up
  (let ((scale (scale-from-tonic note-symbol '(0 2 4 5))))
    (map (lambda (p) (list p 'sixteenth)) scale)))

(define twinkle-var1
  (apply append
    (map (lambda (note-and-duration)
           (let ((n (car note-and-duration))
                 (d (cadr note-and-duration)))
             (if (eq? d 'quarter)
                 (fill-quarter-with-run n)
                 (list note-and-duration))))
         twinkle-theme)))

(play-theme twinkle-theme)
(play-theme twinkle-var1)
```

That's the shape of the thing: state the theme; write a variation that keeps the harmonic ground and rhythmic outline but decorates the surface; state the variation. Mozart's K. 265 has twelve variations on 'Ah! Vous dirai-je, maman' — twelve different surfaces over the same twenty-four-bar frame. If you learn even one of them, the tune will never sound the same to you again.

# Why the three forms matter together

Sonata form, rondo, and theme and variations are three answers to the same question: *how do we make a piece of music that has enough coherence to be one thing, but enough variety to be interesting for five, or ten, or forty minutes?*

Sonata form answers by using two contrasting themes, taking us on a journey, and bringing us home. The variety is in the development; the coherence is in the return.

Rondo answers by having one memorable refrain that keeps coming back, with contrasting episodes between the returns. The variety is in the episodes; the coherence is in the refrain.

Theme and variations answers by staying on one theme the whole time, but showing it in many different lights. The variety is in the transformations; the coherence is in the theme itself.

Every large classical piece is some combination or hybrid of these three answers. A symphony often has a sonata-form first movement, a variation-form or slow second movement, a scherzo or minuet third movement, and a rondo or sonata-form finale — four movements, each answering the coherence-variety question differently, so that across the whole piece the listener has been shown many ways of being one thing that also unfolds. This is one of the deep reasons Western classical music from Haydn to Brahms works on people who have never studied it: the shapes are old, the shapes are shared, and the shapes hold the pieces together the way skeletons hold bodies together.

# Tie back

We started this chapter with three names — sonata form, rondo, theme and variations. We've filled them in with what they are, why they work, and what a listener notices when they arrive. Next chapter is the ear's toolkit: pitch, interval, and the harmonic series — the raw material that all these forms are built out of.

If you have been listening to any of the pieces from the last two chapters — Rach 2, the Chopin nocturnes and waltzes — see if you can name the form the next time you hear a movement start. You will not always be right (composers have been playing with the forms for two centuries), but you will start to notice.

For Diabelli Variations background: William Kinderman, *Beethoven's Diabelli Variations* (Oxford University Press, 1987).\"
