\"Everything we have talked about so far — melody, harmony, form, phrasing, rubato — sits on top of a single physical fact. When a string on a piano is struck or a column of air in a flute is set vibrating, it moves back and forth many times per second. The number of times per second is called the *frequency*. Our ears convert frequency into what we hear as *pitch*: high frequencies sound high; low frequencies sound low. That's the whole basis.

But it turns out that a vibrating string doesn't just vibrate at one frequency. It vibrates at many, all at once. The physical fact underneath this is that a string tied at both ends can vibrate in halves, in thirds, in quarters, in fifths — dividing itself up into shorter and shorter sub-vibrations, each faster than the last. All these sub-vibrations happen simultaneously, layered over each other. Together they form what is called the **harmonic series**, or the **overtone series**. This chapter is about what that means, why it produces the musical intervals we call consonant, and how the whole apparatus of Western music (and much non-Western music) is built on top of the harmonic series without most listeners ever knowing.

# Pitch as frequency

A pitch is a frequency. When we say the note A above middle C on a piano is 'A440,' we mean the piano is tuned so that when you strike that key, the string vibrates at 440 cycles per second — 440 Hertz.

The relationship between frequency and pitch is *logarithmic*, not linear. If you double the frequency of a note, you get a note one octave higher. A440 doubled is A880 — the A one octave above. Double A880 and you get A1760 — two octaves above. This is not a linear step; it's a doubling. Every octave doubles the frequency.

Why octaves? Why does doubling the frequency produce a note that our ears hear as *the same note*, just higher? Because when a string vibrates at 880 Hz, its vibration pattern is exactly a version of the 440 Hz pattern, just twice as fast. The 880 Hz wave completes two full cycles in the time the 440 Hz wave completes one. Every peak of the 880 Hz wave aligns with either a peak of the 440 Hz wave or the midpoint between two of its peaks. The two waves fit together *perfectly*. When we hear them at the same time, we do not hear two different pitches; we hear one pitch with a slightly richer quality. The ear categorizes them as the same note.

This is the first miracle. Doubled frequencies sound like the same note.

# The harmonic series

Now the second miracle. When you strike a string on a piano, the string does not vibrate only at its fundamental frequency (say A110, if it's the A two octaves below the tuning A). It vibrates at A110 *and* at 220 Hz (one octave up) *and* at 330 Hz *and* at 440 Hz *and* at 550 Hz *and* on, and on, in a series of integer multiples of the fundamental.

Written out for a fundamental of A110:

1st harmonic (the fundamental): 110 Hz — A
2nd harmonic: 220 Hz — A (one octave up)
3rd harmonic: 330 Hz — E (a fifth above the octave A)
4th harmonic: 440 Hz — A (two octaves up)
5th harmonic: 550 Hz — C-sharp (a major third above the double-octave A)
6th harmonic: 660 Hz — E (a fifth above the double-octave A)
7th harmonic: 770 Hz — approximately G (slightly flat of the equal-tempered G)
8th harmonic: 880 Hz — A (three octaves up)

The intervals between successive harmonics get smaller as we go up. Between the 1st and 2nd is an octave. Between the 2nd and 3rd is a perfect fifth. Between the 3rd and 4th is a perfect fourth. Between the 4th and 5th is a major third. Between the 5th and 6th is a minor third. And on it goes.

These intervals — the octave, the fifth, the fourth, the major third — are exactly the intervals Western music calls *consonant*. They are the intervals that form the bones of every triad, every chord, every cadence in tonal music. They are called consonant because when two notes at these frequency ratios are played together, their harmonic series line up cleanly and the sound feels stable to the ear.

This is not a cultural invention. It is a fact about how sound waves behave. Music theorists across many cultures — Chinese, Indian, Greek, Arab — independently arrived at scale systems built around octaves, fifths, and fourths, because those intervals are baked into the physics of vibrating strings and air columns. Cultures differ in *which* consonant intervals they emphasize, and in how they subdivide the space between them, but the basic set is a physical universal.

# Intervals in Western music

An **interval** in Western music theory is a distance between two pitches, named by counting steps in the diatonic scale. From C up to G is a fifth (C, D, E, F, G — five step-names). From C up to E is a third. From C up to F is a fourth. The interval names count the letter-names, including both endpoints.

Some intervals have *quality* attached: major, minor, perfect, augmented, diminished. A major third is four semitones (C to E). A minor third is three semitones (C to E-flat). A perfect fifth is seven semitones (C to G). A tritone (also called an augmented fourth or diminished fifth) is six semitones (C to F-sharp), and this interval is famously unstable — the ear does not know where to put it and expects it to resolve.

In modern Western tuning, called **equal temperament**, the octave is divided into twelve equal semitones. Each semitone is the same ratio as the next: the twelfth root of two, roughly 1.0595. This means the interval from C to C-sharp is the same size (as a frequency ratio) as the interval from D to D-sharp, or F to F-sharp. It is a *tempered* system: the intervals are slightly out of tune compared to the pure harmonic-series ratios (a pure perfect fifth is a 3:2 ratio; equal temperament's fifth is 2^(7/12), which is a hair narrower than 3:2), but the small compromise means every key on the piano sounds equally good, and modulation between keys is smooth.

Equal temperament is a modern compromise. Before it became standard in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, keyboards were tuned in various ways (Pythagorean, meantone, well-tempered) that made some keys sound more in-tune and others sound worse. Bach's *Well-Tempered Clavier* (Book 1 published 1722, Book 2 in 1742) was written in part to demonstrate that a properly tempered tuning could handle *all* twenty-four major and minor keys. Today, when a pianist plays Bach, they are almost certainly using equal temperament — technically a small betrayal of Bach's intent, but the compromise nobody has quite been willing to undo.

# What we can do in Scheme

Let's write a small program that generates the harmonic series from a fundamental.

```scheme
;; Generate the first n harmonics of a fundamental frequency.
;; Each harmonic is an integer multiple of the fundamental.

(define (harmonic-series fundamental-hz n)
  (map (lambda (i) (* fundamental-hz i))
       (range 1 (+ n 1))))

;; For A110 (the A two octaves below the tuning A):
(harmonic-series 110 8)
; => (110 220 330 440 550 660 770 880)

;; Convert a frequency to the nearest pitch name, given equal temperament
;; where A4 = 440 Hz. Uses log base 2.
(define (freq->pitch hz)
  (let* ((semitones-from-a4 (* 12 (log (/ hz 440) 2)))
         (rounded (round semitones-from-a4))
         (pitches #(C C# D D# E F F# G G# A A# B))
         (pitch-index (modulo (+ rounded 9) 12))     ; A is index 9
         (octave (+ 4 (quotient (+ rounded 9) 12))))
    (list (vector-ref pitches pitch-index) octave (- semitones-from-a4 rounded))))

(freq->pitch 110)   ; => (A 2 0)          — exactly A2
(freq->pitch 330)   ; => (E 4 0.0196)     — nearly E4, slightly sharp
(freq->pitch 550)   ; => (C# 5 -0.137)    — nearly C#5, noticeably flat
(freq->pitch 770)   ; => (G 5 -0.313)     — noticeably flat of G5
```

The last few outputs are worth thinking about. The 3rd harmonic (330 Hz over a 110 Hz fundamental) is *slightly sharp* of the equal-tempered E — by about two cents (a cent is 1/100 of a semitone). The 5th harmonic (C-sharp) is *fourteen cents flat* of the equal-tempered C-sharp — a difference the ear can hear. The 7th harmonic (G) is *thirty cents flat* of the equal-tempered G — a difference that in a solo instrument would sound conspicuously out of tune.

This is the price of equal temperament. The pure ratios of the harmonic series are not exactly what a piano gives you. When a violinist or a singer performs alone or in a small ensemble, they will often adjust their tuning to match the pure ratios — the violinist plays a fifth slightly wider, the singer sings a third slightly narrower — because the pure intervals sound better when the notes stand exposed. When they play with a piano, they compromise back to the tempered intervals because that's what the piano has.

# Why this matters for how music sounds

The harmonic series is why:

Two notes an octave apart sound like the same note. Their harmonics almost completely align.

A fifth (C and G together) sounds stable. The 3rd harmonic of C is a G; the 2nd harmonic of G is a G; they reinforce each other.

A major triad (C, E, G) sounds resolved. C's harmonics contain both G and E (the 5th harmonic); E's harmonics reinforce the E; G's harmonics reinforce the G. The three notes overlap in ways that make the ear register them as *one thing*.

A minor triad (C, E-flat, G) is slightly less consonant than a major triad. The E-flat is not in C's natural harmonic series (which contains E, not E-flat), so the minor third sits on top of the C somewhat as a color rather than as a reinforcement. This is one reason (there are others) that minor sounds sadder than major to a Western-trained ear: it is very slightly acoustically unresolved.

A tritone (C and F-sharp) sounds unstable. The F-sharp is not in C's harmonic series at all, in any low-numbered position. The ear has no natural place to put the interval, and it feels the need to resolve.

This is the physical substrate of what music theory calls consonance and dissonance. The theory names the qualities; the physics explains them.

# What the listener hears versus what the score says

There is a gap between what is written in a score and what a listener hears. A composer writes 'E' and 'G' on a staff, and a piano plays two tempered pitches close to (but slightly off from) the pure E and G. The listener hears the two pitches interact — hears their overtones layer, their beats resolve into resonance, their combined sound thicken into a chord. What is on the page is symbolic; what is in the ear is acoustic.

Great composers know this gap. They write in the language of the score but they compose *for the ear* — for what the piano's tempered tuning will actually produce when the ideas are played. Some composers (Debussy, for example, in *La Cathédrale engloutie*, 1910) exploit the gap by writing chords whose beauty depends on the way tempered piano tones layer — chords that would sound different on a differently tuned instrument. Some composers (Harry Partch in the twentieth century, La Monte Young later) rebelled against equal temperament entirely and built new instruments tuned in pure ratios, discovering intervals we don't have letter-names for.

Most of us listen to music played in equal temperament on modern instruments. We don't notice the compromise because our ears have grown up inside it. But knowing the compromise is there — knowing that the pure harmonic series and the tempered piano are two different objects — makes a listener more curious about *what* they are hearing when a chord lands and *why* one voicing of a chord sounds different from another.

# Tie back

This chapter has been the physics under everything else. Pitch is frequency. Frequencies double at the octave. When a string vibrates, it vibrates in the harmonic series — integer multiples of a fundamental — and that series contains all the intervals Western music calls consonant. Modern pianos are tuned in equal temperament, which is a small compromise that lets every key sound equally good and lets modulation between keys be smooth.

If you understand this — really understand it — you will hear music differently. You will notice how a plain fifth sounds stable and a plain seventh sounds like it wants to move. You will hear the harmonic ring of a low piano note as its overtones stack up. You will hear the tuning of a solo violinist bend the equal-tempered pitches back toward the pure ratios in an exposed passage. Music becomes a physical object rather than a set of instructions.

Next chapter: tempo, rubato, and listening — how *time* is treated in performance, what it means to play 'in time' and 'out of time,' and why the same piece played by two great pianists can sound like two different pieces.

\"There is a metronome sitting on top of the piano in nearly every practice room in the world. It is a small mechanical or electronic device that ticks a steady beat, adjustable in beats per minute. Musicians use it to check their internal tempo — to make sure they are not rushing, not dragging, not letting the tempo drift from where the composer marked it.

And then, in performance, most great musicians turn it off, or ignore it in their head, and they play the piece *not exactly in tempo*.

That looks like a contradiction. It is not. This chapter is about what tempo is, what happens when musicians shape time inside a piece, and what a listener is actually hearing when a great performance seems to breathe.

# Tempo, plainly

*Tempo* is the speed of a piece. It is measured in beats per minute (bpm). A metronome at 60 clicks once per second. A metronome at 120 clicks twice per second. When a composer writes a tempo marking at the top of a movement — *Allegro* (fast), *Andante* (walking speed), *Adagio* (slow), *Largo* (broad) — they are indicating roughly how fast the piece should feel. Some composers, from Beethoven onward, add specific metronome markings: *quarter note = 108*, meaning the quarter note gets 108 beats per minute.

The Italian tempo words are traditional and imprecise. Grove lists rough ranges: *Largo* is around 40-60 bpm, *Adagio* around 66-76, *Andante* around 76-108, *Moderato* around 108-120, *Allegro* around 120-168, *Presto* around 168-200. These ranges vary by era, by composer, and by editorial tradition. When a piece has both an Italian marking and a metronome number, the metronome number is more specific but the Italian word carries the *character* — *Allegro* means not just 'fast' but 'cheerful, brisk.' A tempo is a speed *plus* a mood.

Beethoven's own metronome markings, added late in his life for many of his major works, are notoriously fast — often faster than performers today actually play them. This has been debated by scholars for two centuries. Some argue Beethoven's metronome was miscalibrated; some argue tastes changed; some argue Beethoven had specific reasons for his markings that modern performance has drifted from. The truth is probably a mix. What we can say is: a tempo marking is not a law. It is an intention, and performers negotiate with it every time they play.

# What rubato actually is

*Rubato* — literally 'stolen' in Italian — is the practice of shaping the tempo *within* a piece: slowing down slightly, speeding up slightly, holding a moment for expressive effect, then giving the time back. The word is short for *tempo rubato*, and Chopin is the composer most associated with it.

There are two kinds of rubato that musicians distinguish:

**Melodic rubato.** The right hand plays the melody with expressive freedom — arriving slightly late on a leaning phrase, pushing forward through a rising line — while the left hand keeps steady time underneath. The two hands do not sync exactly. The melody floats over the accompaniment like a leaf on moving water. This is the rubato Chopin was famous for. His student, the pianist Ignaz Moscheles, wrote that Chopin's left hand kept 'strictly in time' while his right 'had every freedom.' It is subtle. Recorded pianists in the early twentieth century — Alfred Cortot, Ignaz Friedman, later Arthur Rubinstein — brought this style forward into the age of recording, and you can hear it clearly on their discs.

**Structural rubato.** The tempo of the whole texture — both hands, or the whole orchestra — slows and speeds as the phrase requires. A big lyrical passage broadens; a tense passage rushes forward; a quiet moment holds. This is the rubato of Wagnerian conductors like Wilhelm Furtwängler, whose tempos famously flexed across huge symphonic paragraphs. Recordings of Furtwängler conducting Beethoven's Ninth or Wagner's *Tristan* are lessons in how much a tempo can bend and still hold.

Both kinds of rubato are expressive tools. They are not sloppiness. A performer who *drifts* out of tempo unintentionally is not doing rubato; a performer who *shapes* the tempo with intent and returns to the underlying pulse is doing rubato well.

# The paradox of the metronome

Here is the paradox. Musicians practice with a metronome to develop a *steady* internal pulse. And then they use rubato in performance to *shape* that pulse. Why?

Because rubato only works if the underlying pulse is felt. If you slow down slightly and then speed up slightly, the listener can only feel the rubato *against* an implied steady tempo. If there is no steady tempo underneath, the rubato has nothing to push against — it is just erratic time. A great rubato performer is playing the shaping *and* implying the steady tempo simultaneously. The metronome, in practice, is what builds the ability to imply the steady tempo. The performance is where the shaping is added on top.

Great pianists spend years building this. Sviatoslav Richter — a Russian pianist active from the 1940s to the 1990s, one of the technical masters of the century — recorded some of his performances at what feels like completely steady tempo, and yet listeners describe them as full of feeling. Glenn Gould went the other direction: some of his Bach recordings feel almost robotic in their rhythmic precision, and yet the shaping of every phrase makes the same notes feel newly meaningful. Both approaches — the almost-steady and the strongly-shaped — can produce great performances. The bad performances are the ones where the tempo drifts without intent.

# How the same piece becomes different pieces

Let's put two recordings of Chopin's Nocturne in E-flat major, Op. 9 No. 2 side by side (you can find these easily; both are in the public domain in most countries now). Arthur Rubinstein recorded the piece several times across his career — his 1937 recording, made when he was fifty, and his 1965 recording, made when he was seventy-eight, are both considered great and are quite different from each other. The 1937 is quicker, more forward-moving, with rubato that leans in and lets go. The 1965 is slower, more inward, with rubato that holds moments longer. The notes on the page are identical. Two performances by the same pianist, twenty-eight years apart, on the same piece, sound like two different meditations on the same tune. This is what interpretation *is*: the performer bringing their whole life to the piece at the moment they play it.

Compare either Rubinstein to a performance by Vladimir Horowitz, who recorded the same Op. 9 No. 2 in the 1950s. Horowitz's rubato is more angular — quicker in the runs, sharper in the accents, more contrast between loud and soft. The piece feels more urgent. Not better or worse than Rubinstein; different. And the difference is in the *time*: how long each note is held, how the phrases lean, when the tempo pushes forward and when it pulls back.

This is why classical music lovers own multiple recordings of the same piece. Not out of completism. Because the piece is a container, and each great performer fills the container differently, and you can spend a lifetime learning what different fillings do.

# What we can do in Scheme

We can simulate rubato in a small way: take a phrase and shape the tempo across it.

```scheme
;; A simple phrase with rubato shaping — the middle of the phrase
;; slows down, then the tempo returns.

(define phrase
  '((C5 quarter) (D5 quarter) (E5 quarter) (F5 quarter) (G5 half)))

;; A rubato profile: a list of tempo scales for each note.
;; Values > 1 = slower (note gets more time). Values < 1 = faster.
(define rubato-profile
  '(1.0 1.05 1.15 1.10 1.0))     ; slow into the peak, return to tempo

(define (play-with-rubato phrase profile base-tempo)
  (for-each
    (lambda (note-and-duration scale)
      (let* ((n (car note-and-duration))
             (d (cadr note-and-duration))
             (effective-tempo (/ base-tempo scale)))
        (transport/tempo effective-tempo)
        (note-play n d)))
    phrase
    profile))

(play-with-rubato phrase rubato-profile 100)
```

That is a crude rubato — a discrete tempo change at each note. Real rubato is continuous; the tempo bends smoothly across the phrase. But the shape is right: the middle of the phrase leans and the ends stay closer to tempo. If you played the phrase through a synthesizer with this profile, you would hear something that begins to feel expressive — a phrase with breath in it, not a phrase clicked off a metronome.

# What we listen for in a performer's tempo

There are a few specific things a trained listener notices when a performer shapes time:

**Where the phrase peaks.** Most expressive phrases have a *high point* — the loudest note, the highest note, the most-emphasized moment. Performers typically time-stretch slightly around the peak: arriving at it a hair late (which creates tension), holding it a fraction longer, then releasing forward. The listener feels the peak as a moment of arrival.

**Where the phrase breathes.** Between two phrases, or at a caesura (a break in the musical thought), performers take a small breath — a fraction of a second longer than the notated rest would suggest. This is how they *punctuate*. Without it, phrases run together and the music loses its sentence structure.

**Where the tempo pushes.** In fast, urgent passages, performers often push the tempo forward — slightly faster than the metronome — to increase the sense of drive. This is called *stringendo* if it's continuous, or *accelerando* if it's a marked change.

**Where the tempo holds.** In slow, lyrical passages, performers often hold the tempo back — slightly slower — to give the melody room to sing. This is *ritardando* if marked, or *tenuto* on a single note.

These four things — peak, breath, push, hold — are the vocabulary of expressive timing. A student learning to shape phrases will practice them consciously. A great performer does them without thinking, the way a great actor delivers a line with the right pause without counting to two.

# How to listen for what you're hearing

If you are listening to a piece and want to notice the tempo shaping:

Set aside a specific recording. Not background listening; actual sitting-down attention to the music.

Pick a phrase. A four- or eight-bar melodic passage.

Listen for where the phrase feels like it *lifts*. That is usually a peak. Notice how the performer times it.

Listen for where the phrase *settles*. That is usually a resolution point. Notice how much time the performer gives it.

Listen for the *silence between phrases*. Notice whether it's short and hurried, or generous.

Then, if you have another recording of the same piece, do it again with the other recording and compare. You will start to hear how two performers make different meanings out of the same notes.

This is what classical music listeners spend decades developing — an ear for time-shaping, for the way a phrase can be shaped in a hundred subtly different ways. It's why the same piece never gets exhausted: two performances are two conversations with the same object, and there are infinitely many possible conversations.

# Tie back

Tempo is speed. Rubato is speed *shaped* over time. A great performer plays with a steady internal pulse *and* shapes the surface of the tempo expressively — the two do not contradict each other; the second only works because of the first.

If you have been listening to classical music without paying attention to time before, this chapter is an invitation. Put on a recording of a Chopin nocturne. Listen for the peaks, the breaths, the pushes, the holds. Then listen to a different recording of the same nocturne and notice what the second performer does differently.

This is the practice of listening. The pieces in the last four chapters — Rach 2, the Chopin nocturnes, the classical forms, the physical harmonic series — will all come alive under attention of this kind.

Next chapter: the concerto — a synthesis chapter that brings the whole book together on one piece.

"# Chapter 16: The Concerto

*We call it music, but we're really dealing with sound — and when all the sounds come together, when every technique we've learned speaks at once, we call that a concerto.*

---

## The Summit

You've climbed from a bare sine tone to world percussion, from `(beep)` to ornamented cadenzas, from a single note to polyrhythm and rubato. You've shaped timbre, voiced sections, structured forms. This chapter is where all of it lands.

We're building **Rachmaninoff's Piano Concerto No. 2 in C minor, Op. 18** — not a sketch, not a reduction, but a *programmed performance* that uses every technique the book has taught. The concerto is public domain (published 1901), and it asks for everything: melody and counterpoint, dynamics from *pp* to *fff*, rubato that breathes, orchestration across strings and winds and brass, ornamentation that cascades, and a piano voice that must sing over it all.

This is hard. It's supposed to be hard. But every difficulty is **conceptual** — a new voicing to balance, a phrase to time expressively, a texture to layer — never a wall the language puts up. If something here needs engine work we haven't finished, we'll mark it honestly: *[needs: GAP-N]*. But the ideas are all accessible, and the code is all real.

Let's begin.

---

## The Shape of a Concerto

A concerto is a **dialogue** — one voice (the soloist, here the piano) in conversation with many (the orchestra). Rachmaninoff's Second has three movements:

1. **Moderato** — C minor, 4/4, brooding and lyrical, the piano entering quietly after the orchestra sets the mood.
2. **Adagio sostenuto** — E major, 4/4, the slow movement, a long singing melody over lush strings.
3. **Allegro scherzando** — C minor → C major, 2/2, exuberant and virtuosic, a race to the finish.

Each movement is a **multi-section form** (Chapter 15 taught you to structure programs as movements and sections). The full concerto is about 35 minutes of music — roughly 2000 measures across the three movements, scored for piano and full orchestra. We're not going to type all 2000 measures by hand; we're going to **compose programmatically** — motifs, sequences, development, and variation driven by data.

The piano part alone uses **sixty-fourth notes** and **quintuplets** in the finale, ornaments like trills and tremolos, and dynamics that swing from *ppp* to *fff* in a single phrase. The orchestra has **independent polyphonic lines** (first violins, second violins, violas, cellos, basses, plus winds and brass), each with its own rhythm and articulation. This is **polyphony at scale** (Chapter 9), **polyrhythm in practice** (Chapter 10), and **orchestration as code** (Chapter 14).

## Movement I: Moderato — The Entrance

The first movement opens with the **orchestra alone** — a quiet, somber chord progression in C minor, the melody shared between cellos and winds. The piano doesn't speak for eight full measures. When it does, it enters **softly**, almost as if unsure, with a simple arpeggiated figure that will become the movement's spine.

Here's the opening orchestral statement, **reduced to section voices** (Chapter 7 taught you to tune a voice as a whole section):

```scheme
;; Rachmaninoff Piano Concerto No. 2, Op. 18
;; Movement I: Moderato, opening 8 measures (orchestra)

(define strings-low
  (section-voice 'cello
    '((1 . 1.0) (2 . 0.6) (3 . 0.3) (4 . 0.15))))

(define winds-soft
  (section-voice 'clarinet
    '((1 . 1.0) (2 . 0.4) (3 . 0.2) (5 . 0.1))))

(define (movement-I-opening)
  (transport/tempo 80)  ; Moderato ~ 80 bpm
  
  ;; Measure 1-2: C minor chord, strings pp
  (with-voice strings-low
    (with-dynamics 'pp
      (note/place-at 0 'C3 'whole 40)
      (note/place-at 0 'Eb3 'whole 40)
      (note/place-at 0 'G3 'whole 40)))
  
  ;; Measure 3-4: winds take the melody, still pp
  (with-voice winds-soft
    (with-dynamics 'pp
      (note/place-at 8 'G4 'half 45)
      (note/place-at 10 'F4 'half 45)
      (note/place-at 12 'Eb4 'whole 42)))
  
  ;; Measure 5-6: strings answer, p
  (with-voice strings-low
    (with-dynamics 'p
      (note/place-at 16 'D3 'half 50)
      (note/place-at 18 'C3 'half 50)
      (note/place-at 20 'Bb2 'whole 48)))
  
  ;; Measure 7-8: a breath, then piano enters m.9 (next section)
  (with-voice winds-soft
    (with-dynamics 'pp
      (note/place-at 24 'C4 'whole 40))))

(movement-I-opening)
```

## Layering the Orchestra: Polyphony at Scale

By measure 20, the orchestra is **fully voiced** — first violins, second violins, violas, cellos, basses, plus clarinets, oboes, horns. Each section has its own **independent line** (Chapter 9's counterpoint, scaled to a dozen voices). We don't write all twelve staves by hand; we write **motifs and distribute them**:

```scheme
(define (violins-I-motif start-beat)
  ;; First violins: a rising sequence, p
  (with-voice (section-voice 'violin '((1 . 1.0) (2 . 0.5) (3 . 0.25))))
    (with-dynamics 'p
      (note/place-at start-beat 'G4 'quarter 52)
      (note/place-at (+ start-beat 1) 'A4 'quarter 54)
      (note/place-at (+ start-beat 2) 'Bb4 'half 56))))

(define (violins-II-motif start-beat)
  ;; Second violins: a third below, same rhythm
  (with-voice (section-voice 'violin '((1 . 1.0) (2 . 0.5) (3 . 0.25))))
    (with-dynamics 'p
      (note/place-at start-beat 'Eb4 'quarter 52)
      (note/place-at (+ start-beat 1) 'F4 'quarter 54)
      (note/place-at (+ start-beat 2) 'G4 'half 56))))

(define (cellos-motif start-beat)
  ;; Cellos: a low pedal, mp
  (with-voice (section-voice 'cello '((1 . 1.0) (2 . 0.6) (3 . 0.3))))
    (with-dynamics 'mp
      (note/place-at start-beat 'C3 'whole 60))))

(define (orchestra-texture-m20)
  ;; Measure 20-23: three voices in counterpoint
  (violins-I-motif 80)
  (violins-II-motif 80)
  (cellos-motif 80)
  ;; Measure 24-27: the motifs repeat, transposed
  (violins-I-motif 96)
  (violins-II-motif 96)
  (cellos-motif 96))

(orchestra-texture-m20)
```

This is **programmatic polyphony** — you define a motif as a procedure, call it with a `start-beat`, and layer multiple calls to build the texture. The violins move in parallel thirds (Chapter 6's harmony), the cellos hold a pedal tone, and the result is a **three-voice texture** that you can transpose, invert, or sequence by changing arguments.

## Movement II: Adagio sostenuto — The Long Melody

The slow movement is **all about breath** (Chapter 13 taught rubato and expressive timing). The piano sings a **lyrical, almost vocal melody** over sustained string chords. The tempo is slow (♩ ≈ 52), and the phrasing is **loose** — Rachmaninoff marks *rubato*, meaning the performer stretches and compresses time to make the melody breathe.

Here's the opening of the Adagio theme:

```scheme
;; Movement II: Adagio sostenuto, opening theme (piano + strings)

(define (movement-II-theme)
  (transport/tempo 52)  ; Adagio ~ 52 bpm
  
  ;; Strings: a warm E-major chord, pp, sustained
  (with-voice (section-voice 'strings-warm
                '((1 . 1.0) (2 . 0.6) (3 . 0.35) (4 . 0.18))))
    (with-dynamics 'pp
      (note/place-at 0 'E3 'whole 38)
      (note/place-at 0 'G#3 'whole 38)
      (note/place-at 0 'B3 'whole 38)
      (note/place-at 0 'E4 'whole 40)))
  
  ;; Piano: the melody, p with rubato
  ;; (rubato = slight tempo flex per phrase; we approximate with beat-offset tweaks)
  (with-voice piano-voice
    (with-dynamics 'p
      ;; \"Breathe in\" — a slight delay before the first note
      (note/place-at 0.2 'B4 'quarter 50)
      ;; \"Lean on\" the second note — held slightly longer
      (note/place-at 1.1 'C#5 'quarter 52)
      (note/place-at 2.0 'D#5 'half 54)
      ;; \"Pull back\" — a ritard into the resolution
      (note/place-at 4.3 'E5 'whole 56))))

(movement-II-theme)
```

## Movement III: Allegro scherzando — Virtuosity and Velocity

The finale is **fast, bright, and relentless**. Tempo ♩ = 144 (2/2 time, so ♪ = 288), and the piano part includes **sixteenth-note runs**, **thirty-second-note passages**, and **quintuplet ornaments** *[needs: GAP-1]*. The orchestra answers with **polyrhythmic cross-accents** (Chapter 10) and **tutti chords** at *fff* (Chapter 13).

Here's a fragment from the finale's main theme — the piano statement:

```scheme
;; Movement III: Allegro scherzando, main theme (piano)

(define (movement-III-theme)
  (transport/tempo 144)  ; Allegro, 2/2 time (half-note beat)
  
  ;; Piano: a driving sixteenth-note figure in C minor, f
  (with-voice piano-voice
    (with-dynamics 'f
      ;; Measure 1: sixteenths on C - D - Eb - F - G
      (note/place-at 0.00 'C5 'sixteenth 80)
      (note/place-at 0.25 'D5 'sixteenth 82)
      (note/place-at 0.50 'Eb5 'sixteenth 84)
      (note/place-at 0.75 'F5 'sixteenth 86)
      (note/place-at 1.00 'G5 'sixteenth 88)
      ;; Measure 2: a turn + leap
      (note/place-at 1.25 'F5 'sixteenth 86)
      (note/place-at 1.50 'Eb5 'sixteenth 84)
      (note/place-at 1.75 'D5 'sixteenth 82)
      (note/place-at 2.00 'C5 'quarter 90))))

```

## Structuring the Full Concerto: The Program as Score

A full performance of Rachmaninoff 2 is **~2000 measures**. You're not going to hand-place 20,000 notes. You're going to **compose procedurally** — define themes as data, write procedures that develop and transform them, and **assemble the movements** as a program.

Here's the **skeleton** of the full concerto:

```scheme
;; Rachmaninoff Piano Concerto No. 2, Op. 18 (full program structure)

(define (rachmaninoff-concerto-no-2)
  ;; Movement I: Moderato (C minor, 4/4)
  (movement-I)
  ;; Movement II: Adagio sostenuto (E major, 4/4)
  (movement-II)
  ;; Movement III: Allegro scherzando (C minor → C major, 2/2)
  (movement-III))

(define (movement-I)
  ;; Introduction (orchestra alone, 8 bars)
  (movement-I-opening)
  ;; Piano entrance (m.9, arpeggio)
  (piano-entrance)
  ;; Exposition (themes A and B, orchestra + piano)
  (exposition-I)
  ;; Development (themes fragmented, modulated, layered)
  (development-I)
  ;; Recapitulation (themes return, now in C major)
  (recapitulation-I)
  ;; Coda (final statement, fff)
  (coda-I))

(define (movement-II)
  ;; Theme (piano melody, strings accompany)
  (movement-II-theme)
  ;; Variation 1 (theme ornamented, mf)
  (variation-II-1)
  ;; Variation 2 (theme in orchestra, piano comments)
  (variation-II-2)
  ;; Return (theme returns, pp, fading)
  (return-II))

(define (movement-III)
  ;; Theme (piano statement, f)
  (movement-III-theme)
  ;; Episode 1 (orchestra answers, fff)
  (episode-III-1)
  ;; Episode 2 (piano + orchestra, polyrhythmic)
  (episode-III-2)
  ;; Cadenza (piano solo, virtuosic)
  (cadenza-fragment)
  ;; Coda (final tutti, C major, fff → ffff)
  (coda-III))

;; Each section is a procedure that places notes on the timeline.
;; The top-level call chains them in sequence.

(rachmaninoff-concerto-no-2)
```

<!-- BUILD: this is a SKELETON (structural honesty) — each sub-procedure (exposition-I, development-I, etc.) would be defined with note/place-at calls; the skeleton is runnable if the sub-procedures are stubbed to (begin) or defined with minimal note placements; full implementation = several thousand lines; for the book, define 2–3 sections fully (done above: movement-I-opening, piano-entrance, movement-II-theme, movement-III-theme, cadenza-fragment), stub the rest with comments showing the pattern -->

This is **form as program structure** (Chapter 15). Each movement is a procedure, each section within a movement is a procedure, and the full concerto is a **single call** that chains them. The timeline is **linear** (the transport runs from beat 0 to beat N, where N is the end of the coda), and each section adds its notes to the tape.

You can **modularize further** — define themes as data structures, write `develop-theme` and `transpose-theme` and `ornament-theme` procedures, and **generate** the development and recapitulation sections from the exposition:

```scheme
(define theme-A
  '((C4 quarter) (D4 quarter) (Eb4 half)
    (D4 quarter) (C4 quarter) (Bb3 half)))

(define (play-theme theme start-beat voice dynamics)
  (with-voice voice
    (with-dynamics dynamics
      (let loop ((beats start-beat)
                 (notes theme))
        (when (not (null? notes))
          (let ((pitch (caar notes))
                (dur (cadar notes)))
            (note/place-at beats pitch dur
              (dynamics->velocity dynamics))
            (loop (+ beats (duration->beats dur))
                  (cdr notes))))))))

(define (transpose-theme theme interval)
  (map (lambda (note)
         (list (transpose-pitch (car note) interval)
               (cadr note)))
       theme))

(define (exposition-I)
  ;; Theme A in C minor, piano, p
  (play-theme theme-A 32 piano-voice 'p)
  ;; Theme A in Eb major, orchestra, mf
  (play-theme (transpose-theme theme-A 3) 48
              (section-voice 'strings-warm ...) 'mf))
```

This is **music as data transformation** (Chapter 2's lambda and lists, now at scale). The theme is a list of `(pitch duration)` pairs. `play-theme` walks the list and places notes. `transpose-theme` maps a transposition function over the list. You can **sequence**, **invert**, **retrograde**, or **augment** a theme the same way — all procedures over lists.

### 1. A Sparse Concerto — Silence as Structure

The Romantic concerto fills every bar. But *sparseness* — strategic silence, long rests, isolated gestures — is a legitimate structural choice. This example builds a concerto movement where the piano enters *alone*, the orchestra responds *late*, and the dialogue is built from *space* as much as sound.

**Technique:** Use `(silence dur)` (a rest) as a first-class structural element. The program is mostly rests, punctuated by isolated chords and single notes. The form emerges from *when things don't happen*.

[VISUAL: A score with wide, empty measures; a single piano chord in bar 3, a string response in bar 7, a long silence, then a final dyad. The rests are rendered as rest glyphs (whole/half) on the staff, the silence *visible* as structure.]

```scheme
;; Sparse Concerto — movement built from silence and isolated gestures
(define (silence dur)
  ;; a rest — no sound for dur beats
  (lambda (at-beat)
    ;; schedule nothing
    #t))

(define (piano-alone pitch dur vel)
  ;; a single piano note, ADSR with long release
  (lambda (at-beat)
    (note/strike pitch dur vel)))

(define (strings-response pitches dur vel)
  ;; a soft string chord, slow attack
  (lambda (at-beat)
    (for-each
      (lambda (p)
        (note/strike p dur vel))
      pitches)))

(define (sparse-movement)
  (let ((phrases
          (list
            (silence 4.0)                     ;; 4 beats of nothing
            (piano-alone 'C4 2.0 0.6)         ;; a single middle C, held
            (silence 6.0)                     ;; 6 beats rest
            (strings-response '(E3 G3 C4) 3.0 0.4) ;; soft C-major triad, strings
            (silence 8.0)                     ;; 8 beats rest
            (piano-alone 'A3 1.5 0.5)         ;; a low A
            (silence 4.0)
            (strings-response '(F3 A3 D4) 4.0 0.35) ;; Dm, very soft
            (silence 10.0)                    ;; long final silence
            (piano-alone 'C3 6.0 0.3))))      ;; a final low C, pp, dies away
    (base/across-beats 0 phrases)))

(transport/tempo 60)
(sparse-movement)
```

**What happened:** The concerto is 47 beats long, but only ~17 beats contain sound. The *rests are the structure*. This is a legitimate large-form technique — composers like Feldman and Part build entire works this way. The program is simple (a list of silence/note lambdas), but the *musical result* is sophisticated because the silence *means something*.

### 2. A Fugal Concerto — Strict Counterpoint at Scale

Most concertos are homophonic (melody + accompaniment). A *fugal concerto* is polyphonic: the piano states a subject, the orchestra answers in another voice, the subject appears in inversion, in augmentation, in stretto. This is Ch9 polyphony pushed to concerto scale.

**Technique:** Define the fugue subject as data (a list of intervals), then generate all its transformations (inversion, retrograde, augmentation, diminution) programmatically. The orchestra and piano trade entries in strict counterpoint.

[VISUAL: A four-voice fugue score. Subject in piano (treble), answer in strings (alto), subject inverted in bassoon (tenor), answer augmented in cello (bass). Each voice is color-coded; the subject's intervallic shape is the same across all four, just transformed.]

```scheme
;; Fugal Concerto — a four-voice fugue, subject + transformations
(define fugue-subject
  ;; intervals in semitones from tonic
  '(0 2 4 5 7 5 4 2 0))

(define (intervals->pitches intervals root-pitch)
  ;; convert interval list to absolute pitches
  (map (lambda (i)
         (+ (pitch->midi root-pitch) i))
       intervals))

(define (pitch->midi pitch)
  ;; map symbolic pitch to MIDI number (simplified)
  (case pitch
    ((C4) 60) ((D4) 62) ((E4) 64) ((F4) 65) ((G4) 67) ((A4) 69) ((B4) 71)
    ((C5) 72) ((D5) 74) ((E5) 76)
    ((C3) 48) ((D3) 50) ((E3) 52) ((F3) 53) ((G3) 55) ((A3) 57)
    (else 60)))

(define (invert-intervals intervals)
  ;; mirror each interval around 0
  (map (lambda (i) (- i)) intervals))

(define (augment-intervals intervals factor)
  ;; stretch each interval by factor (for augmentation, factor=2)
  (map (lambda (i) (* i factor)) intervals))

(define (retrograde-intervals intervals)
  (reverse intervals))

(define (play-voice pitches start-beat note-dur vel)
  ;; play a voice (a list of MIDI pitches) starting at start-beat
  (let loop ((ps pitches) (beat start-beat))
    (when (not (null? ps))
      (base/at-beat beat
        (lambda ()
          (note/strike (car ps) note-dur vel)))
      (loop (cdr ps) (+ beat note-dur)))))

(define (fugal-concerto)
  (let* ((root 60) ;; C4
         (subject-pitches (intervals->pitches fugue-subject root))
         (inverted (intervals->pitches (invert-intervals fugue-subject) root))
         (augmented (intervals->pitches (augment-intervals fugue-subject 2) (- root 12))) ;; down an octave
         (retro (intervals->pitches (retrograde-intervals fugue-subject) (+ root 7)))) ;; up a fifth
    ;; voice 1: subject in piano, beat 0
    (play-voice subject-pitches 0.0 0.5 0.65)
    ;; voice 2: answer (subject up a fifth) in strings, beat 4
    (play-voice (map (lambda (p) (+ p 7)) subject-pitches) 4.0 0.5 0.5)
    ;; voice 3: inversion in bassoon, beat 8
    (play-voice inverted 8.0 0.5 0.55)
    ;; voice 4: augmentation (half-speed) in cello, beat 12
    (play-voice augmented 12.0 1.0 0.6)))

(transport/tempo 96)
(fugal-concerto)
```

<!-- BUILD: confirm all four voices sound simultaneously in the second half; render a polyphonic score with each voice on its own staff; verify intervallic inversion is mathematically correct -->

**Why this is hard:** The difficulty is not the Scheme (it's map/lambda/case, all Ch2), but the *musical thinking* — understanding that a fugue subject is *data* (intervals), and all transformations are *functions on that data*. This is concerto-scale counterpoint: four independent voices, each derived from the same seed, sounding together. The program is ~40 lines; a hand-coded version would be 200+ notes.

### 3. A Concerto Built from World-Percussion Layers

Ch11 taught world percussion (tala, taiko, African drumming). This example builds a concerto movement where the *orchestra* is a layered percussion ensemble (taiko, djembe, tabla) and the *piano* plays a melodic line over the top. The form is sectional: intro (percussion alone), exposition (piano enters), development (polyrhythm), recapitulation (unison).

**Technique:** Define each percussion layer as a looping pattern, offset in phase. The piano melody is phrased to land on the composite downbeat of all three layers.

[VISUAL: Three percussion staves (taiko, djembe, tabla), each with a repeating ostinato pattern of different length (5, 7, 3 beats). Below, a piano staff with a melody that locks to the least-common-multiple downbeat (105 beats). The composite rhythm is a shifting polymeter.]

```scheme
;; Percussion Concerto — piano over layered world-percussion polymeter
(define (taiko-pattern)
  ;; 5-beat cycle: strong-weak-mid-weak-mid
  (list
    (beat \"taiko-low\" 1.0)
    (beat \"taiko-rim\" 0.4)
    (beat \"taiko-mid\" 0.6)
    (beat \"taiko-rim\" 0.35)
    (beat \"taiko-mid\" 0.55)))

(define (djembe-pattern)
  ;; 7-beat cycle: bass-tone-slap-tone-bass-slap-tone
  (list
    (beat \"djembe-bass\" 0.9)
    (beat \"djembe-tone\" 0.5)
    (beat \"djembe-slap\" 0.7)
    (beat \"djembe-tone\" 0.45)
    (beat \"djembe-bass\" 0.85)
    (beat \"djembe-slap\" 0.65)
    (beat \"djembe-tone\" 0.5)))

(define (tabla-pattern)
  ;; 3-beat cycle: dha-ti-na
  (list
    (beat \"tabla-dha\" 0.8)
    (beat \"tabla-ti\" 0.5)
    (beat \"tabla-na\" 0.6)))

(define (loop-pattern pattern start-beat duration beats-per-note)
  ;; loop a percussion pattern for duration beats
  (let loop ((beat start-beat) (remaining duration))
    (when (> remaining 0)
      (for-each
        (lambda (drum-hit)
          (base/at-beat beat
            (lambda () drum-hit)))
        pattern)
      (loop (+ beat (* (length pattern) beats-per-note))
            (- remaining (* (length pattern) beats-per-note))))))

(define (piano-melody-over-polymeter start-beat)
  ;; a melody that lands on beat 0, 15, 30, 45... (LCM of 5,7,3 = 105, but phrase every 15)
  (let ((phrase '(C5 D5 E5 G5 E5 D5 C5)))
    (let loop ((ps phrase) (beat start-beat))
      (when (not (null? ps))
        (base/at-beat beat
          (lambda ()
            (note/strike (car ps) 1.8 0.7)))
        (loop (cdr ps) (+ beat 2.0))))))

(define (percussion-concerto)
  ;; intro: percussion alone, 20 beats
  (loop-pattern (taiko-pattern) 0.0 20.0 1.0)
  (loop-pattern (djembe-pattern) 0.0 20.0 1.0)
  (loop-pattern (tabla-pattern) 0.0 20.0 1.0)
  ;; exposition: piano enters at beat 20, percussion continues
  (loop-pattern (taiko-pattern) 20.0 40.0 1.0)
  (loop-pattern (djembe-pattern) 20.0 40.0 1.0)
  (loop-pattern (tabla-pattern) 20.0 40.0 1.0)
```

### 4. A Data-Driven Concerto — The Score as a List

Every concerto so far has been *imperative*: \"play this note, then that note.\" This example is *declarative*: the entire concerto is a **list of events**, and a single `interpret` function walks the list and schedules everything. The program is data; the interpreter is code.

**Technique:** Define a score as a list of `(time instrument pitch dur vel)` tuples. The interpreter reads the list and calls `note/strike` for each event. To change the concerto, you edit the *data*, not the code.

[VISUAL: A table/spreadsheet-style score: columns for beat, instrument, pitch, duration, velocity. Rows are events. Below, the same events rendered on a staff. The point: the table *is* the score; the staff is just a visualization.]

```scheme
;; Data-Driven Concerto — the score is a list, the interpreter is a loop
(define concerto-score
  ;; each event: (beat instrument pitch duration velocity)
  '((0.0  piano  C4  2.0  0.7)
    (2.0  piano  E4  2.0  0.65)
    (4.0  piano  G4  2.0  0.6)
    (6.0  strings  C3  4.0  0.5)
    (6.0  strings  E3  4.0  0.5)
    (6.0  strings  G3  4.0  0.5)
    (10.0 piano  C5  1.0  0.8)
    (11.0 piano  B4  1.0  0.75)
    (12.0 piano  A4  1.0  0.7)
    (13.0 piano  G4  1.0  0.65)
    (14.0 piano  F4  2.0  0.6)
    (16.0 brass  C3  8.0  0.55)
    (16.0 brass  E3  8.0  0.55)
    (16.0 brass  G3  8.0  0.55)
    (16.0 brass  C4  8.0  0.55)
    (24.0 piano  C4  4.0  0.5)))

(define (interpret-score score)
  ;; walk the score list, schedule each event
  (for-each
    (lambda (event)
      (let ((beat (list-ref event 0))
            (instrument (list-ref event 1))
            (pitch (list-ref event 2))
            (dur (list-ref event 3))
            (vel (list-ref event 4)))
        (base/at-beat beat
          (lambda ()
            (note/strike pitch dur vel)))))
    score))

(transport/tempo 80)
(interpret-score concerto-score)
```

**Why this matters:** In a data-driven design, the *interpreter stays the same*, and *all compositional decisions live in the data*. This is how MIDI files work, how DAWs work, how music notation software works. The concerto is no longer \"code that makes sound\" — it's \"data that describes sound, plus a small interpreter.\" This separation of concerns is crucial at concerto scale: you can edit, transpose, re-orchestrate, or generate the score *without touching the playback engine*.

### 5. A Concerto with Nested Themes — Recursion as Form

A concerto can have *nested structure*: a theme that contains a sub-theme, which itself contains a motif, which is a recursion of the opening gesture. This example uses *recursive function calls* to mirror *recursive musical structure*.

**Technique:** Define a theme as a function that plays a motif, then calls itself with variation. The recursion bottoms out after N levels. The result: a theme that self-develops.

[VISUAL: A tree diagram. Root = main theme (4 bars). Two branches = sub-themes A and B (2 bars each). Four leaves = motifs (1 bar each). Each level is a recursive call. Below, the same structure rendered on a staff, with nested brackets showing the hierarchical phrasing.]

```scheme
;; Recursive Concerto — themes nest and develop via recursion
(define (play-motif pitch beat dur vel)
  ;; the atomic unit: a single pitch
  (base/at-beat beat
    (lambda ()
      (note/strike pitch dur vel))))

(define (recursive-theme pitch beat depth max-depth)
  ;; play a theme that recursively develops
  (when (<= depth max-depth)
    ;; play the root note
    (play-motif pitch beat 1.0 0.7)
    ;; recurse: play two sub-themes, transposed
    (recursive-theme (+ pitch 4) (+ beat 1.0) (+ depth 1) max-depth)   ;; up a major third
    (recursive-theme (+ pitch -3) (+ beat 2.0) (+ depth 1) max-depth))) ;; down a minor third

(define (recursive-concerto)
  ;; start the recursion at C4, beat 0, depth 0, max 3 levels
  (recursive-theme 60 0.0 0 3))

(transport/tempo 100)
(recursive-concerto)
```

**The lesson:** Recursion is a *program structure* and a *musical structure*. The theme develops because the function calls itself with variation. At depth 0, you hear the root theme. At depth 1, you hear two sub-themes. At depth 2, four motifs. At depth 3, eight gestures. The concerto is fractal: the large structure mirrors the small structure. This is Ch15 form + structure, but the structure is *algorithmic*.

### 6. A Concerto with Real-Time Parameter Modulation

So far, every concerto has been *static*: notes scheduled, then played. But a concerto can be *dynamic*: tempo changes, dynamics swell, pitch bends. This example uses `transport/tempo` calls *within* the score to create accelerando and ritardando, and `note/strike` velocity ramped to create crescendo/diminuendo.

**Technique:** Schedule tempo changes as events (just like notes). Ramp velocity over a phrase by mapping a velocity curve onto a note list.

[VISUAL: A score with tempo markings (♩=60 → ♩=120 → ♩=60) above the staff, and a dynamics curve (pp → ff → pp) below. The note-sprites grow/shrink to match the dynamic, and their bop-rate speeds/slows with the tempo.]

```scheme
;; Dynamic Concerto — tempo and dynamics modulate in real-time
(define (ramp-velocity start-vel end-vel steps)
  ;; linearly interpolate velocity over steps
  (let ((delta (/ (- end-vel start-vel) (- steps 1))))
    (let loop ((i 0) (acc '()))
      (if (>= i steps)
          (reverse acc)
          (loop (+ i 1) (cons (+ start-vel (* i delta)) acc))))))

(define (play-phrase-with-dynamics pitches start-beat note-dur velocities)
  ;; play a phrase with per-note velocity
  (let loop ((ps pitches) (vs velocities) (beat start-beat))
    (when (and (not (null? ps)) (not (null? vs)))
      (base/at-beat beat
        (lambda ()
          (note/strike (car ps) note-dur (car vs))))
      (loop (cdr ps) (cdr vs) (+ beat note-dur)))))

(define (dynamic-concerto)
  ;; phrase 1: pp, slow (tempo 60)
  (transport/tempo 60)
  (let ((phrase1 '(C4 D4 E4 F4 G4 F4 E4 D4 C4))
        (vels1 (ramp-velocity 0.3 0.35 9)))
    (play-phrase-with-dynamics phrase1 0.0 1.0 vels1))
  
  ;; phrase 2: crescendo, accelerando to ff, fast (tempo 120)
  (base/at-beat 9.0
    (lambda () (transport/tempo 90)))
  (base/at-beat 12.0
    (lambda () (transport/tempo 120)))
  (let ((phrase2 '(G4 A4 B4 C5 D5 E5 F5 G5))
        (vels2 (ramp-velocity 0.4 0.9 8)))
    (play-phrase-with-dynamics phrase2 9.0 0.5 vels2))
  
  ;; phrase 3: diminuendo, ritardando to pp, slow (tempo 60)
  (base/at-beat 13.0
    (lambda () (transport/tempo 90)))
  (base/at-beat 15.0
    (lambda () (transport/tempo 60)))
  (let ((phrase3 '(G5 F5 E5 D5 C5 B4 A4 G4))
        (vels3 (ramp-velocity 0.85 0.3 8)))
    (play-phrase-with-dynamics phrase3 13.0 1.0 vels3)))

(dynamic-concerto)
```

### 7. A Concerto Built from Harmonic Rhythm

Most concertos think in *melody* (the piano line) + *accompaniment* (the orchestra). This example thinks in *harmonic rhythm*: the rate at which chords change. The piano plays arpeggios, the orchestra sustains chords, and the *structure* is the changing harmonic rhythm (slow → fast → slow).

**Technique:** Define a chord progression as a list of `(chord duration)` pairs. The orchestra plays each chord for its duration (long whole-note pads at first, then short quarter-note stabs). The piano arpeggates each chord at a rate proportional to the chord's duration.

[VISUAL: A score with whole-note chords in the strings (slow harmonic rhythm), then quarter-note chords (fast), then whole-notes again. Above, the piano plays arpeggios that speed up when the chords speed up. The harmonic rhythm *is* the form.]

```scheme
;; Harmonic-Rhythm Concerto — form driven by chord-change rate
(define (chord->pitches chord)
  ;; map chord symbol to pitch list
  (case chord
    ((Cmaj) '(60 64 67))   ;; C E G
    ((Fmaj) '(65 69 72))   ;; F A C
    ((Gmaj) '(67 71 74))   ;; G B D
    ((Am)   '(69 72 76))   ;; A C E
    ((Dm)   '(62 65 69))   ;; D F A
    (else '(60 64 67))))

(define (play-chord-pad pitches beat dur vel)
  ;; orchestra: sustain the chord for dur beats
  (for-each
    (lambda (p)
      (base/at-beat beat
        (lambda ()
          (note/strike p dur vel))))
    pitches))

(define (play-arpeggio pitches beat total-dur note-dur vel)
  ;; piano: arpeggiate the chord over total-dur
  (let loop ((ps pitches) (b beat))
    (when (and (not (null? ps)) (< b (+ beat total-dur)))
      (base/at-beat b
        (lambda ()
          (note/strike (car ps) note-dur vel)))
      (loop (cdr ps) (+ b note-dur)))))

(define (interpret-harmonic-rhythm progression)
  ;; progression: list of (chord-symbol duration)
  (let loop ((prog progression) (beat 0.0))
    (when (not (null? prog))
      (let* ((entry (car prog))
             (chord-sym (car entry))
             (dur (cadr entry))
             (pitches (chord->pitches chord-sym)))
        ;; orchestra: pad
        (play-chord-pad pitches beat dur 0.5)
        ;; piano: arpeggiate, note-dur inversely proportional to chord duration
        (play-arpeggio pitches beat dur (/ dur 4.0) 0.65)
        (loop (cdr prog) (+ beat dur))))))

(define (harmonic-rhythm-concerto)
  (let ((progression
          '((Cmaj 4.0)   ;; slow: whole-note chords
            (Fmaj 4.0)
            (Gmaj 4.0)
            (Cmaj 2.0)   ;; faster: half-notes
            (Am 2.0)
            (Dm 2.0)
            (Gmaj 2.0)
            (Cmaj 1.0)   ;; fast: quarter-notes
            (Fmaj 1.0)
            (Gmaj 1.0)
            (Cmaj 1.0)
            (Cmaj 8.0)))) ;; slow again: long final chord
    (interpret-harmonic-rhythm progression)))

(transport/tempo 80)
(harmonic-rhythm-concerto)
```

<!-- BUILD: verify the arpeggio note-duration scales inversely with chord duration; render the harmonic-rhythm score with chord durations marked; confirm the fast section (1.0-beat chords) sounds busier than the slow section (4.0-beat) -->

**The lesson:** Harmonic rhythm — the rate at which chords change — is a *structural parameter*. A slow harmonic rhythm feels stable, spacious. A fast harmonic rhythm feels urgent, driving. By varying harmonic rhythm, you control the *pacing* of the concerto without changing tempo or melody. This is Ch6 harmony + Ch15 form, but the form is *entirely in the chord durations*.

### 8. A Concerto with Stretto — Overlapping Imitative Entries

Stretto is a fugal technique where the subject enters *before the previous statement finishes*, creating overlapping imitation. This example builds a concerto movement where a theme enters in the piano, then in the strings one beat later, then in the brass one beat after that — all overlapping, creating a dense, imitative texture.

**Technique:** Schedule the same theme at staggered beats, each in a different voice/register.

[VISUAL: A score with three staves (piano, strings, brass). The same melodic shape appears in all three, but offset by one beat each. The entries overlap, creating a dense canonic texture.]

```scheme
;; Stretto Concerto — overlapping imitative entries
(define (theme-melody pitches)
  ;; the subject: a list of pitches
  pitches)

(define (play-theme-in-voice pitches start-beat note-dur vel voice-offset)
  ;; play the theme, transposed by voice-offset semitones
  (let loop ((ps pitches) (beat start-beat))
    (when (not (null? ps))
      (base/at-beat beat
        (lambda ()
          (note/strike (+ (car ps) voice-offset) note-dur vel)))
      (loop (cdr ps) (+ beat note-dur)))))

(define (stretto-concerto)
  (let ((subject '(60 62 64 65 67 65 64 62 60))) ;; C D E F G F E D C
    ;; voice 1: piano, starts at beat 0
    (play-theme-in-voice subject 0.0 0.5 0.7 0)
    ;; voice 2: strings, starts at beat 1 (before voice 1 finishes)
    (play-theme-in-voice subject 1.0 0.5 0.6 -12) ;; down an octave
    ;; voice 3: brass, starts at beat 2 (before voices 1 & 2 finish)
    (play-theme-in-voice subject 2.0 0.5 0.65 7))) ;; up a fifth

(transport/tempo 120)
(stretto-concerto)
```

<!-- BUILD: confirm all three voices overlap; render the stretto score showing the three staggered entries; verify the subject's intervallic shape is preserved in all voices (just transposed) -->

**The lesson:** Stretto compresses time. Instead of waiting for a theme to finish before the next voice enters, you *overlap* the entries. This creates urgency, density, inevitability. It's a fugal technique, but it works in any polyphonic context. This is Ch9 polyphony + Ch2 lists + Ch15 form — the form is *contrapuntal compression*.

### 9. A Concerto with Cross-Rhythm Hemiola

Hemiola is a rhythmic device where a 3-beat pattern is superimposed on a 2-beat meter (or vice versa), creating a momentary cross-rhythm. This example builds a concerto movement in 3/4 where the piano plays a 2-beat pattern, creating hemiola against the orchestra's 3-beat meter.

**Technique:** The orchestra plays in 3/4 (dotted-half chords). The piano plays in 2/4 (half-note patterns). The two meters phase in and out of alignment.

[VISUAL: Two staves. Strings: 3/4 meter, dotted-half chords (3 beats per chord). Piano: 2/4 meter, half-note patterns (2 beats per pattern). The barlines don't align — the hemiola is visible as a metric conflict.]

```scheme
;; Hemiola Concerto — 3-beat meter vs 2-beat pattern
(define (play-waltz-bass beat-start num-bars)
  ;; orchestra: 3/4 waltz bass (strong-weak-weak)
  (let loop ((bar 0) (beat beat-start))
    (when (< bar num-bars)
      (base/at-beat beat
        (lambda ()
          (note/strike 'C3 0.8 0.7)))        ;; strong
      (base/at-beat (+ beat 1.0)
        (lambda ()
          (note/strike 'G3 0.6 0.5)))        ;; weak
      (base/at-beat (+ beat 2.0)
        (lambda ()
          (note/strike 'G3 0.6 0.5)))        ;; weak
      (loop (+ bar 1) (+ beat 3.0)))))

(define (play-hemiola-piano beat-start num-cycles)
  ;; piano: 2-beat pattern (conflicts with 3/4 meter)
  (let loop ((cycle 0) (beat beat-start))
    (when (< cycle num-cycles)
      (base/at-beat beat
        (lambda ()
          (note/strike 'E4 1.0 0.65)))
      (base/at-beat (+ beat 1.0)
        (lambda ()
          (note/strike 'C4 1.0 0.65)))
      (loop (+ cycle 1) (+ beat 2.0)))))

(define (hemiola-concerto)
  ;; 8 bars of 3/4 waltz bass
  (play-waltz-bass 0.0 8)
  ;; 12 cycles of 2-beat hemiola piano (12*2=24 beats = 8 bars of 3/4)
  (play-hemiola-piano 0.0 12))

(transport/tempo 120)
(hemiola-concerto)
```

**The lesson:** Hemiola is a *metric conflict*. The two parts are playing in different meters, but they resolve at the LCM (least common multiple) of the two cycle lengths. It creates tension and release, a hallmark of Romantic concerto writing. This is Ch10 polyrhythm, but applied vertically (simultaneous conflicting meters) instead of horizontally (offsetting a single meter).

### 10. A Concerto with a Walking Bassline

Jazz concertos often feature a walking bassline: a steady quarter-note bass part that outlines the chord progression, independent of the melody. This example builds a concerto movement where the piano plays a bebop melody, the strings walk a bassline, and the brass punctuate with offbeat chords.

**Technique:** Generate a walking bassline by picking chord tones and passing tones on every beat. The bassline is algorithmic, but it sounds hand-composed.

[VISUAL: Three staves. Bass (strings): walking quarter-notes, every beat filled. Piano: syncopated bebop melody, lots of rests. Brass: offbeat chords on the \"and\" of beats 2 and 4. The walking bass ties it all together.]

```scheme
;; Walking-Bass Concerto — jazz-influenced piano + walking bassline
(define (chord->root chord)
  (case chord
    ((Cmaj7) 48)  ;; C2
    ((Dm7)   50)  ;; D2
    ((G7)    55)  ;; G2
    ((Am7)   57)  ;; A2
    (else 48)))

(define (generate-walking-bass chord num-beats)
  ;; generate a walking bassline for num-beats over chord
  ;; strategy: chord root, fifth, root, passing tone
  (let* ((root (chord->root chord))
         (fifth (+ root 7))
         (passing (+ root 2))) ;; a passing tone (major 2nd above root)
    (case num-beats
      ((4) (list root fifth root passing))
      ((2) (list root fifth))
      (else (list root)))))

(define (play-walking-bass progression start-beat)
  ;; progression: list of (chord duration-in-beats)
  (let loop ((prog progression) (beat start-beat))
    (when (not (null? prog))
      (let* ((entry (car prog))
             (chord (car entry))
             (dur (cadr entry))
             (bass-notes (generate-walking-bass chord dur)))
        (let inner ((notes bass-notes) (b beat))
          (when (not (null? notes))
            (base/at-beat b
              (lambda ()
                (note/strike (car notes) 0.9 0.6)))
            (inner (cdr notes) (+ b 1.0))))
        (loop (cdr prog) (+ beat dur))))))

(define (play-bebop-melody start-beat)
  ;; a syncopated bebop melody
  (let ((phrase '((0.5 67) (1.5 69) (2.0 71) (3.5 72) (4.0 74) (5.5 72) (6.0 71) (7.0 67))))
    (for-each
      (lambda (note-event)
        (let ((offset (car note-event))
              (pitch (cadr note-event)))
          (base/at-beat (+ start-beat offset)
            (lambda ()
              (note/strike pitch 0.4 0.75)))))
      phrase)))

(define (walking-bass-concerto)
  (let ((progression '((Cmaj7 4) (Dm7 4) (G7 4) (Cmaj7 4))))
    (play-walking-bass progression 0.0)
    (play-bebop-melody 0.0)))

(transport/tempo 180)
(walking-bass-concerto)
```

### 11. A Concerto with Metric Modulation

Metric modulation is a tempo technique where the beat subdivides (or multiplies) to create a new tempo that's mathematically related to the old tempo. Example: if ♩=120, and you modulate so that the old eighth-note becomes the new quarter-note, the new tempo is ♩=240. This example builds a concerto movement that modulates from ♩=60 to ♩=90 to ♩=180 via metric modulation.

**Technique:** Schedule tempo changes where the new tempo is a multiple of the old beat subdivision.

[VISUAL: A score with tempo markings: ♩=60 (quarter=60). At bar 4, a marking \"♪ of previous bar = ♩ of this bar\" and ♩=90. At bar 8, \"♪ of previous bar = ♩ of this bar\" and ♩=135. The tempo accelerates by metric relationship, not arbitrarily.]

```scheme
;; Metric-Modulation Concerto — tempo changes via beat subdivision
(define (play-phrase-at-tempo pitches start-beat note-dur vel)
  (let loop ((ps pitches) (beat start-beat))
    (when (not (null? ps))
      (base/at-beat beat
        (lambda ()
          (note/strike (car ps) note-dur vel)))
      (loop (cdr ps) (+ beat note-dur)))))

(define (metric-modulation-concerto)
  ;; section 1: tempo 60, quarter-notes
  (transport/tempo 60)
  (play-phrase-at-tempo '(C4 D4 E4 F4) 0.0 1.0 0.7)
  
  ;; modulation 1: old eighth = new quarter, so new tempo = 60 * 1.5 = 90
  (base/at-beat 4.0
    (lambda () (transport/tempo 90)))
  (play-phrase-at-tempo '(G4 A4 B4 C5) 4.0 1.0 0.75)
  
  ;; modulation 2: old eighth = new quarter, so new tempo = 90 * 1.5 = 135
  (base/at-beat 8.0
    (lambda () (transport/tempo 135)))
  (play-phrase-at-tempo '(C5 B4 A4 G4) 8.0 1.0 0.8)
  
  ;; modulation 3: old eighth = new quarter, so new tempo = 135 * 1.5 = 202.5
  (base/at-beat 12.0
    (lambda () (transport/tempo 202)))
  (play-phrase-at-tempo '(F4 E4 D4 C4) 12.0 1.0 0.85))

(metric-modulation-concerto)
```

<!-- BUILD: verify each tempo change is a 1.5× multiple of the previous; render the score with metric-modulation markings; confirm the perceived acceleration matches the mathematical relationship -->

**The lesson:** Metric modulation makes tempo changes feel *inevitable* rather than arbitrary. The new tempo is not \"faster\" — it's \"the old subdivision.\" This technique (pioneered by Elliott Carter) is common in 20th-century concertos. The program is simple (three tempo changes), but the musical result is sophisticated because the *relationship* between tempos is rigorous.

### 12. A Concerto Built from a Twelve-Tone Row

A twelve-tone concerto uses all twelve pitches of the chromatic scale in a fixed order (the \"row\"), with no pitch repeated until all twelve have sounded. This example builds a concerto movement from a twelve-tone row and its transformations (retrograde, inversion, retrograde-inversion).

**Technique:** Define the row as a list of MIDI pitches. Generate transformations algorithmically. The entire concerto is built from this one row.

[VISUAL: A table showing the prime row (P0), its retrograde (R0), its inversion (I0), and its retrograde-inversion (RI0). Below, a score showing a phrase built from P0, then R0, then I0, then RI0 — all the same twelve pitches, just reordered.]

```scheme
;; Twelve-Tone Concerto — row + transformations
(define twelve-tone-row
  ;; a row: all 12 chromatic pitches, no repeats
  '(60 64 67 63 70 66 69 61 65 68 62 71)) ;; C E G Eb Bb F# A C# F Ab D B

(define (retrograde row)
  (reverse row))

(define (invert row)
  ;; inversion: mirror each interval around the first pitch
  (let ((first (car row)))
    (map (lambda (p)
           (- (* 2 first) p))
         row)))

(define (retrograde-inversion row)
  (reverse (invert row)))

(define (play-row row start-beat note-dur vel)
  (let loop ((ps row) (beat start-beat))
    (when (not (null? ps))
      (base/at-beat beat
        (lambda ()
          (note/strike (car ps) note-dur vel)))
      (loop (cdr ps) (+ beat note-dur)))))

(define (twelve-tone-concerto)
  ;; prime row
  (play-row twelve-tone-row 0.0 0.5 0.7)
  ;; retrograde
  (play-row (retrograde twelve-tone-row) 6.0 0.5 0.65)
  ;; inversion
  (play-row (invert twelve-tone-row) 12.0 0.5 0.7)
  ;; retrograde-inversion
  (play-row (retrograde-inversion twelve-tone-row) 18.0 0.5 0.65))

(transport/tempo 100)
(twelve-tone-concerto)
```

**The lesson:** Twelve-tone technique is *data transformation*. The row is data, and all transformations (retrograde, inversion, transposition) are functions on that data. The concerto is built from one twelve-pitch seed, but it sounds varied because the transformations reorder the pitches. This is Ch2 lists + Ch4 sequence + Ch15 form, but the form is *serialist*.

### 13. A Concerto with a Cadenza — Unmetered Solo

A cadenza is a solo passage, traditionally unmetered (not bound to the beat), where the soloist improvises (or plays a written-out \"improvisation\"). This example builds a concerto movement with a metered orchestral section, then a cadenza where the piano plays freely (no transport/tempo), then the orchestra re-enters.

**Technique:** The cadenza uses *absolute time* (in seconds, not beats). The rest of the concerto uses *musical time* (beats).

[VISUAL: A score. Bars 1–8: orchestra + piano, metered. Bar 9: a fermata (hold), then the word \"cadenza\" and a bracket over 4 bars of piano solo with no barlines. Bar 13: \"a tempo\" and the orchestra re-enters, metered again.]

```scheme
  ;; orchestra + piano, in tempo
  (let ((orch-chords '((0.0 (C3 E3 G3)) (2.0 (F3 A3 C4)) (4.0 (G3 B3 D4)) (6.0 (C3 E3 G3))))

    (for-each
      (lambda (chord-event)
        (let ((beat (car chord-event))
              (pitches (cadr chord-event)))
          (for-each

                (lambda ()

            (lambda ()
```

### 14. A Concerto with Layered Dynamics — pp/mf/ff Simultaneously

Most dynamics are *global* (the whole ensemble gets louder or softer together). But in a concerto, you can have *layered dynamics*: the piano plays ff while the strings play pp. This example builds a concerto movement where three layers (piano, strings, brass) each have independent dynamic curves.

**Technique:** Each voice gets its own velocity ramp, scheduled independently.

[VISUAL: Three staves with independent dynamic markings. Piano: pp → ff. Strings: mf throughout. Brass: ff → pp. The three curves are simultaneous but independent.]

```scheme
;; Layered-Dynamics Concerto — independent dynamic curves per voice
(define (play-voice-with-dynamic-curve pitches start-beat note-dur vels)
  ;; play a voice with per-note velocity from vels list
  (let loop ((ps pitches) (vs vels) (beat start-beat))
    (when (and (not (null? ps)) (not (null? vs)))
      (base/at-beat beat
        (lambda ()
          (note/strike (car ps) note-dur (car vs))))
      (loop (cdr ps) (cdr vs) (+ beat note-dur)))))

(define (layered-dynamics-concerto)
  (let ((phrase-length 8)
        (piano-pitches '(60 62 64 65 67 69 71 72))
        (strings-pitches '(48 50 52 53 55 57 59 60))
        (brass-pitches '(55 57 59 60 62 64 65 67)))
    ;; piano: pp → ff (0.3 → 0.95)
    (let ((piano-vels (ramp-velocity 0.3 0.95 phrase-length)))
      (play-voice-with-dynamic-curve piano-pitches 0.0 1.0 piano-vels))
    ;; strings: mf throughout (0.55)
    (let ((strings-vels (make-list phrase-length 0.55)))
      (play-voice-with-dynamic-curve strings-pitches 0.0 1.0 strings-vels))
    ;; brass: ff → pp (0.9 → 0.35)
    (let ((brass-vels (ramp-velocity 0.9 0.35 phrase-length)))
      (play-voice-with-dynamic-curve brass-pitches 0.0 1.0 brass-vels))))

(define (make-list n val)
  ;; helper: make a list of n copies of val
  (if (<= n 0)
      '()
      (cons val (make-list (- n 1) val))))

(transport/tempo 90)
(layered-dynamics-concerto)
```

<!-- BUILD: confirm the three voices have independent velocity curves; render the score with three dynamic markings (one per staff); verify piano crescendos, brass diminuendos, strings stay constant -->

**The lesson:** Layered dynamics create *textural depth*. The piano can surge forward while the orchestra recedes, or vice versa. This is Ch13 dynamics, but applied *per-voice* rather than globally. It's a concerto-specific technique: the soloist and ensemble are independent dynamic agents.

### 15. A Concerto with Polymeter — 5/4 Piano vs 4/4 Orchestra

We've done polyrhythm (Ch10) and hemiola (earlier in this chapter). This example goes further: *true polymeter*, where the piano is in 5/4 and the orchestra is in 4/4, and they never resolve (no LCM cadence).

**Technique:** Schedule the piano on a 5-beat cycle, the orchestra on a 4-beat cycle. Let them run in parallel for 20 beats (4 piano bars, 5 orchestra bars). The barlines never align.

[VISUAL: Two grand staves. Top (piano): 5/4 time signature, 5 beats per bar. Bottom (orchestra): 4/4 time signature, 4 beats per bar. The barlines are staggered — the two meters are simultaneous but independent.]

```scheme
;; Polymeter Concerto — 5/4 vs 4/4, no resolution
(define (play-piano-5-4 num-bars)
  ;; piano: 5/4 meter (5 beats per bar)
  (let loop ((bar 0) (beat 0.0))
    (when (< bar num-bars)
      ;; a 5-beat pattern: strong-weak-mid-weak-weak
      (base/at-beat beat
        (lambda () (note/strike 'C5 0.8 0.75)))
      (base/at-beat (+ beat 1.0)
        (lambda () (note/strike 'E5 0.6 0.55)))
      (base/at-beat (+ beat 2.0)
        (lambda () (note/strike 'G5 0.7 0.6)))
      (base/at-beat (+ beat 3.0)
        (lambda () (note/strike 'E5 0.6 0.55)))
      (base/at-beat (+ beat 4.0)
        (lambda () (note/strike 'C5 0.6 0.5)))
      (loop (+ bar 1) (+ beat 5.0)))))

(define (play-orchestra-4-4 num-bars)
  ;; orchestra: 4/4 meter (4 beats per bar)
  (let loop ((bar 0) (beat 0.0))
    (when (< bar num-bars)
      ;; a 4-beat pattern: bass on 1, chords on 2 and 4
      (base/at-beat beat
        (lambda () (note/strike 'C3 0.9 0.7)))
      (base/at-beat (+ beat 1.0)
        (lambda ()
          (for-each
            (lambda (p) (note/strike p 0.8 0.5))
            '(E3 G3 C4))))
      (base/at-beat (+ beat 3.0)
        (lambda ()
          (for-each
            (lambda (p) (note/strike p 0.8 0.5))
            '(E3 G3 C4))))
      (loop (+ bar 1) (+ beat 4.0)))))

(define (polymeter-concerto)
  ;; 4 bars of piano 5/4 = 20 beats
  ;; 5 bars of orchestra 4/4 = 20 beats
  ;; they run in parallel, barlines never align
  (play-piano-5-4 4)
  (play-orchestra-4-4 5))

(transport/tempo 120)
(polymeter-concerto)
```

**The lesson:** Polymeter is *metric independence*. The two parts are not in different subdivisions of the same beat (that's polyrhythm) — they're in *different meters entirely*. It creates a floating, unresolved texture. This is Ch10 polyrhythm + Ch5 meter, pushed to the extreme. It's disorienting, which is the point.

### 16. A Concerto with a Ground Bass — Variations Over a Repeating Bass

A ground bass (basso ostinato) is a repeating bassline over which variations are built. Baroque concertos (Vivaldi, Bach) often use this technique. This example builds a concerto movement with an 8-beat ground bass that repeats 8 times, while the piano plays increasingly elaborate variations over the top.

**Technique:** Loop the bassline. For each iteration, the piano plays a different variation (melody, then arpeggios, then trills, then chords).

[VISUAL: A score with the bass staff showing the same 8-note pattern repeating 8 times. Above, the piano staff shows 8 different variations: simple melody, then sixteenth-note runs, then arpeggios, then full chords. The bass is the constant; the piano is the variable.]

```scheme
;; Ground-Bass Concerto — variations over repeating bassline
(define ground-bass
  ;; an 8-beat bassline (MIDI pitches)
  '(48 50 52 53 55 53 52 50)) ;; C D E F G F E D

(define (play-ground-bass num-iterations)
  ;; loop the bassline num-iterations times
  (let loop ((i 0) (beat 0.0))
    (when (< i num-iterations)
      (let inner ((ps ground-bass) (b beat))
        (when (not (null? ps))
          (base/at-beat b
            (lambda ()
              (note/strike (car ps) 0.9 0.6)))
          (inner (cdr ps) (+ b 1.0))))
      (loop (+ i 1) (+ beat 8.0)))))

(define (variation-1 start-beat)
  ;; simple melody
  (for-each
    (lambda (note-event)
      (let ((offset (car note-event))
            (pitch (cadr note-event)))
        (base/at-beat (+ start-beat offset)
          (lambda ()
            (note/strike pitch 0.8 0.7)))))
    '((0.0 60) (1.0 62) (2.0 64) (3.0 65) (4.0 67) (5.0 65) (6.0 64) (7.0 62))))

(define (variation-2 start-beat)
  ;; sixteenth-note run
  (let ((run '(60 62 64 65 67 69 71 72 74 72 71 69 67 65 64 62)))
    (let loop ((ps run) (beat start-beat))
      (when (not (null? ps))
        (base/at-beat beat
          (lambda ()
            (note/strike (car ps) 0.3 0.65)))
        (loop (cdr ps) (+ beat 0.5))))))

(define (variation-3 start-beat)
  ;; arpeggios
  (let ((arp1 '(60 64 67 72))
        (arp2 '(62 65 69 74)))
    (let loop ((ps arp1) (beat start-beat))
      (when (not (null? ps))
        (base/at-beat beat
          (lambda ()
            (note/strike (car ps) 0.4 0.7)))
        (loop (cdr ps) (+ beat 1.0))))
    (let loop ((ps arp2) (beat (+ start-beat 4.0)))
      (when (not (null? ps))
        (base/at-beat beat
          (lambda ()
            (note/strike (car ps) 0.4 0.7)))
        (loop (cdr ps) (+ beat 1.0))))))

(define (variation-4 start-beat)
  ;; full chords
  (for-each
    (lambda (chord-event)
      (let ((offset (car chord-event))
            (pitches (cadr chord-event)))
        (for-each
          (lambda (p)
            (base/at-beat (+ start-beat offset)
              (lambda ()
                (note/strike p 1.8 0.75))))
          pitches)))
    '((0.0 (60 64 67)) (2.0 (62 65 69)) (4.0 (64 67 71)) (6.0 (65 69 72)))))

(define (ground-bass-concerto)
  ;; ground bass loops 8 times
  (play-ground-bass 8)
  ;; variations over each iteration
  (variation-1 0.0)    ;; iteration 1
  (variation-1 8.0)    ;; iteration 2
  (variation-2 16.0)   ;; iteration 3
  (variation-2 24.0)   ;; iteration 4
  (variation-3 32.0)   ;; iteration 5
  (variation-3 40.0)   ;; iteration 6
  (variation-4 48.0)   ;; iteration 7
  (variation-4 56.0))  ;; iteration 8

(transport/tempo 100)
(ground-bass-concerto)
```

**The lesson:** A ground bass is *thematic constancy + surface variety*. The bass is the anchor; the variations are the interest. This is Ch4 variation + Ch15 form, but the form is *additive* (each variation is independent, but they all share the same harmonic foundation). This is a Baroque technique, but it works in any era.
