;; appendix-j-poetry-prose-playable.book.slatl

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(appendix
  :book                "Book of Narrative Games"
  :letter              "J"
  :title               "Poetry, Prose, and Playable Text"
  :dialect             "motoi"
  :audience            :kid
  :also-for            :adult
  :content-rating      :G
  :training-eligible   #t
  :confidentiality     "public"
  :book-version        "1.0.0"
  :prose
"When text arrives, HOW it arrives is half the meaning. A prose block
that pops onto the screen reads flat. The same block that eases in
over three seconds reads considered. The same block that drops from
above, letter-by-letter, reads like a poem being written in front of
you.

This appendix is a decision guide. When to use which text-motion
verb. Which combinations feel right for which content. What NOT to
do (many things).

---

## The three arrival verbs

**motion/drop** — text falls from above and settles into place.

```scheme
(paint-text 40 60 \"The kitchen at dawn.\")
(motion/drop 'text-slot :duration 45 :ease 'ease-out)
```

Feel: gentle, considered, like a leaf falling. Best for prose that
should feel like a thought arriving.

**motion/with-feel** — text arrives with a specific emotional
signature (a shape of motion).

```scheme
(paint-text 40 60 \"You do not know when they will come back.\")
(motion/with-feel 'text-slot 'tender)
```

Feel: parametric. `'tender` is soft ease. `'urgent` is fast slam.
`'reluctant` is slow drag. Different feels for different tones.

**motion/with-pace** — text unfolds character-by-character at a
controllable speed.

```scheme
(motion/with-pace \"You do not know when they will come back.\"
                  40 60 :chars-per-sec 12)
```

Feel: someone typing the text in real time. Slow (5 chars/sec) reads
as thoughtful; fast (30 chars/sec) reads as breathless.

---

## Choosing between them

For prose passages that feel like paragraphs from a book:
`motion/drop` per line.

For lines that carry specific emotional weight (a confession, a
farewell): `motion/with-feel` with a matching feel.

For lines that should feel like they are being SPOKEN or WRITTEN in
the moment (a voice message, a note being read aloud):
`motion/with-pace`.

For lines with no special weight: plain `paint-text` with no
animation.

You can mix them within a scene. The variation itself is meaningful.

---

## Pace as gameplay

Player controls pace by pressing a key between lines.

```scheme
(define (player-paced-poem lines)
  (let ((idx 0))
    (define (show-line)
      (when (< idx (length lines))
        (let ((line (list-ref lines idx))
              (y (+ 40 (* idx 60))))
          (paint-text 40 y line)
          (motion/drop 'text-slot :duration 45)
          (set! idx (+ idx 1)))))
    (show-line)   ;; first line automatic
    (on-key
      (lambda (k)
        (when (eq? k 'space) (show-line))))))
```

Player presses SPACE. The next line drops in. They wait however long
they want.

This is the essential structure of a playable poem. The reader is
also the pacer. Poems that would be over in twelve seconds if
autoplay-ed become three-minute meditations under the reader's
control.

---

## Auto-advance with the option to skip

For hybrid experiences — prose that mostly self-plays but can be
skipped or paused.

```scheme
(define (auto-advance-with-skip lines)
  (let ((idx 0) (paused? #f))
    (define (show-line)
      (when (and (< idx (length lines)) (not paused?))
        (let ((line (list-ref lines idx)))
          (paint-text 40 (+ 40 (* idx 60)) line)
          (motion/drop 'text-slot :duration 45)
          (set! idx (+ idx 1))
          (world/after 150 show-line))))
    (show-line)
    (on-key
      (lambda (k)
        (case k
          ((space)
           (set! paused? (not paused?))
           (unless paused? (show-line)))
          ((right)
           (show-line)))))))
```

Auto-advances every 2.5 seconds. SPACE pauses/unpauses. RIGHT
advances immediately. The player who wants to speed up can; the
player who wants to slow down can.

---

## Lines that linger vs lines that fade

Some lines should stay on screen for the whole scene. Some should
fade after being read.

```scheme
(define (mixed-behavior-poem)
  ;; Line 1 stays.
  (paint-text 40 60 \"The kitchen at dawn.\")
  (motion/drop 'line-1 :duration 45)

  ;; Line 2 fades after 90 frames.
  (world/after 100
    (lambda ()
      (paint-text 40 110 \"A jar of honey with a spoon in it.\")
      (motion/drop 'line-2 :duration 45)
      (world/after 90
        (lambda () (surface/dim 0.0 60)))))    ;; fade

  ;; Line 3 stays.
  (world/after 250
    (lambda ()
      (paint-text 40 160 \"Someone was here.\")
      (motion/drop 'line-3 :duration 45)))
  )
```

Fading lines are ones the reader should HOLD IN THEIR MIND while
reading the next. The honey line fades as 'someone was here'
arrives — the reader connects them mentally.

Do not fade every other line. Choose specific ones.

---

## Spotlight on one word

The equivalent of italic emphasis in prose.

```scheme
(paint-text 40 60 \"You do not know when they will come back.\")
;; Spotlight the word 'when.'
(world/after 60
  (lambda ()
    (surface/spotlight 145 60 30 20 :duration 90)))
```

'When' becomes the emotional center. The reader's eye goes there. In
prose you would italicize it; in playable text you spotlight it.

Once or twice per poem. Not every line.

---

## Motion as meaning

Text can move AFTER arriving. Rain lines fall. Water lines settle.
Wind lines drift.

```scheme
;; A wind line drifts to the right slowly.
(paint-text 40 100 \"the wind through the reeds\")
(motion/move-to 'wind-line 200 100 :duration 300 :ease 'linear)
```

The line 'the wind through the reeds' physically drifts. The
audience feels the wind because the text does. This is what makes
playable poetry different from a printed page.

Use sparingly. If EVERY line moves, motion becomes background noise.
One or two moving lines per poem.

---

## Sound in poetry

Every poem should have exactly one audio element beyond silence.
Maybe an ambient. Maybe one cue on one line. Not both, usually.

```scheme
;; A poem with a single audio cue.
(paint-text 40 60 \"The stone drops.\")
(motion/drop 'line-1 :duration 45)
(audio/play 'stone-in-water :volume 0.4)

;; The rest of the poem is silent.
(world/after 90
  (lambda ()
    (paint-text 40 110 \"The ripples cross the whole face of it.\")
    (motion/drop 'line-2 :duration 45)))
```

One sound cue on one line. The stone drop is heard exactly when the
line arrives. The rest is silence, which lets the reader hear their
own breathing.

If you use ambient, use ONE ambient layer at very low volume
(0.1-0.15). Poetry does not need three layers.

---

## The blank space rule

Playable poems benefit from empty screen space around the text.

```scheme
;; Wide margins.
(paint-text 200 200 \"one small line, centered\")
```

Position the text with wide margins. The white (or paper-colored)
space around the words gives them weight. This is the same principle
as poetry books using large margins.

Cluttered pages read as prose. Sparse pages read as poetry. Choose
your positioning to match your intent.

---

## Combining forms — the prose-with-a-poem

Sometimes a narrative scene has a poetic moment inside it.

```scheme
(define (scene-with-poetic-moment)
  ;; Normal prose lines.
  (paint-text 20 40 \"You climb the hill. You reach the top.\")
  (paint-text 20 70 \"You look at the valley below.\")

  ;; Then a poetic beat.
  (world/after 150
    (lambda ()
      (paint-text 40 150 \"The wind.\")
      (motion/drop 'poetic-1 :duration 60 :ease 'ease-out)))

  (world/after 280
    (lambda ()
      (paint-text 40 200 \"The hawk.\")
      (motion/drop 'poetic-2 :duration 60 :ease 'ease-out)))

  (world/after 410
    (lambda ()
      (paint-text 40 250 \"The distance you did not know you could see.\")
      (motion/drop 'poetic-3 :duration 60 :ease 'ease-out)))

  ;; Then back to prose.
  (world/after 570
    (lambda ()
      (paint-text 20 340 \"You breathe out. You start down.\"))))
```

Normal prose. Then three poetic lines with `motion/drop` and wider
margins. Then normal prose again. The scene has a poem inside it.

This is a great technique for high-emotional beats in an otherwise
prose-heavy game. The shift in TEXTURE tells the reader 'this is
important.'

---

## What NOT to do

**Don't animate every line.** If every line has motion, motion loses
meaning. Reserve motion for lines that need weight.

**Don't use character-by-character pace for prose paragraphs.**
Typewriter-style unfolding is a specific effect — for voice
messages, notes being read, direct messages from characters. It is
annoying for narrative prose.

**Don't spotlight everything.** One or two spotlights per scene.

**Don't run motion during choice text.** When the player is about to
pick a choice, the choice options should be still. Moving text is
harder to read.

**Don't autoplay through emotional beats.** Give the player a moment
to sit with a line before advancing. Even 1-2 seconds of pause
between an emotional line and the next line matters.

---

## Timing reference

For prose:
- 200-300ms per line of arrival animation
- 3-5 seconds of hold before next line

For poetry:
- 500-800ms per line of arrival animation (slower is more considered)
- 5-10 seconds of hold before next line — or player-paced

For dialogue:
- 100-200ms of arrival (fast, feels like speaking)
- Advance on player key press

Tune for your content. Rules of thumb, not laws.

---

## Summary

Three arrival verbs (drop, with-feel, with-pace). Player-paced or
auto-advance. Lines linger or fade. Spotlight for emphasis. Motion
for meaning. Sound sparingly. Blank space matters. Combine forms
for poetic beats inside prose scenes.

The kid who reads this appendix and then reads a paper poem will
suddenly notice how the poet used LINE BREAKS as motion. Playable
text just makes the motion explicit.")

[book:book-of-narrative-games] [chapter:appendix-k-testing-a-story] [book-type:application]

;; appendix-k-testing-a-story.book.slatl

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(appendix
  :book                "Book of Narrative Games"
  :letter              "K"
  :title               "Testing a Story — The Playtest Checklist"
  :dialect             "motoi"
  :audience            :kid
  :also-for            :adult
  :content-rating      :G
  :training-eligible   #t
  :confidentiality     "public"
  :book-version        "1.0.0"
  :prose
"How do you know if your story-game is any good?

Not from the same feeling that told you 'this is my idea, I love it.'
Not from running through it yourself — you know it too well. You
know only from watching someone play who has never seen it.

This appendix is the playtest protocol. Twenty questions to ask.
Body-language cues to watch for. What patterns mean, and what to
do about them.

---

## The setup

Get a friend. Sit next to them. Do not touch the keyboard. Do not
talk unless they ask a direct question. Watch. Take notes silently.

Ideal duration: 30-45 minutes. Long enough that they get past the
opening; short enough that they don't get exhausted. If your game
is longer than 45 minutes, run playtests in chunks — 'today just
the first act.'

Bring water. Playtesting is thirsty work for the tester.

---

## What to watch (body language)

**They lean forward.** They are engaged. The scene is working.

**They lean back.** They are bored. The scene is not working.

**They smile.** A moment of pleasure. Note when. That is a moment to
protect and multiply.

**They frown.** Confusion or displeasure. Note what just happened.

**They look at their phone.** You have lost them. The next minute
had better re-engage them.

**They fidget.** Waiting for something. Your pace is off.

**They mouth the words.** They are reading intently. Good.

**They stop reading.** They are thinking about what they read. Also
good — but do not follow up with three more lines immediately. Let
the moment breathe.

**They laugh.** Note it. Laughs are gold.

**They cry.** Note it. Do not comment. Bring tissues.

---

## After the play — twenty questions

Ask these in order. Do not skip. Do not soften.

### Structure

1. **Which ending did you get?**
   (Ensures they finished. Also tells you which endings players
   gravitate toward.)

2. **Roughly how long did you play?**
   (Their perception, not clock time. If it felt longer than it
   was, pacing is slow. If shorter, pacing is fast.)

3. **Was there a chapter or scene that felt too long?**
   (Direct feedback on pacing bottlenecks.)

4. **Was there a chapter or scene that felt too short?**
   (Often the emotional peaks. If they wanted more, that's a
   signal you had them.)

### Attention

5. **What was the moment you felt most alive?**
   (The scene that made them lean forward, laugh, or cry. This is
   the load-bearing moment of your game.)

6. **Where did you get bored?**
   (The scene where they leaned back. Sometimes multiple. All are
   fixable.)

7. **Did you ever want to quit?**
   (If yes, where? That's where the design is failing them.)

### Choices

8. **Was there a choice that felt fake — like it didn't matter?**
   (Consequence-table failure. Check that choice's downstream
   references.)

9. **Was there a choice you wanted to make but couldn't?**
   (Missing option. Sometimes worth adding.)

10. **Did you feel the game respected your choices?**
    (Vague, but their feeling matters more than the answer's
    precision.)

### Characters

11. **Who was your favorite character? Why?**
    (Watch what they name. Often it's not who you expected.)

12. **Who did you not like? Why?**
    (Not the villain. If they don't like the villain, that's fine.
    If they don't like someone you wanted them to bond with,
    problem.)

13. **Was there a character you wanted to see more of?**
    (Might be a character who should have had a bigger role.)

14. **Was there a character you wanted to see less of?**
    (Might be a character taking up screen time without earning
    it.)

### Feel

15. **Did the game feel like reading, watching, or playing?**
    (No wrong answer, but tells you what genre-analog they
    perceived. Your intent should match.)

16. **What was the tone of the game — light, heavy, funny, sad?**
    (Their perception vs. your intent. Mismatch means voice
    tuning needed.)

17. **Was there anything that felt like a system rather than a
    story?**
    (Ideally no. If yes, that's where your seams are showing.)

### Companion (if applicable)

18. **Did you talk to the [old woman / companion character]?**
    (Zero-answer means she is invisible; frequent-answer means
    she is being useful.)

19. **Did she interrupt at a bad time?**
    (Any yes here means you're triggering her at the wrong
    beats.)

20. **Would you replay this game?**
    (The ultimate question. Not 'did you like it' but 'would you
    do it again.' A yes here means you have made something they
    care about.)

---

## Analyzing the answers

**Convergence.** If three friends give the same answer to a question,
that is a REAL signal. Fix it or protect it.

**Divergence.** If three friends give different answers, the game is
Rorschach-shaped for that dimension. Neither good nor bad
necessarily — but be curious.

**Silence.** If a friend can't remember something (a character, a
choice, a scene), it did not land. Either strengthen it or cut it.

**Enthusiasm.** If they get animated talking about a scene, protect
that scene. Do not touch it. Build outward.

---

## Common findings and their fixes

**'I got bored in the middle.'**
Middle acts sag naturally. Add a peak at the midpoint — a small
revelation, a new character, a scene of unexpected texture.

**'The choices didn't feel like they mattered.'**
Consequence-table failure. Go back to appendix I. Add downstream
references to the choices they mentioned.

**'I didn't understand what to do at [scene X].'**
Missing signposting. Add a small hint in-scene or via the
companion.

**'That character was boring.'**
Body-language check. Does the character have a signature (breath
rate, sway, expression baseline)? If they are just standing still,
they are furniture. See appendix C.

**'The ending felt sudden.'**
Missing setup. Track backward: which scenes were meant to prepare
the ending? Are they doing enough?

**'The ending felt unearned.'**
Player expected a reward for effort. Endings should honor what the
player did, not just what the writer felt like writing.

**'It was too short.'**
Success. Do not artificially extend. Trust the impact of a short
game.

**'It was too long.'**
Cut. Every scene should earn its screen time. Cut the ones that
don't.

---

## The correctness question

'What does correct mean for narrative?'

Not the same as correctness for code. There is no unit test for a
scene. But some heuristics:

**A scene is correct if the emotion the writer intended is the
emotion the player felt.** Playtest reveals this. Alignment good;
misalignment bad.

**A scene is correct if the player can navigate it.** They know
what to do; they can execute; they see the result. Confusion is
correctness failure.

**A scene is correct if it earns its runtime.** A three-minute
scene that could be a thirty-second scene is not correct. Cut.

**A scene is correct if it connects to what came before and prepares
what comes next.** A scene disconnected from the arc is not
correct even if it is beautifully written.

Correctness in narrative is about function AND feeling. Both matter.

---

## After the fix — a second playtest

Get a DIFFERENT friend. Play through the fixed version. Watch
whether the fixed scene works.

Do not use the same friend twice for the same version. They already
know the story; their reactions are contaminated.

Rotating playtesters means every playtest gives fresh signal.

---

## Playtest ethics

**Never argue with a playtester.** Their experience is their
experience. Your intent is not their experience. Take the data.

**Never make them feel bad about their answers.** They are doing
you a favor. Their honest answers are more valuable than their
polite answers.

**Never ask them to play again if they didn't want to.** If they
finished and they're done, thank them and let them go.

**Thank them specifically.** 'I noticed you leaned forward at the
scene with the fisherman — that helped me a lot.' Specific thanks
means you were paying attention. They will play for you again.

---

## Solo playtest — the reset

You cannot playtest your own game with fresh eyes. But you can
approximate it.

Wait three weeks. Come back. Read the game as if you have not
seen it. Notice where you get bored. Notice where you smile.

This is not as good as a real playtester, but it is better than
nothing.

Do not do this the day after you wrote the game. You will just
replay your own intent.

---

## Summary

Playtest with real people. Twenty questions. Watch body language.
Convergence is signal; divergence is Rorschach; silence is failure.
Common findings have common fixes. Never argue with a tester;
thank them specifically.

The game that a playtester says 'I want to play again' is a game
worth shipping. Everything else is iteration.")

someone who has never played a Motoi Scheme program in their life.

They should not need to install anything. They should not need to
create an account. They should click a link, and after a second of

## The card

A card is a self-contained runnable. Wrap your game as a card and
you have something publishable.

```scheme
(define-card 'my-narrative-game
  :title \"the beekeeper's daughter\"
  :author \"your name here\"
  :estimated-time \"25-40 minutes\"
  :audience :teen-and-up
  :description
    \"You come home after six months away. Your sister is missing.\n    You have three days.\"
  :init run-beekeepers-daughter)
```

Metadata fields:
- `:title` — what appears in the browser tab and share preview
- `:author` — you
- `:estimated-time` — helps players decide if they have time
- `:audience` — `:child` `:teen-and-up` `:adult`
- `:description` — one or two lines for the share preview
- `:init` — the function that starts the game

The `:init` function is called when the player loads the card. It
should set up the scene and then start playing.

---

## The share URL

Publishing gives you a URL.

```scheme
;; Publish the card. Returns a URL string.
(define my-url (define-card-publish 'my-narrative-game))
```

The URL is something like `https://motoi.example/play/abc123`. It
is public — anyone with the URL can play. It does NOT require an
account for the player.

Copy the URL. Paste it into a message. Send to a friend. They open
it. They are playing your game.

If you want to unpublish, `(define-card-unpublish 'my-narrative-game)`
takes the URL down. Existing links stop working.

---

## The share preview

When someone pastes your URL into a message, most chat apps generate
a preview. That preview uses your card's title, description, and (if
you set one) a preview image.

```scheme
(define-card 'my-narrative-game
  :title \"the beekeeper's daughter\"
  :description \"You come home. Your sister is missing.\"
  :preview-image 'beehive-illustration
  ;; ... other fields ...
  )
```

`:preview-image` is a named asset in the substrate — either a
pre-existing sprite or an image you uploaded.

Preview matters. It is the difference between someone clicking your
link and someone scrolling past it.

---

## Per-player Cortex

When your published game runs, the runtime gives each player their
own isolated Cortex scope. Player A's `state/first-choice` does not
affect Player B's.

This is automatic. You do NOT need to add player-id namespacing
yourself. Just write `(cortex/write 'state/whatever value)` — the
runtime scopes it to the current player.

Sessions persist per player, too. Player A closes the tab and opens
tomorrow — their Cortex is still there.

---

## Anonymous vs signed-in

Players can play anonymously (default). Their Cortex is scoped to
their browser's anonymous session — persistent for the browser, but
lost if they clear cookies or switch devices.

Players who sign in have a stable identity — their Cortex follows
them across devices.

Your card does not need to know which is which. Write to Cortex; the
runtime handles the scoping.

If your game has a 'save your progress across devices' feature you
want to encourage, add a small note:

```scheme
(unless (or (cortex/read 'system/signed-in?)
            (cortex/read 'system/dismissed-signin-nudge?))
  (paint-text 20 500 \"Tip: sign in to keep your progress across devices.\")
  (paint-text 20 525 \"[press S to sign in, or ESC to dismiss]\"))
```

Small nudge, no pressure. Player who dismisses never sees it again.

---

## The load screen

When someone opens your URL, there is a brief moment of loading.
the Motoi runtime handles that automatically — but if your game has
large assets (audio, sprites), the load may take a few seconds.

Add a loading scene:

```scheme
(define (loading-scene)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (paint-text 300 300 \"loading...\"))

;; Then, when assets are ready:
(define (init-with-loading)
  (loading-scene)
  (async-load-assets
    (lambda ()
      (run-beekeepers-daughter))))
```

The player sees 'loading…' for two seconds instead of a blank
screen. Small detail, big polish.

---

## Analytics — what you learn about players

If you want to see how many people play your game, and how far they
get, wire lightweight analytics:

```scheme
(define (log-scene-entry scene-name)
  (cortex/write 'analytics/last-scene scene-name)
  (cortex/write 'analytics/scenes-visited
    (cons scene-name
          (or (cortex/read 'analytics/scenes-visited) '()))))
```

You (the author) can then query aggregate stats: how many players
reached ch3, how many finished, how many quit at ch5.

DO respect player privacy. Do NOT log the content of things they
type. Do NOT log identifying details. Log only scene ids and
timestamps.

---

## Multi-player narrative (advanced)

For games where two friends play the same story with different
Cortex — say, a two-player mystery where each has separate clues —
use per-player Cortex scoping.

```scheme
(define (player-write key value)
  (let ((pid (or (cortex/read 'system/current-player-id) 'p1)))
    (cortex/write
      (string->symbol
        (string-append \"player/\" (symbol->string pid) \"/\"
                       (symbol->string key)))
      value)))

(define (player-read key)
  (let ((pid (or (cortex/read 'system/current-player-id) 'p1)))
    (cortex/read
      (string->symbol
        (string-append \"player/\" (symbol->string pid) \"/\"
                       (symbol->string key))))))
```

Switch `system/current-player-id` when it's the other player's turn.
Reads and writes go into the right namespace.

For a full two-player system with real-time sync, you need more
infrastructure than this appendix covers. This pattern is for
turn-based couch-coop.

---

## Sharing beyond one friend

If your game gets popular, several things can happen:

**Word of mouth.** Players share the URL themselves. Nothing you
need to do.

**Curated collections.** the runtime's platform may feature your game in
a 'kids' games' or 'first-timer' collection. This is by editorial
review.

**Direct search.** Players search for narrative games by keyword;
your card's title and description determine whether you show up.

Write good metadata. It matters more than you think.

---

## Updates

Your game will get better. You will fix bugs, add scenes, rework
endings. When you republish, existing URLs continue to work — they
point at the newest version.

Player saves may or may not survive the update (see appendix H on
migration). Test carefully.

If your update is BIG — new act, major structural changes — consider
publishing as a new card. Old URL stays with the old version;
players discover the new version separately.

---

## Removing your game

If you want to take your game down, unpublish.

```scheme
(define-card-unpublish 'my-narrative-game)
```

Existing URLs immediately return 'this game is no longer available.'
Cortex data is preserved for a grace period (in case you republish);
after that, it may be deleted.

You can always republish later. `define-card-publish` again — same
card id — gives you a new URL that reads the old Cortex data.

---

## The one-shot cart

For a really small game — a two-minute playable poem, a five-minute
short — you might skip the card wrapper entirely and just share a
raw Scheme file. Anyone with a Motoi Scheme runtime can load and
run it.

This is fine for kids sharing with friends who are already coders.
For sharing with people who are NOT coders, use the card.

---

## The moment

Someone opens your URL. Your kitchen appears. They press A. They
walk through the red door. They are playing YOUR game.

This is the moment the book has been building toward. Everything —
Cortex, story trees, dialogue, body language, camera, sound,
consequences, companion, save slots — was for this.

Send the URL to someone you love. Wait to hear back. Take notes on
their reaction. Then write the next one.

---

## Summary

Wrap in a card. Publish for a URL. Player runs it in a browser
with no install. Cortex scopes per-player. Add a loading scene for
polish. Log analytics respectfully. Multi-player is possible with
extra scoping. Updates preserve URLs. Unpublish takes it down.

Send the link. Wait. Iterate. That is the shape of publishing
narrative games.")

;; ch01-room-door-choice.book.slatl
;; Book of Narrative Games — Chapter 1: A Room, a Door, a Choice
;; Authored 2026-07-16 by narrative-games-engineer-lane from architect design.

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura")
         :note "Base-language narrative teaching. Applies to both dialects.")

(chapter
  :book                "Book of Narrative Games"
  :chapter-number      1
  :title               "A Room, a Door, a Choice"
  :dialect             "motoi"
  :audience            :kid
  :also-for            :adult
  :content-rating      :G
  :author-lane         "narrative-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"
  :training-eligible   #t
  :confidentiality     "public"
  :voice               "sakura-teaching + narrative-craft"
  :book-version        "1.0.0"
  :draws-from-preserved (:book "book-of-games-preserved" :ch 1)
  :provenance          ((:source-path "narrative-games-engineer-lane")
                        (:authored-by "Engineer")
                        (:date "2026-07-16"))
  :prose
"Someone told a story. Someone else asked 'and then what did they do?'
The teller shrugged and said 'depends on what you would have done.' That
is where narrative games come from. Not from computers. From a fire and
two people who could not agree on what the hero should do next.

The oldest computer version is Colossal Cave Adventure, 1976, written
partly to teach a nine-year-old daughter how caves worked. It painted no
pictures. It printed a paragraph, waited for a verb, printed the next
paragraph. The whole world was a linked list of rooms and each room was
a paragraph with exits. That is the whole idea. The rest is decoration.

This chapter builds the smallest possible narrative game: one room, two
doors, one choice. The kid types A or B. The game responds. That is it.
Then we teach the physics of a page — text does not slam onto the
screen; it eases in. The previous room does not vanish; it dims. Not
action physics. Patience physics. The physics of turning a page in a
book someone read to you at bedtime and hoped you would remember.

---

## 1.1 The smallest possible narrative game

```scheme
;; A kitchen. Two doors. One choice.
(define (kitchen)
  (scene/imagine)
  (paint-text 20 40
    \"You are in a small kitchen. A red door stands to the north.\")
  (paint-text 20 70
    \"A blue door stands to the west. Which do you take?\")
  (paint-text 20 120 \"[A] north (red)   [B] west (blue)\")
  (on-key
    (lambda (k)
      (cond
        ((eq? k 'a) (garden))
        ((eq? k 'b) (hallway))
        (else       (kitchen))))))

(define (garden)
  (scene/imagine)
  (paint-text 20 40 \"The red door opens on a garden. Bees.\")
  (paint-text 20 70 \"You stand in tomatoes to your knees.\")
  (paint-text 20 120 \"[press any key to continue]\")
  (on-key (lambda (k) (kitchen))))

(define (hallway)
  (scene/imagine)
  (paint-text 20 40 \"The blue door opens on a hallway. Dust.\")
  (paint-text 20 70 \"A cat sits on the third step of a staircase.\")
  (paint-text 20 120 \"[press any key to continue]\")
  (on-key (lambda (k) (kitchen))))

(big-bang :init kitchen)
```

That is a game. Not a good game — the choices do not compound, the two
rooms are dead ends, and the kid can loop forever. But the shape is
there. `scene/imagine` clears the surface and prepares a new one.
`paint-text x y string` puts characters at pixel coordinates. `on-key`
takes a function that runs on any key press and decides what happens
next. `big-bang :init kitchen` starts the whole thing by running the
kitchen scene.

Read it out loud to yourself: kitchen, choice, garden or hallway, back
to kitchen. That is the same as `while (playing) { describe; wait;
branch; }` in any other language, except we do not have a while-loop.
Each scene calls the next scene. The stack does the loop for us. This is
the Scheme way — continuations, not iterations.

---

## 1.2 What the reader sees

When the kid runs `(big-bang :init kitchen)`, the surface goes to a soft
paper color (default for `scene/imagine`). Three lines of text appear.
Nothing moves. The kid presses A. The screen clears. Two new lines
appear. The garden. The kid presses any key. The screen clears again.
Back to the kitchen.

We have not painted a picture. We have painted words. Words are enough.
When someone reads 'you stand in tomatoes to your knees' they see
tomatoes; the graphics card in their head does the rest. Text adventures
are the most graphically intensive games in history — they run on the
best rendering hardware you own, which is your imagination.

The kid may not see this yet. That is fine. In chapter 4 we will add a
character with a body; in chapter 6 we will add a camera. For now, text
is enough. The eleven-year-old who plays this and gets bored is the same
eleven-year-old who reads the book with the missing pages and invents
the ending herself. That kid is our reader.

---

## 1.3 The physics of the page

Slam a paragraph on the screen and it feels rude. Ease it in and it
feels like a story. We add `tick/ease` — a smooth fade from invisible to
visible over a set number of frames.

```scheme
;; Words that arrive gently.
(define (paint-gently text x y)
  (let ((alpha (tick/ease 0.0 1.0 30)))   ;; ease from 0 to 1 over 30 frames
    (paint-text x y text :alpha alpha)))

(define (kitchen-eased)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (paint-gently \"You are in a small kitchen.\"                 20 40)
  (world/after 15
    (lambda ()
      (paint-gently \"A red door stands to the north.\"          20 70)))
  (world/after 30
    (lambda ()
      (paint-gently \"A blue door stands to the west.\"          20 100)))
  (world/after 50
    (lambda ()
      (paint-text 20 160 \"[A] north (red)   [B] west (blue)\")))
  (on-key
    (lambda (k)
      (cond ((eq? k 'a) (garden-eased))
            ((eq? k 'b) (hallway-eased))))))
```

`world/after n thunk` runs a function n frames from now. We use it to
stagger the arrival of lines. First line at frame 0. Second at frame 15.
Third at frame 30. Choices at frame 50. Half a second, one second, two
seconds. The kid reads at a natural pace and the world responds. This is
a lesson she will feel before she can articulate: the game has time. It
is not screaming at her. It is TELLING her a story.

`surface/paper` sets a warm off-white background — the color of book
pages, not screens. `tick/ease` gives us a smooth 0-to-1 alpha curve. If
we wanted the text to slide in from the left as well, we could add
`motion/drop` or `motion/with-feel` (chapter 14 does exactly that for
poetry).

Change 30 to 8 and the words snap in. Change it to 90 and they arrive so
slowly the kid gets impatient. Somewhere between 20 and 40 is the sweet
spot — fast enough to feel responsive, slow enough to feel considered.

---

## 1.4 Fading out the old scene

When the kid presses A, the kitchen should not vanish. It should dim.
The garden should fade in on top of the dimmed kitchen, then the kitchen
should clear. Three beats: dim, arrive, clear. Half a second each.

```scheme
;; Transition from one scene to the next with a fade.
(define (goto-scene next-scene)
  (surface/dim 0.5 20)               ;; dim to 50% brightness over 20 frames
  (world/after 20
    (lambda ()
      (scene/imagine)                ;; clear surface
      (surface/paper)                ;; fresh page
      (next-scene))))

(define (kitchen-nice)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (paint-gently \"You are in a small kitchen.\" 20 40)
  (world/after 15
    (lambda ()
      (paint-gently \"A red door stands to the north.\" 20 70)))
  (world/after 30
    (lambda ()
      (paint-gently \"A blue door stands to the west.\" 20 100)))
  (world/after 50
    (lambda ()
      (paint-text 20 160 \"[A] north (red)   [B] west (blue)\")))
  (on-key
    (lambda (k)
      (cond ((eq? k 'a) (goto-scene garden-nice))
            ((eq? k 'b) (goto-scene hallway-nice))))))
```

`surface/dim 0.5 20` dims the whole surface to half brightness over
twenty frames — about a third of a second at 60 fps. Then `world/after
20` waits for that dim to complete, clears the surface with
`scene/imagine`, and calls the next scene. The kid sees: kitchen goes
gray, screen clears, garden fades in.

Try changing 0.5 to 0.0 (full black) and 20 to 45 (three-quarters of a
second). The transition is now slow and total, like a chapter break in a
film. Or change 0.5 to 0.9 (barely dim) and 20 to 5 (quick blink). Now
transitions are almost instant, snappy. Both are valid; they set
different rhythms. Fast transitions for chases. Slow transitions for
reflection.

---

## 1.5 The choice as data

Every game we build in this book eventually stores its choices. We start
now, with the simplest possible store.

```scheme
;; Remember the first choice.
(define (kitchen-remembered)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (paint-text 20 40 \"You are in a small kitchen.\")
  (paint-text 20 70 \"A red door stands to the north.\")
  (paint-text 20 100 \"A blue door stands to the west.\")
  (paint-text 20 160 \"[A] north (red)   [B] west (blue)\")
  (on-key
    (lambda (k)
      (cond
        ((eq? k 'a)
         (cortex/write 'first-choice 'red)
         (goto-scene garden-remembered))
        ((eq? k 'b)
         (cortex/write 'first-choice 'blue)
         (goto-scene hallway-remembered))))))

(define (garden-remembered)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (paint-text 20 40 \"The garden. Bees. Tomatoes.\")
  (paint-text 20 70
    \"You will remember this door was red.\")
  (paint-text 20 160 \"[press any key]\")
  (on-key (lambda (k) (goto-scene kitchen-remembered)))))
```

`cortex/write 'first-choice 'red` stores the symbol `red` under the key
`first-choice` in a place that outlives this session. When the kid quits
and comes back tomorrow, `(cortex/read 'first-choice)` still returns
`red`. That is Cortex — the memory of the story. Chapter 3 is entirely
about it. For now, we are just planting the seed. The garden scene tells
the kid 'you will remember this door was red' and it is true — the game
will remember it. In three chapters, the shopkeeper is going to say
'ah, I heard from Mira you came through the red door.' The seed has to
be planted here so it can bloom there.

---

## 1.6 A worked scene: The Kitchen at Dawn

Here is what the shape looks like when we care about the words. Not
placeholder text like 'you are in a small kitchen' — real prose that a
kid or an adult could read out loud.

```scheme
(define (kitchen-at-dawn)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (paint-gently
    \"It is early. The kitchen has that after-rain quiet. A jar of\"
    20 40)
  (paint-gently
    \"honey has been left on the counter with a spoon in it. Someone\"
    20 65)
  (paint-gently
    \"was here and left in a hurry.\"
    20 90)
  (world/after 40
    (lambda ()
      (paint-gently
        \"The RED door leads to the garden. You can hear bees from here.\"
        20 140)))
  (world/after 55
    (lambda ()
      (paint-gently
        \"The BLUE door leads to the hall. You can hear a cat.\"
        20 165)))
  (world/after 80
    (lambda ()
      (paint-text 20 220 \"[A] garden   [B] hall   [C] eat the honey\")))
  (on-key
    (lambda (k)
      (cond
        ((eq? k 'a)
         (cortex/write 'first-choice 'garden)
         (goto-scene garden-at-dawn))
        ((eq? k 'b)
         (cortex/write 'first-choice 'hall)
         (goto-scene hall-at-dawn))
        ((eq? k 'c)
         (cortex/write 'first-choice 'honey)
         (cortex/write 'ate-the-honey #t)
         (goto-scene the-honey-eating))))))
```

Look at what changed. We named the room 'kitchen at dawn' instead of
'kitchen' because time of day is part of setting. We put a jar of honey
on the counter because a room needs one specific object the kid can see.
We added a third choice — eat the honey — which is not a door but is
still a valid action. Text adventures teach a truth about narrative:
every scene is a small negotiation between what the writer wants and
what the reader would do.

The honey scene, if the kid picks C, might set two Cortex flags —
`first-choice = honey` and `ate-the-honey = #t`. Fifteen scenes from
now, someone might notice honey on the kid's chin, or the beekeeper
might say 'you smell sweet.' The seed is dropped here; the bloom comes
later.

---

## 1.7 Common desktop tasks — a shopkeeper's cold-open

An operator sells cast-iron cookware. She wants a five-second onboarding
that makes new customers smile before they even see the catalog. She
writes a narrative-game cold-open.

```scheme
;; A tiny narrative cart the shopkeeper serves as her landing page.
(define-card 'shop-cold-open
  :title \"welcome to the iron shop\"
  :init
  (lambda ()
    (scene/imagine)
    (surface/paper)
    (paint-gently
      \"You walk into a small shop. It smells like beeswax and old fire.\"
      20 40)
    (paint-gently
      \"A woman looks up from a skillet she is seasoning by hand.\"
      20 70)
    (world/after 40
      (lambda ()
        (paint-gently
          \"'You looking for a pan, or for a story about a pan?'\"
          20 120)))
    (world/after 70
      (lambda ()
        (paint-text 20 200 \"[A] a pan   [B] a story   [C] both\")))
    (on-key
      (lambda (k)
        (cond
          ((eq? k 'a) (shop-catalog))
          ((eq? k 'b) (shop-story))
          ((eq? k 'c) (shop-both)))))))
```

Three scenes flowing from here — `shop-catalog` opens the actual
listings, `shop-story` tells a two-minute origin story about how the
shopkeeper's grandmother taught her to season cast iron, `shop-both`
does the story first and then the catalog. The operator is doing what
narrative games have always done: welcoming a stranger, giving them a
choice, treating them like a guest.

This works because the operator has a voice. Her shop is not 'a shop.'
It is a small shop that smells like beeswax and old fire. Every operator
who writes a cold-open should write it in her actual voice — the voice
she uses when a friend walks in the door. The runtime will help her tune the
prose if she asks (chapter 12), but the voice has to be hers.

---

## 1.8 Routing patterns — one page, three shapes

Not every narrative game is a graph of rooms. Sometimes it is a stream
of scenes with no branches at all. Sometimes it is a wide fan of one-shot
scenes off a hub. Three shapes to know from the start:

**The corridor.** Scene 1 leads only to scene 2, which leads only to
scene 3. No branches. Use this when you are telling a story and the kid
is a reader, not a driver. Poems (chapter 14) live here.

**The hub.** One central room with N choices, each of which returns you
to the hub after playing out. Use this for museums, shops, and any place
where the kid is meant to explore rather than progress. Our kitchen with
its two return-here doors is a two-spoke hub.

**The branch.** Every choice leads to a new node with its own choices.
Use this for stories with real stakes. Chapter 2 formalizes this shape
as the story tree.

Most narrative games are a mix. A branch story with a corridor prologue
and a hub-shaped shop in the middle is completely normal. Your job as a
designer is to pick the right shape for each moment.

---

## 1.9 Closing

You have written a game. Not a big one. But a game. A kitchen, two
doors, a choice. The text eases in. The scene dims when you leave. The
choice is stored in a place that will remember it tomorrow.

Change one thing. Add a third door. Or change the kitchen to a bedroom
at 3am. Or make the honey scene actually paint a small yellow flower
with `flower/paint 20 120 :color 'gold`. The reference has hundreds of
verbs; you know six of them now. That is enough to make something
someone else has never seen.

The next chapter formalizes what we did into a story tree — a data
structure the engine reads, not a hand-written cascade of functions. The
kid designs the tree in her head, types it out as nested lists, and the
engine walks it. That is when narrative games start to feel like the
real thing.

For now, run the kitchen. Watch the text arrive. Press A. Press B. Play
your own game for a minute. That is the whole point.")

;; Book of Narrative Games — Chapter 2: The Story Tree

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(chapter

  :chapter-number      2
  :title               "The Story Tree"
  :dialect             "motoi"
  :audience            :kid
  :also-for            :adult
  :content-rating      :G
  :author-lane         "narrative-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"

"In chapter 1 each scene was a function that called the next scene by
name. That is fine for six scenes. For sixty it is a jungle of
functions. You can no longer see the shape of the story because it is
scattered across the code. The writer in you cannot see the game the
programmer in you is writing.

The fix is to move the story out of code and into data. A story becomes
a list of nodes; each node has an id, a text, and a list of choices.
The engine is one small function that reads the current node, paints its
text, waits for a choice, and jumps to whichever node the choice points
at. Now the story is a diagram you could sketch on a napkin. The engine
is 25 lines you write once and never think about again.

This is the physics of story-space: nodes are places, choices are edges,
a playthrough is a path through the graph. Once you see stories that way
you can design bigger ones.

---

## 2.1 A story as a list

Here is our kitchen story, but as data.

```scheme
(define story
  '((:id kitchen
     :text \"You are in a small kitchen. A red door to the north, a\n         blue door to the west.\"
     :choices ((:label \"go north (red)\" :goto garden)
               (:label \"go west (blue)\" :goto hallway)))
    (:id garden
     :text \"Bees. Tomatoes. A watering can that has been left out in\n         the rain and rusted through.\"
     :choices ((:label \"back to the kitchen\" :goto kitchen)
               (:label \"pick a tomato\"       :goto pocket-tomato)))
    (:id hallway
     :text \"Dust. A cat on the third step of a staircase. It watches\n         you without blinking.\"
     :choices ((:label \"upstairs\"           :goto upstairs)
               (:label \"back to the kitchen\" :goto kitchen)))
    (:id pocket-tomato
     :text \"You pocket a tomato. It leaves a warm wet spot on your\n         shirt. You feel obscurely happy.\"
     :choices ((:label \"back to the garden\" :goto garden)))
    (:id upstairs
     :text \"A small landing. The cat did not follow. A window is\n         open. There is a note on the sill in a hand you know.\"
     :choices ((:label \"read the note\"      :goto the-note)
               (:label \"go back down\"       :goto hallway)))
    (:id the-note
     :text \"The note says: 'I am at the beehive. Do not worry about\n         the honey. I will be back before you get bored.'\"
     :choices ((:label \"end for today\"      :goto ending)))
    (:id ending
     :text \"You put the note in your pocket, next to the tomato. You\n         decide to go to the hive.\"
     :choices ())))
```

Six scenes. Two endings (the ending node, and the pocket-tomato node
which loops but does not advance). Every scene has an id, a text, and
zero or more choices. Each choice has a label the kid sees and a goto
that names the next node. That is the whole vocabulary of a story tree.

The story is now a diagram you could draw on paper. Kitchen at the top.
Garden left, hallway right. Garden has pocket-tomato hanging off it.
Hallway has upstairs above it. Upstairs has the-note, which has ending.
That is the shape. Anyone who reads the data can see the shape. Compare
to chapter 1 where the shape was smeared across seven function
definitions — you could not see it without running the game.

---

## 2.2 The engine that walks the tree

We need one function that takes a story and a starting id and does the
right thing. Here is the whole engine.

```scheme
;; Find a node in the story by id.
(define (node-lookup story id)
  (find (lambda (n) (eq? (node-get n :id) id)) story))

(define (node-get node key)
  (cond ((null? node) #f)
        ((eq? (car node) key) (cadr node))
        (else (node-get (cddr node) key))))

;; Paint a node and let the kid choose.
(define (play-node story id)
  (let ((node (node-lookup story id)))
    (if (not node)
        (paint-text 20 40 (string-append \"?? node not found: \" (symbol->string id)))
        (begin
          (scene/imagine)
          (surface/paper)
          (paint-text 20 40 (node-get node :text))
          (paint-choices (node-get node :choices) 20 160)
          (on-key
            (lambda (k)
              (let ((chosen (choice-for-key (node-get node :choices) k)))
                (if chosen
                    (play-node story (node-get chosen :goto))
                    (play-node story id)))))))))

(define (paint-choices choices y0 x)
  (let loop ((cs choices) (i 0))
    (when (not (null? cs))
      (paint-text x (+ y0 (* i 25))
        (string-append \"[\" (number->letter (+ i 1)) \"] \"
                       (node-get (car cs) :label)))
      (loop (cdr cs) (+ i 1)))))

(define (choice-for-key choices k)
  (let ((idx (letter->index k)))
    (if (and (>= idx 0) (< idx (length choices)))
        (list-ref choices idx)
        #f)))

(define (number->letter n)
  (list-ref '(A B C D E F G H) (- n 1)))

(define (letter->index k)
  (case k
    ((a) 0) ((b) 1) ((c) 2) ((d) 3)
    ((e) 4) ((f) 5) ((g) 6) ((h) 7)
    (else -1)))

;; Kick it off.
(big-bang :init (lambda () (play-node story 'kitchen)))
```

Twenty-five lines of engine, plus five of helpers. It never mentions
kitchens, doors, or gardens. It works for any story you write in the
same shape. This is the point of pulling data out of code: the engine
gets reused; the story gets rewritten as often as you like.

Change the story and the engine still works. Add ten more scenes to
`story` and press play again. That is a design win worth pausing on.
Anytime you catch yourself writing the same shape three times in a row,
that shape belongs in data.

---

## 2.3 Marking visited nodes

A kid plays a small tree twice and the second time she should see which
choices she has already tried. We use Cortex to track it.

```scheme
;; Track visited nodes across sessions.
(define (play-node-remembering story id)
  (cortex/write 'last-node id)
  (let* ((visited (or (cortex/read 'visited-nodes) '()))
         (already (member id visited)))
    (cortex/write 'visited-nodes (cons id visited))
    (let ((node (node-lookup story id)))
      (scene/imagine)
      (surface/paper)
      (paint-text 20 40 (node-get node :text))
      (paint-choices-with-visited
        (node-get node :choices) visited 20 160)
      (on-key
        (lambda (k)
          (let ((chosen (choice-for-key (node-get node :choices) k)))
            (if chosen
                (play-node-remembering story (node-get chosen :goto))
                (play-node-remembering story id))))))))

(define (paint-choices-with-visited choices visited x y0)
  (let loop ((cs choices) (i 0))
    (when (not (null? cs))
      (let* ((c (car cs))
             (target (node-get c :goto))
             (seen? (member target visited))
             (label (string-append \"[\" (number->letter (+ i 1)) \"] \"
                                   (node-get c :label)
                                   (if seen? \" (visited)\" \"\"))))
        (paint-text x (+ y0 (* i 25)) label))
      (loop (cdr cs) (+ i 1)))))
```

Now when the kid opens the game tomorrow, the choices she has already
tried are marked with 'visited.' Not disabled — she can still take them,
maybe she wants to revisit — but tagged. She has a sense of the shape
of the space she has already explored. That is a small piece of respect
for her time.

`cortex/read` returns `#f` if the key has never been set. We
`(or ... '())` to default to the empty list. Then `member` checks if a
node id is in the list. `member` returns a tail-list if found, `#f` if
not, which is truthy/falsy — perfect for `if`.

---

## 2.4 Endings and dead ends

An ending is any node whose choices list is empty. The engine should
notice this and offer the kid a way to reset or replay.

```scheme
(define (play-node-with-endings story id)
  (let ((node (node-lookup story id)))
    (scene/imagine)
    (surface/paper)
    (paint-text 20 40 (node-get node :text))
    (let ((choices (node-get node :choices)))
      (if (null? choices)
          (paint-ending-panel)
          (paint-choices choices 20 160))
      (on-key
        (lambda (k)
          (if (null? choices)
              (case k
                ((r) (play-node-with-endings story 'kitchen))   ;; replay
                ((q) (return-to-menu))
                (else (play-node-with-endings story id)))
              (let ((chosen (choice-for-key choices k)))
                (if chosen
                    (play-node-with-endings story (node-get chosen :goto))
                    (play-node-with-endings story id)))))))))

(define (paint-ending-panel)
  (paint-text 20 220 \"~~~ end ~~~\")
  (paint-text 20 260 \"[R] replay from start   [Q] back to menu\"))
```

The kid reaches the ending scene. The engine sees the empty choices
list and paints the ending panel instead. R starts over from the
kitchen. Q returns to whatever menu wraps the game. An ending is not the
end of the code; it is the end of THIS playthrough. Kids should always
have a way back to the beginning.

---

## 2.5 Multiple endings

A tree with multiple endings feels bigger than it is. Ten scenes with
three endings feels like a real story; ten scenes with one ending feels
like a hallway.

Rewrite the story to have three endings — the beehive, the cat's
staircase, and the rusted watering can.

```scheme
(define story-with-endings
  '((:id kitchen
     :text \"A small kitchen. Red door north. Blue door west.\"
     :choices ((:label \"north\" :goto garden)
               (:label \"west\"  :goto hallway)))
    (:id garden
     :text \"Bees. Tomatoes. A watering can rusted through.\"
     :choices ((:label \"back\"                :goto kitchen)
               (:label \"study the can\"       :goto ending-watering-can)))
    (:id hallway
     :text \"Cat on the stairs. Watches you.\"
     :choices ((:label \"upstairs\"            :goto upstairs)
               (:label \"back\"                 :goto kitchen)
               (:label \"sit with the cat\"    :goto ending-cat)))
    (:id upstairs
     :text \"A note on the sill. It mentions the hive.\"
     :choices ((:label \"go to the hive\"      :goto ending-hive)
               (:label \"back\"                 :goto hallway)))
    (:id ending-watering-can
     :text \"You realize the can is your grandmother's. You keep it.\"
     :choices ())
    (:id ending-cat
     :text \"You sit for a long time. The cat allows itself to be pet.\"
     :choices ())
    (:id ending-hive
     :text \"You find the hive. There is honey. There is a friend.\"
     :choices ())))
```

Six scenes, three endings. The kid can replay and get a different
outcome each time. She will not replay unless the first ending felt
weighted enough to make her curious about the others. That is a lesson
for chapter 11 — branches only matter if the endings matter. Do not
make three endings just to have three; make three endings if you know
which one you want the kid to reach first.

---

## 2.6 A worked scene: what the tree feels like when it is small

Here is a five-node story called 'The Return.' A person walks home to
a place she has not been in years. Three endings.

```scheme
(define the-return
  '((:id door
     :text \"You are standing on the porch of a house you have not\n         been to in twelve years. The key still works.\"
     :choices ((:label \"unlock and walk in\"       :goto foyer)
               (:label \"ring the bell instead\"   :goto bell)
               (:label \"turn around and leave\"   :goto ending-leave)))
    (:id foyer
     :text \"It smells like your mother. Nobody is home. The kitchen\n         light is on.\"
     :choices ((:label \"kitchen\"                 :goto kitchen)
               (:label \"upstairs, your old room\" :goto old-room)))
    (:id bell
     :text \"A woman you have not seen in twelve years opens the door.\n         She is smaller than you remembered.\"
     :choices ((:label \"tell her you came\"     :goto ending-reunion)
               (:label \"apologize for the years\" :goto ending-apology)))
    (:id kitchen
     :text \"A note on the fridge in her handwriting. 'If you come\n         home, there is soup on the stove.'\"
     :choices ((:label \"eat the soup\"           :goto ending-soup)))
    (:id old-room
     :text \"The bed is made. Your books are on the shelf, dusted.\n         She kept it.\"
     :choices ((:label \"lie down\"                :goto ending-soup)))
    (:id ending-leave  :text \"You do not go in. That is a decision.\" :choices ())
    (:id ending-reunion :text \"You cry. So does she. It is not fixed. It is started.\" :choices ())
    (:id ending-apology :text \"'I know,' she says. That is all.\" :choices ())
    (:id ending-soup    :text \"The soup is still warm. She knew you were coming.\" :choices ())))
```

Twelve years is specific. 'Smaller than you remembered' is honest. Soup
still warm is a lie the kid can catch — did she know, or did the soup
just happen to be warm? The kid decides. That is what a story tree gives
you room for.

Notice that 'leave' is one of the endings. Sometimes not going in IS
the choice. Do not always force the kid down the story. Let refusal be
a real option. This is a lesson about consent as design: a game that
punishes the kid for opting out is a game that lies about its choices.

## 2.7 Common desktop tasks — an operator's return-policy tree

A shopkeeper has a return policy. She could write it as three
paragraphs of legalese or she could write it as a five-scene story tree.
The kid — I mean, the customer — walks through the tree, and by the end
they know exactly what applies to their situation.

```scheme
(define return-policy-tree
  '((:id start
     :text \"How can I help? Did the piece arrive broken, was it not\n         what you expected, or has it been over 30 days?\"
     :choices ((:label \"arrived broken\"   :goto broken)
               (:label \"not what expected\" :goto not-expected)
               (:label \"over 30 days\"      :goto over-thirty)))
    (:id broken
     :text \"I am sorry. That is on me. Send a photo of the damage\n         and I will make it right same day.\"
     :choices ((:label \"got it, thank you\" :goto ending-broken-yes)))
    (:id not-expected
     :text \"Return for full refund within 14 days. You cover ship.\n         I will refund immediately on receipt — no waiting.\"
     :choices ((:label \"start the return\"  :goto ending-not-expected)))
    (:id over-thirty
     :text \"After 30 days it depends on the piece. If it broke of its\n         own accord, I usually cover 50%. Tell me what happened?\"
     :choices ((:label \"broke on its own\"     :goto ending-repair)
               (:label \"I dropped it\"          :goto ending-drop)))
    (:id ending-broken-yes    :text \"Photo tool below. I will reply within the hour.\" :choices ())
    (:id ending-not-expected  :text \"Return-label form below. Thank you for being kind about it.\" :choices ())
    (:id ending-repair        :text \"Send a photo. I will quote 50%-off repair or replace.\" :choices ())
    (:id ending-drop          :text \"Best I can do is a repair quote. No refund past 30.\" :choices ())))
```

The customer walks through the tree in fifteen seconds. She feels heard.
She has been offered a specific action. She has a real answer, not a
paragraph of maybe. That is what narrative shape does for a shopkeeper
who does not want to write help-center documentation and does want to
treat customers like people.

The shopkeeper wrote each ending in her own voice ('that is on me,'
'no waiting'). If she gave the tree to the runtime and asked for wording
suggestions, the runtime would tune it — but the shape and the values are
the shopkeeper's.

---

## 2.8 Routing patterns for trees

Three shapes worth knowing when you design a tree:

**The lattice.** Some choices lead to the same later node from different
directions. Kitchen and garden both loop back; a save room is reachable
from three floors. Trees with lattices feel richer because the kid can
approach the same scene with different history. Cortex makes this
delicious in chapter 3.

**The gate.** A node the kid cannot reach without a specific past
choice. 'You cannot go through the door unless you took the key' is
implemented by checking Cortex before offering the door. Chapter 8 does
this properly with inventory. For now, just know that a tree with gates
feels more like a world and less like a menu.

**The pruned branch.** Some choices should disappear based on what the
kid has done. If you gave the honey to the bees in scene 2, you cannot
also eat it in scene 5. Filter the choices list before painting it.
This is where `filter` earns its place in your toolkit.

```scheme
(define (available-choices node)
  (filter
    (lambda (c)
      (let ((req (node-get c :requires)))
        (if req
            (cortex/read req)         ;; only if the flag is set
            #t)))                     ;; unconditional
    (node-get node :choices)))
```

Choices with `:requires 'have-lantern` only appear if `(cortex/read
'have-lantern)` is truthy. Choices with no `:requires` always appear.
Ten lines, and now your trees have conditional edges.

## 2.9 Closing

You have replaced code with data. Six scenes now take up eight lines of
list; the engine reads them and does the right thing. You can add
scenes without touching the engine. You can share the story with a
friend and she can rewrite the words without touching Scheme at all.

Try this: write a five-scene story about something that happened to you
this week. It does not have to be interesting to anyone else. It has to
have three choices somewhere and two endings. Load it into the engine
you built. Play it. If your friend plays it and asks 'wait, what did
this really mean?' — you have made a small narrative game.

Chapter 3 is about memory. The story tree walks itself; Cortex
remembers what it walked. When the shopkeeper says 'I heard you came
through the red door,' it is Cortex whispering to her. That is where
narrative games start to feel alive.")

"The trick of a good narrative game is that the story remembers. Not the
kid. The story. She made a choice thirty minutes ago and she has
forgotten it, and then a character three rooms later says 'I heard
about what you did with the fox.' She gets goosebumps. That is not a
literary effect. That is code.

The code is a key-value store called Cortex that survives every kind of
break — the frame ending, the game closing, the phone going to sleep,
the kid coming back tomorrow. Anything you write to Cortex is still
there when she opens the game again. That means the character you built
last night still knows what she did.

This chapter is about using Cortex well. Not just writing to it. Using
it — reading it at the right moments, tagging it with the right keys,
letting it accumulate into a shape that feels like a person's memory
of a person.

## 3.1 The three verbs

You will use three Cortex verbs for the whole book.

```scheme
(cortex/write key value)      ;; remember this
(cortex/read key)             ;; what did you remember?
(cortex/topk n)               ;; the n most recent things you remembered
```

`cortex/write 'saved-the-fox #t` stores the boolean #t under the key
`saved-the-fox`. That's it. Any Motoi Scheme value works: a symbol,
a number, a string, a list, a nested list. Write anything you want to
be able to look up later.

`cortex/read 'saved-the-fox` returns #t if we wrote it, or #f if we
never touched that key. Simple lookup. If you want a default when the
key is missing, use `(or (cortex/read 'saved-the-fox) #f)`.

`cortex/topk 5` returns the five most recently written entries, newest
first. This is how you build a 'previously on…' recap without keeping
your own log. Cortex keeps a log for you.

Those three verbs are 95% of narrative-game memory. Everything else in
this chapter is patterns for using them.

---

## 3.2 The keys have a shape

Do not just scatter keys named `x`, `y`, `flag1`. Give them namespaces.
Future you needs to know what a key means when she reads it in scene 40.

```scheme
;; A good key naming scheme:
;;
;;  'state/*        — world flags: 'state/door-unlocked, 'state/well-poisoned
;;  'inventory      — the kid's stuff (a list)
;;  'past-choices   — an alist of important choices made
;;  'reputation/*   — how NPCs feel: 'reputation/mira, 'reputation/villain
;;  'seen/*         — which scenes have been visited
;;  'save/slot/1    — full snapshot bundles
;;
;; So instead of:
(cortex/write 'red #t)

;; do:
(cortex/write 'state/first-door-red? #t)

;; And instead of:
(cortex/write 'inv (cons 'lantern (cortex/read 'inv)))

;; do:
(cortex/write 'inventory (cons 'lantern (or (cortex/read 'inventory) '())))
```

The namespace tells you the meaning. When you are debugging a game a
month from now and you see `'state/well-poisoned` in a log, you know
exactly what it does. Appendix A tabulates the full recommended
namespace.

The `or` idiom — `(or (cortex/read 'inventory) '())` — is the safe way
to append. If inventory has never been touched, `cortex/read` returns
#f, and #f cannot be `cons`ed onto. We coerce to the empty list first,
then cons. Do this every time you extend a list-shaped Cortex key.

## 3.3 The shopkeeper who remembers

Here is the game we have been building toward. The kid played the
kitchen last night, took the red door, ate the honey. Today she
continues the story. She walks into a shop.

```scheme
;; The shop scene reads Cortex and greets the kid personally.
(define (shop-scene)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (let ((first-choice (cortex/read 'state/first-choice))
        (ate-honey?   (cortex/read 'state/ate-the-honey))
        (has-tomato?  (member 'tomato (or (cortex/read 'inventory) '()))))
    (paint-text 20 40 (shopkeeper-greeting first-choice ate-honey? has-tomato?))
    (paint-text 20 200 \"[A] buy something   [B] tell her about the note\")
    (on-key
      (lambda (k)
        (case k
          ((a) (shop-catalog))
          ((b) (tell-about-note))))))
  (paint-text 20 250 \"[Q] leave the shop\"))

(define (shopkeeper-greeting first-choice ate-honey? has-tomato?)
  (cond
    ((and (eq? first-choice 'garden) has-tomato?)
     \"Oh — Mira said you might come. She could smell tomato on you\nfrom the porch. Sit, sit.\")
    ((eq? first-choice 'garden)
     \"You are the one who came through the garden. Mira told me.\")
    ((and (eq? first-choice 'hall) ate-honey?)
     \"You are the one who ate the honey. It shows around your mouth.\nDo not worry, I laugh, come in.\")
    ((eq? first-choice 'hall)
     \"You are the one who came through the hall. The cat is mine, by\nthe way. She likes you.\")
    (else
     \"Welcome. I do not think we have met.\")))
```

Five possible greetings based on what the kid did last night. The kid
took the garden door AND has a tomato — the shopkeeper knows Mira told
her, and can smell the tomato. The kid took the hall AND ate the honey
— the shopkeeper is amused, notes the honey around her mouth.
Otherwise, the shopkeeper is polite but no history to draw on.

This is the moment the kid feels seen. She did not tell the shopkeeper
anything. The game did. The game had its ear pressed to the door.

If the shopkeeper mentioned facts the kid does NOT recognize — 'you
must have had a fine time with Yolanda' — the illusion breaks and the
kid gets suspicious. Cortex only helps when the writer is honest about
what the game actually knows. Do not fake it.

---

## 3.4 Reading past-choices as an alist

For messier stories with lots of small choices, one flag per choice
gets out of hand. Use a single alist called `past-choices`.

```scheme
;; Instead of many separate flags:
(cortex/write 'state/first-door 'red)
(cortex/write 'state/ate-honey? #t)
(cortex/write 'state/spared-wolf? #t)

;; Use one bundle:
(define (remember-choice key value)
  (let ((old (or (cortex/read 'past-choices) '())))
    (cortex/write 'past-choices (cons (cons key value) old))))

(define (recall-choice key)
  (let ((old (or (cortex/read 'past-choices) '())))
    (cdr (or (assoc key old) '(#f . #f)))))

;; Now:
(remember-choice 'first-door 'red)
(remember-choice 'ate-honey? #t)
(remember-choice 'spared-wolf? #t)

(recall-choice 'first-door)   ;; => 'red
(recall-choice 'ate-honey?)   ;; => #t
(recall-choice 'never-set)    ;; => #f
```

Every choice you make in the story flows through
`remember-choice`. Later, any character can `recall-choice` any past
decision. The alist grows without bound, but Cortex handles that; you
do not need to prune it.

This pattern is worth using early. The first time you catch yourself
adding a fourth `cortex/write 'state/...`, migrate to alist-shape and
you will not regret it.

---

## 3.5 Reputation as a number

Sometimes the past is not a boolean but a magnitude. How much does
Mira trust you? Not 'yes' or 'no' — a number.

```scheme
;; Reputation with an NPC as a signed integer.
(define (rep-change npc delta)
  (let* ((key (string->symbol
                (string-append \"reputation/\" (symbol->string npc))))
         (old (or (cortex/read key) 0)))
    (cortex/write key (+ old delta))))

(define (rep npc)
  (let ((key (string->symbol
               (string-append \"reputation/\" (symbol->string npc)))))
    (or (cortex/read key) 0)))

;; The kid does a kind thing:
(rep-change 'mira +2)

;; The kid does a cold thing:
(rep-change 'mira -1)

;; Mira's dialogue branches on it:
(define (mira-greeting)
  (let ((r (rep 'mira)))
    (cond
      ((> r 5)  \"Oh, it is YOU. Come in, sit, tell me everything.\")
      ((> r 0)  \"Hello again. Nice to see you.\")
      ((= r 0)  \"Hello.\")
      (else     \"You. Well. What is it you want.\"))))
```

Every kindness moves the number up. Every coldness moves it down. Mira
greets accordingly. The kid does not know the exact number — she just
feels that Mira warms up over time, or cools down. That is how
reputation works in life. It is also how it works in some of the best
role-playing games.

Reputation lives in Cortex under `reputation/<npc>`. It survives
sessions. The kid closes the game with Mira at rep 7 and opens
tomorrow with Mira still at 7.

---

## 3.6 The 'previously on…' recap

Long narrative games benefit from a recap the way TV shows do. When
the kid opens the game after two days away, remind her.

```scheme
;; Show a two-second recap of the last three big events.
(define (previously-on)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (paint-text 20 40 \"~~ previously ~~\")
  (let ((recent (cortex/topk 3)))
    (let loop ((es recent) (i 0))
      (when (not (null? es))
        (paint-text 20 (+ 80 (* i 30)) (event->prose (car es)))
        (loop (cdr es) (+ i 1)))))
  (world/after 180                     ;; three seconds
    (lambda () (start-game))))

(define (event->prose entry)
  ;; entry is a cortex log record — a pair of (key . value) plus a timestamp.
  ;; We render it as a short human sentence.
  (let ((key (car entry))
        (val (cdr entry)))
    (cond
      ((eq? key 'past-choices)
       (string-append \"You chose: \" (symbol->string (car val))))
      ((eq? key 'inventory)
       (string-append \"You picked up: \" (symbol->string (car val))))
      ((string-prefix? \"reputation/\" (symbol->string key))
       (string-append \"You dealt with \"
                      (string-drop (symbol->string key) 11)
                      \".\"))
      (else
       \"…something happened.\"))))
```

Three most recent Cortex writes become three lines of prose recap. The
kid sees 'you chose garden, you picked up tomato, you dealt with mira'
and the story wraps back around her shoulders like a familiar blanket.
Three seconds and then the game continues.

You can go fancier with `ai/summarize` — feed it the last 20 entries
and ask for a two-line prose summary. Chapter 12 covers that. For now,
top-3 with hand-crafted rendering is plenty.

---

## 3.7 A worked scene: three shopkeepers, one kid

The kid has been playing for two hours across three sessions. She has
past-choices: took-red-door, ate-honey, spared-wolf, gave-note-to-mira.
Inventory: tomato, lantern, feather. Reputations: mira +4, villain -2,
kestrel +1.

She walks into a village square. Three shopkeepers. Each greets her
based on what THEY would know.

```scheme
(define (village-square)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (paint-text 20 40 \"The square. Three stalls. Three people you know.\")
  (paint-text 20 100 (baker-greeting))
  (paint-text 20 160 (smith-greeting))
  (paint-text 20 220 (herbalist-greeting)))

(define (baker-greeting)
  (cond
    ((> (rep 'mira) 3)
     \"BAKER: 'Oh! Mira sent word ahead. There is a bread for you.'\")
    ((recall-choice 'ate-honey?)
     \"BAKER: 'You are the honey-eater. I have a jar with your name.'\")
    (else
     \"BAKER: 'Morning. Loaves are two coppers.'\")))

(define (smith-greeting)
  (cond
    ((recall-choice 'spared-wolf?)
     \"SMITH: 'I heard about the wolf. That was not a small thing.'\")
    ((recall-choice 'gave-note-to-mira?)
     \"SMITH: 'You brought the note. I owe you a favor.'\")
    (else
     \"SMITH: 'You need an edge sharpened?'\")))

(define (herbalist-greeting)
  (cond
    ((> (rep 'villain) 0)   ;; kid befriended the villain?
     \"HERBALIST: 'You are the one who talks with the wolf. Careful.'\")
    ((< (rep 'villain) -1)
     \"HERBALIST: 'You are the one who stood up to him. Good.'\")
    (else
     \"HERBALIST: 'Fresh mint. Fresh sage. What do you need?'\")))
```

Three greetings, each read from a different corner of Cortex. Nobody
mentions everything — the baker does not know about the wolf, the
smith does not know about the honey. Each shopkeeper knows what a
shopkeeper would know: the baker heard from Mira, the smith heard about
the wolf-and-note, the herbalist has strong opinions about the
villain. This is realism as design: characters know some things, not
all things.

Play this scene four times over four playthroughs and it has four
different textures. The kid never sees the same square twice. The game
did not grow bigger. Cortex just remembered more, and the writers
tapped that.

---

## 3.8 Common desktop tasks — a repeat customer

A shopkeeper's cart. A customer has bought from her twice before. On
the third visit the greeting should be personal.

```scheme
;; Ambient shopkeeper cart — greets a returning customer by history.
(define-card 'shop-personal-greeting
  :init
  (lambda ()
    (let* ((visits    (or (cortex/read 'customer/visits) 0))
           (last-buy  (cortex/read 'customer/last-purchase))
           (fav-color (cortex/read 'customer/fav-color)))
      (cortex/write 'customer/visits (+ visits 1))
      (scene/imagine)
      (surface/paper)
      (paint-text 20 40
        (cond
          ((and last-buy (> visits 2))
           (string-append \"You came back. The \" last-buy
                          \" is treating you well I hope?\"))
          ((= visits 1)
           \"First time in. Welcome.\")
          (else
           \"Welcome back.\")))
      (when fav-color
        (paint-text 20 100
          (string-append \"I set aside a piece in \" fav-color
                         \" — thought of you when it came in.\")))
      (paint-text 20 200 \"[A] browse   [B] special orders\"))))
```

The customer visits for the third time. She bought a cast-iron skillet
last time. Her favorite color, which she once mentioned in chat, was
green. The card greets her: 'you came back — the skillet is treating
you well I hope?' and 'I set aside a piece in green — thought of you
when it came in.'

The customer is a customer. The shopkeeper cannot remember every
detail about every visitor. Cortex CAN. And the operator wrote the
tiny card that lets Cortex whisper the details into her greeting.
This is what turns a shop into a place.

Persistence caveat: `customer/visits` and `customer/fav-color` are
per-customer, so they live in a Cortex scope keyed to the customer id.
Appendix A shows the recommended scoping. For now, know that Cortex
handles per-user isolation for you.

---

## 3.9 Cross-session persistence — the acid test

Here is how you know Cortex is really working across sessions: quit
the game, restart your machine, open the game, and see if it remembers.

```scheme
;; A tiny test — set a value, quit, come back, check it.
(define (test-persistence)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (let ((saved (cortex/read 'test/persisted)))
    (if saved
        (begin
          (paint-text 20 40
            (string-append \"Cortex says: \" saved))
          (paint-text 20 80
            \"That value came from a previous session.\"))
        (begin
          (cortex/write 'test/persisted \"a plum tree in blossom\")
          (paint-text 20 40 \"I wrote a plum tree in blossom to Cortex.\")
          (paint-text 20 80 \"Quit and come back. It will still be here.\")))))
```

Run it once. See the write message. Quit. Run it again. See the plum
tree quoted back at you. That is the whole magic. Any string, symbol,
list, or number you write is still there tomorrow. The story remembers.

The kid who understands this understands the difference between a
video game and a narrative game. A video game resets. A narrative game
keeps you.

---

## 3.10 Closing

Cortex is three verbs and a naming convention. Use them well and the
kid's character grows a body. Six characters remember her from
different angles. The shopkeeper says 'I heard from Mira.' The
herbalist has strong opinions about the villain. The baker set aside
a piece in green.

The physics of memory: story gets heavier the longer you play. In a
narrative game with no memory, every scene weighs the same. In one
with Cortex, scene 40 carries scene 3 on its shoulders. That is why
we play.

Chapter 4 gives characters bodies. Right now they are voices in the
dark. Next they will breathe, and lean, and look at you. Cortex knows
who; the body shows who.")
