"A character with a name and a body of text is a character. A character
with a name and a body of pixels that BREATHES is a person. The
difference is not measurable in pixels or verbs. It is measurable in
what the kid does when the character leaves the room. If she looks up.
If she noticed. If she cares that the room is now empty.

We are going to give characters bodies that do the smallest, quietest
things: breathe, nod, lean, look toward the player. Not action-movie
gestures. The subtle continuous motion that says 'this thing is alive.'
Animation studios call it 'ambient motion' and it is what separates a
statue from a figure. Kids call it 'breathing' because that is what it
looks like.

The physics of body language: two pixels of vertical drift over a
one-second cycle is the difference between a mannequin and a person.

---

## 4.1 Making a character

```scheme
;; Give a name and a body to a character.
(define mira (make-character 'mira))
(entity/pose!  mira 'standing)
(entity/sprite! mira 'girl-in-blue)
(entity/set-pos! mira 200 180)
(entity/tag! mira 'friendly)
```

`make-character` gives us an entity id we can refer to by name. The
symbol `'mira` is a Scheme name; the return value is the entity id.
Elsewhere in the code, if we need to talk about Mira, we use the
variable `mira` — not the symbol.

`entity/pose!` sets the stance — standing, sitting, crouched. This
picks a sprite from the character's sprite sheet, if it has one, or
just tags the pose for later reads.

`entity/sprite!` sets which sprite to render. In the reference,
sprites are named symbols; you can put anything you want there and the
engine substitutes a placeholder shape if the name is unknown. Perfect
for prototyping.

`entity/set-pos!` puts her at pixel coordinates. `entity/tag!` adds
`'friendly` to her tag list for later `filter`ing.

Four lines. Mira exists on the page. But she does not yet breathe. Let
us fix that.

---

## 4.2 Breath

This is the single most important verb in this chapter.

```scheme
;; A gentle rise-and-fall that never stops.
(part/breathe mira 0.3)
```

That's it. `part/breathe mira 0.3` starts a slow ambient motion where
Mira's whole body rises about 2 pixels and falls about 2 pixels every
2 seconds. The 0.3 is the rate — 0.3 Hz, or about one breath every 3
seconds. Slower than a human at rest (about 0.2-0.25 Hz for adults,
faster for kids), which reads on screen as 'calm.' A character in
distress might breathe at 0.6-0.8 Hz — the same amount of movement,
just faster.

Try it. Put Mira on the page. Do not breathe her. Watch her for ten
seconds. She looks like a decal. Add `(part/breathe mira 0.3)`. Watch
her for ten seconds. You cannot look away. Your eye locks onto the
tiny rise-and-fall the way it locks onto a candle flame.

That is what animation studios pay their senior animators to do — the
breath cycle. In our runtime it is one line of Scheme.

---

## 4.3 The (part/*) family

Twelve verbs give a character everything she needs to communicate a
mood without speaking.

```scheme
(part/breathe    ent rate)              ;; ambient rise-fall
(part/nod        ent)                   ;; agreement: two quick down-ups
(part/tilt       ent degrees)           ;; head tilt for curiosity
(part/lean       ent px)                ;; body lean forward or back
(part/turn       ent direction)         ;; face left, right, front, back
(part/look-toward ent x y)              ;; eyes track a point
(part/bow        ent depth)             ;; respect
(part/wave       ent hand)              ;; greet
(part/sway       ent amount)            ;; uncertainty, thinking
(part/step       ent direction)         ;; a single step in that direction
(part/reach      ent x y)               ;; arm extends toward point
(part/expression ent emotion)           ;; face changes: happy, sad, angry
(part/shrug      ent)                   ;; don't know
```

Every one is short. Every one composes with the others. A character can
be breathing (baseline) and tilting her head (curiosity) and looking at
the player (attention) all at once. The runtime layers them.

Study the list. If you are designing a character, ask 'what does she do
when she is thinking?' Maybe she sways slightly (`part/sway mira 3`).
'What does she do when she is confused?' She tilts and looks
(`part/tilt mira 15` and `part/look-toward mira player-x player-y`).
Every character can have a signature — a combination of these gestures
that reads as HER.

---

## 4.4 A scene with body language

Let us give Mira a whole scene where her body is doing the talking.

```scheme
(define (mira-scene)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  ;; The room.
  (paint-text 20 40 \"A small back garden. Mira is looking at a book.\")

  ;; Mira's baseline: breathing, sitting.
  (entity/pose! mira 'sitting)
  (entity/set-pos! mira 240 200)
  (part/breathe mira 0.3)                    ;; slow, calm

  ;; The kid walks in.
  (world/after 60
    (lambda ()
      (part/look-toward mira 60 200)          ;; eyes track to the door
      (part/tilt mira 8)))                    ;; curiosity — head tilts

  ;; The kid says hi.
  (world/after 120
    (lambda ()
      (part/expression mira 'smile)
      (part/wave mira 'right)))                ;; a small wave

  ;; The kid asks a hard question.
  (world/after 240
    (lambda ()
      (part/tilt mira 0)                       ;; head straightens
      (part/lean mira -8)                      ;; leans back
      (part/expression mira 'thinking)
      (part/sway mira 4)))                     ;; sways gently while she thinks
  )
```

Read the code. That is a whole silent conversation. Mira is reading.
The kid walks in — Mira's eyes go to the door and her head tilts. The
kid says hi — Mira smiles and waves. The kid asks a hard question —
Mira straightens, leans back, thinks. No dialogue in this snippet at
all, and yet a scene has happened.

Now imagine putting dialogue on top. Every part-verb is punctuation.
Mira nods on 'yes.' She sways on 'I do not know.' She tilts on the
kid's confusing sentence. The words are the melody; the body is the
rhythm.

---

## 4.5 A character who reacts to the mouse

`part/look-toward` accepts any (x, y). If we pass the mouse position,
Mira watches the mouse. This is a small trick that makes a static
scene feel alive.

```scheme
;; Mira's eyes follow the pointer.
(on-frame
  (lambda ()
    (part/look-toward mira (input/mouse-x) (input/mouse-y))))
```

Every frame, Mira's eyes reposition to look where the pointer is.
Move the pointer left; her eyes go left. Move it up; her eyes go up.
This costs almost nothing and communicates 'she is aware of you' more
strongly than a whole paragraph of description.

You can also do this with the touch position on a tablet, or with the
sensed direction of a controller stick. Whatever the kid's attention
points at, Mira looks at.

Do not overuse this. If every character in the game tracks the mouse
constantly, the effect feels needy — like all the NPCs want your
attention. Use it selectively, for the character whose relationship
with the player is central to the scene.

---

## 4.6 Signatures — every character breathes differently

The bee-keeper breathes slow. The kid breathes fast. The villain
breathes slower than anyone else in the game — that is HOW he is
scary. Signatures come from the parameters.

```scheme
;; Character signatures.
(define (mira-signature)
  (part/breathe mira 0.28)                    ;; calm
  (part/sway    mira 1))                       ;; barely detectable

(define (kid-signature)
  (part/breathe kid 0.55)                     ;; excited
  (part/sway    kid 3))                        ;; fidgets

(define (villain-signature)
  (part/breathe villain 0.15)                  ;; unnervingly slow
  (part/sway    villain 0))                    ;; unmoving

(define (bee-keeper-signature)
  (part/breathe bee-keeper 0.20)               ;; slower than average
  (part/sway    bee-keeper 2))                 ;; a small ambient sway
```

The kid does not know she is decoding breath rates. She just feels
that the villain is unnerving and the kid character is nervous and
Mira is calm and the bee-keeper is slower than everyone else because
he has been breathing to that rhythm his whole life.

Set the signature ONCE when the character enters the scene. It runs
in the background for the whole scene. Layer specific gestures on top
— nods, tilts, waves — without touching the baseline. When the
character leaves, `(part/halt villain)` stops all ambient motion.

---

## 4.7 A worked scene: the meeting on the porch

Two characters. One breath rate each. A page of prose that would take
you five minutes to write and thirty seconds to read.

```scheme
(define (porch-meeting)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (paint-text 20 40 \"The porch. Late afternoon. Two chairs.\")

  ;; Mira, on the left chair.
  (define mira (make-character 'mira))
  (entity/pose! mira 'sitting)
  (entity/set-pos! mira 120 180)
  (part/breathe mira 0.28)

  ;; The kid's father, on the right chair. He has not spoken in a while.
  (define father (make-character 'father))
  (entity/pose! father 'sitting)
  (entity/set-pos! father 280 180)
  (part/breathe father 0.22)

  ;; First minute: silence.
  (world/after 180
    (lambda () (paint-text 20 250 \"MIRA: 'It is a fine sky.'\")))

  ;; Father takes his time to respond.
  (world/after 300
    (lambda () (part/turn father 'left)))       ;; he turns to look at her

  (world/after 360
    (lambda ()
      (part/nod father)
      (paint-text 20 280 \"FATHER: 'It is.'\")))

  ;; A pause.
  (world/after 480
    (lambda () (paint-text 20 310 \"MIRA: 'She came home yesterday.'\")))

  ;; He does not react quickly. He stops breathing for one cycle.
  (world/after 540
    (lambda ()
      (part/halt father)                        ;; a moment without breath
      (world/after 60
        (lambda () (part/breathe father 0.22)))))

  (world/after 660
    (lambda ()
      (part/lean father -6)                     ;; leans back into the chair
      (paint-text 20 340 \"FATHER: 'Did she stay?'\")))

  (world/after 780
    (lambda ()
      (part/nod mira)
      (paint-text 20 370 \"MIRA: 'She stayed.'\")))
  )
```

That is a scene with almost no words. The father's held breath — one
line of `part/halt` — carries more than any adjective. The lean back
after the news comes carries the rest. Mira's nod at the end is a
period. Nobody said anything a screenwriter would love, but a whole
family reunion happened in eight seconds of screen time.

The kid who watches this and understands why it worked will write
better scenes forever. The kid who wrote this and got tears from a
friend who played it will write more games.

---

## 4.8 Common desktop tasks — the operator's little companion

An operator's shop has a mascot: a small cat named Yuzu. Yuzu sits
in the corner of the shop cart, breathes, occasionally looks at the
kid, occasionally does a small stretch. Yuzu is not gameplay. Yuzu is
COMPANY.

```scheme
;; Yuzu the shop cat. Ambient companion.
(define-card 'shop-with-yuzu
  :init
  (lambda ()
    (scene/imagine)
    (surface/paper)
    (paint-text 20 40 \"Welcome. Feel free to look around.\")

    (define yuzu (make-character 'yuzu))
    (entity/sprite! yuzu 'cat-orange)
    (entity/set-pos! yuzu 400 300)
    (part/breathe yuzu 0.35)                    ;; cats breathe faster than us

    ;; Every 15-25 seconds, Yuzu looks at the mouse.
    (define (yuzu-attention)
      (part/look-toward yuzu (input/mouse-x) (input/mouse-y))
      (world/after (+ 900 (random 600))       ;; 15-25s at 60fps
        (lambda () (yuzu-attention))))
    (yuzu-attention)

    ;; Every 30-60 seconds, Yuzu does a small stretch.
    (define (yuzu-stretch)
      (part/reach yuzu (entity/x yuzu) (- (entity/y yuzu) 20))
      (world/after 30 (lambda () (part/halt yuzu)))
      (world/after 30 (lambda () (part/breathe yuzu 0.35)))
      (world/after (+ 1800 (random 1800))
        (lambda () (yuzu-stretch))))
    (yuzu-stretch)))
```

Yuzu does nothing gameplay-relevant. Ever. She just breathes and
occasionally looks at the pointer and occasionally stretches. Customers
who visit the shop feel a small warmth without being able to name
why. That is Yuzu.

Companies once paid millions for animated logo mascots that did less
than this. An operator with fifty lines of Scheme has one that does
more. That is the leverage.

---

## 4.9 Routing patterns — grouping characters by scene

When a scene has three characters, do NOT re-spawn them every frame.
Spawn once at scene entry; halt when the scene ends. Otherwise you
leak entities and their breath-timers pile up.

```scheme
(define scene-characters '())

(define (add-character-to-scene c)
  (set! scene-characters (cons c scene-characters)))

(define (end-scene-clear-characters)
  (for-each part/halt scene-characters)
  (for-each entity/despawn! scene-characters)
  (set! scene-characters '()))

;; Every scene ends with:
(end-scene-clear-characters)
```

Halt breath, despawn entities, reset the list. If you skip this you
will notice the game slowly getting laggier over an hour of play —
every scene's ghost characters still breathing off-screen. Rookie
mistake, easy fix.

---

## 4.10 Closing

You made a character breathe. You gave her a body. You wrote a scene
where two people had a hard conversation using seven part-verbs and
almost no words. That is what body language buys you.

Any character in your story from here on breathes. If she does not
breathe, she is furniture. Cortex tells you WHO she is. Breath tells
the kid that she IS.

Chapter 5 gives her a mouth — full dialogue trees. Now that her body
is alive, her words matter more.")

;; Book of Narrative Games — Chapter 5: Dialogue Trees

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(chapter
  :book                "Book of Narrative Games"
  :chapter-number      5
  :title               "Dialogue Trees"

"A dialogue tree is a story tree scaled down to one conversation. Mira
says something. You pick a reply from a small list. Mira responds. That
loops until someone walks away. Every good NPC in a role-playing game
is one of these trees under the hood.

We built the story-tree engine in chapter 2. The dialogue-tree engine
is the same idea, one level of magnification finer. Nodes are lines an
NPC speaks. Choices are lines the player says back. Everything else is
identical.

The interesting part of dialogue trees is not the code — it is the
craft. What makes a dialogue tree feel like a conversation and not a
menu? Body language on both sides. Silences that mean something.
Choices that stay open long enough for the player to think but not so
long she loses the thread. That is what this chapter is about.

---

## 5.1 The shape of a dialogue node

```scheme
(define chat-with-mira
  '((:id opening
     :npc \"How are you today?\"
     :npc-reaction (nod smile)
     :replies ((:label \"I'm fine.\"        :goto fine-branch)
               (:label \"Tired, actually.\" :goto tired-branch)
               (:label \"I'd rather not say.\" :goto quiet-branch)))

    (:id fine-branch
     :npc \"Good. Come sit.\"
     :npc-reaction (wave-in)
     :replies ((:label \"[sit down]\" :goto seated)))

    (:id tired-branch
     :npc \"Long night? Or long year?\"
     :npc-reaction (tilt lean-forward)
     :replies ((:label \"Long year.\"  :goto year-branch)
               (:label \"Long night.\" :goto night-branch)))

    (:id quiet-branch
     :npc \"Okay. We can just be quiet.\"
     :npc-reaction (nod-slow)
     :replies ((:label \"[sit down anyway]\" :goto seated)
               (:label \"[walk away]\"       :goto ending-walk-away)))

    (:id year-branch
     :npc \"Tell me about it.\"
     :npc-reaction (settle-in)
     :replies ((:label \"[start telling]\" :goto ending-listened)))

    (:id night-branch
     :npc \"Sleep here if you need. There's a bed upstairs.\"
     :npc-reaction (soft-smile)
     :replies ((:label \"[thanks]\" :goto ending-warmth)))

    (:id seated
     :npc \"Better. What did you come to talk about?\"
     :npc-reaction (steady)
     :replies ())    ;; ends the conversation

    (:id ending-listened
     :npc \"[listens for a long time]\"
     :npc-reaction (attentive)
     :replies ())

    (:id ending-warmth
     :npc \"Anytime.\"
     :npc-reaction (soft-smile)
     :replies ())

    (:id ending-walk-away
     :npc \"[nods]\"
     :npc-reaction (nod)
     :replies ())))
```

Nine nodes. Four ways the conversation can end. The reactions are
listed as a small vocabulary — nod, tilt, lean-forward, settle-in —
that our engine will translate into `part/*` verb calls.

Notice that some 'replies' are actions rather than words. `[sit
down]` is not something you say, it is something you do. Bracketed
labels convey action. This is a text-adventure convention borrowed by
every serious RPG. The kid understands the bracket-convention
immediately.

---

## 5.2 The engine that runs a dialogue tree

Reusing the story-tree pattern, one small extension: the NPC's
reactions.

```scheme
(define (play-dialogue tree npc-entity id)
  (let ((node (node-lookup tree id)))
    (scene/imagine)
    (surface/paper)

    ;; Paint the NPC.
    (paint-character npc-entity 300 180)

    ;; Do the NPC's reaction gestures.
    (apply-reactions npc-entity (node-get node :npc-reaction))

    ;; Paint the NPC's line.
    (paint-text 20 40 (string-append (npc-name npc-entity) \": \\\"\"
                                     (node-get node :npc) \"\\\"\"))

    ;; If there are no replies, the conversation is over.
    (let ((replies (node-get node :replies)))
      (if (null? replies)
          (paint-text 20 400 \"[press any key to end]\")
          (paint-choices replies 20 400))

      (on-key
        (lambda (k)
          (if (null? replies)
              (end-dialogue)
              (let ((chosen (choice-for-key replies k)))
                (if chosen
                    (play-dialogue tree npc-entity
                                   (node-get chosen :goto))
                    (play-dialogue tree npc-entity id)))))))))

(define (apply-reactions entity reactions)
  (for-each
    (lambda (r)
      (case r
        ((nod)          (part/nod entity))
        ((smile)        (part/expression entity 'smile))
        ((soft-smile)   (part/expression entity 'soft-smile))
        ((tilt)         (part/tilt entity 10))
        ((lean-forward) (part/lean entity 8))
        ((wave-in)      (part/wave entity 'right))
        ((nod-slow)     (part/nod entity))       ;; runtime uses default speed
        ((settle-in)    (part/lean entity -4))
        ((steady)       (part/lean entity 0))
        ((attentive)    (part/tilt entity 4))
        (else #f)))
    reactions))
```

The engine paints the NPC's body (with breath from the character
signature we set earlier), applies whatever reaction gestures the
node calls for, paints the line, and offers the replies. The kid
picks A/B/C. The engine jumps to the target node and does it again.

`apply-reactions` is a small vocabulary translator. When the tree
says `(nod smile)`, that becomes `(part/nod mira)` and `(part/expression
mira 'smile)`. You can add reactions to the vocabulary by adding cases
to `apply-reactions`. Twelve to fifteen reactions cover 95% of what
a scene needs.

---

## 5.3 Highlighting the currently-focused reply

When the kid is picking a reply, the currently-highlighted one should
be visible. `paint-highlight` is designed for this.

```scheme
(define (paint-replies-highlighted replies focus x y0)
  (let loop ((rs replies) (i 0))
    (when (not (null? rs))
      (let ((label (string-append \"[\" (number->letter (+ i 1)) \"] \"
                                  (node-get (car rs) :label)))
            (y (+ y0 (* i 25))))
        (if (= i focus)
            (paint-highlight x y (+ x 400) (+ y 22)  :color 'soft-yellow)
            #f)
        (paint-text x y label))
      (loop (cdr rs) (+ i 1)))))
```

`paint-highlight` draws a soft-yellow rectangle behind the text at
the given bounds. The currently-focused reply gets highlighted; the
others do not. The kid moves the focus with up/down arrows and
presses ENTER to select. This feels more like a real dialogue system
than press-A-B-C.

Note: at the time of this writing, `paint-highlight` is a
substrate-required verb — it returns a placeholder error record if the
consumer has not wired the substrate. Fall back to a `paint-text` with
a prefix `->` for the focused reply if you need portability:

```scheme
(paint-text x y
  (if (= i focus)
      (string-append \"-> \" label)
      (string-append \"   \" label)))
```

---

## 5.4 Fallbacks when the player hesitates

A dialogue tree that waits forever feels dead. If the player has not
picked a reply within 20 seconds, the NPC should say something. Not
'HELLO?' — something in character. 'Take your time.' Or a quiet look.

```scheme
;; Set a timer at the start of each dialogue node.
(define hesitation-timer 0)

(define (play-dialogue-with-timeout tree npc-entity id)
  (let ((node (node-lookup tree id)))
    ;; ... (paint node as before) ...
    (set! hesitation-timer 0)
    (on-frame
      (lambda ()
        (set! hesitation-timer (+ hesitation-timer 1))
        (cond
          ((= hesitation-timer (* 60 20))
           (npc-gentle-check npc-entity))    ;; 20 seconds
          ((= hesitation-timer (* 60 40))
           (npc-second-check npc-entity))     ;; 40 seconds
          ((= hesitation-timer (* 60 90))
           (npc-give-up npc-entity)))))))     ;; 90 seconds — walks away

(define (npc-gentle-check entity)
  (part/tilt entity 5)
  (paint-text 20 500 \"MIRA: 'Take your time.'\"))

(define (npc-second-check entity)
  (part/lean entity -4)
  (paint-text 20 530 \"MIRA: 'You alright?'\"))

(define (npc-give-up entity)
  (part/turn entity 'front)
  (paint-text 20 560 \"MIRA: 'Come find me when you know.' [walks away]\"))
```

Three tiers of check-in. Twenty seconds — a soft prompt. Forty seconds
— a concerned check. Ninety seconds — the NPC leaves. Each with a
matching body-language beat.

The 20/40/90 numbers are not universal. A scene where the player is
supposed to be thinking hard about a big choice should give them 60/120/300.
A rapid-fire conversation might use 5/10/20. Tune to the mood.

---

## 5.5 Storing dialogue history

You want the NPC to remember what the player said last time. Cortex
handles this beautifully.

```scheme
;; After each reply, log it.
(define (log-reply npc-id reply-label)
  (let* ((key (dialogue-log-key npc-id))
         (log (or (cortex/read key) '())))
    (cortex/write key (cons reply-label log))))

(define (dialogue-log-key npc-id)
  (string->symbol
    (string-append \"dialogue-log/\" (symbol->string npc-id))))

;; Later, an NPC can consult the log:
(define (mira-recall-something)
  (let* ((log (or (cortex/read (dialogue-log-key 'mira)) '()))
         (last-time (if (null? log) #f (car log))))
    (cond
      ((equal? last-time \"I'd rather not say.\")
       \"MIRA: 'You said last time you'd rather not — no pressure now either.'\")
      ((equal? last-time \"Tired, actually.\")
       \"MIRA: 'Are you still tired? Let me put a kettle on.'\")
      (else
       \"MIRA: 'Good to see you.'\"))))
```

Cortex stores every reply keyed by NPC. Mira's next scene reads the
log and adjusts her opening line. The kid feels seen because the game
saw her.

Do not overuse this either. Mira should probably not open with 'you
said the following twelve things last time.' She should recall one
detail if it is emotionally relevant. Restraint is design.

---

## 5.6 A worked scene: twenty lines the kid designs

The exercise for the chapter: the kid writes a full 20-line dialogue
tree with three endings. Here is one, so she has a template.

```scheme
(define chat-with-the-fisherman
  '((:id start
     :npc \"You have not been out here at dawn before.\"
     :npc-reaction (glance-up)
     :replies ((:label \"I couldn't sleep.\"        :goto sleepless)
               (:label \"I wanted to see you.\"     :goto wanted)
               (:label \"Just passing by.\"          :goto passing)))

    (:id sleepless
     :npc \"That is the dock's job, is it not. Sit.\"
     :npc-reaction (pat-the-plank)
     :replies ((:label \"[sit]\"                    :goto sitting)))

    (:id wanted
     :npc \"Why now?\"
     :npc-reaction (still)
     :replies ((:label \"You said you were leaving.\" :goto leaving-branch)
               (:label \"Nothing specific.\"          :goto nothing-branch)))

    (:id passing
     :npc \"Long walk for a passing.\"
     :npc-reaction (small-smile)
     :replies ((:label \"Alright, alright.\"         :goto sitting)))

    (:id leaving-branch
     :npc \"I said maybe.\"
     :npc-reaction (look-out-at-water)
     :replies ((:label \"Are you?\"                  :goto answering)))

    (:id nothing-branch
     :npc \"There's always something.\"
     :npc-reaction (small-smile)
     :replies ((:label \"Alright — I wanted to know if you were staying.\" :goto answering)))

    (:id answering
     :npc \"I have not decided.\"
     :npc-reaction (long-look-at-you)
     :replies ((:label \"Take your time.\"           :goto ending-patience)
               (:label \"Please stay.\"               :goto ending-plea)
               (:label \"I'd stay if you did.\"      :goto ending-commit)))

    (:id sitting
     :npc \"Nothing to say for a while. That's alright too.\"
     :npc-reaction (breathe-with-you)
     :replies ((:label \"[stay for a while]\"       :goto ending-quiet)))

    (:id ending-patience
     :npc \"Thank you. That's what I needed to hear.\"
     :npc-reaction (breath-out-relieved)
     :replies ())

    (:id ending-plea
     :npc \"Then I will think harder.\"
     :npc-reaction (nod)
     :replies ())

    (:id ending-commit
     :npc \"That is a different question.\"
     :npc-reaction (long-look-eyes-shining)
     :replies ())

    (:id ending-quiet
     :npc \"The sun's up. You'd better go.\"
     :npc-reaction (soft-smile)
     :replies ())))
```

Eleven nodes, four endings. Every reaction is a specific gesture that
would translate through `apply-reactions` into `part/*` calls. Every
reply the player picks pushes the conversation into a different
emotional room.

This is what dialogue trees can do when the writer takes them
seriously. It is not 'yes/no/maybe.' It is people saying things they
have been thinking about for weeks.

---

## 5.7 Common desktop tasks — the customer-service dialogue

An operator handles a return. Rather than a flat form, she writes a
five-line dialogue between the customer and 'the shopkeeper's voice.'

```scheme
(define returns-dialogue
  '((:id start
     :npc \"Hi — sorry to hear something's off. What happened?\"
     :npc-reaction (attentive)
     :replies ((:label \"It arrived damaged.\"        :goto damaged)
               (:label \"It's not what I expected.\"  :goto wrong-fit)
               (:label \"I changed my mind.\"          :goto changed-mind)))

    (:id damaged
     :npc \"That is on me. Photo when you can — same-day refund or replacement, your call.\"
     :npc-reaction (regretful-nod)
     :replies ((:label \"Replacement.\"                :goto ending-replace)
               (:label \"Refund.\"                     :goto ending-refund)))

    (:id wrong-fit
     :npc \"I want you to have something you love. Full return within 14 days, I cover ship.\"
     :npc-reaction (gentle-lean)
     :replies ((:label \"Start the return.\"           :goto ending-return-start)))

    (:id changed-mind
     :npc \"Totally fine — no explanation needed. Return within 14 days works.\"
     :npc-reaction (no-judgment)
     :replies ((:label \"Thanks.\"                     :goto ending-return-start)))

    (:id ending-replace       :npc \"Replacement out today. Watch your email.\"    :replies ())
    (:id ending-refund        :npc \"Refund is instant. Should show tonight.\"     :replies ())
    (:id ending-return-start  :npc \"Label in your inbox in a moment.\"            :replies ())))
```

Six nodes. Three endings. The customer feels handled by a person, not
a form. The operator wrote the whole thing in her own voice. The
'shopkeeper's voice' NPC has body-language reactions coded — regretful
nod, gentle lean, no-judgment (which is a slight `part/turn` to
'front' and a `part/expression 'neutral`).

This dialogue tree is one of dozens the shopkeeper writes for her
common customer situations. Each one takes ten minutes. Each one
handles the customer better than a form field. This is why operators
who take narrative games seriously end up with more repeat business —
their customers feel like guests, not tickets.

---

## 5.8 Routing patterns

Three shapes worth naming:

**The interview.** NPC asks; player answers; NPC asks again. Every
reply funnels into the next NPC question. Good for onboarding, for
confessions, for negotiations. All-forward, no loops.

**The wandering.** A node has replies that all loop back to a hub
node, from which new replies branch again. Good for bar conversations,
for asking a wise character many questions in any order.

**The escape.** Every non-terminal node has a `[walk away]` reply
that ends the conversation. Good for social scenes where the player
must feel free to leave without penalty. Do this by default; the
absence of an exit reply is a design smell.

---

## 5.9 Closing

You have a dialogue engine. You have a template for a 20-line
conversation. You have body-language reactions coded into the tree.
Write your first tree tonight. Make it 15 nodes. Make it about
somebody you know. Do not use their real name; use a pretend name.
Play it. It will probably surprise you.

Chapter 6 gives you the camera. Right now the scene is a static frame.
Next we make the frame move.")

"Where the camera looks, the audience looks. That is the whole rule of
cinema. A film director spends four decades learning nuances of it. You
have this chapter and eight verbs. That is plenty for a narrative
game.

Static frame with two characters talking: the audience does not know
where to look, so they look at whoever moved last. Pan the camera to
the speaker: the audience follows. Cut hard on a line: it lands.
Slow-push into a close-up as the character says something quiet: the
audience feels the closeness in their chest.

Everything the camera does is emotional grammar. This chapter teaches
the grammar in Scheme.

---

## 6.1 The eight camera verbs

```scheme
(world/camera-snap!  x y)               ;; instant cut to (x, y)
(world/camera-pan-to x y :duration 90)  ;; smooth pan
(world/camera-follow! ent :ease 0.15)   ;; track the entity
(world/camera-shake! 30 0.98)           ;; shake for 30 frames, damping 0.98
(cine/shot 'close-up  ent  duration)    ;; scripted shot type
(cine/shots list-of-shots)              ;; scripted sequence
(cine/follow ent :ease 0.15)            ;; cine-style follow
(cine/stop)                             ;; stop whatever cine is doing
```

Eight verbs. Each has one job. Together they cover every camera move a
narrative game ever needs.

`world/camera-snap!` cuts instantly. Use for hard emotional beats —
someone opens a door and you cut to the door. `world/camera-pan-to`
moves smoothly. Use for softer transitions — a character walks into
the shot and the camera drifts to follow. `world/camera-follow!` locks
onto an entity for as long as the follow is active. Use for chase
scenes and any sequence where the audience should stay on the
character.

`world/camera-shake!` shakes for effect. Use sparingly — an
earthquake, a slammed door, a moment of shock. Overuse and it becomes
irritating.

`cine/shot` is the cinematographer's move — it composes a specific
shot type. `close-up` frames the head. `mid` frames the torso. `wide`
pulls back to the room. `over-shoulder` looks past a character at
another. Six or so shot types cover most needs.

`cine/shots` runs a list of scripted shots in sequence — a full shot
list, like a storyboard. Chapter 12 uses this for a five-shot
memorial scene.

`cine/follow` is the cine-styled follow with default easing tuned for
narrative pacing (slower than the twitchier arcade follow). `cine/stop`
halts whatever the cine system is doing.

---

## 6.2 Panning to whoever speaks

The most common narrative-camera move: two characters, camera drifts
between them as they take turns.

```scheme
(define (two-shot mira father)
  ;; Start on Mira.
  (world/camera-snap! (entity/x mira) (entity/y mira))

  ;; She speaks.
  (paint-text 20 40 \"MIRA: 'It is a fine sky.'\")

  ;; Wait a beat, then pan to father.
  (world/after 90
    (lambda ()
      (world/camera-pan-to (entity/x father) (entity/y father)
                           :duration 60))))

  ;; He responds.
  (world/after 180
    (lambda ()
      (paint-text 20 80 \"FATHER: 'It is.'\")))

  ;; Pan back to Mira for her next line.
  (world/after 260
    (lambda ()
      (world/camera-pan-to (entity/x mira) (entity/y mira)
                           :duration 60)))
```

Snap to Mira. Beat. Pan to father. Beat. Line. Pan to Mira. Beat.

The 60-frame pan is one second — deliberate but not slow. In a rapid
argument you might use 30 frames (half a second) so the audience feels
the whiplash. In a solemn conversation you might use 120 frames (two
seconds) so the pan itself has weight.

Note the beats. `world/after 90` gives 1.5 seconds after Mira's line
before we start panning. If we pan immediately, the line has no time
to land. This is a common junior-writer mistake — camera moves too
fast, no line gets a moment.

---

## 6.3 The close-up

`cine/shot 'close-up` frames a character's face. Use for lines that
matter — a confession, a revelation, a small kindness. The audience
feels closeness because the frame IS close.

```scheme
;; A three-shot sequence: wide establish, close-up on the important line, wide back.
(define (confession-scene)
  ;; Wide establish — we can see both of them.
  (cine/shot 'wide 'room-center 60)

  ;; Father says something small.
  (world/after 60
    (lambda ()
      (paint-text 20 40 \"FATHER: 'She kept your room.'\")))

  ;; Cut to close-up on Mira as it lands.
  (world/after 150
    (lambda ()
      (cine/shot 'close-up mira 120)))

  ;; Mira's reaction.
  (world/after 180
    (lambda ()
      (part/expression mira 'held-back-tears)
      (part/lean mira -3)))

  ;; Cut back to wide.
  (world/after 320
    (lambda ()
      (cine/shot 'wide 'room-center 30))))
```

Wide, close-up on Mira as father delivers the line, wide again after
her body responds. The kid watching feels the moment — because the
frame framed it.

That is not high art. That is standard film grammar. Wide-close-wide
is the shape of every confession scene in cinema. You can now write it
in Scheme.

---

## 6.4 Follow shots

When a character moves, the camera follows. When they stop, the camera
stops. `world/camera-follow!` handles this.

```scheme
;; A character walks across the room, camera follows.
(define (walking-scene)
  (world/camera-follow! mira :ease 0.15)

  ;; Mira walks to the window.
  (motion/move-to mira 400 180 :duration 240)

  ;; When she stops, unfollow.
  (world/after 240
    (lambda ()
      (cine/stop)
      (world/camera-snap! (entity/x mira) (entity/y mira)))))
```

The `:ease 0.15` parameter is a smoothing factor — 0 is snap-to (no
smoothing) and 1 is very slow. 0.15 means the camera moves 15% of the
way toward its target each frame. Feels smooth without lagging.

Follow shots are the workhorse of adventure games. Chase scenes,
walking-and-talking scenes, exploration. If your camera follows a
character for the whole scene, use `cine/follow` instead of raw
`world/camera-follow!` — the cine version has more natural pacing.

---

## 6.5 Shake — the rare tool

`world/camera-shake!` is a specialty tool. Use it three times per
game, tops.

```scheme
;; A door slams shut behind the player.
(paint-text 20 40 \"You step in. The door slams.\")
(audio/play 'door-slam)
(world/camera-shake! 15 0.9)      ;; short sharp shake, damps fast

;; The villain enters.
(world/camera-shake! 8 0.95)      ;; two frames of subtle unease

;; A wall collapses.
(world/camera-shake! 60 0.98)     ;; longer, slower — earthquake
```

The two numbers are `frames` (how long to shake) and `damping` (how
fast the shake dies down). Short and sharp for slams and pops. Long
and slow for cataclysms.

Never shake during a dialogue line the audience needs to read. The
text becomes unreadable and the moment is ruined. Shake BETWEEN lines,
or before them, or after — never underneath.

---

## 6.6 Scripted shot lists

For big cinematic moments, write a `cine/shots` script.

```scheme
;; The moment the sister comes home. Five shots.
(define homecoming-shots
  '((:shot :type wide      :target room-center :duration 60)   ;; establish
    (:shot :type close-up  :target door        :duration 45)   ;; the door
    (:shot :type mid       :target sister      :duration 90)   ;; she stands there
    (:shot :type close-up  :target father      :duration 60)   ;; his face
    (:shot :type wide      :target room-center :duration 120))) ;; both of them

(cine/shots homecoming-shots)
```

Five shots, total nine seconds of screen time. The audience gets the
whole homecoming in shots — the room, the door, the sister, the
father's face, both together. It IS a scene from a film, running in
your engine.

Bookmark this pattern. Any big moment in your game — first meeting,
reveal, farewell — earns a scripted shot list. Ten minutes of design
work; forty seconds of screen impact.

---

## 6.7 A worked scene: villain enters

The villain has been offscreen for eight chapters. The kid knows their
name. They have never seen them. Here is how to introduce them with
camera work that says 'this is a big deal without me having to
narrate that.'

```scheme
(define (villain-enters)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)

  ;; Wide of the room.
  (world/camera-snap! 320 240)
  (paint-text 20 40 \"A door in the far wall opens.\")

  ;; Slow push to the doorway.
  (world/after 60
    (lambda ()
      (world/camera-pan-to 480 220 :duration 120))) ;; 2-second push

  ;; The villain steps in. Long shadow first.
  (world/after 180
    (lambda ()
      (paint-text 20 80
        \"A long shadow falls across the floor before the man does.\")))

  ;; Reveal.
  (world/after 240
    (lambda ()
      (entity/set-pos! villain 480 220)
      (part/breathe villain 0.15)                    ;; his signature: slow
      (paint-text 20 120
        \"He stops in the doorway. He does not look at anyone but you.\")))

  ;; Cut hard to close-up on the villain's face.
  (world/after 320
    (lambda ()
      (cine/shot 'close-up villain 90)
      (audio/play 'villain-motif :volume 0.4)))

  ;; Beat. Then cut hard to close-up on the kid.
  (world/after 420
    (lambda ()
      (cine/shot 'close-up kid 60)
      (part/breathe kid 0.75)))                       ;; kid's breath speeds up

  ;; Pull back to wide, both of them.
  (world/after 500
    (lambda ()
      (cine/shot 'wide 'room-center 60))))
```

Wide, slow push, shadow reveal, villain reveal, cut to villain
close-up (with motif), cut to kid close-up (with fear breath), pull
back to wide. Eight-and-a-half seconds of camera choreography. The kid
now has a complete impression of the villain without ever hearing
them speak. That is the film-grammar payoff.

The audio motif under the villain close-up is a chapter-9 topic, but
we have to sneak it in here because camera and sound work together —
neither is a solo act.

---

## 6.8 Common desktop tasks — a product-reveal shot for a shop

An operator has a new piece she is excited about. Rather than a static
product page, she writes a five-shot reveal that plays on the shop's
front card.

```scheme
(define-card 'product-reveal-skillet
  :init
  (lambda ()
    (scene/imagine)
    (surface/paper)

    ;; Wide of the workshop.
    (world/camera-snap! 320 240)
    (paint-text 20 40 \"The workshop. Late light.\")

    ;; Push to the workbench.
    (world/after 60
      (lambda ()
        (world/camera-pan-to 200 300 :duration 120)))

    ;; The skillet on the workbench.
    (world/after 200
      (lambda ()
        (paint-text 20 120
          \"A skillet has been seasoned three times over three days.\")))

    ;; Close-up on the surface.
    (world/after 260
      (lambda ()
        (cine/shot 'close-up 'skillet-surface 90)
        (paint-text 20 160 \"You can see your face in it.\")))

    ;; Pull back to the whole piece.
    (world/after 380
      (lambda ()
        (cine/shot 'mid 'skillet 60)
        (paint-text 20 200 \"Ten and a half inches. Cast in Vermont iron.\")))

    ;; Call to action.
    (world/after 500
      (lambda ()
        (paint-text 20 260 \"[A] add to cart   [B] read the story\")))))
```

Six seconds of camera work. The customer sees a workshop, then a
workbench, then a beautifully seasoned pan, then the whole piece, then
gets a specific detail (ten and a half inches, Vermont iron). Then a
call to action.

A photograph would take the customer three seconds. This takes six.
The customer stays for six because the camera IS the story. They
learned the pan's origin. That is worth an extra three seconds. And
maybe an extra sale.

---

## 6.9 Routing patterns

Three camera-shape rules:

**Static in dialogue-heavy scenes.** If the scene is 30 lines of
dialogue, the camera should mostly HOLD. Pan between the two speakers
if you must. Do not push, do not shake, do not follow. Let the words
work. Cine moves are salt; too much and the food is uneatable.

**Movement in movement scenes.** If a character is walking, running,
or fighting, the camera moves with them. Use `world/camera-follow!`
for the whole span. Cut only at scene changes.

**Cuts at emotional beats.** Do not pan into a close-up when a
character delivers a big line — CUT to the close-up. Cuts have more
emotional weight than pans. Save the pans for transitions and reserve
the cuts for the moments you want the audience to feel.

---

## 6.10 Closing

You have a camera. You know when to snap and when to pan. You know
that a close-up on a face is a magnifier for one line of dialogue.
You know that shake is a rare tool, not a spice.

Next time you play a narrative game you love, watch where the camera
looks and when it cuts. That is the film director in your head,
finally clocking in.

Chapter 7 introduces puzzles — the parser, the riddle, the item
combination. Puzzles are the moments the narrative game asks the
player to think hard for thirty seconds. The reward is a scene worth
having thought hard for.")

"A puzzle in a narrative game is a moment where the player has to think
for real. Not pick from three replies — actually think. The reward is
not points; the reward is that a door opens or a character talks to
you in a new way.

Puzzles come in three shapes: the riddle (right answer wins), the
combination (assemble the right sequence of actions), and the wait (do
nothing at the right moment). We will build all three. The riddle
teaches soft-matching. The combination teaches state tracking. The
wait teaches restraint as game design.

Puzzles that are too hard become walls. Puzzles that are too easy are
decorations. The right puzzle sits exactly where the player would have
guessed with a little more thought. That is the target. This chapter
shows the mechanics; craft is a lifetime.

---

## 7.1 The classic riddle

'I speak without a mouth, hear without ears. I have no body, but come
alive with wind. What am I?'

The answer is echo. Or an echo. Or ECHOES. Or 'the echo.' A well-made
puzzle accepts all of those.

```scheme
;; A gate that opens for the right answer.
(define (riddle-gate)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (paint-text 20 40 \"A door with a mouth carved into it. The mouth\")
  (paint-text 20 65 \"speaks: 'I speak without a mouth, hear without\")
  (paint-text 20 90 \"ears. I have no body, but come alive with wind.\")
  (paint-text 20 115 \"What am I?'\")
  (paint-text 20 200 \"[type your answer, then ENTER]\")
  (input/text-buffer 20 240
    :on-submit
    (lambda (answer)
      (if (answer-matches? answer '(\"echo\" \"an echo\" \"the echo\" \"echoes\"))
          (gate-opens)
          (gate-refuses answer)))))

(define (answer-matches? given acceptable)
  (let ((normalized (string-downcase (string-trim given))))
    (any (lambda (a) (equal? a normalized)) acceptable)))
```

`input/text-buffer x y :on-submit fn` shows a text input at (x, y) and
calls `fn` with the typed string when the player presses ENTER. Our
handler normalizes the answer (lowercase, trim whitespace) and checks
against a list.

`answer-matches?` is where you decide how forgiving to be. Strict
match on 'echo'? Or accept 'AN echo,' 'the ECHO,' 'echoes'? The list
above accepts four variants. That covers most kids and most typos.

You could go stricter (only 'echo') or looser (any string containing
'echo'). Looser is friendlier; stricter is puzzle-purer. Kids under
ten play best with looser. Adults playing puzzle-focused games
sometimes prefer stricter — 'you had to have thought of it exactly.'

---

## 7.2 Soft-matching with ai/vector-search

For richer puzzles, use embeddings. 'The answer is the sound that
comes back' should also match 'the answer is echo' — that requires
semantic matching, not string matching.

```scheme
;; Vector-based answer matching.
(define (semantic-match? given target-list threshold)
  (let* ((given-embedding (ai/embed given))
         (best-similarity 0.0))
    (for-each
      (lambda (target)
        (let* ((target-embedding (ai/embed target))
               (similarity (ai/vector-search given-embedding target-embedding)))
          (when (> similarity best-similarity)
            (set! best-similarity similarity))))
      target-list)
    (> best-similarity threshold)))

;; Use it:
(if (semantic-match? answer '(\"echo\") 0.75)
    (gate-opens)
    (gate-refuses answer))
```

`ai/embed` turns a string into a vector. `ai/vector-search` compares
two vectors and returns a similarity score between 0 and 1. Above 0.75
is usually a semantic match; above 0.85 is a near-synonym.

Trade-offs. Semantic match is friendlier for creative writers ('the
returning voice of a canyon' matches 'echo' with high similarity). It
is also slower and requires a network round-trip in some substrates.
For simple riddles, keep string matching. For narrative puzzles where
you want the kid to answer in her own words, use semantic.

A hybrid pattern: string match FIRST (fast, most players hit exact),
fall back to semantic on failure. That is what a good production
puzzle uses.

---

## 7.3 The hint system

If the player guesses wrong twice, offer a hint. If they guess wrong
five times, offer the answer with a small penalty.

```scheme
(define (riddle-with-hints)
  (let ((wrong-count 0))
    (define (on-answer answer)
      (cond
        ((answer-matches? answer '(\"echo\" \"an echo\"))
         (gate-opens))
        (else
         (set! wrong-count (+ wrong-count 1))
         (cond
           ((= wrong-count 2)
            (paint-text 20 300
              \"The door hums: 'The wind is a clue.'\"))
           ((= wrong-count 4)
            (paint-text 20 300
              \"The door sighs: 'You HEAR it in canyons.'\"))
           ((>= wrong-count 6)
            (paint-text 20 300
              \"The door: 'It is an echo. The door opens; a\n         debt is owed.'\")
            (cortex/write 'debt/riddle-door #t)
            (world/after 90 (lambda () (gate-opens))))
           (else
            (paint-text 20 300
              \"The door: 'That is not it. Try again.'\"))))))
    ;; ... input buffer wired to on-answer ...
    ))
```

Two wrong: 'the wind is a clue.' Four wrong: 'you HEAR it in canyons.'
Six wrong: door tells the answer but the player carries a debt.

The debt is a Cortex flag another scene reads later. Maybe the door
comes back at the ending and says 'you owed me — pay now.' The
penalty is not immediate; it is dramatic. That is a narrative game.

Some kids hate hints. Give a scene-start option: 'help me if I get
stuck' vs 'no hints, ever.' Store in Cortex. Now the game respects
their preference for the whole session.

---

## 7.4 The combination puzzle

You have to do three things in some order for the door to open: fill
the well, light the lantern, wait for midnight. Each is a scene the
kid must play through.

```scheme
;; Track completion of three sub-tasks.
(define (check-door-opens)
  (let ((well-filled? (cortex/read 'state/well-filled?))
        (lantern-lit? (cortex/read 'state/lantern-lit?))
        (midnight-passed? (cortex/read 'state/midnight-passed?)))
    (and well-filled? lantern-lit? midnight-passed?)))

;; When any sub-task completes, check the door.
(define (mark-well-filled)
  (cortex/write 'state/well-filled? #t)
  (paint-text 20 400 \"The well is full. Something clicked far away.\")
  (when (check-door-opens) (the-door-opens)))

(define (mark-lantern-lit)
  (cortex/write 'state/lantern-lit? #t)
  (paint-text 20 400 \"The lantern lights. Something warmed far away.\")
  (when (check-door-opens) (the-door-opens)))

(define (mark-midnight-passed)
  (cortex/write 'state/midnight-passed? #t)
  (paint-text 20 400 \"Midnight has passed. Something has changed.\")
  (when (check-door-opens) (the-door-opens)))

(define (the-door-opens)
  (world/after 60
    (lambda ()
      (scene/imagine)
      (surface/paper)
      (paint-text 20 40
        \"You return to the door. It is standing open.\")
      (world/after 60
        (lambda () (next-chapter))))))
```

Three flags. Any can be set in any order. When all three are true, the
door opens the next time the player visits it — or immediately, if
they set the last one while standing at the door.

The 'something clicked far away' feedback is critical. Without it, the
player does not know that filling the well helped. Feedback tells the
player they made progress even though the door has not opened yet.

You can make the puzzle harder by requiring an ORDER: the well before
midnight, the lantern last. Store the order taken and gate on it.
Order-sensitive puzzles are harder to design but more satisfying to
solve — the player feels she really uncovered something.

---

## 7.5 The wait puzzle

The player is being chased. She ducks into a closet. If she moves, she
gets caught. She must sit still and do nothing for eight seconds. The
game is telling her that doing nothing is the correct action. Kids
find this shocking.

```scheme
(define (hide-in-closet)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (paint-text 20 40 \"You duck into the closet and pull the door shut.\")
  (paint-text 20 70 \"You can hear the footsteps outside.\")
  (paint-text 20 100 \"[if you move, you will be found.]\")

  (let ((frames-still 0))
    (on-frame
      (lambda ()
        (if (or (input/pressed? 'up) (input/pressed? 'down)
                (input/pressed? 'left) (input/pressed? 'right)
                (input/pressed? 'a) (input/pressed? 'b))
            (get-caught)
            (begin
              (set! frames-still (+ frames-still 1))
              (when (= frames-still 480)     ;; eight seconds at 60fps
                (footsteps-fade))
              (when (= frames-still 60)
                (paint-text 20 200 \"You breathe as quietly as you can.\"))
              (when (= frames-still 240)
                (paint-text 20 230 \"The footsteps get closer.\"))
              (when (= frames-still 360)
                (paint-text 20 260 \"They stop, right outside the door.\"))
              (when (= frames-still 420)
                (paint-text 20 290 \"Then they walk away.\")))))))))
```

Eight seconds of screen text. The player must not press a single key.
When the footsteps fade, the puzzle is solved. If the player presses
anything, `get-caught` fires and the villain finds her.

This is a puzzle a kid will remember for years. Not because it was
hard to solve mechanically — she just had to sit still — but because
the game asked her to do something counterintuitive and rewarded her
for it.

Trust puzzles like this feel deep because they are asking the player
to trust the game. If the game rewards trust, the player leans in for
the rest of the play. If the game betrays trust, she leaves.

---

## 7.6 A worked scene: the three-key puzzle

The classic. Find three keys. Bring them to the door. But present it
as a story, not a fetch quest.

```scheme
(define (three-keys-puzzle)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (paint-text 20 40 \"A great door. Three locks: brass, silver, bone.\")

  (let ((keys (or (cortex/read 'inventory/keys) '())))
    (paint-text 20 100
      (string-append \"You have: \"
                     (if (null? keys)
                         \"nothing.\"
                         (keys->prose keys))))

    (cond
      ((= (length keys) 3)
       (paint-text 20 160 \"[A] use all three keys\")
       (on-key (lambda (k) (when (eq? k 'a) (door-opens-three)))))
      ((not (null? keys))
       (paint-text 20 160 (string-append \"You still need: \"
                                         (missing-keys->prose keys))))
      (else
       (paint-text 20 160 \"You will need all three to open it.\")))))

(define (keys->prose keys)
  (cond
    ((null? keys) \"\")
    ((null? (cdr keys)) (key->prose (car keys)))
    ((null? (cddr keys))
     (string-append (key->prose (car keys)) \" and \"
                    (key->prose (cadr keys))))
    (else
     (string-append (key->prose (car keys)) \", \"
                    (keys->prose (cdr keys))))))

(define (key->prose key)
  (case key
    ((brass)  \"the brass key\")
    ((silver) \"the silver key\")
    ((bone)   \"the bone key\")))

(define (missing-keys->prose have)
  (let ((missing (filter (lambda (k) (not (member k have)))
                         '(brass silver bone))))
    (keys->prose missing)))
```

The puzzle is state accumulation, gated on a predicate. The prose
around it — 'a great door,' 'you have the brass and the silver' — is
what turns the puzzle into a scene.

Three keys, three subquests to find them. Each subquest is its own
scene. Each scene ends with a `(cortex/write 'inventory/keys (cons
'brass old))` or equivalent. The door scene displays what the player
has and does not have. When they have all three, the option to use
them appears.

The kid who solves this feels she completed a real puzzle. The story
did not tell her the answer; she assembled it herself.

---

## 7.7 Common desktop tasks — a spot-the-detail cart

An operator wants to teach a customer about her craft in an
interactive way. Not a video. A puzzle. 'Look at this piece — find
five things a machine could not have done.'

```scheme
(define-card 'spot-the-craft
  :init
  (lambda ()
    (scene/imagine)
    (surface/paper)
    (paint-text 20 40
      \"This is a hand-forged spoon. There are five details a machine\")
    (paint-text 20 65
      \"cannot produce. Click each one when you find it.\")

    ;; The image (represented here by clickable regions).
    (define found '())

    (define (mark-found detail)
      (unless (member detail found)
        (set! found (cons detail found))
        (paint-text 20 (+ 400 (* (length found) 20))
          (string-append \"[✓] \" (detail->prose detail))))
      (when (= (length found) 5)
        (world/after 60 (lambda () (celebration)))))

    (define hammer-mark-region (make-clickable 100 200 150 250 'hammer-marks))
    (define curl-region        (make-clickable 200 220 240 260 'grip-curl))
    (define patina-region      (make-clickable 300 210 350 280 'darkened-patina))
    (define nick-region        (make-clickable 400 230 430 270 'small-nick))
    (define asymmetry-region   (make-clickable 220 300 320 340 'slight-asymmetry))

    (on-click
      (lambda (x y)
        (cond
          ((region-hit? hammer-mark-region x y) (mark-found 'hammer-marks))
          ((region-hit? curl-region x y)        (mark-found 'grip-curl))
          ((region-hit? patina-region x y)      (mark-found 'darkened-patina))
          ((region-hit? nick-region x y)        (mark-found 'small-nick))
          ((region-hit? asymmetry-region x y)   (mark-found 'slight-asymmetry)))))))
```

The customer sees a spoon. She has to click on five specific parts —
the hammer marks, the grip curl, the darkened patina, the small nick
where the forger tapped once too many, the slight asymmetry that
machines cannot fake. Each click adds a line to a small list.

When she finds all five, the operator's voice comes up: 'That's what
you paid for. Every one of those took me two extra minutes.' The
customer has done a puzzle AND learned about the craft. She is going
to remember this piece.

This is the kind of narrative cart operators write when they take
their customers seriously. Not a form, not a video — a puzzle that
teaches.

---

## 7.8 Routing patterns

Three puzzle-design patterns:

**Give one way, hint at others.** The puzzle has an intended solution.
It also accepts three or four alternate solutions the writer thought
of during design. Each alternate has its own reaction. The player who
finds the intended way feels rewarded; the player who finds an
alternate feels clever.

**Solvable in one session.** A puzzle that requires the player to
close the game and come back tomorrow with a fresh mind is a puzzle
that most players will never solve. Keep the whole logic reachable
within one 20-minute play session. Multi-session puzzles are for
puzzle-focused games, not narrative games.

**No dead ends without notice.** If a player can put themselves in a
state where the puzzle is unsolvable — dropped the key in a well
they can no longer reach, ate the food they needed to give away — the
game must tell them. 'You feel a sinking sense that you have made a
mistake.' Or offer a rewind. Silent dead ends are the number one
reason players quit adventure games.

---

## 7.9 Closing

Three shapes of puzzle. Ways to be forgiving without being mushy. A
hint system that respects the player. A wait puzzle that teaches
trust.

Puzzles in a narrative game are earned pauses. They give the story a
rhythm — a beat where the player must think, then a beat of release
when the door opens. The pace of great narrative games is exactly this
alternation.

Chapter 8 formalizes inventory — the collection of items the player is
carrying, and the world-state that gates what they can do with them.
Every puzzle in every adventure game is really an inventory puzzle
under the hood.")

"An adventure game is a state machine. The player is in a room. The
door is locked. The player picks up a key. The state changes. Now the
door is unlocked, or at least can be. Everything the player does is a
state transition; every scene reads the state to decide what to
render.

Inventory is a subset of world-state — specifically the items the
player is carrying. World-state is the bigger set: what's true about
the world right now. Is the well poisoned? Has the sister come home?
Did the villain die in scene 12? All of that is world-state.

Cortex is our state store. Inventory is one Cortex key holding a list.
World-state is many Cortex keys holding flags. Simple. What's hard is
the discipline of writing scenes that always read state before
rendering, and always update state after significant actions.

---

## 8.1 Inventory as a list

```scheme
;; Add an item to inventory.
(define (pick-up item)
  (let ((inv (or (cortex/read 'inventory) '())))
    (cortex/write 'inventory (cons item inv))
    (paint-text 20 400
      (string-append \"You picked up \" (item->prose item) \".\"))))

;; Drop an item.
(define (drop item)
  (let ((inv (or (cortex/read 'inventory) '())))
    (cortex/write 'inventory (filter (lambda (i) (not (eq? i item))) inv))
    (paint-text 20 400
      (string-append \"You dropped \" (item->prose item) \".\"))))

;; Check if you have something.
(define (have? item)
  (member item (or (cortex/read 'inventory) '())))

;; Item to prose (English article + name).
(define (item->prose item)
  (case item
    ((lantern) \"the lantern\")
    ((key)     \"a small brass key\")
    ((rope)    \"a coil of rope\")
    ((letter)  \"a folded letter\")
    ((feather) \"a white feather\")
    (else      (string-append \"a \" (symbol->string item)))))
```

Four verbs — pick up, drop, have?, item->prose — and you have a
working inventory. Every scene can consult `(have? 'lantern)` before
deciding whether to offer the enter-the-cave option.

The `filter` in `drop` returns a new list with all elements except the
dropped one. This is standard list-processing. If you have multiple
copies of the same item and only want to drop one, use a more careful
`remove-first` — but for narrative games, one copy of each item is
usually plenty.

Notice we do NOT delete an item when it is used. We might read
'you have the lantern' in scene 8 and light the darkness. In scene 15
we still have the lantern. Real inventory only drops when the player
explicitly drops it OR when a scene explicitly consumes it (like
handing over the letter).

---

## 8.2 Consuming items

Sometimes handing over an item removes it from inventory.

```scheme
;; Give an item to someone.
(define (give item npc)
  (drop item)
  (cortex/write (npc-received-key npc item) #t)
  (paint-text 20 400
    (string-append (npc-name npc) \" takes \" (item->prose item)
                   \" from your hand.\")))

(define (npc-received-key npc item)
  (string->symbol
    (string-append \"gift/\" (symbol->string npc)
                   \"/\" (symbol->string item))))

;; Later, Mira can react:
(define (mira-check-gift)
  (cond
    ((cortex/read 'gift/mira/letter)
     \"MIRA: 'The letter — you brought it? Thank you.'\")
    ((cortex/read 'gift/mira/feather)
     \"MIRA: 'The feather. From the hawk on the ridge?'\")
    (else
     \"MIRA: 'You have empty hands. That is fine too.'\")))
```

`give` drops the item from your inventory AND records a Cortex flag
saying you gave THIS item to THIS npc. That flag survives forever.
Ten scenes later, another NPC can say 'Mira told me about the
letter.' The economy of the world tracks itself.

The compound key trick — `gift/mira/letter` — lets you have any
number of gift-relationships without a giant hardcoded flag list.
Every gift is its own flag. Reading them later is a matter of building
the key.

---

## 8.3 World-state flags

Beyond inventory, the world has state that is not carried by anyone.

```scheme
;; Common world-state keys.
;;
;;   'state/door-unlocked?
;;   'state/well-poisoned?
;;   'state/village-burned?
;;   'state/sister-home?
;;   'state/villain-killed?
;;
;; Read them:
(if (cortex/read 'state/sister-home?)
    (paint-text 20 40 \"Your sister is in the kitchen, humming.\")
    (paint-text 20 40 \"The kitchen is empty. She is not back yet.\"))

;; Write them:
(cortex/write 'state/sister-home? #t)
```

Prefer `?`-suffixed boolean keys. They read naturally in code:
`(if (cortex/read 'state/sister-home?) ...)` reads like English.

Prefer flat namespaces. `state/well-poisoned?` is better than
`village/well/water/poisoned?`. Deep hierarchies feel organized but
make the code longer. The narrative game usually has 30-100 flags —
that fits in a flat namespace fine.

---

## 8.4 The inventory bar

Players want to see what they are carrying. Paint a bar at the bottom
of the screen showing current inventory.

```scheme
;; Paint an inventory bar along the bottom.
(define (paint-inventory-bar)
  (let ((inv (or (cortex/read 'inventory) '())))
    (paint-text 20 550 \"CARRYING:\")
    (let loop ((items inv) (i 0))
      (when (not (null? items))
        (paint-text (+ 110 (* i 80)) 550
          (item-icon-or-name (car items)))
        (loop (cdr items) (+ i 1))))))

(define (item-icon-or-name item)
  (case item
    ((lantern) \"[lantern]\")
    ((key)     \"[key]\")
    ((rope)    \"[rope]\")
    ((letter)  \"[letter]\")
    (else      (string-append \"[\" (symbol->string item) \"]\"))))
```

Call `paint-inventory-bar` at the end of every scene's render pass.
The player sees, at all times, what they are carrying. This is a
small courtesy that saves hours of frustration — 'do I have the key?
Where does it show up?'

For a fancier bar, replace the bracketed text with sprite icons via
`entity/sprite!` on a dedicated inventory-bar entity per item. But
text works fine; do not over-engineer.

---

## 8.5 Gating scenes on state

A scene checks state before rendering. If the state does not allow
the scene, redirect or offer a partial version.

```scheme
(define (enter-the-cave)
  (cond
    ((have? 'lantern)
     (scene-cave-lit))
    (else
     (scene/imagine)
     (surface/paper)
     (paint-text 20 40 \"The cave is pitch dark. You cannot see three\")
     (paint-text 20 70 \"feet in front of you.\")
     (paint-text 20 100 \"You back out. You would need a light.\")
     (world/after 90 (lambda () (previous-scene))))))
```

The player can enter the cave with a lantern (full scene) or without
(short warning-and-back). Never let the player walk into a state the
game cannot handle — always give a graceful bounce back.

For multi-item gates:

```scheme
(define (enter-the-tower)
  (cond
    ((and (have? 'key) (have? 'letter))
     (scene-tower-full))
    ((have? 'key)
     (scene-tower-locked-inside))
    (else
     (scene-tower-locked-outside))))
```

Three different scenes based on inventory. Each is fully written; each
reads differently for the player who arrives in that state.

## 8.6 A worked scene: five rooms, seven items

Here is a small puzzle-adventure. Five rooms. Seven items to find.
One exit. The player must assemble a specific combination to leave.

```scheme
;; The five rooms.
(define (kitchen)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (paint-text 20 40 \"KITCHEN. A pot on the stove. A window over a garden.\")
  (paint-text 20 100 (if (have? 'pot) \"\" \"[A] take the pot\"))
  (paint-text 20 130 \"[B] to the garden   [C] to the hall\")
  (on-key
    (lambda (k)
      (case k
        ((a) (unless (have? 'pot) (pick-up 'pot)) (kitchen))
        ((b) (garden))
        ((c) (hall))))))

(define (garden)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (paint-text 20 40 \"GARDEN. Tomatoes. A well. A shed.\")
  (paint-text 20 100 (if (have? 'tomato) \"\" \"[A] pick a tomato\"))
  (paint-text 20 130 (if (have? 'water)  \"\" \"[B] fill a container from the well\"))
  (paint-text 20 160 \"[C] enter the shed   [D] back to kitchen\")
  (on-key
    (lambda (k)
      (case k
        ((a) (unless (have? 'tomato) (pick-up 'tomato)) (garden))
        ((b) (if (have? 'pot)
                 (begin (pick-up 'water) (garden))
                 (begin (paint-text 20 220
                          \"You have no container.\") (garden))))
        ((c) (shed))
        ((d) (kitchen))))))

(define (shed)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (paint-text 20 40 \"SHED. A hoe. A coil of rope. Dust.\")
  (paint-text 20 100 (if (have? 'hoe)  \"\" \"[A] take the hoe\"))
  (paint-text 20 130 (if (have? 'rope) \"\" \"[B] take the rope\"))
  (paint-text 20 160 \"[C] back to garden\")
  (on-key
    (lambda (k)
      (case k
        ((a) (unless (have? 'hoe) (pick-up 'hoe)) (shed))
        ((b) (unless (have? 'rope) (pick-up 'rope)) (shed))
        ((c) (garden))))))

(define (hall)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (paint-text 20 40 \"HALL. Stairs up. A door out (locked).\")
  (paint-text 20 100 (if (have? 'lantern) \"\" \"[A] take the lantern from the hook\"))
  (paint-text 20 130 \"[B] upstairs   [C] to kitchen\")
  (paint-text 20 160
    (if (and (have? 'key) (have? 'lantern) (have? 'rope))
        \"[D] open the door and leave\"
        \"\"))
  (on-key
    (lambda (k)
      (case k
        ((a) (unless (have? 'lantern) (pick-up 'lantern)) (hall))
        ((b) (upstairs))
        ((c) (kitchen))
        ((d) (when (and (have? 'key) (have? 'lantern) (have? 'rope))
               (leave)))))))

(define (upstairs)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (paint-text 20 40 \"UPSTAIRS. A bedroom. A key on the dresser.\")
  (paint-text 20 100 (if (have? 'key) \"\" \"[A] take the key\"))
  (paint-text 20 130 \"[B] back down\")
  (on-key
    (lambda (k)
      (case k
        ((a) (unless (have? 'key) (pick-up 'key)) (upstairs))
        ((b) (hall))))))

(define (leave)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (paint-text 20 40 \"You unlock the door. Rope tied to the doorframe,\")
  (paint-text 20 70 \"lantern in one hand, key in the other. You step\")
  (paint-text 20 100 \"out into the yard. You made it.\"))
```

Five rooms, seven items (pot, tomato, water, hoe, rope, lantern, key),
one exit. The exit needs key + lantern + rope. Water is a red herring
— it makes the world feel real without being required. Tomato is
another red herring — some players will try to bring it, and nothing
bad will happen either way.

Red herrings are important. If every item is required, the puzzle is a
fetch quest. If some items are optional, the player has to think about
which are which. Better yet, some optional items unlock BONUS scenes
— take the tomato home, hand it to the neighbor, get a small
sub-story.

---

## 8.7 The chair — an example of world-state that isn't inventory

There is a chair in the corner. If you sit in it, you fall asleep and
dream of your sister. But you can only sit in it once. This is
world-state, not inventory.

```scheme
(define (the-chair)
  (cond
    ((cortex/read 'state/slept-in-chair?)
     (paint-text 20 200 \"The chair is empty. You have already slept.\"))
    (else
     (paint-text 20 200 \"[A] sit in the chair\")
     (on-key
       (lambda (k)
         (when (eq? k 'a)
           (cortex/write 'state/slept-in-chair? #t)
           (dream-of-sister)))))))
```

The `state/slept-in-chair?` flag survives forever. The player who
comes back tomorrow cannot sit in the chair a second time. The
one-shot dream becomes a one-shot memory.

This is important design: some scenes should not repeat. Dreams,
confessions, deaths, farewells. Gate them with a `state/*` flag and
respect it forever.

---

## 8.8 Common desktop tasks — an operator's virtual bookshelf

An operator sells vintage books. She wants a page where the customer
can 'browse a bookshelf' — pick up a book, read its jacket, put it
back or add to cart. State-tracked so returning customers see which
books they have already read summaries of.

```scheme
(define-card 'browse-bookshelf
  :init
  (lambda ()
    (scene/imagine)
    (surface/paper)
    (paint-text 20 40 \"A shelf of six books. Which one interests you?\")

    (let* ((books '(the-riverside-cook the-copper-tea rustic-tables
                    a-year-in-glass the-quiet-hours night-thoughts))
           (read-titles (or (cortex/read 'browse/read-jackets) '())))
      (let loop ((bs books) (i 0))
        (when (not (null? bs))
          (paint-text 20 (+ 100 (* i 30))
            (string-append \"[\" (number->letter (+ i 1)) \"] \"
                           (book->title (car bs))
                           (if (member (car bs) read-titles)
                               \"  (jacket read)\"
                               \"\")))
          (loop (cdr bs) (+ i 1))))

      (on-key
        (lambda (k)
          (let ((idx (letter->index k)))
            (when (and (>= idx 0) (< idx 6))
              (let ((chosen (list-ref books idx)))
                (cortex/write 'browse/read-jackets
                  (cons chosen (or (cortex/read 'browse/read-jackets) '())))
                (show-jacket chosen)))))))))
```

Six books. The customer picks one. The card records that she read
that jacket. Next time she comes, that book is marked (jacket read).
She can browse jackets she hasn't seen. When she is ready to buy, a
sub-scene lets her add to cart.

The operator did what a bookseller does: made a shelf, let the
customer touch things. State keeps track so the customer doesn't feel
like she is starting from zero on each visit.

---

## 8.9 Routing patterns

**Consumable vs persistent items.** Some items — letters, gifts —
are consumed on use. Others — lanterns, keys — persist. Decide up
front for each item; do not surprise the player mid-game.

**One-shot vs repeatable scenes.** Some scenes happen once ever. Some
repeat. Mark one-shots with `state/*-done?` flags and check them at
scene entry. If a player has already seen the dream, do not offer it
again.

**Explicit vs implicit gates.** Explicit gate: 'you need the key to
open this door — you can see the lock.' Implicit gate: 'the door
looks weird, you cannot figure out how to open it.' Explicit is
kinder for kids. Implicit is more rewarding for puzzle-focused
players. Choose based on your audience.

---

## 8.10 Closing

You have inventory. You have world-state flags. You can gate scenes on
state. You have written a five-room puzzle that a friend could play
in ten minutes.

The state store is the skeleton of your game. Every scene reads it;
every action writes to it. Get this discipline right and everything
downstream — dialogue, camera, sound — has a solid foundation.

Chapter 9 is the sound layer. A soundscape can carry state as well:
music changes as the player approaches the villain, silence lands
when a beat needs weight.")
