"Audio is a full third of a narrative game and gets a fifth of the
attention. That is the imbalance to fix. Not by piling in music — by
using sound with the same discipline you use for camera and body
language.

Three uses for sound in this book: motif (a short phrase attached to a
character or place), texture (ambient background — wind, rain, hearth
crackle), and punctuation (a single sound for a beat). Plus silence:
sometimes cutting the audio is the loudest sound choice you can make.

The physics of sound in narrative: audio is state. When the world
changes, the audio should change with it. When the villain enters, the
music darkens. When they leave, it lifts. The player feels the world
respond.

---

## 9.1 The audio verbs

```scheme
(audio/play name)                     ;; play a named sound one-shot
(audio/play name :loop? #t)           ;; play looping
(audio/play name :volume 0.4)         ;; softer
(audio/halt name)                     ;; stop that specific sound
(audio/halt)                          ;; stop everything
(audio/master-volume level)           ;; global volume 0.0-1.0

(note-strike pitch duration)          ;; play a single note
(note-place-at x y pitch)             ;; note tied to a screen position
```

`audio/play` fires a named sound. Names refer to assets — 'thunder,'
'creak,' 'villain-motif' — that the substrate resolves. If the
substrate does not have that name, it fires a silent placeholder (no
crash, just no sound).

`audio/halt` with a name stops that specific loop. Without a name it
stops everything — useful for scene transitions.

`audio/master-volume` sets the global level from 0.0 to 1.0. Duck to
0.3 during a dialogue-heavy scene to keep music from drowning out
lines, then restore to 1.0 when the scene ends.

`note-strike` and `note-place-at` are for tone-level composition —
building a two-note motif in code rather than using pre-recorded
audio. Useful for scenes where you want a specific pitch relationship
that no library asset will match.

---

## 9.2 A door creaks

The simplest sound cue.

```scheme
(paint-text 20 40 \"You push open the heavy door.\")
(audio/play 'door-creak)
```

Play the creak once, at the moment the text describes the door
opening. Sound and text arrive together. The player's brain fuses
them. They believe the door made that sound.

This is the same trick foley artists have used for a century — a
sound plus a visual, and the audience remembers experiencing the
sound as coming from the visual. Even though you never rendered a
door. You painted text.

Rule of thumb: one sound per sentence. If you play three sounds under
three lines of text, the sounds compete and the player registers
none of them.

---

## 9.3 Ambient loops

A scene has a bed of sound. In the kitchen it might be a hearth
crackling. In the garden it might be birds. In the villain's chamber
it might be a low sub-audible drone.

```scheme
;; A scene with an ambient loop.
(define (kitchen-with-hearth)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (audio/play 'hearth-crackle :loop? #t :volume 0.3)
  (paint-text 20 40 \"You are in a warm kitchen. Something is on the stove.\")
  ;; ... rest of the scene ...
  )

;; When you leave:
(define (leave-kitchen)
  (audio/halt 'hearth-crackle)
  (goto-scene next-room))
```

The hearth loops as long as the player is in the kitchen. When they
leave, the loop stops. If they come back, the loop restarts.

Ambient volume: 0.2-0.4 is a good range. Loud enough to notice, quiet
enough to disappear under dialogue. 0.5 is intrusive; 0.1 might as
well be silent.

Layer two or three ambient sources for depth. Hearth + wind outside
+ a clock ticking. Each at low volume; together they create a
soundscape that feels three-dimensional.

---

## 9.4 The motif

A motif is a short musical phrase tied to a character or place. Every
time that character enters a scene, the motif plays softly. The
player learns the motif over five hours of play and eventually feels
the character before they see them.

```scheme
;; Mira's motif: a soft rising phrase.
(define (mira-enters)
  (audio/play 'mira-motif :volume 0.3)
  ;; ... scene work ...
  )

;; Villain's motif: a slow low drone.
(define (villain-enters)
  (audio/play 'villain-motif :volume 0.5)
  ;; ... scene work ...
  )
```

For pre-recorded motifs, name each one and play it at the entry point.
For code-composed motifs, use `note-strike`.

```scheme
;; Mira's motif in code — three notes.
(define (mira-motif)
  (note-strike 'A4 0.3)
  (world/after 15 (lambda () (note-strike 'C5 0.3)))
  (world/after 30 (lambda () (note-strike 'E5 0.5))))

;; Villain's motif — two low notes.
(define (villain-motif)
  (note-strike 'C2 0.8)
  (world/after 45 (lambda () (note-strike 'F2 0.8))))
```

A three-note rising phrase for Mira. A two-note descending drone for
the villain. Distinct, memorable, brief. The player will remember
these long after they close the game.

You do not need to be a composer. Three or four notes is enough.
Pick pitches that FEEL right — high and rising for the friendly
character, low and slow for the ominous one. Trust your instincts;
you have been listening to music your whole life.

---

## 9.5 Ducking under dialogue

When a character starts talking, drop the background music. Restore
after they finish.

```scheme
(define (mira-says text)
  (audio/master-volume 0.3)                 ;; duck to 30% during speech
  (paint-text 20 40 (string-append \"MIRA: '\" text \"'\"))
  (world/after (* (string-length text) 3)   ;; roughly reading-speed
    (lambda ()
      (audio/master-volume 1.0))))          ;; restore
```

The reading-speed heuristic — three frames per character — is about
right for adult prose. Kids read a bit slower; use 5 frames per
character. Adjust for your audience.

Some voices should NOT be ducked under. When the villain speaks, keep
their motif loud — it should feel oppressive that the music does not
quiet down for them. When Mira speaks, duck. The difference between
'the world respects her voice' and 'the villain overpowers the
world' is baked into the duck logic.

---

## 9.6 Silence as punctuation

Silence is loud. When the villain enters, cut all audio. Two seconds
of nothing, then their motif. The player's ears will strain.

```scheme
(define (villain-enters-with-silence)
  (audio/halt)                              ;; kill everything
  (world/after 120                           ;; two full seconds of silence
    (lambda ()
      (audio/play 'villain-motif :volume 0.4))))
```

Two seconds of silence in a game is a long time. The player who was
half-listening now leans forward. When the motif finally hits, it
lands like a hammer.

Do not overuse this. Once per major moment. If every scene starts
with silence, silence becomes the new ambient and loses its impact.

---

## 9.7 A worked scene: music shifts as you approach the villain

You are walking through a corridor. As you get closer to the villain's
door, the music changes — the warm score drops out; the villain's
drone rises. The physical distance dictates the audio mix.

```scheme
;; Corridor scene with distance-based audio.
(define (villain-corridor)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (audio/play 'warm-strings :loop? #t :volume 0.4)
  (audio/play 'villain-drone :loop? #t :volume 0.0)

  ;; Player moves down the corridor via left/right.
  (define player-x 20)

  (on-frame
    (lambda ()
      (when (input/pressed? 'right)
        (set! player-x (+ player-x 2)))
      (when (input/pressed? 'left)
        (set! player-x (max 20 (- player-x 2))))

      (paint-text player-x 300 \"@\")

      ;; Compute distance to villain door at x = 600.
      (let* ((distance (- 600 player-x))
             (t (max 0 (min 1 (/ (- 600 distance) 600.0))))
             (warm-vol (* 0.4 (- 1 t)))
             (drone-vol (* 0.5 t)))
        (audio/master-volume 1.0)
        (audio/play 'warm-strings :volume warm-vol)
        (audio/play 'villain-drone :volume drone-vol))

      ;; If they reach the door, enter.
      (when (>= player-x 590)
        (villain-scene)))))
```

Two audio layers running simultaneously. As the player walks right,
one layer fades down and the other fades up. The mix is a
distance-parameterized crossfade. By the time the player reaches the
door, they hear only drone.

The player will not notice the crossfade consciously. They will feel
the room getting colder as they walk. Then they will realize they are
holding their breath. That is what a sound designer means when they
say 'sound tells the story.'

---

## 9.8 Common desktop tasks — a shop chime for a returning customer

An operator wants a friendly sound when a returning customer opens
the shop. Not every visitor — only ones who have been here before.

```scheme
(define-card 'shop-greeting-chime
  :init
  (lambda ()
    (let ((visits (or (cortex/read 'customer/visits) 0)))
      (cond
        ((= visits 0)
         (audio/play 'chime-neutral :volume 0.5))
        ((= visits 1)
         (audio/play 'chime-warm :volume 0.5))
        (else
         (audio/play 'chime-warm :volume 0.5)
         (world/after 30 (lambda () (audio/play 'chime-second :volume 0.4)))))
      (cortex/write 'customer/visits (+ visits 1))
      (scene/imagine)
      (surface/paper)
      (paint-text 20 40
        (case visits
          ((0) \"Welcome. First time in.\")
          ((1) \"Welcome back.\")
          (else \"Oh — you again. I have something to show you.\")))
      (paint-text 20 100 \"[A] browse\"))))
```

A first-time customer hears a neutral chime. A second-visit customer
hears a warmer chime. A returning-multiple-times customer hears the
warm chime plus a second note — a small musical hello just for them.

The customer will not consciously register that the chime changed
across visits. They will just feel more welcome. Which is exactly
what the operator wanted.

---

## 9.9 Ten scene cues at a glance

For quick reference when designing a scene, here are ten common
sound cues:

1. **Door creak** — `(audio/play 'door-creak)` at the moment 'the door
   opens' is painted.
2. **Distant thunder** — `(audio/play 'thunder :volume 0.4)` during
   a scene of foreboding.
3. **Kettle whistle** — `(audio/play 'kettle)` in the kitchen after
   a five-second delay.
4. **Cat purr** — `(audio/play 'cat-purr :loop? #t :volume 0.2)`
   whenever the cat is on screen.
5. **Wind in reeds** — `(audio/play 'reed-wind :loop? #t :volume 0.3)`
   at the pond scene.
6. **Footsteps** — `(audio/play 'footsteps :volume 0.5)` when a
   character walks in.
7. **Heartbeat** — `(audio/play 'heartbeat :loop? #t :volume 0.6)`
   under a tension scene, ducking dialogue.
8. **Kettle whistle stops** — `(audio/halt 'kettle)` when someone
   picks it up.
9. **Silence after a slam** — `(audio/halt)` immediately after
   `(audio/play 'door-slam)` for a beat of empty air.
10. **Motif return** — `(audio/play 'mira-motif :volume 0.3)` at the
    end of the game when the player finds her again.

Copy these into your scenes and modify. Appendix F has ten more.

---

## 9.10 Closing

Sound is state. Motif is character. Silence is punctuation. Ambient
is the room breathing.

If you take one thing from this chapter: try running a scene with the
music muted for five minutes. Then run it again with the audio
correct. The difference is enormous, and you will spend the rest of
your career remembering it.

Chapter 10 gives us the villain — and shows how everything we have
built (Cortex, body language, camera, sound) comes together in one
character who must feel real. Villains are the hardest characters to
write and the most rewarding when they land.")

(chapter
  :book                "Book of Narrative Games"
  :chapter-number      10
  :title               "The Villain and Their Face"
  :dialect             "motoi"

"A good villain does not need to shout. A great villain does not need to
speak. The scariest villains in narrative games are the ones the player
FEELS before they see, and never fully understands.

We are going to build a villain out of stillness. Slower breath than
anyone else in the game. A stare that locks and does not blink. A
motif that plays at the edge of hearing when they are near. Cortex
tracks what the player has done, so the villain can reference it —
'so you spared the wolf, did you?' — which is more terrifying than
any threat.

The physics of menace: pause where others move; move where others
freeze; know what nobody should know. That is the shape.

---

## 10.1 The villain's signature

We start where every character starts: signature parameters.

```scheme
;; Create the villain.
(define villain (make-character 'villain))
(entity/pose! villain 'standing)
(entity/sprite! villain 'man-in-dark-coat)

;; Signature: slower breath than everyone else.
(part/breathe villain 0.13)      ;; extremely slow — 8 seconds per cycle
(part/sway    villain 0)         ;; does not sway. Ever.

;; Locked stare.
(part/look-toward villain 400 300)  ;; wherever the kid stands
```

Compare to Mira's 0.28 breath rate. The villain breathes half as
fast. On screen this reads as 'holding still.' The eye picks up
motion; the villain has almost none. The player's gaze rests on him
and finds nothing moving. That is what dread feels like.

The zero sway is deliberate. Every character in your game should have
at least a `part/sway 1` — a barely-visible ambient drift. The
villain has none. He is the only fully-still figure in the game. The
player will notice without knowing why.

The locked stare is the last piece. When Mira looks at the player,
she blinks, adjusts her gaze, glances away. The villain does not.
`part/look-toward villain player-x player-y` and then no other
gaze command for the whole scene. His eyes lock.

---

## 10.2 The villain in the doorway

The reveal scene. Building on chapter 6's camera work.

```scheme
(define (villain-first-appearance)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)

  ;; Silence.
  (audio/halt)
  (world/after 60
    (lambda ()
      (paint-text 20 40 \"You hear nothing. That is the strange thing.\")))

  (world/after 120
    (lambda ()
      (paint-text 20 70 \"You realize the crickets stopped.\")))

  (world/after 180
    (lambda ()
      (paint-text 20 100 \"You look toward the doorway.\")
      (world/camera-pan-to 480 220 :duration 120)))

  (world/after 300
    (lambda ()
      (entity/set-pos! villain 480 220)
      (part/breathe villain 0.13)
      (part/look-toward villain 200 300)          ;; where the kid stands
      (paint-text 20 130
        \"There is a man in the doorway.\")))

  ;; Beat of nothing.
  (world/after 420
    (lambda ()
      (paint-text 20 160
        \"He has been there long enough for you to have noticed.\")))

  (world/after 540
    (lambda ()
      (paint-text 20 200
        \"He does not speak. He does not move.\")
      (audio/play 'villain-motif :volume 0.3)))

  (world/after 660
    (lambda ()
      (paint-text 20 240 \"He knows your name. He does not say it.\"))))
```

Nine seconds of screen time. No dialogue from the villain. Two lines
of description telling the player that he KNOWS. The audio-halt kills
all ambient, then the crickets-stopped line makes the silence
explicit, then the motif enters underneath.

The kid who plays this scene will not forget it. Not because anything
happened. Because nothing happened, and it was worse than something
happening.

---

## 10.3 The villain who remembers

Two chapters from now, the player encounters the villain again. He
mentions what she has done. That is not narrative slack — that is
Cortex working.

```scheme
;; The villain's dialogue reads Cortex and reacts.
(define (villain-speaks-once)
  (paint-text 20 40 \"He tilts his head to look at you.\")
  (world/after 90
    (lambda ()
      (paint-text 20 80 (villain-remembering-line)))))

(define (villain-remembering-line)
  (cond
    ((cortex/read 'state/spared-wolf?)
     \"VILLAIN: 'So you spared the wolf. That was interesting.'\")
    ((cortex/read 'state/killed-wolf?)
     \"VILLAIN: 'The wolf's ghost is with you now. I can see it.'\")
    ((cortex/read 'state/ignored-mira?)
     \"VILLAIN: 'Mira waited. You did not come. I noticed.'\")
    ((> (rep 'mira) 3)
     \"VILLAIN: 'You have friends. Take care of them.'\")
    (else
     \"VILLAIN: 'You have been at this a while. It shows.'\")))
```

Five possible openings. Each references a specific thing the player
did (or did not do). None are threats. All are observations. Which
is worse.

The villain's default line — 'you have been at this a while, it
shows' — is what he says if nothing specific comes up. Even the
default is unsettling. It implies he has been watching.

Do not have the villain reference EVERYTHING the player did. Just
one specific thing per encounter. Overstuffed references feel
like a data dump. One reference feels like a person who has been
paying attention.

---

## 10.4 The villain moves

When the villain moves, everyone else has been still. When everyone
else is moving, the villain has been still. He is always the
opposite of the room.

```scheme
;; A scene where three characters are chatting and the villain enters.
(define (dinner-interrupted)
  ;; Three characters, all breathing, all sway'ing a little.
  (part/breathe mira 0.28)   (part/sway mira 2)
  (part/breathe father 0.22) (part/sway father 1)
  (part/breathe niece 0.35)  (part/sway niece 3)

  ;; The room is alive with small motion.
  (paint-text 20 40 \"Dinner. Three chairs pulled up to a small table.\")

  ;; Villain appears in the doorway.
  (world/after 180
    (lambda ()
      (entity/set-pos! villain 500 200)
      (part/breathe villain 0.13)
      (part/sway    villain 0)
      (part/look-toward villain (entity/x mira) (entity/y mira))))

  ;; The three others FREEZE.
  (world/after 200
    (lambda ()
      (part/halt mira)
      (part/halt father)
      (part/halt niece)
      (paint-text 20 100 \"They stop talking. They stop moving. All at once.\")))

  ;; Ten seconds of the villain being the only thing that breathes.
  (world/after 800
    (lambda ()
      (paint-text 20 140 \"He was there. He is gone. Nobody says anything.\")
      (entity/despawn! villain)))

  ;; Life returns — slowly.
  (world/after 900
    (lambda ()
      (part/breathe mira 0.28)
      (part/breathe father 0.22)
      (part/breathe niece 0.35))))
```

Everyone in the scene breathes and sways. The villain enters. Everyone
else freezes. The villain, who breathes almost imperceptibly, is
NOW the only moving thing in the frame — because he was so still
before, his tiny motion is what the eye locks onto.

Ten seconds. He leaves. Nobody speaks. Life comes back slowly.

This scene has almost no code. Ten `part/*` calls. The choreography of
who moves when tells the story.

---

## 10.5 The villain's face — close-up

Chapter 6 taught close-ups. The villain gets one, and it earns its
weight because you have been building toward it for chapters.

```scheme
(define (villain-close-up)
  ;; Cut hard.
  (cine/shot 'close-up villain 120)

  ;; Full-face view. His breath is on the microphone.
  (audio/play 'breath-close :volume 0.6)

  ;; Two beats of just his face.
  (world/after 90
    (lambda ()
      (part/expression villain 'small-smile)))    ;; the ONLY expression change

  (world/after 180
    (lambda ()
      (paint-text 20 40
        \"He smiles. Not a warm smile. A recognizing smile.\")))

  (world/after 300
    (lambda ()
      (cine/shot 'wide 'room 60))))
```

Four seconds on his face. One expression change — a small-smile that
is not warm. Then pull back to wide.

Do not use `part/expression villain` at any other point in the game.
He has one facial expression the whole game: neutral. This is his
one and only smile. When it arrives, the player feels it as an
event.

Restraint. Every technique you know, held back until the moment it
matters most.

---

## 10.6 A worked scene: the confrontation

The player and the villain finally meet on their terms. The player
has three options. Each ends the game differently.

```scheme
(define (final-confrontation)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)

  ;; Establish.
  (paint-text 20 40 \"The clearing. He was waiting. Of course.\")
  (world/after 60
    (lambda ()
      (entity/set-pos! villain 320 220)
      (part/breathe villain 0.13)
      (part/look-toward villain 320 400)))

  ;; His line — depends on what the player has done.
  (world/after 180
    (lambda ()
      (paint-text 20 100 (villain-final-line))))

  ;; The player's three options.
  (world/after 300
    (lambda ()
      (paint-text 20 200 \"[A] Fight him.\")
      (paint-text 20 230 \"[B] Ask him why.\")
      (paint-text 20 260 \"[C] Turn around and walk away.\")))

  (on-key
    (lambda (k)
      (case k
        ((a) (ending-fight))
        ((b) (ending-conversation))
        ((c) (ending-refuse))))))

(define (villain-final-line)
  (cond
    ((> (rep 'mira) 5)
     \"VILLAIN: 'She sent you, did she?'\")
    ((cortex/read 'state/spared-wolf?)
     \"VILLAIN: 'You spared the wolf. You will not spare me.'\")
    ((cortex/read 'state/found-note?)
     \"VILLAIN: 'You read the note. Then you know why I am here.'\")
    (else
     \"VILLAIN: 'You came alone. That is a kind of courage.'\")))

(define (ending-fight)
  (paint-text 20 300 \"You fight him. He does not resist. He falls.\")
  (paint-text 20 330 \"You do not feel what you thought you would feel.\")
  (world/after 240 (lambda () (credits))))

(define (ending-conversation)
  (paint-text 20 300 \"You ask him why.\")
  (paint-text 20 330 \"He tells you. It takes a long time. You listen.\")
  (paint-text 20 360 \"When he is done, he stands and walks away.\")
  (paint-text 20 390 \"You do not know if you have won. You know something.\")
  (world/after 300 (lambda () (credits))))

(define (ending-refuse)
  (paint-text 20 300 \"You turn around. You walk home. You do not look back.\")
  (paint-text 20 330 \"He calls after you. You do not turn.\")
  (paint-text 20 360 \"The rest of your life happens elsewhere.\")
  (world/after 300 (lambda () (credits))))
```

Three endings, each specific. None triumphant. The FIGHT ending — 'you
do not feel what you thought you would feel.' The CONVERSATION ending
— 'you know something.' The REFUSE ending — 'the rest of your life
happens elsewhere.'

Do not write triumphant villain-defeats. Real narrative games earn
their endings by making them cost. A player who fights and wins
should feel the weight of having taken a life. A player who talks
should feel the discomfort of understanding. A player who walks
away should feel the ache of choosing peace over closure.

None of these are moral judgments. All three are legitimate. The
player chose, and each ending honors the choice they made.

---

## 10.7 Common desktop tasks — the difficult customer

Not every difficult person is a villain. But some customer-service
scenarios feel that way to the operator. Here is a small dialogue
card for handling a customer who is upset and unreasonable — treated
with grace but with limits.

```scheme
(define difficult-customer-tree
  '((:id start
     :npc \"I'm sorry you're upset. Tell me what happened.\"
     :npc-reaction (steady breathe-slow)
     :replies ((:label \"[listen]\" :goto listening)))

    (:id listening
     :npc \"[three-minute pause. She lets him speak.]\"
     :npc-reaction (attentive)
     :replies ((:label \"[when he pauses]\" :goto response)))

    (:id response
     :npc \"I hear you. Here's what I can do: full refund, no questions,\ntoday. Would that resolve it for you?\"
     :npc-reaction (calm)
     :replies ((:label \"[if he accepts]\"    :goto ending-refund)
               (:label \"[if he demands more]\" :goto boundary)))

    (:id boundary
     :npc \"I understand you want more. That is not something I can do.\nThe refund is the offer.\"
     :npc-reaction (still)
     :replies ((:label \"[he takes the refund]\"      :goto ending-refund)
               (:label \"[he continues to demand]\"   :goto ending-decline)))

    (:id ending-refund
     :npc \"Refund is initiated. Thank you for telling me. Take care.\"
     :replies ())

    (:id ending-decline
     :npc \"The refund still stands. I am ending the conversation now.\"
     :replies ())))
```

The operator plays herself: steady, breathing slow, attentive. Three
possible endings. The first two acknowledge the customer's
grievance and resolve it. The third is a hard boundary: 'I am ending
the conversation now.' Restrained, courteous, firm.

Some operators run this card in training mode — they walk through
it themselves before a hard conversation, and by the time they are
on the phone their body-language habits (slow breath, attentive
tilt, steady stillness) come up automatically. That is what a card
like this teaches.

---

## 10.8 Routing patterns

Three villain-design rules:

**Never on schedule.** If the villain shows up in scene 4, 8, and 12,
the pattern deflates them. Have them show up unpredictably — scene
5, then scene 6, then not again for six scenes, then abruptly. Real
menace is unscheduled.

**Only one first appearance.** The reveal scene (like 10.2 above) can
only happen once. After that, every appearance is casual. The player
must never get a second 'first look' at the villain, because they
have already had the definitive one.

**Not always present.** Great villains spend most of the game
offscreen. The player fears them because they know they are out
there. If the villain is in every scene, they become a co-star, and
co-stars are not villains.

---

## 10.9 Closing

Slow breath. Locked stare. Cortex memory. Silence around them.
Restrained expression, used exactly once.

The villain who works is a design achievement. The player will
remember them years later. The techniques in this chapter — plus
everything you learned in chapters 4, 5, 6, 8, 9 — are what make
that memory possible.

Chapter 11 is the hardest chapter in the book. Consequence. The
promise that a branch changes something. Getting this right is why
narrative games sometimes make people cry.")

;; Book of Narrative Games — Chapter 11: Branching That Matters

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(chapter
  :book                "Book of Narrative Games"
  :chapter-number      11
  :title               "Branching That Matters"
  :dialect             "motoi"
  :audience            :kid
  :also-for            :adult
  :content-rating      :PG
  :author-lane         "narrative-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"

"A choice that does not change anything is a lie. Kids catch it faster
than adults. If you offer the player 'kiss her or don't' and the next
scene is identical either way, they will never trust another choice
you offer.

This chapter is the ethics of branching. Every meaningful choice must
alter the game in a way the player LATER encounters. Not immediately.
Not in a rewarded animation right after. LATER — in a scene the
player has almost forgotten was possible.

The physics of consequence: pressure at the start of the game must
be released or paid for by the end. Chekhov called this the gun on
the mantelpiece. In a narrative game every branch is a gun.

---

## 11.1 The three levels of consequence

**Cosmetic** — the choice affects flavor text but not the shape of
the story. 'You wore the blue coat' vs 'you wore the red coat.' The
next scene mentions it once and nothing else changes. Kids catch
this in one playthrough.

**Local** — the choice affects the next scene or two, then falls off.
'You saved Mira' means Mira thanks you next scene, then the story
proceeds as it would have anyway. Adults still notice this pretty
fast.

**Structural** — the choice permanently changes the world. Mira is
alive in some playthroughs; dead in others. The final battle
happens with different allies present. The player who saved Mira in
chapter 3 has a completely different chapter 15 than the player who
didn't.

Aim for structural. Cosmetic is filler. Local is training wheels.
Structural is what narrative games are for.

---

## 11.2 A worked example: the fox

In scene 2 the player finds an injured fox. Three choices: heal it,
kill it, walk past. Each ripples through the game.

```scheme
;; The fox scene, chapter 2.
(define (fox-scene)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (paint-text 20 40 \"A fox lies in the reeds. Something is wrong with\")
  (paint-text 20 65 \"its leg. It watches you steadily.\")
  (paint-text 20 130 \"[A] heal it\")
  (paint-text 20 160 \"[B] kill it\")
  (paint-text 20 190 \"[C] walk past\")
  (on-key
    (lambda (k)
      (case k
        ((a) (cortex/write 'state/fox 'healed) (fox-healed-scene))
        ((b) (cortex/write 'state/fox 'killed) (fox-killed-scene))
        ((c) (cortex/write 'state/fox 'ignored) (fox-ignored-scene))))))
```

Three flag values under `state/fox`. Now the game is going to consult
this flag for the rest of the play.

```scheme
;; Chapter 8: the deep-woods scene.
(define (deep-woods-scene)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (case (cortex/read 'state/fox)
    ((healed)
     (paint-text 20 40 \"The fox from before appears from the trees.\")
     (paint-text 20 70 \"She has grown. Her leg has a bend from where\")
     (paint-text 20 100 \"you set it. She leads you to a path you would\")
     (paint-text 20 130 \"not have found.\")
     (cortex/write 'state/fox-guides #t))
    ((killed)
     (paint-text 20 40 \"Bones in the reeds. You feel a small cold\")
     (paint-text 20 70 \"even though the sun is high.\"))
    ((ignored)
     (paint-text 20 40 \"You cross the reeds. The fox is not there.\")
     (paint-text 20 70 \"Something moves in the underbrush behind you.\")
     (paint-text 20 100 \"You do not turn around.\"))
    (else
     (paint-text 20 40 \"The reeds are quiet.\"))))
```

Six chapters after the fox scene, the woods scene checks the fox
flag. The player who healed the fox has an ally now. The player who
killed the fox feels cold in the sun. The player who ignored the
fox has a wildness at their back.

And then chapter 15, the ending sequence:

```scheme
;; Chapter 15: the final approach.
(define (final-approach)
  (cond
    ((cortex/read 'state/fox-guides)
     (paint-text 20 40 \"You take the fox's path. It saves you six hours.\")
     (paint-text 20 70 \"You arrive rested. You will need it.\"))
    (else
     (paint-text 20 40 \"You take the long way. You are tired when you\")
     (paint-text 20 70 \"arrive. You will feel it in the fight to come.\"))))
```

The fox-healed player fights the villain rested. The fox-killed or
fox-ignored player fights tired. The mechanic backing this could be
as simple as HP: rested = 10 HP, tired = 6 HP. Or a specific ally
present in the final scene: rested = fox at your side, tired = alone.

One choice in chapter 2 changed the shape of chapter 8, chapter 15,
and the final battle. That is structural consequence. That is why
players replay narrative games — to see the other branch.

---

## 11.3 The Chekhov principle

Every important object shown in early scenes should be usable or
referenced by late scenes. If you can't find a use for it, cut it
from the early scene.

Keep a design table:

```
scene 2: fox → healed/killed/ignored (payoff scene 8 + scene 15)
scene 3: letter → given to Mira / kept / burned (payoff scene 12)
scene 5: honey → eaten / given away / left (payoff scene 9 shopkeeper)
scene 7: locked box → opened / left / smashed (payoff scene 14)
```

If any early-scene object has no listed payoff, either invent a
payoff or remove the object. This is where writers spend the most
time — figuring out which small things need to matter later.

Not every object needs a payoff. Setting details are allowed. The
'jar of honey on the counter' in chapter 1 might be pure atmosphere,
never referenced again. But CHOICES — meaningful options the player
picks — should almost always echo forward.

---

## 11.4 Foreshadowing the consequence

The best narrative games telegraph that a choice matters WITHOUT
telling the player which choice is 'right.'

```scheme
;; Scene 2 fox choice, with foreshadowing.
(define (fox-scene-with-weight)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (paint-text 20 40 \"A fox lies in the reeds. Something is wrong with\")
  (paint-text 20 65 \"its leg. It watches you steadily.\")
  (world/after 90
    (lambda ()
      (paint-text 20 100
        \"You feel this is a small moment that will not stay small.\")))
  (world/after 180
    (lambda ()
      (paint-text 20 170 \"[A] heal it\")
      (paint-text 20 200 \"[B] kill it\")
      (paint-text 20 230 \"[C] walk past\"))))
```

'You feel this is a small moment that will not stay small.' That
sentence tells the player the choice will echo. It does not tell
them which choice is right. It just says: pay attention. This is a
gun on the mantelpiece.

Do not do this for every choice. If every choice comes with 'this
will matter,' the player becomes numb. Use it for two or three key
branches in the game. The others should feel casual — and, if you
have done the design work, they will still echo, but as small
touches rather than headline events.

---

## 11.5 The single-playthrough principle

Most players will only play your game once. Design so that ONE
playthrough feels complete and weighted, not so that N playthroughs
combine into one full experience.

This means:
- No single ending should feel like the 'true' ending.
- Every branch should have its own emotional payoff.
- The player who takes the 'wrong' branch (from the writer's
  perspective) should not be worse off — just have a different game.

If you find yourself thinking 'the good ending is the one where they
save everyone,' you have designed a game with one correct branch.
The other branches are punishment routes. Do not do this. Every
branch should be a legitimate story.

---

## 11.6 The impossible fork

Sometimes the player has to make a choice where BOTH options cost
something they care about.

```scheme
;; Save Mira OR save the village. Not both.
(define (impossible-fork)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (paint-text 20 40 \"The bridge is on fire. Mira is at the north end;\")
  (paint-text 20 70 \"the village is at the south end. You can reach\")
  (paint-text 20 100 \"one before the bridge falls. Not both.\")
  (paint-text 20 200 \"[A] Mira\")
  (paint-text 20 230 \"[B] the village\")
  (on-key
    (lambda (k)
      (case k
        ((a) (cortex/write 'state/chose 'mira)
             (cortex/write 'state/village-burned? #t)
             (mira-saved-scene))
        ((b) (cortex/write 'state/chose 'village)
             (cortex/write 'state/mira-dead? #t)
             (village-saved-scene))))))
```

Both choices carry a cost. The player who saves Mira lives with the
village burning. The player who saves the village lives with Mira's
death. Either way the rest of the game is heavy.

Impossible forks work because they respect the player's agency
enough to hurt them with it. This is a hard thing to write. Do it
once in your game, maybe twice. Not every scene.

Never give the impossible-fork player a secret third option. 'What
if the third option is a trick and you save both?' That is a
trick. The player who thought they had to choose feels betrayed by
the game. Impossible forks are impossible.

---

## 11.7 The consequence table (design tool)

Before writing scenes, make a table. Left column: choices. Middle
column: immediate consequence. Right column: downstream scenes it
affects.

```
CHOICE                          IMMEDIATE                DOWNSTREAM
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
heal the fox (ch 2)             fox thanks you           ch 8 fox-guides
                                                          ch 15 rested
                                                          ch 16 fox-at-battle

kill the fox (ch 2)             fox dies                 ch 8 cold-feeling
                                                          ch 15 tired
                                                          ch 16 alone-at-battle

give letter to Mira (ch 3)      Mira reads it            ch 6 Mira warm
                                                          ch 12 Mira acts on info
                                                          ch 15 different plan

burn letter (ch 3)              you feel guilty          ch 6 Mira distant
                                                          ch 12 Mira does not act
                                                          ch 15 original plan

honey scene (ch 5)              you eat/give/leave       ch 9 shopkeeper reacts
                                                          ch 11 bees appear
```

Every row is a story-thread. Design the table BEFORE you write. When
you sit down to write scene 8, you already know what the fox line
should look like — because the table says it. This is why writers
who plan branches this way ship games where every choice matters.

Appendix I is a fuller template for this table. Fill it in for your
own game before you write scene 2.

---

## 11.8 A worked scene: the delayed payoff

In chapter 1 the kid gives water to a stranger on the road. In
chapter 14 that stranger turns out to be a healer who knows her by
face.

```scheme
;; Chapter 1: the road.
(define (road-scene)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (paint-text 20 40 \"An old woman by the side of the road. Waterskin\")
  (paint-text 20 65 \"in her hand. Empty.\")
  (paint-text 20 130 \"[A] give her water\")
  (paint-text 20 160 \"[B] keep walking\")
  (on-key
    (lambda (k)
      (case k
        ((a) (cortex/write 'state/road-water 'gave) (road-thanked))
        ((b) (cortex/write 'state/road-water 'kept) (road-ignored))))))

(define (road-thanked)
  (paint-text 20 200 \"'Bless you,' she says. You do not think much\")
  (paint-text 20 225 \"of it. You have far to walk.\"))

(define (road-ignored)
  (paint-text 20 200 \"She watches you go. You feel it.\"))
```

Fourteen chapters later:

```scheme
;; Chapter 14: the healer's cottage.
(define (healer-cottage)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (paint-text 20 40 \"You reach the cottage. An old woman opens the\")
  (paint-text 20 65 \"door. Her waterskin is full.\")
  (world/after 90
    (lambda ()
      (case (cortex/read 'state/road-water)
        ((gave)
         (paint-text 20 100 \"'You,' she says. 'Come in. There is no charge.'\")
         (cortex/write 'state/free-healing #t))
        ((kept)
         (paint-text 20 100 \"'I remember you,' she says. 'The rate is double.'\")
         (cortex/write 'state/expensive-healing #t))
        (else
         (paint-text 20 100 \"'You are new here,' she says. 'Standard rate.'\"))))))
```

The player who gave water thirteen hours of gameplay ago gets free
healing. The player who kept walking pays double. The player who
never met the old woman (took a different route) pays standard.

The payoff is thirteen hours of gameplay later. The player who was
paying attention feels a shiver of recognition. That is the shiver
narrative games are for.

---

## 11.9 Common desktop tasks — remembering a customer's preference

An operator asks a first-time visitor 'do you like coffee or tea?'
Not because it matters to the transaction. Because next time she
comes in, the shopkeeper's voice starts with 'the kettle is on —
tea, right?'

```scheme
(define-card 'coffee-or-tea
  :init
  (lambda ()
    (let ((known (cortex/read 'customer/prefers)))
      (cond
        (known
         ;; Second+ visit.
         (scene/imagine)
         (paint-text 20 40
           (string-append \"The kettle is on. \"
                          (case known
                            ((tea) \"Tea, right?\")
                            ((coffee) \"Coffee for you.\"))
                          \" Take a seat.\")))
        (else
         ;; First visit.
         (scene/imagine)
         (paint-text 20 40 \"Welcome. Coffee or tea?\")
         (paint-text 20 100 \"[A] coffee   [B] tea\")
         (on-key
           (lambda (k)
             (case k
               ((a) (cortex/write 'customer/prefers 'coffee)
                    (paint-text 20 160 \"Coffee it is.\"))
               ((b) (cortex/write 'customer/prefers 'tea)
                    (paint-text 20 160 \"Tea it is.\"))))))))))
```

The choice from visit 1 pays off in visit 2. The customer feels
remembered. She IS remembered — by Cortex, but she does not need to
know the mechanism. She just knows the shopkeeper's voice remembers
her tea order and that is a small kindness that adds up.

This is what shopkeepers with good memories have always done. Now it
is available to any operator with fifteen lines of Scheme.

---

## 11.10 Closing

Branch matters. Chekhov. Impossible forks. Delayed payoff. The
consequence table.

Write these into your design before you write your first scene. It
is the single most important discipline in narrative games. Skip it
and your game will feel like a menu; keep it and your game will
feel like life.

Chapter 12 opens a strange new tool: an AI companion in the story
itself. Not the villain, not an NPC — a companion whose job is to
reflect what the player has done back to them. Handled well, it is
the deepest tool in the book. Handled badly, it ruins the whole
game. Chapter 12 is careful.")

been playing for a while. She does not have quests. She does not
demand anything. She notices things — 'you have helped every stranger
you met. Is that who you want to be?' — and lets the player sit with
what she said.

She is an AI companion. Not the narrator. Not an NPC with a story
arc. A mirror. The player asks her a question; she reads the last
several Cortex entries and offers a reflection. She talks less than
any character in the game.

This chapter is the shape of that companion. It is also, more
importantly, the ETHICS of that companion. Get it wrong and you have
built a chatbot in a story. Get it right and you have built the
deepest tool in narrative games since the second-person pronoun.

## 12.1 The verbs

```scheme
(afford/deep-think prompt)         ;; long-form reasoning; returns a paragraph
(ask/reasoner question)            ;; single-question consult; returns short answer
(ai/summarize items)               ;; summarize a list of items into prose
(ai/generate prompt :max n)        ;; free-form generation with token cap
(ai/rank items :by criterion)      ;; rank items by a criterion
```

Five verbs. Each has a place. `afford/deep-think` is expensive and
slow — save it for once-a-chapter reflection moments.
`ask/reasoner` is cheap and fast — good for a single question.
`ai/summarize` is what we use for 'previously on…' recaps.
`ai/generate` is when we need free-form prose. `ai/rank` is when we
have a list of options and want a scored order.

All five have real cost. Metering is real. Use sparingly.

---

## 12.2 The reflection scene

The player has just finished a chapter. The old woman appears.

```scheme
(define (reflection-scene)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (paint-text 20 40 \"You reach a bend in the road. An old woman is\")
  (paint-text 20 65 \"sitting on a stone. She looks up.\")

  (world/after 90
    (lambda ()
      (paint-text 20 100 \"'You seem to be thinking,' she says.\")
      (paint-text 20 130 \"'Do you want an ear?'\")))

  (world/after 180
    (lambda ()
      (paint-text 20 200 \"[A] yes\")
      (paint-text 20 230 \"[B] not right now\")))

  (on-key
    (lambda (k)
      (case k
        ((a) (deep-think-with-companion))
        ((b) (skip-reflection))))))

(define (deep-think-with-companion)
  ;; Grab the last 10 Cortex writes and summarize them into a reflection.
  (let* ((recent-events (cortex/topk 10))
         (event-prose (events->prose recent-events))
         (prompt (string-append
                   \"The player has just done these things: \"
                   event-prose
                   \". Offer a single quiet observation about what those\n\"
                   \"choices might mean about who they are becoming. Do not\n\"
                   \"lecture. Do not moralize. One sentence, or two at most.\"))
         (reflection (afford/deep-think prompt)))
    (paint-text 20 300 \"The old woman looks at you for a long moment.\")
    (world/after 90
      (lambda ()
        (paint-text 20 330 (string-append \"'\" reflection \"'\"))))
    (world/after 240
      (lambda ()
        (paint-text 20 400 \"She looks back at the road. You continue.\")))))
```

The player says yes. The companion pulls the last ten Cortex writes,
translates them into prose, and asks the reasoning model for ONE
observation. The prompt asks specifically for no lecture and no
moralizing. The reasoning model returns something like: 'You have
helped every stranger. That is a kind of hunger.' Or: 'You have taken
what you needed but rarely more. That is a rare quality.' Or: 'You
have been kind to the ones you knew and hard on the ones you did
not. Something to sit with.'

The player sits with it. The companion looks back at the road. The
game continues. She does not follow up. She does not ask if the
player wants to talk more. That would be nagging. She has offered
one sentence and returned to silence.

---

## 12.3 Non-negotiable rules for companions

Read these before wiring your own reflection scene:

**She only speaks when asked.** The player must actively choose to
approach her. She does not intrude, does not interrupt gameplay,
does not push notifications. The moment a companion talks without
being asked, they become the game's Clippy — hated and eventually
muted.

**She summarizes, does not judge.** Her observations reflect back
what the player has done. She never says 'you should have done X.'
She might say 'you did not do X — is that a pattern for you?' —
which is a question, not a judgment. Even that is a stretch. Prefer
observations.

**She does not remember the last conversation with the player.** OR
if she does, she only remembers ONE detail. If she brings up
everything the player said last time, the player feels tracked.
Once every three or four reflections she might say 'you mentioned
your sister last time.' That is enough.

**She has quiet mode.** A menu option lets the player disable the
companion entirely for a session or forever. Respect it. The player
who never wants a reflection scene must be able to opt out with one
click.

**She costs money.** The `afford/deep-think` call has a real per-use
cost. If the player is on the free tier, offer a lighter fallback —
a hand-written short observation from a list instead of a live
generation. Never surprise-charge.

---

## 12.4 The wrong companion — a cautionary example

Here is what NOT to do. Read it, notice why it's bad, do the opposite.

```scheme
;; BAD companion behavior — for study only.
(on-frame
  (lambda ()
    (when (= (frame-count) (* 60 60 5))     ;; every 5 minutes
      (interrupt-with-reflection))))         ;; unprompted

(define (interrupt-with-reflection)
  (audio/play 'ding-ding-ding)               ;; loud attention-grab
  (paint-text 20 40 \"HEY! LET'S REFLECT!\")
  (paint-text 20 80 \"You have been playing for 5 minutes.\")
  (paint-text 20 110 \"Here is what I think you should do next:\")
  (paint-text 20 140 (afford/deep-think ...))  ;; unsolicited advice
  (paint-text 20 200 \"[click OK to continue]\"))
```

Everything wrong: unprompted, loud, capitalized, prescriptive,
modal. This companion is a chatbot in a story-suit. Players will hate
it within one session.

Contrast with 12.2: the old woman sits on a rock and asks if the
player wants to talk. The rest is silence unless invited.

---

## 12.5 The lightweight reflection — no AI call

For the free tier, or for players who prefer no AI in their
narrative, offer a lightweight reflection built from Cortex
patterns.

```scheme
;; Free-tier reflection — hand-crafted pattern matching.
(define (lightweight-reflection)
  (let* ((rep-mira (rep 'mira))
         (rep-villain (rep 'villain))
         (kills (or (cortex/read 'stat/kills) 0))
         (helps (or (cortex/read 'stat/helps) 0)))
    (cond
      ((and (> rep-mira 5) (> helps 10))
       \"You have been building bonds. Something is warmer than when\nyou started.\")
      ((and (< rep-villain 0) (> kills 3))
       \"You have chosen to fight when you could have walked away.\nThat is a kind of person.\")
      ((and (> helps 5) (= kills 0))
       \"You have not raised a hand this whole time. Some players\nnever notice they haven't.\")
      ((> (+ helps kills) 15)
       \"You are moving through the world. Many things have touched you.\")
      (else
       \"You are quiet, mostly. That's alright.\"))))
```

Five hand-crafted patterns. Each recognizes a specific Cortex
signature and returns a specific observation. No AI call. No cost.
Ships in the free tier.

The signal is coarser than a live generation, but the shape is the
same: the game reads what you have done and reflects it. Coarse but
free is often better than fine but paid.

---

## 12.6 A one-question consult

`ask/reasoner` is the cheap, quick verb. Use it when the player asks
the companion a specific question and you want a specific answer.

```scheme
(define (ask-the-companion)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (paint-text 20 40 \"'What do you want to know?' she says.\")
  (paint-text 20 100 \"[A] am I doing the right thing?\")
  (paint-text 20 130 \"[B] where should I go next?\")
  (paint-text 20 160 \"[C] never mind\")
  (on-key
    (lambda (k)
      (case k
        ((a) (companion-considers-right-thing))
        ((b) (companion-suggests-next))
        ((c) (skip-question)))))

(define (companion-considers-right-thing)
  (let* ((choices (or (cortex/read 'past-choices) '()))
         (choice-prose (choices->prose choices))
         (answer (ask/reasoner
                   (string-append
                     \"Given a person who did these things: \" choice-prose
                     \". Is there a way to answer their question 'am I doing\n\"
                     \"the right thing?' honestly — not to reassure and not\n\"
                     \"to condemn. One sentence.\"))))
    (paint-text 20 220 (string-append \"'\" answer \"'\"))))
```

The player asks the hardest question. The companion consults a
reasoning model with the full context of what the player has done
and asks for an honest answer — not reassuring, not condemning.
The model returns something like: 'You are doing what you can with
what you know. That is the only honest answer.'

Note the tone-lock in the prompt. Without it the model would tend
toward reassuring platitudes. With it, we get something the player
can sit with.

---

## 12.7 A worked scene: the summary at chapter break

At the end of each chapter, the game offers a chapter-summary the
player can read to feel where they have been.

```scheme
(define (chapter-summary chapter-number)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)
  (paint-text 20 40 (string-append \"~ end of chapter \"
                                   (number->string chapter-number) \" ~\"))
  (paint-text 20 100 \"[A] see what you did this chapter\")
  (paint-text 20 130 \"[B] skip to the next\")
  (on-key
    (lambda (k)
      (case k
        ((a) (show-chapter-summary chapter-number))
        ((b) (next-chapter))))))

(define (show-chapter-summary chapter-number)
  (let* ((this-chapters-events (cortex-events-in-chapter chapter-number))
         (event-prose (events->prose this-chapters-events))
         (summary (ai/summarize event-prose :style 'narrative-recap)))
    (paint-text 20 40
      (string-append \"Chapter \" (number->string chapter-number) \" — recap:\"))
    (paint-text 20 100 summary)
    (paint-text 20 300 \"[press any key to continue]\")))
```

Cortex has been logging every write. `cortex-events-in-chapter`
filters to just the chapter that just ended. `ai/summarize` renders
those events as a two-line prose recap. The player reads it and
feels the shape of the chapter she just played.

This is the same pattern as 'previously on…' — but for the chapter
she just finished, offered as a reflection rather than a reminder.
Some players will skip it. Some will read every one. Respect both.

---

## 12.8 Common desktop tasks — the shopkeeper's end-of-day reflection

An operator wants a nightly card that summarizes her day: what sold,
what didn't, what conversations happened, what she might want to
think about tomorrow.

```scheme
(define-card 'end-of-day
  :init
  (lambda ()
    (scene/imagine)
    (surface/paper)
    (paint-text 20 40 \"End of the day. Want a two-line summary?\")
    (paint-text 20 100 \"[A] yes   [B] not tonight\")
    (on-key
      (lambda (k)
        (case k
          ((a) (day-summary))
          ((b) (fade-out)))))))

(define (day-summary)
  (let* ((today-events (todays-shop-cortex-entries))
         (event-prose (events->prose today-events))
         (summary (ai/summarize event-prose
                                :style 'shopkeeper-diary
                                :max-sentences 2)))
    (paint-text 20 40 \"Today:\")
    (paint-text 20 100 summary)
    (paint-text 20 300
      \"[A] add a note   [B] archive   [C] pull tomorrow's cart\")))
```

The shopkeeper opts in each evening. The card pulls the day's
Cortex entries — orders, customer messages, promotions — and asks
the reasoner for a two-sentence diary entry. The shopkeeper reads it,
maybe adds a personal note, archives.

This is not a spreadsheet. It is a small daily ritual that gives the
shopkeeper a moment to see her shop as a story rather than a series
of transactions. Over months of use, the diary becomes something she
can look back through when she is having a hard week.

---

## 12.9 Routing patterns

**Once per chapter, tops.** A reflection scene is a spice, not a
staple. If every scene has a reflection, none of them land. Reserve
for chapter breaks, meaningful moments, and player-initiated asks.

**Free fallback for expensive verbs.** Any scene that uses
`afford/deep-think` or `ai/generate` should have a hand-crafted
fallback for players who cannot or will not pay. Detect tier at
runtime; branch on it.

**Companion can be muted.** In the game settings, offer 'quiet
mode.' In quiet mode, companion scenes do not appear. This is a
first-class feature, not a hidden toggle. Some players want no AI in
their story; respect them.

---

## 12.10 Closing

The companion is quiet. She notices. She offers one observation. She
returns to silence. That is the shape.

Do this well and your game has a mirror the player can bring their
choices to. Do it badly and your game has a chatbot the player has
to tolerate.

"Two-character dialogue is easy. Three or more is theater. Who is
looking at whom? Who reacts when the third character speaks? Where
does the camera live? Who does the player interrupt?

This chapter is about scenes with three or more speaking characters.
The vocabulary is the same — `part/look-toward`, `part/turn`,
`world/camera-pan-to`, dialogue trees — but arranged as
choreography. We are directing a scene, not scripting a conversation.

The physics of ensemble scenes: every non-speaking character must be
DOING SOMETHING. Otherwise they read as furniture. A listener nods,
tilts, breathes. A listener who ignores becomes cold on purpose.
Nothing is neutral.

## 13.1 Setup — spawning three characters

```scheme
(define (three-character-scene)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)

  ;; Spawn characters at their positions.
  (define mira    (make-character 'mira))
  (define father  (make-character 'father))
  (define niece   (make-character 'niece))

  (entity/set-pos! mira    120 200)
  (entity/set-pos! father  280 200)
  (entity/set-pos! niece   440 200)

  (entity/pose!    mira   'sitting)
  (entity/pose!    father 'sitting)
  (entity/pose!    niece  'sitting)

  ;; Each character's signature breath rate.
  (part/breathe mira    0.28)
  (part/breathe father  0.22)
  (part/breathe niece   0.38)

  ;; Camera on the group.
  (world/camera-snap! 280 200)
  (paint-text 20 40 \"Three chairs at a table. Nobody has started yet.\"))
```

Three characters, three positions, three signature breath rates.
The niece is the youngest, so she breathes fastest. Father is oldest,
slowest. Mira is between them.

The characters are placed left, center, right at the same y. Later
we might elevate some — the niece sits on a stool, the father on the
tallest chair. But start flat and add depth if needed.

The camera starts on the group — the center point between the three
of them. As the scene progresses, we will pan between speakers.

## 13.2 Turn-taking

The heart of ensemble choreography: when A speaks, B and C look at
A. When B responds, A and C look at B.

```scheme
;; Helper: everyone except the speaker looks at the speaker.
(define (turn-to-speaker speaker others)
  (for-each
    (lambda (listener)
      (part/look-toward listener (entity/x speaker) (entity/y speaker)))
    others))

;; The scene proceeds.
(define (dinner-conversation mira father niece)
  ;; Mira speaks.
  (turn-to-speaker mira (list father niece))
  (paint-text 20 100 \"MIRA: 'She's not coming.'\")

  (world/after 150
    (lambda ()
      ;; Father takes the beat.
      (part/lean father -4)                         ;; leans back
      (world/after 60
        (lambda ()
          (turn-to-speaker father (list mira niece))
          (paint-text 20 140 \"FATHER: 'No.'\")))))

  (world/after 400
    (lambda ()
      ;; Niece speaks after the silence.
      (turn-to-speaker niece (list mira father))
      (paint-text 20 180 \"NIECE: 'What do we do?'\")))

  (world/after 500
    (lambda ()
      ;; Mira answers — and looks at niece specifically.
      (turn-to-speaker mira (list father niece))
      (part/look-toward mira (entity/x niece) (entity/y niece))
      (paint-text 20 220 \"MIRA: 'We eat. That's all.'\"))))
```

The pattern: before each line, the speaker faces forward (or wherever
they should look), and the others turn to face the speaker. This one
helper — `turn-to-speaker` — carries the whole scene.

Notice line 4 in Mira's response: after the group turn, we
specifically point Mira at the niece. She is answering the niece's
question, not father's. Small target adjustments like this make the
scene feel real.

---

## 13.3 Reaction beats

When one character says something surprising, the others react. The
reactions carry more emotional weight than the line itself sometimes.

```scheme
;; A hard reveal.
(paint-text 20 100 \"MIRA: 'She said she is not coming back.'\")

(world/after 60
  (lambda ()
    ;; Father: freezes. Breath halts.
    (part/halt father)
    ;; Niece: leans in, curious more than sad.
    (part/lean niece 6)
    (part/tilt niece 8)))

;; Two seconds later, life comes back to father.
(world/after 200
  (lambda ()
    (part/breathe father 0.22)
    (part/turn father 'front)
    (paint-text 20 140 \"FATHER: 'When did she tell you.'\")))
```

Mira drops the news. Father freezes — halted breath. Niece leans in
(children process news physically). Two seconds of silence. Father
returns to breath, turns, asks a question.

Every character reacted. Nobody was furniture. The father's freeze
carries the emotional beat of the scene. The niece's lean is a
smaller register — she does not understand yet.

Design your reactions in advance. For every big line in the scene,
write down what each non-speaker does. This is the same discipline
theater directors call 'blocking.'

---

## 13.4 The player interrupts

In our dialogue trees so far the player has been ONE of the
speakers. In an ensemble scene, sometimes the player is present but
listening. Sometimes they want to break in.

```scheme
;; The player can press 'B' to break into the conversation.
(define (dinner-with-interrupt-option)
  ;; Set the scene as before.
  ;; ...

  (on-key
    (lambda (k)
      (when (eq? k 'b)
        (interrupt-happens)))))

(define (interrupt-happens)
  ;; The current speaker halts.
  (part/halt current-speaker)
  ;; They turn to the player.
  (part/turn current-speaker 'front)
  (part/lean current-speaker 4)      ;; leans forward to hear you
  ;; The others turn to the player too.
  (for-each
    (lambda (c)
      (part/look-toward c (input/mouse-x) (input/mouse-y)))
    (all-characters-except current-speaker))
  ;; Player gets to say their piece.
  (paint-text 20 300 \"You: [type your interruption]\")
  (input/text-buffer 20 340
    :on-submit
    (lambda (text)
      (paint-text 20 380 (string-append \"You said: '\" text \"'\"))
      ;; The characters react.
      (world/after 60
        (lambda () (react-to-interruption text))))))
```

The player presses B. The current speaker halts mid-sentence, turns
to the player, leans forward. Everyone else turns to look at the
player. The player types their interruption. When they submit,
characters react.

`react-to-interruption` can be as simple as everyone nodding, or as
complex as a semantic classification of the interruption content that
triggers different reactions. Chapter 12 gives you the tools; use
what feels right for your scene.

Not every scene needs to allow interruption. In fact most should not
— an ensemble scene that keeps getting derailed by player
interruptions never builds momentum. Reserve interruption for scenes
where the player's voice matters.

---

## 13.5 The camera in ensemble scenes

Camera choices in three-way scenes are trickier than in two-way. Some
options:

**Wide the whole time.** Camera stays on the group; the audience
sees all three faces. Works for scenes where the group dynamic is
the point.

**Cut between close-ups.** Every line gets its own close-up. Feels
cinematic but expensive — twelve cuts in a two-minute scene, and
the player's brain gets tired.

**Pan between speakers.** Camera drifts to whoever speaks. Works
when there are only two active speakers and one silent observer.
Great for tense confrontations where the silent observer's face
holds the emotional weight.

**Follow the focus character.** Pick ONE character whose face is the
scene's emotional throughline. Camera stays on them, watching them
react to what others say. Works for scenes about ONE person even
though many are talking.

Here is the follow-the-focus variant.

```scheme
;; The scene is 'about' the niece — how she absorbs what the adults say.
;; The camera stays on her.
(define (niece-focus-scene)
  (world/camera-follow! niece :ease 0.1)

  ;; Adults have their conversation.
  (mira-says \"She's not coming.\")
  (father-says \"No.\")
  (mira-says \"We eat. That's all.\")

  ;; During all of this, the niece's face is what we see.
  ;; Every time an adult speaks, we watch how she reacts.
  )
```

The audience never sees father's face. Never sees Mira's face. They
see the niece hearing her family talk about the loss. That is a very
different scene from the wide version — even though the dialogue is
identical.

Choosing the camera is choosing whose experience the scene is about.

## 13.6 A worked scene: the three-way negotiation

Two shopkeepers and a customer. The customer wants to trade a piece
from one shop as partial payment on a piece from the other. Neither
shopkeeper wants to say yes first.

```scheme
(define (three-way-negotiation)
  (scene/imagine)
  (surface/paper)

  ;; Three positions.
  (define anna    (make-character 'anna))     ;; shopkeeper 1
  (define bea     (make-character 'bea))      ;; shopkeeper 2
  (define customer (make-character 'customer)) ;; the player character

  (entity/set-pos! anna    100 200)
  (entity/set-pos! bea     500 200)
  (entity/set-pos! customer 300 300)

  (part/breathe anna 0.30)
  (part/breathe bea  0.25)
  (part/breathe customer 0.45)

  (world/camera-snap! 300 220)

  ;; Customer opens.
  (turn-to-speaker customer (list anna bea))
  (paint-text 20 40
    \"YOU: 'I'd take Bea's chair if I could put Anna's lamp against it.'\")

  ;; Anna and Bea look at each other, not at the customer.
  (world/after 120
    (lambda ()
      (part/look-toward anna (entity/x bea) (entity/y bea))
      (part/look-toward bea (entity/x anna) (entity/y anna))))

  ;; Long silence. Both are calculating.
  (world/after 240
    (lambda ()
      (paint-text 20 80 \"[Anna and Bea study each other for a long moment.]\")))

  ;; Anna speaks first.
  (world/after 400
    (lambda ()
      (turn-to-speaker anna (list bea customer))
      (part/lean anna 4)
      (paint-text 20 120 \"ANNA: 'The lamp is worth two-thirty.'\")))

  ;; Bea considers.
  (world/after 550
    (lambda ()
      (part/tilt bea 10)              ;; head tilt: considering
      (part/sway bea 3)))              ;; small sway

  (world/after 700
    (lambda ()
      (turn-to-speaker bea (list anna customer))
      (paint-text 20 160 \"BEA: 'The chair is four hundred. I'd take one-eighty\")
      (paint-text 20 185 \"in cash and the lamp — but Anna, you're too generous.'\")))

  ;; Camera cuts to Anna as she considers.
  (world/after 900
    (lambda ()
      (cine/shot 'close-up anna 90)
      (part/expression anna 'thinking)))

  ;; Anna's decision.
  (world/after 1050
    (lambda ()
      (part/nod anna)
      (paint-text 20 220 \"ANNA: 'Two-ten. Split the difference.'\")))

  ;; Bea nods, deal is done.
  (world/after 1200
    (lambda ()
      (cine/shot 'wide 'group 60)
      (part/nod bea)
      (paint-text 20 260 \"BEA: 'Done. Take the chair. Bring the lamp Tuesday.'\")))

  ;; Customer gets the last beat.
  (world/after 1350
    (lambda ()
      (turn-to-speaker customer (list anna bea))
      (paint-text 20 300 \"YOU: 'Tuesday. Thank you both.'\"))))
```

Twenty-two seconds. Three characters. The audience sees the whole
negotiation in body language — Anna and Bea looking at each other
without speaking, the long calculation, the small tilts and sways.
The dialogue is spare. The choreography carries the scene.

The reader who has been working through this book will now spot every
technique: turn-to-speaker helper, signature breath rates, camera
cuts at emotional beats, `part/tilt` and `part/sway` as thinking
markers, `close-up` when a character considers alone, `wide` when the
group closes a deal.

You can build this scene. You built the tools for it in every
previous chapter.

## 13.7 Common desktop tasks — a three-person shop chat

A customer, the shopkeeper, and a specialist. The customer has a
question the shopkeeper doesn't know the answer to; she pings the
specialist.

```scheme
(define-card 'three-person-consult
  :init
  (lambda ()
    (scene/imagine)
    (surface/paper)

    (define shopkeeper (make-character 'shopkeeper))
    (define specialist (make-character 'specialist))
    (define customer   (make-character 'customer))

    (entity/set-pos! shopkeeper 200 200)
    (entity/set-pos! specialist 400 200)
    (entity/set-pos! customer   300 320)

    (part/breathe shopkeeper 0.30)
    (part/breathe specialist 0.28)
    (part/breathe customer   0.40)

    ;; Customer asks a question.
    (turn-to-speaker customer (list shopkeeper specialist))
    (paint-text 20 40
      \"CUSTOMER: 'Would this work on cast iron?'\")

    ;; Shopkeeper looks at specialist.
    (world/after 120
      (lambda ()
        (part/look-toward shopkeeper (entity/x specialist) (entity/y specialist))
        (part/shrug shopkeeper)))

    ;; Specialist steps in.
    (world/after 240
      (lambda ()
        (turn-to-speaker specialist (list shopkeeper customer))
        (part/nod specialist)
        (paint-text 20 100
          \"SPECIALIST: 'On cast iron, yes, if it's already seasoned.'\")))

    ;; Shopkeeper thanks specialist.
    (world/after 400
      (lambda ()
        (turn-to-speaker shopkeeper (list specialist))
        (part/nod shopkeeper)
        (paint-text 20 140 \"SHOPKEEPER: 'Thank you.'\")))

    ;; Customer takes the answer.
    (world/after 500
      (lambda ()
        (turn-to-speaker customer (list shopkeeper specialist))
        (paint-text 20 180 \"CUSTOMER: 'Great — I'll take it.'\")))))
```

Three characters. Fifteen seconds. The shopkeeper's shrug when asked
is honest — she didn't know. The specialist stepped in. The customer
got the answer she needed. Everyone acted like a real person.

The operator who ships a cart like this is signaling to customers
that her shop is a place where you can ASK — because if the
shopkeeper doesn't know, someone will. That is the difference between
a shop and a store.

---

## 13.8 Routing patterns

**Never more than four active speakers.** Three is comfortable. Four
is manageable. Five gets confusing — the audience loses track of
who is who. If you need a bigger group, have some characters be
non-speaking presence.

**Assign a focus character per beat.** Every moment in the scene
should have ONE character whose face the audience is watching.
Switch focus at emotional beats. Never split attention.

**Let silence carry beats.** In a two-person scene, silence is
awkward. In a three-person scene, silence is dense — everyone is
reacting to what was just said. Trust silence more in ensemble
scenes than you would in two-person.

---

## 13.9 Closing

Ensemble scenes are the hardest thing in narrative games. They are
also the moments players remember. The dinner where nobody spoke
about the thing everyone was thinking about. The negotiation where
two shopkeepers stared each other down. The consult where the
shopkeeper shrugged and asked for help.

Every technique you have — breath, turn, tilt, camera cut, motif —
comes together here. Practice with small scenes. Three people, six
lines. Then scale up.

games — experiences that happen to run on the runtime. Some of the
most memorable things you can make.")
