"# Chapter 13: Nested Wire-Shots

You've learned to collapse a single wire call into one atomic form—fetch, transform, use, all closed by the same paren that opened the journey. Now double it: two wire calls, one nested inside the other, still expressed as a single top-level form. The outer call waits for the inner; the inner closes with data that the outer immediately consumes. No intermediate variable. No orphaned state between hops. No latency compounding across a seam.

This is the nested wire-shot: one form, two flights, zero gaps.

Why it matters in Motoi: a recipe site returns an ingredient list; a second call fetches the pantry inventory for each ingredient; the final answer—\"can I make this?\"—lands in one atomic expression. A news API returns a headline; a knowledge lookup fills the context; the composed summary surfaces in one shot. The disposition we're drilling: when two wire calls depend on each other, nest them in place rather than sequencing them across statements.

The chapter opens gently—simple pairs where the dependency is obvious—and climbs toward genuinely hard nests where three or four calls close each other in a single form.

---

## The Simplest Nest

A city name comes back from one wire call. A weather lookup needs that city. Instead of storing the city in a variable and calling weather in a second statement, nest the city fetch inside the weather call. One form. Two hops. The inner call closes the outer.

```scheme
(surface :say \"Current temperature: ~a°F\"
  :from (fetch (string-append \"https://api.weather.local/temp?city=\"
                              (fetch \"https://api.location.local/city\"))))
```

The inner `(fetch …)` runs first, returns a city string, and immediately closes the URL being built by `string-append`. The outer `fetch` fires with the complete URL. The temperature string closes the `:from` slot. One paren closes the whole interaction.

---

## Nest a Knowledge Lookup Inside a Query

A wire call returns a species name. A local knowledge lookup needs that species to answer a habitat question. Nest the wire call inside the knowledge form.

```scheme
(knowledge/of :category \"habitat\"
              :subject (fetch \"https://api.nature.local/species/random\"))
```

The fetch runs, returns `\"peregrine falcon\"` (or any species), and that string immediately closes the `:subject` slot. The knowledge lookup fires with the complete argument. One form. Two data sources—one remote, one local—both closed by the same outer paren.

---

## Nest a Recall Inside a Wire Call

A speech template needs a topic summary. That summary lives in cortex. The final result gets sent over the wire to a logging service. Nest the recall inside the wire post.

```scheme
(fetch \"https://api.log.local/entry\"
       :method 'POST
       :body (cortex/recall :topic \"favorite-color\"))
```

The `(cortex/recall …)` runs first, returns the stored value, and immediately closes the `:body` slot. The `fetch` fires with the complete POST payload. One form. Two retrievals—one from cortex, one to the wire—nested without intermediate state.

---

## Nest a Computation Inside a Fetch

A conversion endpoint needs a Celsius value. The Celsius value comes from a Fahrenheit fetch. Nest the fetch inside the arithmetic that closes the second URL.

```scheme
(fetch (string-append \"https://api.convert.local/c-to-k?c=\"
                      (number->string
                        (/ (- (string->number
                                (fetch \"https://api.weather.local/temp-f?city=Portland\"))
                              32)
                           1.8))))
```

The innermost fetch returns a Fahrenheit string. `string->number` converts it. The arithmetic `(/ (- … 32) 1.8)` produces Celsius. `number->string` serializes it. `string-append` builds the Kelvin query URL. The outer fetch fires. One form. Four transformations. Two wire hops. Zero intermediate variables.

---

## Nest Two Knowledge Lookups

A question about \"predators of X\" where X comes from a knowledge lookup about \"most common rodent in Y\" and Y comes from a wire call returning a biome name.

```scheme
(knowledge/of :category \"predators\"
              :subject (knowledge/of :category \"common-rodent\"
                                     :subject (fetch \"https://api.geo.local/biome?lat=45.5&lon=-122.6\")))
```

The innermost fetch returns `\"temperate rainforest\"`. The middle knowledge lookup returns `\"deer mouse\"`. The outer knowledge lookup returns `\"owls, snakes, foxes\"`. Three lookups. One form. Each call closes the slot of the call that wraps it.

---

## Nest a Guard Inside a Nested Fetch

Only fetch the second resource if the first returns a non-empty result. Use `when` inside the outer form to guard the second hop.

```scheme
(when (not (string=? (fetch \"https://api.feature.local/enabled?flag=new-ui\") \"\"))
  (fetch (string-append \"https://api.assets.local/bundle?name=\"
                        (fetch \"https://api.feature.local/enabled?flag=new-ui\"))))
```

The first fetch runs. If it returns an empty string, the `when` short-circuits and the whole form returns `#f`. If it returns a feature name, the second fetch fires with that name embedded in the URL. One form. One guard. Two wire hops only if the guard passes.

*[needs: short-circuit semantics for `when` across async fetch completions]*  
<!-- BUILD: runtime must not fire the consequent fetch if the guard fetch returns falsey -->

## Nest a Map Over Fetched Data

A wire call returns a list of city names (as a JSON array). Map a weather fetch over each city. The map closes the outer `surface :say` form.

```scheme
(surface :say \"Temperatures: ~a\"
  :from (map (lambda (city)
               (fetch (string-append \"https://api.weather.local/temp?city=\" city)))
             (json-parse (fetch \"https://api.geo.local/cities?region=PNW\"))))
```

The innermost fetch returns a JSON string of city names. `json-parse` converts it to a list. `map` iterates, firing a weather fetch for each city. The resulting list of temperatures closes the `:from` slot. One form. Multiple wire hops (one + N). Zero intermediate accumulation outside the form.

*[needs: `json-parse` in stdlib and async-aware `map` that waits for all fetches]*  
<!-- BUILD: map must return a promise that resolves when all inner fetches complete -->

## Nest a Filtered Fetch Result Inside Another Call

Fetch a list of product IDs. Filter for IDs above 1000. Fetch details for the first match. Return the product name.

```scheme
(let ((id (car (filter (lambda (n) (> n 1000))
                       (json-parse (fetch \"https://api.store.local/products/ids\"))))))
  (json-ref (fetch (string-append \"https://api.store.local/products/\" (number->string id)))
            \"name\"))
```

The innermost fetch returns a JSON array of IDs. `json-parse` converts it to a list. `filter` keeps IDs > 1000. `car` takes the first. `number->string` serializes it. `string-append` builds the detail URL. The second fetch fires. `json-ref` extracts the name field. One `let` binds the filtered ID; the body is still a single composed expression. One top-level form.

## Nest a Fold Over Fetched Data Inside a POST

Fetch a list of numbers. Fold them into a sum. POST the sum to a logging endpoint. One form.

```scheme
(fetch \"https://api.log.local/sum\"
       :method 'POST
       :body (number->string
               (fold + 0 (json-parse (fetch \"https://api.math.local/numbers\")))))
```

The innermost fetch returns a JSON array of numbers. `json-parse` converts it to a list. `fold` sums them. `number->string` serializes the result. The outer fetch POSTs it. One form. Three transformations. Two wire hops. The fold closes the `:body` slot; the body closes the POST.

## Nest Recall Inside a Conditional Inside a Fetch

If a user preference is set, fetch a personalized resource; otherwise fetch the default. Nest the recall inside the conditional inside the URL builder.

```scheme
(fetch (string-append \"https://api.content.local/\"
                      (if (cortex/recall :topic \"premium-user\")
                          \"premium/feed\"
                          \"standard/feed\")))
```

The `(cortex/recall …)` runs first, returns `#t` or `#f`. The `if` selects the path segment. `string-append` builds the URL. The fetch fires. One form. One recall. One wire hop. The conditional closes the URL; the URL closes the fetch.

## Nest a Fetch Inside a Case Dispatch

A registry lookup returns a capability tier. A `case` dispatch selects which analytics endpoint to call. Nest the registry call inside the `case` test, and nest each fetch inside its branch.

```scheme
(case (system/registry :domain \"analytics-tier\")
  ((premium) (fetch \"https://api.analytics.local/premium/event\" :method 'POST :body \"signup\"))
  ((standard) (fetch \"https://api.analytics.local/standard/event\" :method 'POST :body \"signup\"))
  (else 'nan))
```

The `(system/registry …)` runs first, returns a symbol like `'premium`. The `case` matches the branch. The corresponding fetch fires. One form. One registry lookup. One wire hop. The case closes the fetch; the fetch closes the form.

---

## Triple Nest: Fetch, Knowledge, Fetch

A product category comes from a wire call. A knowledge lookup maps the category to a warehouse region. A second wire call fetches inventory for that region. Three lookups, one form.

```scheme
(fetch (string-append \"https://api.inventory.local/stock?region=\"
                      (knowledge/of :category \"warehouse-region\"
                                    :subject (fetch \"https://api.catalog.local/product/category?id=8472\"))))
```

The innermost fetch returns a category string like `\"electronics\"`. The knowledge lookup returns a region code like `\"west\"`. `string-append` builds the inventory URL. The outer fetch fires. One form. Three data sources—two remote, one local—all closed by the same top-level paren.

## Nest Four Calls: Fetch, Parse, Filter, Fetch

Fetch a JSON array of user IDs. Parse it. Filter for IDs divisible by 10. Fetch profile details for the first match. Return the username.

```scheme
(json-ref (fetch (string-append \"https://api.users.local/profile?id=\"
                                (number->string
                                  (car (filter (lambda (n) (= (modulo n 10) 0))
                                               (json-parse (fetch \"https://api.users.local/ids\")))))))
          \"username\")
```

Four transformations: fetch, parse, filter, fetch. The innermost fetch returns a JSON string. `json-parse` converts it to a list. `filter` keeps IDs divisible by 10. `car` takes the first. `number->string` serializes it. `string-append` builds the profile URL. The second fetch fires. `json-ref` extracts the username. One form. Two wire hops. Four transformations. Zero intermediate bindings outside the expression.

## Nest a Conditional Wire-Shot Inside Another Conditional

If a feature flag is enabled (first fetch), and if the user is premium (recall), fetch the premium content; otherwise fetch standard. Two guards, two fetches, one form.

```scheme
(if (and (string=? (fetch \"https://api.feature.local/enabled?flag=premium-content\") \"true\")
         (cortex/recall :topic \"premium-user\"))
    (fetch \"https://api.content.local/premium\")
    (fetch \"https://api.content.local/standard\"))
```

The first fetch checks the feature flag. The recall checks the user tier. `and` short-circuits if either is false. The `if` selects the content fetch. One form. Up to three lookups (one wire, one recall, one wire). The guards close the `if`; the `if` closes the consequent fetch.

## Nest a Fetch Inside a Let-Bound Transformation

Fetch a temperature in Kelvin. Bind the conversion factor in a `let`. Return the Fahrenheit value as a formatted string. One form (the `let` is the top-level form; the body is a single expression).

```scheme
(let ((k (string->number (fetch \"https://api.weather.local/temp-k?city=Seattle\"))))
  (string-append (number->string (+ (* (- k 273.15) 1.8) 32)) \"°F\"))
```

The fetch runs, returns a Kelvin string. `string->number` converts it. The `let` binds `k`. The body computes Fahrenheit and formats it. One `let` form. One fetch. One transformation. The fetch closes the binding; the transformation closes the body.

## Nest a Fold Over Two Fetched Lists

Fetch a list of prices. Fetch a list of quantities. Zip them and fold to compute total cost. POST the result.

```scheme
(fetch \"https://api.orders.local/total\"
       :method 'POST
       :body (number->string
               (fold (lambda (pair acc)
                       (+ acc (* (car pair) (cdr pair))))
                     0
                     (map cons
                          (json-parse (fetch \"https://api.orders.local/prices\"))
                          (json-parse (fetch \"https://api.orders.local/quantities\"))))))
```

Two fetches return JSON arrays. Two `json-parse` calls convert them to lists. `map cons` zips the lists into pairs. `fold` accumulates the sum of `(price * quantity)` for each pair. `number->string` serializes the total. The outer fetch POSTs it. One form. Two wire reads. One wire write. The fold closes the `:body`; the body closes the POST.

## Nest a Recursive Fetch Chain

Fetch a paginated API. If the response includes a `next` URL, fetch it recursively. Return all accumulated items. (Use named `let` for recursion within a single top-level form.)

```scheme
(let fetch-all ((url \"https://api.data.local/items?page=1\")
                (acc '()))
  (let ((resp (json-parse (fetch url))))
    (let ((items (json-ref resp \"items\"))
          (next (json-ref resp \"next\")))
      (if next
          (fetch-all next (append acc items))
          (append acc items)))))
```

Named `let` establishes the recursive loop. The first fetch runs. The response is parsed. Items and the next-page URL are extracted. If `next` exists, recurse with the new URL and accumulated items. Otherwise return the final accumulation. One top-level form (the named `let`). Multiple wire hops (unknown count until `next` is null). Zero intermediate state outside the recursion.

## Nest a Fetch Inside a Guarded Map

Fetch a list of city names. For each city, fetch weather only if the city name is longer than 5 characters. Return the list of temperatures (with `'nan` for skipped cities).

```scheme
(map (lambda (city)
       (if (> (string-length city) 5)
           (fetch (string-append \"https://api.weather.local/temp?city=\" city))
           'nan))
     (json-parse (fetch \"https://api.geo.local/cities?region=EU\")))
```

The inner fetch returns a JSON array of city names. `json-parse` converts it to a list. `map` iterates. For each city, the guard checks length. If long enough, fetch temperature; otherwise return `'nan`. The map closes the outer form. One top-level `map`. One + N wire hops (where N is the number of long city names). Zero intermediate accumulation outside the `map`.

## Nest a Knowledge Lookup Inside a Filtered Map

Fetch a list of animal names. For each animal, look up its habitat. Filter the results to keep only \"forest\" animals. Return the filtered list.

```scheme
(filter (lambda (pair) (string=? (cdr pair) \"forest\"))
        (map (lambda (animal)
               (cons animal (knowledge/of :category \"habitat\" :subject animal)))
             (json-parse (fetch \"https://api.nature.local/animals\"))))
```

The fetch returns a JSON array of animal names. `json-parse` converts it to a list. `map` iterates, performing a knowledge lookup for each animal and pairing the animal name with its habitat. `filter` keeps only pairs where the habitat is `\"forest\"`. One form. One wire hop. N knowledge lookups. The filter closes the map; the map closes the fetch.

## Nest a Recall Inside a Let Inside a Fetch POST

Fetch a username from a wire call. Recall a stored auth token. Combine them in a JSON payload. POST to a login endpoint. One form.

```scheme
(let ((username (fetch \"https://api.auth.local/username\"))
      (token (cortex/recall :topic \"auth-token\")))

         :method 'POST
         :body (string-append \"{\\\"username\\\":\\\"\" username \"\\\",\\\"token\\\":\\\"\" token \"\\\"}\")))
```

The `let` binds two values: one from a wire call, one from cortex recall. The body constructs a JSON string and POSTs it. One `let` form (the top-level). One wire read. One recall. One wire write. The bindings close the body; the body closes the POST.

Fetch a health-check endpoint that returns a status code as a string. Dispatch on the code: if \"200\", fetch the main resource; if \"503\", return an error message; otherwise return `'nan`.

```scheme
(case (fetch \"https://api.service.local/health\")
  ((\"200\") (fetch \"https://api.service.local/data\"))
  ((\"503\") \"Service unavailable\")
  (else 'nan))
```

The first fetch runs, returns a string like `\"200\"`. The `case` matches the string. The corresponding branch fires. If `\"200\"`, the second fetch runs. One form. Up to two wire hops. The case closes the consequent fetch; the fetch closes the form.

## Nest Three Wire Calls in a Chain

Fetch a user ID. Use it to fetch a profile. Use the profile's region field to fetch regional settings. Return the timezone.

```scheme
(json-ref (fetch (string-append \"https://api.settings.local/region?code=\"
                                (json-ref (fetch (string-append \"https://api.users.local/profile?id=\"
                                                                (fetch \"https://api.auth.local/user-id\")))
                                          \"region\")))
          \"timezone\")
```

Three fetches. The innermost returns a user ID string. The middle fetch returns a JSON profile. `json-ref` extracts the region code. The outer fetch returns regional settings. `json-ref` extracts the timezone. One form. Three wire hops. Six transformations. Zero intermediate bindings outside the nesting.

## Nest a Fold Inside a Fetch POST with a Guarded Map

Fetch a list of transaction amounts. Filter out negative values. Sum the remaining amounts. POST the total to a reporting endpoint.

```scheme
(fetch \"https://api.reports.local/total\"
       :method 'POST
       :body (number->string
               (fold + 0
                     (filter (lambda (n) (>= n 0))
                             (json-parse (fetch \"https://api.transactions.local/amounts\"))))))
```

The innermost fetch returns a JSON array of numbers. `json-parse` converts it to a list. `filter` keeps non-negative values. `fold` sums them. `number->string` serializes the result. The outer fetch POSTs it. One form. Five transformations. Two wire hops. The fold closes the `:body`; the body closes the POST.

## Nest a Conditional Fetch Based on Two Recalls

If the user has both \"premium\" and \"early-access\" flags set in cortex, fetch the beta resource; otherwise fetch the stable resource.

```scheme
(if (and (cortex/recall :topic \"premium\")
         (cortex/recall :topic \"early-access\"))
    (fetch \"https://api.content.local/beta\")
    (fetch \"https://api.content.local/stable\"))
```

Look up all animals in the \"endangered\" category (assume it returns a list). For each, fetch a photo URL from a wire endpoint. Return the list of URLs.

```scheme
(map (lambda (animal)

```


```scheme
   (fetch \"https://api.resources.local/alpha\"))
  ((string=? (fetch \"https://api.config.local/env\") \"beta\")

  (else 'nan))
```

The fetch runs twice (once per test clause). If \"alpha\" matches, the first consequent fetch fires. If \"beta\" matches, the second fires. Otherwise `'nan`. One `cond` form. Up to three wire hops. The tests close the consequent fetches; the cond closes the form.

## Nest a Fetch Inside a Recursive Countdown

Count down from a fetched number to zero, logging each step to a wire endpoint. Use named `let` for recursion. One form.

```scheme
(let countdown ((n (string->number (fetch \"https://api.math.local/random-int?max=10\"))))
  (if (<= n 0)
      'done
      (begin
        (fetch \"https://api.log.local/event\" :method 'POST :body (number->string n))
        (countdown (- n 1)))))
```

The fetch returns a random integer as a string. `string->number` converts it. Named `let` starts the countdown. Each iteration POSTs the current number to the log endpoint, then recurses with `n - 1`. When `n` reaches zero, return `'done`. One top-level named `let`. One initial fetch. N POST fetches (where N is the random integer). Zero intermediate state outside the recursion.

## Nest a Filter Inside a Fold Inside a POST

Fetch a list of scores. Filter out scores below 50. Compute the average of the remaining scores. POST the average to a summary endpoint.

```scheme
       :body (number->string
               (let ((passing (filter (lambda (n) (>= n 50))

```

The innermost fetch returns a JSON array of scores. `json-parse` converts it to a list. `filter` keeps scores >= 50. The `let` binds the filtered list. `fold` sums the scores. `length` counts them. Look up the capital city of a country (from a fetched country code). Look up the timezone of that city. Fetch current time for that timezone.

```scheme
                                                           :subject (fetch \"https://api.geo.local/country-code?ip=203.0.113.42\")))))
```

## Nest a Map with a Let-Bound Fetched Value

Fetch a currency conversion rate. Map over a list of prices (also fetched) to convert each price using the rate. Return the converted list.

```scheme
(let ((rate (string->number (fetch \"https://api.currency.local/rate?from=USD&to=EUR\"))))
  (map (lambda (price) (* price rate))
       (json-parse (fetch \"https://api.prices.local/list?currency=USD\"))))
```

The second fetch returns a JSON array of prices. `json-parse` converts it to a list. `map` multiplies each price by the rate. One `let` form. Two fetches. One map. ## Nest a Guarded Fetch Inside a Fold

Fetch a list of product IDs. For each ID, fetch stock quantity if the ID is even; otherwise use zero. Sum the quantities.

```scheme
(fold (lambda (id acc)
        (+ acc (if (even? id)
                   (string->number (fetch (string-append \"https://api.inventory.local/stock?id=\" (number->string id))))
                   0)))
      0
      (json-parse (fetch \"https://api.catalog.local/product-ids\")))
```

The innermost fetch returns a JSON array of IDs. `json-parse` converts it to a list. `fold` iterates. For each ID, if even, fetch the stock quantity and add it to the accumulator; otherwise add zero. One form. One initial fetch. Up to N additional fetches (where N is the count of even IDs). The fold closes the sum; the sum closes the form.

## Nest a Case Dispatch Over a Knowledge Lookup Inside a Fetch

Look up a user's subscription tier from knowledge. Use `case` to select which analytics event to POST based on the tier.

```scheme
(case (knowledge/of :category \"subscription-tier\" :subject \"user:4523\")
  ((free) (fetch \"https://api.analytics.local/event/free-action\" :method 'POST :body \"click\"))
  ((premium) (fetch \"https://api.analytics.local/event/premium-action\" :method 'POST :body \"click\"))
```

## Nest a Fold Over Two Fetched and Zipped Lists with a Guard

Fetch prices. Fetch availability flags. Zip them. Fold to sum prices only for available items.

```scheme
(fold (lambda (pair acc)
        (if (cdr pair)
            (+ acc (car pair))
            acc))
      0
      (map cons
           (json-parse (fetch \"https://api.prices.local/list\"))
           (json-parse (fetch \"https://api.availability.local/list\"))))
```

Two fetches return JSON arrays. Two `json-parse` calls convert them to lists. `map cons` zips them into pairs `(price . available?)`. `fold` iterates: if the item is available (cdr is truthy), add the price to the accumulator; otherwise skip. One form. Two wire reads. One fold. The fold closes the sum; the sum closes the form.

## Nest a Fetch Inside a Let with a Conditional Guard

```scheme
(let ((url (if (string=? (fetch \"https://api.feature.local/enabled?flag=new-search\") \"true\")
               (fetch \"https://api.config.local/search-url?version=new\")

```

## Nest Four Calls: Fetch, Knowledge, Filter, Fetch

Fetch a biome name. Look up common animals in that biome. Filter for animals longer than 6 characters. Fetch photos for each filtered animal. Return the list of photo URLs.

```scheme
       (fetch (string-append \"https://api.photos.local/animal?name=\" animal)))
     (filter (lambda (name) (> (string-length name) 6))
             (knowledge/of :category \"common-animals\"
                           :subject (fetch \"https://api.geo.local/biome?region=PNW\"))))
```

The knowledge lookup returns a list of animals. `filter` keeps animals with names longer than 6 characters. `map` fires a photo fetch for each. One form. One initial fetch. One knowledge lookup. ## Nest a Recursive Fetch with a Conditional Stopping Condition

Fetch a paginated list. Continue fetching the `next` page until the response has no `next` field or until 5 pages have been fetched. Accumulate all items.

```scheme
(let fetch-pages ((url \"https://api.data.local/items?page=1\")
                  (acc '())
                  (count 0))
  (if (>= count 5)
      acc
      (let ((resp (json-parse (fetch url))))
        (let ((items (json-ref resp \"items\"))
              (next (json-ref resp \"next\")))
          (if next
              (fetch-pages next (append acc items) (+ count 1))
              (append acc items))))))
```

Named `let` with a page counter. Each iteration fetches a page. If the counter reaches 5, stop and return the accumulator. Otherwise parse the response, extract items and the next URL. If next exists, recurse; otherwise return the final accumulation. One top-level named `let`. Up to 5 wire hops. Zero intermediate state outside the recursion.

```scheme
  (cond
    ((string=? status \"200\") (fetch \"https://api.service.local/data\"))
    ((string=? status \"404\") \"Not found\")
    ((string=? status \"500\") (fetch \"https://api.service.local/fallback\"))
    (else 'nan)))
```

## The Summit: Five-Level Nest

Fetch a user's location (lat/lon as JSON). Use the location to look up the biome (knowledge). Use the biome to fetch a list of common plants (wire). Filter plants with names longer than 8 characters. For each plant, fetch a care guide URL. Return the list of URLs.

```scheme
(map (lambda (plant)
       (fetch (string-append \"https://api.garden.local/care?plant=\" plant)))
     (filter (lambda (name) (> (string-length name) 8))
             (json-parse (fetch (string-append \"https://api.plants.local/list?biome=\"
                                               (knowledge/of :category \"biome\"
                                                             :subject (json-ref (json-parse (fetch \"https://api.geo.local/location\"))
                                                                                \"name\")))))))
```

The innermost fetch returns location JSON. `json-parse` converts it. `json-ref` extracts the location name (e.g., \"Portland\"). The knowledge lookup returns a biome string (e.g., \"temperate rainforest\"). `string-append` builds the plant list URL. The second fetch returns a JSON array of plant names. `json-parse` converts it. `filter` keeps names longer than 8 characters. `map` fires a care guide fetch for each. One form. Three wire hops. One knowledge lookup. N care guide fetches. Zero intermediate bindings outside the nesting.

[VISUAL: A dependency graph showing five nested calls: fetch location → parse → extract → knowledge → fetch plants → parse → filter → map(fetch). Each call closes the slot of the call that wraps it. The final closing paren appears as a large bracket encompassing all five levels.]

## Why This Matters

You've now written forty nested wire-shots, each a single top-level form. The disposition you've drilled: when two (or three, or five) calls depend on each other, nest them in place rather than sequencing them across statements. The inner call closes the outer. No intermediate variable. No orphaned state between hops. No latency compounding across a seam.

This is the core of the one-shot habit: a complicated-looking problem—fetch, transform, lookup, fetch again, filter, map, fold—still collapses to a single composed expression. The retrieval expression closes the outer form. Close data, close paren.

---

## Exercises

Write the route/program for each of the following scenarios. Each answer should be a single top-level Scheme form (a `let`, a `map`, a named `let` recursion, etc.—but ONE form).

1. **Nested weather + preference**: Fetch a city name from `https://api.location.local/city`. Recall a temperature unit preference from cortex (`:topic \"temp-unit\"`, returns `'F` or `'C`). Fetch weather from `https://api.weather.local/temp?city=CITY&unit=UNIT` where `CITY` and `UNIT` are filled from the prior calls. Return the temperature string.

2. **Triple knowledge nest**: Fetch a country code from `https://api.geo.local/country?ip=203.0.113.99`. Look up the country's official language (knowledge, `:category \"official-language\" :subject COUNTRY`). Look up a greeting in that language (knowledge, `:category \"greeting\" :subject LANGUAGE`). Return the greeting string.

3. **Paginated sum**: Fetch a paginated list of numbers from `https://api.data.local/numbers?page=1`. Each response is JSON with `{\"numbers\": [...], \"next\": \"...\"}`. Recursively fetch all pages (stop when `next` is null). Sum all the numbers across all pages. Return the sum. (Use named `let` recursion.)

4. **Guarded map + fold**: Fetch a list of product IDs from `https://api.catalog.local/ids`. For each ID, fetch stock quantity from `https://api.inventory.local/stock?id=ID` only if the ID is divisible by 3; otherwise use zero. Sum all the quantities. Return the sum.

5. **Conditional double-fetch**: Fetch a feature flag from `https://api.feature.local/enabled?flag=premium`. If the flag is `\"true\"`, fetch user data from `https://api.users.local/premium/profile?id=42`; otherwise fetch from `https://api.users.local/standard/profile?id=42`. Extract the `\"username\"` field from the JSON response. Return the username.

6. **Five-level nest with filter and map**: Fetch a zip code from `https://api.location.local/zip`. Look up the city for that zip (knowledge, `:category \"city\" :subject ZIP`). Fetch a list of restaurants in that city from `https://api.food.local/restaurants?city=CITY`. Parse the JSON (assume it returns an array of restaurant names). Filter to keep only restaurants with names longer than 10 characters. For each remaining restaurant, fetch a menu URL from `https://api.food.local/menu?name=NAME`. Return the list of menu URLs.

"# Chapter 14: The Speech Shot

The messy way: fetch the data, store it, build the template, fill it, then say it—five steps, five places to forget what you meant, five seams where the answer can go stale. The one-shot way: the retrieval expression *closes* the utterance form. Data and speech collapse to a single paren. No gap, no drift, no orphaned fetch sitting in a variable while the world moves on.

This chapter drills **(surface :say TMPL :from (…))** — the template and its data source folded into one atomic form. The principles from earlier chapters (Close Data Close Paren, Recall In Place, Compose Don't Sequence) all converge here: the work of speaking *is* the work of retrieving, because the retrieve closes the say.

We'll start gentle—a greeting that pulls one fact—and climb to honestly hard cases: guarded multi-source fills, nested wire-shots closing a speech act, maps that become enumerations inside a single utterance. Every example runs alone. Every example is one shot.

---

## The Simplest Speech Shot

You want to greet someone by name. The name lives in a recall. The old way: fetch the name, bind it, build the string, pass it to say. The one-shot way: the recall closes the :from slot, and the whole greeting is one form.

```scheme
(surface :say \"Hello, {name}!\"
         :from (cortex/recall :topic \"user-name\"))
```

One form. The template declares a `{name}` hole. The `:from` supplies the record that fills it. No intermediate variable. No gap between knowing the name and saying it.

[VISUAL: A single arrow from `cortex/recall` flowing directly into the `{name}` slot of the template, both wrapped in one enclosing paren.]

---

## Two Slots, Still One Shot

Now two facts: a name and a city. The template has two holes. The recall returns a record with both keys. Still one form.

```scheme
(surface :say \"Hello, {name} from {city}!\"
         :from (cortex/recall :topic \"user-profile\"))
```

The record has `:name` and `:city`. The template names them in `{curly}` syntax. The surface engine matches keys to holes. One atomic expression produces the filled utterance.

---

## Time In The Template

The current time is a retrieval—`(clock/now)` returns a timestamp. To speak it, close the clock call inside the :from.

```scheme
(surface :say \"The time is now {time}.\"
         :from (list (cons 'time (clock/now))))
```

We construct the data record *in place*. `(list (cons 'time (clock/now)))` builds a single-entry association on the fly. The clock call closes the cons, the cons closes the list, the list closes the :from, the :from closes the say. One shot.

---

## Knowledge In The Template

A question about the world: \"What is the capital of France?\" The knowledge call retrieves the answer. The speech shot says it.

```scheme
(surface :say \"The capital of France is {capital}.\"
         :from (list (cons 'capital 
                           (world/knowledge :query \"capital of France\"))))
```

No intermediate binding. The query closes the cons, the data closes the :from, the :from closes the say. The answer flows directly into the template.

## Registry Fact In Speech

Ask the system registry for a capability, speak the answer.

```scheme
(surface :say \"Your device supports {feature}.\"
         :from (list (cons 'feature 
                           (system/registry :domain \"media/codecs\" 
                                            :key \"vp9\"))))
```

The registry call closes the data slot. If the key exists, the feature name fills the template. One form retrieves and speaks.

## Combining Two Recalls

Two topics, two recalls. Combine them into one data record, in place.

```scheme
(surface :say \"{name} lives in {city}.\"
         :from (let ((profile (cortex/recall :topic \"user-profile\"))
                     (location (cortex/recall :topic \"user-location\")))
                 (list (cons 'name (cdr (assoc 'name profile)))
                       (cons 'city (cdr (assoc 'city location))))))
```

The `let` builds the combined record. The let closes the :from. The :from closes the say. Still one top-level form. The speech act *is* the composition of the two recalls.

## Guarded Speech: When The Data Might Be Missing

If the recall returns `'nan`, we should not fill the template—we should escalate or say nothing. Fold the guard into the one shot.

```scheme
(surface :say (let ((profile (cortex/recall :topic \"user-profile\")))
                (if (eq? profile 'nan)
                    \"I don't have that information yet.\"
                    \"Hello, {name}!\"))
         :from (cortex/recall :topic \"user-profile\"))
```

Wait—this fetches twice. Better: guard *and* supply in one let.

```scheme
(let ((profile (cortex/recall :topic \"user-profile\")))
  (surface :say (if (eq? profile 'nan)
                    \"I don't have that information yet.\"
                    \"Hello, {name}!\")
           :from profile))
```

Now one recall, one guard, one say—but still one top-level let-form. The guard lives *inside* the speech shot's template selection.

```scheme
    ((eq? name-record 'nan)
     (surface :say \"I don't know your name yet.\"))
    (else
     (surface :say \"Your name is {name}.\" :from name-record))))
```

One let-form. The cond picks the branch. Each branch is a complete speech shot. The whole expression is one atomic decision-and-utterance.

"# Chapter 15: Refactor To One

**What it drills:** take a sprawling multi-line sketch and collapse it to a single one-shot form

---

You've sketched something that *works*. It's laid out in steps—define this, compute that, check the other thing, build the answer. Readable. Clear. Each line makes sense.

And yet something nags. Every intermediate `define` is a place for staleness to creep in. Every step is a place to forget a guard. The data flows down the page, but the *closure* doesn't happen until the very end—if it happens at all.

This chapter drills the collapse. We take a multi-step sketch—something you might write on first pass—and fold it into a single atomic form. No intermediate bindings that outlive their use. No gaps where an error can hide. The retrieval expressions close the outer form. Close data, close paren.

The work isn't rewriting for cleverness. It's rewriting for *honesty*: the shape of the code matches the shape of the idea. One question, one form. One decision, one value.

Let's start simple.

---

## The Sketch

Here's a two-step sketch that computes a greeting:

```scheme
;; SKETCH (two steps)
(define user-name \"Keiko\")
(string-append \"Hello, \" user-name \"!\")
```

It works. But `user-name` lives beyond its use. If we wanted to *close* the data at the point of use, we'd write:

```scheme
;; ONE SHOT
(string-append \"Hello, \" \"Keiko\" \"!\")
```

No intermediate. The literal closes the form. If the name came from elsewhere, we'd pull the lookup *into* the form:

```scheme
;; ONE SHOT (lookup in place)
(string-append \"Hello, \" (or (system/env \"USER\") \"friend\") \"!\")
```

The fallback is guarded *inside* the form. No `user-name` binding to forget, no gap between retrieval and use.

---

## Two Guards, One Form

Sketch that checks two conditions before building a message:

```scheme
;; SKETCH (three steps)
(define temp (sensor/read :thermometer))
(define status (if (> temp 30) \"hot\" \"comfortable\"))
(string-append \"The room is \" status \".\")
```

Collapse it:

```scheme
;; ONE SHOT
(string-append \"The room is \" 
               (if (> (sensor/read :thermometer) 30) 
                   \"hot\" 
                   \"comfortable\") 
               \".\")
```

*[needs: sensor/read]*  
<!-- BUILD: wire sensor surface -->

The sensor read happens *inside* the conditional, which happens *inside* the append. One form. The guard and the work are one expression.

---

## Retrieve, Check, Use

Sketch that fetches a user preference, checks it, and acts:

```scheme
;; SKETCH (four steps)
(define pref (cortex/recall :topic \"audio.volume\"))
(define vol (if pref pref 50))
(define clamped (max 0 (min 100 vol)))

```

Collapse:

```scheme
;; ONE SHOT
(string-append \"Volume set to \" 
               (number->string 
                 (max 0 
                      (min 100 
                           (or (cortex/recall :topic \"audio.volume\") 50)))))
```

*[needs: cortex/recall]*  
<!-- BUILD: wire cortex recall for preferences -->

The recall is guarded with `or`, clamped with `max` and `min`, stringified, and appended—all in one closing form. No `vol`. No `clamped`. The data flows inward, and the paren closes at the end.

```scheme
     (filter (lambda (n) (> n 0)) 
             (or (cortex/recall :topic \"measurements\") '())))
```

```scheme
           (cdr (assoc 'items (fetch \"https://api.example.com/items\")))))
```

*[needs: fetch]*

The fetch closes inside the `assoc`, the `assoc` closes inside the map, the map closes inside the fold. One form. No `response`. No `items`. No `values`.

## The Summit: Wire + Recall + Knowledge + Guard + Transform + Speech

Sketch that fetches weather, recalls a preference, looks up knowledge, guards everything, transforms the data, and speaks it:

```scheme
;; SKETCH (eight steps)

(define temp (cdr (assoc 'temperature weather)))
(define unit (cortex/recall :topic \"temperature.unit\"))
(define display-temp (if (equal? unit \"C\") (/ (- temp 32) 1.8) temp))
(define clothing (knowledge/of :category \"clothing\"))
(define suggestion (cdr (assoc 'warm (car clothing))))

```

Collapse to one form:

```scheme

(surface :say 
         (string-append \"It's \" 
                        (number->string 
                          (let ((temp (cdr (assoc 'temperature (fetch \"https://weather.example.com/now\")))) 
                                (unit (cortex/recall :topic \"temperature.unit\"))) 
                            (if (equal? unit \"C\") (/ (- temp 32) 1.8) temp))) 
                        \" degrees. Wear \" 
                        (cdr (assoc 'warm (car (knowledge/of :category \"clothing\")))) 
                        \".\"))
```

*[needs: fetch, cortex/recall, knowledge/of, surface :say]*

All in **one atomic Scheme form**. No `weather`. No `temp`. No `unit`. No `display-temp`. No `clothing`. No `suggestion`. No `message`.

The wire call closes the outer form. The recall closes within the `let`. The knowledge lookup closes within the append. The conditional closes within the `number->string`. The data flows inward, and the paren closes at the speech boundary.

## Exercises

Write the route (one-shot Scheme form) for each:

1. **Recall a list of tasks, filter out completed ones (those with a 'done field set to `#t`), map them to just their 'name field, fold them into a comma-separated string, and speak it.**  
   Use: `(cortex/recall :topic \"tasks\")`, `filter`, `map`, `fold`, `(surface :say ...)`.

2. **Fetch a user profile from `https://api.example.com/user`, extract the 'id field, construct a new URL `https://api.example.com/user/ID/friends`, fetch that, extract the 'friends list, and return the count.**  
   Use: `fetch`, `assoc`, `cdr`, `string-append`, `length`.

3. **Check the registry for \"location\" capability. If present, fetch `https://location.example.com/current`, extract the 'city field, look up knowledge about that city in category \"cities\", and speak the first fact's 'description field. If any step fails, escalate with a clear reason.**  
   Use: `(system/registry :domain \"location\")`, `fetch`, `assoc`, `cdr`, `(knowledge/of :category ...)`, `car`, `(surface :say ...)`, `(escalate :reason ...)`.

4. **Recall a number from \"counter\", increment it by 1, store it back to \"counter\", then fetch a URL `https://api.example.com/log?n=N` where N is the new counter value, and return the response.**  
   Use: `(cortex/recall :topic \"counter\")`, `+`, `(store :counter ...)`, `string-append`, `number->string`, `fetch`.

   Use: `map`, `fetch`, `string-append`, `assoc`, `cdr`, `fold`, `(surface :say ...)`.

6. **Look up knowledge in category \"planets\", map each planet to its 'distance field, filter out any `#f` values, compute the average distance (sum ÷ count), and store the result in `:average-distance`.**  
   Use: `(knowledge/of :category \"planets\")`, `map`, `assoc`, `cdr`, `filter`, `fold`, `/`, `length`, `(store :average-distance ...)`.

**What you've learned:**

The sprawling multi-step sketch—readable but leaky—can *always* collapse to a single closing form. The intermediate `define`s are eliminated. The data flows inward. The guard, the retrieval, the transformation, and the action become one expression.

This isn't cleverness. It's honesty. The shape of the code matches the shape of the idea. One question, one form. One decision, one value. No gaps where staleness or errors can hide.

You've seen it at every scale: from a two-line greeting to an eight-step wire-spanning speech shot. The technique is the same. Close data, close paren. Refactor to one.

"# Chapter 16: The Grand One-Shot

You've climbed through fifteen drills. You've seen the simplest possible one-shot, learned to close data where you fetch it, folded guards and maps and wire-calls into single atomic forms. This is the summit: a genuinely ambitious task—one that spans knowledge lookups, conditionals, internet retrieval, storage, speech, and honest-null handling—still expressed as ONE atomic Scheme form. The lesson is unchanged: no matter how many moving parts the problem has, the solution collapses to a single composed expression. No intermediate variables. No \"step one, step two.\" Just close data, close paren.

The reward is zero gap between fetch and use. No staleness. No orphaned errors. No latency compounding. Even when the task looks impossible to hold in one form, you'll see it collapse.

We'll start near the floor and climb by concept. Every example is a complete, standalone program.

---

## The Warm-Up Grand Shot

The simplest ambitious task: fetch knowledge, guard against null, recall context, and say something—all in one form.

```scheme
(surface :say
         (if (knowledge/of :category \"birds:migration\")
             \"Migration patterns are in the knowledge base.\"
             \"No migration data available.\")
         :to-user)
```

One form. The knowledge lookup closes the `if`, the `if` closes the `:say`. No intermediate step.

---

## Adding Recall In Place

Now fold in a cortex recall. The user asked about their favorite bird; we fetch that preference and use it immediately.

```scheme
(surface :say
         (let ((fav (cortex/recall :topic \"user:favorite-bird\")))
           (if fav
               (string-append \"Your favorite bird is \" fav \".\")
               \"You haven't told me your favorite bird yet.\"))
         :to-user)
```

Still one top-level form. The `let` binds the recall, the `if` guards it, the `string-append` uses it. No gap.

---

## Wire-Shot Inside

Fetch from the internet, use the result immediately. No \"download, then process.\" The wire-call closes the outer form.

```scheme
(surface :say
         (let ((weather (fetch \"https://api.weather.local/current?zip=10001\")))
           (if (and weather (assoc 'temp weather))
               (string-append \"Current temperature: \" 
                              (number->string (cdr (assoc 'temp weather)))
                              \"°F\")
               \"Weather data unavailable.\"))
         :to-user)
```

The `fetch` closes the `let`, the `if` guards the result, the `string-append` formats it. One atomic expression.

---

## Map The Many, Say The Result

The user wants a summary of all their stored book titles. We map over them, format them, and say the result—in one shot.

```scheme
(surface :say
         (let ((titles (cortex/recall :topic \"user:reading-list\")))
           (if (and titles (list? titles) (not (null? titles)))
               (string-append \"Your reading list: \"
                              (fold (lambda (title acc)
                                      (string-append acc title \", \"))
                                    \"\"
                                    titles))
               \"Your reading list is empty.\"))
         :to-user)
```

The `fold` collapses the list, the `if` guards it, the whole thing closes the `:say`. No loop variable. No accumulator living outside the form.

---

## Registry Check In The Guard

Check a capability registry before attempting the wire-call. If the capability isn't present, say so honestly.

```scheme
(surface :say
         (if (system/registry :domain \"network:fetch\")
             (let ((data (fetch \"https://api.facts.local/random\")))
               (if data
                   (string-append \"Random fact: \" (cdr (assoc 'fact data)))
                   \"Fetch succeeded but no fact found.\"))
             \"Network fetch capability not available.\")
         :to-user)
```

The registry check closes the outer `if`. The fetch closes the inner `let`. Still one form.

---

## Store And Say

Fetch data, store it, and confirm—all in one shot. The storage call closes the outer form.

```scheme
(let ((recipe (fetch \"https://api.recipes.local/recipe/12345\")))
  (if recipe
      (begin
        (store :slot \"user:saved-recipe\" :value recipe)
        (surface :say \"Recipe saved.\" :to-user))
      (surface :say \"Recipe not found.\" :to-user)))
```

The `let` binds the fetch, the `if` guards it, the `begin` sequences the store and the say. One top-level form.

---

## Nested Wire-Shots

Two wire calls, one closing the other. The inner fetch provides a parameter for the outer fetch.

```scheme
(surface :say
         (let ((city (cortex/recall :topic \"user:home-city\")))
           (if city
               (let ((weather (fetch (string-append 
                                      \"https://api.weather.local/current?city=\" 
                                      city))))
                 (if weather
                     (string-append \"Weather in \" city \": \" 
                                    (cdr (assoc 'summary weather)))
                     \"Weather data unavailable.\"))
               \"I don't know your home city yet.\"))
         :to-user)
```

The inner `let` closes the outer `if`. The inner `fetch` uses the recalled city. No intermediate variable living outside the form.

---

## Knowledge Lookup With Fallback

Check world knowledge first; if absent, fetch from the internet; if that fails, say so honestly.

```scheme
(surface :say
         (let ((local-knowledge (knowledge/of :category \"history:ancient-rome\")))
           (if local-knowledge
               (string-append \"From knowledge base: \" local-knowledge)
               (let ((remote-data (fetch \"https://api.history.local/ancient-rome\")))
                 (if remote-data
                     (string-append \"From internet: \" 
                                    (cdr (assoc 'summary remote-data)))
                     \"No information available locally or online.\"))))
         :to-user)
```

The nested `let` and `if` forms collapse the fallback logic. One atomic shot.

---

## Map, Filter, Fold In One

The user has a list of books with ratings. We filter for high-rated ones, map to titles, fold into a sentence, and say it—all in one form.

```scheme
(surface :say
         (let ((books (cortex/recall :topic \"user:book-ratings\")))
           (if (and books (list? books) (not (null? books)))
               (let ((high-rated (filter (lambda (b) (>= (cdr (assoc 'rating b)) 4))
                                         books)))
                 (if (not (null? high-rated))
                     (string-append \"Your top-rated books: \"
                                    (fold (lambda (b acc)
                                            (string-append acc 
                                                           (cdr (assoc 'title b)) 
                                                           \", \"))
                                          \"\"
                                          high-rated))
                     \"No books rated 4 stars or higher.\"))
               \"No book ratings stored.\"))
         :to-user)
```

Filter → fold, all closing the outer `:say`. One shot.

---

## Guard Against Multiple Nulls

A genuinely defensive one-shot: check registry, recall context, fetch data, guard each step.

```scheme
(surface :say
         (if (system/registry :domain \"network:fetch\")
             (let ((username (cortex/recall :topic \"user:github-username\")))
               (if username
                   (let ((profile (fetch (string-append 
                                          \"https://api.github.com/users/\" 
                                          username))))
                     (if (and profile (assoc 'bio profile))
                         (string-append \"GitHub bio: \" 
                                        (cdr (assoc 'bio profile)))
                         \"Profile fetched but no bio found.\"))
                   \"I don't know your GitHub username yet.\"))
             \"Network fetch not available.\")
         :to-user)
```

Three guards, one inside the next. Still one form.

## The Honest-Null Grand Shot

When no data is available at any level, return an honest null instead of faking a result.

```scheme
(let ((source-1 (knowledge/of :category \"astronomy:black-holes\"))
      (source-2 (cortex/recall :topic \"user:astronomy-notes\")))
  (if source-1
      (surface :say source-1 :to-user)
      (if source-2
          (surface :say source-2 :to-user)
          (surface :say \"No information available on black holes.\" :to-user))))
```

Two fallbacks, one closing the other. If both are null, we say so honestly.

## Store, Then Fetch Back

Store a value, then immediately fetch it back to confirm. The fetch closes the outer form.

```scheme
(let ((user-note \"Remember to water the basil.\"))
  (begin
    (store :slot \"user:garden-reminder\" :value user-note)
    (surface :say
             (let ((stored (cortex/recall :topic \"user:garden-reminder\")))
               (if stored
                   (string-append \"Stored and confirmed: \" stored)
                   \"Storage may have failed.\"))
             :to-user)))
```

Store → fetch → say, all in one top-level form.

## Conditional Wire-Shot

Only fetch if a precondition is met. The guard closes the outer form.

```scheme
(surface :say
         (let ((has-api-key (cortex/recall :topic \"user:api-key:nasa\")))
           (if has-api-key
               (let* ((base \"https://api.nasa.gov/planetary/apod\")
                      (url  (string-append base \"?apikey=[REDACTED-USE-CORTEX-KEY]\"))
                      (apod (fetch url)))
                 (if apod
                     (string-append \"Astronomy Picture of the Day: \" 
                                    (cdr (assoc 'title apod)))
                     \"Fetch failed.\"))
               \"No API key stored; cannot fetch NASA data.\"))
         :to-user)
```

Guard → fetch → say. One atomic shot.

## Map Over Wire Results

Fetch a list from the internet, map a transformation, say the result.

```scheme
(surface :say
         (let ((posts (fetch \"https://api.blog.local/recent-posts\")))
           (if (and posts (list? posts) (not (null? posts)))
               (string-append \"Recent post titles: \"
                              (fold (lambda (post acc)
                                      (string-append acc 
                                                     (cdr (assoc 'title post)) 
                                                     \"; \"))
                                    \"\"
                                    posts))
               \"No recent posts found.\"))
         :to-user)
```

Fetch → fold → say. One shot.

## Multi-Guard With Escalate

If multiple preconditions fail, escalate with a reason instead of faking success.

```scheme
(surface :say
         (if (system/registry :domain \"network:fetch\")
             (let ((location (cortex/recall :topic \"user:location\")))
               (if location
                   (let ((transit (fetch (string-append 
                                          \"https://api.transit.local/status?loc=\" 
                                          location))))
                     (if transit
                         (string-append \"Transit status: \" 
                                        (cdr (assoc 'status transit)))
                         (escalate :reason \"Transit API returned null\")))
                   (escalate :reason \"User location unknown\")))
             (escalate :reason \"Network fetch unavailable\"))
         :to-user)
```

Three escalate paths, each guarded. One form.

## Fold With Nested Lookup

For each item in a list, perform a knowledge lookup, then fold the results into a summary.

```scheme
(surface :say
         (let ((topics (list \"birds:raptors\" \"birds:songbirds\" \"birds:waterfowl\")))
           (let ((summaries (map (lambda (t) (knowledge/of :category t)) topics)))
             (let ((available (filter (lambda (s) s) summaries)))
               (if (not (null? available))
                   (string-append \"Bird knowledge: \"
                                  (fold (lambda (s acc)
                                          (string-append acc s \"; \"))
                                        \"\"
                                        available))
                   \"No bird knowledge available.\"))))
         :to-user)
```

Map → filter → fold, all in one shot.

## The Kitchen-Sink Grand Shot

Fetch user context, check registry, fetch from internet, store result, recall stored result, say confirmation—all in one form.

```scheme
(let ((username (cortex/recall :topic \"user:name\")))
  (if (and username (system/registry :domain \"network:fetch\"))
      (let ((greeting-data (fetch \"https://api.greetings.local/personalized\")))
        (if greeting-data
            (let ((greeting-text (cdr (assoc 'greeting greeting-data))))
              (begin
                (store :slot \"user:last-greeting\" :value greeting-text)
                (let ((stored (cortex/recall :topic \"user:last-greeting\")))
                  (surface :say
                           (if stored
                               (string-append \"Hello, \" username \"! \" stored)
                               \"Greeting stored but recall failed.\")
                           :to-user))))
            (surface :say 
                     \"Network fetch succeeded but no greeting found.\" 
                     :to-user)))
      (surface :say 
               \"Cannot personalize greeting; missing username or network capability.\" 
               :to-user)))
```

Recall → registry → fetch → store → recall → say. One atomic expression.

## Nested Maps

Map over a list of lists, transforming each inner list, then fold the outer list.

```scheme
(let ((categories (list (list \"fruit:apple\" \"fruit:banana\")
                        (list \"vegetable:carrot\" \"vegetable:broccoli\"))))
  (surface :say
           (let ((summaries (map (lambda (cat-list)
                                   (map (lambda (item)
                                          (knowledge/of :category item))
                                        cat-list))
                                 categories)))
             (let ((flattened (fold append '() summaries)))
               (let ((available (filter (lambda (s) s) flattened)))
                 (if (not (null? available))
                     (string-append \"Food knowledge: \"
                                    (fold (lambda (s acc)
                                            (string-append acc s \"; \"))
                                          \"\"
                                          available))
                     \"No food knowledge available.\"))))
           :to-user))
```

Nested maps, fold, filter, fold again. One shot.

## Conditional Store

Only store if the fetched data meets a condition.

```scheme
(let ((forecast (fetch \"https://api.weather.local/forecast?zip=10001\")))
  (if (and forecast (assoc 'temp forecast))
      (let ((temp (cdr (assoc 'temp forecast))))
        (if (> temp 70)
            (begin
              (store :slot \"user:warm-day-alert\" :value \"It's warm today!\")
              (surface :say \"Warm day alert stored.\" :to-user))
            (surface :say \"Not warm enough to store an alert.\" :to-user)))
      (surface :say \"Forecast unavailable.\" :to-user)))
```

Fetch → guard → conditional store → say. One form.

## Guard With Clock

Only fetch if the current hour is within a certain range.

```scheme
(surface :say
         (let ((hour (cdr (assoc 'hour (clock/now)))))
           (if (and (>= hour 9) (<= hour 17))
               (let ((news (fetch \"https://api.news.local/headlines\")))
                 (if news
                     (string-append \"Headline: \" (cdr (assoc 'headline news)))
                     \"News fetch failed.\"))
               \"News is only fetched between 9 AM and 5 PM.\"))
         :to-user)
```

Clock check → fetch → say. One atomic shot.

## Fold With Counter

Count items that meet a condition while folding.

```scheme
(let ((items (list 3 7 2 9 5 8)))
  (surface :say
           (let ((count (fold (lambda (n acc)
                                (if (> n 5) (+ acc 1) acc))
                              0
                              items)))
             (string-append \"Number of items greater than 5: \" 
                            (number->string count)))
           :to-user))
```

Fold with a conditional accumulator. One shot.

## Multi-Source Fallback Chain

Try four sources in sequence; use the first that succeeds.

```scheme
(surface :say
         (let ((s1 (knowledge/of :category \"botany:ferns\")))
           (if s1
               s1
               (let ((s2 (cortex/recall :topic \"user:botany-notes\")))
                 (if s2
                     s2
                     (let ((s3 (fetch \"https://api.botany.local/ferns\")))
                       (if s3
                           (cdr (assoc 'summary s3))
                           \"No information on ferns from any source.\"))))))
         :to-user)
```

Four-level nested fallback. One form.

## Store Multiple, Recall Multiple

Store two values, recall both, combine into a sentence.

```scheme
(begin
  (store :slot \"user:city\" :value \"Brooklyn\")
  (store :slot \"user:state\" :value \"New York\")
  (let ((city (cortex/recall :topic \"user:city\"))
        (state (cortex/recall :topic \"user:state\")))
    (surface :say
             (if (and city state)
                 (string-append \"You're in \" city \", \" state \".\")
                 \"Location data incomplete.\")
             :to-user)))
```

Store → store → recall → recall → say. One top-level form.

## Fetch, Transform, Store, Confirm

Fetch data, transform it, store the transformed version, recall it, confirm.

```scheme
(let ((raw-temp (fetch \"https://api.weather.local/raw-temp?zip=10001\")))
  (if (and raw-temp (assoc 'kelvin raw-temp))
      (let ((fahrenheit (- (* (cdr (assoc 'kelvin raw-temp)) 9/5) 459.67)))
        (begin
          (store :slot \"user:temp-fahrenheit\" :value fahrenheit)
          (let ((stored (cortex/recall :topic \"user:temp-fahrenheit\")))
            (surface :say
                     (if stored
                         (string-append \"Temperature stored: \" 
                                        (number->string stored) \"°F\")
                         \"Storage may have failed.\")
                     :to-user))))
      (surface :say \"Raw temperature unavailable.\" :to-user)))
```

Fetch → transform → store → recall → say. One shot.

## Conditional Map

Map a transformation over a list, but only if a precondition is met.

```scheme
(let ((numbers (list 2 4 6 8)))
  (surface :say
           (if (system/registry :domain \"math:operations\")
               (let ((doubled (map (lambda (n) (* n 2)) numbers)))
                 (string-append \"Doubled: \"
                                (fold (lambda (n acc)
                                        (string-append acc 
                                                       (number->string n) 
                                                       \" \"))
                                      \"\"
                                      doubled)))
               \"Math operations not available.\")
           :to-user))
```

Registry guard → map → fold → say. One form.

## Fetch With Query String

Build a query string from recalled values, fetch, say result.

```scheme
(let ((city (cortex/recall :topic \"user:city\"))
      (interest (cortex/recall :topic \"user:interest\")))
  (surface :say
           (if (and city interest)
               (let ((events (fetch (string-append 
                                     \"https://api.events.local/search?city=\" 
                                     city 
                                     \"&interest=\"

                     (string-append \"Event: \" (cdr (assoc 'name events)))
```

Recall → recall → string-append → fetch → say. One shot.

## Guard With Honest Escalate

If any precondition fails, escalate instead of pretending to succeed.

```scheme
(if (system/registry :domain \"network:fetch\")
    (let ((api-key (cortex/recall :topic \"user:api-key:weather\")))
      (if api-key
          (let ((data (fetch (string-append 
                              \"https://api.weather.local/secure?key=\" 
                              api-key))))
            (if data
                (surface :say 
                         (string-append \"Secure weather: \" 
                                        (cdr (assoc 'condition data))) 
                         :to-user)
                (escalate :reason \"Weather API returned null\")))

    (escalate :reason \"Network fetch unavailable\"))
```

Three escalate paths. One form.

## Filter, Map, Fold Chain

Filter a list, map a transformation, fold into a sentence—all in one shot.

```scheme
(let ((temps (list 55 72 68 80 45 90)))
  (surface :say
           (let ((warm (filter (lambda (t) (>= t 70)) temps)))
             (if (not (null? warm))
                 (let ((descriptions (map (lambda (t) 
                                            (string-append (number->string t) \"°F\"))
                                          warm)))
                   (string-append \"Warm temperatures: \"
                                  (fold (lambda (d acc)
                                          (string-append acc d \", \"))
                                        \"\"
                                        descriptions)))
                 \"No warm temperatures found.\"))
           :to-user))
```

Filter → map → fold. One atomic shot.

## Store From Wire, Use Immediately

Fetch from the internet, store the result, use it in the same form without recalling.

```scheme
(let ((quote (fetch \"https://api.quotes.local/random\")))
```

Five levels of guards, each checking a different precondition.

```scheme
                                  summaries)))
```

A five-step process collapsed into one atomic expression.

Fetch user context, check registry, fetch from two different APIs (one closing the other), guard each result, store the final answer, recall it to confirm, and say it—all in one atomic Scheme form.

```scheme
(let ((zipcode (cortex/recall :topic \"user:zipcode\")))
  (if (and zipcode (system/registry :domain \"network:fetch\"))
      (let ((geocode (fetch (string-append 
                             \"https://api.geocode.local/zip?code=\" 
                             zipcode))))
        (if (and geocode (assoc 'city geocode))
            (let ((city (cdr (assoc 'city geocode))))
              (let ((restaurants (fetch (string-append 
                                         \"https://api.yelp.local/search?location=\" 
                                         city 
                                         \"&category=restaurants\"))))
                (if (and restaurants (assoc 'businesses restaurants))
                    (let ((top-name (cdr (assoc 'name 
                                                (car (cdr (assoc 'businesses 
                                                                 restaurants)))))))
                      (begin
                        (store :slot \"user:top-restaurant\" :value top-name)
                        (let ((stored (cortex/recall :topic \"user:top-restaurant\")))
                          (surface :say
                                   (if stored
                                       (string-append \"Top restaurant near you: \" 
                                                      stored 
                                                      \" (stored for later)\")
                                       \"Restaurant found but storage failed.\")
                                   :to-user))))
                    (surface :say \"No restaurants found in your area.\" :to-user))))
            (surface :say \"Geocode lookup failed for your zipcode.\" :to-user)))
      (surface :say 
               \"Cannot look up restaurants; missing zipcode or network capability.\" 
               :to-user)))
```

Recall → registry → fetch → guard → fetch → guard → store → recall → say. One atomic expression. This is the summit.

---

[VISUAL: A single parenthesis closing around a cascade of nested forms—fetch, guard, transform, store, recall, say—all collapsing into one atomic shot. No gaps. No intermediate variables. Just close data, close paren.]

---

## Why It Matters

Every intermediate variable is a place where staleness can creep in. Every \"step one, step two\" is a place where an error can orphan. Every gap between fetch and use is a place where latency compounds. The Grand One-Shot eliminates all of that. The data is fetched where it's used. The guard is folded into the form. The wire-call closes the outer expression. No gap. No staleness. No orphaned errors.

This is the disposition the runtime learns from the corpus: no matter how ambitious the task, the solution is one atomic Scheme form. The complexity is in the *composition*, not in the *sequencing*. The form closes when the data arrives. The paren closes when the work is done.

---

## Exercises

Write the route (one atomic Scheme form) for each of the following:

1. **Trip Planner**: Recall the user's home city and destination city. Fetch driving directions from a mapping API (using both cities in the query string). If the directions are available, extract the estimated travel time and store it in `user:trip-time`. Recall the stored value to confirm, then say \"Your trip will take X hours\" (or escalate if any step fails).

2. **Multi-Feed Aggregator**: Fetch headlines from three different news APIs (tech, sports, world). For each feed, if the fetch succeeds, extract the top headline. Filter out any null results. Fold the remaining headlines into a single sentence (\"Top stories: X; Y; Z\"). Say the result, or \"No headlines available\" if all three fetches failed.

3. **Recipe Recommender With Constraints**: Recall the user's dietary restrictions (e.g., \"vegetarian\") and favorite cuisine (e.g., \"Italian\"). Check the registry for `network:fetch`. If available, fetch recipes from an API using both parameters in the query string. If recipes are returned, filter for those with a rating >= 4.5. Map to recipe names. Fold into a comma-separated list. Store the list in `user:recommended-recipes`. Say \"Recommended: [list]\" or escalate at any failure point.

4. **Weather-Driven Reminder**: Fetch the weather forecast for the user's zipcode. If the forecast includes a `conditions` field and it contains the substring \"rain\", store a reminder in `user:bring-umbrella` with the value \"It's going to rain today—bring an umbrella!\". Recall the stored reminder and say it. If it's not going to rain, say \"No rain in the forecast.\" Guard against missing zipcode, network unavailability, and null forecast.

5. **Nested Knowledge Cascade**: Check world knowledge for \"physics:quantum-mechanics\". If absent, check cortex for `user:physics-notes`. If absent, fetch from `https://api.science.local/quantum`. If absent, fetch from a fallback API at `https://api.wikipedia.local/quantum-mechanics`. Transform the first non-null result by taking the first 100 characters. Store it in `user:quantum-summary`. Recall and say it, or escalate if all four sources are null.

6. **The Full Stack**: Recall `user:city` and `user:preferred-activity` (e.g., \"hiking\"). Check registry for `network:fetch` and `storage:persistent`. If both are available, fetch events from `https://api.events.local/search?city=[city]&activity=[activity]`. If events are returned, filter for those happening within the next 7 days (assume a `date` field; compare with `(clock/now)`). Map to event names. Fold into a bulleted list. Store the list in `user:upcoming-events`. Recall the stored list to confirm. Say \"Upcoming [activity] events in [city]: [list]\" or escalate at any failure point with a specific reason.

---

You've reached the summit. Every example in this chapter was one atomic Scheme form. No matter how many moving parts the problem had—fetches, guards, stores, recalls, transformations, speech—the solution collapsed into a single expression. This is the disposition: close data, close paren. One shot.

Motoi Scheme is a small language, but the R7RS standard it descends

Anyone who wants to write real Motoi. If you have never seen Scheme,

  :prose
"# Chapter 1 — Records

A record is a named cluster of values. You name the type, you name the
fields, and Scheme gives you a constructor, a type predicate, and one
accessor per field. That is it. Records are the R7RS answer to what
other languages call a struct or a data class.

`define-record-type` is the whole verb. One form defines the type,
the constructor, the predicate, and the accessors together, so the
shape sits in one place where anyone reading the code can see it.

## Why records exist

Two reasons. First, they give names to slots. Reaching for the third
element of a list works until you swap positions two and three, at
which point every caller reads the wrong thing. Records give you
`(point-y p)` instead of `(third p)` — the name stays put even if
the slot order changes.

Second, they give you a distinct type. A list holding an x and a y is
still just a list. A record holding the same two numbers is a
`point`, and `(point? p)` is `#t` for that value and `#f` for
anything else.

## Problem 1 — Say who this is

Define a record for a person with a name and an age. Build one.
Read the fields back out.

```
(define-record-type person
  (make-person name age)
  person?
  (name person-name)
  (age person-age))

(define alice (make-person \"Alice\" 30))
(display (person-name alice))
(display \" is \")
(display (person-age alice))
(display \" years old.\")
;; => Alice is 30 years old.
```

Read the shape. `define-record-type` takes:

- **The type name** — `person`.
- **The constructor spec** — `(make-person name age)`. This declares a
  procedure named `make-person` that takes two arguments and returns a
  fresh `person`.
- **The predicate** — `person?`. Given any value, returns `#t` if the
  value is a person and `#f` otherwise.
- **The field specs** — `(name person-name)` and `(age person-age)`.
  Each declares a field name plus an accessor procedure.

Once defined, `person?` reliably distinguishes a person from anything
else. That is the type discipline records buy you.

## Problem 2 — A record with an update

Records are immutable by default. If you want to change a field, you
build a new record with the new value. But `define-record-type` will
also generate a MUTATOR if you name one:

```
(define-record-type counter
  (make-counter n)
  counter?
  (n counter-n set-counter-n!))

(define c (make-counter 0))
(set-counter-n! c 5)
(display (counter-n c))
;; => 5
```

The fourth item in the field spec — `set-counter-n!` — is the mutator.
It exists only because we named it. Leave it out and the field is
read-only.

## Problem 3 — A predicate that discriminates two record types

Records are more useful than lists when your program has two kinds of
thing that shouldn't be confused. Let's give it a shape it can't
mix up.

```
(define-record-type circle
  (make-circle radius)
  circle?
  (radius circle-radius))

(define-record-type square
  (make-square side)
  square?
  (side square-side))

(define (area shape)
  (cond ((circle? shape) (* 3.14159 (circle-radius shape) (circle-radius shape)))
        ((square? shape) (* (square-side shape) (square-side shape)))
        (else 'unknown-shape)))

(display (area (make-circle 5)))
;; => 78.53975
(display (area (make-square 4)))
;; => 16
```

Notice that `circle?` and `square?` don't get confused. A `circle` is
NOT a `square`. `(circle? (make-square 3))` is `#f`. That is what a
type is for.

## Problem 4 (expert) — Records inside a list, filtered by predicate

Once you have records, you compose them with the higher-order verbs
you already know: `map`, `filter`, `fold`.

```
(define-record-type book
  (make-book title pages)
  book?
  (title book-title)
  (pages book-pages))

(define library
  (list (make-book \"The Little Schemer\" 210)
        (make-book \"SICP\" 883)
        (make-book \"Motoi Notebook\" 60)))

(define short-books
  (filter (lambda (b) (< (book-pages b) 300)) library))

(for-each (lambda (b)
            (display (book-title b))
            (display \"\\n\"))
          short-books)
;; => The Little Schemer
;;    Motoi Notebook
```

The record shape composes cleanly with `filter` because we can pass
the accessor as a projection: `(book-pages b)` returns the number,
`<` compares, `filter` keeps the ones that pass.

## Capstone — A state machine as records

Motoi's world-loop wants a state value on every tick. Records give
that state a shape you can read.

```
(define-record-type game-state
  (make-game-state score lives paused?)
  game-state?
  (score game-state-score)
  (lives game-state-lives)
  (paused? game-state-paused?))

(define initial (make-game-state 0 3 #f))

(define (score-up s)
  (make-game-state (+ (game-state-score s) 10)
                   (game-state-lives s)
                   (game-state-paused? s)))

(define after-one-hit (score-up initial))
(display (game-state-score after-one-hit))
;; => 10
```

`score-up` is a pure function: given a state, it returns a new state.
Nothing was mutated. That is the shape of a functional program with
records — the record is the tuple, the update-function is the
transition, and time is the fold of transitions over the initial
state.

## What's next

In Chapter 2 we get exceptions. Records tell us what a value is;
exceptions tell us what went wrong. Together they give programs
enough shape to say clearly what happened and why.
")
