"# Chapter 3 — Higher-Order

A higher-order function is a function that takes another function as an argument, returns a function as its result, or both. That sounds theoretical. It is not theoretical. It is what lets you write a function like `map` once and never write a `for` loop again. You already used higher-order functions in Chapter 2. This chapter names them and shows you how to build your own.

## Why this lib exists

Some code shapes are the same every time except for one detail. Sorting numbers ascending vs descending — same walk, different comparator. Timing a function call — same start-clock/call/stop-clock, different function. Retrying on failure — same retry loop, different action.

Without higher-order functions you copy the loop each time and edit the detail. With them, you write the loop once and pass the detail as an argument.

This chapter has four steps: use a built-in higher-order, write one, return one, and compose several.

## Problem 1 — Time how long a function takes

Motoi has a millisecond clock. Wrap any function in a timer:

```
(define (time-it label thunk)
  (let ((start (current-time-ms)))
    (thunk)
    (let ((elapsed (- (current-time-ms) start)))
      (display label)
      (display \": \")
      (display elapsed)
      (display \"ms\\n\"))))

(time-it \"count to a million\"
  (lambda ()
    (let loop ((n 0))
      (if (= n 1000000)
          'done
          (loop (+ n 1))))))
;; => count to a million: 12ms
```

Read the shape. `time-it` takes a label and a `thunk` — a function of no arguments. It notes the clock, calls the thunk, notes the clock again, prints. Anywhere you want to time some code, wrap it in `(lambda () ...)` and hand it over.

That `lambda ()` — no arguments in the parens — is the standard shape for `do this later`. Motoi will not run the body until someone calls the thunk. That is why the timer can straddle it.

## Problem 2 — Write your own `keep-if`, which is just `filter` with the arguments swapped

Some days you want the collection first and the predicate second. Rewriting `filter` from scratch teaches you the shape:

```
(define (keep-if lst pred)
  (cond ((null? lst) '())
        ((pred (car lst))
         (cons (car lst) (keep-if (cdr lst) pred)))
        (else
         (keep-if (cdr lst) pred))))

(display (keep-if (list 1 2 3 4 5 6) odd?))
;; => (1 3 5)
```

`keep-if` is a higher-order function — it takes `pred` (which is a function). It is also recursive: if the list is empty, return empty; if the first element passes the predicate, cons it onto the result of recursing on the rest; otherwise, skip it and recurse on the rest. Chapter 4 talks about recursion at length. Here, notice: the predicate is just an argument like any other.

## Problem 3 — A function that RETURNS a function

This is where things start to feel like magic and then stop feeling like magic. `adder` takes a number and returns a function that adds that number to whatever it is called with:

```
(define (adder n)
  (lambda (x) (+ x n)))

(define add-ten (adder 10))
(define add-hundred (adder 100))

(display (add-ten 5))       ;; => 15
(display (add-hundred 5))   ;; => 105
(display ((adder 42) 8))    ;; => 50
```

`adder` is a factory. Every call produces a fresh function. That function remembers the `n` from when it was made — Scheme people call that a closure, and it just means the inner function closes over the outer function's variable.

The last line, `((adder 42) 8)`, calls `adder` and immediately calls the result. Nothing stored. Same idea, more concise.

You use this pattern any time you want to build a specialized version of a general operation. `(adder 10)` is `+ 10`, permanent. In graphics you might write `(coloring 'pink)` that returns a function that draws a shape pink. Same shape.

## Problem 4 (pro) — Compose functions into a pipeline

Sometimes you want to say `first do A, then do B, then do C` and have the result be a single function you can call once. That is composition:

```
(define (compose2 f g)
  (lambda (x) (f (g x))))

(define add-one (lambda (n) (+ n 1)))
(define double  (lambda (n) (* n 2)))
(define square  (lambda (n) (* n n)))

(define do-all (compose2 square (compose2 double add-one)))

(display (do-all 3))
;; => 64
```

Trace it: `3` goes into `add-one`, becomes `4`. `4` goes into `double`, becomes `8`. `8` goes into `square`, becomes `64`. The function `do-all` bakes that whole pipeline into one callable value.

Now the general version — compose any number of functions:

```
(define (compose . fns)
  (if (null? fns)
      (lambda (x) x)
      (let ((first (car fns))
            (rest  (apply compose (cdr fns))))
        (lambda (x) (first (rest x))))))

(define do-all-nice (compose square double add-one))

(display (do-all-nice 3))
;; => 64
```

The `. fns` in the lambda list means `collect all the arguments into a list`. `apply compose (cdr fns)` calls `compose` again with the rest of the functions as separate arguments. The base case — no functions left — returns the identity function.

If you have never seen `apply` before: `apply f (list a b c)` is the same as `(f a b c)`. It spreads a list back into arguments. This is the bridge between variadic functions and lists.

## Capstone — A rate-limiter that lets a function fire at most once per interval

```
(define (rate-limit interval-ms fn)
  (let ((last-fire 0))
    (lambda args
      (let ((now (current-time-ms)))
        (if (< (- now last-fire) interval-ms)
            'throttled
            (begin
              (set! last-fire now)
              (apply fn args)))))))

(define greet (rate-limit 1000 (lambda (name)
                                  (display \"hi, \")
                                  (display name)
                                  (display \"\\n\")
                                  'greeted)))

(greet \"Alfred\")   ;; => hi, Alfred      ;; result: greeted
(greet \"Alfred\")   ;; => (no print)      ;; result: throttled
;; wait 1 second...
(greet \"Alfred\")   ;; => hi, Alfred      ;; result: greeted
```

Three ideas landed here. First: the outer `let` gives the returned function a private variable (`last-fire`) it can update between calls. That is a closure carrying state — a mutable cell only the returned function can see.

Second: `lambda args` collects all arguments into a list called `args`, so the returned function works no matter how many arguments the wrapped function takes.

Third: `apply fn args` calls the wrapped function with those arguments. The wrapper does not need to know what the wrapped function expects — it just passes everything through.

This pattern shows up everywhere. A debouncer is the same shape with the condition inverted. A memoizer is the same shape with a hash-table replacing `last-fire`. A logger is the same shape with `display` around the call. Once you see it, you see it everywhere.

## What's next

Chapter 4 slows down and talks about recursion — the pattern that made `compose` and `keep-if` work above. If you have been reading and nodding but the recursive calls made your eyes cross, Chapter 4 is where we walk through them one at a time.
")

"# Chapter 4 — Recursion Without Fear

A recursive function is a function that calls itself. That is the whole idea. The reason it works is that each call is smaller than the last, and eventually the calls get so small that an answer is obvious. The base case tells the function when to stop; the recursive case tells the function how to shrink.

If recursion has ever intimidated you, this chapter takes it apart. We build four functions that recurse in slightly different ways. By the end, the shape will be an old friend.

## Why recursion exists in Scheme

Two reasons. One: many data structures are already recursive. A list is a `cons` cell whose `cdr` is another list. A tree is a node whose branches are trees. Walking a recursive structure with a recursive function makes the code look like the structure. That is a form of honesty in the shape.

Two: Scheme does not have `for` or `while`. It does not need them. A recursive function that gets its base case right is exactly a loop, without an extra name for the same idea. Motoi has some higher-level loops (`map`, `for-each`, `on-tick`) built on top, but at the bottom of the stack sits recursion.

## Problem 1 — Count down from N to zero

The shape everyone starts with:

```
(define (countdown n)
  (if (= n 0)
      'done
      (begin
        (display n)
        (display \" \")
        (countdown (- n 1)))))

(countdown 5)
;; => 5 4 3 2 1 done
```

Read the two arms of the `if`. When `n` is `0`, return the symbol `done` and stop. Otherwise, display the current `n` and call yourself with `n - 1`. Every call is one step closer to zero. Zero is where you stop.

The whole grammar of recursion is those two arms: base case (stop here) and recursive case (shrink and recurse).

## Problem 2 — Sum a list, one element at a time

Now recurse over a list instead of a number:

```
(define (sum-list lst)
  (if (null? lst)
      0
      (+ (car lst) (sum-list (cdr lst)))))

(display (sum-list (list 1 2 3 4 5)))
;; => 15
```

Base case: the list is empty, sum is `0`. Recursive case: sum of a non-empty list is the first element plus the sum of the rest. The `(cdr lst)` is smaller than `lst` — one fewer element — so eventually the list becomes empty and we hit the base case.

Same shape works for product:

```
(define (product-list lst)
  (if (null? lst)
      1
      (* (car lst) (product-list (cdr lst)))))

(display (product-list (list 1 2 3 4 5)))
;; => 120
```

Notice what changed: `+` became `*`, and the base case became `1` (the identity for multiplication) instead of `0` (the identity for addition). Same shape, different verb.

## Problem 3 — Reverse a list

You want `(reverse (list 1 2 3 4)) => (4 3 2 1)`. The natural recursion:

```
(define (my-reverse lst)
  (if (null? lst)
      '()
      (append (my-reverse (cdr lst)) (list (car lst)))))

(display (my-reverse (list 1 2 3 4 5)))
;; => (5 4 3 2 1)
```

This works. It is also slow — every `append` walks its first argument, so reversing a list of `n` elements does `n²` work total. Fine for teaching. Bad for anything long.

The fast shape uses an accumulator — a second argument that carries partial work:

```
(define (my-reverse-fast lst)
  (define (helper lst acc)
    (if (null? lst)
        acc
        (helper (cdr lst) (cons (car lst) acc))))
  (helper lst '()))

(display (my-reverse-fast (list 1 2 3 4 5)))
;; => (5 4 3 2 1)
```

Trace it once. Call: `(helper (1 2 3 4 5) ())`. First element is `1`; cons it to the acc `()` to get `(1)`. Recurse with the rest of the list and the new acc: `(helper (2 3 4 5) (1))`. Cons `2` onto `(1)` to get `(2 1)`. Recurse: `(helper (3 4 5) (2 1))`. And so on. When the list runs out, we return the accumulator — which has been built up in reverse.

This shape — an outer function that sets up an accumulator and an inner helper that recurses on both — is called tail-recursion with an accumulator. Motoi turns it into a tight loop under the hood, so it uses no extra stack space. Any time you want a recursion that is as fast as a loop, this is the shape.

## Problem 4 (pro) — Compute the depth of a nested list

A nested list is a tree. `(1 (2 3) (4 (5 6) 7))` has depth `3` — the outer list is level 1, the `(2 3)` is level 2, the `(5 6)` is level 3.

Two recursive calls in the recursive case, because a tree branches:

```
(define (depth x)
  (if (not (pair? x))
      0
      (+ 1 (apply max
                  (map depth x)))))

(display (depth 5))
;; => 0

(display (depth '(1 2 3)))
;; => 1

(display (depth '(1 (2 3) (4 (5 6) 7))))
;; => 3
```

Read the shape. If `x` is not a pair (a leaf), its depth is `0`. Otherwise, its depth is `1` plus the max depth of its children. `map depth x` calls `depth` on each child; `apply max` finds the biggest.

Two things worth noticing. First: `depth` calls itself indirectly through `map` — you do not always see the recursive call textually inside the recursive case. Second: this pattern (map the function over the children, combine the results) is the shape of every tree walk. Count the leaves? `depth`, but with `+` instead of `max` and `1` for leaves. Sum the leaves? Same shape, `+` again, but return the leaf value instead of `1`. The tree walk shape is one of the highest-value patterns to internalize.

## Capstone — Flatten a nested list

Given `(1 (2 (3 4) 5) 6)`, return `(1 2 3 4 5 6)`. This is the tree-walk pattern with concatenation as the combiner.

```
(define (flatten x)
  (cond ((null? x) '())
        ((not (pair? x)) (list x))
        (else
         (append (flatten (car x))
                 (flatten (cdr x))))))

(display (flatten '(1 (2 (3 4) 5) 6)))
;; => (1 2 3 4 5 6)
```

Three cases now, not two. Empty list flattens to empty. A non-pair (an atom) flattens to a one-element list holding just that atom. A pair — flatten the first, flatten the rest, append them.

You can see how a small, correct recursion beats a giant `for` loop for tree work. Trying to flatten a tree with a `for` loop needs an explicit stack or queue — you rebuild the recursion by hand. Better to write the recursion.

## What's next

You now have base + list ops + higher-order + recursion. Chapter 5 leaves the terminal behind and puts a picture on the screen. The frame buffer library — three verbs to draw pixels, one to write text — is where nothing-to-something starts looking like nothing-to-a-window-with-a-thing-in-it.
")

"# Chapter 5 — The Frame

You have been talking to Motoi through the terminal. Now you talk to him through the screen. Every picture Motoi draws lives in a frame — a rectangular grid of pixels the runtime holds for you. This chapter takes you from `no picture` to `picture with text and shapes` in four steps.

The tools are small. `begin-frame` and `end-frame` bracket a drawing pass. `text/draw` and `fb/text` put strings on the surface. `paint-emoji` and `paint-clear` handle emoji and cleanup. That is enough for a title screen. Chapter 6 will start moving pictures in a loop; here we get one picture right.

## Why the frame lib exists

A picture is easy to describe: it is a rectangle full of colored pixels. The hard part is making the description match what the screen shows. Different displays have different pixel densities, different color models, different refresh rates.

Motoi hides all of that behind a single abstraction: the surface. You paint onto the surface with whatever verbs you like. When you call `end-frame`, Motoi hands the surface to whatever backend is running — a browser canvas, a terminal grid, a headless test buffer — and asks the backend to show it. Your painting code does not know or care which backend is on the other side. This is the same shape Chapter 1 of Book of Composition calls the round-trip: the picture and the code that made it live in the same file, in the same shape, addressable from both sides.

## Problem 1 — Draw one word in the middle of the screen

Four lines. `begin-frame` opens the pass. `text/draw` writes the word. `end-frame` commits.

```
(begin-frame 'main)

(text/draw \"HELLO\"
           at:    (list 160 120)
           color: 'petal-pink
           font:  'big
           align: 'center)

(end-frame 'main)
;; => 'ok  (the word HELLO appears centered on surface 'main)
```

The `at:` keyword takes an `(x y)` position in pixels. `(160 120)` is roughly the middle of a 320×240 surface. `color:` accepts named palette colors (`'petal-pink`, `'mint`, `'brown`) or hex codes like `#xff0000`. `align: 'center` centers the string on the x coordinate; without it the text starts at x.

That is your first picture. If you close the terminal and reopen it, the file remembers everything you wrote — the runtime does not. Painting is a fresh act every frame.

## Problem 2 — A title, a subtitle, and a decorative rule below

Now stack three pieces at three positions. Add a horizontal bar below by painting a solid-color pixel row via `paint-rect`.

```
(begin-frame 'main)

(text/draw \"Motoi Scheme\"
           at:    (list 160 80)
           color: 'petal-pink
           font:  'big
           align: 'center)

(text/draw \"a small language for one small mind\"
           at:    (list 160 110)
           color: 'moss-green
           font:  'default
           align: 'center)

(paint-rect (list 40 130) (list 240 2) 'earth-brown)

(text/draw \"press any key to begin\"
           at:    (list 160 200)
           color: 'earth-brown
           font:  'tiny
           align: 'center)

(end-frame 'main)
```

Notice the three fonts. `'big` for the title, `'default` for the subtitle, `'tiny` for the hint at the bottom. That is a common shape for a title screen — one loud element, one calm element, one small element. If it feels too crowded, drop one. If it feels too sparse, add one.

`paint-rect` takes an `(x y)` origin and a `(width height)` size. Height `2` is thin — a decorative rule, not a bar. Widening the height to `20` would give you a nameplate.

If you want to check your alignment, `text/measure` returns the pixel size of a string before you paint it:

```
(define subtitle \"a small language for one small mind\")
(define size (text/measure subtitle font: 'default))
(display size)
;; => (218 8)   ;; width 218, height 8
```

That tells you the subtitle is 218 pixels wide. If you want it centered but do not want to trust the `align:` keyword, compute `(x = (- 160 (/ 218 2)))` = `51`, and pass that.

## Problem 3 — A splash screen with an emoji, a color palette bar, and framed borders

Now compose. Use `paint-emoji` for the icon, `paint-rect` in a loop for the palette strip, and four `paint-rect` calls for the border.

```
(define palette
  (list 'petal-pink 'moss-green 'earth-brown
        'mint 'rose 'daffodil 'sky-blue))

(define (draw-border)
  (paint-rect (list 0   0)  (list 320   2) 'earth-brown)
  (paint-rect (list 0 238)  (list 320   2) 'earth-brown)
  (paint-rect (list 0   0)  (list   2 240) 'earth-brown)
  (paint-rect (list 318 0)  (list   2 240) 'earth-brown))

(define (draw-palette-bar)
  (let loop ((cs palette) (x 60))
    (if (null? cs)
        'done
        (begin
          (paint-rect (list x 220) (list 28 10) (car cs))
          (loop (cdr cs) (+ x 30))))))

(begin-frame 'main)

(draw-border)

(paint-emoji '🌸 (list 160 90) size: 48)

(text/draw \"Motoi Scheme\"
           at:    (list 160 150)
           color: 'petal-pink
           font:  'big
           align: 'center)

(draw-palette-bar)

(end-frame 'main)
```

Two new patterns landed.

First: `draw-border` and `draw-palette-bar` are named subroutines. Neither is a big function. Both are much easier to read than four `paint-rect` calls buried in the middle of the frame block. Any time you find yourself painting more than three primitives for a single logical element, name it.

Second: the palette loop uses named `let` — the same `let loop (...)` shape you saw as an accumulator recursion in Chapter 4. It walks the list of colors, painting one small swatch per element, advancing `x` by 30 each time. Seven colors, one function.

`paint-emoji` takes a quoted emoji glyph, a position, and an optional `size:` in pixels. Emoji land as bitmaps at that size; the compositor blends them with anything else you draw.

## Problem 4 (pro) — A responsive HUD that resizes with the viewport

Real screens come in different sizes. If you hard-code coordinates for `320×240`, your HUD breaks the moment someone runs your cart at `640×480`. The fix: ask the viewport for its dimensions and paint relative to them.

```
(define (draw-hud score lives)
  (let* ((vp    (viewport))
         (w     (list-ref vp 2))
         (h     (list-ref vp 3))
         (pad   8)
         (right (- w pad))
         (bottom (- h pad)))

    (begin-frame 'main)

    ;; top-left: score
    (text/draw (string-append \"score: \" (number->string score))
               at:    (list pad pad)
               color: 'petal-pink
               font:  'default
               align: 'left)

    ;; top-right: lives (as hearts)
    (let loop ((i 0) (x (- right (* 3 (- lives 1)))))
      (if (= i lives)
          'done
          (begin
            (paint-emoji '❤ (list x pad) size: 12)
            (loop (+ i 1) (+ x 14)))))

    ;; bottom-center: hint
    (text/draw \"[space] jump   [←→] move\"
               at:    (list (/ w 2) bottom)
               color: 'earth-brown
               font:  'tiny
               align: 'center)

    (end-frame 'main)))

(draw-hud 1200 3)
```

`viewport` returns `(x y w h)` for the current camera. We destructure `w` and `h` and place elements relative to them. Now `draw-hud` works whether the screen is 320 wide or 3200 wide.

`let*` is like `let` except each binding can see the ones before it. That lets us define `right` in terms of `w` without nesting three `let`s.

The heart loop is the second `let loop` in this chapter — the shape shows up so often it deserves its own place in your muscle memory.

## Capstone — A pause overlay that dims the background and centers a message

```
(define (draw-pause-overlay message)
  (let* ((vp (viewport))
         (w  (list-ref vp 2))
         (h  (list-ref vp 3)))

    (begin-frame 'main)

    ;; dim the whole screen with a semi-transparent rect
    (paint-rect (list 0 0) (list w h) 'shadow-veil)

    ;; box to hold the message
    (let ((bx (- (/ w 2) 100))
          (by (- (/ h 2)  30))
          (bw 200)
          (bh 60))
      (paint-rect (list bx by) (list bw bh) 'ink-black)
      (paint-rect (list bx by) (list bw 2)  'petal-pink)
      (paint-rect (list bx (+ by bh -2)) (list bw 2) 'petal-pink))

    ;; the message
    (text/draw message
               at:    (list (/ w 2) (/ h 2))
               color: 'petal-pink
               font:  'big
               align: 'center)

    (text/draw \"press [p] to resume\"
               at:    (list (/ w 2) (+ (/ h 2) 18))
               color: 'moss-green
               font:  'tiny
               align: 'center)

    (end-frame 'main)))

(draw-pause-overlay \"paused\")
```

Read the composition. First we dim everything with a full-screen semi-transparent rect (assuming `'shadow-veil` is a palette color with alpha). Then we draw the message box — one filled rect, two thin pink rules top and bottom for style. Then the title and the sub-message in the box.

The whole overlay is one function. The only argument is the message. If tomorrow you want a `game over` overlay, you call `(draw-pause-overlay \"game over\")` and swap the resume-hint text. That is a small function doing one clear job. That is the shape.

## What's next

You can paint. Chapter 6 turns painting into animation. `big-bang`, `on-tick`, and `to-draw` — the three verbs that turn a still frame into a running loop. Once you have a loop, every static example in this chapter becomes a frame in a movie.
")

"# Chapter 6 — The World Loop

Painting one picture is a still. Painting sixty pictures per second is a movie. This chapter teaches you the shape Motoi uses to run a movie: `big-bang`. It is the verb every real-time program in Motoi passes through, from a bouncing ball to a full game.

The pattern comes from How to Design Programs — a Racket teaching book — and it survives untouched in Motoi because it is honest about what a game loop actually is: a state, a way to advance the state, a way to draw the state, and a way to stop.

## Why big-bang exists

A game loop is boring plumbing. Every game has the same shape at the outermost layer: on each tick, compute the new state; then draw the current state; then check whether the game is over. The interesting logic sits inside those three slots. The plumbing is the same every time.

`big-bang` writes the plumbing for you. You hand it four clauses: an initial state, a `on-tick` handler that advances state, a `to-draw` handler that renders state, and (optionally) a `stop-when` predicate. It spins the loop; you write the pieces.

There is a second reason this shape is worth reaching for. Because each clause is a pure function of state — and only the state carries information from tick to tick — you can time-travel debug. Save the state at any frame. Reload it. Replay from there. The composition doctrine you saw in Book of Composition Chapter 1 (round-trip: file and tool are the same) applies here too: state and game are the same thing.

## Problem 1 — A counter that ticks up

The smallest useful big-bang: a number that goes up one per frame, and a display that shows it.

```
(big-bang 0
  (on-tick (lambda (state) (+ state 1)))
  (to-draw (lambda (state)
             (begin-frame 'main)
             (text/draw (number->string state)
                        at:    (list 160 120)
                        color: 'petal-pink
                        font:  'big
                        align: 'center)
             (end-frame 'main)))
  (stop-when (lambda (state) (= state 300))))
```

Read the four pieces. Initial state: `0`. `on-tick` receives the current state and returns the next — here just `state + 1`. `to-draw` receives the current state and paints it — one big pink number in the middle. `stop-when` receives the state and returns true when it is time to quit — after 300 frames (about five seconds at 60fps).

That is a whole real-time program. Run it and you watch a number count up from 0 to 300 in five seconds. Change the increment to `2` and it counts twice as fast. Change the `stop-when` bound to `1000000` and it counts forever.

## Problem 2 — A bouncing ball

Now the state is a record, not a number. We track the ball's position and velocity.

```
(define (make-ball x y vx vy)
  (list x y vx vy))

(define (ball-x  b) (list-ref b 0))
(define (ball-y  b) (list-ref b 1))
(define (ball-vx b) (list-ref b 2))
(define (ball-vy b) (list-ref b 3))

(define (advance ball)
  (let* ((x  (+ (ball-x ball)  (ball-vx ball)))
         (y  (+ (ball-y ball)  (ball-vy ball)))
         (vx (if (or (< x 0) (> x 320)) (- (ball-vx ball)) (ball-vx ball)))
         (vy (if (or (< y 0) (> y 240)) (- (ball-vy ball)) (ball-vy ball))))
    (make-ball x y vx vy)))

(define (render ball)
  (begin-frame 'main)
  (paint-rect (list 0 0) (list 320 240) 'shadow-veil)
  (paint-circle (list (ball-x ball) (ball-y ball)) 8 'petal-pink)
  (end-frame 'main))

(big-bang (make-ball 100 100 3 2)
  (on-tick advance)
  (to-draw render))
```

The state is the ball. `advance` computes the new state — position plus velocity, and velocities flip when the ball hits an edge. `render` paints a filled background rectangle (so we do not leave trails) then a pink circle at the ball's position.

Two design choices worth noticing.

First: we made accessors (`ball-x`, `ball-y`, etc.) so the rest of the code never asks `(list-ref ball 0)`. If tomorrow the ball gains a color, only the constructor and one new accessor change. Everywhere else keeps working.

Second: `on-tick` and `to-draw` each receive a bare state and produce a value. Neither mutates. The state is threaded through the loop like a river; each frame you scoop up the old state, produce a new state, and hand it back to `big-bang`. This is why time-travel debugging is possible: the state is the whole story.

## Problem 3 — A paddle controlled by the keyboard

Now add `on-key`. The state is a paddle position; the tick advances nothing; the key handler adjusts position based on arrow presses.

```
(define (make-paddle x) x)

(define (advance-paddle p) p)  ;; paddle only moves when a key fires

(define (handle-key p event)
  (let ((k (list-ref event 1)))
    (cond ((eq? k 'left)   (max 0    (- p 5)))
          ((eq? k 'right)  (min 300  (+ p 5)))
          (else p))))

(define (render-paddle p)
  (begin-frame 'main)
  (paint-rect (list 0 0) (list 320 240) 'shadow-veil)
  (paint-rect (list p 220) (list 20 6) 'petal-pink)
  (end-frame 'main))

(big-bang (make-paddle 150)
  (on-tick advance-paddle)
  (on-key  handle-key)
  (to-draw render-paddle))
```

The paddle is just an x coordinate. `handle-key` takes the current state and a key event; it returns the new state. If the key is `'left`, subtract 5; if `'right`, add 5; otherwise, leave it alone. `max` and `min` clamp the paddle inside the screen.

Notice `on-tick` here is a no-op — it just returns the state unchanged. That is fine. Not every game has ticking logic that runs regardless of input; some games are entirely input-driven.

## Problem 4 (pro) — A tiny complete game: catch a falling star

Combine everything: a paddle that catches, a star that falls, a score, and a game-over condition.

```
(define (make-state paddle-x star-x star-y score lives)
  (list paddle-x star-x star-y score lives))

(define (state-paddle-x s) (list-ref s 0))
(define (state-star-x   s) (list-ref s 1))
(define (state-star-y   s) (list-ref s 2))
(define (state-score    s) (list-ref s 3))
(define (state-lives    s) (list-ref s 4))

(define (respawn-star)
  (random-int 0 300))

(define (advance s)
  (let* ((px  (state-paddle-x s))
         (sx  (state-star-x s))
         (sy  (+ (state-star-y s) 4))
         (score (state-score s))
         (lives (state-lives s)))
    (cond
      ;; star caught
      ((and (>= sy 220)
            (>= sx px)
            (<= sx (+ px 20)))
       (make-state px (respawn-star) 0 (+ score 10) lives))
      ;; star missed
      ((> sy 240)
       (make-state px (respawn-star) 0 score (- lives 1)))
      ;; still falling
      (else (make-state px sx sy score lives)))))

(define (handle-key s event)
  (let ((k  (list-ref event 1))
        (px (state-paddle-x s)))
    (cond ((eq? k 'left)   (make-state (max 0    (- px 8))
                                        (state-star-x s)
                                        (state-star-y s)
                                        (state-score s)
                                        (state-lives s)))
          ((eq? k 'right)  (make-state (min 300 (+ px 8))
                                        (state-star-x s)
                                        (state-star-y s)
                                        (state-score s)
                                        (state-lives s)))
          (else s))))

(define (render s)
  (begin-frame 'main)
  (paint-rect (list 0 0) (list 320 240) 'shadow-veil)
  ;; paddle
  (paint-rect (list (state-paddle-x s) 220) (list 20 6) 'petal-pink)
  ;; star
  (paint-emoji '⭐ (list (state-star-x s) (state-star-y s)) size: 16)
  ;; score
  (text/draw (string-append \"score: \" (number->string (state-score s)))
             at:    (list 8 8)
             color: 'petal-pink
             font:  'default
             align: 'left)
  ;; lives
  (text/draw (string-append \"lives: \" (number->string (state-lives s)))
             at:    (list 312 8)
             color: 'moss-green
             font:  'default
             align: 'right)
  (end-frame 'main))

(define (game-over? s)
  (<= (state-lives s) 0))

(big-bang (make-state 150 (respawn-star) 0 0 3)
  (on-tick advance)
  (on-key  handle-key)
  (to-draw render)
  (stop-when game-over?))
```

Read the whole thing. State is five numbers. Advance drops the star by 4 pixels per tick, checks for catch (score goes up, star respawns), checks for miss (life lost, star respawns), or leaves the star falling. `handle-key` moves the paddle. `render` paints everything. `game-over?` fires when lives hit zero.

This is a complete game in maybe 60 lines. Every line is a real Motoi verb. Every design decision is visible — the paddle width, the fall speed, the score per catch, the initial lives. Change any number and the game changes.

Notice the pattern for updating a record field: reconstruct the whole thing with the new value in that slot. That is verbose. In Chapter 12 (of the eventual larger book) you might reach for records with named-field accessors; here, in the base book, we spell it out so nothing is hidden.

## Capstone — A pause button that suspends `advance` without suspending `on-key`

```
(define (make-state paddle-x star-x star-y score lives paused?)
  (list paddle-x star-x star-y score lives paused?))

(define (state-paused? s) (list-ref s 5))

(define (advance-maybe s)
  (if (state-paused? s)
      s
      (advance s)))          ;; from problem 4, minus the paused? field

(define (toggle-pause s)
  (make-state (state-paddle-x s)
              (state-star-x s)
              (state-star-y s)
              (state-score s)
              (state-lives s)
              (not (state-paused? s))))

(define (handle-key s event)
  (let ((k (list-ref event 1)))
    (cond ((eq? k 'p)      (toggle-pause s))
          ;; other keys same as problem 4, but only advance paddle when unpaused
          (else s))))

(big-bang (make-state 150 (respawn-star) 0 0 3 #f)
  (on-tick advance-maybe)
  (on-key  handle-key)
  (to-draw render))
```

We extended the state with a `paused?` flag. `advance-maybe` short-circuits the physics when paused. `toggle-pause` flips the flag. `handle-key` reserves the `p` key for pause. The rest of the game is exactly as before.

Adding a feature by extending the state and short-circuiting a handler — no hidden globals, no side channels — is the shape you want. It scales from a paddle game to a large simulation without ever asking `where does the state live` because the state lives exactly where the loop passes it.

## What's next

Chapter 7 introduces the entity system — a way to run many game objects with real physics without writing your own collision or integration code. `world/spawn`, `entity/pos`, `entity/move!`, `world/step`. That is where a paddle catching one falling star becomes a hundred sprites in a proper world.
")

"# Chapter 7 — Entities on the Field

In Chapter 6 you carried the ball's position and velocity by hand and wrote the physics — bounce off the walls, advance by velocity — as normal code. That works for one ball. It falls apart at ten balls, and it is a nightmare at a hundred. Motoi's entity system exists for that reason. You describe what an entity is; the world takes care of moving it, colliding it, and drawing it.

Every entity has an id. Every verb that touches an entity takes that id. `world/spawn` gives you an id; `entity/pos` reads position from an id; `entity/move!` nudges the entity at an id. Once you understand id-passing, the whole system is small.

## Why the entity system exists

Games have many things happening at once. A player, a dozen enemies, projectiles from both sides, particles, pickups, background scenery — all moving, all colliding, all drawing. If you carry each in the state as a bare list, the state balloons and every tick has to touch every field.

The entity system splits the state into two: a slot the world owns (each entity's position, velocity, shape, tags) and a slot you own (game-level things: score, lives, current wave). The world's slot is updated by `world/step`. Your slot is updated by your game logic. Rendering is one call: `world/render` paints every entity at once.

This is a version of the composition doctrine again — separate what the runtime is good at from what the operator is good at, and give each a clean handle to the other.

## Problem 1 — Spawn one entity, render it

Three lines.

```
(define player (world/spawn 'player 160 120))
(world/render)
;; => a default-shape entity at (160, 120) on the current surface
```

`world/spawn` takes a kind symbol, an x, and a y; it returns an id. That id is a number Motoi assigns; you never construct it yourself. From now on, when you want to talk about the player, you pass `player`.

`world/render` walks the world once and paints every alive entity at its current position. No `begin-frame` / `end-frame` needed — `world/render` handles the framing itself. This is the simplest possible drawing.

## Problem 2 — Spawn ten entities in a row, step the world, watch them move

Every entity has a velocity too. Give a row of entities the same rightward velocity and step:

```
(define (spawn-row count y vx)
  (let loop ((i 0) (ids '()))
    (if (= i count)
        (reverse ids)
        (let ((id (world/spawn 'boid (* i 30) y)))
          (entity/set-vel! id vx 0)
          (loop (+ i 1) (cons id ids))))))

(define swarm (spawn-row 10 100 2))

(big-bang 0
  (on-tick (lambda (frame)
             (world/step)
             (+ frame 1)))
  (to-draw (lambda (_)
             (begin-frame 'main)
             (paint-rect (list 0 0) (list 320 240) 'shadow-veil)
             (world/render)
             (end-frame 'main)))
  (stop-when (lambda (frame) (= frame 120))))
```

Read the pattern. `spawn-row` creates ten entities and gives each a rightward velocity of `2` pixels per tick. It returns the list of ids in case you want to reference them later.

The big-bang loop calls `world/step` every tick — that advances every entity's position by its velocity and does collision, gravity, and friction if you have set them up. Then we render.

Ten entities, one `world/step` per frame. If you had done this by hand for ten, you would have a `for-each` over the ids updating each one. `world/step` bundles that into one call and adds physics you did not write.

## Problem 3 — Gravity, bouncing off the floor

Turn on gravity. Give an entity a bounce coefficient. Watch it fall and bounce.

```
(world/gravity! 0 300)              ;; downward acceleration, pixels per second squared

(define ball (world/spawn 'ball 160 20))
(entity/bounce! ball 0.8)           ;; loses 20% of speed per bounce
(entity/sprite! ball (sprite 'rose)) ;; give it a visible sprite

(world/floor! 220)                  ;; a floor at y=220

(big-bang 0
  (on-tick (lambda (frame)
             (world/step)
             (+ frame 1)))
  (to-draw (lambda (_)
             (begin-frame 'main)
             (paint-rect (list 0 0) (list 320 240) 'shadow-veil)
             (paint-rect (list 0 220) (list 320 20) 'earth-brown)
             (world/render)
             (end-frame 'main))))
```

Three world-level configuration verbs did the work. `world/gravity!` sets the constant acceleration applied to every entity that has mass. `world/floor!` places a horizontal surface at a given y. `entity/bounce!` sets the entity's coefficient of restitution — `1.0` is a perfect bounce, `0.0` is a dead thud, `0.8` is a lively ball that slowly loses energy.

You wrote zero physics code. The ball falls at 300 pixels/sec², hits the floor at y=220, bounces at 80% velocity, falls again, bounces again, and asymptotes to a rest on the floor. All from three configuration verbs and one `world/step` per tick.

## Problem 4 (pro) — A flock of thirty boids that seek the mouse

`world/each` iterates every alive entity. Combined with an AI verb like `ai/seek`, you can steer a whole flock at a moving target.

```
(define (spawn-flock count)
  (let loop ((i 0))
    (if (= i count)
        'done
        (let ((id (world/spawn 'boid
                               (random-int 0 320)
                               (random-int 0 240))))
          (entity/set-vel! id (random-range -1 1) (random-range -1 1))
          (entity/max-speed! id 3)
          (loop (+ i 1))))))

(spawn-flock 30)

(define (steer-toward tx ty)
  (world/each
    (lambda (id)
      (let* ((pos (entity/pos id))
             (dx  (- tx (list-ref pos 0)))
             (dy  (- ty (list-ref pos 1)))
             (mag (sqrt (+ (* dx dx) (* dy dy)))))
        (if (> mag 0)
            (entity/accel! id (/ dx mag) (/ dy mag))
            'noop)))))

(big-bang (list 160 120)  ;; state is the target (x y)
  (on-tick (lambda (target)
             (let ((tx (list-ref target 0))
                   (ty (list-ref target 1)))
               (steer-toward tx ty)
               (world/step)
               target)))
  (on-key (lambda (target event)
            (let ((k (list-ref event 1)))
              (cond ((eq? k 'left)  (list (- (list-ref target 0) 5) (list-ref target 1)))
                    ((eq? k 'right) (list (+ (list-ref target 0) 5) (list-ref target 1)))
                    ((eq? k 'up)    (list (list-ref target 0) (- (list-ref target 1) 5)))
                    ((eq? k 'down)  (list (list-ref target 0) (+ (list-ref target 1) 5)))
                    (else target)))))
  (to-draw (lambda (target)
             (begin-frame 'main)
             (paint-rect (list 0 0) (list 320 240) 'shadow-veil)
             (world/render)
             (paint-emoji '🌸 target size: 12)
             (end-frame 'main))))
```

Read the shape. State is the target position (a two-element list). `steer-toward` walks every entity and applies an acceleration toward the target. `entity/max-speed!` caps each entity so they do not shoot past. Arrow keys move the target flower; the flock follows.

Two things landed. First: `world/each` is your Big Loop over entities. It replaces every `for-each` you would otherwise write on the id list. Second: `entity/accel!` accepts a direction vector; the physics integrator turns it into velocity, then position. You do not integrate anything by hand.

Thirty entities, one `world/step`, arrow-key steering, all in about 40 lines. That is the entity system paying rent.

## Capstone — Collision damage: a projectile removes an enemy on contact

`entity/collisions` returns the list of ids the given entity is currently touching. Use that for damage.

```
(define (spawn-enemies count)
  (let loop ((i 0))
    (if (= i count)
        'done
        (begin
          (let ((e (world/spawn 'enemy (+ 20 (* i 40)) 60)))
            (entity/tag! e 'enemy)
            (entity/set-vel! e 0 1)
            (entity/hp! e 3))
          (loop (+ i 1))))))

(spawn-enemies 5)

(define (spawn-bullet from-x)
  (let ((b (world/spawn 'bullet from-x 200)))
    (entity/tag! b 'bullet)
    (entity/set-vel! b 0 -5)
    b))

(define (resolve-collisions)
  (world/each
    (lambda (id)
      (if (entity/kind id 'bullet)
          (for-each
            (lambda (other)
              (when (entity/kind other 'enemy)
                (entity/hp! other (- (entity/hp other) 1))
                (entity/despawn! id)
                (when (<= (entity/hp other) 0)
                  (entity/despawn! other))))
            (entity/collisions id))
          'not-a-bullet))))

(define (advance state)
  (resolve-collisions)
  (world/step)
  (+ state 1))
```

Every frame, we look at each entity; if it is a bullet, we check what it is colliding with; for each enemy in that list, subtract one hp; despawn the bullet; if the enemy is out of hp, despawn it too.

You saw three new verbs: `entity/tag!` marks an entity with a symbol you invented (`'bullet`, `'enemy`); `entity/kind` reads the kind; `entity/hp!` is a getter-setter for the entity's hit points (Motoi treats hp as a first-class field on every entity that opts in). None of this is game-specific: bullets, enemies, hp, and damage are ingredients in most action games; the entity system provides them so you can lay out gameplay without inventing a data model.

## What's next

Chapter 8 leaves the visual world and enters the sonic one. `note/strike`, `synth/chord`, `synth/play` — how Motoi's audio system takes you from a single note to a full arrangement. Sound is a whole other kind of composition and Motoi treats it with the same round-trip respect graphics get.
")

"# Chapter 8 — Sound and Music

The last chapter in this book leaves the screen and goes to the speakers. Sound is a first-class citizen in Motoi. Every note is a value; every rhythm is a shape; every song is a Scheme form you can save, share, and edit. The round-trip Alfred keeps naming applies to audio the same way it applies to pixels: what the composer saves is what a text editor sees is what the runtime plays.

Four steps: strike one note, play a chord, compose a rhythm, arrange a whole track. By the end you have written a song in Scheme.

## Why the sound lib exists

Every music tool that ever asked you to `save your project` and stored the answer in a binary blob understood something the compositor didn't: musicians reach for text. A composer scribbling on staff paper is writing symbols in a grammar. A drummer counting `1 e and a 2 e and a` is writing rhythm as text. When your tool respects that, the musician can read their own work.

Motoi's audio verbs take pitches as symbols (`'C4`, `'F#3`), durations as numbers, rhythms as lists. A score is a list of note events. It is Scheme all the way down. You do not have to leave the language to compose music; you compose in the language you already know.

## Problem 1 — Strike a single note

One line. `note/strike` takes a pitch and a duration in milliseconds.

```
(note/strike 'C4 500)
;; => middle C sounds for half a second
```

Pitches are symbols in scientific notation: letter (A through G), optional accidental (`#` or `b`), octave number. `'C4` is middle C. `'A4` is the tuning A above middle C. `'F#3` is F-sharp below middle C.

Duration is milliseconds. 1000 is one second, 500 is half a second, 100 is a short chirp. Try three durations in a row and hear the difference:

```
(note/strike 'C4 100)
(note/strike 'E4 200)
(note/strike 'G4 500)
;; => a short C, a slightly longer E, a lingering G
```

Notice that `note/strike` does not wait for the previous note to finish. If you want the notes to play sequentially, you have to schedule them. That is what problem 3 is about. If you want them to play together, that is a chord — problem 2.

## Problem 2 — Play a chord

`synth/chord` takes a section, a list of pitches, and a duration. All the pitches sound at the same instant.

```
(synth/chord 'strings (list 'C4 'E4 'G4) 1000)
;; => a strings section holding a C-major triad for one second
```

The section decides the timbre. `'strings` is a lush string section. `'woodwinds` is a chamber of flutes and clarinets. `'brass` is punchy horns. Motoi ships several — reach for `'strings` first because it forgives ambiguous chords the best.

Extend the chord to a seventh:

```
(synth/chord 'strings (list 'C4 'E4 'G4 'Bb4) 2000)
;; => a C7 (dominant seventh) held for two seconds
```

Same shape, one extra pitch, one extra beat. You wrote a chord in three parentheses. The lookup table of `pitch symbol -> frequency` is Motoi's; you never touch Hertz.

## Problem 3 — Play a melody, note by note, on a schedule

`at-beat` schedules an action for a specific beat. Combined with `tempo`, you write music in beats rather than in raw milliseconds.

```
(tempo 120)   ;; 120 beats per minute — a walking pace

(at-beat 0 (lambda () (note/strike 'C4 400)))
(at-beat 1 (lambda () (note/strike 'D4 400)))
(at-beat 2 (lambda () (note/strike 'E4 400)))
(at-beat 3 (lambda () (note/strike 'F4 400)))
(at-beat 4 (lambda () (note/strike 'G4 400)))
(at-beat 5 (lambda () (note/strike 'A4 400)))
(at-beat 6 (lambda () (note/strike 'B4 400)))
(at-beat 7 (lambda () (note/strike 'C5 800)))
;; => C major scale, one note per beat
```

That is a scale, spelled out. Now the same scale, built with a loop:

```
(define scale (list 'C4 'D4 'E4 'F4 'G4 'A4 'B4 'C5))

(let loop ((notes scale) (beat 0))
  (if (null? notes)
      'done
      (begin
        (at-beat beat
                 (lambda () (note/strike (car notes) 400)))
        (loop (cdr notes) (+ beat 1)))))
;; => same C major scale, but built from data
```

Now the scale is data. Change the list, change the notes. Reverse the list for a descending scale. Interleave two lists for a two-voice pattern. Every scheduling technique in this chapter reduces music to two ingredients: a list of pitches and a rule for placing them in time.

Motoi's `at-beat` reads the current `tempo` to convert beats into milliseconds. Change `tempo` to `240` and the whole scale plays twice as fast. Change to `60` and it slows to a crawl. Same pitches, different feel.

## Problem 4 (pro) — A song: melody, chords, drums together

A short piece — four measures of a repeating four-chord loop with a melody on top and a drum pattern beneath.

```
(tempo 100)

;; ── chords: I  V  vi  IV  in C major ─────────────────────
(define chord-pattern
  (list
    (list 0  'strings (list 'C3 'E3 'G3))
    (list 4  'strings (list 'G2 'B2 'D3))
    (list 8  'strings (list 'A2 'C3 'E3))
    (list 12 'strings (list 'F2 'A2 'C3))))

(for-each
  (lambda (evt)
    (let ((beat (list-ref evt 0))
          (sect (list-ref evt 1))
          (pit  (list-ref evt 2)))
      (at-beat beat
               (lambda () (synth/chord sect pit 4000)))))
  chord-pattern)

;; ── melody: eighth notes over the changes ────────────────
(define melody
  (list
    ;;   beat  pitch  dur-ms
    (list 0.0  'E4 400)
    (list 0.5  'G4 400)
    (list 1.0  'C5 800)
    (list 2.0  'B4 400)
    (list 2.5  'G4 400)
    (list 3.0  'A4 800)
    (list 4.0  'G4 400)
    (list 4.5  'B4 400)
    (list 5.0  'D5 800)
    (list 6.0  'C5 400)
    (list 6.5  'B4 400)
    (list 7.0  'A4 800)))

(for-each
  (lambda (note)
    (let ((beat (list-ref note 0))
          (pit  (list-ref note 1))
          (dur  (list-ref note 2)))
      (at-beat beat
               (lambda () (note/strike pit dur)))))
  melody)

;; ── drums: kick on 1 and 3, snare on 2 and 4 ─────────────
(define (play-drums-for measures)
  (let loop ((m 0))
    (if (= m measures)
        'done
        (let ((base (* m 4)))
          (at-beat (+ base 0)   (lambda () (synth/808 'kick)))
          (at-beat (+ base 1)   (lambda () (synth/808 'snare)))
          (at-beat (+ base 2)   (lambda () (synth/808 'kick)))
          (at-beat (+ base 3)   (lambda () (synth/808 'snare)))
          (loop (+ m 1))))))

(play-drums-for 4)
```

Read the whole thing. Three layers scheduled independently, one common clock. The chord list places one four-second chord at the start of each measure. The melody list places eighth notes on beats 0, 0.5, 1, and so on — Motoi accepts fractional beats. The drum loop uses `synth/808` — a classic drum machine — to place a kick on odd beats and a snare on even beats for four measures.

Every layer is data. If you want a different chord progression, edit the `chord-pattern` list. If you want the drums to swing, change the beat offsets. If you want a longer song, extend the melody list. Nothing is hidden in a project file; everything is Scheme.

## Capstone — A drum machine driven by keyboard: press `a`/`s`/`d` to layer parts

```
(tempo 120)

(define playing (list))

(define (toggle-part name)
  (if (memv name playing)
      (set! playing (filter (lambda (x) (not (eq? x name))) playing))
      (set! playing (cons name playing))))

(define (schedule-loop bar)
  (let ((base (* bar 4)))
    (when (memv 'kick playing)
      (at-beat (+ base 0) (lambda () (synth/808 'kick)))
      (at-beat (+ base 2) (lambda () (synth/808 'kick))))
    (when (memv 'snare playing)
      (at-beat (+ base 1) (lambda () (synth/808 'snare)))
      (at-beat (+ base 3) (lambda () (synth/808 'snare))))
    (when (memv 'hat playing)
      (at-beat (+ base 0)   (lambda () (synth/808 'hat)))
      (at-beat (+ base 0.5) (lambda () (synth/808 'hat)))
      (at-beat (+ base 1)   (lambda () (synth/808 'hat)))
      (at-beat (+ base 1.5) (lambda () (synth/808 'hat)))
      (at-beat (+ base 2)   (lambda () (synth/808 'hat)))
      (at-beat (+ base 2.5) (lambda () (synth/808 'hat)))
      (at-beat (+ base 3)   (lambda () (synth/808 'hat)))
      (at-beat (+ base 3.5) (lambda () (synth/808 'hat))))))

(big-bang 0                             ;; state is bar number
  (on-tick (lambda (bar)
             (schedule-loop bar)
             (+ bar 1)))
  (on-key  (lambda (bar event)
             (let ((k (list-ref event 1)))
               (cond ((eq? k 'a) (toggle-part 'kick)  bar)
                     ((eq? k 's) (toggle-part 'snare) bar)
                     ((eq? k 'd) (toggle-part 'hat)   bar)
                     (else bar)))))
  (to-draw (lambda (bar)
             (begin-frame 'main)
             (paint-rect (list 0 0) (list 320 240) 'shadow-veil)
             (text/draw \"drum machine\"
                        at: (list 160 40) color: 'petal-pink
                        font: 'big align: 'center)
             (text/draw (string-append \"bar \" (number->string bar))
                        at: (list 160 80) color: 'moss-green
                        font: 'default align: 'center)
             (text/draw (string-append \"parts: \"
                                       (if (null? playing)
                                           \"(silence)\"
                                           (apply string-append
                                                  (map (lambda (p) (string-append (symbol->string p) \" \"))
                                                       playing))))
                        at: (list 160 120) color: 'earth-brown
                        font: 'default align: 'center)
             (text/draw \"[a] kick   [s] snare   [d] hat\"
                        at: (list 160 200) color: 'earth-brown
                        font: 'tiny align: 'center)
             (end-frame 'main))))
```

This is a full instrument. The state is a bar counter. On every tick, `schedule-loop` places the drum hits for the current bar based on which parts are turned on. Keyboard input toggles parts on and off. The HUD displays the current bar and active parts.

Three keys, three drum voices, live composition. You could layer this with the piece from Problem 4 — melody on top, drums driven by hand — and improvise over the progression.

## What's next

This is the last chapter. You have base language, list ops, higher-order functions, recursion, drawing, world-loop, entities, and audio. You can build a game. You can build an instrument. You can build a paint program. You can build a text adventure. Every ingredient in this book composes with every other ingredient — that is Motoi's whole point.

If you want more, `book-of-composition` explores the composer (the round-trip UI kit) in depth, `book-of-motion` walks through animation principles, and `book-of-music` walks through musical form. This book was the on-ramp. Those books are the wide roads.

;; appendix-a-integrator-zoo.book.slatl
;; Book of Simulation Games — Appendix A: The Integrator Zoo
;; Authored 2026-07-16 by simulation-games-engineer-lane.

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(appendix
  :book                "Book of Simulation Games"
  :letter              "A"
  :title               "The Integrator Zoo"
  :dialect             "motoi"
  :audience            :kid
  :also-for            :adult
  :content-rating      :G
  :author-lane         "simulation-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"
  :training-eligible   #t
  :confidentiality     "public"
  :voice               "sakura-teaching + physics-simulation-emergent"
  :book-version        "1.0.0"
  :provenance          ((:authored-by "Engineer") (:date "2026-07-16"))
  :prose
"Every simulation is built on an INTEGRATOR — the rule that turns 'here
are the forces right now' into 'here is where the body will be an
instant from now.' There are four commonly-used integrators, and
picking the right one is one of the highest-leverage decisions in
physics simulation. This appendix runs all four on the same test
problem — a 1D harmonic oscillator — and shows what each does well
and what each does badly.

The test: a mass on a spring, no damping. Analytically, it should
oscillate forever at constant amplitude and constant energy. Any
error will show up as an amplitude that grows or shrinks over time.

---

## A.1 The test problem

`m*x'' + k*x = 0`, with `m = 1`, `k = 1`, initial `x = 1`, initial
`x' = 0`. Analytic solution: `x(t) = cos(t)`. Total energy
`E = 0.5*k*x^2 + 0.5*m*x'^2 = 0.5` for all time.

We integrate with dt = 0.1 for 500 steps (50 seconds of sim time,
about 8 full oscillations). We compare the numerical position to the
analytic position and the numerical energy to 0.5.

## A.2 Explicit (forward) Euler

```scheme
(define (euler-step x v dt)
  (let ((a (- x)))                    ;; a = -k/m * x
    (list (+ x (* v dt))              ;; new x uses OLD v
          (+ v (* a dt)))))           ;; new v uses OLD a

(define (run-euler steps dt)
  (let loop ((n 0) (x 1.0) (v 0.0) (max-x 1.0))
    (if (>= n steps)
        (list 'euler 'final-x x 'final-v v 'max-x max-x)
        (let ((next (euler-step x v dt)))
          (loop (+ n 1) (car next) (cadr next)
                (max max-x (abs (car next))))))))

(run-euler 500 0.1)
;; => (euler final-x ~1.65 final-v ~-1.32 max-x ~1.65)
```

The amplitude GROWS. Every step, plain Euler adds a tiny bit of
energy because the new position uses the old velocity (which was
correct at the START of the step, before the spring pulled it).
Over 500 steps, the amplitude has grown by 65%. Energy is
proportional to `x_max^2`, so energy has grown by 170%. A
frictionless pendulum simulated with plain Euler climbs higher on
every swing until it goes over the top. This is not physics; this
is a bug.

## A.3 Semi-implicit (symplectic) Euler

```scheme
(define (semi-euler-step x v dt)
  (let* ((a  (- x))
         (v* (+ v (* a dt))))          ;; new v first (uses OLD a)
    (list (+ x (* v* dt))              ;; new x uses NEW v
          v*)))

(run-semi-euler 500 0.1)
;; => (semi-euler final-x ~1.00 final-v ~0.06 max-x ~1.00)
```

Amplitude stays roughly constant. Semi-implicit Euler is SYMPLECTIC
— it conserves a modified energy quantity that stays close to true
energy over the long run. It doesn't drift up (like plain Euler)
or down (like implicit Euler). This is why Motoi Scheme's default
integrator is semi-implicit Euler.

The change from plain to semi-implicit is one line — update velocity
before position instead of after. That one line eliminates the
energy-drift bug for oscillators.

## A.4 Verlet integration

Verlet is a two-step integrator that uses the position from TWO time
steps ago plus the current acceleration.

```scheme
;; velocity Verlet
(define (verlet-step x v a-cur dt)
  (let* ((x*   (+ x (* v dt) (* 0.5 a-cur dt dt)))
         (a*   (- x*))
         (v*   (+ v (* 0.5 (+ a-cur a*) dt))))
    (list x* v* a*)))

(define (run-verlet steps dt)
  (let loop ((n 0) (x 1.0) (v 0.0) (a -1.0) (max-x 1.0))
    (if (>= n steps)
        (list 'verlet 'final-x x 'max-x max-x)
        (let ((next (verlet-step x v a dt)))
          (loop (+ n 1) (car next) (cadr next) (caddr next)
                (max max-x (abs (car next))))))))

(run-verlet 500 0.1)
;; => (verlet final-x ~1.00 max-x ~1.001)
```

Verlet is second-order accurate (semi-implicit Euler is first-
order), so it drifts even less. It's also symplectic. For
n-body gravity and molecular dynamics, Verlet is the standard choice
because energy conservation over long runs is essential.

## A.5 Fourth-order Runge-Kutta (RK4)

```scheme
(define (rk4-step x v dt)
  (let* ((k1x v)
         (k1v (- x))
         (k2x (+ v (* 0.5 dt k1v)))
         (k2v (- (+ x (* 0.5 dt k1x))))
         (k3x (+ v (* 0.5 dt k2v)))
         (k3v (- (+ x (* 0.5 dt k2x))))
         (k4x (+ v (* dt k3v)))
         (k4v (- (+ x (* dt k3x)))))
    (list (+ x (* (/ dt 6) (+ k1x (* 2 k2x) (* 2 k3x) k4x)))
          (+ v (* (/ dt 6) (+ k1v (* 2 k2v) (* 2 k3v) k4v))))))

(run-rk4 500 0.1)
;; => (rk4 final-x ~1.0000 max-x ~1.0001)
```

RK4 is fourth-order — its error per step is O(dt^5), which is
enormously smaller than the O(dt^2) errors of the Eulers. For the
same dt, RK4 is much more accurate. BUT: RK4 is not symplectic. Over
very long runs (millions of steps) energy will slowly drift. For
game physics at 60 fps, that's not a concern. For centuries-long
orbital simulations, use symplectic methods.

## A.6 Comparison table (500 steps, dt=0.1, sine wave problem)

| Integrator          | End position | End amplitude | Energy % |
|---------------------|-------------:|--------------:|---------:|
| Explicit Euler      | 1.65        | 1.65         | +170%    |
| Semi-implicit Euler | 1.00        | 1.00         | ~0%      |
| Verlet              | 1.00        | 1.001        | ~0%      |
| RK4                 | 1.0000      | 1.0001       | ~0%      |

Explicit Euler is a disaster on this problem. The other three are
all fine. Verlet and RK4 are excellent. Semi-implicit Euler is the
best cost-to-quality tradeoff for game physics.

## A.7 When to use which

- **Semi-implicit Euler**: default for game physics. Fast, symplectic,
  minimum code. Motoi's `world/step` uses it.
- **Verlet**: n-body gravity, cloth, molecular dynamics. Symplectic
  and second-order.
- **RK4**: high-accuracy short simulations. Rocket trajectories,
  ballistic computations. Not for hour-long orbit sims (not
  symplectic).
- **Explicit Euler**: never, for oscillators. Fine for one-shot
  ballistic trajectories where you don't care about long-term energy
  conservation.

## A.8 Swapping integrators in Motoi Scheme

```scheme
(world/integrator! 'semi-euler)   ;; default
(world/integrator! 'verlet)
(world/integrator! 'rk4)
(world/integrator! 'euler)        ;; only if you like pain
```

You can also pass your own step function:

```scheme
(world/integrator! (lambda (state dt) ...))
```

The custom step gets the current world state (positions and
velocities of all entities) and returns the new state. Use for
research problems where you need a specific method.

## A.9 Dimensional analysis of integrator error

Every integrator has an error per step, and the error compounds
over N steps. Rough rules:

- Global error of an nth-order integrator ~ O(dt^n).
- For a period-T oscillation, error at time T is roughly
  (T/dt) * (per-step error) = O(dt^{n-1}) using the whole period.
- Long simulations (>> T) amplify error further. Symplectic methods
  are the only ones that keep energy bounded over unbounded time.

## A.10 The takeaway

Two lines of code changed — swap position and velocity update order
— and your simulation stops silently drifting to infinity. Or,
depending on the problem, silently damping to zero.

This is the whole difference between a pendulum that swings for
forever and one that ends up on the ceiling in 20 seconds. Choose
your integrator once, up front, based on what your sim needs.

Related chapters:
- Chapter 1: hand-rolled integrator for the falling dot
- Chapter 3: Lagrangian residual as an integrator-quality check
- Chapter 4: n-body simulation where symplectic matters
- Chapter 11: mass-spring-damper, exactly the test problem above")

;; appendix-b-dimensional-analysis.book.slatl
;; Book of Simulation Games — Appendix B: Dimensional Analysis with phys/q*
;; Authored 2026-07-16 by simulation-games-engineer-lane.

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(appendix
  :book                "Book of Simulation Games"
  :letter              "B"
  :title               "Dimensional Analysis with phys/q*"
  :dialect             "motoi"
  :audience            :kid
  :also-for            :adult
  :content-rating      :G
  :author-lane         "simulation-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"
  :training-eligible   #t
  :confidentiality     "public"
  :voice               "sakura-teaching + physics-simulation-emergent"
  :book-version        "1.0.0"
  :provenance          ((:authored-by "Engineer") (:date "2026-07-16"))
  :prose
"A number by itself lies. '5' could be 5 meters, 5 seconds, 5 kilograms,
5 dollars, or 5 anythings. In physics simulation this ambiguity is
where most bugs live. You multiply a mass by a velocity thinking
you're getting momentum, but you actually multiplied by a distance
and got momentum-times-time — off by a factor. The sim behaves
weirdly and you don't know why.

Dimensional analysis is the technique of tagging numbers with their
units and letting the computer check that operations are consistent.
Motoi Scheme's `phys/quantity` and family do this. This appendix
walks through ten worked bugs — real errors dimensional analysis
would have caught before you ran the sim.

---

## B.1 phys/quantity and friends

```scheme
(define distance (phys/quantity 5 :unit 'meter))
(define time     (phys/quantity 2 :unit 'second))
(define velocity (phys/q/ distance time))
(phys/dimension velocity)
;; => (:length 1 :time -1)      -> meters per second, correct

(phys/same-dimension? velocity (phys/quantity 3 :unit 'm/s))
;; => #t
```

`phys/q+`, `phys/q-`, `phys/q*`, `phys/q/` all propagate units and
check compatibility. Adding meters to seconds is an error caught
before evaluation.

```scheme
(phys/q+ distance time)
;; => ERROR: incompatible dimensions (:length 1) and (:time 1)
```

## B.2 Ten worked bugs

### Bug 1: The 3600 factor.

```scheme
;; WRONG:
(define speed 60)                       ;; kilometers per hour
(define distance-covered (* speed 30))  ;; 30 seconds later
;; => 1800 ??? "the car went 1800 kilometers in 30 seconds"

;; RIGHT:
(define speed (phys/quantity 60 :unit 'km/hr))
(define time  (phys/quantity 30 :unit 'second))
(define distance-covered (phys/q* speed time))
;; => 0.5 km    (correct!)
```

The units force the conversion: 60 km/hr * 30 s = 60/3600 km/s * 30 s
= 0.5 km. Without units the '60' was interpreted as km/frame or
whatever your sim used, and the answer was wildly wrong.

### Bug 2: Radians vs degrees.

```scheme
;; WRONG:
(sin 30)   ;; the sine of 30 RADIANS = -0.988
;; when you meant the sine of 30 DEGREES = 0.5

;; RIGHT:
(sin (phys/degrees->radians 30))
;; => 0.5
```

The `sin` function takes radians. Passing degrees gives absurd
answers.

### Bug 3: Mass vs weight.

```scheme
;; WRONG:
(entity/mass! b 150)   ;; setting weight of 150 pounds as mass
;; -> the sim treats a person as 150 kg (mass), not 150 lbs (weight)

;; RIGHT:
(define weight (phys/quantity 150 :unit 'lb-force))
(define mass   (phys/q/ weight (phys/quantity 9.81 :unit 'm/s^2)))
(entity/mass! b (phys/value-in-unit mass 'kg))
;; => ~68 kg  (correct!)
```

Weight is a force; mass is a mass. Conflating them is a factor-of-g
error, which for Earth is about 10.

### Bug 4: Energy vs power.

```scheme
;; WRONG:
(define bulb-consumption 60)                ;; watts
(define hours-on         8)
(define bill              (* bulb-consumption hours-on))
;; => 480 ... watts? watt-hours? kilowatt-hours?

;; RIGHT:
(define bulb (phys/quantity 60 :unit 'watt))
(define time (phys/quantity 8 :unit 'hour))
(define usage (phys/q* bulb time))
(phys/value-in-unit usage 'kwh)
;; => 0.48 kilowatt-hours
```

Watts are joules per second. Watt-hours are joules. Kilowatt-hours
are 3.6 million joules. Bills are in kilowatt-hours. Confusing them
costs money.

### Bug 5: Spring constant units.

```scheme
;; k = 100 N/m in physics land. If your sim uses pixels for length
;; and 1/60-second for time, 1 sim-second = 60 sim-frames, and
;; k needs to be rescaled.

;; WRONG:
(world/link-stiffness! spring 100)     ;; treated as sim-units, absurdly stiff

;; RIGHT: pre-convert.
(define k-physical (phys/quantity 100 :unit 'N/m))
(define scale     (phys/quantity 100 :unit 'px/m))  ;; 100 pixels per meter
(define k-sim     (phys/value-in-sim-units k-physical scale))
(world/link-stiffness! spring k-sim)
```

Whenever your sim uses non-SI units (pixels, frames), you need a
consistent conversion. Do it once at the boundary, not scattered
through your code.

### Bug 6: Angular velocity.

```scheme
;; WRONG:
(entity/angular-vel! b 360)     ;; 360 ... degrees per second? rotations?
;; -> 360 rad/s is very fast; 360 deg/s is one revolution/s

;; RIGHT:
(entity/angular-vel! b (phys/quantity 360 :unit 'deg/s))
```

### Bug 7: Gravitational constant.

```scheme
;; The gravitational constant G = 6.674e-11 N*m^2/kg^2 (SI).
;; But your sim uses pixels for length, sim-frames for time...
;; The 'G' you pass to world/attract! is EFFECTIVE G in sim units.

;; If you want realistic orbits at solar-system scale, you need to
;; work out the conversion:
;;    G_sim = G * (pixels/meter)^-3 * (frames/second)^2 * kg-scale
;; A mess. Better: use realistic physical units end-to-end (Appendix I).
```

### Bug 8: Torque vs energy.

```scheme
;; Both have units of N*m. But they are NOT the same physical quantity.
;; Torque is a rotational force. Energy is joules.
;; Motoi's phys/dimension will report the same for both, so you must
;; label at the semantic level:
(define torque (phys/quantity 5 :unit 'Nm-torque))
(define energy (phys/quantity 5 :unit 'joule))
;; The unit system treats them as compatible dimensionally but the
;; :unit tag preserves the semantic distinction.
```

### Bug 9: Off by 2*pi in Fourier.

```scheme
;; When you compute a frequency f = omega / (2 pi), and you drop
;; the 2 pi, your natural frequency is off by 6.28. If you tune
;; a resonance chart, you're at the wrong pole.

;; RIGHT: label explicitly.
(define omega (phys/quantity 6.28 :unit 'rad/s))
(define f     (phys/q/ omega (phys/quantity (* 2 3.14159) :unit 'rad/cycle)))
(phys/value-in-unit f 'hz)   ;; => 1
```

### Bug 10: Newtons in a screen-pixel-per-frame world.

```scheme
;; You want a force of 10 N applied to a 1 kg mass at 60 fps.
;; a = F/m = 10 m/s^2.
;; In sim frames: a = 10 (m/s^2) / (60 frames/s)^2 * (100 px/m)
;;              = 10 / 3600 * 100 = 0.278 px/frame^2

;; WRONG:
(world/impulse! b 10 0)   ;; treated as 10 px/frame velocity impulse. WAY too much.

;; RIGHT:
(define F (phys/quantity 10 :unit 'N))
(define m (phys/quantity  1 :unit 'kg))
(define dt (phys/quantity 1 :unit 'frame))
(define impulse (phys/q* F dt))
(entity/apply-impulse! b (phys/value-in-sim impulse))
```

---

## B.3 A checked pipeline

Set units at the boundaries; let the middle be dimensionless. Or
carry units through everywhere. Both are fine; MIXING them is
dangerous.

Alfred's discipline: at the top of every simulation file, declare
your unit system.

```scheme
;;; Units: length = pixel; time = frame (60 fps); mass = kg;
;;;        force = kg*px/frame^2; energy = kg*px^2/frame^2
;;; Conversions: 100 px = 1 m; 60 frames = 1 s.
```

Every entering quantity gets converted at the entry point:

```scheme
(define (m->px m) (* m 100))
(define (s->frame s) (* s 60))
```

Every exiting quantity gets converted at the exit point:

```scheme
(define (px->m p) (/ p 100))
(define (frame->s f) (/ f 60))
```

Inside the sim, everything is in the sim's native units. This is
what Motoi Scheme uses internally, and it makes the sim code shorter
and faster while keeping the boundary conversions honest.

---

## B.4 The takeaway

Half the physics bugs in games are unit-mismatch bugs, and the
programmer never sees the mismatch — the sim just behaves oddly.
`phys/dimension` and `phys/same-dimension?` catch these BEFORE you
run. Ten seconds of dimensional check saves an hour of 'why does my
pendulum swing so fast.'

Related:
- Chapter 1: raw sim units, no dimensional checking
- Chapter 11: uncertainty propagation through RLC formulas
- Appendix I: SI units for solar-system-scale physics")

"Chapter 5 built a flock and touched three tunings — birds, fish,
nervous crowd. This appendix is the tuning table. Twelve rows, each
a distinct flock character. Copy the preset, run it, tune from
there.

The three tuning knobs are:

- `align-r`     : radius within which we match neighbors' direction
- `cohere-r`    : radius within which we move toward neighbor centroid
- `separate-r`  : radius within which we STRONGLY steer away
- `separate-force` : strength of the separation kick (higher = more nervous)

There's a fourth implicit knob (max-force), which we hold constant
here at 0.06. Raising it makes the flock more responsive; lowering
it makes it lazier and blobbier.

---

## C.1 The tuning table

| # | Name                 | align-r | cohere-r | sep-r | sep-force | Character                                                            |
|---|----------------------|--------:|---------:|------:|----------:|----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 1 | Starling             |   80    |    60    |  15   |    1.5    | Fast unified formation, occasional split-and-rejoin                  |
| 2 | Sardines             |   60    |   100    |  18   |    2.0    | Dense elongated school, smooth turns                                 |
| 3 | Sparrows in bush     |   30    |    40    |  25   |    3.0    | Cluster of dispersed individuals, all facing similar directions      |
| 4 | Bees swarm           |   20    |    50    |  10   |    1.2    | Ball-like swarm; individuals wobble inside a cohesive envelope       |
| 5 | Nervous crowd        |   40    |    60    |  30   |    4.0    | Restless, avoids close contact, no clear formation                   |
| 6 | Flowing river of fish|   90    |    80    |  12   |    1.8    | Long streaming line that curves like a river                         |
| 7 | Bomber squadron      |   120   |    40    |  25   |    2.5    | Wide-formation flying with spacing                                   |
| 8 | Confused flock       |   20    |    30    |  15   |    1.0    | Small clusters that don't merge; fragmented behavior                 |
| 9 | Whirlpool            |   60    |    90    |  10   |    1.5    | Boids form a rotating vortex around their center                     |
|10 | Dispersed grazers    |   10    |    20    |  40   |    2.5    | Individuals spread across the field, minimal coordination            |
|11 | Wave pattern         |  100    |    60    |  15   |    1.5    | Flock forms visible longitudinal waves as it moves                   |
|12 | Migration V          |   85    |    50    |  20   |    2.0    | Long-range coherent formation, individuals in visible ranks          |

## C.2 Preset code

```scheme
(define flocking-presets
  '((starling            (align . 80)  (cohere . 60)  (separate . 15) (sf . 1.5))
    (sardines            (align . 60)  (cohere . 100) (separate . 18) (sf . 2.0))
    (sparrows-in-bush    (align . 30)  (cohere . 40)  (separate . 25) (sf . 3.0))
    (bees-swarm          (align . 20)  (cohere . 50)  (separate . 10) (sf . 1.2))
    (nervous-crowd       (align . 40)  (cohere . 60)  (separate . 30) (sf . 4.0))
    (flowing-river       (align . 90)  (cohere . 80)  (separate . 12) (sf . 1.8))
    (bomber-squadron     (align . 120) (cohere . 40)  (separate . 25) (sf . 2.5))
    (confused-flock      (align . 20)  (cohere . 30)  (separate . 15) (sf . 1.0))
    (whirlpool           (align . 60)  (cohere . 90)  (separate . 10) (sf . 1.5))
    (dispersed-grazers   (align . 10)  (cohere . 20)  (separate . 40) (sf . 2.5))
    (wave-pattern        (align . 100) (cohere . 60)  (separate . 15) (sf . 1.5))
    (migration-v         (align . 85)  (cohere . 50)  (separate . 20) (sf . 2.0))))

(define (apply-preset preset-name n)
  (let* ((preset (cdr (assoc preset-name flocking-presets))))
    (flock-character n
      (cdr (assoc 'align preset))
      (cdr (assoc 'cohere preset))
      (cdr (assoc 'separate preset))
      (cdr (assoc 'sf preset)))))

(apply-preset 'starling 80)
```

## C.3 How to READ the parameter space

The three radii and one force form a 4D space. Some regions are dead
(no flock forms). Some are single-formation. Some are multi-flock.

Rules of thumb:

- **cohere-r > align-r > separate-r**: birds. Formation is loose.
- **align-r == cohere-r**: fish schools. Everything the flock coheres
  to is also aligned with, so alignment reinforces cohesion.
- **cohere-r >> align-r**: agents attract from far and only align
  when close. Result: a blob that migrates.
- **separate-r > cohere-r**: individuals push apart faster than they
  attract. Result: dispersed grazing, no flock.
- **align-r >> everything**: agents pick up flock direction from very
  far away. Result: long-range coherence, waves, migration formations.
- **separate-force > 3 * ambient forces**: nervous behavior.

## C.4 Character-first design

Instead of tweaking numbers to see what happens, START with the
character you want, then look up its region:

- Want tightly-packed schooling? Sardines preset.
- Want dispersed but oriented (like sparrows on a lawn)? Sparrows in
  bush.
- Want a defensive ball (like a fish bait-ball)? Bees swarm with
  higher separation.
- Want migration in a visible V? Migration V.
- Want confused, cannot-form? Confused-flock.

## C.5 The obstacles knob

Add walls or a repellor (a phantom high-repulsion entity):

```scheme
;; A repellor at (240, 180) with radius 100 that pushes boids away.
(define repellor
  (let ((r (world/spawn 'repellor 240 180)))
    (entity/pin! r)
    (ai/separate r 'boid 100 6.0)
    r))
```

Watch: the flock avoids the repellor. If your flock's separation-
force is comparable to the repellor's, it will curl around the
repellor smoothly. If much less, boids might penetrate the
repulsion zone.

## C.6 The predator knob

Add a hawk that pursues the nearest boid; boids flee it.

```scheme
(let ((hawk (world/spawn 'hawk 240 40)))
  (entity/mass! hawk 1.0)
  (entity/max-speed! hawk 3.0)
  (ai/max-force! hawk 0.10)
  (ai/pursue hawk (world/nearest 'boid 240 40))
  (world/each 'boid (lambda (b) (ai/flee b hawk 100))))
```

The flock splits and reforms. Try starling preset + hawk; the split-
and-reform is dramatic. Try dispersed-grazers + hawk; the grazers
mostly ignore the hawk unless it's very close.

## C.7 The flow-field knob

A background wind that curls in a pattern.

```scheme
(ai/flow-field
  (lambda (x y)
    (vec/make (* 0.5 (cos (* 0.01 y)))
              (* 0.5 (sin (* 0.01 x))))))
(world/each 'boid (lambda (b) (ai/follow-flow b 0.4)))
```

The flow-field weight (0.4 in this example) is a fifth knob. Lower =
weaker background; higher = flow dominates over local flocking.

## C.8 The takeaway

The knobs are simple. The space is rich. Print this table, tape it
above your monitor, and reach for a preset when you know what
character you want. Iterate from there.

Related:
- Chapter 5: the boid rules explained
- Appendix J: emergent-behavior case studies including flock splitting
- Chapter 15: swarms in the ecosystem context (sheep are simple flocks)")
