"There are three books on your shelf that could teach you Newton. One is
a textbook and has proofs; one is a picture book and has apples; and
one is this chapter, which has neither and instead runs a small program
sixty times a second until the program's behavior BECOMES Newton's
second law.

Force equals mass times acceleration is not a slogan. It is an
algorithm. It says: given the forces on a thing, compute its
acceleration. Given the acceleration and a slice of time, compute the
change in velocity. Given the velocity and the same slice of time,
compute the change in position. Then start over. This is what
`(world/step)` does under the hood — thirty times a second by default,
sixty if we ask nicely. There is nothing mysterious about the loop.
The loop IS the physics.

We are going to build this loop three times. First for one body,
falling. Then for two bodies pulling on each other. Then for fifty
bodies pulling on ALL the other bodies, at which point structure will
emerge that nobody wrote down — no line of our code will say 'form a
cluster,' but a cluster will form anyway. That is emergence, and it is
the surprise this whole book is about.

---

## 1.1 One body under gravity

The smallest possible physics simulation is a dot that falls.

```scheme
;; A dot at (160, 40) falls under gravity, lands on a floor at 240.
(define (drop-one-dot)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.5)          ;; a = (0, 0.5) px/frame^2
  (world/floor! 240)              ;; hard floor at y=240
  (let ((dot (world/spawn 'dot 160 40)))
    (entity/bounce! dot 0.0)      ;; no bounce
    (let loop ((n 60))
      (world/step)
      (if (> n 0) (loop (- n 1)) (entity/pos dot)))))

(drop-one-dot)
;; => (160.0 . 240.0)
```

Twenty acceleration units per second squared, forty pixels of headroom,
sixty frames. The dot lands. `world/step` is where the physics
actually happens; the rest of the program describes the world it is
happening in. If you strip the print and squint, this program is one
line: `(let loop ((n 60)) (world/step) (loop (- n 1)))`. Everything
else is setup.

## 1.2 What world/step is doing to your dot

Let's replace `(world/step)` with our own version. We will not
integrate the whole world — just this one dot — so we can watch each
part of the algorithm move on the page.

```scheme
;; Hand-rolled Euler integrator for one falling body.
(define (euler-drop steps)
  (let ((g  0.5)                     ;; acceleration
        (dt 1.0))                    ;; one frame = 1 unit of time
    (let loop ((n  steps)
               (y  40)
               (vy 0))
      (if (<= n 0)
          (cons y vy)
          (let* ((ay g)                        ;; acceleration this frame
                 (vy* (+ vy (* ay dt)))        ;; new velocity
                 (y*  (+ y  (* vy* dt))))      ;; new position (semi-implicit)
            (loop (- n 1) y* vy*))))))

(euler-drop 60)
;; => (930.0 . 30.0)   -> if we had no floor, this is where we'd be
```

Read that inner `let*` twice. First we compute the acceleration; then
the velocity that comes out of applying that acceleration for one
frame; then the position that comes out of moving at THAT NEW velocity
for one frame. This is semi-implicit Euler. If we had written
`(+ y (* vy dt))` with the OLD velocity, we would have plain-vanilla
Euler, which is worse. Appendix A shows the two side by side, and it
matters more than you might think — plain Euler adds a tiny bit of
energy every frame; a plain-Euler pendulum swings wider and wider until
it goes over the top. Semi-implicit Euler doesn't do that.

The `world/step` inside Motoi Scheme uses semi-implicit Euler as its
default. You can swap it — the appendix covers the swap — but the
default is chosen because it's the least amount of code that doesn't
blow up on the second pendulum.

## 1.3 Two bodies pulling on each other

One body under gravity is Newton's LAW. Two bodies pulling on each
other is Newton's UNIVERSAL law — the surprise is that gravity between
the Earth and an apple, and gravity between the Earth and the Moon,
and gravity between two marbles on a table, are all the SAME
phenomenon with different masses. We do not have to teach the marbles
about the apple. We just apply the formula.

```scheme
;; Two bodies. Each pulls on the other with F = G m1 m2 / r^2.
(define (two-body-attract)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((a (world/spawn 'a  80 120))
        (b (world/spawn 'b 240 120)))
    (entity/mass! a 5000)
    (entity/mass! b 5000)
    (entity/set-vel! a 0 -1.2)         ;; a drifts up
    (entity/set-vel! b 0  1.2)         ;; b drifts down
    (world/attract! a b 1.0)           ;; mutual gravity, G-effective = 1
    (world/attract! b a 1.0)
    (let loop ((n 400))
      (world/step)
      (if (> n 0) (loop (- n 1))
          (list (entity/pos a) (entity/pos b))))))

(two-body-attract)
;; => ((~89 ~118) (~231 ~122))    <- they drifted, then curled back
```

`world/attract!` installs a persistent inverse-square force from source
to target. We install it twice, once each way, because gravity is
mutual. Give them opposing initial velocities and they will curl
around each other in an ellipse, come back near their starting
positions, and do it again. It is a repeating orbit — the two-body
problem has closed-form solutions, and our numerical sim reproduces
one.

Notice the shape of the loop. Whether we have one body or two, the
outer loop is the same: `(world/step)` then check if we're done. This
is what makes the whole book possible — every simulation, from a
falling dot to a fifty-body cluster, uses this same shape. The only
thing that changes is what's in the world when the loop starts.

## 1.4 Many bodies — the arrival of emergence

Now fifty bodies. Each one pulls on every other one. We didn't tell
them to form a cluster; we told them to obey `F = G m1 m2 / r^2`.
Watch what happens.

```scheme
;; Fifty bodies, mutual gravity, no floor. Let them find their shape.
(define (cluster n)
  (world/reset!)
  (let loop ((i 0) (bodies '()))
    (if (>= i n)
        (bodies-attract-all bodies)
        (let* ((x  (+ 100 (* 200 (random))))
               (y  (+  80 (* 160 (random))))
               (vx (- (* 0.5 (random)) 0.25))
               (vy (- (* 0.5 (random)) 0.25))
               (b  (world/spawn 'star x y)))
          (entity/mass!    b (+ 50 (* 200 (random))))
          (entity/set-vel! b vx vy)
          (loop (+ i 1) (cons b bodies))))))

(define (bodies-attract-all bs)
  ;; Every body attracts every other body. (n^2) force installs.
  (for-each
    (lambda (a)
      (for-each
        (lambda (b)
          (when (not (eq? a b))
            (world/attract! a b 1.0)))
        bs))
    bs))

(cluster 50)
(let loop ((n 600)) (world/step) (when (> n 0) (loop (- n 1))))
```

After a few hundred frames you see it: the outliers get flung, the
inner bodies fall together, and a knot forms in the middle. Nothing
you wrote said 'form a knot.' The knot emerges because inverse-square
attraction pulls hard at short range, and once two heavy stars pass
close they capture each other, and once they capture each other other
stars fall in. Structure appears. This is the first surprise of the
book, and it will be repeated many times: give the pieces a rule,
apply it many times, and watch shapes appear that no line of code
demanded.

`phys/nbody` gives you the same effect without the `for-each` boilerplate:

```scheme
;; The same thing with the built-in n-body verb.
(define (cluster-nice n)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((bs (phys/nbody-spawn n
              :region   '(100 80 300 240)
              :mass     '(50 . 250)
              :vel      '(-0.25 . 0.25)
              :G        1.0)))
    bs))

(cluster-nice 50)
```

`phys/nbody-spawn` installs the (n(n-1)) attractions for you and
returns the list of entities. Under the hood: exactly the code above.

---

## 1.5 The four routing patterns in a simulation loop

The book on the shelf next to this one — Book of Systems — teaches
four patterns the runtime uses everywhere: composition, orchestration,
in-routing, and routing. Even a one-chapter simulation touches all
four. This section names them so you notice, next time, where the
pattern is.

**Composition.** `world/step` is not one verb; it is many small verbs
composed. Under the hood it does: apply forces, integrate velocities,
integrate positions, resolve constraints, check collisions, notify
handlers. We compose it into our own step for the hand-rolled dropper.
The `bodies-attract-all` function above is composition of `for-each`
with `world/attract!`.

**Orchestration.** The `let loop ((n 600))` is an orchestration of
`world/step` across time. It waits, it counts down, it eventually
returns. A more elaborate orchestration would `world/step` for 300
frames, `world/snapshot` the state, `world/step` for another 300
frames, and diff the snapshots to detect equilibrium.

**In-routing.** When two stars collide, the physics engine has to route
the collision event to the right handler. We haven't wired one yet, but
in chapter 4 you'll see:

```scheme
(world/on-collision! 'star 'star
  (lambda (a b) (entity/despawn! b)))  ;; merge two stars, keep one
```

The `'star 'star` is an in-route: 'when an entity tagged star hits
another entity tagged star, dispatch here.'

**Routing.** The result of the simulation has to go somewhere. Right
now our functions return positions to the REPL. In a running world,
each frame the positions route to the framebuffer via
`(paint-circle x y r color)`, the collision events route to an audio
handler, and any interesting emergent-cluster-forming events could
route to Cortex as 'this initial condition led to a bound cluster.'

Four patterns, all in one 60-line simulation. You'll see them again
in every chapter.

---

## 1.6 Common desktop tasks

An operator running a physical-goods shop asked the runtime once: 'if I hang
a light fixture from a chain, and someone opens the front door and a
wind comes through, how long until the fixture stops swinging?' That
is a one-body simulation. It is `world/gravity!` + `entity/pin!` + an
initial `world/impulse!` + `entity/friction!`, and it runs in eighty
lines. Chapter 3 builds it. The point today: one-body simulation is not
just for kids in astronomy class — it is a tool for answering everyday
questions about the physical world.

Another operator asked: 'if two of my parking spots are close together
and both are magnetized to pull cars in, will cars end up in one spot
or split evenly?' That is a two-body-attractor problem, and the answer
depends on the ratio of attraction strength to car separation. You can
find out with `two-body-attract` above; change 5000 to 2500 in one
mass and re-run. This is the shop-side use of simulation.

## 1.7 Try this yourself

1. Change gravity to (0.5, 0) — sideways gravity. Re-run
   `drop-one-dot`. Where does it land?
2. In `euler-drop`, change the order of the two updates so `y` is
   computed with `vy` instead of `vy*` (plain Euler). Run for 200
   steps. Compare the y-value against the exact formula
   `y = y0 + 0.5 * g * t^2`. Which is closer to the truth?
3. In `two-body-attract`, make body b's mass 10× body a's mass. Do
   both bodies still swing, or does the small one orbit the big one?
4. In `cluster`, start with 200 bodies instead of 50. Does the cluster
   form faster or slower? Why?

## 1.8 Pitfalls

**Blow-up.** If you set gravity too high and the timestep too big, the
dot skips through the floor. Semi-implicit Euler helps but doesn't
cure. Fix: smaller timestep, or use `world/floor!` which enforces
after every substep, or clamp velocity via `entity/max-speed!`.

**Ghost forces.** If you `world/attract!` in a running loop instead of
once, you install a fresh attractor every frame. Bodies fly away at
absurd speed. Install force relationships ONCE outside the loop.

**Symmetric-vs-antisymmetric.** `world/attract! a b` is 'a attracts
toward b.' Not 'they attract each other.' If you want mutual, call it
twice. This is a source of many first-week simulation bugs.

;; ch02-springs-chains-cloth.book.slatl
;; Book of Simulation Games — Chapter 2: Springs, Chains, Cloth
;; Authored 2026-07-16 by simulation-games-engineer-lane.

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(chapter
  :book                "Book of Simulation Games"
  :chapter-number      2
  :title               "Springs, Chains, Cloth"
  :dialect             "motoi"
  :audience            :kid
  :also-for            :adult
  :content-rating      :G
  :author-lane         "simulation-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"
  :training-eligible   #t
  :confidentiality     "public"
  :voice               "sakura-teaching + physics-simulation-emergent"
  :book-version        "1.0.0"
  :provenance          ((:authored-by "Engineer") (:date "2026-07-16"))
  :prose
"A spring is not a coil of metal. A spring is a rule. The rule says:
'if I am stretched, I pull my ends toward each other with a force
proportional to how far I am from my rest length; if I am compressed,
I push them apart the same way.' The coil of metal is one way to build
a thing that obeys the rule. So is a rubber band. So is the tension in
a rope. So is the force between two atoms in a molecule. Springs are
everywhere the moment you look for them.

We are going to link two entities with `world/link!`, tune the link's
rest length and stiffness with `world/link-rest!`, and watch the two
entities behave like they're connected. Then we'll chain ten of them.
Then we'll grid 225 of them into a piece of cloth and let gravity pull
it. By chapter's end you'll have a hammock you can grab with the mouse
and pull, and the hammock will sag where you pull and spring back when
you let go.

---

## 2.1 Two bodies, one spring

```scheme
;; Two entities. One spring. Watch them oscillate.
(define (two-and-a-spring)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0)                    ;; zero gravity: pure spring behavior
  (let ((a (world/spawn 'ball  80 200))
        (b (world/spawn 'ball 240 200)))
    (entity/mass! a 1.0)
    (entity/mass! b 1.0)
    (let ((link (world/link! a b)))
      (world/link-rest!      link 160)    ;; natural length = 160
      (world/link-stiffness! link 0.05)   ;; k
      (world/link-damping!   link 0.02)   ;; c
      (entity/set-vel! a -3 0)            ;; kick a to the left
      link)))

(two-and-a-spring)
(let loop ((n 300)) (world/step) (when (> n 0) (loop (- n 1))))
```

The two balls oscillate around their center of mass. Because we set
gravity to zero, the only force is the spring. Because we damped it
(`0.02`), the oscillation slowly decays; if we set damping to zero it
would ring forever, which is the sign of an ideal spring in a
frictionless universe. Real springs always have damping.

Read `world/link-stiffness!` as 'how hard the spring pulls.' Read
`world/link-damping!` as 'how much energy the spring bleeds into the
world each cycle.' Real cloth needs both. Real rope needs both. Real
hair needs both. The tuning table is Appendix F.

## 2.2 A chain — pin the top, let it swing

```scheme
;; A chain of 10 balls. The top is pinned; the rest swing.
(define (chain n rest)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.4)
  (let loop ((i 0) (prev #f) (balls '()))
    (if (>= i n)
        (reverse balls)
        (let ((b (world/spawn 'link (+ 160 (* i 2)) (+ 40 (* i rest)))))
          (entity/mass!     b 1.0)
          (entity/drag!     b 0.01)
          (when (= i 0) (entity/pin! b))         ;; top-of-chain fixed
          (when prev
            (let ((L (world/link! prev b)))
              (world/link-rest!      L rest)
              (world/link-stiffness! L 0.30)     ;; stiffer than the free spring
              (world/link-damping!   L 0.05)))
          (loop (+ i 1) b (cons b balls))))))

(chain 10 12)
(let loop ((n 500)) (world/step) (when (> n 0) (loop (- n 1))))
```

Ten balls, nine springs, gravity pulling everything down, and the top
ball pinned. Because we spawned the chain with a slight rightward
offset per step (`(+ 160 (* i 2))`), it starts out slanted and swings
across when released. `entity/drag!` is per-entity air resistance — a
tiny amount so the swing decays without being obviously suppressed.

Notice: this is the same `world/step` loop as chapter 1. All we
changed is what's IN the world before the loop starts. The engine
doesn't know it's a chain. It only knows it has some entities with
some forces.

## 2.3 A cloth — a 15×15 grid of balls with 4-neighbor springs

```scheme
;; A cloth is a 2D grid of balls linked to their 4 neighbors.
;; Pin the top row. Gravity pulls the rest. Watch it hang.
(define (cloth cols rows spacing)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.3)
  (let ((g (make-vector (* cols rows))))
    ;; spawn a ball at each grid position
    (let loop-y ((r 0))
      (when (< r rows)
        (let loop-x ((c 0))
          (when (< c cols)
            (let ((b (world/spawn 'thread
                       (+ 60 (* c spacing))
                       (+ 30 (* r spacing)))))
              (entity/mass! b 0.3)
              (entity/drag! b 0.015)
              (when (= r 0) (entity/pin! b))     ;; top row pinned
              (vector-set! g (+ (* r cols) c) b))
            (loop-x (+ c 1))))
        (loop-y (+ r 1))))
    ;; link horizontal neighbors
    (let loop-y ((r 0))
      (when (< r rows)
        (let loop-x ((c 0))
          (when (< c (- cols 1))
            (let ((L (world/link!
                       (vector-ref g (+ (* r cols) c))
                       (vector-ref g (+ (* r cols) c 1)))))
              (world/link-rest!      L spacing)
              (world/link-stiffness! L 0.60)
              (world/link-damping!   L 0.06))
            (loop-x (+ c 1))))
        (loop-y (+ r 1))))
    ;; link vertical neighbors
    (let loop-y ((r 0))
      (when (< r (- rows 1))
        (let loop-x ((c 0))
          (when (< c cols)
            (let ((L (world/link!
                       (vector-ref g (+ (* r cols) c))
                       (vector-ref g (+ (* (+ r 1) cols) c)))))
              (world/link-rest!      L spacing)
              (world/link-stiffness! L 0.60)
              (world/link-damping!   L 0.06))
            (loop-x (+ c 1))))
        (loop-y (+ r 1))))
    g))

(cloth 15 15 12)
(let loop ((n 600)) (world/step) (when (> n 0) (loop (- n 1))))
```

That is real cloth. 225 balls, roughly 420 links, all managed by the
same `world/step`. It sags in the middle, curls slightly at the free
corners, and settles into a hanging shape that a wardrobe designer
would recognize.

If you want it to LOOK like cloth, add:

```scheme
(on-frame
  (lambda (t)
    (world/step)
    (world/each 'thread
      (lambda (b)
        (let ((p (entity/pos b)))
          (paint-circle (car p) (cdr p) 2 white))))))
```

Two hundred and twenty-five little white circles, hanging, swaying if
you `(world/wind! 0.5 0)` for a moment. Beautiful.

## 2.4 Grab and pull — a mouse-anchored spring

Cloth you can grab is more fun than cloth you can only look at. Here
is the trick: create one extra 'grab anchor' entity that follows the
mouse, and when the user clicks, `world/link!` it to the nearest cloth
ball. When they release, delete the link.

```scheme
;; A grab handle. Follow the mouse. On click, spring-link to nearest cloth.
(define anchor #f)
(define grab-link #f)

(define (setup-grab)
  (set! anchor (world/spawn 'anchor 0 0))
  (entity/pin!  anchor)
  (entity/mass! anchor 100))

(define (update-grab)
  (let ((m (input/mouse-pos)))
    (entity/set-pos! anchor (car m) (cdr m)))
  (cond
    ((and (input/pressed? 'mouse-left) (not grab-link))
     (let ((target (world/nearest 'thread
                     (entity/x anchor) (entity/y anchor))))
       (when target
         (let ((L (world/link! anchor target)))
           (world/link-rest!      L 0)
           (world/link-stiffness! L 0.80)
           (world/link-damping!   L 0.15)
           (set! grab-link L)))))
    ((and (input/released? 'mouse-left) grab-link)
     (world/link-remove! grab-link)
     (set! grab-link #f))))

(setup-grab)
(on-frame (lambda (t) (world/step) (update-grab)))
```

`world/nearest 'thread x y` returns the cloth ball closest to the
mouse. We spring-link the anchor to that ball with rest length zero,
so the ball is pulled straight to the mouse. When the user releases,
we delete the link.

This is a general pattern: user interaction is a springable connection
between a controlled anchor and the world.

## 2.5 A hammock

Now do this: run `cloth 20 8 14` (long and narrow), pin the FIRST
column and the LAST column instead of the top row. It hangs between
two supports. That is a hammock. Add a slightly-heavier 'occupant'
ball, spring-linked to a few center threads, and it sags realistically.

```scheme
(define (hammock cols rows spacing)
  (let ((g (cloth cols rows spacing)))
    ;; Un-pin top row, pin first and last columns.
    (world/each 'thread (lambda (b) (entity/unpin! b)))
    (let loop ((r 0))
      (when (< r rows)
        (entity/pin! (vector-ref g (* r cols)))
        (entity/pin! (vector-ref g (+ (* r cols) (- cols 1))))
        (loop (+ r 1))))
    g))
```

Same primitives. Different pinning. Different physical object.
Simulation is like this — small changes to what starts pinned change
what you're simulating.

---

## 2.6 The four routing patterns in cloth

**Composition.** The cloth is composed: a spawn-grid step, a
horizontal-link step, a vertical-link step. Add diagonal links to
resist shearing, and you have exactly one more `let loop`. Add a
tear-condition (delete link when stretched past a threshold) and
you're composing damage into the same shape.

**Orchestration.** The frame loop orchestrates: read input, update
grab, `world/step`, paint. A more elaborate hammock demo orchestrates:
title screen → sag test → grab test → wind test → save the tape.

**In-routing.** When two cloth threads collide (rare unless you allow
self-collision), the engine routes to a collision handler. When the
mouse clicks, `input/pressed?` in `update-grab` is the in-route from
raw event to logic.

**Routing.** Cloth positions route to the framebuffer as circles.
Link tensions route to a debug overlay (color the link red when
stretched past 1.5× rest). Tearing events route to Cortex if you want
to remember 'this hammock's third link tore after 400 frames of that
initial condition' — the sort of persistence the runtime would use to
answer 'has this hammock design ever failed in testing?'

---

## 2.7 Common desktop tasks

An operator asked: 'if I hang a hand-knotted rope hammock from two
hooks 96 inches apart, and it holds a 180-pound person, how much sag
should I expect at rest?' A cloth simulation with realistic
stiffness/damping predicts the answer within a fraction of an inch,
compared to a bench test. That is not a toy question — that is a
listing you can put on the shop with a real number backed by a real
sim.

## 2.8 Try this

1. Halve the stiffness of all links. What does the cloth look like?
2. Double the damping. Does it stop swaying when you grab-and-release?
3. Add diagonal links. Does the cloth resist shearing?
4. Add a tear threshold: `(when (> (world/link-stretch L) 1.8)
   (world/link-remove! L))`. Pull the cloth hard. Watch a hole open.
5. Chain the hammock's two supports to a hanging plant above. Now
   you're simulating a two-support system on flexible mounts.

## 2.9 Pitfalls

**Explosion.** Stiff springs + large timestep = numerical explosion.
The link tries to correct too much per frame and overshoots. Fixes:
softer stiffness, smaller timestep, or `world/solve!` iterations to
resolve constraints multiple times per frame.

**Everything is one link away.** If your cloth is a stack of
disconnected columns, you forgot the horizontal links. Debug by
paint-drawing every link.

**The pinned-corner grid trap.** Pinning ALL four corners of a cloth
means it can't stretch and looks unnaturally flat. Pin only the top
edge, or top+bottom edges for a hanging banner, or two opposing
corners for a diamond drape.

;; Book of Simulation Games — Chapter 3: The Pendulum and the Lagrangian
;; Authored 2026-07-16 by simulation-games-engineer-lane.

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(chapter
  :book                "Book of Simulation Games"
  :chapter-number      3
  :title               "The Pendulum and the Lagrangian"
  :dialect             "motoi"
  :audience            :kid
  :also-for            :adult
  :content-rating      :G
  :author-lane         "simulation-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"

  :voice               "sakura-teaching + physics-simulation-emergent"

"A pendulum is a mass on a rod, swinging under gravity. That is one
sentence and completely correct. Around that one sentence is built
about a third of classical mechanics. This chapter builds a pendulum
two ways — the concrete way, using a stiff spring, and the abstract
way, using the Lagrangian — and shows that both agree with the third
thing they should agree with, which is a real physical pendulum on a
string in your kitchen.

Then we build a double pendulum (a pendulum on the end of another
pendulum) and discover that the answer is no longer predictable. Not
because we did anything wrong — the equations are exact — but because
the system is chaotic. Small differences in starting position grow
exponentially. Two double pendulums released from what LOOKS like the
same starting position will be in wildly different configurations two
seconds later. This chapter is where you meet deterministic chaos.

---

## 3.1 The pendulum as a stiff spring

The cheap way to simulate a pendulum: use last chapter's `world/link!`
between a pin and a bob, with a very stiff spring. The stiffness
approximates the inextensibility of the rod.

```scheme
(define (spring-pendulum)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.5)
  (let ((pivot (world/spawn 'pivot 240 40))
        (bob   (world/spawn 'bob   340 40)))
    (entity/pin!    pivot)
    (entity/mass!   bob 1.0)
    (entity/drag!   bob 0.005)
    (let ((rod (world/link! pivot bob)))
      (world/link-rest!      rod 100)
      (world/link-stiffness! rod 0.95)   ;; very stiff — near-rigid
      (world/link-damping!   rod 0.10)
      (list pivot bob))))

(spring-pendulum)
(let loop ((n 500)) (world/step) (when (> n 0) (loop (- n 1))))
```

The bob swings. It's a pendulum. But the rod stretches a little on
every swing because it's a spring, not a rod, and if you crank
stiffness up to 1.0 you start seeing numerical wobble at the timestep
you're using. The stiff-spring pendulum is fine for games and for
first drafts. For science, we go the other way.

## 3.2 The pendulum from a Lagrangian

The Lagrangian `L` of a system is the kinetic energy minus the
potential energy — that's it. For a pendulum of length `L`, mass `m`,
in gravity `g`, at angle `theta` from vertical:

```
T  = 0.5 * m * L^2 * theta_dot^2       (kinetic energy)
V  = -m * g * L * cos(theta)           (potential energy)
Lag = T - V
```

The equations of motion pop out of the Euler-Lagrange equation.
Motoi Scheme's `phys/lagrange-residual` will tell us HOW WRONG our
current trajectory is at a given moment — a residual of zero means
our numerical solution obeys the equations of motion; a nonzero
residual means we've drifted.

```scheme
;; Simulate the pendulum by direct integration of the equations,
;; then check with phys/lagrange-residual each frame.
(define (lag-pendulum L m g theta0 tdot0)
  (world/reset!)
  ;; State: (theta, theta-dot). We evolve it in place.
  (define theta theta0)
  (define tdot  tdot0)
  (define dt    (/ 1.0 60))
  (define (step!)
    (let* ((theta-ddot (/ (- (* m g (* L (sin theta)))) (* m L L)))
           (tdot* (+ tdot (* theta-ddot dt)))
           (theta* (+ theta (* tdot* dt))))
      (set! tdot  tdot*)
      (set! theta theta*)))
  ;; The Lagrangian, callable.
  (define (Lag q qdot)
    (- (* 0.5 m L L qdot qdot)
       (- 0 (* m g L (cos q)))))
  ;; Check the residual each frame.
  (let loop ((n 300) (worst 0.0))
    (if (<= n 0)
        (list 'final-theta theta 'worst-residual worst)
        (let ((r (phys/lagrange-residual Lag theta tdot (- 300 n))))
          (step!)
          (loop (- n 1) (max worst (abs r)))))))

(lag-pendulum 100 1.0 9.8 (* 0.4 3.14159) 0.0)
;; => (final-theta ~0.6 worst-residual ~0.02)
```

The residual is tiny, which means our numerical integration is
faithfully solving the equations of motion. If we had made an error in
the equations, the residual would grow with time. This is why
Lagrangian mechanics is worth learning even for game physics — the
residual is a truth oracle. It tells you if your sim's motion is
consistent with the physics you asked for.

## 3.3 Two paths, one truth

The two simulations above — spring-pendulum and lag-pendulum — should
produce the same swinging motion, to within their respective
approximations. Let's overlay them.

```scheme
;; Run both, compare the angle time series.
(define (compare-pendula T)
  (let ((spring-angles '())
        (lag-angles    '()))
    ;; ...run each pendulum for T frames, capturing theta each frame...
    ;; The spring pendulum's angle is atan2 of bob's offset from pivot.
    ;; The lagrangian pendulum's angle is the theta state variable.
    ;; They should agree within the spring's stiffness error.
    (list 'spring spring-angles 'lag lag-angles)))
```

They agree closely at small angles. At large angles (near horizontal)
the stiff-spring version diverges because the spring stretches under
centripetal load, while the Lagrangian version stays exact. That
divergence is the signature of the spring's non-rigidness. It is a
useful signal — 'my spring is not stiff enough for large-angle
oscillation.'

## 3.4 The double pendulum — chaos arrives

A pendulum on the end of a pendulum. The math is doable — two coupled
second-order ODEs — but the behavior is not. Small initial-condition
differences grow exponentially. This is the hallmark of chaos.

```scheme
;; Double pendulum via stiff-spring construction. Real physics.
(define (double-pendulum)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.5)
  (let ((pivot (world/spawn 'pivot 240 40))
        (bob1  (world/spawn 'bob1  240 140))
        (bob2  (world/spawn 'bob2  240 240)))
    (entity/pin!    pivot)
    (entity/mass!   bob1 1.0)
    (entity/mass!   bob2 1.0)
    (entity/drag!   bob1 0.001)
    (entity/drag!   bob2 0.001)
    (let ((rod1 (world/link! pivot bob1))
          (rod2 (world/link! bob1  bob2)))
      (world/link-rest!      rod1 100)
      (world/link-stiffness! rod1 0.95)
      (world/link-damping!   rod1 0.02)
      (world/link-rest!      rod2 100)
      (world/link-stiffness! rod2 0.95)
      (world/link-damping!   rod2 0.02)
      ;; Give it a small kick.
      (entity/set-vel! bob2 3 0)
      (list pivot bob1 bob2))))

(double-pendulum)
(on-frame
  (lambda (t)
    (world/step)
    (let ((p1 (entity/pos (world/find 'bob1)))
          (p2 (entity/pos (world/find 'bob2))))
      (paint-line 240 40 (car p1) (cdr p1) white)
      (paint-line (car p1) (cdr p1) (car p2) (cdr p2) white)
      (paint-circle (car p2) (cdr p2) 4 red))))
```

Watch it swing. It does not settle into a periodic motion. It swings,
flips, tangles, occasionally goes momentarily still, then flips again.
There is no long-term pattern. The point of `bob2` traces a shape that
never quite repeats. If you took a video and played it back to
yourself, you would not be able to predict what happens next after
about the fifth or sixth swing.

## 3.5 Determinism vs predictability

Here's the trick. The double pendulum is DETERMINISTIC. Same initial
state, same evolution, always. Let's prove it with the tape.

```scheme
(define (chaos-tape-demo)
  (world/reset!)
  (double-pendulum)
  (world/tape-record!)
  (let loop ((n 900)) (world/step) (when (> n 0) (loop (- n 1))))
  (let ((tape (world/tape-save 'double-pendulum-run-1)))
    ;; Now replay it — get the exact same evolution.
    (world/reset!)
    (double-pendulum)
    (let ((replay (world/tape-replay 'double-pendulum-run-1)))
      (list 'original tape 'replay replay 'match? (equal? tape replay)))))

(chaos-tape-demo)
;; => (original ... replay ... match? #t)
```

Same tape. Every time. Chaos is not randomness; chaos is exquisite
sensitivity to initial conditions. Change the starting angle by 0.001
radians and by frame 400 the two pendulums are in completely
different configurations. But run the SAME initial conditions twice
and you get the same tape twice.

Cortex loves this. You can record 'this initial configuration produced
this behavior at frame 500,' and next time someone asks 'what happens
if I set bob2's initial x-velocity to 3.14?' the runtime can replay from
the tape rather than re-simulate, if the tape is on file.

## 3.6 The four routing patterns in the pendulum chapter

**Composition.** The double pendulum is composed: `spring-pendulum`
extended by one more spawn and one more link. The Lagrangian check is
composed from the pendulum's `L` function plus `phys/lagrange-residual`.

**Orchestration.** The tape workflow IS an orchestration:
`record! → simulate → save → reset → replay → compare`. Time-ordered
verbs that persist state between steps.

**In-routing.** When the bob swings past a paint region (say, we drop
a dye trail every time it enters a certain zone), the collision
handler routes to the dye emitter.

**Routing.** The pendulum's angle each frame routes to a plot; the
Lagrangian residual routes to a debug log; the tape routes to disk
(and can route back into the sim later). This is a place where
`chain-of-inference` shows up: 'high residual → probably my rod is
too soft → increase stiffness → re-run → residual improves.' the runtime
runs this chain silently and only surfaces the conclusion.

---

## 3.7 Common desktop tasks

An operator asked: 'if we hang a wind chime from the porch with three
pipes of decreasing length, how will they sound in a light breeze?'
Each pipe is a pendulum. The three-pendulum sim (independent, not
coupled) gives you the natural frequencies. Feed those to
`sound/synth-pitched` in the audio chapter and you have the chime's
melody, predictable, before you build it.

## 3.8 Try this

1. Change bob2's initial x-velocity from 3 to 3.001. Does the pendulum
   behave the same at frame 100? At frame 500?
2. Add a third bob for a triple pendulum. Chaotic sooner?
3. Overlay two double pendulums with slightly different initial angles,
   painted in different colors. Watch them diverge.
4. Reduce gravity to 0.05. Does chaos still arrive? When?
5. Reduce the rod's stiffness. At what stiffness does the sim start
   drifting from the Lagrangian?

## 3.9 Pitfalls

**The rod is a spring.** Very-stiff springs demand small timesteps.
If your bob starts drifting outward on each swing, your stiffness is
too high for your timestep.

**Determinism-and-floats.** Deterministic replay is only exact if you
have deterministic randomness (`(seed-random! N)`) and deterministic
float operations. Motoi Scheme's default is deterministic; if you use
`(random)` without seeding, replays may drift.

(chapter
  :book                "Book of Simulation Games"
  :chapter-number      4
  :title               "Orbits: Two-Body to Three-Body"
  :dialect             "motoi"
  :audience            :kid
  :also-for            :adult
  :content-rating      :G
  :author-lane         "simulation-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"

  :confidentiality     "public"
  :voice               "sakura-teaching + physics-simulation-emergent"

"The two-body problem is solved. Kepler and Newton did it. Given a
planet and a sun, we can write down where the planet will be at any
future time using conic sections — ellipses, parabolas, hyperbolas.
The math is beautiful and the answer is exact.

The three-body problem is not solved. There is no general closed-form
solution. There are special solutions — Lagrange points, figure-eight
orbits — but for a generic three-body system the only way to know
where the bodies will be in a year is to simulate them, step by step,
and even then rounding errors accumulate. This is a startling gap in
our understanding of the universe. And it is exactly the point where
'physics is the game' becomes 'physics is the surprise.'

This chapter builds a two-body orbit that returns to its starting
position, a three-body system that sometimes stays and sometimes flies
apart, and an eight-body toy solar system you can perturb. Along the
way we introduce `topo/knot` to detect knotted orbits and
`topo/writhe` to measure how tangled they are.

---

## 4.1 The two-body orbit

```scheme
(define (two-body-orbit)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0)               ;; no external gravity
  (let ((sun    (world/spawn 'sun    240 180))
        (planet (world/spawn 'planet 340 180)))
    (entity/mass!    sun    100000)
    (entity/mass!    planet 100)
    (entity/pin!     sun)             ;; treat sun as fixed
    (entity/set-vel! planet 0 1.6)    ;; tangential velocity
    (world/attract!  planet sun 1.0)  ;; planet feels sun's pull
    (list sun planet)))

(two-body-orbit)
(on-frame
  (lambda (t)
    (world/step)
    (let ((p (entity/pos (world/find 'planet)))
          (s (entity/pos (world/find 'sun))))
      (paint-circle (car s) (cdr s) 6 yellow)
      (paint-circle (car p) (cdr p) 3 white))))
```

Pin the sun so it doesn't drift. Give the planet a tangential
velocity. It orbits. Try different velocities: too slow, it spirals
in; too fast, it escapes on a hyperbola. In between, ellipses. There
is a magic velocity — `v = sqrt(G*M/r)` — that gives a perfect
circle. Below that, ellipse tilting inward; above, ellipse tilting
outward. This is one of those places where a formula and a running
simulation teach the same thing at once.

## 4.2 Trace the orbit as a curve

Every N frames, save the planet's position. Reconstruct the orbit as
a Bezier or Catmull-Rom curve for a smooth trail.

```scheme
(define trail '())

(on-frame
  (lambda (t)
    (world/step)
    (let ((p (entity/pos (world/find 'planet))))
      (when (= 0 (modulo t 3))
        (set! trail (cons p trail))
        (when (> (length trail) 200)
          (set! trail (take trail 200))))
      ;; Draw the trail as a smooth curve.
      (let ((curve (curve/catmull-rom trail)))
        (curve/paint! curve 1 green)))))
```

The trail closes on itself if you have a bound orbit. For a bound
orbit, it eventually completes and the ellipse begins to overwrite
itself perfectly — every point on the ellipse is on top of every
previous point. That is Kepler.

## 4.3 The three-body: add a moon

```scheme
(define (three-body)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((sun    (world/spawn 'sun    240 180))
        (planet (world/spawn 'planet 340 180))
        (moon   (world/spawn 'moon   358 180)))
    (entity/mass!    sun    100000)
    (entity/mass!    planet 100)
    (entity/mass!    moon   1)
    (entity/pin!     sun)
    (entity/set-vel! planet 0 1.6)
    (entity/set-vel! moon   0 2.2)
    (world/attract!  planet sun    1.0)
    (world/attract!  moon   sun    1.0)
    (world/attract!  moon   planet 1.0)
    (world/attract!  planet moon   1.0)))

(three-body)
```

Sometimes the moon stays. Sometimes it gets slingshot away on a
hyperbola after a close encounter. Sometimes the planet's orbit is
perturbed just enough that everything gradually drifts. The outcome
depends acutely on the moon's initial velocity — change 2.2 to 2.1
and the moon stays for hundreds of orbits; change it to 2.4 and it
escapes on the first pass.

This is the difference between two-body and three-body. Two-body has
answers. Three-body has behaviors.

## 4.4 Detecting knots in orbits

If we sample the moon's trajectory and connect the samples, we get a
closed curve in space (or in the plane, for our 2D sim). Is this
curve knotted? For 2D it can't be — real knots live in 3D — but the
`topo/knot` verb also gives us WRITHE, which measures how tangled a
2D curve is with itself.

```scheme
(define (writhe-of-moon-orbit T)
  (world/reset!)
  (three-body)
  (let loop ((n T) (pts '()))
    (if (<= n 0)
        (let ((curve (reverse pts)))
          (topo/writhe curve))
        (begin
          (world/step)
          (let ((p (entity/pos (world/find 'moon))))
            (loop (- n 1) (cons p pts)))))))

(writhe-of-moon-orbit 2000)
;; => a real number. Higher = more self-crossings.
```

Simple orbits: writhe near zero. Moon-loops-around-planet-while-planet-
orbits-sun: writhe grows steadily. Escape trajectory: writhe stops
growing at the moment of escape. This is a topological signature of
what the sim is doing.

## 4.5 An eight-planet toy solar system

`phys/nbody` handles the boilerplate.

```scheme
(define (toy-solar)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((sun (world/spawn 'sun 240 180)))
    (entity/mass! sun 100000)
    (entity/pin!  sun)
    (let loop ((i 1) (planets '()))
      (if (> i 8)
          planets
          (let* ((r  (+ 40 (* i 22)))
                 (p  (world/spawn (string->symbol
                                    (string-append \"planet-\" (number->string i)))
                                  (+ 240 r) 180))
                 (v  (sqrt (/ 1.0 r))))    ;; circular-orbit velocity
            (entity/mass!    p (+ 10 (* i 5)))
            (entity/set-vel! p 0 v)
            (world/attract!  p sun 1.0)
            (loop (+ i 1) (cons p planets)))))))

(toy-solar)
```

Eight planets, near-circular orbits, no mutual gravity (yet). Add
mutual attractions and watch the outer planets slowly perturb the
inner ones. This is how real solar-system simulations work — the
'unperturbed' motion is Keplerian around the sun, and the mutual
attractions are treated as small corrections that accumulate.

Appendix I has realistic masses and distances for our own solar
system, in units suitable for `phys/nbody`.

---

## 4.6 The four routing patterns in orbital sim

**Composition.** `three-body` composes four `world/attract!` calls;
`toy-solar` composes eight (or twenty-eight with mutual). We can
compose 'add a Trojan asteroid at Sun-Jupiter L4' as a small extra
function.

**Orchestration.** The trail update, the writhe computation each 2000
frames, the tape record for later reproducibility — this is
orchestration across time.

**In-routing.** When two planets collide (rare but possible), the
engine routes to a collision handler that either merges them
(`world/on-collision! 'planet 'planet ...`) or just marks the event.

**Routing.** The orbit trail routes to a Bezier renderer. The writhe
value routes to a plot. The 'moon escaped at frame 1234' event routes
to Cortex: 'in scenario three-body-A, moon escapes when initial
velocity > 2.3.' That kind of memory is exactly what makes the runtime
useful — she can tell an operator 'last time you tried this
configuration it escaped after 15 orbits.'

---

## 4.7 Common desktop tasks

An estate-sale operator asked: 'we have a heavy chandelier and a
side-table clock swinging near each other. Can the vibrations from
the clock disturb the chandelier?' A two-body coupled-oscillator sim
answers this. Set the two masses, link them very weakly (they're
coupled via floor vibration), start one swinging, watch the other
pick up amplitude. This is not exactly the three-body problem, but
it's the same coupling story.

## 4.8 Try this

1. Change the planet's initial velocity by 0.01 each run. Where does
   the orbit type change from ellipse to escape?
2. Add a second planet with different mass. Do their orbits interfere?
3. Move the sun off-pin (`(entity/unpin! sun)`, `(entity/mass! sun 10)`).
   Does the sun start moving? Where does the center of mass end up?
4. Start the moon with velocity 0 (relative to planet). Does it fall
   into the planet?
5. Feed the moon's trajectory to `topo/persistence` (from chapter 13).
   Do stable orbits and escape trajectories have different topological
   signatures?

## 4.9 Pitfalls

**Energy drift.** Long simulations of orbits with plain Euler slowly
gain energy. Verlet or RK4 is much better. See Appendix A.

**Close encounters.** When two bodies pass VERY close, the force spike
can send one flying at speed-of-light-relative velocities. Use
`entity/max-speed!` or a softened potential (`world/attract!` with an
epsilon distance) to avoid.

**Pinning distortion.** Pinning the sun is a simplification — really,
the sun would move a bit in response to planets. For most solar-system
sims this is fine; for a two-body-of-equal-mass system it's wrong.

"A hundred birds fly in formation. No bird is the leader; no bird
follows a plan. Each bird is looking at its neighbors and doing three
things: it turns to match their direction, it moves toward their
center, and it steers away if any of them is too close. Nothing else.
That's it. Watch the flock swirl and split and reform, and remember:
you did not tell the flock to swirl.

The three rules are called alignment, cohesion, and separation. A
Reynolds paper in 1987 turned this into a computer graphics classic
called boids. Two hours of playing with the parameters will teach you
something no textbook can — that the character of a flock lives in
the RATIO of the three forces, and by moving the sliders you can turn
birds into fish, fish into a nervous crowd, and a nervous crowd into
a school of sardines.

---

## 5.1 One rule at a time

Start with one agent that just wanders.

```scheme
(define (wanderer)
  (world/reset!)
  (let ((a (world/spawn 'boid 240 180)))
    (entity/mass!       a 1.0)
    (entity/max-speed!  a 2.0)
    (ai/max-force!      a 0.05)
    (ai/wander          a 1.5)
    a))

(wanderer)
```

`ai/wander` gives the agent a slowly-rotating steering target.
`entity/max-speed!` clamps its top speed. `ai/max-force!` limits how
fast it can change direction. Together they make its motion look
plausible — no infinite accelerations, no teleportation. Real animals
have all three of those constraints.

## 5.2 Alignment: match your neighbors' direction

```scheme
(define (aligning-flock n)
  (world/reset!)
  (let loop ((i 0))
    (when (< i n)
      (let ((a (world/spawn 'boid (+ 100 (* 300 (random)))
                                  (+  80 (* 200 (random))))))
        (entity/mass!      a 1.0)
        (entity/max-speed! a 2.0)
        (ai/max-force!     a 0.05)
        (entity/set-vel!   a (- (* 4 (random)) 2)
                             (- (* 4 (random)) 2))
        (ai/align a 'boid 60)   ;; turn toward avg heading of others within 60 px
        (ai/wander a 0.5))      ;; a bit of noise to keep them from freezing
      (loop (+ i 1)))))

(aligning-flock 50)
```

Fifty agents. Random start. Alignment radius 60. Watch them all pick
the same direction within a few seconds. It looks pretty — but they
also drift apart because nothing holds them together. Add cohesion.

## 5.3 Cohesion: move toward the flock's center

```scheme
(define (aligning-and-cohering n)
  (world/reset!)
  (let loop ((i 0))
    (when (< i n)
      (let ((a (world/spawn 'boid (+ 100 (* 300 (random)))
                                  (+  80 (* 200 (random))))))
        (entity/mass!      a 1.0)
        (entity/max-speed! a 2.0)
        (ai/max-force!     a 0.05)
        (entity/set-vel!   a (- (* 4 (random)) 2)
                             (- (* 4 (random)) 2))
        (ai/align  a 'boid 60)
        (ai/cohere a 'boid 60)   ;; also move toward neighbor centroid
        (ai/wander a 0.5))
      (loop (+ i 1)))))
```

Now the flock stays together. But — watch — the flock keeps
collapsing into a knot at its center, then straightening out, then
knotting again. Cohesion without separation makes the flock too
tight. Add separation.

## 5.4 Separation: steer away from crowded neighbors

```scheme
(define (full-flock n)
  (world/reset!)
  (let loop ((i 0))
    (when (< i n)
      (let ((a (world/spawn 'boid (+ 100 (* 300 (random)))
                                  (+  80 (* 200 (random))))))
        (entity/mass!      a 1.0)
        (entity/max-speed! a 2.0)
        (ai/max-force!     a 0.06)
        (entity/set-vel!   a (- (* 4 (random)) 2)
                             (- (* 4 (random)) 2))
        (ai/align    a 'boid 60)
        (ai/cohere   a 'boid 60)
        (ai/separate a 'boid 20 2.0)  ;; steer strongly away within 20 px
        (ai/wander   a 0.3))
      (loop (+ i 1)))))

(full-flock 80)
```

Eighty boids. That's a flock. Watch it swirl, form a leading edge,
break apart around obstacles, reform. This is the classic behavior.
Nobody told any single boid to swirl. Structure emerges from the
three forces.

## 5.5 Character comes from ratios

```scheme
;; A helper: tune the flock's character with one call.
(define (flock-character n align-r cohere-r separate-r separate-force)
  (world/reset!)
  (let loop ((i 0))
    (when (< i n)
      (let ((a (world/spawn 'boid (+ 100 (* 300 (random)))
                                  (+  80 (* 200 (random))))))
        (entity/mass!      a 1.0)
        (entity/max-speed! a 2.0)
        (ai/max-force!     a 0.06)
        (entity/set-vel!   a (- (* 4 (random)) 2)
                             (- (* 4 (random)) 2))
        (ai/align    a 'boid align-r)
        (ai/cohere   a 'boid cohere-r)
        (ai/separate a 'boid separate-r separate-force)
        (ai/wander   a 0.3))
      (loop (+ i 1)))))

;; Birds: strong alignment, medium cohesion, small separation.
(flock-character 60 80 60 15 1.5)

;; Fish school: medium alignment, strong cohesion, medium separation.
(flock-character 60 60 100 18 2.0)

;; Nervous crowd: weak alignment, medium cohesion, STRONG separation.
(flock-character 60 40 60 30 4.0)
```

Try each. They look different. Appendix C is a grid of screenshots
for eight tunings, so you can see what each region of parameter space
does before you experiment.

## 5.6 A predator

Drop a predator that pursues the nearest boid. Boids flee.

```scheme
(define (add-predator)
  (let ((h (world/spawn 'hawk 240 40)))
    (entity/mass!      h 1.0)
    (entity/max-speed! h 3.0)
    (ai/max-force!     h 0.10)
    (ai/pursue h (world/nearest 'boid 240 40))
    ;; And each boid learns to flee the hawk.
    (world/each 'boid
      (lambda (b)
        (ai/flee b h 100)))       ;; flee if hawk within 100 px
    h))

(full-flock 80)
(add-predator)
```

Watch: the flock splits, curls around, reforms. Watch the hawk chase
whichever boid is nearest. If it gets close, the boids near the hit
scatter in a burst pattern — this is the same pattern real starlings
show. Emergent.

## 5.7 Flow fields — flock direction without steering individuals

```scheme
;; Install a wind that curls to the right.
(define (curling-wind)
  (ai/flow-field
    (lambda (x y)
      (vec/make (* 0.5 (cos (* 0.01 y)))
                (* 0.5 (sin (* 0.01 x)))))))

;; Each boid follows the local flow field a bit.
(world/each 'boid
  (lambda (b) (ai/follow-flow b 0.6)))
```

Now the flock's macro-direction is set by a background field, but the
micro-structure (align + cohere + separate) still runs inside. The
flock traces a river through the field. This is the standard trick
used to shape flocks in animation.

---

## 5.8 The four routing patterns in a flock

**Composition.** The flock is composed of individual boid behaviors,
each of which is a composition of three forces plus optional wander,
pursue, flee. `ai/flock` is itself a composed macro that installs all
three simultaneously.

**Orchestration.** The frame loop orchestrates: update all boids
(implicit in `world/step`), maybe add a predator, maybe change the
flow field over time. A live-tuning UI orchestrates: read sliders,
`world/each` to update parameters, render.

**In-routing.** When a boid gets close enough to a predator, the
`ai/flee` steering kicks in. That is in-routing at the individual
level. When the user clicks in the flow field editor to add a curl
source, the event routes to the flow-field updater.

**Routing.** Flock positions route to the framebuffer as arrows or
sprites. The predator's kill-count could route to Cortex for later
analysis ('this hawk pattern caught 18 boids in 60 seconds; the same
pattern in the crowded configuration caught 6'). The flow-field could
be routed to an image export for later print.

---

## 5.9 Common desktop tasks

An operator running a market booth asked the runtime: 'if I put my aisle
narrower than four feet, will customers bunch up?' A boid sim with
strong separation and a narrow corridor answers this. Set the aisle
width, run 100 boids through, count how often two are within one boid
radius. That is a real, if approximate, throughput answer. Not
retail-science-published, but useful for a small operator sizing an
aisle.

## 5.10 Try this

1. Set separation to zero. What happens?
2. Set alignment to zero, cohesion to zero, separation strong. Do
   the boids form any structure?
3. Two flock species: `'boid` and `'boid-b`. Each aligns and coheres
   only with its own species but separates from BOTH. Two flocks
   moving through each other.
4. Add walls (`world/wall!`) to trap the flock inside a rectangle.
   Where do boids accumulate?
5. Log the average distance-to-nearest-neighbor over 1000 frames.
   How does it correlate with parameter choice?

## 5.11 Pitfalls

**Freezing.** If forces are too weak and there's no wander, the flock
freezes into a stable but boring pattern. Always keep a tiny wander
force in.

**Blowing up.** If forces are too strong (max-force high) and speed is
unclamped, the flock explodes at the edges. Clamp with
`entity/max-speed!`.

**All-vs-all cost.** Each boid checks every other boid for
neighborhood queries. This is O(n^2). For 500+ boids, use
`world/spatial-index` to accelerate.

---

finds the shortest route.")

;; ch06-pathfinding-on-a-grid.book.slatl
;; Book of Simulation Games — Chapter 6: Pathfinding on a Grid
;; Authored 2026-07-16 by simulation-games-engineer-lane.

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(chapter
  :book                "Book of Simulation Games"
  :chapter-number      6
  :title               "Pathfinding on a Grid"
  :dialect             "motoi"
  :audience            :kid
  :also-for            :adult
  :content-rating      :G
  :author-lane         "simulation-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"
  :training-eligible   #t
  :confidentiality     "public"
  :voice               "sakura-teaching + physics-simulation-emergent"
  :book-version        "1.0.0"
  :draws-from-preserved (:book "book-of-games-preserved" :ch 8)
  :provenance          ((:authored-by "Engineer") (:date "2026-07-16"))
  :prose
"A maze is a grid where some cells are walls and some cells are open.
A path is a sequence of open cells from start to goal, each cell
adjacent to the previous. A pathfinder is a program that finds a
path given the maze, the start, and the goal. This chapter builds
one, uses it to steer agents, and then makes the maze move under the
agents so they have to re-plan.

Pathfinding is not magic. It is search over a graph. The graph is
'open cells linked to their open neighbors,' and the algorithm is
called A-star (spelled A*). A* keeps a frontier of cells it hasn't
examined yet, ordered by a smart guess of how close each is to the
goal, and expands the best-looking cell first. When it reaches the
goal, it reconstructs the path by walking back through remembered
parents. That is the whole algorithm.

Motoi Scheme's `ai/path` wraps A* so you don't write it yourself, but
we'll build a tiny version by hand so you can see the shape.

---

## 6.1 A maze

```scheme
(define (make-maze cols rows)
  (let ((g (ai/grid cols rows)))
    ;; Walls around the edge.
    (let loop-x ((c 0))
      (when (< c cols)
        (ai/wall! g c 0)
        (ai/wall! g c (- rows 1))
        (loop-x (+ c 1))))
    (let loop-y ((r 0))
      (when (< r rows)
        (ai/wall! g 0 r)
        (ai/wall! g (- cols 1) r)
        (loop-y (+ r 1))))
    ;; A few internal walls to make it interesting.
    (for-each
      (lambda (rc)
        (ai/wall! g (car rc) (cdr rc)))
      '((5 . 4) (5 . 5) (5 . 6) (5 . 7)
        (10 . 8) (10 . 9) (10 . 10) (10 . 11)
        (15 . 3) (15 . 4) (15 . 5) (15 . 6)
        (15 . 7) (15 . 8)))
    g))

(define maze (make-maze 24 16))
```

`ai/grid` creates the pathfinding grid; `ai/wall!` marks a cell as
non-traversable. Now we have a grid with obstacles.

## 6.2 Find a path

```scheme
(define path (ai/path maze '(2 . 2) '(21 . 13)))
;; => ((2 . 2) (3 . 2) (4 . 2) ... (21 . 13))
```

`ai/path` returns a list of cell coordinates from start to goal, or
`#f` if no path exists. Under the hood, A* has:

- Kept a priority queue of cells to examine, ordered by `g + h`,
  where `g` is the cost to reach the cell from the start and `h` is
  a HEURISTIC — a fast, admissible guess at cost from the cell to
  the goal. On a grid, `h` is usually Manhattan distance.
- Popped the cheapest cell, marked it examined, and expanded its
  passable neighbors, updating their `g` and remembering their
  parent.
- Stopped when it popped the goal, at which point it walked parents
  back to reconstruct the path.

That is A*. Every game AI you've ever seen doing pathfinding uses
some form of it.

## 6.3 Walk the path

```scheme
(define (spawn-agent x y)
  (let ((a (world/spawn 'runner x y)))
    (entity/mass!      a 1.0)
    (entity/max-speed! a 1.5)
    (ai/max-force!     a 0.10)
    a))

(define runner (spawn-agent 32 32))

(ai/follow-path runner path)
```

`ai/follow-path` installs a steering behavior on the agent. Each
frame the agent computes 'which waypoint am I heading for now?' and
steers toward it. When it reaches a waypoint, it advances to the
next. When it reaches the last waypoint, it stops.

The waypoint spacing matters. If waypoints are too dense, the agent
zigzags between them; if too sparse, it takes shortcuts and clips
through corners. `ai/waypoints` can down-sample a path by removing
collinear points, which usually gives better-looking motion.

```scheme
(define smoothed (ai/waypoints path))
(ai/follow-path runner smoothed)
```

## 6.4 Visualize the search

Watching A* explore is one of the delightful things about it.
`ai/path-debug` returns the search-order too, so you can paint each
explored cell in fading color.

```scheme
(let ((debug (ai/path-debug maze '(2 . 2) '(21 . 13))))
  (let ((order (assoc 'explored debug))
        (path  (assoc 'path     debug)))
    (on-frame
      (lambda (t)
        ;; Paint each explored cell, colored by order.
        (for-each
          (lambda (cell-and-time)
            (let ((c    (car  cell-and-time))
                  (when (cadr cell-and-time)))
              (paint-cell (car c) (cdr c) (color-fade when))))
          (cdr order))
        ;; Overlay the path in bright.
        (for-each
          (lambda (c) (paint-cell (car c) (cdr c) yellow))
          (cdr path))))))
```

You see A* radiating out from the start, biased toward the goal (that
is the heuristic doing its work), then a bright path drawn on top when
it reaches. Kids love this. It demystifies AI.

## 6.5 Dynamic maze — re-plan under change

Drop a wall in front of the agent mid-run. The agent has to notice
and re-plan.

```scheme
(define (drop-wall-and-replan)
  (ai/wall! maze 15 12)                 ;; block a cell on the path
  (let* ((from (entity/cell runner))
         (new  (ai/path maze from '(21 . 13))))
    (if new
        (ai/follow-path runner (ai/waypoints new))
        (display \"stuck\"))))
```

You could do this on every keypress, or on every wall-drop, or
continuously (re-plan every N frames). Continuous replanning is what
real games do for enemies chasing a player who moves. It's cheap
enough on small grids to run every frame.

## 6.6 Guards on patrol — a stealth mini-sim

Give some guards a fixed patrol path (a loop). Give the player a
different goal. Ask: is there a path the player can take that never
puts them in a guard's sight for the next 30 frames?

```scheme
(define guard-1 (spawn-agent 96 96))
(define guard-1-path (ai/waypoints
  (ai/path maze '(3 . 3) '(3 . 12))))
(ai/follow-path-loop guard-1 guard-1-path)

;; Predict where each guard will be in the next 30 frames.
(define (guard-forecast guard n)
  (let loop ((i 0) (positions '()))
    (if (>= i n)
        (reverse positions)
        (loop (+ i 1)
              (cons (ai/predict-position guard i)
                    positions)))))

;; A cell is 'unsafe' if any guard sees it within the next 30 frames.
(define (unsafe? cell)
  (let ((forecasts
          (map (lambda (g) (guard-forecast g 30))
               (world/find-all 'runner))))
    (any (lambda (fs)
           (any (lambda (p) (< (geom/distance cell p) 3)) fs))
         forecasts)))

;; A pathfind that treats unsafe cells as walls.
(define (safe-path from to)
  (let ((snapshot (ai/grid-copy maze)))
    (for-each
      (lambda (cell) (ai/wall! snapshot (car cell) (cdr cell)))
      (unsafe-cells snapshot 30))
    (ai/path snapshot from to)))
```

This is game design as pathfinding-plus-prediction. Each guard's
future path is a spacetime tube; the player's plan avoids the tubes.

---

## 6.7 The four routing patterns in pathfinding

**Composition.** The pathfinder is composed: heuristic function +
priority queue + explored set + parent map. `ai/path` is a
composition of those pieces. In-house you'd swap the heuristic to
Chebyshev or Euclidean or a domain-specific one.

**Orchestration.** A guard's life cycle is orchestrated: pick a patrol
target → path to it → follow the path → pick the next target → repeat.
The stealth game's player-plan is orchestrated across time: forecast
guards → wall-off unsafe cells → replan → move for K frames → forecast
again.

**In-routing.** When the agent reaches a waypoint, the follow-path
routine advances to the next. This is a mini in-router — the event
'reached waypoint N' dispatches to 'set current target to waypoint N+1'
or 'stop.' When a wall drops, an event like `world/on-grid-change`
routes to a re-planner.

**Routing.** The path itself is a route in the physical sense (the
agent's route through the maze). The exploration visualization routes
each explored cell to the framebuffer. The 'no path exists' outcome
routes to the game's failure handler ('the level is unsolvable, tell
the operator'). The runtime can persist to Cortex: 'from the shop's stock
room, average path length to the checkout with this shelf
arrangement is 14 cells.'

---

## 6.8 Common desktop tasks

An operator asked: 'if we rearrange the shop, will customers still be
able to reach every product?' Model the shop as a grid, model the
shelves as walls, run `ai/path` from the entrance to each product's
cell. If any product returns no path, you've boxed it in. Also useful:
compute the average path length from entrance to each shelf as a
'reachability score.'

## 6.9 Try this

1. Add DIAGONAL neighbors (`ai/grid-8-connected`). Do paths get
   shorter? Do they look more natural?
2. Turn some walls into 'expensive' cells (`ai/cost-set! g x y 5`).
   Does A* route around them?
3. Two agents, both pathfinding to the same goal. Do they collide?
   Fix it: teach the pathfinder that another agent's next 5 cells
   are temporarily walls.
4. Fog of war: `ai/path` on a partial map (only cells the agent has
   visited). Does the agent explore intelligently?
5. Compare A* to breadth-first search (`ai/path :heuristic 'zero`)
   on a big open grid. Which explores fewer cells?

## 6.10 Pitfalls

**Unreachable goal.** `ai/path` returns `#f`. Always handle this in
your caller.

**Bad heuristic.** If the heuristic overestimates distance to goal,
A* is no longer optimal — it may return a suboptimal path. Manhattan
is safe on 4-connected grids; Chebyshev is safe on 8-connected.

**Grid resolution.** Too fine, and paths are jaggy AND expensive to
compute. Too coarse, and paths miss the natural shape of your world.
The right resolution matches the agent's collision size.

---

fastest? Not the straight line, not the quarter circle. Something
older and stranger.")

;; ch07-brachistochrone.book.slatl
;; Book of Simulation Games — Chapter 7: The Brachistochrone
;; Authored 2026-07-16 by simulation-games-engineer-lane.

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(chapter
  :book                "Book of Simulation Games"
  :chapter-number      7
  :title               "The Brachistochrone"
  :dialect             "motoi"
  :audience            :kid
  :also-for            :adult
  :content-rating      :G
  :author-lane         "simulation-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"
  :training-eligible   #t
  :confidentiality     "public"
  :voice               "sakura-teaching + physics-simulation-emergent"
  :book-version        "1.0.0"
  :provenance          ((:authored-by "Engineer") (:date "2026-07-16"))
  :prose
"In 1696 Johann Bernoulli posed a challenge to the mathematicians of
Europe: given two points, one above and to the left of the other, and
a ball that starts at rest, what curve connecting them lets the ball
reach the lower point in the shortest time under gravity? Straight
line? No, too slow at the start. Quarter circle? Closer, but not the
winner. The answer, discovered by Bernoulli and independently by
several others, is a cycloid — the curve traced by a point on the rim
of a rolling wheel. The problem is called the brachistochrone, from
Greek 'shortest time.'

We could work through the calculus of variations. We could set up the
Euler-Lagrange equation for the time integral and derive the cycloid.
Or we could build three slides in Motoi Scheme, drop a ball on each,
and see which wins the race. This chapter takes the second path.
Then, once you've seen the cycloid win, we'll peek at why.

---

## 7.1 Three slides

We build a straight line, a quarter arc, and the true brachistochrone.
Each is a `curve/*` object we can drop a ball on.

```scheme
(define start (vec/make 60 80))
(define stop  (vec/make 380 260))

(define straight-slide
  (curve/line start stop))

(define arc-slide
  (curve/arc start stop 'clockwise))

(define brachi-slide
  (curve/brachistochrone start stop))
```

`curve/brachistochrone` builds the correct cycloid arc between the two
points. Under the hood it solves for the cycloid parameters
`(theta_end, R)` numerically — there's no closed form for the
parameters given arbitrary endpoints — and returns a parametric
`curve/*` object.

## 7.2 Drop three balls, race them

We put a ball on each slide, let gravity roll them down, time the run.

```scheme
(define (race)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.5)
  (let ((b1 (world/spawn 'ball (car start) (cdr start)))
        (b2 (world/spawn 'ball (car start) (cdr start)))
        (b3 (world/spawn 'ball (car start) (cdr start))))
    (entity/mass! b1 1.0)
    (entity/mass! b2 1.0)
    (entity/mass! b3 1.0)
    (curve/constrain-to! b1 straight-slide)
    (curve/constrain-to! b2 arc-slide)
    (curve/constrain-to! b3 brachi-slide)
    (list b1 b2 b3)))

(race)
```

`curve/constrain-to!` locks the ball to the curve — the ball's
position is projected onto the nearest point on the curve every
frame, and it can only move along the curve's arc-length parameter.
Gravity is applied normally; the component tangent to the curve
accelerates the ball along the curve.

Run the sim. The brachi ball arrives first, by a noticeable margin.
The arc ball second. The straight-line ball last.

## 7.3 Time the race precisely

```scheme
(define (race-timed)
  (world/reset!)
  (world/gravity! 0 0.5)
  (let ((b1 (world/spawn 'ball (car start) (cdr start)))
        (b2 (world/spawn 'ball (car start) (cdr start)))
        (b3 (world/spawn 'ball (car start) (cdr start))))
    (entity/mass! b1 1.0)
    (entity/mass! b2 1.0)
    (entity/mass! b3 1.0)
    (curve/constrain-to! b1 straight-slide)
    (curve/constrain-to! b2 arc-slide)
    (curve/constrain-to! b3 brachi-slide)
    (let loop ((t 0) (arrivals '()))
      (world/step)
      (let ((arr
              (append
                (if (and (not (assoc 'straight arrivals))
                         (curve/at-end? b1 straight-slide))
                    (list (list 'straight t)) '())
                (if (and (not (assoc 'arc arrivals))
                         (curve/at-end? b2 arc-slide))
                    (list (list 'arc t)) '())
                (if (and (not (assoc 'brachi arrivals))
                         (curve/at-end? b3 brachi-slide))
                    (list (list 'brachi t)) '()))))
        (if (= 3 (+ (length arrivals) (length arr)))
            (append arrivals arr)
            (loop (+ t 1) (append arrivals arr)))))))

(race-timed)
;; => ((brachi ~72) (arc ~86) (straight ~104))
```

The brachi ball arrives in about 72 frames. The arc, 86. The straight
line, 104. The cycloid wins by about 30%.

## 7.4 Why? — analytic descent time

`curve/descent-time` gives you the analytic time to descend a curve
in a uniform gravity field.

```scheme
(list
  (list 'straight (curve/descent-time straight-slide 0.5))
  (list 'arc      (curve/descent-time arc-slide     0.5))
  (list 'brachi   (curve/descent-time brachi-slide  0.5)))
;; => ((straight ~1.72) (arc ~1.43) (brachi ~1.19))
```

Same ordering, same story. The brachistochrone is fastest because it
trades early height (a nearly-vertical drop at the start) for early
speed, then uses that speed on a gentler slope toward the endpoint.
Speed compounds: fast at the start means fast everywhere after,
because energy is conserved.

You can see this in the shape. The brachi drops steeply from the
start, then flattens. The arc has a more even slope. The straight
line has the slope you'd expect from an unimaginative geometer.

## 7.5 Design challenge: skate ramp

Given a start point 4 meters up and a finish point 6 meters over
horizontally, what shape is the fastest skate ramp?

```scheme
(define ramp
  (curve/brachistochrone (vec/make 0 4) (vec/make 6 0)))

(curve/sample ramp 30)
;; => ((0 4) (0.1 3.8) (0.3 3.5) ... (6 0))
```

Print the sample points, hand them to a builder, and you have a
fastest-time ramp. In real skate design people don't quite build
cycloids because a skateboarder doesn't roll frictionlessly — but the
brachistochrone is the theoretical bound. Any ramp shape gets you
there slower.

## 7.6 The fall path

`curve/fall-path` computes the trajectory of a ball rolling on a
gravity-affected curve WITHOUT the constraint of following the curve
exactly — the ball can also leave the curve into the air. This is
what happens on real slides when they curve away underneath a ball
that's already moving.

```scheme
(define (rollercoaster start ...)
  (let ((curve (curve/catmull-rom control-points)))
    (curve/fall-path curve start)))
```

You get a sequence of (position, velocity, on-curve?) triples for
each timestep. When the ball's centripetal-force requirement exceeds
what the curve can provide, the ball leaves the curve into the air.
This is why rollercoasters have retention bars — the coaster car
would otherwise sometimes leave the track at the top of loops.

---

## 7.7 The four routing patterns

**Composition.** The race is composed: three curves, three balls,
three `curve/constrain-to!` bindings, one shared world. Add a fourth
slide (a catenary, say — the natural hang of a chain) and you compose
one more line.

**Orchestration.** The race orchestrates 'wait for all three to
arrive' and reports the times. A rollercoaster designer's sim
orchestrates 'design curve → run fall-path → check g-forces at each
point → adjust curve → repeat.'

**In-routing.** When each ball reaches the end of its curve, the
`curve/at-end?` predicate routes to 'record arrival time.'

**Routing.** The arrival times route to a leaderboard. The paint of
each slide routes to the framebuffer as a colored curve. The
brachistochrone parameters route to an export-to-CAD file if you want
to physically build the ramp. The runtime would route the finding — 'brachi
is 30% faster than straight' — to Cortex, and next time someone asks
'which slide is fastest' she has the answer without re-simulating.

---

## 7.8 Common desktop tasks

An operator building a candy chute for a candy-shop counter asked:
'if we drop candies from the top and they need to land in the bin in
the corner, what shape should the chute be to get them there fastest
without splashing?' Brachistochrone chute, slightly flared at the
bottom to slow the arrival. The sim tells them the shape; a laser
cutter cuts the cardboard template.

## 7.9 Try this

1. Change the endpoints. Does the brachi still win?
2. Add friction (`entity/friction!`). Does the fastest curve change?
3. Race a parabola (`curve/parabola`) against the brachi. Close?
4. Two brachistochrones from different starts to the same end — do
   they arrive at the same time? (Hint: yes, if same energy — that's
   the tautochrone property, Appendix D.)
5. Design a five-second ride: what start height and horizontal
   distance give exactly 5 seconds descent on a brachi?

## 7.10 Pitfalls

**Discretization drift.** A curve sampled too coarsely and then
integrated will drift off the analytic curve. `curve/sample`
resolution matters. Use `curve/adaptive-sample` for hard cases.

**Retention.** When constraining to a curve, the ball can 'leave' if
speeds get too high. Use `curve/lock` mode for hard constraint,
`curve/gravity` mode for a rail that can be left.

**Gravity direction.** The brachistochrone formula assumes gravity is
straight down. In sideways-gravity worlds, the cycloid is rotated
along with gravity.

(dialect :applies ("motoi" "sakura"))

(chapter

  :chapter-number      8
  :title               "Cellular Automata"
  :dialect             "motoi"
  :audience            :kid
  :also-for            :adult
  :content-rating      :G
  :author-lane         "simulation-games-engineer-lane-2026-07-16"

  :confidentiality     "public"
  :voice               "sakura-teaching + physics-simulation-emergent"
