  (piece
    :id \"st-01-dogs-on-brooklyn-streets\"
    :title \"Dogs on Brooklyn streets\"
    :prose
    \"Brooklyn dogs come in every size. There's a big black one that lives
in the brownstone on the corner. Every morning at seven the owner walks
her, and the dog stops at the same fire hydrant, sniffs it for exactly
one second, then keeps going. She has learned the shape of her walk.

There's a small brown one who lives in the third-floor apartment above
the coffee shop. He barks at every skateboard that goes by. His name
is Marbles, or at least that's what the woman who owns him calls when
she stands on the fire escape and whistles.

There are two identical corgis owned by two different families on the
same block. They meet on the sidewalk and stand very still, staring
at each other, until one of the owners laughs and pulls their leash
and everyone moves on.

There's an old golden retriever who walks slower than his owner would
like, and his owner has stopped hurrying him because it's not worth it.
There's a bulldog on Adelphi who doesn't move for cars. There's a
poodle whose ears blow up in the wind like small flags.

The dogs know the block. The block knows the dogs.\")

  (piece
    :id \"st-02-morning-on-the-avenue\"
    :title \"Morning on the avenue\"
    :prose
    \"Six-thirty in the morning on Nostrand Avenue: the deli owner is
propping open the door with a milk crate. The corner store owner is
lifting the metal gate. The woman who runs the copy shop is sweeping
last night's leaves from her doorway. The bus driver at the corner
finishes his coffee.

By seven the street is louder. Delivery trucks. Kids running for the
bus. The man who sells fruit on the corner sets up his stand — apples,
bananas, mangoes, oranges, some tangerines that are more expensive
than the others because they're seedless. He knows every regular by
what fruit they buy.

By eight the pace is what the day will hold. People walking with
purpose. People walking with less. The old man who sits on the folding
chair outside the church is already there. He nods at everyone.

By nine the deli has run out of the bacon-egg-and-cheese with the
extra pepper because the two guys who work construction got there
first and cleaned out the tray. The deli owner promises the next
customer she'll make one to order and it takes three minutes and the
next customer says thanks and it happens.

This is what a morning is.\")

  (piece
    :id \"st-03-summer-rain\"
    :title \"Summer rain\"
    :prose
    \"The rain in July arrives without warning. The sky was blue five
minutes ago; now it's dark and heavy and the first drops are landing
on the sidewalk in fat splats.

Everyone runs. The kids who were playing basketball run inside. The
guys who were sitting on the stoop run under the awning. The woman
with the stroller opens the plastic cover and keeps walking because
her stroller has good wheels.

The street smells like hot pavement getting wet. It's a smell that
some people love and some people don't. Petrichor is the word for it,
but not many people use that word.

The rain lasts nine minutes. When it stops, the sky is still gray but
the sun is working on it. The kids come back out. The stoop empties.
The pavement steams a little.

Fifteen minutes later it's like it never happened, except the leaves
on the trees are darker green and the birds are louder.\")

  (piece
    :id \"st-04-winter-block\"
    :title \"A block in winter\"
    :prose
    \"January in Brooklyn: the block is quieter than any other time of year.
Fewer people out. Cars parked with snow on them from the storm three
days ago that nobody's bothered to clean off. The trees are bare and
you can see the outlines of buildings you don't usually see.

The salt on the sidewalk crunches. Every stoop has been shoveled or
not, and you can tell whose is whose. The building super at the corner
shovels wide and clean. The guy in the middle of the block shovels
narrow. The old woman on the far end has a neighbor who shovels for
her — you can tell because it's the widest and cleanest of them all.

The bodega is warm when you push open the door. The heat gets you
before the smell of coffee does. The owner nods. You buy what you
came for. You go back out into the cold.

The dogs still come out. The big black one still stops at the hydrant.
Her owner's breath fogs. The dog doesn't seem to mind the cold.
Brooklyn is where she lives.\")

  (piece
    :id \"st-05-the-corner\"
    :title \"The corner\"
    :prose
    \"Every neighborhood has a corner. Not every corner, but one specific
one. The one where people wait for the bus. The one where the older
guys stand and talk on Saturday afternoons. The one where the woman
who sells lottery tickets has been sitting for eleven years.

On the corner in Bed-Stuy where Bergen meets Nostrand, there's a
bench. Not officially a bench — a low retaining wall that people
started sitting on years ago. The bricks are worn smooth in the
places where people put their weight.

The corner is where you find out what's going on. Someone got a new
car. Someone's daughter is graduating. Someone's mother is in the
hospital. Someone lost their job. Someone found one.

The corner is not a monument. It doesn't have a name. But everyone
knows it. When someone from the block moves away and comes back to
visit, the corner is where they stop first.\")

  (piece
    :id \"st-06-a-bike-lane\"
    :title \"The bike lane\"
    :prose
    \"The bike lane on Bergen used to be a car lane. Then it was a
protected lane with a green stripe. Now it's a lane with a plastic
divider that some drivers respect and some don't.

The bikes come through in waves. Morning: mostly commuters. They ride
fast. Some of them have earbuds; some don't. They mostly don't look
at pedestrians until the pedestrian is about to be a problem.

Afternoon: delivery riders. Electric bikes with big insulated bags on
the back. They're carrying somebody's dinner. They know the streets.
They ride the fastest.

Weekend: mixed. Kids with training wheels. Adults with expensive
bikes. A grandmother with her granddaughter on a tandem. Someone on
a unicycle.

The bike lane is the most contested piece of the street. Everyone has
an opinion about it — drivers, bikers, pedestrians. The bikers say
drivers park in it. The drivers say bikers ignore stop signs. The
pedestrians say both are true.

Everyone is a little right. That's why it stays hard.\")

  (piece
    :id \"st-07-a-fire-escape\"
    :title \"A fire escape\"
    :prose
    \"The fire escape on the third floor has a plant on it. Not a garden.
One plant. A tomato in a plastic pot. It's from the woman who lives
there. She started it in April. By August the tomato has produced
three tomatoes, one of which she ate and two of which she gave to her
downstairs neighbor.

The fire escape has a metal grating. When you walk on it, it makes a
sound. The plant has to be tied to the railing so it doesn't fall
during storms.

The fire escape is a place for the plant. It's also a place for the
woman to sit on hot evenings when the apartment is too warm. She sits
with her feet through the grating and looks at the street below. Sometimes
she reads. Sometimes she smokes a cigarette even though she says she
quit. Sometimes she just sits.

The fire escape is a fire escape. It's also a small extra room. The
building was built in 1896. The fire escape was added later. The plant
was added last spring. Everything gets layered on.\")

  (piece
    :id \"st-08-the-crossing\"
    :title \"A pedestrian crossing\"
    :prose
    \"The crossing at Fulton and South Portland has been marked with
white paint for as long as anyone remembers. The paint fades. The city
repaints it every few years.

At morning rush hour, cars stop for pedestrians most of the time. Not
always. The lady with the dog is confident — she walks straight into
the crossing and the cars stop. The delivery guy on the bike doesn't
stop; he weaves through. The kid with headphones on doesn't look up.

At noon the crossing is easier. Less traffic. More time.

At night the crossing is a different thing. Nobody is walking. The
occasional cab. A late bus. The white paint is more visible in
headlights than in daylight.

The crossing does a job. It doesn't feel important. But if you took
it away, the block would feel different. Someone would slip through
the traffic somewhere else and get hurt. So the paint stays. And the
cars stop most of the time.

Most things in a city are like this. Small pieces of paint doing a
job. Nobody thinks about them until they're gone.\"))
")

  (piece
    :id \"fd-01-dinner-with-a-teenager\"
    :title \"Dinner with a teenager\"
    :prose
    \"Dinner at seven. The mother has made pasta with red sauce because
that's what everybody will eat. The teenager sits down last, plate
already served, and moves the pasta around without eating for a
minute.

'How was school,' the father asks.
'Fine.'
'Anything happen?'
'No.'

The mother knows something happened. She doesn't push. The teenager
eats three bites, drinks water, and looks at his phone.

'No phone at dinner,' the father says.

The teenager puts the phone face-down on the table with more force
than necessary. Nobody says anything about it.

After dinner the mother is cleaning the pot and the teenager comes
into the kitchen for a glass of water. He stands there a minute.
Then: 'kevin got in trouble today.'

'Yeah?'

'Yeah.'

He doesn't say what for. The mother doesn't ask. She rinses the pot.
He drinks the water. He leaves. She hears his door close.

That was the whole conversation. It was more than she thought she'd
get. Some nights that's what dinner is — a moment in the kitchen after
the plates are cleared where a teenager mentions Kevin.

She smiles a little at the pot. The teenager will be okay. Not because
Kevin got in trouble instead of him — that's not the point. Because
he told her.\")

  (piece
    :id \"fd-02-thanksgiving\"
    :title \"Thanksgiving\"
    :prose
    \"There are ten of them around the table. Twelve if you count the two
cousins who are watching football in the other room. The turkey came
out a little dry because the oven was open too much. Nobody says so.

The grandmother is at the head. She's smaller than she used to be. She
gets tired earlier. But she's here. She wanted to be here.

The uncle who always talks politics is quieter this year because
somebody had a stroke last month and everybody's been thinking about
that.

The aunt who makes the sweet potatoes has outdone herself. Everyone
takes seconds.

A cousin drops a fork. Everyone laughs. The dog under the table
notices but doesn't move because he has learned that food usually
lands where he can reach it eventually.

They go around the table with what they're thankful for. It's a small
tradition. Nobody says anything grand. The grandmother says 'you.'
Just that. She looks at the family.

Then everyone eats pie. Then everyone sits. The cousins come back
from the football room and grab plates too.

It's a small holiday. Nobody made a speech. Nobody had a big fight.
Nobody left early. That's a real success, not the kind you can
photograph.\")

  (piece
    :id \"fd-03-morning-coffee\"
    :title \"Morning coffee\"
    :prose
    \"The father is up at six. He makes coffee in the same pot he's used
for twelve years. He grinds the beans, puts water in, hits the button.

While it's brewing he stands at the window. The street is empty. A
cat crosses it. A car turns the corner. The sky is going gray-blue
from the east.

He pours the coffee into a mug that his daughter made in a pottery
class in high school. It's uneven. It leans a little to the left. He
doesn't use any of the other mugs when he's alone in the kitchen.

His wife comes down at six-forty. She kisses him on the shoulder and
pours her own coffee. She uses a different mug — a plain white one
because she likes plain white.

They stand at the window together. They don't talk. He notices the
cat is back. Different cat. Or the same. He isn't sure.

'You sleep,' she asks.
'Yeah,' he says.
'Good.'

Then they sit at the small table by the window and drink their coffee
and read separately for twenty minutes. He reads the paper. She reads
a novel.

At seven the kids wake up. The morning ends. This particular quiet
is over. They will do it again tomorrow.\")

  (piece
    :id \"fd-04-a-sick-day\"
    :title \"A sick kid\"
    :prose
    \"The kid is home sick. Sore throat, low fever. Not bad enough for
the doctor but bad enough to keep him from school.

The mother is working from home. She's set the kid up on the couch
with the blanket he likes and a small tray with soup and juice. He is
watching a movie he's seen before because when he's sick he doesn't
want new things.

Every twenty minutes she comes over and puts her hand on his forehead.
The fever is holding steady. She gives him a cough drop. He complains
about the taste. She lets him have another kind.

By the afternoon he's asleep. She works quietly at the table so as
not to wake him. When he wakes he's a little better. He asks for
crackers. She brings crackers.

The father comes home at six. He puts a hand on the kid's forehead
too. He asks the mother how the fever was. She tells him. He nods.

They don't do dinner formal. The kid has more soup. The parents eat
sandwiches at the counter. They watch the kid on the couch. He's
watching the same movie again from a different scene.

At eight the mother helps the kid up the stairs. He is heavier than
he was last year. She notices. She kisses his forehead. He is
lukewarm now.

'Feel better,' she says.
'I know,' he says.

Then he falls asleep. She stands in the doorway a minute. Then she
turns off the light.\")

  (piece
    :id \"fd-05-a-cold-day\"
    :title \"The cold day\"
    :prose
    \"The temperature dropped to twelve degrees overnight. Nobody wanted
to go outside. But everybody had to.

The mother put an extra layer on the kid. Long-sleeved shirt under
the sweater. Then a coat. Then a scarf. Then a hat that the grandmother
knitted three winters ago. Then mittens because gloves are for
teenagers.

Getting to the bus stop was a project. The wind blew straight through
Adelphi and cut across their faces. The kid started crying. Not a big
cry. Just the kind of cry you do when your cheeks are freezing.

At the bus stop the mother tucked the scarf higher. She stood in
front of the kid to block the wind. The bus was three minutes late.

When it finally came the driver said 'sorry, it's the cold.' Which
was the same thing all the drivers said. The mother nodded. She got
the kid on. The kid sat by the window and put his forehead against
the glass, which was cold, but he didn't move it.

At school the mother handed the kid off to the teacher and headed
home. The wind was still cutting. She walked with her head down. By
the time she got home her ears were bright red.

She stood in the kitchen with her hat still on and drank a glass of
tap water because she was thirsty. Then she took the hat off and hung
it on the hook. The rest of the day would happen inside.\")

  (piece
    :id \"fd-06-a-body-getting-older\"
    :title \"A body getting older\"
    :prose
    \"The knee has been bothering him for eight months. Not a sudden thing.
A slow thing. Some mornings it's fine. Some mornings it's not.

He's fifty-eight. He knows what this is. He knows the fix might be
physical therapy, might be surgery, might just be that this is how
things go.

He goes to the doctor. The doctor says the imaging shows some wear.
Some inflammation. Try physical therapy first. Six weeks. See how it
goes.

He goes to physical therapy twice a week. The therapist is a woman in
her thirties. She shows him small exercises. She is patient. She
does not talk about how his knee will be like new.

After three weeks the knee is a little better. Not fixed. Better.

He asks the therapist if it will keep getting better. She says maybe.
She says maybe he will learn to work with it. Some knees you fix and
some knees you accept.

He goes home. He does the exercises. He walks less than he used to.
He notices the knee more than he used to.

His wife notices him noticing. She doesn't say anything. She knows
he doesn't want to be babied. But she knows.

This is what getting older is. It isn't dramatic. It's a knee.\")

  (piece
    :id \"fd-07-a-body-learning\"
    :title \"A body learning\"
    :prose
    \"The two-year-old has learned to walk down stairs. Not with holding.
With holding the railing, but not holding the mother's hand.

She goes slow. One foot down. Then the other foot down onto the same
step. Then one foot down. Then the other. She looks up at the mother
every third step to check that the mother is watching.

The mother is watching.

At the bottom the toddler turns around and looks up at the stairs.
Then she looks at the mother. Then she starts back up.

Up is harder than down. She stands at the bottom step and lifts her
foot. She has to lean forward. Her diaper makes it a little awkward.
She grunts.

She gets to the top. She turns around. She starts back down.

The mother has been watching for ten minutes. She hasn't moved. She
hasn't interrupted. The toddler is doing this because she wants to.
Not because anybody made her. The mother knows this is a shape of
work that a two-year-old can do only if the adult doesn't get in the
way.

Twenty minutes later the toddler has done the stairs six times. She
is done. She walks over to the couch and climbs onto it and sits.

The mother sits down next to her. She puts a hand on the toddler's
back.

'Yeah,' she says.

The toddler nods without really understanding what she's agreeing to.
Then she falls asleep.\")

  (piece
    :id \"fd-08-the-weekly-food\"
    :title \"The weekly food\"
    :prose
    \"Sundays are the shopping day for a lot of families. The father goes
because the mother handled dinner. Or the mother goes because the
father is watching football. Or they go together because that's what
they do on Sundays. It varies.

The list is always the same shape: bread, milk, eggs, coffee, some
vegetables, some fruit, one meat, one thing for the week's dinner
plan, snacks for the kids, whatever's on sale.

The store is loud on Sundays. Two-year-olds crying. Teenagers pushing
carts. Older people with lists on paper. Younger people with lists on
phones.

The person shopping thinks about money. Every week is a small
negotiation between want and need. The mangoes are three dollars
each and the kid likes them but it's a lot for a fruit. The cereal is
buy-one-get-one so you get two boxes of cereal you don't quite want.

The checkout is a small ritual. The cashier says hello. The shopper
loads the belt. The bagger — if there's a bagger — packs the bags.
Money moves. The receipt prints.

By the time you leave the store you've been in there fifty minutes
and you're tired. You loaded the bags into the car. You drove home.
You unloaded the bags. You put things away.

Then it's Sunday afternoon and you're not thinking about food again
until dinner. The rhythm holds another week.\"))
")

  (piece
    :id \"rr-01-neighbors-who-dont-know-each-other\"
    :title \"Neighbors who don't know each other\"
    :prose
    \"The couple in 3B and the couple in 3C have lived on the same floor
for six years. They nod at each other in the hallway. They know each
other's names because there's a maintenance sheet on the bulletin
board downstairs. But they don't know each other.

3B is a schoolteacher and a nurse. 3C is a graphic designer and a
paralegal. They would probably like each other. They've never had a
reason to find out.

Once a package for 3C got left at 3B's door. 3B knocked on 3C's door
and handed it over. 'Wrong door,' 3B said. 'Thanks,' 3C said. Both
smiled. That was the longest conversation they've ever had.

The building has an annual holiday party in December. Half the
tenants show up. Neither 3B nor 3C usually does. Once, five years
ago, they were both there for twenty minutes. They didn't talk to
each other. They talked to other people.

This is a specific kind of relationship. Not friendship, not
strangers. Something in between. The building has dozens of them.
Most buildings do.

Neither couple thinks about it much. But when 3B moved out — three
years later, to a house upstate — 3C actually felt something small.
Not sadness. A shape leaving.\")

  (piece
    :id \"rr-02-a-first-date\"
    :title \"A first date\"
    :prose
    \"They agreed to meet at a bar in Fort Greene. Neither had been there
before. Both looked it up beforehand — she looked at the menu, he
looked at the reviews.

She got there five minutes early on purpose. She wanted the seat
facing the door. He got there three minutes early because he was
nervous. He didn't know she was already inside.

They both saw each other at the same time. Small awkward wave. She
stood. He walked over. He hugged her lightly. She hugged back but
kept it short.

They both ordered a drink. Neither wanted a second drink yet but they
both said 'yeah' when the bartender asked.

The conversation was okay. Not amazing. Not bad. They found out they
both grew up in Ohio, in different towns, which was more common than
they expected. He talked about his sister. She talked about her mother.

An hour in he asked if she wanted to walk. She said yes. They walked
along Lafayette. It was cool for June. The trees were full.

At the end of the walk he asked if he could see her again. She said
yes.

Neither of them said 'I had a great time.' They said 'this was nice.'

She got in a cab. He walked home. He was tired but not disappointed.
She was slightly excited but not thrilled.

Six months later they would be dating. A year later they would live
together. Five years later they would decide not to get married. Ten
years later he would remember the walk on Lafayette and the way she
said 'this was nice.'\")

  (piece
    :id \"rr-03-a-shared-bathroom\"
    :title \"A shared bathroom\"
    :prose
    \"Two roommates, one bathroom. He gets up at seven. She gets up at
seven-fifteen. They have worked out a schedule. He is out of the
bathroom by seven-ten. She takes hers from seven-ten to seven-forty.
He uses it again for two minutes at seven-forty-five. She uses it for
five more minutes at seven-fifty-five.

The schedule has evolved over eighteen months. It works now. It
didn't at first. There were three or four incidents. One time she
took thirty extra minutes because she got a work call in there. Once
he used up the last of the toilet paper and didn't replace it.

They talked. They set new rules. Neither of them wanted to be the
one who was harder about it. But they were both firm because a shared
bathroom is a real limit.

Now she buys the toilet paper. He buys the cleaning supplies. The
schedule is unspoken but stable.

They are not close friends. They are polite roommates. This is
enough.

Someday one of them will move out. The other will get a solo
bathroom and appreciate it in a way that only shared-bathroom people
can.\")

  (piece
    :id \"rr-04-a-marriage-of-thirty-years\"
    :title \"A marriage of thirty years\"
    :prose
    \"They have been married thirty years. They finish each other's
sentences half the time. The other half of the time they still argue.

He has certain things she doesn't like: he leaves cabinet doors open;
he can't hear her when she's in another room; he always thinks he's
right about directions when he isn't. She has certain things he
doesn't like: she buys things and doesn't tell him; she interrupts;
she keeps the thermostat too low.

They have found a rhythm around most of it. The cabinets she closes
without saying anything. He shouts her name louder when she's in the
kitchen. The directions she ignores and does what she thinks. The
purchases he lets be. The interrupting she is trying but rarely
succeeds. The thermostat is a fight that resurfaces every winter.

The parts they got right: they laugh a lot. They read next to each
other in bed with different books. They eat breakfast together every
day, even weekends. They know each other's parents (his parents are
dead now, hers still call every Sunday). They have never had a fight
neither remembered how to end.

If you asked either of them why they've stayed, they would give a
short answer. She would say 'he's good.' He would say 'she's the
one.' Neither would elaborate.

Thirty years of small good moments make a bigger shape than either of
them could describe. That's a marriage.\")

  (piece
    :id \"rr-05-a-breakup\"
    :title \"A breakup\"
    :prose
    \"They had been together three years. They both knew for six months
that it wasn't going to last. Neither said it.

They said it on a Sunday afternoon. She said it first. He was ready.
He had been ready for a while.

They sat on the couch and cried a little. Not a lot. There was
relief in it too. They had loved each other. They still did. That
wasn't the problem. The problem was that they wanted different lives.

He offered to move out first. She said she would. He said no, he
would. They argued about who would move out until they both laughed
because it was so predictable of them.

He moved out three weeks later. He rented a smaller apartment two
neighborhoods away. She kept the apartment. She got the couch. He
got the good dishes.

They agreed to not see each other for a while. Then friends.

The first month was hard for both of them. Then it wasn't as hard.
By six months they were texting each other about small things. By a
year they were friends in the way exes sometimes become friends.

Neither dated for a while. Then they both did. Then they both had
new relationships. Then they were people they didn't recognize.

The breakup had been the right thing. Neither of them ever second-
guessed it. But sometimes she would find a small object of his in a
box and feel a tenderness that surprised her. He would too, on his
side.

Some love ends without ending completely. That's a shape too.\")

  (piece
    :id \"rr-06-a-kitchen\"
    :title \"A kitchen\"
    :prose
    \"The kitchen is small. Galley-style. Two people can be in it if they
coordinate. Three is a crowd.

There's a wooden cutting board that has been used enough that it's
warped. There's a knife the mother has sharpened many times that is
slightly shorter than it started. There's a pot on the back burner
that came from her mother.

The kitchen has certain rules. Nothing goes on top of the fridge
because things fall off. The dish drying rack lives on the counter to
the right of the sink. The salt and pepper live on the counter to the
left of the stove.

The kitchen is a working room. It has been used every day for
fourteen years. The paint on one wall is darker where the pan is
always hung. There is a small ring on the counter where a glass
sweated one summer and it stained the surface.

When the family sold the apartment they took the pot and the cutting
board and the knife. They left the rings and the paint. Some kitchen
things travel. Others belong to the room.\")

  (piece
    :id \"rr-07-a-living-room\"
    :title \"A living room\"
    :prose
    \"The living room has a couch that is not new. It has a coffee table
that came from IKEA seven years ago and is still holding up. It has a
rug that was expensive at the time but the price has been amortized
across many afternoons.

The bookshelves have books, but also other things — a framed photo of
the parents at a wedding, three small plants, a set of hardcover
novels from grandma who has died, a candle that was lit once and now
has dust on it.

The lamp on the side table doesn't quite match the other lamp. Nobody
minds.

The TV is on the wall. Underneath it are the game consoles and the
remotes. Behind the couch there is a small stack of books that got
started and never finished.

The room gets tidied on Sundays. During the week it accumulates —
mail, jackets, socks the toddler took off. Sunday is reset day.

If you took a photo of the room every day for a year you would see
it slowly age. New coffee table books. A cushion changed. The rug
darkening slightly. This is how rooms live.\")

  (piece
    :id \"rr-08-a-morning-in-a-family\"
    :title \"A morning in a family\"
    :prose
    \"The alarm goes off at six-fifteen. The mother turns it off. She
lies still for a minute. The father is still asleep.

She gets up. She goes to the bathroom. She brushes her teeth. She
starts the coffee. She checks her phone for six minutes even though
she's promised herself she'll stop doing that.

At six-forty-five she wakes the kids. The first one groans. The second
one says 'no.' She says 'yes.' They get up. They stumble to the
bathroom. There is a brief negotiation about who goes first.

By seven both kids are eating cereal. The mother has made lunches.
The father is in the shower. The dog wants to go out. She takes the
dog out because it's quick and she can do it in her slippers.

By seven-thirty the kids are dressed and the backpacks are packed and
the father is downstairs. Everyone hugs. The father walks the older
kid to school. The mother walks the younger kid to the daycare
around the corner.

By eight-fifteen the house is empty. The mother goes back inside to
finish her coffee. Ten minutes to herself. This is the reward for
the whole morning.

Then she leaves for work. The morning is over. It happens again
tomorrow.\"))
")

  (piece
    :id \"ww-01-october\"
    :title \"October\"
    :prose
    \"October in New York is the best month. The trees turn. The air is
cold in the morning and warm by noon. Everyone is out in coats but
carrying them by afternoon.

The park is full on Saturdays. Everyone knows they only have a few
more good weekends before the winter. The kids kick soccer balls. The
adults walk in twos and threes. The dogs are extra enthusiastic
because the temperature suits them.

The pumpkin spice thing is a joke and also real. The line at the
coffee shop is longer than usual. The scarves come out. The boots
come out.

At night the temperature drops. You put on a heavier jacket. You
notice your breath.

By the last week of the month the leaves are on the ground more than
the trees. The rakes come out. Someone in every block hires a kid to
rake. Someone else does it themselves and complains cheerfully.

The kids in kindergarten make window decorations. The colder mornings
smell like coffee and wet leaves and something else that is just
October.

The world is beautiful in October. Everyone knows. Nobody says it too
much or it will lose the shape.\")

  (piece
    :id \"ww-02-a-heat-wave\"
    :title \"A heat wave\"
    :prose
    \"Three days of ninety-eight degrees. The city becomes a slower
version of itself.

The AC in the bodega is set to sixty-eight. The owner doesn't care
about the electric bill because customers stay longer and buy more.

The subway platforms are unbearable. Everyone stands as close to the
wall as possible for the tiny piece of shade. When the train pulls
in the wind before it is the best moment of the afternoon.

Old people stay inside. The city sends alerts to check on them. The
neighbors do it too, not because of the alert but because that's what
you do.

Kids in the fire hydrant. Kids in the sprinklers at the park. Kids at
the beach.

Dogs are miserable. Owners walk them at seven in the morning and nine
at night. Nobody walks them at noon.

The old air conditioners hum in every window. The people who don't
have air conditioners go to the library or the movies or a friend's.

On the third night a thunderstorm breaks the heat. Everyone opens
their windows. The rain smells sweet. The temperature drops fifteen
degrees in an hour. The city sleeps well.

The next morning the heat wave is over. It felt like an event while
it was happening. Now it's just a memory. Until the next one.\")

  (piece
    :id \"ww-03-a-snowstorm\"
    :title \"A snowstorm\"
    :prose
    \"The forecast said six inches. It got twelve. The mayor called a
snow emergency at eight in the morning. Everything closed.

The kids were the most excited. School was canceled. They got up
early anyway. They put on their snow pants — some had them, some
made do with layers. They went to the park across the street. There
were maybe forty kids there by noon.

The adults were more mixed. The people who worked from home were
mostly fine. The people who had to get somewhere were mostly not.
The bus and train service was reduced. Trains ran but slowly.

The plows came around three in the afternoon. The city plows the
main streets first. The side streets get done later. Sometimes not
until the next day. Everyone knew this. Nobody was surprised.

By evening the snow had stopped and the temperature had dropped. The
snow got crunchier. Kids started coming inside. Adults started
digging out cars. Some cars would stay buried for three days because
their owners weren't going anywhere.

The next morning the city was different. Whiter. Quieter. The rooftops
had a foot of snow on them. The trees looked heavy.

The kid down the block got paid twenty dollars to shovel someone's
sidewalk. That was the going rate. He shoveled five sidewalks and
made a hundred dollars and told his mother it was a good day.

That was the whole storm. It happened once and then it faded into
regular winter.\")

  (piece
    :id \"ww-04-a-slow-work-day\"
    :title \"A slow work day\"
    :prose
    \"Some days at work are slow. The phones don't ring much. The emails
are routine. You get through your inbox by ten and then you have
nothing to do until lunch.

You could take a longer lunch. You could get ahead on things that
have been backlogged. You could reorganize your files. Nobody would
notice.

Or you could take out your phone and scroll for a while and hate
yourself a little.

The office has three of you today. One of the others is on a call.
The other is looking at a spreadsheet.

You go make coffee. You take longer than you need. You put on some
music that you can only listen to when nobody's around. You come
back to your desk.

The mail arrives at two. You have one letter. You open it. It's not
important.

At three the boss comes by. She has three questions. You have three
answers. It takes eight minutes. Then she leaves.

At four you decide you've done enough. You send a status email so it
looks like a full day. You leave at four-thirty.

Some days are slow. Nobody talks about them. Nobody feels good about
them. They're just part of the week.

Tomorrow will be busy. That's usually how it works.\")

  (piece
    :id \"ww-05-a-fast-work-day\"
    :title \"A fast work day\"
    :prose
    \"You wake up already thinking about work. Three big things due today.
The presentation you haven't finished. The client who is going to
call. The document that has to be reviewed.

You skip breakfast. You get to the office at eight instead of nine.
You start with the presentation because it needs the most brain.

By nine you've got the shape of the presentation but it's not clean.
You keep going.

At nine-thirty the client calls. You take the call in the small
conference room. It's a good call — twenty minutes, no drama. You
get back to the presentation.

At ten-forty-five you send the presentation. It's not perfect but it's
sent.

At eleven you start the document review. Twenty pages. You read it
carefully. You mark two things that need to change. You send it back
by twelve-thirty.

You skip lunch. You eat a granola bar at your desk.

The afternoon is a bunch of small fires. Somebody needs a number.
Somebody needs a signature. Somebody needs your opinion.

By six you're tired. You leave. You get home and don't want to
cook. You order in. You watch something on TV that doesn't require
attention.

You go to bed at ten. You sleep well because you're tired.

That was a good work day. Nothing spectacular. Nothing was broken.
Everything moved.\")

  (piece
    :id \"ww-06-a-farmer-market\"
    :title \"A farmers market\"
    :prose
    \"Saturday mornings at the farmers market. It's in a small square
that becomes a market between April and November. Twenty vendors.
They start setting up at six. The crowd arrives at eight.

The tomato guy is your favorite. He's an older man from a farm two
hours north. His tomatoes are always better than what's in the
supermarket. You have paid five dollars for one tomato before, without
regret.

The bread guy has a line. His sourdough is famous in the neighborhood.
If you don't get there by nine there won't be any left.

The flower woman sells small bouquets for ten dollars each. Wildflowers.
Nothing fancy. You buy one every weekend if you have the ten dollars.

The honey guy. The mushroom guy. The lady with the pickles. The couple
who makes cheese. The teenager who sells eggs from her family's farm.

You walk the whole market before you decide what to buy. You have
sixty dollars in cash. You buy some tomatoes, a loaf of bread, a bunch
of flowers, and half a dozen eggs. That takes fifty-four dollars. You
put six back in your pocket.

You walk home with the bag. It smells like tomato and basil. You are
in a specific kind of good mood that only Saturday morning at the
market can produce.

By eleven you're home. You'll eat some of the tomatoes today. Some
tomorrow. The bread will last until Tuesday. The flowers will last
until Thursday. The eggs are for the week.

Sixty dollars. A good spend.\")

  (piece
    :id \"ww-07-a-laundromat\"
    :title \"A laundromat\"
    :prose
    \"The laundromat on Vanderbilt is open twenty-four hours. Most people
go on the weekend. But there are people there all the time.

The woman who runs it during the day is friendly but not chatty. She
knows most of the regulars. She keeps quarters at the counter for the
people who forget to bring them.

The washing machines are big. Big enough for two weeks of laundry.
Everyone who does laundry knows the shape of a two-week wash: three
or four loads, one or two hours per load, then folding.

You sit in a plastic chair and wait. There's a little TV on the wall
playing something with the volume off. The subtitles roll.

You bring a book. You've been meaning to finish it for weeks. You get
through a chapter.

The person next to you is also waiting. Their phone is playing a
video. They apologize and put in earbuds. You nod. They nod back.

At the folding table, at the end, you fold everything. You've done
this so many times that the folding takes ten minutes for a whole
basket.

You carry the folded clothes home. They smell clean. The laundromat
smell — bright and floral and slightly chemical — will be on the
clothes for a day.

It's not a fun trip. It's not exactly a chore either. It's just
laundry. It happens. It gets done.\")

  (piece
    :id \"ww-08-a-small-shop\"
    :title \"A small shop\"
    :prose
    \"The store on the corner sells a little of everything: chips,
candy, phone chargers, batteries, lottery tickets, sodas, aspirin,
sunscreen in summer, gloves in winter.

The owner is Bengali. He has been on this corner for eighteen years.
He knows most of the customers. The customers know him. Some know
his family. Some remember when his kids were small.

The store is small. Six aisles. The counter is at the front. Behind
the counter there is a wall of small items and the lottery machine.

The margins on most things are thin. The margins on lottery tickets
are okay. Everything else keeps the lights on.

The owner works six days a week. His son works the seventh. The son
is in college for engineering. He works the store on Sundays to give
his father a day off.

The lottery is popular. The owner has sold three winning tickets over
his eighteen years. Two small (five thousand and two thousand). One
larger (forty-two thousand). The winners always come back and tell
him. Twice they gave him a small gift as thanks.

Customers come in for something specific. They leave with something
specific plus something they didn't plan on. That's the whole
economics of a corner store. The unplanned item on the way out is
the margin.

The store is unglamorous. It works. It has worked for eighteen years.
It will work for eighteen more if the rent doesn't go up too much.\"))
")

  (piece
    :id \"br-01-hands\"
    :title \"Hands\"
    :prose
    \"Everyone's hands tell a story. The mother of the third-grader has
hands that get cold in fall. She wears a ring her grandmother gave
her, on the fourth finger of her left hand, which used to be a
wedding ring but isn't anymore. She keeps it because she likes it.

The father works with his hands. His fingernails are shorter than most
people's because he cuts them every Sunday. His knuckles are wider
than the fingers because that's how hands go when you use them.

The grandmother's hands are thinner. The skin on the back is loose.
There are age spots. She notices them. She used to hide them. Now she
doesn't.

The two-year-old has hands that are the tiny shape of the adult ones
they will become. Her thumb is proportionally huge. Her fingernails
are barely there.

The teenager's hands are almost adult but not quite. His pinkie is
still small in a way it won't be next year. His palms are always
warm.

Everybody looks at their own hands sometimes without thinking. Notices
a vein, a callus, a small scar from last winter. Hands are the part
of the body you see most. They are also the part that most changes
without you noticing.\")

  (piece
    :id \"br-02-feet-after-a-long-day\"
    :title \"Feet after a long day\"
    :prose
    \"The nurse takes her shoes off at the end of the shift and her feet
hurt in the specific way that only a twelve-hour shift can produce.
The arches. The balls of the feet. The pinky toes, always.

She sits on the couch and rubs one foot with the other for a minute.
Then she rubs one foot with her hands. Then the other.

If she had a bathtub she would soak. She doesn't. She takes a hot
shower with the water pointed at her feet.

Feet after a long day is a specific tiredness. You can't get away from
it. You're just going to have to sit and let it pass.

By nine-thirty the tiredness has migrated. It's no longer in her
feet. It's now a general tiredness. That's actually better. Localized
foot pain is the worst.

She goes to bed. She sleeps. In the morning her feet are fine again.
The body forgets fast.\")

  (piece
    :id \"br-03-a-cold\"
    :title \"A cold\"
    :prose
    \"It starts as a scratchy throat on Thursday. By Friday morning your
head is fuzzy and you know.

You go to work anyway because you have a meeting. You get through the
meeting. You go home at three.

Friday night is where the cold really shows up. You have chills. You
have body aches. You are annoyed. You take some over-the-counter
medicine that makes your mouth taste weird.

Saturday you sleep till eleven. You are worse. You are also better,
in the sense that you have accepted that you are sick and are not
going to fight it.

You eat soup. You drink water. You watch a lot of TV. You take
another dose of the medicine.

Sunday is transition day. Still congested but no longer feverish. You
do very little. You read a little.

Monday you are back at work. Not one hundred percent. Enough. Your
voice sounds different. Your coworkers keep their distance. You
appreciate it.

By Wednesday the cold is basically gone. You forget you had it. A
month from now you won't remember which cold this was. There will be
another one, later.\")

  (piece
    :id \"br-04-a-bedroom\"
    :title \"A bedroom\"
    :prose
    \"The bedroom has a bed. The bed has sheets. The sheets need to be
changed. They will be, on Sunday.

There is a nightstand on each side of the bed. One has a lamp, a
book, a glass of water, and an alarm clock. The other has a lamp, a
different book, a glass of water, and a phone charger.

The closet is small. Half of it is one person's clothes. Half is the
other's. There is a small compromise about what goes on the floor.

The window looks out on the back of another building. There is a
tree between the two buildings. The tree is bigger than either of
them expected.

At night the bedroom is quiet. The heater ticks. Occasionally a car
goes by on the street. Occasionally a siren. Occasionally something
they can't identify — a bird? An engine? A dream?

They have been sleeping in this room for two years. They have never
gotten around to painting it. They will, eventually.

The room is not decorated. The room does not need to be decorated. It
is the room where they sleep. It works.\")

  (piece
    :id \"br-05-a-shower\"
    :title \"A shower\"
    :prose
    \"A shower has a specific ritual. You turn the water on. You wait for
it to get hot. This takes anywhere from ten seconds to two minutes
depending on the building.

You step in. The first hit of hot water on the back of the neck is
one of the small good moments of the day.

You wash your face. You wash your hair. You wash the rest. You do
this in the same order every time without thinking about it.

You stand under the water for an extra minute at the end because it
feels good and there's no reason not to.

You turn the water off. You step out. You use a towel that is not as
clean as it could be but not so dirty you can't use it.

You dress. You feel awake now. The shower did its job.

Some days the shower is where you cry. Some days it is where you make
a decision. Some days it is where you sing. Some days it is just a
shower.

The shower is a small enclosed space where you are alone. That's part
of what it is.\")

  (piece
    :id \"br-06-a-desk\"
    :title \"A desk\"
    :prose
    \"The desk has a laptop. Next to the laptop, a mug that used to have
coffee in it. Next to the mug, a small stack of paper. Next to the
paper, a pen that works and two pens that don't.

There is a plant on the corner. It is doing okay. It gets watered
about once every ten days, which is not enough for some plants but
is fine for this one because it is a pothos.

The chair is not ergonomic. The person sitting in it knows this. They
have thought about buying a better chair. They have not.

There is a picture frame on the desk. In the picture: two people at
a beach. They are smiling. The picture is from three years ago.

There is a lamp. Its cord goes down behind the desk in a way that is
hidden but also a little annoying. Every once in a while it gets
knocked and unplugs. The person plugs it back in and thinks about
routing the cord better and then doesn't.

The desk is where work happens. It is also where snacks are eaten. It
is also where the phone is charged. It is also where the mail sits
before it gets opened.

Desks are small workshops of adulthood. Nobody plans a desk. A desk
happens.\")

  (piece
    :id \"br-07-a-walk-to-the-subway\"
    :title \"The walk to the subway\"
    :prose
    \"It is a six-minute walk from the apartment to the subway. She has
been doing it for three years. She knows every crack in the sidewalk.

She passes the flower shop. It is closed at this hour but the door
smells faintly of jasmine.

She passes the bagel place. It is open. There are people in line. She
does not have time this morning.

She passes the coffee cart. She stops. She orders a small coffee with
one sugar. She hands over three dollars. She gets fifty cents back.
The cart owner nods.

She crosses one street. She waits at the light. The light changes.
She crosses another street.

She goes down the stairs to the subway. Her train arrives in three
minutes according to the sign. She takes out her phone.

Six minutes and thirty seconds since she left the apartment. She has
done this walk more than a thousand times. She could do it in her
sleep. Some days she basically does.

The walk is not remarkable. It is what her mornings are made of.\")

  (piece
    :id \"br-08-a-window\"
    :title \"A window\"
    :prose
    \"There is a window in the kitchen that faces east. In the morning
light comes through it at an angle. This is where the family sits
for breakfast.

The window has a plant on the sill. The plant has been there for
four years. It has grown from a small thing to a medium thing.

Through the window you can see the neighbor's roof. A pigeon lives
there. The pigeon has been there for six months. Whether it is the
same pigeon every day, nobody is sure.

At sunset the light hits the window differently. Golden hour. The
family notices this sometimes. Other times they don't because they
are doing dishes.

The window has a small crack in the corner from something that
happened years ago. Nobody remembers what. The crack is not going to
get bigger. It just is.

You can open the window a few inches for air. Or all the way for a
breeze. In summer they open it in the morning and close it before
evening because the AC has to run.

The window is one of the most-looked-at things in the apartment. But
if you asked the family to describe it they would probably struggle.
It is furniture at this point. It is background.

Windows are like that. You look through them, not at them.\"))

    \"The alarm goes off at six-thirty. He hits snooze once. Then he gets
up.

The apartment is dark. He does not turn on lights. He knows the layout.
He can shower without the light on if he wants to. Sometimes he does.

Today he turns on the bathroom light and looks at himself briefly. He
sees an ordinary face. He turns off the light and gets in the shower.

After the shower he dresses. Jeans, t-shirt, sweater over the t-shirt.
Socks. Shoes. He knows where everything is because he laid it out last
night.

He makes toast and eats it standing at the counter. He drinks coffee
from the mug his sister gave him for a birthday four years ago. He
reads a headline on his phone but not the article.

At seven-twenty he leaves. The lock clicks. The hallway is quiet. The
elevator has one other person on it — a woman with a dog. They nod.

Outside it is cold. He turns up his collar. He walks to the subway.
The Tuesday begins.\")

  (piece
    :id \"mn-02-a-friday-night\"
    :title \"A Friday night\"
    :prose
    \"It's eight-thirty on a Friday. Two friends are on the couch. They
haven't decided if they're going out or staying in.

'Are we going out,' one says.
'Are we,' says the other.
'I don't know.'
'Me neither.'

They order Thai food. The decision is made.

The food arrives forty minutes later. They eat at the coffee table
because that's where they are. They put on a show.

They finish the food. They watch two episodes of the show. Now it's
almost eleven.

'Should we still go out,' one says.
'Should we,' says the other.

They laugh at themselves. They will not go out. That was decided at
eight-thirty; they just didn't want to admit it.

They watch another episode. At twelve one of them falls asleep on the
couch. The other one gets a blanket and puts it over the first one.
Then goes to bed.

Friday nights don't have to be big. Sometimes staying in with a friend
and thai food and three episodes of a show is what a Friday night is.\")

  (piece

    :title \"A child can't sleep\"
    :prose
    \"It's ten forty-five. The seven-year-old is at the top of the stairs.
He is in his pajamas but he is not in bed.

'I can't sleep,' he says.

His mother comes to the bottom of the stairs. 'Bad dream?'

'No. Just can't.'

She goes up. She sits on the edge of his bed. He gets in. She rubs
his back for a minute.

'What are you thinking about,' she asks.

'The volcano book.'

The mother remembers that they read about a volcano yesterday. He was
fascinated and a little scared.

'Volcanoes are far away,' she says. 'Not in Brooklyn.'

'I know.'

'But still?'

'Yeah.'

She sits with him for a while longer. She doesn't say anything else.
He doesn't either. He is not asleep but he is calmer.

She stays until his breathing slows. Then she gets up quietly. She
turns out the light. She closes the door partway.

Downstairs, her partner asks: 'okay?'

'Yeah. Volcano.'

Her partner nods. They both know how kids are.\")

    :title \"A night shift\"
    :prose
    \"The night nurse comes on at seven pm. She works until seven am.

The first hour is settling in. Reviewing the day nurse's notes.
Checking on patients. Meeting the resident.

By nine most patients are settling. Some are sleeping. Some are
watching TV. Some are anxious.

Ten to two is when the alerts come. The heart monitors beep. The IVs
finish. The call button gets pressed. She moves from room to room. She
knows the shape of each patient in a way the day nurse doesn't have
time to.

Two to five is the quiet middle. The patients are asleep. She catches
up on paperwork. She drinks coffee. She talks with the other night
nurse about small things.

Five to seven the shift ends. Patients start waking. The day nurse
arrives at six-forty-five for handoff.

She leaves at seven. Outside the sun is up. She squints. She walks to
the subway. She sleeps most of the day and comes back at seven pm.

Night shift is a different kind of work. Different rhythm. Different
rewards. Some nurses hate it. She loves it. The quiet middle is what
she likes. And knowing the patients in that specific way.\")

    :title \"A Saturday morning\"
    :prose
    \"Saturday morning is nine-thirty before anyone gets up. The whole
week rushes and Saturday makes up for it by refusing to.

The parents get up first. They make coffee. They eat cereal. They read
the paper — the actual paper, delivered to the door. This is one of
their small extravagances.

The kids come down at ten-thirty in pajamas. They ask about breakfast.
The father makes pancakes because Saturday. There is syrup and there
is fruit.

By eleven-thirty everyone is dressed. They discuss what to do. Park?
Yes. Groceries? Yes, after. Lunch? Maybe out.

They walk to the park. It is a fifteen-minute walk. They talk about
the week. The nine-year-old talks the most. The four-year-old
interrupts. The parents mediate.

At the park, an hour. Swings, slides, running. The nine-year-old
climbs the tree that they are told not to climb. Nobody enforces the
rule too hard.

By one o'clock they are back home. They have groceries. They have
lunch. They have their Saturday.

The rest of the day is unstructured. Maybe a movie. Maybe not. That
is what Saturday afternoons are for.\")

    :title \"The late late night\"
    :prose
    \"It is two in the morning. He is in the kitchen making tea. He could
not sleep.

The kettle takes four minutes. He stands by the window. Outside the
street is empty. One car goes by very slowly, then stops at the light
which is red even though there is no traffic. Then it goes.

He pours the tea. He sits at the table.

He drinks the tea. His mind is loud but not focused. The tea is warm.
The kitchen is dim. The refrigerator hums.

He is not doing anything. He is not thinking anything specific. He is
just up.

By three the tea is done. His mind has quieted a little. He goes back
to bed. His partner does not wake up. She rolls over. He lies still.

Ten minutes later he is asleep.

In the morning he will barely remember getting up. He will find the
empty mug in the sink and it will be the only evidence.

Some nights this happens. Not most. But some. He does not fight it.
The tea works.\")

    :title \"First light\"
    :prose
    \"In June, first light is at four forty-five. The sky is not yet blue.
It is a gray-lavender that has no name. If you are awake for it, you
are usually the only person on your block who is.

The birds start about ten minutes before first light. Small ones,
starting quietly. By first light they are louder. By five they are
what everyone would call birds singing.

If you walk outside at four forty-five in June you find a city that
looks strange. Empty streets. No cars. The rustle of the leaves in
the trees. You can hear a train two miles away.

By five-thirty the light is more visible. By six the sky is proper
blue. By six-thirty the first commuters are on the street.

Most people never see first light. That's fine. It happens every day
whether or not anyone is watching.\")

    :prose
    \"In December, last light is at four-thirty in the afternoon. This is
the hardest thing about December. Not the cold. The light going out
so early.

At three-thirty you can feel it coming. The sky is already turning.
The sun is low. Everything gets that late-day slant.

By four the streetlights come on. Some people don't notice. Some people
notice and feel a small sadness. Some people notice and feel nothing.

By four-thirty it is dark. The kids getting out of school walk home
in the dark. The commuters going home walk home in the dark. The
whole afternoon shift ends in the dark.

The stores put on their lights. The subway stations glow. The
apartments have lights in their windows. The city adjusts. It has
done this every December for as long as the city has existed.

By six the darkness is normal. Nobody thinks about it anymore. Winter
begins to feel like winter. There will be short bright days between
storms. There will be days that are just gray from start to finish.
There will be days when the sun is out at three and gone by four-
thirty.

The days will start getting longer by January. Nobody will notice for
a few weeks. By February they will notice. By March they will feel
happy about it.

But right now, in December, last light is early. That's just how it
is.\"))

# Chapter 8 — A touch of geography

Geography grounds conversation. When someone says \"the market opens at 9,\" the market is somewhere. This chapter gives Motoi a small vocabulary for talking about places.

> **Author says**
>
> Geography is one of those topics where knowing a little is much better than knowing nothing. A country's shape, its rivers, its neighbors — those small anchors change what you can talk about.

## The continent list

```scheme
(define continents
  '(africa antarctica asia australia europe north-america south-america))

(display continents) (newline)
```

Output:

```
(africa antarctica asia australia europe north-america south-america)
```

Seven continents.

## A country record

```scheme
(define (make-country name continent capital pop-mil)
  (list 'country name 'in continent 'capital capital 'pop-mil pop-mil))

(display (make-country 'japan 'asia 'tokyo 125)) (newline)
(display (make-country 'brazil 'south-america 'brasilia 213)) (newline)
```

Output:

```
(country japan in asia capital tokyo pop-mil 125)
(country brazil in south-america capital brasilia pop-mil 213)
```

## The distance-between

```scheme
(define (rough-distance from to)
  (list 'from from 'to to 'about 'km-estimate))

(display (rough-distance 'tokyo 'new-york)) (newline)
```

Output:

```
(from tokyo to new-york about km-estimate)
```

## Time zones

```scheme
(define (time-zone-offset city)
  (case city
    ((london tokyo new-york sydney))
    ((london) 0)
    ((tokyo) 9)
    ((new-york) -5)
    ((sydney) 10)
    (else 0)))

(display (time-zone-offset 'tokyo))    (newline)
(display (time-zone-offset 'new-york)) (newline)
```

Output:

```
9
-5
```

## Rivers and mountains

```scheme
(define (feature-of country)
  (case country
    ((japan) '(mount-fuji shinano-river))
    ((egypt) '(nile-river sinai-peninsula))
    ((usa)   '(mississippi-river rockies-appalachians))))

(display (feature-of 'japan))  (newline)
(display (feature-of 'egypt))  (newline)
```

Output:

```
(mount-fuji shinano-river)
(nile-river sinai-peninsula)
```

## What you know now

- Seven continents.
- Country = name, continent, capital, population.
- Rough distance and time zones anchor time-of-day talk.
- Each country has features worth naming.

## Try before you turn the page

```scheme
(display '(geography-anchors-conversation)) (newline)
```

If you can name a country's continent and capital, you're ready for composing-tools-deeper.
